title: Vulnerability Practices among Professionals in Multidisciplinary Settings
methods: Inductive qualitative single-case process study of a weekly multidisciplinary meeting; nonparticipant and participant observation of 20 online meetings (~3 hrs each) over 10 months, 19 semi-structured interviews (~60 min), and 7 group discussions; grounded analysis (Charmaz, 2014) across 27 episodes in six phases; process modeling.
industry: Health care (academic primary care / family medicine clinic)
time_period: 10-month observation period; meetings held online during COVID-19
units: One weekly multidisciplinary team meeting and its episodes of vulnerability practices; professionals (physicians, residents, senior psychologist, psychology interns, nurse, social workers) and patient partners
n_sample: 27 episodes across 20 weekly meetings; 19 interviews; 7 group discussions; ~8-10 participants per meeting
authors: Bouchard, M.; Chreim, S.; Langley, A.; Boivin, A.
theories: containment and interpretation (Petriglieri & Petriglieri, 2010, 2020); holding environments (Winnicott, 1965; Kahn, 2001); ritual theory (Bell, 1992; Johnson, Prashantham, Floyd, & Bourque, 2010)
keywords: holding environments; multidisciplinary settings; professional work; ritual; social support; vulnerability practices
research_question: How and with what perceived effects do professionals in multidisciplinary settings engage in practices that enable the sharing of doubts and insecurities experienced in the performance of their work roles?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Setting (holding environment): a weekly, ritualized multidisciplinary meeting theorized as a precarious "holding environment" that can provide containment (managing difficult emotions) and interpretation (making sense of them).
- Phases: an individual disclosure phase (dominated by social pressure to display vulnerability) and a communal reflection phase (culminating in social support), with "theorizing from the case" bridging the two.
- Ritualized sequence of practices: offering/accepting the mic, storytelling to colleagues, questioning the storyteller, revealing vulnerability, theorizing from the case (boundary setting, categorizing, perspective shifting), validating, advising, and thanking colleagues.
- Core tension: a delicate "Catch-22" between social pressure (to display vulnerabilities) and social support (to contain them).
- Power and authority dynamics: the role of the facilitator, discretion to participate or not, theorizing capability, and position in institutionalized professional hierarchies.
- Feedback loop: participants' appraisals of past episodes (benefits vs. risks) shape their willingness to engage in subsequent episodes.
- Path anomalies: "under-vulnerability" (E19) and "under-validation" (E9), where the typical sequence breaks down.

The paper develops an inductive process model in which a ritualized sequence of vulnerability practices moves professionals from individual disclosure to communal reflection, with theorizing from the case as the pivotal bridge that enables the interpretive function of a holding environment and seeds social support. Whether the setting functions as a "good enough" holding environment is a precarious, ongoing accomplishment: when social pressure to disclose is not matched by social support, and when power and authority dynamics tied to multidisciplinarity intrude, the environment may "hold" some participants more than others.
data_measures: Qualitative data drawn from an academic primary care (family medicine) clinic in Quebec, Canada. The first author observed and recorded 20 weekly online meetings (about three hours each) over 10 months, conducted 19 semi-structured interviews (about 60 minutes on average), and ran 7 participatory group discussions, yielding 93 hours of audio-video recording and 960 single-spaced pages of transcripts and observation notes (quotes translated from French). Using an insider-outsider research team and an inductive approach (Charmaz, 2014), analysis proceeded in six phases: extracting 27 episodes of vulnerability practices across the meetings; identifying roles (facilitator, storyteller, colleagues); open coding of the moves/practices and their chronology; coding perceived effects (benefits and risks); analyzing power dynamics related to seniority and discipline; and developing a theoretical model. Focal constructs were operationalized as coded utterances/moves and participant appraisals illustrated in Tables 1-9.
key_findings: As an inductive qualitative study, the paper reports an emergent process model rather than hypothesis tests. Most episodes (25 of 27) followed a typical ritualized sequence unfolding through an individual disclosure phase and a communal reflection phase, bridged by "theorizing from the case" (boundary setting, categorizing, perspective shifting). A delicate tension between social pressure (to display vulnerabilities) and social support (to contain them) underpins the practices; when balanced, the setting operates as a holding environment that yields perceived benefits — comfort/belonging, normalization and reassurance, and role-based learning. Two path anomalies reveal its precarity: in "under-vulnerability" (E19) the storyteller repeatedly resisted disclosing, and in "under-validation" (E9) colleagues skipped theorizing and validating, leaving the storyteller feeling devalued and reluctant to return. Power and authority dynamics (facilitator role, discretion to participate, theorizing capability, and position in institutionalized hierarchies) shaped who was "held": lower-status participants (residents, social workers, nurses, patient partners) more often reported social discomfort and intimidation, while multidisciplinarity both widened the interpretive resources available (notably patient partners' perspective shifting) and could intensify social pressure. Participants' appraisals of past episodes fed back into their willingness to engage in subsequent ones.
theoretical_contribution: The study introduces the concept of "vulnerability practices" — a ritualized sequence of moves through which group members display, or lead others to display, and address the role-based doubts and insecurities experienced in their work — and derives an inductive process model moving from individual disclosure to communal reflection, with theorizing as the pivotal bridge that constitutes a holding environment. It reconceptualizes holding environments at work not as fixed settings people enter but as precarious, ongoing accomplishments nourished or undermined episode by episode, nuancing prior research that emphasizes the positive effects of vulnerability display by surfacing its risks. It also theorizes how power dynamics tied to multidisciplinarity seep into vulnerability practices, showing how some ritual elements flatten power relations while others do not, and how multidisciplinary epistemic diversity expands the interpretive resources available for role-based learning.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that recognizing sustained engagement in vulnerability practices as "real work" is a practical as well as a theoretical contribution: this recognition may help practitioners (including academics) value such dedicated settings as potential holding environments (or "lifeboats") for coping with the pervasive doubts and insecurities experienced in daily professional work.
limitations: The single-case design was explicitly focused on vulnerability practices in one context where doubts and insecurities about professional roles were the central concern. The activity studied was conducted entirely online during the observation period. The multidisciplinary composition, while offering a rich array of interpretive resources, may also make exchanges appear intimidating or invalidating for some participants.
future_research: The authors call for multi-case studies comparing various contexts, processes, and dynamics of vulnerability practices, and for analysis of how professionals engage in vulnerability practices online versus in person. They also suggest examining other groups spanning diverse disciplinary and seniority statuses to understand how to level the playing field and enhance the benefits of vulnerability practices — for example, rotating the facilitator role among participants of different disciplinary statuses, or organizing groups whose members do not otherwise work together.
abstract: Professional workers are expected to display confidence and mastery in their work roles, and may be hesitant to reveal their doubts and insecurities, especially in multidisciplinary settings characterized by status differences. However, scholars have recognized the benefits of sharing vulnerabilities to create opportunities for social support. We contribute to the literature by revealing how this might be achieved through a ritualized sequence of “vulnerability practices” in a dedicated setting. Based on a qualitative study of a weekly meeting where a multidisciplinary group of professionals shares experiences, we develop a process model that explains how vulnerability practices evolve through phases of individual disclosure and communal reflection bridged by theorizing from experiences. We reveal how a delicate tension between social pressure (to display vulnerabilities) and social support (to contain them) underpins these practices, and how this tension is influenced by power relations associated with multidisciplinarity. We show how participants’ appraisals of past episodes shape their willingness to engage in subsequent episodes, reinforcing or undermining the capacity of the setting to serve as a “holding environment” offering interpretation and containment. We thus reveal holding environments at work to be precarious accomplishments, created and maintained through ritualized vulnerability practices, and imbued by power relations.

title: Not So Fast? Rapid Response to Voice Leads to Perceived Inauthenticity
methods: Mixed-method; three preregistered experiments (n = 3,056). Study 1: qualitative field experiment with doctoral students, two blind coders rating open-ended responses on a tripartite (in)authenticity scale, analyzed via ordered and multinomial logistic regression. Studies 2-3: randomized between-subjects vignette experiments (Study 2 uses executive 360-degree action-plan stimulus sampling), analyzed via one-way and two-way ANOVA and bootstrapped (moderated) mediation estimated with structural equation models.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals: doctoral students evaluating their advisors, and part-time and full-time employees evaluating managers/leaders
n_sample: 3,056 total across three studies (initial samples); final analytic samples of 190 (Study 1), 1,676 (Study 2), and 710 (Study 3)
authors: Chon, D.; Sezer, O.; Flynn, F. J.
theories: attribution theory (Martinko & Gardner, 1987); lay theories of behavior change; leader-centric voice (Morrison, 2023); perceived authenticity (Cha et al., 2019)
keywords: change difficulty; leader-centric voice; perceived authenticity; rate of behavior change; subsequent voice
research_question: When leaders change their behavior in response to leader-centric voice, how does the rate of that change (rapid vs. gradual) influence followers' perceptions of the leader's authenticity and, in turn, followers' willingness to express subsequent voice? The paper further asks whether the difficulty of the requested change moderates this authenticity penalty.
hypotheses:
H1. Leaders who change their behavior rapidly in response to leader-centric voice are perceived as less authentic than leaders who change their behavior gradually.
H2. The negative effect of a rapid change on followers' willingness to express subsequent voice is mediated by perceived authenticity.
H3. The negative effect of a rapid change on perceived authenticity is mitigated when the behavior change is easy (versus difficult).
H4. The negative effect of a rapid change on followers' willingness to express subsequent voice is mitigated when the behavior change is easy (versus difficult).
H5. The negative effect of a rapid (versus gradual) change on followers' willingness to express subsequent voice when the change is difficult (versus easy) is mediated by lowered perceived authenticity.
mechanism_summary: Followers hold lay beliefs that true, authentic change reflects a corresponding transformation of a leader's core sense of self and therefore requires substantial time and effort. When a leader changes rapidly in response to voice, this violates the lay expectation; drawing on attribution and person-perception logic, followers are prompted to seek an alternative explanation and infer that the swift change is a façade to appease them rather than a genuine transformation, so they judge the leader as less authentic. Because authenticity attributions shape observers' own behavior, this authenticity penalty reduces followers' willingness to voice future concerns. The penalty is sharper when the requested change is difficult (which more starkly contradicts the lay belief) and attenuates for easy changes, where a rapid response can instead raise perceived responsiveness.
data_measures: Rate of change (IV) was manipulated through vignettes across contexts: a doctoral advisor's behavior (Study 1), executive action plans written in response to 360-degree feedback and screened via stimulus sampling (Study 2), and a manager, "Mark" (Study 3). Change difficulty (moderator) was manipulated as easy vs. difficult in Study 3. Perceived authenticity (DV) was coded qualitatively in Study 1 by two hypothesis-blind coders on a tripartite scale (-1 = inauthenticity references, 0 = neutral/both/irrelevant, +1 = authenticity references), and measured in Studies 2-3 with a four-item scale adapted from Bailey and Levy (2022) on a 7-point scale (α = .95-.96). Willingness to express subsequent voice (DV, Study 3) used four items adapted from Liang et al. (2012), 7-point (α = .90); perceived responsiveness (exploratory mediator) used three items (α = .93). Analyses used ordered and multinomial logistic regression (Study 1), one-way and two-way ANOVA (Studies 2-3), and bootstrapped simple, mediated, and moderated-mediation models (5,000 resamples) estimated via structural equation models in Stata. Because rate and difficulty were randomized, their effects support causal interpretation; the authenticity-to-voice mediation rests on a measured mediator and is associational at that link.
key_findings: All five hypotheses were supported, and the effect direction is consistent throughout: a faster rate of change lowers perceived authenticity. H1 was supported across studies — in Study 1, a faster (immediate) rate yielded more inauthenticity references (n = 15 vs. 2) and fewer authenticity references (n = 7 vs. 16), with a significant ordered logistic model, x2(1) = 12.88, p < .001 (log odds of authenticity references decreased by 1.37, p = .001); in Study 2, rapid changes were judged less authentic (M = 4.42) than gradual changes (M = 5.09), F(1, 1674) = 105.16, p < .001, robust across all eight stimuli. H3 was supported (Study 3): a significant rate × difficulty interaction on authenticity, F(1, 706) = 8.27, p = .004; when the change was difficult, rapid change was less authentic (M = 3.47) than gradual (M = 4.70), whereas when easy the gap attenuated (rapid M = 4.39 vs. gradual M = 5.06). H4 was supported: a significant interaction on willingness to voice, F(1, 706) = 4.52, p = .034; rapid change reduced subsequent voice under difficult change (M = 4.05 vs. 4.36) but not under easy change. H2 was supported by a significant negative indirect effect of rate on subsequent voice via perceived authenticity (b = -.31, 95% CI [-.42, -.23]). H5 was supported by significant moderated mediation (index b = -.19, p = .008): the negative indirect effect via authenticity was stronger for difficult (b = -.41) than easy (b = -.22) changes. Exploratorily, a rapid easy change also raised perceived responsiveness (a positive indirect path), which can offset the authenticity penalty on subsequent voice when change is easy; for difficult changes both authenticity and responsiveness paths were negative.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to voice research by identifying the rate of a leader's response — not merely whether the leader responds — as a determinant of leader evaluations, challenging the prevailing assumption that faster change is unambiguously better. It surfaces perceived authenticity as an overlooked consequence of how leaders respond to voice and theorizes a recursive dynamic in which authenticity attributions feed back into followers' willingness to voice. It also answers Cha et al.'s (2019) call to address the temporal dimension of authenticity, arguing that authenticity judgments hinge on followers' lay belief that genuine change takes time and effort.
practical_implication: The authors deliberately refrain from simply urging leaders to slow down, because authenticity is only one dimension of leader evaluations: when a change is easy, rapid responders may be seen as less authentic but more responsive, letting employees feel seen and heard. They advise leaders to weigh this trade-off between perceived authenticity and perceived responsiveness when deciding how quickly to change in response to leader-centric voice. Drawing on King et al. (2019), they also suggest leaders may soften the authenticity penalty by proactively communicating how difficult a requested change actually is, shaping followers' expectations before enacting a rapid change.
limitations: The studies are, for the most part, hypothetical vignette experiments; the authors note this and partly address it with a recall design (Study S3) but still do not observe change in real time or within an ongoing leader-follower relationship. In Studies 2 and 3 authenticity is captured with bipolar measures, leaving a possible asymmetry between authenticity and inauthenticity judgments (highlighted in Study 1) only partially examined. The work also does not account for cultural differences and relies primarily on Western-oriented theory and Western samples.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether differences in behavior type (e.g., interpersonal vs. task changes) correspond to differences in difficulty that strengthen or attenuate the authenticity penalty, and on weighted coding of authenticity-related keywords. They suggest longitudinal and experience-sampling designs to study the penalty across multiple timepoints and sub-variants of change rates (e.g., a constant rate vs. a slow start followed by a flurry), further examination of the asymmetry between authenticity and inauthenticity judgments, and replication using non-Western perspectives on authenticity and the self.
abstract: Employees voice their concerns in the hope that leaders will change their behavior. But how do employees evaluate these changes? In the present research, we highlight the rate of behavior change as a key factor in determining leader evaluations: Leaders are seen as less authentic when they change rapidly in response to employee voice because people believe that true change takes time. We investigate this claim with three studies that adopt a mixed-method approach (n 5 3,056). In Study 1, PhD students describe rapid improvement in their advisor’s behavior as less authentic than gradual improvement— even when these changes are desired. In Study 2, we employ a stimulus sampling design to test the robustness of this effect. Followers see rapid improvement as less authentic than gradual improvement across a wide array of leader behaviors. In Study 3, we highlight change difficulty as a moderator and subsequent voice as a downstream consequence: When change is hard, rapid improvement elicits a greater authenticity penalty, which undermines followers’ willingness to voice their concerns in the future.

title: Under Pressure to Be Perfect: How Dehumanizing and Rehumanizing Social Cues Lead to Maladaptive and Adaptive Perfectionism in Professional Ballet
methods: Inductive, qualitative theory-elaboration study; grounded-theory analysis (open, axial, and theoretical coding in NVivo) of 61 semi-structured interviews (avg. 52 min) with professional ballet dancers, 10 follow-up interviews, 5 industry-leader interviews, and ~21 hours of observation.
industry: Professional ballet (elite dance companies)
country: United States (initial fieldwork in the Western United States; dancers drawn from 24 companies)
time_period: 2019-2020 (fieldwork began late 2019; interviews moved to Zoom after the COVID-19 outbreak)
units: Individual professional/semi-professional ballet dancers (plus 5 industry leaders)
n_sample: 61 dancers (aged 17-40, mean 28.5), from 24 companies; plus 10 follow-up and 5 leader interviews
authors: Goodwin, R. D.; Garrett, L. E.; Block, A. P.
theories: organizational dehumanization (Bell & Khoury, 2011; Haslam, 2006); perfectionism: maladaptive vs. adaptive (Stoeber & Otto, 2006; Hamachek, 1978); social information processing theory (Salancik & Pfeffer, 1978)
keywords: adaptive perfectionism; maladaptive perfectionism; organizational dehumanization; performance pressure; professional ballet; rehumanization; self-compassion; social information processing theory
research_question: How do social cues within high-pressure work environments influence workers' experience of different (maladaptive vs. adaptive) forms of perfectionism? The study asks what contextual factors stimulate one type of perfectionism rather than the other.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Performance pressure: a constant, high-stakes condition of the ballet profession that primes perfectionism.
- Dehumanizing cues (organization-signaled): denial of fallibility, denial of agency, denial of subjectivity, denial of individuality.
- Maladaptive perfectionism cycle: perfectionistic concerns and self-destructive behaviors mutually reinforcing, tending toward breakdown or exit.
- Breakdown: a physical/mental turning point that raises receptivity to rehumanizing cues.
- Rehumanizing cues (individual/small-group-signaled): reaffirming fallibility, agency, subjectivity, individuality.
- Adaptive perfectionism cycle: perfectionistic strivings and self-compassionate behaviors mutually reinforcing.
- Relapse / learned response: iterative shifting between the two cycles across a career.

Drawing on social information processing theory, the paper theorizes that dancers internalize social cues about their worth and humanity. When the organization signals that human error, autonomy, feeling, and individuality are unacceptable, dancers internalize dehumanization and slip into a self-reinforcing maladaptive cycle. When individuals or peers signal that mistakes, voice, pain, and uniqueness are legitimate, dancers rehumanize and enter an adaptive cycle. Because performance pressure and dehumanizing cues persist, the two cycles are dynamic and reversible rather than terminal states.
data_measures: Data corpus: 61 semi-structured interviews (average 52 minutes) with professional/semi-professional ballet dancers from 24 companies; 10 follow-up interviews to trace shifts through the emergent model; 5 interviews with industry leaders used only as a credibility check; ~21 hours of nonparticipant observation of classes, rehearsals, and facilities; and autoethnographic insight from an insider-outsider team. Analysis followed grounded-theory principles under a theory-elaboration and problematization approach: line-by-line open coding in NVivo (staying close to informants' own terms), axial coding into second-order themes (e.g., perfectionistic concerns, self-destructive behaviors), and theoretical coding into aggregate dimensions and a process model (Figures 1-2). The design is interpretive; the authors state it is not intended to isolate causal effects.
key_findings: Organizational dehumanizing cues, internalized under performance pressure, elicited perfectionistic concerns and increased self-destructive behaviors (e.g., pushing through injury, eating disorders, substance abuse), forming a vicious maladaptive perfectionism cycle that often culminated in breakdown or exit. Rehumanizing cues that reaffirmed dancers' fallibility, agency, subjectivity, and individuality precipitated a shift toward adaptive perfectionism, marked by perfectionistic strivings and self-compassionate behaviors (boundaries, self-care, self-forgiveness). Dancers moved back and forth between the two cycles over their careers, with relapse always possible; relapses became less frequent, and breakdown less necessary, as dancers learned to resist internalizing dehumanizing cues. The study also surfaces a previously unnamed form of dehumanization — denial of fallibility — alongside the established denials of agency, subjectivity, and individuality.
theoretical_contribution: The paper identifies organizational dehumanization and rehumanization as contextual mechanisms that separate maladaptive from adaptive perfectionism, responding to calls to examine the antecedents and mechanisms of workplace perfectionism. It offers a cyclical, iterative view in which each type of perfectionism is a mutually reinforcing loop of cognitions and behaviors, and — via social information processing theory — challenges the assumption that perfectionism is primarily a stable trait by showing how everyday social cues shape workers' shifting between types. It contributes to the dehumanization literature by proposing the denial of fallibility as a new form of dehumanization, showing that people can internalize dehumanizing cues in self-destructive ways, and positioning a dehumanizing environment as a moderator of whether performance pressure yields adaptive or maladaptive responses.
practical_implication: For leaders, managers, HR professionals, and mentors in high-pressure organizations, the authors argue that person-centered perfectionism interventions are insufficient because they neglect the dehumanizing context; organizations should proactively affirm workers' humanity and avoid sending dehumanizing signals, especially to entry-level professionals seeking to prove themselves. Recommended managerial practices tied to the four forms of dehumanization include: objective, attainable metrics that leave room for making and reporting mistakes; leaders sharing (rather than hiding) weakness; structuring roles to support subordinate agency (e.g., anonymous reporting, active listening); prioritizing well-being through regular breaks and support resources; and aligning work with individual expression and recognition. The authors frame attenuating dehumanization as a moral obligation while maintaining high performance expectations.
limitations: The authors caution that the sample has idiosyncratic features that raise transferability questions: 78% of interviewees were women, which may heighten the salience of replaceability and status denial, and ballet's extreme reliance on the physical body makes its perfectionism more body-focused than in most workplaces. The inductive design is not intended to isolate the causal effects of de- and rehumanization on perfectionism. As with qualitative data generally, there are concerns of biased recall and the possibility that dancers framed their experiences more positively to protect their self-concept.
future_research: The paper calls for research on gendered dynamics of dehumanization and perfectionism; on embodiment and how perfectionism is experienced in the body, including in less physically demanding work; and for deductive/experimental tests (controlling individual differences such as trait perfectionism, conscientiousness, and gender) of the moderating effects of de- and rehumanization. It also invites study of other maladaptive reactions triggered by internalizing dehumanization (e.g., unethical behavior, and the dehumanization-to-unethical-behavior direction), self-compassion as a response to environmentally induced perfectionism and which strategies are most effective, the effects of adaptive vs. maladaptive perfectionism on retention and performance and the organizational costs and benefits of rehumanizing, the nature and degree of performance pressure across competitive industries, and how leaders and institutions dehumanize workers and whether rehumanization fixes or merely perpetuates the harm.
abstract: Research on workplace perfectionism has focused on harmful consequences of workers' perfectionism. However, perfectionism is not a uniform experience. Maladaptive and adaptive perfectionism have different outcomes for worker performance and well-being. While perfectionism appears especially prevalent in high performance pressure environments, minimal research has examined how social cues shape workers' experience of perfectionism. Through an inductive study of professional ballet dancers facing extreme performance pressure, we discovered that social cues influence whether people experience maladaptive or adaptive perfectionism. We found that organizational dehumanizing cues elicited perfectionistic concerns and increased self-destructive behaviors, leading to a vicious cycle of maladaptive perfectionism and an increased likelihood of breakdowns at work. However, rehumanizing cues precipitated a shift toward adaptive perfectionism characterized by perfectionistic strivings and self-compassionate behaviors. We also show how workers can shift back and forth between maladaptive and adaptive perfectionism cycles throughout their careers. We reveal new insights at the intersection of high performance pressure, dehumanization, and perfectionism, offering dehumanization and rehumanization as key mechanisms linking the environment and perfectionism. We also discuss how our findings, though in an extreme context, apply to other high-pressure workplace environments, and open new opportunities to explore the processes of maladaptive and adaptive perfectionism in other domains.

title: The Dualities of Multiple Team Membership: Implications for Team Performance and Adaptability
methods: Quantitative archival study. Unconflated 1-1-1 multilevel (moderated-)mediation models estimated by full-information maximum likelihood, with group-mean and grand-mean centering; Hoberg-Phillips text-based firm-similarity and Blau's-index measures; indirect effects tested with 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo 95% confidence intervals. Observational (non-experimental) design.
industry: Sell-side financial analyst (equity research) teams at the investment bank J. P. Morgan
units: Analyst teams, observed as report-level team performance episodes nested within teams
n_sample: 20,867 team performance episode observations (Level 1) nested within 473 teams (Level 2)
authors: Lang, T.; de Vries, T. A.; Li, H.; Shaw, J. D.
theories: attention-based perspective; categorization-elaboration model (van Knippenberg et al., 2004); social network perspective; team information processing framework (Hinsz et al., 1997)
keywords: external network heterogeneity; external role heterogeneity; internal informational diversity; multiple team membership; team adaptability; team performance
research_question: Through what countervailing mediating mechanisms, and under what team-internal contingency, does team-level multiple team membership (MTM) simultaneously benefit team performance and undermine team adaptability? The paper asks why and when team-level MTM positively or negatively affects distinct dimensions of team effectiveness.
hypotheses:
H1. External network heterogeneity mediates the positive relationship between MTM and team performance.
H2. External role heterogeneity mediates the negative relationship between MTM and team adaptability.
H3. Internal informational diversity moderates the indirect relationship between MTM and team performance (mediated by external network heterogeneity); this positive indirect relationship is stronger when internal informational diversity is high.
H4. Internal informational diversity moderates the indirect relationship between MTM and team adaptability (mediated by external role heterogeneity); this negative indirect relationship is weaker when internal informational diversity is high.
mechanism_summary:
- Moderator: Internal informational diversity (variety of members' knowledge bases and perspectives).

Drawing on the social network perspective, higher team-level MTM gives members access to more diverse, nonredundant external resources (higher external network heterogeneity), which improves team performance. Drawing on the attention-based perspective, higher MTM pushes members to adopt focused, more homogeneous external roles to manage switching costs (lower external role heterogeneity), which impairs the team's capacity to deviate from routines and adapt its output. The team information processing framework identifies internal informational diversity as the lever that lets teams combine and elaborate member inputs, thereby amplifying the beneficial network pathway to performance and buffering (compensating for) the detrimental role pathway to adaptability.
data_measures: Archival authorship data from J. P. Morgan's U.S. firm research report summary files (ProQuest, 2011-2019), linked to I/B/E/S detailed one-year-ahead EPS forecasts. MTM: ratio of reports members authored in external teams to total reports (inside plus outside), aggregated to the team. External network heterogeneity: 1 minus the average Hoberg-Phillips (HP) product cosine similarity across the firms covered by external members. External role heterogeneity: Blau's (1977) index of members' authorship-order (role) distribution outside the team, aggregated following Bunderson and Sutcliffe (2002). Internal informational diversity: mean HP similarity of firms studied by the team's own members. Team performance: forecast accuracy (inverse of absolute forecast error). Team adaptability: number of report updates issued within one month after the focal forecast. Estimation is associational (unconflated 1-1-1 multilevel models); the study makes no causal-identification claim.
key_findings: All four hypotheses were supported. H1: MTM is positively related to external network heterogeneity (B = 27.52, p < .01) and external network heterogeneity is positively related to team performance (B = 1.98, p < .01); the indirect effect of MTM on team performance is positive, 0.53, 95% CI [0.30, 0.75] (the direct MTM-performance effect was non-significant, B = 1.22, p = .06). H2: MTM is negatively related to external role heterogeneity (B = -33.61, p < .01), which is in turn positively related to team adaptability (B = 22.56, p < .01); the indirect effect of MTM on team adaptability is negative, -10.19, 95% CI [-11.56, -8.81]. H3: the external-network-heterogeneity x internal-informational-diversity interaction on performance is positive (B = 11.11, p = .02); the positive indirect relationship is significant only when internal informational diversity is high (+1 SD = 0.81, 95% CI [0.46, 1.15]) and non-significant when low (-1 SD = 0.14, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.50]). H4: the external-role-heterogeneity x internal-informational-diversity interaction on adaptability is negative (B = -106.69, p < .01); the negative indirect relationship is attenuated (weaker) when internal informational diversity is high (+1 SD = -2.21, 95% CI [-4.06, -0.37]) and accentuated when low (-1 SD = -9.46, 95% CI [-11.40, -7.52]).
theoretical_contribution: The study integrates the social network and attention-based perspectives through the team information processing framework to explain the countervailing team-level effects of MTM, identifying external network heterogeneity and external role heterogeneity as previously unexplored mediating mechanisms and distinguishing team performance from team adaptability as effectiveness dimensions affected in opposite directions. It positions internal informational diversity as a shared moderator that governs whether teams can leverage these external-diversity mechanisms. In doing so it extends O'Leary et al.'s (2011) seminal MTM model and contributes an open-systems reading of the categorization-elaboration model, the team boundary-spanning literature, and the diversity-bandwidth trade-off by jointly considering teams' internal and external forms of diversity.
practical_implication: For team leaders, the identified mediators offer intermediate outcomes to monitor and target: leaders can gauge whether members' MTM yields a broad set of external contacts (external network heterogeneity) and whether members vary their external role assignments (external role heterogeneity), and can use levers such as role-rotation schemes and network-aware team composition. For team members, the findings help anticipate the benefits and costs of additional parallel team engagements, including weighing the internal diversity and similarity of teams they contemplate joining. For higher-level administrators, the results inform when to deploy MTM structures: high-performance, knowledge-intensive projects can benefit from MTM, whereas projects requiring rapid adaptation may need alternative or hybrid structures, and continued investment in MTM is more justified when internal informational diversity offsets its adaptability costs.
limitations: The model was tested in a single organization of comparable financial analyst teams, and the competitive industry limited cross-firm interaction, so generalizability to other industries and regions requires replication. The archival design relies on proxies (authorship order for members' roles, and covered firms for external network and role heterogeneity). The conceptualization of team adaptability is relatively broad. Contrary to expectation, team adaptability and team performance were significantly negatively related, so the two effectiveness dimensions may not be fully independent.
future_research: The authors call for replication in other industries (e.g., manufacturing) and regions (e.g., Africa, Europe, Asia) and for alternative operationalizations of the network and role mechanisms. They suggest examining why team performance and adaptability are negatively related (e.g., whether decision-making biases such as confirmation bias impede adaptation) and integrating structural adaptation theory to study which types of team adaptation MTM hinders or enables. Further directions include clarifying the role of autonomy in MTM engagements and identifying alternative mechanisms (e.g., supervisory or organization-level design) behind reduced external role heterogeneity, extending the model to other effectiveness dimensions such as team viability and turnover, and differentiating task-related from demographic diversity as well as short- versus long-term implications.
abstract: Researchers recognize that multiple team membership (MTM) represents a double-edged sword for teams, but the precise mechanisms that explain the countervailing effects and contingencies that modulate these relationships remain underexplored. We argue that team-level MTM allows team members to access heterogeneous external resources through more diverse external-network ties, benefiting team performance. In contrast, we advance ideas that team-level MTM can negatively impact team adaptability by diminishing the heterogeneity of team members' external roles. To reconcile these divergent arguments, we introduce an informational perspective to suggest that teams can strengthen the benefits and mitigate the downsides of MTM when they have high levels of internal informational diversity. Using data from financial forecast reports published by 473 analyst teams in J. P. Morgan from 2011 to 2019, we find support for our integrated theoretical framework. MTM indeed appears to be beneficial for team performance through increased external network heterogeneity, but detrimental for team adaptability through reduced external role heterogeneity. Teams' internal informational diversity was furthermore found to accentuate these indirect benefits of MTM for team performance, while simultaneously attenuating its indirect detriments for team adaptability.

title: When Dirty Work Inspires: The Joint Effect of Work Dirtiness and Perceived Stigma on Pro-Organizational Behavior
methods: Four studies. Three field surveys (Study 1: 179 Chinese nurses, cluster-robust path model; Study 2: 302 U.S. employees, temporally separated waves; Study 4: 194 Chinese employees, two-week daily experience sampling analyzed with multilevel SEM) and one scenario-based experiment manipulating work dirtiness (Study 3: 116 U.S. workers). Moderated-mediation path models with interaction terms probed via the Johnson-Neyman technique.
industry: Multiple occupations/industries (home-healthcare nursing; technology, manufacturing, finance, hospitality, retail, public and social services)
country: China (Studies 1 and 4) and United States (Studies 2 and 3)
time_period: Not reported as calendar dates; Study 4 collected brief daily surveys over two weeks
units: Individual employees (Study 4 also person-day daily reports)
n_sample: Study 1: 179 nurses; Study 2: 302 employees; Study 3: 116 workers; Study 4: 194 employees (1,798 daily observations)
authors: Peng, A. C.; Kim, D.; Schaubroeck, J. M.; Zeng, W.
theories: self-categorization theory (Turner, 1985; Turner, Hogg, Oakes, Reicher & Wetherell, 1987); social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979)
keywords: normative fit; organizational citizenship behavior; organizational identification; perceived occupational stigma; self-categorization theory; work dirtiness
research_question: Why do many individuals performing dirty work engage positively with their jobs and organizations whereas others become disengaged? The paper asks how the experience of performing dirty tasks (work dirtiness) and the perception of occupational stigma jointly determine which identity process, and thus which behavioral response, is triggered.
hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1. Perceived occupational stigma moderates the relationship between work dirtiness and OCB; the relationship is positive when perceived stigma is high and negative when perceived stigma is low.
Hypothesis 2. Organizational identification mediates the interaction effect of perceived occupational stigma with work dirtiness on OCB; the indirect effect of work dirtiness on OCB through organizational identification is positive when stigma perception is high and negative when stigma perception is low.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on self-categorization theory, the authors argue that a work-related social identity becomes salient only when a social category is both accessible and matches social reality. High perceived occupational stigma makes the occupational/organizational category accessible; high work dirtiness then supplies normative fit (behavior matches the negative societal stereotype), activating the social identity and channeling attention toward supporting the organization. When perceived stigma is low, work dirtiness lacks normative fit, so personal identity becomes salient, dirty tasks are appraised as a threat to self-worth, and employees psychologically disengage. Organizational identification is the proximal expression of a salient social identity that carries the interaction into behavior.
data_measures: Work dirtiness was measured with the 12-item scale (three sub-dimensions) of Schaubroeck et al. (2018); Study 3 instead manipulated moral and social dirtiness through a personal-trainer scenario (with a six-item manipulation check), and Study 4 used a nine-item daily version. Perceived occupational stigma used Schaubroeck et al.'s (2018) five-item scale. The mediator, organizational identification, used Mael and Ashforth's (1992) six-item scale (four items in Study 4's daily measure). Pro-organizational behavior used established OCB scales: OCB-I (Podsakoff et al., 1990; Lee & Allen, 2002), OCB-C (Amarnani et al., 2022, reworded to "patients"), and OCB-O (Lee & Allen, 2002). Identification comes from Study 3's experimental manipulation of work dirtiness (causal), whereas Studies 1, 2, and 4 are associational surveys that mitigate common-method bias via cluster-robust errors, temporal separation of waves, and daily experience sampling rather than through causal identification. Interactions were probed with the Johnson-Neyman technique.
key_findings: The work dirtiness × perceived stigma interaction was positive and significant in every study (Study 1: b = .16 on OCB-I, b = .30 on OCB-C; Study 2: b = .10 on OCB-I, b = .24 on OCB-O; Study 3: b = .62 on OCB-O, OCB-I nonsignificant; Study 4 between-person: b = .25 on OCB-I, b = .19 on OCB-O). Consistent with H1, work dirtiness had a positive effect on OCB when perceived stigma was sufficiently high and a negative effect when stigma was low, but support was asymmetric: the positive high-stigma slope was clearest in Studies 1-2, while the negative low-stigma slope was clearest in Studies 3-4 (whose samples skewed toward low stigma). H1 was therefore supported for OCB-C/OCB-O across studies (in Study 4 chiefly for the negative low-stigma half, with less support for the high-stigma part of the interaction) but only partially for OCB-I (the predicted negative low-stigma effect on OCB-I was often nonsignificant). H2 (moderated mediation through organizational identification) was partially supported in Studies 2-4: identification carried the interaction, the negative indirect effect under low stigma was significant in Studies 3-4 but not Study 2, whereas the positive indirect effect under high stigma reached significance only in Study 2. Overall the four studies "largely support" the hypotheses. A supplementary analysis showed the interaction also predicted organizational identity salience, and excluding very-low-stigma participants in Study 4 strengthened the predicted effects.
theoretical_contribution: The paper offers a self-categorization-theory explanation of why incumbents of dirty jobs foster a positive social identity and act pro-organizationally, moving beyond prior work that described what workers think and do after their social identity is presumed already salient to specify when that salience arises — namely through normative fit created by the joint presence of work dirtiness and perceived stigma. It establishes that perceived occupational stigma (a meta-perception about society's view of one's job) is conceptually and empirically distinct from work dirtiness (performing degrading tasks) and that the two operate in concert, reconciling seemingly contradictory prior findings. It also extends the literature's focus from occupational identity to organizational identity and identification as the proximal, tangible social category among the general work population.
practical_implication: For managers, the study implies that symbolic management aimed at reframing tainted work will be more effective when managers also make employees aware of the societal stigma attached to their jobs, because such awareness supplies the normative fit that activates a supportive social identity. Managers are advised to attend especially to employees who do not hold strong occupational stigma beliefs, since these workers are more likely to construe work dirtiness as a threat to personal identity and to withdraw; maintaining regular communication that frames dirty tasks as contributing to the organization and society, and as a marker of professionalism, can help sustain their engagement.
limitations: Three of the four studies relied on self-reports, raising common-method-bias concerns; the authors mitigated this through temporal separation (Study 2), manipulation of work dirtiness (Study 3), and repeated daily measures (Study 4), and note that interaction effects are less susceptible to such bias. The studies were run only in the United States and China, so cultural differences may shape how workers attend to the two aspects of dirty work. Occupational stigma was conceptualized and measured at the individual level, leaving group-shared stigma unmodeled, and the theory and tests focused on between-person processes.
future_research: The authors call for tests using external (non-self-report) ratings of pro-organizational behavior and for examining whether a group's shared perception of stigma has additional impact on the identity processes. They suggest studying incongruent combinations of the two constructs (e.g., tainted occupations performing ordinary tasks, or high work dirtiness in low-stigma occupations), exploring how other forms of societal stigma (such as discrimination or social exclusion) communicate identity information, considering comparative fit (alongside normative fit) as a route to stigmatized-identity salience, and investigating crucial within-person moments that temporarily heighten work dirtiness and activate social identity.
abstract: Research reveals that many employees derive esteem and pride from their work despite indignities attributed to their occupations. Whereas studies have identified what these “dirty workers” think and do to maintain a positive work identity, it remains unclear why they do so whereas others tend to disengage from work. We draw from self-categorization theory to develop a model that conceptualizes how the salience of one’s social identity is determined jointly by engaging in dirty tasks (i.e., work dirtiness) and perceived occupational stigma. When perceiving that others in society stigmatize one’s occupation, high work dirtiness creates a match between one’s behavior and societal expectations linked to one’s job. Based on this mechanism of normative fit, work-related social identity is salient, encouraging pro-organizational behavior. Conversely, we argue that when stigma is perceived as low, individuals experiencing high dirtiness at work become more concerned about their personal identity, reducing engagement with their organization. Results from four studies using survey and experimental designs largely support our hypotheses. This research reconciles seemingly contradictory results concerning employee responses toward dirty work and provides a theoretical explanation for why people with dirty jobs engage positively with their work and organizations.

title: On the Move: The Impact of Internal Mobility and Internal Comobility on Unit- and Organization-Level Outcomes
methods: Longitudinal panel of monthly store-level personnel and sales records from a single Fortune 500 U.S. retail firm (2016–2018). Store and month fixed-effects regressions for established stores (Hypotheses 1–5b) and OLS regression without fixed effects for new stores (Hypothesis 6); a Hausman test favored fixed effects. Design is observational/associational (within-store variation).
industry: Retail (stores of a single Fortune 500 retail firm; over $5 billion revenue, 40,000+ employees)
units: Retail stores (store-month observations)
n_sample: 884 established stores (26,910 store-month observations) and 259 new stores; 1,202 retail locations, 1,143 with sales data
authors: Ray, C.; Nyberg, A. J.; Maltarich, M. A.; Reilly, G.
theories: human capital resources (HCR) theory; human capital theory; social capital theory
keywords: firm-specific human capital; human capital resources; internal comobility; internal mobility; resource reallocation; social capital; unit performance
research_question: Whether, when, and why internal mobility is beneficial or detrimental to unit- and organization-level outcomes: specifically, what the net gains and losses of internal transfers are for the units that receive movers and the units that supply them, and from where within the organization internal movers should be sourced.
hypotheses:
H1. Transfers in are positively related to the performance of the unit they join.
H2. The positive effect of comobile transfers in on the performance of the unit they join is weaker than the positive effect of multisource transfers in.
H3. Transfers out are negatively related to the performance of the unit they leave.
H4. The negative effect of comobile transfers out on the performance of the unit they leave is stronger than the negative effect of multi-destination transfers out.
H5a. The positive effect of multisource transfers in on the performance of the unit they join is stronger in magnitude than the negative effect of multi-destination transfers out on the performance of the unit they leave.
H5b. The positive effect of comobile transfers in on the performance of the unit they join is weaker in magnitude than the negative effect of comobile transfers out on the performance of the unit they leave.
H6. The unit performance effects of transfers in are larger in magnitude in new units than in existing units.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on human capital resources (HCR) theory, the authors argue that internal mobility reallocates firm-specific human and social capital across units, so that adding internally sourced workers enhances a receiving unit's HCR and performance while transfers out dilute the supplying unit's HCR and depress its performance. Multisource transfers in add greater diversity of unit-specific knowledge, whereas comobile transfers in rely more on intact social ties whose redundant knowledge and potential fault lines limit their contribution. Because each transfer in is also a transfer out, the net organizational effect turns on whether gains to receiving units exceed losses to supplying units; these effects should be amplified in new units that have no established HCR, social structure, or path-dependent performance.
data_measures: Data are monthly personnel and sales records for 1,202 retail locations of a single Fortune 500 U.S. retail firm during a 2016–2018 growth period (884 established stores yielding 26,910 store-month observations; 259 new stores). DV: sales = monthly retail sales per store (for H6, Month 6 sales in new stores). IVs: transfers in and out measured as rolling six-month sums of monthly transfers; comobile transfers in/out as the rolling six-month sums of movers who entered/left with at least one other individual from the same prior/current store; multisource transfers in and multi-destination transfers out as movers who entered/left without any other individual from the same store; for new stores, "initial" versions were measured over the store's first three months. Covariates: new hires (rolling six-month sum of external hires), turnover (rolling six-month sum of employees leaving the organization), store size (monthly employee count), and, for new stores, initial budget sales. Estimation: a Hausman test favored fixed effects, so Hypotheses 1–5b used store and month fixed-effects models on established stores, while Hypothesis 6 used OLS regression without fixed effects on new stores (one observation per store). The design is observational/associational, identifying within-store variation rather than an experiment.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: transfers in are positively related to retail sales (b = 6,120.93; SE = 481.08; p < .001), about +$6,121 per transfer in over six months.
- H2 supported: multisource transfers in have a positive, significant effect (b = 8,895.77; SE = 588.84; p < .001) while comobile transfers in are non-significant (b = 274.67; SE = 863.48; p = .75); non-overlapping confidence intervals confirm comobile < multisource.
- H3 supported: transfers out are negatively related to retail sales (b = −5,334.26; SE = 626.22; p < .001), about −$5,334 per transfer out.
- H4 NOT supported: contrary to prediction, comobile transfers out are more weakly negative (b = −4,533.17; p < .05) than multi-destination transfers out (b = −5,268.99; p < .001).
- H5a supported: the positive effect of multisource transfers in (b = 8,895.77) exceeds in magnitude the negative effect of multi-destination transfers out (b = −5,268.99); the difference is significant (diff = 3,626.78; p < .001).
- H5b supported: comobile transfers in (b = 274.67, n.s.) are smaller in magnitude than comobile transfers out (b = −4,533.17, p < .05); the difference is significant (diff = 4,258.50; p < .05).
- H6 partially supported: transfers in are directionally more valuable in new stores (b = 9,272.07) than established stores (b = 6,120.93), but the overall difference is not significant (diff = 3,151.14; p = .08); H6 holds specifically for comobile transfers in, which are significantly more valuable in new stores (diff = 7,965.16; p < .001).
- Net organizational takeaway: reallocating established employees benefits the firm overall only when movers are drawn from a variety of (multiple) source units rather than moved as intact groups.
theoretical_contribution: The study recasts internal mobility as a mechanism for human capital resource (HCR) reallocation across the organization, expanding its theorized scope from individually relevant to organizationally impactful. It distinguishes unit-level attributes of internal mobility (comobile vs. multisource transfers in; comobile vs. multi-destination transfers out) and shows they operate through two distinct means: the diversity of unit-specific knowledge added or removed, versus the transfer of intact social structures. It is the first to theorize and quantify the net effects of internal mobility by simultaneously modeling gains to receiving units and losses to supplying units, thereby capturing organization-level impact, and it extends the macro literature on the reallocation of nonfinancial (human capital) resources.
practical_implication: For managers making staffing and talent-reallocation decisions, the optimal outcome depends on where internal movers are sourced: firms should reallocate employees with firm-specific HCR from a variety of units, sourcing roughly one transfer each from as many units as can reasonably supply them, because transferring more than one worker from any given unit brings substantially less benefit and may be outweighed by disruption to the supplying unit. Because each transfer in is also a transfer out, leaders should weigh the gains to receiving units against the vacancies and HCR losses created in supplying units, taking an organization-level rather than single-unit perspective. The authors caution that this prescription rests on a single study and should be applied cautiously until other studies produce corroborating data.
limitations: The setting is a single U.S. retail organization, so the authors cannot know how far the findings generalize to other industries or contexts. They do not directly test the theorized underlying mechanisms (the unit's social relationships and diversity of knowledge, i.e., changes in unit HCR), relying instead on transfer-type proxies. The measures capture the average number of workers with firm-specific HCR rather than the kind or quality of each mover's human capital. The number of comobile transfers out in the sample is small, limiting inference for that category.
future_research: The authors call for research on the boundary conditions of their theoretical conclusions and on the duration of transfer effects (how long, and with what intensity, effects on HCR persist). They encourage work assessing the kind and quality of employees' firm-specific human capital and more complex configurations of HCR (e.g., means, minima or maxima, variability, and fault lines), and untangling the distinct roles, processes, and value of different mover types (e.g., managers vs. individual contributors). They also encourage directly measuring the quality of transfer relationships and the diversity of knowledge structures to test the proposed mechanisms, and accounting for the causes of transfers into and out of units (e.g., employees being more or less attracted to units based on store performance).
abstract: Internal mobility is commonly used to reallocate talent within organizations. Despite its prevalence and potential implications for organizational performance, most prior work has focused on the individual-level outcomes associated with internal mobility. That is, there has been relatively limited theoretical and empirical attention to the mechanisms that connect internal mobility to unit- and organization-level outcomes, making it difficult to predict when or why internal mobility is beneficial to organizations. To address this oversight, we draw from human and social capital literatures to build theory to predict when and why internal mobility will have unit-level implications. We test this by examining a period of growth in a Fortune 500 company and evaluate gains and losses associated with moving employees within firms, including distinguishing between two types of internal movers—those who come from different units in the organization (solo movers) and those who come from the same unit in the organization (comobile movers). In doing so, we contribute to both internal mobility and strategic human capital resource literatures and provide actionable insights regarding when to source internal movers, and where from.

methods: Editorial essay ('From the Editor'); first-person statement of editorial vision, no empirical data or analysis

research_question: The editorial's guiding question is how AMJ can sustain its commitments to intellectual pluralism, developmental reviewing, and shared editorial stewardship as scale and expectations continue to rise. It asks how editorial models designed for a smaller, more bounded scholarly community must evolve to support the journal's mission under contemporary conditions of growth, complexity, and global participation.

theoretical_contribution: The editorial synthesizes the visions of prior AMJ editors (Beyer, Tsui, and Rynes) into a shared philosophy of editorial leadership as stewardship of a scholarly institution rather than a personal agenda—emphasizing continuity with purposeful evolution, developmental reviewing as a core value, and "big-tent" accessibility to diverse ideas and approaches. title: Anticipatory Impression Management for Potential Adverse Events: Positive Framing in the Wake of Short Seller Attacks on a Competitor
methods: Longitudinal panel; firm and year-quarter fixed-effects OLS regressions with interaction terms; difference-in-differences robustness check; content analysis of earnings-call transcripts using Loughran-McDonald sentiment dictionaries.
industry: Cross-industry; publicly listed U.S. firms whose direct competitor was attacked by a short seller (competitors identified via the Hoberg-Phillips TNIC-3 text-based network industry classification)
units: Firm-quarters (competitors of short-seller-attacked firms), nested in firms
n_sample: 1,989 firms; 344 unique short attacks; 11,824 firm-quarter observations
authors: Song, R.; Connelly, B. L.; Ketchen, D. J., Jr.; Shi, W.
theories: anticipatory impression management (Elsbach, Sutton, & Principe, 1998); awareness-motivation-capability framework (Chen, 1996); theory elaboration (Fisher & Aguinis, 2017)
keywords: anticipatory impression management; awareness-motivation-capability; earnings conference calls; positive framing; product-market similarity; short seller attacks
research_question: Under what conditions does a firm engage in anticipatory impression management—specifically, CEOs' use of positive framing in earnings conference calls—in the wake of a short seller attack on a competitor, a potential event with known adverse consequences? Guided by Chen's (1996) awareness-motivation-capability logic, when is a firm more or less likely to use AIM before such a potential event occurs?
hypotheses:
H1. Following a short seller attack on a competitor, CEO positive framing in earnings conference calls will be higher than it was prior to the attack.
H2. Following a short seller attack on a competitor, a firm's product-market similarity to the attacked firm will be positively associated with CEO positive framing in earnings conference calls.
H3. Following a short seller attack on a competitor, the magnitude of stock price decline at the attacked firm will be positively associated with CEO positive framing in earnings conference calls.
H4. Following a short seller attack on a competitor, a focal firm's recent (prior) stock price performance will be positively associated with CEO positive framing in earnings conference calls.
mechanism_summary: Grounded in AIM theory and Chen's (1996) awareness-motivation-capability (AMC) framework, the study argues that a short seller attack on a competitor raises the specter of a similar attack on the focal firm. When a firm is aware the event might occur, motivated to prevent it, and capable of credibly framing positively, its CEO proactively uses positive framing in earnings calls to deter short sellers before an attack materializes. The paper elaborates AIM from known upcoming events with uncertain consequences to potential events with known adverse consequences, shifting uncertainty from the event's consequences to whether the event occurs.
data_measures: Short attack data came from Insightia (short-seller campaigns, 2007-2022); competitors of attacked firms were identified with the Hoberg-Phillips TNIC-3 text-based network industry classification; earnings-call transcripts came from Thomson Reuters StreetEvents and Capital IQ; stock and accounting data came from CRSP/Compustat. DV, positive framing: CEO positive words minus negative words (Loughran-McDonald 2011 dictionaries; 354 positive and 2,355 negative words), scaled by speech length, coded from the managerial-discussion section of the call. IV: a binary short-attack indicator (0 = four quarters pre-attack on a competitor, 1 = four quarters post). Moderators: product-market similarity (TNIC-3 product-similarity score combined with the two firms' relative market share, min-max normalized); stock price decline of the attacked firm (cumulative abnormal returns, CAR, over a three-day [-1, +1] window, using the absolute value of negative CAR); focal firm's prior performance (quarter-prior stock returns standardized by competitors). Estimation used firm and year-quarter fixed-effects OLS with the moderators entered as interactions with the IV; time-invariant controls were interacted with the IV; a difference-in-differences design served as a robustness check.
key_findings: All four hypotheses were supported. H1: a short seller attack on a competitor has a positive and significant effect on CEO positive framing (β = 0.47, p < .05), corresponding to roughly a 21% increase in positive framing versus pre-attack calls (at zero moderator values). H2 supported: short attack × product-market similarity is positive and significant (β = 0.15, p < .01). H3 supported: short attack × stock price decline is positive and significant (β = 0.94, p < .01). H4 supported: short attack × prior performance is positive and significant (β = 0.23, p < .01), with the marginal effect becoming meaningful only above a threshold of prior performance (significant near the 15th percentile). Results were robust to difference-in-differences estimation. A post hoc analysis found that positive framing is negatively associated with the firm's subsequent short interest (β = -0.06, p < .01), suggesting positive framing can deter short selling.
theoretical_contribution: The study elaborates AIM theory (Fisher & Aguinis's theory elaboration) by extending it from known upcoming events with potentially adverse consequences to potential events with known adverse consequences, thereby shifting the locus of uncertainty from the event's consequences to the event's occurrence. Using Chen's (1996) AMC framework as an organizing logic, it specifies the awareness, motivation, and capability conditions that initiate AIM before a potential event, and it extends AIM to an adversarial audience (short sellers) whom firms seek to deter rather than merely appease. A secondary contribution to short-selling research uncovers a previously overlooked spillover effect of short seller attacks on competitors of the attacked firm and theorizes the ex ante steps firms take in anticipation of short selling.
practical_implication: Viewed from an oversight perspective, boards may encourage CEOs to engage in AIM (positive framing) to pre-empt volatility from anticipated disruptions, and could direct executives' attention to the AMC factors—how similar the attacked competitor is, how severe the attack was, and the firm's own vulnerabilities. More generally, because "good words are worth much, and cost little," firms may treat words as a low-cost first line of defense against short sellers and other hostile actors, though firms with very poor prior performance cannot credibly use positive language and thus lose this tool. The findings may also inform regulators, since short seller attacks that spill over to competitors can carry both corrective and disruptive effects across multiple firms.
limitations: The authors could not fully account for the underlying reasons firms are susceptible to short seller attacks, though a supplementary test suggests spillover is more likely when a competitor is accused of product flaws than of accounting problems. The archival data did not permit direct assessment of the decision-making process that leads to AIM. The model's goodness-of-fit improved only marginally from the baseline to the full model, possibly reflecting nonlinearities or an excess of nonsignificant control variables. The study focuses on the potential for a short seller attack, whereas firms face many other events with negative consequences (e.g., investor activism, employee strikes, buyer demands).
future_research: The authors call for combining actions with words to build a more comprehensive theory of AIM behavior, and for integrating AIM with theories such as protection motivation theory and threat rigidity theory to study long-term, over-time effects. They suggest exploring interorganizational nuances (including framing the potential event as a "selection decision" and drawing on signaling theory), testing the ideas with experimental or policy-capturing designs among CEOs and top executives, using case studies to examine how firms perceive antecedents of short seller attacks, and developing a "multiplex" version of AIM—combined with an attention-based view—that addresses multiple audiences and other threat contexts such as hostile takeovers, market entry, competitive dynamics, and labor disputes.
abstract: Anticipatory impression management (AIM) provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the tactics organizations use to mitigate the potential adverse consequences of known upcoming events. We extend this theorizing to encompass potential upcoming events with known adverse consequences. We posit that a potential event is more likely to induce AIM to the extent that the firm is aware the event might occur, motivated to mitigate its potential consequences, and capable of engaging in tactics that could reduce the event’s likelihood. We test our theorizing in the scenario wherein a competitor has been attacked by a short seller, which raises the specter of a short seller attack on the focal firm. We contend that, following an attack on a competitor, chief executive officers use positive framing in earnings conference calls as an AIM tactic to deter short sellers. Examination of 1,989 firms with a direct competitor attacked by a short seller confirms our ideas. Our study thus extends the boundaries of theory on AIM and broadens research on short selling to encompass principles of attack prevention.

Anticipatory impression management for potential adverse events: Positive framing in the wake of short seller attacks on a competitor. *Academy of Management Journal, 69*(1), 99–122. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2023.0914

title: More-than-capitalist economies: Insights from community supported agriculture, tiny houses and hitchhiking in Denmark
methods: Qualitative focus group study. Seven focus groups (6-9 participants each, 52 in total) conducted Fall/Winter 2023-24 with professional stakeholders mixed across consumption domains and organizational sectors, recruited by first mapping the institutional and organizational landscape of food, housing and mobility in Denmark (public, civil, private). Groups were loosely moderated with open-ended questions on work practices, sustainability approaches, and relationships to consumers, plus a future-imaginaries visioning exercise. Analysis maps mainstream vs. alternative consumption-production relationships and applies Gibson-Graham's 'reading for economic difference' to three in-depth grassroots cases (CSA, tiny house project, hitchhiking).
industry: Food, housing and mobility (three high-emission consumption domains), spanning mainstream actors (supermarkets, food production companies, pension-fund property investors, public transport, private-car lobby) and grassroots actors (food cooperatives, regenerative farms, tiny-house projects, non-profit housing, ridesharing, hitchhiking)
time_period: Fall/Winter 2023-24
units: Professional stakeholders / organizations across food, housing and mobility
n_sample: 52 participants across seven focus groups
authors: Aagaard, L. K.
theories: capitalocentrism critique; diverse economies framework (Gibson-Graham, 2006b, 2020); reading for economic difference; sufficiency
keywords: Community supported agriculture; Consumption-production relationships; Diverse economies; Hitchhiking; More-than-capitalist; Sufficiency; Tiny house
research_question: How can reading for economic difference across the domains of food, housing and mobility reveal the way more-than-capitalist economic activities can show a path towards more sustainable, sufficiency-oriented consumption-production relationships? Concretely: how do grassroots organizations offer alternative approaches to sustainable consumption that exist alongside, and challenge, dominant capitalist models?
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: capitalocentrism vs. diverse / more-than-capitalist economies; efficiency-oriented (profit-driven) vs. sufficiency-oriented (collective) economic models; mainstream vs. grassroots actors
- Method-as-lens: "reading for economic difference" — making subordinated, less-visible economic activities visible and granting them independent agency (the iceberg metaphor)
- Cases (reading for difference across three domains): community supported agriculture (food), a tiny house project (housing), hitchhiking (mobility)
- Cross-cutting dimensions deduced from the cases: 1) spatial (local proximity, direct relationship to land/community over global supply-chain distance); 2) temporal (long-term, flexible engagement with time over immediate, predictable market exchange); 3) relational (face-to-face interaction, interdependency, trust and community over individualism and profit maximization)
- Boundary conditions: the Danish welfare-state context means these cases pursue ecological/relational aims rather than urgent responses to unmet needs (unlike U.S. solidarity economies); none of the cases is fully independent of capitalist structures (each still relies on money and resources)

The paper argues that economic systems are performative — how the economy is conceptualized and enacted shapes which sustainability strategies become possible. Efficiency-oriented sustainability reproduces profit-driven, market-based relationships, whereas sufficiency-oriented practices align with collective, more-than-capitalist forms of organizing. Using Gibson-Graham's diverse economies lens, the three grassroots cases are shown to share spatial, temporal and relational characteristics that decommodify consumption-production relationships and foster ethical and ecological bonds, illustrating a sufficiency-oriented pathway out of the dominant capitalist paradigm.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to diverse economies scholarship by bringing the framework into sustainable consumption research and, rather than studying single sectors or organizations in isolation, reading for economic difference across multiple high-emission domains simultaneously. Its central contribution is a crosscutting framework of three dimensions — spatial, temporal and relational — that travel across food, housing and mobility and serve as anchor points for identifying and framing more-than-capitalist economies as a lens for sustainable, sufficiency-oriented consumption-production relationships.
practical_implication: For more-than-capitalist economies to proliferate from the margins, the paper argues for alternative, collective governance that integrates municipalities, funding bodies and regulatory agencies across public and private sectors. Public funding and subsidies, accessible public land and facilities, and public procurement policies that prioritize cooperatives, CSAs and other sufficiency-oriented enterprises can foster these models, alongside knowledge-sharing networks, hybrid public-grassroots partnerships, and education that brings these economic concepts into public discourse.
limitations: The study is situated in a Danish welfare-state context with relatively low poverty, so the cases pursue slowing societal metabolism and reducing ecological harm rather than responding to injustices of unmet food, housing or mobility needs, limiting transferability to contexts where diverse economies arise as resistance to social, economic and racial exclusion. The paper also frames itself as one initial, exploratory step at the intersection of sufficiency and more-than-capitalist economies, and the long-term social and ecological implications of the cases are not assessed.
future_research: The paper calls for further empirical investigation into the long-term social and ecological implications of more-than-capitalist initiatives, and for assessing the effectiveness of policy interventions that support them so as to refine future regulatory and funding strategies. It also invites continued attention to spatial proximity, long-term engagement and community-building in developing consumption-production relationships for a sustainable future.
abstract: Furthermore, more-than-capitalist economic activities in this landscape are explored. By zooming in on three cases, community supported agriculture, tiny houses and hitchhiking, I draw attention to diverse economies as a lens to reframe consumption-production relationships in a sufficiency-oriented direction. I contribute to this field by proposing three key dimensions in which more-than-capitalist actors share characteristics across food, housing and mobility: 1) spatial; 2) temporal; and 3) relational. Highlighting these, the paper calls for further research and attention to spatial proximity, long-term engagement and community-building in developing consumption-production relationships for a sustainable future.
