title: CEO Activism and Corporate Reputation: How Authenticity and CSR Mitigate Stakeholder Misalignment
methods: Two-study mixed design: Study 1 is a nationally representative survey (n=1050) rating 525 real BLM statements from Fortune 500 companies and Certified B Corps, analysed via OLS regression and structural equation modelling with Sobel tests; Study 2 is a preregistered 2x2 between-subject randomized experiment (n=600) manipulating CEO activism and CSR initiative, analysed via OLS contrasts and mediation analysis.
industry: Fortune 500 companies and Certified B Corps (Study 1); fictitious retail chain 'Supermarket' stimulus (Study 2)
time_period: BLM statements issued largely in late May or June 2020
units: Participants (individual US adults) rating corporate statements
n_sample: Study 1: 1050 participants rating 525 BLM statements; Study 2: 600 participants (150 per experimental group)
authors: Li, L. Z.; Soule, S. A.
theories: cognitive perspective on reputation formation; signalling theory
keywords: CEO sociopolitical activism; corporate social responsibility; moral authenticity; organizational reputation; political ideology; signalling theory
research_question: Under what conditions and through what perceptual mechanisms does CEO activism improve corporate reputation across stakeholders with heterogeneous political ideologies, and how does CSR engagement shape these reputational effects?
mechanism_summary: CEO activism operates as a visible and politically costly signal that deviates from pure shareholder-value focus and risks alienating ideologically opposed stakeholders; this costliness makes the stance credible evidence of the organization's underlying values, which stakeholders interpret as moral authenticity — consistency between espoused values and actions. CSR engagement functions as a congruent, longer-horizon signal of organizational values that reinforces authenticity perceptions when combined with activism, amplifying reputational gains. Because moral authenticity is valued across the ideological spectrum, congruent activism-plus-CSR signals attenuate the reputational penalty that ideologically misaligned stakeholders would otherwise impose, producing a cognitive-interpretive buffer against partisan discounting.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends signalling theory by showing that multiple non-market signals (CEO activism and CSR) interact synergistically when congruent, and integrates the signalling perspective with a cognitive view of reputation formation by introducing stakeholders' political ideology as a previously underexplored interpretive dimension. It reframes CSR not only as a reputation premium but as a reputation buffer that overrides ideological disagreement through perceived moral authenticity, distinguishing this mechanism from Godfrey's moral-capital insurance view by locating the buffering effect in audience heterogeneity and cross-strategy spillovers rather than within-domain wrongdoing.
practical_implication: Leaders considering sociopolitical advocacy can mitigate the risk of alienating ideologically opposed stakeholders by pairing CEO activism with substantive, sustained CSR engagement (e.g., B Corp certification, philanthropic donations), because such congruent signals broaden reputational gains across the ideological spectrum. CSR therefore acts as a reputation buffer that makes activism more viable in ideologically diverse environments.
limitations: Study 1 is correlational and its mediation analysis does not establish causality or rule out alternative mechanisms; the authors did not control for perceptions of inauthenticity or hypocrisy potentially elicited by the Study 2 control; and the CSR initiative was operationalized in a politically neutral domain distinct from the activism stance, which may explain its null direct effect on authenticity. The authenticity mechanism may not generalize to product markets, and experimental vignettes capture only immediate responses from general-public samples rather than diverse organizational stakeholders.
future_research: Examine more contentious and politically costly forms of CSR (e.g., BLM-aligned CSR) to test whether CSR alone can trigger authenticity perceptions in charged domains. Employ non-intrusive methods such as sentiment analysis to trace longitudinal reputational effects in real-world settings, and investigate the antecedents of CEO activism — in particular, why B Corps were less likely than Fortune 500 firms to issue activist statements despite benefiting more from doing so.
abstract: Previous research suggests that the effect of CEO activism depends on its alignment with stakeholders' political ideology. We examine when and why CEO activism can enhance corporate reputation across the ideological spectrum. Integrating signalling theory with a cognitive perspective on reputation formation, we argue that the reputational impact of CEO activism depends on the firm's corporate social responsibility (CSR), which fosters perceptions of organizational authenticity. Using a national survey and an experiment, we find that CEO activism improves corporate reputation through perceived moral authenticity. This effect is stronger when firms hold B Corp certification, engage in philanthropic donations, or are perceived as more socially responsible. Although stakeholders rate firms as more reputable when their political ideology aligns with the CEO's activism, this relationship weakens when firms engage in CSR, thereby signalling authenticity. These findings demonstrate how non-­market strategies interact to shape corporate reputation and inform corporate sociopolitical advocacy among heterogeneous audiences.
apa_citation: Li, L. Z., & Soule, S. A. (2026). CEO activism and corporate reputation: How authenticity and CSR mitigate stakeholder misalignment. *Journal of Management Studies*, 63(5), 2175-2201. https://doi.org/10.1111/joms.70060

title: Female Equity Analysts and Corporate Environmental and Social Performance
methods: Archival empirical analysis combining hand-collected analyst gender data with E&S ratings; panel regressions with firm and year fixed effects; difference-in-differences around broker closures as a quasi-exogenous shock to female (male) analyst coverage; active-learning fine-tuning of FinBERT for E&S-topic classification on 2.4M analyst reports and 120K earnings call transcripts; Structural Topic Modeling (STM) and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) for thematic, cognitive, and linguistic analysis; event-study tests of market reactions to analysts' E&S-related tone
industry: Multi-industry publicly listed firms with analyst coverage (Fama-French 12 industries)
time_period: 2005-2021 (main E&S sample); 2004-2020 (report-level and recommendation samples)
units: Firm-year observations; analyst reports; earnings conference calls
n_sample: 20,423 firm-year observations covering 3,567 unique firms; more than 11,000 sell-side equity analysts; 2.4 million analyst reports; 120,000 earnings call transcripts
authors: Li, K.; Mai, F.; Wong, G.; Yang, C.; Zhang, T.
theories: analyst monitoring / governance role of analysts; gender differences in values and preferences (psychology/economics); information intermediary theory
keywords: FinBERT; RepRisk; analyst coverage; analyst monitoring; analyst reports; cognition; corporate environmental and social performance; earnings conference calls; female equity analysts; readability
research_question: Does female equity analyst coverage causally influence firms' environmental and social (E&S) performance, and through what mechanisms—differences in research activities, thematic focus, cognitive and linguistic approaches, and post-report actions—do female analysts exert this influence compared with their male counterparts?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on psychological and economic evidence that women place greater weight than men on the well-being of others, communities, and the environment, the authors argue that female equity analysts—who already constitute a selected, highly skilled group in a male-dominated profession—are more attentive to corporate E&S issues than male analysts. Through their research activities (writing reports, questioning managers on earnings calls), female analysts identify value-relevant E&S risks and communicate them with greater thematic breadth (regulatory compliance, stakeholder welfare, environment), more sophisticated cognitive processing, and greater clarity. These signals exert governance pressure on management because female analysts are also more willing to downgrade recommendations and target prices after negative E&S content, and investors react more strongly to their negative E&S tones. Together these information-production and monitoring channels lead firms with more female analyst coverage to improve their E&S performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the gender-and-finance literature by showing that female equity analyst coverage causally improves corporate E&S performance, identifying gender diversity among sell-side analysts as an impetus for firms to adopt more environmentally and socially responsible policies. It extends the analyst-monitoring literature by taking a gender lens and uncovering the specific textual, cognitive, and action-based mechanisms through which female analysts influence firm outcomes, thereby explaining observed gender differences in analyst impact first documented by Kumar (2010). Methodologically, it advances the finance/accounting literature on computational linguistics by introducing a data-centric active-learning approach to fine-tune FinBERT on analyst reports and earnings-call transcripts for E&S-topic classification.
practical_implication: The findings imply that firms, brokerages, and regulators interested in strengthening corporate E&S performance should promote gender diversity in the equity analyst profession, since female analysts act as effective external monitors of E&S issues. Investors and asset managers can use female analysts' reports and negative tones as informative signals of firms' E&S risks and are already shown to respond more strongly to them. For corporate management, the evidence suggests that expanding coverage by female analysts increases the likelihood that E&S concerns will be raised publicly and priced into stock recommendations.
limitations: The analysis relies on hand-collected gender inferences and on E&S ratings (e.g., LSEG, ASSET4, KLD, Sustainalytics) that are known to contain measurement noise and inter-rater disagreement. The broker-closure design yields a small, clean treated-control sample, so the economic magnitude of the causal effect should be interpreted with care. The machine-learning pipeline, while extensively validated, still depends on the quality of human-labeled training data and on the coverage of the FinBERT backbone.

title: Organizations as Stages: A Dramaturgical Theory of the Societal Integration of Stigmatized Groups
methods: Conceptual theory development drawing on Goffman's relational perspective on stigma and dramaturgical metaphors; derives a typology of staging forms (concealing and normalizing), identifies structural antecedents, and develops eight propositions
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Lodge, J.; Helms, W. S.; Roulet, T.; Tracey, P.
theories: Goffman's relational perspective on stigma; dramaturgical theory; stigma management
keywords: audiences; dramaturgy; organizations; societal integration; stigma
research_question: How can organizations, conceptualized as "stages," enable the societal integration of stigmatized groups by presenting them to diverse stigmatizing and supportive audiences, and what structural antecedents shape the forms of staging (concealing vs. normalizing) they adopt?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on Goffman's relational view, the authors argue that stigma is constituted through audience evaluations rather than being inherent to attributes, so integration depends on how organizations manage audiences. Organizations function as stages that present stigmatized groups in ways that either conceal stigmatized attributes from hostile audiences (reducing sanctions) or normalize them before sympathetic audiences (eliciting acceptance). The likelihood of concealing is driven primarily by the salience of stigmatized attributes, while normalizing is driven by their institutionalization. Because environments are fragmented and contain both stigmatizing and supportive audiences, organizations frequently must engage in both forms of staging simultaneously, generating tensions when visibility from normalizing undermines concealment efforts.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes three contributions. First, it reconceptualizes the integration of stigmatized groups as an inherently audience-focused process, departing from prior work that treats integration as a consequence of managing group attributes. Second, it develops a structural model in which forms of staging are driven by contextual antecedents (attribute salience and institutionalization) rather than by managerial preferences alone. Third, it theorizes concealing and normalizing as discrete, potentially simultaneous approaches rather than opposite ends of a continuum, and elaborates the dynamics and tensions that arise when organizations engage in both at once.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that societal integration is not automatically achieved by openly celebrating stigmatized groups; in some contexts, deliberate concealment may be the most effective route to integration, an insight often overlooked in DEI debates that emphasize visibility. Integration outcomes depend on how different audiences evaluate stigmatized groups, so attribute-focused initiatives may fail if audience dynamics are ignored. Stigmatized groups can use the framework to anticipate trade-offs when selecting employers or advocacy partners, and organizations should involve stigmatized groups in co-creating staging approaches tailored to their needs.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: Future research could investigate the "dark side" of staging—how organizational actions may unintentionally exacerbate sanctions and deepen stigmatization when forms of staging and audiences are misaligned. Scholars could examine the relative weight of the structural antecedents, consider how organizations' own stigma interacts with that of the groups they support, and explore how technology and social-media-driven context collapse amplify or complicate concealing and normalizing activities.
abstract: This paper theorizes how organizations enable the societal integration of stigmatized groups. Drawing on Goffman’s relational perspective on stigma and his dramaturgical metaphors, we conceptualize organizations as “stages” on which stigmatized groups are presented to diverse audiences. We identify two fundamental forms of staging—concealing and normalizing— through which organizations can reduce sanctions from stigmatizing audiences and elicit acceptance among more supportive ones, thereby ultimately enabling societal integration. Our model specifies the structural antecedents that shape the likelihood of each form of staging, offering a nuanced understanding of when organizations adopt them as well as the tensions that may arise from doing so. Based on this, we extend research on organizations’ management of stigma by advancing a dramaturgical theory of the societal integration of stigmatized groups. Whereas prior work has largely assumed that managing the stigmatized attributes of groups is central (and often sufficient) for their broader integration, we demonstrate that integration ultimately depends on the management of audiences and must therefore be understood as an inherently audience-focused process.

title: How Gender Diversity and Equality in R&D Departments Jointly Affect Firm-Level Innovation Through Innovation Capabilities
methods: Longitudinal panel analysis of a balanced sample of corporate R&D departments from Spain's Technological Innovation Panel (TIP, based on the Community Innovation Survey framework) over 2005-2016; generalized structural equation modelling (GSEM, Stata) estimating all paths simultaneously with Probit (binary implementation quality), Poisson (counts for breadth and use of external knowledge), and Poisson with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors for the new-to-the-market sales share; pseudo-fixed effects via pre-sample (2004) values of dependent variables, plus industry, regional, and year dummies; robustness checks include Heckman-style sample-selection correction, negative binomial and fractional logit alternatives, lagged mediators, separate-equation mediation, and alternative gender-diversity indices (entropy, gender ratio)
industry: Manufacturing firms with in-house R&D departments across all sectors of the Spanish economy
time_period: 2005-2016 (12 years), with pre-sample values from 2004
units: R&D department-firm-year observations
n_sample: 552 R&D departments; 6,624 firm-year observations
authors: Lokshin, B.; Boone, C.; Post, C.
theories: diversity-as-variety vs. disparity (Harrison & Klein); gender inequality and status hierarchies; information/decision-making perspective on diversity; innovation capabilities / dynamic capabilities
keywords: diversity, equity, and inclusion; innovation and learning; technology and innovation management
research_question: How and when does gender diversity in R&D departments influence firm-level innovation—specifically, through which innovation capabilities (the "how"), and under what conditions of gender rank equality at different hierarchical levels of the R&D department (the "when") does this relationship hold?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the information/decision-making perspective on diversity combined with research on inequality, the authors argue that gender-diverse R&D departments can only convert demographic variety into innovation capabilities when men and women are proportionally represented across hierarchical ranks. Gender rank equality reduces the salience of gender and gender stereotypes, fostering a climate in which complementary knowledge, perspectives, networks, and resources can be voiced and integrated. Under these conditions, gender diversity strengthens external knowledge search, external knowledge use, and implementation-process quality, which in turn raise firm-level innovation. When gender rank inequality is high, by contrast, status-based hierarchies suppress communication and collaboration, attenuating or reversing the diversity-innovation link.
theoretical_contribution: First, the paper identifies firm-level innovation capabilities as the missing mechanism linking R&D department gender composition to firm-level innovation, responding to calls to move beyond upper-echelons explanations and to show how workforce diversity shapes organizational capabilities. Second, it brings inequality-as-disparity back into diversity research by demonstrating that numerical gender diversity cannot be understood without jointly considering the distribution of power and authority across hierarchical ranks, thereby helping to reconcile mixed prior evidence on gender diversity and innovation. Third, it extends theorizing on when gender diversity fosters a climate for constructive collaboration by showing that, in groups with meaningful internal hierarchies, gender rank equality is a necessary enabler of gender-based complementarities—advancing the micro-foundations of knowledge integration and dynamic capabilities.
practical_implication: Managers, HR executives, and diversity professionals should recognize that simply increasing the share of women in R&D departments is insufficient and may even hamper innovation when gender rank inequality persists. To realize the innovation benefits of gender diversity, firms must also ensure proportional representation of men and women at all hierarchical levels (researchers, technicians, and support staff) within R&D. These changes should be paired with holistic, firm-wide practices to translate improved R&D capabilities into new-to-the-market product sales.
limitations: The study measures macro-level innovation capabilities and cannot directly observe the micro-level group processes (e.g., psychological safety, relational conflict) through which gender diversity and rank equality shape capabilities. It captures levels rather than changes in gender rank equality, so it cannot disentangle short-run disruption effects from long-run benefits of structural change toward equality. The sales-based innovation outcome is distal and affected by many factors beyond R&D capabilities, and the secondary TIP data anonymize firms, preventing controls for variables such as TMT gender diversity. Results pertain to Spanish manufacturing R&D departments and may not generalize to other countries with different gender gaps or cultural norms.
future_research: Micro-level research should examine what actually happens inside R&D departments under different combinations of gender diversity and gender rank equality, including psychological safety and additional mediating mechanisms. Longitudinal designs capturing changes in gender rank equality over time could separate short-run adjustment costs from long-run benefits. Scholars should also explore more proximal innovation indicators (e.g., patent applications), test whether the framework generalizes beyond gender to other diffuse-status diversity dimensions (race/ethnicity, age, nationality, disability), and conduct cross-country comparative studies to see how societal gender norms condition the department-level findings.
abstract: Innovation research has long shown that firms depend on their R&D personnel to strengthen their innovation capabilities, sparking scholarly interest in how to best staff R&D departments for competitive advantage, with a focus on gender diversity. However, left unexamined are the mechanisms linking gender diversity in R&D departments and firm-level innovation. Further, despite growing interest in the conditions under which diversity may enhance innovation, researchers have not adequately addressed how department-level gender rank inequality—the disproportionate concentration of men and women at various hierarchical ranks—interacts with numerical diversity to affect innovation outcomes. We address both limitations by integrating insights from the information/decision-making perspective on diversity and research on inequality with research on innovation capabilities. Specifically, we develop and test a model explaining how R&D department gender diversity and gender rank equality jointly affect three firm-level innovation capabilities: breadth of external knowledge search, use of external knowledge, and quality of the innovation implementation process.

title: Emancipatory entrepreneurship by a stigmatized social group
methods: Historical qualitative case study; grounded theory analysis of 30 years (1988-2018) of archival documents and 31 semi-structured interviews
industry: Gambling/casino industry
units: First Nations (Indigenous peoples) collective casino ventures
n_sample: 31 interviews (20 First Nations leaders, 11 government/industry informants); ~8000 pages of documents; 19 casinos established
authors: Lu, C.; Zhang, R.; Reay, T.
theories: contentious collective action; entrepreneurship as emancipation; stigma theory
keywords: Emancipation; Entrepreneurship; Interaction; Social group; Stigma
research_question: How does emancipatory entrepreneurship by a stigmatized social group unfold over time?
mechanism_summary: The authors theorize a three-phase process in which a stigmatized group first mobilizes internally by forging a shared collective entrepreneurial identity and narrative, then enters a first wave of contestations with stigmatizing audiences over collective entrepreneurial identity, autonomy, and resource eligibility, which resolves into an interim settlement enabling venture creation. A second wave of contestations centered on venture differentiation and governance then produces adjusted settlements. Drawing on contentious collective action theory, the authors argue that a mix of symbolic and material strategies, combined with partial acquiescence to powerful stigmatizers, enables the group to recalibrate power, legitimate its ventures, and transition stigmatizers into apparently supportive audiences, sustaining the precarious path of emancipatory entrepreneurship over time.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances the EE literature by developing a process model of collective emancipatory entrepreneurship by stigmatized groups, shifting the locus of EE theorizing from individual entrepreneurs to the dynamic interactions between group entrepreneurs and external audiences. It shows that partial acquiescence to stigmatizing audiences, rather than signaling emancipation failure, can be instrumental in forming interim settlements that sustain ventures and enable long-term progress toward emancipation. It further contributes to the entrepreneurship-stigma intersection by highlighting the importance of managing interdependence with stigmatizing audiences, demonstrating that stigmatizers also depend on the obedience of the stigmatized, which creates leverage that group entrepreneurs can exploit.
practical_implication: Stigmatized groups pursuing collective entrepreneurship should anticipate waves of contention with media, government, and public stakeholders and prepare by mobilizing internal unity through shared collective entrepreneurial identities and narratives. They should combine power-based tactics such as protests with actions designed to gain sympathy and support, and work with alternative resource providers like social procurement programs or inclusive business accelerators when mainstream sources are closed. They should also accept that negotiated partial concessions and interim settlements, though uncomfortable, can be critical stepping stones toward longer-term emancipation.
limitations: Not reported in paper.
future_research: The authors call for research in other contexts beyond First Nations casinos to validate and extend the process model of collective emancipatory entrepreneurship, particularly for other stigmatized groups such as women in highly patriarchal societies, undocumented immigrants, and people with histories of mental illness or incarceration. They also invite further study of the dynamics of contestations and settlements in emancipatory entrepreneurship and of how such processes can inform approaches to alleviating oppression via entrepreneurship.
abstract: In the world, marginalized groups such as women in highly patriarchal societies, displaced war victims, and oppressed ethnicities face structural constraints when attempting careers in established corporations. As a result, they may seek entrepreneurship as a way to break free from various constraints, despite stigma and lower power positions. In this study, we examine how a stigmatized social group can engage in emancipatory entrepreneurship through interactions with different stakeholders. We conducted a qualitative study of how First Nations in Canada collectively opened casinos to emancipate from post-colonial policies. By analyzing documents from 1988 to 2018 and 31 interviews with individuals who played major roles in casino creation or are knowledgeable about the process, we found that a stigmatized group will go through waves of contestations with stakeholders interspersed by interim settlements, once they are internally mobilized for collective entrepreneurship. We identified different types of contestations, including contestation around the stigmatized's collective entrepreneurial identity, autonomy, resource eligibility, venture differentiation and governance. Overall, we found that the stigmatized collective entrepreneur can use a mix of symbolic and material strategies to counter the resistance of stigmatizing stakeholders. In so doing, they can gain access to entrepreneurship and preserve the precarious path of emancipatory entrepreneurship.

title: In Defense of an “Ethics Judgment Rule”
methods: Conceptual/normative legal-philosophical argument; doctrinal analysis of Delaware corporate law and the Business Judgment Rule, followed by a normative proposal to incorporate an Ethics Judgment Rule
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Mejia, S.
theories: Business Judgment Rule doctrine; ethics-constrained shareholder value maximization (E-SVM); normative business ethics; shareholder value maximization (SVM)
keywords: Business Judgment Rule; Ethics Judgment Rule; corporate governance; corporate law; shareholder value maximization
research_question: Does the Business Judgment Rule, as commonly understood in Delaware corporate law, actually give corporate leaders the discretion to pursue ethically motivated decisions that are profit-sacrificing, and, if not, how should corporate law be reformed to properly accommodate managers' moral obligations?
mechanism_summary: Mejia argues that although the BJR nominally grants wide deference, its doctrinal tethering to SVM signals to practitioners that courts will only shield ethically motivated decisions when they can be recast as profit-enhancing. This pushes ethically minded leaders either to avoid profit-sacrificing ethical choices or to obfuscate their true motives, which in turn instrumentalizes ethics and corrupts public discourse about the role of morality in business. Incorporating an explicit Ethics Judgment Rule would replace SVM with E-SVM as the standard of review, authorizing good-faith, profit-sacrificing ethical decisions and thereby aligning legal doctrine with the genuine normative structure of corporate moral obligations.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the prevailing business-ethics consensus that the Business Judgment Rule already provides sufficient latitude for ethically motivated corporate conduct, and advances a novel doctrinal proposal—the Ethics Judgment Rule—that reframes the proper standard of managerial review from shareholder value maximization (SVM) to ethics-constrained shareholder value maximization (E-SVM). In doing so, it reconnects normative business ethics with corporate-law doctrine and reconceptualizes corporate success as requiring both profitability and moral integrity.
practical_implication: Adopting an Ethics Judgment Rule would give directors, executives, and managers explicit legal cover to make profit-sacrificing ethical decisions in good faith without fear of liability, freeing them from the pressure to dissemble by recasting moral commitments as profit-enhancing. It would clarify to shareholders, stakeholders, and the broader public that ethics is a non-instrumental constraint on corporate conduct, helping to repair moral discourse in the business community and reorienting conceptions of corporate success toward companies that are both profitable and display moral integrity.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The paper points to the need for further doctrinal work on how an Ethics Judgment Rule could be operationalized within Delaware corporate law, including how courts should evaluate good-faith ethical motivations and how E-SVM should be reconciled with existing fiduciary duties. It also invites continued normative inquiry into the substantive content of corporations' moral obligations and how legal institutions can better articulate the mandatory, non-voluntary dimension of business ethics.
abstract: According to the conventional wisdom among business ethicists, the “Business Judgment Rule” gives corporate leaders the discretion needed to abide by the firm’s moral obligations. In the first part of the paper, I challenge this view: managers have compelling reasons to believe that the Business Judgment Rule (and corporate law more generally) allows corporate leaders to pursue ethically motivated decisions only when these decisions are expected to be profit-enhancing. This is problematic because it instrumentalizes ethics, pushes ethically motivated corporate leaders to dissemble, and corrupts the quality of our public discourse. In response, I propose that corporate law should incorporate ethics into the Business Judgment Rule, explicitly giving managers discretion to make ethically motivated decisions that are profitsacrificing. After responding to concerns about implementing such a rule, I contend that such a rule would be an important step to put corporate ethics in its proper place.

title: Moral Distress in Bioethics and Business Ethics: Knowledge, Action, and Desire in Moral Conditions and Communities
methods: Conceptual and theoretical analysis; comparative review of bioethics and business ethics literatures; development of a taxonomy of moral conditions based on combinations of moral knowledge, agency, and desire.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Michaelson, C. W.; Jameton, A.; Liaschenko, J.
theories: moral community; moral distress theory; moral philosophy; moral psychology
keywords: bioethics; business ethics; decision-making; moral community; moral distress; nursing ethics
research_question: Why is moral distress — a central concept in bioethics — largely absent from business ethics scholarship, and how can importing and extending it illuminate important problems of business ethics and the role of moral communities in shaping moral action?
mechanism_summary: The paper theorizes that ethical outcomes at work arise from the joint configuration of three elements — whether an agent knows the right thing to do, has the agency to act on it, and desires to do so. Different combinations yield a taxonomy of eight moral conditions, with moral distress defined as knowing and desiring the right action yet lacking agency due to institutional constraints. In business, the tension between profit maximization and other moral purposes makes moral distress an ever-present, existential condition that is often reframed as moral rationalization. Morally supportive communities — characterized by shared moral purpose, opportunities for voice, and loyalty — can align knowledge, action, and desire and mitigate distress across both medicine and business.
theoretical_contribution: The article bridges bioethics and business ethics by importing moral distress into business ethics discourse and reframing it as an existential condition of modern business rather than an exceptional event. It develops a novel taxonomy of eight moral conditions based on combinations of moral knowledge, agency, and desire, and theorizes morally supportive communities as a mechanism for cultivating right desires and aligning them with moral knowledge and action.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that organizations in healthcare, business, and beyond should cultivate morally supportive communities that articulate a common moral end beyond profit, remove institutional constraints that impede workers' ability to act on their moral convictions, and create conditions for voice and loyalty so that moral knowledge, agency, and desire can be aligned.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The paper invites further work applying moral distress to additional problems of business ethics, extending business ethics thinking on stakeholder relationships and moral agency back into bioethics, and exploring how different ethical theories apply to distinct relationships (e.g., patients and customers, employees and managers, providers and payers) across healthcare and business settings.
abstract: “Moral distress” was introduced in nursing ethics to describe the experience of having the moral conviction about the right thing to do while having limited agency to enact it. It exists at the intersection of moral philosophy, moral psychology, and moral communities that influence our desires to act. Although moral distress has significantly impacted bioethics scholarship, it has had almost no presence in business ethics scholarship. We argue that moral distress is useful for understanding important problems of business ethics. We claim it may be missing from business ethics discourse not because it is not present but rather because it is ever-present, an existential condition brought on by the tension between profit maximization and other moral purposes. We consider how the moral communities of medicine and business can be morally supportive or distressing and set forth a taxonomy of moral conditions involving the relationship between knowledge, action, and desire.

title: How Deadly Is Financial Leverage? Evidence from Care Homes During the COVID-19 Crisis
methods: Cross-sectional and panel OLS regressions with care home and group fixed effects; propensity score matching; nonlinear (piecewise) specifications; extensive robustness/sensitivity analysis across alternative leverage constructions, samples, and wave definitions
industry: Care homes (nursing homes for older people)
time_period: COVID-19 pandemic, 2020 (first and second waves); financial accounts through fiscal year ending on or before 31 March 2020
units: Care homes and the corporate groups that operate them
n_sample: Working sample of 3,356 care homes operated by 1,045 providers with consolidated audited P&L accounts (broader sample: 7,585 care homes, 4,223 providers; universe: 8,760 care homes, 5,136 providers)
authors: Morris, P.; Phalippou, L.; Wu, B.
theories: agency theory (Jensen and Meckling 1976); financial distress / real effects of leverage; internal capital markets
keywords: COVID-19; IFRS 16; care homes; disclosure; healthcare; lease; leverage; real effects
research_question: How does financial leverage — once measured accurately by consolidating corporate group structures and capitalizing operating leases — affect resident death rates in English care homes during the COVID-19 pandemic, and does this relationship explain the previously documented higher mortality in private equity–controlled care homes?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on Jensen and Meckling (1976) and the broader real-effects-of-leverage literature, the authors argue that highly leveraged operators facing an unanticipated negative shock must cut costs aggressively to preserve debt-service capacity, and in a labor- and care-intensive industry these cost cuts (on PPE, staffing, agency workers) translate directly into higher resident mortality. Because financial flexibility depends on the consolidated group's balance sheet — including off-balance-sheet operating lease obligations — leverage measured at the standalone provider level or without lease capitalization badly mismeasures the true pressure on operators. Once leverage is reconstructed at the corporate-group level with operating leases capitalized (multiplied by 13x, based on REIT comparables), highly leveraged care homes show a first-wave death rate roughly double that of unleveraged care homes, the effect disappears in the second wave (when government support was in place), and the previously observed "PE effect" on mortality is fully absorbed by PE firms' higher leverage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes two contributions. First, it shows that accurate measurement of financial leverage — requiring consolidation at the corporate group level and capitalization of operating leases — is essential for detecting the real, non-financial externalities of debt, and that conventional provider- or brand-level, non-lease-adjusted leverage measures systematically understate financial pressure. Second, it demonstrates that the documented association between private equity ownership and worse stakeholder outcomes (care home mortality) operates primarily through the leverage channel rather than through ownership type per se, reframing the PE-and-healthcare debate as fundamentally a leverage-and-healthcare debate.
practical_implication: For policy makers and regulators (e.g., the UK Care Quality Commission), the paper argues that quality-of-care regulation should be complemented by systematic monitoring of providers' consolidated, lease-adjusted financial leverage, because high leverage generates negative stakeholder externalities during crises. For prospective residents and families trying to assess a care home's financial stability, currently available public data (Companies House, regulator filings) are insufficient without substantial accounting expertise to reconstruct group-level leverage. Accounting standard setters and disclosure regimes should take seriously the distortive effect of excluding operating leases for smaller or unquoted entities.
limitations: Propensity-score matching is difficult in this setting because high- and low-leverage care homes differ systematically on observables, so matches are loose. The lease-capitalization multiple (13x) is based on two UK care-home REITs and may not generalize. The analysis is confined to English care homes over a single pandemic episode, which, while offering strong identification, limits external generalizability. The leverage measure, although carefully constructed, still relies on self-reported financial accounts of varying quality (especially for smaller private entities).
future_research: The authors' framing implies several directions: replicating lease-adjusted, group-level leverage analyses in other jurisdictions and sectors (especially the United States, where data on private companies and operating leases are harder to obtain) to test whether the leverage-mortality channel generalizes beyond English care homes. The broader trend toward privatization of care services across countries invites cross-national comparative work on how ownership structure and financial leverage jointly shape outcomes in essential services. Further research could also examine whether the leverage channel observed here extends to other non-financial externalities of debt (e.g., quality of care in non-crisis periods, worker safety) and whether alternative accounting treatments of operating leases materially change prior empirical findings on leverage and real outcomes.
abstract: private equity firms no longer display higher COVID-19 death rates once their significantly higher leverage is controlled for.

title: The effects of food insecurity on work outcomes.
methods: Multimethod design across three studies: (1) a preregistered online recall experiment on Prolific (N = 375) manipulating food insecurity; (2) a four-wave within-person diary study on Prolific (N = 567) modeling within- and between-person effects via multilevel path analysis; (3) a randomized field experiment in Lahore, Pakistan (N = 196) partnering with a local NGO to distribute food versus matched nonfood packages, analyzed with path analysis in Mplus and 10,000-draw bootstrap for indirect effects.
industry: Mixed employed adults (Studies 1-2: U.S. working adults recruited via Prolific, 31+ hrs/week); Study 3: low-income daily-wage workers served by a Pakistani NGO
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual employees
n_sample: Study 1 N=375; Study 2 N=567; Study 3 N=196
authors: Moy, J. H.; Khan, U. A.; Ong, W. J.; Barnes, C. M.
theories: behavioral inhibition system; reinforcement sensitivity theory
keywords: anxiety; food insecurity; organizational citizenship behavior; task performance; work engagement
research_question: How does food insecurity—insufficient access to safe and nutritious foods—affect core workplace outcomes (task performance, work engagement, and organizational citizenship behaviors), and through what psychological mechanism? Can providing food aid remediate these effects for food-insecure employees?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on reinforcement sensitivity theory (Gray, 1978, 1982; Gray & McNaughton, 2003), the authors argue that food insecurity constitutes a diffuse, nonacute threat that activates the behavioral inhibition system and produces anxiety. Because cognitive capacity is limited, anxiety redirects attention toward monitoring and resolving the threat, leaving fewer attentional and cognitive resources available for work. This depleted bandwidth undermines task performance (which requires focused information processing), work engagement (which requires sustained mental immersion), and OCB (which requires noticing and responding to others' needs). Providing food aid is therefore expected to reduce anxiety and indirectly improve work outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends applied psychology into the grand challenge of food insecurity, challenging the field's implicit WEIRD-centric assumption that food is not a workplace-relevant stressor. It contributes to the food insecurity literature by moving beyond personal and physiological outcomes to show organizational consequences, building a business case for corporate engagement. It also enriches the workplace anxiety literature by identifying a stressor unique to economically disadvantaged workers struggling to meet basic physiological needs.
practical_implication: Organizations have an evidence-based rationale to address employee food insecurity because it improves task performance and engagement through reduced anxiety. Employers can provide free or discounted food, partner with local food banks, host on-site pantries or community gardens, offer transportation to food banks (especially in food deserts), and educate employees about public food-assistance programs such as SNAP. Investing in employees' basic needs may yield higher returns than programs targeting higher-order needs (e.g., meditation, employee resource groups).
limitations: In Study 3, only indirect (not direct) effects of food insecurity on work outcomes were significant, possibly because Pakistan's broader anxiety-inducing context diluted the food-specific signal and a single food package may have been insufficient to substantially reduce food insecurity. The studies rely heavily on self-reported measures, raising common-method concerns (though mitigated by the manipulated IV in Study 3 and within-person design in Study 2). The active nonfood control condition in Study 3 may have created expectancy effects. The research examined only three focal outcomes and did not capture other work-relevant consequences such as turnover or absenteeism.
future_research: Future work should probe boundary conditions of food insecurity's effect on OCB—e.g., whether food-insecure workers extend more citizenship toward similarly situated colleagues than toward others. Researchers could test alternative or additional mediating mechanisms beyond anxiety, such as negative affect or regulatory focus, to map a more complete nomological network. Field experiments should also explore dose-response effects by varying the number and size of food packages, and examine downstream outcomes like turnover and absenteeism.
abstract: Despite its prevalence and importance, the ﬁeld of applied psychology has ignored this problem with the implicit assumption that food insecurity is not an issue relevant to the workplace. Contrary to this view, we hypothesize and demonstrate that food insecurity is detrimental to the three core work outcomes: task performance, work engagement, and organizational citizenship behaviors. To test our hypotheses, we employed a multimethod design across three empirical studies: (a) an experimental recall study, (b) a within-person diary study, and (c) a ﬁeld experiment. Our ﬁndings consistently demonstrate that food insecurity leads to higher anxiety, which subsequently has a negative effect on task performance, work engagement, and organizational citizenship behavior. In our ﬁeld experiment, we further demonstrated that providing food to those experiencing food insecurity can improve work outcomes. This research highlights that food insecurity is a signiﬁcant issue with important implications for the workplace that requires greater attention from both researchers and business leaders.

title: A CEO-Driven Process Model of Firm Responsiveness to Secondary Stakeholder Demands: The Roles of CEO Values and Passion
methods: Conceptual theory-building paper that develops a CEO-driven process model of firm responsiveness to secondary stakeholder demands, integrating stakeholder theory, strategic leadership/upper echelons research, and social-psychological work on values and passion, and illustrating the arguments with brief real-world vignettes (e.g., Trader Joe's vs. Costco/Publix, MEC/CamelBak, Starbucks, Chick-fil-A)
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Neville, F.; Rizzi, G. A.; Lovelace, J. B.
theories: Schwartz values theory; dualistic model of passion (harmonious vs. obsessive); stakeholder theory (salience); strategic leadership / executive cognition; upper echelons theory
keywords: CEO cognition; CEO passion; CEO values; secondary stakeholders; strategic leadership; upper echelons
research_question: What is the process by which a CEO's values and passion shape firm responsiveness to secondary stakeholder demands, and how do firms—and specifically CEOs—come to construct and enact divergent responses to similar, if not identical, secondary stakeholder demands?
mechanism_summary: The model argues that because secondary stakeholder demands arise in situationally weak, value-laden, and emotionally charged contexts, CEOs' personal values and passion — rather than purely rational stakeholder-salience calculations — drive firm responsiveness. Values determine which demands CEOs attend to and deem salient (what they engage with and why), while passion determines the intensity, persistence, and emotional investment with which CEOs engage (how). Harmonious passion tends to produce flexible, reflectively committed responses, whereas obsessive passion can yield rigid, defensive, or escalatory responses even when detrimental to the firm. Because audiences interpret responses through the lens of the leader, values- and passion-infused responses shape divergent social (dis)approval outcomes across otherwise similarly situated firms (multifinality).
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes three contributions. First, it enriches stakeholder theory by incorporating top-executive characteristics — specifically CEO values and passion — into the conceptualization of when and whether a secondary stakeholder demand is perceived as salient and acted upon, moving beyond frameworks developed primarily for primary stakeholders. Second, it advances strategic leadership and Upper Echelons Theory by disentangling values from cognitive bases and specifying the distinctive socio-cognitive and motivational processes through which values (what CEOs engage with) and passion (how intensely they engage) jointly shape executive choice. Third, it offers a micro-foundational lens on firm social (dis)approval by explaining how CEO values and passion shape both firm responses and how audiences interpret those responses, accounting for why similarly situated firms can elicit divergent social evaluations.
practical_implication: Strategic leaders should cultivate greater self-awareness of their natural tendencies to inject personal values and passion into decision-making about secondary stakeholder demands, because such reflexivity can help them evaluate these demands more effectively and avoid responses inconsistent with firm objectives or primary-stakeholder priorities. Boards and top management teams should monitor the extent to which a CEO's personal value commitments and obsessive versus harmonious passions are driving firm responses, and create processes for surfacing value-based assumptions before commitments become hard to reverse. Training and coaching interventions can help executives distinguish harmonious from obsessive passion so that value-driven responses remain flexible and compatible with broader firm strategy.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The authors call for empirical tests of the model using CEO primary data (e.g., Schwartz Value Survey; Vallerand et al.'s passion scale; Cardon et al.'s entrepreneurial passion measure adapted to CEOs), as well as AI-based measurement approaches that apply NLP, sentiment trajectory modeling, and high-arousal language detection to CEO speeches, interviews, earnings calls, and social media to infer values and passion at scale. They suggest verbal protocol ("think aloud") studies in which CEOs or proxies respond to realistic secondary-stakeholder scenarios, and laboratory experiments in which participants assuming stakeholder roles evaluate alternative response postures to trace social (dis)approval and competitive-dynamics consequences. Future work could also examine how CEOs' personal values form a basis for firms' dynamic political management capabilities and non-market competitive advantage.
abstract: Secondary stakeholder demands represent increasingly important strategic issues for firms. However, the principal drivers of firm response remain poorly understood. We extend research on firm responsiveness to secondary stakeholders by introducing a new theoretical perspective to detail the cognitive processes through which key CEO attributes—namely, personal values and passion—shape the trajectories of firm responsiveness. We first outline key aspects of secondary stakeholder demands to explain why CEO values and passion are important determinants of a firm’s response to secondary stakeholder demands. We then explain how a CEO’s values and passion influence the process of firm responsiveness. Finally, we extend our arguments to illustrate how values and passion-infused responses may influence social (dis)approval among key organizational stakeholders. By focusing on the cognitive processes of CEOs, we offer novel theoretical contributions to stakeholder theory, strategic leadership research, and the literature on firm social evaluations.
apa_citation: Neville, F., Rizzi, G. A., & Lovelace, J. B. (2026). A CEO-driven process model of firm responsiveness to secondary stakeholder demands: The roles of CEO values and passion. *Journal of Management*. https://doi.org/10.1177/01492063261416425

title: Leadership and the Virtue of Humanity: Conceptual Clarity, Systematic Review, and Future Research Agenda
methods: Conceptual theorization plus PRISMA 2020 systematic review of empirical leadership studies in Web of Science; title search conducted July 2024 yielding 60 included studies synthesized narratively across six virtuous dimensions.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: No year restriction; Web of Science title search conducted July 2024
units: Empirical academic journal articles (English-language) on leadership and a virtuous dimension of humanity
n_sample: 60 studies (from 183 records screened)
authors: Newstead, T.; Loghman, S.; Newman, A.; Riggio, R.
theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics; higher-order virtues framework; relational leadership / co-creation of leadership; virtue ethics
keywords: compassion; empathy; forgiveness; generosity; humanity; kindness; leadership; love; virtues
research_question: How should the higher-order virtue of humanity be conceptually defined, which lower-order virtues qualify as its virtuous dimensions, and what is empirically known about each of these dimensions in relation to leadership?
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Humanity is a universal, higher-order virtue comprised of — but irreducible to — a set of lower-order virtuous dimensions that together enable meaningful human connection and sustain human community.
- Key constructs: empathy (primarily affective/cognitive), compassion, forgiveness, love (equally affective, cognitive, and behavioral), kindness, and generosity (primarily behavioral).
- Criteria (derived from Aristotelian virtue ethics) used to qualify a lower-order virtue: it must be inherently good, habituated, expressed in relation to others, and represent a golden mean between opposing vices.
- Processual model: leaders' and followers' expression of the six virtuous dimensions mutually shapes the relational co-creation of leadership, which in turn sustains human community (its telos).
- Boundary conditions: situations may demand other higher-order virtues (e.g., courage, justice); the effect of humanity on leader-follower relations is expected to vary with context.

The paper's processual argument is that when leaders and followers reciprocally enact empathy, compassion, forgiveness, love, kindness, and generosity, these dimensions operate in concert rather than isolation, producing the fullest expression of humanity as a higher-order virtue. Grounded in Aristotelian virtue ethics and Newstead's (2022) higher-order virtues framework, the authors argue that humanity — as the golden mean between cruelty and sycophantism — is habituated through practice and is uniquely suited to sustaining organizations through polycrisis because it is the virtue of meaningful human connection itself.
theoretical_contribution: The paper resolves conceptual ambiguity around the virtue of humanity by providing a robust definition, theorizing humanity as a higher-order (meta) virtue, and distilling virtue-ethics criteria for determining which lower-order virtues qualify as its virtuous dimensions. It advances a processual model of leader and follower humanity and, through a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of 60 empirical studies, consolidates what is known about each dimension in relation to leadership and articulates a structured future research agenda.
practical_implication: The authors argue that managers and HR practitioners should consider the virtuous dimensions of humanity in recruitment, selection, promotion, career development, training, and performance management — for example, by hiring, rewarding, and promoting individuals who demonstrate the capacity to lead in ways that express empathy, compassion, forgiveness, love, kindness, and generosity, because doing so promises to help sustain organizations through turbulent times and for the long term.
limitations: The authors identify three limitations in the body of reviewed research: a dearth of empirical work on several dimensions (love, kindness, and especially generosity, for which no empirical leadership studies were found), an overreliance on cross-sectional and self-report data prone to social desirability bias, and a pronounced leader-centrism that neglects follower perspectives and the relational co-creation of leadership. The review itself was restricted to published, English-language empirical articles indexed in Web of Science and relied on title-only search terms.
future_research: The authors propose exploring the outcomes and mechanisms (e.g., social exchange, reciprocity norms, emotional contagion, social identity, psychological safety climate) through which the less-studied dimensions — love, kindness, and generosity — influence workplace outcomes, and addressing leader-centrism by examining follower and relational expressions of humanity. They call for longitudinal, experience-sampling, and experimental designs to move beyond cross-sectional self-report, psychometric work to develop a valid higher-order measure of humanity, articulation of boundary conditions, and replication of the theorization exercise for the other higher-order virtues (courage, justice, prudence, temperance, transcendence, wisdom).
abstract: Humanity – the virtue enabling meaningful human connection – is vital to the leadership we need to survive our polycrisis context. As a prerequisite to sustainable human community, the virtue of humanity is considered universal. It has been claimed as a 'higher-order virtue', comprised of and enacted by – but irreducible to – a suite of 'lower-order virtues' such as compassion and kindness. This claim is evident in widely-adopted virtues catalogues, but we lack consensus on how humanity is defined, and which attributes qualify as its virtuous dimensions. To address this, we develop a robust definition of humanity and apply criteria distilled from virtue ethics to theorize the lower-order virtues that comprise its virtuous dimensions. We thus determine the virtuous dimensions of humanity include empathy, compassion, forgiveness, love, kindness, and generosity. Our processual model illustrates how, when expressed by leaders and followers, these virtuous dimensions represent the fullest expression of the higher-order virtue of humanity and sustain human community. Our systematic review details what is known empirically about each virtuous dimension of humanity in relation to leadership. Drawing on this, we propose a research agenda to advance understanding of how the virtue of humanity might enable the leadership needed today and into the future.

title: Beyond Rugged Individualism?: Exploring the Resilience of Black Entrepreneurs to Chronic Racism
methods: Qualitative, decolonizing research design combining Group Model Building (GMB) workshops with semi-structured interviews. Data collection unfolded in four phases: (1) semi-structured Zoom interviews with 49 Black entrepreneurs (March-June 2023); (2) a first full-day GMB workshop in July 2023 with 12 entrepreneurs and 7 policymakers to co-construct causal loop diagrams of the ecosystem shaping resilience; (3) iterative refinement of the process model; and (4) a second validation workshop. Analysis integrated critical race methodology and critical race theory to foreground participants' lived experiences of racism-related stress and build an emergent process model of resilience to chronic racism.
industry: Diverse small businesses (retail, food service, salons, construction, professional services, creative industries, etc.)
time_period: March 2023 - July 2023 (data collection); reflections spanning COVID-19 pandemic and earlier business history
units: Self-identified Black entrepreneurs with no more than 40 employees who had experienced challenges such as gentrification, recessions, natural disasters, racial unrest, or COVID-19
n_sample: 49 Black entrepreneurs interviewed (10 immigrants from majority-Black countries in Africa and the Caribbean; remainder African American); 12 entrepreneurs plus 7 policymakers participated in the GMB workshop
authors: Nurse, S.; Dasent, K.; Rivera, A.; Ansah, J. P.; Black, J.
theories: critical race methodology; critical race theory; socio-ecological theory of resilience
keywords: black entrepreneur; chronic adversity; entrepreneurship; racism; resilience
research_question: How do individual capacities and systemic factors interact to shape the resilience of Black entrepreneurs in the context of chronic racism, and to what effect?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the socio-ecological theory of resilience and Critical Race Theory, the authors argue that Black entrepreneurs operate within systems built on White normative standards that provide lower foundational institutional support and, combined with in-group discrimination, limit external resources. Because racism is chronic rather than episodic, entrepreneurs cannot simply "bounce back" to a pre-adversity state; instead they must engage in continuous adaptation that repeatedly draws on internal coping mechanisms (self-reliance, hard work, faith). Over-reliance on these personal resources, triggered by the insufficiency of external support, leads to resource depletion, exhaustion, and fluctuating phases of well-being and duress. Strategic partnerships (co-ethnic and cross-racial) can replenish resources and enable periodic disengagement and re-entry, rendering resilience a cyclical, dynamic process whose outcomes are both enabling and costly.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the dominant "bounce-back" conception of resilience and theorizes resilience to chronic racism as a continuous, cyclical process of adaptation in which internal and external coping resources are gained and depleted over time. By integrating critical race theory and critical race methodology with the socio-ecological theory of resilience, it foregrounds racism-related stress as a core construct in entrepreneurship research and shows how insufficient institutional and social support compels over-reliance on individual coping, exposing a grimmer, compensatory face of resilience. In doing so, it advances efforts to decolonize entrepreneurship scholarship, moving beyond race-neutral framings and offering a process model that may transfer to other groups facing chronic, identity-linked adversity.
practical_implication: The authors advocate a dual-strategy policy approach that simultaneously strengthens internal capabilities and addresses systemic barriers. Internally, they recommend building Black-entrepreneur-focused business-to-business networks and cross-group mentorship and sponsorship programs, alongside financial vehicles such as credit unions, Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), and cooperative economic practices (e.g., sousous). Systemically, they call for transparent, race-conscious policies, greater representation of Black individuals and allies in decision-making, disaggregated data on grants and loans by race, and streamlined MWBE certification and government contracting processes to remove biases; the research team also partnered with a CDFI to launch a networking and referral program with forgivable loans as a tangible benefit to participants.
limitations: The sample is drawn predominantly from the Northeast United States and over-represents women, which may constrain the regional and demographic generalizability of the findings. The emergent theory of resilience to chronic racism may be transferable to other marginalized groups facing chronic, identity-linked adversity, but its applicability should not be assumed without careful contextual consideration, as marginalized groups are heterogeneous. The study did not specifically theorize the experiences of Black immigrant entrepreneurs, whose relationship to racism and community support differs from that of African American participants.
future_research: Future work should conduct similar socio-ecological, decolonizing studies with other marginalized groups (e.g., Latinx, women, refugee, or low-income entrepreneurs) to test the transferability of the process model and identify group-specific dynamics. Researchers should examine Black immigrant entrepreneurs in greater depth, including how ethnic-enclave community support reduces reliance on individual coping, and explore other intersectional identities. Empirical testing of specific elements of the resilience process model — particularly the compensatory dynamics between internal and external coping resources — could refine the theory and inform more tailored interventions.
abstract: This study investigates how the resilience process unfolds for Black entrepreneurs in the context of chronic racism, employing a novel qualitative approach that combines Group Model Building (GMB) and semi-­structured interviews with 49 Black entrepreneurs. Drawing on the socio-­ecological theory of resilience and leveraging Critical Race Theory (CRT), the research finds that resilience, shaped by the persistent nature of racism, requires ongoing adaptation rather than a return to a pre-­adversity state. This continuous adaptation can lead to the depletion of coping resources. The study also illustrates how internal and external coping mechanisms interact, showing that over-­reliance on internal coping mechanisms arises due to insufficient institutional and social support. Our research contributes to the literature on Black entrepreneurship, resilience, and race in entrepreneurship, while offering a comprehensive policy approach to both support and empower Black entrepreneurs. We advocate for decolonizing research practices that not only study but actively benefit the communities involved, fostering engaged and transformative scholarship.
apa_citation: Nurse, S., Dasent, K., Rivera, A., Ansah, J. P., & Black, J. (2026). Beyond rugged individualism?: Exploring the resilience of Black entrepreneurs to chronic racism. *Journal of Management Studies*, 63(1), 162-194. https://doi.org/10.1111/joms.13211

title: Carbon Populism and Representative Politics: On Why Fossil Fuel Firms Speaking for ‘The People’ Is a Bad Idea
methods: Qualitative case study of the Australian fossil fuel industry combining semi-structured interviews and document analysis. Data sources: 77 semi-structured interviews (2019-2023) with fossil fuel executives, lobbyists, industry association leaders, politicians (including two former Prime Ministers and a former State Premier), environmental NGO representatives, trade union officials, and industry analysts; 29 industry-association media releases; 57 ministerial press releases/speeches; 133 Hansard records; and 262 media items from The Australian, Sydney Morning Herald, ABC News, The Guardian Australia, and Sky News Australia (total 481 documents). Factiva/Hansard keyword searches on ‘climate change’ and ‘fossil fuel’ over 2009-2024 returned an additional 207 parliamentary documents and 311 media items. Three-stage coding in QSR NVivo: (1) open coding of actors, discourses, phenomena, practices; (2) coding of Saward's (2006, 2010) representative-claim components (maker, subject, object, audience); (3) alignment with political-theory constructs to identify six forms of political representation.
industry: Fossil fuel industries (mainly coal and gas), plus energy generation/retail, industry associations, politics, environmental NGOs, and trade unions
time_period: Interviews 2019-2023; documents/media searches covering 2009-2024
units: Individuals (interviewees) and texts (industry media releases, parliamentary speeches, Hansard records, newspaper articles)
n_sample: 77 interviews; 481 documents (29 industry media releases, 57 ministerial press releases, 133 Hansard records, 262 media items); plus 207 parliamentary documents and 311 media items from keyword searches
authors: Nyberg, D.; Wright, C.; Bowden, V.; Fleming, P.
theories: Corporate Political Activity (CPA); Political Corporate Social Responsibility (PCSR); political representation as claim-making (Saward 2006, 2010); populism theory (Laclau and Mouffe; Moffitt); public sphere / political sphere (Habermas); representative politics / constructivist turn (Saward; Disch; Castiglione and Pollak)
keywords: climate change; corporate political activity; fossil fuel industries; nationalism; populism; representative politics
research_question: How do industries seek to represent ‘the people’ and what are the implications for political decision-making? Specifically, how do fossil fuel industries in Australia construct and represent ‘the people’ in (a) the political sphere where collective and binding decisions are made, and (b) the public sphere where common concerns are deliberated?
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: Carbon populism; representative claim-making (Saward's maker-subject-object-audience schema); political sphere vs. public sphere; national identity; artificial/hegemonic representation.
- Forms of representation in the public sphere: (1) Simulated representation — industry acts ‘as’ the people (e.g., Glencore-funded astroturfing campaigns like ‘Energy in Australia’); (2) Symbolic representation — industry acts ‘on behalf of’ the people through advertising, public relations blitzes, and regional jobs narratives (e.g., the anti-carbon-tax campaign); (3) Staged representation — sympathetic media identifies the industry as standing for the nation.
- Forms of representation in the political sphere: (4) Claims about what counts as legitimate expertise and knowledge; (5) Authorization of policies favourable to the industry; (6) Institutionalized revolving-door and lobbying practices that reinforce industry voice.
- Process / loop: These six representations form a self-reinforcing loop — public-sphere claims about national identity legitimize the industry's political-sphere activity, which authorizes public policy, which in turn enables continued representative claim-making.
- Outcomes: Construction of ‘who we are’ (identity), ‘what we know’ (knowledge), and ‘what we decide to do’ (policy) around carbon-intensive interests; exclusion of citizen participation and voice; hegemonic (rather than legitimate) industry dominance over climate politics.

The central process is performative: by making claims that equate the fossil fuel industry with ‘the people’ and the Australian nation, firms and their allies manufacture an aggregated ‘unity of the people’ that mirrors industry interests. This artificial representation derives from hegemony rather than democratic legitimacy (Laclau and Mouffe), because citizens are neither the formal authorizers of nor accountable audiences for industry's claims. Once industry interests are rendered equivalent with the national interest, the need for extensive overt lobbying diminishes — decarbonization is structurally obstructed without overt prohibition.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of carbon populism — a form of populism in which the future of the nation is discursively and materially bound to carbon-intensive industries — and advances three contributions to management scholarship: (i) it extends Political Corporate Social Responsibility (PCSR) by explaining why firms cannot act as legitimate democratic representatives, since their ‘representative’ claims exclude citizen participation and rest on hegemony rather than legitimacy; (ii) it advances Corporate Political Activity (CPA) research by surfacing how artificial representation across public and political spheres shapes national identity and policy expertise, producing negative democratic externalities; and (iii) it contributes to emerging debates on corporate populism and nationalism and to political-theory discussions of the ‘constructivist turn’ by foregrounding corporate actors as claim-makers largely absent from those literatures.
practical_implication: The authors recommend two measures to combat carbon populism and strengthen representative democracy for decarbonization. First, in the political sphere, expand citizen inclusion through public forums, citizen panels, and climate assemblies (e.g., the French Citizens' Convention for Climate), and devolve power to municipal councils, cooperatives, referenda, and recall elections. Second, in the public sphere, develop alternative digital platforms — not owned by private firms or single individuals — to support public consultation, online voting, real-time policy feedback, and ‘people's platforms’ for broad-based e-democracy. Together these measures would limit the industry's capacity to manufacture an ‘aggregated unity of the people’ that underwrites fossil fuel expansion.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The authors suggest extending the concept of carbon populism to other industries where industry prosperity is rendered equivalent to the national interest — including emerging ‘AI populism’ among US tech firms framing AI leadership as central to national identity amid US-China competition, as well as steel and other sectors facing foreign competition or legislative threats. They also call for further interrogation of the power relations underlying representative politics: who speaks for whom, why, and how social-media algorithms enable agents to reproduce representative claims from unwitting claim-makers.
abstract: Despite growing recognition that countries around the world must transition to a low-carbon economy, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise. One way that decarbonization has been obstructed, we argue, is by fossil fuel firms intentionally conflating their agenda with ‘the people’, evoking notions of national identity, security and prosperity. We develop the concept of carbon populism to explain why big oil, coal and gas firms make representative claims typically associated with democratically elected governments. This adds a significant layer of difficulty for stakeholders endeavouring to enact decarbonization. Drawing on an in-depth study of fossil fuel industries in Australia (mainly coal and gas), we demonstrate how different forms of political representation in the public and political spheres influence national identity, expert knowledge and public policy. These artificial forms of representation legitimize fossil fuel industries’ political activities, authorize public policies that benefit it, and enable the industry to enjoy national dominance. We conclude by arguing that decarbonization can be achieved by rejecting carbon populism in favour of inclusive and participatory democratic representation.
