title: The power of consumer solidarity framing in scaling up social impact
methods: Single exemplary qualitative case study of the French social venture C'est qui le patron?! (CQLP), 2016-2023; inductive process analysis with dual-coding by outsider authors, triangulating 21 founder media interviews, 1.6K Facebook posts with 30K comments, 54 TV/radio reports, 2,736 pages of parliamentary records, 1,823 min of nonparticipant observation, 103 emails, and three semi-structured interviews.
industry: Agri-food / dairy (fair-priced milk consumer co-operative)
units: One social venture (CQLP) and its ecosystem actors (consumers/community, media, retailers, policymakers)
n_sample: 1 focal venture; data includes 21 founder interviews, 1.6K Facebook posts, 54 media reports, 2736 pages of parliamentary transcripts, 3 semi-structured interviews
authors: Snihur, Y.; Bluntz, C.; Bocken, N.
theories: business ecosystems; collective emotional energy; entrepreneurial framing; social movement framing (diagnostic/prognostic/motivational)
keywords: Ecosystem actors; Energized solidarity framing; Scaling up; Social entrepreneurship; Social impact
research_question: How do social entrepreneurs use entrepreneurial framing to mobilize ecosystem actors to scale up social impact?
mechanism_summary: The paper develops a process model in which an entrepreneur's energized solidarity framing — articulating a societal problem (diagnostic), a collaborative consumer-based solution (prognostic), and a motivational call to fairness — infuses a mundane purchase with shared moral meaning. Positive and negative emotional energizing generates collective momentum first within the community, which is then amplified by the media, engaged by market actors seeking legitimacy, and taken up by policymakers. Reinforcing feedback loops between entrepreneur, community, media, market actors, and politicians sustain engagement over time and drive nationwide scaling outside the venture's direct control.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on scaling up social impact by theorizing a distributed process in which a social entrepreneur's framing of a solution is progressively taken up and energized by heterogeneous ecosystem actors, enabling nationwide impact under resource scarcity. It also advances entrepreneurial framing research by introducing a social-emotional perspective — showing how shared emotions and energized solidarity framing, not cognition alone, mobilize diverse ecosystem actors and enable change.
practical_implication: Rather than confronting incumbents NGO-style, social entrepreneurs can combine consumer-solidarity content with emotional energizing to maneuver between community, media, retailers, and policymakers, adopting fair pricing even in price-competitive sectors. Skillful framing that avoids direct attacks and cultivates both social and traditional media engagement can help small ventures trigger systemic change, as illustrated by cases such as Fairphone, Fairafric, and Yuka.
limitations: The findings rest on a single exemplary case (CQLP) in France, so the distributed scaling-up process may unfold differently in other settings. Boundary conditions include the publicized nature of the French milk crisis, the concreteness of milk as a consumer product, and founder Nicolas Chabanne's skill with media and willingness to cooperate with incumbents; framing may be less effective where crises are not publicized, media is state-controlled, or founders lack such skills.
future_research: More work is needed on cognitive and emotional dynamics around social and environmental problems, including conditions under which emotional energy dissipates rather than accumulates. Comparative and cross-national studies could examine how energized framing interacts with deep versus up scaling, whether it transfers across product categories, and how authenticity is preserved when powerful actors co-opt the frame. Future research could also build on identity-based typologies to ask which social entrepreneurs are most likely to pursue distributed scaling processes.
abstract: This distributed process of scaling up social impact unfolds outside the venture's direct control, relying on community enactment as well as engagement and energizing from the media, incumbent retailers and competitors, as well as politicians. We contribute to research on scaling up social impact by explaining how and why entrepreneurial framing can mobilize diverse ecosystem actors. We also advance entrepreneurial framing research by offering a social-emotional explanation of how framing can enable change.

title: A Design for All: De-Neurotypicalizing Business Schools and Achieving Substantive Performativity
methods: Conceptual essay; theoretical argumentation drawing on the performativity, neurodiversity, and business school literatures
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Spoor, J. R.; Jameson, T. P.; Billsberry, J.; Vogus, T. J.
theories: performativity theory
keywords: business schools; de-neurotypicalization; diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI); neurodivergent; neurodiversity; neurotypical; performativity; substantive performativity; symbolic performativity; universal design
research_question: The essay addresses the open conceptual challenge of how organizations can realize the radical implications of performativity and transition from symbolic to substantive performativity, focused specifically on how business schools can move beyond symbolic DEI gestures to substantively redress the exclusion of neurodivergent students, staff, and faculty.
mechanism_summary: The paper articulates a conceptual mechanism rather than an empirical one. The authors argue that applying universal design principles — Universal Design for Learning (UDL) in the classroom and Universal Design for Work (UDW) in the workplace — drives a process they call de-neurotypicalization, which challenges and changes the implicit neurotypical assumptions embedded in business school culture, curriculum, teaching, and work practices. De-neurotypicalization, in turn, enables business schools to move from symbolic performativity (declarations, awareness campaigns, narrow accommodations) to substantive performativity that alters core structures and processes. The mechanism is theorized as one in which deep analysis of an underrecognized problem (neurotypical business schools) surfaces anomalies, generates paradigm shifts (e.g., regarding effective leadership), and enables practice shifts (e.g., new pedagogical practice and broader conceptions of accommodation through universal design).
theoretical_contribution: The authors develop the novel concept of de-neurotypicalization to illustrate how specific mechanisms (e.g., universal design) enable organizations to intentionally design for substantive performativity, building upon Marti and Gond (2018) to show how a new approach challenges existing practices, surfaces anomalies, and generates paradigm and practice shifts. They advance theory on DEI in business schools by illustrating the importance of intentional design and creating capabilities (e.g., universal design) that enable DEI efforts to be bundled rather than fragmented. The essay also provides the foundations for a fuller theory of the double empathy problem by showing how design choices, content choices, and norms can exacerbate it and how ad hoc, individualized interventions fail to redress it.
practical_implication: Business schools should apply universal design principles to both learning (UDL) and work (UDW) — including transparent workload allocation, flexible work arrangements, explicit feedback structures, multiple means of participation, and varied forms of assessment — to move from symbolic to substantive performativity on neuroinclusion. By embedding these practices and aligning internal workplace practices with classroom pedagogy, business schools can simultaneously improve outcomes for neurodivergent students, staff, and faculty, benefit neurotypical members of the community, and better prepare future leaders to build neuroinclusive organizations. Doing so also positions business schools to meet AACSB and stakeholder expectations for meaningful DEI commitment.
limitations: Not reported in paper.
future_research: Future empirical research should examine how symbolic performativity (e.g., declaring support for neurodiversity) and substantive performativity (e.g., neuroinclusive curriculum, pedagogy, and workplace practices) affect disclosure, neurodivergent enrolment and employment, and the growth of neurodivergent employment over time. Further conceptual and empirical work is needed to test the proposed mechanism of universal design. Researchers should also examine the extent to which the proposed benefits of de-neurotypicalization and inclusive universal design extend to other marginalized groups as well as to neurotypical students, and whether and how spillover benefits across minoritized identities (e.g., LGBTQ+) materialize.
abstract: Neurodivergent people experience significant disadvantages obtaining and maintaining employment. Locating our analysis at the intersection of the performativity, neurodiversity, and role of business school literatures, we argue that business schools exacerbate these issues by being designed and operated around neurotypical culture, curriculum, and teaching practices. Substantively redressing these issues and making business schools neuroinclusive requires more than the symbolic performativity that is typically the case with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives. Instead, there is an urgent need to move to substantive performativity through a process that we call de-neurotypicalizing the business school. De-neurotypicalization involves challenging and changing the implicit neurotypical assumptions that pervade business school education and work practices. A key mechanism is applying universal design principles to both learning and work. By taking substantive actions toward de-neurotypicalization, we argue that business schools will make business education genuinely open to both neurodivergent and neurotypical people. Our analysis also advances theory on DEI in business schools by illustrating that universal design offers an inclusive solution to broader equity concerns.

title: BOP’s dilemma: is jugaad an innovation or an invisible burden?
methods: Qualitative phenomenological study; 29 semi-structured in-depth interviews with BOP consumers; thematic analysis (open and axial coding) supported by NVIVO 14, yielding 115 open codes, 26 categories and nine themes
industry: Informal-sector occupations at the Bottom of the Pyramid (street vendors, laborers, barbers, shopkeepers, cleaners, cycle mechanics, homemakers, etc.)
country: India (Belpahar, Odisha and Kharagpur, West Bengal)
time_period: July 2023 to September 2023
units: BOP consumers practicing jugaad
authors: Sutar, J.; Mukherjee, S.
theories: bounded rationality; expectation-confirmation model
keywords: Bottom of the Pyramid; Bounded rationality; Consequences; Continuance intention; Environmental risk; Expectation confirmation model; Health and safety risk; Jugaad; Social unacceptance
research_question: RQ1: What are the consequences of practicing jugaad at the BOP? RQ2: What motivates jugaad practitioners to continue with its usage despite adverse consequences?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the expectation-confirmation model, the authors argue that BOP consumers form expectations about a jugaad solution at adoption and then evaluate post-use performance, with confirmation of expectations shaping satisfaction, perceived usefulness and continuance intention. However, they show that in BOP jugaad contexts this chain is disrupted in two ways: satisfied users may nevertheless abandon jugaad when health, safety or social-unacceptability risks materialize and override functional benefits; and dissatisfied users may persist because bounded rationality, financial scarcity and the absence of safer alternatives force them to satisfice rather than optimize, cognitively recalibrating expectations downward so that compromised functionality is accepted as "good enough." Jugaad is therefore reinterpreted as a necessity-driven, context-specific practice in which continuance reflects structural deprivation and social negotiation as much as positive evaluation.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends the expectation-confirmation model (ECM) to resource-constrained BOP settings by demonstrating a satisfaction–CI mismatch: satisfaction is a necessary but insufficient condition for continuance because health, safety and social-unacceptability consequences moderate the relationship, and dissatisfaction does not trigger discontinuance when viable alternatives are absent. It also extends bounded rationality theory into informal, survivalist BOP economies, showing that persistence with hazardous jugaad reflects satisficing under structural constraints rather than attitudinal endorsement. Finally, it unveils the social-acceptability and stigma dimensions of jugaad at the BOP, reframing it as a socially negotiated practice marked by aspiration and image management rather than a purely functional adaptation.
practical_implication: Businesses serving BOP markets should design affordable products that address both functional and aspirational needs, and can leverage the resourcefulness of jugaad for circular-economy branding and sustainability-driven segments. Policymakers, labor unions and social-initiative groups can reduce risks by running awareness campaigns, conducting safety audits in informal workplaces, training BOP consumers in safer alternatives, and institutionalizing affordable substitutes such as solar energy, low-cost water filtration and safer transport in place of hazardous electrical, water and vehicular jugaad. Municipal waste departments and urban planners can integrate jugaad practitioners into formal recycling and waste-management systems, while design-led capacity-building programs can elevate the cultural value of repurposed products and mitigate the stigma of jugaad as "the poor's way."
limitations: The study did not develop and validate measurement scales for the proposed constructs (environmental impact, social acceptability, maintenance costs), leaving the propositions untested in a structural model. The two regional sites (Odisha and West Bengal) turned out to be culturally similar, so intended cross-cultural comparisons were not achievable, and the sample is male-skewed because women were more reluctant to participate, limiting gendered insight. The cross-sectional design also cannot capture how jugaad practices and continuance intentions evolve as technologies, incomes and infrastructure change over time.
future_research: Future work should develop measurement scales and test the propositions as hypotheses in a structural model, and replicate the study in culturally distinct BOP regions to examine cross-cultural differences in jugaad. Researchers should pursue greater gender balance and examine gender as a moderator of jugaad practices, motivations and challenges in BOP communities. Longitudinal and comparative (urban vs. rural) designs are needed to track how jugaad and its social acceptability evolve as access to technology, education, infrastructure and awareness changes.
abstract: Purpose – This study aims to explore the consequences of jugaad at the Bottom of the Pyramid (BOP) and to examine the motivations behind continuance intention (CI) following its adoption. Design/methodology/approach – This qualitative phenomenological study used 29 in-depth interviews with BOP consumers. Thematic analysis yielded 26 categories and nine themes. The expectation-confirmation model (ECM) and bounded rationality (BR) serve as the theoretical lens through which the authors understand the rationale behind the CI of jugaad. Findings – Despite its utility, jugaad carries safety risks, frequent failures, and social stigma, putting BOP consumers in a dilemma of whether to persist. The study reveals a paradox where certain jugaad repurpose waste, while certain other jugaads pollute the environment. The study found that social unacceptance often outweighs functional benefits, showing that jugaad’s CI is shaped by nuanced, context-specific trade-offs. Originality/value – This study extends ECM by showing that BOP consumers may continue with jugaad despite dissatisfaction, driven by BR and limited alternatives. Satisfaction alone does not ensure CI. Safety concerns, social stigma, and aspirations shape CI. The findings offer key insights for policymakers and businesses engaging with BOP markets.

title: Designing Dual-Purpose Organizations: The Role of Soft Governance
methods: Conceptual / theory-building paper. The authors develop an integrative process model of dual-purpose organizing by synthesizing the organization design, hybrid organizing, and goal multiplicity literatures; they introduce and define the construct of 'soft governance' and articulate its interaction with formal design across the sorting, structuring, and socialization phases of organizing.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Szerb, A.; Kivleniece, I.; Aggarwal, V. A.
theories: goal multiplicity / multi-objective organizing; hybrid organizing; micro-foundations of organizing; organization design theory
keywords: aggregation problem; consolidation problem; coordination problems; dual-purpose organizations; goal heterogeneity; hybrid organizing; informal design mechanisms; nonhierarchical decision-making; organization design; soft governance
research_question: How can organization design—and in particular the agentic deployment of informal mechanisms (soft governance)—address the distinctive coordination challenges (an aggregation problem and a consolidation problem) that arise in dual-purpose organizations pursuing commercial and social objectives simultaneously?
mechanism_summary: DPOs are conceptualized as facing two unique coordination problems: an aggregation problem rooted in heterogeneous individual and organizational preferences, and a consolidation problem arising because dual purposes cannot be collapsed into a single meta-goal, producing nonhierarchical and opaque decision rules. Formal design mechanisms (incentives, supervisory structures, task allocation) are necessary but insufficient under these conditions. Soft governance—the intentional, agentic deployment of informal mechanisms—complements formal design by shaping the informal decision-making structure of the organization across the three organizing processes: during sorting it attracts and screens members with aligned preferences through tacit signaling; during structuring it supplies informal feedback and authority where formal rules are ambiguous; and during socialization it diffuses and converges local decision rules via peer interactions, enabling micro-level choices to cohere with macro-level dual-purpose goals.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces and develops the construct of "soft governance," defined as the deliberate, agentic deployment of informal mechanisms (informal roles, authority, rewards, and interaction structures) that shape an organization's informal decision-making structure. By extending the scope of organization design to encompass intentionally cultivated informal elements, the authors challenge the dominant assumption that informal structures merely emerge as byproducts of formal design and show that soft governance can complement formal processes to resolve coordination challenges that are endemic to dual-purpose organizing. The integrative process model bridges the hybrid-organizing, goal-multiplicity, and organization-design literatures, recasting informal structure as a "designable" component of the organization.
practical_implication: The framework offers managers of DPOs a diagnostic lens for identifying when formal mechanisms are likely to fail and a categorization of informal mechanisms that can complement or substitute for them. Achieving coordination under goal ambiguity, the authors argue, requires not just formal structure but also the strategic, agentic construction of informal scaffolding such as informal roles, recognition-based rewards, and deliberately cultivated interaction patterns. The insights may also extend to other pluralistic organizational settings, including multinational firms and nonmarket forms of organizing, where goal divergence and decision ambiguity are endemic.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The authors call for comparative empirical studies that examine the relative effectiveness of specific soft governance mechanisms—for example, when and why informal roles outperform recognition-based rewards, or how different interaction patterns affect the convergence of decision rules across levels. They further invite research into the coevolution of individual and organizational goals over time, and into how soft governance operates in other pluralistic or contested settings beyond DPOs, such as multinational firms and nonmarket organizations.
abstract: Although the phenomenon of dual-purpose organizations (DPOs)—market-based organizations that pursue both private (commercial) and broader social objectives simultaneously— has been explored extensively in prior literature, the role of organization design in addressing the distinct coordination problems inherent to DPOs has been largely overlooked. We develop a theoretical framework that conceptualizes how design considerations can influence organizational outcomes for DPOs. We identify two central coordination challenges faced by DPOs: an aggregation problem, in which heterogeneous individual preferences and organizational goals must be effectively aligned; and a consolidation problem, in which the dual-purpose nature of DPOs prevents the consolidation of goals into a single organizational meta-goal, resulting in nonhierarchical decision-making structures. We argue that formal organization design processes and mechanisms alone may fail to resolve these coordination problems, and we conceptualize the role and notion of soft governance, which we define as the agentic deployment of informal design mechanisms that shape an organization’s informal decision-making structure. Our core contribution lies in developing an integrative model of dual-purpose organizing that demonstrates how soft governance may complement formal organization design in alleviating the coordination problems inherent in DPOs, thereby supporting their stability and growth.

title: Values, risk and biodiversity-friendly action: perceived consumer effectiveness matters
methods: Cross-sectional online survey analyzed with structural equation modelling (SEM); mediation via risk perception and moderation tests of perceived consumer effectiveness; bootstrapping with 2,000 resamples for indirect effects
industry: Consumer / general population (not industry-specific)
time_period: August 2022
units: Individual adult consumers aged 18-75, recruited via an online panel with quotas for gender, age, and region
authors: Uusitalo, O.; Rouhiainen, H.; Salimi, M.
theories: Perceived consumer effectiveness; Pro-environmental behaviour (PEB) framework; Schwartz value theory (egoistic, altruistic, biospheric orientations); Value-Belief-Norm theory
keywords: Biodiversity loss; Pro-environmental behaviours; Risk perception; Sustainable consumption; Value orientations
research_question: What are the antecedents of biodiversity-respectful consumer behaviours, and how do value orientations, risk perception of biodiversity loss, and perceived consumer effectiveness jointly shape environmental citizenship/activism, sustainable consumption, and biodiversity-friendly food choices?
mechanism_summary: Grounded in value-belief-norm reasoning, the study argues that stable value orientations shape consumers' cognitive appraisal of biodiversity loss as a risk, which in turn activates pro-environmental actions. Biospheric values (valuing nature intrinsically) strongly elevate risk perception, whereas altruistic values (prioritizing human others) reduce it because biodiversity loss appears distant and indirect relative to immediate human needs. Risk perception then drives three types of behavior. Perceived consumer effectiveness — the belief that one's actions can make a difference — amplifies the translation of risk perception into activism, sustainable consumption, and food choices, functioning as a self-efficacy-like moderator of agency.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends the pro-environmental behaviour literature by distinguishing biodiversity-respectful consumption from more familiar climate-oriented behaviours and showing that biospheric values, not altruistic values, are the dominant value-based driver of biodiversity loss risk consciousness. It contributes a moderation account in which perceived consumer effectiveness amplifies the link between risk perception and high-effort sustainable behaviours, advancing understanding of why value-behaviour gaps persist for indirect, hard-to-observe environmental threats. The counterintuitive negative effect of altruistic values highlights that nature must be incorporated as a distinct moral object in theories of sustainable consumption.
practical_implication: Marketing managers, public campaigners, and policymakers should frame biodiversity loss in terms of both its direct and indirect impacts on human and natural well-being and make the consumer's own potential impact salient. Communications should activate biospheric values, clearly convey the risks of biodiversity loss, and emphasise consumers' agency through active citizenship, sustainable consumption, and biodiversity-respectful food choices (e.g., plant-based, organic, or locally sourced products). Firms can use these insights to design non-greenwashed green marketing that connects product claims to concrete biodiversity outcomes.
limitations: Model fit was only marginal on some indices (e.g., TLI = 0.89), suggesting the specified pathways may omit relevant constructs. The data are cross-sectional and self-reported, limiting causal inference about value–risk–behaviour links. The Finnish sample, characterized by tradition and conformity-oriented values and relatively pro-environmental attitudes, may not generalize to populations with different cultural value profiles.
future_research: The authors call for strengthening the model by adding mediators such as moral obligation, eco-anxiety, or biodiversity knowledge, and moderators such as social influence, cultural factors, or personality traits. Longitudinal and experimental designs are needed to establish causality and test specific interventions, and subgroup analyses across demographics and awareness levels would test robustness. Future work should also disaggregate egoistic values (hedonic vs. financial) and altruistic values (local vs. global) and experiment with framing biodiversity loss as a personal or community issue; comparative cross-country studies involving different value orientations are also encouraged.
abstract:
Purpose – Exploiting natural resources, including the escalating production and consumption of goods, significantly impacts the environment, manifesting in crises such as biodiversity loss. This paper aims to examine the antecedents of biodiversity-respectful consumer behaviours and provide novel insights for marketing about how to promote biodiversity-respectful consumer behaviour.
Design/methodology/approach – Using structural equation modelling, this study examines the relationships among value orientations, risk perception of biodiversity loss, perceived consumer effectiveness and three types of pro-environmental behaviours, based on a survey of 1,000 Finnish consumers.
Findings – Results indicate a weak positive link between egoistic values and risk perception of biodiversity loss, while altruistic values exhibited a negative association. Biospheric values showed a strong positive effect on risk perception, which in turn positively influenced environmental citizenship, activism, sustainable consumption and biodiversity-friendly food choices. Additionally, perceived consumer effectiveness enhanced the relationship between risk perception and pro-environmental actions.
Practical implications – The results point to the importance of framing and communicating environmental problems in terms of their direct and indirect impacts on both human and natural well-being. It also emphasises the need for marketing managers to consider the context of biodiversity loss and leverage perceived consumer effectiveness in promoting consumer practices mitigate biodiversity loss.
Originality/value – This study highlights the critical role of biospheric values and perceived consumer effectiveness in fostering biodiversity-friendly behaviours. The results suggest that biospheric values strongly induce biodiversity loss risk consciousness, which is significantly associated with multiple types of environmentally sound and biodiversity-friendly behaviours. Altruistic values were found to be negatively related to biodiversity loss risk perception. Biodiversity-respectful consumer behaviour may involve characteristics that are distinct from the factors underlying other types of pro-environmental behaviours. Consumers may be unable to handle the connections between perceived risks and the actual outcomes in situations where the consequences of environmental destructions are indirect and difficult to observe.
apa_citation: Uusitalo, O., Rouhiainen, H., & Salimi, M. (2026). Values, risk and biodiversity-friendly action: Perceived consumer effectiveness matters. *Journal of Consumer Marketing*, 43(1), 108-121. https://doi.org/10.1108/JCM-01-2025-7548

title: Ecosystem initiation: a key policy challenge for circular economy transition
methods: Multiple case study (six circular ecosystem cases across Australia and the Netherlands); 19 semi-structured interviews with key informants across ecosystem functional groups, supplemented by secondary data (websites, media posts, reports); deductive thematic coding in NVivo 14 against a synthesized seven-function circular ecosystem framework.
industry: Hospitality (hotels, commercial white linen); recreational parkland/light industrial manufacturing; industrial materials exchange; retail textiles/denim; road construction/asphalt polymers
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Circular economy ecosystems (six cases); interviewees drawn from local government, businesses, knowledge providers, suppliers, and consumers
n_sample: 6 cases; 19 interviews
authors: Vogel, R.; Geissdoerfer, M.
theories: business ecosystems (Moore; Adner; Baldwin et al.); circular economy; ecosystems theory
keywords: Circular economy; Circular economy transitions; Circular ecosystems; Industrial ecology; Local government
research_question: Why and how might local government initiate and orchestrate a circular economy ecosystem?
mechanism_summary: Local government, acting through empowered officers, can serve as initiator, orchestrator, and context-specific participant in a circular economy ecosystem. By convening autonomous but interdependent stakeholders around a focal CE value proposition, local government helps establish the market-sector conditions (innovation, knowledge diffusion, supply structure, regulatory support, cultural legitimacy, and demand) required for circular practices to scale. The mechanism works when actors in each of the seven functions cooperate and co-create value, and when dominant values, norms and culture shift to support circularity; absent such agency and cultural alignment, CE initiatives remain confined to niche markets.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances ecosystem theory for the circular economy on two fronts. First, it identifies that local government has the agency to initiate and orchestrate circular ecosystems and may take up other context-specific functional roles beyond regulation. Second, it proposes a novel circular ecosystem framework with seven functions as the organizing principle (rather than stakeholders/actors), categorizing business and technology, social and behavioral, and policy and regulation perspectives, and introducing "dominant values, norms and culture" as an explicit function — offering a more nuanced conceptual and definitional basis for analyzing circular ecosystems.
practical_implication: For local governments, the guidance framework clarifies the range of roles — initiator, orchestrator, knowledge partner, procurer, cultural advocate — available to facilitate a CE transition within their jurisdictions. For firms, investors, and civil-society actors, the framework shows how to purposefully assume or shift between ecosystem roles to maximize collective value creation, de-risk investment, and capture first-mover advantages in emerging circular economy sectors.
limitations: The findings are based on a parsimonious set of case studies, all of which are mature circular ecosystems with successful outcomes, introducing a survivorship bias. Although the authors purposefully sought diversity across market sectors, the selection is limited to two developed economies (Australia and the Netherlands) and to the specific sectors sampled, constraining transferability of the findings.
future_research: The authors recommend (1) investigating circular ecosystems that have failed and the reasons for failure; (2) examining which market sectors are best suited for local government to establish circular ecosystems; and (3) testing the proposed analytical framework — particularly whether foregrounding societally dominant values, norms, and culture usefully explains circular ecosystem dynamics — through longitudinal case studies and agent-based modelling.
abstract: The circular economy (CE) is increasingly viewed as a key pathway to sustainable development, but its uptake remains behind expectations. We explore the concept of circular economy ecosystems to advance our understanding of the market sector conditions necessary for the adoption of circular economy practices by producers, consumers and other stakeholders within an ecosystem. Our methodology is a multiple case study with data collection through semi-structured qualitative interviews of key informants instrumental in the initiation of the ecosystem cases, enriched by secondary data. We identify the special conditions necessary for establishing a circular economy ecosystem and the implications for stakeholders, with a special focus on local government. We deduct a novel framework to analyse and understand the agency involved in a circular economy ecosystem. Our framework depicts seven functions with actors from each function potentially involved in the circular ecosystem. Finally, the article outlines the limitations of our work, and testable propositions and methodological avenues for longitudinal case studies, and agent-based modelling to empirically validate and refine the proposed concepts, advancing the research frontier on circular ecosystems.

title: Mitigating Disability Bias in Hiring: The Role of Inclusion-Focused Generative AI in Complex HR Decisions
methods: Preregistered two-experiment design with HR professionals recruited via Prolific. Study 1 used a between-subjects design with two counterbalanced certificate-allocation conditions (COMdw, COMdk) on nine binary hiring decisions. Study 2 used a 2 x 2 factorial design crossing AI type (standard GAI vs. inclusion-focused GAI) with certificate allocation (COMdw vs. COMdk); inclusion-focused GAI prompts were built on OpenAI's GPT-4 via API (v.2024.01). Hypotheses tested with chi-square and Fisher's exact tests against a 50/50 neutrality benchmark, plus logistic regression with propensity-score matching for robustness. Supplementary text analyses used TextBlob sentiment, type-token ratio for lexical diversity, and LDA topic modeling of participants' written rationales.
industry: Cross-industry (HR professionals in engineering, management, healthcare, retail, IT, utilities, finance)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: HR professionals making binary hiring decisions between hypothetical candidates varying in disability status and certification
n_sample: Study 1: 117 HR professionals (after exclusions from 140 recruited); Study 2: 238 HR professionals (after exclusions from 260 recruited)
authors: Yang, Miles M.
theories: construal level theory; extended mind perspective
keywords: construal level theory; disability bias; fairness in hiring; generative AI; inclusive HRM
research_question: How can organizations harness the potential of generative AI while ensuring equitable, inclusive hiring decisions? Specifically, does decision complexity amplify disability bias, and does inclusion-focused GAI (designed with diversity, fairness, and inclusion principles) reduce such bias more effectively than standard GAI, particularly under complex decision conditions?
mechanism_summary: Grounded in Construal Level Theory, the paper argues that complex, ambiguous hiring decisions induce greater psychological distance and higher-level (abstract) construals, triggering stereotype-consistent evaluations that disadvantage disabled candidates. Inclusion-focused GAI, designed with diversity-fairness-inclusion prompts, functions as an external cognitive scaffold (per the Extended Mind perspective) that reduces psychological distance and redirects evaluators toward concrete, job-relevant competencies. This competency-anchored construal displaces heuristic stereotype use, mitigating disability bias most strongly in high-complexity contexts where bias risk is greatest.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends Construal Level Theory by demonstrating that psychological distance—typically treated as an individual cognitive tendency—can be externally regulated through AI framing, operationalizing CLT in a technologically mediated context. Drawing on the Extended Mind perspective, it reconceptualizes inclusion-focused GAI as an active cognitive intervention and ethical scaffold rather than a passive decision aid, positioning AI as a "fairness infrastructure" alongside structured interviews and standardized rubrics that embeds equity and accountability into hiring systems.
practical_implication: Organizations should embed diversity, fairness, and inclusion prompts into GAI hiring tools to guide evaluators toward competency-based judgments, particularly in complex, cognitively demanding decisions where bias risk peaks. Inclusion-focused GAI should be deployed as a strategic partner rather than a replacement for human judgment, enabling bias auditing through logged prompts and outcomes; however, calibration is needed to avoid overcompensation (e.g., the 70.2% hiring rate for disabled candidates in COMdk).
limitations: Psychological distance was theorized but not directly manipulated, leaving the CLT mechanism inferred rather than empirically isolated. The controlled lab setting with hypothetical candidates may not reflect real-world hiring conditions involving time pressure, team dynamics, or organizational norms. The analysis focused solely on disability bias and did not include an AI-only condition to isolate algorithmic judgment from human decision-making.
future_research: Future work should design GAI prompts that explicitly manipulate CLT mechanisms such as temporal and social framing, and test their interaction with organizational culture and individual cognition. Field studies in naturalistic recruitment contexts are needed, as are extensions to other bias domains (race, age, gender) and to alternative human-AI configurations that address privacy, transparency, and unintended effects. Calibration research is needed to prevent inclusion-focused GAI from producing inverted bias or overcompensation.
abstract: This research investigates how inclusion‐focused generative AI (GAI), designed with diversity, fairness, and inclusion princi ples, mitigates disability bias in hiring—particularly under complex, cognitively demanding conditions. Drawing on Construal Level Theory, two experiments with HR professionals (N = 117; 238) compared standard, inclusion‐focused, and control conditions. Inclusion‐focused GAI significantly reduced bias by emphasizing job‐relevant competencies and lowering psy chological distance. The study introduces a fairness‐oriented AI design that advances accountability and inclusion in HR systems, offering implications for equitable hiring, bias auditing, and the strategic use of ethical AI in talent acquisition.

title: Participative pricing, food affordability, and nutritional adequacy: evidence from India
methods: Cross-sectional analysis of NSSO 2022-23 Consumption Expenditure Survey microdata; log-level OLS regressions, generalized linear models with log link, and logistic regressions; simulated PWYW (50/75/100/150% of baseline) and SYOP (+/-20% band) counterfactual pricing scenarios with interactions between pricing scenarios and MPCE income quintiles; separate urban/rural models; standard errors clustered at PSU level
industry: Household food consumption (all food categories: wholegrains, tubers, vegetables, fruits, dairy, protein, added fats, sugars, spices, processed)
units: Households (urban and rural) from NSSO HCES
n_sample: 261,746 households (155,014 rural and 106,732 urban); analytic sample 256,016
authors: Zeeshan, Z.; Khan, M. T.
theories: Engel's law; participative pricing (pay-what-you-want, set-your-own-price); price elasticity and consumer discretion
keywords: Affordability; Consumer behavior; Food expenditure; Income elasticity; India; NSSO; Nutritional adequacy; Participative pricing
research_question: How do participative pricing mechanisms (PWYW and SYOP) influence household food expenditure patterns across income groups; can they improve affordability for diverse and nutritious food categories; and how do participative pricing responses differ across urban and rural households in India?
mechanism_summary: Participative pricing shifts part of the pricing decision from the seller to the buyer, introducing consumer discretion over prices. Under PWYW, simulated fixed-fraction discounts interact with existing affordability constraints: lower prices do not automatically raise quantities because households reallocate their budgets across food categories, with urban and higher-income households being more elastic than rural or low-income ones. Under SYOP, consumer-set prices within a narrow acceptance band allow higher-income consumers to channel spending toward nutrient-dense foods, but binding affordability constraints prevent lower-income households from doing the same. The heterogeneity across income and sector reflects differences in budget slack, market access and price elasticity rooted in Engel's-law reasoning about food shares and household welfare.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends participative pricing research beyond digital commerce and cultural industries to food affordability in a developing-country context, formalizing PWYW and SYOP as counterfactual pricing regimes over national survey microdata. It reframes the policy question from "how much to cut prices" toward "how to allocate pricing discretion and complementary access supports," showing that bounded consumer discretion (SYOP) outperforms uniform discounts (PWYW) for affordability when budgets are tight. In doing so, it integrates participative pricing with nutrition-transition and food-security literatures in low- and middle-income countries.
practical_implication: Policymakers and retailers should pair flexible pricing with complementary interventions: tiered "community pricing" bands anchored by a suggested price, simple eligibility (e.g. ration-card verification) for reduced bands and brief SYOP windows to learn willingness-to-pay. Urban, higher-income households respond to PWYW-style discounts, while rural and low-income households require structural supports (market access, subsidies, income transfers) to benefit. Programs should track affordability rates (<=30% MPCE), basket diversity and sector-specific take-up, iterating floors and bands accordingly.
limitations: Price variation is simulated through PWYW fractions and SYOP bands rather than observed in live markets, so external validity depends on how floors, reference prices and eligibility are implemented in practice. The analysis focuses on expenditure rather than directly mapping quantities to nutrients, which would require additional assumptions beyond the scope of the study. The design is cross-sectional, precluding observation of learning, persistence or seasonal adjustment in consumer behavior.
future_research: Future work should run live pilots or staggered rollouts to capture dynamic learning, persistence and seasonal effects under actual participative pricing. Short panels could identify how floors, reference prices and eligibility rules shape affordability and basket composition. Extensions could map expenditure changes more explicitly to nutritional intake and calorie adequacy, and test community pricing bands in field experiments across regions.
abstract: Purpose – This study investigates the impact of participatory pricing mechanisms, specifically pay-what-you-want (PWYW) and set-your-own-price (SYOP), on household food expenditure and affordability in India. This study aims to understand how these pricing models affect consumer behavior across various food categories and income groups in both urban and rural settings. Design/methodology/approach – Using data from the NSSO 2022–23 Consumption Expenditure Survey (CES), this study uses log-level ordinary least squares regressions, generalized linear models with a log link and logistic regressions. These models incorporate interactions between pricing scenarios (for PWYW, as well as SYOP quintiles) and income groups (measured by monthly per capita expenditure quintiles). A comprehensive set of control variables at the household level was included to ensure robust estimates. Findings – The results indicate that PWYW pricing leads to nonlinear changes in food expenditure. Urban households exhibit elastic responses, with higher-income groups reallocating their spending more significantly in response to discounts, whereas rural households display inelastic behavior under similar pricing conditions. Under the SYOP model, lower-income households face severe affordability constraints, whereas higher-income consumers demonstrate increased spending on nutrient-dense foods. These heterogeneous responses suggest that price flexibility alone may not uniformly improve food affordability and nutritional adequacy across different socio-economic contexts. Originality/value – This research extends the existing literature on pricing strategies by applying participative pricing models to food expenditure and nutritional adequacy in a developing country context. The study offers actionable insights for policymakers and industry stakeholders, underscoring the need for targeted interventions that integrate flexible pricing with complementary social and economic support measures.

title: From a Portfolio of Journals to a System of Knowledge Production
methods: Editorial essay (From the AOM Editors). Develops a conceptual framework — the knowledge production value cycle — that maps the seven AOM journals onto four quadrants (generation, synthesis, education, application) and illustrates inter-journal linkages with a running example on the venting literature.
industry: na
time_period: na
units: na
n_sample: na
authors: Cronin, Matthew A.; Galvin, Benjamin Martell; George, Elizabeth; Gruber, Marc; Lindebaum, Dirk; Markman, Gideon D.; Miller, C. Chet; Rose, Elizabeth L.; Thatcher, Sherry M. B.; Wood, Geoffrey T.
theories: disciplined imagination (Weick, 1989); full-cycle research (Chatman & Flynn, 2005); knowledge production system / value cycle framework
keywords: AOM journals; application; education; generation; knowledge production system; scholarly impact; synthesis; value cycle
research_question: Not reported in paper
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: The seven AOM journals function not as a portfolio but as an integrated knowledge production system organized into a value cycle of generation, synthesis, education, and application.
- Key constructs: knowledge generation (AMD, AMJ, AMR), knowledge synthesis (AMR, AMC, Annals), education (Annals, AMLE), application (AMP, AMLE).
- Process / phases: discoveries (AMD) seed empirical investigation (AMJ) and unit-theory development (AMR); these feed synthesis (AMC, Annals); synthesized knowledge informs pedagogy (AMLE) and practitioner-facing prescriptions (AMP); application surfaces new puzzles that restart the cycle.
- Boundary conditions: a single paper need not serve all readers; clarity about which quadrant(s) a paper occupies determines for whom its findings are credible, useful, and usable.

The essay argues that scientific impact is amplified when authors recognize how their paper's function relates to other quadrants of the cycle — between-journal hand-offs are themselves part of the value chain, with the output of one journal becoming the input to another. A worked example follows the venting construct from a counterintuitive AMD discovery, through AMJ empirical work and AMR theorizing, into AMC curation and Annals integration, and finally into AMLE pedagogy and AMP practitioner translation.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: Reframes the AOM journal portfolio as an interdependent knowledge production system rather than a collection of independent outlets, articulating the distinct epistemic function of each journal within a generation–synthesis–education–application value cycle. Positions inter-journal linkages — not within-paper rigor alone — as the locus of cumulative scholarly impact, and invites authors to write with explicit awareness of how their work feeds and is fed by adjacent quadrants.
practical_implication: Authors and reviewers should locate each paper within the value cycle and clarify what function it serves, who its audience is, and how its findings can be leveraged by papers in other quadrants. This reframing dissolves the false dichotomy between managerial-application impact and citation-based impact: all four quadrants are necessary, and clarity of function makes findings more usable for researchers, educators, students, and practitioners alike.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editors invite the AOM community to enact the value-cycle perspective in concrete authorship and review practices — making explicit how individual papers connect across journals, integrating AMLE pedagogical lessons into practitioner-oriented AMP work, and using application-phase failures to surface new discoveries that restart the cycle.

title: Socialization as a Political Arena: A Multi-Agent Interactionist Perspective to Understand Political Skill and Newcomer Socialization Rates
methods: Four-wave longitudinal field survey of newcomers nested within supervisors at a large Chinese IT corporation; latent growth curve modeling of role clarity, task mastery, and social integration trajectories over the first six months of employment, with two-month intervals between waves; moderated-mediation path analysis using Mplus 8.6 with a sandwich estimator (TYPE = COMPLEX) to handle multilevel nesting and FIML for missing data; Monte Carlo bootstrap with 20,000 replications for indirect and conditional indirect effects; supplemented by two cross-lagged panel studies (each n = 200) for causal inference and discriminant validity, plus interpretive interviews with 40 newcomers.
industry: Information technology — a large IT corporation that recruited campus hires in 2019; supplemental Studies A and B used 200 newcomers each from an IT company and a university alumni network
time_period: Four waves spanning the first six months after newcomer entry — Time 0 (before first day), Time 1 (second month), Time 2 (fourth month), Time 3 (sixth month); 2019 cohort
units: Organizational newcomers (employee-rated IVs/mediators/moderator) nested in their direct supervisors (supervisor-rated adjustment outcomes at T1, T2, T3)
n_sample: 1,197 newcomers nested in 550 supervisors (final response rate 85.1%); two supplemental studies of 200 newcomers each; supplemental interviews with 40 newcomers
authors: Deng, Yingxin; Lin, Weipeng; Song, Yifan; Wang, Mo; Cai, Di; Liu, Jia
theories: interactionist perspective on newcomer socialization rates (Reichers, 1987); multi-agent perspective on socialization (supervisor vs. veteran colleagues); person-by-situation interaction perspective; political skill theory (Ferris et al., 2005, 2007)
keywords: growth rates of adjustment; horizontal social interaction; interaction frequency; interactionist perspective; newcomer socialization; political skill; prosocial climate for newcomers; role clarity; social integration; socialization rates; supervisor; task mastery; vertical social interaction; veteran colleagues
research_question: How and when does newcomers' political skill shape their socialization rates, and through which social-interaction-based mechanism — vertical interactions with one's supervisor versus horizontal interactions with veteran colleagues — does it transmit its effects into different adjustment dynamics (early-entry adjustment states vs. growth rates of role clarity, task mastery, and social integration), conditional on a prosocial climate for newcomers?
hypotheses:
H1. Newcomer political skill positively predicts interaction frequency with (a) supervisor and (b) veteran colleagues.
H2. Interaction frequency with supervisor positively predicts growth rates of (a) role clarity, (b) task mastery, and (c) social integration.
H3. Interaction frequency with veteran colleagues positively predicts growth rates of (a) role clarity, (b) task mastery, and (c) social integration.
H4. Newcomer political skill has positive indirect effects on growth rates of (a) role clarity, (b) task mastery, and (c) social integration via interaction frequency with supervisor.
H5. Newcomer political skill has positive indirect effects on growth rates of (a) role clarity, (b) task mastery, and (c) social integration via interaction frequency with veteran colleagues.
H6. Prosocial climate for newcomers moderates the positive effects of political skill on interaction frequency with (a) supervisor and (b) veteran colleagues, such that the effects are stronger when prosocial climate is high.
H7. Prosocial climate for newcomers moderates the positive indirect effects of political skill on growth rates of (a) role clarity, (b) task mastery, and (c) social integration via interaction frequency with supervisor, such that the effects are stronger when prosocial climate is high.
H8. Prosocial climate for newcomers moderates the positive indirect effects of political skill on growth rates of (a) role clarity, (b) task mastery, and (c) social integration via interaction frequency with veteran colleagues, such that the effects are stronger when prosocial climate is high.
mechanism_summary:
- Moderator: Prosocial climate for newcomers (T1, newcomers' psychological perception that insiders care about their needs and adjustment).
- Controls: age, gender, education, Big Five personality, proactive personality, and interaction quality with each agent.

The interactionist perspective holds that interaction frequency is "the primary mechanism through which newcomers are transformed into insiders," and that frequent interactions and rapid socialization arise when newcomer interpersonal characteristics (political skill) and the social environment (insider prosociality) jointly favor adjustment. Politically skilled newcomers can both initiate and prolong interactions with insiders and inspire insiders to interact with them, but vertical and horizontal channels carry different content: supervisor interactions deliver authoritative, structured, holistic information that crystallizes early-entry understanding of roles, tasks, and norms, whereas veteran-colleague interactions supply detailed, diverse, sometimes fragmentary information whose value compounds over time as newcomers integrate it into a sophisticated cognitive schema — producing growth in adjustment rather than immediate states. A prosocial climate amplifies both pathways by making insiders responsive and signaling that interaction returns are high.
data_measures:
Data come from a four-wave longitudinal field survey of 1,197 newcomers nested in 550 supervisors at a large Chinese IT corporation (2019 campus cohort), with two-month intervals across the first six months after entry. Focal constructs were operationalized as follows:
- IV — newcomer political skill (T0): Ferris et al.'s (2005) 18-item scale, 7-point Likert (Cronbach's alpha = .91).
- Mediators — interaction frequency with supervisor and with veteran colleagues (T1): McAllister's (1995) four-item scale, 5-point Likert (alpha = .89 and .87, respectively).
- Moderator — prosocial climate for newcomers (T1): De Dreu and Nauta's (2009) three-item scale, 5-point Likert (alpha = .96).
- DVs (supervisor-rated at T1, T2, T3), modeled via latent growth curve modeling as intercepts (early-entry states) and linear slopes (growth rates): role clarity (Rizzo, House, & Lirtzman, 1970), task mastery (Morrison, 1993a), and social integration (Jokisaari & Nurmi, 2009), each three items, 5-point Likert.
- Controls: age, gender, education, Big Five personality, proactive personality, and interaction quality with each agent.

Moderated-mediation path analysis was estimated in Mplus 8.6 with a sandwich estimator (TYPE = COMPLEX) to handle the newcomer-in-supervisor nesting and FIML for missing data; indirect and conditional indirect effects used Monte Carlo bootstrapping with 20,000 replications. The primary design is longitudinal and associational; two supplemental two-wave cross-lagged studies (n = 200 each) strengthen causal inference, though the authors note causality still cannot be firmly established.
key_findings:
Support was heterogeneous across the two social-interaction pathways, and this differentiation is the paper's headline result:
- H1a/H1b supported: newcomer political skill positively predicted interaction frequency with supervisor (γ = .12, p < .001) and veteran colleagues (γ = .11, p < .001).
- H2a–c NOT supported: interaction frequency with supervisor did not significantly predict growth rates (slopes) of role clarity, task mastery, or social integration.
- H3a–c supported: interaction frequency with veteran colleagues positively predicted growth rates of role clarity (γ = .06), task mastery (γ = .07), and social integration (γ = .05).
- H4a–c NOT supported: political skill's indirect effects on growth rates via supervisor were non-significant (CIs included zero).
- H5a–c supported: political skill's indirect effects on growth rates via veteran colleagues were positive and significant (.006, .008, .006).
- H6a/H6b supported: prosocial climate positively moderated political skill's effect on interaction frequency with supervisor (γ = .10, p < .001) and veteran colleagues (γ = .08, p = .012), with effects stronger when prosocial climate was high.
- H7a–c NOT supported (moderated mediation of growth rates via supervisor); H8a–c supported (moderated mediation of growth rates via veteran colleagues, significant only at high prosocial climate).

Supplementary analyses showed that interaction frequency with supervisor (but not with veteran colleagues) positively predicted early-entry states (intercepts) of all three adjustment outcomes (role clarity γ = .10; task mastery γ = .13; social integration γ = .12), and these indirect effects were significant and stronger under high prosocial climate. Net pattern: veteran-colleague interactions transmit political skill into growth rates of adjustment, whereas supervisor interactions transmit it into early-entry states — the effect is differentiated by agent, not uniform.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates two previously disconnected social-interaction-based mechanisms in the political skill literature (vertical vs. horizontal) into a single multi-agent interactionist model and shows that they map onto distinct adjustment dynamics — supervisor interactions to early-entry states and veteran-colleague interactions to growth rates — thereby reconciling disparate views about how political skill operates and overcoming the literature's prior treatment of social contacts as undifferentiated. By identifying prosocial climate for newcomers as a moderator, it advances a person-by-situation account in which newcomer adjustment is a joint function of newcomer social skill and insider prosociality, and extends the political skill nomological network into the underexamined newcomer socialization domain.
practical_implication: Organizations can incorporate political-skill training into newcomer orientation, design mentoring programs and social events that maximize early-entry interaction with supervisors and sustained interaction with veteran colleagues, and recognize the differential roles each agent plays at different stages of adaptation. Because prosocial climate is critical for politically skilled newcomers to socialize effectively, firms should establish formal procedures, anonymous newcomer-feedback systems, and reward structures that motivate supervisors and veterans to attend to newcomer needs and integrate insider prosociality into performance evaluation.
limitations: Adjustment outcomes were rated only by supervisors, so multi-source replication (newcomer, coworker) is needed; cross-lagged supplemental analyses strengthen but do not establish causality, and reverse-direction effects (e.g., better adjustment reducing reliance on insider interactions) cannot be ruled out. All data were collected in China, a high-collectivism, high-power-distance setting where political skill and deference to supervisors may be especially salient, limiting cross-cultural generalizability. Other interpersonal constructs (emotional intelligence, emotional regulation, impression management) were not controlled for, and the conscientiousness measure showed alpha below conventional benchmarks.
future_research: Future studies should replicate the model with multi-source adjustment data and in non-Chinese contexts to test cultural generalizability, control for additional interpersonal-skill confounds (emotional intelligence, emotional regulation, impression management) while parsing variance overlap with proactive personality and Big Five traits, and examine alternative moderators such as psychological safety climate or the level of organizational politics. Researchers should also empirically test the qualitative speculations about why vertical interactions matter for early-entry states and horizontal interactions for growth rates, and explore reciprocal dynamics in which political skill is itself shaped over time through interactions with insiders.
abstract: Integrating two social-interaction-based perspectives (i.e., vertical vs. horizontal social interactions) on political skill, the current research examined how organizational newcomers might leverage their political skill to promote their socialization rates through frequent interactions with different agents of socialization (i.e., supervisor vs. veteran colleagues). Using a four-wave longitudinal study with a sample of 1,197 organizational newcomers nested in 550 supervisors, we found that newcomer political skill had positive indirect effects on growth rates of adjustment outcomes via interaction frequency with veteran colleagues (but not with supervisor), while it had positive indirect effects on early-entry adjustment states via interaction frequency with supervisor (but not with veteran colleagues). Moreover, these effects were stronger when the level of prosocial climate for newcomers was high. Two supplemental studies, each using repeated-measures data from 200 organizational newcomers, provide stronger causal inference of the impact of newcomer political skill that is contingent on prosocial climate for newcomers, and rule out alternative explanations. Furthermore, we conducted supplemental interviews with 40 newcomers to provide an in-depth discussion on the differential roles of vertical (newcomer–supervisor) versus horizontal (newcomer–veteran colleagues) interactions in transmitting newcomer political skill into different adjustment dynamics (i.e., early-entry adjustment states vs. growth rates of adjustment).

Socialization as a political arena: A multi-agent interactionist perspective to understand political skill and newcomer socialization rates. *Academy of Management Journal*, 68(1), 108-137. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2022.0669

title: Information-Based Competition: The Case of Rival Owners in Rating Agencies
methods: Pooled OLS regressions of MSCI ESG ratings on rival-MSCI common institutional ownership with industry-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered by industry-year; firm-year panel from 2013-2019 with 12,634 firm-year observations on 2,787 firms; moderation tests for rival/target ESG media controversies and ESG awards; robustness checks include Heckman selection models, firm fixed effects, random effects, alternative industry classifications (FIC-100 vs MSCI IVA), benchmarking against ESG risk incidents and ASSET4 evaluations, quasi-natural experiments around MSCI's 2010 acquisition of KLD and Thomson Reuters' 2009 acquisition of ASSET4, ITCV omitted-variable analysis, and decomposition by dedicated/transient/quasi-indexer investors.
industry: U.S. publicly traded firms across industries (rivals identified using Hoberg-Phillips fixed industry classification FIC-100); rating agency MSCI ESG Research
time_period: 2013-2019 (sample period set by MSCI ESG Ratings Time Series database coverage and availability of all data sources)
units: Firm-year observations of target firms covered by MSCI ESG Research; rival-MSCI common institutional owners with >=1% ownership stakes in both MSCI and the rival firm
n_sample: 12,634 firm-year observations on 2,787 unique firms
authors: DesJardine, Mark R.; Li, Boshuo; Shi, Wei
theories: awareness-motivation-capability framework (Durand, Hawn & Ioannou, 2019); common ownership theory (Connelly et al., 2019); competitive dynamics theory (Chen & Miller, 2015); information intermediary / coverage bias literature (Sharkey et al., 2023); reputation theory (Bundy, Iqbal & Pfarrer, 2021)
keywords: ESG awards; ESG media controversies; ESG ratings; MSCI; common ownership; competitive dynamics; information intermediaries; information-based competition; institutional investors; rating agencies; reputational opportunities; reputational threats
research_question: How and when do competitive forces operating through information intermediaries shape the information that stakeholders receive about a firm — specifically, do firms receive less favorable ESG ratings from rating agencies in which their rivals' institutional investors hold greater ownership stakes, and how is this rating bias amplified or attenuated by reputational threats (rival/target ESG media controversies) and reputational opportunities (rival/target ESG awards)?
hypotheses:
H1. The level of common ownership that rivals' institutional investors hold in a rating agency is negatively associated with the target firm's ESG rating issued by that agency.
H2a. This negative relationship is stronger when the rivals face more ESG media controversies.
H2b. This negative relationship is weaker when the target firm faces more ESG media controversies.
H3a. This negative relationship is stronger when the rivals have won more ESG awards.
H3b. This negative relationship is weaker when the target firm has won an ESG award.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: target firm-MSCI CIO, rival/target firm-other agency CIO, target firm-rival CIO, market overlap, size similarity, target/rival firm financial and governance characteristics, ESG compensation/board/regulatory enforcement, industry-year fixed effects.

The theorized mechanism is that institutional investors who simultaneously own significant stakes in MSCI and in firms outside the rating industry have both motive (portfolio returns benefit when their portfolio firms appear better than rivals on ESG) and means (legal "advisor" status, opaque ESG rating processes, executive incentives to placate large investors) to tilt MSCI's ESG ratings against the portfolio firms' rivals. The bias intensifies when reputational stakes are high — rival ESG media controversies create motivation to repair rivals' reputations via ratings, and rival ESG awards heighten raters' receptivity to negative information about less-decorated peers — and weakens when target firms themselves are already drawing reputational scrutiny or have countervailing ESG awards that buffer their ratings.
data_measures: Data are archival firm-year panels (2013-2019) assembled around ESG ratings from MSCI ESG Research. Dependent variable: MSCI ESG rating, the MSCI ESG Ratings Time Series database's seven-point letter grade (AAA-CCC) converted to integer scores 6-0 and averaged per firm-year. Independent variable: rival-MSCI common institutional ownership (rival-MSCI CIO), computed via Equation 1 as the average product of an investor's ownership in MSCI and in the target firm's industry rivals, summed across institutional owners holding at least 1% of both MSCI and a rival (Thomson Reuters 13F Holdings); rivals are identified with the Hoberg-Phillips fixed industry classification (FIC-100). Moderators: rival and target firm ESG media controversies (RepRisk; natural log of 1 plus ESG risk incidents weighted by severity and reach) and rival and target firm ESG awards (ASSET4; rival awards = percentage of commonly owned rivals winning at least one award, target awards = a binary indicator). Controls drawn from Compustat, Thomson Reuters Insider Filings, ISS, BoardEx, Violation Tracker, and 10-K/EDGAR capture other common-ownership ties, market overlap, size similarity, and target and rival financial, governance, and ESG characteristics. Estimation is pooled OLS with industry-year fixed effects and standard errors clustered by industry-year; explanatory variables are deliberately not lagged, which the authors note weakens causal inference. The design is associational: endogeneity is addressed but not resolved through Heckman selection models, firm and random effects, alternative (MSCI IVA) industry classifications, benchmarking against ESG risk incidents and ASSET4 evaluations, ITCV omitted-variable analysis, and quasi-natural experiments around MSCI's 2010 acquisition of KLD and Thomson Reuters' 2009 acquisition of ASSET4.
key_findings: All five hypotheses are supported. H1: rival-MSCI CIO is negatively related to the target firm's MSCI ESG rating (b = -0.231, p < .001; Model 1); moving rival-MSCI CIO from its 25th to 75th percentile lowers the ESG rating by 0.82, roughly 67% of its standard deviation. H2a: the interaction of rival-MSCI CIO with rival ESG media controversies is negative (b = -0.242, p < .001; Model 2), so the negative effect strengthens when rivals face more controversies. H2b: the interaction of rival-MSCI CIO with target firm ESG media controversies is positive (b = 0.014, p < .001; Model 3), so the effect weakens when the target itself faces controversies. H3a: the interaction of rival-MSCI CIO with rival ESG awards is negative (b = -1.056, p < .001; Model 4), strengthening the effect when rivals win awards. H3b: the interaction of rival-MSCI CIO with target firm ESG awards is positive (b = 0.066, p < .001; Model 5), weakening the effect when the target wins an award. The main effect and moderators hold across Heckman selection, firm fixed effects, random effects, an alternative (IVA) industry classification, and the KLD and ASSET4 quasi-natural experiments (post-acquisition KLD-score effect b = -0.531, p < .10). Benchmarking shows rival-MSCI CIO predicts the gap between MSCI ratings and objective ESG signals (MSCI-incident difference b = -0.033, p < .01; MSCI-ASSET4 difference b = -0.034, p < .10) but is unrelated to raw ESG risk incidents or ASSET4 evaluations themselves, consistent with a rating-bias rather than a real-performance interpretation. In untabulated decomposition the negative main effect holds for the environmental (b = -0.346, p < .001) and social (b = -0.207, p < .01) subratings but is nonsignificant for governance (b = -0.038, n.s.). Supplementary tests concentrate the effect among dedicated institutional investors (b = -0.931, p < .01) relative to transient investors (b = -0.249, p < .05; Wald test of difference p = .039), with the moderating effects largely driven by dedicated investors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces information-based competition — competition waged by manufacturing, assembling, and disseminating information that shapes stakeholders' perceptions of other organizations — as a new construct in competitive dynamics research, and adds a dynamic dimension by theorizing the reputational threats and opportunities under which outside actors leverage their influence over information intermediaries. It extends the information-intermediary literature by showing that bias originates not only from rated firms and direct economic exchange partners but also from the rivals' common investors, and contributes to the common-ownership literature by uncovering an indirect channel — boundary-spanning ownership in publicly traded rating agencies — through which common owners profit from competitive intervention.
practical_implication: Firms should manage information flows with intermediaries by disclosing ESG activities transparently in standardized formats, enabling stakeholders and privately owned raters to assess them directly and limiting common-owner influence. Socially responsible investors should use ESG ratings from multiple agencies and account for the ownership/governance structures of those agencies when weighting them. Regulators (notably the SEC) could weigh whether the conflicts of interest introduced by common owners of ESG rating agencies warrant disclosure and internal-control requirements of the kind the SEC applies to rating-agency conflicts.
limitations: The empirical strategy does not lag explanatory variables (because investor influence is theorized to operate during current holding periods), which the authors acknowledge weakens causal claims; endogeneity is mitigated through Heckman selection, ITCV, and quasi-natural experiments rather than fully resolved. The setting is U.S. firms rated by a single agency (MSCI), with robustness checks against ASSET4 aligning with the theory. The two channels of investor influence — direct intervention versus executive pacification of investors — could not be empirically separated.
future_research: Scholars should explore information-based competition along three dimensions: the actor engaging in it (institutional vs. individual investors, formal officeholders inside intermediaries), the type of intermediary (social media platforms like X, online review aggregators like Yelp), and the tie through which influence is exerted (ownership, formal position, advertising). Future work could disentangle whether common-owner influence operates through investor-initiated intervention or executive-initiated pacification, examine information-based competition in non-rating contexts, and probe how multiple competing information sources interact in shaping firm reputations and competitive dynamics.
abstract: This study extends competitive dynamics research by theorizing how and when information about a firm may be shaped by competitive forces operating through information intermediaries. Arguing that ownership bestows investors with influence over information intermediaries from which investors can profit, we suggest that firms receive less favorable ratings from rating agencies in which their rivals' investors have greater ownership. Building on research in this vein, we develop a dynamic theory of information-based competition that suggests the rating discounts a firm receives from rating agencies owned by its rivals' investors are shaped by the reputational threats and opportunities faced by the firm and its rivals, which motivate and enable investors to use information intermediaries to intervene in competitive dynamics. Analyses of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) ratings of 2,787 firms by a leading ESG rating agency support these ideas. Our study introduces the concept of information-based competition and illuminates the conditions under which investors engage in information-based competitive attacks.
