title: Uprooting Loneliness: A Theory of Continuity-Breaking Self-Narrative Change
methods: Inductive, interpretivist qualitative study grounded in narrative inquiry. Data collected over 15 months via 90-120 minute semi-structured video interviews with 61 senior executives recruited from an international business school's alumni population. Pilot interviews with 7 executives preceded the main study. Analysis used iterative first-order, axial, and theoretical coding (Locke, 2001; Salda~na, 2009), case summaries, narrative causality (Carton, 2018), and circling between data and the literatures on self-narratives, work loneliness, and attachment. Theoretical saturation was reached at interview 46; data collection stopped at 61.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: 15 months of data collection (specific calendar dates not reported); informants reported persistent loneliness experiences of at least two years' duration
units: Senior executives (e.g., CEOs, CFOs, CHROs, CMOs, COOs, partners, presidents, directors) who self-reported sustained or repeated loneliness in their work roles
n_sample: 61 executives in the formal study (28 holding constraining self-narratives, 24 having transitioned to connecting self-narratives, 9 in the midst of change), plus 7 pilot interviewees
authors: Petriglieri, Jennifer Louise; Sheprow, Elizabeth
theories: attachment theory; narrative inquiry; psychodynamic perspective; relational scripts; self-narrative theory; threshold theory
keywords: attachment theory; connecting self-narrative; constraining self-narrative; continuity-breaking self-narrative change; emotional threshold; executives; narrative inquiry; persistent loneliness; relational scripts; self-narratives; self-referential insight; work loneliness
research_question: Why and how do people engage in continuity-breaking self-narrative change related to their work? The authors examine this question in the empirical context of executives experiencing persistent work loneliness.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: self-narratives and their central themes; constraining vs. connecting relational scripts ("If I am self-reliant, then I will be less vulnerable to others who could undermine my success" vs. "If I am open, then I will be more connected to others, and this will aid my success"); deprived vs. enriched relational realities; persistent/painful vs. short-lived/unpleasant loneliness.
- Triggering conditions: an accumulation of distressing loneliness, often catalyzed by a precipitating work event, that pushes informants past an emotional threshold beyond which loneliness becomes intolerable and rhetorical justification and relational compensation can no longer keep it tolerable.
- Process / phases: (1) constraining self-narrative maintained through enactment of self-isolating behavior, rhetorical justification of loneliness as the price of success, and relational compensation outside work; (2) crossing an emotional threshold when loneliness becomes intolerable; (3) self-referential insight that loneliness is partly an agentic construction; (4) translating insight into experimental relational actions, or hitting an impasse driven by fear; (5) oscillation between competing relational scripts; (6) connecting self-narrative in which the alternative script replaces the original and other stories of self are updated.
- Practices: enacting guarded/self-isolating behaviors vs. open/affiliative behaviors; rhetorical justification; relational compensation in nonwork life; gradual experimentation ("almost by stealth"); seeking help; building "circles of confidence."
- Emergent outcomes: continuity-breaking self-narrative change creating "disjuncture between past and present selves"; reconstruction of work realities even when little in the work environment has changed; loneliness moves from persistent and painful to short-lived and unpleasant.

The central process is that persistent loneliness becomes "rooted in the self" via constraining relational scripts that yoke success to self-reliance and invulnerability. Continuity-breaking change is triggered by a coalescence of external precipitating events and an internal emotional shift across a threshold; this distress drives a self-referential insight that loneliness is partly self-constructed, which in turn fuels experimentation with connecting scripts that develop in parallel, compete with, and ultimately supplant the original ones as the central themes of the self-narrative — at which point informants update other stories of self and reconstruct their relational realities at work.
data_measures:
- Data corpus: 61 semi-structured video interviews (90-120 minutes each) with senior executives, conducted over 15 months and preceded by 7 exploratory pilot interviews; all interviews were audio-recorded and professionally transcribed. Informants were recruited from an international business school's alumni population and had confirmed sustained or repeated work loneliness of at least two years' duration.
- Coding: descriptive first-order codes that closely reflected informants' own terms (Locke, 2001) were grouped into axial codes by similarity and difference, then into three theoretical codes that became the three findings sections; detailed per-informant case summaries (averaging eight single-spaced pages) supplemented the coding.
- Construct operationalization: relational scripts were coded as if-then contingencies about who informants felt they needed to be to elicit or avoid responses from others; two forms were induced as the central themes of two self-narratives, and informants were coded as holding constraining (28), connecting (24), or in-transition (9) self-narratives.
- Process analysis: narrative causality (Carton, 2018) was applied to the 33 informants in the midst of, or having completed, the change to map their own attributions of what precipitated what. The design is interpretivist and purposefully subjective; the authors state they cannot claim the changes objectively occurred as informants narrated them.
key_findings:
- Relational scripts — if-then contingencies about relating to others — formed the central theme that connected and unified all other stories in executives' self-narratives. A constraining script ("If I am self-reliant, then I will be less vulnerable to others who could undermine my success") anchored constraining self-narratives; a connecting script ("If I am open, then I will be more connected to others, and this will aid my success") anchored connecting ones.
- Constraining self-narratives led executives to construct deprived relational realities and to experience persistent, painful loneliness, which they rendered tolerable through self-isolating behavior, rhetorical justification (storying loneliness as the price of success), and relational compensation in nonwork relationships.
- Continuity-breaking change began when accumulated distress, often catalyzed by a precipitating work event, pushed informants across an emotional threshold past which loneliness became intolerable. This triggered a self-referential insight that their loneliness was partly self-constructed (an agentic construction), which drove experimentation with connecting relational actions.
- Insight was necessary but not sufficient: some informants who reached the threshold and had the insight could not act, held back by strong fear of others' reactions, and remained at a painful impasse; others oscillated between the competing scripts, and a subset described themselves as still stuck in that oscillation.
- For those who changed, the connecting script developed in parallel to, competed with, and eventually replaced the constraining one as the central theme; informants then updated their other stories of self and reconstructed enriched relational realities, and their loneliness shifted from persistent and painful to short-lived and unpleasant — even though little in their work environment had changed.
- Theoretically, the study surfaces that relational scripts change not through gradual revision of an existing script but through the parallel development, competition, and replacement of an alternative script.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a theory of continuity-breaking self-narrative change that complements existing work on narrative continuity by showing how people create disjunctions between past and present selves. It contributes to research on work loneliness by theorizing loneliness as partly an agentic construction in which people psychologically invest, and shifts the field's perspective from a static phenomenon to a dynamic process. It expands attachment theory by mapping how relational scripts — the cognitive elements of attachment systems — change through parallel development, competition, and replacement rather than gradual revision, and it advances a contextualized view of relational scripts as domain-specific (e.g., to work) rather than only global or relationship-specific.
practical_implication: Workplace interventions that focus solely on the work environment are unlikely to be sufficient to combat the loneliness epidemic. Organizations should pair opportunities to connect with interventions that help workers question their assumptions about who they need to be and how they need to act in relation to others at work, and create opportunities for self-reflection. Senior executives, in particular, should recognize that the bargains they have made between self-reliance and success can produce persistent loneliness, and that humanizing oneself at work can paradoxically aid leadership effectiveness.
limitations: The findings are drawn from an elite sample of executives recruited from an international business school's alumni population, raising questions about generalizability to non-executives or to workers with job (rather than career) orientations. The method is purposefully subjective and relies on narrative causality, so it cannot establish that the changes described actually occurred objectively as informants recounted them. Data were collected at a single point in time rather than longitudinally, although the authors mitigate this by sampling informants at different stages of the process.
future_research: Future studies could investigate cultural and collective dynamics of continuity-breaking self-narrative change — for example, whether senior executives' updated self-narratives diffuse to surrounding workers, paralleling contagion effects in loneliness. Researchers could examine self-narrative change among workers at different career stages, compare workers with different orientations to work, and explore how loneliness in one life domain affects relational behavior in others. Scholars are also encouraged to examine threshold-crossing levels of other social emotions (anger, shame, envy) as triggers of self-narrative change, and to investigate interindividual variance in whether and when people cross such thresholds.
abstract: Through an inductive study of executives reporting persistent loneliness at work, we examine how problematic work experiences can be rooted in the self through narratives, and the process by which they can be uprooted. In the case of loneliness, we found that relational scripts formed the central theme of executives' self-narratives, which informed how they acted and felt at work. Some executives drew on constraining scripts that portrayed self-isolating behavior as necessary for success. This led them to construct a deprived relational reality that rendered loneliness a persistent feature of their working selves. Our study reveals the process through which people changed this constraining self-narrative. For the executives we studied, it began when people crossed an emotional threshold, past which loneliness became intolerable. This prompted the insight that loneliness was partially an agentic construction, and drove experimentation with connecting scripts that, over time, replaced the constraining ones. As this occurred, people made deliberate efforts to construct more relationally enriching work realities and updated their other stories of self. Building on these findings, we develop a theory of continuity-breaking self-narrative change that reveals how people can create disjunctions between past and present selves.

title: The Moral Case Revisited: Moral Framing as a Double-Edged Sword for Motivating Majority Group Leaders to Support DEI
methods: Multi-study experimental package combining a critical-incident recall study with random assignment (Study 1, n=581 full-time leaders on Prolific), a field experiment within a single firm's annual engagement survey using a three-condition (control, economic, moral) between-subjects design (Study 2, n=782), and a preregistered 2 (issue-selling frame: economic vs. moral) x 2 (problem-solving autonomy: low vs. high) between-subjects online experiment with White U.S. leaders (Study 3, n=821). Six supplementary studies on OSF cover scale validation, gender-equity replication, alternative mechanisms, and de-moralization vs. moralization comparisons. Hypotheses tested via two-way ANOVA, simple-effects tests, and Hayes (2022) PROCESS macro Models 4 and 7 for moderated mediation with 5,000 bootstrapped samples; psychological standing and psychological reactance modeled as simultaneous mediators.
industry: Cross-industry full-time managerial leaders for Studies 1 and 3 (Prolific panels); Study 2 conducted within a single power-tools and specialty-construction-materials supplier (~9,000 employees, ~$3.4B revenue) headquartered in the southeastern United States
country: United States (Studies 2 and 3); United States or United Kingdom (Study 1)
time_period: Not reported in paper for exact data-collection dates; Study 2 used the firm's annual engagement survey with manipulations informed by 2022 prior-year survey comments
units: Individual leaders (full-time managers, including lower-, middle-, and senior-level managers); Study 2 includes 645 lower-level, 116 middle-level, and 21 senior-level managers
n_sample: Study 1 n=581 (60% White, 66% male); Study 2 n=782 business leaders (~65% White, ~72% male); Study 3 n=821 White U.S. leaders; supplementary studies range from 201 to 486 leaders
authors: Preston, McKenzie C.
theories: focus theory of normative conduct; issue selling theory; moral framing theory; psychological reactance theory
keywords: DEI; diversity equity and inclusion; gender equity; issue selling; majority group leaders; moral framing; moral framing double-edged sword; problem-solving autonomy; psychological reactance; psychological standing; racial equity
research_question: When and why is employees' moral framing of DEI issues effective at motivating majority group leaders (e.g., White or male leaders) to support DEI initiatives, and how can issue sellers reconcile moral framing's competing effects on these leaders' psychological standing and psychological reactance?
hypotheses:
H1: Moral framing for DEI issues (vs. control and economic framing) is positively associated with majority group leaders' psychological standing.
H2: Moral framing (vs. control and economic framing) has a positive indirect effect on majority group leaders' DEI issue support through psychological standing.
H3: Moral framing (vs. control and economic framing) is positively associated with majority group leaders' psychological reactance.
H4: Moral framing (vs. control and economic framing) has a negative indirect effect on majority group leaders' DEI issue support through psychological reactance.
H5: When issue sellers highlight majority group leaders' problem-solving autonomy for how to address a DEI issue, moral framing has a stronger positive indirect effect on issue support through psychological standing.
H6: When issue sellers highlight majority group leaders' problem-solving autonomy for how to address a DEI issue, moral framing has a weaker negative indirect effect on issue support through psychological reactance.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the focus theory of normative conduct, the paper theorizes moral framing as an interpersonal normative cue that simultaneously conveys social approval (legitimizing leaders' engagement) and prescriptive expectation (an obligation to act). Approval focus elevates psychological standing — particularly for majority group leaders, who otherwise lack identity-based stakes — and increases DEI support. Obligation focus elevates psychological reactance, especially for majority group leaders who feel implicated by historical injustices, reducing support. Highlighting leaders' problem-solving autonomy cognitively reframes moral appeals from "I should" to "I could," amplifying the standing pathway and dampening the reactance pathway, and producing a positive overall effect of moral framing on DEI support.
data_measures: Three main between-subjects experiments plus six OSF supplementary studies. Study 1 (recall, n=581 full-time leaders on Prolific) randomly assigned a moral vs. economic recall frame; Study 2 (field experiment, n=782) embedded a three-condition (control/economic/moral) design in a firm's annual engagement survey; Study 3 (preregistered online experiment, n=821 White leaders on Prolific) crossed issue frame (economic vs. moral) with problem-solving autonomy (low vs. high). Mediators: psychological standing (three items adapted from Sherf et al., 2017) and psychological reactance (three items adapted from Hong & Page, 1989), on 5-point scales. Dependent variable, leader DEI issue support: Hussain et al. (2023) three-item issue-support and five-item voice-endorsement scales (Study 1); a behavioral DEI-engagement index of willingness to volunteer for a racial-equity task force, mentoring, and attending a college recruiting event to attract more racial-minority employees (Study 2); and budget-allocation ($20,000 across four items) and time-allocation (30 minutes across four issues) behavioral intentions plus the three-item support scale (Study 3). Moderators: leader race (White = 1, racial minority = 0; Studies 1-2) and highlighted problem-solving autonomy (Study 3). Moral-frame and autonomy manipulations were checked with Mayer et al. (2019) and a one-item discretion measure. Hypotheses tested with two-way ANOVA, simple-effects tests, and Hayes (2022) PROCESS Models 4 and 7 (5,000 bootstrap samples) with standing and reactance as simultaneous mediators; random assignment supports causal inference, though mediators and dependent variables were measured concurrently from the same source.
key_findings:
Study 1 (recall, n=581): supported H1-H4 for majority (White) leaders but not for racial-minority leaders. Moral (vs. economic) framing raised White leaders' psychological standing (F(1,577)=20.49, p<.001, H1) and psychological reactance (F(1,577)=52.34, p<.001, H3); the indirect effect on issue support was positive via standing (b=0.22, 95% CI [0.12, 0.32], H2) and negative via reactance (b=-0.13, 95% CI [-0.21, -0.06], H4), with both moderated-mediation indices significant.
Study 2 (field experiment, n=782): supported H1-H4 for White leaders — moral framing (vs. control and economic) raised both standing and reactance, and the positive (standing) and negative (reactance) indirect effects on issue support and behavioral DEI engagement were stronger for White than racial-minority leaders.
Study 3 (online experiment, n=821 White leaders): the standing pathway was null — H1 not supported (p=.134) and H2's standing-mediated indirect effect nonsignificant — which the author attributes to the vignette design; the reactance pathway held — the moral-vs-economic reactance contrast was significant (p=.002, H3) and H4's negative reactance-mediated indirect effect was significant (though the Study 3 discussion characterizes the standing main effects as yielding null results for both H1 and H3). H5 and H6 were supported across all three issue-support measures: highlighting problem-solving autonomy strengthened the standing pathway and weakened the reactance pathway, shifting moral framing's total effect on issue support from significantly negative (autonomy not highlighted) to significantly positive (autonomy highlighted).
Supplementary studies (Table 8, six studies): support was heterogeneous across DEI subdomains and robustness checks — a gender-equity recall study supported only the reactance pathway while a gender-equity vignette supported both pathways; a de-moralization vignette showed partial standing-pathway and full reactance-pathway support; a moral-vs-economic comparison found no significant interaction; and two alternative-mechanism studies found no significant effects of moral framing on the tested alternatives.
theoretical_contribution: The paper complicates the prevailing view that moralizing DEI issues uniformly empowers leaders, recasting moral framing as a double-edged sword whose net effect on majority group leaders depends on whether their attention is directed to social approval or prescriptive obligation. It introduces a dual-pathway psychological model — psychological standing (granting moral license) and psychological reactance (imposing moral obligation) — to explain when moral appeals galvanize versus alienate majority group leaders, and it advances the issue-selling literature by introducing "highlighting problem-solving autonomy" as a novel persuasion tactic that converts moral framing's liability into an asset.
practical_implication: For majority group leaders, the findings underscore the value of recognizing one's psychological reactions to moral appeals and actively reframing them around problem-solving autonomy and shared responsibility rather than coercion. For issue sellers (employees, students, activists), moral framing should be paired with explicit emphasis on the leader's discretion to design and select DEI solutions; over-prescriptive moral demands ("you should adopt initiative X") risk triggering reactance and reducing support, while presenting a menu of viable initiatives sustains both legitimacy and behavioral freedom. The author also illustrates the implication for university leaders facing student activism on contested issues (e.g., racial justice, geopolitical conflicts).
limitations: Mediator and dependent-variable data were collected at the same time from the same source, raising common-method concerns; the author calls for designs that manipulate mediators or use multi-source data. The studies offer limited examination of issue-seller demographic and status characteristics (e.g., organizational status, tenure, position) beyond race and gender. Study 3's vignette-based design produced weaker effects on psychological standing than the real-employee-communication contexts of Studies 1 and 2, yielding null results on H1 and H2 in Study 3 (H2 receives only partial support across the full set of studies). The supplementary studies on gender equity show only partial replication of the standing pathway, suggesting boundary conditions across DEI subdomains.
future_research: Future work could investigate how moral characteristics (e.g., moral awareness) shape majority group leaders' susceptibility to moral framing, and whether moral framing translates into effective — not just declared — DEI advocacy. Researchers could examine how distinct moral values (fairness vs. harm) channel leaders toward "non-discrimination" initiatives like bias training versus "resource" initiatives like targeted recruiting. Additional avenues include retaliatory responses toward moral issue sellers, the welfare consequences of leaders' choices among autonomy-granted initiatives, and contextual factors that shape whether moral and economic frames interact rather than substitute.
abstract: Employees’ use of moral frames to sell the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives is gaining popularity over business-case frames. Yet, it remains unclear when and why moral framing is effective at motivating majority group leaders (e.g., White, male leaders) to support DEI initiatives. Drawing on the focus theory of normative conduct, I argue that employees’ use of moral frames can be a double-edged sword for motivating majority group leaders to support DEI initiatives. On the one hand, moral framing can heighten majority group leaders’ psychological standing, thereby increasing their support for DEI initiatives. On the other hand, moral framing can trigger psychological reactance for majority group leaders, thereby reducing their support for DEI initiatives. To reconcile these competing pathways, I argue that, when employees emphasize majority group leaders’ problem-solving autonomy concerning how to address DEI issues, moral framing has a stronger effect on psychological standing and a weaker effect on psychological reactance, thus enhancing majority group leaders’ overall support for DEI initiatives. I find support for these predictions across several studies that cover racial and gender equity issues, and discuss theoretical and practical implications.

title: The Gendered Complexity of Sponsorship: How Male and Female Sponsors’ Goals Shape Their Social Network Strategies
methods: Four studies combining survey and experimental data from U.S. online panels (CloudResearch; Prolific). Studies 1a/1b: vignette surveys with independent-samples t-tests and ANOVA on number of goals, plus quantitative content-coding of open-ended goal statements (Study 1b preregistered). Study 2 (preregistered): survey with rating/ranking measures analyzed via ANOVA and Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney tests. Study 3: 2 (participant gender) x 3 (goal condition: control, single protege-centric, dual protege-/sponsor-centric) between-subjects randomized experiment with cognitive network activation (network density) as the outcome, analyzed via ANOVA.
industry: Working adults across a range of industries recruited via online panels; sponsorship vignettes set in investment banking (Studies 1a-1b), with work context unspecified in Study 3
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals (full-time employees / managers reporting experience providing sponsorship)
n_sample: Study 1a: 215; Study 1b: 619; Study 2: 307; Study 3: 591 (four online-panel samples)
authors: Campbell, E. L.; Shea, C. T.
theories: cognitive network activation (Krackhardt, 1987; Smith et al., 2012); gendered expectations / communality-agency and role congruity (Abele, 2003; Eagly & Karau, 2002); goal systems theory (Kruglanski, Fishbach, & Köpetz, 2023; Kruglanski et al., 2002); goal-setting / goal pursuit (Locke & Latham, 1990; Latham & Locke, 2007); social capital theory (Bourdieu & Wacquant, 1992; Burt, 1992)
keywords: cognitive network activation; gender differences; goal complexity; network closure; social capital; sponsorship
research_question: How do male and female sponsors’ goals differ in complexity, and how do those goal differences shape the social networks they cognitively activate when deciding whether and how to provide sponsorship (mobilizing social capital on a protege’s behalf)?
hypotheses:
The paper uses an abductive design and states no formally numbered hypotheses; it advances the following theorized predictions (summarized in Figure 1, its theoretical model):
- Male sponsors experience lower goal complexity than female sponsors — pursuing fewer goals, more focused on benefiting themselves (sponsor-centric), and therefore experiencing less goal conflict.
- Female sponsors, constrained by gendered expectations about communality, experience greater goal complexity — pursuing more (and more conflicting) goals that balance the needs of multiple constituencies (protege-centric and sponsor-centric).
- These goal differences shape cognitive network activation: when balancing protege-centric and sponsor-centric goals, female sponsors activate networks higher in closure (higher density), whereas male sponsors, focused on a sponsor-centric self-advancement goal, activate sparse, low-density networks.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on goal systems theory and work on social capital and cognitive network activation, the authors argue that because women face gendered expectations to be communal and other-oriented, female sponsors set more numerous and more conflicting goals (balancing their own and their proteges’ interests), whereas men, held to agentic expectations, set fewer, more self-beneficial goals. Greater goal complexity leads women — when goals conflict — to cognitively activate denser, higher-closure networks (which offer cooperation, social support, and lower-risk mobilization), while men activate sparse, information-rich networks that serve their own advancement regardless of goals. Because gender is measured rather than manipulated, the gender-to-goals link is associational; Study 3 supplies the experimental link from goals to network activation.
data_measures:
- Data: Four online-panel samples of U.S. full-time employees / managers reporting experience providing sponsorship (Studies 1a and 3 via CloudResearch; Studies 1b and 2 via Prolific), using vignette/scenario surveys and, in Study 3, a randomized experiment; all materials and data are posted on OSF.
- Number of Goals: participants list goals in an open-ended box and self-count them; a research assistant independently recounted goals blind to gender (IRR = .964).
- Goal content (Study 1b): a research assistant blind to condition content-coded each goal statement on warmth, other-orientation, dominance, competence, self-benefit, and mentorship mentions (0 = not at all, 1 = a little, 2 = a lot), then averaged per participant.
- Perceived opportunity (Study 2): ratings (1-5) and rankings of six items forming sponsor-, protege-, and firm-focused composites (alpha = .885 / .819 / .724); prior sponsorship experience on a 1-5 scale.
- Network activation (Study 3): a name generator (up to 10 real contacts); Network Density (closure) computed from pairwise tie strength among named contacts; Percent Women and Network Homophily.
- Identification: Studies 1a-2 are associational gender comparisons (t-tests, ANOVA, Mann-Whitney). Study 3 randomly assigns goal conditions, so the goals-to-network-activation link is experimentally identified; sponsor gender is a measured attribute, not manipulated.
key_findings:
Across four studies, men approached sponsorship with lower goal complexity than women, but the support pattern differs by study and several theorized effects were null or only marginal.
- Study 1a (n = 215): Women reported significantly more goals than men (M = 3.130 vs. 2.460; t(213) = -2.446, p = .015, d = .334). No gender difference in goal specificity (p = .888) or word count (p = .471); women spent more time on the task (p = .035).
- Study 1b (n = 619, preregistered): The gender effect on number of goals was only marginal — women reported more goals than men (M = 2.576 vs. 2.399; F(1,613) = 3.23, p = .073). A marginal protege-gender main effect emerged (p = .053), but the protege-gender x participant-gender interaction was non-significant (p = .337). Exploratory content coding found no gender differences in warmth, other-orientation, dominance, competence, or mentorship mentions (all p > .50); the only significant content difference was self-benefit, with men’s goals rated higher on self-benefit than women’s (M = 0.321 vs. 0.219; t(616) = 2.263, p = .024, d = .182) — i.e., women’s goals were rated as focusing less on benefiting themselves.
- Study 2 (n = 307, preregistered): Men were more likely than women to perceive sponsorship as an opportunity to benefit themselves (F(1,305) = 4.34, p = .038; M = 2.961 vs. 2.681), while women were more likely to perceive it as an opportunity to benefit proteges (F(1,305) = 8.52, p = .004; M = 4.645 vs. 4.426); there was no gender difference for firm benefit (p = .249). Rankings concurred (own advancement ranked higher by men, Z = -2.35, p = .019; protege advancement ranked marginally higher by women, Z = -1.87, p = .061). Men’s self-benefit perception rose with sponsorship experience (slope = .238, p = .008) but women’s did not (p = .387).
- Study 3 (n = 591, experiment): A significant participant-gender x goal-condition interaction on network density emerged (F(1,585) = 4.268, p = .014). Women activated denser (higher-closure) networks than men only in the dual-goal condition (M = 0.771 vs. 0.615, p = .013); densities did not differ by gender in the control (0.710 vs. 0.691) or single-goal (0.664 vs. 0.670) conditions. Within women, the dual-goal condition was denser than the single-goal condition (p = .028); men showed no differences across conditions (p = .101), activating sparse networks regardless of goals. Men also activated more gender-homophilous networks (M = 0.713 vs. 0.545, p < .001) and networks with a far smaller share of women (M = 0.014 vs. 0.545, p < .001). The authors flag the null gender difference in the control condition as unexpected.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances a sponsor-centric (rather than protege-centric) account of sponsorship, disentangling it from mentorship by treating social capital as the unique resource sponsors expend, and identifies sponsors’ goals / goal complexity as a microlevel cognitive mechanism that links gender to how sponsors mobilize their networks. It establishes a novel connection between goal pursuit and cognitive network activation in sponsorship, showing gender differentiates how individuals interact with their social capital. It also refines the gender-and-work literature by showing gendered patterns are nuanced: men’s goals are more self-beneficial but do not differ on broader communality/agency dimensions (warmth, other-orientation, dominance, competence), challenging the notion that gendered expectations exert uniform pressure on behavior.
practical_implication: Within its own stated managerial and organizational implications, the paper cautions against broad calls for all leaders to simply provide more sponsorship: doing so may lead male leaders (but not female leaders) to sponsor with their own needs in mind, potentially producing inequities in who benefits from providing sponsorship. To support equitable sponsorship, firms could design goal-based interventions and make sponsorship’s purpose explicit — articulating the goals of sponsorship and differentiating them from the goals of mentorship — to give leaders clearer cognitive guidance.
limitations: Focusing exclusively on the sponsor’s perspective is both a strength and a limitation. The studies examine goal pursuit and network activation only after a high-quality protege has been selected, leaving possible sponsor-gender differences in protege selection unexamined. The reliance on online-panel survey and experimental designs risks lower external validity and generalizability, which the authors offset by sampling working supervisors with sponsorship experience and by using cognitive activation of real network contacts. The work also isolates cognitive processes under the sponsor’s control rather than actual network mobilization or downstream sponsor effectiveness.
future_research: The authors call for research on how other sponsor and protege characteristics intersect to shape sponsors’ goals and strategies (e.g., race and ethnicity, disability status); on gender differences in protege selection and in actual network mobilization (not just cognitive activation); on how specific occupational and organizational norms and cultures shape sponsors’ decision-making; on how the configurations of sponsors’ cognitively activated networks affect their effectiveness as sponsors (an open empirical question); and on sponsors’ decision-making using alternative methods, including whether these gendered tendencies are intentional or occur through more unconscious processes.
abstract: Providing sponsorship, when senior colleagues (sponsors) mobilize resources in their social network on junior colleagues’ (prot eg es) behalf, is consequential to the effective functioning of organizations. Yet, the psychological processes underlying male and female sponsors’ goals, priorities, and strategies for activating resources in their networks for proteges are not well understood. We conduct four studies to examine male and female sponsors’ goals and the resulting impact on their approach to activating resources in their social network. Studies 1a and 1b provide converging, initial evidence that men approach sponsorship with less complexity than women, by setting fewer goals that focus more on benefiting themselves. Study 2 provides additional evidence: male sponsors are more likely than female sponsors to perceive sponsorship as an opportunity to benefit themselves while female sponsors perceive sponsorship as an opportunity to benefit their proteges. Study 3 experimentally links the differences in goal pursuit to sponsors’ social network strategies: when asked to balance prot eg e-centric and sponsorcentric goals, women cognitively activate networks higher in closure, but men activate sparse networks regardless of their goals. The implications of these network activation configurations for understanding the sponsorship process are discussed.

title: Catalyzing Categories: Category Contrast and the Creation of Groundbreaking Inventions
methods: Observational panel analysis of USPTO utility patents (1975-2013); OLS regressions with focal-patent and year fixed effects; matching estimators; instrumental-variable regressions using retroactive USPTO reclassification orders as exogenous variation in category contrast.
industry: Utility patents across all USPTO technology classes (all technological sectors)
units: Utility patents (focal inventions), analyzed as patent-year observations
n_sample: 3,127,467 patents
authors: Carnabuci, G.; Kovács, B.
theories: category contrast theory (Carnabuci, Operti & Kovacs, 2015); recombinant innovation / knowledge recombination (Fleming, 2001); sociology of categories (Hannan et al., 2019)
keywords: catalyzing categories; category contrast; groundbreaking inventions; idea-creation; idea-positioning
research_question: Where do groundbreaking inventions come from? Specifically, how does the categorical structure of an institutionalized classification system — in particular, the category contrast of the patent class in which an invention is classified — shape whether that invention has a groundbreaking (path-creating) rather than consolidating (path-reinforcing) technological impact?
hypotheses:
Central hypothesis: The lower the contrast of the category in which an invention is classified, the more groundbreaking its impact — holding invention characteristics and other factors constant, an invention is more likely to spur descendant inventions that break away from its technological predecessors as the contrast of its category decreases.
Idea-creation mechanism prediction: Inventions classified in low-contrast categories generate descendant inventions that exhibit greater (a) boundary spanning, (b) novelty, (c) originality, and (d) atypical combinations.
Idea-positioning mechanism prediction: When a focal invention is classified in a low-contrast category, patent examiners afford its descendants greater leeway to frame their claims and patent text as novel, distinctive, and broad — departing from, rather than consolidating, the focal invention’s lineage.
mechanism_summary: Low-contrast categories comprise more heterogeneous knowledge and offer more ambiguous evaluation criteria. Through idea-creation, building on an invention classified in a low-contrast category leads descendant inventions to combine it with more novel, atypical, original, and boundary-spanning knowledge inputs, opening technological paths that diverge from the status quo. Through idea-positioning, the ambiguity of low-contrast categories gives applicants and their attorneys greater latitude during the patent examination negotiation to frame descendants as distinctive departures rather than consolidations, so the codified patent text emphasizes novelty, uniqueness, and breadth. Both pathways raise the likelihood that a focal invention spurs groundbreaking technological trajectories.
data_measures:
Data: USPTO utility patents granted 1975–2013 (drawn from PatentsView), excluding patents reclassified during the observation window; final sample of 3,127,467 focal patents.
Dependent variable: Consolidation–disruption (CD) index (Funk & Owen-Smith, 2017), the proportion of overlap between a descendant’s and the focal patent’s backward citations, computed yearly using 1-, 3-, and 5-year windows and ranging from −1 (maximally consolidating) to +1 (maximally groundbreaking).
Independent variable: Category (patent-class) contrast (Carnabuci, Operti & Kovács, 2015), derived from the share of a class’s patents that are cross-classified into other primary classes, with exponential discounting (parameter 0.9).
Mechanism variables: Boundary spanning, Novelty, Originality, and Combination atypicality of descendants (idea-creation); changes in independent-claim word counts and claim number, and text similarity to closest patents (Arts et al., 2018), plus descendant classification patterns (idea-positioning).
Controls: Class size, technological fertility, average age of cited patents, count of descendants’ backward citations, and focal patent’s inventor productivity, with year and focal-patent fixed effects.
Identification: Patent and year fixed effects, matching estimators, and an instrumental-variable regression using retroactive USPTO reclassification orders (1999–2013) as exogenous variation in contrast (instrument passes Stock–Yogo, Kleibergen–Paap, and Anderson–Rubin tests). The design is observational; the IV provides the causal test. Implication measures use patent economic value from stock-price reactions (Kogan et al., 2017), citation lag, and next-generation CD.
key_findings: The central hypothesis is robustly supported: category contrast is negatively related to the CD index across all three windows (Contrast ≈ −0.047 [CD1], −0.052 [CD3], −0.059 [CD5] with patent fixed effects; ≈ −0.031 / −0.031 / −0.032 with matched-strata fixed effects), so lower contrast means more groundbreaking impact; the effect strengthens over longer windows, and a one-standard-deviation increase in contrast reduces CD by about 1.1% of its standard deviation. The idea-creation mechanism is supported (Table 4): lower contrast yields descendants with greater boundary spanning (−0.061), novelty (−0.006), originality (−0.074), and atypical combinations (−0.013), all significant. The idea-positioning mechanism receives only partial support in the claims-change test (Table 5): higher contrast lengthens (narrows) descendant claims for the shortest independent claim (+11.389) and the average claim word count (+11.455), both significant, but the change in the number of independent claims is not significant (0.035, ns) — the authors explicitly label this "partial support." Remaining idea-positioning tests are supported: higher contrast increases text similarity to closest patents (Table 6: +0.025 full, +0.035 matched) and makes descendants more likely to stay in the focal patent’s class, remain in its prior-art class, and cite its prior art (Table 7, all six models). The instrumental-variable regression supports causal interpretation (Table 8): exogenous increases in contrast significantly reduce groundbreaking impact (second-stage Contrast on CD = −0.213). Results are robust across contrast quintiles (a monotonic effect that flattens at high contrast), alternative contrast measures, pre-/post-AIPA subsamples, extreme-value exclusions, logit specifications for the most groundbreaking patents, and class-year aggregation / GLS. On material consequences, low-contrast categories spur descendants with higher economic value (Table 10: Contrast = −$15.349M; a one-SD contrast increase corresponds to roughly $1.4M lower average descendant value) and greater value dispersion (a one-SD contrast increase lowers the probability of a very-high-value descendant by 24.6% and of a very-low-value one by 5.6%), longer-lasting impact (citation lag rises as contrast falls), and more groundbreaking next-generation descendants (Table 9: −0.007).
theoretical_contribution: The paper offers a novel theoretical perspective on the genesis of groundbreaking inventions: an invention’s impact depends not only on its content but on how it is categorized, with low-contrast "catalyzing categories" fostering breakthroughs through idea-creation and idea-positioning. It also contributes to the sociology of categories literature by showing that low-contrast (fuzzy) categories — usually viewed as inefficient and disadvantageous for information search — can catalyze groundbreaking inventions, challenging the prevailing view that classification in high-contrast categories is always more beneficial.
practical_implication: For the design of institutionalized classification schemes such as patent systems, the study surfaces a tension in the paper’s own terms: maximizing category contrast improves information-search efficiency but may reduce the collective capacity to generate groundbreaking inventions. Digitized classification schemes that maintain crisp categorical boundaries could, in doing so, diminish disruptive innovation.
limitations: As with all observational research, isolating the theorized mechanisms is challenging: the authors lack direct data on inventors’ search behavior and must rely on proxies for idea-positioning, and the main outcome (the CD index) is an indirect, though widely validated, measure. They cannot compare the relative magnitude of the idea-creation and idea-positioning channels, endogeneity remains a concern because inventions cannot be randomly assigned to categories, and the empirical test is limited to patent data, which have known limitations and biases.
future_research: The authors call for measuring the mechanisms more directly through interviews, experiments, or case studies; testing the argument in other domains (e.g., how academic classification into disciplines shapes groundbreaking science); examining whether inventions can simultaneously consolidate and break ground across different technology streams and how category contrast affects different groups of inventors (e.g., "outsiders"); exploring how technological cycles drive shifts in contrast; and pursuing the intellectual-property-strategy questions the study raises about whether low- versus high-contrast categories favor strategically broadening patent scope or the activity of patent assertion entities.
abstract: We hypothesize that “low-contrast categories” (those lacking sharp differentiation from adjacent categories) catalyze the creation of groundbreaking inventions by influencing two key stages in the life of an invention: (1) idea-creation and (2) idea-positioning. During “idea-creation,” low-contrast categories increase the likelihood that descendant inventions will combine the focal invention with more (a) boundary-spanning, (b) novel, (c) original, and (d) atypical knowledge inputs. During “idea-positioning,” they allow greater leeway in articulating how descendant inventions depart from the focal invention’s lineage and chart new technological directions. We find robust support for our hypothesis using data from the United States Patent and Trademark Office’s classification system spanning nearly four decades. Further analyses demonstrate that the catalyzing effect of low-contrast categories has important material consequences: inventions classified in low-contrast categories spur descendant inventions that generate substantially higher economic value and exert more enduring technological impact than those in high-contrast categories. By introducing the concept of catalyzing categories, this study offers a novel theoretical perspective on the genesis of groundbreaking inventions and the role of categorical structures in the inventive process.

title: Cross-Sector Relational Realignments after an Institutional Crisis: Checking the Instrumentalization of Corporate-Nonprofit Partnerships
methods: Multilevel mixed-effects (MLM) logit panel regression with random effects for nonprofit type and firm fixed effects; robust standard errors clustered by nonprofit type. Eight-year (2010-2017) firm-nonprofit dyadic panel of Brazilian publicly listed firms and registered nonprofits, with partnerships coded from annual reports via Python NLP; associational before/after (Operation Carwash) design (difference-in-differences deemed unsuitable). 54 semi-structured interviews illustrate the mechanisms.
industry: Publicly listed nonfinancial firms across 20 industries and registered nonprofits of all social missions
time_period: 2010-2017 (four years before and after Operation Carwash, 2014)
units: Firm-nonprofit dyad-years
n_sample: 10,488,578 dyad-year observations (approx. 440 firms per year; 820,000 registered nonprofits; 6,067 nonprofits cited in annual reports)
authors: Gama, M. A. B.; Gatignon, A.
theories: institutional change; nonmarket strategy; organizational legitimacy; stakeholder management
keywords: corporate political influence; corporate-nonprofit partnerships; government corruption scandals; institutional crisis; instrumentalization; nonmarket strategy; nonprofit legitimacy
research_question: How do revelations of government corruption scandals influence corporate-nonprofit partnerships by altering the institutional context and shifting the benefits and risks for both parties?
hypotheses:
H1. A corporate-nonprofit partnership is more likely to emerge after the disclosure of a government corruption scandal.
H2. The positive effect of a government corruption scandal on the likelihood of a corporate-nonprofit partnership is weaker if the firm is directly (H2a) or indirectly (H2b) tainted by the scandal.
H3. The positive effect of a government corruption scandal on the likelihood of a corporate-nonprofit partnership is weaker for trade associations (H3a) and education and research (E&R) nonprofits (H3b) relative to other nonprofit missions.
H4. The positive effect of a government corruption scandal on the likelihood of a corporate-nonprofit partnership is weaker when the nonprofit has more political capital.
mechanism_summary: A highly mediatized government corruption scandal erodes institutionalized trust in government and shifts perceived value toward nonprofits, raising the joint benefits of socioeconomic-development partnerships and making partnerships more likely overall. The same crisis, however, heightens legitimacy risks: nonprofits avoid firms tainted directly or indirectly (state ownership, politically connected boards) to protect their own legitimacy, and the nonprofits most exposed to accusations of enabling corporate political influence — trade associations, E&R nonprofits, and those with more political capital — become especially cautious, "checking" their own instrumentalization to preserve the appearance of disinterested public service.
data_measures: Setting/design: an eight-year (2010-2017) firm-nonprofit dyadic panel spanning four years before and after Operation Carwash (2014) in Brazil. DV: corporate-nonprofit partnership, coded 1/0 from firms' annual reports (and available corporate-foundation reports) using Python NLP over 3,524 corporate and 252 foundation reports; the candidate nonprofit set (6,067 nonprofits) was cross-checked against the IPEA database of ~820,000 registered nonprofits. IV: Post (2014-2017 = 1). Moderators: tainted directly (dummy for the eight directly implicated firms); SOE (>49.9% government ownership); political board ties (count of political positions from 39,452 board-member résumés); trade association and E&R nonprofit (IBGE classifications); nonprofit political capital (count of positive nonprofit-government ties extracted from 324,150 Factiva articles via Python NLP and a 60% LIWC cutoff). Firm-, nonprofit-, and dyad-level controls (fines, compliance communication/department, campaign and municipal donations, ROA, market-to-book, leverage, size, nonprofit board ties, government resources, geographic scope, collaborative experience, established relationship). Estimation: multilevel mixed-effects (MLM) logit panel regression with random effects for nonprofit type and firm fixed effects, robust standard errors clustered by nonprofit type, across 10,488,578 dyad-year observations. The design is associational (Operation Carwash affected all firms, leaving no clean control group, so difference-in-differences was rejected); 54 semi-structured interviews illustrate the mechanisms.
key_findings: H1 is supported: the post-Operation Carwash period positively predicts partnership formation (b = 3.57, p < .001; margins ≈ +2.32%, roughly 246 additional partnerships). H2 is partially supported. H2a is supported: being directly tainted weakens the effect (tainted-directly × post b = -0.36, p < .01; ≈ 44.05% less likely, 51 fewer partnerships for the eight implicated firms). H2b is only partially supported, depending on the indirect-taint measure: state ownership weakens the effect (SOE × post b = -0.38, p < .001; ≈ 0.7% less likely, 14 fewer partnerships for the 21 SOEs), but political board ties × post is only b = -0.001, p < .1, which the authors state does not support the hypothesis. H3 is supported: the effect is weaker for trade associations (H3a: b = -0.55, p < .001; ≈ 19 fewer partnerships) and for E&R nonprofits (H3b: b = -0.45, p < .001; ≈ 8 fewer partnerships). H4 is supported: more nonprofit political capital weakens the effect (b = -1.22, p < .001; ≈ 14 fewer partnerships). Results hold across numerous robustness tests (alternative partnership coding, continuous scandal-intensity measures, alternative fixed-effects and estimation specifications, and sample restrictions).
theoretical_contribution: The study advances a more dynamic view of nonmarket strategy and stakeholder management by showing that an institutional crisis triggers a realignment of firms' partnerships across nonmarket sectors — political and nonprofit arenas jointly, not just within each — so cross-sector ties must be theorized together. It "checks" the instrumentalization of corporate-nonprofit partnerships, revealing the limits of leveraging nonprofits for reputational repair or political influence (even for firms not directly implicated) and showing how nonprofits actively resist co-optation to protect their legitimacy. It integrates corporate political activity with corporate social responsibility and specifies the institutional and organizational contingencies (taint, sector proximity to firms or the state, political capital) that determine when using nonprofits for political influence backfires.
practical_implication: The findings can help firms and nonprofits adapt more quickly — or act more proactively and intentionally — in crafting partnership strategies when such scandals occur, and help managers better understand the benefits and risks of nonmarket ties from different perspectives. They can also support policymakers and society in recognizing the sometimes opaque implications of firms' relationships with the nonprofit sector for government and public trust.
limitations: The design observes only partnerships that could have formed (realized and counterfactual dyads), not whether a firm or nonprofit declined a potential partnership or the reasons for doing so, and it cannot directly observe which combinations of firm and nonprofit characteristics drove collaboration; identifying explicit empirical measures of the potential benefits and risks to both parties, and how these jointly evolve after a scandal, is untenable. In addition, the scale of Operation Carwash — implicating an unusually broad set of high-profile politicians and businesspeople — is rare, which limits generalizability.
future_research: The authors call for a configurational approach to extend the theory; tests of generalizability to other, likely smaller-scale, corruption scandals and to other institutional changes that introduce political uncertainty and devalue corporate political ties (e.g., Taiwan's Sunflower Movement); and cross-country analyses as anti-government and anti-corporate sentiments rise globally. They also point to examining the longer-term sustainability of the observed effects (whether they persist if attitudes swing back toward indifference about corporate political influence) and how results might change if nonprofits themselves faced government opposition or allegations of financial misconduct.
abstract: We examine how government corruption scandals influence corporate-nonprofit partnerships by altering the institutional context in ways that reshape the value of nonmarket relationships. We analyze these dynamics following Operation Carwash (2014) in Brazil, using comprehensive data on all publicly listed firms and registered nonprofits from 2010 to 2017. We find that partnerships became more common after the scandal's disclosure, as firms and nonprofits sought to collaborate on socioeconomic development. However, firms seen as directly or indirectly implicated in the scandal struggled to form partnerships due to risks to nonprofits' legitimacy. Moreover, nonprofits perceived as closely aligned with firms (i.e., trade associations) or the state (i.e., education and research nonprofits or those with political capital) were especially cautious about entering partnerships to avoid appearing complicit in advancing corporate political influence. Our findings thus "check" the instrumentalization of corporate-nonprofit partnerships in two ways: by examining how it unfolds after an institutional crisis and by revealing how nonprofits resist being used as vehicles for corporate reputational repair or political gain. We show that such crises can trigger a broader realignment of corporate partnerships with nonmarket actors, highlighting the need to study shifts across nonmarket sectors, and not just within them.

title: Special Research Forum—Our Transformational Era: Implications for Management and Organizations
methods: Editorial introduction to a Special Research Forum; narrative synthesis of 10 studies spanning deductive, abductive, and inductive approaches.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Studies in the Special Research Forum
n_sample: 10 studies (selected from 100 submissions)
authors: Gruber, M.; Langley, A.; Roberson, Q.; von Krogh, G.
theories: cognitive science; collective action; identity theory; institutional theory; knowledge-based views
keywords: governance and stakeholders; identity, inclusion, and human flourishing; researching forward; technology and knowledge work; transformational era
research_question: How are technological advances and mounting societal challenges transforming management and organizations, and how can scholars study these ongoing shifts—including by "researching forward"—to challenge, change, and advance existing theory or develop new theory?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Technology and the changing nature of knowledge and work: how algorithmic systems, digital tools, and categorization processes are reshaping expertise, innovation, and learning.
- Identity, inclusion, and human flourishing in the workplace: how evolving organizational practices and ideologies influence worker dignity, mental health, and equitable career advancement.
- Governance, stakeholders, and the reconfiguration of institutional relationships: how organizations respond to legitimacy threats, community mobilization, and shifting stakeholder expectations.

The editorial organizes 10 Special Research Forum studies into three thematic clusters and argues that they share a deeper commonality: the urgent need to rethink foundational assumptions about how organizations operate, for whom they exist, and how they should evolve amid dramatic external and internal shifts. It frames organizational transformation as simultaneously technological, epistemological, and deeply human, and introduces "researching forward" as a stance that narrows the gap between retrospective theorizing and the forward-looking concerns of practice.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The forum demonstrates the analytical potential of bridging micro- and macro-level insights and integrating diverse theoretical lenses—including identity theory, cognitive science, institutional theory, collective action, and knowledge-based views—to understand organizations in transformation. Beyond diagnosis, the editors argue the Special Research Forum offers direction: new models, practices, and priorities for scholars and practitioners. The editorial advances the notion of "researching forward" (real-time, prospective, and engaged designs) as a way to make scholarship more relevant to unfolding transformational trends.
practical_implication: The editors urge scholars to move beyond studying phenomena retrospectively and to articulate the practical and policy implications of their work more clearly to a broad and diverse audience, engaging more directly with practice. For practitioners who seek to lead, study, and engage with organizations, the forum offers new models, practices, and priorities to help navigate technological, human, and institutional transformation in ways that are adaptive, ethical, and future-facing.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editors highlight significant opportunities for scholars to study the nonlinearity of institutional and sociopolitical change and its consequences for organizations and for humanity's ability to address collective grand challenges. They encourage "researching forward" through real-time studies, collaborative inquiry, field experiments, prospective case studies, and "racing designs," and call for further work on the links among work arrangements, mental illness, and individual and organizational strategies for managing it.

title: Interlacing Situated and Algorithmic Modes of Knowledge Work: A Workplace Jurisdiction Perspective
methods: Single-case, three-year ethnographic study (November 2019-September 2022) of a hospital radiology workflow; grounded, inductive process analysis (Langley narrative; four-step coding) of interviews, non-participant observation, and documents.
industry: Healthcare (academic medical center; radiology department)
time_period: November 2019 to September 2022
units: Occupational groups in a radiology workflow (image processing lab members, radiologists, radiographers, referring physicians, managers, IT specialists)
n_sample: 34 interviews; ~192.5 hours of observation; 9 public + 535 internal documents
authors: Kim, B.; Rezazade Mehrizi, M. H.; Bailey, D. E.
theories: situated versus algorithmic modes of knowledge work (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1986; Suchman, 1987); workplace artifacts / practice-based coordination (Barley, 1996; Bechky, 2003a); workplace jurisdictions (Abbott, 1988; Bechky, 2003a; Pine & Mazmanian, 2017)
keywords: algorithmic knowledge claims; algorithmic technologies; interlacing practices; knowledge work; situated and algorithmic modes; workplace jurisdictions
research_question: How does the algorithmic mode of knowledge work become integrated with the situated mode of knowledge work across the flow of work to create new workplace jurisdictions?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / modes: situated mode vs. algorithmic mode of knowledge work; expert knowledge claims vs. algorithmic knowledge claims; workplace jurisdiction as the legitimate division and coordination of work among occupations.
- Reorganizing interlacing practices: (1) redefining tasks and interactions (co-developing detailed image-processing protocols with radiologists); (2) reorchestrating workplace artifacts through technology (reprogramming the PACS workflow engine to auto-route images and results).
- Enacting interlacing practices: (3) systematically using algorithmic technologies (Vitrea, ISP) to construct accurate, consistent image-processing results; (4) embedding algorithmic knowledge claims into expert knowledge claims (prefilling radiology reports with standardized templates).
- Consequences for jurisdiction creation: unique combinatory expertise developed; distinct value added to the flow of work; a new task area created.
- Triggering conditions: temporally constrained, interdependent knowledge work whose situated mode left algorithmic capabilities dormant and whose idiosyncratic expert claims spawned demands for standardization and replicability.

A low-status group of radiographers (the image processing lab, IPL), established merely to relieve radiologists of routine tasks, used four interlacing practices to weave the situated and algorithmic modes of knowledge work together. It first reorganized task boundaries and the technological infrastructure of the workflow, then enacted systematic algorithmic-technology use and embedded algorithmic knowledge claims into radiologists’ reports. By establishing and reinforcing a new structure of coordination and securing downstream occupations’ legitimization of its algorithmic knowledge claims, IPL created a new workplace jurisdiction whose boundaries simultaneously demarcated its distinctive expertise and connected occupations across the flow of work.
data_measures: Three-year ethnography at "Southern" (pseudonym), the radiology department of one of six Dutch university medical centers. Corpus: roughly 192.5 hours of non-participant observation (167.5 hours seated beside IPL members across 37 days, plus 25 hours across the broader workflow), 34 semi-structured interviews (9 IPL members, 8 radiologists, 1 referring physician, 14 managers, 2 IT specialists), and 544 documents (9 public and 535 internal, chiefly evolving image-processing protocols and Vitrea/ISP manuals), triangulated with on-site member checks. Analysis was grounded and inductive in four steps (immersing in the case; defining the analytical focus around the situated/algorithmic gap; conceptualizing interlacing practices; operationalizing jurisdiction-creation outcomes), building an in-depth process narrative (Langley, 1999). Focal constructs were coded from the data: algorithmic vs. expert knowledge claims, algorithmic technologies (Vitrea, ISP) vs. workflow technology (PACS), and the four interlacing practices.
key_findings: As an inductive study, the paper reports an emergent process model rather than hypothesis tests. Despite its low status and a mandate merely to offload routine, time-intensive tasks, the IPL created a new workplace jurisdiction over algorithmic image processing and won legitimacy from radiologists, referring physicians, and managers. Jurisdiction creation manifested in three interrelated acts: unique combinatory expertise developed (anatomical/pathological knowledge combined with skilled use of Vitrea and ISP), distinct value added to the flow of work (standardized and enriched reports, alleviated radiologist workload, improved inter-occupational coordination), and a new task area created (IPL formalized as a separate section with its own section head and 5% extra compensation). The four interlacing practices were co-constitutive and mutually reinforcing, generating a positive feedback loop that expanded interlacing onto new tasks (task protocols grew from 1 to 13 over the observation window). Four triggering conditions enabled the process: temporally constrained work performed interdependently across occupations, whose situated mode left algorithmic capabilities dormant and whose idiosyncratic expert knowledge claims spawned growing demands for standardization and replicability.
theoretical_contribution: The study makes two contributions, both emphasizing a trans-group focus. First, it introduces interlacing practices as a means of integrating the algorithmic mode of knowledge work with the situated mode across the flow of work, through a new structure of coordination and downstream occupations’ legitimization of algorithmic knowledge claims, moving beyond the literature’s focus on the local interface between an algorithm and a single focal user group. Second, it shows how interlacing creates a new workplace jurisdiction by proactively and simultaneously altering an occupation’s (human) relational and non-relational aspects, leveraging novel technology both to develop unique expertise within a group and to improve inter-occupational coordination, thereby revealing the duality of jurisdictional boundaries that demarcate and connect.
practical_implication: For managers of professional knowledge work adopting algorithmic technologies, the study suggests approaching adoption holistically by comprehensively reorganizing the workflow before or in conjunction with deploying the technologies, rather than relying on local quick fixes. Managers can support cross-occupational knowledge sharing (for example, by assigning roles or creating a cross-functional team to reassess the workflow) and collaborate with IT specialists so that integration minimally disrupts the flow of work. Creatively reallocating the tasks that algorithmic technologies tackle, preferably to a nonexpert group upstream while experts retain authority to validate and modify algorithmic knowledge claims, can break the vicious cycle of limited use and limited value and even upskill rather than weaken an occupation.
limitations: The authors caution that their case represents one of various possible sociotechnical constellations, so the specificities of a single-case setting may have shaped the theorization. For example, the referring physicians who played a crucial role in IPL gaining legitimacy were located in the same organization as IPL members and radiologists.
future_research: The paper explicitly calls for research on whether IPL’s workplace jurisdiction will be formalized in the public or legal realm, including developments in legal protections and professional associations; on how jurisdiction creation through interlacing unfolds when occupations sharing a flow of work are located across different organizations; and on the conditions under which interlacing is or is not likely to create a jurisdiction, such as settings where professional accountability is not crucial or non-professional settings where the algorithmic mode may substitute for, rather than complement, the situated mode.
abstract: Algorithmic technologies are challenging to integrate into knowledge work; they produce knowledge claims profoundly differently from the situated mode in which experts work. Because knowledge work is often accomplished through the flow or sequential progression of work across multiple occupations, knowledge claims must be legitimized and accepted across those occupations and not by just a single focal user group. Yet, we know little about the deeper changes that organizations must make regarding who has the legitimate expertise to produce knowledge claims and what counts as valuable knowledge when the algorithmic mode of knowledge work enters the workplace. To explore this, we draw on workplace jurisdictions as the foundation for dividing and coordinating work among occupations to study how the algorithmic mode of knowledge work becomes integrated with the situated flow of work, creating a new workplace jurisdiction. Our three-year ethnographic study of the radiology workflow in a medical center shows that interlacing practices weave together the two distinct modes of knowledge work by reorganizing existing relations among tasks, workplace artifacts, and technologies and enacting those reorganized relations. Contrary to the literature’s focus on the interface between algorithmic knowledge claims and a single focal user group, our study proposes a trans-group focus that refines scholarly understanding of how organizations can integrate algorithmic technologies with situated practices of professionals and their knowledge claims, as well as how new workplace jurisdictions emerge around technologies.
