title: Vicarious Experimentation: Do Innovators Learn by Being Imitated?
methods: Quantitative observational study of 438 original-sequel video-game dyads; OLS regression with genre, publisher, and sequel-release-year fixed effects and robust standard errors; interaction terms test two moderators; robustness checks include Oster (2019) unobservable-selection bounds, Heckman selection correction, two-stage least squares, and alternative measures/specifications.
industry: Console video game industry (PlayStation 2 games across 28 genres)
time_period: 2000-2013 (PS2 console lifespan)
units: Original-sequel game dyads (innovator firms' game series)
n_sample: 438 original-sequel game pairs (drawn from 3,051 PS2 games)
authors: Kim, S.; Posen, H. E.; Ganco, M.
theories: absorptive capacity (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990); causal ambiguity (Lippman & Rumelt, 1982; Rivkin, 2000); knowledge spillovers (Cohen & Levinthal, 1989); organizational learning (March, 1991; Levinthal & March, 1993); strategic experimentation (Felin & Zenger, 2009; Gans et al., 2019; Ries, 2011); vicarious experimentation (novel construct); vicarious learning (Argote & Miron-Spektor, 2011; Haunschild & Miner, 1997)
keywords: causal ambiguity; imitation; learning by being imitated; organizational learning; strategic experimentation; vicarious experimentation; vicarious learning; video game industry
research_question: How and what can innovators learn from being imitated? The paper asks whether an innovator's product being near-cloned by imitators functions as a source of quasi-experimental learning that improves the quality of its next-generation product, and identifies the boundary conditions under which this effect holds.
hypotheses:
H1. The extent of vicarious experimentation is positively related to the quality of the next generation of the innovator's original product (controlling for the quality of the original product).
H2. The positive relationship between the extent of vicarious experimentation and the quality of the innovator's next-generation product is stronger if the imitators have higher prominence in the market.
H3. The positive relationship between the extent of vicarious experimentation and the quality of the innovator's next-generation product is weaker if the innovator's tacit knowledge is disrupted by changes in the product development unit.
mechanism_summary: Being imitated supplies the innovator with a set of quasi-experiments it does not run itself: an imitator's near-clone holds the original's core features fixed while varying peripheral features, so the innovator's original acts as the control and the near-clone as the treatment. By observing these peripheral variations and their market feedback, the innovator can reduce causal ambiguity and infer which feature changes improve performance, then retain, add, or delete features in its sequel. The learning is amplified when imitators are prominent — their products generate more visible, comprehensive, and reliable observational data — and it depends on the innovator retaining the tacit, product-specific knowledge (a form of absorptive capacity) needed to interpret and integrate the insights; disrupting the development unit erodes that knowledge and dampens the benefit.
data_measures:
- Data: 438 original-sequel game dyads drawn from a base of 3,051 PS2 games (2000–2013, 28 genres), combining MobyGames, Metacritic, and IGDB; near-clones are later games that retain the original's core features (released between the original and the sequel). An additional 5,449 games on other consoles (e.g., Wii, Xbox) support cross-platform-imitation tests.
- DV — sequel quality: average critics' rating scores (0–100) from MobyGames and Metacritic.
- IV — vicarious experimentation: aggregated angular separation (Jaffe, 1986) of IGDB game-keyword vectors between each near-clone and the original (peripheral-feature variation with core features fixed), summed over the near-clone pool.
- Moderator — imitator prominence: average of imitator firms' market shares in the focal genre in year y–1 (with entropy-based, award-winning, and average-clone-sales alternatives).
- Moderator — loss of tacit knowledge: dummy = 1 if the game development unit changed between original and sequel (with developer-retention alternatives).
- Controls: quality and sales of the original game, years since the original, generation in the series, genre concentration (HHI), genre popularity, development-team size (plus an imputation dummy), and average game-feature popularity; genre (28), publisher (46), and sequel-release-year (10) fixed effects.
- Identification: associational OLS with robust standard errors; the authors state the results do not establish strict causality and instead bound unobservable selection (Oster, 2019), apply Heckman correction and two-stage least squares, and run alternative-explanation tests.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: vicarious experimentation is positively associated with sequel quality (Model 2: b = 0.17, p < .01; Model 3: b = 0.16, p < .01); a 1.0 SD increase in vicarious experimentation corresponds to roughly a 0.1 SD improvement in sequel quality in the main-effects model.
- H2 supported: the vicarious experimentation × imitator prominence interaction is positive and significant (Model 4: b = 0.04, p < .05) — the learning effect is driven by prominent imitators.
- H3 supported: the vicarious experimentation × loss-of-tacit-knowledge (development-unit change) interaction is negative and significant (Model 4: b = -0.29, p < .05) — the benefit disappears when the development studio changes.
- In the fully specified Model 4 the main effect of vicarious experimentation is not significant (b = 0.019, ns), confirming that imitator prominence and tacit-knowledge retention act as boundary conditions rather than the effect operating unconditionally; for prominent (top-20%) imitators with an unchanged development unit, a 1.0 SD increase corresponds to about a 0.3 SD increase in sequel quality.
- Robustness: results hold under alternative IV measures (imitation counts, unique feature bundles), alternative prominence measures (entropy of market shares, award-winning status, average clone sales), Oster (2019) bounds (δ = 76.05), Heckman selection correction, two-stage least squares, feature-removal-only cases, and cross-platform-imitation checks, although some alternative specifications weaken slightly.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces "vicarious experimentation" as a novel mechanism, reframing being imitated not as mere knowledge leakage but as a source of targeted, causal, and actionable learning for the innovator. It positions the construct at the intersection of vicarious learning and learning from one's own experimentation — the innovator's original is the control and the imitator's near-clone is the treatment — thereby extending the strategy-as-experimentation perspective to experiments the focal firm does not control and specifying causal-ambiguity-based boundary conditions (near-clonal peripheral variation, imitator prominence, and tacit-knowledge retention). In doing so it foregrounds innovator agency in imitation research, which has traditionally cast innovators as passive parties whose knowledge is expropriated.
practical_implication: From a managerial perspective, the study suggests firms may need to change their mindset about being imitated: rather than dismissing imitators as copycats with little to offer, innovators can study imitators' near-clones as opportunities to learn and improve their next-generation products. It also highlights the managerial importance of internal organizational factors — particularly retaining the tacit, product-specific knowledge of the original development team — because organizational changes that disrupt the development unit can inhibit the ability to learn from vicarious experimentation.
limitations: The authors note that the interplay between competition and imitation is complex and not fully isolated, so the extent of competition may still shape how innovators learn from vicarious experiments. They do not fully examine the broader set of mechanisms (e.g., shifts in customer perceptions, competitive responses from rivals, and recombined knowledge spillovers) through which being imitated can affect an innovator, and they do not resolve whether being imitated benefits the innovator or the imitator more. Finally, the results do not establish strict causality — finding instruments or natural experiments for imitation remains difficult — so the design relies on extensive controls, unobservable-selection analysis (Oster, 2019), and tests ruling out alternative explanations.
future_research: The authors call for research that disentangles imitation and competitive dynamics in more detail, and that develops a more comprehensive framework for how the interdependent mechanisms of being imitated jointly shape an innovator's outcomes over time. They encourage further work to explore causal relationships in imitation, and to weave together the strategy-as-experimentation, entrepreneurial-decision-making, Carnegie-tradition, and quasi-experimentation perspectives on which vicarious experimentation draws.
abstract: Strategy scholars conventionally view imitation as a one-way knowledge transfer from an innovating firm to an imitating firm. We propose that being imitated also serves as a source of learning for the innovator. An innovator learns by being imitated—observing the imitator’s choices and outcomes and comparing them to its own. A key challenge in such learning, and in vicarious learning more broadly, is causal ambiguity in identifying the factors that drive observed performance outcomes. We theorize that an innovator’s learning by being imitated is particularly effective in overcoming causal ambiguity when it takes the form of vicarious experimentation, where an imitator’s near-clone of the innovator’s product functions as a quasi-experimental treatment from which the innovator can learn. This concept extends the logic of strategic experimentation by highlighting how firms can learn from experiments they do not control. We test our theory in the video game industry, demonstrating that vicarious experimentation enhances the quality of the innovator’s next-generation product and offering support for the theorized boundary conditions under which this effect holds.

title: The Limits of Pivoting: A Culturally Informed Model of Resource Commitments during Repeated Organizational Transformation
methods: Longitudinal, inductive qualitative case study (real-time ethnography) of a single publicly listed micro-cap venture; grounded, four-stage process analysis of 150 ethnographic observations, 75 semi-structured interviews, and 245 archival documents by an insider-outsider team.
industry: Medical-technology entrepreneurial venture (pivoting across sports, sleep, and medical-cannabis products)
time_period: Real-time fieldwork February 2013-December 2015 (venture founded 2008)
units: A single entrepreneurial venture and its employee and investor stakeholders
n_sample: 1 venture (Respiro, pseudonym); 75 interviews, 150 ethnographic observations, 245 archival documents
authors: Knight, E.; Grimes, M. G.; Gehman, J.
theories: cultural toolkit / culture in action (Swidler, 1986); narrative theory (Vaara et al., 2016); relational models theory (Fiske, 1991; Bridoux & Stoelhorst, 2016); stakeholder theory (Parmar et al., 2010; Freeman, 1984)
keywords: entrepreneurial runway; organizational transformation; pivoting narratives; repeated pivoting; resource commitments; stakeholder orientations
research_question: How do different and changing narratives affect employees' and investors' resource commitments as a venture repeatedly pivots? The study asks why some stakeholders sustain and others withdraw their human and financial resource commitments across successive organizational transformations.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Pivoting narratives (two types the CEO circulated simultaneously): a *revolutionary* narrative (a "clean break" from the past, a *proximate* future with no further change needed, *individual* agency) versus a *scientific revision* narrative (a process that *connects with* the past, a *distal* future of continuous experimentation, *collective* agency).
- Narrative elements coded across both narratives: "the past" (break from / connect with), "the future" (proximate / distal), and "source of agency" (individual / collective).
- Stakeholder orientations: *market pricing* (an extractive basis of exchange — valuing interactions for personal or professional benefit) versus *communal sharing* (a generative basis of exchange — valuing contribution to shared purpose), identified across both employees and investors.
- Cultural resonance: the degree of fit between a pivoting narrative and a stakeholder's orientation, which shifts over time and across pivots.
- Resource commitments (emergent outcomes): human (extra-role effort, tenure) and financial (capital-raise participation, buy/hold/sell decisions), aggregating to the venture's entrepreneurial "runway."

The process model holds that resource commitments flow not from a narrative alone but from its cultural resonance with a stakeholder's orientation. Revolutionary narratives promise proximate, specific deliverables that resonate with market-pricing stakeholders and produce a short-lived surge of resources; because repeated pivots break those promises, resonance collapses and these stakeholders withdraw. Scientific-revision narratives frame pivots as connected, collective experiments toward a distal purpose, resonating with communal-sharing stakeholders whose expectations are actualized rather than violated by continued change, so their commitments persist across repeated pivots and sustain the venture's runway.
data_measures: Real-time, longitudinal ethnographic case study of "Respiro" (a pseudonym), a publicly listed Australian micro-cap medical-technology venture that pivoted from patent licensing to sports products (SportsPro) to sleep applications (SleepPro) to medical cannabis. The data corpus comprised 150 ethnographic observations, 75 semi-structured interviews (including the CEO nine times and 11 employees), and 245 archival documents (company announcements, investor presentations, board materials, and 624 comments across investor discussion-forum threads), collected February 2013-December 2015 by an insider-outsider team (the first author served on the board). Analysis proceeded inductively in four stages: (1) constructing a timeline of pivots and human/financial resource flows; (2) identifying the two pivoting narratives and their three elements; (3) identifying stakeholders' orientations (market pricing vs. communal sharing); and (4) linking the cultural resonance of narratives to resource commitments over time (Table 4 color-coded each stakeholder's reactions across the three pivots). The design is interpretive and process-oriented rather than causal-identification-based.
key_findings: Respiro's CEO advanced two pivoting narratives that circulated simultaneously; over time the scientific-revision narrative became dominant. The revolutionary narrative initially resonated with market-pricing-oriented stakeholders (e.g., the CFO Julia, marketing staff, and day traders), raising short-term human and financial resource commitments; but across repeated pivots its broken promises destroyed that resonance, and these stakeholders curtailed extra-role effort, divested, refused capital raises, and eventually left the venture. The scientific-revision narrative resonated with communal-sharing-oriented stakeholders (e.g., Liz, Nadine, and mission-driven investors), who sustained or increased their human and financial commitments across all three pivots despite lackluster financial performance, because repeated pivots confirmed rather than violated the narrative's promise of continuous, collective experimentation toward a broad purpose. The central finding is that cultural resonance between narrative and stakeholder orientation — not the narrative type alone — governed whether commitments were temporary or sustained, so scientific-revision narratives paired with communal-sharing orientations enabled repeated pivoting by sustaining the entrepreneurial runway.
theoretical_contribution: The study develops a culturally informed process model of resource commitments during repeated organizational transformation, extending transformation research beyond single change episodes to show how the residual effects of prior pivots constrain later ones and how pivoting narratives can narratively sustain (or erode) stakeholder support across successive change. It theoretically elaborates the concept of the entrepreneurial "runway," reconceptualizing it as resources contributed by both employees and investors (human as well as financial capital) that are dynamically constructed and reconstructed through pivoting narratives rather than a fixed function of cash and burn rate. It also extends stakeholder theory by showing how within-group differences in stakeholders' orientations (market pricing vs. communal sharing) shape the cultural resonance of narratives and thereby their sustained access to resources.
practical_implication: For entrepreneurial leaders of ventures that must pivot repeatedly, the study surfaces a cultural "toolkit": framing change as "scientific revision" — repositioning strategic goals as hypotheses, strategic action as tests, strategic failure as learning, and strategic change as pivoting — helps leaders maintain stakeholder engagement and sustain resource commitments across repeated transformations without rendering themselves culpable, whereas revolutionary "clean break" narratives tend to secure only short-lived commitments that collapse once repeated change exposes broken promises.
limitations: Insights derive from a single micro-cap venture, raising questions of generalizability; the authors position the findings as most applicable to organizations closest to Respiro and as inviting re-theorization when extended to organizations farther from this template, such as larger corporations. Only two of the four stakeholder orientations from prior relational theory — market pricing and communal sharing — were observed in the case, leaving authority ranking and equality matching unexamined.
future_research: The authors call for research into how different cultural contexts shape the effectiveness of pivoting narratives and into the limits and resilience of scientific-revision narratives over extended periods, as well as extensions across a broader range of industries and organizational sizes (including large corporations) to test whether the narrative and orientation effects are universal. They also invite study of other pivoting narratives built on alternative metaphors of change (e.g., disruptive innovation, evolutionary change, high-impact social mission), settings in which all four stakeholder orientations are present, and other forms of capital (technological, intellectual, social, and institutional) beyond the human and financial resources examined here.
abstract: In contrast to models of organizational transformation that focus on one-time episodes of change, this study reveals limits to the number of transformations an organization can make without losing the support of key stakeholder groups. To better understand the process of repeated transformation, we study an extreme case of a medical technology startup with a history of pivoting, focusing on the degree to which employees and investors continued to support the venture. Although new ventures are often advised to be highly adaptive, we find that repeated pivoting introduces relational liabilities for even highly flexible organizations. Drawing on our analysis, we develop a culturally informed process model of resource commitments that reveals how differences in pivoting narratives and stakeholder orientations affect the flow of support from employees and investors, even as the organization repeatedly pivots. Our model contributes to existing theories of organizational transformation, offering an enriched understanding of how organizations can narratively sustain resource commitments to enable continuous adaptation.
apa_citation: Knight, E., Grimes, M. G., & Gehman, J. (2025). The limits of pivoting: A culturally informed model of resource commitments during repeated organizational transformation. *Academy of Management Journal, 68*(5), 1130–1162. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2023.0314

title: Would Archimedes Shout “Eureka” with Algorithms? The Hidden Hand of Algorithmic Design in Idea Generation, the Creation of Ideation Bubbles, and How Experts Can Burst Them
methods: Two experimental studies. Pilot Study 1: between-subjects laboratory experiment (exploitation Google Search vs. exploration XYZ), independent-samples t-test and OLS regression. Study 2: preregistered field experiment via a global online ideation challenge, two-way ANOVA, OLS regression, simple-slope analysis, parametric-bootstrap Monte-Carlo mediation, and NLP sentence-embedding + DBSCAN semantic cluster analysis of aggregate idea diversity.
industry: Sustainability challenge domains: reducing overconsumption (Pilot Study 1) and reducing household food waste in the food industry (Study 2); creators from diverse professional backgrounds
country: Pilot Study 1: not reported (undergraduate students); Study 2: creators based across more than 40 countries
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals (idea generators / creators); ideas clustered at the aggregate level
n_sample: 104 participants (Pilot Study 1, laboratory); 245 creators (Study 2, field experiment)
authors: Lazar, M.; Lifshitz, H.; Ayoubi, C.; Emuna, H.
theories: algorithmic confirmation bias (Nickerson, 1998); cognitive entrenchment / lock-in (Dane, 2010); exploration-exploitation design logic; filter bubble / ideation bubble (Pariser, 2011); recombinant innovation (Hargadon & Sutton, 1997; Carnabuci & Operti, 2013)
keywords: algorithmic confirmation bias; algorithmic design; domain expertise; exploration-based algorithms; idea creativity; idea generation; ideation bubbles; recombinant innovation
research_question: Does domain expertise still matter for idea generation in the algorithmic age, and how does algorithmic design logic—exploitation-based versus exploration-based—shape whether experts generate more creative ideas (individually) and greater diversity of ideas (at the aggregate level)? As the paper frames it in its discussion: "What role does expertise play in idea generation with algorithms?"
hypotheses:
Hypothesis 0 (baseline). In the idea generation process, using algorithms based on exploration design logic leads individuals to generate ideas that are more creative, compared to algorithms based on exploitation design logic.
Hypothesis 1a. Algorithm design logic and domain expertise interact to affect idea creativity, such that individuals with high levels of domain expertise will generate ideas that are more creative when using exploration-based algorithms (compared to those with low levels of domain expertise).
Hypothesis 1b. The recombinant innovation process mediates the interactive effect of algorithm design logic and domain expertise on the generation of creative ideas.
Hypothesis 2. Algorithm design logic and domain expertise interact to affect the diversity of ideas, such that those with high levels of domain expertise will contribute to greater diversity of ideas when using exploration-based algorithms (compared to those with low levels of domain expertise).
mechanism_summary:
- Mediator(s): Recombinant innovation (reconfiguring the topics in the algorithm-provided information set into new combinations)
- Moderator(s): Domain expertise (years of prior experience in the sustainability domain)

Exploitation-based algorithms surface popular, familiar, relevance-optimized information that triggers "algorithmic confirmation bias," locking experts into prevailing knowledge and suppressing creative recombination. Exploration-based algorithms instead surface diverse, uncommon information; domain experts, drawing on their deep knowledge reservoir, can synthesize these distant elements through recombinant innovation to generate more creative ideas. Beyond the individual level, experts using exploration-based algorithms can burst dominant "ideation bubbles" (bounded clusters of similar ideas) and form new, less conventional ones, thereby expanding the diversity of ideas and heterogeneity of thought at the aggregate level.
data_measures: Pilot Study 1 (laboratory, N = 104 undergraduate students): random between-subjects assignment to Google Search (exploitation) or XYZ (exploration) before generating an idea to reduce overconsumption; idea creativity rated by three blind domain-expert evaluators on six 7-point items ("original," "novel," "unique," "practical," "feasible," "applicable"); controls for age and gender. Study 2 (preregistered field experiment on Freelancer, N = 245 creators across 40+ countries, household food-waste challenge): same exploitation-vs-exploration manipulation; idea creativity scored by the same expert panel; domain expertise measured as self-reported years of prior experience in the sustainability domain (continuous; 37% novices with zero years); recombinant innovation quantified via a ratio approach (number of topics combined weighted by pairwise co-occurrence frequency, following Fleming & Sorenson, 2004); diversity of ideas measured with NLP sentence embeddings plus DBSCAN density-based semantic clustering (counting ideation bubbles); controls for age, gender, general digital-tool use, task motivation, and geographic region. Both studies use randomized experimental assignment, supporting causal identification of the design-logic effect.
key_findings:
- Baseline H0 supported in BOTH studies: exploration (XYZ) produced more creative ideas than exploitation (Google Search). Pilot Study 1: M = 4.77 (SD = 0.76) vs. M = 3.35 (SD = 1.27), t(102) = 2.13, p = .04; OLS b = .43, p = .04. Study 2: M = 4.33 (SD = 0.79) vs. M = 4.03 (SD = 0.88), t(243) = 2.75, p = .01; OLS b = .31, p = .01. (Abstract summary: XYZ increased idea creativity by ~14% in the lab and ~11% in the field.)
- H1a supported (tested in Study 2 only, which measured expertise): positive algorithm-design × domain-expertise interaction on idea creativity (two-way ANOVA F(1,241) = 5.63, p = .02; OLS interaction b = .05, p = .01). Simple slopes — under exploration, expertise related positively to creativity (b = .04, p = .01); under exploitation, the relationship was non-significant (b = −.01, p = .57).
- H1b supported (Study 2 only): recombinant innovation mediated the interactive effect. Exploration produced significantly greater recombinant innovation (b = .05, p < .001); the design × expertise interaction on recombinant innovation was significant only at the 10% level (b = .01, p = .09); recombinant innovation in turn predicted idea creativity (b = 1.38, p = .03); positive indirect effect = 0.01, 90% CI [0.01, 0.02].
- H2 supported (Study 2 only): domain experts enhanced aggregate idea diversity, and the effect was stronger under exploration. Semantic clustering — with exploration (XYZ), experts' ideas formed five clusters vs. two for novices; with exploitation (Google Search), experts formed two clusters vs. one for novices — i.e., experts burst dominant ideation bubbles and formed new, less conventional ones.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the future-of-work debate on the relevance of expertise by unveiling the central role of domain expertise in reaping algorithms' benefits for idea generation: exploration-based design mitigates algorithmic confirmation bias and enables experts to conduct productive recombinant innovation, which the paper operationalizes in an algorithmic context. It extends the creativity/grand-challenges discourse by showing experts' benefits manifest beyond the individual level, fostering diversity of ideas and heterogeneity of thought, and introduces the concept of "ideation bubbles" (the output analogue of filter bubbles). Finally, it advances the conversation on how algorithms shape knowledge work by shifting attention from efficiency to idea generation and revealing the "hidden hand" of algorithmic design logic.
practical_implication: For creators, managers, and organizations, the paper suggests that during early ideation stages, exploration-based approaches that reveal diverse information may be more valuable for creative idea generation than standard exploitation-based tools. Practitioners can customize interfaces or adjust parameters in algorithmic tools (e.g., temperature settings in generative AI) to promote exploration when seeking creative solutions, strategically pair domain experts with exploration-based algorithms to maximize recombinant innovation, and monitor the distribution of ideas across solution spaces to help burst dominant thought patterns.
limitations: The empirical focus is a single search algorithm (Google Search) and its modification, which does not encapsulate the full spectrum of algorithmic tools. The design documents only the short-term effect of algorithms on idea generation rather than dynamics over repeated interaction. The study examines domain expertise specifically and focuses on the early idea-generation phase and on individuals.
future_research: The authors call for examining a broader range of algorithmic tools (e.g., interactive and collaborative algorithms such as LLMs, including prompting for narrower/broader search or different personas); investigating long-term and repeated algorithm exposure and whether effects magnify or induce different biases across expertise types; exploring how different forms of expertise shape the ability to leverage algorithms; studying different algorithmic designs and interfaces at different stages of the innovation process (generation vs. evaluation/implementation) and their short- versus long-term effects; and extending from individuals to teams and collaborative creativity.
abstract: Does “eureka” still ring true in the algorithmic age? This paper investigates algorithmic design and its impact on idea generation. The use of algorithms transforms knowledge work processes, redefining experts’ roles across industries. While experts are typically viewed as the cornerstone of knowledge work, an emerging debate is underway about whether expertise is still necessary in the idea generation process for creativity and innovation. Integrating creativity, expertise in knowledge work, and algorithmic design literatures, we theorize on the interplay between expertise and algorithmic design in idea generation. We suggest that the prevailing algorithmic design, focusing on information exploitation, is misaligned with the recombinant innovation processes needed for idea generation, especially for experts. We design an exploration-based modification to the prevalent exploitation-based algorithm—Google Search. We hypothesize that when using exploration-based algorithms, experts can overcome confirmation bias and generate more creative ideas through recombinant innovation. Moving beyond the individual level, experts are central to bursting “ideation bubbles”—clusters of similar ideas—thus enhancing idea diversity. We test our theory in a laboratory study and a field experiment through a global ideation challenge in sustainability launched on Freelancer. Findings offer insights into designing and using algorithms to augment human expertise for innovation.

The hidden hand of algorithmic design in idea generation, the creation of ideation bubbles, and how experts can burst them. *Academy of Management Journal, 68*(5), 881–906. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2023.1307

title: Navigating Mental Illness at Work Using Disengagement and Engagement Pathways
methods: Inductive qualitative study using the Gioia grounded-theory methodology. Two-phase design: a sensitizing phase (171 blog posts; 252 Reddit threads, 1,119 posts) followed by a main phase of 59 semi-structured interviews with 57 employed adults diagnosed with mood and/or anxiety disorders; initial open coding then axial coding into an emergent process model.
industry: Varied occupations (e.g., bus driver, chemical engineer, chief technology officer, consultant, lawyer, professor, teacher, restaurant server, touring musician)
time_period: November 2020 to July 2021
units: Employed adults diagnosed with mood and/or anxiety disorders
n_sample: 59 interviews with 57 participants (two interviewed twice)
authors: Rosado-Solomon, E. H.; Thatcher, S. M. B.; Strizver, S. D.
theories: embodiment (Heaphy & Dutton, 2008); social identity and stigma (Goffman, 1963); work (dis)engagement (Kahn, 1990; Demerouti et al., 2001)
keywords: disengagement; distraction; embodiment; employee well-being; engagement; image preservation; mental illness at work; suffering reduction
research_question: How do employees with mental illness navigate their symptoms vis-a-vis work — that is, how do they experience their conditions and manage their symptoms alongside the demands of paid employment?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: Onset of episodic mental illness symptoms arising from an omnipresent chronic condition, which interferes with expected work behaviors
- (Dis)engagement actions: Disengagement (physical, task, social) and engagement (physical or task, social), enacted by employees who are aware of symptom onset and able to respond
- Mechanisms: Suffering reduction (an active process curtailing the aversive experience of symptoms), image preservation (avoiding stigma/discovery of one's condition), and distraction (diverting attention from aversive symptoms)
- Outcomes: Wellness outcomes (survival, subjective well-being) and work-related outcomes (acceptable performance, avoiding discrimination, continued employment)
- Boundary condition (non-independence): Disengagement and engagement are not opposite ends of a spectrum — some employees disengaged (e.g., physically or from a task) while simultaneously increasing engagement (e.g., socially)

When employees with mood or anxiety disorders experience a symptom onset, those able to respond temporarily (dis)engage from work rather than passively absorbing a conflict between symptoms and job demands. Distinct types of disengagement (physical, task, social) and engagement (physical/task, social) connect to valued wellness and work outcomes through three explanatory mechanisms — suffering reduction, image preservation, and distraction. Disengagement is especially crucial because it gives employees the time and space to enact symptom-management strategies while still meeting "good enough" performance standards; the two pathways frequently co-occur as employees navigate a fluctuating, embodied condition.
data_measures: Data: 59 semi-structured interviews with 57 participants (two interviewed twice; 55 recorded and transcribed verbatim, others documented via notes; interviews 43–84 minutes, average 61), all US adults diagnosed with a mood and/or anxiety disorder prior to March 2020, holding varied occupations. A prior sensitizing phase drew on 171 anonymous blog posts and 252 Reddit threads (1,119 posts from 781 users) to refine the interview protocol. Analysis: inductive grounded-theory coding following the Gioia methodology — initial open coding kept close to participants' own language, followed by axial coding that consolidated open codes into higher-order categories and specified relationships among (dis)engagement types, mechanisms, and outcomes, iterating between coding and extant literature. The design is interpretive/associational; the authors explicitly state their data do not allow causal inferences (e.g., for the distraction-to-work-outcomes link).
key_findings:
- In response to symptom onset, employees temporarily altered their work engagement: most disengaged (physical, task, or social), while others increased engagement (physical/task or social). The two were not mutually exclusive and often co-occurred within the same individual.
- Disengagement was crucial in enabling employees to balance symptom management with stable, acceptable job performance (frequently framed by participants as "good enough" rather than optimal performance).
- Three mechanisms linked (dis)engagement to outcomes: suffering reduction (connecting all disengagement types, and social engagement, to wellness outcomes, and physical/task disengagement to work-related outcomes); image preservation (connecting social and physical disengagement to avoiding discrimination); and distraction (connecting physical/task and social engagement to survival).
- The work-related impact of increased engagement via distraction was not conclusive and is represented by a dashed line in the model.
- A small minority (n = 5) who could not deploy effective (dis)engagement — due to poor self-awareness, uniquely severe symptoms, or work constraints — generally suffered poor wellness and work outcomes.
- A few participants experienced symptoms as sometimes adaptive for performance (e.g., mania, anxiety), but this positive impact was excluded from the theoretical model for lack of sufficient data.
theoretical_contribution: The study augments a mental-illness-at-work literature previously criticized as atheoretical and disclosure-dominated, theorizing how employees actively navigate tensions between symptoms and work obligations rather than merely deciding whether to disclose. It broadens the (dis)engagement literature (Kahn, 1990; Bakker et al., 2008) by showing that distinct types of disengagement and engagement affect wellness and work outcomes through different mechanisms, and that disengagement and engagement can co-occur rather than being opposite, mutually exclusive states. It extends the embodiment literature by articulating that the cognitive, affective, and somatic experiences of mental illness are tightly intertwined and cannot be divorced when studying the body at work.
practical_implication: Because outcomes differ as a function of symptoms, (dis)engagement actions, and context, one-size-fits-all approaches to employees' mental illness symptoms are unlikely to be effective. The authors' central implication for managers is to trust that when employees temporarily disengage, it is likely done with the best of intentions for the organization. Managers can also support employees by recognizing that social disengagement (via image preservation) and social engagement (via suffering reduction and distraction) are legitimate ways to manage symptoms — for instance, informal small talk can be beneficial for some employees — and managers across industries should reconsider employment restrictions for those with a history of mental illness.
limitations: The sample was overwhelmingly Caucasian (~80%), limiting the ability to examine how intersectional racial or ethnic backgrounds shape experiences of mental illness at work. The study could not determine whether simultaneous combinations of (dis)engagement types were distinctly beneficial for particular outcomes, as this was beyond its scope. The authors also did not explicitly investigate the temporal dynamics of (dis)engagement across short- versus long-term symptom episodes.
future_research: The authors call for intersectional work on how cultural, racial/ethnic, and gender differences (e.g., men with mental illness and pressure to suppress emotions) shape these experiences. They suggest quantitative studies — such as latent profile analysis — of how different combinations of (dis)engagement types relate to work and well-being outcomes, and longitudinal (qualitative and quantitative) analysis of short- versus long-term symptoms and how employees learn which (dis)engagement behaviors suit their symptoms. They further propose examining whether the model extends to other employees who experience tension between their lived experience and job expectations (e.g., other stigmatized or chronically ill workers, those going through divorce), and delineating the boundary conditions that distinguish mental-illness-specific components from those applying to all employees.
abstract: Nearly 20% of adults in the United States experience mental illness, or chronic conditions that influence the way people think, feel, and act, that may initially seem incompatible with the demands of work. Yet, many employees with mental illness are professionally successful. The present research builds theory about mental illness at work by investigating how employees with mental illness experience their conditions and how they navigate their symptoms vis-a-vis their employment. Based on 59 interviews with participants that have diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders, our findings elucidate that employees temporarily alter their work engagement—either by pulling back through various types of disengagement (physical, task, social) or by increasing their engagement in various elements of their work. Our findings show that disengagement is crucial in enabling employees with mental illness to balance symptom management and stable job performance. Our theoretical model specifies types of disengagement and engagement and the mechanisms that explain their relationship to wellness and work outcomes, including suffering reduction, image preservation, and distraction. These findings provide a nuanced view of the ways employees with mental illness navigate their symptoms, with implications for better understanding how mental illness influences affective, cognitive, and embodied experiences at work.

title: Subordinating Humanism: How Colliding Beliefs about a Living Wage Shape Personal Fulfillment and “Professional-Class” Identities in Working-Class Jobs
methods: Qualitative, inductive single-organization field study; 77 semi-structured interviews with 64 participants (51 workers, 13 managers) across two U.S. sites of one firm, in three waves (2017–2018), supplemented by site-visit observations and documents; inductive thematic analysis (open then focused coding; Charmaz, 2014).
industry: Financial technology services (a single firm, pseudonym 'WageCo')
time_period: 2017–2018 (three data-collection waves)
units: Individual workers and managers within one organization (two sites)
n_sample: 64 participants (51 workers, 13 managers); 77 interviews
authors: Seegars, L.; Lee, S. S.; Reid, E. M.; Ramarajan, L.
theories: humanistic management (Pirson, 2017; Town, Reina, Brummans & Pirson, 2024); identity theory (Gecas, 1982; Burke & Stets, 2009); market-based ideology / shareholder value capitalism (Fligstein & Goldstein, 2022); social class and work (Gray & Kish-Gephart, 2013; Williams, Blair-Loy & Berdahl, 2013); work role identity (Ibarra, 1999; Pratt, Rockmann & Kaufmann, 2006; Ramarajan & Reid, 2013)
keywords: autonomy; humanistic management; identity work; living wage; market-based ideology; overwork; professional-class identity; working-class jobs
research_question: How does the introduction of a humanistic practice — here, a living wage — into a context dominated by market-based ideology affect managers' and workers' identities?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Market-based ideology (wages tied to performance and external market value) versus humanistic ideology (pay as a means to human welfare and a good life); workers' and managers' beliefs about deservingness; working-class versus professional-class work-role identities, the latter defined by autonomy and overwork.
- Process / phases (three-phase model): (1) Status quo — market-based ideology in which financially insecure working-class workers, and their managers, treat that insecurity as normal and "deserved" for such jobs; (2) Destabilizing — a living wage is introduced, delivering financial security and fulfillment, but its decoupling of pay from performance collides with the entrenched market-based ideology, sparking workers' undeservingness concerns and threatening managers' ability to enact their role identities; (3) Restabilizing — managers demand, and workers embrace, professional-class traits, resolving the dissonance while subordinating the humanistic practice.
- Practices: Managers convey escalated expectations through performance reviews and revised hiring criteria, invoking labels such as "be your own CEO" (autonomy) and rejecting the "clockpuncher" (overwork); workers take on autonomy and overwork out of gratitude/reciprocity, relief from feelings of undeservingness, and felt pressure.
- Emergent outcomes: Workers adopt elements of a professional-class identity while the actual tasks of their working-class jobs stay the same; managers reaffirm their identities as shapers of performance despite losing control over wages; the humanistic practice is subordinated to market-based ideology through identity work.

The paper theorizes a reciprocal, multilevel process of humanistic transformation and subordination. A humanizing pay practice produces genuine resource gains and personal fulfillment, but because it is embedded in a market-based context, both parties read the raise through market logic and question whether it was earned. To restore a sense of deservingness, managers use their remaining control over hiring and performance expectations to demand professional-class conduct, and workers internalize autonomy and overwork to "deserve" the wage. Through this identity work, market-based ideology reasserts its dominance and the living wage's humanistic intent is subordinated — even though workers' underlying jobs are unchanged.
data_measures: Data corpus: 77 semi-structured interviews with 64 participants (51 workers and 13 managers; 13 participants interviewed twice) across two sites of a single U.S. financial-technology firm ("WageCo"), gathered in three waves in 2017–2018, plus two site visits with observations and organizational documents treated as supplemental data. Analysis: inductive coding (Charmaz, 2014) — analytical memos, open coding of all interview data into broad themes, then focused coding of emergent constructs (fulfillment, conflict with market-based ideology, undeservingness, autonomy, overwork; coding scheme in Online Appendix C), with managers and workers analyzed as separate subgroups and construct prevalence tallied (e.g., 27 of 51 workers described autonomy, 30 of 51 described overwork). The design is interpretive and associational rather than causal.
key_findings:
- Intended humanistic effect realized: the living wage moved workers from financial insecurity to greater financial security and personal fulfillment outside work.
- Unintended clash: decoupling pay from performance contradicted WageCo's entrenched market-based, pay-for-performance ideology, leading both workers and managers to view the raise as undeserved.
- Resolution via identity work: managers demanded, and workers embraced, two professional-class traits — autonomy ("be your own CEO") and overwork (distancing from the "clockpuncher") — while the jobs' actual tasks and definitions stayed the same; managers simultaneously reaffirmed their own role identities as shapers of performance despite their weakened control over wages.
- Net result: the humanistic living-wage practice was ultimately subordinated to market-based ideology.
- Heterogeneity across workers (not uniform): the transition was amplified for the lowest-level workers, who received the largest increases and expressed undeservingness far more often (58.3% of lowest-level vs. 25.9% of higher-level workers); construct prevalence was 27 of 51 workers describing autonomy, 30 of 51 overwork, and 16 describing both. A minority of workers with prior professional/managerial experience or credentials, or who were hired after the announcement, did not feel undeserving (they saw the pay as commensurate with their qualifications), yet they still upheld market-based ideology and demanded that other workers "prove" they deserved the wage.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances humanistic-management scholarship by documenting both the genuine benefits of a living wage (real improvements in workers' lives outside work) and how such a humanistic practice can be subordinated to a dominant market-based ideology, and by surfacing the psychological and identity roots of market-based-versus-humanistic tension — showing that worker and manager identities, not only structures, can drive resistance to humanistic management. It also contributes to theory on class and work identity: changes in pay-setting can spark transitions toward new class-based work-role identities even when job tasks remain the same, and taken-for-granted market beliefs about self-worth shape both workers' identity work and managers' identity control. On this basis the authors argue that scholars of work identity must take wages more seriously in accounts of what it means "to be" a given type of worker.
practical_implication: For leaders, managers, and workers interested in living wages and humanism, the paper argues that living wages have clear benefits and should be implemented wherever feasible, but their humanistic intent can be undone by the prevalence of market-based ideology. Leaders should explicitly affirm and protect the humanistic rationale of a new practice, train managers to enact it in concrete practices such as performance reviews and hiring, and pay particular attention to reassuring workers in the lowest-level jobs, who are most prone to viewing themselves as undeserving. Because market-based ideology is deeply entrenched, the authors caution that humanistic initiatives cannot be introduced piecemeal but should be part of a broad, ambitious organizational transformation of governance, power, and formal and informal practices, and that leaders should be externally facing and advocate for more organizations to embrace humanistic management.
limitations: The authors studied a single organization and relied primarily on interview data, which is subject to self-enhancing reports and retrospective sensemaking. The interview data cannot establish the CEO's true motivations for the living wage (he may have simultaneously held a market-based belief that better-paid workers would be more productive), and as a single case the study cannot say whether the opposite move — from humanistic to market-based pay — would be similarly or oppositely destabilizing. An explicit boundary condition is national context: the study was situated in the United States, where market-based pay practices are taken for granted, so in countries with more social-welfare infrastructure the demand that living-wage recipients take on professional-class identities may be less likely.
future_research: The authors call for quantitative work on how introducing a living wage alters labor supply, work hours, and turnover, and for tracking whether people adjust psychologically over time and whether the professional-class identity enactment tapers off. They encourage further unpacking of the meaning of autonomy in working-class jobs, including the positive processes that may emanate from embracing autonomy even when the underlying job does not change. They also invite research on when workers' and managers' views of undeservingness diverge (identity asymmetry), on whether workers' broader social-class identity is altered, and on a systems-psychodynamic perspective for understanding the underlying anxieties and social defenses that can produce such subordination.
abstract: In a society dominated by market-based ideology and management practices that prioritize financial considerations, some organizations are shifting toward humanistic ideology and practices that emphasize human welfare. To examine this transformation in pay-setting, we studied a U.S. company that introduced a living wage for its low-wage workers. Interviews with 64 participants across two sites revealed both intended and unintended effects. Motivated by humanistic aims, the living wage was designed to reduce financial insecurity; indeed, workers felt more financially secure and fulfilled in their personal lives. However, its humanistic intent conflicted with the dominant market-based ideology linking wages to performance, raising concerns about whether these workers deserved higher pay. To resolve this tension, managers and workers altered expectations for workers to reflect two aspects of professional-class roles: autonomy and overwork. As workers internalized these expectations, they adopted elements of professional-class identities while remaining in working-class jobs. Simultaneously, managers reaffirmed their own role identities as shapers of performance despite their weakened control over wages. These findings inform a multilevel model conceptualizing how a transformative humanistic practice can be subordinated to market-based ideology through identity work. We contribute to research on humanistic management and the interconnections between wage, class, work roles, and identity.

title: Distributed Knowledge and the Creation of Public Value: Community-Based Organizing and Wildfire Management in Northern California
methods: Original longitudinal panel of 321 Northern California communities (1998–2018); two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (TWFE DiD) and 2SLS instrumental-variable DiD with community fixed effects (climate shocks / SPEI as the instrument); polychoric PCA to classify collaboration types; GIS geospatial matching; Goodman-Bacon decomposition robustness.
industry: Community-based wildfire management / fire prevention planning (public value creation)
country: United States (seven northernmost counties of California)
units: Communities (human settlements); community–year (community–fire dyad) observations
n_sample: 321 communities (103 with fire prevention plans, 218 controls); 6,741 community–year observations
authors: Stein, D.; Minniti, M.
theories: collective action theory (Ostrom, 1990, 2010); distributed / local knowledge (Hayek, 1945); public value creation (Mahoney, McGahan & Pitelis, 2009; Cabral et al., 2019); public–private collaborations (Quelin, Kivleniece & Lazzarini, 2017)
keywords: collective action; cross-level collaborations; distributed knowledge; local knowledge; public value; public–private collaborations; self-organizing communities
research_question: How and why do self-organizing communities create public value — often achieving outcomes superior to those of higher-level public organizations alone — and how do the breadth of stakeholder participation and cross-level collaborations with higher-level public organizations shape this value creation?
hypotheses:
H1. More public value is created in communities that self-organize than in communities that rely solely on existing public organizations.
H2. More public value is created in communities that, in addition to self-organizing, rely on the participation of more stakeholders than in communities relying on fewer stakeholders — though this relationship is nonlinear.
H3. More public value is created in communities that, in addition to self-organizing, collaborate with higher-level public organizations than in communities that do not.
H3a. More public value is created in communities that, in addition to self-organizing, collaborate more actively with higher-level public organizations than in communities that do not collaborate as actively.
mechanism_summary:
- Mediator (theorized, not directly tested): mobilization of otherwise-idle distributed local knowledge (Hayek, 1945)
- Instrument: climate shocks (largest month-over-month drop in SPEI over the preceding 15 fire seasons), used to instrument a community's propensity to self-organize
- Reinforcing conditions: the number of participating stakeholders and the extent of cross-level collaboration reinforce the self-organizing effect on public value

The paper argues that self-organizing communities function as repositories of distributed local knowledge — the decentralized, place-specific understanding held by community stakeholders (Hayek, 1945) — that would otherwise remain idle. When communities self-organize and, in particular, collaborate across hierarchical levels with higher-level public organizations, they mobilize this local knowledge and combine it with the "global," place-neutral best-practice knowledge of higher-level agencies, enabling contextualized solutions, reducing market frictions, and creating public value in the form of fewer property losses, even without formal contracts. Because the number of stakeholders and the intensity of cross-level collaboration shape how much knowledge is pooled, they reinforce the self-organizing effect. The authors are explicit that they cannot test the knowledge mechanism directly; it is inferred from FPP content and the pattern of results, so alternative mechanisms (better coordination, stronger incentive alignment, or a richer resource environment) cannot be ruled out.
data_measures:
Data: an original longitudinal (panel) dataset of community-based fire prevention plans (FPPs) in the seven northernmost counties of California, 1998–2018. The authors identify 321 communities (human settlements); 103 had adopted an FPP by 2018 and 218 serve as controls, yielding 6,741 community–year (community–fire dyad) observations. FPP participant lists were hand-coded for stakeholder counts and collaboration structure; QGIS/GIS geospatial (nearest-neighbor) matching linked communities to CAL FIRE fire perimeters; property-loss data come from the National Wildfire Coordinating Group, CAL FIRE, and the National Fire Incident Reporting System.
DV: property loss (proxy for public value) = number of public and private structures destroyed by wildfires per community-year, entered with an inverse hyperbolic sine transformation.
IVs: fire prevention community and fire prevention plan (dummies); stakeholders (count of represented organizations plus unaffiliated individuals; robustness uses ind. stakeholders and org. stakeholders separately); cross-level collaboration (binary; the FPP references a collaboration with a higher-level public organization); cross-level diversity (Blau's 1977 index); and extensive / concentrated / limited cross-level collaboration (latent components from a polychoric PCA of collaboration characteristics).
Identification: two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) difference-in-differences (DiD) and 2SLS instrumental-variable DiD with community fixed effects; the instrument is climate shocks (the largest month-over-month decrease in SPEI over a community's preceding 15 fire seasons). Controls: fire risk, community-at-risk (CAR) designation, SPEI, per-capita income, education, ln(acres burned), ln(distance to nearest fire), and fire-management jurisdictions. Robustness: Goodman-Bacon decomposition of the staggered DiD and alternative climate-shock windows (8, 10, 15 years).
key_findings:
Hypothesis 1 is supported: communities that self-organize (create an FPP) experience fewer property losses than communities that do not. In the TWFE DiD, FPP communities see about 5% less property loss per year after plan creation (fire prevention plan b = -0.05, p < .05; no pre-creation difference, b = -0.01, p > .10), and the finding holds in the 2SLS IV DiD (fire prevention plan b = -1.06 / -1.39 / -0.97, p < .05 / .01 / .10 across the 8-, 10-, and 15-year climate-shock windows). The IV also shows FPP-adopting communities are higher-risk on average (fire prevention community b > 0, p < .05–.10), yet the plan itself reduces losses.

Hypothesis 2 is only partially supported. The loss-reducing effect of broader stakeholder participation holds — more stakeholders is associated with less property loss (stakeholders b = -0.01, p < .10 in the TWFE DiD; b = -0.22, p < .05 in the 2SLS IV) — but the hypothesized nonlinear/diminishing-returns pattern is NOT found in the main analysis (stakeholders² not significant). The predicted nonlinearity emerges only in robustness tests using individual- and organization-level stakeholder counts (ind. stakeholders² b = 0.00, p < .10; org. stakeholders² b = 0.01, p < .05).

Hypothesis 3 is supported in the 2SLS IV analysis but not in the unadjusted TWFE DiD: cross-level collaboration is non-significant in the TWFE DiD (b = -0.01, p > .10), whereas in the IV model communities with a cross-level collaboration experience about 51% less property loss (b = -0.72, p < .05).

Hypothesis 3a is supported, with the benefit concentrated in the most active collaborations: extensive cross-level collaborations are associated with the largest loss reductions / best outcomes (b = -0.07, p < .05 in the TWFE DiD; b = -3.15, p < .10 and b = -2.11, p < .05 in the IV); concentrated collaborations show smaller reductions (b = -0.43, p < .05; b = -0.22, p < .10); and limited collaborations are mixed (one positive coefficient, b = 1.04, p < .05, alongside b = -0.18, p < .05, in the IV, though b = -0.05, p < .10 in the TWFE DiD). Robustness (Goodman-Bacon decomposition) confirms FPP communities experience 4%–7% less property loss, and cross-level diversity is associated with less property loss (b = -1.01 / -2.64, p < .05) with a nonlinear component (b = 2.85, p < .05).
theoretical_contribution: The study extends Ostrom's theory of collective action and commons governance by explaining how and why self-organizing communities achieve outcomes superior to those of higher-level public organizations alone, and by positioning the self-organizing community as a distinct organizational form that creates public value rather than merely a context for, or beneficiary of, it. It advances research on public value and public–private collaboration by showing that noncontractual, cross-level collaborations between communities and higher-level public organizations enhance public value, and that their effectiveness is contingent on the type of collaboration (extensive, concentrated, or limited). It also reframes such collaborations as reducing not only resource constraints but also knowledge constraints, theorizing self-organizing communities as repositories of distributed local knowledge (Hayek) whose privileged access to place-specific knowledge is a source of strategic advantage.
practical_implication: For policy, the results support distributed governance: self-organizing communities can be effective producers of public value both independently and alongside higher-level public organizations, and top-down policies that impose homogeneous best practices may underperform because of context mismatch — so local initiatives developed together with state and federal authorities tend to yield better outcomes. The authors suggest these lessons may generalize to other public-value domains they name (public education, water distribution, sewage systems, roads and waste management, and healthcare and public safety). For practice, managers can leverage community-based organizing and other noncontractual, relational governance mechanisms when formal contracts are incomplete or infeasible because coordination costs are high.
limitations: First, the quasi-experimental 2SLS DiD design mitigates but does not fully remove endogeneity — some communities may be more fire-prone for unobservable reasons (though the authors argue this bias likely works against them, since FPP communities are typically those at greatest initial fire risk). Second, public value is difficult to define and measure; the property-loss proxy captures both public and private structures but is not a comprehensive measure and may diverge from alternative operationalizations. Third, the knowledge mechanism cannot be tested directly — FPP content is only an indirect measure of knowledge — so alternative explanations (better coordination, stronger incentive alignment, or a richer resource environment) cannot be ruled out.
future_research: First, future work could test the theory's boundaries in other contexts — settings where community engagement matters less or information asymmetries are less pronounced — and check whether the extensive/concentrated/limited collaboration typology generalizes beyond wildfire management. Second, researchers could test the relative importance and interplay of stakeholder engagement, cross-level collaboration, and subsequent decision-making and resource use, and investigate the specific content and forms of local knowledge leveraged, how it is disseminated, whether the nature of particular stakeholders outweighs broad participation, and whether improved coordination or stronger incentive alignment are the main drivers. Third, future studies could dig into communities' histories and leadership structures to unpack the origins of self-organizing.
abstract: We build on extant theories of collective action and public–private collaborations to unpack the distinctive role self-organizing communities may play alongside other organizations in the creation of public value. We suggest that, when communities self-organize to address a common goal and, in particular, when they collaborate with higher-level public organizations, they discover more and better opportunities to reduce market frictions. Using an original longitudinal dataset of community-level fire prevention plans in Northern California from 1998 to 2018, we find that communities taking local actions and coordinating them with state and federal organizations manage wildfires better and experience fewer property losses than communities that do not organize. The number of stakeholders participating in these collaborations and the extent of the collaborations across hierarchical levels reinforce this effect. We conjecture that one possible mechanism explaining why self-organizing and cross-level collaborations tend to yield positive outcomes may be because they allow stakeholders to benefit from otherwise idle local knowledge. Unpacking the role played by self-organizing communities and their cross-level collaborations is important because it may enable contextualized solutions and prevent the potentially ineffective application of homogenous practices to heterogeneous problems, even in the absence of formal contracts.

title: Temporary Regulations and Institutional Change: Insights from the Brazilian World Cup Experience
methods: In-depth qualitative single-case process study (2014 FIFA World Cup, Brazil) with an abductive approach; historical timeline reconstruction plus Gioia-style open and axial coding into first-order concepts, second-order themes, and aggregate theoretical dimensions.
industry: Sports mega-events and beer sales/consumption in football stadiums (Brazilian beer industry)
time_period: Media data 1995-2023; focal event 2014 FIFA World Cup; interviews December 2018-May 2021
units: Institutional actors around beer regulation in Brazilian stadiums (professionals, fans, legislators, FIFA, government, football clubs, beer industry)
n_sample: 52 semi-structured interviews (31 professionals + 21 fans); plus 611 news articles, 66 legal/governmental documents, industry and FIFA reports, and participant observation at 8 matches
authors: Bitektine, A.; Dolbec, P.-Y.; Martins, M.; Kruidenier, S.
theories: institutional theory (institutional work; institutional maintenance); practice theory (Schatzki, 2010; Shove, Pantzar & Watson, 2012)
keywords: counter-normative practice; institutional change; institutional learning; institutional maintenance; institutional work; temporary regulations
research_question: How and why can temporary regulatory changes—regulations adopted for a limited time and typically misaligned with prevailing societal understandings—lead to lasting institutional change? The study asks what path of institutional change temporary regulation initiates, what institutional work such change requires, and what creates variance in temporary-regulation outcomes, using Brazil's temporary legalization of beer sales and consumption in stadiums during the 2014 FIFA World Cup.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Institutional system (practice lens): three recursively aligned elements—understandings, regulations, and practices—sustained by ongoing institutional (maintenance) work.
- Triggering condition: an exceptional circumstance (the 2014 FIFA World Cup and FIFA's demands) prompts a temporary regulation (the Lei Geral da Copa / World Cup Law) that legalizes a counter-normative practice (beer sales and consumption in stadiums) misaligned with prevailing understandings and the durable ban.
- Tension 1 (introducing the temporary regulation): resolved by "discursively countering critiques" (sovereignty critiques; beer-and-violence critiques) and "using power" (FIFA's use of power; governmental use of executive power); allows the counter-normative practice to be performed.
- Tension 2 (managing the temporarily allowed counter-normative practice): resolved by "preventing negative outcomes"—redesigning practice performances (new stadium-security model, stewards, command-and-control standardization) and redefining practice participants from "fan" to "client"—and by "constructing the outcome as 'success'"; generates institutional learning and new understandings.
- Tension 3 (new understandings versus old understandings and regulations): resolved by "undermining practice contentiousness," "presenting the practice as a solution" (economic and security problems), "linking the issue to macro-social discourses" (consumer rights/freedoms; local and international isomorphism), and "exploiting legal ambiguity" (judicial hierarchy; countering legalistic arguments); enables revision of durable regulations and lasting legalization.

A temporary regulation opens a legally protected, publicly visible, time-bounded space in which a counter-normative practice can be performed and widely observed. Actors performing institutional maintenance work to contain the practice's expected negative outcomes—though not seeking institutional change—unintendedly generate new societal understandings (that beer in stadiums does not necessarily cause violence; learning about "how things can be done differently"). Once the temporary regulation lapses and the durable ban returns, interested actors leverage these new understandings to revise durable regulations, producing lasting institutional change with changed practices, understandings, and regulations. The account thus locates institutional maintenance work as an unintended driver of change and offers one resolution to the paradox of embedded agency.
data_measures: Data corpus: 52 semi-structured interviews (December 2018-May 2021) with two sets of interviewees—31 professionals (beer producers, stadium security personnel, venue managers, public administrators, journalists, academics, activists) and 21 football fans sampled across five host states; 611 newspaper articles from Folha de S. Paulo, O Estado de S. Paulo, and O Globo covering 1995-2023 (124 tied to emergent themes); 66 legal and governmental documents (bills, laws, parliamentary hearings) plus Senate hearing videos; beer-industry data (Sicobe, Euromonitor, Passport, Hoovers) and FIFA regulations, bid, and inspection reports; and participant observation at eight FIFA-organized matches. Analysis: abductive, iterating between theory and data; a reconstructed historical timeline of beer regulation; open coding into first-order concepts (e.g., "Training and deploying stewards," "Dissociating beer and violence"), axial coding into second-order themes, and abstraction into aggregate theoretical dimensions organized by the three tensions. Interpretive process design; no causal-identification strategy is claimed.
key_findings: The temporary World Cup Law legalized beer sales and consumption in stadiums for the event only; when it terminated, the durable ban returned, but the new understandings the episode generated persisted. During the event, actors' institutional maintenance work (a preventive FIFA security model, stewards, standardized command-and-control, redefining fans as "clients," and the discursive construction of the World Cup as a "success") kept violent episodes relatively infrequent despite the taken-for-granted beer-violence link; the observed outcome—"the drink was released and there was no increase in violence"—unsettled that link. These new understandings ("beer in stadiums does not necessarily lead to violence") were then leveraged after the event by legislators, football clubs, stadium operators, and the beer industry—through undermining contentiousness, presenting the practice as an economic and security solution, linking to macro-social discourses, and exploiting legal ambiguity—to push for permanent legalization. The result was lasting institutional change: by the study's end thirteen states had authorized beer sales and consumption in stadiums, with the Supreme Federal Court upholding several such state laws (ADI decisions). The paper also shows the outcome is not deterministic—the 2010 South Africa "swift justice" courts illustrate a temporary regulation that lapsed because a negative narrative blocked favorable new understandings.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances institutional theory by identifying a previously unexplored path of institutional change that runs through temporary regulation—distinct both from durable-regulation paths and from temporary organizing—showing that temporary regulations can destabilize a stable institutional order and create a bounded, publicly visible space for practice variation and institutional learning. It extends research on institutional work by demonstrating that institutional maintenance work, performed by actors with no intention of changing institutions, can unintendedly drive lasting change (a solution to the paradox of embedded agency) even in highly visible and tightly controlled settings. It also foregrounds institutional learning about "how things can be done differently"—rather than learning for conformity—as a precursor to institutional change, and identifies facilitating factors such as high public visibility, broad participation, media attention, and the construction of outcomes as "success."
practical_implication: The authors argue that temporary regulations can be a valuable tool for policymakers and regulators, facilitating learning, reducing uncertainty, and complementing experimental and "experimentalist" approaches to regulatory change by piloting alternative practices as time-bounded experiments before committing to durable rules—illustrated with environmental/emission standards and artificial-intelligence governance. They note a parallel use in private governance (temporary self-regulation, e.g., the Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety). They also caution that temporary regulations can be misused to establish states of exception and erode rights (e.g., the U.S. Patriot Act), so their use should be checked by the regulatory review of democratic institutions.
limitations: The authors note that qualitative theory-building from a single context faces limitations and that care is required when discussing transferability. The durable institutional change stemming from a temporary regulation is not deterministic: they identify at least five factors that must be met—overcoming maintenance-work resistance (e.g., through use of power), broad societal observation of the counter-normative practice, outcomes broadly perceived as favorable, generation of novel understandings that challenge the ones supporting existing durable regulations, and legal or political opportunities for renegotiating durable regulations. Not all temporary regulations produce lasting change, as the South Africa "swift justice" counter-example shows.
future_research: The paper explicitly calls for (1) further exploration of the time and temporality of regulation—for example, the effect of temporariness on actors' decisions to support or tolerate counter-normative institutional arrangements; (2) empirical validation of the boundary conditions and generalizability of the findings—including how "success" is socially constructed when relevant actors do not share interests, cannot coordinate, or lack power, and the effect of varying durations and public visibility of the temporary regulation; and (3) deeper study of the role of institutional learning in institutional change, which has so far been largely limited to learning for institutional maintenance.
abstract: While institutional theory has extensively examined how durable regulations contribute to institutional change, little is known about how temporary regulations—pervasive in modern societies—can transform institutions. This study examines how and why temporary regulations can lead to lasting institutional change by analyzing Brazil's temporary legalization of beer sales and consumption in stadiums during the 2014 FIFA World Cup. Using extensive qualitative data, we develop a process model explaining how the introduction of a temporary regulation creates an opportunity for society to experience a counter-normative practice and learn from it. During this period, multiple institutional actors—while pursuing objectives far removed from considerations of institutional change—perform various types of institutional work to contain the practice's expected negative outcomes. This institutional work unintendedly generates new societal understandings about the practice's risks and consequences, which interested actors then leverage to achieve lasting institutional change. We advance institutional theory by identifying an unexplored path of institutional change through temporary regulations, demonstrating how temporary regulations can enable practice variations and institutional learning, and revealing how institutional maintenance work can drive change. Our insights suggest that temporary regulations can be valuable policy tools for reducing uncertainty and enabling learning about alternative institutional arrangements.
