title: Bearing, Belittling, or Befriending Doubt: Understanding Doubt’s Generative versus Corrosive Effect on Entrepreneurs’ Early-Stage Idea Validation
methods: Inductive, longitudinal qualitative study using a grounded theory approach; 308 weekly interviews (~134 hours) with 35 early-stage entrepreneurs (29 in the primary sample) across six incubation cohorts, with archival and participant-observation data; analyzed via open and axial coding, constant comparison, temporal bracketing, visual mapping, and insider-outsider coding.
industry: Early-stage entrepreneurs developing varied business ideas (e.g., art, tech, sustainability, medical) in an incubation program
time_period: 2018-2021 (six consecutive incubation cohorts over roughly three and a half years)
units: Individual early-stage entrepreneurs
n_sample: 29 primary analytic sample (308 interviews with 35 entrepreneurs in total)
authors: Cholakova, M.; Yalcin, U.; Andriopoulos, C.
theories: attribution theory (Weiner, 1985, 2010, 2018); corrosive doubt / opportunity evaluation (McMullen & Shepherd, 2006); generative doubt / pragmatist inquiry (Locke, Golden-Biddle & Feldman, 2008); goal-disengagement theory (Brandstätter & Bernecker, 2022); self-regulation and goal-striving theory (Carver & Scheier, 1998; Gollwitzer, 2012)
keywords: attribution; doubt; doubt regulation; idea validation; idea-related doubt; self-desirability; self-feasibility; self-related doubt
research_question: How do different types of doubt emerge as entrepreneurs work to validate an early-stage idea, and how and why do their responses to these doubts play a corrosive or a generative role in their ability to identify the value of the idea and sustain their commitment to that goal?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Trigger: perceived lack of desired goal progress (a shared starting point across participants).
- Causal attribution (Weiner): the progress shortfall is read as internal–controllable, internal–uncontrollable, or external–uncontrollable.
- Types of doubt made salient: idea-related doubts; self-related doubts — self-feasibility (ability) and self-desirability (personal attractiveness/motivation).
- Doubt regulation responses (practices): embracing, normalizing, downplaying.
- Emergent orientations to further goal-directed effort: mastering (engagement), yearning (disengagement), curtailing (disengagement).

When entrepreneurs perceive a shortfall in goal progress, the causal attribution they make renders particular doubts salient and shapes how they regulate them. An internal–controllable attribution (insufficient effort) yields aspirational self-doubts alongside idea doubts that entrepreneurs embrace, freeing cognitive capacity to question and refine their product-market beliefs, surface interim proof of concept, and maintain self-desirability beliefs (a mastering orientation). An internal–uncontrollable attribution (lack of ability) yields ruminative self-feasibility doubts that entrepreneurs normalize; these hijack attention from idea doubts, limit proof of concept, and erode self-desirability into gradual disengagement (a yearning orientation). An external–uncontrollable attribution preserves self-confidence but leads entrepreneurs to downplay idea doubts, so they under-engage, gain little clarity, and disengage by conditioning effort on external factors (a curtailing orientation). The cycle repeats, with embracing making doubt generative and normalizing or downplaying making it corrosive for identifying the idea's value and sustaining commitment.
data_measures: Data comprised 308 weekly follow-up interviews (~134 hours of audio) plus intake interviews with 35 entrepreneurs (29 in the primary analytic sample) followed across six consecutive incubation cohorts, triangulated with archival materials (training slides, business model canvases, newsletters, press) and 116 pages of participant-observation memos. Analysis was inductive and interpretive with no causal-identification strategy: open coding in NVivo, constant comparison, and axial coding; doubt and confidence were coded on a continuum, with doubts further distinguished by direction (self vs. idea); temporal bracketing isolated episodes of lower-than-desired progress as comparative units; visual mapping and an insider–outsider coding procedure (Gioia et al., 2013) supported the emergent process model.
key_findings: The study surfaces a doubt-regulation process model with three recurrent paths, distinguished by how entrepreneurs attributed a perceived lack of goal progress. (1) Mastering (generative): internal–controllable attributions produced aspirational self-doubts and embraced idea doubts, letting entrepreneurs surface interim proof of concept, maintain self-desirability beliefs, and sustain commitment. (2) Yearning (corrosive): internal–uncontrollable attributions produced ruminative self-feasibility doubts that were normalized; attention stayed trapped on the self, proof of concept remained limited, self-desirability doubts emerged, and entrepreneurs disengaged by passively hoping and indulging in positive fantasies. (3) Curtailing (corrosive): external–uncontrollable attributions preserved self-confidence but led entrepreneurs to downplay idea doubts, gain little clarity, and disengage by conditioning effort on external factors and procrastinating. Across paths, self-feasibility and self-desirability doubts resurfaced after action had commenced, and only the embracing response made doubt generative for identifying the idea's value and sustaining goal commitment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes three contributions to research on doubt in entrepreneurial action. First, it shows empirically that self-feasibility doubts (about one's ability) resurface after entrepreneurial action has commenced, alongside idea-related doubts, rather than being resolved beforehand as opportunity-evaluation accounts assume. Second, by drawing on self-regulation and goal-striving theory, it demonstrates limits to entrepreneurial motivation, showing how resurfacing self-desirability doubts erode sustained commitment. Third, it integrates the previously divergent corrosive and generative perspectives on doubt into a doubt-regulation process model that specifies the conditions (causal attributions) under which and the mechanisms (embracing, normalizing, downplaying) through which doubt becomes generative or corrosive.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that supporting entrepreneurs in making effort-based (internal, controllable) attributions and in embracing—rather than ruminating over or dismissing—their doubts could help them keep engaging in idea validation and avoid premature disengagement. They point to interventions that build entrepreneurial self-efficacy and foster growth mindsets as potentially useful in early-stage support and education settings.
limitations: The authors note that their sample is composed mostly of novice entrepreneurs with little prior entrepreneurial experience, so the triggers for progress reflections may partly be artifacts of the milestones set by the incubator. They can only speculate about the origins of participants' attributions (e.g., perceived self-efficacy), which were not directly measured, and they cannot yet demonstrate whether entrepreneurs who embraced their idea doubts avoid classic decision-making biases over the longer term.
future_research: The paper calls for longitudinal research on whether entrepreneurs who embrace idea doubts still fall prey to classic decision-making biases over time, and for engagement with the literature on effective reasoning strategies under uncertainty. It suggests examining psychological-ownership reappraisal and whether "market-approved" representations of an idea retain enough personal desirability to warrant continued effort, as well as how intra- and inter-individual progress comparisons, their timing, and accompanying emotions shape what makes a progress shortfall a trigger. It also points to the role of founders' prior background and experience, the origins of attributions in perceived self-efficacy, and intervention-based designs in the pre-entry learning period to prevent premature abandonment of ideas.
abstract: Doubt in the early-stage entrepreneurial process is pervasive. However, we argue that our understanding of the types of doubt individuals experience during entrepreneurial action— and how their responses to these doubts affect their ability to determine the value of their ideas and remain committed to this goal—remains incomplete. When entrepreneurs set out to validate their ideas, doubt is typically framed in one of two ways: as corrosive or as generative. In both perspectives, the focus is on idea-related doubts, overlooking the possibility that once entrepreneurial action commences, self-related doubts about one's abilities or motivation may resurface. Furthermore, while the generative approach provides valuable insights into how entrepreneurs can engage with idea doubts, it tells us little about why some individuals can do so while others may not. To address these questions, we followed early-stage entrepreneurs weekly during an incubation program. We found that they experienced not only idea-related but also self-related doubts. Their responses to these doubts— namely embracing, downplaying, or normalizing them—shaped their ability to make progress toward their goal and influenced their commitment to it. Ultimately, this commitment was underpinned by the emergence of three distinct orientations toward expending further goal-directed effort: mastering, curtailing, or yearning.

title: Constraints, Competencies, or Choices? How Lay Theories of the Gender Gap Impact Diversity Support
methods: Multimethod, five studies. Study 1a: hybrid inductive-deductive open-ended coding of survey responses and newspaper reader comments, with two-rater interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa). Study 1b: exploratory factor analysis (principal axis factoring, oblimin rotation) plus second-order CFA scale development. Study 2: hierarchical and k-medoids cluster analysis of locus/controllability attributions. Study 3: two-wave field survey with OLS regression and 10,000-resample bias-corrected bootstrapped serial mediation (lavaan). Study 4: preregistered experiment (scientific human-capital-report manipulation) with one-way ANOVA and mediation. Design is correlational (Study 3) plus an experimental causal test (Study 4).
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: News-article reader comments from articles published 2015-2020 (Study 1a); survey data-collection dates not otherwise reported
units: Individual working adults (online-panel participants) and online newspaper commenters
n_sample: Study 1a: 300 (Sample A) plus 685 online comments coded to 779; Study 1b: 361; Study 2: 190; Study 3: 450; Study 4: 680
authors: Flynn, E.
theories: attribution theory (Weiner, 1985; Weiner, Perry & Magnusson, 1988); lay theories / naïve scientist perspective (Hong, Levy & Chiu, 2003)
keywords: attribution theory; controllability; diversity initiative support; gender gap; lay theories; personal choice
research_question: Beyond demographics and ideology, do employees form lay theories about why the gender gap persists, and how do those lay theories shape support for (versus resistance to) diversity initiatives? Specifically, through what attributional process (locus and controllability of the gap, and women's resulting perceived responsibility) does each lay theory affect diversity initiative support?
hypotheses:
H1. Endorsement of the organizational barriers theory is negatively related to attributions that the gender gap stems from factors (a) internal to and (b) controllable by women themselves.
H2. Endorsement of the dispositional factors theory is positively related to attributions that the gender gap stems from factors internal to women.
H3. Endorsement of the personal choice theory is positively related to attributions that the gender gap stems from factors (a) internal to and (b) controllable by women themselves.
H4. Attributions that the gender gap stems from factors (a) internal to and (b) controllable by women are positively related to beliefs that women are responsible for the gender gap.
H5. Belief in women's responsibility for the gender gap in career attainment is negatively associated with support for diversity initiatives.
H6. The organizational barriers theory has two positive indirect effects on diversity support due to decreased (a) internality and (b) controllability attributions, both of which predict lower responsibility assigned to women.
H7. The dispositional factors theory has one negative indirect effect on diversity support due to increased internality attributions, which predict greater responsibility to women.
H8. The personal choice theory has two negative indirect effects on diversity support due to increased (a) internality and (b) controllability attributions, both of which predict greater responsibility to women.
H9. The personal choice theory is more detrimental to diversity initiative support relative to the dispositional factors theory.
H10. The personal choice theory is more likely to be endorsed for gender gaps than for racial gaps in career attainment.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on classic attribution theory (Weiner, 1985), the paper argues that lay theories differ in the locus (internal vs. external) and controllability they imply for the gender gap, and that these two dimensions jointly determine how responsible women are held for the gap, which in turn drives diversity support. Attributing the gap to organizational barriers implies external, uncontrollable causes, lowering women's responsibility and raising support. Attributing it to dispositional factors implies internal (but not necessarily controllable) causes, raising responsibility and lowering support via one path. Attributing it to personal choices implies causes both internal to and controllable by women, producing the highest responsibility and lowest support via two paths — making the personal choice theory the most undermining.
data_measures: Five studies triangulate qualitative and quantitative data. Study 1a inductively-deductively coded open-ended explanations for the gender gap from a Prolific working-adult sample (Sample A) and archival newspaper reader comments (Sample B; NYT, WSJ, Washington Post), with two blind raters and Cohen's kappa reliability. Study 1b developed a lay-theory scale from an initial 50 items via EFA and second-order CFA, yielding a 30-item measure of three theories (organizational barriers, dispositional factors, personal choices; with a competence subdimension). Study 2 measured the locus and controllability implied by each first-order category (three items each, alpha approximately .97) and cluster-analyzed them. Study 3 (two-wave field survey, controlling for age, gender, race, political orientation, internal motivation to control prejudice, and diversity experience) measured the 30-item lay theories, locus/controllability attributions (four items each, alpha .93/.95), women's responsibility (three items, alpha .94; adapted from Tang et al., 2020), and diversity initiative support (three items, alpha .94; adapted from Bell et al., 2000). Study 4 manipulated lay theory (four conditions: organizational barriers, dispositional factors, personal choices, control) via an annual-report message and measured attributions, responsibility, diversity initiative support (alpha .96), and diversity prioritization (ranking). Causal identification rests on the randomized Study 4 experiment; Study 3 is explicitly correlational.
key_findings: In the Study 3 field survey (N = 450) the author reports full support for H1–H10. Organizational barriers was negatively associated with internal (b = −0.48, p < .001) and controllable (b = −0.55, p < .001) attributions (H1). Dispositional factors was positively associated with internal (b = 0.20, p = .002) but not controllable (b = 0.14, p = .058) attributions (H2). Personal choices was positively associated with internal (b = 0.25, p < .001) and controllable (b = 0.21, p = .002) attributions (H3). Internality (b = 0.33) and controllability (b = 0.19) positively predicted responsibility (H4), and responsibility was negatively associated with diversity support (b = −0.16, p = .033; H5). The predicted indirect effects held (H6–H8), the negative controllability path was significant for personal choices only (H9), and personal choice was endorsed more for gender than racial gaps (b = 1.18, p < .001; H10). Two unexpected direct effects emerged: organizational barriers had a positive direct effect on support (b = 0.36, p < .001) and personal choices a negative direct effect (b = −0.13, p = .021). The Study 4 experiment (N = 680) supported H2–H8 (H6 only partially, via decreased controllability rather than locus) but did NOT support H1 (the organizational-barriers message did not lower attributions relative to control) or H9 (the negative indirect effects of personal choices did not differ in size from dispositional factors). Dispositional-factors and personal-choice messages causally raised internality and controllability attributions, increasing women's perceived responsibility and lowering both diversity support and prioritization.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces "gender gap lay theories," shifting explanations of diversity support from perceiver characteristics (self-interest, ideology) to attributional sensemaking about why groups achieve less, and offering a more dynamic, malleable account of support. It identifies attribution of the gap to personal choice — rather than competence or discrimination — as a novel driver of the maintenance of gender inequality that reinforces the gender hierarchy while appearing gender-neutral. It shows that gender gaps are attributed to personal choice more than racial gaps, implying diversity resistance varies by target group, and it extends organizational attribution theory by showing internal factors differ in perceived controllability (traits vs. choices), which is consequential for how much blame women receive.
practical_implication: For organizational leaders, the findings suggest that assessing and targeting employees' beliefs about why the gender gap persists is key to increasing diversity initiative support and efficacy. Because lay theories form partly from workplace observation, leaders should be attuned to the rhetoric they use: for example, rather than emphasizing that women leave at higher rates (which can increase internal attributions), they can acknowledge how their own incentive structures and ideal-worker norms make advancement harder for women (increasing external attributions). Organizations are also advised to incorporate awareness of how gender gap lay theories shape diversity attitudes into diversity training, addressing the gap between lay and academic understandings of how controllable women's career choices actually are.
limitations: The Study 3 design is correlational, limiting causal claims (addressed by the Study 4 experiment), and the samples skewed female and White, which the author frames as a conservative test. Diversity-support measures were global, so the type of initiative might moderate the relationships, and the boundaries between lay-theory categories (and between individual-level choice and group-level norms, or choices vs. demands) are hard to define precisely. In Study 4 there was little evidence that manipulating the organizational-barriers theory shifted attributions, and the dispositional-factors and choice conditions became unexpectedly positively associated with support after attributions were controlled.
future_research: The author calls for research on whether lay theories differ depending on which aspect of the gender gap is highlighted (e.g., STEM vs. top leadership) and on how work-family decisions are construed (choices vs. demands). Further work should clarify the role of locus and controllability attributions, examine whether ambivalence toward diversity reflects interactions between lay theories and self-interest or ideology, and test whether lay theories explain why some initiatives (e.g., leadership training vs. diversity slates) are supported more than others. Additional stated directions include how gender gap lay theories form within organizations (culture, leader rhetoric, ideal-worker norms) and studying gender gap attributions from the organization's perspective.
abstract: Resistance to diversity initiatives can undermine their effectiveness. I advance insight into diversity support by identifying lay theories about why the gender gap persists. I identify three gender gap lay theories, which differ in the implied locus and control women have over the gap. These attributions shape women’s perceived responsibility, which, in turn, undermines diversity initiative support. Attributing the gap to organizational barriers is positively associated with diversity support because it implies the causes are external and uncontrollable by women. Attributing the gap to dispositional factors (e.g., traits) is negatively associated with diversity support because it implies the causes are internal to women (but not necessarily controllable). Finally, attributing the gap to women’s personal choices is negatively associated with diversity support because it implies the causes are both internal to and controllable by women; thus, it is most undermining overall. I test these ideas in five multimethod studies, which generally support my theory. I also find gender gaps are attributed to personal choice more than racial gaps are. Overall, this project suggests that, beyond demographics and ideology, sensemaking about the causes of gender inequality and, in particular, the belief that it is due to personal choice, significantly undermines diversity support.

title: Understanding I-Deals through the Social Ledger Lens: The Role of Trust and Hindrance Networks
methods: Two-study, multisource, multiwave (time-lagged) field design; multilevel path modeling in Mplus 8.4; relative weight analysis (RWA) for relative importance; Monte Carlo resampling (20,000 draws) for (moderated) indirect effects; simple-slopes and Johnson-Neyman probing of cross-level moderation. Associational (non-experimental) design.
industry: Midsize restaurants / food service (Study 1); large retail business (Study 2)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employees nested within supervisor-led workgroups (multisource: employee, coworker, supervisor)
n_sample: Study 1: 305 employees in 57 workgroups/supervisors; Study 2: 502 employees and 101 supervisors
authors: Jahantab, F.; Anand, S.; Vidyarthi, P. R.; Erdogan, B.
theories: social comparison theory (Buunk & Gibbons, 2007); social exchange theory (Blau, 1964); social ledger model (Labianca & Brass, 2006)
keywords: hindrance network centrality; idiosyncratic deals (i-deals); negative asymmetry; network density; social ledger model; task performance; trust network centrality
research_question: How does an employee’s position in the workgroup’s social networks — centrality in the trust network (a social asset) versus the hindrance network (a social liability) — and the density of those networks shape the employee’s ability to secure i-deals, and how do i-deals transmit these network effects to task performance?
hypotheses:
H1. Centrality in the workgroup’s trust network is positively related to i-deals.
H2. Centrality in the workgroup’s hindrance network is negatively related to i-deals.
H3. Relative to trust network centrality, hindrance network centrality is more strongly related to i-deals (negative asymmetry).
H4. Centrality in the trust network indirectly and positively affects task performance via i-deals.
H5. Centrality in the hindrance network indirectly and negatively affects task performance via i-deals.
H6. Hindrance network density moderates the relationship between trust network centrality and i-deals such that when the hindrance network is dense, this positive relationship is stronger.
H7. Hindrance network density moderates the indirect relationship between trust network centrality and task performance via i-deals such that when the hindrance network is dense, this positive indirect relationship is stronger.
H8. Trust network density moderates the relationship between hindrance network centrality and i-deals such that when the trust network is dense, this negative relationship is stronger.
H9. Trust network density moderates the indirect negative relationship between hindrance network centrality and task performance via i-deals such that when the trust network is dense, this negative relationship is stronger.
mechanism_summary: Under the social ledger model, being central in the trust network confers reputation, influence, and privileged access to private information, which raise both the employee’s confidence to seek an i-deal and the leader’s willingness to grant one at low perceived social cost; being central in the hindrance network marks the employee as difficult, lowering coworker acceptance and leader support. Because hindrance ties are rarer and more diagnostic than trust ties, they weigh more heavily (negative asymmetry). Integrating social comparison theory, a contrasting network context sharpens the salience of one’s centrality, so a dense hindrance network amplifies the benefit of trust centrality (and, symmetrically, a dense trust network was predicted to amplify the harm of hindrance centrality). Finally, per social exchange theory, employees who obtain i-deals reciprocate with greater task performance, carrying the network effects downstream.
data_measures:
Two field studies. Study 1: 305 employees nested in 57 supervisor-led workgroups across 70 midsize restaurants in a Southwestern U.S. city; multisource and time-lagged (employees reported network ties and i-deals at Time 1; supervisors rated task performance one month later at Time 2). Study 2: 502 employees and 101 supervisors in a large retail business in Iran, using a multisource, three-wave design.
- I-deals: Study 1, 6-item scale from Rousseau, Hornung, and Kim (2009) (α = .82); Study 2, 9 items adapted from Rosen et al. (2013) (α = .70).
- Trust network centrality: in-degree from a single sociometric item (Lau & Liden, 2008) — coworkers checkmarked those with whom they "talk about confidential work-related matters"; scored as the count of times a focal employee was named.
- Hindrance network centrality: in-degree adapted from Sparrowe et al. (2001) — Study 1, coworkers named those they "avoid because he or she is difficult for me to work with"; Study 2, "[Name] hinders my work"; scored as count of times named.
- Network density: number of direct ties divided by the maximum possible ties in the group (Burt, 1992).
- Task performance: supervisor-rated 4-item scale (Tsui, 1984; Tsui & Gutek, 1984) (α = .87).
- Controls: LMX (Graen & Uhl-Bien, 1995), employee age, sex, dyadic tenure, and group size; Study 2 additionally controlled status, neuroticism, emotional intelligence, proactive personality, and group justice climate.
Analysis used multilevel path modeling (Mplus 8.4), relative weight analysis for relative importance (H3), and Monte Carlo resampling for (moderated) indirect effects. The design is associational and time-lagged; the authors caution it is not experimental or longitudinal and cannot rule out reverse causality.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: trust network centrality was positively related to i-deals (Study 1 γ = 0.14, p < .05; Study 2 γ = 0.12, p < .05).
- H2 supported: hindrance network centrality was negatively related to i-deals (Study 1 γ = −0.31, p < .01; Study 2 γ = −0.41, p < .01).
- H3 supported (negative asymmetry): hindrance centrality explained far more variance in i-deals than trust centrality (Study 1: 58.80% vs. 8.41%, ΔR² = 50.39; Study 2: 55.89% vs. 25.62%, ΔR² = 30.27).
- H4 supported: positive indirect effect of trust centrality on task performance via i-deals (Study 1 b = .02, 95% CI [.001, .054]; Study 2 b = .03, 95% CI [.001, .062]).
- H5 supported: negative indirect effect of hindrance centrality on task performance via i-deals (Study 1 b = −.05, 95% CI [−.113, −.015]; Study 2 b = −.11, 95% CI [−.154, −.073]).
- H6 supported: hindrance network density strengthened the positive trust-centrality → i-deals relationship (Study 1 γ = 0.24, p < .01; Study 2 γ = 0.28, p < .01); the relationship was positive under high hindrance density and nonsignificant under low density.
- H7 supported: the positive indirect trust-centrality → task-performance effect (via i-deals) held when hindrance density was high and was nonsignificant otherwise.
- H8 not supported: trust network density did not moderate the hindrance-centrality → i-deals relationship (Study 1 γ = 0.04, ns; Study 2 γ = 0.02, ns).
- H9 was not tested because H8 failed.
- Unexpected: in Study 1, hindrance network density × hindrance centrality was significant (γ = −0.30, p < .01) — hindrance centrality's negative relation with i-deals was stronger when the hindrance network was dense.
- Supplementary (Study 2): the model held for i-deals that were "asked for and granted," but not for i-deals "asked for" alone or "granted without being asked," reinforcing i-deals as employee-initiated and successfully negotiated.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes three contributions in its own terms. First, it integrates i-deals research into the social network perspective, relocating the driver of i-deals from individual traits and dyadic factors (e.g., proactivity, LMX) to the broader workgroup network structure. Second, it theorizes and empirically substantiates the long-assumed but previously untested negative asymmetry of the social ledger — hindrance (negative) ties outweigh trust (positive) ties in explaining i-deals. Third, it introduces network density as a moderator by integrating the social ledger model with social comparison theory, showing that a contrasting tie context (e.g., dense hindrance ties) amplifies the value of one's centrality in the opposing (trust) network.
practical_implication: For managers, HR, and line managers, i-deals are a tool to motivate performance when the interests of employees, coworkers, workgroups, leaders, and the organization are aligned. Social structure can enable or bar access: employees central in trust networks — and especially those not central in hindrance networks — are advantaged, and trusted employees are further advantaged when hindrance ties are prevalent in the group. Because employees with the greatest need for customized arrangements (e.g., someone caring for a sick parent) may be structurally disadvantaged, managers can grant flexible schedules to help move such employees out of the hindrance network, but must do so carefully and with clear communication to the whole team. At the organizational level, HR and line managers should weigh workgroup member composition and train employees to build positive ties (trust, friendship, advice) while minimizing negative ties.
limitations: The time-lagged design is not experimental or longitudinal, so reverse causality cannot be ruled out (e.g., i-deal recipients may later attract social ties). The theorized social-comparison mechanics were not directly measured. In Study 1, the hindrance measure may have confounded avoidance with hindrance. Some potentially relevant controls (e.g., ties outside the workgroup, leaders' personality, team-level factors) were omitted, and centrality — an aggregation of many coworkers' reactions — may be relatively insensitive to a focal employee's recent i-deal.
future_research: The authors call for empirically verifying the underlying social-comparison mechanisms — for example, tracing the co-evolution of network development and i-deals negotiations over time and using realistic experimental designs to clarify causality. They suggest examining additional employee-level (ties outside the workgroup, past performance), leader-level (leaders' personality, psychological process in granting i-deals, leader's-leader exchange [LLX]), and workgroup/organization-level factors (team potency, turnover rate). They also encourage testing other outcomes such as employee innovation and creativity, counterproductive work behavior, and turnover, and investigating how social networks develop and i-deals are dispensed in virtual environments and in multicultural workgroups.
abstract: Individually negotiated customized work arrangements or idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) are an increasingly common practice in contemporary organizations. We propose that these deals are created and implemented in the social context of the workgroup and that one’s position in the web of social relationships serves as a strategic advantage or barrier to accessing i-deals. Drawing on the social ledger model, we propose that being central in the trust network is positively associated with i-deals, whereas being central in the hindrance network is negatively associated with i-deals, with indirect effects on employee performance. Further, we predict that i-deals are affected more strongly by centrality in the hindrance network than by centrality in the trust network. Finally, we theorize that trust network density strengthens the negative relationship between hindrance network centrality and i-deals and that hindrance network density strengthens the positive relationship between trust network centrality and i-deals. Results of multilevel modeling and relative importance analyses in two field studies employing data from 305 employees and 57 supervisors in the United States and 502 employees and 101 supervisors in Iran provided support for our model. Implications and future directions for social network and i-deals research are discussed.

title: Diversity Incentives Can Increase Women’s Aspirations to Lead
methods: Four preregistered experiments: a field experiment (Study 1) analyzed with OLS (linear probability) regressions and cluster-robust standard errors clustered at the manager level; an incentive-compatible online experiment (Study 2) with OLS and robust standard errors; and two online vignette experiments testing mediation via 10,000-sample bootstrapped indirect effects (Study 3A) and moderation via a 2x2 between-subjects design (Study 3B); analyzed in R 4.2.2.
industry: Global telecommunications and engineering company (Study 1 field site); online-panel participants (Studies 2, 3A, 3B)
country: European and Latin American offices (Study 1 field site); online-panel samples not reported by country (Studies 2, 3A, 3B)
time_period: December 2022 annual performance-review cycle (Study 1); online-study timing not reported
units: Individual female employees (Study 1) and individual online participants (Studies 2, 3A, 3B; Study 2 also included men)
n_sample: 2,035 (Study 1 field experiment); 920 (Study 2); 578 (Study 3A); 997 (Study 3B); total online n = 2,495
authors: Kirgios, E. L.; Chang, E. H.
theories: economic signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al., 2011); identity threat / stereotype threat (Branscombe et al., 1999; Steele et al., 2002); social role theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002)
keywords: costly signaling; diversity incentives; expected managerial support; gender diversity; identity threat; leadership aspirations
research_question: Will gender diversity incentives — payouts to managers or executives conditional on progress toward a diversity goal — increase or decrease the leadership aspirations of the women they target? The paper asks how "targets" (women), not just incentivized "actors" (managers), respond when they learn an organization has tied executive or managerial pay to gender diversity goals.
hypotheses:
H1. Diversity incentives will increase female employees' leadership aspirations relative to (a) diversity goals alone or (b) communicating diversity values with no mention of goals or incentives.
H2. Diversity incentives will increase female employees' leadership aspirations via increased expectations of managerial support.
H3. Diversity incentives will decrease female employees' leadership aspirations relative to (a) diversity goals alone or (b) communicating diversity values with no mention of goals or incentives.
H4. Diversity incentives will decrease female employees' leadership aspirations via increased expectations of backlash and stigma.
(H1/H3 and H2/H4 are competing positive-vs-negative predictions drawn, respectively, from an economic signaling account and the dominant identity-threat account.)
mechanism_summary: Drawing on an economic signaling perspective, the authors argue that because diversity incentives are literally costly, they act as a credible organizational signal that leaders will support women's advancement. This raises women's expectations that managers will sponsor them (e.g., nominate them as high-potential, assign visible projects), helping women cross a minimum confidence threshold for expressing leadership aspirations. This costly-signal mechanism competes with the dominant identity-threat account, in which incentives imply women cannot succeed on their own and thus trigger stigma, backlash concerns, and lowered aspirations. The four studies adjudicate between these accounts and locate the mediating role of expected support.
data_measures:
- Study 1 (field experiment, n = 2,035 female employees at a global telecommunications and engineering firm): DV = binary self-evaluation item "I want to manage/continue managing others" (yes = 1/no = 0), embedded in the December 2022 annual performance review; OLS linear-probability regression with cluster-robust standard errors clustered at the manager level; preregistered controls (employee functional-area fixed effects, job stage, tenure, prior-year aspirations, manager gender/tenure/job stage); intention-to-treat (non-responses coded 0), with robustness dropping non-responses (n = 1,549) and coding them as 1.
- Study 2 (incentive-compatible online experiment, n = 920 after preregistered comprehension-check exclusions; includes men): DV = actual decision to apply to be a "leader" in a Niederle & Vesterlund (2007)-style number-grid task with real bonus consequences; OLS with robust standard errors.
- Study 3A (mediation vignette, n = 578 women): DV = 7-point willingness to seek a promotion; mediator = expected managerial support (three-item scale adapted from Ragins & McFarlin's 1990 mentor-roles scale, Cronbach's α = .91); 10,000-sample bootstrapped mediation plus Sobel test.
- Study 3B (moderation vignette, n = 997 women): 2x2 between-subjects (diversity incentives yes/no × manager historical support low/high); DV = 7-point willingness to seek a promotion; preregistered two-sample t tests and an OLS interaction model.
Randomized assignment supports causal interpretation of the treatment effects (the paper flags that manager gender, being non-randomized, cannot be interpreted causally).
key_findings:
- H1 supported across studies (positive effect of incentives). Study 1: women in the goal + incentives condition were 4.9 percentage points more likely to want to lead than control (regression-estimated +11.3%; 95% CI [0.006, 0.091], p = .025) and 4.8 pp more likely than the goal-alone condition (+11.7%; p = .025); the diversity goal alone did not differ from control (estimated change = 0.001, p = .970). Study 2: women's leadership-application rates were significantly higher in the goal + incentives condition (b = .137, SE = .058, p = .018; +13.7% vs. control, +13.3% vs. goal alone), whereas men showed no significant increase (directionally lower, b = −.099, p = .075); significant condition × gender interaction (b = .236, SE = .080, p = .003). Study 3A: incentives raised willingness to seek promotion (M = 6.031 vs. 5.678, t(576) = 3.745, p < .001).
- H2 supported. Study 3A: incentives increased expected managerial support (M = 5.435 vs. 4.862, t(575) = 6.788, p < .001); the bootstrapped indirect effect excluded zero (95% CI [0.191, 0.390]; Sobel b = 0.279, p < .001), with expected support accounting for an estimated 79.1% of the total effect. Study 3B: incentives significantly boosted aspirations when managers had low historical support (M = 5.937 vs. 5.412, t(500) = 4.513, p < .001) but not when support was already high (t(493) = 1.560, p = .119); significant incentives × historical-support interaction (b = .371, SE = .152, p = .015).
- H3 not supported — no evidence that incentives decreased women's aspirations in the field or online. H4 was not empirically tested, because no support for H3 emerged.
- Exploratory: the aspiration boost carried no measurable "quality cost" (no cross-condition difference in the manager-rated quality of women expressing aspirations); in Study 1, women under female managers were less willing to lead at baseline, and the goal-alone effect was stronger for them (goal-alone × female-manager interaction b = 0.111, p = .012), while the goal + incentives effect was less clearly dependent on manager gender.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates an economic, cost-based signaling perspective into research on the consequences of diversity initiatives, challenging the dominant identity-threat / stereotype-threat view that identity-conscious policies decrease women's aspirations. By showing that "targets" (women), not only incentivized "actors" (managers), respond to diversity incentives — and that a costly positive signal shifts women's beliefs that they will be supported — it bridges demand-side and supply-side explanations of the gender leadership gap and repositions women as strategic actors reading organizational signals. It also extends signaling theory by examining how receivers respond to a costly positive signal in an environment of otherwise negative signals, and when such signals matter most (more when a manager's historical support is low, i.e., when a concordant prior signal is absent).
practical_implication: The authors suggest organizations can raise women's aspirations to lead by instituting and communicating gender diversity incentives, rather than trying to change women's self-assessments or beliefs about their own ability. They caution that organizations should be prepared to follow through on such commitments — insincere commitments to diversity can harm marginalized members' sense of belonging, and raising aspirations without real pathways may itself be harmful — so firms should ensure the structures to make good on commitments exist before adopting diversity incentives.
limitations: Study 1 examined a single, male-dominated engineering firm with relatively low baseline gender diversity, which may inflate the benefit of learning about incentives and limit generalization to other industries or less male-dominated firms; the cooperating field partner may also be anomalous. The field study could not directly test the hypothesized mechanism (the firm collected no expected-support items) and provided no data on actual promotions, leaving long-run and behavioral effects unknown. Study 2's high comprehension-check exclusion rate may select for attentive participants, and its low-contact design may mute identity-threat and backlash concerns. Only short-run effects were studied, H4 (backlash/stigma) was never empirically tested, and manager gender was not randomly assigned, precluding causal claims about manager-gender effects.
future_research: The authors call for field research on heterogeneity that would predict when and whether the effects generalize to other industries and less male-dominated firms; on when diversity goals alone act as effective costly signals (depending on goal ambition, advertising, audience, norms, and organizational history); on how majority-group members (men) respond in the field to incentives targeting minorities; on the demand-side impact of incentives (managers' evaluations and actual promotions) and their longer-term effects; on the "separating equilibrium" dynamics of whether firms adopt incentives without intending to follow through, muddying the signal; and on how manager gender shapes women's leadership aspirations.
abstract: To boost diversity, organizations are increasingly using “diversity incentives,” or payouts for managers or executives dependent on progress toward a specific diversity goal. Diversity incentives can affect both actors—managers incentivized to meet the goal— and targets—marginalized group members who are the focus of the incentivized goal. Whereas the effects of incentives on actors are well documented, it is unclear how targets will be affected. We examine how gender diversity incentives affect women’s aspirations to lead. On one hand, diversity incentives may generate identity threat and concerns about backlash among women; on the other, they may be viewed as costly signals of organizational support for women’s leadership aspirations. A preregistered field experiment (n 5 2,035) shows that communicating the existence of organizational diversity incentives increases women’s aspirations to lead by 11.3% relative to sharing a goal-free diversity statement and by 11.7% relative to communicating diversity goals alone. We replicate these findings across three preregistered experiments (total n 5 2,495) and provide evidence that diversity incentives increase women’s expectations of receiving sponsorship from their managers, thereby increasing their willingness to state leadership aspirations. Our findings contribute to our understanding of the drivers of female leadership aspirations.

title: Emotional Signaling: How Helpers’ Emotional Expressions Affect Attributions of Motives, Relationship Quality, and Reciprocation
methods: Multi-study experimental design: a pilot study (N=266) validating the social-engagement dimension of nine discrete emotions; Study 1, a critical-incident recall study (N=221 working adults); Study 2, a video-based lab experiment with a student actor (N=86 undergraduates); Study 3, a preregistered text-vignette in-basket experiment (N=305; N=243 analytic, excluding a no-emotion control). Four emotion conditions (pride, contempt, gratitude, sympathy) modeled as a socially-engaging-vs-disengaging dummy. CFA measurement models; path analysis in Mplus 8 with bias-corrected bootstrapping (10,000 resamples) for indirect effects.
industry: Not industry-specific; general working adults (Prolific Academic) and undergraduate business students (Study 2)
country: United States (Studies 1-3); United States and Canada (pilot)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual recipients of workplace help (working adults; undergraduate students in Study 2)
n_sample: Pilot 266; Study 1 221; Study 2 86; Study 3 305 (243 excluding control condition)
authors: Lee, S. H.; Johnson, M. D.
theories: attribution theory (Heider, 1958; Kelley & Michela, 1980); emotions as social information (EASI) framework (van Kleef, 2009); social engagement–disengagement of discrete emotions (Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Kitayama et al., 2006); social exchange theory / norm of reciprocity (Blau, 1964; Gouldner, 1960); social-functional perspective of emotions (Keltner & Haidt, 1999; Methot et al., 2017)
keywords: attribution of instrumental motives; attribution of prosocial motives; emotional signaling; interpersonal helping; reciprocation; relationship quality; socially disengaging emotions; socially engaging emotions
research_question: When and how do recipients of help attribute different motives to a helper, and how do the helper’s discrete emotional expressions during helping (pride, contempt, gratitude, sympathy) shape those motive attributions and, in turn, the recipient’s relationship quality with and reciprocation toward the helper?
hypotheses:
H1. Recipients are more likely to attribute helping to prosocial motives when helpers express socially engaging emotions (gratitude or sympathy) rather than socially disengaging emotions (pride or contempt).
H2. Recipients are more likely to attribute helping to instrumental motives when helpers express socially disengaging emotions (pride or contempt) rather than socially engaging emotions (gratitude or sympathy).
H3. The attribution of prosocial motives is positively associated with the recipient’s relationship quality with the helper.
H4. The attribution of instrumental motives is negatively associated with the recipient’s relationship quality with the helper.
H5. The attribution of prosocial motives is positively associated with the recipient’s reciprocation toward the helper.
H6. The attribution of instrumental motives is negatively associated with the recipient’s reciprocation toward the helper.
H7. The effect of expressions of discrete emotions on (a) relationship quality and (b) reciprocation is mediated by the attribution of prosocial motives.
H8. The effect of expressions of discrete emotions on (a) relationship quality and (b) reciprocation is mediated by the attribution of instrumental motives.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the emotions-as-social-information (EASI) framework and the social engagement–disengagement dimension of discrete emotions, the paper argues that a helper’s expressed emotions are a salient, immediately accessible cue that signals how the helper is oriented toward the recipient. Socially engaging emotions (gratitude, sympathy) signal interest in and concern for the recipient, prompting attributions of prosocial motives; socially disengaging emotions (pride, contempt) signal status distance and self-orientation, prompting attributions of instrumental motives. Through the lens of social exchange theory and the norm of reciprocity, these attributed motives — especially the attribution of prosocial motives — then determine whether the recipient values the relationship and feels obligated to reciprocate.
data_measures: Identification rests on experimental manipulation of the helper’s expressed emotion with random assignment to four conditions (Study 2 uses student-actor videos; Study 3 uses text-based scenario descriptions plus a no-emotion control; Study 1 uses recalled critical incidents). Mediation is tested via path analysis (Mplus 8) with bias-corrected bootstrapping (10,000 resamples). Mediators: attribution of prosocial motives via a four-item measure (Grant, 2008) and attribution of instrumental motives via a six-item measure (Allen & Rush, 1998), reused across studies. DVs: relationship quality via coworker exchange quality (Sherony & Green, 2002) in Studies 1 and 3 and a two-item peer-evaluation measure in Study 2; reciprocation operationalized behaviorally as interpersonal citizenship behavior (Settoon & Mossholder, 2002) in Study 1 and as incentivized reward-, resource-, time-allocation, and recommendation decisions in Studies 2-3. Study 1 controls for reputational information (morality, compassion), Kelley covariation cues (consistency, distinctiveness, consensus), locus of causality, relative status, and helping norms; Studies 2-3 model affect and perceived character as competing mediators.
key_findings:
Coefficients are reported in Study 1 / Study 2 / Study 3 order; all are standardized path estimates.
- H1 SUPPORTED: expressing socially engaging (vs. disengaging) emotions increased attributions of prosocial motives (b = 0.16, p = .039 / b = 1.21, p < .001 / b = 1.00, p < .001).
- H2 SUPPORTED: socially engaging emotions decreased attributions of instrumental motives (b = -0.54 / -0.65 / -0.84; all p <= .001) — that is, socially disengaging emotions raised instrumental attributions.
- H3 SUPPORTED: attribution of prosocial motives was positively associated with relationship quality (b = 0.18, p = .004 / 0.39 / 0.42; both p < .001).
- H4 NOT SUPPORTED: attribution of instrumental motives was not significantly related to relationship quality in any study (b = -0.02, p = .698 / b = -0.10, p = .256 / b = 0.04, p = .405).
- H5 SUPPORTED: attribution of prosocial motives was positively associated with reciprocation (b = 0.17, p = .022 / 0.40 / 0.49; both p < .001).
- H6 NOT SUPPORTED: attribution of instrumental motives was not significantly related to reciprocation (b = -0.04, p = .361 / b = -0.09, p = .361 / b = -0.10, p = .253).
- H7a and H7b SUPPORTED: the effect of socially engaging emotions on both relationship quality and reciprocation was significantly mediated by the attribution of prosocial motives (bootstrap CIs excluded zero in all three studies).
- H8a and H8b NOT SUPPORTED: the attribution of instrumental motives did not significantly mediate either outcome.
Alternative mediators were weaker than the attribution of prosocial motives and not uniformly significant: in Study 2 the indirect effect through positive affect was significant but the one through negative affect was not, and in Study 3 perceived morality and compassion were significant for relationship quality but weaker or nonsignificant for reciprocation. Net result: only the attribution of prosocial motives (not instrumental motives) consistently drove downstream relationship quality and reciprocation.
theoretical_contribution: First, the paper advances social exchange theory by challenging the presumption of reciprocity: reciprocation of ostensibly positive behavior involves an interpretive element, and it is the helper’s emotional signals of social (dis)engagement — not merely the material benefits exchanged — that give the transaction relational meaning and regulate the norm of reciprocity. Second, it reintegrates an affective perspective into the interpersonal-helping literature by shifting attention from the recipient’s experienced emotions to the helper’s expressed emotions, explaining why helping does not always elicit favorable responses. Third, it extends attribution theory by identifying discrete emotional expressions embedded within the exchange as a salient, accessible source of social information from which recipients infer motives when traditional attributional cues (reputation, behavioral norms) are unavailable.
practical_implication: For leaders — often seen by subordinates as symbolic representatives of the organization and holding greater access to resources for helping — it is important to express emotions that signal prosocial motives when helping in order to strengthen reciprocal bonds, and to cultivate an affective culture that normalizes socially engaging (rather than disengaging) emotions during helping. For employees giving help, good deeds may not be reciprocated when accompanied by emotional signals that recipients do not attribute to prosocial motives; deep-acting emotion regulation and perspective-taking may help elicit authentic socially engaging emotions. For recipients of help, greater awareness of how they process these emotional signals — and, where maintaining the relationship holds practical value, regulating their own attributional processes — can guide their responses.
limitations: There is a risk of common method bias, particularly in Study 1, where focal variables were measured from the same source at the same time (mitigated by inserting controls between mediators and dependent variables and by using different scale formats and in-basket decisions in Studies 2-3, but not fully eliminated). Given the ephemeral nature of emotions, the studies were conducted primarily in controlled settings; while the pilot and Study 1 offer real-work evidence, they cannot establish the real-world frequency of emotional expressions during helping. The studies also focused primarily on anticipatory (rather than reactive) help and on task-related helping.
future_research: The authors call for extending the framework to naturalistic field settings and to reactive help and non-task-related helping domains (e.g., emotion helping), where different emotional expressions may elicit different motive attributions. They suggest examining the broader relational context and temporal dynamics in which episodes of helping are embedded, the role of helpers’ emotion regulation and whether recipients reappraise emotional signals, how virtual/electronic communication alters perceptions of expressed emotions, and how combinations of simultaneously expressed (mixed) emotions and additional discrete emotions (e.g., pity, guilt, disgust, anger) convey social engagement or disengagement.
abstract: Research has shown that interpersonal helping offers many social benefits for the helper, yet these social benefits depend on the recipients’ responses. Whether helping is perceived favorably by recipients depends on the underlying motives they attribute to the helper, which raises the questions of when and how recipients may attribute different motives to helping. To explain when and how those receiving help make these attributions, we adopt a social-functional approach to emotions to examine the impact of the social information conveyed through discrete emotional expressions. We draw on the framework of emotions as social information to theorize that the helper’s emotional expressions act as signals of social engagement or disengagement that differentially impact the recipient’s attribution of motives and reactions to help. Across three studies, we find that helpers’ expressions of socially engaging emotions (gratitude and sympathy) lead to greater attributions of prosocial motives, whereas expressions of socially disengaging emotions (pride and contempt) lead to greater attributions of instrumental motives. We find that the effect of these expressed emotions on relationship quality and reciprocation toward the helper is mediated by the recipient’s attribution of prosocial motives but not by the attribution of instrumental motives.

title: Autonomous, Yet Interdependent: Designing Interfaces across Routine Clusters
methods: 12-month ethnographic single-case study of the reorganization of agile (Scrum) software development at a medium-sized high-tech manufacturing firm ('Technology Innovation Corporation'). Data comprise ~1,000 pages of fieldnotes and 122 hours of audio from 2-3 days/week of observation, 35 formal interviews (30 during fieldwork plus 5 follow-ups two years later), ~6,300 pages of documents and ~2,000 emails, and ~163,000 digital trace actions from Jira. Inductive process analysis in five steps: identifying routine clusters, constructing an event timeline of reorganization, classifying emerging interdependencies via Thompson's (1967) pooled/sequential/reciprocal typology, inductively coding four interface design practices, and modeling the dynamics linking reorganization, interdependencies, and interface design work across three analytical periods.
industry: High-tech manufacturing (agile software development for industrial machines such as cellphone-display cutters and laser battery-pack welders)
time_period: November 2016 - October 2017 (primary fieldwork), with trace data and follow-up interviews extending to 2021
units: Two agile (Scrum) software development teams ('Team Alpha' and 'Team Beta') embedded in one medium-sized firm ('Technology Innovation Corporation', a pseudonym)
n_sample: 2 teams (~10-12 developers, product owners, and Scrum masters in total) within 1 firm
authors: Mahringer, C. A.; Danner-Schröder, A.
theories: interdependence theory (Thompson 1967); organizational design; practice and process ontology; routine dynamics
keywords: Scrum; agile software development; autonomy; interdependence; interface design; organizational design; pooled, sequential, and reciprocal interdependence; resources; routine clusters; routine dynamics
research_question: The paper asks: (1) How do interdependencies emerge during the reorganization of routine clusters? (2) How does the process of designing interfaces to manage those interdependencies unfold?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering conditions: Reorganization of work into two semi-autonomous routine clusters through replication of routines across teams and the sharing of scarce resources (actors and artifacts such as software code).
- Key constructs / tensions: Autonomy aspiration vs. emergent interdependence; pooled, sequential, and reciprocal interdependencies (Thompson 1967); divisibility vs. indivisibility of shared resources; transitory vs. patterning interventions.
- Practices ("interface design work"): analyzing interdependencies, reconfiguring resources, mitigating interferences, and reconfiguring schedules — differentiated along two dimensions: durability (transitory vs. patterning) and design elements (artifacts vs. timing).
- Process / phases: (1) implementing the second cluster and discovering emergent pooled interdependencies; (2) iterative harmonization that escalates pooled interdependencies into sequential and, under time pressure, reciprocal ones; (3) stabilization of interfaces that allows the clusters to operate relatively autonomously.
- Emergent outcomes: Stabilized interfaces between the clusters and a mutually constitutive relationship between resourcing, patterning, and performing.

Because contemporary organizations operate in flux, interdependencies between routine clusters are not exogenously given but emerge as actors replicate routines and share resources across clusters. These emergent pooled interdependencies trigger "interface design work": actors analyze interdependencies and mitigate interferences through transitory adjustments within routine performances, while reconfiguring resources and reconfiguring schedules produce more durable patterning of interfaces. Harmonizing one interdependence often creates new and more complex ones — pooled interdependencies can escalate into sequential ones when reconfiguration work must precede regular work, and sequential interdependencies compress into reciprocal ones under time pressure. Through iterative cycles of creating and harmonizing interdependencies, routine participants themselves act as endogenous designers who eventually stabilize interfaces, disentangling the clusters.
data_measures: Data corpus: a 12-month ethnographic single-case study at "Technology Innovation Corporation" (TIC, a pseudonym), a medium-sized high-tech manufacturing company, drawing on four data sources collected between November 2016 and October 2017 — participant observation (two to three days per week; ~1,000 pages of fieldnotes and 122 hours of audio), 35 formal interviews (30 during fieldwork plus 5 follow-ups two years later, covering at least one member of each of teams Alpha and Beta), ~6,300 pages of documents and ~2,000 emails, and ~163,000 digital-trace actions logged in the Jira issue-tracking system. Analysis proceeded inductively in five steps: abstracting each team's routine cluster and identifying its routines by coding the data with in vivo codes tied to the actors' own language (e.g., Sprint, Refinement, Review, Retrospective routines); constructing an event timeline (Langley, 1999) of the reorganization; classifying the emerging cross-cluster interdependencies with Thompson's (1967) pooled/sequential/reciprocal typology; inductively coding four interface-design-work practices and cross-classifying them by durability (transitory vs. patterning) and design element (artifacts vs. timing); and modeling the dynamics linking reorganization, interdependencies, and interface design across three analytically bracketed periods. Interpretive, process-oriented design; no measurement scales, statistical estimation, or causal-identification strategy is claimed.
key_findings: The study surfaces a process model in which designing interfaces between routine clusters is an endogenous and iterative process of creating and harmonizing emergent interdependencies, carried out by routine participants themselves rather than by detached, exogenous designers. Reorganizing work into two envisioned-autonomous clusters — by replicating Team Alpha's Scrum routines in the new Team Beta and sharing scarce resources (the shared actor "Austin-Blake" and Alpha's code) — generated pooled interdependencies across the clusters. Actors harmonized these through "interface design work," which the authors resolve into four practices: analyzing interdependencies and mitigating interferences (transitory work) and reconfiguring resources and reconfiguring schedules (patterning work), further split by whether they act on artifacts or on timing. A central finding is directional: harmonizing one interdependence tended to create new, more complex ones, so that pooled interdependencies proliferated into sequential ones (when reconfiguring a shared resource had to precede regular Sprint work) and then into reciprocal ones once several harmonizing efforts were temporally compressed under a synchronized joint release date — reciprocal interdependence emerging when sequential interdependence is temporally compressed. Disentangling the clusters therefore paradoxically produced heightened entanglement before, over three periods, the teams stabilized the interfaces so the clusters could operate relatively autonomously; resourcing, patterning, and performing are theorized as mutually constitutive.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances routine dynamics, interdependence, and organizational design research by reframing interface design as an endogenous, iterative process of creating and harmonizing emergent interdependencies, performed by routine participants rather than by detached exogenous architects. It uncovers "interface design work" as four distinct practices differentiated along two dimensions — durability (transitory vs. patterning) and design elements (artifacts vs. timing) — and theorizes a mutually constitutive relationship between resourcing, patterning, and performing. Third, it unpacks the role of resources in interface design, showing that sharing scarce resources generates pooled interdependencies that can escalate into sequential and reciprocal forms, such that disentangling routine clusters may paradoxically produce heightened forms of entanglement before stable autonomy is achieved.
practical_implication: For organizations reorganizing work into more autonomous units, the study suggests that designing the interfaces between those units is less an up-front architectural task than an ongoing, endogenous one: because interdependencies surface as routines are performed and resources are shared, the routine participants themselves are positioned to harmonize them. The paper details four practices through which they do so — analyzing interdependencies, reconfiguring resources, mitigating interferences, and reconfiguring schedules — combining transitory fixes within ongoing routines with more durable patterning of shared artifacts and timing. It also shows that sharing scarce, indivisible resources can escalate pooled interdependencies into sequential and reciprocal ones, so on the paper's account treating interface design as continuous, participant-led work rather than fixed up-front coordination is what sustains the autonomy such reorganization is meant to create.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that their theoretical insights rest on a single 12-month ethnographic case study of two agile (Scrum) software development teams in one high-tech manufacturing firm, so the findings are bounded by this particular context. The setting is one in which both teams valued autonomy and operated with high mutual respect, shared scarce (rather than freely copiable) resources, used Scrum routines that combine task decomposition with regular collective-reflection meetings, and involved only two clusters that replicated essentially the same routines. The authors flag each of these features as scope conditions rather than general properties, noting in particular that the absence of power asymmetries and the presence of Scrum-enabled reflection may have shaped how interface design work unfolded in ways that would not necessarily transfer to other settings.
future_research: The authors identify four boundary conditions inviting further work: (a) settings with more than two clusters sharing resources, or with orchestrated resource allocation across multiple clusters, and settings where resource allocation shifts over time; (b) reorganizations in which autonomy is less central, or which involve clusters with entirely different routines or temporal rhythms, potentially collapsing into a single cluster; (c) contexts where routines are not based on Scrum or task decomposition, and where routines afford less collective reflection, to clarify how task decomposition and reflection shape interface design; and (d) cases of lower mutual respect or power asymmetries between clusters, where breakdowns or alternative resolutions might emerge.
abstract: This paper examines the process of designing interfaces between routine clusters in a world in flux in which interdependencies are emergent. We reveal that designing interfaces is an endogenous and iterative process of creating and harmonizing interdependencies. In our ethnographic study of the reorganization of agile software development, actors implemented a second routine cluster, which they envisioned to work autonomously. Because the teams shared resources, however, they created interdependencies across the two routine clusters that challenged their autonomy. Our findings contribute to research on routine dynamics, interdependence, and organizations design. They do so, first, by showing how the dynamics of designing interfaces are driven by the emergent nature of interdependencies, which routine participants may endogenously harmonize through routine performances. Second, our findings detail the practices through which “interface design work” is accomplished. Although some of these practices imply transitory variations in routine performances, others change the patterning of interfaces more sustainably. Third, resources play an important role in designing interfaces because making them readily available may require their reconfiguration. Moreover, the pooled interdependencies that flow from shared resources can escalate into more complex types of interdependence.
