title: Faking It with the Boss’s Jokes? Leader Humor Quantity, Follower Surface Acting, and Power Distance
methods: Three studies testing a moderated-mediation model in which leader humor quantity (LH quantity) increases follower surface acting and indirectly worsens follower emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction, with follower power distance moderating the first stage. Study 1 is a one-week field experiment with 88 leader-follower dyads at organizations in Southern China, randomly assigning leaders enrolled in a leadership course to a LH quantity intervention or control condition with follower-reported outcomes (Time 2 surveys) and ANOVA plus Mplus 8.5 single-level regression with robust standard errors and bias-corrected bootstrapping (10,000 resamples) for indirect effects. Study 2 is a pre-registered 2 (LH quantity: low vs. high) x 2 (power distance: low vs. high) between-subjects laboratory experiment in 49 focus groups (n = 198 students/employees in the U.S.) led by a trained professional actor-moderator delivering scripted puns and power-distance norms, analyzed via cluster-robust regression accounting for nested groups. Study 3 is a pre-registered three-wave correlational field study at a Southern China technology firm (n = 126 employees) combining employee surveys (Times 1 and 2, separated by ~1 week) with company pulse-survey records (Time 3) for outcomes; analyses use Mplus 8.5 path models (Hayes Models 4 and 7), CFAs, controls for leader humor quality, LMX, charismatic leadership, positive affect, demographics, and 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Supplemental mini meta-analyses across studies, plus exploratory tests of LH quantity x LH quality interactions, mediation, and additive models.
industry: Mixed organizations of Chinese part-time professional-degree managers and their direct subordinates (Study 1); university bookstore focus-group context with student and local-employee participants in the northeastern United States (Study 2); a single technology firm with a project-based structure based in Southern China (Study 3).
country: Study 1: Southern China; Study 2: northeastern United States; Study 3: Southern China
time_period: Study 1: one workweek (Time 1 leader manipulation, Time 2 follower outcomes one week later); Study 2: ~30-minute in-person experimental session; Study 3: three waves spanning approximately two weeks (Time 1, Time 2 ~5 workdays later, Time 3 ~1 week after Time 2).
units: Leader-follower dyads (Study 1); individual focus-group participants nested in 49 groups led by a focus-group leader (Study 2); employees reporting on focal managers within a single firm (Study 3).
n_sample: Study 1: 88 leader-follower dyads (42 control, 46 LH quantity); Study 2: 198 participants across 49 focus groups; Study 3: 126 employees with complete data across all three time points.
authors: Hu, Xiaoran; Parke, Michael R.; Peterson, Randall S.; Simon, Grace M.
theories: emotion regulation (Diefendorff & Gosserand, 2003; Elfenbein, 2007); emotional labor theory (Grandey, 2000; Grandey & Gabriel, 2015; Morris & Feldman, 1996); experience of power and social hierarchy (Magee & Galinsky, 2008); leader humor research (Cooper, 2005; Cooper, Kong, & Crossley, 2018); power distance values (Hofstede, 1980; Kirkman et al., 2009)
keywords: emotion regulation; emotional exhaustion; emotional labor; field experiment; follower surface acting; job satisfaction; laboratory experiment; leader humor quality; leader humor quantity; leader-follower relationships; multi-wave field study; power distance
research_question: Why and when does leader humor quantity (LH quantity) — irrespective of its quality — increase follower surface acting and, through this emotion-regulation pathway, impair follower emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction; and how does follower power distance moderate these effects?
hypotheses:
- H1: Leader humor quantity increases follower surface acting (positive main effect).
- H2: Leader humor quantity has a positive indirect effect on follower emotional exhaustion, mediated by follower surface acting.
- H3: Leader humor quantity has a negative indirect effect on follower job satisfaction, mediated by follower surface acting.
- H4: Follower power distance moderates the positive effect of leader humor quantity on follower surface acting, such that the effect is stronger for high-power-distance followers and weaker for low-power-distance followers (first-stage moderation).
- H5: Leader humor quantity's (a) positive indirect effect on follower emotional exhaustion and (b) negative indirect effect on follower job satisfaction, via surface acting, are moderated by follower power distance, such that the indirect effects are stronger (weaker) for followers with high (low) power distance.
mechanism_summary:
- Mediator: Follower surface acting — masking, faking, or suppressing felt emotions to display positive emotions (amusement, happiness, interest) toward the leader.
- Moderator: Follower power distance — the extent to which followers accept unequal power distribution between leaders and followers (first-stage moderator on LH quantity to surface acting).
- Controls: Leader humor quality, follower positive affect, deep acting, leader-member exchange (LMX), charismatic leadership, follower/leader demographics.

Drawing on emotional labor theory and the experience of power, the authors argue that leader humor signals a strong positive display rule (laughing, smiling, amusement) that followers — as lower-power actors dependent on leaders for resources and acceptance — feel obliged to meet. Because humor is unexpected and individualized, frequent expression creates frequent discrepancies between followers' naturally occurring affect and the expected display, making surface acting (rather than deep acting) the available response-focused regulation strategy. Surface acting then drains cognitive resources and produces inauthenticity, increasing exhaustion and reducing satisfaction. The effect is amplified for high-power-distance followers because (a) compliance with leader display standards is more instrumental to their goals and (b) leader humor more sharply violates their counter-normative expectation that leaders maintain social distance.
data_measures:
The moderated-mediation model is tested across three studies.
- Study 1 (one-week field experiment, 88 leader-follower dyads, Southern China): Leader humor quantity (IV) was manipulated by randomly assigning leaders to an LH quantity intervention vs. a control condition (coded 1/0), with a leader-rated modified Cooper et al. (2018) three-item scale as a manipulation check (α = .90). Follower surface acting (mediator) used an adapted discrete-emotions emotional labor scale (Hu & Shi, 2015) capturing how often followers display amusement, happiness, and interest they do not genuinely feel (α = .91). Emotional exhaustion (DV) used a six-item Wharton (1993) scale (α = .94); job satisfaction (DV) a modified three-item scale (Tepper, 2000) (α = .92). Follower power distance (moderator) used three items from Dorfman and Howell (1988) (α = .62). Controls: follower positive affect (α = .87) and deep acting (α = .93). Identification strategy in the paper's terms: a field experiment with random assignment; ANOVA plus Mplus 8.5 path models (Hayes Models 4 and 7) with 10,000-resample bias-corrected bootstrapping for indirect effects.
- Study 2 (pre-registered laboratory experiment, 198 participants nested in 49 focus groups, northeastern United States): a 2 (LH quantity: low vs. high) × 2 (power distance: low vs. high) between-subjects design in which a trained actor-moderator delivered scripted humor and power-distance norms; both LH quantity and power distance were manipulated, with LH quality and power distance manipulation checks. Analyzed with cluster-robust standard errors in Mplus 8.5 to account for the nested (clustered) groups.
- Study 3 (pre-registered three-wave field study, 126 employees, a Southern China technology firm): LH quantity measured with the Cooper et al. (2018) three-item scale; power distance with the six-item Dorfman and Howell (1988) scale; surface acting with a modified version of the Study 1 scale; outcomes drawn from both employee surveys and company pulse-survey records; controls include LH quality, LMX, positive affect, charismatic leadership, and demographics. The paper describes this study as correlational (associational), not experimental.
key_findings:
Leader humor quantity had no significant main effects on follower well-being outcomes; its effects on emotional exhaustion and job satisfaction operated indirectly through surface acting.
- Study 1 (n = 88 dyads): H1 supported — LH quantity increased surface acting (ANOVA F(1, 86) = 5.50, p = .021; regression b = 0.27, p = .005). Surface acting positively predicted emotional exhaustion (b = 0.43, p < .001) and negatively predicted job satisfaction (b = -0.24, p = .013); H2 and H3 supported (indirect effects via surface acting). H4 supported (LH quantity × power distance on surface acting, b = 0.31, p = .016; positive at high power distance, non-significant at low). H5a and H5b supported.
- Study 2 (n = 198 in 49 groups): H1 supported (b = 0.30, p < .001). Surface acting positively predicted emotional exhaustion (b = 0.34, p < .001) and negatively predicted job satisfaction (b = -0.15, p = .029); H2 and H3 supported. H4 supported (interaction b = 0.36, p < .001; positive at high power distance, non-significant at low). H5a and H5b supported.
- Study 3 (n = 126): H1 supported (b = 0.32, p = .002). H2 supported (surface acting related to company-recorded emotional exhaustion, b = 0.16, p = .037), but H3 not supported (surface acting did not relate to job satisfaction). H4 supported (interaction b = 0.16, p = .015). H5a supported for both the company-recorded and employee-survey measures of emotional exhaustion; H5b not supported for job satisfaction.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the dominant positive view of leader humor on follower well-being by theoretically and empirically distinguishing leader humor quantity from leader humor quality, identifying surface acting as a novel emotion-regulation mechanism through which expressing humor frequently can backfire, and positioning follower power distance as a key moderator of when LH quantity is most damaging. Beyond leader humor research, the work contributes to emotional labor theory by showing that a positively intended leader behavior — not just negative interpersonal events — can elevate surface acting, and to the broader humor literature by adding "how much" and "to whom" as risks alongside the traditional "what kind."
practical_implication: Leaders should scale back the frequency of humor expression and adopt a "less is more" approach — focusing on fewer, higher-reward humor attempts to capture the benefits of humor quality while avoiding the emotional-labor costs of humor quantity, especially because followers are often surface-acting positive feedback that masks the harm. Managers should also calibrate humor to follower power-distance values: high-power-distance followers are more likely to fake positive responses and bear well-being costs, so managers can use existing surveys (e.g., Kirkman et al., 2009 scale) to gauge follower values before expressing humor.
limitations: Sample sizes were modest in Study 1 (n = 88) and Study 3 (n = 126), reducing power to detect direct effects of LH quantity on well-being and possibly affecting measure reliability; the Dorfman-Howell (1988) power distance measure had Cronbach's alpha below the 0.70 threshold in Studies 1 and 3, although within the range reported in prior work. Study 3 was correlational, could not rule out nesting effects given anonymized data, and relied on employees as the source for all model variables, raising common-method-bias concerns despite time separation and supplemental tests.
future_research: Future studies should examine other boundary conditions (e.g., perceived appropriateness of leader humor, follower's own sense of humor, group humor norms, humor styles such as self-enhancing vs. self-defeating) and additional mechanisms beyond surface acting and positive affect — such as follower appreciation of humor attempts — to reconcile the joint effects of LH quantity and LH quality. Within-person/event-level designs that track multiple humor episodes throughout a day, larger and cross-cultural samples with stronger power-distance measures, and disentangling leader power from follower power distance would help specify the optimal ratio of high- versus low-quality humor and identify factors (e.g., leaders explicitly acknowledging display rules) that mitigate the harms of LH quantity for high-power-distance followers.
abstract: Most scholarly work concludes that leader humor positively affects emotional outcomes for followers. However, two interrelated issues with past research make this view incomplete: (a) studies often conflate the act of expressing humor with the humor’s effectiveness, and (b) existing research overlooks follower emotion regulation. In addressing these issues, we generate and test new theory that challenges the theoretical consensus, highlighting why and when leader humor expression has emotional costs for followers. Specifically, we theorize that leader humor quantity, irrespective of its quality, puts pressure on followers to engage in “surface acting” to fake or exaggerate positive emotions. We further propose that these surface acting responses are more likely to occur when followers hold high power distance values, such that followers more willingly comply with expectations to display positive emotions in response to leader humor expression. This increase in surface acting then leads to more emotional exhaustion and less job satisfaction for followers. Results from three studies—incorporating a field experiment, a laboratory experiment, and a multi-wave field study—provide support for these hypotheses. We close with a discussion of how our findings provide a unique counterpoint regarding the effects of leader humor on follower emotional outcomes.

title: Hiding and Seeking Knowledge-Providing Ties from Rivals: A Strategic Perspective on Network Perceptions
methods: Mixed methods: two between-subjects online experiments (Experiment 1 N=248; Experiment 2 N=259 with 2x2 design) testing rivalry-induction and hiding/seeking intentions and behaviors; plus a two-wave field study using cognitive social network data from 73 employees of a chemical company headquarters, analyzed with MRQAP (dyadic level) and OLS / negative binomial regression (individual level for career outcomes).
industry: Online experiments: working adults across various industries (e.g., 13% health care, 12% education); field study: a leading global chemical company (Taiwan-Japan joint venture) supplying agrochemicals, textile, food, pharmaceutics, metals, construction, and electronics products.
country: United States (online experimental panels) and Asia (field study; Taiwan-Japan international joint venture).
time_period: Field-study network data collected in two waves one year apart, with archival career-outcome data drawn three and four years after the wave-2 survey.
units: Individual employees and dyads (i.e., perceiver-target pairs within the same organization); reduced to 69 individuals for the longitudinal career-outcome regressions after attrition.
n_sample: Experiment 1: 248 participants; Experiment 2: 259 participants; field study: 73 employees (5,329 dyads = 73*73 - 73), reduced to 69 individuals for career-outcome models.
authors: Kilduff, Martin; Wang, Kun; Lee, Sun Young; Tsai, Wenpin; Chuang, You-Ta; Tsai, Fu-Sheng
theories: cognitive social network theory; social psychology of rivalry; structurally equivalent rivalry theory
keywords: career outcomes; cognitive social networks; errors of omission; knowledge hiding; knowledge-providing ties; network perceptions; rivalry; structural equivalence
research_question: Do individuals in organizations hide their knowledge-providing ties from those they perceive as rivals, and do they actively seek to detect the knowledge-providing ties of those rivals — and does success in this hiding and seeking translate into career advantage? More foundationally, does the perception of structural equivalence engender rivalry and motivate action toward perceived rivals?
hypotheses:
The two experiments test underlying assumptions (that perceived structural equivalence engenders rivalry, and that people take action toward structural equivalents) rather than numbered hypotheses; the four formal hypotheses are tested in the field study.
- H1a (Seeking hypothesis): The more an individual considers a coworker as a rival, the fewer the errors of omission in the individual's perception of the coworker's knowledge-providing relationships.
- H1b (Hiding hypothesis): The more an individual is considered a rival by a coworker, the more errors of omission there are in the individual's perception of the coworker's knowledge-providing relationships.
- H2a: The more that individuals minimize errors of omission in their perceptions of their rivals' knowledge-providing relationships, the more likely it is that individuals will achieve favorable career outcomes.
- H2b: The more that individuals increase errors of omission in their rivals' perceptions of the individuals' knowledge-providing relationships, the more likely it is that individuals will achieve favorable career outcomes.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism extends structurally equivalent rivalry theory: when ego perceives a coworker to share many of the same knowledge providers, this triggers rivalrous feelings of competitive threat. Rivalry then motivates two complementary forms of strategic network manipulation — minimizing one's own errors of omission with respect to the rival's knowledge ties (seeking) and maximizing the rival's errors of omission with respect to one's own ties (hiding). Hiding success is hypothesized to confer career benefits because protected knowledge sources support innovative work, while seeking success is hypothesized to provide informational advantage through awareness of rivals' resources. The experiments validate the assumption that perceived structural equivalence ignites rivalry and prompts action; the field study shows these processes operate in a real organization even after controlling for actual structural equivalence, common friendship ties, and direct knowledge-sharing ties.
data_measures:
- Experiments (U.S. working adults via CloudResearch online panels; between-participants designs). Experiment 1 (N=248): perceived coworker's knowledge network manipulated (structural equivalence vs. non-equivalence) using a name-generation technique; sense of rivalry = two items averaged (r=.77); hiding and seeking intentions on 7-point items. Experiment 2 (N=259): 2 (coworker gender) x 2 (perceived structural equivalence) design; rivalry = three items (Cronbach's alpha=.78); hiding intention = two items, seeking intention = one item; hiding and seeking behaviors coded 1/0 from participants' free-text replies to the coworker.
- Field study (73 headquarters employees; two-wave survey one year apart). Structurally equivalent rivalry = an asymmetric rivalry index (0-100%) measuring the percentage overlap between ego's and alter's perceived knowledge-receiving ties, split into rivalry-with-alter-as-perceived-by-ego (tests H1a) and rivalry-with-ego-as-perceived-by-alter (tests H1b). Dyadic DV: ego's errors of omission (false negatives) — ties reported by alter but not detected by ego. Individual DVs: number of projects led and percentage compensation increase, taken from company archives three and four years after wave 2. Seeking-from-rivals and hiding-from-rivals indices weight each false-negative rate by the rivalry index. Controls include actual structural equivalence, direct knowledge tie, friendship tie, common friends, ego/alter network size, false positives, and same department/rank/tenure/gender.
- Estimation: dyadic hypotheses (H1a, H1b) via double-Dekker semi-partialling MRQAP; individual hypotheses (H2a, H2b) via negative binomial regression (projects led) and OLS (compensation increase). The field design is associational; no causal-identification strategy is claimed.
key_findings:
- Experiments (assumption tests, largely convergent across both studies): perceived structural equivalence significantly increased a sense of rivalry (Experiment 1: F(1,246)=8.37, p=.004; Experiment 2: F(1,256)=10.84, p<.001) and hiding intention (Experiment 1: p=.013; Experiment 2: p=.002). Seeking intention rose significantly in Experiment 1 (p=.039) but not in Experiment 2 (p=.951) — a divergence between the two experiments. In Experiment 2, structurally equivalent participants disclosed their knowledge providers less (p<.001) and sought their coworker's providers more (p=.050). Rivalry mediated the effects of structural equivalence on hiding/disclosing (both experiments) and on seeking intention in Experiment 1.
- Field study (formal hypothesis tests, MRQAP). H1a supported: rivalry as perceived by ego was associated with fewer errors of omission (b=-19.031, p=.001) — egos detected rivals' knowledge-providing ties. H1b supported: rivalry as perceived by alter was associated with more errors of omission in ego's perceptions (b=4.234, p=.001) — alters successfully hid their ties from those who saw them as rivals. Both held after controlling for actual structural equivalence and common friends.
- Career outcomes (H2a, H2b) were mixed at best. Seeking from rivals did not predict project leadership (n.s.) but predicted a higher t+4 compensation increase (b=3.640, p=.047), not t+3 (b=4.019, p=.339) — partial support for H2a. Hiding from rivals predicted more projects led at t+3 (b=21.351, p=.005) and t+4 (b=11.190, p=.004) but did not significantly predict compensation (t+4 only marginal, b=7.828, p=.099) — partial support for H2b.
- Convergence/divergence: experiments and field study align on the core hiding-and-seeking patterns tied to perceived rivalry; the main divergence is seeking (significant in Experiment 1 and in the field-study H1a test, but non-significant in Experiment 2), alongside weak and inconsistent career-outcome effects.
theoretical_contribution: The paper provides the first empirical test of two foundational but previously untested assumptions of structural-equivalence research: that perceived structural equivalence engenders rivalry, and that individuals take strategic action toward those perceived as structural equivalents. It bridges the social-psychological literature on dyadic rivalry with the network literature on structural equivalence, and contributes a new perspective on cognitive social networks by showing that errors in network perception are not merely cognitive limitations but partly the outcome of strategic deception (hiding) and detection (seeking) in pursuit of competitive advantage.
practical_implication: Encouraging individual-level competition for valued goals such as salary increases or promotions can have the unintended consequence of stifling the cooperation organizations require, because rivalrous employees devote effort to concealing their knowledge sources and probing those of others. Managers may need to make knowledge-sharing relationships more transparent and to design incentives that reward collaboration over the maintenance of exclusive knowledge ties, while balancing the motivational benefits of competition against the corrosive effects of rivalry.
limitations: The field-study sample is relatively small (73 employees, 69 retained for individual-level career outcomes), limiting statistical power particularly for the conservative two-tailed career-outcome tests. The study captures hiding and seeking outcomes through observed network-perception data rather than directly observing tactics in real time, and the three- to four-year lag between independent variables and career outcomes introduces noise that may obscure effects. Mutual rivalry was rare in the empirical context, so the seeking-trumps-hiding interaction result should be interpreted with caution.
future_research: Future work could establish the causal chain from perceived structural equivalence through rivalry to hiding and seeking using longitudinal observational designs, identify the specific tactics individuals use to conceal knowledge providers and to detect rivals' contacts, and examine whether individual gains from hiding and seeking damage broader organizational productivity. Researchers could also investigate boundary conditions in non-competitive settings (e.g., mentorship dyads, multiplex relationships) and extend the framework to firm-level effects of false-positive and false-negative network perceptions.
abstract: Rivalry is endemic in society and organizations, fueling competitive intentions and behaviors. According to social network theory, rivalry emerges among people who, like siblings, have many of the same connections to others. For this structurally equivalent rivalry to have its effects, the individual must see the other person as a rival. We ask whether, in the context of competition, people seek to identify the knowledge providers of their rivals while striving to hide their own knowledge providers from perceived rivals. We conducted two experiments that showed, for the first time, that structural equivalence does induce feelings of rivalry and does lead people to take action with respect to perceived rivals, namely to hide and seek knowledge providers. Our analysis of timeseparated social network and outcome data from all 73 employees in the headquarters of a chemical company found support for these patterns of hiding and seeking in relation to perceived rivals. We also found limited evidence that career outcomes may be influenced by individuals' success in hiding and seeking. Bringing together research on rivalry and network cognition, we provide a new approach to the strategic deployment of deception and detection in social networks.

title: Constructing Envelopes: How Institutional Custodians Can Tame Disruptive Algorithms
methods: Inductive grounded-theory qualitative analysis combining 1,512 newspaper articles, 1,185 pages of nine U.S. Congressional hearing transcripts, 39 semi-structured interviews with 29 actors, and a secondary dataset of 90,322 newspaper articles; coding via Gioia methodology with temporal bracketing into three phases.
industry: U.S. securities trading (financial markets)
units: Custodian and noncustodian actors (guardians, reformers, regulators, high-frequency traders, challengers) responding to high-frequency trading
n_sample: 140 individuals identified as publicly responding to high-frequency trading; 39 interviews with 29 individuals
authors: Marti, E.; Lawrence, T. B.; Steele, C. W. J.
theories: envelope theory; institutional custodianship; social dynamics of algorithms
keywords: U.S. securities trading; disruptive algorithms; envelopes; fairness; high-frequency trading; institutional custodians
research_question: How do custodians construct envelopes around algorithms that threaten to disrupt valued elements of organizational fields?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper. This is an inductive, grounded-theory study (Corbin & Strauss, 2008) in which all concepts emerged inductively and no a priori hypotheses were tested; the authors instead develop an empirically grounded process model of how institutional custodians construct envelopes around disruptive algorithms.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: institutional custodians vs. disruptive algorithms; values, governance, and practices of the field vs. impacts, inputs/outputs, and usage of algorithms; "envelope" as a boundary delimiting interactions
- Process / phases: Phase 1 (2009–2010, normative layer — guardians couple values to algorithmic impacts); Phase 2 (2010–2014, governance layer — reformers couple governance to algorithmic inputs/outputs); Phase 3 (2014–2016, practice layer — regulators couple legitimate practices to algorithmic usage)
- Triggering conditions: attention-increasing events (Aleynikov arrest 2009, Flash Crash 2010, publication of Flash Boys 2014) that heightened anxiety and fueled political contests
- Practices: rhetorical work (guardians), diagnostic and showcasing work (reformers via IEX, whistleblowing), enforcement actions and rule-making (regulators)
- Emergent outcomes: a three-layered envelope that transformed high-frequency trading from a disruptive threat into "an unproblematic part of the field"
- Boundary conditions: tightly bounded field; relatively passive algorithm-developing firms; well-connected custodians with clear roles

The process model shows custodians constructing envelopes through a "conjunctive" rather than linear sequence: each layer coupled a field element to an algorithmic aspect, with established layers motivating and resourcing subsequent custodians. Different custodian types drew on heterogeneous resources — guardians on prominence, reformers on technical expertise, regulators on formal authority — and their cumulative work delimited the algorithm's interactions with the field without any single actor needing to fully understand the algorithm's inner workings.
data_measures: Inductive, grounded-theory analysis (Corbin & Strauss, 2008) in which all concepts emerged inductively. The data corpus drew on four sources: (1) a "primary newspaper dataset" of 1,512 articles on high-frequency trading from the five highest-volume U.S. outlets (Chicago Tribune, Los Angeles Times, New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and Washington Post) for January 2009 to December 2016; (2) nine U.S. Congressional hearing transcripts (1,185 pages); (3) 39 semi-structured interviews with 29 actors (33 hours in total); and (4) a "secondary newspaper dataset" of 90,322 articles from 639 U.S. newspapers referring to the 140 individuals identified as publicly responding to high-frequency trading. Analysis proceeded through five sequential (though iterative) steps. Step 1 identified 133 individuals from the primary newspaper dataset and coded the 260 statements they made in terms of whether they highlighted positive or negative social and economic impacts of high-frequency trading; drawing additionally on the Congressional-hearing transcripts, the authors identified 140 individuals in total who publicly responded to high-frequency trading. Step 2 grouped individuals into five actor types — three custodian types (guardians, reformers, regulators) and two noncustodian types (high-frequency traders, challengers) — operationalizing each actor's position through dictionary-based content analysis (WordStat) of three resources: public prominence (the number of 2009–2016 newspaper articles mentioning the actor), specialization in high-frequency trading (the share of an actor's articles that mentioned it, using an 18-keyword dictionary), and prior participation in public discussions of financial markets. Step 3 identified key political contests and used temporal bracketing (Langley, 1999) to distinguish three phases, coding data in NVivo from open codes to first-order categories, second-order themes, and aggregate dimensions (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013). Step 4 searched for commonalities across custodians' work, theorized as a "coupling" of one element of the field to one aspect of high-frequency trading. Step 5 analyzed how each coupling constrained high-frequency trading, theorized as a "layer" of the envelope.
key_findings:
The study develops an empirically grounded process model in which custodians in the field of U.S. securities trading constructed an envelope around high-frequency trading algorithms out of three interconnected "layers," each built in a distinct phase:
- Normative layer (Phase 1, 2009–2010): guardians (high-profile politicians, journalists, and pundits) coupled the value of fairness for retail investors to the impacts of high-frequency trading through rhetorical work, establishing a normative reference point for evaluating those impacts.
- Governance layer (Phase 2, 2010–2014): reformers (highly specialized actors) coupled the governance of the field to the inputs and outputs of high-frequency trading by diagnosing how it produced unfair impacts and showcasing alternatives such as the IEX trading venue.
- Practice layer (Phase 3, 2014–2016): regulators coupled legitimate practices to the usage of high-frequency trading through routinized surveillance, enforcement actions, and industry self-regulation.
Each phase was set off by an attention-increasing event — the July 2009 arrest of Sergey Aleynikov, the "flash crash" of May 2010, and the March 2014 publication of Flash Boys — that heightened anxiety and fueled a political contest between one custodian type and one noncustodian type, in which custodians proved more successful than noncustodians. Construction was "conjunctive" rather than linear: a layer established in one phase motivated and resourced custodians in subsequent phases. Jointly, the three layers transformed high-frequency trading from a disruptive threat to the field into an unproblematic part of it, allowing the algorithms to operate while mitigating their harmful impacts, without any single actor fully understanding the algorithms' inner workings.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on the social dynamics of algorithms by generating empirically grounded process theory of how envelopes around algorithms are constructed, showing actors can work around algorithmic opacity by leveraging field-specific expertise rather than mastering code. It contributes to institutional custodianship research by identifying envelope construction as a third custodial response — distinct from buffering institutions and intervening in threats — that allows custodians to steer institutional change when threats make change unavoidable.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that actors lacking deep technological expertise or access to proprietary algorithms can still meaningfully influence the algorithmic transformation of society by coupling familiar field elements (values, governance arrangements, practices) to specific aspects of algorithms (their impacts, inputs/outputs, usage). Custodians can thereby tame disruptive algorithms without halting their adoption.
limitations: The high-frequency trading firms played a relatively passive role during the studied period, leaving open how proponents of algorithms work to counteract envelope construction. The field of U.S. securities trading is also relatively tightly bounded, limiting generalizability to algorithms that span multiple, less well-bounded fields (e.g., Google search algorithms).
future_research: Future work should explore how proponents of algorithms actively resist or counter custodial efforts, and how envelopes can be constructed around algorithms that traverse multiple fields or that disrupt less well-bounded fields. Researchers can also examine how exogenous shocks and adaptive algorithm development trigger new cycles of envelope-maintenance work.
abstract: The infusion of algorithms into organizational fields—accelerated by advances in artificial intelligence—can have disruptive effects that trigger defensive responses. One important response involves establishing a boundary around an algorithm to delimit its interactions with its environment—in engineering terms, constructing an "envelope." Yet, we know little about the process through which such envelopes are constructed. We address this issue by exploring how institutional custodians construct envelopes around disruptive algorithms. We empirically examine custodians' responses to the high-frequency trading algorithms that disrupted the field of U.S. securities trading, focusing on the years 2009–2016. Our inductive analysis shows that custodians created an envelope with interconnected normative, governance, and practice "layers" that jointly constrained high-frequency trading. Each layer emerged as custodians "coupled" one element of the field (e.g., its values) to one aspect of the disruptive algorithms (e.g., their impacts). Our study contributes to research on the social dynamics of algorithms by generating novel theory of how envelopes around algorithms are constructed, and to research on institutional custodianship by highlighting the constructing of envelopes as a custodial response to a wide range of threats—including, but not restricted to, disruptive algorithms.

title: Avoidance and Aggression in Stakeholder Engagement: The Impact of CEO Paranoia and Paranoia-Relevant Cues
methods: Longitudinal panel of 925 CEOs in 774 S&P 1500 firms over 2010-2017 (3,823 firm-year observations); CEO paranoia operationalized via a newly developed and validated content-analytic dictionary applied to earnings call transcripts (six components: anxiety, distrust, fear, obsession, suspicion, threat); Tobit regression for left-censored lobbying breadth and negative binomial regression for count-valued competitive actions, with two-digit SIC and year fixed effects, Heckman-style selection correction (inverse Mills ratio), robustness-of-inference-to-replacement (RIR), and two-stage residual inclusion (2SRI) endogeneity checks.
industry: S&P 1500 firms (multi-industry, with two-digit SIC dummies)
units: CEO-firm-year observations from earnings calls
n_sample: 3,823 firm-year observations covering 925 CEOs across 774 firms
authors: Ridge, Jason W.; Hill, Aaron D.; Ingram, Amy; Kolomeitsev, Sergei; Worrell, Dan L.
theories: psychology of paranoia and safety behaviors (Chan & McAllister, 2014; Freeman et al., 2001, 2002); trait activation theory (Tett & Burnett, 2003; Tett & Guterman, 2000); upper echelons theory (Hambrick & Mason, 1984)
keywords: CEO paranoia; aggression; avoidance; competitive actions; content analysis; lobbying breadth; paranoia-relevant cues; regulatory rulings; rival attacks; stakeholder engagement; trait activation; upper echelons theory
research_question: How does CEO paranoia affect firms' engagement with powerful external stakeholders (government and competitors), and how do paranoia-relevant cues (regulatory rulings and rival attacks) activate the trait to shift CEOs from avoidance toward more aggressive engagement?
hypotheses:
- H1: CEO paranoia is negatively related to government lobbying breadth (predicted negative direct effect).
- H2: CEO paranoia is negatively related to firm competitive actions (predicted negative direct effect).
- H3: There will be a positive interaction effect of paranoia and regulatory ruling severity on lobbying breadth, such that the negative CEO paranoia–lobbying breadth relationship is mitigated as regulatory ruling severity increases (predicted positive interaction).
- H4: There will be a positive interaction effect of paranoia and rival attacks on competitive actions, such that the negative CEO paranoia–competitive actions relationship is mitigated as rival attacks increase (predicted positive interaction).
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Firm size, market performance (Tobin's Q), tax aggressiveness, governmental subsidies and contracts, lobbying expenditures, blockholder ownership, TMT power, CEO compensation and pay sensitivity, perceived political and nonpolitical risk, inverse Mills ratio, year and two-digit SIC dummies.

Drawing on upper echelons theory and trait-activation logic, the paper argues that CEO paranoia — anchored in hypervigilance, rumination, self-as-target bias, and sinister attribution bias — manifests primarily in avoidance safety behaviors that reduce engagement with external stakeholders perceived as threatening. When trait-relevant cues (severe regulatory rulings against the firm; rival attacks on the firm) signal that avoidance has failed to provide protection, the trait activates an alternative response: aggression, defined as direct engagement intended to deter further targeting. Empirically, paranoia is negatively associated with lobbying breadth (avoidance of government), and this relationship flips toward aggression as regulatory rulings become more severe; the predicted negative direct effect on competitive actions is not supported, but the activation interaction with rival attacks is positive and significant.
data_measures:
- Data: CEO earnings-call transcripts from CapitalIQ, linked to Execucomp and to control/outcome data from the Center for Responsive Politics, Thomson-Reuters, Compustat, USAspending.gov, goodjobsfirst.org, and RavenPack; sample of S&P 1500 firms over 2010-2017 (925 CEOs, 774 firms, 3,823 firm-year observations).
- IV — CEO paranoia: a newly developed content-analytic dictionary of six components (anxiety, distrust, fear, obsession, suspicion, threat) applied to CEO speech in earnings calls, then summed to a yearly measure; validated via management-faculty ratings (retaining components with >75% agreement), a single-factor solution (eigenvalue 1.16, 67% of variance), within-CEO reliability (Cronbach's α = 0.83), and correlations with related content-analytic measures.
- DV — lobbying breadth (government engagement): standardized and summed count of the number of agencies and pieces of legislation a firm targeted with lobbying expenditures (Ridge et al., 2017).
- DV — competitive actions: RavenPack count of eight action types (new product, capacity, pricing, marketing, acquisitions, alliances, market expansion, legal).
- Moderator — regulatory rulings: penalty amount in millions of U.S. dollars for assessed rulings (goodjobsfirst.org). Moderator — rival attacks: count of RavenPack competitive actions in which the focal firm is the target.
- Estimation: Tobit regression for the left-censored lobbying-breadth outcome and a negative binomial model for the count-valued competitive-actions outcome, with two-digit SIC and year dummies and an inverse Mills ratio; dependent variables measured at t+1 and predictors at t. The design is observational; the paper addresses endogeneity through diagnostics and robustness checks — robustness of inference to replacement (RIR) and two-stage residual inclusion (2SRI, using sadness and negativity as instruments) — rather than claiming clean causal identification.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: CEO paranoia is negatively and significantly related to lobbying breadth (coefficient –105.82, p = .02); a one-standard-deviation increase in paranoia corresponds to roughly a 7% decrease in lobbying breadth (avoidance of government).
- H2 not supported: the CEO paranoia coefficient for competitive actions is positive (opposite the predicted negative direction) and not statistically significant (p = .30).
- H3 supported: a positive, significant interaction of CEO paranoia and regulatory ruling severity on lobbying breadth (0.13, p < .01); at higher ruling severity the negative paranoia–lobbying relationship weakens and flips toward positive (aggression).
- H4 receives some support: a positive, significant interaction of CEO paranoia and rival attacks on competitive actions (2.25, p = .01), but the practical effect is small and the interaction strengthens an already-positive (statistically non-significant) main effect rather than weakening a negative one.
- Overall, the effects of CEO paranoia differ by stakeholder: the avoidance-then-activation pattern holds for government engagement (H1, H3), whereas the predicted avoidance of competitors is not supported (H2).
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends upper echelons theory by integrating trait activation, showing that CEO traits — typically treated as stable predictors of stable outcomes — manifest differently when triggered by trait-relevant cues, opening a more dynamic view of how CEOs engage stakeholders over time. It introduces CEO paranoia as a previously overlooked but consequential trait in a literature dominated by self-assured, attention-seeking executive characterizations, and theorizes how paranoia produces stakeholder-specific patterns of avoidance and aggression. Methodologically, it develops and validates the first content-analytic measure of paranoia in management research, derived from psychology and applicable beyond CEOs to other linguistic populations.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that CEO paranoia has tangible firm-level consequences — for example, a one-standard-deviation increase in CEO paranoia is associated with roughly a 7% decrease in lobbying breadth, and small lobbying changes can carry meaningful tax-rate and contracting consequences. Boards, advisors, and shareholders should recognize that paranoid CEOs may avoid information exchange with regulators yet swing aggressively when targeted, while also potentially fostering bright-side outcomes such as more prudent risk management, supply-chain diversification, and verification practices.
limitations: The paper focuses only on two stakeholder types (government and competitors), so generalization to other stakeholders (boards, suppliers, investors, partners) is uncertain, and CEO paranoia is shown to operate differently across different stakeholders, suggesting context-specific contingencies the study cannot fully unpack. The negative direct effect of paranoia on competitive actions is not supported, indicating boundary conditions on the avoidance argument. The empirical setting is the relatively stable 2010-2017 economic period within S&P 1500 earnings-call discourse, raising concerns about extension to post-pandemic or other firm-level contexts; CEO selection and other endogeneity concerns are addressed but cannot be fully eliminated.
future_research: The authors call for studies extending CEO paranoia to other stakeholder relationships (cooperative-strategy partners, acquisitions, investors, boards, suppliers, buyers), examining tournament-theory and structural-interdependence dynamics within TMTs, and exploring how paranoia interacts with agency-theoretic accounts of executive decision-making. They encourage further validation of the content-analytic paranoia measure across different settings and populations, exploration of "bright" versus "dark" sides of subclinical paranoia (e.g., risk-management benefits vs. missed partnerships), and broader application of trait-activation logic to other CEO traits whose outcomes may also be cue-dependent rather than uniformly stable.
abstract: We develop and test theory regarding the effect of CEO paranoia, defined as stable tendencies toward suspicion, feelings of ill will or resentment, mistrust, and belief in external control or influence, on firm stakeholder engagement. We theorize that because CEOs higher in paranoia have tendencies toward hypervigilance and the biases of self-as-target and sinister attributions they typically avoid engagement with external stakeholders. Further, we argue that CEOs higher in paranoia are subject to paranoid activation when confronted with trait-relevant cues that confirm suspicions of being targeted by a malevolent external entity (here, regulatory rulings or rival attacks), thus eliciting a shift away from avoidance to a more aggressive engagement with those stakeholders. To do so, we develop a content-analytic measure of CEO paranoia following both theory and evidence in psychology and methodological best practices, finding evidence that broadly supports our premise. In total, our study draws attention to how the manifestation of CEO paranoia changes the way CEOs engage stakeholders over time, contributing to understanding in multiple ways.

title: Fairness Judgments in the Context of Structural Sexism: The Role of Beliefs in Individual and Structural Causes of Success
methods: Twelve preregistered vignette experiments (online via MTurk, Prolific, Connect; one lab study) using 2x2 factorial designs and a within-person design. Participants assumed the role of a senior manager observing a junior manager's allocation decision (raw performance vs. adjusting for structural sexism). Analyses used OLS regression and multilevel/random-coefficient modeling in R with Johnson-Neyman simple-slopes tests, regression-based path analysis with 5,000 bootstraps in Mplus 8.10 for mediated moderation, and an internal meta-analysis (psychmeta) across studies.
industry: Vignette experiments simulating workplace allocation decisions (bonuses, management training program, employee-of-the-year award, firefighter promotion) with junior-manager allocators
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Adult observers (online and lab participants) judging managerial allocation decisions
n_sample: Across 12 studies, k=11 / N=3,748 in the internal meta-analysis of common-procedure conditions; focal Studies 1-4 had N=330 (within-person), 1,067, 366, and 672
authors: Tedder-King, Alyssa; Sherf, Elad N.
theories: attribution theory; distributive justice / organizational fairness; equity theory; meritocracy
keywords: beliefs in causes of success; diversity equity inclusion; equity; fairness judgments; meritocracy; performance indicators; social justice; structural sexism
research_question: When and how do observers' beliefs in the individual versus structural causes of success shape their fairness judgments of managerial allocations that adjust (vs. fail to adjust) raw performance indicators in light of evidence of structural sexism?
hypotheses:
- H1: When observers' beliefs in individual causes of success are stronger (weaker), they judge managers who adjust allocations to address structural sexism as less (more) fair than managers who allocate based on raw performance. (Predicted: stronger individual beliefs → adjusting judged less fair.)
- H2: When observers' beliefs in structural causes of success are stronger (weaker), they judge managers who adjust allocations to address structural sexism as more (less) fair than managers who allocate based on raw performance. (Predicted: stronger structural beliefs → adjusting judged more fair.)
- H3: The effects of beliefs in causes of success on fairness judgments (i.e., Hypotheses 1 and 2) emerge only when information about structural sexism in a key performance indicator (KPI) is available in the context of the decision.
- H4: Observers' fairness judgments of a manager are positively related to that manager's performance evaluations.
- H5: Fairness judgments mediate the effect of allocation (raw performance vs. adjusting for structural sexism) on the manager's performance evaluations, and the indirect effect is moderated by observers' beliefs in individual and structural causes of success.
mechanism_summary:
- Mediator: Fairness judgments mediating the effect of allocation condition on performance evaluations
- Controls: Participant gender; luck (random) beliefs

Drawing on equity theory and the meritocratic ideal, the authors argue that "equity" entails causal judgments about which contributions count, and that observers vary in how they interpret causally ambiguous structural barriers. When information about gender-based structural barriers in a key performance indicator is salient in the decision context, observers with stronger structural beliefs (rigged worldview) view raw indicators as misrepresenting women's contributions and thus judge adjustments as fairer; observers with stronger individual beliefs (rewarding worldview) treat raw indicators as merit-aligned and judge adjustments as less fair. When information about structural barriers is absent, or when barriers are not gender-based, beliefs lose their moderating power. Fairness judgments in turn drive performance evaluations of the allocator.
data_measures:
- Data source: 12 vignette experiments (10 preregistered), run online via MTurk, Prolific, and Connect plus one lab study; focal Studies 1-4 used U.S. adult observers (N = 330 within-person, 1,067, 366, 672) who role-played a senior manager evaluating a junior manager's allocation decision (bonus, employee-of-the-year award, management-training program, or firefighter promotion).
- IV — allocation condition: dummy-coded (raw performance = 0; adjusting for structural sexism = 1), randomly assigned.
- Mediator / DV — fairness judgments: three-item scale from Colquitt, Long, Rodell, and Halvorsen-Ganepola (2015) (sample item "To what extent did the junior manager act fairly?"), rated 1-7.
- DV — manager performance evaluation: recommended bonus out of $500 (participants told the average bonus was $250).
- Moderators — beliefs in causes of success: causal-attributions-of-financial-uncertainty scale (Krijnen et al., 2022) with the stem adapted to job success; individual beliefs = three-item "Rewarding" factor, structural beliefs = three-item "Rigged" factor, rated 1-7. Presence/absence of the KPI-disparity report (Study 2), gender-based vs. non-gender-based barriers (Study 3), and subjective vs. objective barriers (Study 4) were experimentally manipulated moderators.
- Controls: participant gender and luck ("Random" factor) beliefs.
- Identification: random assignment to the allocation (and information/barrier) conditions provides experimental identification of allocation effects, but success beliefs were measured, not manipulated, so their moderating role is correlational rather than causally identified. Estimation used OLS regression in R (multilevel / random-coefficient modeling for the within-person Study 1) with Johnson-Neyman simple-slope tests; H5 mediated moderation used regression-based path analysis with 5,000 bootstraps in Mplus 8.10; an internal meta-analysis (psychmeta) pooled the common-procedure conditions (k = 11, N = 3,748).
key_findings:
- H1 (stronger individual beliefs → adjusting judged less fair) received heterogeneous support: supported in Study 1 (within-person) but not supported in Studies 2, 3, or 4, where the predicted slope reversal did not obtain (e.g., Study 3 allocation × individual-beliefs interaction b = −0.05, p = .750, n.s.).
- H2 (stronger structural beliefs → adjusting judged more fair) was supported in all four focal studies: allocation × structural-beliefs interaction γ = 0.62 (Study 1), b = 0.47 (Study 2), and b = 0.51 (Study 4), all p < .001, plus support in Study 3's gender-based-barrier condition. Observers with stronger structural beliefs judged adjusting as fairer; those with weaker structural beliefs judged it less fair.
- H3 (belief effects emerge only when KPI structural-sexism information is present) was supported in Study 2 (report present vs. absent) and Study 3 (three-way allocation × information × structural-beliefs interaction b = 0.75, p = .008).
- H4 (fairness judgments positively related to manager performance evaluations) was supported in every study that tested it (Study 1 γ = 50.43; Study 2 b = 41.27; Study 4 b = 44.87; all p < .001).
- H5 (fairness judgments mediate allocation → performance evaluation, moderated by beliefs) received partial support: the moderated indirect effect held for structural beliefs but was weaker or absent for individual beliefs (Study 1 partially supported for individual, supported for structural; Study 4 not supported for individual, partially supported for structural).
- Overall, structural beliefs moderated fairness judgments more consistently than individual beliefs, and only when contextual information about gender-based structural barriers was made salient.
theoretical_contribution: The paper broadens the equity principle by showing that fairness judgments of equitable allocations depend on observers' beliefs in the causes of success and on contextualized information about structural barriers, rather than being a fixed weighting of raw performance indicators. It theoretically separates two related-but-distinct manifestations of meritocratic ideals (individual vs. structural causes of success) and demonstrates that structural beliefs play a more consistent moderating role than individual beliefs once contextual information is made salient — bridging organizational fairness research with social-justice and meritocracy scholarship.
practical_implication: Organizational leaders pursuing DEI goals should provide salient, contextualized evidence of gender-based disparities in specific performance indicators rather than relying on equal-pay-for-equal-work framings; doing so leverages observers' structural beliefs and reduces pushback against adjustments. Framing barriers as objective features of the work environment (e.g., equipment design) is especially likely to broaden support, including from observers with weaker structural beliefs. Justifications consistent with observers' success beliefs may help managers anticipate and mitigate perceived unfairness around adjustments.
limitations: The studies use vignette experiments rather than real organizational allocations, so external validity is limited; success beliefs were measured rather than experimentally manipulated, so causal inferences about their moderating role are constrained. All samples were drawn from the United States, where individual beliefs are stronger and structural beliefs more dispersed than elsewhere, and norms vary across cultures. Theorizing focused on gender, leaving intersectional and other-group barriers (e.g., race, LGBTQ+) unexamined; some measurement choices (preference for the merit principle scale, beliefs in causes of success) showed psychometric difficulties.
future_research: Future work should validate and develop independent manipulations of individual versus structural beliefs, test the framework with field-level organizational allocation data, and examine whether the findings extend to recipients (not just observers) and to allocations of less-tangible, non-zero-sum resources such as respect. Researchers can extend the lens to other marginalized groups and intersectional identities, examine how exposure to structural barriers (e.g., reverse mentoring) shapes belief endorsement over time, and integrate the framework with affirmative-action research that has emphasized individual but not structural beliefs.
abstract: Due to structural sexism, women frequently encounter barriers that result in lower rankings on performance indicators such as productivity data and appraisals by others. The fairness literature offers unclear predictions about the extent to which observers would judge allocations that fail (vs. attempt) to account for such structural barriers as fair. We suggest that past conceptual discussions and empirical designs did not factor in the causal ambiguity embedded in information about structural barriers and the variance in how individuals interpret such information. Hence, we propose that beliefs in the causes of success, anchored in the endorsement of meritocratic ideals, shape fairness judgments by determining the weight given to performance indicators and structural barriers. Such effects emerge in the presence of information about structural barriers in the context of the decision, a feature that is absent from past studies. We discuss our theory and findings in the context of calls for bridging organizational fairness and social justice research and for a nuanced understanding of people's responses to violations of the meritocratic ideal within organizations.
apa_citation: Tedder-King, A., & Sherf, E. N. (2024). Fairness judgments in the context of structural sexism: The role of beliefs in individual and structural causes of success. *Academy of Management Journal*, 67(5), 1234-1272. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2022.0776

title: Screening Theory and Its Boundaries: Investigation of Screen Credibility, Necessity, and Salience in the Context of Corporate Venture Capital
methods: Archival panel study using competing risks survival models with partial likelihood estimation and time-varying covariates, predicting CVC funding termination at the firm-venture-year level; Heckman two-stage selection correction (multinomial first stage with industry diversifying CVC intensity as exclusion), difference-in-differences using institutional-investor mergers as an exogenous shock, and ITCV/RIR omitted-variable robustness checks; supplementary policy-capturing scenario study (Study 2) with 41 experienced CVC decision-makers analyzed via hierarchical linear modeling; data integrated from VentureXpert, Thomson Reuters 13F, Compustat, BoardEx, USPTO, SDC M&A, and FactSet; QSs identified following Bushee (1998) by portfolio turnover and holding concentration.
industry: Diversifying corporate venture capital investments by U.S. publicly traded firms (excluding financial services); top CVC industries were business services (24.8%), computers and communications (19.1%), and electronic equipment (11.2%); ventures across 197 different industries
time_period: Ventures receiving initial CVC funding between 2000 and 2014, tracked through 2019 (five years of subsequent funding)
units: CVC firm-venture pairs (firm-year observations) for the survival model; CVC decision-makers for the policy-capturing study
n_sample: 3,358 ventures funded by 294 CVC firms, yielding 4,051 CVC firm-venture pairs and 17,825 pair-year observations with 627 CVC funding terminations; 41 CVC decision-makers in Study 2
authors: Zhang, Jiamin; Shi, Wei; Connelly, Brian L.
theories: absorptive capacity (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990; Zahra & George, 2002); information economics / information asymmetry (Qian, Crilly, Wang, & Wang, 2021); screening theory (Riley, 2001; Stiglitz, 1975; Arrow, 1973)
keywords: CVC funding termination; corporate venture capital; diversifying CVC; industry holdings; industry-specific knowledge; information asymmetry; market heat; quality shareholders; screen credibility; screen necessity; screen salience; screening theory
research_question: When and under what boundary conditions do corporate venture capital (CVC) decision-makers use the industry shareholdings of their firm's quality shareholders as an informational screen to inform CVC funding-termination decisions in industries where the firm does not yet compete?
hypotheses:
- H1 (fundamental screen): Investment in an industry by a firm's quality shareholders (QSs) is *negatively* associated with the firm's termination of CVC funding in that industry.
- H2 (screen credibility): The negative H1 relationship is amplified (i.e., negatively moderated) by the concentration of QS shareholdings; the relationship is stronger for highly concentrated QSs than for less concentrated (dispersed) QSs.
- H3 (screen necessity): The negative H1 relationship is attenuated (i.e., positively moderated) by market heat; in hot markets the relationship is less negative.
- H4 (screen salience to the screener): The negative H1 relationship is amplified (i.e., negatively moderated) by the firm's industry-specific knowledge; when the firm is highly familiar with an industry, the relationship is more negative.
mechanism_summary:
- Screen credibility: QS industry concentration (concentrated vs. dispersed QS shareholdings, split via Herfindahl-Hirschman index and orthonormalized).
  - Screen necessity: market heat (log of successful exit events — IPOs/acquisitions — in the venture's industry in the prior year).
  - Screen salience to the screener: industry-specific knowledge (CVC firm's supply-chain industry experience, ratio of customers/suppliers in the venture's industry to total in non-competing CVC-funded industries).

The mechanism is informational: under uncertainty about diversifying-CVC industries, decision-makers scan secondary cues and use their own QSs' concentrated shareholdings as an "industry quality" screen because QSs face costly screening equilibria and possess deep industry expertise. The screen's efficacy is conditioned by three systems-perspective boundaries — whether the screen is credible (concentrated QSs are more dependable signalers than dispersed ones), whether it is necessary (cold markets demand the screen; hot markets substitute for it), and whether it is salient to the screener (high industry-specific knowledge complements the external cue, allowing decision-makers to absorb and act on it).
data_measures:
- Data sources: CVC deals from VentureXpert; institutional ownership from Thomson Reuters 13F; financials from Compustat; boards from BoardEx; patents from USPTO; acquisitions from SDC M&A; customer-supplier links from FactSet. Sample: diversifying CVC by U.S. public firms (financial services excluded), ventures receiving initial funding 2000-2014 and tracked through 2019.
- DV — CVC funding termination: coded as terminated if the CVC firm did not invest in any subsequent funding round (following Guler, 2007; Ma, 2020; Zheng & Xia, 2018).
- IV — QS industry holdings: the weighted sum of a firm's quality shareholders' shareholdings in the venture's industry; QSs identified following Bushee (1998) by portfolio turnover and holding concentration.
- Moderator (screen credibility) — QS industry concentration: concentrated vs. dispersed QS industry holdings from a Herfindahl-Hirschman-index median split, orthonormalized via the modified Gram-Schmidt procedure.
- Moderator (screen necessity) — market heat: natural log of the number of successful exit events (IPOs/acquisitions) in the venture's industry in the prior year.
- Moderator (screen salience) — industry-specific knowledge: supply-chain industry experience, the ratio of the CVC firm's customers/suppliers in the venture's industry to those in its other (non-competing) CVC-funded industries, from FactSet.
- Estimation: competing-risks survival model with partial likelihood estimation and time-varying covariates (sub-hazard of funding termination), robust standard errors clustered by firm. Endogeneity is addressed with a Heckman two-stage selection correction (multinomial first stage; exclusion restriction = industry diversifying CVC intensity), a difference-in-differences design using institutional-investor mergers as a shock, and ITCV/RIR omitted-variable checks; the authors frame these as alleviating endogeneity rather than establishing strictly exogenous identification. Study 2: a policy-capturing scenario study of 41 experienced CVC decision-makers (orthogonal fractional factorial design) analyzed with hierarchical linear modeling.
key_findings:
- Main study (competing-risks model; 17,825 firm-venture-year observations, 627 terminations): all four hypotheses supported.
  - H1 supported: QS industry holdings is negatively related to CVC funding termination (b = -0.263, p < .001); a one-SD increase lowers termination likelihood by about 23%.
  - H2 supported: concentrated QS industry holdings is negatively associated with termination (b = -0.739, p < .01), dispersed QS holdings is not significant (b = -0.101, ns), and the two coefficients differ (z = 2.04, p < .05).
  - H3 supported: the market heat × QS industry holdings interaction is positive (b = 0.061, p < .01) — hot markets attenuate the negative relationship.
  - H4 supported: the industry-specific knowledge × QS industry holdings interaction is negative (b = -0.127, p < .05) — internal industry knowledge amplifies the negative relationship.
- Study 2 (policy-capturing, n = 41) corroborates the main effect and H2-H3: negative QS main effect (p < .001), negatively moderated by QS concentration (p < .001), positively moderated by market heat (p < .01); the industry-specific-knowledge moderation (H4) was negative but only marginally significant (p = .065).
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends screening theory by introducing a systems-level set of boundary conditions — screen credibility, screen necessity, and screen salience to the screener — that specify when a screen is activated within the decision-making process, addressing the long-standing critique that screening theory lacks conceptual precision and is often conflated with signaling theory. The framework provides scholars with screen-specific constructs (rather than only context-specific moderators) to apply screening theory rigorously across new domains and clarifies that screening focuses on receivers' differential reliance on cues, whereas signaling focuses on senders' decisions to send cues. The study also contributes to the CVC literature by uncovering quality shareholders as a previously unrecognized class of informational influencers on CVC funding-termination decisions.
practical_implication: Investor-relations departments may want to actively cultivate "quality shareholders" — patient, concentrated institutional investors — whose industry holdings serve as a brain-trust-like informational resource for corporate decision-makers, particularly in CVC units evaluating diversifying ventures. CVC managers should weight QS industry signals more heavily in cold markets and when the firm has internal industry expertise to interpret them, and less heavily when concentrated QS positions are absent or when hot-market dynamics already justify continued funding. Policymakers should be aware that increased QS presence in boardrooms can carry externalities by shaping corporate venturing decisions beyond what QSs themselves intend.
limitations: The authors do not directly observe whether CVC decision-makers know about and use QS shareholdings, nor whether the screen actually improves decision quality; the design infers screening processes from outcomes, supplemented by hypothetical scenarios in the policy-capturing study. The theory is developed from the CVC firm's perspective only and does not capture quality-of-information concerns, post-termination disposition of equity stakes, or how different institutional-investor types might create competing screens simultaneously. Despite difference-in-differences, ITCV, and Heckman corrections, the absence of a strictly exogenous shock means causal inference remains qualified.
future_research: Scholars could enrich screening theory by examining additional screen-specific constructs (e.g., screen valence, screener transparency, screens based on stock vs. flow information, quality- vs. intent-based screens) and by reconciling screens with opposing valences (e.g., short-seller interest vs. insider ownership). Future policy-capturing studies could extend to entrepreneurs, top managers of CVC firms, and QSs themselves to unpack the screening process from multiple actors' perspectives, and could explore initial CVC funding decisions rather than only termination. Researchers should also assess how QS investment patterns affect target ventures' operations and entrepreneurial perceptions, and investigate the simultaneous influence of different institutional-investor types on industry screening.
abstract: Screening theory explains how decision-makers search for and use external cues to overcome information asymmetry problems under conditions of uncertainty. We introduce screen credibility, screen necessity, and screen salience to the screener as boundary conditions that determine screen efficacy. We test our ideas in the context of corporate venture capital (CVC) funding aimed at industries where firms do not yet compete. These decisions are fraught with uncertainty, so we suggest that CVC decision-makers use the industry shareholdings of a firm's quality shareholders, who are knowledgeable about many industries, as a screen to help them decide whether to continue or terminate CVC funding in that industry. We also hypothesize that screen credibility, screen necessity, and screen salience to the screener condition the fundamental screening relationship. Analysis of CVC funding termination over a period of two decades confirms our ideas. A policy-capturing study administered to executives with CVC experience offers additional support. Our study thus extends screening theory by identifying the factors that activate a screen within the decision-making process. We also add a unique element to the empirical body of CVC research as we uncover the influence of corporate ownership on CVC decision-making.
