title: Polishing the Gilt Edge: Elite Category Endurance and Symbolic Boundaries in U.S. Luxury Hotels, 1790–2015
methods: Inductive, longitudinal historical case study combining grounded-theory qualitative analysis of archival texts, 25 semi-structured interviews, and ~120 hours of observations with semiotic chain analysis and LDA topic modeling of ~16,000 pages of press and trade-publication text spanning 1790–2015.
industry: U.S. hotel industry, focusing on the luxury hotel category vis-à-vis nonluxury (upscale, midscale, economy) tiers
time_period: 1790–2015 (225 years), with archival press coverage from 1853–2015
units: Luxury hotel category-level discourse drawn from popular and trade press, industry rating systems, books by hoteliers/historians, performance data, expert interviews, and on-site observations
n_sample: ~16,000 pages of archival text; 25 semi-structured interviews; one dozen on-site visits; ~120 hours of conference observation; LDA model with 24 topics (13 used in findings)
authors: Lockwood, Christi; Glynn, Mary Ann; Giorgi, Simona
theories: category theory (Durand & Paolella, 2013; Hsu & Grodal, 2021); cultural consonance (Giorgi, Maoret, & Zajac, 2019); semiotic code analysis (Granqvist, Grodal, & Woolley, 2013; Weber et al., 2008); symbolic boundaries (Bourdieu, 1984; Lamont & Molnár, 2002)
keywords: cultural consonance; elite category endurance; elite exclusivity; luxury hotels; oppositional appropriation; semiotic code; social partitioning; symbolic boundary; temporal translation
research_question: How does an elite market category endure over the very long term in the face of recurrent industry- and society-driven threats to its status? Specifically, how is the symbolic boundary that distinguishes the elite from the nonelite discursively constructed, settled, disrupted, and redefined across historical periods?
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: elite exclusivity vs. cultural consonance; symbolic boundary as a temporary "settlement" encoded in a semiotic code of oppositions (connotations and denotations) between luxury and nonluxury.
- Process / phases: three historical periods — Grand Hotel Period (1790s–1920s, luxury = opulence), Chain Hotel Period (1930s–mid-1990s, luxury = cosmopolitanism), Lifestyle Hotel Period (late 1990s–2015, luxury = originality) — each demarcated by symbolic boundary settlement followed by disruption.
- Practices (three discursive mechanisms): social partitioning (drawing the boundary around an idealized elite clientele), oppositional appropriation (selectively absorbing elements from the nonelite category), and temporal translation (reinterpreting the category's own past for the present).
- Triggering conditions: industry shifts (e.g., chain hotels, lifestyle hotels) and societal sociocultural movements (modern progressive, artisanal) that heighten the tension between exclusivity and consonance.
- Emergent outcomes: a new symbolic boundary settlement and a new semiotic code that re-partitions luxury from nonluxury, sustaining elite category endurance.

Across all three periods the three mechanisms interlock — one is "primary" at category emergence (social partitioning), growth (oppositional appropriation), or maturity (temporal translation), while the other two play supporting roles. The process resembles a punctuated equilibrium of long stable settlements separated by brief disruption-and-redefinition phases, with a notable correspondence between the primary settlement mechanism and the source of the next disruption.
theoretical_contribution: The paper recasts elite category endurance as an active, ongoing cultural accomplishment rather than an inertial property of status hierarchies, showing how symbolic boundaries adapt by holding elite exclusivity and cultural consonance in productive tension. It identifies three novel, interlocking discursive mechanisms — social partitioning, oppositional appropriation, and temporal translation — and exposes a periodicity in which each mechanism takes the lead at a different phase of the category's evolution. It also bridges debates between impermeable and porous category boundaries by showing that elite symbolic boundaries oscillate between sharp definition in stable times and greater fluidity under threat.
practical_implication: Managers of elite categories and luxury brands should monitor shifts in broader societal tastes and values, not just competitive moves, because cultural consonance is as crucial to enduring eliteness as exclusivity. Sustaining elite status calls for organizational ambidexterity: preserving continuity with the category's storied past while selectively absorbing nonelite practices and reinterpreting tradition to align with contemporary values.
limitations: The study is based on a single category (luxury) within a single industry (U.S. hotels), which constrains generalizability across sectors and national settings. The analysis takes a broad-brush, category-level approach to public discourse and does not deeply track individual organizations, specific actors, or membership-level boundary dynamics.
future_research: The authors call for replication of the symbolic boundary settlement–disruption framework in other cultural-industry contexts (restaurants, retail, watches, wine, haute couture, "masstige" brands) and in non-cultural or credence-good settings. They also encourage cross-national comparisons of how class structures shape boundary dynamics and finer-grained tracking of which actors and organizations come to influence elite category discourse over time.
abstract: We conducted an inductive study of discourse associated with the U.S. luxury hotel category, from its beginnings in 1790 through 2015, to explain how cultural processes contribute to elite category endurance. Analyzing data from historical archives, interviews, and observations, we use both qualitative and quantitative methods to reveal how the endurance of an elite category is an ongoing cultural accomplishment that occurs via periodic redefinition of its "symbolic boundary"—that is, the set of meanings and practices that distinguish the elite from nonelite. Modeling the boundary in terms of semiotic codes of opposition, we find that the encoding of the symbolic boundary serves as a temporary settlement that conveys both the category's elite exclusivity and its cultural consonance with broader societal beliefs, tastes, and practices. Over time, however, with industry and societal changes, tensions erupt in the balance between the needs for exclusivity and consonance, propelling a redefinition of what it means to be elite. Our research extends current theorizations of elite category endurance by revealing how the elite symbolic boundary is neither permanent nor unassailable; rather, we show how it changes to enable long-term elite category endurance.

title: Balancing “Protective Disguise” with “Harmonious Advocacy”: Social Venture Legitimation in Authoritarian Contexts
methods: In-depth, single-case qualitative study using process research (Langley, 1999) and Gioia-style open coding; 45 semi-structured interviews across four rounds, 93 media texts, 12 public speeches/interviews, and field-visit observations, with theory-building through process-tracing.
industry: Disability-rights social venture (registered as NGO, positioned as accessibility consultancy) and its key audiences (government, corporate employers, nondisabled employees, NGOs)
time_period: Organizational history 2011-2020; primary fieldwork during two visits in February and April 2018
units: One focal social venture ("Amal," pseudonym) plus actors in its audience environment
n_sample: 45 interviews; 93 media texts; 12 public speeches/interviews; field observations from two visits
authors: Neuberger, I.; Kroezen, J.; Tracey, P.
theories: optimal distinctiveness (Deephouse, 1999; Zhao et al., 2017); organizational legitimacy (Suchman, 1995; Deephouse et al., 2017; Suddaby, Bitektine, & Haack, 2017); social venture legitimation (Ruebottom, 2013; Nicholls, 2010)
keywords: authoritarian contexts; disability inclusion; harmonious advocacy; optimal assimilation; protective disguise; social venture legitimation
research_question: "How do new social ventures gain legitimacy in authoritarian contexts?"
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: protective disguise vs. harmonious advocacy; political vs. cultural manifestations of authoritarianism; "fitting in" vs. advocating for beneficiaries
- Legitimation challenges: (a) political manifestation — social activism perceived as threat to national interests; (b) cultural manifestation — entrenched beliefs and practices that devalue the human rights of marginalized groups
- Protective disguise practices: (1) cloaking social mission under rhetorical alignment with regime goals (economic prosperity, national stability, tourism); (2) camouflaging social action through an innocuous organizational design (positioning as a commercial accessibility consultancy rather than a human-rights NGO)
- Harmonious advocacy practices: (3) experiential construction of social problems (community days, blindfolded simulations, ambassador stories that build empathy); (4) reactive campaigning for social mission (leveraging conducive events such as the 2017 disability law and the "Year of People with Disabilities," while explicitly shielding government from criticism)
- Emergent outcomes: venture perceived as nonthreatening, then as worthy of support; growing audience backing
- Boundary conditions: continuous balancing required; ventures may need to pivot back toward disguise during crackdowns and forward toward advocacy during conducive periods

The process Amal followed shows that legitimation in authoritarian contexts is underpinned by a continuous balancing of disguise and advocacy that the authors label "optimal assimilation." Disguise is necessary because confrontation triggers regime aggression; advocacy is necessary because pure disguise prevents the venture from acting on its mission. Disguise lays the platform that makes later, carefully calibrated advocacy possible, and the two strategies are continuously rebalanced in response to political-cultural dynamics.
theoretical_contribution: The paper builds a process model of social-venture legitimation in authoritarian contexts that identifies "protective disguise" and "harmonious advocacy" as the two overarching strategies and "optimal assimilation" as the governing principle — a counterpart to "optimal distinctiveness" in democratic contexts. It addresses the democratic-society bias in organizational-legitimacy research by showing that core assumptions (e.g., the evaluative benefits of "standing out," the four-state progression toward "accepted") do not transfer to authoritarian regimes, where ventures occupy a liminal zone between "debated" and "proper" and political elites uniquely bestow or withdraw legitimacy.
practical_implication: Social ventures operating in authoritarian regimes should resist transplanting democratic-context playbooks: confrontational framing, hero/villain rhetoric, and overt rights-based campaigning can endanger founders and trigger forced closure. Founders should instead cloak their mission in language that aligns with regime priorities, adopt an innocuous organizational form (e.g., a service-providing consultancy), and use empathy-building experiential activities plus reactive campaigning tied to government-initiated events to advance their cause without attracting unwanted political attention.
limitations: The study rests on a single case in one authoritarian context (post-revolutionary Egypt), focused on a relatively less politically contentious issue (disability inclusion); the findings may differ for ventures tackling more sensitive issues (e.g., free speech, LGBTQ rights) or operating in other authoritarian or hybrid regimes (China, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Albania, Nigeria). The authors also flag that whether "optimal assimilation" is the morally best path is a normative question they cannot answer.
future_research: Comparative work across authoritarian and hybrid regimes is needed to test whether the disguise-advocacy balance generalizes. Future studies should examine more politically and culturally contentious causes, explore how a commercial vs. social orientation shapes legitimation under different regimes, and investigate the state's role as a uniquely powerful audience whose interdependency with other audiences shapes legitimacy judgments — even in democracies.
abstract: This paper seeks to advance understanding of how new social ventures can gain legitimacy in authoritarian contexts. Through a study of a new disability rights organization in post-revolutionary Egypt, we theorize how authoritarianism poses distinct challenges for social ventures that require different legitimation strategies than those commonly reported in the literature. Specifically, we use our case study to build a theoretical model that suggests social ventures need to achieve “optimal assimilation” by balancing “protective disguise” with “harmonious advocacy.” By explicitly theorizing social venture legitimation in authoritarian contexts, we advance the budding literature on social venture legitimation that has so far predominantly considered legitimation in more democratic contexts. Moreover, our study shows that organizational legitimacy may need to be conceptualized differently when examining social ventures—and indeed other forms of organization—in authoritarian regimes.
apa_citation: Neuberger, I., Kroezen, J., & Tracey, P. (2023). Balancing “protective disguise” with “harmonious advocacy”: Social venture legitimation in authoritarian contexts. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(1), 67-101. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.0517

title: Toward a Configural Theory of Job Demands and Resources
methods: Three cross-sectional and time-lagged survey studies of employees; fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) supplemented by OLS regression of configuration membership scores on outcomes.
industry: Diverse occupations (MTurk workers; MBA alumni and a major technology company; Prolific Academic online panel)
time_period: Study 2 collected during the COVID-19 pandemic; calibration data drawn from the past 10 years of published management research
units: Full-time employees
n_sample: 199 (Study 1); 124 (Study 2); 412 (Study 3)
authors: Ong, W. J.; Johnson, M. D.
theories: Job demands–resources (JDR) model; bad-is-stronger-than-good principle; demand–control–support model; person-centered/configural theory
keywords: autonomy; configurations; emotional demands; engagement; exhaustion; fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis; job demands–resources; person-centered approach; social support; workload
research_question: Which configurations of job demands and resources are sufficient to produce the presence and absence of exhaustion and engagement (and other strain outcomes), and do these configurations exhibit equifinality and causal asymmetry that variable-centered models cannot detect?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the demand–control–support extension of JDR theory and the "bad-is-stronger-than-good" cognition literature, the authors theorize that several qualitatively different configurations of high demands and low resources can be equally sufficient to produce exhaustion (equifinality), and that the configurations producing an outcome are not the inverse of those producing its absence (causal asymmetry). They predict that high-workload/low-autonomy and high-workload/low-social-support combinations are each sufficient for exhaustion, that some configurations of multiple high demands cannot be buffered by any resource, and that there are more pathways to negative than positive outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reinterprets the JDR model in configural terms, replacing the additive/multiplicative variable-centered logic with set-theoretic propositions about equifinal and causally asymmetric configurations of demands and resources. It shows that certain demands (high workload combined with emotional demands) cannot be buffered by any resource, that the absence of social support can itself function as a demand, and that there are more configurations sufficient for exhaustion than for engagement, instantiating a "bad-is-stronger-than-good" pattern within JDR theory.
practical_implication: Managers should diagnose employees' overall configurations of job demands and resources rather than intervening on any single demand or resource in isolation: simply lowering workload will not help an employee whose exhaustion comes from low social support, and adding social support will not help when high workload combines with high emotional demands. Because exhaustion has multiple sufficient pathways but its absence has none, prevention is more tractable than cure.
limitations: Studies 1 and 2 measured demands, resources, and outcomes at the same time from the same source, raising common-method concerns (addressed in Study 3 with time-lagged measurement). The observational design leaves the causal ordering of JDRs and outcomes open, and samples were drawn primarily from the United States, which may limit cross-cultural generalizability. The set of demands and resources examined was finite and did not include nonwork antecedents of strain.
future_research: The authors call for longitudinal designs that test lagged effects between JDRs and outcomes, replications in non-U.S. and especially collectivistic cultural contexts to test whether social support and autonomy play different buffering roles, and extensions to additional outcomes such as performance. They also suggest examining antecedents of configuration membership (e.g., personality traits, organizational and national institutions) and identifying configuration-specific mediating mechanisms.
abstract: Job demands–resources research has largely adopted a variable-centered approach to test main and interactive effects of demands and resources on employee outcomes. However, this approach cannot detect distinct configurations of job demands and resources that may lead to the same outcomes, and the many multiplicative models attempting to do so have received little support. We take a person-centered theoretical approach to examine configurations of demands and resources that are sufficient to produce exhaustion, engagement, and other strain outcomes. Using fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis across three studies, we find three equifinal configurations sufficient to produce exhaustion: (a) high workload and emotional demands, (b) low social support, and (c) high workload and low autonomy. We also find evidence for causal asymmetry in both exhaustion and engagement. Our person-centered approach yields more theoretically consistent results compared to a variable-centered approach. The findings highlight that certain job demands may only be buffered by specific resources, and that certain configurations of demands cannot be buffered at all.
apa_citation: Ong, W. J., & Johnson, M. D. (2023). Toward a configural theory of job demands and resources. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(1), 195–221. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.0493

title: The Impact of Communist Ideology on the Patenting Activity of Chinese Firms
methods: Panel analysis of 1,298 non-state-owned Chinese listed manufacturing firms (5,731 firm-year observations) over 2000-2017. Random-effects negative binomial regression for patent applications (count outcome) and logit model with standard errors clustered by firm for patent infringement (binary outcome). Propensity score matching (PSM) addresses endogeneity of Party membership; robustness checks include coarsened exact matching (CEM), entropy balancing, full-sample estimation, alternative measures, and impact-threshold-of-confounding-variable analysis.
industry: Non-state-owned manufacturing firms (industry grouping based on three-digit classification by China Securities Regulatory Commission)
time_period: 2000-2017 (explanatory variables 2000-2016; dependent variables 2001-2017)
units: Firm-year observations of listed non-SOEs on the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges
n_sample: 1,298 firms; 5,731 matched firm-year observations (9,262 in full sample)
authors: Xu, Dean; Zhou, Kevin Zheng; Chen, Shihua
theories: Imprinting theory (Marquis & Tilcsik, 2013; Stinchcombe, 1965); Political ideology in business research; Upper echelons theory (Hambrick, 2007; Hambrick & Mason, 1984)
keywords: Chinese Communist Party; Maoist communist ideology; board chairs; ideological decay; non-state-owned enterprises; patent infringement; patenting activity; secondhand ideological imprinting
research_question: Why does Maoist communist ideology continue to affect the patenting behavior of Chinese Communist Party members—including younger members who never directly experienced the Maoist era—and through what specific imprinting mechanism does this ideological influence persist amid decades of decoupling between Party policy and Maoist doctrine?
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Founder chair, government/SOE experience, overseas experience, chair ownership, R&D intensity, state shares, firm size, firm age, ROA, industry competition (1 − HHI), city-level GDP growth, Internet development, provincial legal development, year and industry dummies

Drawing on imprinting theory, the authors argue that older Party members carry firsthand Maoist imprints from the politically sensitive 1960s–1970s, while younger Party members—who joined under Dengism—acquire Maoist orientations only indirectly, through "secondhand imprinting" by older Party-member peers in their elite social and role category. Maoist beliefs (anti-private-property, anti-IPR, devaluation of scientific work and intellectuals) translate into lower patent application volumes and higher patent infringement propensity. Higher education and younger age weaken this effect (ideological decay), but a high regional presence of older Party-member directors reactivates Maoist influence among younger chairs (offsetting age-based decay), though it does not offset education-based decay.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends imprinting theory by empirically demonstrating secondhand imprinting in a setting where the original imprinting environment has disappeared—showing that older Party-member directors in the same regional elite category pass Maoist ideological imprints onto younger Party-member board chairs who never experienced the Maoist era directly. It contributes to the political ideology literature by modeling the interplay between ideological decay (via age, education) and ideological persistence (via secondhand imprinting) within a single integrated framework, departing from the Western liberal/conservative dichotomy that dominates extant work.
practical_implication: When assessing Chinese non-SOEs as innovation partners or rivals, observers should weigh board chairs' ideological background (CCP membership) alongside their age, education, and the demographic composition of older Party-member directors in their regional social network—because firms led by Party-member chairs file fewer patents, more often violate other firms' patent rights, and may instead diversify into multiple industries as an alternative growth strategy. Education in particular appears to robustly counteract Maoist ideological influence on innovation.
limitations: The study isolates Maoist ideological elements, but these are intermixed with broader Chinese cultural features (e.g., Confucian skepticism of individualism and IPR; historically modest cultural emphasis on science and technology) that also bear on innovation activity. The authors caution against overgeneralizing the ideology effect to all corporate decisions, noting that when evidence is unambiguous Party members often act pragmatically (e.g., founding private firms after SOE collapse).
future_research: Cross-national comparisons of how different versions of communist ideology shape firm behavior in China, Cuba, Vietnam, and former Soviet Bloc countries would test the generalizability of the secondhand-imprinting mechanism. Future work could also examine how a board chair's home province, prior SOE/planned-economy experience, or other contextual moderators interact with political ideology to shape innovation orientations.
abstract: The Chinese Communist Party began decoupling its policies and practices from Maoist communist ideology more than four decades ago. Yet, why does Maoism continue to have an impact on the behavior of Party members? In this study, we argue that, although the influence of Maoist ideology has become weaker among younger Party members and Party members with higher educational attainment, such ideological decay is countered by a process of secondhand ideological imprinting. Based on data from 1,298 nonstate-owned Chinese listed firms for 2000–2017, we find that firms with Party-member board chairs file fewer patent applications and are more likely to commit patent infringement. These effects are weaker if a board chair is younger or has higher educational attainment. Importantly, the moderating effect of young age is reduced as the presence of older Party-member corporate directors in a region becomes more prominent. However, the moderating effect of education appears to be unaffected by the presence of older Party-member directors. These findings generate fresh insights on the dynamics of ideological decay and persistence.
apa_citation: Xu, D., Zhou, K. Z., & Chen, S. (2023). The impact of communist ideology on the patenting activity of Chinese firms. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(1), 102–132. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.0810

title: Does Job Satisfaction Rise and Fall with the Economy? Cross-Sectional, Longitudinal, and Experimental Evidence That Job Satisfaction Increases during Recessions
methods: Three studies: (1) OLS regressions on repeated cross-sectional GSS data with national and state unemployment rates, standard errors clustered by year (and by state-year); (2) hierarchical/multilevel linear models with autoregressive residuals and individual fixed effects on longitudinal BHPS panel data; (3) randomized between-subjects experiment manipulating economic conditions via newspaper articles, with bootstrapped mediation analysis (lavaan).
industry: Cross-industry working adults (16/17-category NAICS classifications used as controls)
time_period: Study 1: GSS waves 1974–2016 (data over four decades); Study 2: BHPS/Understanding Society 1991–2013; Study 3: online experiment (article adapted from 2021)
units: Individual employed adults (survey respondents and experiment participants)
n_sample: Study 1: 23,335 respondents; Study 2: 12,859 respondents; Study 3: 512 participants
authors: Bianchi, Emily C.; Martin, Chris C.; Li, Ren
theories: Cornell model / frame-of-reference theory of job satisfaction (Smith, Kendall, & Hulin, 1969); impressionable years hypothesis; investment model (Rusbult & Farrell, 1983); system justification / compensatory control (Kay et al., 2009)
keywords: economic conditions; job satisfaction; recessions; salience of alternative jobs; sense-making; unemployment rate
research_question: Do macroeconomic conditions outside the workplace shape how satisfied people are with their jobs? Specifically, the authors ask whether job satisfaction rises during recessions (when unemployment is high) and falls during booms, and whether this relationship is driven by the reduced salience of alternative jobs.
hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1. There is a positive relationship between the unemployment rate and job satisfaction (predicted positive: higher unemployment, higher job satisfaction).
- Hypothesis 2. The positive relationship between the unemployment rate and job satisfaction is mediated by the reduced salience of alternative jobs (predicted positive indirect effect: higher unemployment lowers the salience of alternative jobs, which in turn raises job satisfaction).
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Age, age squared, gender, income, linear time trend; industry and occupation; tenure (Study 3); state dummies (Study 1 state models).

When job alternatives are plentiful and salient, jobs are judged against higher reference standards and comparisons surface their negative features, depressing satisfaction (the Cornell frame-of-reference and investment models). During recessions, scarce and unreachable alternatives become less salient, so people focus on the positive features of their existing jobs and use system-justifying, compensatory-control strategies to view their situation more favorably. Study 3's mediation confirms that worse economic conditions lower the salience of alternatives, which in turn raises job satisfaction.
data_measures:
- Study 1 data source: the General Social Survey (GSS), a nationally representative repeated cross-sectional survey of American adults; 23,335 respondents interviewed in one of 29 waves administered between 1974 and 2016, retained if they were working full time at interview and had valid data on all independent and dependent variables (55.1% male, 81.2% White, mean age 40.5 years, SD = 12.1).
- Study 1 IV: economic conditions operationalized as the national unemployment rate, chosen because it tracks job availability and perceptions of the economy more tightly than GDP, stock market performance, or inflation-adjusted indicators, and because it is only modestly correlated with year (r = −.21 over the study window). A second set of models used the state unemployment rate (range 2.3% to 15.3%), obtained as restricted state-level data from the National Opinion Research Center and merged on state of current residence and survey year, giving a slightly smaller sample (n = 20,890).
- Study 1 DV: a single GSS item — "On the whole, how satisfied are you with the work you do—would you say you are very satisfied, moderately satisfied, a little dissatisfied, or very dissatisfied?" — recoded so higher values reflect greater job satisfaction. Because this item measures work rather than job satisfaction and is single-item, the authors validated it in a separate 250-person Amazon Mechanical Turk survey against the Brayfield and Rothe (1951) 5-item scale (r = .76, p < .001).
- Study 1 controls and estimation: age, age squared, gender, log inflation-adjusted income (built from GSS category midpoints), and a linear time trend; fuller models added the 16 industry categories of the North American Industry Classification System 2007 and six 2010 occupational categories, and the state models added state dummy variables. All models are ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions with random errors clustered by year for national analyses and by state-year for state analyses.
- Study 2 data source: the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and its Understanding Society continuation, collected 1991–2013 by the Institute for Social and Economic Research at the University of Essex; all 12,859 original BHPS respondents (regional and other oversamples excluded), averaging 7.7 years per participant and 98,153 to 99,314 year-observations depending on the measure.
- Study 2 IV and DV: the UK national unemployment rate from Eurostat (M = 6.49, SD = 1.66 over the period) as the IV; job satisfaction measured by the single item "All things considered, how satisfied or dissatisfied are you with your present job overall?" from 1 ("not satisfied at all") to 7 ("completely satisfied"), asked only of respondents employed at the time of the survey. Controls: age, age squared, and log inflation-adjusted annual labour income (imputed variables wfiyrl in the BHPS and w_fimnlabgrs_dv in Understanding Society) at level 1, and the time-invariant gender variable at level 2.
- Study 2 estimation: hierarchical linear models with random coefficients and a first-order autoregressive residual structure, chosen because the intraclass correlation for job satisfaction was .30, with standard errors clustered by person and non-consecutive waves treated as gaps. A companion specification entered a dummy variable for every participant (individual fixed effects) to absorb all observed and unobserved person-level variation and so test within-person fluctuation. A supplementary model restricted the sample to respondents with no spells of unemployment during the study — reported as 8,587 participants in Table 4, Model 4, while the Sample section describes this restricted sample as 8,617 respondents, or 67% of the sample.
- Study 3 design and manipulation: a randomized between-subjects experiment on 512 usable Amazon Mechanical Turk respondents (700 recruited; 188 excluded for failing an attention check or taking more than two standard deviations longer than average), all currently employed, mean age 35.87 (SD = 8.75), mean tenure 14.33 years (SD = 4.80). Under a memory-recall cover story, participants were randomly assigned to read a modified New York Times article reporting a bad economy ("New Unemployment Claims Rose Again Last Week", 112 words, adapted from a 2021 article) or a good economy ("Job Openings Are Everywhere", 114 words), viewing it for at least 30 seconds; the manipulation was modeled on Hill et al. (2012, Study 2) and checked with two items on job-market strength and the perceived unemployment rate.
- Study 3 measures: DV = Brayfield and Rothe's (1951) 5-item job satisfaction scale, 1 ("strongly disagree") to 7 ("strongly agree"), sample item "I feel fairly well satisfied with my present job". Mediator = Miller's (1997) 6-item Attention to Alternatives Index, adapted from the salience of alternative romantic partners to the salience of other possible jobs, sample item "I often think about other job opportunities", same 1–7 response format. Controls: age, age squared, gender, income, job tenure, the 17-category North American Industry Classification System, and the 6-category Census Occupational Classification system.
- Study 3 estimation: mediation estimated with the lavaan R package, with indirect-effect significance assessed using bias-corrected accelerated bootstrap 95% confidence intervals from 5,000 resamples based on the product of coefficients for each path; because bias-corrected bootstrapping can inflate Type I error, the authors also ran a joint-significance test with Monte Carlo confidence intervals (5,000 iterations).
- Identification: only Study 3 randomly assigns economic conditions, which the paper describes as allowing a more direct test of causality. Studies 1 and 2 are associational — the paper states that the correlational nature of these datasets precluded it from establishing causality. Study 2's individual fixed effects and continuously-employed subsample rule out stable person-level confounds and cyclical change in workforce composition, but the design remains observational rather than a causal identification strategy.
key_findings:
- Hypothesis 1 was supported in each of the three studies, but the paper emphasizes that the magnitude of the effects is relatively small.
- Study 1 (national unemployment rate, OLS): higher unemployment predicted greater job satisfaction with only a linear time trend (b = 0.011, SE = 0.005, p < .05), after adding age, age squared, gender, and income (b = 0.011, SE = 0.004, p < .05), and after adding industry and occupational controls (b = 0.010, SE = 0.004, p < .05). Model R² ranged from 0.015 to 0.043.
- Study 1 (state unemployment rate with state dummies, n = 20,890): higher state unemployment predicted greater job satisfaction with a time trend only (b = 0.009, SE = 0.003, p < .01), with individual-level characteristics added (b = 0.008, SE = 0.003, p < .01), and with industry and occupational controls added (b = 0.007, SE = 0.003, p < .01).
- Study 1 robustness with alternative indicators: substituting other economic measures for the unemployment rate, the paper reports that indicators linked to perceptions of the economy were predictive of job satisfaction — inflation-adjusted median income divided by 10,000 (b = −0.005, SE = 0.002, p < .05), consumer confidence (b = −0.033, SE = 0.014, p < .05), consumer sentiment (b = −0.010, SE = 0.004, p < .01), and the Consumer Price Index (b = −0.0064, SE = 0.0019, p < .01) — whereas indicators not tightly tied to consumer perceptions were not (real per capita GDP in 1,000s: b = −0.005, SE = 0.004, n.s.; S&P 500: b = 0.000, SE = 0.000, n.s.).
- Study 2 (BHPS multilevel models): worse economic conditions were associated with greater job satisfaction (b = .013, SE = .003, p < .001), and the result held with age, age squared, gender, and income controlled (b = .012, SE = .003, p < .001). The individual fixed-effects specification also found higher unemployment associated with higher job satisfaction (b = .064, SE = .003, p < .001), showing the relationship holds within the same people over time. Restricting the sample to continuously employed respondents reproduced the effect (b = .018, SE = .004, p < .001), so the pattern is not explained by cyclical change in the composition of the workforce.
- Study 3 (experiment, preliminary test of Hypothesis 1): participants who read the bad-economy article reported greater job satisfaction (M = 4.83, SD = 0.89) than participants in the comparison condition (M = 4.68, SD = 0.88), t(510) = 1.94, p = .05 — the Results sentence labels this comparison group the "control condition", although the design contrasts a bad-economy with a good-economy article. Controlling for age, age squared, gender, tenure, and income, worse economic conditions continued to predict higher job satisfaction (b = 0.20, SE = 0.08, p = .01). Manipulation checks worked as intended: the bad-economy group rated the job market as weaker (M = 5.52, SD = 1.66 vs. M = 6.04, SD = 1.08; t(510) = 4.23, p < .001) and estimated unemployment as higher (M = 5.99, SD = 1.24 vs. M = 5.65, SD = 1.55; t(510) = 2.74, p < .01).
- Hypothesis 2 was tested only in Study 3 — Studies 1 and 2 contained no measure of the mediator — and was supported there. The indirect effect of economic conditions on job satisfaction through the salience of alternatives was significant (b = 0.12, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.04, 0.23], p < .01), with bad economic conditions reducing the salience of alternatives (b = −0.29, SE = 0.11) and the salience of alternatives negatively related to job satisfaction (b = −0.42, SE = 0.04); the total effect was 0.18 (SE = 0.08), CI [0.03, 0.34]. Similar results emerged with and without controls, and the joint-significance test with Monte Carlo confidence intervals also excluded zero.
- The reverse mediational pathway (job satisfaction as the mediator and salience of alternatives as the outcome) produced much weaker evidence: indirect effect b = −0.11 (SE = 0.06), CI [−0.257, 0.003], p = .072.
- Post hoc analyses in Studies 1 and 2 found that life satisfaction fell with the economy even as job satisfaction rose, which the authors read as evidence that the affective boost during downturns is limited to work rather than extending to all domains of life.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends job-satisfaction research—which has focused almost exclusively on situational conditions inside the workplace—by showing that contextual conditions outside organizations also shape workplace attitudes. It contributes to work on the psychological effects of recessions and provides theoretical and empirical support for the idea that adverse societal events can promote positive (not just disengaging) sense-making processes that bolster workplace attitudes.
practical_implication: Organizations may benefit from acknowledging and addressing external economic events rather than ignoring them. Because employees seem driven to view their jobs favorably during downturns, efforts to raise satisfaction may be well-received then, and hiring during recessions may yield workers who rate their jobs more highly. Conversely, firms should attend more to satisfaction during booms, when salient alternatives make dissatisfaction costlier and turnover easier.
limitations: The magnitude of the effects is relatively small, plausibly because countervailing forces—greater workplace stress and job insecurity during recessions—depress satisfaction at the same time the identified sense-making processes elevate it. The correlational nature of the first two studies' datasets precluded the authors from establishing causality; by manipulating rather than measuring economic conditions, Study 3 allowed "a more direct test of causality" and tested the mediator.
future_research: Future work could simultaneously capture the competing forces that elevate and depress satisfaction during downturns, and examine when the elevating factors dominate. Researchers could also test moderation by personality (e.g., need for cognitive closure) or demographics (recessions are unevenly experienced, e.g., low-wage workers), and explore additional psychological mechanisms such as tempered expectations or gratitude, and why alternatives undermine satisfaction.
abstract: While recessions have many adverse consequences for individuals and organizations, we propose that they have positive implications for job satisfaction. We argue that during bad economic times, people will be less attuned to other possible jobs, and more likely to see their own jobs favorably. We find support for these predictions across three studies. Study 1 (n 5 23,335) utilizes a large cross-sectional survey of American adults collected over four decades and finds that job satisfaction increases during recessions and declines during booms. Study 2 (n 5 12,859) replicates this result using a large longitudinal survey of British adults and finds that job satisfaction rises and falls with the unemployment rate even within the same people. Finally, Study 3 (n 5 512) uses an experimental design and finds that the relationship between economic conditions and job satisfaction is mediated by the reduced salience of alternative jobs. While scholars have long recognized that job satisfaction is affected by situational features inside organizations, our findings suggest that conditions outside the workplace can also influence how people think about and evaluate their jobs.

Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental evidence that job satisfaction increases during recessions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(2), 688–709. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.0405

title: Do I Dare? The Psychodynamics of Anticipated Image Risk, Leader-Identity Endorsement, and Leader Emergence
methods: Multistage mixed-methods design across four studies (plus supplementary studies B and C): a longitudinal field survey of MBA consulting teams (Study 1), a quantitative experiment manipulating lay theories (Study B), an exploratory qualitative survey (Study 2), a multisource field survey of employee-supervisor dyads (Study 3), and a podcast-based experiment (Study 4). Quantitative analyses use multivariate regression and PROCESS macro moderated-mediation models with bootstrapped indirect effects; qualitative data thematically coded.
industry: Study 1: multidisciplinary MBA student consulting teams addressing business challenges; later studies span a variety of industries (online/MTurk workers, Air Force cadets, employee-supervisor dyads)
time_period: Study 1 data collected in 2017; project published 2023
units: Individuals (within consulting teams, dyads, and online/virtual worker samples)
n_sample: Study 1: 411 individuals in 83 teams; Study 2: 327 workers (plus 119 cadets); Study 3: 377 employee-supervisor pairs; Study 4: 448 virtual workers
authors: Lee Cunningham, Julia; Sonday, Laura; Ashford, Susan J.
theories: identity work (Brown, 2015, 2017; Caza, Vough, & Puranik, 2018); lay theories / implicit theories (Dweck, 2006); psychological/ego defense (Cramer, 2000; Freud, 1936)
keywords: anticipated image risk; identity work; lay theories of leadership ability; leader-identity endorsement; leadership emergence; psychodynamic defense
research_question: Why don't more people internalize a leader identity and emerge as leaders? Specifically, how does anticipated image risk—individuals' belief that leading might harm how others see them—reduce leader-identity endorsement and thereby leadership emergence, and how do lay (fixed vs. malleable) theories of leadership ability moderate this process?
hypotheses:
The quantitative components state six formal hypotheses, tested across Studies 1, B, 3, and 4. Study 2 is exploratory and qualitative and advances no a priori hypotheses.
- Hypothesis 1. When individuals anticipate that leadership will be risky for their image, they will be less likely to emerge as leaders.
- Hypothesis 2. When individuals anticipate that leadership will be risky for their image, they will be less likely to endorse a leader identity.
- Hypothesis 3. Individuals' endorsement of a leader identity is positively associated with their leadership emergence.
- Hypothesis 4. Anticipating image risk has a negative indirect effect on leadership emergence, through leader-identity endorsement.
- Hypothesis 5. The negative effect of anticipated image risk on leader-identity endorsement is less pronounced for those who hold a malleable view than for those who hold a fixed view of leadership ability.
- Hypothesis 6. The negative indirect effect of anticipated image risk on leadership emergence through leader-identity endorsement will be stronger for those who hold a fixed view of leadership than for those who hold a malleable view of leadership ability.
mechanism_summary: When individuals anticipate that leading will damage their image, ego/self-protection prompts a psychodynamic form of identity work in which they decline to endorse "leader" as a self-descriptor ("that's just not who I am"), neutralizing the threat while avoiding seeing themselves as lacking courage. Reduced leader-identity endorsement in turn lowers leadership emergence. A fixed lay theory of leadership ability strengthens this negative path because reputational damage is seen as permanent and growth as impossible, whereas a malleable view buffers it. The qualitative study specifies three concrete image concerns (bossy, unqualified, different) underlying the construct, with fear of seeming unqualified the most debilitating.
data_measures:
The dominant method is quantitative (Studies 1, B, 3, and 4), with Study 2 supplying qualitative construct elaboration.
- Study 1 (longitudinal field survey; one of the two studies testing all six hypotheses, alongside Study 4): 411 first-year MBA students working in 83 multidisciplinary consulting teams of four to six at a large U.S. midwestern university in 2017, surveyed by the MBA program office three weeks before team formation (Time 1) and just as the seven-week project completed (Time 2), roughly 10 weeks apart. IV anticipated image risk in leadership: 5-item Likert scale from Zhang et al. (2020), alpha = .75, measured at Time 1 (sample item: "If I step up and attempt to lead the team, others in the group will think less of me"). Moderator lay theories of leadership ability: the four-item "implicit theory of leadership" scale from Hoyt et al. (2012), which substitutes "leadership" for "intelligence" in Dweck's (1999) implicit-theory measure, alpha = .84, coded so that high scores represent a fixed view. Mediator leader-identity endorsement: a newly developed 4-item measure administered at Time 2 (sample items "I see myself as a leader" and "Being a leader is very important to my sense of who I am"), also used by Lanaj et al. (2021, 2022). DV leadership emergence: three peer-rated items from Lord, Foti, and De Vader (1984) as used by DeRue et al. (2015), alpha = .93, with every team member rating each other member's contribution to team leadership and the ratings averaged. Controls: age and gender (in all studies), plus leadership self-efficacy (Paglis & Green, 2002; alpha = .76) to test incremental validity. Estimation: multivariate regression with mean-centered predictors and an interaction term, plus PROCESS model 4 (simple mediation) and model 7 (first-stage conditional process) with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (Hayes, 2017). The authors state the Study 1 data are correlational, so the design is associational rather than causally identified.
- Study B (Online Appendix B; preregistered experiment, n = 324, nonoverlapping sample): experimentally manipulated lay theories of leadership ability in order to test the first stage of the model causally rather than by measurement.
- Study 2 (qualitative, exploratory): 327 full-time workers from a variety of industries recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk for a 15-minute survey paying $1.00, answering deliberately open-ended, non-priming questions about what, if anything, makes them feel uncomfortable (or comfortable) using the label "leader." Research assistants and one author first performed "complete coding" of everything relevant to what makes "leader" an uncomfortable identity, then a second, focused coding of image-risk mentions, with multiple codes allowed per response and periodic coder meetings after batches of 10 to 20 responses; disagreements were resolved by an author. Codes mentioned by at least three respondents were clustered into themes that all authors refined for internal homogeneity and external heterogeneity. 285 respondents (87%) named at least one source of discomfort, and 88 (31% of those) mentioned image-related concerns. A separate survey of 119 Air Force cadets was used to check whether the themes replicated in a different sample.
- Study 3 (multisource field survey): 377 focal employee–supervisor pairs, combining 233 pairs obtained by snowball sampling through an undergraduate management course at a midwestern U.S. university with 144 pairs recruited via the paid Positly.com pool; the authors confirmed the two data sets showed identical patterns before combining them. Employees rated the three specific image-risk scales developed from the Study 2 themes (fear of seeming bossy alpha = .93, fear of seeming different alpha = .94, fear of seeming unqualified alpha = .90) on 7-point agreement scales following the stem "If I step up and attempt to lead in my team at work ...", and rated their own leader-identity endorsement with the Study 1 measure (alpha = .88); supervisors independently rated the employee's leadership emergence with the Study 1 three-item measure (alpha = .86). Controls: age, gender, narcissism, extraversion, leadership self-efficacy, and prior discomfort in leading. Mediation was tested with PROCESS model 4 and 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Predictor and mediator were separated within the survey, but the authors state that common method variance bias is still possible.
- Study 4 (preregistered randomized experiment): 448 virtual workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk (500 targeted; 4 excluded a priori for not reading instructions and 47 for completion times outside 12 to 33 minutes), paid $2.50, randomly assigned to one of two otherwise-identical eight-minute podcasts presenting leadership as riskier than people think (high-risk) or less so (low-risk), with the script built around the three specific image concerns from Study 2 and an "expert" voice reinforcing the framing. Leader-identity endorsement used the Study 1 measure (alpha = .92) plus Bergami and Bagozzi's (2000) five-diagram circles measure of self-identity congruence as a constructive replication with a different operationalization. Because participants did not actually interact in a team, leadership emergence was operationalized as willingness to lead ("If given the opportunity, I would like to step up and lead this group," alpha = .88). Lay theories of leadership ability were measured (as in Study 1), not manipulated. Controls: age, gender, and six preregistered podcast-perception items (difficulty, credibility, persuasiveness, and so forth); a separate pilot (n = 200) confirmed the manipulation moved both general and specific image risk.
key_findings:
Support is heterogeneous across studies, so it is reported per study rather than pooled. The mediation chain (Hypotheses 2, 3, and 4) held in every study that tested it, but Hypothesis 1 failed in Study 3 and the lay-theory moderation (Hypotheses 5 and 6) failed in Study 4; the authors themselves write that "the data offer mixed support" for the moderation argument.
- Study 1 (n = 411; correlational field survey): all six hypotheses supported. H1 — anticipated image risk negatively predicted peer-rated leadership emergence at Time 2 (Table 3, Models 7, 8, and 9; B = -.166, SE = .065 in Model 8). H2 — image risk negatively predicted leader-identity endorsement at Time 2 (B = -.17, SE = .07, p = .018). H3 — endorsement was positively related to peer-rated emergence (B = .28, SE = .04, p < .001). H4 — the indirect effect was significant (effect = -.05, SE = .02, 95% CI [-.103, -.005]) alongside a significant direct effect (effect = -.14, SE = .06, p = .017), which the authors read as partial mediation. H5 — the image-risk-by-lay-theory interaction on endorsement was significant (B = -.30, SE = 0.12, p = .013), with simple slopes negative and significant for a fixed view (+1 SD; B = -.31, SE = .10, p = .002) but null for a malleable view (-1 SD; B = .02, SE = .10, p = .871). H6 — the conditional indirect effect was significant under a fixed view (effect = -.08, SE = .03, 95% CI [-.144, -.025]) but not under a malleable view (effect = .005, SE = .03, 95% CI [-.06, .063]); index of moderated mediation = -.08, SE = .04, 95% CI [-.165, -.005].
- Study B (n = 324; preregistered, lay theories manipulated): supported H2 and H5 per the paper's summary table — inducing a malleable view of leadership ability attenuated the negative influence of anticipated image risk on leader-identity endorsement. (The Limitations section additionally describes Study B as finding further support for Hypotheses 5 and 6, whereas Table 1 marks H6 as not tested there.)
- Study 2 (qualitative, n = 327): three specific image concerns emerged — fear of seeming bossy (the most frequently referenced: domineering n = 28, undemocratic n = 6, prone to corruption n = 4, harsh n = 3, selfish n = 3), fear of seeming unqualified (incongruent personality, lacking expertise, expected to have all the answers; reminiscent of imposter syndrome), and fear of seeming different (leaders seen as always in the spotlight, n = 22; not wanting to be looked up to, n = 5). Notably, the fear was not confined to negative evaluation: being singled out positively, even idolized, was also discomforting. The 119 Air Force cadets converged on the same three themes.
- Study 3 (n = 377 employee–supervisor dyads): H1 was not supported — none of the three specific image risks significantly and negatively predicted supervisors' ratings of leadership emergence. H2 was supported for each risk entered separately (fear of seeming bossy B = -.19, SE = .04; fear of seeming different B = -.18, SE = .05; fear of seeming unqualified B = -.32, SE = .04; all p < .001), but when all three were entered simultaneously only fear of seeming unqualified remained significant (B = -.40, SE = .06, p < .001). H3 was supported (employee-rated endorsement was positively related to supervisor-rated emergence). H4 was supported for each risk entered separately (bossy effect = -.04, 95% CI [-.066, -.017]; different effect = -.07, 95% CI [-.097, -.041]; unqualified effect = -.04, 95% CI [-.065, -.016]), but only the fear-of-seeming-unqualified indirect effect survived controlling for the other two (effect = -.08, SE = .02, 95% CI [-.121, -.048]). H5 and H6 were not tested in this study.
- Study 4 (n = 448; image risk manipulated): H1 supported — participants assigned to the high-risk condition were less willing to lead in the upcoming group task (B = -.43, SE = .15, p = .004; M = 3.99 vs. 4.35, t(446) = 2.40, p = .017). H2 supported with the preregistered controls (B = -.30, SE = .13, p = .024), although the uncontrolled t-test on endorsement was not significant (M = 3.86 vs. 4.08, t(446) = 1.70, p = .089). H3 supported (B = .90, SE = .03, p < .001). H4 supported (indirect effect = -.27, SE = .12, 95% CI [-.503, -.039]). H5 and H6 were not supported: the manipulation-by-lay-theory interaction was non-significant (B = -.13, SE = .15, p = .379) and so was the index of moderated mediation (index = -.11, SE = .14, 95% CI [-.395, .169]), even though the simple slopes trended as in Study 1 (fixed view B = -.41, SE = .19, p = .03; malleable view B = -.17, SE = .19, p = .357). The authors suggest the null interaction may be a methodological artifact of manipulating image risk while only measuring lay theories.

Convergence and divergence across methods: the quantitative studies converge on the core account — H2, H3, and H4 were supported wherever tested, and the randomized Study 4 supplies causal evidence that anticipated image risk lowers leader-identity endorsement and emergence. They diverge on the outcome link and the moderator: H1 held in Studies 1 and 4 but failed in Study 3, where emergence was supervisor-rated rather than peer-rated or self-reported, and the lay-theory moderation held in Study 1 (and, for H5, in Study B) but not in Study 4. The qualitative Study 2 converged with and extended the quantitative work by specifying the content of image risk and supplying the three-factor scale used in Study 3, where fear of seeming unqualified proved the most debilitating of the three concerns.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts leader-identity scholarship from a lasting "once and for all" construction toward situational, fluid endorsement, and introduces a rarely invoked ego-defense (psychodynamic) explanation for why people deny a leader identity. It advances the concept of metaperception—how people think others think of them—as an underexplored driver of identity, and elaborates image risk from a molar construct into three specific reputational concerns (seeming bossy, unqualified, different).
practical_implication: Organizations seeking more leadership at all ranks should reckon with negative, outdated stereotypes of leaders as aggressive or domineering and foster a consensus that leadership is independent of formal title. They should also promote a malleable view of leadership ability—reinforcing that leadership is a learnable skill and praising attempts to lead—to help employees circumvent the ego-defense response that suppresses leader-identity endorsement and emergence.
limitations: The studies emphasize within-person perceptions over social context, leaving out other context-specific variables (e.g., perceived organizational support, hierarchy) that may shape image risk and endorsement. Study 1 used single-source survey measures vulnerable to common method variance, and support for the lay-theory moderation hypotheses (H5, H6) was mixed across studies—significant in Studies 1 and B but not when image risk was manipulated and lay theories measured in Study 4.
future_research: Scholars could further test the moderating role of lay theories across varied, multisource settings to clarify when this mindset matters, and probe additional context variables (e.g., organizational support, hierarchy) shaping image risk. Researchers might examine the full range of anticipated reactions (negative, neutral, positive), whether people over- or accurately estimate social backlash, and why fear of seeming unqualified is the most debilitating concern.
abstract: Although many organizations value leadership across levels, individuals are reluctant to step up and lead. We explore how anticipated image risk (i.e., individuals' beliefs that the act of leading might harm their image with others) and lay beliefs about leadership ability (i.e., that this ability is fixed versus malleable) may diminish individuals' endorsement of a leader identity and thus their leadership emergence. Across MBA consulting teams, supervisor–employee dyads, and virtual workers, we find that lay theories of leadership ability moderate the negative relationship between anticipated image risk in leadership and leader-identity endorsement, which affects subsequent leadership emergence (Study 1). Using qualitative survey data, Study 2 identifies three specific image concerns that individuals associated with leading: seeming bossy, seeming unqualified, and seeming different from one's peers. Study 3 tests whether a newly developed measure of three specific image risks similarly predicts leader-identity endorsement and emergence. Last, in Study 4 we experimentally manipulate the anticipation of image risk to show its causal impact on leader-identity endorsement and emergence.

title: Leveraging Knowledge Diversity in Hierarchically Differentiated Teams: The Critical Role of Hierarchy Stability
methods: Multilevel (mixed-effects) modeling of cross-sectional field survey data with random intercepts for organization; three-way (moderated-moderation) interaction tested via Dawson and Richter's slope-difference procedure; moderated mediation tested via nonparametric bootstrapping (10,000 draws); supplementary dyadic round-robin analysis.
industry: Work teams across 13 industries (e.g., information technology, hospitality, health care, finance, manufacturing, government)
time_period: All data collected within a three-month period
units: Intact work teams (data from team members and supervisors)
n_sample: 156 teams comprising 995 individuals from 110 organizations
authors: Gray, Steven M.; Bunderson, J. Stuart; van der Vegt, Gerben S.; Rink, Floor; Gedik, Yeliz
theories: hierarchy stability; status hierarchy / status characteristics
keywords: hierarchy stability; knowledge diversity; status hierarchy; team information sharing; team performance
research_question: When and how does a team's status hierarchy constrict versus amplify the relationship between knowledge diversity and team information sharing (and, in turn, team performance), and does hierarchy stability determine which effect prevails?
hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1. Hierarchy stability moderates the moderating effect of status hierarchy on the relationship between knowledge diversity and team information sharing, such that status hierarchy will weaken (make more negative) the diversity–information-sharing relationship as hierarchy stability increases and will strengthen (make more positive) that relationship as hierarchy stability decreases.
- Hypothesis 2. Hierarchy stability moderates the moderating effect of status hierarchy on the indirect relationship between knowledge diversity and team performance through its effect on team information sharing, such that status hierarchy will weaken that indirect effect as hierarchy stability increases and will strengthen it as hierarchy stability decreases.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that status hierarchy has two countervailing effects on diverse teams: a constricting effect (high-status members' perspectives dominate, low-status members feel inhibited) and an amplifying effect (hierarchy offers status-enhancement incentives for sharing unique knowledge). Drawing on the concept of hierarchy stability, the authors propose that stable hierarchies activate four constricting dynamics—greater dominance of one perspective, reduced accountability of high-status members, increased personal risk to low-status members, and weakened status-enhancement incentives—so that diversity's benefit to information sharing (and downstream performance) is weakest when status differences are large and stable. The empirical three-way interaction supports this: knowledge diversity was negatively related to information sharing when status hierarchy and stability were both high, and only marginally positive when hierarchy was high but unstable.
data_measures:
- Data source: a multi-source field survey of intact work teams, recruited through the personal contacts of students in an MBA thesis course coordinated by one of the authors and collected with a standardized, coordinator-monitored procedure (a convenience sample; students could not sample their own organizations). Three temporally separated surveys were used: team-member survey 1 (hierarchy stability, job roles, educational background, demographics, and round-robin dyadic ratings of influence, prominence, and respect); team-member survey 2 two weeks later (team process variables, including team information sharing); and a supervisor survey roughly two weeks after that (team performance). All data were collected within a three-month period.
- Sample attrition: 198 teams approached, 170 teams (1,243 members, 122 organizations) provided data, 1,095 members responded (88%; average within-team response rate 92%), and after excluding teams with missing diversity, round-robin, supervisor, or member data the final sample was 156 teams / 995 individuals / 110 organizations (79% team response rate).
- IV — knowledge diversity: mean of the standardized Blau (1977) index scores for educational-background diversity (subject area of the highest degree, nine listed options plus a tenth category created from open-ended answers) and job-role diversity (open-ended current job position). The two dimensions correlated r = .48.
- Moderator — status hierarchy: peer round-robin 7-point ratings of each member's influence, prominence, and respect (following Anderson et al., 2001). Each member's mean peer rating per item was computed, then the within-team standard deviation of each of the three dimensions, then the mean of those three dispersion scores; Cronbach's alpha = .83.
- Second-stage moderator — hierarchy stability: a 6-item 7-point scale the authors developed because only experimental manipulations existed (e.g., "The pecking order in this team is stable"; reverse-scored items such as "In this team, it is relatively easy to move up in the hierarchy"). Cronbach's alpha = .67, cross-checked with Guttman's lambda-6 = .73 and omega = .76; in a separate online validation study the scale correlated r = .68 (p < .001) with the Hays and Bendersky (2015) measure.
- Mediator — team information sharing: 6-item scale from De Dreu (2007), 1 (never) to 7 (very often); Cronbach's alpha = .82; aggregation to the team level supported by ICC(1) = .27, ICC(2) = .69, median r-wg(j) = 0.84.
- DV — team performance: supervisor ratings on a 3-item scale that compares the focal team with other teams in the same organization with similar composition, tasks, and customers, 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree); Cronbach's alpha = .78; correlated r = .78 (p < .001) with Edmondson's (1999) measure in an online validation study.
- Controls: task routineness/stability (Jehn, Northcraft, & Neale, 1999), membership stability (Wageman, Hackman, & Lehman, 2005), team status mean, and team size.
- Supplementary dyadic data: a roster measure of dyadic advice giving ("I give advice to" each teammate, 3-point scale) as a proxy for dyadic information sharing; knowledge uniqueness scored 0-2 on shared educational background and job role, then reverse-scored; member status group-mean centered. 5,811 dyadic observations, with random intercepts for information provider and information receiver.
- Estimation: multilevel (mixed-effects) models with a random intercept for organization to absorb organization-level nonindependence; the three-way interaction probed with Dawson and Richter's (2006) four-step slope-difference procedure; moderated mediation tested with nonparametric bootstrapping (10,000 draws) and robust standard errors clustered on organization using the R "mediation" package. An a priori Monte Carlo power analysis indicated at least 140 cases were needed to detect a moderate slope difference; post hoc power was 84%.

The design is associational, not causally identified: it is a cross-sectional field survey whose only design safeguards are multiple sources (members and supervisors) and temporal separation of measures. The authors state plainly that they cannot assert causality with their field study and cannot rule out the reverse possibility that information sharing shapes hierarchy or hierarchy stability.
key_findings:
- Main effects (Table 2, Model 1): knowledge diversity was unrelated to team information sharing (B = -0.00, SE = 0.04, p = .941), as was status hierarchy (B = -0.01, SE = 0.04, p = .785). Hierarchy stability had a positive main effect on information sharing (B = 0.10, SE = 0.04, p = .008), a result the authors flag and revisit in the Discussion. About 22% of the variance in information sharing was between organizations.
- No two-way interaction was statistically significant: knowledge diversity x status hierarchy was null (B = 0.00, SE = 0.05, p = .923; Model 2), and none of the three two-way interactions in Model 3 reached significance.
- Hypothesis 1 supported: the knowledge diversity x status hierarchy x hierarchy stability interaction predicting team information sharing was negative and significant (B = -0.13, SE = 0.06, p = .017; Model 4). Simple slopes: knowledge diversity was negatively related to information sharing when status hierarchy and hierarchy stability were both high (Est. = -0.21, SE = 0.10, t = -2.02, p = .046) and only marginally positively related when status hierarchy was high and stability low (Est. = 0.17, SE = 0.09, t = 1.84, p = .069). Those two slopes differed significantly (slope difference a: Est. = -0.32, SE = 0.13, t = -2.50, p = .015). Neither low-hierarchy slope was significant (high stability Est. = 0.10, p = .294; low stability Est. = -0.06, p = .461).
- Hypothesis 2 supported: the indirect effect of knowledge diversity on team performance via team information sharing was negative when status hierarchy and stability were both high (Est. = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.23, 0.00], p = .046) and only marginally positive when status hierarchy was high and stability low (Est. = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.20], p = .068); the two indirect effects differed significantly (Est. = -0.18, p = .008). Both low-hierarchy indirect effects were non-significant (high stability Est. = 0.05, p = .261; low stability Est. = -0.03, p = .511).
- The support is asymmetric and the paper says so: the constricting effect of a stable steep hierarchy in knowledge-diverse teams is clearly evidenced, whereas the authors judge it less clear that low hierarchy stability exerts an amplifying effect, since both instability-side estimates were only marginal (p = .069 and p = .068).
- Robustness: five additional checks — excluding all control variables (Model 5), a bias-corrected Blau index, industry fixed effects, Sundstrom et al. (1990) team-type fixed effects, and adding task interdependence — each supported both Hypothesis 1 and Hypothesis 2.
- Supplementary dyadic analysis (5,811 dyads, Table 6): knowledge uniqueness was negatively related to advice giving (B = -0.04, SE = 0.01, t = -4.69, p < .001), so commonly held knowledge was discussed more than unique knowledge, and higher-status members gave more advice overall (B = 0.26, SE = 0.02, t = 11.17, p < .001). The knowledge uniqueness x member status interaction was null (B = 0.02, SE = 0.01, t = 1.53, p = .126), while member status x hierarchy stability was negative and significant (B = -0.04, SE = 0.02, t = -2.00, p = .046) and the three-way interaction was significant (B = -0.03, SE = 0.01, t = -2.03, p = .042; and B = -0.03, SE = 0.01, t = -2.07, p = .038 without controls).
- The dyadic result is only partly consistent with the theory, and the paper states this: high-status members were more likely to share information with teammates from different knowledge backgrounds when hierarchy stability was low than when it was high (t = -2.32, p = .020), but low-status members showed no such difference (t = 0.51, p = .607) — a finding the authors describe as "not consistent with our theoretical arguments."
- The authors further note that the pattern in Figure 1 suggests the information-sharing effects of hierarchy stability were more pronounced in steep homogeneous teams than in steep knowledge-diverse teams, contrary to the agnostic stance they had taken in theorizing.
theoretical_contribution: The study integrates the historically separate diversity (horizontal differentiation) and hierarchy (vertical differentiation) literatures, showing that the information-sharing and performance benefits of knowledge diversity cannot be understood without accounting for status hierarchy and its stability. It extends hierarchy-stability research—previously focused on homogeneous teams, where stability is beneficial—by demonstrating that stability can instead be detrimental in knowledge-diverse teams with steep hierarchies.
practical_implication: Managers of knowledge-diverse teams should ask, in order, how important diverse-knowledge exchange is, whether status differences exist, and whether the status hierarchy is stable. Where status differences are unavoidable, managers should deliberately destabilize the hierarchy—rotating leadership, changing roles, refreshing membership, and structuring interactions to require all members' input—to keep diverse knowledge flowing.
limitations: Hierarchy stability was measured via team-member perceptions rather than directly observed changes in the hierarchy. The temporally separated but cross-sectional field design cannot establish causality or rule out reverse effects of information sharing on hierarchy. The aggregated team-level information-sharing measure cannot decompose high- versus low-status sharing or unique versus common information content (partially addressed by a supplementary dyadic analysis that still did not capture actual content exchanged).
future_research: Future work should test the correspondence between perceived and actual hierarchy stability and whether they predict different outcomes, use (field) experiments or longitudinal designs to probe the reciprocal information-sharing/hierarchy relationship, examine why stability effects appear stronger in homogeneous than diverse teams, and capture the actual content of information exchanged across diversity, hierarchy, and stability conditions.
abstract: Past research has been equivocal about the information sharing and performance effects of knowledge diversity in teams. In an attempt to resolve this equivocality, scholars have suggested that status hierarchy may play a role, proposing that status differences can constrict team-level information sharing in diverse teams by privileging the knowledge of higher-status members and discounting the knowledge of lower-status members. Although there is some evidence to support this notion, there is also evidence to suggest that status differences may amplify information sharing in diverse teams by offering status enhancement incentives to members who share unique knowledge. In this paper, we reconcile these different predictions by suggesting that the effects of status hierarchy on the relationship between knowledge diversity and team information sharing will depend on the stability of the hierarchy. Using a diverse sample of 156 teams across 110 organizations, we found that status differences constricted information sharing in knowledge-diverse teams when hierarchy stability was high and amplified information sharing in knowledge-diverse teams when hierarchy stability was low. These information sharing effects, in turn, affected team performance. Our study highlights how hierarchy stability is critical for understanding whether status differences constrict or amplify information sharing in knowledge-diverse teams.
