title: The Role of Attribution in Learning from Performance Feedback: Behavioral Perspective on the Choice between Alliances and Acquisitions
methods: Event-history (survival) analysis estimating the hazard rate of a firm switching from an alliance to an acquisition, using a Cox model with firm fixed effects and standard errors clustered on firms; alliance performance measured by cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) relative to a social aspiration level via a spline; robustness via linear probability, conditional logit/multinomial logit, alternative aspiration levels, and alternative samples.
industry: Cross-industry; equity alliances/joint ventures and acquisitions by large U.S. corporations (SDC Joint Ventures and Alliances and Mergers and Acquisitions databases; COMPUSTAT/CRSP)
time_period: 1994–2017 (with 1989–1993 used to measure prior experience)
units: Firm-quarter observations (firms whose most recent transaction was an alliance, at risk of switching to an acquisition)
n_sample: 13,535 firm-quarter observations (39,570 before filtering); 4,017 alliance-to-acquisition switches; models estimated on n = 26,005
authors: Lee, Jaemin; Lee, Joon Mahn; Kim, Ji-Yub (Jay)
theories: attribution theory (Weiner, 1979, 1986; Sedikides & Alicke, 2012); performance feedback theory / behavioral theory of the firm (Cyert & March, 1963; Greve, 2003b); self-serving attribution (Mezulis et al., 2004; Shepperd et al., 2008)
keywords: acquisitions; alliances; aspiration level; attribution; diffusion of responsibility; governance mode choice; performance feedback; self-serving attribution
research_question: How does the causal attribution of past alliance performance influence a firm's subsequent choice between acquisitions and alliances, and how do three attribution-relevant factors—the diffusion of responsibility, the perceived capability of partners, and the ambiguity of performance information—moderate the effect of alliance performance feedback on that choice?
hypotheses:
- Baseline Hypothesis 1a. When a firm's alliance performance is below its aspiration level for alliances, the lower the alliance performance, the more likely the firm will subsequently make an acquisition (predicted sign on ALL < ASP: negative).
- Baseline Hypothesis 1b. When a firm's alliance performance is above its aspiration level for alliances, the higher the alliance performance, the less likely the firm will subsequently make an acquisition (predicted sign on ALL > ASP: negative).
- Hypothesis 1a. When alliance performance is below the aspiration level, the larger the number of alliance partners, the less likely a decrease in alliance performance will increase the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition (predicted interaction sign: positive).
- Hypothesis 1b. When alliance performance is above the aspiration level, the larger the number of alliance partners, the less likely an increase in alliance performance will decrease the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition (predicted interaction sign: positive).
- Hypothesis 2a. When alliance performance is below the aspiration level, the more experienced the alliance partner(s) with alliances, the more likely a decrease in alliance performance will increase the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition (predicted interaction sign: negative).
- Hypothesis 2b. When alliance performance is above the aspiration level, the more experienced the alliance partner(s) is with alliances, the less likely an increase in alliance performance will decrease the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition (predicted interaction sign: positive).
- Hypothesis 3a. When alliance performance is below the aspiration level, the higher the variability in alliance performance, the less likely a decrease in alliance performance will increase the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition (predicted interaction sign: positive).
- Hypothesis 3b. When alliance performance is above the aspiration level, the higher the variability in alliance performance, the more likely an increase in alliance performance will decrease the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition (predicted interaction sign: negative).
- The paper also states an explicit asymmetry expectation: the number of alliance partners is predicted to increase self-serving bias when alliance performance is below the aspiration level but to decrease it when performance is above the aspiration level, whereas partner alliance experience and alliance performance variability are predicted to produce symmetrical effects for success and failure.
mechanism_summary: The paper integrates attribution theory into the four-step performance feedback process (evaluation, attribution, search, change). Because managers make self-serving attributions, poor alliance performance attributed to external causes "may not deter managers from making alliances again, nor encourage them in searching for an alternative to alliances to the same degree as when attributed to internal causes," weakening the baseline below-aspiration prediction; conversely, crediting themselves for successful alliances leads managers to believe they will succeed again, which decreases their search for alternatives and reinforces the baseline above-aspiration prediction that stronger performance makes a subsequent acquisition less likely. The three moderators shift how strongly self-serving attribution manifests: more partners and higher performance variability amplify external attribution of failure (weakening the push toward acquisitions), while highly capable partners make blaming them less credible (strengthening the push toward acquisitions after failure).
data_measures:
- Data sources: firms listed on the 1994 Fortune 500 list; their alliances (including alliances made by their subsidiaries, because alliance and acquisition decisions are typically made by headquarters) from the SDC Joint Ventures and Alliances database, and their acquisitions from the SDC Mergers and Acquisitions database, for deals announced and completed between 1994 and 2017. The 1989-1993 window supplies prior alliance and acquisition experience, and the study period starts in 1994 because SDC is known to be unreliable prior to 1989. Duplicate deal entries were eliminated and announcement dates were verified against major business news outlets such as Financial Times and Bloomberg News; SDC and news dates matched for about 77% of alliances, and news dates took precedence where they disagreed. Main analyses include only equity alliances and joint ventures, excluding nonequity forms such as licensing and manufacturing arrangements, marketing agreements, and research collaborations. Quarterly demographic and financial data on sample firms and alliance partners come from the COMPUSTAT/CRSP merged database.
- DV: the unobserved hazard rate for a firm that used an alliance at t to change to an acquisition at t+1, coded 1 if the first event the firm made at t+1 was an acquisition and 0 otherwise; the estimation sample is restricted to firm-quarter observations in which the firm's most recent transaction was an alliance (so the firm is at risk of switching governance mode).
- IV (alliance performance): cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) around the alliance announcement, measured over a [-1, +1] event window, with normal returns from the market model estimated on the CRSP value-weighted index over a 100-day period ending 10 days before the event. CAR was chosen because stock market reaction is regarded as salient performance feedback by managers and because its short window avoids the confounding that accounting measures suffer.
- IV (performance feedback): alliance performance relative to a social aspiration level, measured as the average CAR of every alliance made by all other firms (not only Fortune 500 firms) in the same industry, defined by the 2-digit SIC code of the firm's primary industry, during the year prior to the focal alliance. A spline splits performance into ALL < ASP (focal CAR minus the aspiration level when CAR falls below it, 0 otherwise) and ALL > ASP (focal CAR minus the aspiration level when CAR exceeds it, 0 otherwise). Where a firm made more than one alliance in a quarter, the last alliance's performance was used. The social aspiration specification was chosen partly because it gave the best model fit relative to historical and weighted aspiration levels.
- Moderator (diffusion of responsibility): alliance partner number, the total number of partners that participated in the focal alliance.
- Moderator (perceived capability of partners): partner alliance experience, the average of the total number of alliances completed by each partner during the five-year period prior to the focal alliance.
- Moderator (ambiguity of performance information): alliance performance variability, the standard deviation of the performance of all the alliances the firm made during the five-year period prior to the focal alliance.
- Controls (Table 3): alliance experience and acquisition experience (numbers of prior alliances and acquisitions completed in the previous five years), alliance performance variability and acquisition performance variability, partners' alliance experience, alliance partner number, firm performance (return on equity), divestiture experience (number of divestitures completed in the previous five years), financial slack (equity-to-debt ratio), unabsorbed slack (working capital to total sales), absorbed slack (selling, general, and administrative expenses to sales), diversification (number of different SIC codes reported), average past acquisition performance (average CAR of all acquisitions the firm made in the previous five years), partner firm performance (average return on equity of the alliance partners in the focal firm's alliances over the previous five years), and industry alliance density and industry acquisition density (numbers of alliances and acquisitions in the focal firm's industry over the previous five years).
- Estimation and identification: hazard rates were estimated with the Cox model, with firm identifiers included to control for potential heterogeneity and robust standard errors clustered on firms; Table 3 reports n = 26,005 and states that all models include firm fixed effects. The design is associational, not quasi-experimental: the paper names no instrumental-variable, difference-in-differences, regression-discontinuity, natural-experiment, or randomized strategy, and instead supports inference through a comprehensive control set, firm-level heterogeneity controls, a Schoenfeld-residuals test that found no violation of the proportional-hazards assumption, and a discussion of sample-induced endogeneity (all sample firms made both alliances and acquisitions during the study period). Multicollinearity was assessed via variance inflation factors, the highest being 3.7.
key_findings:
- Both baseline hypotheses were supported. The coefficients on ALL < ASP and ALL > ASP are negative and statistically significant in Models 2-5 (Model 2: ALL < ASP = -.055; ALL > ASP = -.094), so alliance performance further below the aspiration level raised, and performance further above it lowered, the hazard of subsequently making an acquisition. Model 2 implies that a decrease in alliance performance below aspiration of one dollar per share increases the likelihood of subsequently making an acquisition by 5.35%.
- Hypothesis 1a supported: the interaction of ALL < ASP with alliance partner number is positive and statistically significant (.008, Model 3), so a larger number of partners weakened the push from alliance failure toward acquisition.
- Hypothesis 1b supported: the interaction of ALL > ASP with alliance partner number is positive and statistically significant (.012, Model 3), so a larger number of partners weakened the extent to which alliance success deterred acquisition. Table 4, Panel A shows the marginal effects of both ALL < ASP and ALL > ASP are smallest at the high level of alliance partner number.
- Hypothesis 2a supported: the interaction of ALL < ASP with partner alliance experience is negative and statistically significant (-.003, Model 4), so more experienced (more capable) partners strengthened the push from alliance failure toward acquisition.
- Hypothesis 2b supported: the interaction of ALL > ASP with partner alliance experience is positive and statistically significant (.003, Model 4), so more experienced partners weakened the extent to which alliance success deterred acquisition. Table 4, Panel B shows the marginal effect of ALL < ASP is greatest, and that of ALL > ASP smallest, at the high level of partners' alliance experience.
- Hypothesis 3a supported: the interaction of ALL < ASP with alliance performance variability is positive and statistically significant (.253, Model 5), so more variable prior alliance performance weakened the push from alliance failure toward acquisition.
- Hypothesis 3b supported: the interaction of ALL > ASP with alliance performance variability is negative and statistically significant (-.433, Model 5), so more variable prior alliance performance amplified the negative relationship between above-aspiration performance and subsequent acquisition. Table 4, Panel C shows the marginal effect of ALL < ASP is smallest, and that of ALL > ASP greatest, at the high level of variability.
- Reported effect magnitudes from the interaction plots: below the aspiration level, a decrease in alliance performance from the mean to two standard deviations below the mean increased the multiplier of the hazard rate of making an acquisition by 24.65% at a low alliance partner number but by only 0.003% at a high one; above the aspiration level, an increase of two standard deviations decreased the multiplier by 48.60% at a low partner number versus 11.26% at a high one. For partner alliance experience, the same below-aspiration decrease produced a 50.11% increase in the hazard multiplier at a high level of partner alliance experience versus only 5.69% at a low level.
- The authors summarize the moderator results as follows: a larger number of alliance partners decreased the likelihood that a firm would turn to an acquisition when the alliance failed, but a successful alliance was more likely to prompt a change to an acquisition as the number of partners increased; firms were more likely to turn to an acquisition after a failed alliance when partners were experienced (perceived as highly capable) than when they were inexperienced, while a successful alliance was less likely to trigger a change to an acquisition when partners were inexperienced than when they were experienced; and highly variable past alliance performance made firms less likely to switch to an acquisition after both failed and successful alliances.
- The authors caution that the kinked baseline curve on its own - the coefficient on ALL > ASP being significantly smaller (more negative) than that on ALL < ASP - cannot be taken as evidence of self-serving attribution, because other behavioral processes such as organizational inertia or threat rigidity could produce similar results; the three moderator tests are what tease out the attribution mechanism. A supplementary test that used the partners' strongest past alliance performance as the aspiration level found no significant interaction between that expectation-based performance feedback measure and the partners' perceived capability, which the authors read as ruling out an expectation-based alternative explanation for Hypothesis 2b.
- Results were robust across a linear probability model with firm fixed effects, a multinomial logistic estimation conditioned on firms, and a logistic estimation conditioned on firms; historical and weighted aspiration levels; samples that include nonequity alliances or minority acquisitions; quarterly return on assets in place of CAR; five alternative CAR event windows; alternative four-, seven-, and ten-year windows for the moderator measures; an alternative dependent variable based on the last rather than the first event in a quarter; dropping quarters in which firms made more than one alliance; dropping observations with no alliance or acquisition in the focal quarter; and alternative methods for handling tied failure events.
theoretical_contribution: The study is the first to explicitly integrate the attribution process into performance feedback theory, showing that a firm's response to prior performance is significantly shaped by how managers attribute that performance and arguing that core predictions of performance feedback theory may require revision. By identifying three attribution-influencing moderators, it uncovers the theoretical mechanisms by which attribution operates and helps explain enduring inconsistent findings on whether failure triggers strategic change. It also extends corporate strategy research by providing the first behavioral account of the alliance-versus-acquisition choice, departing from economic and agency perspectives.
practical_implication: Governance-mode decisions (alliances vs. acquisitions) are not purely rational or opportunistic but can be distorted by managerial heuristics and biases such as self-serving attribution. Managers and stakeholders should be aware that conditions enabling blame-shifting—many alliance partners, highly variable performance histories, or weakly capable partners—can suppress learning from alliance failure, so that failed alliances "could barely facilitate strategic change when the conditions promoting self-attribution were present."
limitations: The study examines only the choice between acquisitions and alliances and cannot observe internal development (organic growth), which typically goes unannounced. Its performance measure (CAR), though most suitable here, may not generalize to other metrics. The theory focuses on the focal firm's attribution and does not integrate the partner firm's view, and although results are robust across alternative aspiration-level specifications, slack resources may also influence how attributions are formed.
future_research: Future work could study settings where organic growth or other performance metrics can be reliably measured and tightly linked to specific actions, more fully integrate a partner's view "using appropriate methods," examine how attribution processes differ across alternative aspiration-level specifications, and explore how attribution and slack search jointly shape other types of organizational change such as managerial succession or foreign-market entry mode.
abstract: The causal attribution of performance has not been explicitly considered in the performance feedback literature, despite its potential value in learning from prior performance. In this study, we develop a theory concerning the attribution in learning from performance feedback and explore how the attribution of past alliance performance can influence a firm's choice between future acquisitions and alliances. We also examine the mechanisms by which attribution manifests by exploring how three theoretical factors, known to influence attribution, can moderate the relationship—the diffusion of responsibility, the perceived capability of partners, and the ambiguity of performance information. We find strong evidence supporting our predictions. This study contributes to the performance feedback literature by integrating attribution with performance feedback theory. It also extends research on corporate strategy by providing a behavioral account of the choice between acquisitions and alliances.

title: With Head and Heart: How Emotions Shape Paradox Navigation in Veterinary Work
methods: Inductive grounded-theory study (Strauss & Corbin, 1990; Gioia et al., 2013); semi-structured interviews (n=63 veterinarians, 93 total interviews), ~239 hours of nonparticipant observation, and archival data, analyzed iteratively to build a four-dimension process model.
industry: Veterinary medicine (private veterinary clinics)
time_period: Data collected 2009–2015, with follow-ups and additional interviews in 2019
units: Individual veterinarians navigating the business–care paradox
n_sample: 63 veterinarians (93 interviews; ~239 observation hours; 79 emotion-laden instances across 53 vets in 12 clinics)
authors: Pradies, Camille
theories: emotional labor (Hochschild, 1983); paradox theory; social emotions (Zietsma & Toubiana, 2018)
keywords: business–care paradox; emotional labor; emotions; intuition; microfoundations; paradox navigation; salience
research_question: How do emotions shape the ways in which individuals navigate paradox? The study examines this through veterinarians confronting the business–care paradox—the opposing yet interrelated business and care goals embedded in their work.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: The business–care paradox, made salient each time a client interaction pits profitability against the care of a pet.
- Phase 1 — Emotional salience of paradox: Social bonds (perceived deservingness of pet owners) surface social emotions (empathy, compassion, guilt), creating a personal connection to paradoxical tensions and an impetus to consider both sides.
- Phase 2 — Flexible emotional labor between demands: Vets intuit "room to maneuver" and either justify downplaying or justify following emotions, opting for cost or care; organizational billing norms influence the direction.
- Phase 3 — Emotional traces following response: Decisions leave emotional fatigue (focus on cost) or emotional energy (focus on care) that linger after the consultation.
- Phase 4 — Ongoing learning from emotions: Traces drive vets to construct "workable barriers" that block fatigue while preserving exceptions, enabling learning over repeated exposure.
- Influencing factors / boundary conditions: Social bond between vet and client; perceived strictness of organizational billing norms.

Pradies theorizes paradox navigation as an emotionally fueled process rather than a purely cognitive or rational act. Emotions make paradox personally felt (not merely "seen" cognitively), and intuition—a swift, unconscious process—drives flexible iteration between competing demands. The emotional traces left by each response accumulate into learning, so that over time individuals adjust their workable barriers to balance energy and fatigue while sustaining engagement with both poles.
data_measures: Inductive grounded-theory study (Strauss & Corbin, 1990; Locke, 2001) of veterinarians in France navigating the business–care paradox; constructs were built inductively from the data rather than measured, and the design is interpretive — there are no variables, no estimation, and no causal identification strategy. Data corpus: semi-structured interviews with 63 veterinarians, plus follow-up interviews in 2019 with roughly half of the initial informants, for a total of 93 interviews; approximately 239 hours of overt, nonparticipant observation (Pratt & Sala, 2021) inside clinics, where the author shadowed nearly all the vets she interviewed and, with informant permission, recorded 73% of consultations using a camera (later a tablet) on a tripod or a voice recorder on the vet's desk; and archival data from the French veterinary press (Semaine Vétérinaire, Dépêche Vétérinaire, the Medical Board Journal), which was deliberately not coded to answer the research question and used only to understand the French veterinary context. Sampling used elements of theoretical sampling, starting from an "open sampling" strategy to retain theoretical flexibility; among the vets interviewed, 59% were partners, 30% employees, and 6% freelance professionals; average tenure was 14 years (range 1–49); 37% were men and 63% women; 70% worked exclusively with pets and small animals. Interviews lasted 70–80 minutes on average, were conducted in French, and were recorded and transcribed verbatim, with only relevant quotes translated into English. The analytic corpus was narrowed via a summary table of consultations: among 195 observations and 123 consultations recalled in interviews, 151 instances were identified in which clients had little economic means and business–care tensions surfaced (53 observed, 98 recalled); of these, 79 instances carried coded signs of emotional arousal (17 observed, 62 recalled), spread across 53 vets in 12 clinics, and those 79 were the primary focus of inquiry. The remaining tension instances showed no evidence of emotional arousal and were excluded from the formal analysis, serving instead as contrast cases. The focal construct — social emotions arising in interaction (Zietsma & Toubiana, 2018) — was operationalized through the signs catalogued in Table 1: nonverbal emotional display in interactions (facial expression, prosodic features such as pitch, volume, lengthened vowels, pauses and hesitations, and gestures and posture) and emotional statements while recalling exchanges (evaluative comments and quoted speech, in which a vet speaks as if she were the client). Coding proceeded in four steps in the Gioia et al. (2013) tradition: (I) open coding of interviews and field notes, plus a thick description per observed vet joining interview and observation transcripts, to identify consultations involving emotions; (II) refining first-order concepts, yielding codes such as "feeling that one's action may be causing harm and distress to the pet and pet owner" and "putting oneself in the shoes of the pet owner"; (III) integrating first-order concepts into second-order themes by iterating between empirical themes and relevant literature on social emotions, emotional labor (Hochschild, 1983), and emotional traces (Rivera, 2015) — with the author coining her own label, "intuiting room to maneuver regarding the balance between demands," because the prevalent intuition codes were not reflected in existing studies; and (IV) building a theoretical model, which produced four aggregate dimensions (Figure 2), with the full first-order/second-order/aggregate data structure in Figure 1 and exemplary quotes per theme in Table 2. Validity procedures were triangulation of observational and interview data (Jick, 1979), regular meetings with external colleagues to discuss first-order concepts and emerging constructs to reduce single-coder bias, and member checks in 2019 in which informants confirmed that the model accurately represents their experiences.
key_findings:
The study's central finding is that emotions make paradox salient by surfacing a personal connection to paradoxical tensions, trigger flexible emotional labor while responding to paradox, and leave emotional traces that foster ongoing learning — assembled into an emotionally informed model of paradox navigation with four aggregate dimensions.

Emotional salience of the paradox. Clinics had routine protocols for cost–care dilemmas (payment in multiple installments, or a lower level of care for less money), but these protocols were not always used in consultations where social emotions surfaced. The social bond between vet and client — manifested as the perceived deservingness of pet owners and pets, judged from a pleasant demeanor, loyalty to the clinic, or a strong connection with the animal — influenced whether vets experienced social emotions in the form of empathy, compassion, or guilt; vets said they would not "go out of their way" for clients they perceived as undeserving, and made the "strict minimum" effort for vindictive ones. Where those emotions arose, they surfaced a personal connection to tensions: vets described feeling attached to care and upset at the organizational routine focused on cost, and feeling personal ownership of the cost–care problem, treating the paradox as their own issue to solve rather than the client's. The contrast cases sharpen this: consultations without signs of emotional arousal ran much like nonparadox consultations — staying calm, asking diagnostic questions, no hesitation during payment — and there the client was left holding responsibility for the cost.

Flexible emotional labor between demands. Experiencing salience emotionally in turn led vets into flexible emotional labor that was fundamentally intuitive rather than deliberative: they intuited "room to maneuver," relying on gut feeling ("So much is based on how I feel about it in my gut") and on balancing care and cost on average across clients over a day, month, or year. The direction of the response tracked that intuition. When vets intuitively sensed room to maneuver, they justified following emotions — emphasizing that they were giving away their personal time, or emphasizing their values and humanity — and decided to focus on care, providing discounted or free services. When they sensed little room to maneuver, they justified downplaying emotions — emphasizing the value of their professional work and expertise, and that care comes with costs — and decided to focus on cost, billing in line with the organization's guidelines. Perceived organizational billing norms shaped the direction: where norms were perceived as strict, vets tended to justify downplaying their emotions; where perceived as loose, vets were more inclined to follow them. Neither intuition nor the organizational setting alone dictated the outcome, and the justificatory work was "far from linear" — one vet reported having "justifications that go both ways" and falling back into the paradox.

Emotional traces following response. Responses left feelings that lingered after the consultation ended. A focus on cost left emotional fatigue: vets described feeling drained when reducing care to focus on cost, and feeling fatigued when clients suffered as a result of expensive care they had chosen. A focus on care left emotional energy: vets described feeling energized when focusing on care and a spur of relief when prioritizing care over cost.

Ongoing learning from emotions. Those traces became a source of learning. Eager to avoid fatigue, vets realized the importance of constructing protective barriers — "armor myself a little more," a "warning signal" to "get back to your role" — while also learning to remain open to emotions by emphasizing exceptions, because occasional care-focused consultations were energizing and reconnected them to why they chose the profession ("those exceptions are important, as long as they stay exceptions"). The resulting "workable barrier" holds a double balance: too much protection forgoes energizing experiences, too little risks overexposure to fatiguing ones and to financial problems. Over time individuals adjust their workable barriers from repeated exposure to paradoxes, so learning to navigate paradox entails reaching a dynamic equilibrium not only between responses but also between emotional traces. The author is explicit that some links are suggested rather than demonstrated: the feedback from decision patterns over time into the intuitive process, and from the workable barrier back into experiencing social emotions, are drawn as gray dashed arrows indicating relationships the findings suggest but do not fully show, and the "decision to focus on cost" and "decision to focus on care" boxes are implicit in the vets' emotional labor rather than separately evidenced.
theoretical_contribution: The study enriches the microfoundations of paradox theory by explaining how emotions shape both the salience of paradox and individuals' responses to it. It theorizes an affective route to salience (driven by a desire to sustain social bonds), positions intuition as the key driver of flexible responses, and extends Smith's (2014) dynamic-equilibrium model to show that learning to navigate paradox entails balancing emotional traces, not just responses. More broadly it answers calls to address the dominant rational focus of paradox scholarship by foregrounding emotionality alongside rationality.
practical_implication: Practitioners benefit from being attuned to their emotions when confronting paradoxical tensions, since learning to navigate paradox involves reaching a dynamic equilibrium between emotional traces (energy and fatigue), and building a "workable barrier" should be a conscious act. Management educators should highlight emotional awareness and intelligence as key skills in paradox navigation.
limitations: As with other qualitative studies, the single French veterinary context raises questions about generalizability, though the dynamics may transfer to other professional settings where occupational values are pitted against business imperatives. Findings are likely most applicable to organizational members with high autonomy. It is also difficult to verify whether consultations categorized as lacking social emotions were truly devoid of emotion or whether emotions were repressed.
future_research: Future work could examine how varying levels of emotional intensity produce different levels of salience over time, explore emotions and paradox at the organizational level (e.g., via multiple case studies of emotion norms), and investigate how individual backgrounds, work orientations, or affective commitments shape emotional experiences of paradox.
abstract: Emotions are part of everyday life, and paradox scholars have long acknowledged that navigating paradox—that is, opposite, interrelated, and enduring tensions—is inherently emotional. Yet, how such emotions shape the ways in which individuals navigate paradoxes remains unclear. Drawing on an in-depth qualitative study of 63 veterinarians facing the business–care paradox, I develop an emotionally informed model of how individuals navigate paradox at work. I find that emotions: (a) make paradox salient by surfacing a personal connection to paradoxical tensions, (b) trigger flexible emotional labor while responding to paradox, and (c) leave emotional traces that foster ongoing learning. In so doing, I surface how emotions shape the way paradoxes are recognized and experienced. My model invites paradox scholars to consider the centrality of emotions in paradox navigation, thus moving beyond emotions as something to be avoided and instead embracing their generative potential. Foregrounding emotions offers rich theoretical opportunities for future work.

title: Inside-Out, Outside-In, or All-in-One? The Role of Network Sequencing in the Elaboration of Ideas
methods: Mixed but dominantly quantitative: exploratory interviews (40 R&D scientists/engineers, 30 R&D managers) inform construct development, followed by hypothesis-testing on a multi-survey design. Three surveys of scientists/engineers, managers, and directors; network data via name-generator/-interpreter and alter–alter matrix questions; a scenario-based question (NASA technology-readiness stages) measures timing of network mobilization. An inside-out network sequencing (IONS) index combines dispersion and consistency components. Ordered probit models predict the ordinal innovation rating, standard errors clustered by rank, IV and moderators mean-centered; robustness via Poisson model on an alternative count DV.
industry: Corporate R&D in a large, technology-intensive, Fortune-500 multinational firm (anonymized as 'Neptune') spanning diverse product markets and technologies
country: Multinational firm with R&D sites in Asia, Europe, and North America (single firm, anonymized)
time_period: Survey wave with innovation performance ratings obtained six months after the survey (data circa 2020; collection year not explicitly stated)
units: Individual R&D scientists and engineers and their ego networks of advice/support ties
n_sample: 301 R&D scientists and engineers (final analytic sample; 61% response rate, 48% of the original population)
authors: Ter Wal, Anne L. J.; Criscuolo, Paola; Salter, Ammon
theories: network mobilization / timing effects (Mannucci & Perry-Smith, 2021; Perry-Smith & Mannucci, 2017); network theory of innovation / structural holes (Burt, 2004); social circles (Dunbar, 1998; Kadushin, 1968); social cohesion around relationships (Reagans & McEvily, 2003; Tortoriello et al., 2012)
keywords: all-in-one network mobilization; idea elaboration; inner-circle ties; innovation performance; inside-out network sequencing; outer-circle ties; outside-in network sequencing; shared third-party ties
research_question: How does the sequence in which R&D scientists and engineers mobilize feedback and support from colleagues for the elaboration of novel ideas affect their innovation performance? In particular, does mobilizing inner-circle ties before outer-circle ones ("inside-out" sequencing) outperform "outside-in" or "all-in-one" approaches, and is this advantage stronger in less supportive work environments?
hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1. Inside-out network sequencing in idea elaboration is positively associated with individual innovation performance.
- Hypothesis 2. The association between inside-out network sequencing and innovation performance is stronger when individuals operate in less supportive work environments.
mechanism_summary: Inner-circle ties (those sharing many third-party connections with the idea creator) bring greater commitment and information redundancy, so they patiently digest ill-defined, ill-structured early-stage ideas, supply candid constructive feedback, and surface logical inconsistencies before creators grow wedded to flawed directions. Exposing immature ideas to outer-circle ties too early risks dismissive reactions and "false negatives," whereas these nonredundant outsiders become valuable later, once ideas are robust enough to withstand external scrutiny and to validate fit with the wider organization. Sequencing inner-before-outer therefore lets individuals secure early feedback while shielding fragile ideas, mitigating the dual risk of dropping good ideas or persisting with bad ones. The contrast between circles—and hence the payoff to careful sequencing—sharpens in unsupportive contexts where outer-circle skepticism is most damaging.
data_measures:
Data come from one large technology-intensive Fortune-500 multinational R&D organization (anonymized as "Neptune"). Three online surveys were sent to all 622 senior R&D scientists and engineers (61% response, n = 370), 969 R&D managers (43%), and 80 R&D directors (46%); responses were linked to Neptune archival HR records and individual innovation performance ratings via an algorithm converting respondent emails to anonymous IDs. After dropping cases with incomplete data on the study variables, the analytic sample is 301 scientists and engineers (48% of the original population). Individuals with higher innovation ratings were overrepresented relative to the full population, so population weights are included in the regressions (results are robust without weights). Exploratory interviews with 40 R&D scientists/engineers and 30 R&D managers preceded and informed the survey design.

DV: innovation performance is Neptune's annual performance review rating, in which a committee of line managers compares performance-review documents within rank and allocates individuals to one of three bands under a forced distribution; ratings were obtained six months after the survey. A robustness DV is the self-reported number of projects in the prior year that reached the implementation stage-gate (mean = 1.12, SD = 1.11), available for a subset (n = 212). IV: inside-out network sequencing (IONS), an index with two components — dispersion, the extent to which tie mobilization is spread across the four idea-elaboration stages (Stirling, 2007), and consistency (0-1), whether ties sharing more third parties are mobilized before ties sharing fewer. Network data came in three steps: four name-generator questions soliciting up to 11 contacts, a name-interpreter question (rank, division, communication frequency), and an alter-alter matrix. Inner- versus outer-circle status is operationalized structurally as f_ij, the fraction of i's ties also held by j (respondents averaged 2.3 shared third-party ties, SD = 1.63); relational tie strength is not measured. Timing comes from a scenario-based question asking, for each listed contact, at which of four stages of idea elaboration — wording adapted from NASA technology-readiness levels, from "Almost immediately after first getting the idea" to "After validation in a lab/trial environment" — the respondent would first disclose a recent idea. Moderators: emphasis on accountability (own scale; four-item accountability factor from the R&D managers' survey, α = .61, averaged by division and site); lack of innovation support (six-item supervisory-support scale adapted from Greenhaus, Parasuraman, and Wormley, 1990, α = .92, reverse-coded and averaged across the division leaders nominated as critical decision-makers); lack of organizational slack (four-item Danneels, 2008 scale, α = .81, reverse-coded, from the R&D directors' survey); reluctance to cannibalize (five-item Chandy and Tellis, 1998 scale as adapted by Danneels, 2008, α = .70, reverse-coded, R&D directors). Controls: relative speed to promotion, junior rank, job tenure, managerial support, research-portfolio time horizon, gender, intrinsic motivation, Burt network constraint, network prominence, and sectoral dummies.

Estimation is an ordered probit of the three-band rating (a Wald test rejected the parallel-regression assumption, χ2 = 35.92, p < .001), with standard errors clustered by rank because ratings follow a forced distribution within seniority ranks, and with IONS and the moderators mean-centered. The paper claims no causal-identification strategy: the design is associational, reporting associations between survey-measured sequencing and performance ratings collected six months later, and the scenario-based measure captures expected rather than actual mobilization behavior.
key_findings:
Hypothesis 1 is supported. In Model 2 the coefficient for inside-out network sequencing is positive and significant (β = 0.63, p < .01); an increase from its mean to 1 SD above the mean raises the probability of receiving the highest innovation rating by 9.3% (from 0.47 to 0.51) and reduces the probability of the lowest rating by 7.6% (from 0.28 to 0.24). The effect holds over and above network constraint, which is itself negatively associated with individual performance. The raw bivariate pattern is weaker and not linear: bottom-rated individuals show lower IONS (0.461) than middle- and top-rated ones (0.489, t = 1.289, p = .099), while bottom- and middle-rated (0.470) do not differ significantly from top-rated (0.485, p = .289).

Hypothesis 2 is supported for all four indicators of a less supportive work environment, added as interaction terms in turn across Models 3-6: IONS × emphasis on accountability (β = 1.83, p < .01), IONS × leaders' lack of innovation support (β = 0.42, p < .001), IONS × lack of organizational slack (β = 1.01, p < .001), and IONS × reluctance to cannibalize (β = 1.02, p < .001). The paper states two range restrictions on the marginal effects. For lack of innovation support, the difference in the predicted probability of a top rating between supportive and unsupportive contexts is significant only where IONS is low (< 0.35; 20% of the sample), which the authors read as a performance penalty for not sequencing inside-out rather than an amplified benefit of doing so, since the benefits of high IONS are similar in supportive and unsupportive contexts. For reluctance to cannibalize, the moderation is significant only for individuals with higher IONS (> 0.35; 80% of the sample).

Robustness: a Poisson model on the alternative count DV (projects reaching the implementation stage-gate, n = 212) also yields a positive IONS coefficient (β = 0.36, p < .001), a 1 SD increase raising the predicted count by 15.6%. Entered separately, both index components are positive and significant (dispersion β = 0.33, p < .001; consistency β = 0.32, p = .002). Hypothesis 1 continues to hold when controlling for the previous year's self-reported rating (β = 0.84, p < .001, n = 251) and when junior R&D professionals are excluded (β = 0.83, p < .001). When IONS is recomputed weighting shared third-party ties by communication frequency, all results remain substantively unchanged except the moderating effect of reluctance to cannibalize — the one reported result that is not robust to that respecification.
theoretical_contribution: The study introduces "network sequencing" as a temporal, behavioral dimension of networks distinct from network structure and position, showing that *when* individuals involve which contacts—not just *whom* they are connected to—explains differences in innovation performance over and above network constraint. It connects to and extends research on strategic networking behaviors by demonstrating that creative individuals outperform peers by making "savvy choices of who to involve when." Third, it shows that network mechanisms such as feedback and support are time- and alter-dependent and may backfire if mobilized at the wrong time, unpacking idea elaboration into substages in which strong/inner and weak/outer ties play different roles.
practical_implication: Because network sequencing matters yet many individuals make poor mobilization choices, organizations should inform and train R&D talent to deliberately sequence their networks—seeking early input from committed inner-circle ties to nurture ideas in "safe spaces" before exposing them to outer-circle scrutiny, while avoiding cleaving too closely to the inner circle and engaging outer-circle ties once ideas mature. Such training is especially valuable in units lacking innovation support, where engaging outsiders too early is costly; careful management of slack, autonomy/accountability balance, cannibalization concerns, and supportive leadership can each reduce the risk of squandering creative talent.
limitations: The study is based on a single organization with relatively homogeneous HR practices, limiting generalizability, and it examines only intra-organizational networks. The scenario-based measure of mobilization timing captures expected rather than actual behavior and cannot establish whether the reported approach generalizes across different ideas, contexts, or situations. The innovation-performance measure has a short (single-year) time horizon, and inner/outer-circle ties are operationalized structurally (shared third parties) without directly observing tie strength; the paper also does not explore why sequencing differences arise.
future_research: Future work could examine network sequencing in other organizational contexts and across organizational boundaries, and use more direct methods (e.g., diary-based monitoring) to capture how individuals seek feedback for different ideas. Researchers could disentangle tie strength from social cohesion in sequencing effects, study how idea radicalness and longer-horizon (radical) innovation call for different sequencing strategies, and investigate antecedents of sequencing choices such as confidence, political skill, personality, and cognition.
abstract: The structure of advice and support networks within organizations has a profound impact on the elaboration of novel ideas. We explore how the sequence in which individuals expose ideas to their network contacts affects their innovation performance. We argue that, during idea elaboration, inside-out network sequencing—that is, mobilizing input and support from inner-circle ties before outer-circle ones—yields an innovation performance advantage over outside-in network sequencing and all-in-one mobilization of network contacts. Inside-out network sequencing generates valuable early feedback and support from inner-circle ties that actively engage with ill-defined, ill-structured, and uncertain ideas, and delays exposure to outer-circle ties until ideas can better withstand criticism from beyond the social circle where they emerged. We further contend that the benefits of inside-out network sequencing are amplified in environments that lack support for innovation. Using an analysis of survey data and archival innovation performance records for 301 research and development scientists and engineers in a large multinational firm, we find support for our predictions.

title: Pay Transparency as a Moving Target: A Multistep Model of Pay Compression, I-Deals, and Collectivist Shared Values
methods: Two studies. Study 1: preregistered 2x2 between-subjects online business-simulation experiment (managerial agency in pay compression). Study 2: multisource, firm-level field study analyzed with multilevel structural equation modeling (2-2-1-2 MSEM) in Mplus, with Monte Carlo tests of (conditional) serial indirect effects.
industry: Medical device distribution firms (Study 2); managers recruited via Prolific (Study 1)
country: China (Study 2); United States and United Kingdom (Study 1)
time_period: Endogenous variables measured over the past year; two-phase data collection
units: Firms (with employer and employee survey + archival pay data); individual managers in Study 1
n_sample: Study 1: 117 managers (final); Study 2: 645 employees in 111 firms
authors: Wong, Man-Nok; Cheng, Bonnie Hayden; Lam, Leon Wai-Yuan; Bamberger, Peter A.
theories: compensating wage differentials (CWD) theory (Rosen, 1974, 1986); social comparison theory (Gibbons & Buunk, 1999); transparency-privacy model (Bernstein, 2017)
keywords: collectivist shared values; compensating wage differentials; i-deals; pay transparency; transparency-privacy model; variable pay compression
research_question: Whether, how, and when does firm-level pay transparency become a "moving target" — that is, through what multistep process does transparency lead managers and employees to shift remuneration from more observable forms (variable pay) to less observable ones (nonmonetary i-deals), and under what conditions is this process amplified?
hypotheses:
The quantitative components test six numbered hypotheses (Hypothesis 5 is split into 5a and 5b), summarized in the Figure 1 theoretical model. Study 1 tested only Hypotheses 1 and 5a; Study 2 tested the full model (Hypotheses 1–6).
- Hypothesis 1. Firm-level pay transparency is positively associated with variable pay compression.
- Hypothesis 2. Variable pay compression is positively associated with firm-level rates of employee i-deal requests.
- Hypothesis 3. Firm-level pay transparency is indirectly associated with firm-level rates of employee i-deal requests via variable pay compression.
- Hypothesis 4. Firm-level pay transparency is indirectly associated with firm-level i-deal grants via variable pay compression and firm-level rates of employee i-deal requests.
- Hypothesis 5a. Firm-level collectivist shared values moderate the effect of firm-level pay transparency on variable pay compression, such that this positive relationship is amplified among firms characterized by more collectivist shared values.
- Hypothesis 5b. Firm-level collectivist shared values moderate the effect of variable pay compression on firm-level rates of employee i-deal requests, such that this positive relationship is amplified among firms characterized by more collectivist shared values.
- Hypothesis 6. Firm-level collectivist shared values moderate the indirect effect of firm-level pay transparency on firm-level rates of employee i-deal grants via variable pay compression and firm-level rates of employee i-deal requests, such that this positive indirect relationship is amplified among firms characterized by more collectivist shared values.
mechanism_summary: Building on Bernstein's (2017) transparency-privacy model, the authors argue that making pay more observable pressures managers to avoid controversy over visible pay differentials by compressing variable pay. Consistent with compensating wage differentials theory, this compression motivates employees to seek redress through less observable, particularistic rewards (i-deals), and those requests are in turn granted — thereby "hiding" reward dispersion in discreet forms. Drawing on social comparison theory, firms with more collectivist shared values heighten the salience of observability and social monitoring, amplifying the compression-to-i-deal-request stage of the serial indirect effect. The field study supported Hypotheses 1–4 and 6 (and 5b), while Hypotheses 5a was not supported.
data_measures:
The dominant component is the quantitative Study 2 field study; Study 1 is a preregistered experiment supplying randomized evidence for the first link only.
- Study 1 (preregistered online business-simulation experiment): 117 managers in the final sample (120 recruited via Prolific, screened on managerial experience; two failed embedded attention checks and one reported suspicion) from the United States and United Kingdom. A 2 × 2 between-subjects design randomly assigned participants to pay communication policy (pay transparency vs. pay secrecy) crossed with shared values (collectivist vs. individualist), both delivered as written framing of a five-person online sales team in which every participant was in fact assigned the manager role. After viewing an identical set of first-round performance scores for four "subordinates" (one made a high performer), participants allocated a £10 performance-based bonus pool, so the resulting distribution was attributable entirely to their own decision-making. The dependent variable, variable pay compression, was operationalized as the additive inverse of variable pay dispersion, that is, the Gini coefficient (Donaldson & Weymark, 1980; Pfeffer & Langton, 1993) multiplied by −1.0, so that 0 indicates complete compression and −1.0 absolute inequality. Manipulation checks used a 6-item pay transparency scale (α = .88) tapping pay process, pay outcome, and pay communication transparency, and a 2-item collectivist shared values scale (α = .84); both manipulations were effective, with no transparency × collectivism interaction on either check. Estimation: 2 × 2 ANOVA. Syntax, data, and materials are posted at https://osf.io/nuvge/.
- Study 2 (multisource, firm-level field study): 645 salespeople nested in 111 medical device distribution firms in China, collected in two phases about one week apart. Owners or CEOs of 135 firms were surveyed first (111 participated, firm-level response rate 82.22%), then the 805 salespeople whose contact details they supplied (645 responded, 80.12%, with three to 15 employees per firm). All items were back-translated into Mandarin Chinese, and the measurement reference period for every endogenous variable was the past year. Firm-level pay transparency (employer-rated) used Arnold and colleagues' (2018) 12-item scale covering pay process, pay outcome, and pay communication transparency across four pay components, modeled as a second-order factor (CFI = .97, TLI = .96, RMSEA = .09, SRMR = .04). Variable pay compression (archival) was computed from employer-reported bonus plus incentive pay per employee in RMB, again as −1.0 × the Gini coefficient. Firm-level i-deal requests (employee-rated) used Ho and Tekleab's (2016) 5-item frequency scale (four developmental items, one benefit item; 1 = never to 5 = frequently), aggregated to the firm (developmental ICC1 = .27, ICC2 = .68; benefit ICC1 = .31, ICC2 = .73). Firm-level i-deal grants (employer-rated) used the same five items rated for extent granted in the past year (1 = not at all to 5 = to a great extent; developmental reliability .91). Firm-level collectivist shared values (employee-rated) used two items from Wagner and Moch's (1986) collectivist values scale aggregated under a direct consensus model (mean rwg = .71, ICC1 = .29, ICC2 = .70). Controls: number of employees, firm revenue, tenure diversity, age diversity, education diversity, gender diversity, mean organizational tenure and its quadratic term, and base pay compression. Estimation: a 2-2-1-2 multilevel structural equation model (Preacher, Zyphur, & Zhang, 2010) fitted to item-level data in Mplus 8.4 with full-information maximum likelihood, plus Monte Carlo tests of the indirect and conditional indirect effects with 20,000 replications.
On identification, the authors treat Study 1's random assignment as evidence that pay transparency drives managers' compression decisions, and state that because Study 2 applied a field study design no comparable causal assertion can be made about the association between variable pay compression and i-deals; that part of the model is associational. To probe reverse causation they also collected an independent cross-lagged sample of 69 medical device distribution firms in China, and Appendix A reports a supplementary experiment testing whether compression drives transparency.
key_findings:
Support is reported per study because the two studies tested different subsets of the model. The dominant Study 2 supported Hypotheses 1, 2, 3, 4, 5b, and 6 and rejected Hypothesis 5a; Study 1 supported Hypothesis 1 and did not support Hypothesis 5a.
- Study 2 (645 employees in 111 firms; 2-2-1-2 MSEM). Hypothesis 1 supported: firm pay transparency was positively related to variable pay compression (γ = .05, p = .010). Hypothesis 2 supported: variable pay compression was positively related to both developmental (γ = 1.08, p = .000) and benefit (γ = 1.14, p = .004) i-deal requests. Hypothesis 3 supported: the Monte Carlo indirect effects of pay transparency via compression were significant for developmental (indirect effect = .05, 95% CI [.01, .11]) and benefit (indirect effect = .05, 95% CI [.01, .12]) i-deal requests. Hypothesis 4 supported: requests predicted grants (developmental γ = 1.54; benefit γ = .94; both p = .000) and the serial indirect effects were significant for developmental (.08, 95% CI [.01, .17]) and benefit (.05, 95% CI [.01, .11]) i-deal grants. Hypothesis 5a rejected: the latent pay transparency × collectivist shared values interaction was not related to variable pay compression (γ = −.03, p = .242). Hypothesis 5b supported: the variable pay compression × collectivist shared values interaction was positively related to developmental (γ = 1.56, p = .001) and benefit (γ = 1.86, p = .002) i-deal requests, with the compression-to-request slopes steeper in firms with more collectivist shared values. Hypothesis 6 supported: the serial indirect effect on developmental i-deal grants was .15 (95% CI [.03, .30]) at high versus .01 (95% CI [−.06, .07]) at low collectivist shared values, difference .14 (95% CI [.02, .32]); for benefit i-deal grants it was .10 (95% CI [.02, .21]) versus .00 (95% CI [−.06, .05]), difference .10 (95% CI [.02, .23]). In the firm-level descriptive statistics, pay transparency correlated significantly with variable pay compression (r = .20, p = .037), but its correlations with both developmental and benefit i-deal requests and grants were not significant. The indirect-effect model explained 18%, 20%, 13%, 61%, and 39% of the variance in variable pay compression, developmental requests, benefit requests, developmental grants, and benefit grants respectively. Results were essentially unchanged when the control variables were removed.
- Study 1 (117 managers; 2 × 2 ANOVA). Hypothesis 1 supported: managers in the pay transparency condition compressed subordinates' variable pay more (M = −.17, SD = .11) than those in the pay secrecy condition (M = −.27, SD = .16), F(1, 113) = 18.93, p = .000, η² = .14, power = .99, recalling that higher values indicate greater compression. Hypothesis 5a not supported: the pay transparency × collectivist shared values interaction was only marginally significant, F(1, 113) = 3.22, p = .076, η² = .03, power = .43, and the interaction pattern ran contrary to the prediction. The collectivist-versus-individualist difference in compression was significant under pay secrecy (M = −.21 vs. M = −.33, difference in means = .12, p = .005) but small and nonsignificant under pay transparency (M = −.15 vs. M = −.18, difference in means = .03, p = .804).
Convergence and divergence: the experiment and the field study converge on the first link, with Hypothesis 1 supported in both, and converge on the failure of the manager-side moderation, with Hypothesis 5a unsupported in both; the collectivist amplification instead appeared only at the employee-driven compression-to-request stage in Study 2. Supplementary analyses reported in the appendices found no support for an association between variable pay compression and employees' requests or managers' grants for higher pay (financial i-deals), and confirmed robustness to the full three-item collectivism measure and to a coefficient-of-variation dispersion measure. In the independent 69-firm cross-lagged sample, pay compression was not associated with subsequent pay transparency (γ = .40, p = .573), while pay transparency was positively associated with concurrent variable pay compression (γ = .03, p = .011).
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends Bernstein's (2017) transparency-privacy theory from the individual to the firm level, explicating a previously undescribed multistep mechanism by which transparency indirectly (rather than intentionally) produces hiding of reward differentials. It contributes to i-deals research by identifying pay compression as a firm-level antecedent of i-deal requests and grants and by isolating collectivist shared values as a boundary condition that counterintuitively amplifies the transparency–privacy paradox.
practical_implication: Because pay transparency can trigger unintended pay compression and a downstream rise in nonmonetary i-deal grants, leaders should anticipate these externalities — e.g., emphasizing to managers that justifiable pay differences benefit their own performance, and monitoring i-deal allocation so hidden rewards are not used as a "back door" for gender- and ethnicity-based disparities. Effects are especially pronounced in collectivist contexts, where managers should make pay policies more transparent and procedurally clear.
limitations: Study 1's experimental design cannot rule out reciprocal causation between compression and transparency, and its short-term managerial role may not generalize to real-life decisions. Study 2 used field data from small firms in a single industry (medical device distribution) and a single occupation (salespeople) in one country, limiting generalizability to larger firms, other industries, and contexts where vertical/tournament pay dynamics matter.
future_research: Future work should test the causal link between pay compression and i-deals via experimental or quasi-experimental designs, examine pay compression as a mechanism linking transparency to outcomes like collective performance and human-capital sorting, and pursue cross-industry and cross-cultural samples. Researchers could also unpack the dominant mechanism behind the collectivist amplification effect and study pay "noticeability" at the individual level.
abstract: Drawing from research on the transparency-privacy dilemma in management, we theorize that firm-level pay transparency elicits a multistep process involving managers and employees that shifts the dispersion in remuneration from more to less observable forms, thus making pay transparency a “moving target.” We posit a serial indirect effect of pay transparency on firm-level rates of i-deal grants (a less observable form of remuneration) via variable pay compression and heightened rates of employee i-deal requests, with this indirect effect amplified in firms characterized by collectivist shared values. First examining the role of managerial agency and collectivist shared values in the pay transparency–compression relationship in a simulation-based experiment, we test the overall model in a multisource field study using a sample of 111 medical device distribution firms. Our findings demonstrate that: (a) firm-level pay transparency is predictive of greater pay compression, (b) firm-level rates of i-deal grants are largely explained by this pay compression via its effects on employee i-deal requests, and (c) this sequential effect is amplified in firms with more collectivist shared values. Accordingly, we explicate how transparency triggers unintentional hiding, and suggest that accompanying more transparent pay may be an increased reliance upon rewards that, by their very nature, are less transparent.

title: Learning Down to Train Up: Mentors Are More Effective When They Value Insights from Below
methods: Five studies: three survey studies (Study 1 cross-sectional; Study 2A correlational; Study 2B two-wave pre-registered longitudinal) testing the downward-learning -> engagement link via OLS/Tobit/Poisson regression and mediation; a field study (Study 3) linking mentors' learning direction to archival mentee outcomes via multilevel ordinal logistic and OLS regressions; and an online experiment (Study 4) manipulating learning direction, with multilevel mediation and moderated-mediation analyses. Confirmatory factor analyses establish discriminant validity of the new scale.
industry: Working professionals/supervisors across diverse industries (Prolific Academic samples); software engineers and data scientists mentoring novice coders at an online programming boot camp (field study)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual mentors (and matched mentees), via Prolific Academic surveys/experiments and a field setting
n_sample: Study 1 n=499; Study 2A n=776; Study 2B n=400 (364 at Time 2); Study 3 = 278 mentor-mentee pairs (50 matched mentors); Study 4 = 439 mentors and 295 mentees
authors: Zhang, Ting; Wang, Dan J.; Galinsky, Adam D.
theories: growth mindset; learning orientation; social hierarchy and power
keywords: downward learning; learning direction; learning orientation; mentor engagement; mentoring effectiveness; social hierarchy
research_question: What motivates potential mentors to engage with and be effective for their mentees? The paper asks whether mentors' "learning direction"—specifically the belief that those lower in a hierarchy are valuable sources of knowledge—predicts mentor engagement and mentoring effectiveness, above and beyond related constructs like learning orientation and growth mindset.
hypotheses:
H1a. The downward learning of mentors will positively predict their engagement (i.e., time invested) with their mentees.
H1b. Mentors' downward learning will positively predict viewing mentoring as a worthwhile opportunity to learn knowledge and skills from their mentees.
H1c. Perceiving mentoring as a worthwhile learning opportunity will mediate the relationship between mentors' downward learning and their engagement with their mentees.
H2a. The downward learning of mentors will positively predict mentee learning experiences and outcomes.
H2b. Increased mentoring engagement will explain the relationship between mentors' downward learning and mentees' learning.
Additional unnumbered prediction developed for Study 4: the downward learning manipulation will have a greater impact on mentor engagement and on the learning experiences and outcomes of mentees when mentors have greater positional power.
mechanism_summary: Believing that people below oneself in a social hierarchy hold valuable knowledge reframes mentoring from a costly obligation into a two-way learning opportunity. This reframing raises mentors' engagement (the time and effort they invest), which in turn improves mentees' learning outcomes and their perceptions of advice and support. Because power tends to reduce perspective-taking, the downward-learning manipulation has its strongest effects for mentors high in positional power.
data_measures:
- Data: five studies. Studies 1 (n = 499), 2A (n = 776), 2B (n = 400 at Time 1, 364 at Time 2), and 4 (439 mentors, averaging 7.55 years of industry experience) recruited full-time working professionals from Prolific Academic, while Study 4's separate mentee sample of 295 were "individuals seeking jobs" recruited on the same platform; Study 3 matched survey responses from mentors at "MissionCode," an online programing boot camp, to archival records of student performance (278 mentor-mentee pairs from 50 matched mentors).
- IV, learning direction (Studies 1-3): three parallel items per direction, rated 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree, e.g., "I learn a lot by interacting with those who have [LESS/the SAME amount of/MORE] power than I do"; downward-learning alphas were .87 (Study 1), .88 (Study 2A), .91 (Study 2B), and .84 for the abridged two-item version used in Study 3.
- IV, learning direction (Study 4): manipulated. Mentors wrote three to five sentences about "a time in which you learned from someone with less power than you" (downward condition) versus "more power than you" (upward condition).
- DV/mediator, mentor engagement: the number of a prospective mentee's questions (out of 20) that mentors said they would take the time to answer (Studies 1-2B); the word count of the advice message actually written to a mentee (Study 4).
- Mediator, mentoring as an opportunity to learn knowledge and skills: six items adapted from Ragins and Scandura (1999) (alpha = .85). A competing mediator, mentoring as an opportunity to learn social and cultural information, used five items (alpha = .87).
- DV, mentee learning outcomes (Study 3): hireability rated by a third-party mock interviewer who had never met the student (0 = "no," 1 = "maybe," 2 = "yes") and technical competence rated on the same interviews (1 = poor to 5 = excellent).
- DV, mentee learning experience (Study 4): mentees rated the quality of the advice received (overall quality, useful, clear, actionable, detailed, concrete; adapted from Zhang & North, 2020) and the support received (an adaptation of Edmondson's 1999 psychological-safety items plus encouraging/motivating/supportive), each collapsed into a single highly correlated dimension (alpha = .98).
- Moderator, mentor hierarchical position: a 1-10 ladder measure of positional power within the organization (Anderson et al., 2012).
- Controls: learning orientation (Vandewalle et al., 2001), growth mindset (Dweck, 2000), power distance (Farh et al., 2007), intellectual humility (Leary et al., 2017), Big Five traits (Lang et al., 2011), mentor self-perceived coding knowledge (Study 3), and demographics.

Estimation follows the design of each study: OLS with Tobit and Poisson specifications as robustness checks in Study 1, OLS with Tobit specifications in Studies 2A and 2B, multilevel ordinal logistic regression (hireability) and multilevel OLS (technical skill) with test and interviewer fixed effects plus mentee and mentor random effects in Study 3, and multilevel models treating each piece of advice and each mentee rater as random intercepts with bootstrapped mediation in Study 4. Only Study 4 is a randomized experiment, and the paper presents it as the study that "sought causal evidence"; the other four designs are associational. Study 2A collected all variables at one time point, which the authors note may have overinflated the relationship, motivating the pre-registered two-wave Study 2B in which predictors were measured at Time 1 and the outcome and mediators two weeks later. In Study 3, matches were based only on overlap in scheduling availability rather than self-selection, but the authors still acknowledge that the mentor-mentee relationship could run in the reverse direction.
key_findings:
- H1a supported in all three survey studies: downward learning positively predicted mentor engagement in Study 1 (b = 0.16, t(494) = 3.15, p = .002; b = 0.13, t(486) = 2.53, p = .01 with related constructs and demographics controlled), Study 2A (b = 0.20, t(772) = 4.71, p < .001; b = 0.15, t(760) = 3.52, p < .001 with controls), and Study 2B (b = 0.15, t(360) = 2.37, p = .019; b = 0.14, t(348) = 2.18, p = .03 with controls).
- Lateral learning never significantly predicted engagement in any of the three studies. Upward learning did so only in Study 1 before controls (b = 0.11, t(494) = 2.12, p = .03) and was no longer significant once the related constructs were added.
- H1b supported in both studies that tested it: downward learning positively predicted viewing mentoring as a worthwhile opportunity to learn knowledge and skills in Study 2A (b = 0.22, t(772) = 5.15, p < .001) and Study 2B (b = 0.32, t(360) = 5.57, p < .001), with the effect surviving controls in both.
- H1c supported in both studies: the indirect effect through perceiving mentoring as a worthwhile learning opportunity was significant in Study 2A (95% CI [0.02, 0.06]) and Study 2B (95% CI [0.05, 0.14]). The competing mediator, mentoring as a chance to learn social and cultural information, produced no significant indirect effect in either study.
- H2a supported for hireability but only marginally for technical skill in the Study 3 field data: mentors scoring higher on downward learning had more hireable mentees (B = 0.39, t = 3.63, p < .001, odds ratio = 1.47; a one-unit increase raised the odds of a mentee moving from "maybe" to "yes, I'd hire" by 72%), while downward learning only marginally predicted mentees' technical ability (B = 0.09, t = 2.11, p = .05). Neither upward nor lateral learning predicted either outcome.
- H2a and H2b supported experimentally in Study 4: the downward-learning manipulation increased mentor engagement (word count M = 35.78 vs. 29.33; b = 0.14, t(437) = 3.02, p = .003), mentees' ratings of advice quality (4.49 vs. 4.24; b = .08, t(435) = 2.57, p = .01), and mentees' ratings of received support (4.39 vs. 4.19; b = 0.07, t(435) = 2.09, p = .04), with significant bootstrapped indirect effects of mentor engagement on perceived advice ([0.06, 0.29]) and on perceived support ([0.08, 0.27]). The manipulation check was significant but small (M = 4.86 vs. 4.62, t(437) = 1.93, p = .05, d = .18).
- Moderation by mentor positional power appeared only in the experiment, not in the surveys. In Study 4 the manipulation interacted with hierarchical position for engagement (b = 0.10, t(435) = 2.21, p = .03), advice quality (b = 0.07, t(434) = 2.17, p = .03), and support (b = 0.11, t(434) = 3.38, p < .001), with simple slopes significant at +1 SD and null at -1 SD. Exploratory tests in Studies 2A and 2B found no significant moderation by mentors' positional power.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces "learning direction" as a new construct that shifts learning from a task-related construct (learning orientation) to a relational one—who one believes one can learn from across a hierarchy. It extends work on learning orientation and growth mindset (which focus on the self) by showing that downward learning predicts mentor engagement and effectiveness independent of those constructs, and integrates research on social hierarchy, mentoring, and advice to explain what makes mentors effective.
practical_implication: Organizations typically motivate mentors by emphasizing benefits to mentees, which is insufficient because mentorship still feels like a costly obligation. Instead, they should highlight the learning value mentees offer to mentors. The research identifies an easy-to-implement intervention: having mentors reflect on times they learned from someone below them in a hierarchy shifts their learning direction and boosts engagement, especially for those in positions of power.
limitations: In the field study (Study 3), although mentor-mentee matches were based only on scheduling availability, the authors acknowledge the relationship between mentors' downward learning and student outcomes could partly run in reverse, with mentee performance shaping mentors' reported learning direction. The field sample of matched mentors was small and predominantly male, motivating the controlled, gender-diverse experiment in Study 4.
future_research: Future work should examine downward learning beyond mentoring (e.g., how leaders' downward learning affects their own and their team's productivity and innovation), and explore optimal learning directions across career stages and roles. Researchers are also encouraged to study the conversational-level process through which downward learning improves mentee outcomes—disentangling content of knowledge exchanged from relational rapport—and to extend learning direction to nontraditional sources of learning.
abstract: Although mentorship is vital for individual success, potential mentors often view it as a costly burden. To understand what motivates mentors to overcome this barrier and more fully engage with their mentees, we introduce a new construct, “learning direction,” which captures the beliefs people have about which individuals within a hierarchy— upward, lateral, or downward—are valuable sources of knowledge. Although most mentors believe knowledge resides higher up in hierarchies, the current research demonstrates mentors are more engaged and effective when they value insights from below. Our first three studies found that downward learning predicted mentor engagement (Study 1) because downward learning-directed mentors viewed mentoring as a worthwhile opportunity for their own learning (Studies 2A and 2B). A field study examined downstream consequences on mentees’ learning outcomes, finding that downward learning-directed mentors trained more hireable mentees (Study 3). A final experiment established causality while also demonstrating that learning direction is open to intervention: reflecting on a downward learning experience increased mentor engagement, which enhanced the mentorship experience for their mentees (Study 4). We extend theories on learning orientation to learning direction and demonstrate that beliefs about the hierarchical sources of learning are critical to successful mentoring.
