title: May I Please Go the Extra Mile? Citizenship Communication Strategies and Their Effect on Individual Initiative OCB, Work–Family Conflict, and Partner Satisfaction
methods: Three studies. Study 1: inductive qualitative interviews (constant comparative analysis) with married couples to identify communication strategies. Study 2: multi-source (employee + partner) cross-sectional survey, hierarchical linear regression and relative weights analysis. Study 3: between-subjects experimental vignette study, ANOVA with Tukey's HSD.
industry: Knowledge-work occupations (e.g., management, sales, professional services, government, attorney, financial planner)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Married/partnered employees and their partners (couples)
n_sample: Study 1: 22 individuals (11 couples), expanded by 6; Study 2: 192 employee–partner pairs; Study 3: 922 participants
authors: Bolino, Mark C.; Flores, Marisa L.; Kelemen, Thomas K.; Bisel, Ryan S.
theories: dual concern theory (Pruitt & Rubin, 1986; Beitler, Scherer, & Zapf, 2018); social exchange perspective on OCB (Organ, 1990)
keywords: citizenship communication strategies; dual concern theory; individual initiative; organizational citizenship behavior; partner satisfaction; work–family conflict
research_question: How do employees communicate with their partner at home when engaging in individual initiative OCB, and how do these citizenship communication strategies affect the employee's OCB, their work–family conflict, and their partner's satisfaction?
hypotheses:
Study 1 was inductive and advanced no a priori hypotheses. The three hypotheses below were developed for the Study 2 survey, and Hypothesis 3 was retested experimentally in Study 3.
- Hypothesis 1. The self-concerned citizenship communication strategies of (a) projecting payoffs and (b) invoking prior conversations are positively related to OCB.
- Hypothesis 2. Whereas the self-concerned citizenship communication strategies of (a) projecting payoffs and (b) invoking prior conversations are positively related to work–family conflict, the other-concerned communication strategies of (c) providing early notice, (d) seeking permission, and (e) negotiating logistics are negatively related to work–family conflict.
- Hypothesis 3. The other-concerned citizenship communication strategies of (a) providing early notice, (b) seeking permission, and (c) negotiating logistics are positively related to partner satisfaction.

The authors state that they do not specify a prediction regarding the use of self-concerned strategies in relation to partner satisfaction, and that they do not directly test dual concern theory itself; the theory is used as a framework for categorizing the strategies and generating these predictions.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on dual concern theory from the conflict-management literature, the authors argue that self-concerned strategies emphasize the employee's own career goals and the rewards of OCB, whereas other-concerned strategies prioritize accommodating the partner. Self-concerned strategies should facilitate OCB but strain home life, while other-concerned strategies should reduce work–family conflict and raise partner satisfaction. Empirically, the trade-off is asymmetric: invoking prior conversations and projecting payoffs raise OCB (and invoking prior conversations raises work–family conflict; projecting payoffs lowers partner satisfaction), while seeking permission and providing early notice raise partner satisfaction but do not reduce work–family conflict and (for seeking permission) lower OCB.
data_measures:
- Study 1 (qualitative strategy discovery): 22 individuals from 11 married couples, purposively sampled from personal and professional networks against inclusion criteria (married; the individual or spouse employed full time in a knowledge-work industry; at least one child under age 10). Semi-structured, 10-question interviews of 45 to 60 minutes, digitally recorded and professionally transcribed. Two of the authors applied modified principles of constant comparative analysis (familiarization, then data reduction, then iterative open coding into categories) to derive the five strategy categories. Validation used member checking with three participants plus an expansion sample of three demographically divergent couples (n = 6), in which all five strategies appeared and no additional category could be identified.
- Study 2 (multi-source survey, the hypothesis-testing core): 192 employee–partner pairs recruited via Qualtrics panels, retained from 428 initial focal-employee responses after exclusions for missing partner data, missing employee data, and a speed check (7.5 minutes average per person). The five citizenship communication strategies (IVs) were measured with a new 25-item scale, five items per strategy, developed following Hinkin (1998), Colquitt et al. (2019), and Anderson and Gerbing (1991), employee-rated from 1 = "never" to 5 = "always" (alphas .89 to .93; a five-factor structure fit best in CFA). Individual initiative OCB was Bolino and Turnley's (2005) 15-item scale, rated by the employee's partner on a 5-point scale (alpha .93). Work–family conflict was Netemeyer et al.'s (1996) 5-item scale, completed by both employee and partner on 7-point scales (alphas .95 each, r = .73) and averaged to capture the couple's shared experience. Partner satisfaction was operationalized as relationship satisfaction using Norton's (1983) 6-item scale completed by the partner (alpha .97). Controls: employee gender, weekly hours worked, job tenure, relationship length, number of children, employee job satisfaction (Cammann et al., 1983), partner-rated employee communication competence (Arroyo & Segrin, 2011), and OCB itself when predicting work–family conflict and partner satisfaction. Estimation was hierarchical linear regression with one-tailed significance tests, supplemented by relative weights analysis. The design is cross-sectional and associational; the authors state they cannot draw definitive conclusions regarding causality.
- Study 3 (between-subjects experimental vignette): 922 employed participants recruited on Prolific (962 recruited, 40 excluded as not currently employed), resident in the United States, working at least 30 hours per week, and married or living with a partner, randomly assigned to 1 of 10 conditions (roughly 92 per condition) crossing the five communication strategies with a more depleting OCB (staying late at the office) and a more enriching OCB (attending a work-related dinner together). The manipulation was a hypothetical message received from the participant's partner. The dependent variable was partner communication satisfaction, measured with the five-face Kunin (1955) scale plus an item on how satisfied the participant would be receiving the message, on a 5-point scale (alpha .88). Realism checks (mean 4.61) and items on whether the focal OCB was discretionary were also collected. Analysis was ANOVA with Tukey's HSD comparisons.
key_findings:
Support was partial and the pattern differs by outcome and by study, so it is reported per study rather than pooled.
- Study 2 (OCB): Hypotheses 1a and 1b were both supported. Projecting payoffs (b = .15, p < .05) and invoking prior conversations (b = .25, p < .01) were positively related to partner-rated individual initiative OCB. Unhypothesized, seeking permission was negatively related to OCB (b = -.20, p < .01, one-tailed).
- Study 2 (work–family conflict): only Hypothesis 2b was supported, with invoking prior conversations positively related to work–family conflict (b = .18, p < .05). Hypothesis 2a was not supported (projecting payoffs, b = .00, ns), and none of the three other-concerned strategies reduced conflict, so Hypotheses 2c (providing early notice, b = -.04, ns), 2d (seeking permission, b = .13, ns), and 2e (negotiating logistics, b = .04, ns) were not supported.
- Study 2 (partner satisfaction): Hypotheses 3a (providing early notice, b = .23, p < .01) and 3b (seeking permission, b = .20, p < .05) were supported; Hypothesis 3c (negotiating logistics, b = -.02, ns) was not. Unhypothesized, projecting payoffs significantly decreased partner relationship satisfaction (b = -.20, p < .05, one-tailed).
- Study 2 (relative weights analysis): invoking prior conversations (49%) and projecting payoffs (26%) were the strongest predictors of OCB; invoking prior conversations was the most potent predictor of work–family conflict (37%); for relationship satisfaction the employee's general communication competence dominated (61%), with providing early notice (19%) and seeking permission (11%) next. Post hoc tests found no significant interactions among the strategies.
- Study 3 (partner communication satisfaction): communication strategy had a significant between-subjects effect, F(4, 917) = 5.28, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .02. Seeking permission was the most satisfying strategy (M = 3.51) and invoking prior conversations the least (M = 3.13), while projecting payoffs (M = 3.34) did not differ significantly from seeking permission. Hypothesis 3b held here, but providing early notice (M = 3.24) and negotiating logistics (M = 3.14) were associated with relatively lower satisfaction, so Hypotheses 3a and 3c were not supported and Hypothesis 3 was partially supported. There was a main effect of OCB type (dinner M = 3.40 vs. staying late M = 3.15) but no significant strategy-by-OCB-type interaction, and gender moderated nothing in either Study 2 or Study 3.

Convergence and divergence across methods: only seeking permission's positive link to partner satisfaction held in both the survey and the experiment. Providing early notice was supported in Study 2 but not in Study 3, where it produced relatively lower communication satisfaction, and negotiating logistics was unsupported in both. The Study 1 qualitative finding that couples treat OCB as effectively non-discretionary converged with Study 3, where participants rated the scenario behavior as at least somewhat expected ("is an expected part of the job," mean 3.27; "is above and beyond job requirements," mean 3.97). The authors report two robustness caveats: the invoking prior conversations link to work–family conflict was not significant when work–family conflict was measured with the partner rating alone, and the projecting payoffs link to OCB became only marginally significant (p = .08) when controls were omitted. Taken together, no single strategy was positive for both OCB and home-life outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: By identifying the *content* of partner communication specific to OCB, the paper extends partner-communication and work–family research—previously focused on how communication is enacted (e.g., demand–withdraw, assertive–passive)—into the citizenship domain. It demonstrates that there is no single communication strategy beneficial for both work (OCB) and home (reduced conflict, higher partner satisfaction), and shows that employees and their partners conceptualize OCB as involuntary for achieving family goals, deepening the literature on felt pressure to engage in citizenship.
practical_implication: Organizations and managers should recognize that "extra-role" behavior is often experienced as non-discretionary by employees and their partners, raising justice concerns. Employees can strategically match communication to their priorities: emphasizing seeking permission and providing early notice to protect home life, or projecting payoffs and invoking prior conversations to enable OCB—while being mindful of each strategy's costs. Organizations should encourage, but not compel, good citizenship.
limitations: The Study 1 qualitative sample was relatively young, well educated, predominantly White, and seemingly happily married, possibly surfacing mainly constructive strategies and limiting transferability. Study 2 data were cross-sectional, precluding causal inference, and OCB was partner-rated rather than fully objective. The research focused on one resource-consuming OCB type (individual initiative) and on one-way (employee) communication rather than dyadic exchange.
future_research: Scholars could examine dysfunctional or post-hoc communication strategies, collect reciprocal dyadic data using the actor–partner interdependence model, and study how OCB may generate work–family enrichment rather than only conflict. Additional work could investigate antecedents of citizenship communication (e.g., personality, organizational norms) and whether these strategies extend to other OCB types and targets such as coworkers and managers.
abstract: Organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) contributes to organizational effectiveness, but it can also create a burden for employees and their partners. In three studies, we examine how employees communicate with their partner about engaging in OCB and how this affects employees' OCB, their work–family conflict, and their partner's satisfaction. In Study 1, we use qualitative data to identify five ways employees communicate with their partner in order to engage in individual initiative OCB (e.g., staying late at work, volunteering for special assignments). In Study 2, using dual-concern theory, we hypothesize that self-concerned citizenship communication strategies will not only increase OCB, but also increase work–family conflict, and we predict that other-concerned communication strategies will reduce work–family conflict and increase partner satisfaction. Using survey data from employees and their partners, these hypotheses were partially supported. Finally, in Study 3, we use experimental vignette methodology to provide causal evidence that citizenship communication strategies influence partner satisfaction. Together, these studies increase our understanding of how employees communicate with their partner about OCB, indicate that there is no single communication strategy that has positive implications for both OCB and home life, and suggest that employees and their partners tend to think of OCB as involuntary for achieving family goals.

title: Double Weaving: A Bottom-Up Process of Connecting Locations and Scales to Mitigate Grand Challenges
methods: Inductive, longitudinal single-case study of the nonprofit CINI; participatory fieldwork plus 40 years of archival records; over 1,200 documents (~9,000 pages), 225 days of participant observation, 42 open-ended semi-structured individual interviews and 17 group interviews; Gioia-style first-/second-/third-order coding (24 first-order categories, 8 second-order themes, 4 aggregate dimensions), visual mapping, narratives, and triangulation.
industry: Nonprofit / NGO sector addressing child malnutrition (health, nutrition, education, protection)
country: India (West Bengal and Jharkhand; CINI headquartered near Kolkata)
time_period: Archival data 1974–2014 (40 years); fieldwork 2012–2017
units: Single organization (Child In Need Institute, CINI) and the actors it connects across locations and scales
n_sample: 1 organization (longitudinal case); ~5 million beneficiaries in 2013 scaling to over 7 million by end of fieldwork
authors: Chatterjee, Arijit; Ghosh, Anjan; Leca, Bernard
theories: grand challenges / wicked problems (Ferraro, Etzion, & Gehman, 2015; George et al., 2016); human geography of space, locations, and scales (Lefebvre, 1974/1991; Marston et al., 2005; Delaney & Leitner, 1997); process / inductive theory building (Langley, 1999; Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013); scaling social innovation (Westley et al., 2014; Bansal, Kim, & Wood, 2018)
keywords: child malnutrition; double weaving; grand challenges; grassroots organization; locations and scales; scalar asymmetry; scaling; spatial turn
research_question: How can a grassroots organization work within and across locations and scales to mitigate a grand challenge? The study uses a spatial lens that treats space as both horizontal (locations) and vertical (scales), asking how a resource-poor local organization can connect dispersed actors and resources to address a system-wide, "wicked" problem.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / dimensions: Scaling out, scaling up, scaling down (three directional components) plus reinforcing (a process driver) — the four broad activity types that comprise double weaving.
- Process / phases: Scaling out (local intervening, disseminating) → scaling up (synchronizing, strategic linking) → scaling down (collective capacity building, anchoring) → reinforcing (diagnosing, consolidating), iterating recursively through multiple cycles.
- Triggering conditions: Grassroots interventions lack financial resources and access to policy-making, which triggers a need to scale up to higher-scale actors; successful scaling up builds on credible disseminated outcomes of local interventions.
- Boundary conditions: A cooperative case with no contestation/conflict; norms of freely shared knowledge; and a long, nested four-decade scaling path from community to government.

Double weaving is theorized as a multidirectional, recursive process in which a focal organization "weaves" actors and resources horizontally across locations and vertically across scales at the same time, analogous to two fabrics woven and interwoven for strength. Reinforcing (continuous diagnosing of root causes and consolidating of what works while discarding what fails) drives and sustains scaling out, up, and down, giving the process continuity and durability. Rather than seeking shared consensus among all stakeholders, the organization weaves actors around specific problems on which agreement can be more easily managed, navigating scalar asymmetries of power and contextual familiarity.
data_measures: Inductive, longitudinal single-case study of CINI combining archival records with participatory fieldwork; the design is interpretive and process-oriented, and no causal identification is claimed. Archival corpus: CINI's records covering the 40 years since its inception (1974–2014), over 1,200 documents totaling around 9,000 pages — 160 quarterly board-meeting minutes (1,800 pages), 40 annual general meeting minutes, 39 annual reports, 31 audited financial accounts, 32 statutory filings, 147 government/donor grant agreements and related communications, three commemorative books, and 820 units of other materials (training materials, newsletters, project reports, audio-visuals) — supplemented by reports located in the National Library archives in Kolkata and by netnography. Fieldwork (participant observations and conversations, 2013–2017): 225 days as a participant-observer stationed at CINI's headquarters, 15 days of field visits to eight project locations, and five observed training programs for government fieldworkers (25 days), recorded in six field diaries (about 200 pages each), 117 hours of conversation audio recordings, and 100 photographs. Interviews (conducted during 2015–2017): 42 open-ended semi-structured individual interviews and 17 group interviews with CINI's cofounder and chairman, unit and functional heads, fieldworkers, board members, child development project officers, and a former state government secretary. Constructs were coded in five nonlinear, concurrent, iterative steps: (1) chronicling CINI's scaling activities as a narrative series of events and actions; (2) axial coding of the field data through questioning and constant comparison, using phrasal descriptors (e.g., "socio-technical intervention") and yielding 24 first-order categories after several cycles of refinement; (3) grouping those categories under eight second-order themes, some drawn from respondents' own language (e.g., "synchronizing"); (4) free-hand drawing and visual mapping to capture the space–time aspects of the themes; and (5) theoretical coding classifying the themes into four third-order aggregate dimensions — scaling out, scaling up, scaling down, and reinforcing — and settling on the double weaving metaphor. Triangulation across archives, observation, and interviews was reinforced by the third author, who never visited the field and coded as an outsider to balance "etic" and "emic" perspectives; coding disagreements were resolved by revisiting the data and often approaching informants for empirical validation.
key_findings: The study surfaces "double weaving" as an ongoing recursive process through which a resource-poor grassroots organization mitigated the grand challenge of child malnutrition: three directional components—scaling out, scaling up, and scaling down—plus reinforcing as a process driver, iterating through multiple rounds. Scaling out (local intervening plus disseminating) diffuses social innovations within and across locations, but grassroots organizations lack the financial resources and policy access needed to extend it, so scaling out triggers a need for scaling up; successful scaling up builds on successful scaling out because disseminating outcome histories builds credibility and attracts the attention of higher-scale actors. Scaling up (synchronizing plus strategic linking) requires acknowledging the asymmetry of power across scales and complying with the mandates and expectations of higher-scale actors rather than lecturing officials on what they should do; it secures access to financial resources and policy-making, and the resulting policy changes and resource allocations are what allow the partnership to extend into scaling down. Scaling down (collective capacity building plus anchoring) channels those higher-scale policies and resources into superior grassroots interventions, completing one weaving cycle and enabling the next. Reinforcing—continuous diagnosing of root causes together with consolidating, which strengthens what worked and discards what did not (the Life Cycle Approach and, after decades of trial and error, Premix were retained; a farming project was dropped for lack of requisite knowledge and a university's large-sample randomized control proposal was rejected on ethical grounds)—runs throughout the process rather than preceding it, which is why the study treats diagnosing and mitigating as concomitant rather than sequential. The study also reports a second, opposite asymmetry: higher-scale actors have less familiarity with local contexts than lower-scale actors, an asymmetry lower-scale actors can use to access them. Double weaving does not rest on shared consensus among stakeholders; the focal organization instead weaves actors and resources around specific problems on which consensus can be more easily managed. Reported outcomes: CINI collaborated with four government agencies and 28 partners in total in 1980, rising to 18 and 95 by 2000 and 61 and 173 by 2016; after becoming Jharkhand's nodal agency for deprived children its outreach increased from two million to four million in two years; and by the end of the fieldwork it was reaching over seven million beneficiaries. As higher-scale actors developed confidence in CINI, weaving cycles that had initially begun at the grassroots often began at higher scales instead.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to grand-challenges research by showing that identifying a grand challenge and its root causes is inseparable from engaging with it, and by treating diagnosing and mitigating as concomitant rather than sequential. It advances the "spatial turn" in organizational research by developing the under-theorized scalar (vertical) dimension alongside locations (horizontal), and extends scaling research—which has treated scaling as a unidirectional process—by theorizing scaling down as a complement to scaling out and up and by foregrounding scalar asymmetry.
practical_implication: For grassroots organizations with limited resources, the case offers lessons on scaling social impact: pair local interventions with disseminating credible outcomes to attract higher-scale actors, synchronize with the mandates and expectations of those actors (rather than lecturing them), and use scaling down to channel resources and policy into superior grassroots interventions. Lower-scale actors can exploit asymmetries—using higher-scale actors' resources and policy access while supplying the local contextual familiarity those actors lack.
limitations: The authors flag three boundary conditions of a single-case study. First, the case features collaboration and cooperation without the contestation or conflict often inherent in grand challenges. Second, CINI members freely shared knowledge, whereas many settings involve closely guarded ideas and inter-firm rivalry. Third, the nested, four-decade scaling path highlights how slow the process can be and may not generalize to contexts with faster, politically accountable pathways.
future_research: Future work could compare less emotionally intense and vivid issues (e.g., preventable diseases such as malaria) with child malnutrition; examine the conditions under which knowledge diffuses widely given the tension between sparse networks for idea brokering and dense networks for implementation; and study grand challenges from a higher-scale actor's perspective. Researchers could also examine more closely how actors exploit scalar asymmetries across scales.
abstract: Grand challenges are system-wide problems. While top-down approaches to mitigating grand challenges may have potentially far-reaching impact, such initiatives from the higher scales can fail because of limited knowledge of ground realities. At the same time, resilient local efforts to address societal challenges can have limited reach. How can a grassroots organization work across locations and scales to address a grand challenge? We report the findings of a longitudinal case study of the Child In Need Institute, a nonprofit organization that successfully scaled its impact to reach over seven million beneficiaries. Based on 40 years of archival data and four years of intensive fieldwork, our findings reveal “double weaving” as a recursive process of diagnosing and addressing problems by connecting actors and resources across locations and scales. The double weaving process gives researchers a framework to explore the complex interplay between locations and scales that is necessary to address grand challenges. Our study contributes to research on grand challenges and scaling, advancing the spatial turn in organizational studies by developing the scalar dimension, and expanding research that has primarily focused on locations.

title: Identity Multiplicity and the Formation of Professional Network Ties
methods: Logit regression on dyad-level data (26,234 dyads) from 401 part-time MBA students across three cohorts; standard errors clustered simultaneously by ego and alter; KHB mediation tests; LSA of identity-map text to operationalize identity homophily; cohort fixed effects.
industry: Subjects employed across finance (35%), healthcare/pharmaceuticals (10%), technology (8%), and consulting (7%); context is a part-time MBA program
time_period: Three MBA cohorts entering summer 2020, fall 2020, and fall 2021; network survey at end of first semester
units: Dyads (pairs of classmates within a section)
n_sample: 401 subjects; 26,234 dyads (13,082 for reciprocated-tie models)
authors: Ingram, Paul
theories: homophily / value homophily (McPherson, Smith-Lovin, & Cook, 2001); identity theory (Stryker & Burke, 2000); individuation (Maslach, 1974; Kang & Bodenhausen, 2015); social identity theory (Tajfel, 1981; Tajfel & Turner, 1986)
keywords: homophily; identity homophily; identity multiplicity; individuation; professional network ties; racial difference
research_question: How does identity multiplicity—the extent to which personal identities draw on multiple elements—predict the incidence of professional network ties, and does it particularly promote ties between individuals of different races?
hypotheses:
- H1: The likelihood that two individuals will form a network tie increases as their identity multiplicity increases (positive).
- H1a: The relationship between identity multiplicity and the formation of a network tie is mediated by individuation of the people in a dyad (positive mediation).
- H1b: The relationship between identity multiplicity and the formation of a network tie is mediated by identity homophily, indicated by the similarity of personal identity elements of individuals in a dyad (positive mediation).
- H2: The likelihood that two individuals of different race will form a network tie increases as their identity multiplicity increases (identity multiplicity positively moderates the otherwise negative effect of racial difference).
- H2a: The effect of identity multiplicity to increase the likelihood that two individuals of different race will form a network tie is mediated by their individuation (positive mediated moderation).

All five predicted paths are signed positive in the paper's theory diagrams (Figures 1A–1C), with racial difference on its own entering negatively via similarity-based attraction.
mechanism_summary: Identity multiplicity makes a person harder to categorize, which prompts interlocutors to individuate them—perceiving them as a unique person rather than a category representative—and individuation drives attraction, engagement, and the initiation of ties. Simultaneously, more identity elements raise the odds of sharing salient elements with an alter (identity homophily), creating bases of attraction and interaction. KHB tests indicate individuation and identity homophily jointly mediate ~82% of the identity-multiplicity effect (full mediation). Because individuation reduces negative racial stereotyping, identity multiplicity is especially potent for forging interracial ties—what the author labels the "Grunitzky effect."
data_measures:
Dyad-level analysis of 401 part-time MBA students at a prestigious university in a large U.S. city, drawn from three cohorts entering in summer 2020 (28% of subjects), fall 2020 (37%), and fall 2021 (35%): 26,234 dyads for sent ties and 13,082 for reciprocated ties. Every measure comes from assignments and surveys embedded in a required first-semester leadership course. Network data were collected by an online survey at the end of the first semester, approximately four months after subjects first came together, using the roster (or "whole network") method within class section: each subject was shown a list of all alters in their own section and asked to indicate who they considered part of their professional network.
- DV — Professional Network Tie: coded 1 if a tie existed between the members of a dyad. The average subject reported a tie with 41.6% of others; counting only reciprocated ties, where both ego and alter recognize the tie, lowers the rate to 25.2%. Both sent and reciprocated ties are analyzed.
- IV — Dyadic Identity Multiplicity: the count of gray and green elements on the identity maps of ego and alter, that is, the salient identity elements they share openly or would feel comfortable sharing. In a class exercise subjects drew "identity maps" (what Ramarajan called intrapersonal identity networks) with "me" as the central node and more important identities nearer the center, then color-coded each element gray (shared openly in the program), green (would feel comfortable sharing), or red (kept hidden). Red elements enter the models separately as Dyadic Hidden Identity; results are comparable if they are folded into the multiplicity count.
- Mediator — Dyadic Individuation: the sum of ego's and alter's Uniqueness, where an individual's Uniqueness is a function of the extent to which the (stemmed) words on their identity map are used less often by other subjects. The measure follows Maslach (1974), who found that experimentally individuated subjects gave more unique self-descriptions; the author needed a measure of individuation separate from identity multiplicity because the element count itself proxies both individuation and the chance of shared identity.
- Mediator — Identity Homophily: generated by latent semantic analysis (LSA) of all text a subject entered on their identity map, implemented with the semantic routine in Stata; the dyad's value is the cosine distance between ego's and alter's scores on the 110 LSA components. LSA captures semantic rather than literal overlap (e.g., matching "ALS" to "cancer", distinguishing "working class" from "upper class"). This operationalization is original to the paper.
- Moderator — Different Race: an indicator variable; Different Sex is carried as a parallel indicator.
- Foci and controls: three foci — Same Study Group (school-assigned through a process based on randomization with demographic and industry diversity constraints), Shared Club Memberships, and Seating-Chart Neighbors — plus Met Face-to-Face, Dyadic Self-Monitoring (Snyder and Gangestad's 18-item measure summed across the dyad), Dyadic Need for Cognition (Cacioppo et al.'s 18-item instrument in Cohort 3; four need-for-cognition items from the Growth Mindset Profile in Cohorts 1–2, scaled by the cohort mean), and cohort fixed effects. Table 4 adds each of 11 further psychometric and personality variables one at a time.

Estimation is logit regression, chosen because Professional Network Tie is dichotomous, with standard errors clustered simultaneously by ego and alter to handle the autocorrelation induced by the same subjects recurring across dyads; mediation is tested with the Karlson–Holm–Breen (KHB) method for comparing coefficients of nested nonlinear probability models. The design is associational rather than causally identified: identity multiplicity is measured from subjects' own identity maps, not manipulated, and the paper claims no experiment, instrument, or quasi-experiment for its focal predictors. What leverage the setting provides is organizational control — sections and study groups were assigned by constrained randomization, and seating charts, club memberships, and face-to-face contact are all observed. The reverse-causality alternative that ties reshape identity salience is addressed by robustness analyses rather than by design: adding indicators for MBA-program-specific identity elements (Models 7–8), restricting the sample to the 74% of subjects who agreed more with maintaining their professional self than with re-inventing themselves in the program (Model 9), and restricting to Cohort 3, whose identity maps were collected before subjects had met each other (Model 10).
key_findings:
The author concludes that "the models in Table 2 support all of the hypothesized relationships which are represented in Figure 1C," and every hypothesis test does return a coefficient of the predicted positive sign. The one qualification the results section itself records is that the mediation half of H2a did not reach significance.

H1 supported. In the base model (Table 2, Model 1) Dyadic Identity Multiplicity has a positive and significant coefficient (0.016, SE 0.006); a one-standard-deviation increase is associated with a 15% increase in the likelihood of a network tie.

H1a and H1b supported. With both mediators added (Model 3), Dyadic Individuation (0.115, SE 0.048) and Identity Homophily (3.001, SE 0.821) are both positive predictors of a tie: a one-SD increase raises tie likelihood by 17% and 7%, respectively. KHB tests indicate that individuation mediates 81% (p < .001) and identity homophily 19% (p < .001) of the identity-multiplicity effect on their own, and 82% (p < .001) combined; once the mediators are included the Dyadic Identity Multiplicity coefficient is not significantly different from 0, which the author reads as full mediation.

H2 supported. The Dyadic Identity Multiplicity × Different Race interaction is positive and significant (Model 2: 0.017, SE 0.006), and the magnitude is substantively important. Taking main effect and interaction together, a different-race dyad one SD below the mean on identity multiplicity is only 88% as likely to form a professional network tie as a same-race dyad; at the mean there is no significant difference; one SD above the mean it is 19% more likely to form a tie than a comparable same-race dyad. The author describes this as identity multiplicity effectively reversing the influence of racial homophily and names it the "Grunitzky effect."

H2a supported in part. Its moderation component holds: the Dyadic Individuation × Different Race interaction is positive and significant (Model 5: 0.073, SE 0.028), so that a one-SD increase in Dyadic Individuation raises tie likelihood by 15% in a same-race dyad and 27% in a different-race dyad — which the paper describes as in line with part of the H2a argument, that individuation moderates the negative impact of racial difference. Its mediation component does not hold: a KHB test indicates individuation mediated about 12% of identity multiplicity's moderation of racial difference, but that estimate is not significant (p = .37), so the unmediated influence of Dyadic Identity Multiplicity on racial homophily remains in place. The author speculates that the unexplained portion reflects a form of individuation not captured by an operationalization based on unique words in the identity map.

Ancillary and robustness results. Shared Club Memberships positively predicts ties (Model 4: 0.675, SE 0.129) and KHB indicates it mediates about 4% of the Identity Homophily effect (p < .01) — consistent with foci being one channel through which identity homophily operates, while leaving identity homophily with a substantial effect that shared club joining cannot explain. Model 6 re-estimates Model 5 on reciprocated ties with comparable results and a larger Identity Homophily coefficient (4.758, SE 1.176), where a one-SD increase makes a tie 12% more likely. Self-monitoring has a strong positive effect on tie formation and need for cognition is unrelated to it, and neither displaces identity multiplicity; the key results also hold across the four reverse-causality models of Table 3 and the addition of each of the 11 psychometric and personality controls in Table 4 (among which promotion, locomotion, and extraversion were positively related to tie formation, and prevention marginally so). Online Appendix replications using tie multiplexity and tie strength as dependent variables are consistent with Table 2, and indicate that identity multiplicity predicts the existence of a tie rather than its multiplexity or strength.
theoretical_contribution: The paper brings personal identity directly into network-formation theory, advancing the "bring the individual back in" agenda by treating self-articulated identity (not demographic proxies) as a determinant of ties. It introduces "identity homophily," extending value homophily beyond race and gender to any self-identified element, and theorizes individuation as an original, tested mechanism linking identity to tie formation and to the transcendence of racial categories.
practical_implication: Individuals who want richer, more diverse professional networks should cultivate identity multiplicity—e.g., by joining multiple affinity groups rather than focusing on one, and by experimenting with and refining authentic identity narratives. Organizations can leverage existing identity-based affinity groups to build cross-demographic ties that enhance creativity, decision-making, collaboration, and inclusion.
limitations: The data do not capture off-campus socializing, so the exact location where each tie formed is unobserved (though the author argues this does not threaten the hypotheses). The reverse-causality concern—that ties reshape identity salience—is addressed through several robustness analyses but cannot be fully ruled out, particularly over longer time periods.
future_research: Future work could analyze the structure of identity maps (e.g., path distance or eigenvector centrality of elements) to study how the importance and interconnection of identity elements shape networking. Researchers could examine networking agency and goal achievement as a function of identity multiplicity, apply text analysis of large identity corpora (e.g., college essays) to study identity homophily at scale, and explore implications for tie efficacy and overall network structure (e.g., modularity).
abstract: How does personal identity multiplicity—a self-perception with more elements—help an individual connect with others? I argue that identity multiplicity increases the likelihood of establishing professional network ties through two mechanisms: individuation, or the tendency of a potential network partner to view one as an individual as opposed to a representative of a category; and identity homophily, or the attraction and interaction opportunities that emerge as a function of shared identity elements with a potential partner. The benefits of identity multiplicity are particularly strong for promoting interracial ties as individuation reduces racial stereotyping. I find support for these ideas in an analysis of the creation of network ties of mid-career professionals.

title: Structuring the Start-Up: How Coordination Emerges in Start-Ups through Learning Sequencing
methods: Inductive, longitudinal multiple-case study of five early-stage start-ups followed for 22 months; data from 52 participant-observation visits (240+ hours), 96 semistructured interviews across three rounds, and archival sources; within-case and cross-case analysis with replication logic and member checks.
industry: Early-stage digital start-ups (all building a digital platform, or a digital brand in one case)
country: Norway (start-ups recruited from coworking spaces; authors at NHH Norwegian School of Economics and BI Norwegian Business School)
time_period: Followed for 22 months (revenue/growth data spanning 2017–2020)
units: Start-ups (firms)
n_sample: 5 start-ups
authors: Jones, Marius; Schou, Peter Kalum
theories: emergent coordination (Okhuysen & Bechky, 2009); organizational learning / learning styles (Bingham & Davis, 2012; Miner, Bassof, & Moorman, 2001)
keywords: coordination; emergent coordination; learning sequencing; organizational learning; start-ups
research_question: The paper asks: (a) How do start-ups develop coordination over time? and (b) How does successful coordination affect organizational performance?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: Early-stage start-ups lack the institutionalized scaffolding (roles, routines, rules, plans) that the emergent-coordination literature assumes is already present, so they must learn to coordinate from a rudimentary starting point.
- Process / phases (the "best practice" learning sequence): (1) *Anticipating coordination* (anticipatory learning) — foreseeing coordination needs before crises emerge; (2) *Steal with pride* (vicarious learning) — importing ready-made frameworks and practices from peers and competitors; (3) *Experimental implementation* (experimental learning) — minimal roll-outs, then scaling mechanisms that prove functional; (4) *Combine and simplify* (trial-and-error learning) — layering and simplifying mechanisms to fit the start-up and avoid over-formalization.
- Key constructs (coordination mechanisms scored per case): rules and plans, routines, and roles (Okhuysen & Bechky, 2009).
- Emergent outcomes: Coordination mechanisms that improve performance, indexed by market growth, received funding, and employee job satisfaction.
- Boundary conditions: Learning styles complement and prompt one another (path-dependent sequencing); start-ups may restart the sequence at junctures such as rapid scaling or pivots.

Across the five cases, the high performer (Freya) executed the full anticipatory→vicarious→experimental→trial-and-error sequence, while lower performers stalled by relying on improvised, unstructured solutions or by failing to combine and simplify. The central process insight is that, lacking pre-existing scaffolds, start-ups must learn coordination *deliberately*: each learning style makes a distinct contribution, and styles feed into one another (e.g., anticipatory learning motivates vicarious search; vicarious learning supplies frameworks for experimentation). Coordination is thus reframed as a state reached through learning rather than something that emerges from institutionalized scaffolds.
data_measures: Data corpus: five early-stage digital start-ups (pseudonyms Freya, Odin, Frigg, Balder, Thor), theoretically sampled on internal characteristics from an initial population of roughly 120 start-ups across eight coworking spaces, retaining ventures that were small (fewer than seven members), young (under three years), and immature (little or no revenue) and that "all had a digital aspect," after excluding accelerator participants, remote teams, and consultancy-focused ventures. Over 22 months the authors collected 52 participant-observation visits (over 240 hours) written up as field notes, 96 semistructured interviews across three rounds (93 hours of recordings, taped and transcribed), and archival sources including social media posts, newspaper articles, and publicly available revenue data from an official database. Operationalization: coordination was scored per case on Okhuysen and Bechky's (2009) three mechanism types (rules and plans, routines, roles) using a two-level score, one level for a mechanism being present and a higher level for a mechanism present and experienced by members as highly functional, with presence assessed from participant-observation field notes and members' experience from interview data, then aggregated into an overall rating (Table 2). Organizational outcomes were scored on market growth (somewhat successful = positive sales growth across the period; highly successful = yearly sales growth above 50%), received funding, and employee job satisfaction rated from interviews with employees rather than founders or top managers (Table 3). Each case was then scored across the four learning styles on a three-level scale adapted from Murray, Kotha, and Fisher's (2020) scoring system, running from no or very few examples, through some examples or many examples in individual teams, to many examples across the whole start-up (Tables 5–8). Coordination mechanisms and performance were scored at both the midpoint and the end of data collection. Analysis: within-case case stories written by the first author, independently read and checked by the second author acting as an "outsider" coder, then cross-case comparison using replication logic against the identified high performer, with triangulation across data sources, member checks in a follow-up interview round, and explicit consideration of alternative explanations. The design is inductive and interpretive; the authors report a "link" between coordination mechanisms and outcomes and claim no causal identification.
key_findings: The study surfaces a four-stage learning sequence through which start-ups build coordination: anticipating coordination (anticipatory learning), then steal with pride (vicarious learning), then experimental implementation (experimental learning), then combine and simplify (trial-and-error learning), producing coordination mechanisms (roles, routines, rules and plans) that the authors associate with better performance. Each style makes a unique contribution and the styles both complement and prompt one another (anticipatory learning motivates vicarious learning; vicarious learning inspires experimental learning), so the authors suggest learning sequences may be path dependent. Support is heterogeneous across the five cases and is reported case by case: only the high performer Freya ran the full sequence; Frigg and Balder anticipated less vigilantly than Freya and stole with pride only in individual teams while mixing in improvised solutions, and both failed to scale mechanisms across the whole start-up (Frigg attempted to combine and simplify but not organization-wide; Balder never reached combine and simplify at all); Odin skipped anticipation and vicarious learning entirely, substituting improvisational learning, and only then implemented and simplified its own improvised mechanisms such as a client checklist, a slower path because it learned only from its own mistakes, and it did not combine mechanisms; the low performer Thor stopped at unstructured improvisation and built no meaningful coordination mechanisms. Outcomes tracked this ordering: Freya doubled its revenue every year from 2017 to 2020, raised four rounds of venture funding totaling 15 M USD, and had the most satisfied members, whereas Thor had no sales growth, received no funding, and closed down before the end of data collection. Two findings are flagged as surprising: coordination problems arose even in start-ups of four to eight people, and these small start-ups struggled to diffuse mechanisms organization-wide unless they deliberately tested them first (Freya designated a "shepherd" to own implementation), which contrasts with prior work assuming mechanisms spread through informal interaction. Start-ups may restart the sequence at junctures such as rapid scaling, as Freya did on reaching 28 members while expanding into new markets. The authors weigh three alternative explanations and judge each unlikely: Freya's market being less volatile, initial team formation, and founder characteristics or prior start-up experience (Freya's founders had no prior entrepreneurial experience, and the medium performers had similar outcomes despite large variation in experience).
theoretical_contribution: The paper's core contribution is a processual theoretical framework explaining how start-ups learn to coordinate by sequencing complementary learning styles, addressing a literature on start-up coordination that has been dominated by static, top-down "blueprint" explanations. It extends the emergent-coordination literature by showing how coordination emerges from an immature state with underdeveloped routines and roles—through deliberate learning rather than from pre-existing scaffolds—and adds to the organizational learning literature by demonstrating how different learning styles interact in learning sequences, with one style compensating for shortcomings in another.
practical_implication: Start-ups should not fear having clear roles, rules, plans, and routines and should deliberately seek to implement them rather than staying unstructured. Entrepreneurs are advised to anticipate coordination needs early, learn from peers, and continuously combine and simplify coordination mechanisms to fit their current situation while avoiding bureaucratic rigidity.
limitations: As an inductive multiple-case study, the work is limited in its knowledge claims, especially regarding performance outcomes, and the authors cannot fully rule out alternative explanations (e.g., market volatility, team-formation effects, founder experience). Because only the high performer restarted its learning sequence within the study window, the authors' ability to theorize iterative sequences and recovery from coordination crises is constrained, and the data are limited on how start-ups recover from such crises.
future_research: The authors call for larger-scale, quantitative work to test whether the learning styles are additive and sequential (does order matter, or can styles be reordered?) and whether the findings replicate in a larger population of start-ups. They also encourage research on how specific learning styles contribute to distinct aspects of coordination, how start-ups restart learning sequences as they scale, and how start-ups recover from coordination crises.
abstract: To succeed in growing and scaling their organization, start-ups must establish roles, routines, rules, and plans that coordinate organizational activities. However, early-stage start-ups often lack such coordination mechanisms. Through a longitudinal qualitative multiple-case study of five start-ups, we develop a theoretical framework for how start-ups develop and improve coordination over time. We find that start-ups establish coordination through a learning sequence consisting of four distinct learning styles. To develop coordination successfully, start-ups anticipate coordination problems before they escalate, steal ideas and frameworks from others, experimentally implement coordination, and combine and simplify coordination mechanisms. By providing a processual understanding of how start-ups develop coordination, we contribute to the literature on coordination in start-ups, which has tended toward static explanations. We also add to the literatures on emergent coordination and organizational learning, as we highlight the role of deliberate learning in developing coordination, and how different learning styles link together to create learning sequences.

title: Gaining Organizational Adoption: Strategically Pacing the Position of Digital Innovations
methods: Two-year ethnographic field study (inductive, grounded process research) of 54 firms in a digital health accelerator; data include participant observation, 150 interviews, and firm-level documents, coded temporally to induct a process model.
industry: Digital health (care management, diagnostics, patient education, treatment, wellness)
time_period: 2016 to 2018 (2017 and 2018 accelerator cohorts)
units: Entrepreneurial firms participating in a digital health accelerator (pseudonym 'Cure')
n_sample: 54 entrepreneurial firms (58 new use cases)
authors: Karp, Rebecca
theories: disruptive innovation theory; effectuation / customer-led innovation; jurisdiction and occupational expertise; literature on pacing in entrepreneurial action
keywords: digital innovations; disruptive innovation; embedded approach; entrepreneurship; market-centric approach; new use cases; organizational adoption; strategic pacing
research_question: Given that adoption decisions inside customer organizations involve a plurality of members with divergent views rather than a single executive, how do entrepreneurial firms gain organizational adoption for their (often disruptive) digital innovations?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: "new use cases" (extensions that expand an innovation's relevance); the single-versus-multiparty difference in organizational adoption; the tension between revealing value-adding disruptive functionality and threatening members' expertise, roles, and jurisdiction.
- Two approaches: an *embedded approach* (deep, on-site engagement with customers to co-develop use cases) versus a *market-centric approach* (scanning competitors and the market, demonstrating expertise, magnifying claims, comprehensively rolling out functionality).
- Practices of strategic pacing (embedded firms only): (i) concealing disruptive functionality, (ii) restraining claims that an innovation displaces work, and (iii) shifting the velocity of deployment based on impact to members' expertise.
- Triggering conditions: deep engagement surfaces how an innovation threatens members' jurisdiction, prompting firms to withhold or slow disruptive elements; threats from *outside* a focal business unit require concealing functionality, whereas threats from *within* a unit can be managed by restraining claims alone.
- Emergent outcome: firms using the embedded approach with strategic pacing generally gained adoption (paid pilots); market-centric firms sparked executive interest but generally failed to gain adoption.

Across 54 firms, identifying unmet customer needs was necessary but insufficient for adoption. The embedded approach gave entrepreneurs contextual insight into how diverse organizational members would receive an innovation, enabling them to strategically pace deployment—temporarily concealing disruptive, value-adding features and restraining claims that the innovation would automate or replace members' work—so as to appease audiences whose expertise or jurisdiction the innovation threatened. The digital nature of the innovations made this selective, reversible "switching on and off" of functionality feasible.
data_measures:
The corpus is two years of field data collected while the author was embedded in the digital health accelerator Cure (a pseudonym) from 2016 to 2018, covering all 54 entrepreneurial firms that matriculated through the 2017 or 2018 cohorts (28 firms in year one, 26 in year two; no selected firm declined). Each cohort was tracked for 12 months — a two-month vetting period before program entry, the six months of participation in Cure, and four months after program completion — a window calibrated to informants' report that closing a deal generally took seven months (10 at most). Three types of field data were collected: (1) ethnographic observation of entrepreneurs' internal team interactions and of their interactions with customer executives and customer users as they developed and attempted to sell new use cases; (2) 150 interviews, ranging from 30 minutes to two hours, with the CEOs or founders of all 54 firms (involving multiple members of each firm) plus executives and influencers at prospective customer organizations; and (3) firm-level data comprising applications at program entry and exit, revised technology development plans, product strategies, and periodic alumni surveys of revenue, new contracts, funding, and hiring after program completion, together with strategic planning documents, acceptance evaluations, blog posts, press releases, product requirements, and product design documentation. Table 1 reports descriptives for all 54 firms: digital health sector, cohort, CEO gender, firm age, initial revenue and funding at program entry, number of founders, and prior startup experience.

Analysis began with open coding of field notes and interviews; all field data were then temporally ordered and coded (Van de Ven & Poole, 1995), with attention to whether and how entrepreneurs identified and developed new use cases. To rule out less plausible opportunities, only use cases "at risk for adoption" — those to which firms had actually committed resources in the form of capital or labor — were traced, yielding 58 new use cases (most firms pursued adoption for one; four firms pursued two). Coding the adoption activities firms enacted produced two patterns: an embedded approach (vetting knowledge extensibility, dedicating team members, strategic pacing) and a market-centric approach (market scanning, demonstrating market expertise, magnifying claims with comprehensive rollout), with activity definitions, representative data, and frequencies in Tables 2 and 4 and firm-level activity distributions in Appendix A (Table A1). Adoption was assessed in two steps. First, the desirability of each new use case was checked with customers and with other experts such as investors and accelerator mentors — deliberately not customers alone, following Christensen and Bower (1996) — by asking whether it addressed "real" problems, could solve unmet needs, and filled gaps in the market. Second, adoption itself was operationalized as whether an entrepreneurial firm contracted with a customer for a paid live pilot during the study window, a proxy justified by informants' report that pilots resulted in fuller deployment in nearly 80% of cases. The process model was then induced by comparing all process differences between the embedded and market-centric approaches, including activities entrepreneurs avoided as well as those they conducted. The design is inductive process research: the paper reports descriptive adoption rates and qualitatively evaluates alternative explanations rather than estimating causal effects.
key_findings:
All 54 firms identified ways to extend their innovations into new use cases capable of satisfying unmet customer needs, so developing a desirable use case was necessary but not sufficient to gain adoption; what separated outcomes was the process used. Twenty-one of the 54 firms employed an embedded approach and strategically paced deployment, while approximately two-thirds pursued a market-centric approach. Table 5 reports that 70% of the 21 embedded-process use cases were adopted by at least one customer versus 30% of the 37 market-centric use cases: firms deploying an embedded process generally gained organizational adoption, and firms using a market-centric process, at least during the study window, generally did not, despite sparking the interest of customer executives. The pattern is general rather than uniform — Appendix Table A1 records both embedded-process firms that did not gain adoption and market-centric firms that did. The share of use cases targeted at new customer segments was similar across processes (55% embedded vs. 60% market-centric), so the difference is not one of market ambition.

The central emergent finding is strategic pacing, and the puzzle it explains is that customer executives explicitly demanded innovations that would tangibly show how their work processes are disrupted, yet firms that comprehensively fulfilled those calls generally did not gain adoption, whereas firms that withheld disruptive, value-adding functionality did. Strategic pacing unfolded in three ways — concealing functionality embedded within a use case that some organizational members found threatening to their expertise and role, restraining claims that a use case could displace or substitute for members' work, and shifting the velocity at which a use case could be fully introduced — and was observed in 85% of embedded-process firms. The embedded process supplied the contextual insight that made pacing possible: dedicating team members built relationships with organizational members spanning roles, levels, and professions, which revealed that executives were rich sources of information on an innovation's future potential while middle managers, line workers, and professionals had a stronger grasp of what an organization would currently adopt and could and did successfully advocate against adoption. The digital nature of the innovations was what made pacing practicable, since functionality could be built robustly and then switched off or on customer by customer.

A conditional finding refines the model. When features diminished the perception of users' expertise held by those working outside the focal department or business unit, entrepreneurs both concealed functionality and restrained claims that the innovation substituted for the organization's processes or technology; when the threat came from within the business unit, rolling out full functionality while restraining substitution claims and positioning the use case as a tool for the affected users was sufficient. There were no cases in which a use case threatened a department or business unit without also unsettling views of a user's expertise, and identifying a pathway for affected members to demonstrate expertise at new tasks was a critical input into how quickly a use case could be fully rolled out. Several alternative explanations for the adoption difference were evaluated and not supported: initial funding and revenue levels, founder gender, subsector alignment, founder experience, and whether firms sold to existing or new customer organizations did not explain which firms gained adoption, and market-centric firms did develop use cases in high demand among customer executives.
theoretical_contribution: The core contribution is a theoretically grounded process model explaining how entrepreneurial firms gain organizational adoption for digital innovations through strategic pacing, extending research that typically picks up after the adoption decision or assumes adoption is made by a few individuals. It reconceives pacing as a *strategic* tool (slowing the introduction of disruptive elements to manage internal stakeholders) rather than only a reflective device for managing market uncertainty, and shows that threats to members' expertise and jurisdiction from outside versus inside a focal business unit call for different tactics (concealing functionality vs. positioning alone).
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs seeking organizational adoption should engage deeply with customers not merely to identify unmet needs but to gain contextual awareness of how diverse organizational members will react, and should strategically pace deployment—building disruptive functionality robustly but withholding or slowly releasing it, and positioning innovations as complements or aids—until affected members can demonstrate expertise in new ways.
limitations: The study examines digital health and does not test whether the observations generalize to other contexts (e.g., financial services or fields further afield), nor whether strategic pacing works for non-digital innovations whose features cannot be flexibly turned off. It also does not address the long-term effects of an embedded process and strategic pacing.
future_research: Future work could examine how these dynamics transition over time as firms gain scale or market dominance and may shift from an embedded to a market-centric process, whether an embedded process and strategic pacing enable other forms of entrepreneurial growth such as funding, and how entrepreneurs foster adoption of disruptive innovations in other regulatory and industry settings.
abstract: Scholars have long suggested that, to foster adoption for their innovations, entrepreneurs should engage with customers to better understand their unmet needs. Yet, customers frequently reside in organizations, and organizational members may not be aligned in their views regarding the benefits an innovation offers. Decision-making within organizations is rarely under the purview of a single executive and various members can wield influence. Given this plurality, how do entrepreneurial firms gain organizational adoption for their innovations? I explore how 54 entrepreneurial firms, all participating in a digital health accelerator, attempted to gain organizational adoption for their innovations. I show that, when entrepreneurs pursued an embedded process, they developed ways to expand the relevance of their innovations for new customers through new use cases, but strategically paced and withheld disruptive aspects of their innovations to appease different audiences within customer organizations. Firms that leveraged a market-centric process also expanded the relevance of their innovations. Despite sparking the interest of executives, firms using a market-centric approach did not gain adoption. By unpacking the process by which some entrepreneurs discovered how to strategically pace the deployment of their digital innovations, I contribute a mechanism that explains how digital innovations gain organizational adoption.

title: Opening Up AMJ’s Research Methods Repertoire
methods: Editorial essay; the five methods experts each selected a research approach deserving more attention, illustrating it with published examples, resources, and evaluation criteria.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Langley, Ann; Bell, Emma; Bliese, Paul; LeBaron, Curtis; Gruber, Marc
theories: performativity of methods; process and temporality in organization studies
keywords: microethnography; multilevel theorizing; researching forward; visual methods
research_question: Not reported in paper
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: AMJ's mission welcomes all empirical methods, yet some valuable methodologies remain underrepresented in its pages; the 23rd editorial team signals openness by adding methods experts and inviting innovative submissions.
- Visual methods: moving beyond words and numbers to study visible, material features of organization through images, video, object interviewing, photo-elicitation, semiotics, and quantitative content analysis.
- Microethnography ("video ethnography"): capturing meaning-making in situ through detailed examination of "small" activities, drawing on conversation analysis, context analysis, and participant observation.
- Incorporating time into quantitative analyses: moving from treating time as a control toward trajectory- and growth-model thinking that theorizes change over time.
- Multilevel theorizing: routinely testing and reporting when within-level effects differ from between-level (emergent or incremental) effects.
- Researching forward: engaged, real-time, forward-looking inquiry (field experiments, action research, collaborative and inside-out research) that helps practitioners "live forward" rather than only explaining the past.

These five illustrations are a "selected sampling of possibilities." Underpinning them is a performative view of method: what we know cannot be separated from how we come to know it, so widening the variety of methods we draw on enriches the knowledge and theory the field can generate.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The editorial advances a performative understanding of research methods—rejecting the conventional assumption that method choice merely flows from a fixed ontological and epistemological stance, and instead positing that methods help constitute reality. On this view, broadening AMJ's methods repertoire is itself a route to richer organizational knowledge and theory.
practical_implication: Authors are encouraged to submit work drawing on less-established methods, with assurance that the editorial team will recruit qualified reviewers to judge it on its merits. Researchers using participative, action-research, or inside-out approaches are asked to be transparent about their relationships with research sites and how those relationships may shape findings.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editors invite greater use of visual analysis (qualitative and quantitative), microethnographic study of micro-level interaction, trajectory-based and emergent-effect modeling that exploits existing nested data, and forward-looking engaged methods such as field experiments and collaborative inquiry, hoping to see these better represented in AMJ.
