title: Betwixt and Between: National and Organizational Identification of Host Country Managers Working in MNE Subsidiaries
methods: Cross-sectional single-source survey of host country managers in domestic firms vs. MNE subsidiaries in Korea. Latent profile analysis (LPA) classifies respondents into four dual-identity profiles; three-step BCH covariate analysis tests profile-membership hypotheses (H1-H2), supplemented by propensity score matching; treatment effect regression addresses nonrandom assignment for continuous-DV hypotheses (H3-H6); Heckman selection regression tests the interaction effect on acculturative stress (H7). Cluster-correlated robust variance estimates account for nonindependence within firms.
industry: Large multinational and domestic firms across 21 Korean Standard Industrial Classification industries (manufacturing as reference category)
country: Republic of Korea (South Korea); MNE subsidiaries headquartered in 11 parent countries
time_period: Survey conducted in 2015
units: Individual managers (Korean nationals) nested in firms
n_sample: 843 managers (219 in 19 domestic firms; 624 in 60 MNE subsidiaries); H7 model uses 624 MNE-subsidiary managers
authors: Lee, Khan-Pyo; Kim, Minyoung; You, Chi-Yeon
theories: acculturation profile model (Berry, 1997; Berry et al., 2006); liability of foreignness (Zaheer, 1995); social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1986; Hogg, 2016; Hornsey, 2008)
keywords: MNE subsidiaries; acculturative stress; dual identities; host country managers; identity conflict; liability of foreignness; national identification; organizational identification
research_question: How do the dual identity patterns of host country managers working in foreign MNE subsidiaries—in terms of the interrelationship and relative strength of their national and organizational identities—differ from those of domestic firm managers, and how do these distinctive patterns relate to the identity-related (acculturative) stress they experience within the foreign-owned firm?
hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1. Compared to those working in domestic firms, host country managers working in MNE subsidiaries are less likely to present the integrated identity profile than the national identity profile.
Hypothesis 2. Compared to those working in domestic firms, host country managers working in MNE subsidiaries are less likely to present the organizational identity profile than the national identity profile.
Hypothesis 3. The level of national identification among host country managers working in MNE subsidiaries is stronger than that among those working in domestic firms.
Hypothesis 4. The level of organizational identification among host country managers working in MNE subsidiaries is weaker than that among those working in domestic firms.
Hypothesis 5. The difference in the level of national identification between host country managers of MNE subsidiaries and domestic firm managers is smaller when their perceived career prospects in the organization are more positive.
Hypothesis 6. The difference in the level of organizational identification between host country managers of MNE subsidiaries and domestic firm managers is smaller when their perceived career prospects in the organization are more positive.
Hypothesis 7. National identification and organizational identification interact in predicting the acculturative stress of MNEs' host country managers, such that the relationship between national identification and acculturative stress is more positive when organizational identification is lower.
The authors state two deliberate non-predictions: they have no a priori reason to expect foreign and domestic firm managers to differ in the likelihood of presenting the diffuse identity profile, and they proposed no separate hypotheses about differences in the level of acculturative stress across the four identity profiles.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that because host country managers' national and organizational identities cross-cut each other (whereas domestic managers' identities are nested), foreign ownership and control heighten the salience of national identity and pose distinctiveness/value threats to it. These threats promote subgroup (national) identification and inhibit superordinate (organizational) identification, making the national profile more likely and the integrated/organizational profiles less likely than for domestic managers. Strong national plus weak organizational identification then exposes managers to greater acculturative stress; high organizational identification neutralizes the positive national-identification–stress link, while more positive perceived career prospects attenuate the foreignness effects.
data_measures:
Data come from a single online questionnaire survey administered in 2015 to Korean national managers working in large domestic firms and in MNE subsidiaries in South Korea. To keep the two groups comparable, the sampling frame was limited to domestic firms and to Korean subsidiaries of firms on the 2015 Forbes Global 2000 list; a firm counted as domestic if no single foreign entity owned more than 10% of its stake (the threshold defining foreign direct investment in Korea's official statistics) and as an MNE subsidiary if it was majority or wholly owned by an MNE headquartered abroad. Contact managers recruited from professional MBA programs at two Korean business schools enlisted managers at 19 domestic firms and 60 MNE subsidiaries; the authors listed the identified managers alphabetically and selected every second person. Of 1,512 questionnaires sent, 897 (59.3%) were returned, and after excluding responses with missing data the final sample is 219 managers of 19 domestic firms plus 624 managers of 60 MNE subsidiaries headquartered in 11 countries. All respondents were Korean nationals with at least one year of tenure in their firm. Survey items were back-translated following Brislin (1986) and rated on 7-point Likert-type scales from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Operationalization of the focal constructs: national identification uses three items from Mlicki and Ellemers (1996) (a = .88), including "I am glad that I am Korean" and "I feel strong ties with Koreans"; organizational identification uses five items from Mael and Ashforth (1992) (a = .87), including "This firm's successes are my successes", with "this firm" specified to MNE subsidiary respondents as the subsidiary rather than the MNE as a whole. Dual identity profile membership is not measured directly but derived from a latent profile analysis using the national and organizational identification items as indicators. Acculturative stress uses five items adapted from Rodriguez et al. (2002), retaining only the pressure-to-acculturate dimension (a = .90), including "It bothers me because I feel pressured to conform to foreign [the parent country's] ways of doing things"; the other dimensions of that instrument were dropped as less relevant to managers working in their own country. The independent variable, foreign-owned firm, is a dummy coded 1 for managers in foreign MNE subsidiaries and 0 for those in domestic firms. The moderator, perceived career prospects, uses three items from Reiche, Kraimer, and Harzing (2011) (a = .90). Controls are organizational prestige (five items from Mael & Ashforth, 1992; a = .87, aggregated to firm level), corporate social responsibility (five items from Lichtenstein et al., 2004; a = .90, aggregated to firm level), perceived organizational support (six items from Shanock & Eisenberger, 2006; a = .86), female gender, age, organizational tenure, job level (six categories), job function (11 categories) and 21 Korean Standard Industrial Classification industry dummies; organizational identification is controlled in the national identification models and vice versa. The acculturative-stress model adds foreign language anxiety (two items adapted from Miller et al., 2011; a = .94) and cultural distance computed from GLOBE country scores using Kogut and Singh's (1988) formula.

The design is a cross-sectional, single-source survey and the paper claims no experimental or quasi-experimental identification. What it does address is the nonrandom assignment of managers into foreign versus domestic employment: Hypotheses 1 and 2 are tested with a three-step BCH covariate analysis of latent profile membership (Bolck, Croon, & Hagenaars, 2004) and supplemented by propensity score matching; Hypotheses 3-6 with treatment effect regression (Maddala, 1983); and Hypothesis 7 with Heckman selection regression (Heckman, 1979) estimated on the 624 MNE-subsidiary managers only, because domestic firm managers rarely face the need to adapt to a foreign organizational culture. The treatment and selection equations use female gender, previous international experience (logged years abroad) and foreign language anxiety, and cluster-correlated robust variance estimates address nonindependence among responses within a firm. The authors state that the cross-sectional data make it difficult to verify the causality between identification patterns and acculturative stress, so the estimates should be read as associational; they judge the risk of common method variance to be low because the independent variable is objective and because common method variance deflates rather than manufactures interaction effects.
key_findings:
The paper reports that the results corroborate its hypotheses; Hypotheses 1-5 and 7 are supported at conventional levels and Hypothesis 6 only marginally.

Hypotheses 1 and 2 supported. Latent profile analysis favored a four-profile solution (the Lo-Mendell-Rubin test was significant at p < .01 for four profiles and insignificant for five), and the profile means for national and organizational identification (3.32 and 2.76; 5.32 and 3.62; 4.25 and 4.89; 5.88 and 5.66) corresponded to the diffuse, national, organizational and integrated profiles. In the BCH covariate analysis with the national profile as the baseline, the foreign-owned firm coefficient is negative and significant for the integrated versus national contrast (b = -1.26, p = .02; odds 0.28 times lower than for domestic counterparts) and for the organizational versus national contrast (b = -1.18, p = .02; odds 0.31 times lower). Consistent with the paper's explicit non-prediction, the coefficient for the diffuse versus national contrast is small and not significant (b = 0.13). Propensity score matching reproduced both signs: the average treatment effect is -0.15 (p < .01) for the integrated versus national profile and -0.13 (p = .03) for the organizational versus national profile.

Hypotheses 3 and 4 supported. In the treatment effect regressions, the foreign-owned firm coefficient on national identification is positive and significant (b = 1.07, p < .01), meaning MNE-subsidiary managers score 1.07 points higher on the 7-point national identification scale than domestic firm managers, and the coefficient on organizational identification is negative and significant (b = -1.51, p < .001), i.e., 1.51 points lower.

Hypothesis 5 supported, Hypothesis 6 marginal. The foreign-owned firm x perceived career prospects interaction on national identification is negative and significant (b = -0.20, p < .01), so the positive effect of the firm's foreignness on national identification is weaker for managers with more positive perceived career prospects. The corresponding interaction on organizational identification is positive but only marginally significant (b = 0.10, p = .08); the authors treat this as corroborating Hypothesis 6, note that the interaction is not significant in the focal-variables-only specification (which they attribute to a suppression effect from omitting national identification), and separately discuss the lower statistical significance of this moderating effect. The plotted effects show the foreign-domestic gap in both national and organizational identification narrowing as perceived career prospects rise.

Hypothesis 7 supported. In the Heckman selection model on the 624 MNE-subsidiary managers, national identification is positively and significantly related to acculturative stress (b = 0.38, p = .02) and the national identification x organizational identification interaction is negative and significant (b = -0.07, p = .04). The marginal-effects plot shows national identification positively and significantly related to acculturative stress when organizational identification is low but insignificantly related when it is high; the authors report that the interaction effect size was not large but was substantial enough to change the direction of the effect, neutralizing the positive national identification-acculturative stress relationship at high organizational identification.

Robustness and post hoc results. Reconstructing the four profiles with midpoint, median and mean cut-offs instead of latent profile analysis reproduced the Hypotheses 1-2 results; separately excluding subsidiaries of U.S.- and Japanese-headquartered MNEs yielded similar results; and adding pay satisfaction as a control did not significantly affect the results. A post hoc latent profile analysis on the foreign firm managers alone produced mean acculturative stress of 3.08 (diffuse), 3.49 (national), 3.31 (organizational) and 3.08 (integrated), with stress significantly higher among those presenting the national profile than among the integrated (p < .01) and diffuse (p = .09) profiles.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to international management in three ways: it uses a counterfactual framework to show how host country managers' dual-identity patterns differ from domestic managers' (rather than studying host country managers in isolation); it identifies an internal, human-resource source of the liability of foreignness (low organizational identification and acculturative stress) overlooked by prior work focused on external-environment sources; and it shows that host country managers' persistent strong national identity implies the MNE is a multicultural "mosaic" rather than a "melting pot," so imposing a common corporate identity may backfire.
practical_implication: Rather than substituting host country managers with parent country nationals, MNEs should adopt measures that raise host country managers' organizational identification and reduce acculturative stress—notably well-developed global talent-management programs that provide clear, credible career development paths across the worldwide organization. A dual identity approach that acknowledges distinct national affiliate identities while cultivating a common ingroup identity is recommended over a "one-company" global identity approach.
limitations: The theoretical premise that nationality is a subjectively important identity may not hold where perceived "nation-ness" is low or in less-developed host countries, so foreignness may constitute less of a liability in such settings. The authors also raise Korea's collectivist culture as a possible influence, but argue there is little reason to expect individualism–collectivism to change how people react to identity threats, so the main thesis "could still hold in individualistic countries as well"—something they note needs testing in future studies. The single-source, cross-sectional data likely deflate the interaction effect (common method variance) and make it difficult to verify the causal direction between identification patterns and acculturative stress.
future_research: Future work should explore how perceived nation-ness and sociocultural divides shape attitudes toward foreignness, and test whether the main thesis holds in more individualistic and in considerably less-developed host countries. Longitudinal designs collecting identification and acculturative-stress data at different time points are needed to address common method variance and establish causality in MNE subsidiary contexts.
abstract: This study investigates the patterns of dual identities of host country managers working in multinational enterprise (MNE) subsidiaries and how these patterns relate to their feelings of identity-related stress within the foreign-owned firms. Drawing on the acculturation literature, we classify the patterns of dual identities based on membership in nation and organization into four identity profiles: (a) diffuse (weak national and organizational identification), (b) national (strong national and weak organizational identification), (c) organizational (weak national and strong organizational identification), and (d) integrated (strong national and organizational identification). We submit that perceived conflict between the dual identities renders MNEs' host country managers less likely to present the integrated and the organizational identity profiles and more likely to present the national identity profile than domestic firm managers. MNEs' host country managers also identify more strongly with their nation and less strongly with their organization than domestic firm managers do. The combination of strong national identification and weak organizational identification among MNEs' host country managers exposes them to greater acculturative stress within foreign organizations. The results of an analysis of a sample of 843 Korean managers working in 19 Korean firms and 60 MNE subsidiaries in Korea corroborate our hypotheses.

title: On the Status Shocks of Tournament Rituals: How Ritual Enactment Affects Productivity, Input Provision, and Performance
methods: Quantitative causal-inference design using difference-in-differences (DID) with player, season, player-by-season, and game fixed effects, plus a regression discontinuity design (RDD) and coarsened exact matching as robustness checks; standard errors clustered by player-by-season.
industry: Professional sports (men's professional basketball, NBA)
country: United States (NBA; league also includes one Canadian franchise)
time_period: 1983/84 to 2016/17 NBA seasons
units: Player-game observations; treatment = All-Star Game participants, control = 'Almost All-Stars'
n_sample: 33,507 game-level observations from 1,676 player-seasons (734 treatment, 942 control)
authors: Maoret, Massimo; Marchesini, Giacomo; Ertug, Gokhan
theories: interaction ritual theory (Collins, 2004); status / signaling theory
keywords: emotional energy; ritual enactment; status shocks; tournament rituals
research_question: Beyond the well-established informational "signaling" pathway, is there another process through which a status shock causally affects winners' subsequent performance? The authors ask whether participating in the ritualistic conferment of a status-boosting award ("ritual enactment") increases tournament winners' productivity and the inputs they receive, and how durable that effect is.
hypotheses:
- H1: All else equal, participating in the ritualistic conferment of prestige will cause an increase in the productivity of tournament ritual winners (predicted positive).
- H2: All else equal, participating in the ritualistic conferment of prestige will cause tournament ritual winners to have an advantage in the inputs they receive (predicted positive).
- H3a: All else equal, participating in the ritualistic conferment of prestige will cause an increase in tournament ritual winners' overall performance (predicted positive).
- H3b: The positive effect of participating in the ritualistic conferment of prestige on tournament ritual winners' overall performance will decrease over time (predicted negative time trend).

H1 and H2 are the two proximal consequences the paper attributes to the emotional-energy boost generated by ritual enactment; H3a is their aggregate performance consequence and H3b its predicted decay.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on Collins's (2004) interaction ritual theory, the authors argue that physically enacting a prestige-conferring ritual charges winners with emotional energy, which raises their drive to convert inputs into outputs (productivity) and, by creating an EE gap relative to non-participating input providers, attracts greater deference and resources (more touches/usage) from teammates. Because EE is transitory, the performance gain decays over subsequent games. The NBA setting separates ritual enactment from signaling because the All-Star announcement and the game occur weeks apart and coaches/teammates already have little uncertainty about player quality.
data_measures:
Longitudinal sample of NBA players' game-level performance from the 1983/84 to the 2016/17 seasons, a range chosen because game-level data are incomplete before 1983/84 and the All-Star selection process changed substantially after 2016/17. All performance, roster, demographic, and ASG voting/participation data come from Basketball-Reference.com. The estimation window is 20 games per player-season: the 10 games before and the 10 games after the ASG. Treatment group = the 24 players selected to participate in the ASG each season (starters or reserves), restricted to those with nonzero ASG playing time. Control group = "Almost All-Stars," players ranked in the top 10 of fan voting who were not selected to participate. Final sample = 1,676 player-seasons (734 treatment, 942 control; 424 unique players) and 33,507 game-level observations.
- IV: the interaction Participation in the ASG x Post ASG. Participation in the ASG is a dummy coded 1 for treatment-group players in the focal season; Post ASG is a dummy coded 1 for games played after the ASG in that season.
- DV, overall performance (H3a/H3b): NBA Efficiency Rating, the composite the NBA officially uses to assess a player's performance in each game, computed as Points + Rebounds + Steals + Assists + Blocked Shots - Turnovers - Missed Shots.
- DV, productivity (H1): NBA Efficiency Rating per Minute Played and NBA Efficiency Rating over Usage, both constructed as ratios of overall performance to the level of input received.
- DV, inputs received (H2): Minutes Played for inputs from coaches; Touches per Minute and Usage Rate for inputs from teammates. Touches is an official NBA statistic aggregating the actions a player can take while possessing the ball (pass, shoot, draw a foul, commit a turnover), used because actual passes received are available only from 2013/14 onward; the two correlate at r = .91. Touches is scaled by minutes played to keep teammate inputs orthogonal to the coach's input. Usage Rate is the percentage of offensive plays that involve the focal player.
- Mediator: emotional energy is not measured. Its proxy is in-ritual exposure, tested as Post ASG x Number of minutes played in the ASG, with that variable set to 0 for control-group players.
- Controls: NBA Experience, Tenure with Team, Ln(1 + Number of Previous ASG Selections) as the player's status stock, PER in Previous Season as underlying quality, Game Won, Home Game, Progressive Game Number, and Participation in the ASG x Progressive Game Number to absorb differential trends across the two groups. Age is excluded because it correlates with NBA Experience at r = .91.

The paper claims causal identification and names its strategies explicitly. The main design is difference-in-differences (Bertrand, Duflo, & Mullainathan, 2004) with player, season, and game fixed effects, plus a stricter specification that replaces the player and season fixed effects with Player x Season fixed effects; robust standard errors are clustered by Player x Season. H3b is tested with a spline regression that splits Progressive Game Number into pre-ASG and post-ASG segments, each interacted with the treatment dummy. Supporting identification checks are a placebo DID that substitutes the All-Star announcement date for the ASG date (to separate ritual enactment from signaling), alternative control groups including all other players, coarsened exact matching, a "41st chair" comparison of Almost All-Stars against all other players, and a regression discontinuity design around the fan-voting cutoff using Relative Votes from Threshold with second-order polynomials fitted separately on each side of the cutoff.
key_findings:
H1 supported. Participation in the ASG x Post ASG is positive and significant for NBA Efficiency Rating per Minute (b = 0.034, p < .001, Model 2) and unchanged under the stricter Player x Season fixed effects (b = 0.034, p < .001, Model 3); for the alternative productivity measure, NBA Efficiency Rating over Usage, the coefficient is 0.043, p < .01 (Models 4 and 5). After the ASG the baseline treatment-control gap is amplified by 117% in NBA Efficiency Rating per Minute (from 0.029 to 0.063) and by 123% in NBA Efficiency Rating over Usage (from 0.035 to 0.078), which the authors translate into a 15% and a 12% increase relative to the within-season standard deviation of productivity.

H2 supported for teammate-provided inputs but not for coach-provided playing time. The coefficient on Participation in the ASG x Post ASG for Minutes Played is statistically nonsignificant (b = 0.079, p = .783, Model 6, confirmed in Model 7), so ASG participants do not seem to receive more playing time from coaches. Teammate inputs do increase: Touches per Minute (b = 0.069, p < .001, Models 8 and 9, with the treatment-control difference amplified by 147%, from 0.047 to 0.116) and Usage Rate (b = 0.668, p < .01, Model 10), corresponding to a 19% and a 13% increase in within-season standard-deviation terms. In the discussion the authors read the coach null as an indication that occupying a higher position in a formal structure such as an organizational hierarchy might shield certain individuals from the influence of ritual enactment.

H3a supported. Participation in the ASG x Post ASG is positive and significant for overall NBA Efficiency Rating (b = 1.314, p < .001, Model 11, which includes Player x Season and game fixed effects).

H3b supported. In the spline specification the post-ASG boost (b = 1.375, p < .001, Model 12) declines by approximately 0.15 after every game: Participation in the ASG x Progressive Game Number post ASG is negative and significant (b = -0.15, p < .001), while the corresponding pre-ASG trend is not significant (b = -0.03, p = .45), so the decay is specific to the post-ritual window. Plotted in five-game bins, the effect is positive and statistically significant for the first five games after the ASG (b = 0.915, p = .003); the 5-to-10-game bin is smaller and not statistically significant, and the downward trend continues in the 10-15 and 15-20 bins, which the authors describe as a halo effect of limited duration.

Mechanism and robustness evidence. Consistent with the emotional-energy account, Post ASG x Number of minutes played in the ASG is positive and significant (b = 0.06, p < .001), so the performance boost is amplified by a player's exposure during the ritual. The placebo DID that uses the All-Star announcement date instead of the ASG date produces no statistically significant changes in productivity, inputs received, or overall performance, which the authors treat as ruling out signaling as a credible alternative explanation. The RDD confirms a discontinuity at the voting cutoff: All-Stars just above it have an NBA Efficiency Rating 3.91 points higher across the 10 games after the ASG than players who barely missed selection (p < .001, Model A-1), and the result holds across four progressively narrower intervals (b = 3.45, p < .01 in the narrowest, Model A-4). Comparing Almost All-Stars with all other players who did not make the top 10 yields no statistically significant difference, supporting the assumed "41st chair effect," and the main results also hold with all other players as the control group and under coarsened exact matching.
theoretical_contribution: The paper's primary contribution is introducing "ritual enactment" as a novel, symbolic/social process—distinct from informational signaling—through which status shocks causally affect performance. It shows status shocks affect not just audiences' perception of output quality but the production of output itself (input acquisition and the transformation of inputs into outputs), and it distinguishes status "shocks" from self-reinforcing status "stocks," demonstrating that the ritual-enactment advantage is of limited duration.
practical_implication: Managers can use ceremonial, prestige-conferring events (not merely announcing winners or paying incentives) to generate motivational and performative boosts among employees, and could organize smaller-scale tournament-ritual-like events within teams or organizations. Because such events may reallocate resources via shifting deference, managers should monitor whether the resulting distribution stays fair and effective for organizational goals.
limitations: The authors cannot measure emotional energy directly, so EE is inferred rather than observed (they provide indirect support via in-ritual exposure). Because the chosen input providers (coaches and teammates) have low uncertainty about player quality, the design isolates ritual enactment but precludes a direct comparison of the magnitude and duration of signaling versus ritual enactment within the same setting.
future_research: Future work could compare the relative magnitude and duration of signaling versus ritual enactment in settings where audiences hold quality uncertainty, examine how formal/informal social structures (e.g., hierarchy, ideology) condition ritual-enactment effects, and study the interaction between status stocks and status shocks. Scholars could also investigate which ritual characteristics (formal vs. informal, public vs. private, field-level vs. organizational) and individual differences amplify or dampen the effect, and whether the framework extends to rituals routinely enacted within organizations.
abstract: We propose a novel process through which status shocks may enhance performance. Specifically, we theorize that, when status shocks include a ritualistic conferment of social prestige—such as in the case of “tournament rituals”—participating in that ritual enactment may increase tournament winners’ productivity and improve the inputs they receive, thereby improving their overall performance. We also consider the duration of that performance improvement, finding a decay that is consistent with our theorized mechanisms that are based on emotional energy. Our study shows that status shocks may carry not only informational value, as signals of quality, but also symbolic and social value that change the behavior of individuals who receive these shocks and of the input providers with whom they interact. We employ difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity designs on game-level data from the National Basketball Association to provide causal evidence for our hypotheses.

title: I Don’t Need a Degree, I’ve Got Abs: Influencer Warmth and Competence, Communication Mode, and Stakeholder Engagement on Social Media
methods: Quantitative observational study; six months of scraped Instagram data on 488 fitness/nutrition influencers (2,928 influencer-month observations) analyzed with Hausman–Taylor random effects regression and Wald tests comparing standardized coefficients; LIWC content analysis and rater-coded image classification for cue measures.
industry: Fitness and nutrition industry influencers (experience-good services) on Instagram
time_period: July 1 to December 31, 2019 (six months)
units: Social media entrepreneurs (influencers); influencer-month observations
n_sample: 488 influencers; 2,928 influencer-month observations
authors: Roccapriore, Ashley Y.; Pollock, Timothy G.
theories: customer engagement (van Doorn et al., 2010); multimodal communication / semiotics (Messaris, 1997; Meyer et al., 2018); warmth and competence (Fiske, Cuddy, & Glick, 2007; Abele & Wojciszke, 2014)
keywords: multimodal communication; social judgments; social media influencers; stakeholder engagement; warmth and competence
research_question: (a) Do images and words vary in their relative influence on stimulating different levels of stakeholder engagement, and (b) do warmth and competence cues vary in their relative influence on these outcomes? The paper asks how communication mode and content shape behaviors that differ in the cognitive effort they require.
hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1a. Image-based cues will have a stronger positive relationship with the influencer’s number of followers compared to word-based cues (predicted positive, images > words).
- Hypothesis 1b. Word-based cues will have a stronger positive relationship with followers’ positive interaction with the influencer compared to image-based cues (predicted positive, words > images).
- Hypothesis 2a. Competence cues will have a stronger positive relationship with an influencer’s number of followers compared to warmth cues (predicted positive, competence > warmth).
- Hypothesis 2b. Warmth cues will have a stronger positive relationship with followers’ positive interaction with the influencer compared to competence cues (predicted positive, warmth > competence).
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Post/reply/comment word counts, posting activity, profile age, traditional credentials, rater-coded attractiveness and fitness, video and deleted posts, gender, race

Because images are processed rapidly and unmediated and offer heuristic "proof" (iconicity, indexicality), they exert more influence on the low-effort decision to follow, while words' syntactic determinacy lets them convey the specific arguments and trust cues needed for the higher-effort decision to interact. Parallel logic applies to content: competence cues credibly signal underlying ability and matter most for following an experience-good provider, whereas warmth cues build the liking, trust, and authenticity that drive cognitively effortful positive interaction. Statistical-significance patterns supported H1b and H2a; the relative effect-size hypotheses (H1a, H2b) were not significant due to wide confidence intervals.
data_measures:
- Data source: secondary Instagram data on fitness and nutrition industry influencers, scraped via an API six days a week (Sunday excluded) from July 1 to December 31, 2019, yielding 52,148 influencer posts, 8,730,714 follower comments, and 620,505 influencer replies to comments, aggregated to influencer-months. The sample was built from key-term Instagram searches (trainer, online trainer, online coach, fitness coach, fitness coaching) plus stratified random sampling on pre-study followership size, giving an initial pool of 1,002 and a drawn sample of 502; removing influencers who stopped posting in the final three months left 488 influencers and 2,928 influencer-month observations (models are estimated on n = 2,916). A March 2019 visit to the Arnold Fitness Expo motivated the study but is not part of the analytic data.
- DV 1 (lower-level engagement): number of followers at the end of each month, taken from the influencer’s profile and log-transformed because of extreme right-skew (raw skew 7.19, reduced to −0.21; raw range 40 to 12,895,427).
- DV 2 (higher-level engagement): positive interactions = the count of positive affect words used by others in the comments on the influencer’s posts, coded with the LIWC positive affect dictionary.
- IV word-based competence cues: three-variable index of analytic words in the influencer’s posts, analytic words in replies to comments, and first-person singular pronouns in posts, coded with the LIWC analytic and pronoun dictionaries.
- IV word-based warmth cues: three-variable index of positive affect words in posts, positive affect words in replies, and other-inclusive first-person plural and second-person pronouns in posts.
- IV image-based competence cues: rater-coded counts of before-and-after transformation posts and of self-portrait or workout-demonstration posts; three raters each independently coded 500 posts (Cronbach’s α = 0.91 for before-and-after images, 0.73 for self-portraits).
- IV image-based warmth cues: rater-coded counts of group images (three or more individuals) and personal-life images; images fitting neither the warmth nor the competence category were excluded.
- Composite construction: every component variable was converted to a z-score. Word-based cues = mean of the six word z-scores; image-based cues = mean of the four image z-scores; competence cues = mean of its three word-based and two image-based z-scores; warmth cues = the same for its warmth components. Construct validity was checked with 93 Instagram users recruited on Prolific who rated eight messages on 1–5 warmth and competence scales.
- Controls: post, reply, and comment word counts; posts, comments, and replies in the period; video posts; deleted posts; traditional credentials (binary, any certification or degree listed in the profile); rater-panel attractiveness and fitness dummies (eight raters; α = 0.61 and 0.79); age of profile; gender; race (α = 0.81).
- Estimation: Hausman–Taylor random effects regression in Stata 16 (xthtaylor), chosen because the theory concerns between-influencer rather than within-influencer variation and the data contain time-invariant and nearly time-invariant measures. Variables were assigned to exogenous and endogenous, time-variant and time-invariant categories so the estimator could absorb an unobserved fixed effect — Instagram’s proprietary placement algorithm. The four focal cue measures were standardized so their coefficients could be compared with Wald tests.

The design is observational and associational: the paper reports relationships between cues and engagement, and its own language throughout is relational rather than causal. Hausman–Taylor does construct instruments for the endogenous regressors automatically, but the paper frames this as a way to retain time-invariant variables while accounting for the unobserved algorithm effect, not as a causal identification strategy. Endogeneity is addressed defensively rather than by design, through a robustness of inference to replacement (RIR/ITCV) analysis using Stata’s konfound command, alongside winsorizing skewed variables at a 1% cutoff, models with lagged dependent and independent variables, models dropping controls, tests for curvilinear cue effects, and substituting Apple and Android emoticon dictionary text before LIWC coding.
key_findings:
- Hypothesis 1a not supported. Image-based cues have a positive, significant relationship with number of followers (b = 0.02, p = 0.04) while word-based cues do not (b = −0.02, p = 0.54); because the hypothesis is about relative effect sizes, the decisive test is the Wald comparison, and the two coefficients are not significantly different (χ² = 1.29, p = 0.26), which the authors attribute to the wide confidence interval (−0.08 to 0.04) on word-based cues. For the significant path, each 1 SD increase in image-based cues corresponds to 1,498 additional followers, a 1.74% increase.
- Hypothesis 1b supported. Word-based cues have a positive, significant relationship with positive interactions (b = 545.49, p = 0.00) and image-based cues a positive, marginally significant one (b = 50.99, p = 0.07); the Wald test shows the word-based coefficient is significantly larger (χ² = 11.89, p = 0.00). Each 1 SD increase raises positive interactions by 36.8% for word-based cues and 3.4% for image-based cues.
- Hypothesis 2a supported. Competence cues have a positive, significant relationship with number of followers (b = 0.05, p = 0.02) while warmth cues do not (b = 0.00, p = 0.64), and the Wald test shows the competence coefficient is significantly larger (χ² = 6.26, p = 0.01). Each 1 SD increase in competence cues corresponds to 4,353 additional followers, a 5.1% increase.
- Hypothesis 2b not supported. Warmth cues have a positive, significant relationship with positive interactions (b = 141.43, p = 0.00) while competence cues do not (b = 78.00, p = 0.29), but the Wald test finds no significant difference between the two coefficients (χ² = 0.66, p = 0.42), again attributed to the wide confidence interval on competence cues (−67.05 to 222.99).
- Net pattern: the direction and statistical-significance pattern is consistent with all four predictions, but only the two comparisons that cleared the Wald test — Hypotheses 1b and 2a — are counted as supported. The authors characterize the overall result as general support for the expected pattern of relationships even though some effect sizes were not significantly different from one another.
- Post hoc within-mode and within-content comparisons (online supplement). For number of followers: image-based competence cues are positive and significant (b = 0.03, p = 0.01) while word-based competence cues are not (b = 0.02, p = 0.38), with no significant difference between them (χ² = 0.13, p = 0.72); image-based warmth cues are nonsignificant (b = 0.01, p = 0.17) while word-based warmth cues are negatively and significantly related (b = −0.04, p = 0.03), a sign opposite to what was anticipated, and the two differ significantly (χ² = 4.75, p = 0.03). For positive interactions: word-based competence cues are significant (b = 244.67, p = 0.02) while image-based competence cues are not (b = −0.94, p = 0.98); both image-based (b = 41.00, p = 0.03) and word-based (b = 307.31, p = 0.00) warmth cues are significant, with the word-based coefficient significantly larger (χ² = 8.75, p = 0.00). Overall, image-based competence cues had the largest positive relationship with lower-level engagement and word-based warmth cues the largest with higher-level engagement.
- Robustness. Winsorizing at 1% left the pattern intact except that image-based cues lost significance with followers and competence cues became slightly less significant (still p < .05). With lagged dependent variables, and separately with lagged independent variables, the only change was that the marginally significant image-based-cues-to-positive-interactions relationship became nonsignificant. Tests for curvilinear cue effects were all nonsignificant. The RIR/ITCV analysis identifies only image-based cues as a possible omitted-variable concern (5.03% of cases for followers, 7.38% for positive interactions), and the authors conclude that endogeneity does not appear to be an issue.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances multimodal communication research by separating communication mode from content—conflated in prior work—and showing that a mode's or cue's effectiveness depends on the cognitive effort the targeted engagement behavior requires. It extends the "Big Two" social-judgment literature by demonstrating that the long-assumed primacy of warmth over competence is conditional: competence cues dominate low-effort engagement, warmth cues dominate high-effort engagement. It also extends entrepreneur–stakeholder engagement research from one-to-one dyads to one-to-many online interactions.
practical_implication: Influencers and entrepreneurs should use images and videos demonstrating competence to grow their following, and deploy both image- and word-based warmth cues to stimulate higher-level engagement such as positive interactions. They should avoid self-focused rhetoric and general cheerleading, instead using other-directed language; posts need not be long, but regular, attentive interaction is crucial for cultivating online relationships and monetization opportunities.
limitations: Findings may not generalize beyond the visual, business-to-consumer fitness and nutrition context, and may differ in B2B settings or where visual evidence is less dramatic. Because data covered a fixed window with small monthly variation in followership and predictors, the authors could not compare within-influencer changes over time. Some images contain words, and Instagram's proprietary algorithm is an unobserved factor only partially addressed by the Hausman–Taylor design.
future_research: Longitudinal designs tracking entrepreneurs from founding onward could reveal how engagement processes evolve as followerships grow. More granular measures of image-based cues could give a more robust understanding, given that some images also contain words. Scholars should also examine how image-based competence cues affect investor decisions in computer-mediated settings such as crowdfunding.
abstract: In this study we consider whether (a) image- and word-based communication modes and (b) warmth and competence cues vary in their relative influence on different levels of stakeholder engagement on social media. Specifically, we explore social media fitness influencers’ abilities to attract followers and get followers to positively interact with them via posts and comments. We theorize that differences in the ways each communication mode is processed, and differences in how competence and warmth cues are perceived, will lead to different relative effects on lower- and higher-engagement behaviors. Using the social media platform Instagram, we followed 488 social media entrepreneurs in the fitness and nutrition industry for six months, and found that images have a positive relationship with less cognitively effortful engagement (following) whereas words do not have a significant relationship, and words have a stronger relationship than images with more cognitively effortful engagement (positive interactions). We also found that competence cues have a stronger positive relationship than warmth cues with the number of followers, and warmth cues have a positive relationship with positive interactions, whereas competence cues do not. Our findings have implications for research on multimodal communication, social judgments, and entrepreneur–stakeholder engagement.

title: Creative Jolts: Exploring How Entrepreneurs Let Go of Ideas During Creative Revision
methods: Inductive multiple-case study (Eisenhardt, 1989); longitudinal one-year tracking of 12 early-stage entrepreneurs via 85 semi-structured personal interviews, 42 phone interviews, and 376 mobile-app entries; experience-sampling-inspired data collection; multistep grounded analysis with temporal narratives, LIWC/PANAS-X affect coding, and cross-case comparison.
industry: Early-stage ventures across diverse domains (online travel, fitness, education, fundraising, food delivery, etc.) based in London coworking spaces
time_period: Approximately one year of observation per venture (six to 13 months); fieldwork spanning 2016–2017
units: Early-stage entrepreneurs (founders/cofounders who were primary inventors of the venture idea)
n_sample: 12 entrepreneurs; six experienced creative jolts, yielding seven jolt episodes analyzed
authors: Toivonen, Tuukka; Idoko, Onyaglanu; Jha, Harsh Kumar; Harvey, Sarah
theories: assumptive worlds (Parkes, 1975; Janoff-Bulman, 1989); idea journey / creative revision (Perry-Smith & Mannucci, 2017); jolts and shocks / unfolding model (Lee & Mitchell, 1994); sensemaking (Weick, 1993)
keywords: assumptive worlds; autonomous creators; creative jolt; creative revision; entrepreneurs; idea journey; letting go of ideas; trigger feedback
research_question: How do creators let go of ideas during creative revision (in order to allow new ideas to emerge and develop)? The paper studies how autonomous creators—early-stage entrepreneurs—navigate the disruptive episodes through which they relinquish ideas.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: *Trigger feedback* — negative, subtractive, core-directed feedback from a credible source (trusted/high-status mentor) that is perceived as threatening the idea or the venture's core mission.
- Key constructs / tensions: the *creative jolt* (an episode of cognitive and emotional upheaval); *assumptive worlds* that must be broken down before letting go; the persistency paradox between flexible revision and rigid commitment.
- Process / phases: (1) *existential crisis* — shattered assumptions plus a heightened emotional state, branching into *existential dread* (threat to idea) or *existential awakening* (threat to mission); (2) *reappraisal* — sensemaking via *reaching out* (diversifying through new networks) or *reaching in* (reflecting on core values with close peers); (3) *resolution* — discarding core aspects and reorienting via *recreation* (a fundamentally new idea) or *restoration* (return to the original mission).
- Emergent outcomes: a dramatic, generative shift onto a new idea trajectory, accompanied by emotional repair.

Creative jolts loosen creators' attachment to ideas by breaking down the assumptive worlds underpinning them, opening a "gap in meaning" that motivates a sensemaking search through which a new idea emerges. Negative affect (dread) and emotional ambivalence (awakening) supply the motivation, while reaching out and reaching in supply the cognitive raw material for reconstruction—so that the remains of the old idea define the opening into which the new one grows.
data_measures: Inductive multiple-case design (Eisenhardt, 1989) following 12 early-stage entrepreneurs — founders or cofounders who were the main inventors of the focal venture idea and so operated as relatively autonomous creators — recruited through four London coworking spaces. Scoping interviews produced structured profiles of 20 potential participants, of whom 12 met the criteria of having worked one to 12 months on a nascent idea they had conceptualized and of being regular users of a space they had joined in the previous three to six months (seven solo founders; five members of two-person founding teams). Observation ran approximately one year per venture, varying from six to 13 months. Three complementary data sources were used, in a design inspired by the experience sampling method (Larson & Csikszentmihalyi, 2014): 85 detailed semi-structured personal interviews of one to two hours tracking the entrepreneur's changing business model, interactions, salient conversations and emotions; 42 phone interviews of 10 to 20 minutes; and 376 substantive mobile-app entries over the 13-month observation period (average 31 per entrepreneur, range two to 70), prompted each evening and used mainly to flag key interactions for follow-up in the next interview. Constructs were built through a multistep inductive analysis. (1) In-depth within-case analysis of each of the 12 entrepreneurs, without theoretical preference or a priori hypotheses, yielding temporal narratives (Langley, 1999) of each idea journey. (2) The challenging feedback interactions the authors label trigger feedback were treated as events (Abbott, 1990), and episodes were built that began with trigger feedback and ended when the entrepreneur viewed the challenge to the idea as resolved; these episodes were labeled creative jolts and became the study's unit of analysis, with three authors independently charting each candidate episode into expansive quote tables and case narratives that were then reconciled across the group, plus comparison tables of interactions that did not trigger a jolt. (3) Systematic coding of emotional expressions, drawing on the emotive-response literature, the PANAS-X affect schedule (Watson & Clark, 1994) and the 2015 LIWC dictionary, produced a coding structure of 16 affective responses — six positive, six negative, four other — with LIWC-flagged emotion words used as a guide to subsequent manual inductive coding rather than mechanically counted, supplemented by interviewer notes. (4) Cross-case comparison of the individual jolt episodes identified consistent themes, temporal patterns and shifts. Data analysis took approximately six months. The design is interpretive and process-based; no causal identification is claimed.
key_findings: Of the 12 entrepreneurs followed, six engaged in ordinary creative revision — elaborating and refining ideas with relatively neutral emotions and incremental changes while retaining the core of the focal idea, with a few also ignoring or dismissing highly critical feedback — while the other six changed their ideas more radically, letting go of core aspects of the original idea; one of these experienced two episodes, yielding seven creative jolt episodes in total. Jolts were rare: across a year of observing many feedback interactions for every entrepreneur, only seven instances led to a creative jolt. Jolts were initiated by trigger feedback that creators perceived as threatening their idea or their venture's core mission. A credible source (someone deeply trusted, or high in status or power) was a precondition, but criticism from a credible mentor alone was insufficient: trigger feedback also focused on the core of an idea rather than a specific strategy or implementation plan, was subtractive rather than additive, and was aimed at an idea the creator was clear and confident about. Critical feedback lacking those characteristics — additive, or aimed at a missing plan rather than the core — did not trigger a jolt: Emily (Zelda) elaborated and improved her idea by developing a strategy for scaling, while Clayton (Digital Lemon), whose respected football-chairman critic was suggesting he wait or offer a larger equity portion rather than purely subtracting, "did not substantially change his plans in response to this feedback." Jolt episodes then unfolded through three phases — existential crisis, reappraisal, resolution — along two pathways that creators tended to follow consistently, without shifting between pathways from phase to phase, although the constituent activities were not exclusive to a pathway. Where trigger feedback was read as threatening the idea, creators experienced existential dread: shattered assumptions plus emotional turmoil, with LIWC-driven coding showing a shift from dominant positive emotions (self-assurance, hope, excitement) to dominant negative emotions (fear, anger, frustration), and actions that arrested or even reversed development of the idea. They reappraised by reaching out — diversifying their information and networks and seeking disconfirmation of the trigger feedback — and resolved through recreation, letting go of the original idea and embracing a fundamentally new one (GymForUs moved from matching gym buddies to connecting users with personal trainers; BaysWater narrowed to connecting Syrian refugee students in Turkey with peers and refugee academics after learning a large university already delivered its value proposition). Where trigger feedback was read as threatening the mission, creators experienced existential awakening: assumptions were shattered but also opened up to new possibilities or to a side-tracked original mission, accompanied by emotional ambivalence in which relief and hope coexisted with uncertainty and fear. They reappraised by reaching in — reflecting on core values and rationale, sometimes alone and sometimes with a close circle who understood the founding mission — and resolved through restoration, discarding significant and sometimes successful aspects of the venture in order to return it to its original core mission (Doorstep Radish forsook the sales drive that had grown it to roughly 600 home and business customers and 2,000 boxes per month; SuperCharge shifted from B2C to B2B to pursue its cultural-shift mission). Both resolutions were generative and both entailed letting go of something fundamental to the idea, but the study cannot establish that the new path was more novel or more useful than the original. Resolution was accompanied by emotional repair, with LIWC coding showing emotional expressions becoming more positive and increasing relief, hope and happiness. The overarching finding is that jolts did not stop creators from progressing along their idea journeys; they jolted those journeys onto a different trajectory, abruptly pushing creative work in substantially new, even radical, directions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper conceptualizes the previously unexamined *destructive* counterpart of idea generation—how letting go of ideas unfolds through creative revision—and introduces the creative jolt as a distinct, affectively charged, multi-phase episode that pushes ideas onto radically new trajectories. It shifts research attention from how ideas are generated and selected toward the processes by which "openings" for new ideas are constructed, arguing that ideas alone are not enough and that commitment/rigidity can paradoxically enable radical change once shaken.
practical_implication: Autonomous creators and the mentors, accelerators, and coworking communities supporting them should recognize that highly critical, core-directed feedback can trigger an agonizing but generative period rather than mere failure. Supporting creators through the emotional upheaval—via opportunities to reach out to diverse networks and reach in to core values—can help them work through the process of letting go, though the study cannot establish whether letting go improved outcomes for creators.
limitations: The analysis deliberately focused on cases where creators let go of ideas, so it cannot establish whether letting go improved outcomes or whether persistence would have succeeded. The study is confined to autonomous creators (individual founders or primary cofounders), so collective- or team-level jolt dynamics could not be elaborated. Findings rely partly on retrospective interviewing, mitigated but not eliminated by the longitudinal, near-real-time design.
future_research: Future work should map creators' emotional journeys more completely and examine how upheaval is prompted across different creators and contexts (e.g., organizational settings where support is withdrawn after a project is greenlit). Scholars could probe the nature of assumptive worlds and how creators emotionally prepare for their destruction, whether jolts can arise from positive triggers, and how jolts unfold at the team or collective level.
abstract: Creative revision involves sharing nascent ideas and soliciting feedback. This process has been portrayed as providing instrumental feedback that enables autonomous creators to shape and progress their ideas in a mostly positive, developmental way. However, creative revision also entails destruction—letting go of some ideas to make way for the new. Research has suggested that abandoning some aspects of ideas will be affectively challenging for creators, but has yet to elaborate how they navigate that challenge. In a longitudinal qualitative study of entrepreneurial ventures over a one-year period, we uncovered a novel phenomenon: the creative jolt—an episode of cognitive and emotional upheaval through which creators let go of their original ideas and allowed new ones to emerge, so that their ideas shifted in dramatic ways. We elaborate the processes through which creative jolts shape the trajectories of creative ideas. Our study captures the rollercoaster of heightened affect and cognitive disorientation experienced by autonomous creators as they try to bring nascent ideas to life.
apa_citation: Toivonen, T., Idoko, O., Jha, H. K., & Harvey, S. (2023). Creative jolts: Exploring how entrepreneurs let go of ideas during creative revision. *Academy of Management Journal, 66*(3), 829–858. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.1054

title: Rekindling the Fire and Stoking the Flames: How and When Workplace Interpersonal Capitalization Facilitates Pride and Knowledge Sharing at Work
methods: Two studies. Study 1: source- and time-separated two-wave field survey with round-robin reports, analyzed via multilevel path analysis (Mplus 8.3, MLR estimator, parametric bootstrapping). Study 2: 10-day experience sampling field experiment with a daily randomized capitalization manipulation, analyzed via multilevel path analysis with random slopes.
industry: Study 1: a privately owned mechanical-gear manufacturing company; Study 2: working professionals across diverse industries and occupations (e.g., nurse, chef, pharmacist, HR advisor)
time_period: Study 1: two survey waves one month apart; Study 2: two daily surveys across 10 consecutive workdays
units: Individual employees (disclosers)
n_sample: Study 1: 448 focal disclosers matched to 1,989 round-robin knowledge-sharing reports across 44 teams; Study 2: 105 participants providing 787 paired daily observations
authors: Watkins, Trevor; Kleshinski, Catherine E.; Longmire, Natalie H.; He, Wei
theories: attribution theory; social-functionalist model of emotions; theory on capitalization
keywords: effort attribution; knowledge sharing; perceived coworker responsiveness; pride; social-functionalist model of emotions; workplace interpersonal capitalization
research_question: How and when does workplace interpersonal capitalization (sharing personal work-related positive events with coworkers) serve the instrumental function of spurring disclosers' knowledge sharing? The paper asks whether capitalization is not only socioemotional but also instrumental, with pride as the linking mechanism, effort attribution as a first-stage boundary condition, and perceived coworker responsiveness as a second-stage boundary condition.
hypotheses:
H1: The association between workplace interpersonal capitalization and pride is moderated by effort attribution, such that the association is positive when effort attribution is high, but not when effort attribution is low.
H2: The positive association between pride and knowledge sharing is moderated by responsiveness, such that the association is stronger when responsiveness is high (versus low).
H3: The positive indirect association of workplace interpersonal capitalization on knowledge sharing via pride is moderated by effort attribution and responsiveness, such that the association is stronger when effort attribution and responsiveness are both high (versus when either or both are low).
mechanism_summary: Integrating capitalization theory with the social-functionalist model of emotions, the authors argue that disclosing a positive work event "rekindles the fire" of past achievement, drawing attention to the self and activating self-enhancement that elicits pride—but only when the event is attributed to one's own effort, a marker of work-goal progress. Pride in turn motivates disclosers to "stoke the flames" by sharing knowledge, a prototypical prestige-seeking behavior through which individuals convert valued achievements into higher social status. This prestige-seeking pathway holds only when disclosers perceive coworkers as responsive, because responsiveness signals that knowledge sharing will be rewarded with status. The full model is a two-stage moderated mediation in which the indirect effect is strongest when both effort attribution and responsiveness are high.
data_measures:
Study 1 data: a two-wave, source- and time-separated survey (waves one month apart) at a privately owned mechanical-gear manufacturing company in Eastern China; 524 full-time employees across 44 working teams were invited, yielding 448 matched focal disclosers and 1,989 round-robin coworker reports (85.50% response rate). All English scales were back-translated into Chinese. IV: workplace interpersonal capitalization = the 5-item Watkins (2021) measure referenced to the past two weeks, self-reported at Time 1 (α = .93). First-stage moderator: effort attribution = two Tracy and Robins (2007) items, "caused by your effort" and "caused by your behaviors and actions," at Time 1 (α = .94). Mediator: pride = the seven achievement-oriented pride items from Tracy and Robins (2007) (accomplished, achieving, confident, fulfilled, productive, self-worth, successful), self-reported at Time 2 with the capitalization referenced in the item stem (α = .96). Second-stage moderator: responsiveness = the 3-item Gable et al. (2012) scale at Time 2 (α = .90). DV: knowledge sharing = the 7-item Srivastava, Bartol, and Locke (2006) scale, completed by each discloser's teammates about the discloser in a round-robin design and aggregated to the discloser (α = .97; Rwg(j) = .96, ICC(1) = .68, ICC(2) = .95). Controls: Time 1 pride, coworker friendship, task interdependence, positive event frequency, team tenure. Estimation: multilevel path analysis in Mplus 8.3 with the MLR estimator accounting for individuals nested in teams, fixed slopes and grand-mean-centered predictors, with moderated mediation tested by parametric bootstrapping (20,000 resamples, 95% CIs).
Study 2 data: a 10-day experience sampling field experiment with UK working professionals recruited on Prolific and screened for regular coworker interaction, a full-time 9-to-5 schedule, and daily commuting; the final sample was 105 participants and 787 paired morning/afternoon observations (mean 8.77 pairs per person). Capitalization was manipulated daily via a constrained random matrix approach: each morning half the participants were assigned to the capitalization condition (coded 1; instructed to recall a past personal work-related positive event and share it that morning with one pre-selected coworker) and half to a control condition (coded 0; a typical conversation topic), with each participant assigned to each condition five times in a within-person randomized order. Effort attribution used the same two items in the morning survey (daily α = .91); because attributions do not apply to control cases, the authors followed Leslie et al. (2012) and multiplied the group-mean-centered raw score by the condition value, so the variable represents variation in effort attribution among capitalization cases against control cases as a baseline rather than a true interaction term. Pride used the same seven items in the afternoon survey (daily α = .96); knowledge sharing used three Srivastava et al. (2006) items self-reported in the afternoon (daily α = .91). Responsiveness was a Level 2 moderator measured in the entry survey with the 3-item active-constructive perceived responses to capitalization attempts scale from Gable et al. (2004) (α = .71). Controls: day of week, sine and cosine weekly-cycle terms, morning pride, event pleasantness, days since the positive event, trait self-esteem (α = .77), coworker tenure. Estimation: multilevel path analysis in Mplus 8.3 with a random slope for the pride-to-knowledge-sharing path, group-mean-centered Level 1 and grand-mean-centered Level 2 predictors, and parametric bootstrapping (20,000 resamples); a chi-square test of independence confirmed the manipulation (χ²(1) = 572.16, p < .001).
Identification: the authors state that Study 1 is correlational in nature and does not sufficiently establish causality. Study 2's randomly assigned daily manipulation and the temporal precedence of its measurement support only a partial causal claim; the authors say explicitly that they can speak to causality only in the front half of the model, where capitalization was manipulated. The pride-to-knowledge-sharing stage and the responsiveness moderation remain associational in both studies.
key_findings:
All three hypotheses were supported in Study 1 and again in Study 2, but the shape of the second-stage (responsiveness) moderation differed between the two studies.
H1 supported in both studies. Study 1: the capitalization × effort attribution interaction on pride was significant (γ = .09, p = .001, Δpseudo-R² = 3%), with the simple slope positive and significant at higher effort attribution (γ = .16, p = .001) and non-significant at lower effort attribution (γ = -.03, p = .488). Study 2: the effort attribution variable predicted pride (γ = .16, p = .001, Δpseudo-R² = 3%) alongside a positive capitalization-manipulation effect (γ = .28, p < .001), and the simple slope was positive and significant at higher effort attribution (γ = .47, p < .001) but non-significant at lower effort attribution (γ = .10, p = .181). The authors note that across both studies capitalization and pride were unrelated when effort attribution was lower.
H2 supported in both studies, with different interaction shapes. Study 1: responsiveness moderated the pride-to-knowledge-sharing association (γ = .10, p = .041, Δpseudo-R² = 1%); pride was significantly associated with knowledge sharing at higher responsiveness (γ = .14, p = .031) but not at lower responsiveness (γ = -.03, p = .775). Study 2: the cross-level interaction was significant in the predicted direction (γ = .13, p = .004; generalized R² = .07, i.e., 7% of Level 1 variance in knowledge sharing), and pride was positively associated with knowledge sharing at higher responsiveness (γ = .66, p < .001) and also, more weakly, at lower responsiveness (γ = .39, p < .001). So pride and knowledge sharing were positively associated only at higher responsiveness in Study 1, whereas in Study 2 they were positively associated at both levels but more strongly at higher responsiveness; the authors attribute the difference to the different levels of analysis (between-individual vs. within-individual) and report that the zero-order responsiveness-knowledge sharing correlation was positive in both studies (Study 1: r = .50; Study 2: r = .38, both p < .001).
H3 supported in both studies, though the Study 1 test was weaker. Study 1: the difference in indirect effects across moderator levels was only marginally significant (difference = .02, 95% CI [-0.002, 0.052]; 90% CI [0.002, 0.046]); the indirect effect differed from zero only when both moderators were higher (ab = .02, SE = .01, 95% CI [0.002, 0.051]) and was non-significant when both were lower and in both mixed cells. Study 2: the difference was significant (difference = .27, 95% CI [0.126, 0.435]); the indirect effect was positive and significant when both moderators were higher (ab = .31, SE = .07, 95% CI [0.177, 0.464]), non-significant when both were lower (ab = .04, SE = .03, CI spanning zero), still significant when effort attribution was higher but responsiveness lower (ab = .18, SE = .05, 95% CI [0.097, 0.287]), and non-significant when effort attribution was lower but responsiveness higher (ab = .07, SE = .05, 95% CI [-0.024, 0.163]), which the authors read as the indirect path being more sensitive to effort attribution than to responsiveness.
Variance explained: the Study 1 predictors accounted for 27% of the variance in pride and 30% in knowledge sharing; the Study 2 model explained an incremental 9% and 14%. In Study 2, days since the positive event was unrelated to pride, indicating comparable pride whether the disclosed event had occurred the previous day or weeks to months earlier.
theoretical_contribution: The paper broadens the concept of capitalization by theorizing its instrumental potential, challenging the long-standing assumption that capitalization is a purely socioemotional process and that the characteristics of the disclosed event are inconsequential. By positioning effort attribution as a boundary condition, it shows that only effort-attributed events activate the instrumental process. It also contributes to the social-functionalist model of emotions by qualifying the assumed evolutionary, universal pride–knowledge sharing link with the boundary condition of responsiveness, demonstrating that the link is not as unbounded as previously theorized.
practical_implication: Because sharing good news at work can indirectly promote knowledge sharing, organizational leaders—especially in knowledge-intensive and innovation-oriented organizations—should encourage employees to share positive events (e.g., in meetings or via workspace design) and coach employees to respond responsively when they are targets of capitalization. Leaders should be cautious, however, since capitalization can backfire through unfavorable social comparison or undermining, and overly controlling reactions (e.g., financial rewards) can reduce intrinsic motivation.
limitations: Study 1 is correlational and cannot fully establish causality; it is set in a single manufacturing organization in China, limiting generalizability, and cannot fully assess whether a given team member was both a capitalization and a knowledge-sharing target. The model does not explain why or when disclosers come to perceive responsiveness in coworkers, and the authors did not directly theorize the instrumental downsides of workplace interpersonal capitalization.
future_research: Future work could examine other characteristics of the disclosed positive event beyond effort attribution, explore the "half-life" of capitalization-elicited pride over time, develop theory on the antecedents of perceived responsiveness, and test whether the instrumental capitalization process generalizes to non-work contexts such as romantic relationships, religious groups, schools, or families. Researchers are also encouraged to study the potential costs and net effects of sharing good news at work.
abstract: Sharing positive events with others is a phenomenon referred to as “capitalization.” Extant theory on capitalization considers the process of disclosing positive events as socioemotional in nature. However, individuals capitalize in the context of workplace relationships that serve instrumental functions, pointing to the possibility that the process of capitalization may at times be instrumental as well. In this paper, we integrate theory on capitalization with the social-functionalist model of emotions to develop a model that explains how workplace interpersonal capitalization serves the instrumental function of spurring knowledge sharing. We identify pride as a linking mechanism between workplace interpersonal capitalization and knowledge sharing, and we argue that experiencing pride is contingent on employees disclosing positive events that they attribute to their own efforts. We also identify perceived coworker responsiveness as a boundary condition qualifying the association between pride and knowledge sharing. A sourceand time-separated field study and an experience sampling field experiment with a daily intervention provide support for our hypothesized model. Overall, our work broadens the concept of capitalization and contributes to the social-functionalist model of emotions.

Rekindling the fire and stoking the flames: How and when workplace interpersonal capitalization facilitates pride and knowledge sharing at work. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(3), 953–978. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2021.1022
