title: “Distinctive from What? And for Whom?” Deep Learning-Based Product Distinctiveness, Social Structure, and Third-Party Certifications
methods: Longitudinal panel of artist-years; convolutional neural network (CaffeNet/AlexNet) extracts 4,096-dimensional feature vectors of artworks, with cosine distance to three reference points (prior competitors, current competitors, past self); negative binomial regression (NBREG, Stata MP 15.1) with robust standard errors, artist and year fixed effects, one-year lags, and supply-/demand-side status moderators.
industry: Fine art (modern-art painting and drawing); third-party certification via galleries and salons
country: Europe (works/exhibitions catalogued in the Database of Modern Exhibitions)
units: Artists (artist-year observations); 12,193 artworks analyzed
n_sample: 153 artists
authors: Banerjee, Mitali; Cole, Benjamin M.; Ingram, Paul
theories: optimal distinctiveness theory (Deephouse, 1999; Zhao et al., 2017); reference-point and categorization perspectives (Bourdieu, 1983; Cattani et al., 2014); social structure / status theory (Zuckerman, 2017; Podolny, 1993)
keywords: deep learning; optimal distinctiveness; product distinctiveness; reference points; social structure; supply-side and demand-side status; third-party certifications
research_question: How do a producer's distinctiveness and its position in social structure jointly shape the third-party certifications it receives? The paper centers on two questions: distinctive compared to what reference point (prior competitors, current competitors, or one's own past), and for whom — i.e., how supply-side (peer) and demand-side (audience) status moderate the rewards to distinctiveness.
hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1. Artists experience more exhibition opportunities if their work is distinctive when compared to prior competitors (predicted positive).
- Hypothesis 2. Artists experience more exhibition opportunities if their work is distinctive when compared to current competitors (predicted positive).
- Hypothesis 3. Artists experience fewer exhibition opportunities as a function of their distinctiveness from current competitors to the extent they are in the middle of, as opposed to low or high in, the status hierarchy derived from the peer network (predicted U-shaped moderation by supply-side peer-network status).
- Hypothesis 4. Artists experience more exhibition opportunities as a function of their distinctiveness from current competitors to the extent that they are higher in market status (predicted positive moderation by demand-side market status).
- Hypothesis 5. Artists' exhibition opportunities have an inverted U-shaped relationship to their distinctiveness from their past self.
- Hypothesis 5a. The distinctiveness from one's past self is positively moderated by an artist's market status.
mechanism_summary: The paper theorizes that distinctiveness from each reference point is rewarded by certifiers up to a point, but a producer's autonomy to differentiate is constrained by two "pulls" of social structure. Supply-side peer pressure to conform is non-monotonic: high- and low-status artists are rewarded for distinctiveness from current competitors, while middle-status artists are penalized (a U-shaped pattern). Demand-side market status is theorized to license distinctiveness from one's own past and, in Hypothesis 4, to reward distinctiveness from current competitors as well; the latter interaction instead emerged with "the opposite directionality than predicted," which the authors rationalize post hoc as high-status producers risking alienation of the peers and audiences on whom their legitimacy depends.
data_measures:
- Sample construction: 361 modern artists born before 1900 listed in the Benezit Dictionary of Artists (2016) under a set of modern-art movements, intersected with the 13,301 artists catalogued in the Database of Modern Exhibitions (DoME) and with the Getty Research Institute's Union List of Artist Names, yielding 153 artists.
- Artwork corpus: 12,193 artworks with known creation years, hand-collected per artist from the Artstor collection and supplemented via Google image search, TinEye, and AskArt; plus a reference corpus of the first 2,000 19th-century images returned by Artstor.
- Feature extraction: CaffeNet (AlexNet architecture) convolutional neural network pretrained on 1,034,908 nonart ImageNet images; input is a 224 × 224 matrix of RGB pixels, output a 4,096-dimensional feature vector per artwork.
- DV (third-party certifications): count of exhibition opportunities afforded to each artist per year, 1905–1916, from DoME; alternative DV is the count of unique cities in which those exhibitions took place.
- IVs: distinctiveness from prior competitors = the artist-year average cosine distance of the artist's works from the 2,000 19th-century works; distinctiveness from current competitors = average cosine distance from the works created one year earlier by the artist's coexhibition alters (a moving one-year window); distinctiveness from past self = average cosine distance from the artist's own works created five to 15 years earlier. Where an artist produced no work in a given year, the most recent prior year's work is used.
- Moderators: supply-side peer-network status = eigenvector centrality in the cumulative artist-to-artist coexhibition network; demand-side market status = the artist's exhibitions in previous years weighted by each venue's eigenvector centrality in the valued venue × venue network.
- Controls: career age; peer-network brokerage (1 minus the local clustering coefficient); artist and year fixed effects.
- Estimation: negative binomial regression (NBREG, Stata MP 15.1) with robust standard errors, all independent variables lagged one year, and one-tailed tests for the hypotheses; 1,694 artist-year observations in the controls-only model and 1,683 in every model containing the distinctiveness measures.

The design is an observational longitudinal panel and the paper claims no causal-identification strategy: artist and year fixed effects are described only as controlling for historical influences and stable artist attributes, so the estimates are associational. Seven robustness checks are reported — dropping artist-years with no artwork by the artist; an alternative 19th-century corpus of 9,923 representational works from the Louvre's Departement des Peintures; peer-network ties restricted to the last three years; dropping the quadratic interaction term; degree-centrality and betweenness-centrality versions of market status; and adding a lagged DV — which the authors describe as leaving the results broadly robust.
key_findings:
- Main effects (Table 2, DV = exhibition count; Model 5, the fully nested main-effects model): support for Hypothesis 1 (p < .001) and for Hypothesis 2 (p < .10), so distinctiveness from prior competitors and from current competitors each predict more exhibitions. Hypothesis 5 receives only partial support in this model (p < .05 on the linear term, not significant on the squared term); the authors read Model 5 as showing a monotonic rather than inverted-U benefit of diverging from one's past self.
- Supply-side moderation (Model 6): Hypothesis 3 is supported. The interaction of distinctiveness from current competitors with peer-network status is negative (p < .10) and the interaction with peer-network status squared is positive (p < .01) — a U-shape in which middle-status artists gain the fewest exhibition opportunities from distinctiveness from peers — and the adjusted Wald test is significant (p < .01).
- Demand-side moderation of distinctiveness from current competitors (Model 7): Hypothesis 4 is not supported, since neither the interaction coefficient nor the adjusted Wald test is significant.
- Demand-side moderation of distinctiveness from past self (Model 8): the Hypothesis 5a interaction is positive and highly significant (p < .001), as is the adjusted Wald test (p < .001).
- Fully nested model with all interactions (Model 9, Table 2): Hypothesis 1 (p < .001), Hypothesis 3 (p < .10 and p < .001), Hypothesis 5 (p < .01 and p < .01) and Hypothesis 5a (p < .001) are supported, with the predicted inverted U for distinctiveness from past self emerging once market status is in the model. Hypothesis 2 falls just out of significance, so support for it depends on the model specification. Hypothesis 4 is significant in the direction opposite to that predicted (coefficient = −3.37, p < .001): higher market status lowers rather than raises the reward for distinctiveness from current competitors.
- Alternative DV (Table 3, unique exhibition cities): results overlap substantially with Table 2 in significance and directionality, with two differences in Model 9, both on the peer-status variable. The simple effect of peer-network status shows the same U-shaped curvilinear directionality but its first term loses significance, and that loss carries over to the first interaction term with distinctiveness from current competitors, whose predicted curvilinear directionality is otherwise unchanged.
- Marginal effects: for distinctiveness from prior competitors, artists at the median are predicted to have 2.05 exhibitions, versus 1.88 at the 25th percentile and 2.17 at the 75th percentile.
theoretical_contribution: The study refines optimal-distinctiveness and status research by specifying which reference point matters and for whom, and by being the first (to the authors' knowledge) to empirically test Zuckerman's (2017) distinction between supply-side and demand-side conformity pressures. It also advances method and theory in aesthetic/sensorial markets by using a deep-learning measure of whole-product distinctiveness that does not rely on predefined categories, making previously unfalsifiable arguments (e.g., Bourdieu, 1983) empirically testable.
practical_implication: Innovators competing for certifications should choose their referent for differentiation strategically given their status: high-market-status producers are better off differentiating from their own past work, while those without such status (e.g., new entrants) benefit more from differentiating from current competitors, and middle-status peers are better off converging closer to their contemporaries.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The authors note the framework and deep-learning approach can be extended beyond fine art to other visually driven industries (fashion, architecture, advertising) and, via tools for sound and text, to music, film, and publishing; distance can also be computed to any theoretically interesting reference point (e.g., a particular movement or artist), and image- and text-recognition techniques could be combined to study how distinctiveness across modalities jointly affects certification.
abstract: How do producers’ distinctiveness and social structure influence third-party certifications? We argue that producers compete against prior and current competitors, and against their past selves. In the context of 153 artists active during a key period of the emergence of modern art (1905–1916), we utilize a convolutional neural network used in computer vision to extract feature vectors of artworks, and measure quantitative distance of these artists’ works from canonical reference points. We find that artists are rewarded for distinctiveness from prior and current competitors and their past selves (up to a point). However, artists’ autonomy to differentiate themselves depends on their position in the social structure, which we divide into supply-side artist-to-artist networks, and demand-side artist-to-gallerist networks. Artists with high or low supply-side status receive higher rewards for distinctiveness from current competitors than do artists with middle supply-side status. Artists with higher demand-side status receive higher rewards for distinctiveness from their own past, but lower rewards for distinctiveness from current competitors. These results show that peers strive to constrain each other to conform to positions of gravity within product space, and that market audiences deploy either higher or lower constraints on a producer’s identity depending on the reference point.

title: A Spillover Model of Dreams and Work Behavior: How Dream Meaning Ascription Promotes Awe and Employee Resilience
methods: Three studies: (1) a morning-of field study of business-school alumni; (2) a single-day morning-afternoon study; (3) a two-week experience sampling study. Hypotheses tested via structural equation / path analysis (Studies 1-2) and multilevel path models in Mplus 8.4 with group- and grand-mean centering and bootstrapped indirect effects (Study 3).
industry: Full-time employees across occupations (no single focal industry); Study 1 used business-school alumni
time_period: Single-week (Study 1), five-week recruitment (Study 2), and two-week daily (Study 3) windows; year not reported in paper
units: Working individuals (employees / business-school alumni)
n_sample: Study 1: 119 alumni; Study 2: 63 employees; Study 3: 411 employees retained for multilevel analysis
authors: Belinda, Casher D.; Christian, Michael S.
theories: appraisal theories of emotion; appraisal-tendency theory; dream-spillover model
keywords: appraisal-tendency theory; awe; dream meaning ascription; dreams; epistemic curiosity; goal progress; resilience; sleep
research_question: How and for whom do dreams spill over to shape daily work behavior? Specifically, the authors ask how ascribing meaning to recalled dreams elicits waking awe that promotes employee resilience and goal progress throughout the workday, and whether trait epistemic curiosity moderates the awe-resilience link.
hypotheses:
- H1: Positive dream meaning ascription is positively related to morning awe.
- H2: Morning awe is positively related to employee resilience.
- H3: Morning awe mediates the relationship between positive dream meaning ascription and employee resilience.
- H4: Employee resilience is positively related to work goal progress.
- H5: Morning awe and employee resilience sequentially mediate the relationship between positive dream meaning ascription and work goal progress.
- H6: Epistemic curiosity moderates the relationship between morning awe and employee resilience, such that this relationship is more (less) positive for employees who are high (low) in epistemic curiosity.
- H7: Epistemic curiosity moderates the indirect effect of positive dream meaning ascription on employee resilience, via awe, such that this effect is more (less) positive for employees who are high (low) in epistemic curiosity.
- H8: Epistemic curiosity moderates the sequential indirect effect of positive dream meaning ascription on work goal progress, via awe and resilience, such that this effect is more (less) positive for employees who are high (low) in epistemic curiosity.
mechanism_summary: Integrating research on dream meaning ascription with appraisal theories of emotion, the authors argue that forming the belief that a dream carries meaning triggers core awe appraisals—perceptions of vastness and a need for cognitive accommodation—giving rise to awe. Through an appraisal-tendency mechanism, awe induces a "small-self" frame that makes subsequent work stressors feel less threatening, increasing resilience and downstream goal progress. Because awe requires expanding one's existing ways of knowing, its benefits accrue mainly to employees high in epistemic curiosity.
data_measures:
Three self-report survey studies of full-time U.S. employees residing in Eastern Standard Time, each timed so that dream recall, meaning ascription, and awe were captured shortly after awakening: Study 1, a single morning-of survey of business-school alumni (119 alumni who recalled a dream); Study 2, a single-day morning-afternoon MTurk study (63 employees who recalled a dream); Study 3, a two-week twice-daily experience sampling MTurk study (411 participants passed the attention check; the final analytic sample was 1,321 dream-recall days across 215 participants who recalled dreams on at least four study days). Items were rated 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree) unless noted.
- Dream meaning ascription (IV, morning survey, all three studies): two single items adapted from Morewedge and Norton (2009) under the stem "To me, my dreams from last night ...", capturing positive ("Have a good meaning") and negative ("Have a bad meaning") ascription separately.
- Morning awe (mediator): the two items "Awe" and "Wonder". Studies 1 and 2 used a dream referent, "My dreams from last night made me feel a sense of ..." (α = .77 and .88); Study 3 shifted the referent to the morning itself, "This morning, I have felt a sense of ..." (α = .95), so that waking awe could be distinguished from awe felt during the dream.
- Resilience (mediator / proximal DV): Study 1 used three items adapted from Tugade and Fredrickson (2004) appraising a one-minute essay each participant wrote about their most important current work problem (α = .85); Studies 2 and 3 used four afternoon items adapted from Sinclair and Wallston (2004) under the stem "At work today, I ..." (α = .82 and .86).
- Work goal progress (distal DV, Studies 2 and 3): two afternoon items adapted from Wanberg, Zhu, and Van Hooft (2010) (α = .96 and .95).
- Trait epistemic curiosity (moderator, Study 3 preliminary survey): three items from Litman and Spielberger (2003) (α = .89). Study 3 additionally measured appraisals of dream vastness with two items adapted from Piff et al. (2015) and Shiota et al. (2007) (α = .94) as a manipulation-free check on the awe appraisal.
- Controls in every study: sleep quantity (self-reported hours slept), sleep quality, and trait positive affect (three items from Watson, Clark, and Tellegen, 1988). Studies 1 and 2 supplement the survey data with quantitative text analysis of open-ended problem, dream, dream-meaning, and dream-cause responses, including sentiment scoring against the bing and NRC lexicons.

The design is associational rather than causally identified: there is no randomization, instrument, or quasi-experiment anywhere in the three studies. What identification leverage exists comes from timing and centering — dream measures are collected between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. and outcomes after work in Studies 2 and 3, controls for sleep and trait positive affect are carried in every path, and Study 3 group-mean centers its Level 1 predictors so estimates reflect within-person deviations from each employee's own average (Level 2 predictors are grand-mean centered). Studies 1 and 2 were estimated as path models with 10,000 bootstrapped samples for indirect effects; Study 3 was estimated as a multilevel path model in Mplus 8.4 (replicated in Stata's generalized SEM) with Monte Carlo confidence intervals based on 20,000 draws. Study 3's baseline mediation model was preregistered; the moderator hypotheses were not.
key_findings:
Every hypothesis a given study tested was supported in that study, but the studies tested different subsets: Study 1 tested only H1-H3, Study 2 tested H1-H5, and the moderation predictions H6-H8 were tested only in Study 3.

Study 1 (N = 119, standardized estimates): a 1-SD increase in positive dream meaning ascription was associated with a .29-SD increase in morning awe (p = .001; H1 supported), and a 1-SD increase in morning awe with a .25-SD increase in resilience (p = .005; H2 supported); the indirect effect of positive dream meaning ascription on resilience via awe was significant and positive (0.07, 95% CI [0.010, 0.174]; H3 supported). The model accounted for 11.65% of the variance in morning awe and 6.39% in resilience. Negative dream meaning ascription was unrelated to morning awe (-.00, p = .999) and had no significant indirect effect on resilience (-0.00, 95% CI [-0.048, 0.041]).

Study 2 (N = 63, standardized estimates): H1-H5 all supported — positive dream meaning ascription to morning awe (+.45 SD, p < .001), morning awe to resilience (+.28 SD, p = .015), indirect effect on resilience 0.09 (95% CI [0.002, 0.246]), resilience to work goal progress (+.41 SD, p < .001), and the sequential indirect effect of positive dream meaning ascription on goal progress via awe and resilience 0.05 (95% CI [0.005, 0.141]). Negative dream meaning ascription's indirect effects on resilience (-0.03, 95% CI [-0.129, 0.009]) and on goal progress (-0.02, 95% CI [-0.079, 0.004]) were not significant. In the text analysis, positive sentiment in participants' dream-meaning reports correlated with morning awe (r_bing = .36, p = .003; r_NRC = .36, p = .004), whereas positive sentiment in their general dream descriptions and dream-cause reports did not.

Study 3 (1,321 dream-recall days across 215 employees, unstandardized within-person estimates): H1-H5 replicated — positive dream meaning ascription to morning awe (γ = 0.21, p < .001), morning awe to resilience (γ = 0.07, p = .035), indirect effect on resilience 0.02 (95% CI [0.002, 0.029]), resilience to work goal progress (γ = 0.47, p < .001), and the sequential indirect effect on goal progress 0.01 (95% CI [0.001, 0.014]). Negative dream meaning ascription again produced no significant indirect effect on either outcome. The awe-resilience slope varied significantly across individuals (τ = .04, p = .005) and trait epistemic curiosity moderated it in the predicted direction (γ = 0.07, p = .010), reducing the slope variability by 21.32%: morning awe raised workday resilience for employees high in epistemic curiosity (γ = 0.12, p = .002) but had no appreciable effect for those low in it (γ = 0.01, p = .885). This is the H6 pattern, although the results text labels that paragraph "Hypothesis 5." The conditional indirect effects were likewise significant at high but not low epistemic curiosity, for resilience (0.03, 95% CI [0.012, 0.040] vs. 0.00, 95% CI [-0.012, 0.014]; H7 supported) and for work goal progress (0.01, 95% CI [0.005, 0.022] vs. 0.00, 95% CI [-0.009, 0.008]; H8 supported).

These relationships hold over and above the sleep quantity and quality controls, which the authors report were of little empirical consequence in their studies. Study 3 robustness checks reproduced the results under alternative operationalizations of positive dream meaning ascription, and neither openness to experience nor perspective taking interacted with morning awe to predict resilience, leaving epistemic curiosity as the operative moderator. A supplemental internal meta-analysis of dream-recall rates across Studies 1-3 and one supplemental study estimated that roughly 40% of employees would recall a dream on any given workday morning (40.18%, 95% CI [27.96, 52.39]).
theoretical_contribution: The paper augments the organizational sleep literature by delineating a psychological (rather than purely biophysiological) pathway—dream meaning ascription—through which sleep spills over into waking behavior. It advances research on emotions by positioning awe as a linchpin between dreams and behavior, and on resilience by showing that resilience can result from emotions occurring prior to stressful encounters, challenging the directional assumption of transactional appraisal theories that appraisal precedes emotion.
practical_implication: Because roughly 40% of working people recall dreams on a given morning and tend to make sense of them, managers and employees benefit from treating sleep as a meaning-laden process. Low-effort practices such as keeping a dream journal or imagery-rehearsal techniques can elicit meaningful dreams and awe; organizations can also cultivate awe directly (e.g., biophilic job design, leadership storytelling).
limitations: Convenience sampling in the time-separated studies (Studies 2-3) may have increased attrition, and analyses rely primarily on self-report data. The time-separated designs lacked a third measurement period, and dream meaning ascription was measured with single items; focusing on dream-recall days created potential selection bias addressed through multiple robustness checks.
future_research: Future work could combine biophysiological and dream-spillover perspectives—e.g., examining dreams as a moderator that offsets or exaggerates the effects of sleep deprivation, or parsing other aspects of sleep. Researchers might use probability sampling, objective and other-report outcome measures, and additional measurement periods, and examine how work outcomes vary solely as a function of dream recall.
abstract: Sleep and employee behavior are linked. While the dominant explanations for this link involve physiology and cognitive resources, we offer a different perspective. We suggest that dreams, or psychological experiences during sleep, spill over to affect employee behavior. This spillover effect, we argue, results from the interplay between dreaming, meaning creation, and emotion. Taking a morning-of perspective, we theorize that recalling and ascribing meaning to dream experiences elicits awe—an epistemic emotion produced by appraisals of vastness and a need for cognitive accommodation. In turn, because awe reduces individuals’ focus on themselves and their concerns, we argue that experiencing awe upon awakening increases employee resilience, and ultimately goal progress, throughout the workday. However, because awe entails a felt need to expand one’s existing ways of knowing, employees may vary in their receptivity to awe. We therefore argue that the link between awe and resilience hinges on trait epistemic curiosity, or employees’ inherent desire to seek and acquire new knowledge. Across three studies—including a morning-of field study, a single-day morning–afternoon study, and a two-week experience sampling study—we find that ascribing positive meaning to dreams elicits awe, which in turn promotes resilience, and ultimately goal progress, throughout the workday.

title: Communication Miscalibration: The Price Leaders Pay for Not Sharing Enough
methods: Four preregistered studies (n = 1,812) combining archival, survey, and experimental methods: Study 1a content-codes 2,717 qualitative comments from 360-degree leadership assessments (chi-square); Study 1b surveys a nationally representative U.S. sample (one-sample t-test); Study 2 is a between-subjects experiment with a multicategorical mediation (PROCESS Macro Model 4); Study 3 uses polynomial regression and response-surface analysis with block-variable mediation.
industry: General working population / employed adults across diverse organizational contexts (not industry-specific)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual employees / followers evaluating their leaders' communication
n_sample: n = 1,812 across four studies (Study 1a: 2,717 comments on 924 leaders; Study 1b: 354; Study 2: 312; Study 3: 222)
authors: Flynn, Francis J.; Lide, Chelsea R.
theories: curse of knowledge; empathic concern / social judgment; prosocial signaling
keywords: communication calibration; downward communication; empathic concern; leadership ability; over-communication; under-communication
research_question: How does the perceived quantity of a leader's downward communication—specifically the (mis)calibration between how much employees perceive and prefer their leader to communicate—shape followers' evaluations of that leader's ability, and why is under-communication penalized more severely than over-communication?
hypotheses:
- H1: Employees will identify under-communication as a leadership weakness more often than over-communication.
- H2: When leaders' communication is perceived to be well-calibrated, employees will provide more favorable evaluations than when it is miscalibrated.
- H3a: Under-communicating managers will be perceived as having less empathy than over-communicating managers.
- H3b: Under-communicating managers will be perceived as having less leadership ability than over-communicating managers.
- H4: The negative effect of under-communication on leadership evaluations will be mediated by a perceived lack of empathy.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on social judgment and helping-behavior research, the authors argue that employees read communication quantity as a prosocial signal of a leader's empathic concern. Because of the "curse of knowledge," leaders systematically underestimate how much their followers want and are therefore seen as under-communicating more often than over-communicating. Under-communication sends a stronger negative signal—that the leader neither helped nor even engaged the employee—whereas over-communication signals a misguided but well-intentioned effort. Consequently, perceived under-communication lowers perceived empathy, which in turn lowers perceived leadership ability, producing an asymmetric penalty.
data_measures: Study 1a: an archive of 360-degree leadership assessments from participants enrolled in an online executive education program at a large private university in the United States; the analysis used direct reports' written answers to an open-ended "areas for improvement" prompt, and two independent coders unaware of the study hypotheses applied a predefined rubric, coding each comment on a binary scale (1 = Yes, 0 = No) first for whether communication was mentioned and then for whether it referenced under-communication ("a lack of communication") or over-communication ("a surplus of communication"), yielding 2,717 usable comments for 924 leaders. Study 1b: a nationally representative U.S. panel recruited through Bovitz, Inc.; communication miscalibration was measured with three items on 1-9 scales whose midpoint represented well-calibrated communication, recoded so that larger values indicate over-communication and averaged into a composite (alpha = .86), then compared against the scale midpoint with a one-sample t-test. Study 2: a between-subjects vignette experiment with full-time employed Prolific Academic participants who read purported assessment feedback describing a fictional leader as communicating too little, too much, or just the right amount; perceived leader empathy was measured with seven items adapted from the empathic concern subscale of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (Davis, 1983; alpha = .92) and perceived leadership ability with three items adapted from Haslam and Ryan (2008) (alpha = .96), both on 5-point likelihood scales, with the Study 1b communication items serving as the manipulation check (alpha = .96); mediation was tested with the PROCESS Macro Model 4 (Hayes, 2022) using a multicategorical predictor that compared each experimental condition to the well-calibrated baseline. Study 3: an online survey of alumni of an MBA program at a private university on the West Coast of the United States; perceived communication quantity (four original 9-point items covering frequency, duration, amount of information, and overall amount; alpha = .82) and preferred communication quantity (the same four items rephrased with "should"; alpha = .67) were measured separately, alongside leader empathy (the Study 2 seven items; alpha = .89), leadership ability (three items on a 7-point agreement scale; alpha = .96), and an exploratory job-satisfaction measure (alpha = .91); calibration was modeled with polynomial regression and response-surface analysis (Edwards & Parry, 1993) following Humberg, Nestler, and Back (2019), with mediation estimated through the Edwards and Cable (2009) block-variable approach and 5,000 bootstrapped samples. All four studies were preregistered. Only Study 2 manipulates communication (mis)calibration; the authors state that the correlational data in Studies 1a and 1b limit their ability to make causal claims, and note in the discussion that the experiment addresses reverse causality and omitted variables while the other studies offer greater generalizability and ecological validity.
key_findings: H1 was supported in each of the three studies that tested it. Study 1a: under-communication was listed as a key leadership weakness in 421 comments (15.5%) versus 46 comments (1.7%) for over-communication, chi-square(1, n = 2,717) = 327.7, p < .001, a relative difference approaching a full order of magnitude. Study 1b: mean communication ratings (M = 4.26, SD = 1.41) fell significantly below 5, the midpoint representing well-calibrated communication, t(353) = -9.87, p < .001, d = .52; of the 273 managers rated as miscalibrated, 74.7% were seen as under-communicating versus 25.3% as over-communicating, chi-square(1, n = 273) = 131.6, p < .001. Study 3: perceived communication quantity (M = 5.66, SD = 1.63) was significantly lower than preferred quantity, t(221) = -8.74, p < .001, d = .59, a negative mean difference of -.88, 95% CI [-1.08, -0.68]. H2 was supported in Studies 2 and 3: in Study 2, perceived leadership ability was highest for the well-calibrated leader (M = 4.08, SD = .86) relative to the under-communicating leader (M = 2.20, SD = .97; p < .001) and the over-communicating leader (M = 3.60, SD = .79; p < .001), F(2, 309) = 130.0, p < .001, eta-squared = .46; in Study 3 the response surface met all four congruence criteria, with the first principal axis slope not differing from 1 (b = .86, 95% CI [0.35, 1.36]), its y-intercept not differing from 0 (b = .18, 95% CI [-0.60, 0.96]), the curvature of the line of incongruence significant and negative (a4 = -.49, p = .001, 95% CI [-0.78, -0.20]), and the slope of that line at the origin non-significant (a3 = -.06, p = .77). H3a was tested only in Study 2 and supported there: perceived empathy was significantly lower for the under-communicating leader (M = 2.93, SD = .78) than for the over-communicating leader (M = 3.64, SD = .65; p < .001) and the well-calibrated leader (M = 3.62, SD = .65; p < .001), F(2, 309) = 35.32, p < .001, eta-squared = .19, while empathy did not differ between the over-communicating and well-calibrated leaders (p = .99). H3b was supported in both studies that tested it: perceived leadership ability was significantly lower for under-communicating than for over-communicating leaders in Study 2 (p < .001) and in Study 3 (M = 4.98, SD = 1.61 vs. M = 5.72, SD = 1.38; t(201) = 2.93, p = .004, d = .47). H4 was supported, but asymmetrically in Study 2: the indirect effect of communication quantity on perceived ability through perceived empathy was significant for the under-communicating versus well-calibrated contrast (b = -.43, SE = .07, 95% CI [-0.58, -0.29]) but not for the over-communicating versus well-calibrated contrast (b = .01, SE = .06, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.12]); in Study 3, the block-variable indirect effect of calibration on perceived ability via perceived empathy was significant (b = .33, SE = .10, p = .001, 95% CI [0.16, 0.53]) and remained significant when controlling for employees' job satisfaction (b = .23, SE = .08, p = .005, 95% CI [0.09, 0.41]).
theoretical_contribution: The paper shows that the trade-offs of communication miscalibration are asymmetric in leadership evaluations: under-communication "looms larger" than over-communication and is judged as a more significant failing, so not all forms of miscalibration are equal. It documents a robust perceptual bias whereby leaders are seen as under-communicating far more often than over-communicating, and it identifies perceived empathic concern as the psychological mechanism linking communication quantity to leadership evaluations—remedying prior downward-communication research that offered no account of how much communication is "the right amount."
practical_implication: Leaders cannot trust their intuition when calibrating the quantity of downward communication; they should adopt independent mechanisms—soliciting employees' idiosyncratic preferences, establishing routine rather than ad hoc communication patterns, and "pretesting" messages for calibration. In most cases leaders should err toward communicating more, accepting the relatively minor risk of being seen as over-communicating to send a stronger signal of empathy and concern.
limitations: The samples were primarily American, so the findings cannot account for cultural differences (e.g., high-context or high-power-distance cultures) that might shape judgments of communication calibration. The theorizing and measures focus exclusively on leadership evaluations as the outcome, leaving aside other objectives such as supporting employee autonomy, and the studies isolate communication quantity while not modeling the qualitative dimension (content, style, delivery) of communication.
future_research: Future work should examine how the quantitative and qualitative dimensions of leader communication interrelate and which matters more in particular cases, including whether qualitative miscalibration signals incompetence rather than low empathy. Researchers should also test whether under-communication can function as deliberate "tough love" that serves employees' developmental or autonomy needs, and how communication expectations vary with hierarchical distance between leaders and direct versus indirect reports.
abstract: Leaders may be seen by their followers as miscalibrating the quantity of their communication—sharing too much or too little. We propose that leaders are more likely to be seen as under-communicating than over-communicating, even though under-communication is more heavily penalized. In Study 1a, we examine 2,717 qualitative comments from archived leadership assessments and find that leaders are nearly 10 times as likely to be criticized for under-communicating than for over-communicating. In Study 1b, we obtain further evidence of this bias using a representative sample of U.S. adults. In Study 2, we manipulate communication (mis)calibration, showing that leaders who under-communicate are viewed as less qualified for a leadership role because they are viewed as less empathic. In Study 3, we use separate measures of employee perceptions of their manager's communication as well as their preferences. When there is a lack of congruence between perceived and preferred communication, employees judge their leaders as lacking empathy and, in turn, leadership ability.

title: The Technological Entrainment of Moral Issues: The Case of Genomic Data Markets
methods: Inductive process / grounded theory case study of the emerging U.S. genomic (DNA) data market; data from 55 semi-structured interviews (57 people), 19 days of field observation, and 914 archival documents, analyzed through open coding, narrative construction, and process modeling.
industry: Genomic (DNA) data exchange market (health care, biomedical research, genealogy, forensics)
time_period: Data collected October 2016 to May 2022; archival documents span 2008-2022
units: Organizations and actors (clusters) engaged in genomic data exchange in a single emerging digital market
n_sample: 55 interviews with 57 people, 224 hours of field observation, 914 archival documents
authors: Gray, Barbara; Briscoe, Forrest; Diaz Ferraro, Celeste
theories: cultural and institutional entrepreneurship; technological framing; theory of morally contentious markets
keywords: digital markets; exchange rules; genomic data; institutional entrepreneurship; moral issues; morally contentious markets; technological entrainment
research_question: What role does technology play in shaping the rules of exchange in digital markets fraught with moral conflicts? The authors investigate this in the emerging U.S. market for human genomic data, where exchange generates moral conflicts over privacy and ownership.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: technological entrainment of moral issues; moral conflicts over privacy and ownership of personal (genomic) data; exchange rules; technological framing (designers encoding values into technologies); competing actor clusters (Right-to-Science, Trusted Brokers, Walled Gardens).
- Process / phases: a four-step entrainment process involving the progressive synchronization of (1) framings, (2) technical policies, (3) technologies/software, (4) exchange platforms, and ultimately market participant behaviors.
- Triggering conditions: entrepreneurial technology-development "moves" by actors seeking to advance their preferred exchange rules in an emergent digital market.
- Emergent outcomes: particular moral stances become "baked into" technological designs, which then dictate the rules participants must follow; a technologically mediated coercive isomorphism that locks in some moral stances and forecloses others.

Through inductive grounded theorizing, the authors show that as actors develop technical policies, software, and exchange platforms, their preferred moral stances on privacy and ownership become progressively synchronized and embedded in the material technology itself. Once these interlocking technologies are widely distributed, they impose de facto exchange rules behind the scenes, rendering discursive or rhetorical contestation ineffectual and making the entrained moral order path-dependent and hard to reverse.
data_measures:
The data corpus has three parts. First, 55 semi-structured interviews with 57 people (eight interviewed more than once) conducted between October 2016 and December 2021, comprising 4,314 minutes of audio: 16 GA4GH leaders plus staff and representatives of member and field organizations, and 39 representatives of other industry sectors (scientific researchers, bioinformaticians, health care practitioners and administrators, IT specialists, security experts, ethics specialists, venture capitalists, academic researchers); all were recorded and transcribed except five, for which contemporaneous notes were kept. Second, 19 days (224 hours) of field observation from October 2017 to November 2021 at GA4GH conferences and workgroup meetings, patient advocacy conferences and training workshops, organizational leadership meetings, a bioinformatics technical training workshop, and a GenoPri conference on genetic data cybersecurity, yielding 42 sets of field notes. Third, 914 archival documents, news articles, websites, and videos produced between 2008 and 2022, comprising 293 organizational documents, 141 websites and blogs, 101 scholarly journals and 32 reports, 45 transcripts and video files plus 3 unedited video recordings, 126 U.S. regulatory documents, 81 industry news articles, 82 mass media news articles, and 10 press releases. Sources are cited in the findings as I-XXX (interviews), O-XXX (observations), and A-XXX (archival documents).

Interviewees were identified first by snowball sampling and later by theoretical sampling as the authors' knowledge of the market evolved. The study period was bracketed from 2008, when genomic sequencing costs dropped over 1,000-fold, through May 2022, and the genomic data market was selected as an extreme case. Coding proceeded in stages: a chronology of the main actors and events; open coding of interview transcripts for key players, the moral stances they adopted, actions taken to create exchange rules, and any agreements that emerged, captured in a code book and supported by memo-writing; construction of narratives of events, moves, and proposed exchange rules for each moral issue; a deliberate shift away from narratives and templates toward temporal sequencing of the policies and technologies each cluster created or used; axial coding to tease out the relationships linking the coded constructs (supporting linkage evidence is reported in Online Supplement E); and finally the generation of a means-ends process model. The design is inductive grounded theorizing and claims no causal identification: entrainment is traced as a temporal, path-dependent progression linking framings, policies, technologies, platforms, and behaviors, not estimated as an effect. Only the Right-to-Science and Trusted Brokers clusters could be observed in detail; the secretive Walled Gardens cluster was excluded from the analysis.
key_findings:
The central emergent finding is a four-step process of technological entrainment, observed in both clusters studied. In Step 1 technical policies are entrained to the moral stances carried in entrepreneurs' framing of the purpose of exchange; in Step 2 technologies (software) are built to align with those policies, and in Step 2a further technologies are yoked to existing ones by interoperability requirements, so that adopting one technology entails adopting its predecessors and the policies they encode; in Step 3 exchange platforms adopt the resulting interlocking technology suites; and in Step 4 the behaviors of data providers and data users are passively entrained, so that participation itself enacts de facto exchange rules. The process baked particular moral stances on privacy and ownership into technological designs, which then dictated the rules participants had to follow, an outcome the authors characterize as a technologically mediated coercive isomorphism that operates behind the scenes and can render discursive or rhetorical argument ineffectual. Notably, this enactment happened independently of what market participants themselves thought was appropriate, and the rules were largely implicit rather than explicitly labeled as exchange rules.

The two clusters ran the same steps but with markedly different reach, so the downstream steps did not play out uniformly. In the Right-to-Science cluster, a framing of data providers as "partners" entitled to share in scientific advancement was encoded in GA4GH's Framework for Responsible Data Sharing, its Data Security and Infrastructure Policy, and its 2015 consent policy and broad-consent clauses, which in turn catalyzed Machine Readable Consent (2020), the Data Use Ontology (2018) and the Data Use Oversight System, the Direct Connect API, and Passports (2021). Exchange platforms such as the Broad Institute's AnVIL/Terra adopted interlocking suites of these technologies. By the end of 2021 GA4GH counted over 2,000 organizational members, mostly U.S.-based but with over 50 other countries represented, and by 2022 its technologies and standards were in use by the governmental genomics programs of 16 nations, by multicountry driver projects (ELIXIR, H3Africa, the 100K Cohort Consortium), by Amazon Web Services, and by the NIH in its All of Us initiative and its genomic database access tools. The de facto rules enacted were relatively broad consent and no compensation for data providers, and relatively expansive, less restrictive, and unpaid access for data users.

In the Trusted Broker cluster, a framing centered on preserving individual rights produced sticky policies, dynamic consent, and a bilateral consent and trusted mediator framework, implemented through blockchain immutable ledgers, smart contracts, micropayments, Blockstack, and data trust or "Mediator of Individual Data" arrangements. But no specific policies were universal across these firms, organizations disagreed over whether and where blockchain was appropriate (a trade group report concluded it was not appropriate for genomic data), and each organization assembled the components differently, leaving very little interoperability between organizations: entrainment here was intraorganizationally strong but interorganizationally weak. Step 3 was not a separate step for this cluster, because the organizations developing the technology were themselves the exchange platforms. Behavioral impact on the overall market was correspondingly limited: as of 2021 none of the Trusted Broker organizations had grown to the scale of the largest Right-to-Science initiatives (such as NIH's All of Us) or Walled Gardens (such as 23andMe or Geisinger's MyCode), although the cluster's technology choices did appeal to patient advocacy organizations (the Genetic Alliance chose to partner with LunaDNA in 2019) and to some indigenous groups.

The authors trace this asymmetry back to the clusters' moral stances: the Right-to-Science stance favoring greater data sharing led to policies geared toward maximal interoperability both between technologies and between organizations, whereas the Trusted Broker stance favoring data-provider control did not necessitate harmonization and instead favored technologies that limited the ease with which data could move outside a given platform's purview. Greater coordination of technology development in the Right-to-Science cluster appeared to have significant consequences for that cluster's relative growth and hence for the relative scope of impact of its idealized exchange rules, and more market participants appeared to be behaviorally enacting the Right-to-Science approach. The authors are explicit, however, that the exchange rules for the market were not settled once and for all: the rules and the moral outcomes they promote differed by cluster and simply coexisted as three separate market segments, counting those promulgated by the Walled Gardens.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces "technological entrainment of moral issues" to explain how the material (not merely symbolic) aspects of technology processes constitute the moral order of digital markets. It extends theories of morally contentious markets and cultural/institutional entrepreneurship by showing technology as a constitutive force—rather than only a cultural resource imbued with meaning—through which exchange rules and moral legitimacy are determined, and it surfaces exchange-platform organizations and technology developers as central (if less visible) moral entrepreneurs.
practical_implication: Because exchange rules are set implicitly through upstream technology development, policy attention and early regulatory action should focus on the exchange-technology-development process before institutionalization, opening it to broader, inclusive, multiparty societal dialogue rather than leaving it to actors with vested interests and technical capabilities. Civil society and collective-action efforts (e.g., data trusts) could champion alternative exchange technologies that protect collective privacy and ownership interests.
limitations: The study focuses on a single emerging market (U.S. genomic data) and could observe only the Right-to-Science and Trusted Brokers clusters in detail; the secretive "Walled Gardens" cluster (e.g., direct-to-consumer testing firms like 23andMe) was excluded from the analysis because of limited access to their exchange technology and its development.
future_research: Future work could compare technology-centered entrainment with sociocultural models of moral and institutional entrepreneurship, examine how the two relate, combine, or compete to produce market- or field-level settlements, and explore whether entrainment constitutes a fourth form of moral-controversy settlement. Researchers could also investigate the role of platform organizations, the legitimacy and exclusionary implications of converting moral questions into technical ones, and the dynamics of Walled Gardens in market evolution.
abstract: This research considers the role of technology in shaping the moral foundations of emerging digital markets. Through an inductive process study, we examine the development of the market for genomic (DNA) data—an emergent digital market plagued by moral conflicts over privacy and ownership. Drawing on interview, archival, and observational data, we analyze how rules for exchanging genomic data emerged, and how entrepreneurial technology-development moves influenced those rules. Our findings reveal a four-step process, which we call the technological entrainment of moral issues, involving the progressive synchronization of framings, technical policies, technologies (software), exchange platforms, and market participant behaviors. This process baked particular moral stances on privacy and ownership into technological designs, which then dictated the rules market participants were required to follow to engage in exchange. We conclude that when markets are digital, technology processes central to exchange end up controlling many moral aspects of exchange. Our study contributes to theories of morally contentious markets and cultural or institutional entrepreneurship by illuminating how those theories can incorporate material (not only symbolic) aspects of technology processes and better explain the emerging moral order within the rapidly expanding realm of digital markets.
apa_citation: Gray, B., Briscoe, F., & Diaz Ferraro, C. (2023). The technological entrainment of moral issues: The case of genomic data markets. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(4), 1123-1151. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.1202

title: Signaling Legitimacy: Why Mixed-Gender Coalitions Outperform Single-Gender Coalitions in Advocating for Gender Equity
methods: Three experiments (a field-based experiment plus two fully randomized online experiments, Study 3 pre-registered with stimulus sampling) manipulating coalition gender composition; analysis of variance (ANOVA) for main and interaction effects and bootstrapped mediation tests in Stata 16.1.
industry: Working adults / managers across organizations (general workforce, not industry-restricted)
time_period: Study 1 November 2018; Study 2 March 2019; Study 3 August 2021
units: Individual managers / participants assessing advocacy coalitions
n_sample: Study 1: 707 managers; Study 2: 974 participants; Study 3: 1,553 responses
authors: Hussain, Insiya; Tangirala, Subrahmaniam; Sherf, Elad N.
theories: legitimacy theory (Suddaby, Bitektine, & Haack, 2017; Suchman, 1995); signaling theory (Spence, 1973)
keywords: coalition legitimacy; gender equity advocacy; issue legitimacy; legitimacy; mixed-gender coalitions; signaling
research_question: Does the gender composition of an employee advocacy coalition affect managers' support for gender equity issues, and why are mixed-gender coalitions more persuasive than women-only or men-only coalitions?
hypotheses:
- H1: Women-only and mixed-gender coalitions are perceived to have greater coalition legitimacy in raising gender equity issues than are men-only coalitions.
- H2: Men-only and mixed-gender coalitions lend gender equity issues greater issue legitimacy than do women-only coalitions.
- H3: Mixed-gender coalitions receive greater managerial support when advocating gender equity issues via (a) greater coalition legitimacy than men-only coalitions and (b) greater issue legitimacy than women-only coalitions.
- H4: Overall, mixed-gender coalitions receive greater managerial support than both men-only and women-only coalitions via the sum of their effects on coalition legitimacy and issue legitimacy.
- H5: Mixed-gender coalitions earn greater managerial support for gender equity (vs. nongender equity) issues via (a) coalition legitimacy when compared with men-only coalitions, and (b) issue legitimacy when compared with women-only coalitions.
mechanism_summary: The paper integrates signaling theory and legitimacy theory to argue that a coalition's gender composition signals two distinct forms of legitimacy. The presence of women signals coalition legitimacy (the messengers have material stake and are the appropriate spokespersons), while the presence of men signals issue legitimacy (the issue is strategically important rather than a niche "women's" concern). Because women-only coalitions convey the former but not the latter and men-only coalitions the reverse, only mixed-gender coalitions signal both, making them uniquely effective at winning managerial endorsement for gender equity issues.
data_measures:
- Study 1 (n = 707 U.S. working adults in managerial roles, recruited via Qualtrics, November 2018): a field-based experiment in which each participant named three women and three men coworkers; two of those real colleagues were then randomly selected to form a women-only, men-only, or mixed-gender coalition proposing a salary-negotiation training program to address a gender pay gap.
- Study 2 (n = 974 U.S. MTurk participants, March 2019): a 3 (coalition gender composition: women-only vs. men-only vs. mixed-gender) x 2 (issue type: control vs. gender equity) between-subjects randomized experiment using an audio simulation in which participants played a store manager at "SoleStyle" and heard two voiceover actors advocate either the gender equity training or a customer-service training (control).
- Study 3 (n = 1,553 U.S. MTurk responses, August 2021): a pre-registered between-subjects experiment with stimulus sampling; participants played a regional manager at "Westfield" and saw one of four gender equity proposals (onsite childcare, eliminating salary negotiation as a basis for pay increases, a candidate pool for leadership at least 50% women, an annual women's leadership conference), with coalition composition manipulated via named and photographed employees drawn from the 10K U.S. Adult Faces database.
- Coalition legitimacy: three items adapted from Sherf et al. (2017) in Studies 1-2, e.g., whether the two employees together are the right spokespeople for the issue (1-7; alpha = .83 in Study 1, .87 in Study 2); five items from the authors' own content-validation study in Study 3 (alpha = .90).
- Issue legitimacy: four author-developed items in Studies 1-2 capturing whether the issue is critical, applicable, and of strategic relevance to the organization at large (1-7; alpha = .88 in Study 1, .85 in Study 2); five validated items in Study 3 (alpha = .94).
- Issue support: eight behavioral-intention items in Study 1 (1 = "Extremely unlikely" to 9 = "Extremely likely"; alpha = .97); dollars allocated to the program from a $50,000 discretionary budget in Study 2 (scaled in thousands); five items in Study 3 (alpha = .95).
- Exploratory moderators (Study 3 only): modern sexism (five items from Swim et al., 1995; alpha = .90) and social dominance orientation (eight items from Ho et al., 2015; alpha = .90).
- Identification and estimation: coalition gender composition was randomly assigned in all three studies (Study 1 a field-based experiment with real colleagues, Studies 2 and 3 fully randomized online experiments), and the authors note that Study 1's design allowed better causal inference than a purely correlational study while still leaving unmeasured coworker characteristics uncontrolled. Effects were tested with ANOVA for main and interaction effects plus bootstrapped indirect effects (10,000 replications, bias-corrected 95% CIs) in Stata 16.1; the legitimacy scales were validated in a separate three-sample study reported in Online Supplement B.
key_findings:
- Study 1 (n = 707): H1 supported — coalition composition affected coalition legitimacy, F(2, 704) = 6.59, p = .002, with women-only (M = 5.10; contrast = 0.33, p = .004) and mixed-gender coalitions (M = 5.16; contrast = 0.39, p = .001) rated higher than men-only coalitions (M = 4.77). H2 supported but with a weak men-only contrast — F(2, 704) = 4.16, p = .016; mixed-gender (M = 5.47; contrast = 0.29, p = .005) and men-only coalitions (M = 5.38; contrast = 0.21, p = .046) raised issues seen as more legitimate than women-only coalitions (M = 5.18), a contrast the authors themselves call not very strong.
- Study 1 mediation: H3a supported (indirect effects on issue support via coalition legitimacy, relative to men-only: women-only 0.11, 95% CI [0.03, 0.20]; mixed-gender 0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.23]); H3b supported (via issue legitimacy, relative to women-only: men-only 0.12, 95% CI [0.00, 0.25]; mixed-gender 0.17, 95% CI [0.05, 0.30]); H4 supported (summed indirect effects favoring mixed-gender over women-only, 0.19, 95% CI [0.02, 0.36], and over men-only, 0.18, 95% CI [0.01, 0.35]). There was no main effect of composition on issue support, F(2, 704) = 1.42, p = .241.
- Study 2 (n = 974): H1 supported in the gender equity condition — composition x issue type interacted on coalition legitimacy, F(5, 968) = 14.67, p < .001, with women-only (contrast = 0.82, p < .001) and mixed-gender coalitions (contrast = 0.74, p = .001) above men-only (M = 4.77), and no differences in the control condition. H2 was only partially supported: the interaction on issue legitimacy was significant, F(5, 968) = 5.21, p = .006, and mixed-gender coalitions exceeded women-only ones (M = 4.92 vs. 4.47; contrast = 0.45, p = .002), but men-only coalitions did not differ from women-only ones (M = 4.53; contrast = 0.05, p = .697).
- Study 2 mediation: H3a supported in the gender equity condition (via coalition legitimacy vs. men-only: women-only 1.09, 95% CI [0.43, 2.04]; mixed-gender 0.99, 95% CI [0.39, 1.86]); H3b supported only for the mixed-gender comparison (via issue legitimacy vs. women-only: mixed-gender 1.41, 95% CI [0.41, 2.65]; men-only 0.17, 95% CI [-0.87, 1.23], nonsignificant); H4 supported (total indirect effects favoring mixed-gender over women-only, 1.30, 95% CI [0.04, 2.71], and over men-only, 2.23, 95% CI [0.94, 3.55]); H5 supported (indices of mediated moderation vs. women-only 2.05, 95% CI [0.56, 3.65]; vs. men-only 2.93, 95% CI [1.38, 4.52]), with none of these effects present in the control condition. There was again no main effect of composition on issue support, F(2, 971) = 0.51, p = .601.
- Study 3 (n = 1,553, pre-registered): H1 supported — F(2, 1,550) = 102.45, p < .001, with women-only (M = 5.66; contrast = 0.90) and mixed-gender coalitions (M = 5.60; contrast = 0.84) above men-only (M = 4.76), both p < .001. H2 supported — F(2, 1,550) = 12.13, p < .001, with men-only (M = 5.43; contrast = 0.35) and mixed-gender coalitions (M = 5.41; contrast = 0.33) above women-only (M = 5.08), both p < .001. H3a and H3b were supported (e.g., mixed-gender vs. men-only via coalition legitimacy, 0.27, 95% CI [0.20, 0.35]; mixed-gender vs. women-only via issue legitimacy, 0.23, 95% CI [0.11, 0.34]), and H4 was supported (mixed-gender over women-only, 0.21, 95% CI [0.07, 0.35]; over men-only, 0.26, 95% CI [0.12, 0.40]). H5 was tested only in Study 2, since issue type was manipulated there alone.
- Study 3 exploratory moderation: modern sexism interacted with composition on coalition legitimacy, F(2, 1,547) = 44.30, p < .001 — the women-only and mixed-gender advantage over men-only persisted but was weaker at high modern sexism (contrasts 0.55 and 0.63) than at low (1.65 and 1.24) — and on issue legitimacy, F(2, 1,547) = 3.25, p = .039, where men-only coalitions outscored women-only ones only among higher-sexism participants (contrast = 0.40). Social dominance orientation similarly attenuated the coalition-legitimacy advantage, F(2, 1,547) = 30.81, p < .001, but did not interact on issue legitimacy, F(2, 1,547) = 1.35, p = .26.
- Overall pattern: H1, H3a, H3b, and H4 were supported in all three studies; H2 was supported in Studies 1 and 3 but only partially in Study 2, where the men-only versus women-only difference in issue legitimacy was null (and it was weak, p = .046, in Study 1); H5 was supported in the one study that tested it. Coalition composition never produced a significant total (unmediated) effect on managerial support, which the authors attribute to the two mediators operating in opposing directions in a pattern of inconsistent mediation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends signaling and legitimacy theories by distinguishing messenger legitimacy (coalition legitimacy) from message legitimacy (issue legitimacy) and showing that the characteristics conferring one need not confer the other, so advocacy coalitions must be composed to convey both simultaneously. It contributes to research on employee coalitions by specifying who should be part of them, and to work on men's allyship by moving beyond individual confrontation of sexism to the collective, coalition-based context.
practical_implication: Employees advocating for gender equity should be strategic in selecting coalition partners, deliberately recruiting mixed-gender coalitions rather than relying on gender-homophilous (women-only) groups, because including men alongside women helps the coalition signal both that it is a credible messenger and that the issue is strategically important to the business. The authors caution, however, that their findings are descriptive rather than prescriptive.
limitations: The studies were experimental and thus limited by their simulated nature despite using immersive paradigms. The threshold of male representation required for a coalition to appear sufficiently "mixed" remains an open empirical question, and the main effect of coalition composition on managerial support was not significant across studies because the two mediators operated in opposing (suppressing) directions.
future_research: Future studies could use qualitative comparative case study approaches to examine how coalition gender composition shapes legitimacy and support over time, investigate the threshold at which a social group is viewed as properly represented rather than tokenistic, and explore additional boundary conditions of the theory.
abstract: Employees often engage in collective grassroots efforts to bring about gender equity in the workplace. Such coalition-based advocacy is largely driven by women, which has led to debate about whether men's involvement as allies can help. Integrating literatures on signaling and legitimacy, we propose that the demographic composition of a gender equity advocacy coalition matters: men-only groups lack "coalition legitimacy," or the perception that they are the "right" spokespersons for gender equity issues, whereas women-only groups struggle to convey "issue legitimacy," or the perception that gender equity is of strategic importance within business organizations. By contrast, mixed-gender coalitions signal both forms of legitimacy, and are thus uniquely effective. We demonstrate these effects over three studies: managers reporting on advocacy coalitions comprising their colleagues (Study 1), an audio-based study showing that the proposed effects are unique for gender equity issues (Study 2), and a stimulus sampling study involving multiple policy proposals (Study 3). Our findings highlight the different forms of legitimacy that women and men bring to the table when selling gender equity issues. We discuss implications for who should be recruited to gender equity advocacy coalitions, and why.

title: Corporate Proximity and Product Market Reentry: The Role of Corporate Headquarters in Business Unit Response to Product Failure
methods: Discrete event history analysis (complementary log-log model) of business unit–product market–year observations in the U.S. medical device industry; mediated moderation analyses using executive career-path data and text analysis of annual reports.
industry: Medical device industry (FDA-regulated)
units: Business unit–product market–year observations (229 reentries, 157 business units, 686 product markets)
n_sample: 4,760 business unit–product market–year observations
authors: Kim, Cheon Mok (John); Cunningham, Colleen; Joseph, John
theories: attention-based view; behavioral theory of the firm; strategic human capital; theories of search
keywords: business unit search; corporate attention; corporate headquarters; corporate proximity; organizational learning; product failure; product market reentry; vertical linkages
research_question: Whether and how a corporate office shapes business unit search following product failure in multiunit hierarchical organizations—specifically, how the hierarchical, geographic, and cognitive proximity of business units to the corporate headquarters conditions a unit's likelihood of reentering a product market after a prior product failure.
hypotheses:
- H1. Compared to market-related exits, product failure-related exits are associated with a greater likelihood of product market reentry.
- H2. Greater corporate proximity increases the (positive) relationship between product failure-related exit and product market reentry.
- H3a. The effect of corporate proximity increases more for products in established product markets compared to nonestablished product markets.
- H3b. The effect of corporate proximity increases more for product failure-related exits involving technical errors compared to those involving user errors.
- H3c. The effect of corporate proximity increases more for severe product failures compared to nonsevere failures.
mechanism_summary: The paper draws on the behavioral theory of the firm, theories of search, strategic human capital, and the attention-based view to argue that variation in failure response stems partly from how proximate business units are to corporate headquarters. Corporate proximity improves a unit's local search process through two channels—vertical linkages that transfer corporate resources and assistance, and corporate attention directed at the unit's problem—thereby increasing the likelihood the unit persists and reenters the failed product market. These effects are amplified when the product market is established and when failures are technical and severe, conditions that increase the corporate office's ability and motivation to support problem-solving.
data_measures:
Data sources: the Medical Device Register (MDR) supplies business unit product portfolios, employees, revenue, location and ownership at the business unit–year level; the FDA Medical Device Reporting database supplies adverse events; LexisNexis Corporate Affiliations supplies the corporate hierarchy; Compustat supplies corporate financials. Stand-alone firms and units that could not be matched to Corporate Affiliations are excluded, giving 4,760 business unit–product market–year observations (229 reentries, 157 business units, 686 product markets).

- DV — Product market reentry: binary variable set to 1 in the year a business unit offers a product in a market where it offered none the previous year but had offerings in prior years (coded from the MDR), 0 otherwise.
- IV — Experience of product failure: indicator set to 1 if the focal business unit had any FDA-reported adverse event in the focal product market within the preceding three years (including the focal year). Exits not involving a product failure are treated as market-related exits and serve as the base category.
- Focal moderator — Corporate proximity: composite built by z-standardizing and summing three subindicators. Hierarchical proximity is the number of hierarchical layers between unit and corporate office (distance 0–4, reverse-coded). Geographic proximity is great-circle distance in miles between the two offices, logged and reverse-coded against the sample maximum (8.84). Cognitive proximity combines corporate similar product experience (correlation in product shares across 19 medical specialty areas) and corporate product failure experience (0/1/2 shared adverse-event experience). Individual dimensions are also entered separately in the Online Appendix.
- Contingency moderators — Established product markets: age of the FDA product code since the product market was introduced. Technical error-driven vs. user error-driven product failure: cause coded from the FDA Medical Device Reporting database. Severe product failure: coded 1 when the adverse event involved serious injury or death and 0 when it involved only a malfunction, using the FDA severity categorization.
- Mechanism proxies — Vertical linkages: a link is assumed where a unit executive previously held or concurrently holds a corporate office position, tracked through the MDR executive directory (average 0.75 links per unit–year dyad). Corporate attention: mentions of the unit in the firm's annual report normalized by total report pages, from 479 annual reports covering 91 business units.
- Controls: performance above and below aspirations (splined), unit importance, unit age, number of products in the medical specialty, focus in medical specialty, reentry experience, product failure in other products, corporate size, corporate ROA, corporate slack, corporate reentry experience, number of business units, device regulatory class, number of incumbents, and exit and entry by other firms, plus year and medical specialty fixed effects.

Estimation is a discrete event history analysis using a complementary log-log model, with all explanatory and control variables lagged one year and mean-centered before forming interactions, and robust standard errors. The design is explicitly non-experimental: the authors state that random assignment was infeasible and argue that omitted variable bias and reverse causality are less salient because the timing of product failure is largely exogenous and corporate structure and location rarely change. They address non-random exit with inverse propensity weighting (trimming non-overlapping propensity scores and weighting by 1/(1 − p)), report balance diagnostics, and run a falsification test using future values of the explanatory variables. No formal causal-identification design (instrument, difference-in-differences, or discontinuity) is claimed.
key_findings:
- H1 supported. Experience of product failure is positively associated with the likelihood of reentry (Model 2, b = 0.755, p = .015). Product failure-related exit more than doubles the reentry likelihood, raising it by 2.2 percentage points, from 2.0% to 4.2%.
- H2 supported. Corporate proximity positively moderates the relationship between product failure-related exit and reentry (Model 3 interaction b = 0.253, p = .002). Product failure raises the reentry likelihood by 4.1 percentage points (from 1.1% to 5.2%) for a unit one standard deviation above mean proximity, versus 2.2 percentage points (from 1.7% to 3.9%) for a unit at mean proximity.
- Unhypothesized result. Corporate proximity has a direct negative effect on reentry (Model 3, b = −0.142, p < .001): units closer to headquarters are less likely to reenter following a market-related exit. The authors did not predict this and offer it as a post hoc observation.
- H3a supported. The three-way interaction of product failure, corporate proximity and established product market is positive (Model 4, b = 0.042, p = .032). In established markets (one standard deviation above the mean) a one standard deviation increase in proximity raises post-failure reentry by 3.2 percentage points (1.8% to 5.0%), against 0.7 percentage points (1.9% to 2.6%) in less established markets.
- H3b supported. The proximity–failure interaction is positive only for technical error-driven failures (b = 0.360, p = .019; +2.8 percentage points, 2.9% to 5.7%); the authors fail to find statistical evidence of the interaction for user error-driven failures (p = .138).
- H3c supported. The interaction is positive for severe failures (b = 0.346, p = .005; +2.9 percentage points, 3.8% to 6.7%); no statistical evidence is found for nonsevere failures (p = .451).
- Mechanism evidence is supportive but indirect. In the vertical-linkages split sample the proximity–failure interaction is positive for units with vertical linkages (p = .028) and negative for units without them (p = .006), though the authors caution that the latter coefficient is large and noisily estimated because of the small number of reentries in that subsample. In the mediated moderation analysis, corporate attention positively moderates the effect of product failure (p < .001); when proximity and attention are entered together the proximity moderation is no longer statistically distinguishable from zero (p = .270) while the failure-by-attention interaction remains positive (p = .032); and corporate proximity is positively associated with corporate attention (p < .001).
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to the behavioral theory of the firm and organizational learning by drawing renewed attention to corporate proximity as a determinant of business unit response to failure, theorizing and empirically demonstrating two operative mechanisms (vertical linkages and corporate attention). It advances the corporate headquarters literature by treating proximity as a multidimensional construct (beyond geographic distance) and by showing corporate influence as a contingent phenomenon shaped by failure characteristics. It also contributes to the literature on determinants of persistence in product entry by positioning corporate proximity as a driver of persistence.
practical_implication: Understanding how structural variation shapes reentry is of value to managers making decisions about proximity via structural design, location, and managerial hiring across units. Although executives rarely relocate corporate headquarters or units, they may channel and redirect attention through changes to structure or cognitive ties, and may configure proximity levers to support performance-enhancing reentry following failure.
limitations: Because the authors only have access to annual data on entry and exit, they cannot capture more granular reentry events (e.g., reentry in the same year as exit) that may also reflect learning. While product failures may cause exits, they do not always do so, so the authors cannot claim exits were caused by a preceding failure in every case (though such "false positives" make the test more conservative). The empirical setting is a single industry over a historical window.
future_research: Future research could examine conditions under which the effects of hierarchical, geographic, and cognitive proximity might diverge (e.g., successful exploration may require close hierarchical but distant cognitive proximity). More work is needed on the performance consequences of proximity's effects on failure response, how and when firms should adjust proximity choices, and how different configurations of proximity levers can create performance-enhancing levels of reentry.
abstract: Understanding how organizations respond to failure is important to management research, yet prior studies have offered contrasting findings for whether, in a multiunit hierarchical organization, a corporate office improves business unit search following product failure. To better understand how a corporate office affects business unit search, we focus on the role of corporate proximity (hierarchical, geographic, and cognitive) between the corporate office and constituent units. We argue that corporate proximity improves a business unit’s local search process through two mechanisms—vertical linkages and corporate attention—that positively condition the likelihood of persisting; that is, reentering a product market after having experienced a prior product failure in that market. We find support for our theory using data on reentry in the U.S. medical device industry following exit from the market due to product failure. We also explore how age of the product market and characteristics of the failure—cause and severity— further moderate corporate proximity’s role in business unit reentry. Overall, our study offers a better understanding of how complex organizations respond to failure, thereby contributing to literatures on search, corporate headquarters, and product entry.
