title: The Benefits and Burdens of Work Moralization on Creativity
methods: Mixed quantitative design: two field surveys (employee self-reports plus supervisor creativity ratings) analyzed with path analysis in lavaan, and a preregistered online experiment manipulating work moralization and value congruence, with indirect effects tested via bootstrapped PROCESS models.
industry: Environmental management organization (Study 1); sanitation plant (Study 2); online working adults designing parks (Study 3 experiment)
time_period: Field data collected in 2019; preregistered online experiment
units: Employees (Studies 1-2, with supervisor ratings of creativity in Study 2); working adults (Study 3 experiment)
n_sample: 134 employees (Study 1); 590 employee-supervisor dyads (Study 2); 379 working adults (Study 3)
authors: Kundro, Timothy G.
theories: regulatory focus theory; value congruence
keywords: cognitive flexibility; creativity; moral rumination; regulatory focus theory; value congruence; work moralization
research_question: How does work moralization—the degree to which individuals integrate moral considerations into their work tasks—influence employee creativity, and under what conditions (value congruence) is its effect a benefit versus a burden?
hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1. Work moralization is positively related to rumination.
Hypothesis 2. There is a negative indirect effect of work moralization on creativity through rumination.
Hypothesis 3. Work moralization is positively related to cognitive flexibility.
Hypothesis 4. There is a positive indirect effect of work moralization on creativity through cognitive flexibility.
Hypothesis 5. The indirect effect of work moralization on creativity through rumination is less negative (positive) when value congruence is high (low).
Hypothesis 6. The indirect effect of work moralization on creativity through cognitive flexibility is more positive (negative) when value congruence is high (low).
Hypothesis 7. The effect of work moralization on creativity is more positive (negative) when value congruence is high (low).
mechanism_summary: Grounded in regulatory focus theory, work moralization is theorized as a double-edged sword: it can trigger prevention-focused moral rumination that drains the cognitive resources creativity requires, while simultaneously prompting promotion-focused cognitive flexibility that enables creative associations. Value congruence is the critical moderator that tips the balance—when employees perceive their values align with the organization's, they are least likely to ruminate and most likely to become cognitively flexible, so work moralization yields higher creativity; when values are misaligned, the burden side dominates.
data_measures:
Study 1 surveyed employees of an organization responsible for environmental management in 2019: approximately 250 employees were invited and 134 provided complete responses to the core measures (approximate response rate 50%). Unless otherwise noted, all measures used 7-point scales from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Work moralization was captured with a three-item measure the author developed for this paper following Hinkin's (1998) recommended procedures (a = .75), retaining the items "In my eyes, performing my work tasks correctly is a matter of right and wrong; I see ethics as a critical component of my work; To me, performing my job correctly is morally important." Content validation with 120 MTurk working adults showed strong definitional correspondence (average 6.27 out of 7), and a 10-factor CFA on 232 MTurk working adults supported convergent and discriminant validity against calling orientation, workplace meaning, reflective and perceptual moral attentiveness, internalized and symbolic moral identity, moral awareness, and performance and family considerations. Moral rumination used three items adapted from Trapnell and Campbell (1999) to target moral topics at work (a = .85; sample item "At work, I ruminate about the morality of my behaviors"), and cognitive flexibility used three items from Martin and Rubin (1995) (a = .63; sample item "I consider alternatives when dealing with work problems"). Study 1 was estimated by path analysis in lavaan, modeling work moralization as a simultaneous predictor of rumination and cognitive flexibility.

Study 2 invited all 862 employees of a sanitation plant in the southeastern United States in 2019; 622 returned complete employee surveys and supervisors rated 590 of them six weeks later (total response rate 68%). Work moralization (a = .79), moral rumination (a = .89), and cognitive flexibility (a = .61) reused the Study 1 items. Creativity was supervisor-rated with three items from Zhou and George (2001) (a = .97; sample item "This employee comes up with creative solutions to problems"). The model was estimated by path analysis with observed variables in MPlus using clustered standard errors to handle employees nested within supervisory units (average four employees per supervisor), with indirect effects calculated from 10,000 bootstrapped samples. Demographic controls were excluded from the core analyses because they were not correlated with both the predictors and the dependent variable and had no specific theoretical rationale; supplementary models added age, gender, race, and tenure, and separately added moral identity internalization and cognitive engagement as controls.

Study 3 was a preregistered 2 (considerations: moral versus logistical) x 2 (value congruence: high versus low) between-subjects online experiment; 400 working adults were recruited from MTurk and 379 retained after preregistered exclusions (one participant who did not generate three ideas, 17 who wrote nonsense responses, three who failed an attention check). Participants generated three ideas for a municipal park. Work moralization was manipulated by instructing participants to apply moral (versus logistical) considerations to the flora and fauna on the site, and value congruence by telling participants that a consultant "Q-Sort" audit had rated each value they had personally listed as "very highly" valued by the organization (85th-88th percentile) or "not at all" valued (12th-15th percentile); both manipulation checks were significant. Moral rumination (a = .96) and cognitive flexibility (a = .88) used the same three items as the field studies, and creativity was scored by two trained research assistants who rated each idea from 1 (not at all creative) to 5 (very creative), with substantial interrater agreement (ICC2 = .74) and composites formed by averaging the two judges per idea and then the three ideas. Moderated mediation for Hypotheses 5-7 was tested with first-stage models using PROCESS Model 8 and 10,000 bootstrapped samples, a deviation from the preregistered Model 7 so that the direct effects in Hypothesis 7 could be estimated.

On identification, the author states plainly that the two field studies are cross-sectional, that time-lagged surveys were not possible given field-site constraints, and that causal inferences could not be assessed from them, so those estimates are associational. Causal evidence rests on the randomized experiment, in which work moralization and value congruence were manipulated; the author describes this as providing stronger evidence of causality than survey data alone and as an episodic test of the model, and frames the three studies together as a constructive replication.
key_findings:
Study 1 (n = 134) supported both hypotheses it tested. Work moralization was positively and significantly related to moral rumination (b = .21, p = .01), supporting Hypothesis 1, and positively and significantly related to cognitive flexibility (b = .25, p = .003), supporting Hypothesis 3; both effects held in supplementary models controlling for age, gender, and organizational tenure (b = .19, p = .038 and b = .25, p = .005). Because supervisor evaluations of creativity could not be collected at this site, Study 1 did not test the indirect effects on creativity.

Study 2 (n = 590 employee-supervisor dyads) supported Hypotheses 1 through 4. Work moralization was again positively and significantly related to rumination (b = .15, p < .001) and to cognitive flexibility (b = .13, p = .007); in the path model, rumination was negatively related to supervisor-rated creativity (-.08, p < .05) and cognitive flexibility was positively related to it (.08, p < .05). The indirect effect of work moralization on creativity through rumination was significant and negative (indirect effect = -.02, 95% CI [-.043, -.002]), supporting Hypothesis 2, and the indirect effect through cognitive flexibility was significant and positive (indirect effect = .02, 95% CI [.001, .046]), supporting Hypothesis 4. Both indirect effects persisted in supplementary models controlling for demographics and, separately, for moral identity internalization and cognitive engagement, although several of these robustness estimates are reported at 90% rather than 95% confidence intervals. The author reports that work moralization had an overall nonsignificant effect on creativity in this study, consistent with the two offsetting pathways. A one-way ANOVA on the subset who reported job type found no significant differences in work moralization across job types (F[8, 287] = 1.71, p = .096).

Study 3 (n = 379) reproduced the pattern under random assignment and added the moderation, but with weaker support on the cognitive flexibility pathway than the field studies gave. Moralization positively predicted rumination (b = .49, SE = .18, p = .006), supporting Hypothesis 1, and produced a significant negative indirect effect on creativity through rumination (indirect effect = -.03, SE = .015, 95% CI [-.062, -.004]), supporting Hypothesis 2. Its effect on cognitive flexibility was only marginal (b = .24, SE = .13, p = .064), and the positive indirect effect through cognitive flexibility was likewise marginal (indirect effect = .02, SE = .012, 90% CI [.001, .043]); the author explicitly records Hypotheses 3 and 4 as supported at p < .10 in this study rather than at conventional significance. All three moderation hypotheses were supported. The work moralization x value congruence interaction on rumination was significant (b = -1.98, SE = .35, p < .001), and the indirect effect through rumination was more negative when value congruence was low (indirect effect = -.07, SE = .04, 95% CI [-.141, -.003]) than when it was high, where it was not significant (indirect effect = .02, SE = .02, 95% CI [-.001, .059]); the index of moderated mediation was significant (.09, SE = .05, 95% CI [.004, .187]), supporting Hypothesis 5. The interaction on cognitive flexibility was also significant (b = .63, SE = .25, p = .01), with the indirect effect through cognitive flexibility significant and positive under high value congruence (indirect effect = .04, SE = .02, 95% CI [.01, .08]) but not significant under low value congruence (indirect effect = -.01, SE = .02, 95% CI [-.04, .03]); the index of moderated mediation was significant (.044, SE = .02, 95% CI [.01, .10]), supporting Hypothesis 6. The interaction on creativity itself was significant (b = .37, SE = .14, p = .01): the effect of moralization on creativity was positive and significant when value congruence was high (b = .28, SE = .10, p = .01) but nonsignificant when it was low (b = -.09, SE = .10, p = .39), supporting Hypothesis 7. As in Study 2, the overall effect of moralization on creativity was nonsignificant. Supplementary analyses ruled out effort as an alternative explanation: the interaction did not predict time spent writing ideas (b = 43.12, SE = 29.18, p = .14) or the length of the responses (b = 51.30, SE = 55.94, p = .36). Parallel analyses on global regulatory focus measures showed the same interaction pattern on prevention focus (b = -1.86, SE = .32, p < .001) and promotion focus (b = .73, SE = .28, p = .01).

Taken together, the author's stated integration is that work moralization has a negative indirect effect on creativity through rumination and a positive indirect effect through cognitive flexibility, a double-edged sword with no reliable overall effect on creativity in either study that measured it, and that value congruence determines which side dominates: when value congruence is high the cognitive flexibility path is significant and positive while the rumination path is not, and when value congruence is low the reverse holds. The support pattern is not uniform across studies. Hypotheses 1 and 2 were supported at conventional significance wherever they were tested, whereas Hypotheses 3 and 4 were fully supported in the two field studies but only marginally (p < .10) in the experiment, and Hypotheses 5 through 7 were tested only in Study 3.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the largely held assumption that moralizing work generally harms creativity, showing instead that work moralization can—and often does—positively influence creativity through offsetting cognitive pathways. It contributes to regulatory focus theory by demonstrating that morality is itself a key predictor of promotion- and prevention-focused cognitions, and it introduces a conceptualization of work moralization that advances research on organizational ethics.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that encouraging employees to view their work in moral terms will dampen creativity. Because value congruence determines whether moralization sparks cognitive flexibility or rumination, cultivating alignment between employee and organizational values can help employees who moralize their work translate that orientation into creative, rather than draining, cognitive outcomes.
limitations: The author notes that the field studies could not establish causal inference, motivating the preregistered experiment as stronger causal evidence. Further evidence is needed to investigate the effects of work moralization on creativity and the role of the proposed moderator across additional contexts.
future_research: Future work should investigate how work becomes moralized in the first place, how the content of work moralization influences an individual's behavior, and the antecedents of work moralization in more depth, and should test whether the effects found here apply to other domains outside creativity.
abstract: Although morality has long been considered an important and integral element of organizational life for employees, research has suggested that moral considerations reduce creativity. However, evidence has hinted that morality may not always be a burden and instead could spark creativity. I develop a model that investigates how work moralization—or the degree to which individuals integrate moral considerations into their work tasks—influences employee creativity. Drawing on regulatory focus theory, I argue that work moralization can lead to prevention-focused cognitions (i.e., moral rumination), which impair and redirect the cognitive resources needed for creativity. However, I also posit that work moralization can lead to promotion-focused cognitions (i.e., cognitive flexibility), leading employees to adopt cognitive approaches that increase creativity. Moreover, integrating research on value congruence, I suggest that work moralizers are the least likely to ruminate—and the most likely to become cognitively flexible—when they perceive that their values are aligned with those of their organization, which ultimately fosters higher levels of creativity. I test my theoretical model with two field studies and a preregistered experiment. This research challenges the consensus that moral considerations generally have a negative impact on creativity, and contributes to research on organizational ethics and creativity.

title: The Glass Wall and the Gendered Evaluation of Role Expansion in Freelancing Careers
methods: Three studies. Study 1A: archival panel/event-history of K-pop songwriter careers, Cox proportional hazard regression of the hazard of a new release with year, role, and songwriter fixed effects. Study 1B: 2x2 mixed-design survey experiment of K-pop songwriters, OLS with participant fixed effects and bootstrapped moderated-mediation. Study 2: 2x2 between-subjects resume experiment of U.S. film workers, OLS with heteroscedasticity-robust errors and bootstrapped moderated-mediation.
industry: Creative freelancing: K-pop (Korean popular music) songwriting (Studies 1A, 1B) and U.S. film production (Study 2)
time_period: Study 1A songs written January 2000-September 2012 (debut cohort January 2003-September 2012); Studies 1B and 2 survey timing not reported
units: Songwriters (archival careers), K-pop songwriter survey participants, and general-population participants evaluating film-worker resumes
n_sample: Study 1A: 8,168 songwriters who debuted (6,401 male, 1,767 female); Study 1B: 78 K-pop songwriters (156 participant-scenario observations); Study 2: 313 U.S. participants (of 400 recruited from Prolific Academic)
authors: Lee, Yonghoon G.; Koval, Christy Zhou; Lee, S. Susie
theories: career progression paradox (O'Mahony & Bechky, 2006); gender stereotypes / gender bias; generalist discount (Zuckerman et al., 2003); social role theory (Eagly, 1987)
keywords: freelancing careers; gendered evaluation; generalist discount; glass wall; nonstandard work; perceived agency; progressive role expansion; role expansion
research_question: How is gender bias manifested in freelancing careers that advance outside formal organizations, and specifically, does progressive role expansion (starting as a specialist and later expanding into new work roles) yield the same career benefits for women as for men, or do women face a "glass wall"?
hypotheses:
H1: Gender will moderate the relationship between role expansion and perceived agency, such that role expansion for female freelancers will be perceived to be less agentic than for male freelancers.
H2a: Perceived agency has a positive relationship with perceived competence.
H2b: Perceived agency has a positive relationship with perceived commitment.
H3a: The indirect relationship between role expansion and perceived competence via perceived agency is moderated by gender, such that this indirect effect is weaker for women compared to men.
H3b: The indirect relationship between role expansion and perceived commitment via perceived agency is moderated by gender, such that this indirect effect is weaker for women compared to men.
H4: Compared to men's role expansion, women's role expansion will result in a lower increase in the chance of having new work opportunities.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that progressive role expansion can signal agency—taking control of one's career—but that gender stereotypes act as an evaluative anchor on how that expansion is read. Because women are stereotyped as communal, emotional, and lacking self-control, their role expansion is attributed to situational pressures or impulsiveness rather than purposeful career-crafting, so it is perceived as less agentic than men's. Reduced perceived agency in turn lowers perceived competence and commitment—the cues clients use to award work—producing an invisible "glass wall" that blocks women from converting role expansion into new opportunities. The effect is conditioned by situational ambiguity, which is endemic to freelancing.
data_measures:
- Study 1A (archival panel): the Korean Music Copyright Association (KOMCA) copyright-holder list, cross-checked against ManiaDB.com, Melon.com, and Bugs.co.kr, yielding 73,753 songs written between January 2000 and September 2012 and a monthly panel of the 8,168 songwriters who debuted between January 2003 and September 2012. DV = the hazard rate of having a new release, with months since the latest release as analysis time. IVs: Generalist debut = 1 if the songwriter debuted performing more than one of the three copyright-recognized roles (melodist, arranger, lyricist); Role expansion = 1 for periods during and after a specialist debutant first performed a role they had never performed before; Female = 1 for female songwriters, coded from the three public databases plus a majority vote of three native-Korean coders (the three coders agreed in 82.42% of cases and matched the public databases in 93.42%). Controls: Recent activity, Tenure, Prior releases, Performer experiences, Genre specialization (the sum of squared genre shares of a songwriter's songs over the prior three years), Prior success (hit songs on Melon.com's monthly top-100 chart), Experiences with majors, Success as a performer, Success of performers, plus Genre, Year, and Role fixed effects. Estimation: Cox proportional hazard regression with robust standard errors clustered by songwriter, time-dependent coefficients for the covariates that violated the proportional-hazard assumption (Schoenfeld residual test), and a stratified songwriter-fixed-effects model as a robustness check. This study is archival and observational; the paper presents it as a field study and makes no experimental-identification claim for it.
- Study 1B (survey experiment): 78 K-pop songwriters recruited from Korean online platforms (Mule.co.kr, KakaoTalk Open Chats, Instagram, Facebook, Clubhouse) in a 2 (target gender: male vs. female, between-subjects) x 2 (roles: specialized vs. expanded, within-subjects) mixed design, giving 156 participant-scenario observations. Perceived agency = eight items (e.g., "willing to take a stand," "independent," "dominant"), 1-5, alpha = .80; Perceived competence = five items ("competent," "capable," "skillful," "masterful," "intelligent"), 1-5, alpha = .88; Perceived commitment = four items adopted from Heilman and Okimoto (2008), 1-9, alpha = .86. The survey was run in Korean using Brislin's (1970) back-translation, and participants rated how people in the K-pop industry would generally respond rather than their own opinions, to alleviate social-desirability concerns. Estimation: OLS with participant fixed effects, standard errors clustered by participant, and bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 resamples (Preacher & Hayes, 2008).
- Study 2 (resume experiment): 400 U.S. participants recruited from Prolific Academic, 313 retained after a manipulation check, in a 2 (gender: male vs. female) x 2 (role expansion: yes vs. no) between-subjects design. Participants read the resume of a cinematographer, Steven or Sarah, who either continued taking cinematographer projects or had recently added a production designer role while keeping a cinematographer role. The same three scales as Study 1B were used (agency alpha = .70, competence alpha = .84, commitment alpha = .84). Estimation: linear regression with heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors, plus the same 10,000-resample bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals. Random assignment gives Studies 1B and 2 experimental control over the manipulated cues, and the paper states that Study 2's fully between-subjects design "allowed us to draw a more conservative causal claim than the fixed effects model used in Study 1B."
key_findings:
- Study 1A (8,168 debutants; 1,847 specialist debutants for the role-expansion test): Generalist debut reduced the hazard of a second release by about 21%, consistent with the value of starting specialized; Female had a significant negative effect on the likelihood of a second release (p < .01) but the Female x Generalist debut interaction was not significant (p = .15). In the role-expansion analysis, the simple effect of Role expansion was positive and significant on the hazard of a new release (b = 0.41, p < .01), the simple effect of Female was not significant (p = .28), and the Role expansion x Female interaction was negative and significant (b = -0.45, p < .01), supporting H4. For male specialists, expanding into a new role increased the hazard of a new release by approximately 40%, whereas for female specialists there was no statistical difference between remaining a specialist and expanding. Results were robust to controls and to songwriter fixed effects.
- Study 1B (78 K-pop songwriters, 156 observations): H1 supported - the Expanded x Female interaction on perceived agency was negative and significant (b = -0.31, p < .05) while the simple effect of Expanded was positive and significant (b = 0.24, p < .01), and women who expanded were rated less agentic (M = 2.73, SD = 0.61) than men who expanded (M = 3.18, SD = 0.66), t(76) = 3.12, p < .01. H2a supported (perceived agency to perceived competence, b = 0.42, p < .01). H2b not supported - no predictor had a statistically significant effect on perceived commitment. H3a supported - the indirect effect of Expanded on perceived competence via perceived agency was significant in the male condition (b = 0.102, 95% BC CI [0.015, 0.253]) but not the female condition (b = -0.027, 95% BC CI [-0.144, 0.026]), and the two differed significantly (b = -0.129, 95% BC CI [-0.329, -0.014]). H3b not supported - neither indirect effect on perceived commitment was significant and their difference was not either (b = -0.039, 95% BC CI [-0.389, 0.294]).
- Study 2 (313 U.S. participants): H1 supported - the Role expansion x Female interaction on perceived agency was negative and significant (b = -0.31, p < .05); here the pattern ran through the female condition, where role expansion lowered perceived agency (M = 2.48, SD = 0.53) relative to no role expansion (M = 2.75, SD = 0.56), t(153) = 3.06, p < .01, while the male comparison was null (M = 2.66 vs. 2.62), t(160) = -0.40, p = .69, and female role expansion was rated less agentic than male role expansion, t(152) = -2.07, p < .05. H2a supported (agency to competence, b = 0.30, p < .01) and H2b supported (agency to commitment, b = 0.48, p < .01). H3a supported - the indirect effect of role expansion on perceived competence via perceived agency was negative and significant in the female condition (b = -0.082, 95% BC CI [-0.152, -0.031]) but null in the male condition (b = 0.011, 95% BC CI [-0.040, 0.068]), difference significant (b = -0.093, 95% BC CI [-0.192, -0.023]). H3b supported - the indirect effect on perceived commitment was negative and significant in the female condition (b = -0.130, 95% BC CI [-0.274, -0.045]) but null in the male condition (b = 0.017, 95% BC CI [-0.064, 0.115]), difference significant (b = -0.147, 95% BC CI [-0.334, -0.036]).
- Support was therefore partial and study-dependent: H1, H2a, and H3a held in both experiments and H4 held in the archival study, but H2b and H3b were supported only in Study 2 (U.S. general population) and not in Study 1B (K-pop songwriter peers), which the authors conjecture reflects industry insiders assuming a baseline level of commitment for any songwriter.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces the "glass wall"—an invisible barrier disadvantaging women who pursue lateral role expansion within professional careers—as a complement to the glass ceiling, glass cliff, and glass escalator that operate inside organizational hierarchies, extending gender-bias theory to nonstandard, organization-free work. It identifies the gendered evaluation of role expansion via perceived agency as the underlying mechanism, and contributes to the generalist-discount/advantage debate by showing that gender stereotypes anchor whether generalism is read as competent agency or as erratic situational drift.
practical_implication: Freelancers (especially women) may mitigate the bias by presenting their practice under an incorporated business name to shift client attention from demographic cues to work portfolios. Clients are cautioned that stereotype-tainted evaluations lead to suboptimal hiring and that female generalists may be an undervalued labor pool; policymakers could accredit licensing schemes that let women credibly signal agentic investment in acquiring new work roles.
limitations: The empirical setting is confined to high-skill creative freelancing (music and film), so generalizability to low-skill platform work (e.g., Uber, Mechanical Turk) and to part-time or transitional freelancing remains untested. Both focal industries are male-dominated, which heightens the salience of gender and may inflate the observed bias, leaving open whether the glass wall appears in female-dominated industries.
future_research: Future work should test whether the glass wall extends beyond high-skill creative freelancing to low-skill gig work and to traditional careers being reformed toward greater worker autonomy, and whether it appears in female-dominated industries. Scholars are also encouraged to examine additional parallel paths to the glass wall—including demand-side algorithmic matching and supply-side self-selection into specialization—and how they may reinforce one another.
abstract: People pursuing careers outside organizations often face a career progression paradox: they must develop expertise to find new work opportunities, but such expertise is largely acquired through accumulating work experience to which they seldom have access. Research has proposed that progressive role expansion—starting one's career specialized in a single work role and later expanding into new work roles—would be helpful to navigate this challenge. However, we propose that when women engage in lateral role expansion within professional careers, they face a "glass wall"—an invisible barrier that limits their work opportunities due to a gendered evaluation of role expansion. Specifically, role expansion by female (vs. male) freelancers is seen as less agentic, and such difference undermines female freelancers' perceived competence and commitment. Three studies using different methods (archival data and experiment), industries (music and film), and samples (Korean and American) show that female (vs. male) freelancers who expand into new work roles are seen as less agentic and have less chance of finding new work opportunities. Although women who pursue careers outside of organizations may become unshackled from gender biases embedded within traditional organizational hierarchies, we suggest that they still face obstacles in the new forms of work.

title: How Organizations Influence Interpersonal Trust Repair: The Case of a French Antiterrorist Unit
methods: Inductive, qualitative grounded-theory study of a single organization (GIGN); three data-collection strategies — 42 semi-structured interviews plus follow-ups, semi-overt participant observation, and archival data; open/axial/theoretical coding to build a process model.
industry: Elite antiterrorist / paramilitary special-forces unit (Groupe d'Intervention de la Gendarmerie Nationale, GIGN)
time_period: Fieldwork from 2014, with interviews and follow-up conversations spanning roughly four years
units: GIGN operatives (officers and noncommissioned officers), candidates, instructors, and one psychiatrist
n_sample: 42 formal semi-structured interviews (17 officers, 25 NCOs) plus participant observation of ~50 candidates and 15 instructors (~360 hours) and archival documents
authors: Sala, Gabriel R.; Pratt, Michael G.
theories: interpersonal trust repair (Kim, Dirks, & Cooper, 2009; Kramer & Lewicki, 2010); organizational responses to wrongdoing and reinstatement (Stewart & Brown, 2014; McCarter & Caza, 2010; Frey, 2022); third-party / 'third wave' trust (Dirks & de Jong, 2021)
keywords: interpersonal trust repair; organizational practices; organizational wrongdoers; reintegration; trust templates; trust violation rules
research_question: What role, if any, does an organization play in facilitating interpersonal trust repair among its members — that is, how might an organization broker the relationship between a wrongdoer and the person(s) whose trust has been violated? The authors examine this in an elite antiterrorism organization, the GIGN.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: trust as "capital" eroded by mistakes; the dilemma that high-stakes interdependent work both requires trust and makes it fragile; trust violations versus trust repair.
- Organizational practices: communicating trust standards through selection and socialization; conducting debriefing sessions about violations; using practice, drills, and simulations; team-leader assessments of trust repair; and role assignments on missions.
- Core mechanisms (the "why"): (a) establishing trust violation rules based on trust standards, (b) detecting violations and assigning blame, (c) providing a trust repair template and opportunities, and (d) rendering and communicating an organizational trust judgment (first by the mission team leader, then by all team leaders).
- Emergent outcomes: full, partial, or failed interpersonal trust repair, with downstream consequences for whether and how violators are reintegrated into mission teams.
- Boundary conditions: the "mesh size" (tightness) of trust violation rules and the rigidity of the repair template vary with the organization's task requirements (e.g., how consequential, complex, and interdependent the work is).

The paper theorizes a "Big O" (organizational) process model in which the organization, not just the trustor–trustee dyad, structures interpersonal trust repair. Because all GIGN mistakes are treated as trust violations and repaired through a single standardized process that mirrors selection and socialization (fix character before competence), the organization can repair and reintegrate scarce expert operatives relatively quickly and unambiguously, signaling restored trust to future teammates via mission assignments.
data_measures:
Three data-collection strategies were used and triangulated: semi-structured interviews, semi-overt participant observation, and archival data gathering. The first author completed 42 formal, one-on-one semi-structured interviews — a final interview sample of 17 officers and 25 NCOs, all but two informants male — conducted in French in an isolated room at GIGN headquarters, averaging one hour (range 30 to 180 minutes), transcribed to English and back-translated for accuracy; three officers and three NCOs were interviewed repeatedly (three up to 30 follow-up conversations each over four years) to clarify aspects of the work and provide member checks, with informal conversations captured in field notes. The protocol was modified over time as the research question shifted toward trust repair, and the final interview count was set by "theoretical saturation." Semi-overt participant observation covered the selection process ("pre-stage") over a five-week period at an average of 12 hours per day (about 360 hours), living and training alongside about 50 candidates and 15 instructors, with video diaries, audio records, and field notes usually written within 24 hours of leaving the field. Archival documents — news articles about GIGN interventions, documentaries about the unit and its selection and training processes, and the specialized magazine Gend'info — supplied context but were explicitly not subject to formal analysis. Sampling was purposeful and evolved with the emerging theory: an initial wave of 10 interviews on trust formation redirected the study to trust repair, after which sampling broadened to former mission members who now train and evaluate operatives, junior and senior members (six months to over 15 years of tenure), and one psychiatrist.

Focal constructs were operationalized through grounded-theory coding rather than measurement instruments. Open coding stayed close to informants' language (e.g., losing "percentages" of "trust capital"), and open codes were then aggregated into axial codes: statements about carrying rocks as punishment or having a "Godfather" mentor were grouped under "socialization practices"; statements such as "all mistakes erode trust," "multiple mistakes eat up trust capital more quickly," and "there are no unforgivable mistakes" were combined into "trust violation rules"; and codes on looking for "character" during selection, the "necessity of admitting your own mistakes," the importance of "competence" in training, and the use of practices, drills, and simulations became "trust repair template." The focal outcome was coded from informants' own trust statements — "I would trust him on any mission," "I would only let that operative drive the car," "I would not go with that operative on a mission" — abstracted to full, partial, or no trust repair. Axial codes were then mapped visually on a whiteboard, organizational practices at the top and interpersonal trust repair dynamics at the bottom, and the mechanism linking each pair was induced. Trustworthiness procedures included an insider-outsider approach with the second author as "devil's advocate," regular peer debriefings during collection, multiple member checks with key informants, and newly gathered data on three "intact" trust repair incidents illustrating the whole model, obtained where possible from both the trust violator and the organizational actor running the repair. The design is inductive and theory-elaborating; it makes no causal-identification claim and reports no statistical estimates.
key_findings:
The central emergent finding is a process model in which the organization, not only the trustor-trustee dyad, structures interpersonal trust repair. Five organizational practices — communicating trust standards through selection and socialization, debriefing about trust violations, practice and training (drills and simulations) to reaffirm trust standards, team-leader assessment of trust repair, and role assignment on missions — work through four mechanisms: (a) establishing trust violation rules, (b) detecting trust violations and assigning blame, (c) providing a trust repair template and opportunities, and (d) rendering and communicating an organization trust judgment, first by the team leader of the mission in which trust was violated and then by all team leaders. Taken together, the organization supplies a process for how, when, and where individuals can repair trust following a violation.

Two trust standards operate at the GIGN: an operative has the trust of others if they demonstrate excellence in character and competence, in that order, and if their "trust bank" is at 100% prior to a mission. These standards underlie three trust violation rules: all mistakes, whether in drills or missions, are trust violations that erode trust capital; violations become harder to rectify as they recur, with dishonesty and lying by omission treated most severely; and no mistake is unforgivable, so the trust bank can be restored to 100%. Because missions and training cannot be stopped mid-stream, detection and blame assignment occur collectively in post-mission debriefings involving everyone who took part, with the team leader charged with ensuring that all mistakes are identified and blame assigned. That collective judgment is expected to be final and is not open to debate, so justifying, rationalizing, or deflecting blame is treated as unacceptable — which, the authors argue, keeps the team from being bogged down by blame denial.

The trust repair template is standardized and public: violators must first acknowledge the violation and take the blame, reaffirming good character, and only then perform flawlessly in subsequent practice, drills, and simulations, reaffirming competence. This two-stage sequence mirrors the character-then-competence ordering of pre-stage and stage probatoire, and reaffirming character alone is necessary but not sufficient — "the debriefing alone is not enough." The same template applied to all violators regardless of the personal relationships they had with team members or leaders. Against the dyadic literature's expectation that repair tactics shift with violation type and relationship, the authors report being struck by the similarity in patterns of how trust was repaired across all situations, and found that violators who successfully went through the standardized organizational process were fully trusted again on subsequent missions.

Repair outcomes are rendered and signaled through role assignment. Full trust repair is communicated by allowing the violator back on missions without restrictions in an important role, at which point mistakes are forgotten and the violator's "slate" is wiped clean. Partial trust repair is communicated by assignment to less central, more peripheral roles. Failed repair is communicated by no longer assigning the violator to missions or by cancelling missions already assigned; the person is then socially ostracized (not greeted in corridors, not invited to eat with others in the cafeteria) and ultimately transferred out of the GIGN or quits. Partial trust repair is explicitly provisional and transitory, converting over time into either full repair — if the operative shows "progress and willingness to improve" — or failure if the template is ignored again. The difference between partially repairing trust and failing to do so resides primarily in the number of current infringements against the template, not the number of mistakes committed over time: many mistakes can all be repaired, but continual failure to repair them via the template makes trust irreparable. Outright failure was described as very uncommon, and the authors note that the GIGN does attempt to keep its operatives given the rarity of their expertise.
theoretical_contribution: The study develops a process model of how organizations influence interpersonal trust repair, contributing to the "third wave" of trust research that looks beyond the trustor–trustee dyad to third parties such as the organization. It shows that what is usually treated as a dyadic, idiosyncratic phenomenon can in fact be collective and standardized, and it bridges the trust-repair literature with research on how organizations deal with wrongdoers (discipline, reinstatement, reintegration).
practical_implication: Coworkers are unlikely to fully trust reinstated violators on the strength of an organizational "stamp of approval" alone; managers should attend to reintegration, not just punishment. The authors suggest that shared agreement on what counts as a violation and how it is repaired, transparency in detection and the remediation process, and trust in the organization and its practices are conditions that make organizationally directed trust repair effective.
limitations: As a theory-elaborating qualitative study of a single antiterrorist unit, transferability and generalizability are constrained; findings apply most directly to similar elite, paramilitary, or project-team organizations that must retain experts after trust violations. The sensitive nature of the missions prevented the researchers from attending violation-detection and blame-assignment meetings or tracking specific incidents in real time, and the studied organization already had functional trust standards, rules, and templates in place.
future_research: Future work could track individuals longitudinally to identify additional ways organizations become involved at different points in the repair process, follow a comparable organization to see how trust standards, rules, and templates form, and examine cases where organizational attempts to repair interpersonal trust fail. Researchers might also probe boundary conditions such as the "mesh size" of violation rules and the rigidity of repair templates across contexts.
abstract: Organizations that increasingly rely on interdependent teams, such as project teams, often imply work that is important, improvisational, and interdependent. However, these are the very same task conditions where trust is most fragile and in need of repair. As a result, organizations may wish to intervene in repairing interpersonal trust among members. Through an inductive qualitative study of a French antiterrorist unit, we move beyond dyadic treatments of interpersonal trust repair to theorize a model that elucidates the organizational practices that can be used to guide members through the trust repair process. We also induce core mechanisms, such as establishing trust violation rules and providing trust templates, that explain why these organizational practices work to repair interpersonal trust. We suggest how this organizationally directed trust repair process can lead to full, partial, or failed trust repair for trust violators, with consequences on whether and how these violators may be reintegrated into the organization. We conclude by discussing the contributions of our research on trust repair, as well as on how organizations treat organizational wrongdoers, and suggest several avenues for future research.

title: “We Can’t Compete on Human Rights”: Creating Market-Protected Spaces to Institutionalize the Emerging Logic of Responsible Management
methods: Inductive, abductive qualitative case study of the global apparel industry post-Rana Plaza; at least two semi-structured interviews per firm (CSR and purchasing managers), documentary evidence, and 63 industry events, analyzed via iterative NVivo and table coding (Gioia approach).
industry: Apparel/garment retailing (fast fashion, branded retailers, department stores, supermarkets, sports/outdoor)
country: Germany and the United Kingdom (with transnational field-level data)
time_period: 2015–2019 (firm interviews March 2016–August 2018; field events 2016–2019)
units: Lead-firm apparel MNCs plus field-level stakeholders (governments, NGOs, unions, multi-stakeholder initiatives)
n_sample: 20 apparel retailers and brands (drawn from a larger project on 79 leading apparel MNCs), plus 40 formal and 33 informal stakeholder interviews
authors: Schuessler, Elke S.; Lohmeyer, Nora; Ashwin, Sarah
theories: institutional logics (Thornton, Ocasio, & Lounsbury, 2012); institutional work (Lawrence, Suddaby, & Leca, 2009)
keywords: corporate social responsibility; global supply chains; institutional logics; institutional work; labor standards; market logic; responsible management
research_question: To what extent can multinational corporations address societal challenges through voluntary CSR, and how can firm- and field-level actors overcome the systemic constraints of the dominant market logic to institutionalize the emerging logic of responsible management?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: tension between the emerging responsible management logic and the highly institutionalized market logic; the "market-protected space" as an institutionally bound space that suspends the dominance of the market logic on selected issues.
- Approaches identified: (a) prioritizing the market logic, (b) accommodating responsible management within the market logic, and (c) prioritizing responsible management in market-protected spaces.
- Institutional work (process): restraining the jurisdiction of the market logic; infusing the responsible management logic with nonmarket elements; maintaining market-protected spaces against resistance.
- Boundary conditions: construction relies on pre-institutionalized market-constraining actors (e.g., trade unions) to act as legal representatives of rights holders; spaces are fragile, contested, and require continuous maintenance.

Through three interlocking forms of institutional work, firm- and field-level actors jointly construct a binding institutional infrastructure that brackets the market logic on selected issues (e.g., fire/building safety, living wages) so that responsible management can be prioritized rather than merely accommodated. The authors theorize this as a multilevel mechanism for institutionalizing an emerging logic within a field dominated by a highly institutionalized rival logic, framed as cyclical embedding and disembedding of the market (Polanyi) rather than linear progress.
data_measures:
- Firm-level corpus: at least two semi-structured interviews per firm across the 20 German and UK apparel retailers and brands — 20 with CSR managers (782 pages of transcript) and 20 with purchasing managers (405 pages) — conducted between March 2016 and August 2018, plus 13 follow-up interviews (69 pages) covering 13 firms in 2018–2019; 83 firm communication documents (corporate, sustainability and progress reports, supplier codes of conduct, responsible purchasing and human rights policies, modern slavery statements) plus corporate website content and press releases.
- Field-level corpus: 40 formal stakeholder interviews (743 pages) with trade unions, NGOs, industry experts, investors, legal experts, government representatives and importers, plus 33 informal talks, collected 2015–2019; notes from 63 industry events (430 pages) attended between 2016 and 2019; and 230 newsletters (210 pages of text) systematically collected from the UK Ethical Trading Initiative and the German Textile Partnership.
- Coding of the focal constructs: an inductive process moving iteratively between data, emerging themes and academic literature (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013; Locke, 2001; Strauss & Corbin, 1998). Field material was first read closely to build a timeline of key events. Firm-level interviews and CSR-related firm documents were then coded in the actors' own terms as in vivo codes — capturing the aims of their responsibility efforts, to whom they attributed responsibility for labor standards, and where they saw the locus of intervention — which were grouped into first-order concepts, then second-order themes, then three aggregate dimensions corresponding to the three approaches (Figure 1). Several rounds of coding used NVivo plus coding in tables.
- Second analytic stage: with the construction of market-protected spaces identified as the core phenomenon, the authors zoomed into data from responsibility-prioritizing firms, added the entire field-level dataset, and related second-order codes to one another to specify conditions and actors, core mechanism, and consequences, connecting these to the institutional-logics dimensions of Thornton and Ocasio (2008) and Thornton et al. (2012).
- Identification: no causal-identification strategy is claimed and none is used. The design is interpretive and inductive, theorizing a process from qualitative data rather than estimating effects. Interview data were triangulated against documentary evidence, NGO studies and news coverage, and initial findings were tested at stakeholder workshops in Berlin, Geneva, Oslo and Dhaka and with the ILO Better Work program.
key_findings:
- Three approaches by which MNCs addressed responsible management demands were apparent in the data, differing in the meaning given to each logic and in organization- and field-level structures and practices: (a) prioritizing the market logic — deflecting responsibility, baseline CSR standards and minimum supplier compliance, joining business-led initiatives and lobbying against binding regulation; (b) accommodating responsible management within the market logic — acknowledging responsibility, formalizing CSR procedures (CSR veto rights on supplier onboarding, CSR information systems, win-win investments), and supporting voluntary industry standards and MSIs; (c) prioritizing responsible management in market-protected spaces — redefining labor standards as "pre-competitive", changing core business practices (notably responsibility-focused KPIs for purchasing staff), and developing a binding institutional infrastructure through lobbying for stricter regulation and forging sectoral agreements with unions.
- The pattern across firms is skewed rather than uniform: the first two approaches were pursued by the majority of firms and only a small number pursued the third; within that group, responsibility-focused purchasing KPIs were practiced by only a handful even of the most advanced firms. Only the third approach counts as an attempt to institutionalize responsible management as separate from the market logic. All market-prioritizing firms in the sample were based in Germany and were members of the Business Social Compliance Initiative (BSCI).
- Two field initiatives are the paper's prime examples of market-protected spaces: the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh (2013, signed by over 200 mostly European MNCs and the global union federations IndustriALL and UNI) and ACT (2015). Their "bindingness" rests on union enforcement — for the Accord, a multistage grievance procedure ending in final and binding arbitration — which prevents signatories from undercutting one another on safety.
- Four enabling conditions were identified: the Rana Plaza collapse as a focusing event that shifted the basis of attention; the UNGPs creating a deepening "shadow of the law" and a new source of legitimacy beyond profit; strengthened market-restraining actors (global union federations, the ILO as independent chair, international human rights lawyers) becoming a new source of authority; and strengthened progressive CSR managers gaining new internal power and status. The focusing event alone was not sufficient — contestation, including union threats of public campaigns, was required to push reluctant firms to accept union involvement and sign the Accord.
- The construction of market-protected spaces ran through three forms of institutional work: restraining the jurisdiction of the market logic (a new meaning of responsible management prompting a search for alternative templates, found in binding sectoral agreements); infusing the responsible management logic with nonmarket elements (a binding institutional infrastructure providing a new basis of norms and strategy, and changed core business practices providing alternative formal and informal control mechanisms such as supplier-list transparency and responsibility-focused purchasing KPIs); and maintaining the spaces against resistance.
- Resistance was persistent and the spaces proved fragile: German business associations lobbied aggressively against due diligence legislation, BSCI initially withheld any recommendation that members join the Accord, and the BGMEA opposed extending the Accord beyond its five-year mandate, with the Accord's presence in Bangladesh subsequently challenged in the courts. This pushback strengthened firm-level actors sceptical of the responsibility agenda, so responsible management continued to be resisted even inside responsibility-prioritizing firms, whose CSR managers feared that without continued maintenance work the spaces "might simply fall back to business as usual".
- The authors are explicit about the limit of what they observed: field-level transformation requires time, and they state they were not able to fully observe the downstream institutionalization effect in their data, seeing only the "seeds" of institutionalization from which nonmarket dimensions of the responsible management logic could eventually diffuse. They likewise conclude that catastrophic events such as Rana Plaza do not, on their own, catalyze a change in dominant logics.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by specifying an alternative way to address tensions between conflicting institutional logics when one logic (the market) is highly institutionalized and dominant. It advances the concept of a "market-protected space" held in place by a binding institutional infrastructure as a distinct alternative to voluntary CSR, and theorizes the multilevel institutional work required to construct and maintain such spaces, informing debates on the limits of CSR.
practical_implication: Binding sectoral agreements—rather than the proliferation of small-scale voluntary projects—can restrain the market in ways that materially benefit peripheral stakeholders such as workers. Firms must align internal incentives (e.g., purchasing managers' KPIs) with responsible management demands, and policy-makers should strengthen market-restraining actors and provide binding regulation, since catastrophic events alone do not shift dominant logics.
limitations: The study examines only one issue (labor standards) in one industry (apparel), so the observed dynamics may be context-specific and not immediately transferable to other grand challenges. The market-protected spaces studied were temporary and fragile, leaving open how the institutional work can scale and stabilize beyond these spaces.
future_research: The authors call for comparative studies of market-protected spaces across grand challenges (e.g., environmental issues), examining which stakeholders can become key allies in restraining the market. Further work could analyze the multilevel political struggles around creating and maintaining such spaces from an open-polity perspective, how practices diffuse from these spaces into organizations, and why firms adopt different approaches cross-nationally.
abstract: To what extent are multinational corporations able to address societal challenges through voluntary corporate social responsibility (CSR)? Based on an in-depth qualitative study of how apparel multinational corporations have addressed labor standards violations since the deadly 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse, we show how CSR managers navigate the tension between the emerging responsible management logic and the highly institutionalized market logic, revealing how some go beyond accommodating responsible management within the market by prioritizing responsible management in market-protected spaces. We theorize the construction of market-protected spaces as a multilevel mechanism for institutionalizing an emerging logic in the context of a field dominated by the market logic via three forms of institutional work: restraining the jurisdiction of the market logic, infusing the responsible management logic with nonmarket elements, and maintaining market-protected spaces against resistance. A “marketprotected space” is an institutionally bound space that suspends the dominance of the market logic on selected issues based on a binding institutional infrastructure that allows prioritizing responsible management—unlike voluntary CSR, which still prioritizes the market logic. The concept of a market-protected space maps a path for policy-makers, managers, and other actors interested in institutionalizing responsible management in the global economy.

title: Publishing Multimethod Research in AMJ: A Review and Best-Practice Recommendations
methods: Editorial (From the Editors). Structured review of all 238 articles published in AMJ between 2020 and the present, classifying the 60 multimethod papers into five design archetypes, followed by editor-observed pitfalls and best-practice recommendations.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Wellman, Ned; Tröster, Christian; Grimes, Matthew; Roberson, Quinetta; Rink, Floor; Gruber, Marc
theories: Methodological fit (Edmondson & McManus, 2007); Scientific reasoning (deduction vs. induction)
keywords: deductive reasoning; inductive reasoning; methodological fit; methodological triangulation; multimethod research; theoretical contribution
research_question: How can authors capitalize on the benefits of multimethod research—the use of more than one methodology in a single research project—while surmounting its limitations and meeting AMJ's publishing standards? The editorial asks what archetypes of multimethod work currently appear in AMJ, what pitfalls undermine such submissions, and how authors can enhance the boldness and rigor of multimethod designs.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Building blocks: two forms of scientific reasoning, deduction (applying established principles via syllogistic argument to derive testable conclusions) and induction (moving from empirical experience toward theory), which methods orient toward but rarely conform to exclusively.
- Five archetypes (from a review of 60 multimethod papers): methodological triangulation for hypothesis testing (45/60, 75%), methodological triangulation for theory development (2/60, 3%), test and explore (5/60, 8%), explore and test (5/60, 8%), and full research cycle (3/60, 5%).
- Common pitfalls: (1) poor justification for mixing methods, (2) poor "methodological fit" between a method and the maturity of the relevant theory, and (3) poor theoretical complementarity between studies.
- Recommendations: employ less common archetypes, explain why and how methods are combined, ensure theoretical and operational alignment, and use appendices/online supplements thoughtfully.

The editorial argues that more methods are not inherently better: value arises only when multiple methods are integrated so the end product exceeds the sum of its qualitative and quantitative parts. Because the field is heavily skewed toward triangulation for hypothesis testing, the authors contend that groundbreaking theoretical contributions are more likely to emerge from the rarer inductive–deductive combinations (test and explore, explore and test, full research cycle), and that fit between method and theory maturity governs whether a multimethod design pays off.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The editorial provides a field-level taxonomy of five multimethod design archetypes in AMJ and reframes the value of multimethod work around theoretical contribution rather than methodological multiplicity. It positions "methodological fit" and "theoretical complementarity" as the conditions under which combining methods generates new theory, rather than redundant or fishing-expedition findings.
practical_implication: Authors are advised to justify their choice of methods early, align studies theoretically and operationally (including explicit aggregation logic for meso designs), "storyboard" projects around rising action, climax, and falling action, partner with coauthors of complementary methodological expertise, and move non-central material to appendices or online supplements.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editorial encourages authors to adopt the less common inductive–deductive archetypes (test and explore, explore and test, and the full research cycle) to increase the theoretical boldness of their submissions, noting these designs are underused partly because few researchers possess expertise in both inductive and deductive methods.

title: When People Build Networks That Hurt Their Performance: Structural Holes, Cognitive Style, and the Unintended Consequences of Person–Network Fit
methods: Randomized longitudinal field experiment over a 2.5-year project in one business unit; a full-day executive-education treatment provided exogenous opportunities to form bridging ties. Two-stage analysis using panel regressions with individual random effects, and an instrumental-variable approach (treatment as instrument for network constraint) to identify performance effects. Cognitive style measured with the Kirton adaption–innovation inventory; innovative performance rated by supervisors at four time points.
industry: Semiconductor design and manufacturing (a business unit that designs, develops, and produces prototypes of innovative semiconductor components)
time_period: 2.5-year research project; networks and performance measured at four time points spanning roughly 13 months before to 7 months after the treatment
units: Employees of a single business unit of a global semiconductor company
n_sample: 172–187 employees tracked across waves; 74 invited to the treatment and 102 to the control group
authors: Carnabuci, Gianluca; Quintane, Eric
theories: adaption–innovation theory of cognitive style (Kirton); complementary versus supplementary person–network fit; social capital theory; structural holes / brokerage theory (Burt)
keywords: adaptors and innovators; cognitive style; innovative performance; network brokerage; person–network fit; structural holes
research_question: Do people build the network structure in which they perform best? Specifically, are adaptors more likely than are innovators to build bridging relationships across structural holes, even though brokerage benefits adaptors' performance more than innovators'?
hypotheses:
- H1 (baseline hypothesis; stage 2): The more adaptive (innovative) an individual's cognitive style, the more (less) building bridging relations across structural holes will enhance his or her innovative performance.
- H2 (main hypothesis; stage 1): The more adaptive (innovative) an individual's cognitive style, the less (more) likely he or she is to build bridging relations across structural holes.
mechanism_summary: The paper advances a two-stage person–network fit model. People perform best in networks that "complement" (combine productively with) their cognitive style, but they tend to build networks that "supplement" (align with and reinforce) their cognitive style. Because adaptors prefer well-defined, consensus-based, stable interactions, they avoid forming the bridging ties across structural holes that would most benefit their idea-implementation strengths; innovators, who gain little from brokerage, nonetheless keep building ever-new bridging relations. When complementary and supplementary fit are misaligned, people build networks that detract from rather than enhance their performance.
data_measures: Data come from a 2.5-year research project in the Italian business unit of a global semiconductor company (roughly 170 employees, 13 functional departments, five hierarchical levels), combining about 30 months of field observation and 25 half-hour interviews with four online survey waves at Time 1 (13 months before the treatment), Time 2 (six months before), Time 3 (one month after) and Time 4 (seven months after), plus a Time 1' mini-wave collecting time-invariant traits. Treated is a binary variable coded 1 if the employee took part in the full-day executive-education intervention. Network constraint, the stage 1 dependent variable and the stage 2 explanatory variable, is Burt's (1992: 62–64) constraint computed on the valued information-exchange network at each wave (roster-based single name generator with a 1–4 frequency name interpreter), where higher values indicate fewer bridging relations across structural holes; the natural logarithm of constraint is used in the analyses. Innovative performance is the average of the innovation-dimension items of Welbourne, Johnson, and Erez's (1998) performance scale, rated by each employee's direct supervisor at every wave, translated and back-translated into Italian, and demeaned at the supervisor level to absorb supervisor-level rating heterogeneity. Cognitive style is the Italian version (Prato Previde, 1991) of Kirton's (1976) adaption–innovation inventory, 33 items rated from 1 (very hard) to 4 (very easy) (Cronbach's alpha = .80), where high values indicate innovators and low values adaptors (observed range 45–95, mean about 75, SD 9.2); it is mean-centered before the multiplicative terms are constructed. Balance-check and control variables include departmental dummies (the reported models control for manufacturing), tenure, hierarchical rank, gender, network size, and self-monitoring. Identification rests on the paper's randomized longitudinal field experiment: employees were allocated by disproportionate stratified random assignment at the department level, with 74 invited to the treatment and 102 to the control group (44 actually attended). Estimation uses random-effects panel regressions with standard errors clustered around departments; individual fixed effects are not possible because treated and control groups do not change over time. Model 4 is a random-effects instrumental-variable panel regression using treated as an instrument for post-treatment constraint and for its interaction with cognitive style, and an intention-to-treat correction (invitation to the treatment as an instrument for actual treatment) handles the 33 noncompliers and three always-takers. The authors report that the instrument set is strong for constraint but weak for the constraint x cognitive style interaction (Sanderson–Windmeijer F = 1.67) and add a LIML estimator as a robustness check. Analytic samples are 268 observations (Model 1), 209 (Model 2) and 180 (Models 3 and 4).
key_findings: The randomized treatment worked as intended: Model 1 shows a negative and significant effect of treatment on post-treatment constraint (b = -0.05, SE = 0.03), mean post-treatment constraint was 0.27 (SD 0.16) in the treatment group versus 0.35 (SD 0.18) in the control group (t test of the difference in means, p = .002), treated employees' networks were over 20% more brokering, and treated employees formed on average 2.6 more new bridging ties one month after the intervention and three more after seven months. Stage 1 (H2) is supported: the Treated x Cognitive style (innovator) interaction is negative and highly significant for post-treatment constraint (b = -0.05, SE = 0.02), so that given the same set of bridge-formation opportunities adaptors were significantly less likely than innovators to leverage them. Predictive margins show that treated and untreated adaptors (one SD below the mean) had statistically indistinguishable post-treatment constraint, whereas treated innovators (one SD above the mean) reduced their constraint by about one third relative to control innovators; descriptively, adaptors created an average of 2.5 new bridging ties against 7.4 for innovators. Stage 2 (H1) is supported, but only at the 10% level: the Cognitive style (innovator) x Constraint interaction on innovative performance is positive both in the random-effects panel model (b = 0.14, SE = 0.08, p < .10) and in the instrumental-variable model (b = 0.43, SE = 0.26, reported p = .071), while the constraint main effect is negative (b = -0.12, SE = 0.06 in Model 3; b = -0.36, SE = 0.17 in Model 4). Because higher constraint means fewer bridging ties, the positive interaction means adaptors' performance benefits from bridging structural holes while innovators draw no or even negative returns: a markedly adaptive employee (two SD below the mean) moving from a highly constrained to a highly brokering network is predicted to gain nearly 60% in innovative performance (from 2.74 to 4.35 on a 1-to-5 scale), and a slightly adaptive one (one SD below) gains 16% (3.41 to 3.81), whereas for an innovator one SD above the mean the same shift has hardly any effect (3.56 to 3.53) and for one two SD above the mean it lowers performance by 16% (from 3.85 to 3.23). Robustness checks using all 12 department dummies, two-way clustering, the intention-to-treat correction, a fully interacted stratification model, and lagged dependent-variable specifications are consistent in direction and significance, with the exception that the treatment x cognitive style interaction loses significance when all departments are controlled for (b = -0.04, SE = 0.02, p = .10).
theoretical_contribution: The study extends the cognitive-microfoundations stream of network theory by showing that cognitive style shapes the brokerage–performance relationship in a more complex, counterintuitive way than prior contingency accounts: it governs not only who benefits from structural holes but also who builds them, and the two are misaligned. By integrating network formation and network performance within a single explanatory framework, it explains why large numbers of employees build networks that are not good for their performance, contributing to both structural-holes and person–environment fit research.
practical_implication: Organizations investing in network-building interventions should tailor them to employees' cognitive styles rather than encouraging brokerage uniformly. Adaptors should be helped to bridge structural holes (which they avoid but benefit from), whereas innovators are better served by deepening cohesive networks optimized for idea implementation; even a single day of executive education can shift employees' network positions.
limitations: Evidence is from a single business unit of one semiconductor company in Italy, which may limit generalizability across settings and industries. Individual-level fixed effects could not be modeled because treatment varied between rather than within employees, so the design relies on random assignment and instrumental-variable estimation; noncompliance and always-takers required an intention-to-treat correction.
future_research: Future work could test the two-stage complementary-versus-supplementary fit model by replicating the analyses across other empirical settings and with other dimensions of person–network fit, and examine additional cognitive or dispositional traits that drive how people build networks misaligned with their own performance.
abstract: Extant research shows that individual cognitive style affects whether employees benefit most from a brokering or a dense network. But do people build the network structure in which they perform best? We address this question by advancing a novel two-stage explanatory model that explicitly disentangles the network formation process from its performance effects. We hypothesize that "adaptors" (i.e., individuals inclined to focus on implementable solutions through commonly accepted and well-defined approaches) perform best when their network spans structural holes. Yet, these same individuals systematically forego opportunities to build relations across structural holes. By contrast, "innovators" (i.e., individuals inclined to focus on envisioning creative solutions that break away with established approaches) draw no or even negative performance returns from structural holes. Nevertheless, their inclination is to build ever-new bridging relations. We test and find support for this counterintuitive hypothesis through a randomized longitudinal field experiment enabling us to disentangle empirically both stages of our theorized process model. Our findings help illuminate why people may build networks that hurt their performance, shed a new light on the role of individual cognitive style in shaping network advantage, and bear concrete implications for organizations aiming to leverage networks to enhance employees' performance.
