title: On the Plurality and Politics of Ally Work: Liberalism and Self, Relational, and Organizational Ally Work
methods: Multi-study, pre-registered survey design. Study 1 developed and validated a 23-item ally work scale (EFA, CFA, convergent/discriminant validity) across MTurk, Prolific, and Lucid samples. Studies 2-4 tested hypotheses using hierarchical linear regression with interaction terms; Study 4 was time-separated to address common method bias.
industry: Working adults across a diverse array of industries and occupations (mix of for-profit, plus undergraduate business students in Study 2a)
time_period: March 2021 - November 2021
units: Individual employees (and undergraduate business students)
n_sample: Hypothesis-testing studies total n = 1,076 working adults (Studies 2-4); plus additional scale-development samples in Study 1
authors: Dang, Carolyn T.; Joshi, Aparna
theories: perceived affordance theory (Gibson, 1979); self-classification / tripartite self theory (Brewer & Chen, 2007); theory of political ideology as motivated cognition (Jost et al., 2009)
keywords: ally work; diversity and inclusion; extra-role behavior; motivated cognition; perceived affordances; political ideology
research_question: What motivates employees in positions of relative social advantage to engage in ally work, and how does political ideology—filtered through contextual affordances—shape the distinct self, relational, and organizational modalities through which ally work is enacted within organizations?
hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1a. Political liberalism is positively related to self ally work.
Hypothesis 1b. Political liberalism is positively related to relational ally work.
Hypothesis 1c. Political liberalism is positively related to organizational ally work.
Hypothesis 2. The relationship between political liberalism and engagement in self ally work is strengthened when individuals perceive a higher (versus lower) degree of personal accountability for diversity efforts.
Hypothesis 3. The relationship between political liberalism and engagement in relational ally work is strengthened when individuals perceive colleague diversity as higher (versus lower).
Hypothesis 4. The relationship between political liberalism and engagement in organizational ally work is strengthened when individuals perceive that the organization is politically liberal (versus conservative).
mechanism_summary: The paper theorizes that political ideology operates as motivated cognition: a liberal (vs. conservative) ideology functions as a "higher-order want" and "perceptual filter" that leads advantaged employees to "see" their organizations as arenas of marginalization where progress requires challenging the status quo, motivating engagement across all three ally-work modalities. Perceived affordances act as a "push" that narrows liberals' choice set toward modality-specific action. Empirically, liberalism showed a consistent positive main effect on all three modalities, and perceived organizational liberalism amplified liberals' organizational ally work; however, the personal-accountability and colleague-diversity moderation hypotheses were not supported, and personal accountability instead promoted self work among more conservative-leaning employees.
data_measures:
Four studies of U.S. self-report survey data collected in 2021. Study 1 built the measure: an initial pool of 15 self, 15 relational, and 12 organizational items (1 = Never to 5 = Always) was sorted by 20 practitioners and scholars, reduced by principal axis factor analysis with varimax rotation in two online-panel samples (MTurk n = 303; Prolific n = 331) to a 23-item scale (7 self, 7 relational, 9 organizational), cross-validated by CFA in Mplus 8.1 on a Lucid sample (n = 596), and checked for convergent and discriminant validity on a Prolific sample (n = 189). The hypothesis tests used Study 2a (124 undergraduate business students), Study 2b (319 MTurk working adults), Study 3 (374 working adults recruited through online classified advertisements in 12 U.S. cities, cross-sectional), and Study 4 (263 working adults completing both waves; n = 259 in the reported regressions), recruited via a university listserv, social media, and classified advertisements in 30 U.S. cities.
- DV(s): self, relational, and organizational ally work, measured with Study 1's 23-item self-report scale (alphas .90-.96 across studies).
- IV: political ideology, a single-item self-placement on a 7-point liberal–conservative spectrum (1 = Very liberal to 7 = Very conservative), reverse-scored so that higher values signify greater liberalism.
- Moderators: personal accountability for diversity (single item on whether all employees are responsible for developing and implementing solutions to diversity issues, 1-5); colleague diversity (self-reported percentage of day-to-day colleagues in each of seven racial/ethnic, gender, and sexual-orientation categories, averaged into an index and log-transformed for the interaction term); perceived organizational political ideology (single item on the same 7-point liberal–conservative spectrum, reverse-scored).
- Controls: gender, race/ethnicity, LGBTQ+ status, social class (10-rung ladder), and managerial status. Studies 2a and 2b additionally entered social identity, personal benefit, collectivism, social dominance orientation, activism orientation, locus of control, and relative deprivation as competing predictors.

Estimation was hierarchical linear regression with political ideology entered in the last step, with interactions tested using the PROCESS Macro for SPSS (v.4, Model 1) with 5,000 resamples and probed with the Johnson–Neyman technique. Studies 2-4 were pre-registered. The design is associational: the paper claims no causal-identification strategy, and Study 4's four-week temporal separation of the Time 1 predictors from the Time 2 ally-work measures is presented as a remedy for common method bias rather than as identification.
key_findings:
Hypotheses 1a-1c were supported in each of the four hypothesis-testing samples: greater liberalism predicted higher engagement in all three modalities. Study 2a incremental variance was ΔR² = .14 for self (p < .001), .04 for relational (p = .002), and .10 for organizational work (p < .001); Study 2b, ΔR² = .04 (p < .001), .01 (p = .039), and .01 (p = .020). Study 3 coefficients were b = .15 for self (p < .001), .10 for relational (p = .001), and .12 for organizational work (p = .001); Study 4, b = .18 (p < .001), .08 (p = .019), and .16 (p < .001). Social dominance orientation was the only competing predictor in Studies 2a and 2b that also predicted ally work.

Hypothesis 2 was not supported in either study that tested it. The political ideology x personal accountability interaction was significant but negative, opposite to the prediction (Study 3 b = -.07, p = .003; Study 4 b = -.07, p = .011): the positive effect of liberalism on self work declined as personal accountability rose and became nonsignificant at higher levels of accountability (above 4.11 in Study 3, above 4.12 in Study 4). Personal accountability's positive effect on self work was instead strongest among moderately-to-less-liberal and conservative-leaning employees and nonsignificant among polarized liberals.

Hypothesis 3 was not supported, and the pattern was discrepant across the two studies that tested it. In Study 3 the political ideology x colleague diversity interaction was significant and negative (b = -.13, p = .001): liberalism's positive effect on relational work weakened as colleague diversity increased and became nonsignificant above 3.34, the reverse of the prediction. In Study 4 the same interaction was nonsignificant with the log-transformed measure (b = .07, p = .062) and significant only with the untransformed measure (b = -.003, p = .033); the paper reports that when graphed this pattern differed from Study 3 and instead matched the hypothesis, with liberalism's positive effect on relational work strongest at higher colleague diversity (above 2.81).

Hypothesis 4 was supported and replicated. The political ideology x organizational ideology interaction was positive and significant in Study 3 (b = .06, p = .004) and Study 4 (b = .07, p = .002): the positive effect of liberalism on organizational ally work became increasingly positive as perceived organizational liberalism rose (above 3.47 in Study 3, above 3.14 in Study 4). Among the least liberal employees (below 2.40 in Study 3, below 3.39 in Study 4), higher perceived organizational liberalism was associated with a decline in organizational ally work.

Robustness checks left the results unchanged when controls were omitted, and the non-hypothesized affordance-by-ideology interactions were nonsignificant in both Studies 3 and 4. In Study 4, adding openness to experience and moral-foundations covariates left liberalism's effect significant for self (b = .15, p < .001) and organizational work (b = .14, p = .001) but rendered its effect on relational work nonsignificant (b = .06, p = .092).
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances a pluralistic tripartite framework that disaggregates ally work into self, relational, and organizational modalities operating at different levels of the social self, and develops a validated measure of these constructs. It identifies political ideology-as-motivated-cognition as a general motivational mechanism for ally work that is portable across multiple intersecting social categories, moving beyond prior identity-specific or social-identity-based accounts. By introducing perceived affordances, it shows how organizational context conditions—and sometimes reverses—the behavioral expression of ideology.
practical_implication: Managers can encourage allyship by creating affordances tailored to specific modalities (e.g., signaling organizational openness to structural change to elicit organizational ally work). Because self work is relatively accessible and self-focused, affording personal accountability can engage even conservative-leaning or politically ambivalent employees in self-directed change. Where employees resist organizational ally work, leaders are advised to move cautiously and use subtler messaging.
limitations: Ally work was assessed only from the focal employee's self-reports, raising questions about whether liberals are "aspirational allies" whose self-reported ally work aligns with observers' reports. The colleague-diversity hypothesis yielded discrepant patterns, suggesting unmeasured moderators the data could not test; the authors call for further research into how task interdependence and other job characteristics shape these effects.
future_research: Future work should examine how organizational factors such as leadership and culture might offset exogenous political influences on discretionary diversity behaviors, and study ally work within specific identity relations and from beneficiaries' perspectives. Researchers could investigate when it is useful to combine versus distinguish the three modalities, the strong self–organizational correlation, and the political ramifications and potential polarization effects that ally work may produce.
abstract: We theorize that ally work (actions by employees belonging to advantaged social groups to support employees belonging to disadvantaged social groups) can be organized into three modalities: self ally work that is oriented toward developing skills and capabilities, relational ally work that is focused on building positive work relationships, and organizational ally work aimed at changing organizational practices to support disadvantaged coworkers. Drawing from the theory of political ideology as motivated cognition, across multiple pre-registered field studies we found that employees who were more liberal-leaning (vs. conservative-leaning) reported higher engagement in all three modalities. We also examined whether contextual affordances amplified the liberalism effect. Specifically, we tested whether personal accountability for diversity, colleague diversity, and organizational ideology directed liberals toward greater engagement in self, relational, and organizational work, respectively. As hypothesized, more liberal-leaning employees reported higher engagement in organizational ally work in more ideologically liberal organizations. However, the hypothesized effects of personal accountability were not supported. Notably, personal accountability had a positive effect on self ally work among more conservative-leaning employees. The moderating effects of colleague diversity were also mixed across studies. Highlighting both the plurality and politics of ally work, we discuss theoretical and practical implications of our findings.

title: Positioning Research on Novel Phenomena: The Winding Road From Periphery to Core
methods: Editorial (From the Editors); develops a core–periphery conceptual framework and a four-scenario typology to guide authors in positioning research on novel phenomena.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Dencker, John C.; Gruber, Marc; Miller, Toyah; Rouse, Elizabeth D.; von Krogh, Georg
theories: core-periphery knowledge structures (Lyles & Schwenk, 2000; Borgatti & Everett, 2000); legitimate distinctiveness / optimal distinctiveness (Navis & Glynn, 2011)
keywords: core-periphery structure; incremental novelty; legitimacy; method alignment; novel phenomena; novelty; positioning research; radical novelty; theory elaboration
research_question: Not reported in paper
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: A key priority of the 2023–2025 AMJ editorial term is to publish research on novel phenomena — "regularities that are unexpected, that challenge existing knowledge ... and that are relevant to scientific discourse" — yet such research is risky because all novelty starts at the periphery and must be connected to, and legitimized through, a field's core conventional knowledge.
- Key constructs: Core vs. periphery of a field's knowledge structure; novelty and legitimacy; positioning; the review process as a legitimacy-conferring interaction between authors, reviewers, and editors.
- Typology of four scenarios (Figure 1), defined by whether the peripheral/novel element resides only in the phenomenon or also in the theory and/or methods:
  - Incremental Novelty: phenomenon is peripheral; theory and methods are core. Strategy — justify the importance of the novel phenomenon and show how knowledge advances significantly.
  - Method Alignment: phenomenon and methods are peripheral; theory is core. Strategy — justify why the novel method is needed, connect it to core methods used in other fields, and show it fulfills a need core methods cannot.
  - Theory Elaboration: phenomenon and theory are peripheral; methods are core. Strategy — make a compelling case for the inadequacy of the core theory and a clear connection to core theories, especially when the novel theory recombines existing concepts.
  - Radical Novelty: phenomenon, theory, and methods all peripheral. Strategy — mitigate complexity by using core elements where possible and weigh the trade-off between parsimony and transparency.
- Boundary conditions: Complexity and risk rise as more elements move to the periphery; radical novelty is the most rewarding but the riskiest, and a single article may be unable to communicate all novel elements parsimoniously.

The editorial advances a normative, programmatic argument grounded in core–periphery knowledge structures: a field's core represents conventional, legitimate knowledge while the periphery is unconventional and only partly legitimate, and "all novel phenomena are peripheral, yet not all peripheral phenomena are novel." Because the core "defines what is feasible" and supplies selection criteria, authors must anchor novel elements to it, since "the core can serve as a legitimacy anchor" that is comprehensible and acceptable to the field. Positioning therefore involves striking a balance between the novel and the conventional and persuading reviewers and editors — who confer legitimacy through the review process — that the novelty makes an important, well-connected contribution.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not test a theory but stakes out an editorial position and a generative framework: it situates research on novel phenomena within a core–periphery structure and derives a four-scenario typology (incremental novelty, method alignment, theory elaboration, radical novelty) with scenario-specific positioning strategies. Its central idea is that novel phenomena are peripheral ideas that must be connected to a core conventional knowledge set and legitimized through interactions between authors, reviewers, and editors, offering authors and gatekeepers a shared vocabulary for diagnosing where a study's novelty lies and how to legitimize it.
practical_implication: Authors are advised to identify precisely what is novel relative to the extant literature, validate the importance of the novel aspect, and connect peripheral elements (phenomenon, theory, methods) to core conventional knowledge as anchoring points. The editors recommend tailoring strategy to the scenario, considering a "portfolio approach" that mixes peripheral and core projects (especially for junior scholars facing promotion), and weighing whether all three dimensions need to be novel — including the option of separating theory from empirics or targeting a better-fit outlet such as AMR or Academy of Management Discoveries. Reviewers and editors are urged to guard against institutional gatekeeping that goes beyond legitimate critique of logic and ideas.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: As editors, the team commits to seeking out and developing research on novel phenomena during transformational times, to watching for institutional gatekeeping, and to minimizing the risk inherent in studying novelty. They encourage authors to engage in such research despite low base rates of publication success, anticipating that artificial intelligence (von Krogh et al., 2023) and attention to transformational times (Gruber, 2023) can help authors recognize and position novel research opportunities.

title: Hierarchical Team Structures Limit Joint Gain in Interteam Negotiations: The Role of Information Elaboration and Value-Claiming Behavior
methods: Four experimental negotiation studies (between-teams designs) with interactive team-on-team negotiations; manipulation checks via one-way ANOVA, and mediation/serial-mediation tested with PROCESS bootstrapping; Study 4 uses a moderation-of-process design manipulating information elaboration.
industry: Business negotiation simulations completed by MBA and undergraduate business students
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Negotiating teams nested within team-on-team negotiation groups
n_sample: Study 1: 318 MBA students; Study 2: 990 undergraduates; Study 3: 368 undergraduates (164 teams); Study 4: 623 undergraduates (282 teams)
authors: Doyle, Sarah P.; Chung, Seunghoo; Lount, Robert B., Jr.; Swaab, Roderick I.; Rathjens, Jake
theories: fixed-pie bias in negotiation (De Dreu, 2003); information elaboration / information processing in teams (Van Knippenberg et al., 2004); intrateam hierarchy (Greer et al., 2018; Magee & Galinsky, 2008)
keywords: fixed-pie bias; hierarchical team structures; information elaboration; interteam negotiation; joint gain; value-claiming behavior
research_question: When and why do formal hierarchical structures within negotiation teams shape a team's ability to maximize joint gain in negotiations between teams that have integrative potential?
hypotheses:
- H1: Negotiations between two teams with formal hierarchical structures will result in lower joint gain as compared to negotiations between two teams with egalitarian structures.
- H2: The negative relationship between hierarchical team structures and joint gain will be mediated by intrateam information elaboration.
- H3: The negative relationship between hierarchical team structures and joint gain will be serially mediated by intrateam information elaboration and the use of value-claiming behaviors.
mechanism_summary: Formal intrateam hierarchy restricts the free flow and exchange of information within teams, reducing intrateam information elaboration. Lower elaboration reinforces the "fixed-pie" assumption that one party's gain is the other's loss, which fosters competitive value-claiming behavior between teams and ultimately lowers joint gain. Study 4's manipulation of information elaboration shows that providing elaboration instructions attenuates the harmful effect of hierarchy, supporting the proposed causal role of the elaboration-then-value-claiming pathway.
data_measures:
Four randomized between-teams experiments with interactive team-on-team negotiations. Hierarchy was manipulated with written instructions telling teams either to designate one leader with decision-making authority over team decisions or to share leadership and influence equally, and was checked with three self-report items on equal power, influence, and leadership (α = .91–.94).
- Study 1: 318 MBA students (156 teams, 78 negotiation groups) negotiating the Cartoon multi-issue simulation; hierarchy (40 groups) vs. egalitarian (38 groups), with leaders self-selected by the team. Joint gain was calculated by aggregating the profit both parties earned from the agreement (maximum $5,080,000).
- Study 2: 990 undergraduates (949 retained; 390 teams, 195 negotiation groups) negotiating The Sweet Shop; hierarchy (63 groups), egalitarian (66), a control condition given no structure instructions (66), and a solo-vs-solo condition (70), with leaders randomly assigned. Joint gain = points summed across both teams (maximum 21,000). Intrateam information elaboration was coded from the video recordings by four assistants blind to hypotheses and condition, using five items reflecting behaviors identified in Van Ginkel and Van Knippenberg (2008) on a 5-point scale (α = .71); interteam value-claiming behavior was coded from the same videos by six different assistants on three items (α = .88).
- Study 3: 368 undergraduates (164 teams, 82 negotiation groups); hierarchy (27 groups), egalitarian (26), and blended (29, one hierarchical and one egalitarian team), with leaders self-selected. Information elaboration was video-coded with the Study 2 items (α = .72); value claiming was coded from written transcripts using the system of Weingart, Olekalns, and Smith (2004) and scored as the proportion of a team's statements that were value-claiming (Cohen's κ = .814).
- Study 4: 623 undergraduates (282 teams, 141 negotiation groups) negotiating The Player online via Zoom during the Covid-19 pandemic, in a 2 (team structure: hierarchy vs. egalitarian) × 2 (information elaboration instructions: yes vs. no) between-teams design. Joint gain = points summed across five issues (maximum 14,400); value claiming was video-coded with the Study 2 items (α = .81).

Team-level measures were aggregated to the negotiation group level before analysis. Mediation and serial mediation were estimated with PROCESS Models 4 and 6 using contrast codes, 5,000 bootstraps, and 95% confidence intervals; Study 4 used PROCESS Model 7 for moderated mediation. Random assignment identifies the effect of the hierarchy manipulation, but the paper states plainly that the relationship among information elaboration, value-claiming behavior, and joint gain is correlational in Studies 2 and 3 and limits causal inference; Study 4's moderation-of-process design (Spencer, Zanna, & Fong, 2005), which manipulates information elaboration directly, is the paper's basis for a stronger causal claim about the mediator.
key_findings:
H1 was supported in Studies 1–3 and held in Study 4 as a main effect that was qualified by the elaboration-instructions manipulation. Study 1: hierarchical negotiations achieved lower joint gain (M = 4,272,054.71, SD = 695,025.74) than egalitarian ones (M = 4,606,335.53, SD = 430,731.55), F(1, 75) = 6.40, p = .014, d = 0.58. Study 2: hierarchy (M = 16,674.60) was below egalitarian (M = 17,280.30), t(260) = 2.42, p = .016, d = 0.42, and below control (M = 17,393.94), t(260) = 2.88, p = .004, d = 0.50, while egalitarian and control did not differ; every team condition beat solo negotiators (M = 15,974.64), but the team advantage was 46% smaller when teams had a formal hierarchy. Study 3: hierarchy (M = 16,574.07) was below egalitarian (M = 17,826.92), t(79) = 2.36, p = .021, d = 0.69, and the blended condition (M = 16,672.41) also fell below egalitarian, t(79) = 2.21, p = .030, d = 0.61, without differing from hierarchy, indicating that one hierarchical team was sufficient to limit joint gain. Study 4: a significant main effect of team hierarchy on joint gain, F(1, 137) = 4.48, p = .036, alongside a significant hierarchy × instructions interaction, F(1, 137) = 10.98, p = .001.

H2 was supported in the two studies that tested it directly. Study 2: significant indirect effect of hierarchy on joint gain through intrateam information elaboration (effect = −385.55, 95% CI [−635.03, −178.86]); hierarchy lowered elaboration (b = −0.36, SE = 0.09, p < .001) and elaboration raised joint gain (b = 1,081.94, SE = 218.45, p < .001), with the direct effect no longer significant (b = −168.62, p = .532). Study 3: indirect effect = −369.56, 95% CI [−940.20, −38.56]; hierarchy lowered elaboration (b = −0.41, SE = 0.13, p = .003) and elaboration raised joint gain (b = 895.05, SE = 437.23, p = .044), with the direct effect not significant (b = −883.29, p = .114).

H3 was likewise supported in Studies 2 and 3. Study 2 serial indirect effect = −57.06, 95% CI [−133.70, −8.21], with elaboration reducing value claiming (b = −0.39, SE = 0.10, p < .001) and value claiming reducing joint gain (b = −413.96, SE = 159.05, p = .010); hierarchical negotiations showed more value claiming than egalitarian ones (M = 3.23 vs. 2.91), t(188) = 2.63, p = .009, d = 0.44, though exploratory contrasts found no hierarchy–control difference on value claiming (p = .271). Study 3 serial indirect effect = −272.00, 95% CI [−610.04, −53.49], with elaboration reducing value claiming (b = −0.06, SE = 0.02, p = .003) and value claiming reducing joint gain (b = −11,696.69, SE = 2,397.32, p < .001).

Study 4 supported the proposed causal role of information elaboration, but conditionally. Without elaboration instructions, hierarchical negotiations achieved lower joint gain (M = 11,422.86) than egalitarian ones (M = 12,682.35), t(137) = 3.80, p < .001, d = 0.96, and displayed more value claiming (M = 3.23 vs. 2.81), t(135) = 3.02, p = .003, d = 0.83. With elaboration instructions the two structures no longer differed on joint gain (M = 12,402.78 vs. 12,125.00), t(137) = 0.86, p = .394, or on value claiming (M = 2.94 vs. 3.04), t(135) = 0.76, p = .451. The indirect effect of hierarchy on joint gain via value claiming was significant only in the no-instructions condition (effect = −267.20, 95% CI [−620.88, −39.09]) and not in the instructions condition (effect = 65.48, 95% CI [−80.16, 392.60]); index of moderated mediation = 332.67, 95% CI [23.21, 929.64]. In Study 4 the main effects of hierarchy and of elaboration instructions on value-claiming behavior were both nonsignificant (p = .106 and p = .723), the main effect of elaboration instructions on joint gain was nonsignificant, F(1, 137) = 0.83, p = .364, and the hierarchy manipulation did not significantly shift coded information elaboration, F(1, 135) = 2.98, p = .086.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends team-negotiation research—which had focused predominantly on the benefits of teams over solo negotiators and treated teams as monolithic—by theorizing how within-team hierarchy undermines intrateam information elaboration and interteam joint gain. It bridges the literatures on intrateam hierarchy and interteam collaboration, showing that formal hierarchies can harm value creation across teams (not just within them), and contributes to work on hierarchical dynamics in teams and on multiteam systems by identifying when and why teams leave valuable resources unused.
practical_implication: Contrary to the common advice from negotiation-training organizations that teams should appoint a single leader with decision-making authority, simply assigning members to leader and follower roles (or allowing self-selection) can inhibit information elaboration, promote competitive behavior between teams, and leave resources unused. Teams with leaders should deliberately take time to engage in information elaboration; egalitarian teams do not perform worse than competitive hierarchical counterparts, offering reassurance for sending more egalitarian teams to the table.
limitations: The studies used MBA and undergraduate student samples in simulated business negotiations, raising generalizability concerns relative to more-complex, hostility-laden real-world negotiations. Effects of hierarchical differentiation may be contingent on the leader's negotiation expertise. The team sizes studied were small, and findings may not extend to larger teams, to status (rather than formal) hierarchies, or to negotiations lacking integrative potential.
future_research: Future work could leverage real-world samples or more difficult-to-resolve negotiations with pre-existing hostilities, examine how leader expertise and leadership styles condition the effects, and study informal status hierarchies and alternative hierarchical shapes in larger teams. Researchers could also measure the fixed-pie bias more directly and examine how hierarchically structured teams perform across tasks with different coordination needs, including purely distributive (single-issue) settings.
abstract: Although teams of negotiators are widely assumed to be better at unlocking integrative solutions compared to individual negotiators, the interteam negotiation context is characterized by unique challenges that can make effective collaboration between teams difficult. We extend our theoretical understanding of interteam negotiations by offering novel insights about when and why teams realize their potential in integrative negotiations. Specifically, we propose a theoretical model that explains how hierarchical team structures reduce information elaboration within teams, which reinforces "fixed-pie" assumptions that prompt the reliance on value-claiming behaviors between teams and lower high-quality outcomes such as the joint gain achieved. Across four studies, each involving interactive team-on-team negotiations, we provide support for the hypothesized effects of formal intrateam hierarchies on joint gain, and test a useful intervention to mitigate the harmful effects of hierarchically structured teams at the negotiation table. Contributions to the literatures on team negotiations, interteam collaboration, and hierarchical differences within teams are discussed.

Hierarchical team structures limit joint gain in interteam negotiations: The role of information elaboration and value-claiming behavior. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(5), 1586–1616. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.1381

title: Signaling Diversity Debt: Startup Gender Composition and the Gender Gap in Joiners’ Interest
methods: Two studies. Study 1: field data from a job-matching mobile app; linear probability models (LPM) with robust standard errors clustered by job advertisement and job seeker, plus job-level fixed effects. Study 2: preregistered 2x2 (job seeker gender x diversity debt signal) between-subjects online experiment with mediation analysis (bootstrapped indirect effects).
industry: Tech/startup employers; jobs dominated by IT/engineering (39%) and marketing (21%) in Study 1; a simulated 'ScaleIT' startup profile in Study 2
country: Netherlands (Study 1 field data); United States (Study 2 experiment)
time_period: Platform activity 2015–2017 (Study 1)
units: Study 1: job seekers' interest decisions on job advertisements. Study 2: individual experiment participants (joiners)
n_sample: Study 1: 522,451 decisions by 8,340 job seekers across 1,978 job ads from 311 startups. Study 2: 597 participants
authors: Engel, Yuval; Lewis, Trey; Cardon, Melissa S.; Hentschel, Tanja
theories: identity threat (Kroeper et al., 2022; Murphy et al., 2007); lack of fit model (Heilman, 1983, 2012); signaling of employer information (Cable & Turban, 2001); tokenism (Kanter, 1977a, 1977b)
keywords: diversity debt; gender gap in interest; identity threat concerns; joiners; lack of fit; startup gender composition; tokenism
research_question: Why are women underrepresented among startup "joiners" (nonfounder employees), and how does information about a startup's existing gender composition—especially signals of "diversity debt"—shape the gender gap in joiners' interest in applying?
hypotheses:
H1: There is a gender gap in interest for startup jobs such that, all else equal, women joiners are less interested in applying than men joiners.
H2: Startup gender composition information moderates the gender gap in joiners' interest in applying; the proportion of women in a startup is positively associated with interest for women joiners while men joiners remain unaffected.
H3: Startup gender composition information moderates the indirect effect of joiner gender on interest in applying through identity threat concerns; when the proportion of women in a startup indicates diversity debt (vs. no diversity debt), identity threat concerns are triggered for women joiners but not for men joiners, and identity threat concerns are in turn negatively associated with joiners' interest (for both men and women).
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the lack of fit model, the paper argues that the masculine gender-typing of startups leads women joiners to form more negative fit expectations and lower interest than men (H1). Job seekers update these expectations using organizational gender composition as a signal, so a higher proportion of women raises women's (but not men's) interest (H2). At the extreme—when a skewed composition signals diversity debt (token representation)—tokenism logic predicts it triggers identity threat concerns in women, which mediate the link to lower interest, reproducing underrepresentation in a self-reinforcing vicious cycle (H3).
data_measures: Study 1 uses proprietary archival data from a job-matching mobile application for tech startups (platform activity 2015-2017; 97% of jobs posted in the Netherlands), covering 522,451 decisions by 8,340 job seekers on 1,978 job advertisements from 311 startups. DV: interest in applying, a binary variable capturing whether a job seeker pressed the "tick" (= 1) or the "cross" (= 0) on a viewed advertisement. IV: job seeker gender, coded algorithmically from first names using the genderize.io API with an 85% probability threshold (0 = man, 1 = woman). Moderator: company gender composition, the proportion of women employees that startups were required to report on every advertisement, scaled 0 (0% women) to 1 (100% women). Controls include a woman (co)founder, gender composition in the company background photo, industry gender composition, company size and age, average employee age, prior external investment, job title, job level, job commitment, net share of feminine wording, job seeker work experience, skills fit, language fit, weeks from posting to rating, and calendar year. Estimation: linear probability models with robust standard errors clustered simultaneously by job advertisement and job seeker, plus fixed effects models holding time-invariant job advertisement and job seeker characteristics constant, with a logit specification as a robustness check. Study 1 is observational, and the authors note that the control variables are unlikely to have a causal interpretation themselves; the mechanism is instead tested experimentally in Study 2. Study 2 is a preregistered 2 (job seeker gender: men, women; self-reported) x 2 (startup gender composition signal: diversity debt, no diversity debt; randomly assigned) between-subjects experiment with 597 Prolific participants residing in the United States, pre-screened for openness to startup employment. The manipulation varied only the gender composition line on an otherwise identical fictitious "ScaleIT" employer profile: 95% men/5% women versus 60% men/40% women. Primary DV: application intentions, Highhouse et al.'s (2003) 5-item scale (alpha = .89), with application decision and behavioral interest as binary secondary measures. Mediator: identity threat concerns, six items from Kroeper et al. (2022) rated 1 "not at all" to 5 "an extreme amount" (alpha = .95); anticipated fairness (alpha = .92) and perceived startup viability (alpha = .88) were measured as alternative mediators. Analysis: two-way ANOVAs plus a moderated mediation model with percentile bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals from 5,000 resamples.
key_findings: Study 1 supports H1 and H2. For H1, holding other factors constant, the probability of expressing interest in applying is about 3% lower for women than for men (Table 3, Model 2: b = -0.03, SE = 0.01), which the authors call sizeable against the 17% baseline interest rate. For H2, the interaction between job seeker gender and the proportional representation of women is positive and significant (b = 0.04, SE = 0.01, p < .001) and survives a fixed effects specification; the slope linking women's representation to interest is positive and significant for women (b = 0.05, SE = 0.01, p < .001) but not for men (b = 0.01, SE = 0.01, p = .612). Marginal effects show the gender gap reaching about 4% at 0-20% women and closing to statistical insignificance as representation approaches about 60% women. In exploratory robustness checks the quadratic term is not significant (no curvilinear effect), but using Kanter's categories women's predicted probability of interest is 12% when startups show 0-15% women versus 17% (15-35%), 15% (35-50%), and 17% (50-100%), and threshold analysis places a tipping point near 30% women; the authors flag these as exploratory and draw no strong conclusions. The H1 gap and the H2 moderation do not significantly vary between masculine, feminine, and gender-neutral industries. Study 2 supports H3 and replicates the moderation. Gender interacted significantly with the composition signal on identity threat concerns, F(1, 593) = 48.65, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .08, and on application intentions, F(1, 593) = 8.00, p = .005, partial eta-squared = .01. Under the diversity debt signal women reported higher identity threat concerns (M = 3.37, SD = 1.23 vs. M = 2.14, SD = 0.83; p < .001, d = 1.18) and lower application intentions (M = 3.18, SD = 1.05 vs. M = 3.81, SD = 0.63; p < .001, d = 0.74). Men showed no significant difference in identity threat concerns across conditions (M = 1.91, SD = 0.83 vs. M = 1.69, SD = 0.59; d = 0.29); their application intentions did differ significantly (M = 3.65, SD = 0.80 vs. M = 3.92, SD = 0.64; d = 0.37), a difference the paper describes as substantially smaller than the one observed for women. The negative indirect effect of job seeker gender on application intentions via identity threat concerns was significant in both conditions (no diversity debt: b = -0.18, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.26, -0.11]; diversity debt: b = -0.60, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.75, -0.46]) and significantly more negative under the diversity debt signal (index of moderated mediation = -0.42, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.56, -0.29]), so Hypothesis 3 is supported. Parallel models show the indirect effects via anticipated fairness and perceived startup viability are not conditional on the gender composition signal.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates a gender lens into research on "joiners," bringing together the lack of fit model, tokenism, and identity threat to explain the self-reinforcing role of organizational gender composition in women's startup underrepresentation. It extends the prior focus on founder–employee gender congruence by showing that organization-level gender composition—a signal of past hiring behavior—is a meaningful informational cue, and positions women's identity threat concerns as the primary mechanism linking diversity debt signals to lower interest, thereby reconciling mixed prior evidence on supply- and demand-side drivers of gender sorting.
practical_implication: Startups have an active role in shaping their own recruitment pipelines rather than attributing women's underrepresentation to a "pipeline problem." Because signaling diversity debt deters women through identity threat concerns, firms could counteract it with "identity safe cues"—for example, sincere text that explicitly recognizes the current lack of gender diversity alongside a concrete commitment to change, rather than generic diversity statements that can backfire.
limitations: Study 1 captures only initial expressions of interest, not whether applicants and companies reached a final employment agreement, and the reported gender composition was holistic (not broken down by job level) and of unverified accuracy. The Study 2 diversity debt manipulation (5% women) was deliberately strong, raising a possible (though mitigated) risk of demand effects.
future_research: Future work could test "identity safe cues" and other interventions to break diversity debt's self-reinforcing cycle, examine whether hiring women early indirectly improves later recruitment of women via signaling, and jointly study the perspectives of job seekers and startups (e.g., given evidence that startups prefer to hire male employees).
abstract: Women are underrepresented in startups, but research on “joiners”—nonfounder employees attracted to startup work—offers limited explanations for why such underrepresentation occurs and how it persists. We argue that, even among joiners, women are less interested than men in applying for startup jobs and that this gender gap is associated with differential reactions to information about the gender composition of prospective employers. We analyze unique field data obtained from a job-matching mobile-application platform for startups, finding the hypothesized gender gap and showing that women, but not men, are sensitive to information about organizational gender composition, especially for startups signaling “diversity debt”—that is, no or only a token representation of women. A preregistered experiment further reveals that women’s identity threat concerns mediate these effects. Gender disparities in startups are reproduced in a vicious cycle as existing underrepresentation deters women from applying. Our findings have implications for research and practice concerning joiners, the underrepresentation of women in entrepreneurship, and startups’ ability to shape the gender composition of their applicant pools.

title: Free to Be Me? Evolving Gender Expression and the Dynamic Interplay between Authenticity and the Desire to Be Accepted at Work
methods: Inductive narrative analysis (narrative inquiry) building theory from 100 semi-structured interviews with 25 transgender employees across four waves; iterative grounded-theory-style coding between literature and emergent themes.
industry: Wide range of occupations and sectors (construction, health care, education, consulting, creative industries) across public, private, and nonprofit organizations
time_period: Two-year period, four interview points at six-month intervals
units: Transgender employees (eight transwomen, seven transmen, eight genderqueer, two agender) undergoing a gender transition while employed
n_sample: 25 participants; 100 interviews total
authors: Hennekam, Sophie; Ladge, Jamie J.
theories: authenticity (Hewlin et al., 2020); gender performativity (Butler, 2009); identity transitions (Caza et al., 2018; George et al., 2022)
keywords: authenticity; gender expression; gender performativity; identity transitions; tempered gender expression; transgender employees
research_question: "How does authenticity evolve over time during a gender identity transition within a work context?" The study asks how transgender employees express, revise, and stabilize an authentic gender at work as they undergo a gender transition.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: a dynamic interplay between the desire to express a gender that feels authentic and the desire to feel accepted by others at work; "tempered gender expression" (softening typical masculine/feminine manifestations to balance acceptance with feeling "authentic enough").
- Process / phases: an evolving, nonlinear identity-transition journey in which psychological, physical, relational, and behavioral movements progress and regress at different speeds.
- Practices: a trial-and-error approach to gender performativity through which individuals learn what feels authentic as they perceive others' reactions.
- Emergent outcomes: an "authentic enough" gender expression treated as a compromise rather than a stable endpoint; authenticity reconceived as an ongoing continuum.

Authenticity is theorized not as alignment with an ex ante core self but as a relational, socially constructed process activated through feedback from workplace interactions. Transgender employees temper their gender expression in response to perceived gender norms, learning iteratively which expressions feel authentic and elicit acceptance, so that even after gaining acceptance the process of self-evaluation continues.
data_measures:
Data: 100 semi-structured narrative interviews with 25 transgender employees in the Netherlands, conducted at four points in time at six-month intervals over a two-year period. Thirty-one individuals participated in the first wave, 27 in the second, and 25 completed all four interviews. Participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling via moderators of online forums for the transgender community, received no compensation, and remained with the same employer throughout the study. Interviews averaged 75 minutes (range 45 to 140 minutes); 66 of the 100 were conducted via Skype and the rest face to face. All interviews were conducted in Dutch by one author and translated verbatim into English by two native English-Dutch speakers, and the interviewing author kept a research diary recording contextual cues such as tone and facial expressions.

Operationalization: transition stage was classified from each participant's own answer to the question asked at the beginning of every interview, "Where do you feel you are in your transition?" Answers such as "I'm only starting" were categorized as initiating, "somewhere in the middle" as performing, and "I feel I'm done for now" as continuing. Participants' self-described gender categories and pronouns (eight transwomen, seven transmen, eight genderqueer, two agender) were used as each participant described them rather than assigned by the researchers.

Analysis: Riessman's five-step approach to narrative inquiry (attending, telling, transcribing, analyzing, reading), woven with elements of grounded theory in which the authors iterated back and forth between common themes and the literature. Each participant's narrative was first reconstructed in short form across the four interviews; each author then independently open-coded a subset of 16 transcripts (the same four participants across four time periods), coding "narrative segments" that captured key turning points rather than each line of text, with disagreements resolved by returning to the transcripts. Second-order coding refined common themes by iterating between literature and data until no additional insights emerged, and the reading stage involved checking the initial interpretation back with each participant. The design is inductive and interpretive; the study builds theory from participants' narratives and claims no causal identification strategy.
key_findings:
The model traces gender expression and authenticity across three transition stages. In the initiating stage, participants expressed a provisional, imagined authentic gender at work, driven by three turning points: a sense of readiness gained by trialing possible selves in personal spheres, the realization that they needed to express their imagined authentic gender identity at work, and the desire to be seen by others at work as they saw themselves. All participants felt they needed to express what they envisioned as their authentic gender, and prioritized this even though they anticipated negative reactions and career repercussions.

In the performing stage two narratives emerged with opposite perceived reactions. Participants who identified within the gender binary "did gender" by expressing themselves in stereotypically conforming ways, which elicited positive reactions in the form of perceived understanding and support from coworkers. Some were accepted so warmly that they reinforced the display into "overdoing gender," and over time reported a lost sense of self, feeling they were playing a character that did not accurately reflect their gender identity. Participants who identified as nonbinary (genderqueer, gender fluid, or agender) "undid gender," and their nonconforming expression was met with perceived resistance: being actively ignored or excluded, denied access to gendered spaces such as bathrooms, and confronted with confusion and discomfort. The two paths then converged. Conforming participants began experimenting with less-conforming displays, felt more positive about themselves, but perceived others' reactions shifting from acceptance to social resistance, so both groups adopted a trial-and-error approach driven by two mechanisms: the subjectivities of authenticity and the perceived reactions of others reflecting prevailing gender norms.

As a consequence of perceived negative reactions from colleagues, many participants shifted from prioritizing their own desire for authentic gender expression ("What do I want?") to taking others' perceptions into account ("How does that make others feel?"), and tempered their gender expression by softening typical masculine or feminine manifestations. They perceived that this tempering elicited greater levels of social acceptance at work.

In the continuing stage, most participants settled on an "authentic enough" gender expression, a middle ground or compromise balancing feeling authentic with feeling accepted; they considered their transition successful when they felt "authentic enough" while feeling accepted, and many were unsure whether a clear endpoint existed at all. Some re-evaluated options, with several who had planned a medical transition no longer feeling the need for one while others who had opted only for a social transition began considering a medical one. A small subset instead exercised "self-authorship," adhering firmly to their internal identity regardless of gender norms and perceived negative reactions, and did not engage in trial and error.

Overall, the transition process is nonlinear: psychological, physical, behavioral, and relational movements do not necessarily move in the same direction or at the same speed. Participants progressed in their transition when they perceived others' reactions as positive and regressed when those reactions were perceived as resistant. Contrary to prior work suggesting that individuals disengage from relationships in which they feel misunderstood, participants did not withdraw from colleagues who did not see them as they saw themselves, but instead adapted their gender expression so that it became acceptable to others.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes three contributions to the authenticity and identity-transition literatures: (1) it introduces "tempered gender expression," challenging the assumption that individuals always strive for full authentic self-expression; (2) it positions authenticity as an ongoing trial-and-error continuum rather than a binary state with a clear endpoint; and (3) it shows that identity transitions evolve in a less linear fashion than prior research suggests, with interrelated movements that advance and set back.
practical_implication: Organizations should not expect transgender employees to know in advance how they wish to express their gender, and should handle these sensitive transitions with adequate support. Raising awareness, training managers, and establishing clear guidelines are key to improving the transition experiences of transgender employees, especially given that many HR departments lacked proper training or knowledge.
limitations: The study took place only in the Netherlands, making generalization to countries with different legislation, perceptions, and attitudes difficult. The sample is limited by the challenge of recruiting individuals willing to commit over time and was drawn via LGBT social-media communities, which may introduce bias. The authors also could not fully capture how other social identities (age, class, race, sexual orientation) intersect with gender identity.
future_research: Future work could replicate the study across national contexts with distinct cultural and historical origins, examine how transition experiences vary by intersecting identities such as race and class, and explore the temporal dynamics of how gender expressions and others' reactions evolve, including how gender expression continues to evolve after a transition is seemingly "over."
abstract: This study examines how the gender expression of transgender individuals evolves as they transition in the context of work. We draw from interviews with 25 transgender employees conducted at four points in time over a two-year period as they initiated, performed, and continued their gender transition. Contributing to the literature on authenticity and identity transitions, our findings challenge the assumptions that individuals know how to express an authentic self and that authenticity has an endpoint by pointing to the evolving and relational nature of authenticity that involves a trial-and-error approach in which transgender individuals learn to become authentic as they engage in various forms of gender performativity. Further, we position authenticity as a continuum, as individuals may temper their gender expression to elicit acceptance and express a gender that feels "authentic enough" as they contend with the impact of prevailing gender norms and expectations in the workplace. Finally, the findings suggest that the identity transition process evolves in a nonlinear way and involves a dynamic interplay between the desire to express one's gender in a way that feels authentic and the desire to feel accepted by others.
apa_citation: Hennekam, S., & Ladge, J. J. (2023). Free to be me? Evolving gender expression and the dynamic interplay between authenticity and the desire to be accepted at work. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(5), 1529-1553. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.1308

title: Wearing Your Worth at Work: The Consequences of Employees’ Daily Clothing Choices
methods: Mixed-methods within-person design: a set of within-person experimental studies (Study 1A/1B) plus a 10-day experience-sampling field study (Study 2) analyzed via multilevel random-coefficient path modeling with a Bayesian estimator in Mplus 8.3.
industry: Online retail, online service, brand design, and information technology firms
time_period: 10-day daily experience-sampling (ESM) study
units: Full-time professional employees (daily-level observations nested within individuals)
n_sample: 808 daily observations from 84 participants (Study 2 field study); 65 (Study 1A) and 123 (Study 1B) in the experiments
authors: Kim, Joseph K.; Holtz, Brian C.; Vogel, Ryan M.
theories: enclothed cognition theory (Adam & Galinsky, 2012); sociometer theory (Leary & Baumeister, 2000; Leary, 2005)
keywords: dress aesthetics; dress conformity; dress uniqueness; enclothed cognition; goal progress; social avoidance; sociometer theory; state self-esteem; work clothing
research_question: Whether, why, and when employees’ daily clothing choices have implications for their daily state self-esteem and subsequent task and relational work behaviors.
hypotheses:
- H1: Within individuals, (a) daily perceived dress aesthetics is positively related to state self-esteem, and (b) this relationship is mediated by the symbolic meaning of personal attractiveness.
- H2: Within individuals, (a) daily perceived dress conformity is positively related to state self-esteem, and (b) this relationship is mediated by the symbolic meaning of belongingness.
- H3: Within individuals, (a) daily perceived dress uniqueness is positively related to state self-esteem, and (b) this relationship is mediated by the symbolic meaning of distinctiveness.
- H4: Within individuals, morning interaction frequency moderates the effect of daily perceived dress (a) aesthetics, (b) conformity, and (c) uniqueness on state self-esteem, such that when interaction frequency is high (vs. low), the relationships are stronger.
- H5: Within individuals, the positive effects of daily perceived dress (a) aesthetics, (b) conformity, and (c) uniqueness on goal progress are mediated by state self-esteem.
- H6: Within individuals, morning interaction frequency moderates the positive indirect effects of daily perceived dress (a) aesthetics, (b) conformity, and (c) uniqueness on goal progress (via state self-esteem), such that when interaction frequency is high (vs. low), the indirect effects are stronger.
- H7: Within individuals, the negative effects of daily perceived dress (a) aesthetics, (b) conformity, and (c) uniqueness on social avoidance are mediated by state self-esteem.
- H8: Within individuals, morning interaction frequency moderates the negative indirect effects of daily perceived dress (a) aesthetics, (b) conformity, and (c) uniqueness on social avoidance (via state self-esteem), such that when interaction frequency is high (vs. low), the indirect effects are stronger.

Study 1B tested the mediation predictions H1b, H2b, and H3b; Study 2 tested H1a, H2a, and H3a together with Hypotheses 4 through 8.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on enclothed cognition theory, the authors argue that the clothes employees wear "embody" symbolic meanings that activate associated psychological processes. Integrating sociometer theory, those meanings (attractiveness, belongingness, distinctiveness) carry relational value that the sociometer registers, raising or lowering state self-esteem on a given day. Heightened state self-esteem then promotes motivated task behavior (goal progress) and reduces relational withdrawal (social avoidance). Because the sociometer is socially attuned, the authors predict that interaction frequency strengthens the effect of each of the three dress dimensions on state self-esteem (Hypotheses 4a–4c), since dress is more readily compared and observed on days with more interpersonal interaction.
data_measures:
- Study 1A (pre-registered online experiment): 65 employed US adults recruited from Prolific, 15 removed for failing attention checks, final n = 50. Participants viewed eight gender-aligned photographs of clothing that a pilot study had classified as high or low in aesthetics, conformity, and uniqueness (2 x 2 x 2) and selected, from a 21-item adjective list (9 focal terms, 12 distractors), the words the clothes would symbolize if worn to a business-casual office. Analyzed with chi-square tests for independence using Yates's correction.
- Study 1B (pre-registered within-person experiment): 140 new Prolific panelists, 17 removed, final n = 123, randomly assigned to an aesthetics, conformity, uniqueness, or control condition. All participants changed clothes twice — into a common baseline outfit and then into the condition outfit — and uploaded a photo each time; after each change they rated, on 5-point scales, personal attractiveness (three adjectives retained from Study 1A), belongingness (three terms), distinctiveness (three items), and state self-esteem (nine items adapted from Heatherton & Polivy, 1991). Analyzed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs and within-subjects mediational analyses using 10,000 bootstraps (Montoya & Hayes, 2017).
- Study 2 (10-day experience-sampling field study): 84 employees of four South Korean organizations returned 2,297 of 2,730 possible surveys (84.1%), yielding 808 complete daily observations. Three surveys per day, separated by at least two hours: T1 at the start of the workday (the three dress variables), T2 at lunch (interaction frequency, state self-esteem), and T3 at the end of the workday (goal progress, afternoon social avoidance). Items were rendered into Korean using Brislin's (1970) translation–back-translation procedure and answered on 5-point scales unless otherwise noted.
- Study 2 measures: dress aesthetics = three newly developed items ("Today, what I am wearing is aesthetically pleasing"; a = .93) and dress conformity = three newly developed items ("Today, what I am wearing conforms to norms at my workplace"; a = .83), both constructed with Hinkin and Tracey's (1999) procedure; dress uniqueness = three items adapted from Gurel and Gurel's (1979) clothing individuality measure (a = .78); interaction frequency = a single item asking how many times the participant had physically interacted with colleagues since arriving at work, on a 6-point scale from (1) never to (6) five or more times; state self-esteem = nine items from Heatherton and Polivy (1991), three each from the performance, social, and appearance dimensions (a = .81); goal progress = a 6-item measure from Wanberg, Zhu, and Van Hooft (2010) (a = .89); afternoon social avoidance = a 5-item measure from Woolum et al. (2017) (a = .92).

Identification rests on random assignment only in Study 1B; Study 2 is a non-experimental within-person field design with no manipulation. To isolate within-person effects and control between-person confounds the authors group-mean centered all predictors, temporally separated the T1/T2/T3 measures to fix the ordering of the variables, and controlled for survey day (1–10), the sine and cosine of the weekday, and prior levels of state self-esteem, goal progress, and social avoidance. Estimation used multilevel random-coefficient path modeling with a Bayesian estimator in Mplus 8.3, with random slopes on all hypothesized paths, fixed slopes on controls, full-information Bayesian handling of missing dependent-variable data, one-tailed p-values per Bayesian convention, and 95% credible intervals.
key_findings:
- Study 1A: chi-square tests confirmed the intended symbolic associations. High-aesthetics photos were rated significantly more often as "good-looking," "attractive," and "stylish"; high-conformity photos as "fits in," "belonging," and "included in the group"; high-uniqueness photos as "original," "unique," and "distinctive" (all p < .001 for both the male and the female stimulus sets).
- Study 1B: all three mediation predictions were supported. H1b — the aesthetics manipulation raised felt personal attractiveness relative to control (F[1, 58] = 26.26, p < .001, eta-squared = .31), and attractiveness mediated the effect on state self-esteem (indirect effect = .86, SE = .37, 95% CI [0.18, 1.64]). H2b — belongingness rose in the conformity condition (F[1, 57] = 6.18, p = .02, eta-squared = .10) and mediated the effect (indirect effect = .69, SE = .20, 95% CI [0.32, 1.09]). H3b — distinctiveness rose in the uniqueness condition (F[1, 58] = 43.75, p < .001, eta-squared = .43) and mediated the effect (indirect effect = .89, SE = .41, 95% CI [0.13, 1.71]). A supplemental analysis found that the need for competence also mediated the uniqueness–self-esteem link (indirect effect = .22, SE = .11, 95% CI [0.04, 0.47]); the identity and other self-determination variables were unaffected by the manipulations.
- Study 2, main effects on state self-esteem: H1a was supported (dress aesthetics, g = .17, p < .001, 95% CrI [0.116, 0.224]) and H3a was supported (dress uniqueness, g = .05, p = .02, 95% CrI [0.001, 0.100]), but H2a was not supported (dress conformity, g = .02, p = .25, 95% CrI [-0.043, 0.096]).
- Study 2, moderation by interaction frequency: only H4b was supported. The dress conformity x interaction frequency term was significant (g = .06, p = .02, 95% CrI [0.004, 0.115]), with conformity positively related to state self-esteem on high-interaction days (g = .16, p = .02) and negatively but non-significantly related on low-interaction days (g = -.11, p = .05; difference = .27, p = .02). H4a (aesthetics, g = .03, p = .17) and H4c (uniqueness, g = .01, p = .41) were not supported.
- Study 2, indirect effects on goal progress: state self-esteem was positively related to goal progress (g = .41, p < .001). H5a and H5c were supported (aesthetics, g = .07, p < .001; uniqueness, g = .02, p = .02) while H5b was not (conformity, g = .01, p = .25). Of the conditional indirect effects, only H6b was supported: conformity's indirect effect was stronger on high-interaction days (g = .07, p = .02) than on low-interaction days (g = -.05, p = .05; difference = .11, p = .02). H6a and H6c were not supported.
- Study 2, indirect effects on afternoon social avoidance: state self-esteem was negatively related to social avoidance (g = -.26, p < .001). H7a and H7c were supported (aesthetics, g = -.04, p < .001; uniqueness, g = -.01, p = .02) while H7b was not (conformity, g = -.01, p = .25). Only H8b was supported: conformity's indirect effect on social avoidance was stronger on high-interaction days (g = -.04, p = .02) than on low-interaction days (g = .03, p = .05; difference = .07, p = .02). H8a and H8c were not supported.
- Convergence and divergence across methods: the experiments and the field study agree that dress aesthetics and dress uniqueness raise state self-esteem through their symbolic meanings, but they diverge on conformity — the Study 1B manipulation did raise belongingness and, through it, state self-esteem, whereas in Study 2 conformity had no unconditional main effect and mattered only on days with frequent colleague interaction. A supplemental Study 2 analysis found no support for a conformity x uniqueness congruence effect; only the dress-uniqueness-squared term was significant (g = .08, p = .02), a slightly accelerating effect of dress uniqueness on state self-esteem.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends enclothed cognition theory from specific, universally meaningful garments (e.g., a doctor's lab coat) to ordinary, day-to-day work clothing applicable to employees in virtually any workplace, and adopts an actor-centric, within-person lens rather than the observer-centric view dominant in the organizational dress literature. It extends sociometer theory by showing that controllable daily choices—not just external events or stable physical attributes—drive state self-esteem, and by providing empirical support for the idea that both fitting in (belongingness) and standing out (distinctiveness) can foster self-esteem.
practical_implication: Investing modest morning effort to dress in clothing that is aesthetically pleasing and unique—and, when interactions are expected, conforming to organizational norms—can meaningfully improve how employees feel about themselves and behave at work. Managers can offer soft guidance and organizationally branded items that help employees fit in while leaving room for self-expression, rather than imposing rigid dress codes.
limitations: All Study 2 measures were self-reported, raising common-method-variance concerns, though the authors temporally separated variables, lagged mediators/outcomes, and group-mean centered within-individual variables to mitigate this. The field-study effects were somewhat small in magnitude, and the study did not use objective indicators of dress or behavior.
future_research: Future studies could assess work behavior with objective indicators (e.g., sales) or other-source reports, and rate attire through a more objective lens (e.g., trained coders) to further reduce common-method-variance concerns. Researchers could examine the dimensionality of clothing with greater specificity, including how particular or personalized clothing attributes convey relational value differently across organizational and cultural contexts (a possible congruence effect).
abstract: Do the clothes worn to work impact employees’ thoughts and behaviors? Despite the universal necessity of wearing clothes and the fact that employees make decisions about this daily, organizational scholars have not yet addressed this question. We integrate sociometer and enclothed cognition theories to propose that aspects of clothing—their aesthetics, conformity, and uniqueness—hold symbolic meanings that have implications for employees’ state self-esteem and subsequent task and relational behaviors (i.e., goal progress, social avoidance). We first provide evidence for the nature of the symbolic meanings associated with these three dimensions of work clothing in a set of within-person experimental studies. The results of a 10-day field study of employees from four organizations generally supported our predictions, showing that daily clothing aesthetics and uniqueness had effects on state self-esteem and downstream behavioral consequences. The effects of daily clothing conformity emerged under the condition of greater interaction frequency with others in the workplace. Our manuscript contributes to both major theories from which we draw, and further offers theoretical and practical contributions to the literature on organizational clothing.
