title: Tempering Temperance? A Contingency Approach to Social Movements’ Entry Deterrence in Scottish Whisky Distilling, 1823–1921
methods: Historical longitudinal panel of county-year whisky distillery foundings; multiple-imputation negative binomial regression with clustered standard errors, era and region dummies, and interaction terms.
industry: Scottish whisky distilling industry
time_period: 1823–1921 (county-level observations)
units: County-year observations of whisky distillery foundings
n_sample: 2,744 county-year observations
authors: Lander, Michel W.; Roulet, Thomas J.; Heugens, Pursey P. M. A. R.
theories: cognitive legitimacy / organizational ecology (Hannan & Carroll, 1992; Suchman, 1995); social movement theory (private vs. public politics; Reid & Toffel, 2009)
keywords: cognitive legitimacy; contested industries; countermobilization; entry deterrence; private and public politics; social movements
research_question: How does social movement opposition affect entrepreneurial entry in contested industries, and how does the effectiveness of movements' contestation depend on the fit between their private/public politics strategies, their mass/elite mobilization tactics, and external contingencies (cognitive legitimacy and incumbent countermobilization)?
hypotheses:
- H1: The greater the mass of a social movement engaging in a private politics strategy, the stronger its negative effect on entrepreneurial entry.
- H2: The greater the degree of political elite mobilization by a social movement engaging in a public politics strategy, the stronger its negative effect on entrepreneurial entry.
- H3: In counties with a large ancestral population, the negative effects of social movement contestation through both local elite-driven public politics and mass-driven private politics on entrepreneurial entry will be weaker.
- H4: In counties with stronger incumbent countermobilization, the negative effect of social movement contestation through national-level elite-driven public politics on entrepreneurial entry will be weaker.
mechanism_summary: Movements pursuing private politics deter entry by getting the public to internalize a negative frame, so a critical mass of supporters raises the social cost of entry; movements pursuing public politics deter entry by enlisting political elites who can signal forthcoming restrictive regulation. These effects are contingent on context: ancestral populations endow the industry with cognitive legitimacy, while incumbent countermobilization in the national legislative arena blunts elite-driven public politics — and, as Hypothesis 4 predicts, can even spur further entry.
data_measures: Hand-collected historical archival panel of Scottish county-years, 1823-1921 (2,744 county-year observations). Distillery founding and failure dates come primarily from Hume and Moss (2000), complemented by Smith (2002), Townsend (2004), and Udo (2006); independent and control variables were coded from yearbooks, census reports, and ledgers in the Glasgow University Archives and the National Archives of Scotland; temperance data come from The Scottish Temperance League Register and Abstainers' Almanac (1857-1921) and The Scottish Permissive Bill & Temperance Association records (1859-1921), with county-level STL membership traceable from 1856 and SPBTA membership from the association's formation in 1858. DV: Whisky distillery foundings, the annual count of all new distilleries founded in a county. IVs: STL member proportion (H1) = total STL membership in a county divided by the number of county inhabitants, lagged one year; SPBTA local elite members (H2) = county count of SPBTA members holding local office (provosts, council members, bailies, sheriffs, constables, justices of the peace); SPBTA MP members (H2) = count of SPBTA Members of Parliament. Moderators: Ancestral populations (H3) = count of all distilleries founded between 1680 and 1823 that failed before the relaxation of licensing constraints in 1823; SLTDA membership (H4) = county count of local organizations belonging to the Scottish Licensed Trade Defense Association; SWASS (H4) = count of Scottish Whisky Associations active in the county. The nonhypothesized cross-tactic mechanisms are controlled directly as SPBTA member proportion and STL reverend members (Church of Scotland reverends who joined the STL). Further controls: era dummies (1823-1840 reference, 1841-1860, 1861-1880, 1881-1900, 1901-1921) and whisky-region dummies, log county inhabitants, total whisky production, whisky retained for consumption and its change, technological advancements, economic depression year, industry age, local distillery failure, World War I, duty per gallon, numbers of positive and negative legislative acts, residual population, time-varying residual population density and its square, and De antiquo density and its square. Estimation is negative binomial regression, preferred over Poisson given overdispersion, with clustering on county; STL member proportion and STL reverend members have missing data and are handled by multiple imputation (Stata mi impute nbreg, 10 imputations, with M20 to M50 robustness checks); interaction terms are interpreted using Zelner's (2009) simulation method rather than from their standard errors. The design is associational. The authors state that because ancestral populations is a county-level constant they cannot estimate fixed-effects models, and substitute era and region dummies instead; no causal identification strategy is claimed.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: in counties with a greater ratio of STL members, organizational founding rates were lower (STL member proportion b = -0.364, SE = 0.156, Model 5). The nonhypothesized alternative for the private politics movement, elite enlistment captured by STL reverend members, had no significant downward effect on founding rates, which the authors read as further support for the contingency logic behind H1.
- H2 not supported: elite mobilization by the public politics movement had no significant direct effect on foundings at either level (SPBTA local elite members b = 0.007, SE = 0.024; SPBTA MP members b = -0.011, SE = 0.176; Model 5). The nonhypothesized alternative, SPBTA mass membership, also had no significant downward effect, ruling out a counterhypothesized effect.
- H3 rejected, with significant counterhypothesized effects in the opposite direction: large ancestral populations strengthened rather than weakened contestation. The interaction of STL member proportion with ancestral populations is negative and significant (b = -0.031, SE = 0.009, Model 6), and so is the interaction of SPBTA local elite members with ancestral populations (b = -0.009, SE = 0.004, Model 6). Zelner simulations show that where ancestral populations are large the effect of STL mass membership on founding turns negative and significant at higher membership levels, and that SPBTA local elite membership carries a sizeable negative effect once it exceeds the enlistment of 130 local elites.
- H4 supported, but only for whisky trade-specific countermobilization: the interaction of SPBTA MP members with SWASS is positive and significant (b = 5.635, SE = 1.716, Model 7), and including it turns the main effect of SPBTA MP membership negative and significant (b = -5.645, SE = 1.770). The parallel interaction with the broader-trade SLTDA is not significant (b = 0.024, SE = 0.019).
- The main effect of ancestral populations is consistently positive and significant across all regression models (b = 0.071, SE = 0.018 in the full model), which the authors interpret as a reservoir of cognitive legitimacy that aspiring entrants benefit from by association.
- Supplementary ARIMA analyses show that STL religious-elite membership positively predicted later mass membership (0.762, p < .001) and that SPBTA mass membership positively predicted SPBTA local elite membership (0.273, p < .001), indicating that mass and elite support are intertwined.
theoretical_contribution: The paper builds a contingency theory of social movements' entry deterrence in established-but-contested industries, distinguishing the constituencies (mass vs. elite) that make private versus public politics strategies effective. It theorizes and tests two external contingencies — ancestral-population cognitive legitimacy and incumbent countermobilization — showing that contestation is a two-way, coevolutionary process whose outcomes depend on the internal fit between strategy and tactics and on engagement with these external conditions.
practical_implication: For activists, the effective tactic depends on strategy: mass mobilization matters most for private politics, while enlisting political elites matters most for public politics, and elite leverage is strongest where an industry is historically well-anchored. For incumbents in contested industries, national-level countermobilization can defend sociopolitical legitimacy and may even encourage new entry by making the regulatory environment appear less hostile.
limitations: The historical data preclude fixed-effects estimation and limit the ability to capture how movements adapted their framing or deployed specific tactics (petitions, boycotts, townhall meetings) over a long period. The authors also could not systematically capture the active lobbying behind incumbent countermobilization or countermobilization efforts aimed specifically at private-politics framing.
future_research: Future work could develop finer-grained understanding of contestation strategies and their supporting constituencies, theorizing about the fit between new combinations of internal and external contingencies. Scholars could adopt a more granular historical approach to trace how movement and countermobilization dynamics, including specific tactical repertoires, unfold over prolonged periods.
abstract: What makes social movements successfully deter entry in contested industries? We develop a contingency framework explaining how movements' success depends on the internal fit between their private and public politics strategies with the tactics of mass and elite mobilization. We also highlight the importance of how these tactics fit with external conditions like the cognitive legitimacy of the industry and industry countermobilization. When movements rely on a private politics strategy to condemn an industry in the eyes of the public, social movement mass will be decisive. Alternatively, when movements use a public politics strategy to push for regulatory intervention, mobilization of elites is crucial. We develop our understanding of external contingency factors by exploring how cognitive legitimacy residuals from local ancestral populations affect both mass-driven private politics and elite-driven public politics, and how nationallevel industry countermobilization efforts affect elite-driven public politics strategies. We test these ideas in a historical study of the Scottish whisky distilling industry during the rise of temperance movements (1823–1921). We contribute to the social movements literature by showing how movements' entry deterrence in contested industries depends on the internal fit between their strategies and mobilization tactics, as well as on their engagement with external contingencies.

title: The Award Goes To… Someone Else: A Natural Quasi-Experiment Examining the Impact of Performance Awards on Nominees’ Workplace Collaboration
methods: Two-study quantitative design at one Chinese company. Study 1 is a longitudinal natural quasi-experiment using 160,830 archival collaboration records of 494 employees over eight months (two months before to six months after a 2016 award announcement), estimated via difference-in-differences (DID) and difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) OLS regressions with extensive fixed effects (hour-of-day, received-date, sender, receiver). Study 2 is a multisource field study matching post-2022-ceremony employee survey data (598 respondents, 7- and 5-point Likert scales) with 34,911 archival collaboration records over two months, testing mediation via multiple regression and indirect-effect analysis.
industry: Single technology/software company (largest market share in its industry; research and sales departments studied, plus 27 local offices)
time_period: Study 1 collaboration records Nov 26, 2015–Jul 26, 2016 (award announced Jan 26, 2016); Study 2 survey after the Jan 23, 2022 award ceremony with collaboration records for the following two months
units: Individual employees (and their dyadic collaboration records) classified as winners, nonwinner nominees, or non-nominees
n_sample: Study 1: 494 employees / 160,830 collaboration records (103 nominated, 30 winners); Study 2: 598 survey respondents (81 winners, 109 nonwinner nominees, 408 non-nominees) / 34,911 collaboration records
authors: Liao, Hui; Feng, Qiang; Zhu, Li; Guan, Olivia Zhishuang
theories: affective events theory (Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996); functional theory of counterfactual thinking (Roese, 1997; Roese & Epstude, 2017); social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954)
keywords: collaboration responsiveness; counterfactual thinking; employee awards; negative affect; nonwinner nominees; social comparison; structural proximity
research_question: How does being nominated for but failing to receive an award affect "nonwinner nominees'" collaboration responsiveness to colleagues—both to winners in particular and to others in general—compared with non-nominees, and through what mediating mechanisms, boundary conditions, and temporal dynamics?
hypotheses:
H1a. Following an award announcement, failing to receive the award has a significantly positive indirect effect on nonwinner nominees' collaboration responsiveness to others in general through causal-inference counterfactual thinking.
H1b. Following an award announcement, failing to receive the award has a significantly negative indirect effect on nonwinner nominees' collaboration responsiveness to others in general through negative affect.
H2a. Following an award announcement, failing to receive the award has a significantly negative effect on nonwinner nominees' collaboration responsiveness to winners.
H2b. Following an award announcement, failing to receive the award has a significantly negative indirect effect on nonwinner nominees' collaboration responsiveness to winners through negative affect.
H3. Following an award announcement, structural proximity moderates the negative effect of failing to receive the award on nonwinner nominees' collaboration responsiveness to winners, such that the effect is stronger when the two parties are more structurally proximal to each other.
H4. In the long run, failing to receive an award has a significantly positive effect on nonwinner nominees' collaboration responsiveness to others in general.
mechanism_summary: Integrating social comparison theory with the functional theory of counterfactual thinking, the authors argue that a "near-miss" experience triggers two opposing forces in nonwinner nominees. Causal-inference counterfactual thinking ("if I had performed a little better, I would have won") motivates them to raise collaboration responsiveness to improve future winning chances, while the contrast effect generates negative affect that depresses responsiveness, especially toward winners. Because negative affect is short-lived but motivation is durable, the net effect is reduced responsiveness to winners in the short run (amplified by structural proximity) but elevated responsiveness to others in general in the long run.
data_measures:
Study 1 draws on archival records from the company's collaborative work management system. DV: collaboration responsiveness, operationalized as the proportion of received collaboration requests processed within one working day; the raw processing-time lag was heavily right-skewed, so it was dichotomized at the company's implicit 24-hour response norm. IV: receiver-group indicators rNominee (nonwinner nominee) and rWinner (winner), interacted with After ("1" if the request was sent after the January 26, 2016 announcement) and, in the triple-difference models, with sWinner ("1" if the sender is a winner). Moderators: three structural-proximity indicators for whether sender and receiver are in the same department (M1), the same section (M2), or the same local office (M3). Controls: whether the collaboration was flagged important, whether it was routine, same-unit indicators, receiver demographics (gender, age, marital status, education), prior-year performance score, and tenure; the time-invariant controls are absorbed in the fixed-effects specifications. The paper names its own identification strategy: a difference-in-differences (DID) model for responsiveness to colleagues in general and a difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) model for responsiveness to winners, each estimated as a linear probability model with hour-of-day, received-date, sender, and receiver fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the receiver and sender level. Sensitivity analyses use placebo announcement dates, alternative conversion rules for the DV (winsorization at the 95th/90th/80th percentiles, log transformation, dichotomization at the median and 75th percentile), an attrition-restricted sample, and propensity score matching of nominees to comparable employees.

Study 2 matches a post-ceremony employee survey with archival collaboration records from the same company. The survey went to all research and sales employees immediately after the January 23, 2022 award ceremony (598 completed responses, 28.6% response rate) and was matched by email address and system ID to 34,911 collaboration records from the following two months. Mediators (5-point scales): negative affect, three items from the circumplex model of affect ("disappointed," "frustrated," "angry"; a = .73); causal-inference counterfactual thinking, a single item, "If I had performed just a little better, I would probably have won the award," adapted from Rye et al. (2008). Competing mediators were also measured: role modeling and rivalry (one item each) and benign envy and malicious envy (six items each; Cronbach's alpha .95 and .86). Controls: education and gender. Mediation was tested with multiple regression plus bootstrapped indirect effects (5,000 replications), and a supplemental Prolific validation study (n = 200) correlated the shortened scales with their full versions (r = .84 to .96). Because the Study 2 mediators are survey-reported and the mediation models are regression-based, these mediation estimates are associational rather than quasi-experimentally identified as in Study 1.
key_findings:
Study 1 (160,830 collaboration records; DID/DDD). The short-run effect of failing to receive the award on nonwinner nominees' overall collaboration responsiveness to others in general was nonsignificant relative to non-nominees (rNominee × After = .01 to .05 across specifications), matching the authors' expectation that the two mechanisms offset each other. H2a was supported: the DDD coefficient on sWinner × rNominee × After was significantly negative in all four specifications (-.25, -.24, -.25, -.23), meaning the announcement reduced the share of winners' requests that nonwinner nominees answered within one working day by 23 to 25 percentage points, about 30% of the average; the corresponding effect on winners was nonsignificant and statistically different from the nominee effect. H3 was supported for two of the three structural-proximity operationalizations: working in the same section (moderating effect = -.29, p = .02) and working in the same local office (-.29, p = .02) each strengthened the negative effect, each corresponding to a 29-percentage-point reduction, while the same-department moderator was nonsignificant, which the authors attribute to departments being too coarse a unit. H4 was supported: relative to non-nominees, the effect on nonwinner nominees' responsiveness to others in general was nonsignificant in months 1-2 (.02) but significantly positive in months 3-4 (.11, an 11-percentage-point increase, about 14% of the sample average) and months 5-6 (.12); in parallel, the negative effect on responsiveness to winners (-.25 in months 1-2) was no longer significant in months 3-4 (.03) or months 5-6 (.08).

Study 2 (598 survey respondents matched to 34,911 collaboration records; regression-based mediation) supported all three mediation hypotheses. H1a: being a nonwinner nominee was positively related to causal-inference counterfactual thinking (b = .18, p < .001), which was positively related to collaboration responsiveness (b = .01, p < .05); the indirect effect on responsiveness to others in general was positive and significant (indirect effect = .001, bootstrap 95% CI [.0001, .0017]), equal to 6.4% of the direct effect. H1b: being a nonwinner nominee was related to higher negative affect (b = .16, p < .001), which reduced responsiveness to others in general (b = -.05, p < .001); the indirect effect was negative and significant (-.0071, 95% CI [-.0089, -.0055]), equal to 49.1% of the direct effect. H2b: negative affect also reduced responsiveness to winners (b = -.05, p < .01), producing a significant negative indirect effect (-.0081, 95% CI [-.0144, -.0022]), equal to 6.3% of the direct effect. The authors report that both hypothesized mechanisms still hold after controlling for the competing mediators (role modeling, rivalry, benign envy, and malicious envy), and that winning an award did not significantly change winners' own collaboration responsiveness relative to non-nominees in either the short or the long run.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes a finer distinction within nonrecipients—separating nonwinner nominees from non-nominees—and shows that those who come closer to a desired outcome behave differently than those who do not, extending social comparison theory and the star-performer literature (e.g., how "losing stars" can harm "winning stars"). It introduces collaboration responsiveness as a novel outcome to the employee awards literature, identifies a dual mediating mechanism (causal-inference counterfactual thinking and negative affect) that holds beyond competing mechanisms such as role modeling, rivalry, and benign/malicious envy, establishes structural proximity as a boundary condition, and uses a longitudinal design to reveal the temporal dynamics of awards effects.
practical_implication: Because awards programs act as a double-edged sword in the short term but yield net-positive long-run collaboration effects, managers should actively promote collaboration between nonwinner nominees and winners—especially immediately after announcements and especially when the two are structurally proximate—to protect winners' performance and retention. Managers can also help nonwinner nominees curb episodic negative affect by showing appreciation for their contributions and providing supervisory support, encouragement, feedback, and resources, lessening frustration and disappointment.
limitations: The study examines only one facet of collaboration (responsiveness to received requests) and does not test other facets such as initiating collaborations, value contributed, or tie persistence. Data were collected in China, a highly collectivistic culture, though the authors argue collaboration is prevalent in organizations even in noncollectivistic cultures, and the awards combined social recognition, feedback, and financial incentives. The authors describe the two mediators' effect sizes as meaningful while acknowledging they are two of many potential mechanisms, and the DID framework cannot rule out individual differences that change after the announcement; the temporal turning-point results are exploratory.
future_research: The authors call for examining additional facets and outcomes of collaboration (e.g., initiating requests, performance, withdrawal, unethical behaviors), additional boundary conditions (e.g., cultural context, award type including purely symbolic awards), and additional mediators (e.g., rivalry, perceived fairness/attributions). They also encourage replicating the quasi-experimental design to test the generalizability of the exploratory temporal pattern, studying "surprise" awards whose nominees are not notified, and exploring employee collaboration during the nomination stage.
abstract: Employee awards programs are prevalent in organizations. This research examines a group of employees who have received relatively less attention in the employee awards literature: those who are nominated for but fail to receive an award. Integrating social comparison theory with the functional theory of counterfactual thinking, we argue that nonwinner nominees go through complex motivational states and affective experiences, which influence their collaboration responsiveness to colleagues. We conducted a field quasi-experiment using 160,830 collaboration records of 494 employees over eight months (Study 1) and a multisource study using survey data and 34,911 collaborative records of 598 employees over two months (Study 2). The results revealed that, compared to non-nominees, nonwinner nominees have lower collaboration responsiveness to winners following the award announcement, especially when they have a higher structural proximity to winners. However, in the long run, nonwinner nominees have higher collaboration responsiveness to others in general. Furthermore, being nominated for but failing to receive an award simultaneously induces nonwinner nominees to experience higher causal-inference counterfactual thinking and negative affect, which exert opposing impacts on nonwinner nominees’ collaboration responsiveness. This research advances the understanding of the impact, influencing mechanisms, boundary conditions, and temporal dynamics of employee awards on workplace collaboration.

title: Resource Idling and Capability Erosion
methods: Longitudinal archival panel of Texas oil drillers (Drillinginfo, RigData, Texas Railroad Commission, EIA). Firm capabilities estimated as residual intrinsic drilling speed from a project-level OLS first stage. H1 tested with firm fixed-effects regressions plus treatment-effect analysis (propensity score matching, inverse probability weighting, doubly robust estimation); H2-H4 tested with firm fixed-effects logit models of rig idling, standard errors clustered by firm.
industry: Onshore oil and gas drilling (drilling contractors operating rig fleets)
units: Drillers, rigs; firm-year level (capability erosion) and rig-month level (idling decisions)
n_sample: 102 drillers and 1,396 rigs; 301,536 rig-month observations in the idling logit models
authors: Ross, Jan-Michael; Li, Toby X.; Hawk, Ashton; Reuer, Jeffrey J.
theories: real options theory; resource-based view
keywords: automation; capability erosion; demand uncertainty; human capital; real options; resource idling; sunk costs
research_question: Why would some firms persist with continued operations when facing unfavorable economic conditions? Specifically, how does anticipated capability erosion from temporarily idling resources function as a sunk cost that shapes firms' decisions to idle versus continue operations under demand uncertainty?
hypotheses:
- H1: The extent of resource idling has a negative effect on a firm's capabilities (i.e., capability erosion).
- H2: Demand uncertainty has a negative impact on the likelihood of resource idling.
- H3: The negative impact of demand uncertainty on the likelihood of resource idling will be magnified for firms with superior capabilities.
- H4: The negative impact of demand uncertainty on the likelihood of resource idling will be magnified for resources with greater reliance on human capital (as opposed to automation).
mechanism_summary: The paper integrates the resource-based view with real options theory to argue that temporarily idling resources erodes existing capabilities through reduced utilization, organizational forgetting, layoffs, and the breaking of coordinated routines. Because this erosion is a sunk cost that cannot be costlessly reversed upon reactivation, forward-looking firms treat idling like outright exit and rationally persist ("hysteresis") under demand uncertainty rather than idle. The dissuading effect of uncertainty on idling is amplified for firms with superior capabilities (which face larger strategic sunk costs) and for firms reliant on human capital rather than automation (whose capabilities are more vulnerable to erosion). All four hypotheses receive empirical support.
data_measures: Archival panel data on Texas oil drilling assembled from Drillinginfo, RigData, the Texas Railroad Commission, and the U.S. Energy Information Administration, covering 102 drillers and 1,396 rigs from 2001 to 2018; the capability erosion analysis is at the firm-year level (n = 1,836) and the idling analysis at the rig-month level (n = 301,536). A driller's capabilities are measured as its intrinsic speed capability in drilling: a first-stage project-level OLS regresses the drilling rate for a given well (total well depth divided by drilling days) on well type, project size, contract type, field oil demand, and field and year dummies, and the residuals are standardized within each field-year subgroup and averaged to the firm-year. Extent of idling is the proportion of a driller's total rigs that are "stacked" relative to its fleet in year t; the rig-level dependent variable is a binary indicator equal to 1 if the driller stacks a given rig in month t by suspending its drilling operations and releasing the associated crew, and 0 otherwise. Demand uncertainty is the market forecast error from a GARCH model estimated on monthly U.S. oil demand for 2001-2018, that is, the absolute percentage difference between predicted and observed industry output; human capital reliance is a dummy equal to 1 if the focal rig is the traditional fully human-operated type and 0 if automated. Controls are grouped at the firm, environment, and rig levels (Table 1). H1 is estimated with firm fixed-effects regression, which the authors call identification by adjustment, with idling in year t lagged relative to capabilities in t + 1, and is complemented by treatment effect analysis, which they call identification by balancing, using propensity score matching, inverse probability weighting, and doubly robust estimation with drillers matched on size, age, number of clients, resource heterogeneity, technological sophistication, and human capital reliance. H2 to H4 are estimated with firm fixed-effects logit models of the binary idling decision, with standard errors clustered by firm. The authors note that idling decisions are not randomly assigned across firms, so identification rests on fixed effects, the lag structure, and balancing on observed covariates rather than on random or exogenous assignment.
key_findings: All four hypotheses are supported. H1 is supported: the extent of resource idling in year t is negatively related to a driller's capabilities in year t + 1 (b = -10.122, p = .005; firm fixed effects, n = 1,836 firm-years), and the treatment effects analysis corroborates this, with drillers that idled at least one rig in year t showing lower capabilities in t + 1 than drillers that idled none (treatment-control differences of -1.619 under propensity score matching, -1.502 under inverse probability weighting, and -0.992 under doubly robust estimation; all p values below .02), a pattern that also holds using capabilities at t + 2. H2 is supported: demand uncertainty has a significant negative effect on the likelihood of idling a rig (b = -6.581, p = .008; rig-month logit, n = 301,536). H3 is supported: the interaction between demand uncertainty and firm capabilities is negative and significant (b = -0.002, p = .026), and the marginal effects plot shows the negative effect of uncertainty on idling is more pronounced for high-capability drillers. H4 is supported: the interaction between demand uncertainty and human capital reliance is negative and significant (b = -0.812, p = .039), with the negative effect of uncertainty on idling more pronounced for rigs relying on human capital than for automated rigs. Supplemental analyses find negative and significant coefficients for both partial ("warm stacking") and complete ("cold stacking") idling, with the larger coefficient and economic magnitude for complete idling, and an ordinal logit in which uncertainty reduces the degree of idling, an effect strengthened both by superior capabilities and by greater reliance on human capital.
theoretical_contribution: The study introduces capability erosion as a previously unacknowledged form of sunk cost relevant to firms' investment decisions under uncertainty, thereby extending the resource-based view's attention from capability building toward the maturity stage of the capability lifecycle. By explicating how capability erosion operates as a sunk cost within a real options framework, it demonstrates a theoretical synergy between the resource-based view and real options theory and identifies a new, internally generated source of hysteresis. It also contributes to the resource reconfiguration literature by introducing temporary contraction as a reversible deviation from a current configuration.
practical_implication: What seems to be an operational decision to navigate cyclical markets (idling resources) can be highly strategic, because it influences a firm's existing capabilities and its ability to benefit from future growth opportunities. Managers, especially at firms with superior capabilities or heavy reliance on human capital, should weigh anticipated capability erosion and reactivation costs against short-term cash-flow savings before idling resources in a downturn.
limitations: The study is limited to a single industry with usage-specific resources and firms exposed to the same environmental shocks (oil price movements). The data cannot directly observe capability buildup in other value-chain activities (e.g., R&D) or other idling-related factors such as union contracts and labor relations dynamics. The authors note the context may be conservative, as predictions could be even stronger in more knowledge-intensive industries.
future_research: Future work could examine resource idling in other cyclical industries (mining, aircraft, shipping), study different forms of idleness and erosion of newly built rather than established capabilities, and explore exogenous events offering varying managerial discretion (pandemics, disasters, political crises, wars). Researchers could also incorporate capabilities into real options analyses of hysteresis, develop more refined measures of automation and complementary knowledge assets, and study initiatives that curate resources and enhance recovery from erosion.
abstract: Why would some firms persist with continued operations when facing unfavorable economic conditions? Although prior studies have investigated the roles of uncertainty and sunk costs as sources of inertia, an unacknowledged type of sunk cost associated with temporary suspensions of operations is related to the erosion of existing capabilities. Building on the resource-based view and real options theory, we argue that resource idling contributes to capability erosion and that the anticipated capability loss motivates firms to refrain from idling their resources under demand uncertainty in the first place. The negative effects of uncertainty on resource idling are likely to be particularly strong for firms with superior capabilities and for those having a greater reliance on human capital. Using data on oil drilling contractors in Texas, the empirical evidence lends support to our theoretical arguments. Our insights suggest that resource idling shapes the development path of capabilities and risks jeopardizing firms' competitive advantages. The seemingly operational decision of temporarily idling resources can therefore be quite strategic for a firm, and "hysteresis," or inertia in continuing operations, can preserve firms' capabilities.

title: Reaching for the Stars: How Gender Influences the Formation of High-Status Collaboration Ties
methods: Binary logistic regression on a matched-sample, dyadic (star-nonstar-year) panel with firm and year fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the star-nonstar dyad level; nearest-neighbor matching of female to male nonstars on tenure, prior patents, and competence area.
industry: Pharmaceutical research and development (R&D) laboratories
country: United States (American R&D departments of the 42 largest pharmaceutical companies)
units: Star-nonstar scientist dyad-years (first-time collaboration risk set)
n_sample: 2.04 million female nonstar observations matched to an equal number of male nonstar observations
authors: Rua-Gomez, Carla; Carnabuci, Gianluca; Goossen, Martin C.
theories: Blau's structural theory of proximity (Blau, 1952, 1977); social capital theory (Lin, 2002; Oldroyd & Morris, 2012); status expectation theory (Foschi, 2000; Ridgeway & Smith-Lovin, 1999)
keywords: collaboration ties; gender; geographic proximity; high-status connections; network proximity; social capital; star scientists; third-party ties
research_question: How do two structural factors—geographic proximity and network proximity—differently affect men's versus women's chances of forming high-status collaboration ties with star scientists, and how does the star colleague's own gender condition these effects?
hypotheses:
- Baseline Hypothesis (i). Being geographically colocated with a star scientist increases a nonstar scientist's likelihood of forming a collaboration tie with that star scientist.
- Hypothesis 1. Female nonstar scientists are less likely than male nonstar scientists to form a collaboration tie with a star scientist with whom they are geographically colocated.
- Hypothesis 2a. The effect postulated by Hypothesis 1 is weaker if the star scientist is a woman.
- Hypothesis 2b (competing with 2a). The effect postulated by Hypothesis 1 is stronger if the star scientist is a woman.
- Baseline Hypothesis (ii). Having third-party ties in common with a star scientist increases a nonstar scientist's likelihood of forming a collaboration tie with that star scientist.
- Hypothesis 3. Female nonstar scientists are more likely than are male ones to form a collaboration tie with a star scientist with whom they share common third-party ties.
- Hypothesis 4a. The effect postulated by Hypothesis 3 is weaker if the star scientist is a woman.
- Hypothesis 4b (competing with 4a). The effect postulated by Hypothesis 3 is stronger if the star scientist is a woman.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on status expectation theory and Blau's structural argument about spatial proximity, the authors argue that colocation rewards stereotypically male agentic self-promotion, so women profit less than men from being geographically near a star (H1, supported). Network proximity instead lets a third party convey stereotype-congruent, person-specific endorsements that override gender bias, so women benefit more than men from third-party ties (H3, supported). Because female stars share female nonstars' minority status yet also face a "favoritism threat," the star's gender amplifies the network-proximity advantage for female nonstars while leaving the colocation disadvantage persistent regardless of star gender.
data_measures:
- Data sources: European Patent Office (EPO) patent applications — both granted applications and failed ones — for the American R&D departments of the 42 largest pharmaceutical companies (all PhRMA members in 1985), with scientists traced through the inventor names appearing on firms' patent applications; Mergent WebReports for firm financial and operational data; U.S. Social Security Administration first-name records for scientist gender (96% matched, raised to 99.5% through manual searches of LinkedIn, public profiles and Google, with the residual 0.5% classified as male). A dozen field interviews with star and nonstar scientists informed the setting.
- DV — First-time collaboration: dyadic dichotomous variable set to 1 if the star and nonstar scientist collaborated for the first time in the current year, observed as coauthorship of a patent application.
- Star status: the 5% most productive R&D scientists within each firm, based on a five-year count of patent applications.
- IV — Geographic colocation: dichotomous, set to 1 if star and nonstar belong to the same geographic cluster, assigned by a "city clustering algorithm" run on the location data in each scientist's most recent patent application (median distance 12 miles for colocated dyads versus 725 miles for non-colocated ones).
- IV — Third-party ties: dichotomous, set to 1 if the star and nonstar had at least one collaborator within the firm in common, identified from patent applications filed during the five years before the current year.
- Gender variables: Female nonstar dummy; in some models, four star–nonstar gender-dyad dummies with Male star–male nonstar as the reference category.
- Controls: star tenure, star prior patents, star current projects, nonstar tenure, nonstar prior patents, potential star collaborators, and same competence area, plus firm and year dummies; skewed controls entered log-transformed.
- Identification (in the paper's terms): a matched-sample design using nearest-neighbor matching — each female nonstar–star–year observation matched to a male nonstar paired with the same star, firm and year, within a 5% range on tenure, prior patents and same competence area (matches found for 89% of female nonstars) — estimated with binary logistic regression carrying firm and year fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the star–nonstar dyad level (4,098,128 observations). The authors describe the study as nonexperimental and caution against interpreting the estimates as evidence of causality. Robustness checks include rare-event logistic regression, a Cox proportional hazards event-history model, dyad-level random effects, looser matching margins and the unmatched sample, alternative colocation and third-party-tie measures, and a replication on USPTO data.
key_findings:
Support is heterogeneous across the eight hypotheses; coefficients below are logit coefficients with signs as reported by the paper.
- Baseline Hypothesis (i) supported: geographic colocation raises the probability of forming a first-time tie (model 1: b = 1.756, p < .001) — in marginal terms, colocation increases that probability by nearly 5.8 times.
- Hypothesis 1 supported: the Geographic colocation × Female nonstar interaction is negative (model 4: b = −0.343, p < .001); colocation raises the tie probability 4.9 times for a female nonstar versus 6.8 times for a male nonstar.
- Hypotheses 2a and 2b both unsupported: a Wald test cannot reject equality between Male star–female nonstar × Geographic colocation (b = −0.324, p < .01) and Female star–female nonstar × Geographic colocation (b = −0.562, p < .01) in model 8 (χ² = 1.22, p = .270), so women's colocation disadvantage persists irrespective of the star's gender; the authors read this as the minority-status homophily and favoritism-threat mechanisms cancelling each other out.
- Baseline Hypothesis (ii) supported: common third-party ties raise the probability of forming a first-time tie (model 1: b = 2.369, p < .001) — by a factor of 10.6.
- Hypothesis 3 supported: the Third-party ties × Female nonstar interaction is positive (model 4: b = 0.294, p < .001); a third-party tie raises the likelihood of collaboration nine-fold for male nonstars but more than twelve-fold for female nonstars.
- Hypothesis 4b supported and Hypothesis 4a not: Female star–female nonstar × Third-party ties (b = 0.645, p < .001) is significantly larger than Male star–female nonstar × Third-party ties (b = 0.260, p < .001) in model 8 (Wald χ² = 6.52, p = .011), so third-party ties are especially beneficial for female nonstars when the star is also a woman — the paper estimates this catalyzing effect is over 50% larger with a female than a male star.
- Unhypothesized direct effect: female nonstar scientists are 10% less likely than their male peers to form ties with star scientists (model 1: b = −0.101, p < .01).
- Post hoc: splitting stars at median organizational tenure, Female star–female nonstar × Geographic colocation is negative and significant in the below-median-tenure subsample but positive and nonsignificant in the above-median-tenure subsample — colocation raises a female nonstar's chance of tying to a recently hired female star by a factor of 3.4 versus 6.1 for a long-tenured female star. The third-party effect is largest among female nonstars with few prior patents and those whose main competence area differs from the star's.
theoretical_contribution: The paper moves beyond the established finding that women have reduced access to high-status social capital to specify the structural mechanisms that amplify or reduce that disadvantage, showing that men and women rely on different pathways (colocation vs. third-party ties) into high-status networks. It advances understanding of how status heterophily shapes tie formation by integrating social-psychological accounts of gender stereotyping into Blau's structural theory, and reframes the debate on high-status women from whether they help other women toward the conditions under which they do so.
practical_implication: Organizations should pair sensitization to agency-stereotype bias in face-to-face settings with interventions that deliberately build third-party (sponsorship) ties between low-status women and high-status colleagues, since such ties are an especially powerful lever when women's competence is hard to signal. The increasing geographic dispersion of knowledge work may itself narrow the gender gap in high-status connections.
limitations: The nonexperimental design precludes strong causal claims; proximity may follow rather than precede collaboration intentions, and matched nonstars may differ on unobserved dimensions. EPO patent data may miss collaborations that never result in a patent filing, risking false negatives in the tie-formation measure, and the study does not examine gendered differences in failed collaborations.
future_research: The authors call for field or lab experiments to establish causation, studies of how the theorized effects change over time as the share of (star) women rises and organizations grow more geographically dispersed, and research on how virtual collaboration technologies and remote work shape men's and women's ability to signal competence and form high-status ties.
abstract: Extant research has shown that it is harder for women than for men to form high-status connections in the workplace. Extending this line of research, we examine how two structural factors—geographic and network proximity—affect men's and women's chances of forming high-status connections. Using data on the formation of collaboration ties with star scientists within the research and development laboratories of the 42 largest pharmaceutical companies between 1985 and 2010, we show that women who are geographically colocated with a "star" colleague are less likely to form a tie with that colleague compared to male peers who are similarly colocated, and that this difference persists irrespective of the star's gender. Conversely, women benefit more than men do from network proximity, as indicated by the presence of common third-party ties, and this difference widens if the star colleague is also a woman. By illuminating how geographic and network proximity affect the chances of forming high-status connections differently for women than for men, our study goes beyond the notion that women have reduced access to workplace social capital and expands consideration to the structural factors that underpin—that is, amplify or reduce—that disadvantage.

title: Distilling Authenticity: Materiality and Narratives in Canadian Distilleries’ Authenticity Work
methods: Inductive grounded qualitative study of the Canadian whisky industry; 92 semi-structured interviews with distillery representatives and audience members plus in situ observations and archival documents, analyzed via constant comparison.
industry: Canadian whisky industry (incumbent and micro-distilleries)
units: Distilleries (incumbents and micro-distilleries) and their audience members (critics, bloggers, restaurateurs, retailers, connoisseurs)
n_sample: 92 semi-structured interviews across distilleries plus archival and observational data
authors: Voronov, Maxim; Foster, William M.; Patriotta, Gerardo; Weber, Klaus
theories: authenticity as an organizational resource; materiality and narratives in organizations; prefigurative materiality (Schatzki) / practice theory
keywords: anchoring; authenticity; authenticity claims; authenticity work; experiential closeness; materiality; narratives; reinforcement
research_question: How do organizations’ material endowments enable and constrain their authenticity claims, and how does the interplay of materiality and narratives shape the authenticity work through which producers craft and sustain believable authenticity claims?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: authenticity work; authenticity claims (combinations of narratives and material artifacts); material endowments (product features, key people, architectural design); the tension between tradition-based and originality-based bases of authenticity.
- Process / mechanisms: *Anchoring* — central product features tie producers to a prefigured base of authenticity, making some claims natural and others requiring greater narrative effort; *Reinforcement* — other material endowments (human embodiments, architectural design) bolster the integrity and persuasiveness of claims.
- Triggering conditions: differential material endowments (e.g., incumbents’ access to aged liquid vs. micro-distilleries’ lack thereof) prefigure which authenticity claims are credible.
- Emergent outcomes: relatively stable authenticity profiles; experiential closeness between producers and audiences that heightens perceived authenticity; authenticity as a competitive resource or liability.

Materiality is prefigurative: rather than being a blank canvas, an organization’s material endowments inform the selection and audience reception of authenticity narratives. Producers exercise agency by skillfully (re)combining narratives and materiality to overcome the constraints of anchoring or to reinforce an existing base of authenticity, conferring plasticity to authenticity claims and generating audience buy-in.
data_measures:
Data: 92 semi-structured interviews with distillery representatives and audience members, collected between 2015 and 2019 in the Canadian whisky industry. Distillery interviewees came from incumbent distilleries (several decades to more than a century old) and micro-distilleries (typically under ten years old), three of which sourced aged liquid from an incumbent under contract distilling; sampling deliberately spanned differences in age, size, ownership structure, geographical location, relative reputation, and reliance on in-house versus contract distilling, and deliberately targeted elite audience members who codify what counts as authentic (retailers, bloggers, restaurateurs, connoisseurs). Table 2 reports the audience interviews as critics and bloggers (10), restaurateurs and bartenders (11), retailers (9), government (2), connoisseurs (7), and others (4). Interviews used open-ended questions from a protocol reproduced in Appendix A, ran 1 to 1.5 hours, and were recorded and transcribed verbatim; protocols were refined as themes emerged, and interviewing continued until it added little new information. The first author additionally logged more than 70 hours of in situ observation of routine distillery operations and public events — 8 distillery tours, 17 tastings or informal visits, and 4 whisky festivals with masterclasses and tastings — and the team assembled archival material comprising 25 distillery websites, 180 newspaper articles, more than 500 whisky blog entries and reviews, 12 social-media accounts, and 11 books on the Canadian and international whisky industries. Distilleries are reported under pseudonyms except where quotes come from public-domain sources.

Operationalization: the focal construct — a distillery's authenticity claim — was coded inductively rather than scored on an instrument. Claims were classified into two bases: authenticity as tradition (continuity, loyalty to original roots, adherence to received practice and methods of production) and authenticity as originality (uniqueness, novelty, virtuosity in production or the resulting products). Table 4 then profiles every distillery on both bases across four evidence streams — "For each distillery, tradition and originality claims are assessed, as high, medium, low, or absent, for each data source" (interviews, observations, website or social media, and blogger or media coverage). Material endowments were coded into the three categories the authors identified as most salient in the whisky field: the aged liquid as manifest in whisky product features, the key people involved in whisky-making, and the architectural design of the distilleries. Each distillery was then assessed for which of these endowments it possessed or lacked, with follow-up interviews or emails where information was missing.

Analysis: a three-phase grounded analysis using constant comparison (Locke, 2001), iterating between raw data and emerging theory. Phase one open-coded authenticity claims, comparing narratives across interviews, website descriptions, and formal and informal presentations during distillery visits and whisky festivals, and searched the corpus for authenticity vocabulary such as "genuine," "traditional," "honest," "faithful," and "original," plus sensitizing synonyms drawn from prior management, sociology, and anthropology work ("pure," "real," "believable," "sincere," "skilled"); within-case comparison established that each distillery made relatively consistent claims, and cross-case comparison surfaced the incumbent–micro divide. Phase two identified the role of materiality and made cross-distillery comparisons of available and absent endowments. Phase three linked the phase-one narratives to the phase-two endowments. Trustworthiness was addressed by presenting tentative interpretations back to interviewees at several points, writing reports for distilleries and audience members, and resolving interpretive disagreements by consensus or by returning to informants (Lincoln & Guba, 1985). The design is inductive and interpretive: it builds theory from cross-case comparison of naturally occurring variation across distilleries and claims no causal identification strategy — there is no experiment, instrument, or quasi-experimental design, and the incumbent–micro contrast is analytic rather than statistical.
key_findings:
Audiences used two widely shared criteria to assess authenticity in whisky-making — tradition and originality — which in this industry are understood not as mutually exclusive opposites but as interdependent qualities. Within-case comparison showed each distillery tended to make relatively consistent claims emphasizing one base; cross-case comparison showed that most incumbent distilleries emphasized tradition while most micro-distilleries emphasized originality (Table 4). The pattern is a tendency rather than a rule: Innovative Spirits, an incumbent, claimed originality strongly in interviews, and two of the three micro-distilleries that sourced aged liquid from incumbents (Clean Air Spirits and Spirit of Adventure) claimed tradition strongly.

Anchoring: material product features anchored which claims a distillery could credibly narrate. The most important material manifestation was whether the product is made with well-aged liquid — on balance, abundant stocks of well-aged liquid made distilleries more likely to construct narratives emphasizing tradition, while limited access to such stocks made them more likely to emphasize originality (Table 5). Incumbents holding vast aged inventories (two owned more than 1.5 million barrels each) could narrate the Canadian whisky-making heritage naturally, but their interviewees reported that the same inventory limited their ability to construct desirable alternative narratives. That constraint was costly, because connoisseurs found the traditional smooth Canadian style "boring" and some dismissed it pejoratively as "brown vodka"; anchored to the aged liquid, incumbents were unable to construct flavor-profile narratives that would counter the perception. Micro-distilleries, conversely, had not produced whisky aged enough to credibly evoke the refinement that signals tradition — their releases were typically seen as less refined and were characterized as "harsh" — so most claimed originality instead, foregrounding higher alcohol content, unusual flavor profiles, grains that are difficult to work with or obtain, and appeals to a foreign (usually Scotch) whisky-making tradition.

Anchoring was strongly suggestive rather than deterministic, and both groups did authenticity work to mitigate it, with mixed results. Heritage Brands, an incumbent, recombined material elements into an annually released collection promoted as using extra-long barrel aging, unusual combinations of distillates, special distillation techniques, and higher alcohol content; these products generated positive reactions from most audience interviewees and showed that incumbents could appeal to connoisseurs. Micro-distilleries lacking aged stock sourced liquid from incumbents, but this mitigation carried a reported cost: because they made whisky in largely the same manner as the incumbents they sourced from, they were to a large extent re-anchored to tradition claims, lost part of their ability to claim originality, and increasingly constructed tradition-based narratives — responding by stressing their own contributions, such as finishing sourced liquid in unusual barrels, or by pointing to future originality from in-house experiments not yet released.

Reinforcement through human embodiments: what made distillery employees effective embodiments was not their mere existence but their visibility, accessibility, and willingness to interact, and audience interviewees generally concurred that master blenders and distillers were the most compelling embodiments. Incumbents mainly deployed historical figureheads and brand ambassadors, and both underperformed — most audience members found references to historical figures unconvincing, and brand ambassadors, whose background was typically bartending or sales rather than whisky-making, were often seen as less knowledgeable and less effective, with one whisky writer dismissing them as "salespeople." Incumbent informants attributed the dearth of active embodiments to organizational complexity that isolated master blenders in production from customer-facing activities; Alex, the master blender at Heritage Brands, was the only incumbent master blender regularly available for such interactions and was received warmly. Among micro-distilleries, founders or cofounders usually doubled as the whisky-makers, making them readily available embodiments of originality claims and allowing greater closeness with audiences, whereas incumbents' lack of present-day embodiments and emphasis on brand promotion often distanced them from theirs.

Reinforcement through architectural design: design reinforced claims mainly by conveying transparency and visibility of production. Incumbent buildings, many standing since founding in the mid-19th century and some classified as historically significant landmarks, are typically large structures in industrial districts built for efficient manufacturing rather than for tours; audience members described them as factories and as "industrial plants" with "no romance." The more consequential problem, according to audience members, was the failure to use the design to let visitors see the whisky-making process, which they named the most significant missed opportunity to showcase authenticity; over the study period incumbents responded by opening or planning visitor centers. Micro-distilleries, newly built and often sited in visitor-accessible areas or near the farms supplying their grain, were designed so that production could be entered or seen through a glass wall, reinforcing originality and the grain-to-glass story, and small size itself signaled authenticity to some consumers. One whisky writer dissented, arguing that entertaining visitors is not transparency and that some micro-distillers do not know enough to be transparent about anything else.

Overall, the findings suggest that micro-distilleries were more effective than incumbents at authenticity work: despite distinguished pasts, iconic founders, and abundant artifacts essential to the tradition of Canadian whisky-making, incumbents did not enjoy an authenticity advantage in the eyes of audience members over upstart micro-distilleries that seemingly had fewer of those material resources. Because material endowments anchored producers to a particular base of authenticity, relatively stable authenticity profiles emerged that generated clarity about producers' identities and conferred consistency to their action, so that authenticity-based advantage rested less on owning prestigious endowments than on the agentic work of combining narratives and materiality to anchor, reinforce, or mitigate claims.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends understanding of authenticity as a valued organizational resource by identifying anchoring and reinforcement as two mechanisms through which materiality both constrains and facilitates authenticity narratives. It theorizes materiality as prefigurative—shaping which claims are credible rather than merely amplifying chosen claims—and surfaces audience members’ experiential closeness as a route through which material artifacts enhance perceived authenticity. It reframes resource advantage as a matter of how organizations use endowments in authenticity work rather than mere ownership.
practical_implication: For producers in industries where authenticity matters, competitive advantage depends less on owning prestigious material endowments than on skillfully combining materiality and narratives to construct credible claims. Incumbents anchored to tradition may need to demonstrate innovation, while newer entrants can leverage approachable makers and architectural design to build experiential closeness; material endowments can be a resource or a liability depending on the authenticity work performed.
limitations: The study relied on audience members’ accounts of what they deem authentic and deferred to their subjective understandings of how materiality matters, building on an audience-centric view of authenticity. It focuses on a single, tradition-rich industry (Canadian whisky) where a product’s perceived authenticity is tightly tied to that of its producer, which may limit transferability.
future_research: Future research could examine how the challenge of balancing different bases of authenticity plays out across industries, and settings where material bases differ or where the product–organization tie is looser (e.g., high-technology or sharing-economy contexts). Scholars could also study how the meaning of material artifacts is negotiated in situ and how authenticity work and an organization’s primary authenticity claim change over time in response to internal and external factors.
abstract: Authenticity is increasingly seen as a source of competitive advantage in many industries. Accordingly, authenticity work, the organizational efforts to develop and sustain believable authenticity claims, has emerged as an important organizational practice. We examined the interplay of materiality and narratives underpinning producers’ authenticity work in the context of incumbent and micro-distilleries operating in the Canadian whisky industry. We found that producers’ material endowments, especially central product features, anchored which authenticity claims they could credibly narrate. Other material endowments, such as key people and architectural design, were used to reinforce the integrity of authenticity claims. Our study extends our understanding of authenticity as a valued organizational resource. First, we identify two mechanisms, anchoring and reinforcement, through which materiality both constrains and facilitates organizations’ authenticity narratives. Second, our research brings to the fore how audience members’ experiential closeness to producers colors their perceptions of authenticity, and we show how material artifacts can enhance such closeness. Third, our findings highlight the competitive value of authenticity by unpacking how producers’ material endowments may constitute a resource or a liability.
apa_citation: Voronov, M., Foster, W. M., Patriotta, G., & Weber, K. (2023). Distilling authenticity: Materiality and narratives in Canadian distilleries’ authenticity work. *Academy of Management Journal, 66*(5), 1438–1468. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.0017

title: Triggers, Traps, and Disconnect: How Governance Obstacles Hinder Progress on Grand Challenges
methods: In-depth interpretive longitudinal case study combining ethnographic observation, semi-structured interviews, and archival documents; ~500 hours of observation, 30 interviews, and extensive documentary material analyzed in three iterative steps (open coding, axial coding, theoretical abstraction) to develop a process model.
industry: Multistakeholder water-health partnership spanning nonprofit, mining, agriculture, government (local, state, federal), academic, and consultancy organizations
time_period: 2008-2018 (historical context 2008-2017; real-time fieldwork in 2018)
units: One multistakeholder initiative (WaterHealthOrg) and its 25 partner organizations
n_sample: 1 case study; 30 semi-structured interviews; ~500 hours of observation; multiple archival documents
authors: Couture, F.; Jarzabkowski, P.; Lê, J. K.
theories: grand challenges (Ferraro, Etzion, & Gehman, 2015; George et al., 2016); multistakeholder governance (Dentoni et al., 2018; Provan & Kenis, 2008); path dependence theory (Sydow, Schreyögg, & Koch, 2009, 2020)
keywords: broadening practices; collective response; containing practices; governance obstacles; governance traps; grand challenges; multistakeholder governance; path dependence; water health
research_question: How are multistakeholder governance obstacles addressed in practice? What are the implications of this for the collective’s ability to mitigate grand challenges?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering conditions: Socioenvironmental triggers (e.g., contamination events, fish deaths, coral bleaching, regulatory debates) that shift the salience of the grand challenge and surface interpretive, structural, and relational governance obstacles.
- Key practices: Broadening practices (stretching the scope by including new activities to incorporate shifting interpretations) and Containing practices (counteracting broadening by limiting scope and keeping focus on agreed activities).
- Process / phases: Three sequential cycles — Developing a collective response (Cycle 1), Protecting a collective response (Cycle 2), Leveraging a collective response (Cycle 3) — each generating positive feedback that narrows the group’s remit.
- Emergent outcomes: Governance traps (D1–Dn) — cumulative lock-in dynamics whereby participants struggle to generate knowledge, develop activities, or deviate from the established response path.
- Boundary conditions: Tool-centric collective responses (e.g., the report card) and tightly coupled multistakeholder initiatives in shifting, evaluative grand challenges.

The process model explains how repeated cycles of trigger → obstacle → broadening/containing practice → narrowed remit produce a cumulative, self-reinforcing path-dependent dynamic. As actors become increasingly skilled at taming governance obstacles to keep the group cohesive, they progressively decouple the collective response from the grand challenge it was intended to mitigate — even external shocks that ought to break the path end up reinforcing it.
data_measures: Data corpus: a single longitudinal interpretive case study of WaterHealthOrg drawing on the qualitative "big three" — over 500 hours of ethnographic observation (an intensive three-month colocation at the partnership's headquarters plus seven punctuated visits in 2018), 30 hour-long semi-structured interviews with partners, science panel members, staff, and proximal third parties, and 495 archival documents (meeting minutes, internal working papers, report cards, media reports, strategy documents, and scientific studies). Contextualized retrospective data covered the historical context (2008-2011) and WaterHealthOrg's first five years (2012-2017), complemented by real-time fieldwork (2018). Coding: interpretive analysis unfolded over three steps — collating and coding data in an ATLAS.ti database to surface two central practice clusters (broadening and containing); temporal bracketing to link triggers, governance obstacles, and practices over time; and visual mapping to reconstruct the cyclical process and abstract the governance-trap dynamic. Five focal constructs were defined in a coding table: triggers, governance obstacles, broadening practices, containing practices, and governance traps.
key_findings: The study surfaces a conceptual process model of how working through multistakeholder governance obstacles erodes a collective's ability to mitigate a grand challenge. Socioenvironmental triggers (contamination events, mass fish deaths, coral bleaching, regulatory debate) raise the grand challenge's salience and surface interpretive, structural, and relational governance obstacles; to avoid group paralysis or dissolution, participants deploy broadening and containing practices that narrow the group's remit while generating positive feedback. Across three cycles — developing (2008-2012), protecting (2013-2016), and leveraging (2016-2018) a collective response — members grew increasingly skilled at taming obstacles and consolidating their response (the water-health report card), producing cumulative, self-reinforcing governance traps. The central finding is directional: increasing the ability to respond collectively simultaneously decreases the ability to mitigate the grand challenge, generating a progressive disconnect between the report card and actual water-health improvement. Contrary to path-dependence accounts, external shocks that could have broken the response path instead reinforced it, as each new trigger was interpreted as one more governance obstacle to be tamed.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of governance traps to explain why multistakeholder initiatives addressing grand challenges so often produce unintended consequences, and theorizes the cumulative, self-reinforcing nature of these traps by connecting them to path-dependence theory. It extends path-dependence work by showing that exogenous shocks, rather than breaking a response path, can reinforce it in interorganizational settings, and nuances optimistic accounts of multistakeholder governance as a panacea for wicked problems.
practical_implication: For policymakers, communities affected by grand challenges, and organizational theorists designing interventions, the study highlights that consolidating a multistakeholder collective response — even successfully — risks decoupling the response from the underlying problem. Practices such as exchanging knowledge with external stakeholders, encouraging activities that deviate from the established path, and critically examining whether the response still fits the evolving challenge may help avoid governance traps.
limitations: The study is bounded by its single-case design focused on one grand challenge (degrading water health in the Great Barrier Reef) and one tightly affiliated multistakeholder initiative whose collective response revolved around a specific commensuration tool (the report card). The cyclical, path-dependent dynamics observed may unfold differently in more loosely affiliated collectives, social movements, online platforms, or initiatives with different membership compositions.
future_research: Future research should examine whether the disconnect documented here also emerges in collective responses to other grand challenges (e.g., the COVID-19 pandemic, catastrophic disasters, climate-related field-configuring events), study longer-term implications of participant selection for multistakeholder initiatives, and test whether commensuration strategies, collective tools, and information practices enable or hinder progress on grand challenges. Comparative work on more loosely affiliated collectives could clarify boundary conditions for the self-reinforcing dynamics.
abstract: In this paper, we adopt a multistakeholder governance perspective to study how people collectively respond to a grand challenge. Specifically, we show how working through governance obstacles—that is, coordinating and collaborating challenges arising from a multistakeholder governance approach to responding to grand challenges—can erode actors’ ability to mitigate these wicked problems. We illustrate this process through an in-depth case study of WaterHealthOrg, a multistakeholder initiative established to address degrading water health in Australia’s critical Great Barrier Reef region. Our findings reveal how, in an effort to avoid group paralysis or dissolution, actors employ specific practices to address governance obstacles. By doing so, actors set off a cumulative self-reinforcing process, driving them to consolidate rather than critically reflect on and adapt their collective response. Drawing on these insights, we develop a conceptual process model of how efforts to manage multistakeholder governance obstacles can generate governance traps that shape participants’ ability to collectively respond and, ultimately, mitigate grand challenges.
apa_citation: Couture, F., Jarzabkowski, P., & Lê, J. K. (2023). Triggers, traps, and disconnect: How governance obstacles hinder progress on grand challenges. *Academy of Management Journal*, 66(6), 1651-1680. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2020.1716
