title: Who Is Leaving and Why? The Dynamics of High-Quality Human Capital Outflows
methods: Longitudinal panel of administrative store-month records analyzed with a panel vector autoregression (PVAR) model with three lags; impulse response functions decomposed via 2,000 Monte Carlo simulations to estimate cumulative dynamic effects of exit events on subsequent unit-level voluntary turnover.
industry: Retail (large national U.S. retailer)
time_period: January 2014 through October 2015 (22-month store-month panel)
units: Store-months from 1,620 stores (Nall = 29,358 unit-months used in PVAR; 35,640 total observations)
n_sample: 1,620 stores
authors: Sajjadiani, Sima; Kammeyer-Mueller, John; Benson, Alan
theories: context-emergent turnover (CET) theory (Nyberg & Ployhart, 2013); psychological contract theory (Morrison & Robinson, 1997); signaling theory; social comparison theory; turnover event theory (Laulié & Morgeson, 2021)
keywords: dismissals; high performers; human capital outflows; layoff announcements; panel vector autoregression; turnover event theory; voluntary turnover
research_question: How do different types of employee exit events—dismissals, layoff announcements, and voluntary turnover—differentially affect subsequent unit-level voluntary turnover, and how is this dynamic shaped by the quality (performance) of the human capital leaving the work unit?
hypotheses:
- H1a: Dismissals will have the weakest effect of all turnover events on subsequent turnover.
- H1b: Layoff announcements will have the strongest effect of all turnover events on subsequent turnover.
- H1c: Voluntary turnover will have a greater effect than dismissals but less than layoff announcements on subsequent voluntary turnover.
- H2a: Higher leaver performance moderates (decreases) the negative relationship between unit-level dismissals and subsequent unit-level voluntary turnover.
- H2b: Higher leaver performance moderates (increases) the positive relationship between unit-level layoff announcements and subsequent unit-level voluntary turnover.
- H2c: Higher leaver performance moderates (increases) the positive relationship between unit-level voluntary turnover and subsequent unit-level voluntary turnover.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on turnover event theory, the authors argue that exit events trigger a disruption-then-recovery phase whose strength is a function of the event's novelty, disruption, and criticality. Layoff announcements signal an uncontrollable, psychological-contract-violating threat, producing strong and immediate spillover quits; voluntary turnover signals viable alternatives and produces moderate but longer-lasting contagion; dismissals largely remove disruptive workers and only weakly (and briefly) depress subsequent quits. The PVAR estimates show these dynamic effects are concentrated within performance strata—high-performer exits beget high-performer quits and low-performer exits beget low-performer quits—revealing a similarity-based "multiplier" structure that individual-level turnover models cannot detect.
data_measures:
- Data source: administrative personnel records from a single large U.S. retailer; 1,620 stores that operated continuously from January 2014 through October 2015 were aggregated into a store-month panel (stores averaged 93.6 workers per month).
- Exit-event and hiring rates: each event was operationalized as the count of the exit (or hire) occurrences in a store-month divided by the store's headcount. Dismissal rate counts dismissals for poor performance, poor attendance, lack of integrity, or rule/policy violations; voluntary turnover rate counts voluntary quits; hiring rate counts external new hires only.
- Layoff announcement rate (focal IV): measured from the layoff rate three months later, because layoffs in this organization were typically announced about three months before positions were eliminated.
- Human capital quality (moderator): annual supervisor performance evaluations on a five-point scale, available only for employees with at least one year of tenure; high performers coded 1 if performance is above the unit's average and 0 otherwise, then interacted with the turnover dummies and aggregated to unit-month rates for high- and low-performer exits.
- Controls: demographic ratios (White, women, and manager ratios), seasonal and full-time ratios, internal mobility, average hourly pay, and quarter dummies; dependent variables were residualized on these controls, and results held with and without them.
- Analysis and identification: panel vector autoregression (PVAR) with three lags estimated via a system of GMM equations; identification uses a theory-based variable ordering (layoff announcements, dismissals, hiring, then voluntary turnover) for same-period effects, with impulse response functions and 2,000 Monte Carlo simulations producing cumulative dynamic effects over twelve months. This is a dynamic time-series decomposition, not a design-based causal identification.
key_findings:
- Hypotheses 1a, 1b, and 1c were supported. Dismissals had the weakest effect: a 1 SD increase (about 1.1 workers) in the dismissal rate was associated with a significant decrease in the next month's voluntary turnover (bM1 = -0.07, p < .001), with no significant effect thereafter (cumulative -0.07 SD). Layoff announcements had the strongest and most immediate effect: a 1 SD increase (0.42 positions) raised voluntary turnover across the first two months (bM1 = 0.24, p < .001; bM2 = 0.09, p < .05; cumulative +0.34 SD). Voluntary turnover had a moderate but longer-lasting effect: a 1 SD increase (2.78 workers) had no first-month effect but raised turnover over the next three months (bM2 = 0.06, p < .01; bM3 = 0.12, p < .001; bM4 = 0.03, p < .001; cumulative +0.23 SD). In worker-level terms, one exit produced a cumulative -0.17 quits following a dismissal, +2.2 quits following a layoff, and +0.23 quits following a quit.
- Hypothesis 2a received only marginal support: dismissing low performers was associated with a slight one-month decrease (0.04 SD, about 0.11 workers) in subsequent voluntary turnover, whereas dismissals of high performers had no significant effect.
- Hypotheses 2b and 2c were not supported: leaver performance did not significantly moderate the layoff-announcement or the voluntary-turnover relationships, and none of the leaver-performance moderation predictions received significant support.
- Supplementary analyses showed that the "multiplier" effect is stratified by performance similarity: high-performer exits beget subsequent high-performer quits and low-performer exits beget low-performer quits (e.g., dismissing one high performer led to about 0.30 additional high-performer quits and 0.08 fewer low-performer quits; Table 6).
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends turnover event theory by jointly modeling dismissals, layoff announcements, and voluntary turnover as endogenous, coevolving elements of a dynamic system rather than as independent outcomes, and by separating layoff announcements from layoff events themselves. It generates and tests TET-grounded predictions about how novelty, disruption, and criticality differentiate the magnitude and duration of subsequent voluntary turnover, and it shows that "turnover begets turnover" is not uniform but stratified by performance similarity—a mechanism prior collective-turnover work had not articulated.
practical_implication: Managers should treat layoff announcements as the single most potent driver of subsequent voluntary turnover, especially when high performers are among those being laid off, and weigh the announcement decision accordingly. Because the consequences of departures multiply among similar workers, organizations underestimate the true human capital cost of losing high performers; retention investments in high performers therefore yield compounding returns. Dismissals targeted at clearly poor performers can be a net stabilizer of the unit.
limitations: Findings are drawn from a single large U.S. retailer with relatively low task complexity and modest human capital investment, which may attenuate the magnitude of disruption effects; generalizability to higher-complexity or higher-tenure settings is uncertain. Human capital quality is operationalized via annual supervisor performance ratings, available only for employees with at least one year of tenure, and the authors lacked objective performance measures or a measure of perceived dismissal fairness. Other plausible sources of heterogeneity (job level, full- vs. part-time status) could not be modeled.
future_research: Replicate the dynamic framework in occupations with higher task complexity, longer training, and greater human capital investment, where event novelty, disruption, and criticality should be larger. Use more objective performance metrics and direct measures of event novelty, disruption, and criticality to test the theorized mechanism more cleanly. Explore why exit events spill over within performance strata—e.g., the role of social-network homophily, social comparison, and signaling among similar workers.
abstract: This study proposes a unified, dynamic framework based on turnover event theory to evaluate the effects of dismissals, layoff announcements, and voluntary turnover on subsequent work-unit voluntary turnover. Applying our approach to 1,620 retail stores over 22 months, we show that modeling exit events as a dynamic and interdependent system adds to our ability to predict subsequent human capital outflow. Dismissals had the weakest total effect on subsequent voluntary turnover, layoff announcements had the strongest and most immediate effects, and voluntary turnovers had moderate but lasting effects. We also find that these three exit reasons each exhibit a distinct pattern of subsequent turnover intensity and longevity. Based on characteristics of work units in our setting, our results correspond to a cumulative worker-level average effect of 0.17 quits following dismissals, 0.23 quits following quits, and 2.2 quits following a layoff. We find that these "multiplier" effects are concentrated among workers of similar performance: high performer exits beget high performer quits, just as low-performer exits beget low-performer quits. Our findings suggest analyses offering individual-level estimates of turnover will generally underestimate the broader, work-unit level consequences of individual exit events on similar workers.

title: “Can I Sell You Avocadoes and Talk to You About Contraception?” “Well, It Depends Which Comes First”: Anchor Roles and Asymmetric Boundaries
methods: Inductive qualitative grounded-theory study using 53 one-on-one interviews and 10 focus groups across four waves (2016-2021) with 73 Tanzanian peer education agents; supplemented by clinic-staff and HealthOrg interviews, on-site observations, and 29 internal documents. Coded for boundary permeability and flexibility on 216 interrole-boundary instances using a Gioia-style first-order/second-order/aggregate-dimension structure with axial coding.
industry: Self-employed petty trading and subsistence farming combined with a volunteer community role as peer education agents (PEAs) providing family planning counseling for an INGO (HealthOrg)
country: Tanzania (Dar es Salaam, Mara, Mbeya, Morogoro, Mwanza, Njombe, and other regions)
time_period: 2016 to 2021 (four waves of data collection)
units: Individual Tanzanian peer education agents who simultaneously held a self-employment work role and a family-planning community role
n_sample: 73 PEA volunteers (53 one-on-one interviews of 42 participants; 10 focus groups with 40 participants; 9 overlapping); 216 coded interrole-boundary occurrences for 24 participants
authors: Shulist, P.; Rivera-Santos, M.; Kistruck, G. M.; Nguni, W.
theories: boundary theory (Ashforth, Kreiner, & Fugate, 2000; Nippert-Eng, 1996); role theory (Biddle, 1979, 1986; Katz & Kahn, 1978); work-family/work-work boundary literature (Allen, Cho, & Meier, 2014; Dumas & Sanchez-Burks, 2015)
keywords: Global South; Tanzania; anchor role; asymmetric boundaries; interrole boundaries; multirole interactions; peer education agents; role contrasts; role theory; work-community roles
research_question: What type of interrole boundary do individuals in the Global South construct between contrasting work and community roles, given that role contrasts predict strong boundaries while the dense networks and poverty of Global South contexts predict weak ones?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Role contrasts (script leeway, knowledge intensity, other- vs. self-interested orientation); boundary strength (permeability and flexibility); the novel concept of "anchor role" — the role that initially sets the stage for a specific social interaction.
- Triggering conditions: A multirole interaction is triggered when role holders have both the ability (dense, overlapping social networks; co-located work and community roles) and the motivation (poverty, time scarcity, care for the community role) to bring two roles together with the same person.
- Practices: When anchored in the work (self-employment) role at one's place of business, role holders enacted permeable, flexible boundaries — freely surfacing the PEA role during work interactions. When anchored in the PEA role (e.g., at the clinic or during community education), role holders enacted strong, narrow boundaries and refrained from work-related behaviors.
- Emergent outcomes: Asymmetric (in)compatibility between two highly contrasted roles, producing relationally embedded asymmetric boundaries within the same relationship — strong when anchored in the community role, weak when anchored in the work role.
- Boundary conditions: Asymmetry emerges when (a) role holders have ability and motivation for multirole interactions and (b) role contrasts produce divergent rather than symmetric (in)compatibility between the two roles.

The process logic departs from existing boundary theory by showing that highly contrasted roles need not be uniformly incompatible. A socioeconomic backdrop of poverty, time scarcity, and dense overlapping networks creates a constant integrative pressure to combine roles, but whether that pressure yields a weak boundary depends on the anchor role: when the anchor role's expectations are relatively simple and self-interested (work), bringing in the other-interested community role creates limited expectation violation; when the anchor role is highly scripted, knowledge-intensive, and other-interested (the PEA role), bringing in work-related behaviors triggers norm violations, confusion, and doubt, leading to a strong boundary.
data_measures: Design: inductive, grounded-theory qualitative study of 73 focal Tanzanian participants who simultaneously held a self-employment work role (petty trading, subsistence farming) and a peer education agent (PEA) community role providing family planning counseling for an INGO (HealthOrg). Data were collected across four waves (2016-2021): in the first two waves, 40 participants took part in 10 group interviews; from wave three onward the authors switched to 53 one-on-one semi-structured interviews of 42 participants (11 followed up for a second interview, and nine also appeared in group interviews, yielding 73 total). Interviews were conducted in Kiswahili and translated into English by a bilingual native-speaking coauthor. Supplementary data included on-site observations at ventures, clinics, and community events; interviews with six clinic staff; 17 meetings with HealthOrg staff; 29 internal documents (over 1,200 pages); and informal community conversations recorded in field notes. Analysis followed the Gioia methodology (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013), aggregating first-order categories into second-order themes and theoretical dimensions, supported by memo-writing, regular team discussions, and "devil's advocate" challenges. To probe the emergent asymmetry, the authors isolated the 216 occurrences of participants speaking about interrole boundaries and, for 24 participants, coded the anchor role (PEA or self-employment) and boundary strength along its two dimensions—permeability and flexibility—each rated high, moderate, or low (Table 3), then applied axial coding (Corbin & Strauss, 2015) to relate role contrasts to boundary outcomes. The design is interpretive rather than causal-identifying; no statistical estimation is claimed.
key_findings: Boundaries between the work and community roles were "asymmetric" rather than uniformly strong or weak: they were strong when a social interaction was anchored in the community (PEA) role but weak when anchored in the self-employment (work) role, where the "anchor role" is the role that initially sets the stage for a given interaction (and can change from interaction to interaction, even with the same person). Anchored in self-employment, participants displayed high permeability and high flexibility, freely surfacing PEA counseling while trading or farming; anchored in the PEA role (e.g., at the clinic), they displayed mixed/low permeability and low flexibility, largely refraining from work behaviors. Table 3 shows the pattern held for nearly all 24 coded participants—most had stronger boundaries when PEA-anchored, and none had a weaker overall boundary when PEA-anchored. Two interdependent factors produced the asymmetry. First, the socioeconomic features of the Global South—overlapping community networks (the ability) plus poverty, time scarcity, and the importance of family planning (the motivation)—created a constant background pressure to integrate roles; this was a necessary boundary condition that acted the same regardless of anchor role and so did not itself drive the asymmetry. Second, three role contrasts—contrasting script leeway, contrasting knowledge intensity, and contrasting orientation—drove the asymmetry by producing divergent (in)compatibility: integrating work behaviors when anchored in the PEA role created significant potential for norm violations, confusion, and doubt in motives (yielding a strong boundary), whereas integrating PEA behaviors when anchored in self-employment created only limited such potential (yielding a weak boundary). The study thus introduces the "anchor role" and "relationally embedded asymmetric boundaries," showing that highly contrasted roles need not be mutually or symmetrically incompatible.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to role theory and boundary-setting by (1) showing that role contrasts do not always render two roles mutually incompatible — contrasts can produce *asymmetric* (in)compatibility; (2) introducing the construct of the "anchor role" and showing that it has a direct, substantial influence on whether an interaction stays single-role or becomes multirole; and (3) theorizing that relationally embedded asymmetric boundaries are not unique to the Global South but extend to work-family (especially family business), work-work (e.g., nurse-manager), and friendship-coworker pairings whenever ability, motivation, and divergent role contrasts coexist.
practical_implication: The findings highlight that combining community and work roles imposes substantial tensions on individuals living in poverty that international NGOs often overlook, because INGOs focus on their donor agreements and ignore that time spent on volunteer roles directly subtracts from livelihood income. Designers of community-health and similar volunteer programs should seek positive spillovers between the community and work roles (e.g., selecting volunteers whose work has some alignment with the community role) and avoid scaling community programs without acknowledging interrole tensions.
limitations: Connections to participants were made through the partner INGO HealthOrg, which may have introduced selection biases despite efforts to diversify by gender, location, and experience. The three observed role contrasts all worked to constrain the PEA role rather than the self-employment role, leaving open the possibility that in other pairings contrasts could constrain the work role instead. The strength of dyadic relationships was not directly measured and may moderate the magnitude of asymmetry, and the study does not theorize how specific role contrasts differentially impact permeability versus flexibility.
future_research: Future work should investigate the magnitude (not just existence) of asymmetric boundaries, including how strong dyadic relationships might attenuate or amplify them; examine settings with "competing" role contrasts that point to opposing anchor-role asymmetries (e.g., a financial planner volunteering at an animal shelter); explore whether ambiguity about which role anchors an interaction produces distinct boundary dynamics; and theorize how specific role contrasts (e.g., knowledge intensity, professionalism) selectively impact the "when" versus "where" dimensions of boundary flexibility.
abstract: Role theory generally predicts that when the demands and norms of two roles are highly contrasted, individuals will construct a strong boundary to separate the roles. However, such predictions are grounded primarily in the Global North, emphasizing role pairings including “work–family” and hybrid “work–work.” Comparatively, the Global South is characterized by a lack of public services that creates a highly contrasted, highly salient, and yet understudied role pairing—“work–community.” Additionally, the socioeconomic features of the Global South (e.g., dense and overlapping community networks, financial poverty) call into question whether existing predictions surrounding boundary strength are likely to hold. We conducted a qualitative study of 73 Tanzanian participants who had both a self-employed work role and a family planning counselor community role. We found that highly contrasted roles can be simultaneously perceived as both incompatible and compatible. Specifically, the boundaries we observed were neither uniformly strong nor weak, but rather of asymmetric strength: strong when a social interaction was anchored in the community role, but weak when anchored in the work role. The specific role contrasts we identify, and the importance of role anchoring we observe, have important implications for role theory and boundary-setting more broadly.

title: Calling Oneself and Others In: Brokering Identities in Diversity Training
methods: Inductive qualitative study combining ethnography and grounded theory ("methodological bricolage") over 18 months at a large private Midwestern university's diversity training program. Data: ~75 hours of ethnographic observation, 41 semi-structured interviews with 36 participants (ICT staff, consultant, experienced/beginner/student peer trainers), and trainer documentation (guides, slides, handouts). Open and focused coding with two coders, axial coding for relationships, member checks, and peer debriefing.
industry: Higher education (organization-wide diversity training program at a large private Midwestern university)
time_period: Approximately 18 months (2016-2018 training cycles)
units: Diversity trainers (volunteer staff, faculty, and student peer trainers) and ICT program staff/consultant
n_sample: 36 participants across 41 semi-structured interviews (plus ~75 hours of observation)
authors: Sugiyama, Keimei; Ladge, Jamie J.; Bilimoria, Diana
theories: cultural brokerage (Jang, 2017; Press, 1969); identity work (Snow & Anderson, 1987; Caza, Vough, & Puranik, 2018); self-efficacy (Bandura, 1977, 1989)
keywords: brokering identities; brokering self-efficacy; calling in; cultural brokerage; diversity training; identity work; social justice-oriented training
research_question: How do trainers draw from their own identities to bridge across differences in demographic and cultural identities within social justice-oriented training contexts?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: trainer identity awareness, brokering identities, diversity repertoire, brokering self-efficacy
- Process phases: (1) Calling oneself in — marshaling identity resources and managing personal risks; (2) Modeling identity work — exemplifying brokering for trainees; (3) Calling others in — accommodating others' identities and encouraging perspective-taking
- Triggering conditions: emotionally charged moments, trainee resistance, offensive remarks, intercultural and demographic differences in the training room
- Emergent outcomes: enriched diversity repertoire, enhanced brokering self-efficacy, refined identity awareness extending beyond the training context
- Boundary conditions: trainers' own privileged/marginalized identities shape personal risks managed; intersectional identities differentially expose trainers

Trainers approach diversity training as cultural brokers who deliberately deploy their own privileged and marginalized identities to bridge across differences. The process is reciprocal and recursive: calling oneself in (drawing on personal stories while regulating triggers and vulnerabilities) is mirrored by calling others in (accommodating trainees' starting points and inviting perspective-taking), with modeling identity work as the connective tissue. Repeated practice builds a stockpile of stories and tactics (diversity repertoire) that strengthens brokering self-efficacy, which feeds back into sharpened identity awareness — explaining why trainers persist despite emotional costs and continue brokering beyond the training room.
data_measures: Data come from three primary sources gathered over roughly 18 months (three training cycles, 2016–2018) at the ICT diversity-training program: approximately 75 hours of ethnographic observation (including the first author's own experience as an active trainer), trainer documentation (training guides, presentation slides, and handouts), and 41 semi-structured interviews spanning 36 participants — experienced, beginner, and student peer trainers plus ICT staff and the external consultant, with key informants interviewed twice. Constructs were built inductively: open coding staying close to interviewees' expressions, then focused coding to synthesize and narrow the data dictionary to core codes, with the other authors and a second coder conducting axial coding to clarify relationships among codes and categories. Theoretical sampling deepened emerging themes, and credibility was checked through member checks (with the ICT, trainers, and the advisory committee) and peer debriefing.
key_findings: The study surfaces a grounded model of brokering identities — the process by which diversity trainers bridge across demographic and cultural differences by working on their own and others' identities. A trainer's initial identity awareness (their perception of their own identities relative to others') informs two reciprocal components: calling oneself in (marshaling identity resources and managing personal risks) and calling others in (accommodating others' identities and encouraging perspective-taking), linked by modeling identity work, through which trainers exemplify brokering for trainees. Through ongoing practice, trainers build a diversity repertoire that enhances their brokering self-efficacy (their belief in their ability to bridge differences), which in turn feeds back to refine identity awareness and often extends the brokering process beyond the training program. The authors argue that this gained self-efficacy and sharpened identity awareness explain why trainers persist in the emotionally exhausting work despite the challenges and controversies they face.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reframes diversity trainers as cultural brokers whose identity work — not just their static identity characteristics — drives the training process, contributing to diversity training research that has previously treated trainer identities as categorical inputs to which trainees react. It elaborates identity work theory by showing that identities can be intentionally used to create identity-implicating experiences for others (not only to repair or secure one's own self-concept), and extends cultural brokerage by foregrounding what brokers themselves gain: brokering self-efficacy and refined identity awareness that sustain effort across cycles.
practical_implication: Organizations should recognize that calling in (versus calling out) requires modeling identity work and gives well-meaning participants an example to follow when they lack self-efficacy to engage across differences. Diversity trainers — especially underrepresented employees who bear disproportionate emotional labor — need ongoing debrief or affinity-group support and tangible organizational rewards rather than relying on volunteer goodwill.
limitations: The study is grounded in a single social justice-oriented training program at one large private Midwestern university, which constrains generalizability to other training designs, sectors, and national contexts. The first author's dual role as researcher and active trainer enabled deep ethnographic access but also introduces interpretive proximity that the authors mitigated through member checks, peer debriefing, and triangulation rather than eliminate.
future_research: Future work could examine how trainees draw on the trainer's example in their own brokering, how possible selves operate in diversity training, and how intersectional differences across trainers' identities shape the personal risks they manage and the identity-implicating experiences they create. Researchers could also study cultural brokering in adjacent diversity-oriented initiatives such as mentoring, coaching, and hiring, and follow when individuals engage and disengage from brokering across different roles.
abstract: Diversity training is a common initiative in organizations, yet also the focus of much debate. Legislative attempts have been made to eliminate diversity training, while research has presented mixed findings and contradictions. Although much is known about designs, pedagogies, and trainee outcomes of diversity training, we know far less about the diversity trainer, who bears the brunt of delivering training amid existing controversies. In this study, we examine the diversity trainer’s experience, bringing to light the important use of the trainer’s own identities in navigating the emotionally charged minefield of educating about bias and bridging across cultural and demographic differences. Through this qualitative investigation, we develop a grounded model that illustrates the process of brokering identities, a form of identity work diversity trainers engage in that involves their deliberate efforts to call themselves and others in during diversity training. We highlight the brokering self-efficacy trainers gain from their identity work, which helps to explain why diversity trainers continue to engage in the process of brokering identities despite the challenges and controversies they may face.

title: Seeing the Forest and the Trees: Exploring the Impact of Inter- and Intra-Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Embeddedness on New Venture Creation
methods: Longitudinal panel analysis of 5,016 MSA-year observations (1994-2016) using linear models with multiple-way fixed effects (Stata reghdfe with state and year fixed effects; robust standard errors). Structural embeddedness operationalized as directional in-degree ego network density of inter-MSA VC firm investment ties; cultural embeddedness operationalized as corporate density and religiosity. Hypotheses 2-3 tested via interaction terms with the squared structural embeddedness term; robustness via fixed-effect Poisson, multilevel modeling, 2SLS using media coverage as instrument, alternative embeddedness measures, and sample splits at the inflection point.
industry: Cross-industry regional entrepreneurial ecosystems operationalized as U.S. metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs); inter-EE ties based on independent U.S. venture capital firm investments.
time_period: 1994-2016 (with 1990-1994 used to construct initial five-year moving-window network measures)
units: Metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) as proxies for entrepreneurial ecosystems; 272 MSAs across 23 years
n_sample: 5,016 MSA-year observations
authors: Xu, L.; Yang, S.; Liu, Y.; Newbert, S. L.; Boal, K.
theories: double embeddedness (Baker & Faulkner, 2009); entrepreneurial ecosystems (Stam, 2015; Spigel, 2017; Wurth, Stam, & Spigel, 2022); social network theory / structural embeddedness (Granovetter, 1985; Uzzi, 1997, 1999; Gulati, 1998)
keywords: corporate density; cultural embeddedness; double embeddedness; entrepreneurial ecosystems; inter-EE network; intra-EE; new venture creation; religiosity; structural embeddedness; venture capital mobility
research_question: Whether, how, and why does an entrepreneurial ecosystem’s position within the larger network of EEs — together with its internal cultural features — shape EE-level new venture creation? Specifically, how do inter-EE structural embeddedness and intra-EE cultural embeddedness (corporate density, religiosity) jointly determine regional new venture creation?
hypotheses:
- H1: An inverted U-shaped relationship exists between structural embeddedness and new venture creation.
- H2: The sociocognitive forces resulting from corporate density moderate the relationship between structural embeddedness and new venture creation such that the inverted U-shaped curve steepens as corporate density increases.
- H3: The social interaction due to religiosity moderates the relationship between structural embeddedness and new venture creation such that the inverted U-shaped curve flattens out as the level of religiosity increases.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Network size, elite and second-tier universities, regional unemployment rate, regional income per capita, region heat (VC-backed IPOs), state and year fixed effects.

The central mechanism is double embeddedness. As an EE becomes more structurally embedded in the inter-EE network, it gains access to valuable, tacit inflowing resources (knowledge, referrals, business models), increasing new venture creation up to an optimal point; beyond that point, inflows become redundant and competition rises, depressing new venture creation — yielding an inverted-U relationship. Corporate density steepens this curve because public companies act as resource integrators that magnify the value of inflowing resources via spawning and spillovers, then constrain novelty at high embeddedness. Religiosity flattens the curve because intra-EE social interaction creates localized trust and access to private (faith-based) resources, reducing reliance on inflowing resources at both low and high levels of structural embeddedness.
data_measures:
Longitudinal MSA-year panel of 5,016 observations (1994-2016; 272 MSAs). Inter-EE ties are built from independent U.S. venture capital firm investments (VentureXpert / SDC Thomson Financial, 1990-2016, five-year moving window); intra-EE and control data are drawn from Compustat, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, the U.S. Census Bureau, the U.S. Religion Census, and the Academic Ranking of World Universities.
- DV: New venture creation = total number of new business establishments in each MSA at time t, natural-log transformed (U.S. Census Bureau).
- IV: Structural embeddedness = directional in-degree ego network density of inter-MSA VC investment ties (mean-centered), with a squared term to model nonlinearity.
- Moderators: Corporate density = number of publicly traded companies per 100,000 population (Compustat); Religiosity = total congregational membership per 10,000 population (U.S. Religion Census); both mean-centered.
- Estimation: linear model with multiple-way (state and year) fixed effects via Stata reghdfe with robust standard errors; moderation tested through interactions with the squared IV term (Haans et al., 2016).
- Identification: primarily associational; a 2SLS specification instruments structural embeddedness and its square with prior-year media coverage as a robustness check for endogeneity, though the authors note reverse causality cannot be entirely ruled out. Further robustness comes from fixed-effect Poisson, multilevel modeling, five alternative embeddedness measures, and sample splits at the inflection point.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: structural embeddedness is positively related to new venture creation (b = 0.75, p < .001) and its squared term is negatively related (b = -1.65, p < .001), confirming an inverted U; the curve peaks at 57.8% ego-network density (about 86,387 new ventures).
- H2 supported: the interaction of the squared structural-embeddedness term with corporate density is negative (b = -0.22, p < .001), steepening the inverted U as corporate density rises (apex increases from 75,782 at the 25th percentile to 90,811 at the 75th).
- H3 supported: the interaction of the squared structural-embeddedness term with religiosity is positive (b = 0.11, p < .001), flattening the inverted U as religiosity rises (apex falls from 128,285 at the 25th percentile to 65,097 at the 75th).
- All three hypotheses received strong support, and results held across fixed-effect Poisson, multilevel modeling, 2SLS, five alternative embeddedness measures, and inflection-point sample splits.
theoretical_contribution: First, the paper applies a double embeddedness framework to EE research, showing that EE-level new venture creation depends not only on internal EE characteristics but also on the inter-EE network of ties — directly answering Wurth et al.’s (2022) call to study the “forest” alongside the “trees.” Second, it advances embeddedness theory by modeling a nonmonotonic, inverted-U effect of structural embeddedness moderated by two dimensions of cultural embeddedness, integrating prior linear/independent treatments into a unified contingent model and identifying a “Goldilocks” zone of inter-EE ties. Third, by integrating network and entrepreneurship literatures it provides a contextualized network view that scholars can apply to other regional-level entrepreneurial outcomes.
practical_implication: Policy-makers seeking to stimulate regional entrepreneurship should justify policies that attract extra-regional VC investment — especially in EEs with many public companies, where the benefits of inflowing resources are magnified, and to a lesser degree in highly religious EEs where such benefits are muted. Policy-makers should monitor returns to external VC and cap incentives to avoid over-embedding their EEs beyond the optimal level. The best policy considers both the forest (inter-EE ties) and the trees (intra-EE features) and identifies the EE-specific combination of factors that maximizes new venture creation.
limitations: The study operationalizes EEs as MSAs, which is one of several possible conceptualizations (e.g., small towns, incubators, university systems, technology hubs), so the results are influenced by this choice. It relies on VC firm mobility to capture inter-EE ties, even though other resource flows (board members, migrants, musicians, etc.) may also matter. Despite a 2SLS analysis using media coverage as an instrument, reverse causality between new venture creation and VC inflows cannot be ruled out entirely. The findings rest on U.S. data and an assumption of geographic inertia in entrepreneurs’ location choice, limiting generalizability.
future_research: Future work should define and measure EEs in alternative ways (small towns, incubators, university systems, technology hubs) to test whether the inter- and intra-EE effects on new venture creation hold in other contexts. Scholars should explore novel types of inter-EE ties (e.g., flows of board members, migrants, knowledge, organizational practices) and richer data sets to assess whether different resource flows generate distinct effects. Researchers should examine how the documented network-based mechanisms operate in other countries, at other levels of analysis, and for other regional outcomes (product development, scaling, customer reach), and should investigate cross-EE founding decisions.
abstract: Research on entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs) has tended to focus on the role that characteristics internal to the EE play in determining EE-level outcomes. Notwithstanding the insights that academics, policy-makers, and entrepreneurs have gleaned from these studies, prior research has yet to explain whether, how, and why these outcomes might also be impacted by an EE’s position within the larger network of EEs. Given broad acceptance for the important role that networks play in facilitating entrepreneurship at the firm level, we contend that adopting a network-based view of EEs may also help predict and explain aggregate entrepreneurial outcomes at the EE level. Specifically, we adopt a double embeddedness lens to examine the impact of both inter-EE (i.e., structural embeddedness) and intra-EE (i.e., cultural embeddedness) factors on EE-level new venture creation. Using a longitudinal sample of regional data in the United States from 1994 to 2016, we develop and test hypotheses where the relationship between structural embeddedness and new venture creation follows an inverted “U” shape that is itself moderated by cultural embeddedness. We conclude by discussing how these findings inform theory and practice in this area.

title: The Effects of Between-Group Pay Dispersion
methods: Two multiwave field studies plus a supplementary qualitative study. Study 1: multilevel path analysis (Mplus 8.3, MLR estimator, TYPE=TWOLEVEL with province-mean centering) on store-level objective pay data plus multisource surveys (employees, group leaders, store managers, archives); BGPD and WGPD measured via coefficient of variation. Study 2: branch-level path-analytic model on two-wave perceptual survey data with construct-level BGPD/WGPD measures; controls for pay communication, pay secrecy, interactional justice, and within- vs. between-group comparison tendencies. Qualitative study: thematic coding of interviews/focus groups with managers and group leaders to triangulate the explained-WGPD mechanism.
industry: Retail stores (Study 1; sales and support workgroups in a children's products, education, and entertainment chain) and bank branches (Study 2; service and marketing frontline groups in a large state-owned bank)
country: China (Study 1: 18 provinces of mainland China; Study 2: one Eastern Chinese city)
time_period: Study 1: January-February 2018 (objective pay and turnover from January 2018; multisource surveys in February 2018; performance over first half of 2018). Study 2: two-wave survey collected in January 2022.
units: Stores (Study 1) and bank branches (Study 2) as the focal unit of analysis; individual employees, group leaders, and store managers aggregated to the store/branch level
n_sample: Study 1: 205 stores comprising 4,234 employees, 1,899 group leaders, and 303 store managers. Study 2: 123 bank branches. Qualitative supplement: managers and group leaders interviewed at the focal retail company.
authors: Zhang, Z.; He, W.; Park, T.-Y.; Xing, Z.; Wu, X.
theories: distributive justice climate (Bowen, Gilliland, & Folger, 1999; Colquitt, 2001); explained pay dispersion theory (Shaw et al., 2002; Trevor, Reilly, & Gerhart, 2012); multiple social comparison theory (Brockner & Wiesenfeld, 1996; Festinger, 1954; Goodman, 1974); social identity and self-categorization theory (Turner, 1975; Turner, Hogg, Oakes, Reicher, & Wetherell, 1987); strategic HRM/workforce differentiation (Becker, Huselid, & Beatty, 2009; Lepak & Snell, 2002; Lepak et al., 2007)
keywords: between-group pay dispersion; distributive justice climate; horizontal pay dispersion; intergroup helping; multiple social comparison; organizational performance; social identity; voluntary turnover; within-group pay dispersion
research_question: When and how does between-group pay dispersion (BGPD) — pay-level differences between employees at the same job level but in different functional job groups — affect employees' shared distributive justice perceptions and, ultimately, organizational performance? Specifically, how does the size of explained within-group pay dispersion (WGPD) moderate the relationship between BGPD and the distributive justice climate, and how is this interaction transmitted through intergroup helping and voluntary turnover rates?
hypotheses:
H1. The relationship between BGPD and distributive justice climate is moderated by WGPD, such that the relationship is positive when WGPD is high and negative when WGPD is low.
H2. The BGPD × WGPD interaction on distributive justice climate is extended to organizational performance via intergroup helping, such that the indirect relationship between BGPD and organizational performance (through distributive justice climate and intergroup helping) is positive when WGPD is high and negative when WGPD is low.
H3. The BGPD × WGPD interaction on distributive justice climate is extended to organizational performance via voluntary turnover rates, such that the indirect relationship between BGPD and organizational performance (through distributive justice climate and voluntary turnover rates) is positive when WGPD is high and negative when WGPD is low.
mechanism_summary: The process draws on multiple social comparison and self-categorization theories: employees compare both within-group (proximal in-group referents) and between-group (out-group referents) pay. Because BGPD reflects ambiguous job-value differences, employees use the legitimacy of explained WGPD as an external cue when judging BGPD's fairness. When BGPD and explained WGPD align (both large signal meritocracy/differentiation; both small signal harmony/collaboration), a "strong situation" emerges and a high distributive justice climate forms. That climate then increases intergroup helping and reduces voluntary turnover, lifting organizational performance.
data_measures:
- Study 1 (205 retail stores): objective monthly pay and voluntary-turnover data from company archives combined with multisource surveys of employees, group leaders, and store managers. BGPD = coefficient of variation of the groups' average pay levels within a store; WGPD = the store average of each group's within-group pay coefficient of variation, treated as a proxy for "explained WGPD." Distributive justice climate = four-item Colquitt (2001) scale aggregated to store level; intergroup helping = two items from Farh et al.'s altruism scale rated by group leaders; voluntary turnover rate = departing over total employees (archival); organizational performance = objective first-half-year goal completion (archive) plus a subjective seven-item Sparrowe et al. (2001) rating by store managers.
- Study 2 (123 bank branches): two-wave perceptual survey; BGPD and WGPD measured with newly developed three-item perceived-dispersion scales contrasting service versus marketing groups; distributive justice climate = four-item scale (Trevor & Wazeter, 2006); controls add pay-system communication, pay secrecy, interactional justice climate, and within- versus between-group pay-comparison tendencies.
- Qualitative study: 34 face-to-face interviews across seven stores, thematically coded into two umbrella constructs (legitimacy of pay-dispersion bases; collective-level pay-comparison processes).
- Both quantitative studies estimate associational path-analytic models (Mplus, MLR/ML); no causal-identification strategy is claimed, and the authors note Study 1's cross-sectional design cannot establish the justice-to-performance causal direction.
key_findings:
- Study 1: the BGPD × WGPD interaction on distributive justice climate was significant (B = 6.62, p < .01); the BGPD slope was positive and significant at high WGPD (simple slope = .60, p < .001) and negative but nonsignificant at low WGPD (simple slope = −.19, ns) — H1 supported. H2 was supported: the indirect BGPD-to-performance effect via distributive justice climate and intergroup helping was positive and significant at high WGPD for both subjective and objective performance. H3 was supported only for the objective performance measure (indirect effect via distributive justice climate and voluntary turnover positive at high WGPD) and was nonsignificant for subjective performance. The BGPD main effect on distributive justice climate was nonsignificant.
- Study 2 (bank branches) replicated the significant BGPD × WGPD interaction (B = 0.57, p < .01) and supported H1, but the significant conditional slope fell in the opposite tail: negative and significant at low WGPD (simple slope = −.46, p < .01) while positive but nonsignificant at high WGPD (simple slope = .10, ns). A three-way BGPD × WGPD × between-group-pay-comparison interaction was significant (B = 0.84, p < .01). Study 2 did not test the performance-outcome hypotheses (H2, H3).
- Convergence with the qualitative study: interviews confirmed that WGPD rested on normatively acceptable bases (individual performance, tenure, human capital) and that employees engage in between-group pay comparison and use WGPD's legitimacy as a frame of reference when judging BGPD fairness, supporting the model's premises.
theoretical_contribution: The paper refines horizontal pay dispersion theory by decomposing it into a job-based (BGPD) and a person-based (WGPD) form, and shows that the desirable effects of "explained" WGPD spill over to make BGPD perceived as fair when the two are aligned. It extends multiple social comparison and self-categorization theories from the individual level to a collective, group-to-group comparison process and validates a nested pay-comparison mechanism in which in-group (WGPD) cues frame the interpretation of out-group (BGPD) cues. It also contributes to strategic HRM and compensation literature by clarifying that workforce differentiation (large BGPD) and workforce harmony (small BGPD) can each be desirable when consistently aligned with WGPD and the organization's strategic intent.
practical_implication: Organizations should design pay structures with a uniform strategic orientation: increasing BGPD (to reflect job-related inputs) is fair and performance-enhancing only when each group also operates a dispersed, person-based WGPD that legitimately rewards employee KSAOs, tenure, and performance. Senior executives should communicate strategic intent to middle managers and align job-based fixed pay with performance-based variable pay. Managing BGPD legitimately may also help address gender pay gaps that arise from occupational segregation between groups.
limitations: Both studies were conducted in large Chinese firms with relatively explainable WGPD, which limits generalizability to small firms, contexts where WGPD is illegitimate, and individualistic cultures with different distributive norms. The collective-level WGPD measure (averaging group WGPD scores) may be sensitive to skewed within-store WGPD distributions. The Study 1 design is cross-sectional and cannot establish whether justice perceptions cause performance or vice versa.
future_research: Future work should test the model in small-sized companies and in Western/individualistic cultures, operationalize legitimate versus illegitimate WGPD separately following Trevor et al. (2012), and develop alternative collective-level WGPD measures robust to within-unit skewness. Researchers should also extend the theory to cross-functional or heterogeneous-job groups (e.g., top management teams, medical teams) where within-group differences themselves reflect job-function differences, and use longitudinal or experimental designs to establish causality. Pay-transparency settings offer another avenue: how BGPD effects change before and after pay disclosure.
abstract: Although allocating resources (e.g., pay) between different job groups is a critical strategic decision, relevant research is limited. Focusing on the form of pay allocation across job groups, we consider the organizational consequences of between-group pay dispersion (BGPD). Building on the multiple social comparison literature, we propose that employees construe both large and small BGPD as fair when it is aligned with the size of explained within-group pay dispersion (WGPD). We also propose that the interaction effect of BGPD and WGPD on the distributive justice climate be extended to organizational performance via intergroup helping and employee stability (voluntary turnover rates). We present supportive evidence of the hypotheses using two multiwave studies (Study 1: 205 retail stores located in China and comprising 4,234 employees, 1,899 group leaders, and 303 senior managers, featuring objective pay data; Study 2: 123 bank branches of a large state-owned bank in China) and a supplementary qualitative study.

title: Longing for the Road Not Taken: The Affective and Behavioral Consequences of Forgone Identity Dwelling
methods: Three studies. Study 1: multi-wave, multi-source field study (four time periods, employee-coworker dyads) testing a moderated serial-mediation model via structural equation modeling in Mplus with bootstrapped indirect effects. Studies 2a and 2b: online randomized experiments using an experimental-causal-chain approach with writing-reflection manipulations, analyzed via ANOVA/ANCOVA.
industry: Employees across many occupations (e.g., social worker, truck driver, architect, nurse, engineer, accountant); occupationally diverse, not industry-specific
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employee-coworker dyads (Study 1); full-time individual employees (Studies 2a, 2b)
n_sample: 316 dyads (Study 1); 183 (Study 2a); 174 (Study 2b)
authors: Burgess, Rachel; Colquitt, Jason A.; Long, Erin C.
theories: cognitive-motivational-relational theory (Lazarus, 1991); identity construction / identity work (Ashforth & Schinoff, 2016; Alvesson & Willmott, 2002)
keywords: forgone identity dwelling; helping behavior; identity construction; job crafting; locus of control; longing; withdrawal behavior
research_question: Do employees continue to dwell on forgone professional identities—the occupational "roads not taken"—long after the identity construction process should have rendered them moot, and if so, what are the affective (longing) and behavioral (withdrawal, helping, job crafting) consequences of such dwelling?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on Lazarus's (1991) cognitive-motivational-relational theory, the authors argue that dwelling on a forgone professional identity triggers primary and secondary appraisals that produce longing—a secondary emotion blending sadness and happiness. The sadness component creates an avoidance action tendency (more withdrawal, less helping because the employee is distracted from the here and now), while the happiness/approach component motivates job crafting to recover unfulfilled values from the forgone path. Because internal-locus employees believe they can shape their own work lives, longing more strongly translates into job crafting for them, which in turn circulates back to reduce withdrawal and increase helping (a serial indirect effect). The field study and two experimental-causal-chain studies converge on these linkages.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the "forward progress" assumption in identity construction theory by showing that "identity echoes" from forgone professional identities continue to shape employee reactions after a current work identity is established, representing a lingering incoherence such models assume is resolved. It extends Obodaru's (2012, 2017) work on alternative selves by introducing identity dwelling as the mechanism through which forgone identities exert influence, and it foregrounds an affective construct—longing—to complement the predominantly cognitive and qualitative identity construction literature, addressing its noted "methodological myopia."
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that employees increasingly carry forgone professional identities and dwell on "what could have been," and should surface these through mentoring, coaching, or developmental conversations. They can then craft work contexts—providing flexibility, autonomy, and delegating tasks aligned with employees' forgone identities—to channel longing toward beneficial job crafting. Locus-of-control training that cultivates a more internal mindset may further encourage positive behavioral reactions to forgone identities.
limitations: Participants may have faced multiple forks in the road and thus multiple forgone identities, but only the most salient was assessed, so findings may miss nuance. The forgone identity dwelling and longing measures were created for this study and need continued use to establish broader construct validity. There may also be reciprocal causation in the dwelling–longing relationship, since cognition and emotion are highly integrated.
future_research: Researchers could examine dwelling on other selves (past, ideal, ought selves) and the cognitive—not just affective—consequences of identity dwelling, drawing on work on repetitive thought. They should probe reciprocal causality between longing and job crafting (e.g., virtuous cycles versus disenchantment) using cross-lagged panel data, and consider how identification strength, occupational prestige, and domain-specific locus of control shape who dwells on forgone identities.
abstract: The literature on identity construction has argued that employees work to create coherent and distinctive identities that encapsulate individual characteristics and professional and organizational memberships. Models of identity construction have suggested that a past career decision—choosing one professional “road” while leaving behind a “road not taken”—should lose its salience over time. We challenged that consensus by introducing the construct of forgone identity dwelling—thinking about and reflecting on a professional path that could have been. Our field and experimental studies showed that employees did dwell on forgone professional identities, even when the decision events that resulted in them were years in the past. Drawing on cognitive-motivational-relational theory, we showed that forgone identity dwelling resulted in longing—a yearning for something missing. Such longing created a “double-edged sword” for the behavioral consequences of forgone identity dwelling. On the one hand, longing was associated with increased withdrawal behavior and decreased helping behavior because employees were distracted from the here and now. On the other hand, longing was associated with job crafting that in turn reduced those reactions—particularly for employees with an internal locus of control. We discuss the implications of our work for models of identity construction.

title: Applying Coleman’s Boat in Management Research: Opportunities and Challenges in Bridging Macro and Micro Theory
methods: Conceptual 'From the Editors' essay; develops editorial guidance by using Coleman's (1990) boat as an organizing framework and illustrating three theoretical pitfalls with published exemplars, not empirical data.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Cowen, Amanda P.; Rink, Floor; Cuypers, Ilya R. P.; Grégoire, Denis A.; Weller, Ingo
theories: Coleman’s boat / macro–micro mechanisms framework (Coleman, 1990; Hedström & Ylikoski, 2010); microfoundations (Felin, Foss, & Ployhart, 2015)
keywords: Coleman’s boat; aggregation; macro–micro bridging; microfoundations; multilevel theory; situational mechanisms; transformational mechanisms
research_question: What recurrent theoretical challenges prevent management researchers from successfully bridging the macro and micro domains, and how can Coleman's (1990) "boat" framework help authors specify the situational, action-formation, and transformational mechanisms that connect levels of analysis?
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Coleman's boat organizes macro–micro linkages into four arrows — macro-level associations (Arrow 4), situational mechanisms (Arrow 1, macro-to-micro), action-formation mechanisms (Arrow 2, within micro), and transformational mechanisms (Arrow 3, micro-to-macro) — and sound cross-level theory must engage the situational and transformational arrows rather than rely on multilevel methods alone.
- Pitfall 1 — Multilevel methods versus multilevel theory: using a mix of macro and micro variables (or clustered errors/fixed effects) as the only "bridge" between levels without theorizing why the methods are needed.
- Pitfall 2 — Misapplication of micro theory: borrowing psychological constructs (e.g., social identity, imprinting, narcissism, anthropomorphizing) without attending to their central assumptions, trait–state distinctions, or whether they translate to the organizational level.
- Pitfall 3 — Insufficiently nuanced contextualization of micro theory: testing micro processes in abstract or experimental settings too detached from the macro organizational context that shapes them (Arrow 1).
- Pitfall 4 — Neglect of aggregation mechanisms: failing to specify the micro-to-macro aggregation logic (Arrow 3), despite equifinality and the non-additive nature of how individual behavior "sums up" to macro outcomes.

The essay's central process claim is that empirically combining macro and micro variables is insufficient: authors must theoretically articulate the situational mechanisms by which macro context shapes individual affect, behavior, choices, and cognition, and the transformational/aggregation mechanisms by which micro-level dynamics produce macro-level outcomes. Using Coleman's boat as an organizing device, the editors argue that explicating these mechanisms — and treating aggregation as an integral, equifinality-aware part of theorizing — is what turns boundary-spanning empirics into robust, integrated cross-level theory.
theoretical_contribution: The essay extends the use of Coleman's (1990) boat beyond merely motivating microfoundations research, showing it can guide bidirectional bridging (using macro perspectives to contextualize micro processes, and modeling how micro phenomena aggregate to macro outcomes) and can diagnose the specific theoretical elements — situational and transformational mechanisms — needed to connect levels. It synthesizes recurring cross-level pitfalls editors observe at AMJ into an actionable framework for building integrated macro–micro theory.
practical_implication: For authors and reviewers, the piece offers concrete guidance: do not substitute sophisticated multilevel methods for multilevel theory; engage the central assumptions of borrowed micro theories; contextualize micro processes within macro realities; and make aggregation logic explicit. The editors also suggest that realizing the promise of boundary-spanning work may require new approaches to doctoral training and macro–micro coauthor collaborations.
limitations: The intention is explicitly not to catalogue limitations of macro or micro research, and the essay focuses primarily on mechanistic cause–effect cross-level relationships, acknowledging that other cross-level forms (composition, compilation, clustering, mutual dependencies) receive less treatment.
future_research: The editors encourage authors to make aggregation an integral part of their theorizing, to extend (rather than merely apply) micro theories at the macro level, and to cross-fertilize the micro literature by introducing new contingency factors and collective/organizational outcomes; they also call for theorizing that connects meso-level dynamics to micro and macro levels.

title: Here Comes the Sun: The Impact of Incidental Contextual Factors on Entrepreneurial Resource Acquisition
methods: Mixed-methods, archival-primary. Study 1: binary logistic regression of Demo Day funding on interday change in sunshine across 1,335 startups (171 Demo Days), errors clustered at the cohort level, with city/sector/accelerator fixed effects and probit/LPM-OLS robustness. Study 2: randomized between-subjects mood-induction experiment (n=92) with three-step, Sobel, and bootstrap mediation tests.
industry: Early-stage / seed-stage technology startups graduating from accelerators (industry fixed effects across sectors)
country: Europe (~a dozen major cities); experiment used a US West-Coast accelerator pitch with online participants
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Startups (Study 1); individual prospective investors / participants (Study 2)
n_sample: 1,335 startups across 171 Demo Days (archival); 92 participants (experiment)
authors: Dushnitsky, Gary; Sarkar, Sayan
theories: affect-as-information theory (Schwarz & Clore, 1983; Schwarz, 2012)
keywords: affect-as-information theory; entrepreneurial resource acquisition; incidental contextual factors; investor mood; seed-stage investment; sunshine; uncertainty
research_question: What explains seed-stage investment patterns, and what factors affect investors' decisions to fund highly uncertain startups? The paper asks specifically whether incidental contextual factors outside the investor–startup pair — namely a daily change in sunshine on Demo Day — systematically shape seed-stage resource acquisition.
mechanism_summary: Affect-as-information theory holds that people confuse incidental feelings (e.g., a sunshine-induced good mood) with integral feelings about the focal task, so that under intense uncertainty an investor's mood "tips the balance" toward more favorable subjective probability assessments of a startup. A sunnier Demo Day lifts investors' mood, which raises their evaluation of an otherwise opaque seed-stage venture and increases the likelihood of funding; the effect attenuates as uncertainty falls (mature startups, high-human-capital founders) because more objective information then displaces mood as the input to judgment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces a third class of explanation for seed-stage investment patterns — incidental contextual factors situated outside the investor–startup pair — to complement the two dominant streams that locate variation in startup characteristics or investor traits. It demonstrates that funding-outcome variation can emerge even across a homogeneous pool of investors and startups, simply because some pairs are randomly exposed to contextual shocks, and it imports affect-as-information theory into entrepreneurship to specify mood as the mechanism, bounded by the level of uncertainty.
practical_implication: Rather than ignoring incidental contextual factors, investors and accelerators should heed their effect, since transient conditions such as weather accrue in a foreseeable way on funding decisions. While one cannot control the sun, accelerators could design Demo Days (e.g., refreshment choices or "walking" Demo Days) to manage investors' mood, and scholars/practitioners should collect data on the context in which pairs are situated, not only on startups and investors.
limitations: The arguments are calibrated to seed-stage investment and its intense uncertainty, so the affect-as-information logic need not extend to later-stage deals where a VC committee already knows the startup. The archival analysis captures funding outcomes for hundreds of accelerator graduates but lacks detailed data on the individual investors who attended, and the outcome is measured only as a binary funding variable.
future_research: Future work could trace individual investors' movements to directly map how incidental contextual factors shape their decisions, and examine whether daily sunshine operates through entrepreneurs as well as investors. It could also test generalizability to other geographies and other contextual factors (e.g., choice of refreshment), and explore richer outcome measures such as premoney valuation.
abstract: This paper focuses on investment decisions in nascent, seed-stage startups, where information is scarce and uncertainty is intense. Entrepreneurship literature has shown that investment is a function of the investor–startup pair; some studies have investigated startup characteristics, while others have focused on investor traits. We complement extant work by studying factors beyond the investor–startup pair; namely, incidental contextual factors such as changes in the physical environment. Drawing on affect-as-information theory, we conjecture that, in the face of intense uncertainty, sunnier days may affect investors' mood and result in a greater likelihood of investment. Archival and experimental analyses inform our predictions. The former utilizes proprietary data on 1,335 startups graduating from European accelerators. Every accelerator holds a "Demo Day," where startups pitch to investors. We find that graduating on a sunnier day increases the likelihood of investment. This effect is stronger under intense uncertainty, where (a) startups are nascent, or (b) founders have limited human capital. An experimental study where prospective investors evaluate a Demo Day pitch yields further insights. We find a positive sunshine–investment association, and show that the association is mediated by investors' mood. Our findings complement extant work and contribute insights regarding seed-stage investment decisions.

title: “I Go Here…But I Don’t Necessarily Belong”: The Process of Transgressor Reintegration in Organizations
methods: Longitudinal, inductive, grounded-theory case study (Glaser & Strauss, 1965; Strauss & Corbin, 1998) of cadet transgressors at a U.S. military service academy; iterative open and axial coding of interviews plus Langley (1999) process narratives, supplemented by surveys, journals, and informal observation.
industry: Military service academy (officer training; strict honor code forbidding lying, cheating, or stealing)
time_period: 111 interviews conducted over 48 months
units: Cadet transgressors who committed honor-code violations, plus their mentors and honor officers
n_sample: 23 cadets, 10 mentors, and 4 honor officers (111 interviews)
authors: Frey, Erin L.
theories: integration / membership and belonging (O’Reilly, Caldwell, & Barnett, 1989; Leary, 2010); liminality (Turner, 1967; Ibarra & Obodaru, 2016); organizational socialization (Van Maanen & Schein, 1978); reintegration (Goodstein, Butterfield, Pfarrer, & Wicks, 2014)
keywords: belonging; institutional belonging; integration; liminality; membership; relational belonging; transgressor reintegration
research_question: How do retained transgressors—organizational members who violated core values and so became "structural insiders but moral outsiders"—attempt to reintegrate and come to feel like full insiders again, and what makes them feel more, or less, reintegrated?
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: A transgression decouples membership and belonging, throwing the retained transgressor into liminality (structural insider, moral outsider) and producing precarious membership and precarious belonging.
- Restoration attempts (membership): Compliance behaviors aimed at obtaining institutional endorsements to feel secure in perceptions of membership.
- Restoration attempts (belonging): Investment in relationships aimed at strengthening relational belonging, while institutional belonging depends on endorsements from institutional actors.
- Emergent outcome: Belonging splits into relational belonging and institutional belonging; both, plus restored membership, are necessary for high reintegration.
- Boundary condition: Because belonging restoration depends on positive perceived interactions with many actors, transgressors often restore membership but not belonging, so high reintegration is rare (only 3 of 23 cadets).

Frey advances a process-with-variance model in which reintegration is an intrapsychic, perceptual process driven by transgressors’ own interpretations of interactions rather than by objective, triangulated behaviors. Transgressors use distinct logics—compliance to restore membership versus relational investment to restore belonging—and because lack of restoration in even one element (membership, relational belonging, or institutional belonging) blocks full reintegration, feeling highly reintegrated is difficult to achieve even in resource-intensive programs.
theoretical_contribution: The study conceptualizes transgressor reintegration from the transgressor’s own perspective, foregrounding its liminal starting point and the driving forces (restoring membership and belonging) rather than merely listing features of reintegration. It recasts integration from a static construct into a dynamic, perceptual, and negotiated process that can be formed, threatened, modified, and regained, and it differentiates belonging into relational and institutional types that are complements, not substitutes—offering new leverage for research on socialization, undersocialization, belonging, and nested relational phenomena.
practical_implication: To give employees a genuine second chance, managers must support both restoring perceptions of membership (e.g., bestowing institutional endorsements such as desirable assignments, promotions, and access to perks) and fostering belonging (e.g., coaching peers and supervisors on how to interact with and affirm the transgressor). Managers should also balance transgressor affirmation against good-standing members’ justice perceptions to avoid backlash.
limitations: Pre-violation integration data are retrospective because first interviews occurred after violations, so cadets’ recollections of initial integration may be inaccurate or colored by present feelings. The author could not collect data from transgressors’ interaction partners (personal acquaintances or institutional actors), leaving open whether transgressors’ perceptions are accurate, and the data are not fine-grained enough to definitively map specific actors to specific types of belonging.
future_research: Survey-based quantitative work could test whether transgressors’ recollections of pre-transgression integration are accurate and whether their perceptions of others’ treatment generally align with reality. Researchers could more systematically identify which types or features of organizational actors foster relational versus institutional belonging, and examine how the observed dynamics differ in organizations with little or no formal structure around transgressor reintegration.
abstract: When organizational members violate important organizational standards, they may face termination, or they may instead be retained by the organization and given a second chance. Retained transgressors experience the tension of liminality: they maintain their affiliation to the organization, making them structural insiders, but they have committed a transgression, making them moral outsiders. How might transgressors attempt to reintegrate and feel like full organizational insiders once again? And what makes transgressors feel more, or less, reintegrated? Previous work has studied reintegration from victims’ or third-parties’ perspectives, but little is known about transgressor reintegration. To build theory on transgressor reintegration, I studied transgressors at a military service academy. Through waves of qualitative data collection and inductive analyses, I find that transgressions threaten transgressors’ integration, leading transgressors to feel precarious in their perceptions of membership and their feelings of belonging. Transgressors attempt to restore both elements, but use distinct approaches for each. Because belonging restoration requires positive interactions with many organizational actors, transgressors can—and, in my data, frequently do—experience restoration of membership but not belonging. Therefore, it may be relatively rare for transgressors to feel highly reintegrated following transgressions, even in organizations that devote considerable resources to reintegration.
