title: Fast or Slow: How Temporal Work Design Shapes Experienced Passage of Time and Job Performance
methods: Multi-study quantitative design: two between-subjects MTurk experiments (Studies 1a, 1b), a naturalistic field study in a garment factory (Study 2), a multilevel organizational field study of knowledge workers and supervisors (Study 3), and a three-wave time-lagged online survey (Study 4). Analyses use one-way ANOVA, CFA, and bootstrapped/Bayesian mediation in Mplus 8.0.
industry: MTurk working adults (Studies 1a, 1b, 4); Chinese garment-factory sewing machinists and support workers (Study 2); knowledge workers at an international logistics company (Study 3)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: individual employees (with supervisor-matched dyads in Studies 2 and 3)
n_sample: Study 1a = 116; Study 1b = 118; Study 2 = 96; Study 3 = 211 employees / 34 supervisors; Study 4 = 270
authors: Zhao, Helen H.; Deng, Hong; Chen, Rocky Peng; Parker, Sharon K.; Zhang, Wei
theories: attentional gate theory (Zakay & Block, 1995; Matthews & Meck, 2016; Walsh, 2003); work design / job characteristics model (Hackman & Oldham, 1976; Parker, 2014)
keywords: attentional gate; experienced passage of time; job performance; task segmentation; temporal predictability; temporal work design; work design
research_question: Is it possible to alter employees' experienced passage of time via work design—and, if it is possible, are there any performance benefits of doing so?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on the attentional-gate perspective, the paper argues that temporal and non-temporal information compete for the same neural resources, so when work design directs attention away from temporal cues, employees process the passage of time less and therefore experience time as passing faster. Temporal predictability removes uncertain "fore-periods" that draw attention to time, and task segmentation inserts categorically different markers that restore diminishing task attention before it drifts to temporal cues. The resulting faster, more pleasant time experience is treated as an intermediate work experience that, in turn, improves job performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends work design theory beyond enrichment-based mechanisms (the job characteristics model and its relational and motivational extensions) by introducing two attention-based temporal work characteristics—temporal predictability and task segmentation—that shape outcomes not by enriching jobs but by redirecting attention away from temporal cues. It establishes experienced passage of time as a previously neglected intermediate work experience linking work design to performance, and connects work design research to the emerging management literature on time.
practical_implication: Managers can design work time, not just work content, to help employees stay focused: eliminate or reduce uncertain wait times (e.g., giving idle "standby" workers other tasks), design better-scheduled meetings, and punctuate the workday with categorically different temporal markers/breaks timed to when attention wanes. Because these levers are flexible and cheap relative to job enrichment, they are especially valuable for simple, standardized, routinized jobs that are hard to enrich, but segmentation should be customized and used cautiously for complex jobs.
limitations: The authors identify only two temporal work characteristics rather than an exhaustive set, and they do not examine boundary conditions (e.g., individual differences such as mindfulness, or whether segmentation is self-initiated versus externally imposed). Although the design attempts to establish the temporal precedence of experienced passage of time over performance, reverse causality—performance shaping experienced time—cannot be fully ruled out. The two experiments (Studies 1a, 1b) are relatively weak in external validity.
future_research: Future work should explore additional temporal work characteristics that alter experienced passage of time (e.g., unusual schedules such as night shifts for ER doctors or air traffic controllers, including chronotype differences), investigate boundary conditions and moderators such as mindfulness and whether segmentation is self-initiated or imposed, and further disentangle the causal ordering between experienced passage of time and job performance.
abstract: Experienced passage of time, the extent to which employees perceive the passage of work time as being fast or slow, is a fundamental aspect of work experience. We identify two novel temporal work design characteristics that can speed up employees' experienced passage of time: temporal predictability and task segmentation. Jobs with high temporal predictability do not make employees go through uncertain wait times before embarking on their next task. High task segmentation occurs when a large chunk of work time is segmented by categorically different temporal markers. We tested a model in which temporal predictability and task segmentation affect experienced passage of time, which in turn influences job performance, with five studies: two experiments that established the internal validity of temporal predictability and task segmentation (Studies 1a and 1b), a naturalistic field study in a factory that investigated the natural consequences of distinct temporal work design (Study 2), an organizational field study that constructively replicated the model using a sample of knowledge workers and their supervisors (Study 3), and an online survey in which we connected our model with the broader work design literature (Study 4). Altogether, the studies support a new temporal approach to work design.

title: Unpacking Firm External Dependence: How Government Contract Dependence Affects Firm Investments and Market Performance
methods: Longitudinal archival panel study of U.S.-based manufacturing firms, using government-contract data from USASpending.gov, firm and financial data from Compustat, political-activity controls, propensity score matching, Heckman-style selection correction, and fixed-effects models with robust standard errors and time dummies.
industry: U.S.-based manufacturing firms in SIC codes 2000-3999
time_period: 2009-2014, with predictors measured at time t and dependent variables at time t+1
units: Firm-year observations for U.S.-based manufacturing firms
n_sample: 1,142 firm-year observations in the reported fixed-effects models
authors: Abdurakhmonov, Mirzokhidjon; Ridge, Jason W.; Hill, Aaron D.
theories: resource dependence theory (Pfeffer & Salancik, 1978); resource orchestration (Helfat et al., 2007; Sirmon et al., 2007, 2011)
keywords: dependence scope; dependence stability; dependence supplementation; firm investment; government contracts; government dependence; market performance; resource dependence theory; resource orchestration
research_question: How does dependence on government contracts affect firms' internal investment decisions and market performance, and how do the scope, supplementation, and stability of that dependence condition these relationships?
mechanism_summary: The mechanism integrates RDT and resource orchestration: as firms become more dependent on one government revenue source, resource configurations become more tailored to that customer's idiosyncratic demands, reducing autonomy, narrowing search for alternative investments, and lowering investors' expectations of future market opportunities. The results generally support a negative association between government dependence and Tobin's Q, and support a negative association with capital expenditures but not directly with R&D. Scope weakens the negative market-performance relationship; supplementation and stability weaken the negative market-performance relationship but strengthen the negative investment relationship, with capital investment partially mediating the dependence-performance link.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends RDT by moving beyond the external management of dependence to examine the internal firm dynamics that accompany dependence relationships. By integrating resource orchestration, it explains how dependence can shape resource search, selection, configuration, and deployment, and it treats dependence as heterogeneous rather than homogeneous through the concepts of scope, supplementation, and stability.
practical_implication: The study warns that government contracts can provide stable revenue while also creating investment and market-performance risks when they dominate a firm's revenue base. Managers and investors should assess not only the level of government dependence but also whether the dependence is spread across agencies, supplemented by new contracts, or locked into longer-term arrangements, because these features change how the market and internal investment choices respond.
limitations: The paper focuses on U.S.-based manufacturing firms and on government contracts as one specific source of external dependence, so the findings may not generalize directly to other industries or dependence relationships. The authors also note that other contextual factors, such as industry concentration or firms' ability to resist inertial forces, may add further nuance to how government dependence affects investment and market perceptions.
future_research: Future research should examine government dependence beyond manufacturing, including how industry concentration, political shocks, consumer boycotts, and market position shape the risks attached to contract stability. The authors also call for work on other dependence relationships, such as dependence on major business customers, and on other RDT approaches such as acquisitions and alliances.
abstract: We advance resource dependence theory (RDT) by answering calls for theorizing on both how being dependent on external entities for resources affects firms and the heterogeneous nature of such dependencies. Specifically, we theorize how internal firm dynamics and performance are affected by resource dependence by integrating resource orchestration (RO) into RDT. Building on RO, we argue that as the degree to which a firm is dependent upon a single source of revenue increases (a core tenet of RDT), the firm adjusts internally by reducing investments and the market responds negatively as well. Further, we argue that the heterogeneous nature of such dependence—namely, dependence scope (the spread of dependence throughout the entity with which the dependence relationship resides), dependence supplementation (the addition of new relationships within the prior dependence relationship), and dependence stability (the expected length of the dependence relationship)—moderates the relationship between the level of dependence and these outcomes. We find broad support for our theorizing in a longitudinal sample of manufacturing firms’ dependence upon governmental contracts for revenue. Collectively, we advance understanding of RDT by adding nuance to both explanatory mechanisms underlying dependence and conceptualizations of firms’ external dependence relationships, posing theoretical and practical implications.

title: Undertrusted, Overtrusted, or Just Right? The Fairness of (In)Congruence between Trust Wanted and Trust Received
methods: Two-study quantitative design. Study 1 uses a multisource, three-wave field study of employee-supervisor dyads, analyzed with polynomial regression, response surface methodology, block-variable indirect effects, and supplemental molecular overtrust/undertrust analyses. Study 2 uses a 2 x 2 scenario experiment manipulating trust wanted and trust received, with post hoc pairwise comparisons and robustness checks against alternative mechanisms.
industry: Study 1: administrative, nonacademic roles in two large public universities. Study 2: employed adults in a scenario set in a professional services firm.
time_period: Study 1: three survey waves separated by four weeks and six weeks; calendar dates not reported. Study 2: date not reported.
units: Employees and supervisors in Study 1; employed Prolific Academic participants in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1: 396 employee Time 1 responses, 342 Time 2 responses, and supervisor ratings for 333 employees; analyses ranged from 342 to 291 employees. Study 2: 225 participants.
authors: Baer, Michael D.; Frank, Emma L.; Matta, Fadel K.; Luciano, Margaret M.; Wellman, Ned
theories: fairness and need rule theorizing (Deutsch, 1975; Leventhal, 1976a); person-environment fit / needs-supplies fit; social exchange theory (Blau, 1964)
keywords: citizenship behavior; feeling trusted; need rule; overall fairness; task performance; trust received; trust wanted
research_question: When employees receive more or less supervisor trusting behavior than they want, do they judge the supervisor as less fair, and do those fairness perceptions explain downstream task performance and citizenship behavior? The paper also asks whether congruent high wanted/high received trust is perceived as fairer than congruent low wanted/low received trust.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a need-rule fairness process. Trusting behaviors are treated as socioemotional resources that vary in how much employees want them, so deficiency and excess both signal that the supervisor is not sufficiently mindful of the employee's needs. Congruence between wanted and received trust increases perceived overall fairness, with high-high fit judged especially fair because it requires more active supervisor effort. Those fairness perceptions then support higher supervisor-rated task performance and citizenship behavior through the social-exchange logic linking fair treatment to reciprocation.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper challenges the prevailing assumption in the feeling-trusted literature that more supervisor trust is uniformly beneficial for employees. It introduces overtrust and undertrust as meaningful forms of trust misfit, showing that low received trust can be fair when low trust is wanted and that excess trust can be unfair when it violates the employee's needs.

The study also foregrounds the neglected need rule in fairness theory and links it to person-environment fit. By shifting from trusting intentions to trusting behaviors, it shows why employee reactions to being trusted depend on the match between supervisor behavior and employee preference, not simply the absolute amount of trust received.
practical_implication:
Supervisors should not assume that allocating as much trust as possible will always improve employee reactions or performance. Trusting behaviors are effortful and can impose demands, so supervisors need to attend to whether employees actually want those responsibilities and whether they have enough support to carry them.

The findings suggest that overtrusting employees who do not want additional trusting behaviors may be worse than wasted effort because it can reduce perceived fairness and harm performance. Supervisors may be better served by increasing the support and developmental benefits that make employees more willing to accept higher trust.
limitations:
Study 1 measured trust wanted and trust received from employees, so the design cannot show whether employees' perceptions aligned with supervisors' trusting intentions. The field study also did not control for distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational justice rule adherence, although Study 2 experimentally addressed this concern with alternative-mechanism checks.

The model is largely agnostic about time beyond the three-wave field design and the scenario experiment. It does not directly examine how employees recalibrate desired trust over time, how trust levels are negotiated between employees and supervisors, or why some employees want less trust.
future_research:
Future studies could compare supervisor-rated trusting intentions with employee perceptions of trusting behavior to test whether and when the two diverge. Research could also examine whether other justice rules interact with need-rule adherence, such as whether high informational or procedural justice offsets the unfairness of unwanted trust.

Additional work could study trust recalibration and negotiation over time, antecedents of lower trust wanted, and other outcomes of overtrust or undertrust. The paper specifically points to possibilities such as unwelcome obligations, need for achievement, need for impact, engagement, self-esteem, and spillovers from excess autonomy.
abstract: The nascent literature on feeling trusted has focused on the notion that it is a benefit to employees and their organizations, with several studies demonstrating a link to improved job performance. It is not surprising, therefore, that the prevailing assumption is that employees will react positively when their supervisors trust them more as opposed to less. Recent research, however, has suggested that the benefits of feeling trusted are accompanied by strains, which some employees may be unwilling to bear. Drawing on seminal theorizing on fairness, we propose that employees will perceive their supervisors as being more mindful of their needs—acting more fairly—when there is a fit between trust wanted and trust received, even when the fit is at low levels of trust. By extension, when trust received exceeds or falls short of an employee’s desire for trust, the employee should perceive the supervisor as less fair. We build a model in which the overall fairness perceptions resulting from the trust wanted–received interplay influence employee performance. Our model is supported by a multisource, three-wave field study and an experiment.

title: Maintaining Strategic Ambiguity for Protection: Struggles over Opacity, Equivocality, and Absurdity around the Sicilian Mafia
methods: In-depth historical process study of the Sicilian Mafia from 1963 to 2018. The authors analyze a large archival corpus of oral sources, judicial documents, parliamentary reports, laws and debates, letters and diaries, media material, book interviews and essays, and DIA/DNA reports; they use historical reconstruction, line-by-line coding, aggregation of Mafia strategies and state responses, bracketing into three struggles, and process-model development.
industry: Clandestine/criminal organization: the Sicilian Mafia, including illegal activities such as trafficking and extortion and legal activities such as the building sector
country: Italy, centered on Sicily and the Italian state
units: Historical events, actions, texts, and interpretations involving Mafiosi, pentiti, and Italian state representatives
n_sample: More than 25,000 pages of empirical material
authors: Cappellaro, Giulia; Compagni, Amelia; Vaara, Eero
theories: ambiguity and sensemaking (Daft & Weick, 1984; Feldman, 1989, 1991; Weick, 1995); clandestine organizations and secrecy (Scott, 2013a, 2015; Costas & Grey, 2014; Dufresne & Offstein, 2008); strategic ambiguity (Eisenberg, 1984; Eisenberg & Witten, 1987)
keywords: absurdity; clandestine organizations; equivocality; opacity; public scrutiny; secrecy; silence; silencing; strategic ambiguity; strategic ambiguity maintenance
research_question: How do organizations that need to protect themselves from outside scrutiny maintain strategic ambiguity? The paper also asks how such organizations interact with external audiences and change their strategies over time.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / ambiguity types: strategic ambiguity as opacity, equivocality, and absurdity; opacity means lack of a conceptual schema, equivocality means multiple possible interpretations, and absurdity means unreasonable or paradoxical interpretations.
- Organizational strategies: protective silence, targeted silencing, one-sided disclosing, obfuscating, untargeted silencing, hyperbolic disclosing, stereotyping, and renewed protective silence.
- External audience responses: state representatives elaborate a tentative interpretation, prioritize one interpretation, and then attempt to merge paradoxical interpretations.
- Process sequence: the 1963-1983 struggle over opacity shifts to the 1984-1993 struggle over equivocality after state representatives make progress in defining the Mafia; the 1994-2018 struggle over absurdity follows after the Maxi Trial validates one interpretation of the Mafia as a violent criminal organization.
- Process outcome: the Mafia maintains strategic ambiguity by changing strategies when state representatives make progress in dissipating ambiguity, ultimately neutralizing audience efforts and producing paralyzing confusion.

The process model treats strategic ambiguity maintenance as an antagonistic, relational struggle between an organization seeking protection and external audiences seeking to reduce ambiguity. The Mafia first withholds cues through silence, then offers multiple and conflicting cues through one-sided disclosure and obfuscation, and finally overwhelms audiences with paradoxical interpretations while returning to concealment. Each shift occurs after state representatives partially dissipate the previous form of ambiguity, which prompts the organization to move toward a harder-to-dissolve form.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances strategic ambiguity research by theorizing maintenance, rather than one-time creation, of ambiguity as a long-term process of interlinked struggles between organizations and external audiences. It introduces opacity, equivocality, and absurdity as progressively harder-to-dissolve types of ambiguity and shows how discursive and nondiscursive strategies, especially silence, silencing, and hyperbolic disclosing, shape these struggles. It also extends research on clandestine organizations by linking secrecy and ambiguity as mutually reinforcing conditions.
practical_implication: For state representatives and other audiences trying to scrutinize clandestine or controversial organizations, the study implies that ambiguity reduction is not a one-shot interpretive task: progress can trigger new organizational strategies that reintroduce confusion. It also warns that insider disclosures may help audiences build an interpretation, but those disclosures can be one-sided, hyperbolic, or strategically confusing, so audiences should attend to how such disclosures shift the ongoing struggle over ambiguity.
limitations: The authors identify the Sicilian Mafia as an extreme and revealing case, so the model should not be automatically generalized to all organizations. The findings apply most directly to organizations that maintain ambiguity for protective purposes in antagonistic relationships with external audiences, especially when survival or control is at stake; they may apply less to organizations using ambiguity to mobilize stakeholder support. The study is also limited by the secrecy of clandestine organizations and by its focus on speech produced for external audiences rather than informal day-to-day conversations among Mafia members.
future_research: Future research could compare this case with organizations and institutional settings that vary in secrecy, stakes, and the availability of illicit strategies such as violence or intimidation. Scholars could also examine contexts where external audiences are less powerful than the state, or respond through disapproval rather than criminalization. The authors further suggest insider-oriented studies of clandestine organizations, using discourse analysis or ethnography, to examine how strategies are chosen and how they affect internal organizational life.
abstract: In spite of an increasing interest in ambiguity, our knowledge of how organizations maintain strategic ambiguity to protect themselves from public scrutiny is still in its infancy. Through an in-depth historical study of the Sicilian Mafia between 1963 and 2018, we develop a model of strategic ambiguity maintenance. We focus on three struggles between the Mafia and state representatives, and show how these struggles centered on different types of ambiguity: ambiguity as opacity, equivocality, and absurdity. We elaborate on the strategies enacted by the Mafia and the responses by state representatives and their implications for ambiguity over time. The main contribution of our paper is that it advances understanding of the maintenance of strategic ambiguity by organizations that need to protect themselves from public scrutiny. More specifically, it enriches our knowledge of the key process dynamics, the types of struggles, and the discursive and nondiscursive strategies employed in the process. Our analysis also extends research on clandestine organizations and illuminates the relationship between (strategic) ambiguity and secrecy.
apa_citation: Cappellaro, G., Compagni, A., & Vaara, E. (2021). Maintaining strategic ambiguity for protection: Struggles over opacity, equivocality, and absurdity around the Sicilian Mafia. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(1), 1-37. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1086

title: How Temporal Focus Shapes the Influence of Executive Compensation on Risk Taking
methods: Panel firm fixed-effects regressions of CEO-year data from 2003 to 2016; CEO temporal focus is measured with LIWC analysis of earnings call language, with IPTW, 2SLS, alternative text-source, random-effects, and alternative-DV robustness checks.
industry: S&P 1500 firms across industries; largest divisions are manufacturing, services, and finance, insurance, and real estate.
units: CEO-year observations
authors: DesJardine, M. R.; Shi, W.
theories: behavioral agency model; prospect theory; temporal focus
keywords: behavioral agency model; executive compensation; merger and acquisition investment; risk taking; temporal focus
research_question: The paper asks how CEOs' present and future temporal focus shape the relationship between current/prospective option wealth and strategic risk taking. It tests this question in the context of M&A investment, where CEOs' compensation incentives and temporal attention jointly condition acquisition spending.
mechanism_summary: The BAM predicts that CEOs endow current option wealth and therefore become risk averse with it, while prospective option wealth is not endowed and therefore encourages risk taking. DesJardine and Shi argue that present-focused CEOs intensify this pattern because attention to the here-and-now strengthens endowment of current wealth and weakens attachment to prospective wealth. Future-focused CEOs reverse the pattern because attention to future outcomes makes prospective wealth psychologically endowed and shifts attention away from current wealth.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the behavioral agency model by making its implicit temporal assumption explicit: option wealth affects risk taking differently depending on where CEOs direct temporal attention. It shows that present focus strengthens the BAM's predicted current-wealth/risk and prospective-wealth/risk relationships, while future focus weakens or reverses them. The study also contributes to temporal focus research by showing that temporal focus does not have a uniform relationship with risk taking; its implication depends on whether the relevant incentive is current or prospective wealth.
practical_implication: Boards and investors should not treat option pay as having uniform incentive effects across CEOs. If the goal is to discourage risk taking, the paper suggests that stronger current option wealth may fit present-focused CEOs, while stronger prospective option wealth may fit future-focused CEOs. The practical implication is that option-pay design should be matched to CEO temporal focus because temporal focus can change not only the strength but also the direction of risk-taking incentives.
limitations: The authors note that their BAM-based argument does not account for CEOs' focus on other stakeholders' interests, even though risk-taking activities may create short-term stakeholder harms and long-term stakeholder gains. They also focus on temporal focus rather than other temporal characteristics such as time horizon or temporal depth. Finally, because the study uses archival textual data, it cannot eliminate the possibility that text analysis imperfectly captures psychological constructs or that alternative mechanisms explain the observed pattern.
future_research: Future research could examine whether CEO stakeholder orientation alters the joint influence of option wealth and temporal focus on M&A investment. It could also explore how time horizon and temporal depth interact with temporal focus in compensation-risk relationships. The authors further suggest that primary data could help test the psychological mechanism more directly, including the alternative possibility that future-focused CEOs become more excited about future prospective gains.
abstract: The behavioral agency model (BAM) posits that executives endow current wealth, but do not endow prospective wealth. As a result of this endowment effect, executives are risk averse with current wealth and risk seeking with prospective wealth. These relationships, however, assume that all executives perceive and attend to current and future outcomes similarly, which is at odds with research on temporal orientations. Drawing on the concept of temporal focus, we theorize that present-focused CEOs adhere to the BAM’s endowment effect, while exhibiting even stronger relationships between current and prospective wealth and risk taking. In contrast, by nature of being forward-looking, future-focused CEOs endow prospective wealth instead of current wealth, thereby reversing the main relationships of the BAM. Using a sample of 7,700 CEO-year observations from 2003 to 2016, we find empirical support for our arguments in the context of merger and acquisition investment. Findings from this study advance the BAM by showing that the relationship between wealth type and risk taking hinges on CEOs’ temporal focus.

title: Turned Down and Taking Off? Rejection and Turnover in Internal Talent Markets
methods: Archival quantitative study of rejected internal job applications at HealthCo. Logistic regression models estimate voluntary exit within six months of rejection, with robust standard errors clustered by individual; robustness checks use a 12-month turnover window, relaxed sample restrictions, cumulative rejection-experience measures, reapplication analyses, winner-similarity analyses, and external-interview-pool composition.
industry: Health services company
time_period: 2013 to 2017, with six-month post-rejection turnover window in the main analysis
units: Unsuccessful internal job applications/rejections submitted by HealthCo employees
n_sample: 9,355 unsuccessful internal applications/rejections submitted by 8,160 employees in the main restricted sample; full data contained 53,089 unsuccessful internal applications submitted by 15,601 employees
authors: Dlugos, Kathryn; Keller, JR
theories: intraorganizational mobility literature (Vardi, 1980; Landau & Hammer, 1986); job matching literature (Keller, 2018; Weller, Hymer, Nyberg, & Ebert, 2018); social comparison research (Schaubroeck & Lam, 2004; Lockwood & Kunda, 1997)
keywords: hiring manager interview; internal advancement; internal hiring; internal rejection; internal talent markets; intraorganizational mobility; voluntary turnover
research_question: When are internal job applicants who are rejected more or less likely to leave the firm voluntarily, and how do hiring-manager interview decisions and internal-versus-external selection outcomes inform rejected candidates' perceptions of future internal advancement?
mechanism_summary: Drawing on intraorganizational mobility research, the paper argues that rejection is not only a closed opportunity but also an informational event. Being interviewed by the hiring manager signals that the candidate met many criteria for the job and may meet criteria for similar jobs later; being rejected in favor of another internal candidate signals that similar future jobs may still be filled internally. The main logistic models support both predictions: rejected candidates were 1.43 times less likely to exit after a hiring-manager interview and 1.23 times less likely to exit when the winner was internal. Supplementary analyses are consistent with the proposed mechanism, showing that these rejection contexts are also associated with greater reapplication to similar jobs and that external interview-pool composition is associated with higher exit.
theoretical_contribution: The paper adds a rejection-side boundary condition to job-matching accounts of internal talent markets, which typically emphasize the value created by successful internal matches. It extends rejection research by showing that internal rejection is not uniformly negative: the evaluation and selection context supplies information about future internal opportunities. It also updates intraorganizational mobility theory by showing how employees in contemporary, market-based internal labor systems learn about advancement prospects through participation in internal job markets rather than only through formal bureaucratic rules.
practical_implication: Firms can potentially reduce post-rejection turnover by managing the informational consequences of internal hiring processes. The authors do not recommend interviewing every internal candidate or always hiring internally; instead, they suggest strategically interviewing key internal candidates and providing guidance about future internal opportunities when an external candidate is selected. Managers should recognize that rejected candidates and observing colleagues may treat interview and winner decisions as signals about whether internal advancement remains possible.
limitations: The study is based on one large, relatively flat U.S. health services organization that openly values internal mobility, so the informational meaning of interviews and internal winners may differ in smaller, more hierarchical, or less internally focused organizations. The archival design cannot directly measure employees' perceptions, affective reactions, or full career histories, and turnover is an imperfect proxy for value destruction. The main sample restriction helps isolate focal rejection effects but excludes employees who apply again within six months, so robustness analyses are needed to assess sensitivity to multiple-rejection histories.
future_research: Future work could compare internal talent markets with other matching mechanisms such as slotting, job rotations, and succession planning, where employees may not know they were rejected. Researchers could provide a fuller financial accounting of value creation and destruction by jointly measuring match value and the costs of rejected-candidate exits. Pairing archival data with surveys would allow direct tests of perceived advancement prospects, affective reactions, and how sequences of rejection and success over time shape employee mobility.
abstract: Internal talent markets—created when firms post open jobs and invite current employees to apply—enhance the value of an organization’s human capital by generating complementary person–job matches. Yet these markets generate more internal rejections than matches, as not all internal applicants are hired. We develop theory to explain when rejections are more or less likely to deplete an organization’s human capital resources through voluntary turnover. Drawing on the extant intraorganizational mobility literature, we argue that variations in post-rejection turnover are shaped by the information that the market provides employees about their likelihood of future internal advancement, despite being rejected in the present. Specifically, we argue that hiring manager decisions about whom to interview and hire provide information to rejected internal candidates about their ability to meet the criteria to be hired for similar jobs in the future and the likelihood that those jobs will be filled internally. Analyzing 9,355 rejections in a single firm over a five-year period, we find that rejected employees are significantly less likely to exit when they are interviewed by the hiring manager (compared to being rejected earlier) and when they are rejected in favor of another internal candidate (compared to an external candidate).

title: The Two Towers (or Somewhere in Between): The Behavioral Consequences of Positional Inconsistency across Status Hierarchies
methods: Archival quantitative study of Hollywood performers. The authors build artistic and commercial status measures from IMDb film participation, Box Office Mojo and WorldwideBoxoffice data, and film-award records; then estimate two-stage Heckman probit models in STATA 15 predicting whether performers appear in films that could enhance their lagging secondary status.
industry: Hollywood film industry / U.S. films
time_period: 1996-2015 performer-film observations, using film and status-history data from 1990-2015
units: Hollywood performers and performer-film observations
n_sample: 1,012 performers; 9,229 performer-film observations
authors: Han, Jung-Hoon; Pollock, Timothy G.
theories: cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1957); status hierarchy/status multiplicity theory (Sauder, Lynn, & Podolny, 2012); status inconsistency theory (Lenski, 1954; Stryker & Macke, 1978)
keywords: artistic status; commercial status; embeddedness; multiple status hierarchies; status hierarchy prestige; status inconsistency
research_question: How do actors respond to status inconsistencies across multiple status hierarchies, and how do hierarchy prestige, high primary status, and embedded professional networks condition attempts to improve lagging status? The paper examines this question in Hollywood, where performers can occupy different positions in artistic and commercial status hierarchies.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that pluralistic value systems create multiple status hierarchies, and that actors experience dissonance when their standing is inconsistent across those hierarchies. In Hollywood, artistic status is treated as more prestigious than commercial status, so performers with higher artistic than commercial status are more likely to pursue commercial-status-enhancing films. Performers with higher commercial than artistic status are less likely to pursue artistic-status-enhancing films, suggesting that hierarchy-level prestige changes both motivation and perceived feasibility. High artistic status dampens secondary-status pursuit, while embeddedness strengthens pursuit for artistic-primary performers but further constrains commercial-primary performers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reconnects contemporary status research with the older status inconsistency tradition by showing that actors' positions across multiple hierarchies can shape behavior. It theorizes value systems as a generalizable basis for multiple status hierarchies and introduces the idea that hierarchies themselves can be ranked by prestige. It also clarifies how high primary status and embeddedness act as boundary conditions whose effects depend on whether the actor's primary hierarchy is more or less prestigious.
practical_implication: Managers and organizational actors should treat status as a multi-hierarchy social approval asset rather than a single ranking. The findings imply that actors' strategic options depend on whether their primary status lies in a more or less prestigious hierarchy and whether embedded ties enable or constrain movement. This affects whether it is more productive to invest in secondary-status enhancement or to maintain and deepen primary status.
limitations: The authors note that the Hollywood setting is useful because artistic and commercial status hierarchies are visible, but it may be idiosyncratic because its status orderings are unusually stark. They also cannot observe opportunities performers were offered, roles they rejected, or roles they pursued but did not obtain; they only observe films in which performers appeared. Finally, other performers' status may influence film choices, but the study focuses on directors and writers because of their earlier involvement and role in shaping films.
future_research: Future research should examine contexts where status orderings are less stark or based on different values. Studies with individual-level decision-process data or dynamic designs could observe opportunities, refusals, and relationship formation more directly. The authors also call for work on the relative value of status-consistent versus status-inconsistent actors, whether status gains in one hierarchy affect status in another, and the cognitive mechanisms through which actors adjust to status inconsistency.
abstract: We examine how actors react to status inconsistencies across multiple status hierarchies. We argue that pluralistic value systems create multiple status conferral mechanisms, and that hierarchies’ prestige varies as a function of the values they represent. While status inconsistency, in general, increases the likelihood that actors will pursue opportunities that can boost their lagging status, their status hierarchies’ unequal prestige influences the magnitude and direction of actors’ responses to their status inconsistency. Further, their ability to respond is constrained by their relative standing in their primary status hierarchy and the extent to which they are embedded in particular professional networks. Using the artistic and commercial status of Hollywood performers, we found that status-inconsistent performers were more likely to appear in films that could boost their lagging status in the commercial hierarchy when they possessed relatively higher artistic than commercial status. Moreover, being high-status decreased the likelihood a performer would pursue opportunities that could improve their lagging status only when they were high status in the artistic status hierarchy, while embeddedness only decreased the likelihood when their primary status hierarchy was commercial.

title: When Does Pay for Performance Motivate Employee Helping Behavior? The Contextual Influence of Performance Subjectivity
methods: Three quantitative studies: a multisource field survey of leader-employee dyads in nine Chinese firms, a two-wave survey of employees in six Chinese firms, and a laboratory experiment manipulating PFP intensity and performance subjectivity.
industry: Study 1 covers financials, consumer services, consumer goods, industrials, telecommunications, and health care; Study 2 covers consumer goods, industrials, and technology; Study 3 uses a simulated consulting task.
country: China; Study 3 uses a Chinese university sample.
time_period: Study 2 used two waves separated by two weeks; Study 3 used a 40-minute task plus a 20-minute survey; dates for Study 1 and Study 3 are not reported.
units: Full-time employees and indirect leaders in Chinese firms, plus undergraduate participants assigned to experimental teams.
n_sample: Study 1: 323 matched leader-employee dyads; Study 2: 176 full-time employees; Study 3: 140 participants in 32 four-person teams and 4 three-person teams.
authors: He, Wei; Li, Shao-Long; Feng, Jie; Zhang, Guanglei; Sturman, Michael C.
theories: expectancy theory (Vroom, 1964; Lawler, 1971); heuristic processing literature / dual-processing theory (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Kahneman, 2011)
keywords: employee helping behavior; expectancy theory; helping-performance expectancy; heuristic processing; pay for performance; performance subjectivity
research_question: When does pay for performance motivate, rather than undermine, employee helping behavior, and why does performance subjectivity change that relationship? The paper asks whether subjective performance appraisal makes employees perceive helping as connected to performance evaluation and thus as instrumentally valuable under PFP.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is expectancy-based. When performance criteria are subjective, employees have fewer clear objective signals about what will be rewarded and are more likely to infer heuristically that helping coworkers can improve performance evaluations. Under higher PFP intensity, that perceived helping-performance link makes helping behavior more instrumentally valuable, producing a conditional positive PFP effect on helping rather than the conventional crowding-out or tradeoff prediction.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the simple claim that PFP undermines extra-role behavior by showing that PFP can increase helping when performance is subjectively evaluated. It shifts PFP theory from the "pay" component alone to the "performance" component, especially the appraisal context, and extends expectancy theory by showing how domain-specific expectancy perceptions can shape the direction, not only the amount, of individual effort.
practical_implication: Organizations should not treat purely objective performance indicators as automatically superior when they also want employees to help coworkers. Hybrid appraisal systems that combine objective and subjective indicators may better motivate comprehensive work outcomes, but managers need systematic training to reduce rater bias when subjective measures are used. Organizations can also strengthen helping-performance expectancy by formally incorporating extra-role behaviors into appraisal or incentive practices.
limitations: The studies examine short-term PFP rather than long-term incentive systems such as deferred compensation or stock options. The field data do not separate within-team from cross-team helping, and the conceptual model does not fully incorporate team-level influences. The authors also note alternative mechanisms such as justice perceptions and affective reactions, and the studies do not directly compare in-role task performance and extra-role helping as parallel outcomes.
future_research: Future studies should examine leadership and team context as boundary conditions, especially because leaders' beliefs about extra-role behavior may shape whether subjectivity increases helping-performance expectancy. Research should also investigate performance appraisal criteria, indicator accuracy, and the joint effects of performance basis and measurability. Longitudinal studies and field experiments could track changes in PFP intensity, objective task performance, and helping behavior over time.
abstract: An extensive body of literature has demonstrated the incentive effect by which pay for performance (PFP) motivates employees’ in-role task performance. Nonetheless, scholars have also posited that PFP is likely to demotivate employees’ extrarole behaviors. Drawing upon expectancy theory (Vroom, 1964) and the heuristic processing literature (Kahneman, 2011), we examine the relationship between PFP and employee helping behavior. We perform this examination not only by considering the “pay” component (e.g., PFP intensity) but also by scrutinizing the “performance” component; namely, performance subjectivity, which refers to the extent to which the criteria or indicators used to measure employee performance in the performance appraisal system are subjective. Specifically, we propose that PFP has a conditional positive effect (i.e., in the context of high performance subjectivity) on employee helping behavior, and further theorize and test the underlying psychological mechanism by which individual perceived helping–performance expectancy accounts for the interactive effects between PFP and performance subjectivity on employee helping behavior. The empirical results of three studies employing distinctive methodologies provide general support for our hypotheses. Taken together, our research challenges the conventional wisdom that PFP undermines employees’ extra-role behaviors by providing new insight into understanding when and why PFP motivates employee helping behavior.

title: Do the Hustle! Empowerment from Side-Hustles and Its Effects on Full-Time Work Performance
methods: Two quantitative studies. Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of full-time employees with side-hustles and OLS regression to test side-hustle complexity, motives, and empowerment. Study 2 uses an experience-sampling method design with employee-coworker dyads, multilevel CFA, multilevel path modeling in Mplus, previous-day controls, and Monte Carlo confidence intervals for serial indirect effects.
industry: Participants worked across varied side-hustles and full-time jobs, including Uber or Lyft driving, event photography, completing surveys online, selling goods online, teaching, software engineering, sales, and nursing; Appendix A reports O*NET job families.
time_period: Study 1 used three surveys separated by three weeks each. Study 2 used a 10-day experience-sampling design with evening, midday, and end-of-day surveys; calendar dates are not reported.
units: Full-time employees with side-hustles in Study 1; focal employee-coworker dyads in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1: 337 employees. Study 2: 80 employee-coworker dyads and 507 complete dyad-day observations after listwise deletion; the method also reports 2,124 raw observations.
authors: Sessions, Hudson; Nahrgang, Jennifer D.; Vaulont, Manuel J.; Williams, Raseana; Bartels, Amy L.
theories: affective shift model (Bledow et al., 2011); job characteristics theory (Hackman & Oldham, 1976); role enrichment theory (Greenhaus & Powell, 2006)
keywords: affective shift; attention residue; positive affect; psychological empowerment; role enrichment; side-hustle complexity; side-hustle engagement; side-hustles
research_question: What makes side-hustles psychologically empowering, and how does empowerment from side-hustles spill over into full-time work performance? The paper asks whether side-hustle complexity and side-hustle motives shape empowerment, and whether daily empowerment enriches or conflicts with full-time work through affective and cognitive pathways.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines enrichment and conflict. More complex side-hustles give workers opportunities for autonomy, skill use, task identity, significance, and feedback, which are expected to support psychological empowerment, especially when some motives make workers more responsive to those opportunities. Daily empowerment then increases side-hustle engagement; the affective component spills into full-time work as positive affect and improves performance, while the cognitive component produces attention residue that can distract from full-time work. The authors find that both pathways operate, but the positive affect pathway is stronger overall, and negative affect from full-time work strengthens later side-hustle engagement through affective shift.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper shifts side-hustle research away from the assumption that side work mainly drains resources and harms full-time work. It uses role enrichment theory to show that side-hustle empowerment can generate resources that carry into full-time work, while still modeling attention residue as a conflicting pathway.

It also extends job characteristics theory to side-hustles by showing that side-hustle complexity and motives jointly explain empowerment. Finally, it extends affective shift theorizing across work domains, not only within a single workday or single job context.
practical_implication:
Managers should be cautious about blanket assumptions that side-hustles are necessarily harmful to full-time work performance. The findings suggest that side-hustles can produce empowerment and positive affect that benefit full-time work, although managers still need to account for attention residue and other workplace distractions.

For employees, the results imply that the type of side-hustle and the reason for pursuing it matter. Side-hustles with higher motivating potential may be more likely to generate empowerment, but employees still need to weigh these benefits against other uses of limited nonwork time, including family, leisure, volunteering, and sleep.
limitations:
The studies use survey designs, so causal inference remains limited even though the authors use temporal separation, source separation, previous-day controls, and theoretically grounded ordering. Study 1 relies on worker perceptions of side-hustle characteristics rather than objective work-characteristics data.

The message-board recruitment strategy may have attracted people especially interested in side-hustles, and the authors could not know how many eligible workers saw the postings but did not participate. The model also does not provide a clear account of hours worked on side-hustles, because side-hustle hours had small or difficult-to-interpret indirect effects and may be endogenous to engagement.
future_research:
Future work could examine how employees craft fit between side-hustles and full-time work, including whether side-hustles supplement or complement unmet needs from full-time jobs. Research could also study congruence in knowledge and skills across side-hustles and full-time work, because overlap may provide training benefits but may also reduce detachment from full-time work.

The authors also call for alternative theoretical perspectives, including challenge-hindrance stress, conservation of resources, and boundary theory. Future designs could use objective work-characteristics data, coworker ratings of side-hustle characteristics, experimental ESM, or before-and-after designs following workers as they adopt side-hustles.
abstract: Side-hustles, income-generating work performed alongside full-time jobs, are increasingly common as the gig economy provides opportunities for employees to perform supplementary work. Although scholars have suggested that side-hustles conflict with full-time work performance, we assert that psychological empowerment from side-hustles enriches full-time work performance. We argue that side-hustle complexity—the motivating characteristics of side-hustles—positively relates to empowerment and that side-hustle motives moderate this relationship. A study of 337 employees supports these assertions. We then investigate the spillover of side-hustle empowerment to full-time work performance in a 10-day experience-sampling method study of 80 employee–coworker dyads. We address an affective pathway in which daily side-hustle empowerment enriches full-time work performance through side-hustle engagement and positive affect at work. We also consider a cognitive pathway wherein side-hustle empowerment distracts from full-time work performance through side-hustle engagement and attention residue—persistent cognitions about side-hustles during full-time work. Overall, performance enrichment from side-hustles was stronger than performance conflict. We also consider affective shift from full-time work to side-hustles, finding negative affect from full-time work strengthens the relationship between side-hustle empowerment and engagement. Combined, our two studies examine the source of side-hustle empowerment and how side-hustle empowerment influences affective and cognitive experiences during full-time work.
apa_citation: Sessions, H., Nahrgang, J. D., Vaulont, M. J., Williams, R., & Bartels, A. L. (2021). Do the hustle! Empowerment from side-hustles and its effects on full-time work performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(1), 235-264. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0164

title: Distinguishing Voice and Silence at Work: Unique Relationships with Perceived Impact, Psychological Safety, and Burnout
methods: Two-study quantitative design. Study 1 is a psychometric meta-analysis of voice, silence, perceived impact, psychological safety, and burnout relationships, using artifact corrections, random-effects estimates, Mplus path tests, relative weight analysis, and moderator analyses for operationalization and methodological differences. Study 2 is an interval-contingent six-month panel of full-time working respondents analyzed with multilevel CFA and hierarchical linear models in R/lme4, including one-month lagged predictors and person-level averages.
industry: Study 1: published and unpublished primary studies on employee voice and silence. Study 2: full-time workers across multiple industries, including construction, education, energy, finance, health care, insurance, law enforcement, manufacturing, publishing, and retail.
country: Study 1: not reported as a single country. Study 2: United States.
time_period: Study 1: studies available through September 2019. Study 2: six consecutive monthly surveys, Times 1-6; calendar months not reported.
units: Primary studies and effect sizes in Study 1; full-time working respondents in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1: 162 relevant papers, including 123 published and 39 unpublished. Study 2: 405 respondents contributing 1,620 of 2,025 possible lagged observations.
authors: Sherf, Elad N.; Parke, Michael R.; Isaakyan, Sofya
theories: behavioral activation system and behavioral inhibition system perspective (Carver, 2006; Elliot, 2006; Gray, 1982); exit, voice, loyalty, and neglect model (Farrell, 1983; Hirschman, 1970; Withey & Cooper, 1989)
keywords: behavioral activation system; behavioral inhibition system; employee burnout; perceived impact; psychological safety; silence; voice
research_question: The paper asks whether employee voice and silence are best understood as opposite behavioral choices or as distinct constructs with different antecedents and consequences. It further asks whether perceived impact is more closely tied to voice, psychological safety is more closely tied to silence, and silence has a stronger relationship with burnout than voice.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in the distinction between behavioral activation and behavioral inhibition. Voice is theorized as an activation-oriented behavior aimed at improvement, opportunity, and reward, making perceived impact the more relevant environmental cue. Silence is theorized as an inhibition-oriented behavior aimed at avoiding interpersonal risk or harm, making psychological safety the more relevant cue. Because repeated silence involves suppression, vigilance, and tension, the authors argue that it should relate more strongly to burnout than voice relates to reduced burnout.
theoretical_contribution:
The article shifts the voice-silence debate from whether the constructs are distinct to how and why they differ. By grounding voice in BAS regulation and silence in BIS regulation, it explains why the two behaviors can coexist at the person level and why low voice should not be treated automatically as high silence.

The paper also clarifies the nomological networks of voice and silence. Across a meta-analysis and a six-month panel, perceived impact aligns more strongly with voice, psychological safety aligns more strongly with silence, and silence shows the stronger burnout relationship, giving silence a more independent theoretical status rather than treating it as a residual of voice.
practical_implication:
Leaders should not infer that frequent voice means employees are not withholding other concerns. The findings imply that managers need to examine both what employees say and what they may be suppressing, especially on risky or sensitive issues.

The paper also suggests that organizations need separate practices for increasing voice and reducing silence. Opportunities that make voice feel impactful may not reduce silence if employees still perceive interpersonal risk, while safety-oriented tools may reduce withholding without necessarily making employees believe their input will matter.
limitations:
The meta-analysis depends on the quality and scope of the underlying studies, and some construct subcategories could not be compared because too few primary studies included them. The authors also note that Study 1 included mostly cross-sectional evidence, limiting strong causal inference.

Study 2 used self-reported measures, which can introduce percept-percept inflation, although the one-month lagged design reduces this concern. The study also omitted some contextual influences, such as industry or job factors, and the authors state that experimental designs would be needed to strengthen internal validity.
future_research:
Future research could examine when voice and silence function more similarly or differently across issue content, personality traits, targets, and organizational contexts. The authors specifically point to sensitive issues, extraversion, leader versus peer targets, and strong voice climates as conditions that may change how voice and silence relate.

The paper also calls for research on other BAS- and BIS-aligned antecedents, other outcomes such as performance, and the role of time frame. In particular, future studies could test whether the distinction between voice and silence differs across person, monthly, and issue levels and whether observed level differences are conceptual or methodological.
abstract: Scholars continue to debate whether voice and silence are opposites or distinct constructs. This ambiguity has prevented meaningful theoretical advancements about employees’ voice and silence at work. We draw on the behavioral activation and behavioral inhibition systems perspective to provide a conceptual framework for the independence of voice and silence and explicate how two key antecedents—perceived impact and psychological safety—more strongly relate to voice and silence, respectively. We further differentiate voice and silence by identifying their distinct effects on employee burnout. In Study 1, a meta-analysis, we demonstrate that voice and silence are independent (Mr 5 2.15) and that perceived impact (psychological safety) relates more strongly to voice (silence) than to silence (voice). We also find that silence has a significantly stronger association with burnout compared to voice. In Study 2, we constructively replicate these findings in an interval-contingent panel study across six months. Taken together, this article helps shift the conversation of whether voice and silence are distinct constructs to how they differ and why such differences matter.
apa_citation: Sherf, E. N., Parke, M. R., & Isaakyan, S. (2021). Distinguishing voice and silence at work: Unique relationships with perceived impact, psychological safety, and burnout. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(1), 114-148. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.1428

title: Resource Dependence, Uncertainty, and the Allocation of Corporate Political Activity across Multiple Jurisdictions
methods: Panel linear regression with firm, state, and year fixed effects on firm-state political contribution data, supplemented by interviews with executives, political consultants, and government officials.
industry: Large publicly traded firms in environmentally intensive industries, including chemical, oil and gas, energy, and manufacturing.
country: United States; firm-state observations across all 50 U.S. states.
units: Firm-state observations of corporate political activity in states where firms had an environmentally intensive presence.
n_sample: 5,990 firm-state observations.
authors: Sutton, T.; Devine, R. A.; Lamont, B. T.; Holmes, R. M., Jr.
theories: Milliken's uncertainty typology (Milliken, 1987); environmental enactment / sensemaking (Weick, 1969, 1988); resource dependence theory (Pfeffer & Salancik, 1978)
keywords: corporate political activity; environmentally intensive industries; political contributions; resource dependence theory; response uncertainty; state uncertainty
research_question: The paper asks how different types and sources of uncertainty affect firms' allocation of corporate political activity across multiple government jurisdictions on which they depend. It focuses on whether state uncertainty and response uncertainty strengthen or weaken the relationship between jurisdictional dependence and political contributions.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that dependence makes a jurisdiction consequential for the firm, but uncertainty shapes whether and how managers act on that dependence. State uncertainty makes government behavior less predictable and therefore strengthens the dependence-CPA relationship when negative national media coverage or oppositional SMO resources heighten concern about policy backlash. Response uncertainty disrupts managers' confidence about how to influence politicians, so TMT turnover and politician turnover weaken the dependence-CPA relationship. Local media tenor was hypothesized to strengthen the relationship but was not supported empirically.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends resource dependence theory by restoring the distinction between dependence and uncertainty and by integrating Milliken's distinction between state uncertainty and response uncertainty. It shows that uncertainty does not uniformly increase dependence management: state uncertainty strengthens political action in dependent jurisdictions, whereas response uncertainty weakens it. It also contributes to corporate political activity research by modeling state-level political contributions across multiple jurisdictions rather than treating political activity as only a national-level strategy.
practical_implication: Managers in environmentally intensive firms should treat political dependence as jurisdiction-specific and monitor the sources of uncertainty that make some jurisdictions more problematic than others. The findings also suggest that response uncertainty after TMT or politician turnover may need explicit management, because disruption in political knowledge and relationships can reduce firms' ability to respond to important political dependencies.
limitations: The empirical setting is U.S. state-level political contributions by large publicly traded firms in environmentally intensive industries, so the findings should be read in relation to that institutional and regulatory context. The study examines political contributions rather than lobbying or other forms of corporate political activity. It also notes that state uncertainty and response uncertainty may be related differently in contexts such as buyer-supplier relationships, where interpersonal ties can be both monitoring and control mechanisms.
future_research: Future research could examine whether state and response uncertainty have similar effects on other dependence-management strategies such as mergers, joint ventures, board appointments, and lobbying. Scholars could also study how the sources of uncertainty vary across contexts and whether state and response uncertainty interact when the same relationships both reveal uncertainty and provide the means for response. Additional work on state-level politics and non-contribution forms of CPA would help test how broadly the paper's arguments generalize.
abstract: This paper contributes to the resource dependence theory and corporate political activity literatures by distinguishing dependence from uncertainty and explaining how two different types of uncertainty have opposite effects on dependence management. We explain how some environmental factors increase the state uncertainty associated with firms' dependence on government jurisdictions, whereas other factors increase response uncertainty. We hypothesize that, due to the historical influence of the media and social movement organizations on politics, negative national media tenor and oppositional social movement organization resources increase state uncertainty (i.e., government's likely behavior toward firms becomes less predictable), strengthening the relationship between firms' dependence on jurisdictions and their use of political contributions in those jurisdictions. Further, we hypothesize that top management team turnover and politician turnover increase response uncertainty (i.e., the effectiveness of firms' efforts to manage their dependence becomes less clear), weakening the relationship between dependence and political contributions. We find support for our theory in an examination of state-level political contributions of firms in environmentally intensive industries from 2009 to 2016. Interviews with senior executives, political consultants, and senior government employees directly involved in corporate political activity help illustrate the hypothesized relationships.
apa_citation: Sutton, T., Devine, R. A., Lamont, B. T., & Holmes, R. M., Jr. (2021). Resource dependence, uncertainty, and the allocation of corporate political activity across multiple jurisdictions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(1), 38-62. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1258

title: Gaining Legitimacy by Being Different: Optimal Distinctiveness in Crowdfunding Platforms
methods: Quantitative study of U.S.-based Kickstarter campaigns. The authors use latent Dirichlet allocation topic modeling to measure narrative distinctiveness, computer-aided text analysis to measure contribution claims, LexisNexis newspaper coverage to measure market category familiarity, and OLS regressions with robust standard errors; robustness tests use pledged funding and alternative distinctiveness/category-coverage operationalizations.
industry: Rewards-based crowdfunding campaigns on Kickstarter in technology, art, food, and theater market categories.
time_period: Campaigns launched between May 2009 and September 2017.
units: Crowdfunding campaigns / new ventures.
n_sample: Final sample of 28,425 campaigns across 39 market categories; main regression models report n = 26,724 after exclusions.
authors: Taeuscher, Karl; Bouncken, Ricarda; Pesch, Robin
theories: cultural entrepreneurship theory (Lounsbury & Glynn, 2001, 2019); optimal distinctiveness / legitimate distinctiveness; organizational legitimacy and institutional theory (Aldrich & Fiol, 1994; Scott, 1995; Suchman, 1995)
keywords: cognitive legitimacy; contribution claims; crowdfunding platforms; entrepreneurial stories; market category familiarity; normative legitimacy; optimal distinctiveness; organizational legitimacy; resource acquisition
research_question: How do new ventures gain legitimacy and attract critical resources when their entrepreneurial stories need both distinctiveness and legitimacy? The paper asks whether distinctiveness in crowdfunding narratives supports resource acquisition from crowdfunders, and whether contribution claims and market category familiarity condition that relationship.
mechanism_summary: The theoretical mechanism is that crowdfunders are a novelty-expecting audience, so distinctive entrepreneurial stories can signal novelty and normative appropriateness while also differentiating a venture in a crowded platform market. In this context, the authors argue that the normative and competitive benefits of distinctiveness exceed its cognitive liabilities, making the expected relationship positive rather than inverted U-shaped. Contribution claims and unfamiliar market-category membership provide alternative sources of normative legitimacy, so the marginal benefit of distinctiveness is lower when those alternatives are present. The regression evidence is consistent with this account: distinctiveness is positively associated with backers and funding, the interaction with contribution claims is negative, and the interaction with category coverage is positive.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper challenges the common assumption in optimal distinctiveness research that distinctiveness necessarily undermines legitimacy. It separates cognitive legitimacy from normative legitimacy and argues that distinctiveness can reduce comprehensibility while increasing normative fit for audiences that expect novelty.

The study also advances cultural entrepreneurship theory by identifying audience novelty expectations, contribution claims, and market category familiarity as contingencies in the distinctiveness-resource acquisition relationship. This shifts the optimal distinctiveness question from a universal preference for moderate distinctiveness toward a context-dependent assessment of competitive benefits, normative benefits, and cognitive liabilities.
practical_implication:
For crowdfunding-seeking entrepreneurs, the findings suggest that strongly differentiated narratives can improve crowdfunding performance when the audience expects novelty. Entrepreneurs may also benefit from contribution claims that resonate with community-oriented norms, although those claims partly substitute for the legitimating value of distinctiveness.

The findings further imply that category positioning matters. Ventures in familiar categories may need stronger narrative distinctiveness to be seen as novel, while ventures in unfamiliar categories may already receive some legitimacy from category-level novelty.
limitations:
The study does not directly measure normative or cognitive legitimacy, so legitimacy remains a theorized latent mechanism rather than an observed mediator. The empirical context is limited to U.S.-based Kickstarter campaigns in selected technology, art, food, and theater categories, which constrains generalization to other funding settings, countries, and audiences.

The measures also depend on text-analytic operationalizations: LDA captures narrative distinctiveness, CATA captures contribution claims, and newspaper coverage proxies market category familiarity. These measures are appropriate for large-scale platform data, but they remain proxies rather than direct measures of how audiences interpret legitimacy.
future_research:
Future research could test the proposed legitimacy mechanisms more directly in settings with observable proxies for normative and cognitive legitimacy or through experiments. Such work could examine whether audiences actually perceive distinctive ventures as more novel, more normatively appropriate, and still sufficiently comprehensible.

Additional studies could test whether the findings generalize to other novelty-seeking audiences, such as corporate innovation contests, cultural industries, startup competitions, app marketplaces, and other online markets. Research could also examine whether similar relationships hold for forms of differentiation other than entrepreneurial stories, such as product portfolios or product features.
abstract: How do new ventures gain legitimacy and attract critical resources? An increasing body of cultural entrepreneurship research has highlighted an “optimal distinctiveness” trade-off: new ventures need to be distinctive from their peers to stand out, yet distinctiveness counteracts the attainment of organizational legitimacy. In this paper, we challenge the underlying assumption that distinctiveness necessarily counteracts the attainment of legitimacy and propose that distinctiveness can become a source of legitimacy. This proposition matters because it fundamentally alters the relationship between distinctiveness and resource acquisition from certain audiences. We build on these theoretical arguments to examine new ventures’ resource acquisition from crowdfunders, one of the most important audiences for new ventures. Analysis of 28,425 crowdfunding campaigns across 39 market categories strongly supports our arguments, showing that higher levels of distinctiveness lead to superior crowdfunding performance. We further demonstrate that the legitimating effect of distinctiveness intensifies under the absence of alternative sources of legitimacy. Our study contributes by uncovering a new mechanism and three contingencies for the “optimal distinctiveness” trade-off.
