title: Too Unsafe to Monitor? How Board–CEO Cognitive Conflict and Chair Leadership Shape Outside Director Monitoring
methods: Two-stage mixed-methods design. Study 1 is an inductive multi-case study of five Australian corporations using video observations of board meetings and semi-structured interviews with board meeting participants. Study 2 is a multisource survey study of 310 outside directors from 64 Dutch boards, analyzed as a multilevel moderated-mediation model with bootstrapped confidence intervals.
industry: Study 1: membership-based Australian financial corporations, including credit unions, a superannuation fund, and a health insurance provider. Study 2: Dutch corporations participating through a board research and feedback tool.
time_period: Study 1: 2013 and 2014. Study 2: survey timing not reported.
units: Board–CEO disagreement episodes, outside directors, CEOs, board meeting participants, and boards.
n_sample: Study 1: five corporations, seven videotaped board meetings, over 17 hours of video footage, and interviews with 39 outside directors, four CEOs, and one CFO. Study 2: 310 outside directors from 64 Dutch boards.
authors: Veltrop, Dennis B.; Bezemer, Pieter-Jan; Nicholson, Gavin; Pugliese, Amedeo
theories: agency theory (Fama & Jensen, 1983; Jensen & Meckling, 1976); group conflict and cognitive conflict theory (Jehn, 1995; de Dreu & Weingart, 2003); participative leadership (Arnold et al., 2000); psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999)
keywords: board psychological safety; boardroom dynamics; board–CEO cognitive conflict; chair participative leadership; corporate governance; director monitoring; outside directors
research_question: How and why does board–CEO cognitive conflict affect outside directors’ engagement in monitoring, and what role does the board chair play in shaping that relationship? The paper also asks whether board psychological safety explains why participative chair leadership helps boards handle cognitive conflict more constructively.
mechanism_summary:
- Focal tension: Outside directors are expected to monitor the CEO partly because their outsider status brings divergent views, but those same divergent views can create board–CEO cognitive conflict.
- Study 1 process: In observed disagreement episodes, low participative chair leadership was associated with directors withdrawing, talking over one another, or failing to seek further information from the CEO; more participative chairs solicited views, structured discussion, and helped directors remain engaged.
- Study 2 tested relationships: Board–CEO cognitive conflict is the predictor, director monitoring is the outcome, board psychological safety is the mediating climate, and chair participative leadership is the moderating board-leadership condition.
- Mechanism: Participative chairs signal that divergent views will be heard and respected, which helps preserve psychological safety during conflict and supports continued director monitoring.

The central process is not that cognitive conflict automatically improves monitoring. The paper argues that cognitive conflict can undermine monitoring when a psychologically unsafe board climate leads directors to reject one another’s views or detach from the monitoring process. Chair participative leadership attenuates this negative relationship by creating conditions in which outside directors continue to challenge, seek information, and deliberate with the CEO.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper refines agency-based corporate governance theory by showing that two standard prescriptions, appointing outside directors and using an independent chair, are insufficient unless boardroom dynamics allow directors to monitor effectively. It shifts attention from the chair mainly as a counterweight or resource for the CEO to the chair as leader of the board itself.

It also imports psychological safety and group conflict insights into board research. By linking board–CEO cognitive conflict, participative chair leadership, psychological safety, and director monitoring, the study specifies a board-level socio-psychological mechanism that helps explain why formal independence may not translate into effective monitoring.
practical_implication:
Boards should not assume that adding independent outside directors or relying on an independent chair will automatically strengthen monitoring. Chairs need to manage disagreement episodes by inviting contributions, withholding premature dominance, and making sure directors’ concerns are heard.

The findings imply that attention to boardroom discussion climate matters alongside structural governance indicators. A chair who counterbalances the CEO but dominates board discussion may weaken the very monitoring role that outside directors are expected to perform.
limitations:
The qualitative study is based on observed episodes in five Australian financial institutions, and the authors note that video cameras and researcher presence may have affected board behavior. The interview evidence also relies partly on directors’ recollections and sensemaking of sensitive boardroom dynamics.

The quantitative study is cross-sectional and based on boards that voluntarily enrolled, so self-selection and reverse causality cannot be fully ruled out. The participating boards were mostly composed of outside directors and had separate CEO and chair roles, limiting direct generalization to settings with CEO duality or different power balances.
future_research:
Future studies could examine whether director monitoring observed in this model actually reduces agency costs or improves firm-level outcomes. Research could also study CEO personality, CEO behavior, board norms around challenging management, and other types of board conflict.

Additional work could test the model in governance systems with CEO duality, lead directors, more insider-heavy boards, or different institutional settings. Longitudinal and processual designs would help assess how board–CEO conflict, psychological safety, and monitoring evolve over time.
abstract: Research into boards of directors has provided mixed support for the view that outside directors’ independence or leadership by an independent chair improves monitoring. In this study, we use a micro-level approach to provide a better understanding of why outside directors have difficulty in monitoring the CEO. We highlight that an important reason for this lies in the boardroom dynamics associated with (a) outside directors’ cognitive conflict with the CEO and (b) the chair’s leadership of the board. Our inductive analyses of video observations of board meetings in five Australian corporations revealed the importance of chair participative leadership during disagreement episodes in the boardroom. Follow-up in-depth interviews of board meeting participants highlighted the importance of psychological safety as a key mechanism explaining why participative board chairs appear so effective in dealing with board–CEO cognitive conflict. We corroborate these results with a second, large-scale survey study involving data on 310 outside directors from 64 Dutch boards. Whereas prior work has mostly focused on the chair’s relationship with the CEO, we instead highlight the importance of the chair’s role as the leader of the board and identify board psychological safety as an important element shaping director monitoring within the confines of the boardroom.

title: Best Not to Know: Pay Secrecy, Employee Voluntary Turnover, and the Conditioning Effect of Distributive Justice
methods: Two quantitative field studies. Study 1 used a time-lagged employee survey of working executive MBA students and multiple regression with Johnson-Neyman and Monte Carlo moderated-mediation tests. Study 2 used firm-level manager and employee survey data, aggregated distributive justice climate, and Tobit regression to model firm voluntary turnover rates.
industry: Study 1 participants worked in fields including medicine, manufacturing, education, and banking; Study 2 sampled state-owned, private, and multinational firms from Dongguan City's registered firm list.
time_period: Study 1 and Study 2 data were collected in different years, reported as 2018 and 2013 respectively.
units: Study 1 employees; Study 2 firms and nonmanagerial employees aggregated to the firm level.
n_sample: Study 1: 196 participants; Study 2: 86 firms and 2,035 employees.
authors: Alterman, Valeria; Bamberger, Peter A.; Wang, Mo; Koopmann, Jaclyn; Belogolovsky, Elena; Shi, Junqi
theories: organizational justice theories (Brockner & Wiesenfeld, 1996; Cropanzano & Folger, 1991); uncertainty management theory (van den Bos & Lind, 2002)
keywords: distributive justice; employee turnover intentions; firm voluntary turnover rates; organizational trustworthiness; pay secrecy; procedural justice; uncertainty management theory; voluntary turnover
research_question: How and when does pay secrecy affect employee turnover-related outcomes, and does distributive justice condition the relationship between pay secrecy, organizational trustworthiness, turnover intentions, and firm voluntary turnover rates?
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that pay secrecy functions as a procedural justice cue that is also confounded with uncertainty. Under uncertainty management theory, employees triangulate pay secrecy with distributive justice to assess organizational trustworthiness. When distributive justice is high, lower pay secrecy provides clearer evidence of fair pay-related treatment and is associated with higher trust and lower turnover-related outcomes; when distributive justice is low, pay secrecy can preserve trust at the individual level by allowing employees to discount aversive fairness information, although this protective pattern did not become significant for firm voluntary turnover rates in Study 2.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends organizational justice theory by showing that procedural and distributive justice cues do not always compound when the procedural cue is also uncertain. It positions organizational trustworthiness as a global fairness judgment linking pay secrecy and turnover-related outcomes, and it extends pay secrecy research from individual attitudes to firm-level voluntary turnover rates.
practical_implication: Organizations considering pay transparency should attend to employees' distributive justice perceptions rather than assuming that transparency or secrecy has a uniform turnover effect. The findings suggest that higher pay secrecy is especially risky when employees generally perceive pay outcomes as fair, whereas additional pay-range or pay-procedure information may help reduce uncertainty when full transparency is not feasible.
limitations: The authors note that the study excludes pay level transparency because of lack of variance, relies partly on self-report measures, and may have limited generalizability beyond Chinese or East Asian contexts. They also acknowledge possible reverse causality, a single manager rating for firm pay secrecy practice, limited firm-level sample size, and the absence of firm-level organizational trust as a mediator.
future_research: Future research should examine pay level transparency, multiple justice dimensions, cross-cultural generalizability, other employee populations, enterprise ownership differences, and additional firm-level controls such as union status, diversity, pay-for-performance policies, and organizational climate. The authors also call for stronger longitudinal designs, multiple manager ratings, firm-level mediating mechanisms, justice climate strength, supervisor-focused justice climate, other outcomes such as performance and counterproductive behavior, and turnover quality among good versus poor performers.
abstract: Building on uncertainty management theory, we develop and test a model explicating how and when secrecy in pay communication may affect employee turnover-related outcomes (i.e., employee turnover intentions and firm voluntary turnover rates). Underlying this model is the notion that employees triangulate perceptions of pay secrecy (i.e., a pay-related procedural justice cue that also reflects uncertainty) with their own or others' perceptions of distributive justice as a basis for assessing organizational trustworthiness, with the latter serving as an important driver of voluntary turnover intentions and behavior. Results of two studies (Study 1 at the individual level and Study 2 at the firm level) indicate that, rather than being universal, the relationship between pay secrecy and turnover is contingent upon perceptions of distributive justice, with turnover intentions (at the individual level via organizational trustworthiness) and voluntary turnover rates (at the firm level) differentially affected by pay secrecy under conditions of higher and lower levels of distributive justice. These findings suggest an important extension to organizational justice theories; namely that, when procedural justice cues are confounded with uncertainty (as they are with pay secrecy), the assumed compounding interaction between procedural and distributive justice cues may be replaced by a more antagonistic interaction.
apa_citation: Alterman, V., Bamberger, P. A., Wang, M., Koopmann, J., Belogolovsky, E., & Shi, J. (2021). Best not to know: Pay secrecy, employee voluntary turnover, and the conditioning effect of distributive justice. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(2), 482-508. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.0231

title: How Technological Overlap between Spinouts and Parent Firms Affects Corporate Venture Capital Investments in Spinouts: The Role of Competitive Tension
methods: Empirical quantitative study using probit regression models on dyad-year datasets of potential corporate investor-venture and corporate investor-spinout investment ties. The analyses use VentureXpert, founder career histories, patent data, patent litigation data, FDA medical device approvals, M&A/alliance data, and Compustat, with robust standard errors clustered at the dyad level, industry segment and year fixed effects, corporate-investor fixed-effect specifications, and multiple robustness checks.
industry: U.S. medical device industry.
units: Potential dyad-years between corporate investors and ventures or spinouts; realized CVC investment deals are coded within those dyads.
n_sample: The paper reports 45 corporate investors; 679 ventures after patent-data restriction; 190,315 potential corporate investor-venture dyad-years with 259 realized CVC deals; and 69,815 potential corporate investor-spinout dyad-years with 91 realized CVC deals.
authors: Bae, Joonhyung; Lee, Joon Mahn
theories: competitive dynamics and competitive tension (Chen et al., 2007); entrepreneurship and employee entrepreneurship literature; knowledge transfer and knowledge protection in interfirm relationships
keywords: competitive risks and benefits; competitive tension; corporate venture capital investments; litigiousness; parent firms; spinouts; technological knowledge; technological overlap
research_question: How does technological overlap between a spinout and its parent firm affect a corporate investor's likelihood of investing in the spinout? The paper also asks when this negative relationship is amplified by competitive risks or mitigated by competitive benefits from access to parent-firm knowledge.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is a competitive-tension process. When a spinout's technology overlaps strongly with its parent firm's knowledge base, corporate investors anticipate that the parent firm may retaliate through legal or market-based actions, making the investment riskier. That risk is stronger when the parent firm is litigious, but it can be offset when the corporate investor expects strategic benefits from indirectly accessing a competitor's knowledge through the spinout.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends employee entrepreneurship research by showing that technological inheritance can be a liability for spinouts, not only a resource endowment or reputational advantage. It identifies a downside of spinout-parent similarity: overlap may trigger competitive tension that reduces external corporate investment.

The paper also contributes to competitive dynamics by theorizing the transitivity of competitive tension through interfirm networks. Rather than treating competitive tension only as a dyadic rival relationship, it shows how tension between a parent firm and a spinout can shape a third party's decision to form an investment relationship.
practical_implication:
For corporate investors, the findings indicate that spinout investments involve a balance between access to useful external technologies and competitive risks from parent-firm reactions. Spinout-parent technological overlap, parent-firm litigiousness, and the investor's potential benefit from indirect access to parent-firm knowledge are central conditions in that balance.

For spinouts, the results imply that close technological inheritance from a parent firm may make CVC funding harder to secure when corporate investors anticipate retaliation risks. Parent firms' reputations for enforcing intellectual property rights can shape how attractive their spinouts look to outside corporate investors.
limitations:
The empirical setting is the U.S. medical device industry, where intellectual property protection and patent litigation are especially salient, so the risk-benefit balance may differ in industries with weaker formal protection regimes. The paper also cannot provide decisive performance implications for whether corporate investors actually create value by accessing spinout knowledge.

The analysis focuses on patented technological knowledge and CVC investment ties, so it does not capture the full range of competitive actions, tacit knowledge conflicts, or governance choices in other forms of external knowledge acquisition. The dyad-level data also cannot fully represent the network structure of triadic competitive tension.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether the same mechanism operates in industries where parent-firm retaliation has weaker deterrent effects or where corporate investors are less sensitive to intellectual property litigation. It could also test when expected benefits from spinout knowledge translate into better corporate-investor performance.

Additional work could study competitive tension across other governance modes, such as R&D alliances, acquisitions, or other external knowledge acquisition relationships. The paper also points to future research on ongoing post-founding knowledge inheritance through founders' social ties with former colleagues at parent firms.
abstract: Drawing on the literature on entrepreneurship and competitive dynamics, we investigate how technological overlap between spinouts and parent firms influences corporate investors’ decisions regarding investments in spinouts. We suggest that a high level of technological overlap between a spinout and its parent firm deters potential corporate investors from making an investment in the spinout because of competitive tension arising from anticipated hostile actions by the parent firm. We further suggest that these negative effects are contingent on the tradeoffs between competitive risks and benefits. Our findings show that the negative effects are amplified when parent firms have a strong litigiousness in claiming their intellectual property rights. However, we find that the negative effects are mitigated when corporate investors can expect benefits from gaining indirect access to parent firms’ technological knowledge. Using a sample of corporate venture capital investments in the U.S. medical device industry, we find evidence that supports our hypotheses.

title: Antecedents and Consequences of Employee and Asset Restructuring
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of NYSE-listed firms using Compustat data. The authors classify employee, asset, and combination downsizing/upsizing with both a 5% cutoff and decile approach; estimate logistic regressions for restructuring antecedents; and estimate dummy-variable panel regressions of industry-adjusted stock returns with heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation controls.
industry: Corporations listed on the New York Stock Exchange across industries; industry-adjusted returns use S&P/Global Industry Classification industry components
country: United States / U.S.-based corporations reporting in U.S. dollars
time_period: 1980 through fiscal year 2016, with later return windows curtailed to 1980-2015 or 1980-2014 depending on the test
units: Firm-year observations of publicly traded corporations; restructuring events/categories by employee, asset, and combination changes
n_sample: 61,853 sets of observations for 4,627 firms after filters
authors: Cascio, Wayne F.; Chatrath, Arjun; Christie-David, Rohan A.
theories: institutional theory / neo-institutional theory (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983, 1991; Scott, 1987, 1995, 2013)
keywords: downsizing; employment and asset restructuring; firm performance; industry-adjusted returns; institutional theory; political uncertainty; upsizing
research_question: Are the antecedents of restructuring common across downsizing and upsizing, and are the performance consequences of employee and asset restructuring related to prior firm performance? The paper asks these questions for two restructuring forms (downsizing and upsizing) and two restructuring types (employees and assets).
mechanism_summary: Guided by institutional theory, the authors argue that restructuring is shaped jointly by efficiency considerations and institutional forces. Company performance and managerial foresight capture normative/efficiency pressures; the economy and political uncertainty capture coercive pressures; and industry effects plus technology capture mimetic processes. The evidence links these antecedents to downsizing and upsizing decisions, then links prior performance trends to subsequent industry-adjusted returns: restructuring after difficult performance is associated with stronger ex post performance than restructuring under more benign conditions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends institutional theory by showing that efficiency considerations and institutional forces jointly predict both downsizing and upsizing, not only employee downsizing. It also refines institutional theory by showing that trends in prior company performance, not only contemporaneous performance, forecast subsequent firm performance after restructuring. The design further highlights time as a research-design issue because market responses to restructuring vary across the 37-year sampling period.
practical_implication: Managers should consider company performance, managerial foresight, the economy, political uncertainty, industry competition, and technology before restructuring, with attention to recent and prior performance trends. The paper cautions against treating employee downsizing as an easy lever to restore profitability because it is frequent in the sample but has the lowest payoff among downsizing categories. It also suggests that upsizing does not automatically produce better stock market performance when undertaken from high profitability.
limitations: The study uses archival data rather than an experimental design, so it identifies statistically significant associations rather than causal effects. The sample consists of publicly traded firms, and privately held firms may behave differently. The authors also could not observe different downsizing motives and goals, such as declining demand versus efficiency improvement.
future_research: Future studies should account explicitly for sampling periods because restructuring-performance relationships vary over time. Qualitative research using in-depth case studies and interviews with senior executives could provide richer evidence about unmeasured variables, tacit knowledge, and firm-specific restructuring decisions. Future work could also examine motives and goals for downsizing more directly.
abstract: We examine two forms of employment and asset restructuring: downsizing and upsizing. Guided by institutional theory, we focus on two important questions: (a) are the antecedents of restructuring common across downsizing and upsizing? and (b) are the performance consequences of such restructuring related to prior firm performance? To answer these questions, we use primary data from companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange over a 37-year period (1980–2016). Our results suggest that six key antecedents play a prominent role in both downsizing and upsizing, although they differ in magnitude and direction in how they affect each form of restructuring. However, in both instances they reflect efficiency considerations (company performance and managerial foresight), as well as institutional forces (the economy, political uncertainty, industry, and technology), just as neo-institutional theory suggests. In addition, prior performance plays a central role in restructuring decisions, in both the upsizing and downsizing of assets and employees. The evidence suggests that it is not just current-year performance but also the trend in company performance over the prior two years that forecasts subsequent firm performance; thus, our findings extend and refine institutional theory.

title: Leading by Doing: Does Leading by Example Impact Productivity and Service Quality?
methods: Empirical quantitative study using two-time-point, three-year panel data from retail stores. The study combines employee survey measures, accounting-based productivity data, and secret-shopper service-quality evaluations, and analyzes the store-year panel with year and retail-store fixed-effects regressions, confirmatory factor analyses, bootstrapped conditional indirect effects, and endogeneity/reverse-causality checks.
industry: Retail chain selling wellness products, including health care, cosmetics, cleaning, pharmaceuticals, and perfumes.
time_period: Three-year panel; exact calendar years not reported. Employee surveys were followed by a three-month lag, and productivity and service quality were averaged over six months after that lag.
units: Retail stores and store-year observations, with employee survey responses, accounting-based productivity data, and secret-shopper service-quality evaluations.
n_sample: 233 retail stores, 8,137 employees, and 699 store-year observations.
authors: Eldor, Liat
theories: engagement theory (Kahn, 1990, 1992); social learning theory (Bandura, 1977); strategy-based resource management framework (Sirmon, Hitt, & Ireland, 2007; Sirmon, Hitt, Ireland, & Gilbert, 2011)
keywords: charismatic leadership; employee engagement; leading by example; organizational core values; productivity; resource management; service quality
research_question: The paper asks whether leading by example creates business-level value by improving productivity and service quality at the store level. It also asks whether employee engagement mediates this effect and whether written manifestation of organizational core values strengthens the engagement pathway.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines strategy-based resource management with leadership and social learning arguments. Leading by example is treated as a practical organizational resource: by visibly performing employee activities, leaders clarify desired behavior, support social learning, and encourage employees to invest more fully in their roles. Core value manifestation adds a conceptual resource that explains why the demonstrated behavior matters for the organization's goals, strengthening engagement and, through engagement, productivity and service quality.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper develops leading by example as a distinct leadership construct rather than treating it as a catchphrase or a subset of charismatic leadership. It extends leadership research by showing that a doing-oriented leadership practice has business-level associations with productivity and service quality beyond a rhetorically oriented leadership style.

The paper also contributes to resource management theory by showing how practical and conceptual resources can work together. Leading by example and core value manifestation jointly enhance engagement, linking micro-level employee motivation to store-level performance outcomes.
practical_implication:
Managers should treat leading by example as a substantive leadership practice rather than a peripheral personal style. The findings imply that leaders can support productivity, service quality, and employee engagement by visibly demonstrating expected frontline behaviors.

The paper also suggests that leading by example works better when paired with clear written communication of organizational core values. Leadership training and promotion criteria should therefore value managers who both model desired behaviors and connect those behaviors to organizational purpose.
limitations:
The study uses multisource, three-year panel data and a three-month lag, but the author states that this design still does not fully support causal inference. Employees' subjective ratings may also imperfectly capture actual leading by example and may be affected by social desirability or employee-leader relations, although anonymity and confidentiality were used to reduce these concerns.

The study examines leading by example mainly in relation to charismatic leadership, while other leadership characteristics such as ethical leadership and behavioral integrity may also affect business performance. It is also limited to one retail chain of medium-sized stores in Israel, which constrains direct generalization to larger organizations, other industries, and other national contexts.
future_research:
Future research could use experimental designs to test the causal effects of leading by example more decisively. Researchers could also examine how leading by example differs from or interacts with ethical leadership, behavioral integrity, and other leadership constructs.

The author calls for work on other ways of manifesting core values, such as leader speeches, conferences, and videos, and for further refinement of the core value manifestation construct. Future studies could also test cascading processes at higher organizational levels and examine leading by example in other contexts, such as high technology or cultures with different authority norms.
abstract: This paper presents a research model for the creation of organizational value through leading by example. I argue that leading by example serves as a unique value-creation driver by enhancing engagement, productivity, and service quality at the business level. Using a strategy-based resource management framework, I also argue that there are synergies between leading by example and the manifestation of organizational core values. My theory is grounded in the strategy-based notion that combining organizational resources—leading by example (practical element) and organizational core values (conceptual element)—optimizes employee engagement, which in turn enhances productivity and service quality. I examine my model empirically using two-time-point panel data derived from three different sources (employees, financial data, and secret shoppers) in a sample of 233 retail stores. The findings provide evidence that leading by example improves productivity and service quality (after taking into account the potential influence of charismatic leadership). The indirect effect of leading by example on productivity and service quality (through engagement) is even stronger when manifestation of organizational core values is high. Contributions to theory, research, and practice are presented.

title: How Voice Emerges and Develops in Newly Formed Supervisor–Employee Dyads
methods: Four-wave longitudinal survey of newly formed supervisor-employee dyads in a Chinese manufacturing firm. Employees and supervisors reported proactive personality before working together; employees reported voice across three later waves; supervisors reported change goal congruence. The authors used cross-level polynomial regressions with response surface modeling, mixed-effects growth models for linear and quadratic voice slopes, and block-variable mediation tests.
industry: Manufacturing; production-line and production-support employees
time_period: First six months after dyad formation, with Time 0 proactive personality measures and three later voice waves spaced three months apart
units: Newly formed supervisor-employee dyads / employees nested within work units
n_sample: 403 employees within 82 work units
authors: Li, Alex Ning; Tangirala, Subrahmaniam
theories: interactional concepts of personality (Carson, 1969; Mischel, 2004); proactivity theory / proactive motivation (Grant & Ashford, 2008; Parker & Collins, 2010); trait activation theory (Tett & Burnett, 2003)
keywords: change goal congruence; leader-member exchange; linear voice trajectory; new supervisor-employee dyads; proactive personality; quadratic voice trajectory; trait activation; voice
research_question: How does voice emerge and develop over time in newly formed supervisor-employee dyads? The paper asks whether employees' proactive personality predicts initial voice and whether supervisor-employee congruence in proactive personality shapes later linear and nonlinear voice trajectories through perceived change goal congruence.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that newly formed dyads initially create uncertainty and opportunity, activating proactive employees to speak up before dyadic norms have solidified. Over time, supervisors and employees become social situations for each other: congruent proactive personalities create mutual trait activation and shared change goals, supporting voice growth and acceleration. Incongruence produces frustration, perceived mismatch in change priorities, and self-deflating voice trajectories. Change goal congruence explains why proactive personality fit translates into both positive linear and nonlinear voice development.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts voice research from a snapshot view to a temporal dyadic model, showing that employee traits have stronger independent effects early in a relationship and later operate jointly with supervisor traits. It extends supervisor-employee dyad research beyond LMX by showing that voice can follow self-amplifying or self-deflating trajectories rather than merely stabilizing as affiliative relationships do. It also identifies change goal congruence as a proximal mechanism linking proactive personality fit to voice development.
practical_implication: Organizations should attend to the social fit between supervisors and employees, not only the technical fit between employees and job demands, because shared proactivity can support sustained voice. Supervisors cannot assume early voice will persist automatically; the paper suggests they need to cultivate repeated successful voice exchanges and recognize whether their change goals align with employees'. The findings also imply that proactivity at only one hierarchical level may be insufficient to sustain voice when adjacent-level partners do not share similar change orientations.
limitations: The authors note that the China setting may shape the results because higher power distance could make supervisor traits more salient than in lower power-distance contexts. They also state that the study cannot definitively establish causality and that random assignment in quasi-experimental designs would strengthen causal inference. The temporal design modeled linear and nonlinear trends across the first six months, but voice may also shift after critical events or follow cyclical ebb-and-flow patterns not captured here.
future_research: Future research should compare proactive personality fit effects across national contexts that vary in power distance and use designs with random assignment of supervisors and employees where possible. Researchers should study voice over longer horizons to identify when it reaches equilibrium and what events disrupt or reset that equilibrium. The authors also encourage work on how the basis, content, quality, and novelty of voice shift as employees move from outsider-like early perspectives to insider on-the-job experience.
abstract: We develop and test theory regarding how voice emerges and develops in new supervisor– employee dyads. We propose that employees higher in proactive personality speak up more in early stages of interactions in their dyads. The subsequent path that their voice takes—that is, increasing in a virtuous positive trajectory or decreasing in a vicious negative trajectory—is determined by whether their proactive personality matches their supervisors’. For instance, when paired with supervisors who are not similarly proactive, they confront low congruence on change-related goals in the working relationship; hence, rather than building off their initial voice and developing a positive voice trajectory, frustration might lead their voice to decay in a negative trajectory. This theory is supported in a sample of 403 newly formed dyads. Employees higher in proactive personality were more likely to speak up to their supervisors immediately after beginning to work together. Supervisor–employee congruence in proactive personality predicted how voice changed in the dyads in the ensuing six months. Dyadic (in)congruence in proactive personality drove the linear (negative) positive trend in voice and enabled voice growth to pick up momentum and nonlinearly (decelerate) accelerate over time. We discuss our findings’ implications for theory and practice.

title: Strength and Weakness in Numbers? Unpacking the Role of Prevalence in the Diffusion of Reverse Mergers
methods: Empirical quantitative study of U.S. reverse mergers using generalized structural equation modeling. The analyses model weekly counts of new reverse mergers, stock-market returns, and negative media coverage, using negative binomial specifications for count outcomes, a linear specification for stock-market valuations, controls for regulatory changes, shell availability, IPO activity, investor sentiment, analyst recommendations, and bootstrapped mediated effects.
industry: U.S. reverse merger and public-shell market, where private firms go public by merging with publicly listed shell companies.
time_period: Reverse merger population data cover 2001-2012; the weekly diffusion models run from August 1, 2002, to December 31, 2012.
units: Reverse merger events, weekly counts of new reverse mergers, stock-market returns for reverse merger firms, and media articles evaluating reverse mergers.
n_sample: The core database contains 1,904 reverse mergers from 2001 to 2012. The stock-market evaluation analysis uses 1,466 firms, and the media analysis identifies 267 articles.
authors: Naumovska, Ivana; Zajac, Edward J.; Lee, Peggy M.
theories: informational social influence; normative social influence; organizational legitimacy and institutional theory; practice diffusion theory
keywords: controversial practices; practice diffusion; practice prevalence; reverse mergers; social influence; strength in numbers; third-party evaluations; weakness in numbers
research_question: What does the prevalence of a controversial practice imply for its subsequent diffusion? The paper asks whether reverse merger prevalence creates only a direct "strength in numbers" effect among potential adopters or also a mediated "weakness in numbers" effect through negative third-party evaluations by investors and the media.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is a competitive mediation process. Growing prevalence directly informs potential adopters that reverse mergers may be valuable, increasing adoption through informational social influence. At the same time, because reverse mergers are controversial and challenge accepted IPO norms, growing prevalence attracts skeptical attention from investors and the media, lowering stock-market evaluations, increasing negative coverage, and indirectly reducing later adoption through normative social influence.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to practice diffusion research by separating prevalence effects into two pathways that can diverge for controversial practices. It shows that prevalence can simultaneously produce a direct strength-in-numbers effect among potential adopters and an indirect weakness-in-numbers effect through third-party evaluators.

The paper also endogenizes third-party evaluations in diffusion theory. Rather than treating media and investor reactions as exogenous influences on adoption, it theorizes and tests how those reactions arise partly from the practice's own growing prevalence and from the declining status of past adopters.
practical_implication:
For potential adopters, the findings imply that widespread use of a controversial practice should not be read only as evidence of value or legitimacy. Reverse merger prevalence also changed how investors and media evaluated the practice, which in turn shaped the practical viability of future adoption.

For regulators, investors, and media evaluators, the study shows why rapid diffusion of a counternormative financial practice can signal both growing market demand and rising legitimacy concerns. Monitoring should therefore consider not only the number of adopters but also the status and quality signals of those adopters.
limitations:
The study focuses on reverse mergers in the United States, a visible and controversial financial-market practice where investor and media evaluations are consequential. Its theoretical scope is therefore strongest for practices that contravene established legitimacy pillars, are visible to third-party evaluators, and can plausibly threaten relevant actors in the organizational field.

The empirical design treats regulatory actions as controls rather than fully modeling them as mediators, and the authors note that the analyses did not allow them to adequately model regulatory actions' mediating role. The results also depend on a long enough observation window to see third-party contestation emerge after prevalence increases.
future_research:
Future research should examine contingencies that strengthen either the direct or mediated pathway, including differences in practice controversy, prospective adopters' vulnerability to third-party evaluations, and adopters' uncertainty about a practice's economic value. The framework could also be applied to noncontroversial practices, where the authors expect complementary rather than competitive mediation.

The paper points to research on multiwave diffusion, practice adaptation, abandonment, and symbolic abandonment of controversial practices. It also calls for work on how adopters shield controversial practices from opposing third-party evaluators through framing, persuasion, knowledge transfer, or adaptation.
abstract: A common prediction in research on practice diffusion is a “strength in numbers” effect (i.e., that a growing number of past adopters will increase the number of future adopters). We advance and test a theoretical perspective to explain when and how practice prevalence may also generate a “weakness in numbers” effect. Specifically, to explain the diffusion of reverse mergers—a controversial practice that allows a private firm to go public by merging with a publicly listed “shell company”—we suggest that prevalence affects their diffusion in a complex way based on two divergent social influence pathways, creating (a) a direct, positive effect of practice prevalence on potential adopters, who view prevalence as evidence of the practice’s value; and (b) an indirect, negative effect mediated through third-party evaluators (i.e., investors and the media), who view prevalence as a cause for concern and skepticism. We also highlight the utility of this theoretical framework by analyzing how a decline in the status of past adopters exerts a negative effect on diffusion through both social influence pathways. Employing structural equation modeling techniques, we find support for the hypothesized relationships, and we discuss the implications of the study for future research on practice diffusion.
apa_citation: Naumovska, I., Zajac, E. J., & Lee, P. M. (2021). Strength and weakness in numbers? Unpacking the role of prevalence in the diffusion of reverse mergers. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(2), 409-434. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0716

title: Salient Expectations? Incongruence across Capability and Integrity Signals and Investor Reactions to Organizational Misconduct
methods: Empirical quantitative event-study design using irregular financial restatements, prior alliance announcements, cumulative abnormal returns, generalized linear regression with firm-clustered robust standard errors, and a Heckman two-stage correction for selection into restatement.
industry: Publicly traded software and chemical/pharmaceutical firms.
units: Irregular financial restatement events by publicly traded firms, with first-stage selection modeled across all Compustat firms in the focal industries.
n_sample: 935 irregular financial restatements; first-stage selection model over 3,477 firms.
authors: Paruchuri, Srikanth; Han, Jung-Hoon; Prakash, Puneet
theories: signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al., 2011); social evaluations literature on capability and integrity judgments
keywords: alliance announcements; capability signals; integrity signals; interdimensional incongruence; investor reactions; irregular financial restatements; organizational misconduct; signal sets; signaling theory
research_question: How do investors respond when a firm has salient positive capability signals before revealing a negative integrity signal? The paper asks whether the salience of prior alliance announcements aggravates investor reactions to irregular financial restatements, and whether firm size and diversification weaken that reaction.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that irregular financial restatements act as negative integrity signals, while prior alliance announcements act as positive capability signals. When alliance announcements are salient, investors process them together with the restatement, producing interdimensional incongruence between capability and integrity. Because integrity judgments have primacy over capability judgments, investors reassess the prior capability signals through the negative integrity signal and impose larger valuation penalties. These penalties are weaker for larger firms. Diversification weakens the frequency-based salience effect, but the paper does not find a significant extremity-by-diversification interaction.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends signaling theory by shifting signal incongruence from intradimensional inconsistency among similar signals to interdimensional inconsistency between capability and integrity signals. It also contributes to social evaluations research by showing that integrity judgments can mar capability judgments, and to organizational misconduct and alliance research by showing when normally positive alliance announcements can intensify negative investor reactions.
practical_implication: Managers cannot assume that making capabilities salient will protect firms when integrity failures emerge. The findings imply that firms with highly visible alliance activity may face sharper investor penalties after irregular financial restatements, especially when they are smaller or less diversified.
limitations: The authors note that the empirical design cannot directly capture the microfoundational mechanism through which audiences resolve incongruence. They also focus on irregular financial restatements, investor reactions, frequency and extremity as forms of salience, and two alliance-intensive industries, which may limit generalizability to other forms of misconduct, other stakeholders, other salience mechanisms, or industries where alliances are less important.
future_research: Future research could compare negative-integrity/positive-capability incongruence with other interdimensional combinations, including negative capability signals with positive integrity signals. The authors also call for experimental or policy-capturing work on audience processing, research on ambiguous misconduct, errors, accidents, non-investor stakeholders, alliance characteristics, other strategic initiatives, external shocks, and industries where alliances are less central.
abstract: Research in signaling theory has recently begun to explore how audiences process signal sets and the incongruence across the signals within. However, prior studies have assumed homogenous compositions of signal sets, and thus unidimensional signal incongruence, although social evaluations tend to involve simultaneous processing of different dimensions. In this study, we examine audiences' responses to the interdimensional incongruence between capability and integrity signals, particularly by focusing on how the salience of positive capability signals aggravates investor reactions to organizational misconduct, a negative integrity signal. Using irregular financial restatements as the negative integrity signals and prior alliance announcements as the positive capability signals, we find that investors react more negatively to restatements by firms whose alliance announcements are more salient—that is, the firms that announce more frequently and firms that create more positive expectations from those announcements. We also find that firm size and level of diversification weaken these negative effects. We contribute to research on signaling theory, social evaluations, organizational misconduct, and alliances.

title: Microfoundations of Framing: The Interactional Production of Collective Action Frames in the Occupy Movement
methods: Qualitative real-time process study of the interaction between Occupy London and St. Paul's Cathedral. The authors used participant observation, 44 semi-structured interviews, informal conversations, documents, media/social-media materials, NVivo coding, temporal bracketing, visual mapping, and grounded theorizing to build a process model of collective action frame emergence, ascendance, and escalation.
industry: Social movement and religious-institutional setting: Occupy London, St. Paul's Cathedral, the Church of England, and the City of London financial-establishment context.
time_period: A year-long interaction beginning with Occupy London's October 15, 2011 protest and extending through the October 14, 2012 anniversary Evensong stunt; participant observation covered the 4.5 months of occupation plus post-eviction events.
units: Movement-target interactions between Occupy London and St. Paul's Cathedral, with Occupy activists, St. Paul's/Church of England respondents, meetings, platform performances, letters, media, and social-media materials.
n_sample: 280 hours of participant observation, more than 40 informal conversations, 44 semi-structured interviews with 28 Occupy activists and 16 St. Paul's/Church of England respondents, and documentary/social-media data.
authors: Reinecke, Juliane; Ansari, Shahzad (Shaz)
theories: interaction ritual and emotional energy (Collins, 2001, 2004); interactional framing / frame analysis (Goffman, 1974); social movement framing theory (Snow et al., 1986; Benford & Snow, 2000)
keywords: collective action frames; emotional attachment; frame amplification; frame laminations; frame sacralization; interactional framing; movement-target interactions; social movements
research_question: How can the microprocesses of framing in movement-target interactions lead to the emergence and escalation of an unanticipated collective action frame? The paper asks this through the case of Occupy London, whose original "capitalism is crisis" frame targeting the financial establishment shifted into a "what would Jesus do?" frame targeting St. Paul's Cathedral and the Church of England.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: collective action frames, interactional frames, frame laminations, keying, frame breaks, misframing, grievance construction, and movement-target interaction.
- Process / phases: emergence, ascendance, and escalation of the WWJD collective action frame across eight interaction episodes from the initial encounter to the anniversary Evensong stunt.
- Situational mechanisms: emotional attachment to the frame, frame sacralization, and frame amplification through media and public audiences.
- Emergent outcome: an initially unintended religious-moral frame displaced the original anti-capitalist frame and turned a potential ally into a target.
- Boundary conditions: the model is grounded in a physically copresent, materially salient, highly public movement-target encounter.

The process begins with an accidental encounter in which St. Paul's became drawn into Occupy's activity frame after protesters were blocked from the London Stock Exchange. Misframing and frame breaks created a new grievance against St. Paul's; protesters then attached emotionally to the WWJD frame, sacralized it through Christian symbolism and the cathedral setting, and amplified it through media-facing performances. These mechanisms reinforced each other over time, making the new frame increasingly salient even though it diverted attention from Occupy's original target.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to social movement and organization theory by shifting attention from strategic deployment of ready-made collective action frames to the interactional production of frames in concrete situations. It theorizes collective action frames as emergent, contested, and endogenous to movement-target interactions rather than as context-free tools that movements simply choose and deploy.

The paper also identifies situational mechanisms that explain how interactional frames become collective action frames. Emotional attachment, sacralization, and amplification show how emotions, moral meaning, material setting, and third-party audiences can transform local interactional dynamics into a movement-level frame trajectory.
practical_implication:
For movement actors, targets, and intermediaries, the study shows that seemingly local interactional choices can redirect a movement's grievance, target, and public identity. Actors who treat framing as only a strategic communications problem may miss how emotional reactions, sacred meanings, material settings, and media feedback can bind participants to a frame that no one originally intended.

For organizations facing activism, the findings imply that responses such as symbolic welcome, legal distancing, public statements, or silence can become frame breaks that reshape the conflict. Managing such encounters requires attention to the interaction order, not only to formal stakeholder positions or message content.
limitations:
The authors acknowledge that their model is built around a setting marked by physical copresence between a movement and its target. This may limit direct extension to virtual communities and social-media-based movements, where amplification and emotional dynamics may operate through different material and sensory conditions.

The case is also an unusually public, symbolic, and religiously charged encounter involving Occupy London and St. Paul's Cathedral. The resulting model is most directly grounded in situations where movement-target interaction is observable, emotionally intense, materially salient, and open to media amplification.
future_research:
Future research can examine how broader cultural meaning systems are reworked at the interactional level and how interactional meanings scale up to affect those systems. The authors specifically invite work on how collective meaning structures and micro-interactional meaning making recursively connect in other movements and contentious settings.

The paper also calls for more research on multimodal framing processes. Scholars could study how verbal, visual, material, sensory, embodied, and digital modes combine in framing, including how online platforms, building design, spatial arrangements, images, gestures, and immersive encounters shape collective action frames.
abstract: Social movement scholars have typically focused either on how social movements strategically use collective action frames to confront targets and mobilize supporters or on how targets respond to social movements. Few have captured the interactional dynamics between the two. This oversight tends to obscure how an extant collective action frame may shift or how a new one may arise during such interactions. To address this issue, we focus on movement–target interactions and illuminate the microfoundations of framing that produce a new collective action frame. Drawing on real-time participant observations, we examine how an unintended collective action frame emerged and escalated during a year-long interaction between the Occupy London movement and St. Paul’s Cathedral, Church of England. Occupy protesters shifted from a “capitalism is crisis” frame targeting the U.K.’s financial establishment to a “what would Jesus do?” frame targeting the Church of England. We develop a process model based on the interplay of frame laminations and three situational mechanisms—emotional attachment to a frame, frame sacralization, and frame amplification—derived from an analysis of framing in movement–target interactions to explain the emergence and escalation of an unexpected collective action frame.
apa_citation: Reinecke, J., & Ansari, S. (2021). Microfoundations of framing: The interactional production of collective action frames in the Occupy movement. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(2), 378-408. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.1063

title: Workplace Interpersonal Capitalization: Employee Reactions to Coworker Positive Event Disclosures
methods: Three empirical quantitative studies plus one supplementary experiment. Study 1 used a dyadic field survey and path analysis; Study 2 used a 2 x 2 online experiment with ANOVA and bootstrapped indirect effects; Study 3 used a two-week experience-sampling design with multilevel path analysis.
industry: University/workplace and student contexts rather than a single industry: Study 1 sampled university employees, Study 2 sampled students, the supplementary study sampled full-time workers, and Study 3 sampled working adults.
country: United States and United Kingdom across the reported studies.
time_period: No calendar data-collection period is reported; Study 3 used a two-week diary study over 10 consecutive working days.
units: Discloser-responder dyads, student participants, full-time worker scenario participants, and daily coworker conversations nested within responders.
n_sample: Study 1: 284 discloser-responder dyads; Study 2: 225 participants; supplementary study: 213 participants; Study 3: 82 participants and 644 conversations.
authors: Watkins, Trevor
theories: capitalization theory (Gable et al., 2004; Gable & Reis, 2010); social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954; Smith, 2000)
keywords: competition; envy; inspiration; interpersonal citizenship behavior; positive event disclosures; social comparison theory; social undermining; workplace interpersonal capitalization
research_question: How do employees respond when coworkers disclose personal work-related positive events, and how does perceived competition with the disclosing coworker shape responders' emotional and behavioral reactions?
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a social-comparison process. Positive event disclosures provide upward comparison information; when competition is low, the discloser's success appears more attainable or co-beneficial, eliciting inspiration and motivating interpersonal citizenship behavior. When competition is high, the same disclosure highlights opposed outcomes, eliciting envy and motivating social undermining as a way to reduce the comparison threat.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts capitalization theory from a discloser-centered account to a responder-centered account. It shows that capitalization is not uniformly constructive in workplaces: under competition, disclosure of good fortune can backfire by producing envy and social undermining. The paper also extends workplace social comparison research by showing that privately disclosed, less visible positive events can trigger consequential comparisons.
practical_implication: Employees should be attentive to competitive cues before sharing positive work events with coworkers, because the benefits of capitalization depend on whether outcomes feel aligned or opposed. Managers can reduce the risk of envy and undermining by deemphasizing competition and designing performance metrics or reward structures that support information and resource sharing.
limitations: The author notes selection bias in Study 1 because participants chose which coworker to invite, and Study 1 was correlational rather than causal. Study 2 did not fully test whether personal sharing has unique effects, although the supplementary study addressed self-disclosure versus third-party disclosure. The field studies also reported relatively low levels of competition, limiting what can be inferred about highly competitive workplaces.
future_research: Future research should examine how the content and type of capitalization shape responder reactions, including whether positive events reflect hard work, luck, first news, or information the responder already knew. The paper also calls for work on who does or does not capitalize at work, and what contexts encourage or discourage positive event disclosure.
abstract: “Capitalization”—the process of sharing a personal positive event with others— provides disclosers with many advantages such as increased self-esteem, relationship quality, and relationship trust. Existing theory on capitalization has been developed within the context of close relationships where individuals typically maintain aligned outcomes. However, when outcomes are opposed such as when individuals are competing, capitalization may not be an effective relationship behavior as currently conceptualized. In this work, I examine the consequences of capitalization within the workplace, a context that is characteristically competitive. I build a model of workplace interpersonal capitalization, defined as the process of sharing personal work-related positive events with coworkers. Drawing from social comparison theory, I posit that hearing a coworker disclose work-related positive events causes an employee to experience either inspiration or envy as a function of the degree to which the disclosing coworker is viewed as a competitor. Furthermore, I explain how these inspirational and envious reactions motivate interpersonal citizenship behavior and social undermining, respectively. Overall, I establish distinct responder-based reactions and postulate competition as a key boundary condition that alters the effects of capitalization.
apa_citation: Watkins, T. (2021). Workplace interpersonal capitalization: Employee reactions to coworker positive event disclosures. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(2), 537-561. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.1339

title: Deploying Human Capital Resources: Accentuating Effects of Situational Alignment and Social Capital Resources
methods: Empirical quantitative archival study of professional cycling teams using cross-classified mixed models. The study analyzes race-level characteristics, individual cyclist competencies, team HCR stocks, deployed start-list HCRs, shared team task-specific experience, and episodic start-list performance across the 2015 Union Cycliste Internationale World Tour, with separate models for mountain and sprint HCR deployment and performance.
industry: Professional cycling / elite team sport.
time_period: 2015 Union Cycliste Internationale World Tour season, with prior 2013-2014 data used to index cyclist competencies and shared team task-specific experience.
units: Cyclists, cycling teams, races, and deployed start lists; the focal performance unit is repeated deployed start-list performance cross-nested within teams and races.
n_sample: 448 riders from 17 World Teams who competed in 26 races, yielding 442 deployed HCR performance episodes; mountain and sprint performance analyses used 204 and 187 observations, respectively.
authors: Wolfson, Mikhail A.; Mathieu, John E.
theories: human capital resource complementarity (HCRC) theory (Wolfson & Mathieu, 2018); human capital resources (Ployhart et al., 2014); social capital resources and shared team task-specific experience; social entrainment theory
keywords: HCR deployment; deployed HCR alignment; human capital resource complementarity; human capital resources; shared team task-specific experience; situational characteristics; social capital resources; team performance
research_question: How do accumulated human capital resource stocks translate into performance through deployment decisions across changing task situations? The paper asks whether aligning deployed HCRs with race characteristics improves start-list performance and whether social capital resources, operationalized as shared team task-specific experience, strengthen that alignment-performance relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cross-level deployment process. Teams with stronger HCR stocks have more options for composing start lists, but performance gains depend on whether those deployed competencies match the specific race demands. Social capital resources matter because members with greater shared task-specific experience can coordinate interdependent work more effectively, allowing aligned HCRs to become performance advantages rather than merely available talent.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends human capital resource complementarity theory by making deployment a central mechanism between HCR stocks and performance. It shifts attention from the accumulation of valuable human capital to the question of how organizations compose and recompose teams across changing situations.

It also bridges strategic human capital research and team composition research by treating start-list composition as the concrete vehicle through which HCRs are mobilized. The paper further identifies SCRs, especially shared team task-specific experience, as a boundary condition that helps explain when HCR-situation alignment yields superior performance.
practical_implication:
Organizations should not assume that accumulating high-quality talent is sufficient for competitive advantage. They need deployment systems that match members' competencies to task demands and that preserve enough shared experience for team members to coordinate effectively under pressure.

For managers, the results imply that staffing decisions should consider both competence-task fit and prior working relationships among deployed members. HR information systems and team assignment processes can be useful when they track not only individual skills but also members' prior shared task experience.
limitations:
The authors note that professional cycling offers objective measures and dynamic deployment situations, but it may limit generalizability because competencies and situational demands are unusually visible and well defined. Findings may not transfer directly to settings where task demands, individual competencies, or alignment requirements are harder to observe in advance.

The study indexes competencies using prior performance and measures SCRs through shared race experience, so these are proxies rather than direct measures of underlying ability or coordination processes. The models also include relatively few predictors, leaving room for other individual and team factors such as personality, leadership, and training interventions.
future_research:
Future research should examine the costs and benefits of HCR deployment over time, including underutilization, development costs, burnout, and whether superstar-focused or team-wide competence strategies perform better in different contexts. The authors also suggest studying multiple team memberships as a mechanism for flexible deployment and as a possible source of role stress.

Longer temporal designs could examine how collective turnover, leavers, replacements, and dynamic team membership reconfigure both HCRs and SCRs. Future studies should also investigate patterns and antecedents of shared team task-specific experience, including whether leaders sometimes need to sacrifice short-term performance to develop future deployment options.
abstract: Researchers and organizational leaders alike have long known that securing human capital (HC) is critical for organizational success. The bulk of research in this domain has addressed issues regarding the accrual of HC stocks. However, there has been a dearth of research exploring the underlying mechanisms through which accrued HC stocks translate to competitive advantage. We expand on Wolfson and Mathieu’s (2018) human capital resource complementarity (HCRC) theory by incorporating the deployment of human capital resources (HCRs) as well as the role of social capital resources (SCRs) in the form of members’ shared team task-specific experience in predicting performance. We empirically test HCRC theory-derived hypotheses using a sample of 448 cyclists from 17 world teams who competed in 26 races during the 2015 season of the Union Cycliste Internationale World Tour. Our results revealed that higher-level HCR stocks indirectly led to deployed HCR performance through deployed HCR alignment with situational characteristics. Furthermore, SCRs acted as a critical boundary condition for the value of aligning deployed HCRs with situational characteristics such that the alignment of deployed HCRs was only advantageous when paired with relatively high levels of SCRs. Implications for future theory building, research, and practice related to HCR deployment are discussed.
apa_citation: Wolfson, M. A., & Mathieu, J. E. (2021). Deploying human capital resources: Accentuating effects of situational alignment and social capital resources. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(2), 435-457. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.0500

title: Marriage of Unequals? Investment Quality Heterogeneity, Market Heat, and the Formation of Status-Asymmetric Ties in the Venture Capital Industry
methods: Empirical quantitative study of U.S. venture capital syndication using VentureXpert data. The authors construct factual lead-follower syndication ties and matched counterfactual alternatives, then estimate conditional logit models and fixed-effects linear probability models with clustered standard errors, robustness checks for sampling, lead definition, nonlead investors, status measures, valuation measures, market heat measures, and selection.
industry: Venture capital syndication / VC industry.
country: United States; U.S.-based portfolio companies and U.S.-based independent VC partnerships.
time_period: Deals from 1990 to 2017, with 1985-1989 data used to construct initial rolling-window measures.
units: Lead VC-follower VC candidate ties within investment rounds, comparing factual followers with matched counterfactual followers.
n_sample: 4,886 factual observations and 40,491 counterfactual observations, from 2,950 discrete investment rounds; final model tables report 45,377 observations.
authors: Zhelyazkov, Pavel I.; Tatarynowicz, Adam
theories: behavioral finance account of market heat and countercyclical risk aversion; network dynamics in VC syndication; status homophily and status leakage in interorganizational relationships
keywords: VC syndication; conditional logit; market heat; status homophily; status-asymmetric ties; valuation trend; venture capital firms; venture performance trajectory
research_question: What drives the formation of upward- versus downward-status-asymmetric ties among venture capital firms? The paper asks how the performance trajectory of the venture and the heat of the external market jointly shape whether lower-status leads attract higher-status followers or higher-status leads bring in lower-status followers.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a directed status-exchange process. A high-performing venture gives a lower-status lead a compelling opportunity that can compensate a higher-status follower for status-leakage and governance risks, making upward-status ties more likely. A poorer-performing venture makes higher-status followers less attractive or less attainable, while lower-status followers may accept a weaker opportunity for access to a high-status lead. Hot markets strengthen the upward-status pathway because investors attend more to upside opportunities, but the paper does not find the corresponding market-heat amplification for downward-status ties.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to network dynamics by treating VC syndication as a directed network rather than an undirected alliance network, separating upward- and downward-status-asymmetric tie formation. It shows that the internal performance trajectory of the collaboration target matters alongside lead and follower characteristics and the external market context.

The paper also refines status theory by showing that status homophily is not the only default in interorganizational matching. High-status actors can use their position to bring lower-status partners into less promising ventures, while lower-status actors can sometimes reach higher-status partners by controlling access to high-performing ventures, especially in hot markets.
practical_implication:
For lower-status VC leads, the findings imply that a strong portfolio-company trajectory can be used strategically to attract higher-status syndication partners, particularly when market heat makes investors attentive to upside opportunities. For higher-status leads, the study suggests that weaker ventures may still be syndicated by reaching down the status hierarchy, but this can reinforce unequal access to high-quality deal flow.

For entrepreneurs and syndicate participants, the results imply that the status composition of later funding rounds is not only about investor prestige. It also reflects the venture's recent valuation trajectory, the lead investor's status position, and whether the market context makes missing high-growth deals more salient than avoiding weak ones.
limitations:
The authors emphasize that the study is based on econometric modeling of archival data, so it cannot make definitive causal claims about the operating mechanisms despite controls, fixed effects, and supplemental analyses. They also note that the data reveal accepted syndication ties, not the full set of invitations and rejections, so the first-stage invitation process and second-stage acceptance process cannot be separated.

The paper further acknowledges that focusing on the lead VC may understate the roles of nonlead investors and entrepreneurs in shaping follower selection. Valuation data are also sparse in VentureXpert, which restricts the analyzable sample and leaves possible selection issues that robustness tests can reduce but not fully eliminate.
future_research:
Future research could use experiments or venture-game designs to manipulate status asymmetry, venture performance trajectory, and market heat directly, allowing stronger causal tests of the mechanisms. Survey-based or multistage designs could distinguish which potential partners are approached from which invitations are accepted.

The authors also call for more work on directed network dynamics, including reciprocity, role specialization in VC syndication, and the different consequences of inbound versus outbound interorganizational ties. Additional research could examine how nonlead investors and entrepreneurs influence follower selection and how entrepreneurs trade off valuation and investor status across venture life-cycle stages.
abstract: In this study, we investigate the emergence of status-asymmetric ties among venture capital firms. In particular, we highlight the venture's performance trajectory as a powerful antecedent of upward-status asymmetries (in which a lower-status actor brings a higher-status alter into a venture) as well as downward-status asymmetries (in which a higher-status actor brings in a lower-status alter). We hypothesize that lower-status firms tend to bring higher-status alters into ventures on a better performance trajectory, whereas higher-status firms tend to bring lower-status alters into poorly performing ventures. Furthermore, we argue that these effects will be moderated by market heat, which affects whether investors would focus on the upside or downside of deals. We test our hypotheses in a longitudinal analysis of venture capital syndication patterns in the United States between 1990 and 2017. We find support for most of our predictions and document that the ability of lower-status lead investors to bring higher-status followers into good ventures is particularly accentuated in hot markets, which can heighten market participants' concerns about missing good deals. We thus highlight the interplay between the internal and the external contexts in shaping the formation of status-asymmetric relationships.
