title: Lenient Reactions to Misconduct: Examining the Self-Conscious Process of Being Lenient to Others at Work
methods: Three empirical quantitative studies: a three-wave field study of police officers, an online experiment using MTurk task-evaluation behavior, and an experimental recall study. The analyses use scale measures, ANOVA/MANOVA/MANCOVA, structural equation modeling, and bias-corrected bootstrapped indirect effects.
industry: Police organizations in Study 1, plus online workplace-task and workplace-recall contexts in Studies 2 and 3 rather than one single industry.
country: United States for the police-officer field study; the MTurk experiments specify native English-speaking or full-time-working participants but do not report a country.
time_period: Study 1 measured leniency over the past six months and used three surveys separated by approximately one month; Study 3 asked participants to recall incidents over the past four months. No calendar collection dates are reported.
units: Employees or participants acting as leniency grantors toward workplace misconduct, with outcomes measured as pride, guilt, engagement, exhaustion, and forgiveness moderation.
n_sample: Study 1: 249 Time 1 police officers and 176 Time 3 respondents; Study 2: 176 MTurk participants after attention-check exclusions; Study 3: 185 MTurk participants after exclusions.
authors: Zipay, Kate P.; Mitchell, Marie S.; Baer, Michael D.; Sessions, Hudson; Bies, Robert J.
theories: moral psychology (Blasi, 1984; Narvaez & Lapsley, 2009); theory of self-conscious emotions (Tracy & Robins, 2004; Tracy, Robins, & Tangney, 2007)
keywords: engagement; exhaustion; forgiveness; guilt; leniency; pride; self-conscious emotions; workplace misconduct
research_question: How does being lenient toward others' workplace misconduct affect the leniency grantor's self-conscious emotions and subsequent energy states at work? The paper also asks whether forgiveness changes the extent to which leniency produces pride and guilt.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an affective appraisal process. Leniency aligns with an ideal-self aspiration to be benevolent, which can evoke pride and increase engagement. At the same time, leniency can conflict with an ideal-self aspiration to be rule-abiding and a good organizational steward, which can evoke guilt and increase exhaustion. Forgiveness changes this appraisal by strengthening the pride pathway and weakening the guilt pathway.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper reframes leniency as a double-edged experience for the person granting it, not simply as a benevolent alternative to punishment. It integrates moral psychology and punishment perspectives by showing that the same lenient act can be appraised as both self-confirming and self-sanctioning.

The paper also extends research on workplace misconduct by shifting attention from victims, wrongdoers, and observers to the grantor who decides how to respond. It highlights self-conscious emotions as a mechanism through which employees evaluate their own workplace behavior against competing ideal-self aspirations.
practical_implication:
Organizations should recognize that employees who address misconduct with leniency may experience a complex emotional process rather than a simple relief from punishment decisions. Support systems after misconduct should therefore consider the grantor as well as victims and wrongdoers.

The findings also suggest that forgiveness may help grantors experience the positive side of leniency while reducing its guilt-related costs. The paper cautions, however, that efforts to promote forgiveness should not encourage disregard for organizational standards.
limitations:
The paper notes that Study 1's time-lagged field design makes it difficult to link emotions to specific leniency events, and the month-long separation may have allowed guilt to dissipate. Study 1 also did not collect detailed information on the particular misconduct incidents, so some incidents may fall near the boundaries of the paper's misconduct definition.

The results are not fully consistent across studies, especially for the main effects of leniency on pride and guilt. Study 3 may also include selection bias because participants had to recall recent lenient and nonlenient incidents, and recall designs may favor self-serving or emotionally accessible events.
future_research:
Future research should examine antecedents of leniency, including close relationships with wrongdoers, unethical climates, self-oriented versus other-oriented motives, and moral identity. It should also compare leniency with punishment decisions to see whether punishers experience parallel self-conscious emotions.

The paper calls for work on how misconduct characteristics, such as severity, intent, and interpersonal versus organizational direction, shape reactions to leniency. It also suggests examining additional outcomes, including citizenship, voice, support, retaliation, avoidance, coordination, workgroup trust, team performance, and climate of hostility.
abstract: How employees address others' misconduct is a common aspect of organizational life. Although some employees adhere to punishment standards when addressing misconduct, not all do. Instead, some are lenient. We propose that being lenient generates a self-conscious affective process that has countervailing effects for grantors. Drawing from the theory of self-conscious emotions and moral psychology, we propose that leniency elicits feelings of pride that enhance engagement and also elicits feelings of guilt that enhance exhaustion. Taken together, we propose that leniency indirectly influences energy states through self-conscious emotions. A multistudy approach was utilized to test these predictions. The results from Study 1 (a multiwave field study of police officers in the United States) and Study 2 (an experiment) largely supported our predictions. In Study 3 (an experiment), we extended our model to consider a theoretically relevant moderator. Grantors' forgiveness was predicted to impact the extent to which feelings of pride and guilt are experienced from leniency. As predicted, our results showed that the impact of leniency on pride was strengthened by forgiveness and the impact of leniency on guilt was weakened by forgiveness.
apa_citation: Zipay, K. P., Mitchell, M. S., Baer, M. D., Sessions, H., & Bies, R. J. (2021). Lenient reactions to misconduct: Examining the self-conscious process of being lenient to others at work. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(2), 351-377. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0123

title: Employer–Employee Matching and Complementary Assets: The Role of Cross-Organization Collaborations
methods: Empirical quantitative study using CV career histories and Scopus publication records for U.K. life-science academics. The authors estimate a multinomial logit model for mobility choices and difference-in-differences OLS models with individual fixed effects and robust standard errors for postmobility productivity and new-colleague collaboration outcomes.
industry: Academic life sciences / U.K. university biology departments.
time_period: 1995-2009 analysis window.
units: Academic researchers, faculty-year observations, mobility events, and coauthor-collaboration measures.
n_sample: 349 active research academics; the mobility subsample includes 156 movers, of whom 66 moved to a coauthor's organization.
authors: Campbell, Benjamin A.; Di Lorenzo, Francesco; Tartari, Valentina
theories: employer-employee matching theory; human capital theory; social capital theory
keywords: academic scientists; complementary assets; cross-organization collaborations; employee mobility; employer-employee matching; postmobility performance
research_question: How do cross-organization collaborations shape employer-employee matching when complementary assets are important to productivity? The paper asks whether prior collaborations increase mobility to collaborators' organizations and whether such moves improve postmobility productivity through better matching with prior and new colleagues.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a matching process in which cross-organization collaboration creates relational capital before hiring occurs. Prior collaboration gives both the employee and the receiving organization more direct information about general human capital and fit with complementary assets, reducing uncertainty in mobility decisions. After mobility, prior collaborators also help the mover integrate with new colleagues, so productivity gains are not limited to continued work with old coauthors.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to employer-employee matching theory by showing how collaboration across organizational boundaries can reveal fit with a receiving unit's complementary assets before a move occurs. It extends strategic human capital theory by treating complementary assets as central to both selection into mobility and postmove adaptation.

The paper also refines social capital theory by distinguishing cross-organization collaboration from general social ties. The authors argue that this hybrid form of relational capital combines features of internal and external relational capital, giving richer information about both employee quality and the employee's likely fit with organizational assets.
practical_implication:
For managers, the findings imply that cross-organization collaborations can operate as a hiring pipeline when productivity depends on fit with complementary assets. Such collaborations provide information about whether a potential employee can work productively with the receiving organization's people and resources, not just whether the person has high general ability.

The implication is not one-sided: collaborations may also increase outbound mobility by making employees visible to better-fitting employers. The authors therefore frame collaboration investment as potentially beneficial at the collective level, especially for organizations with idiosyncratic complementary assets that can attract better-fitting hires.
limitations:
The authors state that the evidence has limited causal interpretation because mobility events are not randomly assigned and omitted variable bias remains possible despite fixed effects, controls, and CV-based individual information. They also note that the academic life-sciences context has unusual transparency, autonomy, and persistent postmove collaboration opportunities, which may limit generalizability.

Additional limitations concern measurement and mechanism visibility. The study can classify within- and cross-organization coauthorships, but it cannot fully distinguish types of new collaborations, organizational onboarding ability, nonhuman complementary assets, or the dynamic evolution of matching after initial hiring.
future_research:
Future research should pursue stronger causal designs and richer data that can rule out alternative explanations for mobility and productivity changes. The authors also call for work that parses new collaborations by topic area, seniority, star status, and specialist versus generalist roles.

Further work could examine organizational heterogeneity in onboarding and integration, distinguish selection from treatment when hiring prior collaborators, and study how complementary assets shape matching after initial entry. The paper also suggests examining long-term postmobility publication trajectories, movement into administrative roles, involuntary turnover, and organization-level effects of investing in cross-organization collaborations.
abstract: Building on human capital theory and social capital theory, we theorize that cross-organization collaborations generate a rich and distinct source of relational capital that enhances employer–employee matches when complementary assets are important in the production process. We test our theory in the context of academic scientists where collaborations within and across organizations are common channels to access complementary assets. We find that cross-organizational collaborations are positively related to an individual’s decision to move to a previous coauthor’s organization. Additionally, moving to an organization where an individual had a direct collaboration is positively related to postmobility performance. This suggests that prior collaboration facilitates better employer–employee matches. We unpack this finding and show that the postmobility performance increase is not only driven by increased productivity with prior coauthors, it is also driven by novel collaborations with new colleagues. Together, our findings suggest that cross-organization collaborations facilitate hiring employees who can integrate well with the complementary assets of the entire unit.
apa_citation: Campbell, B. A., Di Lorenzo, F., & Tartari, V. (2021). Employer–employee matching and complementary assets: The role of cross-organization collaborations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(3), 799-823. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.0207

title: Why Activist Hedge Funds Target Socially Responsible Firms: The Reaction Costs of Signaling Corporate Social Responsibility
methods: Multi-year U.S. firm panel study using logistic regression models to estimate whether CSR score predicts activist hedge fund targeting, with industry CSR and financial communication vagueness as moderators and robustness checks using instrumental-variable probit, matched samples, alternative CSR measures, and geographic-distance analysis.
industry: Firms listed in the MSCI KLD index across industries, with industry measured using two-digit SIC codes.
units: Targeted and non-targeted firm-year observations
n_sample: 506 targeted firms and 1,106 non-targeted control firms; 14,962 firm-year observations
authors: DesJardine, M. R.; Marti, E.; Durand, R.
theories: corporate governance; instrumental corporate social responsibility; signaling theory
keywords: activist hedge funds; corporate governance; corporate social responsibility; reaction costs; signaling
research_question: The paper asks why activist hedge funds target socially responsible firms and whether CSR can create reaction costs when unintended audiences interpret CSR signals negatively. It tests whether higher CSR increases the likelihood of activist hedge fund targeting, and whether this relationship depends on industry CSR norms and the vagueness of firms' financial communication.
mechanism_summary: CSR usually functions as a signal to intended stakeholders that a firm is willing and able to act with a long-term orientation and attend to stakeholder interests. DesJardine, Marti, and Durand argue that activist hedge funds are an unintended audience that can read the same CSR signal as evidence of wasteful intentions and capabilities. This makes socially responsible firms more attractive targets for campaigns that seek short-term shareholder-value reorientation. CSR is less salient when it blends into a high-CSR industry, but more informative when financial communication is vague.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends CSR research by showing that CSR signals need not only generate goodwill; they can also invite costly negative reactions from audiences that interpret stakeholder orientation as poor business character. It contributes to signaling theory by introducing reaction costs as a third signaling cost, distinct from production costs and penalty costs because it arises when unintended audiences react negatively to true signals. It also contributes to corporate governance research by showing that signaling can create, rather than merely reduce, governance conflicts.
practical_implication:
The paper warns that socially responsible firms can face activist pressure before activists later suppress CSR activities. For policy-makers, the authors suggest that protecting firms targeted by activist hedge funds could relieve pressures that undermine CSR. For socially responsible firms, the findings highlight the value of attracting socially minded and long-term shareholders who may moderate profit-centered activist interventions.

For sustainability-oriented investors, the paper suggests reassessing whether investments in activist hedge funds align with their values. More broadly, policy-makers and investors need to weigh the potential efficiency gains of activist hedge funds against their negative effects on CSR and the long-term prosperity of targeted firms.
limitations: The authors note that they examine average reaction costs created by hedge fund activism but do not directly measure the reaction costs borne by each firm. They also assume substantial similarity among activist hedge funds, even though hedge funds differ in investment horizons, tactics, and campaign size. Finally, the analysis examines one context: hedge fund targeting based on CSR signals.
future_research: Future research could directly measure the resources firms allocate to responding to activist campaigns and examine whether firms differ in their capacity to absorb reaction costs. It could also study how variation among activist hedge funds moderates the relationship between CSR signaling and targeting. More broadly, future work could examine reaction costs from other unintended audiences, such as social movements, customer watchdogs, or regulators, and explore how firms balance reaction costs against the benefits of true signals.
abstract: We develop and test a theory of how unintended audiences create reaction costs for firms that use corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a signal. We introduce and define reaction costs as costs that signal senders incur when unintended audiences react negatively to a true signal that was intended for another audience. We argue that activist hedge funds—an unintended audience—treat CSR as a signal that firms have wasteful intentions and capabilities, which prevent firms from maximizing shareholder value in the short term. On that basis, we hypothesize that activist hedge funds are more likely to target firms with higher levels of CSR, thus imposing reaction costs on these firms. We further argue that this relationship is weaker when firms operate in industries with high levels of CSR, and stronger when firms’ financial communication is vague. Using data on activist hedge fund campaigns in the U.S. between 2000 and 2016, we find supporting results. Our study shows that CSR signals may be costlier than previously assumed and contributes to research on CSR, signaling, and corporate governance.
apa_citation: DesJardine, M. R., Marti, E., & Durand, R. (2021). Why activist hedge funds target socially responsible firms: The reaction costs of signaling corporate social responsibility. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(3), 851-872. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.0238

title: The Use of Agency Workers Hurts Business Performance: An Integrated Indirect Model
methods: Empirical quantitative study using four-year store-level panel data from a retail chain. The authors combine archival staffing data, regular-employee and agency-worker surveys, accounting data, and secret-shopper service-quality scores, then estimate store, year, manager, and geographical-cluster fixed effects regressions plus bootstrapped conditional indirect effects.
industry: Retail service chain selling food, cleaning goods, nature and wellness items, and personal care merchandise.
time_period: Four-year panel; exact calendar years not reported.
units: Retail stores and store-year observations, with staffing records, worker surveys, accounting data, and secret-shopper evaluations.
n_sample: 270 stores; fixed-effects tables report 1,080 store-year observations.
authors: Eldor, Liat; Cappelli, Peter
theories: diversity theory; self-categorization theory (Hogg & Terry, 2000); social identity theory (Tajfel, 1978; Tajfel & Turner, 1986; Ashforth & Mael, 1989)
keywords: agency temps; business performance; self-categorization theory; social identity theory; social integration practices; workplace identification
research_question: The paper asks whether greater use of agency temps in a blended workplace hurts store-level business performance by lowering the regular workforce's identification with the workplace. It also asks whether shared instrumental values and social integration practices buffer this indirect negative relationship.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is identity-based. When regular employees work alongside lower-status agency temps, the workplace is perceived as lower status, which weakens regular employees' workplace identification. Lower workplace identification then reduces motivation to act on behalf of the store, harming service quality and private-label sales. Shared instrumental values and social integration practices are theorized to reduce this identity threat by explaining the business value of agency workers and blurring the "we-they" boundary between regular and agency workforces.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends research on agency temps from individual job attitudes to store-level business outcomes. It shows that the negative association between agency-worker use and performance operates through workplace identification, not only through prior explanations based on job security or advancement threats.

It also connects social identity theory, self-categorization theory, and diversity research to blended employment arrangements. The paper treats employment status differences as a contemporary workplace distinction that can create identity threat, while also showing how workplace-level practices may mitigate that threat.
practical_implication:
Managers should not assume that agency temps improve performance simply by increasing flexibility or lowering labor costs. The findings suggest that extensive use of agency temps can carry hidden store-level costs through the regular workforce's reduced identification with the workplace.

The paper also implies that managers can partly offset these costs by communicating why agency workers are needed and by using social integration practices. The authors caution, however, that integration practices operate in a legal and policy context where treating agency workers too similarly to regular employees may create employment-law concerns.
limitations:
The authors state that they cannot rule out all confounding factors and that designs where agency-worker use is more clearly exogenous would be useful. The study is also limited to one form of nonstandard employment, agency workers, and different nonstandard arrangements may affect regular employees differently.

External validity is bounded by the empirical context: a retail service chain in Israel with low-wage frontline work. The authors also note that fixed-effects analysis limited the study to factors operating within stores and that they could not compare individual performance outcomes with business-level outcomes.
future_research:
Future research should examine other occupations, industries, and nonstandard work arrangements, including contractors and outsourced on-site operations. The authors call for a broader taxonomy of nonstandard employment by type, industry, cost effects, and business outcomes.

They also suggest examining whether regular employees accept buffering practices, whether agency temps affect other attitudes and behaviors such as commitment, citizenship, and prosocial behavior, and whether other organization-level outcomes such as innovation and productivity are affected. Further work should also study the process through which employment externalization and alternative work arrangements are introduced into workplaces.
abstract: The use of agency temps in the workplace has been the subject of considerable research interest, much of it focused on the effects that using temps have on the job attitudes of regular employees. We advance this stream of research by examining the effects of using agency temps on business performance. We find first that, when otherwise identical workplaces make greater use of temporary help provided by agencies, the identification of the employee or "regular" workforce with their workplace declines because the perceived status of the workplace declines. This, in turn, leads to lower store-level service quality and sales. This effect is independent of the notion suggested in earlier studies that temp workers threaten the job security and opportunities for advancement of regular employees. Finally, we find that these negative effects can be mitigated by workplace-level strategies associated with shared instrumental values and social integration practices. We examine these relationships using a range of employeeand store-level data sources over time from a retail chain.

title: Sizing Up Entrepreneurial Potential: Gender Differences in Communication and Investor Perceptions of Long-Term Growth and Scalability
methods: Three empirical quantitative studies combining linguistic text analysis, archival field data, regression and mediation models, and an investor experiment. Study 1 codes pitch videos from early-stage entrepreneurs using the Brysbaert Concreteness Index and linguistic category model. Study 2 codes VC funding applications and estimates logistic, OLS, and mediation models. Study 3 experimentally manipulates concrete versus abstract pitch descriptions and founder gender among accredited investors.
industry: Technology entrepreneurship, early-stage startups, and venture capital funding evaluations.
country: United States: Study 1 used a Mid-Atlantic technology entrepreneurship pitch workshop, Study 2 used a West Coast VC firm, and Study 3 used investors attending a U.S. entrepreneurial investment conference.
time_period: Study 2 covers funding requests received by the VC firm in 2018; other study collection dates are not reported in paper.
units: Entrepreneur pitches, startup funding applications, and investor evaluations of venture descriptions.
n_sample: Study 1: 129 early-stage entrepreneurs; Study 2: 1,284 funding applications from 243 female and 1,041 male founders; Study 3: 238 active and experienced investors.
authors: Huang, Laura; Joshi, Priyanka; Wakslak, Cheryl; Wu, Andy
theories: construal level theory; entrepreneurial decision making and investor cognition; gendered communication
keywords: communicative abstraction; concrete language; construal level theory; entrepreneurial funding; female entrepreneurs; investor perceptions; likelihood of investment; long-term growth and scalability
research_question: The paper asks whether gender differences in entrepreneurs' communication style help explain gender disparities in entrepreneurial funding outcomes. Specifically, it examines whether female entrepreneurs use more concrete and less abstract language than male entrepreneurs, whether investors read communicative abstraction as a signal of long-term growth and scalability, and whether that perception affects investment likelihood.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism links gendered communication to investor cognition. The authors argue that women entrepreneurs tend to communicate more concretely, while abstract communication is interpreted by investors as a sign that a venture is oriented toward long-term growth and scalability. In the field corpus, female founder gender is associated with lower abstraction, abstraction is associated with stronger growth perceptions, and growth perceptions are associated with greater investment likelihood. In the experiment, manipulating pitch abstraction provides causal evidence that abstract descriptions increase perceived long-term growth orientation and, through that perception, willingness to invest.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to research on gender and entrepreneurship by identifying communicative style as a behavioral pathway that can partly explain gender disparities in investor funding decisions. It does not reduce the disparity only to investor bias or venture type; instead, it shows how apparently success-oriented investor criteria can still generate gendered outcomes when they reward a communication style more commonly used by men.

It also contributes to entrepreneurial resource acquisition and communication research by showing that the level of linguistic abstraction matters for investment evaluation. The paper extends construal-level arguments into entrepreneurial pitching by linking abstract communication to perceptions of long-term growth, scalability, and investment worthiness.
practical_implication:
The findings imply that entrepreneurs, particularly women entrepreneurs, should attend not only to the factual content of a pitch but also to the level of abstraction used to communicate venture potential. When investors are evaluating long-term growth and scalability, more abstract framing may help signal a broader, future-oriented venture trajectory.

The paper also cautions that investor reliance on communicative abstraction can appear economically reasonable while still producing gendered consequences. Because women entrepreneurs in the studies tended to communicate less abstractly, perceptions of long-term growth and scalability may partly reflect communication style rather than only the venture's underlying potential.
limitations:
The authors identify Study 2's correlational design as a key limitation because unobserved differences between ventures or founders could explain associations between abstraction, perceived growth, and funding outcomes. Study 3 addresses part of this problem experimentally, but the overall evidence remains focused on investor perceptions in venture-backed, growth-oriented settings.

The scope is also limited to entrepreneurial investment contexts where venture capital or equity investors seek financial returns from long-term scalable growth. The paper acknowledges that other investors, such as microfinance institutions or social-mission organizations, may value different communication styles and decision criteria.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether the effects of abstract and concrete communication differ for female entrepreneurs, social-mission ventures, or settings where concrete communication may be advantageous. Additional work could also study other resources that early-stage entrepreneurs seek, such as advice, introductions, human capital, and intellectual capital.

The authors also call for research on how entrepreneurs can modify speech abstraction and whether different ways of achieving abstraction have different consequences. Such work could clarify when impression management through abstract communication is beneficial and when concrete communication better supports entrepreneurial outcomes.
abstract: Female entrepreneurs have been found to face disadvantages when compared with male entrepreneurs, especially in acquiring the financial resources needed to sustain and grow their ventures. Across three studies, we examine how disparities in funding outcomes may be due to differences in how entrepreneurs communicate their ventures, whereby female entrepreneurs have a tendency to use more concrete language when describing their ventures than their male counterparts. We find that the use of abstract speech affects investors' perceptions of which ventures are oriented toward long-term growth and scalability, which in turn affects the likelihood that a venture will receive investment. We conclude with a discussion of the important role of communication style as a key mediating mechanism in influencing investor cognition.
apa_citation: Huang, L., Joshi, P., Wakslak, C., & Wu, A. (2021). Sizing up entrepreneurial potential: Gender differences in communication and investor perceptions of long-term growth and scalability. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(3), 716-740. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.1417

title: Political Dynamics in Organizational Identity Breach and Reconstruction: Findings from the Crisis in UNICEF Germany
methods: Longitudinal qualitative case study of UNICEF Germany using participant and nonparticipant observations, 44 semistructured interviews, internal documents, media texts, and abductive coding to build a process model.
industry: Nonprofit humanitarian and relief organization.
units: Organizational members, board and management actors, workshops, meetings, documents, and media texts at UNICEF Germany.
n_sample: 44 semistructured interviews
authors: Jacobs, C. D.; Kreutzer, K.; Vaara, E.
theories: hybrid identities; organizational identity breach and reconstruction; political perspective on organizational identity
keywords: hybrid organizations; identity reconstruction; organizational identity breach; political dynamics; power balance
research_question: The paper asks how organizational politics shape processes of organizational identity breach and reconstruction. It also asks what political strategies organizational actors employ when wrestling with consensus and conflict over organizational identity.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / orientations: Organizational identity breach, organizational identity reconstruction, managerialist identity beliefs, and idealist identity beliefs.
- Process / phases: Build-up of identity tensions, revelation of identity breach, identity reconstruction, and enactment of the reconstructed identity.
- Political strategies: Normalizing identity beliefs and masking controversial practices; revealing identity violations and defending prevailing identity beliefs; arguing for alternative identity constructions and forging a compromise; enforcing and maintaining the compromise.
- Political effects: Distorted, reversed, restored, and effectuated power balance, paired respectively with disguised conflict, open conflict, orchestrated consensus, and sustained consensus.
- Triggers: Increasing tensions reaching a breaking point, crisis pressure for reconciliation, and the urge to conclude reconstruction and move on.

The process begins when managerialist actors normalize fundraising- and efficiency-oriented identity beliefs while masking practices that idealist actors may contest. Whistleblowing and media attention then reveal perceived identity violations, allowing idealists to reverse the power balance and force open conflict over what UNICEF Germany stands for. Reconstruction occurs through negotiation between activist-educator and professional-fundraiser identity constructions, producing a compromise that is later enforced publicly and maintained backstage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances organizational identity research by theorizing identity breach and reconstruction as political processes rather than merely cognitive or cultural disruptions. It contributes a four-phase process model linking political strategies to changing power balances and forms of consensus or conflict. It also extends research on hybrid identities by showing how idealist actors can use breach and reconstruction to restore a more favorable balance against managerialist dominance.
practical_implication:
For hybrid organizations, the case shows that hidden identity tensions and distorted power balances can build into a public identity breach. The UNICEF Germany reconstruction suggests one pathway through which inclusive mission review, open argument over alternative identity constructions, and compromise formation were associated with restored consensus after a breach.

The study also shows that reconstructed identity settlements require continued enactment and maintenance. Enforced consensus can conceal unresolved tensions again, so the practical lesson is less a one-time communication response than sustained attention to the political work behind organizational identity.
limitations: The authors caution that the model is based on a revealing but idiosyncratic single case in a German hybrid nonprofit organization. They note that the boundary conditions may differ in organizations with other goal sets, such as profit orientation or public value generation. The analysis also focuses mainly on intraorganizational dynamics, even though media and other external constituencies shaped the breach and reconstruction process.
future_research: Future research could examine organizational identity breach and reconstruction in settings beyond hybrid organizations and beyond the German context. Comparative work could study how external stakeholders perceive and influence breaches, how different hierarchical or professional groups experience breach, and how similar processes unfold across sectors or strategic groups. The authors also call for deeper study of masking, silencing, framing, discursive microprocesses, and the darker side of organizational identity construction.
abstract: This paper elucidates the political dynamics of organizational identity breach and reconstruction. Drawing on the revealing case of UNICEF Germany, we develop a process model of four phases of identity breach and reconstruction: build-up of identity tensions, revelation of identity breach, identity reconstruction, and enactment of the reconstructed identity. Our analysis explains how each phase was characterized by specific political strategies employed by the managerialist and idealist organizational members, the effects of these strategies on the power balance and consensus or conflict over organizational identity, and how particular triggers explain shifts from one phase to another. By so doing, our analysis advances our understanding of organizational identity breach and reconstruction as political processes, and paves the way for new studies of political identity dynamics in other contexts.

title: Who Will Board a Sinking Ship? a Firm–Director Interdependence Perspective of Mutual Selection between Declining Firms and Director Candidates
methods: Empirical quantitative study of candidate-declining-firm dyads using Chinese public firms under special treatment. The authors construct a choice-based matched sample with propensity score matching and estimate Cox proportional hazard models with controls for candidate characteristics, firm characteristics, turnaround actions, outgoing directors' capital, industry fixed effects, and years after ST filing; robustness checks use alternative observation windows, logit models, alternative capital measures, and alternative candidate samples.
industry: Public firms under special treatment in China; models include industry fixed effects based on China's official industry classifications.
time_period: Firms receiving *ST designation due to organizational decline from 2004 to 2016, with observation windows running from the year before *ST designation until release from special treatment or public-trading ban.
units: Candidate-*ST-firm dyads and year-candidate-*ST-firm observations for new outside director appointments.
n_sample: 242 *ST firms; 315 individuals who joined these firms as new outside directors; 1,890 matched candidate-*ST-firm dyads; 6,782 year-candidate-*ST-firm observations.
authors: Jiang, Han; Xia, Jun; Devers, Cynthia E.; Shen, Wei
theories: firm–director interdependence perspective; mutual selection between firms and director candidates; resource dependence theory (Pfeffer & Salancik, 1978)
keywords: declining firms; director candidates; firm–director interdependence; human capital; mutual selection; organizational social capital; resource dependence theory; social capital
research_question: Which director candidates will join declining firms, and why? The paper asks how declining firms' organizational dependence on candidates and candidates' personal dependence on declining firms jointly shape director appointments.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a mutual-selection process. Declining firms want resource-rich directors for turnaround, but director candidates also assess reputational risk, career development, positional returns, and experience-based returns. Candidates with moderate social or human capital are most likely to match with declining firms because they are attractive enough to be invited but still personally dependent enough to accept; candidates with very high endowments face lower personal dependence and greater downside risk.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper advances board research by moving director appointment theory beyond a firm-centric selection model. It develops a firm–director interdependence perspective in which director appointments depend on the match or mismatch between firms' organizational dependence and director candidates' personal dependence.

It also extends resource dependence theory by theorizing dependencies across levels: firms depend on directors' personal resources, while individual directors depend on firms for positional and experience-based returns. This helps explain why firms may not obtain the directors they most desire.
practical_implication:
For declining firms, the findings imply that attracting turnaround directors is not only a question of identifying high-resource candidates. Firms must consider whether those candidates have enough personal dependence on the opportunity to accept the appointment.

For director candidates, the study clarifies why joining a distressed firm can be attractive at moderate levels of social or human capital but risky at high levels. Organizational social capital changes this calculus by altering both the firm's need for candidates' resources and the reputational risks candidates face.
limitations:
The authors note that the RDT-based interdependence perspective is not the only possible explanation for mutual selection. Two-sided matching theory, social network theory, status-based matching, and person-organization fit could further explain how firm-director matches form.

The empirical design relies on secondary information from financial reports of public firms. This limits insight into the specific contents of candidates' social and human capital, the candidate pool firms considered, and the firms candidates targeted.
future_research:
Future research could compare the RDT-based account with two-sided matching theory, social network theory, and person-organization fit explanations of firm-director mutual selection. It could also examine other candidate-level and firm-level features, such as personal ties with incumbent or outgoing upper echelons and fit between firm culture and candidate values.

The authors also call for primary data collection and qualitative approaches that can more directly capture the interdependence and mutual selection process. Such work could clarify what candidate resources firms consider, what director opportunities candidates target, and how these judgments unfold before appointment.
abstract: We develop a firm–director interdependence perspective to theorize director appointments as the outcome of a mutual selection process in which firms and director candidates select each other based on their organizational and personal dependencies. We apply this perspective to address a puzzle regarding director appointment in declining firms: Declining firms are often motivated to bring in director candidates with high resource endowments to help enact turnarounds, but these candidates may not join a declining firm’s board due to the potential uncertainties and reputational loss of doing so. Drawing on the firm–director interdependence perspective, we predict that director candidates’ social capital and human capital have inverted U-shaped effects on their likelihood of joining a declining firm. Moreover, the declining firm’s organizational social capital differently moderates the effects of candidates’ social capital and human capital. Evidence from a sample of public firms under special treatment (*ST) in China supports our theoretical predictions.

title: Understanding When and Why Cover-Ups Are Punished Less Severely
methods: Three empirical studies using quantitative experimental and quasi-experimental designs: a Prolific critical incident field study with a 2 x 2 between-subjects design, a University of Pennsylvania laboratory experiment with a behavioral punishment measure, and an MTurk online experiment testing moderated mediation through perceived group loyalty.
industry: Organizational cover-up contexts involving full-time employees, student laboratory participants, and online workers evaluating work-related or task-related unethical behavior.
country: United States laboratory and online task contexts; Study 1 participant country is not reported in the paper.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual third-party evaluators judging personal cover-ups, relational cover-ups, or baseline unethical actions.
n_sample: Study 1 final sample of 385 participants; Study 2 final sample of 273 participants; Study 3 final sample of 502 participants.
authors: Kundro, T. G.; Nurmohamed, S.
theories: attribution theory; group loyalty; in-group favoritism; social identity theory
keywords: attribution theory; cover-ups; group loyalty; punishment; social identity; unethical behavior
research_question: The paper asks when and why in-group third parties punish cover-ups less severely than out-group third parties. It specifically examines whether punishment depends on cover-up type: concealing one's own unethical act versus concealing another group member's unethical act.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is attributional and identity-based. In-group third parties interpret relational cover-ups as evidence that the transgressor risked personal sanction to protect the group, increasing perceived group loyalty and reducing punishment severity. Personal cover-ups do not receive the same credit because they appear self-serving and harmful to the group. Across the studies, in-group leniency emerges for relational cover-ups but not for personal cover-ups.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to behavioral ethics by showing that cover-ups are not a unitary category of unethical behavior: personal and relational cover-ups elicit different punishment responses. It extends social identity research by identifying a boundary condition for in-group favoritism, showing that in-group third parties are more lenient only when the cover-up can be read as loyal to the group. It also advances work on prosocial unethical behavior by shifting attention from first-person motives to third-party punishment judgments.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that internal decision makers will punish all cover-ups consistently. Internal review boards or managers may punish relational cover-ups less severely when they view the actor as loyal, which can unintentionally signal that covering for peers is more permissible. The authors suggest involving out-group third-party input and balancing loyalty with fairness and care when evaluating cover-ups.
limitations: The authors note that mechanisms beyond group loyalty may also explain punishment differences, including perceived incompetence or other judgments. They also acknowledge that the baseline unethical actions in Studies 2 and 3 were limited in severity compared with the wider range of incidents recalled in Study 1. The paper does not fully address how rank, leadership responsibility, or punishment of the original wrongdoer may alter responses to cover-ups.
future_research: Future research could examine when in-group third parties punish personal cover-ups more severely, including situations where out-group observers are present. It could also compare cover-ups with other intentional unethical acts to clarify the role of intentionality and initial wrongdoing severity. Additional work could investigate high-ranking transgressors, leaders who oversee cover-ups, and whether the original wrongdoer in a relational cover-up is punished differently from the person who conceals the act.
abstract: Cover-ups of unethical actions are undesirable and often costly. However, existing theory is unclear on when and why some cover-ups are punished less severely by in-group third parties compared to out-group third parties. Drawing on theories of attribution and social identity, we theorize that the punishment of cover-ups by inand out-group third parties depends on the type of cover-up: specifically, whether individuals conceal their own unethical transgressions (personal cover-ups) or the unethical transgressions of another individual (relational cover-ups). By highlighting this distinction, we hypothesize and find across three studies that in-group third parties punish relational—but not personal—cover-ups less severely than out-group third parties. Moreover, we theorize and find support for the mediating role of perceptions of group loyalty. Our theory and results reveal the ways in which different forms of cover-ups can escape severe punishment, and offer important theoretical contributions for research on unethical behavior, social identity, and loyalty.

title: Minimal and Adaptive Coordination: How Hackathons’ Projects Accelerate Innovation without Killing it
methods: Comparative qualitative field study of 13 assistive technology hackathon projects. The authors triangulated real-time observations, field notes, video recordings, 90 formal and informal interviews, post-hackathon interviews, photographs, work artifacts, online documentation, and secondary materials, then reconstructed project timelines and used inductive comparative process analysis.
industry: Assistive technology hackathons in makerspaces, focused on hardware-based product development for disability-related challenges.
time_period: Late 2015 and early 2016
units: Thirteen project teams and 54 participants across two comparable assistive technology hackathons.
n_sample: 13 projects; 54 participants interviewed at least once; 90 formal and informal interviews.
authors: Lifshitz-Assaf, H.; Lebovitz, S.; Zalmanson, L.
theories: coordination theory; innovation process theory; temporality in organizations
keywords: accelerated innovation; adaptive coordination; coordination; hackathons; minimal basis for coordination; new product development; temporal ambiguity; temporality
research_question: The paper asks how accelerated new product development projects can produce functioning innovations under extreme time pressure when existing innovation and time-pressure research would predict failure. It examines how project teams in assistive technology hackathons deal with temporal ambiguity and how different coordination patterns shape whether they produce fully functioning, basic functioning, or nonfunctioning products.
mechanism_summary:
- Context / triggering condition: Ad hoc 72-hour assistive technology hackathons create high time pressure and temporal ambiguity because only the beginning, end, and challenge are defined.
- Full coordination path: Seven projects import and compress familiar organizational innovation temporal structures, establish a full basis for coordination around methods, materials, and measurements, and continue rich realignment when problems emerge.
- Adaptive coordination path: Three projects let new temporal structures emerge, begin with only a minimal high-level product design, and gradually increase alignment through swift sensing, brief updates, nudges, and adjustment to one another's work.
- Minimal coordination path: Three projects also begin with a minimal basis for coordination but do not increase alignment enough to integrate separate development efforts.
- Outcomes: Full coordination projects fail to produce working products; adaptive coordination projects produce fully functioning products; minimal coordination projects produce only basic functioning products.

The process mechanism is not that less coordination is always better. Rather, under accelerated innovation conditions, early full coordination can lock teams into a detailed solution path and reduce flexibility when ambiguity re-emerges. A minimal basis for coordination preserves flexibility, but only adaptive coordination adds enough later alignment to integrate components into fully functioning products.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to innovation process theory by showing that acceleration need not mean compressing existing innovation stages into a shorter time frame. In this setting, projects succeeded when they allowed new temporal structures to emerge and sustained ambiguity long enough to adapt to unexpected development hurdles.

It contributes to coordination theory by identifying adaptive coordination as a distinct mode between full coordination and minimal coordination. Adaptive coordination combines an initially minimal basis for coordination with later swift sensing and adjustment, explaining how ad hoc teams can maintain flexibility without losing integration. It also extends temporality research by showing how actors' enactment of temporal structures affects coordination processes and innovation outcomes.
practical_implication:
For organizations using hackathons, innovation sprints, or crisis-driven accelerated development, the study cautions against simply compressing familiar agile routines into a shorter schedule. Teams may need visible workflows, rapid experimentation, and brief adjustment interactions rather than early closure around a fully specified design.

The findings are especially relevant for urgent health care or assistive technology innovation, where speed matters but premature alignment can prevent adaptation. Managers and organizers should create conditions that let participants see one another's work and adjust quickly without forcing extensive meetings or detailed upfront plans.
limitations:
The authors explicitly caveat that the study concerns acceleration under changed temporal conditions without clear temporal structures; the findings do not apply when a new innovation process has become routinized with a stable temporal structure. The setting is also bounded to two comparable U.S. assistive technology hackathons in visible makerspaces, where participants could directly observe one another's work.

The model therefore may travel less directly to settings that lack an equivalent visible workflow for sensing and adjustment. Because the study is qualitative and processual, it explains how the observed projects coordinated under temporal ambiguity rather than estimating population-level effects.
future_research:
Future work should examine coordination in other ambiguity-heavy contexts, including innovation and entrepreneurship settings beyond hackathons. The paper also calls for research on whether conceptual closure remains necessary in contemporary innovation processes as digital fabrication, open-source tools, and rapid prototyping reduce experimentation costs.

Further research can study other contemporary ways of organizing for innovation, including remote or virtual accelerated work where visible workflow must be produced through digital technologies. The paper also calls for work on new ways of leveraging human creative capabilities to innovate and solve scientific, technological, and social problems in combination with machines.
abstract: The innovation journey of new product development processes often spans weeks or months. Recently, though, hackathons have turned the journey into an ad hoc sprint of only a couple of days using new tools and technologies. Existing research predicts that such conditions will result in a failure to produce new working products, yet hackathons often lead to functioning innovative products. To investigate this puzzle, we closely studied the product development process of 13 comparable projects in assistive technology hackathons. We found that accelerating innovation created temporal ambiguity, as it was unclear how to coordinate the challenging work within such an extremely limited and ad hoc time frame. Multiple projects worked to reduce this ambiguity, importing temporal structures from organizational innovation processes and compressing them to fit the extremely limited and ad hoc time frame. They worked in full coordination to build a new product. They all failed. Only projects that sustained the temporal ambiguity—by working with a minimal basis for coordination and allowing new temporal structures to emerge—were able to produce functioning new products under the intense time pressure. This study contributes to theories on innovation processes, coordination, and temporality.

title: Institutional Intermediaries and Firm Choices in Response to Regulations
methods: Empirical quantitative study using issue-specific data on Chinese power plants' choices between public and private intermediaries in the Cleaner Production program. The analysis uses logit models with company-clustered standard errors, interaction models for institutional contingencies, robustness checks, and field evidence from policy archives and 21 interviews with firms, intermediaries, and government officials.
industry: Power plants in China's power sector, including electricity corporations and energy-intensive industries.
time_period: Cleaner Production program participation from 2004 to 2012; supplementary interviews were conducted from December 2016 to April 2017.
units: Power plants choosing public or private intermediaries for Cleaner Production program auditing and certification.
n_sample: 530 power plants owned by 147 companies; supplementary field evidence from 21 interviews.
authors: Liu, Ning
theories: bridging and buffering roles of intermediaries; government-business relations theories; information and certification support; institutional intermediary literature
keywords: China; Cleaner Production program; bridging and buffering roles; certification support; firm choices; government regulations; information support; institutional intermediaries
research_question: The paper asks how firms choose between public and private institutional intermediaries when responding to government regulations. It examines how firms match organizational needs to intermediaries' bridging or buffering roles and to the information or certification support those intermediaries provide, and how regulatory and political conditions alter those choices.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an alignment process between firm needs and intermediary strengths. Public intermediaries are theorized to be more valuable when firms need bridging support: learning policy requirements or lending credibility to novel prosocial technologies. Private intermediaries are theorized to be more valuable when firms need buffering support: selective information disclosure or enough legitimacy to avoid heightened regulatory scrutiny. The results support public-intermediary selection for inexperienced firms and firms with novel technologies, private-intermediary selection for firms with noncompliance records, a stronger inexperience-public intermediary association during regulatory change, and private-intermediary selection by less-connected firms mainly where government intervention is stronger.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to institutional intermediary research by integrating two dimensions that are often treated separately: support content, namely information versus certification, and intermediary role, namely bridging versus buffering. This 2 by 2 framework clarifies why intermediaries do not simply improve connectivity but can also preserve distance between firms and regulators.

It also contributes a dynamic account of firm-intermediary-regulator triads. The findings show that intermediary value depends not only on intermediary type but also on firm needs and institutional contingencies such as regulatory change and government intervention.
practical_implication:
For managers, intermediary choice should be treated as a strategic compliance decision rather than a purely administrative contracting decision. Firms that need policy learning or credible endorsement may benefit more from public intermediaries, while firms facing scrutiny or lacking government linkage may seek the buffering functions associated with private intermediaries.

For policy-makers, the study implies that regulation is shaped by more than dyadic firm-regulator interaction. Intermediaries can translate, certify, filter, or buffer regulatory meanings and effects, so policy design and implementation need to account for the incentives and roles of third parties.
limitations:
The paper states that its empirical setting concerns situations in which firms must, or typically do, select an intermediary to obtain sociopolitical regulatory legitimacy. Generalizability is therefore bounded, and the author calls for evidence from other industries, societal contexts, and geographic settings.

The findings are also mixed across contingencies: regulatory changes did not strengthen the noncompliance-private intermediary relationship, and political commitment did not strengthen the novel technology-public intermediary relationship. Although the paper runs robustness and reverse-causality checks, the core evidence remains observational and centered on intermediary choice rather than downstream performance.
future_research:
Future research could test the framework in similar regulatory contexts such as food safety testing and financial accounting, and in more complex make-or-buy or keep-and-switch decisions where not using an intermediary is also possible. Additional work could examine policy-change sequences and whether responses to earlier reforms create residual structures that affect later responses.

The paper also calls for research on intermediaries' own private interests and evolution over time. Case studies or event-based designs could trace whether intermediaries become more firm allied, regulator allied, or neutral as political turbulence, public sector privatization, or anticorruption campaigns reshape the institutional environment.
abstract: This study develops a nuanced framework to unpack the heterogeneous mechanisms of institutional intermediaries’ efforts by aligning their bridging and buffering roles with the information and certification support they offer to clients. I further examine how these mechanisms explain firms’ intermediary choices in response to government regulations. Using a novel dataset of power plants across China, I find that the theorized intermediation mechanisms and the ways in which firms assess them are partially bounded by institutional complexities. Firms’ inexperience with regulations and their adoption of novel technologies are positively related to those firms’ selection of public intermediaries, with the former relationship strengthened when regulatory changes suggest a continuous need for policy updating. Meanwhile, firms’ noncompliance records and a lack of institutional linkage to the government are positively related to their reliance on private intermediaries’ buffering competency, with the latter relationship evident only in settings with an interventionist government. These findings contribute to the literature on the complex and dynamic value of intermediaries and firms’ intermediary choices at the intersection of management and government.

title: Performance Benefits of Reciprocal Vicarious Learning in Teams
methods: Quantitative field study of MBA consulting project teams using whole-network, within-team survey measures of dyadic vicarious learning, aggregated team measures of external learning, sponsor-rated team performance, and tobit regression models with robustness checks excluding controls.
industry: MBA consulting project teams working on client organization projects.
country: MBA students from a large university in the midwestern United States, working on client projects around the world.
time_period: Seven-week consulting project period, with surveys before, midway through, and near the end of the project.
units: MBA consulting project teams
n_sample: 62 teams in the final performance-analysis sample; 88 teams and 450 individuals in the initial network sample.
authors: Myers, C. G.
theories: network-based view of team learning; shared mental models; team learning; vicarious learning
keywords: external learning; reciprocity; team learning networks; team performance; vicarious learning
research_question: The paper asks how reciprocity in dyadic vicarious learning relationships among team members affects team performance. It also asks whether team vicarious learning reciprocity changes whether external learning helps or harms team performance.
mechanism_summary: Myers argues that reciprocal vicarious learning gives team members a more robust map of one another's expertise and perspectives than one-way knowledge sharing. In reciprocal learning dyads, members can ask questions, compare experiences, and refine shared lessons, strengthening shared mental models and cross-understanding. These relational and cognitive resources are expected to improve performance directly and to help teams absorb external learning without overtaxing members' time and attention. Empirically, reciprocity positively predicts team performance, and external learning is more beneficial in high-reciprocity teams but more harmful in low-reciprocity teams.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances team learning research by shifting attention from aggregate team-level learning volume to the dyadic network distribution of vicarious learning ties. It challenges the common one-way sharer-recipient assumption in knowledge-sharing and advice-seeking research by theorizing learning as potentially bidirectional within dyads. It also contributes a weighted-network approach for measuring reciprocity in workplace relationships, preserving tie strength rather than reducing reciprocity to binary mutual ties.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat learning in teams as only a matter of increasing knowledge sharing or external information search. Teams may gain more from structures and routines that foster reciprocal learning relationships, especially when projects require external learning from clients, experts, or other teams. Mentoring, team meetings, and project routines may be more useful when they encourage bidirectional learning rather than one-way advice transfer.
limitations: The study uses MBA student consulting teams, which offered strong response rates and realistic client work but may have inflated performance ratings and unusually high vicarious learning reciprocity because the project was embedded in an educational program. Team members also had little prior experience working together and no formal assigned hierarchy, limiting direct generalization to long-tenure or hierarchical organizational teams. The study focuses on dyadic reciprocity and does not examine generalized reciprocity across larger networks.
future_research: Future research should examine reciprocity in other team environments where performance, reciprocity, density, and centralization vary more widely. It should study how prior shared experience, team tenure, formal power differences, and hierarchy shape reciprocal vicarious learning. Additional work should directly measure mediating processes, examine antecedents of reciprocity, and explore generalized forms of reciprocity beyond immediate dyadic reciprocation.
abstract: Team members' vicarious learning from other members' knowledge and experience is a critical component of learning and performance in interdependent team work contexts. Yet, our understanding of vicarious learning among individuals in teams is still quite limited, as this learning is often oversimplified (as one-way knowledge-sharing) or aggregated (as a collective, team-level property), resulting in incomplete and inconsistent findings. In this paper, I extend these views by exploring the underlying distribution of dyadic vicarious learning relationships in teams, specifically using a network approach to examine the consequences of reciprocity in team members' vicarious learning with one another (i.e., where both individuals in a given dyad learn vicariously from each other's knowledge and experience). Using a novel method for calculating weighted reciprocity in networks in a study of MBA consulting project teams, I demonstrate that greater team vicarious learning reciprocity is associated with greater team performance, and also moderates the performance consequences of teams' external learning efforts, offering a potential reconciliation of conflicting results in prior research. In doing so, this paper advances research on vicarious learning in teams, while also providing conceptual and empirical tools for studying learning and other interpersonal workplace interactions from a network perspective.

title: Social Network and Temporal Myopia
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a 2012 stratified probability survey of CEOs of private manufacturing firms in China's extended Yangtze Delta region. The authors measure CEO ego-network closure with network constraint, model planning horizons and planning practices with multinomial logit, OLS, and logit models, include industry, city, and interviewer fixed effects, cluster robust standard errors by city, and run robustness checks with four-digit industry fixed effects, exclusion of recent contacts, network-composition controls, and perceived price elasticity.
industry: Private manufacturing firms in textiles, machinery, automobile and vehicle parts, pharmaceutical products, and communication technologies.
country: China, specifically the extended Yangtze Delta region.
time_period: 2012 survey, with some firm covariates and business-success measures drawn from the years around the survey.
units: CEOs, their ego business networks, and the private firms they led.
n_sample: 700 CEOs/firms and 4,464 named business contacts.
authors: Opper, Sonja; Burt, Ronald S.
theories: network closure and structural holes perspective; social network theory; temporal myopia in strategic management
keywords: China; business success; long-run planning; network closure; social networks; strategic planning; temporal myopia
research_question: The paper asks how the social network surrounding a business leader is associated with temporal myopia in strategic planning. More specifically, it examines whether network closure around CEOs is linked to shorter planning horizons and to weaker performance benefits from long-run planning.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that closed networks expose managers to redundant information and stronger pressure to adopt majority views, making present-oriented, familiar, and incremental planning more likely. Open networks, by contrast, provide more heterogeneous information and weaker conformity pressure, which the authors argue supports foresight and longer-run strategic planning. The evidence is associational: the authors explicitly treat causality as unresolved because the design is cross-sectional.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper adds a network perspective to research on temporal myopia in strategic management by shifting attention from individual cognitive traits to the social situation surrounding the decision-maker. It argues that myopia can emerge from network structure, especially the information redundancy and conformity pressures of closed networks.

It also extends social network theory by identifying temporal myopia and planning horizon as outcomes associated with network closure and structural holes. The paper reframes the familiar broker "vision advantage" as not only a creativity or opportunity advantage but also a planning advantage.
practical_implication:
For managers whose firms need long-run strategic plans, the findings imply value in maintaining relatively open business networks with diverse contacts not tightly connected to one another. For managers embedded in close-knit networks, the paper suggests actively disrupting established advice networks and adding diverse contacts to increase information heterogeneity.

The authors also caution that closed-network managers may be more successful with shorter planning horizons than with poorly designed long-run plans. Short-run planning is not always irrational, but relying on it as a long-run strategy is risky in competitive and changing environments.
limitations:
The central limitation is the cross-sectional research design, which cannot determine causality or fully rule out endogeneity. The authors use controls, network-history checks, industry fixed effects, and robustness tests, but they still call causal corroboration unresolved.

The sample is also concentrated in China's extended Yangtze Delta region and consists mainly of medium-sized, owner- or founder-led private manufacturing firms. The authors therefore caution that the association may differ in large public companies, professionally managed firms, and other institutional or cultural contexts.
future_research:
Future research should examine contingencies that protect people in closed networks from temporal myopia, including whether external knowledge sources increase diversity inside closed networks or are rejected as unfamiliar. The authors also call for longitudinal employee data, laboratory or field experiments, and comparative studies across cultural and institutional settings.

Additional work should test whether the network-closure association generalizes to larger firms and professional managers who answer to boards, shareholders, and external stakeholders. Such work could refine the boundary conditions before the findings are used to extend theory or guide practice.
abstract: This paper examines the link between the social networks surrounding business leaders and temporal myopia in strategic planning. Specifically, we hypothesize that processes characteristic of being embedded in a closed network are associated with a lack of foresight and a tendency to neglect long-run strategic planning. Using a probability sample of 700 CEOs in China, we show that network closure is associated with temporal myopia, which is evidenced in various measures of business planning. We show that managers embedded in closed networks are less experienced in long-run planning and are also less successful in implementing long-run business plans. Our contribution to the literature is twofold: we add a network perspective to the literature on temporal myopia in strategic management and, more significantly, by grounding temporal myopia in the network surrounding a person, we separate temporal myopia from the person. Myopia emerges from the social situations we create or in which we find ourselves.
