title: When Putting Work Off Pays Off: The Curvilinear Relationship between Procrastination and Creativity
methods: Three-study quantitative design. Studies 1 and 2 are laboratory experiments in which participants were randomly assigned to low, moderate, or high procrastination temptation by varying the salience of funny YouTube videos during creativity tasks; independent raters scored creative output, and Study 2 coded problem restructuring and activation of new knowledge as incubation mediators. Study 3 is a field survey of employees and supervisors at a South Korean furniture company, analyzed with random coefficient modeling, curvilinear tests, two-lines tests, and moderation by intrinsic motivation and creative requirement.
industry: Studies 1 and 2: behavioral laboratory creativity tasks at a large U.S. university. Study 3: office employees across departments at a furniture company.
time_period: Studies 1 and 2 used 30-minute task sessions; calendar dates for all studies were not reported.
units: Undergraduate students, graduate students, office employees, and direct supervisors.
n_sample: Study 1: 119 undergraduate students. Study 2: 126 graduate students. Study 3: 170 employees with direct-supervisor creativity ratings.
authors: Shin, Jihae; Grant, Adam M.
theories: motivational equifinality (Kruglanski et al., 2015); self-determination theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000); theories of incubation and time
keywords: activation of new knowledge; creative requirement; creativity; incubation; intrinsic motivation; problem restructuring; procrastination
research_question: Does procrastination have an inverted-U-shaped relationship with creativity, such that moderate procrastination can increase creative output relative to low or high procrastination? The paper also asks whether problem restructuring and activation of new knowledge explain this effect, and whether intrinsic motivation or creative requirement determines when moderate procrastination is beneficial.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is an incubation process. Low procrastination can make people start too quickly and remain tied to obvious initial framings, while high procrastination leaves too little time and too much deadline pressure for creative restructuring. Moderate procrastination creates enough distance from the task introduction and deadline for people to reframe the problem and access remote knowledge. This process is expected to support creativity only when intrinsic motivation or creative requirement keeps the task active in the back of the mind rather than allowing full disengagement.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper challenges the dominant treatment of procrastination as uniformly dysfunctional by showing that moderate delay can benefit creativity under bounded conditions. It extends creativity research by identifying procrastination as a behavioral antecedent of incubation, and by distinguishing the creative benefits of moderate delay from the efficiency costs of delay.

The study also contributes to motivation theory by showing that intrinsic motivation need not simply prevent procrastination. Instead, intrinsic motivation shapes how attention is allocated during procrastination, while creative requirement can substitute for intrinsic motivation by giving employees a reason to keep a creative problem mentally active.
practical_implication:
Managers should not treat all procrastination as equivalent. When novel and useful ideas are needed, a moderate delay after initial task exposure may help employees incubate ideas, especially when they are intrinsically interested in the work or when the job clearly requires creativity.

The findings do not justify open-ended delay. The authors emphasize that procrastination still reduces task efficiency and that useful creative procrastination requires actual work, sufficient task exposure, and limits that prevent last-minute rushing.
limitations:
The mediators and moderators were tested in separate studies, so the full moderated mediation model was not examined in one integrated design. The studies also do not directly compare different motives for procrastination or the content of alternative activities undertaken while procrastinating.

Additional limitations include partial mediation in Study 2, limited theory about what time intervals count as moderate versus high procrastination, a cross-sectional field study, and a focus on individual rather than group procrastination and creativity.
future_research:
Future research should test the full model in a single design and examine whether different motives for procrastination, such as dissatisfaction with initial ideas versus self-regulatory failure, change its creative consequences. Studies could also test how mindless, moderately interesting, or highly intrinsically motivating alternative activities affect incubation.

The authors call for richer timing theory, experience-sampling designs, research on group-level procrastination and creativity, and studies of organizational antecedents such as deadline design. They also suggest examining additional mechanisms, including selective forgetting, idea selection, and feedback from weak ties.
abstract: Although it is widely assumed that procrastination is counterproductive, delaying task progress may have hidden benefits for creativity. Drawing on theories of incubation, we propose that moderate procrastination can foster creativity when employees have the intrinsic motivation and opportunity to generate new ideas. In two experiments in the United States, we tempted participants to engage in varying degrees of procrastination by making different numbers of funny YouTube videos easily accessible while they were supposed to be solving business problems. Participants generated more creative ideas in the moderate rather than low or high procrastination conditions. This curvilinear effect was partially mediated by problem restructuring and the activation of new knowledge. We constructively replicated and extended the curvilinear effect in a field study with Korean employees: procrastination predicted lower task efficiency but had an inverted-U-shaped relationship with creativity. Employees who procrastinated moderately received higher creativity ratings from their supervisors than employees who procrastinated more or less, provided that intrinsic motivation or creative requirement was high. We discuss theoretical and practical implications for time management, creativity, and motivation in organizations.

title: Publishing Original Research in AMJ: Advice to Prospective Authors
methods: Editorial essay explaining AMJ's originality standards by summarizing editors' and reviewers' perspectives on data use, conceptual originality, and text overlap.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Tihanyi, Laszlo; DeCelles, Katherine A.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: conceptual core; data overlap; original data; original research; original text; salami slicing
research_question: The editorial asks when a submission is considered original by AMJ. It focuses on how editors and reviewers evaluate originality in relation to data reuse, the manuscript's conceptual core, and overlap in text.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: AMJ seeks original empirical research that adds value to management knowledge, and originality is judged across data, conceptual contribution, and text.
- Original data: Original data are important but neither sufficient nor necessary; authors must transparently disclose related papers, overlapping data, shared variables, and concurrent submissions.
- Conceptual core: AMJ submissions should be substantively new in research question, theoretical model, and literature focus, rather than unsolicited revisions or incremental variants of rejected or related manuscripts.
- Original text: Manuscripts should avoid plagiarism, self-plagiarism, and uncredited reuse, and literature reviews should present an independent and fair interpretation of prior work.
- Submission strategy: Authors are advised to put forward their strongest integrated paper rather than fragmenting data sets into minimally publishable pieces.

The process logic is editorial rather than causal: transparency helps editors assess overlap fairly, a new conceptual core distinguishes original submissions from repackaged work, and original writing protects the integrity of scholarly contribution. The essay links these standards to AMJ's goals of fairness, inclusivity, and reliable accumulation of knowledge.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a new theory. Its contribution is to clarify AMJ's evaluative standard for originality, especially the idea that publishable originality requires more than different data cuts, added variables, or revised analyses; it requires a substantively distinct conceptual core.
practical_implication: Prospective AMJ authors should disclose related manuscripts and data overlap fully, ensure consistency in reported sample sizes and response rates across papers from the same data effort, and remove or properly attribute overlapping text. They should also submit the strongest integrated version of a project rather than holding back theoretical ideas or splitting findings into smaller papers that weaken scope and impact.

title: Amplifying Voice in Organizations
methods: Three-study quantitative design: two online vignette experiments testing amplification against alternative peer responses, followed by a pre-post field intervention in a nonprofit educational organization using mixed-model analysis of employee status ratings.
industry: Online working-adult samples plus a nonprofit educational organization serving people with developmental disabilities
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual observers and employees evaluating voicers, responders, ideas, and team-member status
n_sample: Study 1: 1,188 working adults; Study 2: 1,501 MTurk participants; Study 3: 77 preintervention and 75 postintervention employees
authors: Bain, Kristin; Kreps, Tamar A.; Meikle, Nathan L.; Tenney, Elizabeth R.
theories: competitive altruism theory (Hardy & Van Vugt, 2006; Willer, 2009); status characteristics theory (Berger, Cohen, & Zelditch, 1972)
keywords: amplification; competitive altruism; employee voice; gender; idea quality; status; status characteristics; voice recognition
research_question: How do peers' responses to employee voice shape observers' evaluations of the voiced idea, the voicer's status, and the responder's status? The paper asks whether amplification, defined as public endorsement of another person's contribution with attribution, can create status gains for both the person being amplified and the person doing the amplifying.
mechanism_summary:
- Boundary conditions / intervention target: Voice type, voicer gender, and responder gender are tested in the experiments; initially lower-status employees are the target of the Study 3 field intervention.

The proposed mechanism is social evaluative rather than purely individual: amplification signals that a peer regards the voiced contribution as worth considering, which can raise perceived idea quality and thereby increase the voicer's status. For amplifiers, the mechanism draws on competitive altruism: publicly crediting someone else's contribution appears prosocial and group-oriented, allowing the amplifier to gain status without taking attention away from the voicer. Across studies, the effects held for promotive and prohibitive voice and for both men and women.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends voice research by shifting attention from manager recognition to peer responses during the voice process. It contributes to status theory by showing that voice episodes need not be zero-sum: voicers and amplifiers can both gain status when a peer publicly endorses and attributes a contribution. It also suggests that peer amplification can help ideas and contributors that might otherwise be overlooked, including prohibitive voice and voices from lower-status group members.
practical_implication: Organizations can train employees to amplify peers' contributions in meetings, especially when some employees' ideas are not being heard. The field intervention suggests that low-status employees can learn to use amplification and may gain status in their work groups. The findings also reassure employees that amplifying a colleague need not lower their own standing relative to self-promotion or adding another idea.
limitations: Studies 1 and 2 use experimental vignette methods, which provide control but may not capture the full information and social history present in real meetings. Study 3 improves realism but uses a pre-post design in one small nonprofit organization, with employees selected by a manager rather than randomly assigned. The authors also could train amplifiers but could not control which voicers were amplified.
future_research: Future work should examine when amplification has stronger or weaker effects, including contexts with strong subgroup faultlines, competition, or only one idea under consideration. The authors call for research on whether status gains persist over time and whether explicit attribution helps voicers receive longer-term recognition. They also suggest studying group-level consequences, such as performance, decision quality, psychological safety, future voice, and gendered relationships between idea quality and status.
abstract: We extend the field’s understanding of voice recognition by examining peer responses to voice. We investigate how employees can help peers get a status boost from voicing, while also raising their ownstatus, by introducing the conceptof amplification—public endorsement of another person’s contribution, with attribution to that person. In two experiments and one field study, we find that amplification enhances status both for voicers and for those who amplify voice. Being amplified was equally beneficial for voicers who framed their ideas promotively and prohibitively (improvement-focused and problem-focused, respectively; Study 1), and for men and women (Study 2). Furthermore, amplified ideas were rated as higher quality than nonamplified ideas. Amplification also helped amplifiers: participants reading experimentally manipulated meeting transcripts rated amplifiers as higher status than those who self-promoted, stayed quiet, or contributed additional ideas (Studies 1 and 2). Finally, in an intervention in a nonprofit organization, select employees trained to use amplification attained higher status in their work groups (Study 3). Overall, these results increase our understanding of how social actors can capitalize on instances of voice to give a status boost to voicers who might otherwise be overlooked, and help organizations realize the potential of employees’ diverse perspectives.

title: Getting the Picture Too Late: Handoffs and the Effectiveness of Idea Implementation in Creative Work
methods: Two-study quantitative design. Study 1 is an archival study of U.S. films released from 1990 to 2016, using writer and director credits to classify handoff types and random-intercept models to predict Rotten Tomatoes critic scores. Study 2 is an MTurk experiment manipulating late, no, early, serialized late, and separate no-handoff conditions in an advertisement-creation task, with independent raters assessing creativity and product coherence and multilevel mediation tests for psychological ownership and product coherence.
industry: Study 1: U.S. film industry. Study 2: online creative advertising task for a soft pretzel made with cricket flour.
time_period: Study 1 films released from 1990 to 2016; Study 2 online experiment timing not reported in paper.
units: Films in Study 1; individual MTurk participants and independent raters in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1: 5,676 films. Study 2: 600 U.S. participants, with 600 U.S. consumers as independent raters.
authors: Berg, J. M.; Yu, A.
theories: creative cognition; psychological ownership theory
keywords: creative work; handoffs; idea implementation; product coherence; psychological ownership
research_question: The paper asks when and from whom creative ideas can be handed to implementers without reducing the creativity of the final product. It specifically tests whether late handoffs of relatively mature ideas reduce implementers' final-product creativity compared with no handoffs, early handoffs, and serialized late handoffs.
mechanism_summary: Berg and Yu argue that implementers receiving late handoffs enter only after an idea has become relatively mature, leaving less opportunity to shape the idea, invest the self in it, or develop a unified product vision. This weakens psychological ownership and product coherence, which in turn reduces the creativity of the finished product. Serialized late handoffs are theorized to be less costly because an earlier handoff makes ownership seem more open and may encourage the implementer to carry forward a coherent trajectory rather than overwrite a single predecessor's mature plan. Empirically, late handoffs predicted lower creativity in both studies; mediation in Study 2 supported psychological ownership for most late-versus-other comparisons and product coherence for all four late-versus-other comparisons.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts idea implementation research from a primarily social-political focus on winning support for one's own ideas toward the production side of building handed-off ideas into tangible creative products. It extends handoff theory in creative work by distinguishing no, early, late, and serialized late handoffs according to idea maturity and prior handoff structure. It also contributes to psychological ownership research by showing how the timing and structure of creative-process handoffs can shape implementers' ownership, product coherence, and downstream creativity.
practical_implication: Managers should avoid giving implementers mature creative ideas only at the implementation stage when those implementers have had no role in earlier development. When possible, implementers should enter before ideas become detailed plans, so they can develop ownership and a coherent vision. If late handoffs are necessary to use specialized skills, making implementers aware of an earlier handoff may reduce some creativity costs by framing their role as the next step in a sequence rather than as taking over a single creator's mature plan.
limitations: The authors note that generalizability may be limited by the film-industry setting in Study 1 and the advertising task in Study 2, both of which involve aesthetic final products. Their framework assumes one principal individual drives each creative stage, while many real projects involve co-led stages, changing groups, repeated entries and exits, or shared ownership. Study 2 measured psychological ownership after the final ads were completed and measured product coherence from the final products, limiting direct evidence on the cognitive and motivational processes during implementation.
future_research: Future research should test whether the handoff effects generalize to other creative and organizational contexts, especially settings where final products are less aesthetic. Researchers could examine shared ownership, co-led stages, varying group size and stability, repeated handoffs, and relationships between handoff givers and receivers. Additional work should directly measure ownership, coherence, and related cognitive processes during implementation and investigate when late handoffs may help because they bring in unique specialized skills.
abstract: Past research on idea implementation has focused on employees trying to win social support for their own ideas, yet employees are often handed ideas to implement that were developed by others. We propose and test hypotheses on such handoffs, focusing on how handing employees relatively mature ideas to implement may lead them to build less creative final products. We tested our hypotheses using two studies: an archival study of 5,676 movies in the U.S. film industry and a complementary experiment. Results suggest that late handoffs yielded less creative final products than no or early handoffs, meaning it was costly to creativity when employees implemented relatively mature ideas without driving at least some of their prior development. However, “serialized late handoffs”—wherein implementers were handed relatively mature ideas after an earlier handoff between two other individuals—were less costly to creativity than late handoffs from one other individual. Mediation results suggest that late handoffs reduced implementers’ creativity by restrictingtheirsenseofpsychologicalownershipandthecoherenceoftheirfinalproducts. This research advances theory on idea implementation, handoffs, and psychological ownership in creative work.

title: Stakeholder Orientation and Divestiture Activity
methods: Longitudinal U.S. public-firm panel using negative binomial models with robust standard errors and firm and year fixed effects for divestiture counts, plus simultaneously estimated OLS regressions with firm fixed effects and Wald tests for selloff, spinoff, relatedness, distance, and alliance-partner comparisons.
industry: Publicly traded U.S. companies covered by Thomson Reuters Asset4 across industries.
units: Firm-year observations and divestiture events
n_sample: 909 firms; 7,143 firm-year observations; 3,720 divestitures by 592 companies
authors: Bettinazzi, E. L. M.; Feldman, E. R.
theories: corporate strategy; governance adaptation; stakeholder theory
keywords: corporate strategy; divestiture activity; selloffs; spinoffs; stakeholder orientation; stakeholder theory
research_question: The paper asks whether stakeholder orientation explains firms' divestiture activity and whether this relationship varies across modes and types of divestiture. It examines whether lower stakeholder orientation makes divestitures, especially selloffs, a less costly alternative to internal governance adaptation when stakeholder conflicts arise.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a governance-cost comparison. Firms with higher stakeholder orientation have routines, relationships, and reputations that make internal conflict resolution less costly, so they undertake fewer divestitures. Firms with lower stakeholder orientation have weaker capabilities for stakeholder engagement and compromise, making divestiture a more attractive response to unresolved stakeholder conflicts. Selloffs, especially of unrelated or distant businesses and to nonpartner acquirers, are theorized as more costly stakeholder-disrupting responses that should therefore concentrate among lower-stakeholder-orientation firms.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes by framing divestitures as an intermediate governance response between internal adaptation and liquidation. It extends stakeholder theory into corporate strategy by showing how stakeholder orientation can shape firm-boundary decisions, not only stakeholder treatment or performance. It also differentiates divestiture types as progressively costly responses to governance failure.
practical_implication: The analysis implies that managers should treat divestiture decisions as stakeholder-governance decisions, not only portfolio or financial decisions. Firms with stronger stakeholder orientation may be better positioned to resolve conflicts internally or use less disruptive divestiture paths, such as spinoffs or sales to alliance partners. For firms considering selloffs, relatedness, geographic distance, and acquirer relationships matter because they shape the stakeholder costs of separating a business.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The authors suggest future studies could examine whether divestitures resolve misalignments among stakeholders in divesting firms by creating better alignment within acquiring firms. They also call for work on the interplay between governance and scope, including managerial agency, motivation, and perceptions of stakeholders in divestiture and other scope-changing transactions. They note that in-depth qualitative methods could help study these managerial perceptions and motivations.
abstract: We conceptualize divestitures as a costly alternative to the internal resolution of conflicts among stakeholders, albeit one that avoids the more costly liquidation of the firm. In firms that have lower stakeholder orientation (defined as the extent to which management focuses attention on and integrates the interests of multiple stakeholders in its decisionmaking), divestitures will be less costly than the internal resolution of stakeholder conflicts, while the opposite will be true in firms that have higher stakeholder orientation. Consistent with this argument, we document a negative relationship between stakeholder orientation and divestiture activity, using a unique dataset of 909 U.S.-based, publicly listed firms from 2002 to 2015. This negative relationship is more pronounced for selloffs than for spinoffs, for selloffs of businesses that are unrelated to or located far from the divesting firm, and for selloffs to acquirers that are not alliance partners of divesting firms. The core contribution of this paper is to treat different types of divestitures as increasingly costly responses to conflicts among stakeholders, thereby populating the theoretical middle ground between negotiated adaptations of firms’ governance structures and total firm failure. In so doing, this paper contributes to research at the intersection of stakeholder theory and corporate strategy.

title: Unpacking Political Ideology: CEO Social and Economic Ideologies, Strategic Decision-Making Processes, and Corporate Entrepreneurship
methods: Empirical quantitative study using three-wave, multi-informant surveys of Iranian SMEs. The authors validate social and economic ideology scales, estimate OLS models for direct effects, use PROCESS bootstrapping for mediation tests, and conduct ITCV and two-stage least squares checks for potential endogeneity.
industry: Small and medium-sized enterprises from 10 industries across six Iranian provinces.
time_period: Three-wave survey: T1 measured CEO social and economic ideologies and controls; T2 occurred three months later for strategic decision-making; T3 occurred another six months later for corporate entrepreneurship.
units: CEOs, TMT members, and SMEs; firm-level corporate entrepreneurship is modeled through CEO and TMT survey responses.
n_sample: 192 firms from 10 industries, with an average of 4.12 TMT members responding per firm.
authors: Chin, M. K.; Zhang, Stephen X.; Jahanshahi, Asghar Afshar; Nadkarni, Sucheta
theories: CEO-TMT interface; corporate entrepreneurship; political psychology; upper echelons theory
keywords: CEO economic conservatism; CEO social conservatism; corporate entrepreneurship; executive political ideology; political ideology; social and economic ideologies; strategic decision-making processes; upper echelons research
research_question: How do CEO social and economic ideologies independently shape strategic decision-making processes and corporate entrepreneurship? The paper asks whether separating these two ideological dimensions explains firm-level strategic outcomes better than the unitary liberal-conservative view developed mainly in the U.S. context.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level. CEO social conservatism promotes reliance on experience-based intuition in the TMT, which helps identify and implement corporate entrepreneurship opportunities under uncertainty and time pressure. CEO economic conservatism reduces cooperative strategic decision-making by emphasizing competition and individualized goals, which impairs the TMT's ability to coordinate and implement corporate entrepreneurship. The results show opposing indirect effects: social conservatism increases corporate entrepreneurship through intuition, while economic conservatism decreases it through reduced cooperation.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper advances executive political ideology research by replacing a unitary conservatism-liberalism spectrum with a two-dimensional account of social and economic ideology. This matters especially outside high ideology-constraint contexts such as the United States, because social and economic conservatism may be distinct or negatively correlated.

It also contributes to upper echelons theory by specifying strategic decision-making processes as mechanisms linking CEO ideology to firm outcomes. For corporate entrepreneurship research, it highlights the potential value of intuitive decision-making under uncertainty and connects corporate entrepreneurship to behavioral strategy.
practical_implication:
The study implies that CEOs should recognize how their ideological tendencies shape TMT decision processes. Socially liberal CEOs may need to deliberately create room for experience-based intuition when speed and uncertainty are central to corporate entrepreneurship.

Economically conservative CEOs may need to compensate for competitive and individualistic tendencies by designing shared goals and rewards that support cooperative strategic decision-making. This is especially relevant when corporate entrepreneurship requires coordination across units.
limitations:
The authors note that the study is conducted in Iran to address the prior U.S. focus, but it does not directly compare countries with different degrees of ideology constraint. Therefore, the cross-national scope of the two-dimensional ideology argument remains to be tested more directly.

The paper also does not explain why TMT members follow CEOs' ideological tendencies in strategic decision-making. In addition, the ideology scales were adapted to avoid controversial issues that are illegal or socially unacceptable in some contexts, which improves contextual fit but may limit comparability.
future_research:
Future research could compare the strategic implications of social and economic ideology across countries with different ideology constraints, including single-party contexts such as China. It could also examine whether the two ideology dimensions explain other outcomes such as organizational culture, citizenship behavior, turnover intentions, strategic flexibility, diversification, and mergers and acquisitions.

The authors call for more work on the black box of upper echelons theory, including the motivations that lead TMT members to behave consistently with CEO tendencies. Future studies could also examine how combinations of social and economic ideologies within TMTs create different group dynamics and strategic outcomes.
abstract: We integrate political psychology and upper echelons research to introduce an alternative conceptualization of executive political ideology by separating the two distinct ideologies: social and economic. We theorize and test how the two ideologies exert distinct effects on a critical strategic outcome: corporate entrepreneurship. We examine this contention in Iran, a political context that sharply deviates from the exclusively studied U.S. context. We find that social and economic conservatism exert opposing effects on corporate entrepreneurship through distinct strategic decision-making processes; CEO social conservatism positively affects corporate entrepreneurship by promoting intuitive strategic decision-making, whereas CEO economic conservatism negatively affects corporate entrepreneurship by impairing cooperative strategic decisionmaking. These results highlight the need to separate social and economic ideologies, especially in non-U.S. contexts, and inform the underlying strategic decision-making processes through which executive ideology shapes strategic behaviors. The promising results also underscore the importance of examiningthestrategicimplicationsofexecutivepoliticalideologyindiversepoliticalcontexts that differ from the U.S. context.

title: From the Editors—Improving the Transparency of Empirical Research Published in AMJ
methods: Editorial essay; the editors discuss how AMJ authors, reviewers, and editors can improve research transparency across micro-quantitative, macro-quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods scholarship.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: DeCelles, K. A.; Howard-Grenville, J.; Tihanyi, L.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: open science; preregistration; qualitative transparency; reproducibility; research transparency; trustworthiness
research_question: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Contribution and transparency are mutually reinforcing because empirical claims are meaningful only when readers and reviewers can evaluate how the research was conducted, analyzed, and reported.
- Quantitative transparency: Authors can strengthen trust through multiple studies, preregistration, open or reviewer-accessible data, shared materials, code, output, detailed sample-selection explanations, and supplementary robustness checks.
- Qualitative transparency: Authors should explain why, where, and how data were collected, their relation to the field, their ontological stance, and the analytical path through which concepts and mechanisms emerged.
- Editorial responsibility: AMJ editors and reviewers should evaluate transparency in relation to epistemological and methodological diversity rather than equating any single practice, such as open data, with quality.
- Boundary conditions: Transparency should preserve human-subject protections, confidentiality, double-blind review, and the distinct constraints of proprietary organizational data and international research settings.

The editorial argues that AMJ's contribution standard depends on transparent research processes, not polished or perfect results. It positions transparency as a field-wide practice involving authors, reviewers, editors, and readers, with different appropriate forms for quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies. Its process logic is pragmatic rather than causal: more visible research choices improve trust, enable correction of the scientific record, and support stronger theoretical conversations.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes to management-methods discourse by decoupling transparency from any single template and emphasizing fit between transparency practices, methodology, and epistemological assumptions. It argues that transparency supports both trustworthiness and theoretical impact by helping readers inspect evidence, understand research journeys, and build on published work responsibly.
practical_implication: Prospective AMJ authors should make research decisions, materials, analyses, and deviations visible where appropriate, while protecting confidentiality, anonymity, and human subjects. Reviewers and editors should examine supplementary evidence carefully, resist requests to retrofit hypotheses to results, and assess research quality together with transparency rather than treating transparency practices as automatic proof of rigor.
limitations: The editorial explicitly notes that it does not resolve all transparency issues facing management research. It flags unresolved tensions around incentives, tenure pressures, field-site constraints, null-hypothesis significance testing, results-blind reviewing, international human-subject protections, preprint dissemination, and preserving double-blind review when supplementary materials are hosted online.
future_research: The editorial invites continued collective learning about transparency practices across journals, methods, and subfields. It identifies mixed-methods research, cross-national human-subject protections, preregistration evaluation, anonymous sharing infrastructures, and responsible engagement with pre-peer-review dissemination as areas where the management field still needs better practices.

title: Covering in Cover Letters: Gender and Self-Presentation in Job Applications
methods: Four-study quantitative program across three studies: LIWC analysis of real job cover letters and self-reported job outcomes, LIWC analysis of MBA admissions self-descriptions and callback outcomes, an experiment on applicant cover-letter revision, and a yoked experiment in which hiring-experienced evaluators rated cover letters.
industry: Job applications, MBA admissions, and entry-level hiring simulations rather than a single conventional industry
country: Canada and the United Kingdom are explicitly reported for some samples; Study 1 MTurk country is not reported in paper
time_period: Study 1 used application materials from the past year; other collection windows are not reported in paper
units: Individual job seekers, MBA applicants, undergraduate job applicants, and hiring-experienced evaluators
n_sample: Study 1: 257 participants; Study 2: 1,215 applications; Study 3A: 402 participants; Study 3B: 360 evaluators
authors: He, Joyce C.; Kang, Sonia K.
theories: prescriptive gender stereotypes; professional image construction model (Roberts, 2005); social identity-based impression-management; social role theory
keywords: cover letters; covering; gender discrimination; gender-management strategies; hiring outcomes; occupational gender segregation; prescriptive gender stereotypes; social identity-based impression-management
research_question: How do job seekers manage gender impressions when applying for gender-incongruent jobs, and what consequences do these strategies have for hiring outcomes? The paper specifically asks whether women applying for male-dominated jobs cover by reducing feminine language, whether anticipated gender discrimination motivates this behavior, and whether evaluators penalize it through lower liking and hireability.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism begins with devaluation threat: women applying to male-dominated jobs anticipate gender discrimination and attempt to signal fit by downplaying feminine cues. This social identity-based impression-management strategy conflicts with prescriptive gender stereotypes, so evaluators interpret women who use less feminine language as less likeable and less hireable. The result is an ironic reinforcing cycle in which women respond to anticipated discrimination in a way that can reduce their chances of entering male-dominated jobs.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends Roberts's professional image construction model by showing that social identity-based impression-management can backfire when the identity being managed is governed by strong prescriptive stereotypes. It contributes to social role theory by specifying a context in which women adopt counterstereotypic self-presentation to signal job fit but are penalized for violating gender prescriptions. It also offers a supply-side and demand-side mechanism for occupational gender segregation: women's coping behavior and evaluators' prescriptive expectations interact to perpetuate underrepresentation.
practical_implication: The authors argue against placing responsibility on women to navigate biased hiring systems through careful self-presentation. Organizations should change hiring structures and signals, including anonymized recruitment, changes in how applicants are presented to hiring managers, group-based hiring processes, and job postings that genuinely value historically devalued traits. Employers also need to follow through on such signals by valuing candidates who possess more feminine traits rather than treating inclusive language as symbolic.
limitations: The paper reports that it cannot determine whether the observed gender-management strategies apply across job levels or mainly to relatively entry-level jobs. It also did not test how gendered wording in job advertisements shapes applicant self-presentation, because the experimental postings were tightly controlled. The authors further note that they measured devaluation threat through anticipated gender discrimination but did not run competing tests against legitimacy threat.
future_research: Future research should examine whether women use similar strategies when applying for more senior jobs and whether the same backlash persists at later career stages. The authors call for work on how gendered job-advertisement language affects applicants' gendered language in application materials, and on the relative roles of devaluation and legitimacy threat. They also suggest studying men's gender-management strategies, noncisgender applicants' experiences, and intersections of gender with age, social class, and race.
abstract: Despite decades of research and intervention efforts, gender-based occupational segregation remains a significant problem. An emerging body of research has suggested that one way women overcome gender discrimination when applying for male-dominated jobs is by deliberately managing gender impressions. However, social role theory and research on prescriptive stereotypes have suggestedthat these attemptsto manage gender may backfire. In this research, we theorize that, while women actively respond to anticipated sexism using social identity–based impression-management (SIM) strategies (e.g., attempting to appearlessfeminineincoverletters),theseactionscanactuallybackfirebecause theyclash with prescriptive gender stereotypes. Across three studies, we investigate the motivations, techniques, andoutcomesofmanaging genderinjob applicationsfordifferentkindsofjobs. We find that women, but not men, manage gender when applying for gender-incongruent (i.e., male-dominated) jobs by using less feminine language, and that, paradoxically, they are less likely to be hired when they do so. The current research contributes to our understanding of the consequences of SIM strategies and shows that women’s coping behaviorinresponsetoexisting genderinequalitiesinthe labormarket isa novel and ironic mechanism through which occupational gender-segregation is perpetuated.

title: Seeing the Glass as Half Full or Half Empty: The Role of Affect-Induced Optimistic and Pessimistic States on Justice Perceptions and Outcomes
methods: Four quantitative studies: a 10-workday experience sampling study of employee-coworker dyads using multilevel path analysis, followed by three MTurk experiments using a causal-chain design to manipulate state affect, optimistic/pessimistic states, and justice rule adherence or violation.
industry: Study 1 participants worked in manufacturing, finance, real estate, education, health care, and other industries; Studies 2A-2C participants worked in retail, finance, real estate, education, health care, and other industries.
country: Study 1 country is not reported; Studies 2A-2C used full-time employed adults based in the United States via MTurk.
time_period: Study 1 collected three employee surveys per day and one coworker survey per day across 10 workdays; experimental study dates are not reported.
units: Focal employees and coworkers in Study 1; full-time employed adult MTurk participants in Studies 2A-2C.
n_sample: Study 1: 101 focal employee-coworker dyads and 873 usable observations; Study 2A: 273 participants; Study 2B: 199 participants; Study 2C: 184 participants.
authors: Hill, Edwyna T.; Matta, Fadel K.; Mitchell, Marie S.
theories: Carver and Scheier's (1998) optimism and pessimism framework; organizational justice theory; social exchange / reciprocity logic
keywords: citizenship behavior; counterproductive behavior; justice perceptions; optimistic state; pessimistic state; state affect; task performance
research_question: How do employees' affect-induced optimistic and pessimistic states shape their perceptions that supervisors adhere to or violate justice rules, and how do those perceptions influence performance behaviors? The paper asks what cognitive lenses explain the subjective "eye of the beholder" in justice perceptions beyond supervisor behavior itself.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that momentary affect produces valence-congruent optimistic or pessimistic states, which act as perceptual lenses for interpreting supervisor behavior. Optimistic states make employees more likely to see supervisor behavior as adhering to justice rules, supporting task performance and citizenship behavior. Pessimistic states make employees more likely to see supervisor behavior as violating justice rules, supporting counterproductive behavior. The ESM results and causal-chain experiments indicate that affect operates through these states rather than directly overriding justice perceptions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a more precise account of the "eye of the beholder" in organizational justice by specifying optimistic and pessimistic states as the cognitive lenses through which employees interpret supervisor behavior. It extends Carver and Scheier's optimism-pessimism framework into workplace justice research and conceptualizes optimism and pessimism as dynamic states rather than only stable traits. It also shows that justice rule adherence and violation have differentiated behavioral consequences: adherence predicts productive behaviors, whereas violation predicts counterproductive behavior.
practical_implication: Supervisors should not assume that adhering to justice rules is sufficient for employees to perceive them as just, because employees' current affective states can color their interpretations. The findings imply that managers should attend to work conditions that foster positive affect and reduce negative affect, since these states can indirectly shape justice perceptions and performance behaviors. Supervisors may also need to monitor whether their own view of justice-relevant behavior diverges from employees' perceptions.
limitations: The ESM study relies on self-rated independent and mediating variables, so common-method variance remains a concern despite temporal separation and group-mean centering. Study 1 uses coworker-rated performance rather than supervisor-rated performance, and the experiments measure behavioral intentions rather than actual workplace behavior. The paper also focuses on overall justice perceptions, leaving open whether the same affect-induced lens operates similarly across specific justice dimensions and longer-term entity justice perceptions.
future_research: Future research could examine whether discrete emotions, nonwork recovery, or other perceiver factors produce optimistic and pessimistic states that shape justice perceptions in specific events such as layoffs, pay cuts, or policy changes. Studies could also test whether these states influence other interpersonal processes, including perceived support, ostracism, incivility, leader affect, and team performance. Additional research could compare event-level and entity-level justice perceptions and investigate how employees react when supervisor behavior contradicts their optimistic or pessimistic expectations.
abstract: In this paper, we develop and test theory to explain how employees’ perceptions of supervisor justice behavior are subjectively influenced by optimistic and pessimistic states. We propose that state affect gives rise to optimistic and pessimistic states, which color justice perceptions and impact performance behaviors (i.e., task performance, citizenship behavior, counterproductive behavior). Results from an experience sampling study and a set of experimental studies showed that state positive affect fosters an optimistic state that promotes perceptions of justice rule adherence, which influences task performance and citizenship behavior, whereas state negative affect promotes a pessimistic state that promotes perceptions of justice rule violation, which influences counterproductive behavior. Interestingly, state affect does not have a direct relationship with justice perceptions, which points to a new perspective on affect and justice.

title: Swift Sense of Community: Resourcing Artifacts for Rapid Community Emergence in a Temporary Organization
methods: Single qualitative case study of Camp Magic, a five-day sleepaway summer camp, using participant observations, staff meeting observations, staff interviews, informal camper interviews, pre-camp surveys, training observations, and theory-elaboration coding informed by sense of community, high-quality connections, and resourcing theory.
industry: Seasonal non-profit sleepaway summer camp.
time_period: One five-day camp season, with pre-camp training sessions during the preceding academic year.
units: Camp staff, campers, staff-camper dyads, bread tag recipient subgroups, and the organization-wide camp community.
n_sample: 50 staff members and 120 campers; qualitative data included 47 staff interviews, 73 camper informal interviews, 50 hours of participant observations, 11 hours of staff-meeting observations, and 12 hours of training observations.
authors: Livne-Tarandach, R.; Jazaieri, H.
theories: high-quality connections; resourcing theory; sense of community
keywords: high-quality connections; resourcing artifacts; swift sense of community; symbolizing; temporary organizations
research_question: The paper asks how a sense of community can be cultivated in transitory, temporary organizational structures where members' interactions are short-lived. It examines how a swift SOC can emerge when there is low familiarity, limited shared work history, and no expectation of future interactions.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Swift sense of community, brief supportive connections, momentary positive regard, widespread influence, resourcing artifacts, and the tension between dyadic care and broader availability.
- Process / phases: Initial resourcing, embracing resourcing, reinterpreting resourcing, and expanding resourcing.
- Practices: Staff and campers imbue bread tags with layered meanings, distribute them, wear them publicly, personalize them, and use them to invite brief supportive connections.
- Emergent outcomes: Positive regard, fulfillment of needs, bottom-up, top-down, and lateral influence, subgroup membership and responsibility, and eventually organization-wide membership and responsibility.
- Boundary conditions: The process is observed in a caring, secluded, five-day temporary organization with high openness to improvisation and broad willingness to disclose distress.

The process begins when a staff member uses a bread tag to make a brief supportive connection with a homesick camper more durable. Staff then embrace the artifact for coordination, using it to signal homesickness and adjust care without repeated probing. Campers reinterpret the artifact as membership in a homesick peer subgroup and later expand it into a symbol of care for many forms of distress across campers and staff. Through these layered acts of symbolizing, the artifact scales dyadic moments into a web of organization-wide supportive connections.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends sense-of-community research by showing that a swift SOC is not merely a faster version of conventional SOC, but a qualitatively different form built on momentary positive regard and widespread influence, including lateral peer influence. It contributes to resourcing theory by identifying symbolizing as a resourcing mechanism through which actors imbue artifacts with layered meanings that can generate both stability and change. It also extends high-quality connections research by explaining how brief dyadic connections can become durable and aggregate into a new social order.
practical_implication: Temporary organizations can cultivate swift community by leaving room for members to improvise, notice distress, and repurpose simple artifacts as visible supports for connection. Leaders should pay attention to organizational openness, because the Camp Magic process depended on staff and campers being able to recognize problems, disclose difficult emotions, and adopt emergent practices quickly. The findings also suggest that community-building in short-lived organizations may depend less on deep prior relationships than on small, emotionally meaningful, and publicly visible moments of support.
limitations: The authors note that Camp Magic is an extreme and caring context, so the process may look different in less care-centered temporary organizations such as movie sets, seasonal festivals, or construction sites. The secluded setting helped reveal the micro-processes of swift SOC emergence, but limited the study's ability to observe spillover effects beyond the camp. The study also focuses on emergence during a five-day period and does not establish whether swift SOC endures after members leave the temporary organization.
future_research: Future research could examine the consequences of swift SOC for relational coordination, voice, word of mouth, and organizational reputation. Researchers could study how vulnerability and present-moment attention enable brief supportive connections, and compare spontaneous versus deliberately engineered swift SOC. Additional work could examine contradictory symbolizing, regeneration of social orders through familiar meanings, spillover beyond the original setting, and whether swift SOC erodes or persists over time.
abstract: Relational sense of community (SOC) research suggests that SOC depends on the depth of relationships cultivated between members over time. The rise of temporary organizations—transient work arrangements with limited expectations for future interactions— implored us to consider how a swift SOC can emerge in temporary organizations, where the cultivation of relationships may be challenging. We introduce a broader relational approach and draw on high-quality connections and resourcing theories to examine how a swift SOC emerges. Utilizing rich data sources, our qualitative analyses present a swift SOC cultivated in five days in a sleepaway summer camp. We find that this swift SOC was built on brief supportive connections that were made durable by resourcing artifacts. Resourcing artifacts creates scaffolds that mobilize actors to create a web of connections, leading to an organization-wide swift SOC. We propose that a swift SOC can emerge through four intertwined resourcing artifact phases: initial resourcing, embracing resourcing, reinterpreting resourcing, and expanding resourcing. During these phases, individuals imbue artifacts with new meaning and resource artifacts for (a) dyadic connection, (b) staff coordination, and (c) membership in a subgroup and (d) an organization-wide community. We demonstrate symbolizing and momentary connections as novel resourcing mechanisms enabling this process.

title: The Double-Edged Sword of Leadership Task Transitions in Emergency Response Multiteam Systems
methods: Inductive qualitative study of six live-actor mass-casualty incident scenarios at an emergency medical response academy. The authors used audio and video recordings, focused ethnographic reconstruction, temporal bracketing, coding of task and leadership task transitions, medical-professional coding of quality/order/speed of care, and iterative process-model development.
industry: Emergency medical response and mass-casualty incident simulation
time_period: One full-day capstone exercise; calendar date not reported
units: Emergency-response multiteam systems, sectors, paramedics, and leadership task-transition episodes
n_sample: Six live-actor mass-casualty incident scenarios; 13 paramedics per scenario; 1,107 task transitions, 501 leadership task transitions, and 209 linked episodes
authors: Luciano, Margaret M.; Fenters, Virgil; Park, Semin; Bartels, Amy L.; Tannenbaum, Scott I.
theories: functional leadership; hierarchical leadership; multiteam systems theory; shared leadership
keywords: MTS-environment interface; emergency response; functional leadership; hierarchical leadership; leadership task transitions; multiteam systems; shared leadership; task-based cycles
research_question: How do leadership task transitions influence multiteam system effectiveness in complex and dynamic environments? The paper further asks how MTSs function in such environments, and how leadership task transitions influence that functioning and, in turn, effectiveness.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / setting: Emergency response multiteam systems with system- and sector-level task-based cycles under a formal hierarchical leadership structure.
- Environmental pressures: Dynamic complexity creates pressure to gain awareness; dynamic challenge creates pressure to make progress.
- Process trigger: Shifts in the dominant environmental pressure prompt leadership task transitions, defined as temporary movement to or from tasks designated for a leader position.
- Beneficial pathway: Leadership task transitions rapidly reallocate effort toward awareness or progress, helping the MTS alleviate the current dominant pressure.
- Harmful pathway: The same transitions disrupt one or more task-based cycles by interrupting updating, awareness, leader tasks, enabling, worker tasks, or progress.
- Boundary conditions: Rapid restoration of the disrupted cycle mitigates harm; restoration is less successful when cycle activity is high or multiple cycles are disrupted.

Leadership task transitions operate as a double-edged process. They help the MTS manage the environment by moving effort to the pressure that most urgently needs attention, but they also pull effort away from the baseline task-based cycles that keep the system internally coordinated. The net effect depends on whether the disrupted cycle can be restored quickly and completely.
theoretical_contribution: The paper builds process theory on how leadership task transitions affect MTS effectiveness, explaining why fluid leadership can be simultaneously beneficial and harmful inside a formal hierarchy. It reframes the MTS-environment interface from a single external influence into shifting, opposing pressures of dynamic complexity and dynamic challenge. It also advances MTS theory by foregrounding task-based cycles, enabling scholars to examine taskwork alongside the more established focus on teamwork and system-level processes.
practical_implication: Emergency-response MTS members should not treat "stay in your lane" as an absolute rule; brief transitions can be useful when environmental pressures shift. However, members should avoid transitions during high cycle activity, avoid leading outside their zone when they lack awareness, and restore the disrupted cycle quickly by reestablishing updating, awareness, direction, enabling, work, and progress.
limitations: The study is based on one emergency-response training exercise with paramedic students in simulated mass-casualty incidents, so transferability is strongest for similar emergency response MTSs. The MTS had clear formal hierarchy, shared training, low competency separation, and low structural dynamism; systems with flatter structures, high information transparency, different competencies, or more structural change may show different dynamics.
future_research: Future research should test the boundary conditions of the theory in other emergency settings and in non-emergency organizational crises where dynamic complexity and dynamic challenge shift over time. Scholars could examine MTSs with different leadership structures, information transparency, competency separation, and structural dynamism, and could study when repeated task transitions become leader role transitions. The paper also calls for work on individual differences, learning, adaptability, and transferability to teams, matrix organizations, and other organizational forms.
abstract: Multiteam systems (MTSs) operating in complex and dynamic environments often have a formal hierarchical leadership structure. However, it is unclear whether individuals should stick exclusively to performing their designated tasks within the hierarchical leadership structure, or if, instead, they should switch between different types of tasks to align efforts with changes in the environment. We refer to such task switching—an individual shifting to or from tasks designated for a particular leader position—as leadership task transitions. Our qualitative study of six MTSs responding to live-actor mass-casualty incidents revealed that leadership task transitionsare a double-edged sword as they can simultaneously help manage the MTS–environment interface and harm MTS internal functioning. More specifically, leadership task transitions benefit the MTS by rapidly reallocating effort to alleviate the dominant environmental pressure at that time. However, they also harm the MTS by disrupting its internal task-based cycles. Rapidly restoring the disrupted cycles mitigates this harmful effect, but such cycle restoration is not successful when there is a high level of cycle activity or when multiple areas of the MTS are disrupted. Our findings generate new knowledge on how and why leadership task transitions impact MTSs. Implications and future directions are discussed.

title: Constraints and Opportunities of Stigma: Entrepreneurial Emancipation in the Sex Industry
methods: Inductive qualitative study based on interviews, observations, and social media and archival materials. The authors iterated between data and literature, built entrepreneur biographies, coded constraints and opportunities, and developed a process model of entrepreneurial emancipation in stigmatized industries.
industry: Canadian sex industry, including escorting, pornography, erotic webcam, erotic domination/BDSM, erotic massage, sex shops, burlesque, and sex work support.
units: Women and transgender entrepreneurs in the sex industry, plus sex work employees, activists, counselors, clients, observations, and social media posts.
n_sample: 83 interviews with 68 people, including 48 interviews with 39 entrepreneurs and 35 interviews with 29 other industry actors; 94 hours of observations; 52,610 Twitter messages plus other archival materials.
authors: Ruebottom, T.; Toubiana, M.
theories: dirty work; entrepreneurship-as-emancipation perspective; stigma
keywords: edifying practices; entrepreneurial emancipation; entrepreneurs; reframing practices; sex industry; stigma; stigmatized industries; structural, cognitive, and emotional emancipation
research_question: What are the negative and positive impacts of stigma for entrepreneurs in stigmatized industries, and can entrepreneurship emancipate entrepreneurs from the negative impacts of stigma? The paper studies this question in the Canadian sex industry, where stigma simultaneously constrains entrepreneurs and creates opportunities they can actualize.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constraints: Undesirable market exchanges, identity devaluation, and shaming.
- Opportunities created by stigma: Satisfying unmet demand, establishing ethical standards, and redefining oneself.
- Edifying practices: Humanizing practices by self-focused entrepreneurs and ethical pioneering practices by other-focused entrepreneurs.
- Reframing practices: Reframing as authentic for self-focused entrepreneurs and reframing as significant for other-focused entrepreneurs.
- Emergent outcomes: Structural, cognitive, and emotional emancipation, each confined to the stigmatized-industry context and threatened by interactions outside it.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. Stigma pushes the sex industry underground and devalues those who work in it, creating structural, cognitive, and emotional constraints. Entrepreneurs actualize the opportunities embedded in these constraints through edifying practices that improve exchanges and reframing practices that infuse positive value into stigmatized identities. These practices loosen constraints and produce context-specific emancipation, but the gains are fragile when entrepreneurs interact with banks, insurers, family members, strangers, or other external audiences that continue to apply stigma.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to stigma research by showing that stigma is not only a constraint but can also create entrepreneurial opportunities, especially where stigmatized industries produce unmet demand and space for ethical differentiation. It extends entrepreneurship-as-emancipation theory by distinguishing structural, cognitive, and emotional emancipation and by showing that entrepreneurship can be emancipatory in some contexts and dimensions but not others.

It also contributes to dirty work research by showing how reframing works together with structural, market-oriented practices. Reframing does not only protect identity; it also helps entrepreneurs deflect shaming and reduce negative affect, while remaining dependent on validating contexts and social bonds.
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs in stigmatized industries may find viable opportunities by serving underserved customers, improving ethical standards, and building identities that counter the devaluation attached to their work. The findings also caution that these emancipatory gains are context-specific: external audiences such as banks, insurers, family members, strangers, or other outsiders can threaten them when they continue to apply stigma.
limitations:
The study focuses on an extreme case: women and transgender entrepreneurs in the Canadian sex industry. The authors explicitly confine the sample to this group to ensure analytic precision, so the findings should not be treated as a full account of all sex-industry entrepreneurs or all stigmatized industries.

The authors also acknowledge that their presence and social distance from participants may have affected how entrepreneurs presented themselves. The model is grounded in a qualitative, context-specific case and therefore theorizes transferability rather than statistically generalizing across industries or countries.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether the model holds in other stigmatized domains, such as cannabis, cadaver commerce, used car sales, or psychic services. The paper specifically encourages work on how different types of physical, social, or moral stigma shape different opportunities for redefining oneself and changing market exchanges.

Further studies could also examine when reframing breaks down, how durable different reframing responses are, and how social bonds inside or outside the stigmatized industry validate or threaten cognitive and emotional emancipation. More work is needed on how stigmatized contexts and entrepreneurial practices interact in hidden or controversial spaces.
abstract: Entrepreneurs work not only in socially accepted and valued domains but also in highly contested, stigmatized industries. Despite the extreme constraints of working in stigmatized domains, entrepreneurs manage to thrive. The fact that entrepreneurs in these industriesappear to overcome the constraints of stigmaraises questionsabout the actual impacts ofstigma onentrepreneursandtheirventures. Ourqualitativestudy ofentrepreneursinthe sex industry in Canada reveals that the many constraints faced by entrepreneurs in stigmatized industries also create opportunities. Actualizing such stigma-based opportunities loosens the constraints of stigma and enables entrepreneurs to experience structural, cognitive, and emotional emancipation. However, such emancipation is confined to the context, and thus threatened by interactions with those outside the industry. Based on our findings, we develop a model of entrepreneurial emancipation in stigmatized industries.

title: The Hidden Cost of Prayer: Religiosity and the Gender Wage Gap
methods: Multimethod empirical design combining an integrative review of religion and gender scholarship, cross-national country-level path analysis, U.S. state-level path analysis, U.S. state longitudinal multilevel analysis, and two online experiments using wage-allocation decisions and policy-blocking interventions.
industry: Not reported in paper
country: Study 1 uses 140 countries worldwide; Studies 2a and 2b use the 50 United States; Study 3 uses English-fluent full-time employees with supervisory responsibilities recruited through Prolific Academic.
time_period: Study 1 religiosity data were collected between 2006 and 2008; Study 2b uses Gallup religiosity data from 2008-2016 and gender wage gap data from 2009-2018; timing for Study 3 experiments is not reported in paper.
units: Religion-and-gender articles and passages, countries, U.S. states, annual state wage-gap measurements, and individual supervisors/managers making wage-allocation decisions.
n_sample: Integrative review: 133 articles and 1,041 passages. Study 1: 140 countries. Study 2a: 50 U.S. states. Study 2b: 500 annual state measurements. Study 3a: 91 participants. Study 3b: 143 participants.
authors: Sitzmann, Traci; Campbell, Elizabeth M.
theories: biosocial theory; gender differentiation; patriarchy; religiosity as a cultural value; social role theory
keywords: agency; gender differentiation; gender wage gap; gender-egalitarian interventions; patriarchy; religiosity; sexuality; social domains
research_question: How and why does cultural religiosity, regardless of which religion is predominant, relate to the gender wage gap? The paper asks whether religiosity widens wage inequality through three forms of gender differentiation: social domains, sexuality, and agency.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that religiosity works as a broad cultural value that legitimizes differentiated expectations for men and women. Religious cultures are theorized to assign men to public and professional domains, regulate women's sexuality more than men's, and grant men greater agency and decision-making authority. These forms of differentiation can shape organizational wage allocation by devaluing women's workplace contributions, reducing women's accumulated human capital, and limiting women's ability to change unequal systems. Field studies support indirect associations through these mechanisms, while the experiments show that explicitly egalitarian policies can interrupt the wage-allocation effect.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges management scholarship's prevailing view of religion as mainly benevolent for organizations by theorizing and testing a systematic inequality-producing effect. It contributes to religion-and-organization research by treating religiosity as a cross-religion cultural value rather than comparing discrete faith traditions. It also extends work on patriarchy, social role theory, and biosocial explanations of gender roles by identifying social domains, sexuality, and agency as cross-cultural mechanisms linking religiosity to wage inequality.
practical_implication: Managers in religious cultures should not assume that religious inclusion is automatically neutral for wage equality. The experiments suggest that policies supporting equitable parental leave, prohibiting sexual harassment, and promoting inclusive leadership development can block gender-differentiated wage allocation. Organizations can also audit pay equity, increase transparency, and strengthen accountability where cultural norms may make unequal valuation of men's and women's work seem natural.
limitations: The authors note that the global sample lacks complete data for every country, and missingness may reflect development stage, censorship, or other external conditions. The theory contrasts religious and secular cultures, but religiosity is measured on a continuum, and some mediator indicators were collected after wage-gap data. The sexuality indicators rely on online searches for rape and pornography, which may miss non-digital behavior, censorship, or differences in whether people seek information online.
future_research: Future research should examine whether separation between church and state reduces gender inequality and whether religiosity affects other organizational phenomena beyond the gender wage gap. Additional work could study how pornography consumption, rape, and broader sexualization relate to wage inequality. The authors also call for integrating cultural tightness-looseness to test whether religious cultures impose tighter behavioral expectations on women than on men.
abstract: Religion is a preeminent social institution that meaningfully shapes cultures. Prevailing theory suggests that it is primarily a benevolent force in business, and differences across world religions preclude examining effects that thread across religions. We develop a theoretical account that fundamentally challenges these assumptions by explaining how and why religiosity—regardless of which religion is prominent—differentiates based on gender, widening the gender wage gap. Guided by an integrated review of the religion literature, we specify three dimensions of gender differentiation—social domains, sexuality, and agency—that explain why religiosity widens the gender wage gap. A series of studies tested our theoretical model. Two studies showcased the predictive power of religiosity on the gender wage gap across 140 countries worldwide and the 50 United States via gender-differentiated social domains, sexuality, and agency, explaining 37% of the variance in the wage gap. U.S. longitudinal data indicated that the gender wage gap is narrowing significantly faster in secular states. Moreover, experiments allowed for causal inference, revealing that gender-egalitarian interventions blocked the effect of religiosity on the gender wage gap. Finally, theoretical and empirical accounts converge to suggest that religiosity's effect on the gender wage gap applies across the major world religions.

title: Networks, Creativity, and Time: Staying Creative through Brokerage and Network Rejuvenation
methods: Empirical quantitative study of the Doctor Who production world using cross-sectional regressions and a conditional fixed-effects panel model; creativity was assessed by expert judges, while network openness, content heterogeneity, and network stability were computed from artist-episode collaboration and content data.
industry: British science-fiction television production, specifically the Doctor Who production world
units: Core artists and artist-episode creative contributions
n_sample: 200 individual artists and 866 artist-episode observations from episodes produced between 1963 and 2014
authors: Soda, Giuseppe; Mannucci, Pier Vittorio; Burt, Ronald S.
theories: network dynamics and creativity; social network theory; structural holes and brokerage theory (Burt, 1992, 2004)
keywords: content heterogeneity; creativity; network rejuvenation; network stability; new ties; open networks; structural holes
research_question: The paper asks when open networks and heterogeneous network content continue to support individual creativity over time. It specifically examines whether network stability weakens the creative benefits of brokerage and content heterogeneity, and whether adding new ties rejuvenates those benefits.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that open networks and heterogeneous content provide nonredundant perspectives and raw material for creative recombination, but stable network membership can make creators cognitively and socially rigid. When artists add new ties, newcomers create a positive shock that disrupts established mental models and collaboration routines, making creators more able to use the advantages of brokerage and heterogeneous content. The panel results show that openness and heterogeneity foster creativity mainly when they are coupled with low network stability.
theoretical_contribution: The paper adds a dynamic view to network-creativity theory by showing that the benefits of brokerage and content heterogeneity depend on how network composition changes over time. It also separates network structure from network content, arguing that open networks offer a vision advantage beyond access to heterogeneous knowledge. The study further suggests that short-term network rejuvenation can explain how individuals sustain creative performance across longer creative careers.
practical_implication: Managers and creative professionals should not treat a nonredundant network as a static asset. Sustained creativity may require keeping collaboration structures open to newcomers, even when existing teams or products are successful. The implication is to balance brokerage and continuity with periodic renewal that introduces fresh perspectives and disrupts rigid routines.
limitations: The study is set in the Doctor Who production world, a creative, project-based context with fixed roles, so the findings may travel most directly to settings such as consulting, scientific research, and new product design. The analysis focuses on one product category, which helps control product- and company-level confounds but may miss collaboration networks spanning other product domains. Because the data are archival, the study cannot directly measure the cognitive and social mechanisms through which network stability and structural holes shape creativity.
future_research: Future research could examine how much network change is too much across different time horizons, since short-term rejuvenation and long-term instability may have different effects. Scholars could also study alter-centric network dynamics, including how changes in collaborators' ties affect a focal creator's creativity. Additional work using laboratory studies or ad hoc surveys could directly test the cognitive rigidity, social rigidity, and newcomer-shock mechanisms proposed here.
abstract: In this paper, we adopt a dynamic perspective on networks and creativity to propose that the oft-theorized creative benefits of open networks and heterogeneous content are less likely to be accrued over time if the network is stable. Specifically, we hypothesize that open networks and content heterogeneity will have a more positive effect on creativity when network stability is low. We base our prediction on the fact that, over time, network stability begets cognitive rigidity and social rigidity, thus limiting individuals' ability to make use of the creative advantages provided by open networks and heterogeneous content. On the contrary, new ties bring a positive "shock" that pushes individuals in the network to change the way they organize and process knowledge, as well as the way they interact and collaborate—a shock that enables creators to accrue the creative advantages provided by open network structures and heterogeneous content. We test and find support for our theory in a study on the core artists who worked on the TV series Doctor Who between 1963 and 2014.
