title: Too Many Peas in a Pod? How Overlaps in Directors’ Local and Global Status Characteristics Influence Board Turnover in Newly Public Firms
methods: Pooled firm-year archival study of newly public firms using hand-collected director and CEO data from SEC filings, supplemented with database and web sources; mixed effects negative binomial regression in Stata 16.0, with GEE and omitted-variable robustness checks.
industry: U.S. IPO start-ups across multiple industries, including business services, chemical and allied products, instruments and related products, electronic and other electric products, and retail.
time_period: Firms that went public between 2001 and 2005, observed for up to five years after IPO.
units: Newly public firms and their board-year observations
n_sample: 218 firms
authors: Acharya, Abhijith G.; Pollock, Timothy G.
theories: status characteristics theory (Bunderson, 2003; Ridgeway, 2006); status homophily (Lazarsfeld & Merton, 1954; McPherson et al., 2001)
keywords: board expertise overlap; board tenure overlap; board turnover; global status homogeneity; local status hierarchy; newly public firms; status characteristics theory
research_question: How do overlaps in directors’ locally valued status characteristics (board tenure and functional expertise) and global status characteristics shape board turnover in newly public firms? The paper asks whether board-level status structures stabilize boards by clarifying deference relationships or destabilize them when too many directors share the same status characteristics.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is conditional rather than uniformly stabilizing. When directors differ in tenure or expertise, those characteristics can create distinct spheres of influence and deference patterns; when overlap is high, those characteristics lose differentiating power and can increase board turnover. Global status homogeneity has mixed effects: it initially appears to reduce turnover, but in the fuller models it increases turnover while attenuating the positive tenure-overlap effect at higher levels of tenure overlap.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends status characteristics theory by shifting attention from whether an individual possesses a valued status characteristic to what happens when multiple group members share the same characteristic. It also theorizes nested local and global status hierarchies, showing that status characteristics can have different implications depending on whether their value is local to the board or recognized in the broader director labor market. For corporate governance research, it moves beyond formal board structure to explain board turnover through informal board social structures.
practical_implication: For newly public firms, board composition should not be treated as a simple exercise in adding high-status or similarly credentialed directors. The findings suggest that maintaining board stability may require enough heterogeneity in tenure, expertise, and status characteristics for deference structures and distinct spheres of influence to form. Firms refreshing boards during transitions should consider how new appointments affect the board’s informal social order, not only whether appointees look prestigious on paper.
limitations: The study uses archival data, so it cannot directly observe boardroom interaction, directors’ perceptions of the local status hierarchy, or the actual decision processes behind director exits. The dependent variable does not distinguish voluntary from involuntary exits because such information is limited for newly public firms. The sample also has limited variance in diffuse status characteristics such as race, gender, and nationality, and it focuses on young U.S. firms during a period that included SOX and the 2008 financial crisis.
future_research: Future research could examine individual director-level responses to board status hierarchies, including whether committee chairs, board chairs, or directors with specialized skills react differently to hierarchy and overlap. Scholars could also study the consequences of board turnover and refreshment, the interaction of diffuse and specific status characteristics, and how board fault lines are created and activated. Additional work using experiments, ethnography, surveys, policy capturing, or qualitative comparative analysis could directly observe board dynamics and test whether these mechanisms travel to older firms, other time periods, and outcomes beyond board turnover.
abstract: Drawing on status characteristics theory, we explore how boards’ social structures influence board turnover. We theorize that (a) understanding directors’ relative standing and spheres of influence in the local status hierarchy creates deference structures that reduce conflict and enhance stability, thereby reducing board turnover; and (b) shared performance expectations and attraction based on homophily in the global status hierarchy can also reduce conflict and enhance stability and thus serve as another means of reducing board turnover. Using five years of post-initial public offering data on 218 firms that went public between 2001 and 2005, we find that overlaps in directors’ local status characteristics captured by their shared tenure and expertise and directors’ global status homogeneity increase the likelihood of board turnover. However, the directors’ global status characteristics shape the relative salience of the positive or negative effects of boards’ local status characteristics, leading to different effects on board turnover.
apa_citation: Acharya, A. G., & Pollock, T. G. (2021). Too many peas in a pod? How overlaps in directors’ local and global status characteristics influence board turnover in newly public firms. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1472-1496. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1144

title: Zoning Out or Breaking Through? Linking Daydreaming to Creativity in the Workplace
methods: Two empirical quantitative studies: a weeklong daily-life diary study analyzed with multilevel structural equation modeling and a multisource survey study analyzed with multilevel path analysis and moderated mediation tests.
industry: Study 1 drew professionals from a wide range of industries; Study 2 sampled employees in three technology consulting companies.
country: Study 1 was conducted in South America; Study 2 country was not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 collected daily surveys from Monday to Friday; Study 2 time period was not reported in paper.
units: Professional employees and supervisors.
n_sample: Study 1 retained 169 individuals; Study 2 included 117 professional employees and 46 supervisors.
authors: Baer, M.; Dane, E.; Madrid, H. P.
theories: identity and identification; mind wandering and daydreaming
keywords: cognitively demanding work; creativity; daydreams; mind wandering; professional identification
research_question: The paper asks whether daydreaming, a form of imaginative mind wandering, can produce creative benefits in workplace settings rather than only performance costs. It examines whether cognitively demanding work elicits problem-oriented and bizarre daydreams, and whether professional identification conditions their effects on creativity and performance.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that cognitively demanding work stimulates or overloads employees' cognition, drawing the mind toward imaginative daydreams. Problem-oriented daydreams can directly generate novel and useful ideas for existing work problems, while bizarre daydreams may become creatively useful when highly professionally identified individuals treat them as material for problem finding or idea generation. Without professional identification, the same daydreaming can undermine broader performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reframes workplace mind wandering by showing that daydreaming can be a source of creativity rather than only a liability. It differentiates problem-oriented and bizarre daydreams and identifies professional identification as a boundary condition shaping whether employees convert daydreaming into creative value.
practical_implication: Organizations that depend on creativity should be cautious about treating daydreaming only as distraction or deviance. The findings suggest that professionally identified employees may benefit from more license to daydream and from reduced stigma around discussing ideas that emerge from such episodes.
limitations: The authors state that the two studies do not establish the causal ordering of cognitively demanding work, daydreaming, and creativity. They also note that the designs measured quotidian and generalized tendencies rather than specific daydreaming episodes.
future_research: Future research could use experimental designs and finer-grained experience sampling to test causal ordering and episode-level dynamics. The authors also call for direct tests of the mechanisms linking cognitively demanding work to different daydream types and of whether problem-oriented and bizarre daydreams map onto different stages or forms of creativity.
abstract: Much has been written about the liabilities of mind wandering in the workplace. Given its prevalence, however, mind wandering may carry underappreciated benefits—especially with respect to creativity. Examining this possibility, we hypothesize that mind wandering involving imaginative thoughts, also known as “daydreams,” has the potential to spur creativity. We develop a theoretical model in which we examine two facets of daydreams based on their content: problem-oriented daydreams and bizarre daydreams. In addition, we specifyanantecedentconditionthat produces such daydreams(cognitively demanding work; Studies 1 & 2) as well as a boundary condition of the effects of daydreaming on creativity (professional identification; Study 2). Taken together, the studies reported here largely support our theoretical model. Cognitively demanding work reliably elicits both facets of daydreams. However, only problem-oriented daydreams relate to creativity directly; the relationship between bizarre daydreams and creativity is entirely dependent onprofessionalidentification. Inaddition, weobserve negative relationshipsbetween both facets of daydreams and performance more generally when employees lack professional identification (Study 2). Our results indicate that among professionally identified individuals, daydreaming carries noteworthy benefits for creativity but can also impair performance in the absence of identification.
apa_citation: Baer, M., Dane, E., & Madrid, H. P. (2021). Zoning out or breaking through? Linking daydreaming to creativity in the workplace. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1553-1577. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1283

title: Institutional Translation Gone Wrong: The Case of Villages for Africa in Rural Tanzania
methods: Longitudinal qualitative case study of Villages for Africa's macrocredit initiative in rural Tanzania, using observations, interviews, meetings, documents, video materials, and historical/contextual analysis.
industry: Rural development and macrocredit village enterprises.
time_period: The macrocredit project from 2008 to its collapse in 2016, with aftermath followed until the beginning of 2020.
units: Villages for Africa, the Village Enterprise Incubator, four village enterprises, villagers, regional politicians, investors, documents, and observations.
n_sample: Four villages; 109 interviews; 141 formal observation hours by the first author; 1,186 pages of written material; and 67 minutes of video materials.
authors: Claus, L.; Greenwood, R.; Mgoo, J.
theories: history and collective memory in organization studies; institutional theory; institutional translation theory (Wedlin & Sahlin, 2017); reactance theory (Brehm, 1966)
keywords: cultural assimilation; cultural detachment; high-distance translation; history; institutional translation; macrocredit; mzungu; reactance effect
research_question: The paper asks why ideas that appear to have been successfully moved across high institutional distance may later disappear. It examines this question through Villages for Africa's macrocredit initiative in rural Tanzania, focusing on how an initially accepted development idea became rejected after adoption.
mechanism_summary:
- Contextual conditions: Historical suspicion of the mzungu coexisted with hope and admiration for foreign-backed development initiatives.
- Preadoption translation: VFA culturally detached the macrocredit idea from its foreign origins through local surrogates, political cooptation of elders, localized customization, and ceremonial affirmation.
- Postadoption translation: Villagers culturally assimilated the idea through inclusive-exclusivity, materialization of social norms, and emotive celebration, creating a locally owned interpretation of the village enterprises.
- Collision and aftermath: Requests for repayment and renewed VFA involvement triggered in-group shaming, historically anchored vilification, anger, and reluctance to reengage with foreigners.

The process is not a simple failure of initial adoption. The paper argues that cultural detachment helped VFA gain acceptance, while cultural assimilation made the idea meaningful and locally owned for villagers. The same dual success later produced a reactance effect: when VFA reappeared to advise the enterprises and request repayment, villagers interpreted this as a violation of local ownership and as another instance of mzungu exploitation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a process model of high-distance translation failure that distinguishes preadoption cultural detachment from postadoption cultural assimilation. It shows that the conditions enabling successful translation across very different sociocultural contexts can also heighten later rejection when recipients' locally owned interpretation collides with the proponent's assumptions. The paper also extends institutional translation theory by foregrounding history, sociocultural categories, and emotional registers as forces that shape both translation strategies and translation breakdown.
practical_implication: Organizations moving social or business ideas across high institutional distance should not assume that local acceptance means shared understanding. The study suggests that proponents need to communicate their own sociocultural assumptions, including meanings attached to contracts, ownership, repayment, entrepreneurship, and accountability, while still translating those assumptions into recipient-language and recipient-context terms. It also implies that historically charged relationships can remain latent until a triggering event makes them central.
limitations: The study is a single qualitative case of failure in rural Tanzania, and the authors explicitly note that generalizing from one failed case is difficult. The data predominantly capture local informants' perspectives, and the authors acknowledge that their longitudinal narrative was influenced by the third author's interpretations and field relationships. The empirical setting is also a high-distance development context, so the model should be tested against other forms and degrees of institutional distance.
future_research: Future research could examine whether the strategies and processes identified here characterize all high-distance translation contexts, and whether they are unique to such contexts compared with low-distance translations. Scholars could also study high sociocultural distance within countries, including racial, class, religious, ideological, or migration-related divides. The paper further calls for longer-term studies of translation, including how adapted ideas may be translated back into their context of origin as a form of reverse innovation.
abstract: Why do ideas that have been successfully moved across highly different contexts subsequently disappear? To answer this question, we use longitudinal data on the organization Villages for Africa that introduced “macrocredit” loans to rural Tanzanians that would enable them to establish their own village enterprises. Several years after the implementation of the idea, it collapsed. Our findings allow us to make two key contributions. First, we provide a process model of high-distance translation that shows how proponents can strategically introduce an idea across highly different contexts by “culturally detaching” it from its institutional origins, leading to the idea being “culturally assimilated” into the recipient context. However, although cultural detachment and cultural assimilation indicate the successful translation of an idea, the means of doing so can later prompt its rejection. We call this the “reactance effect” of translations across highly different contexts. Second, we showcase the role of history for translation theory more generally. History—particularly the historical relationship between the sociocultural categories of the mzungu (Swahili for “foreigner”) and the villagers— influenced the way in which the macrocredit idea could be introduced to villagers and played a key role in its subsequent rejection.
apa_citation: Claus, L., Greenwood, R., & Mgoo, J. (2021). Institutional translation gone wrong: The case of Villages for Africa in rural Tanzania. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1497-1526. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1089

title: Who Should Become a Business School Associate Dean? Individual Performance and Taking on Firm-Specific Roles
methods: Dominantly quantitative panel analysis of business school professors, using logit models for becoming an associate dean and OLS fixed-effects models for log salary, with robustness checks and exploratory qualitative interviews/surveys of associate deans and deans.
industry: Business school professors in accounting, economics, finance, information systems, management, marketing, and operations at top U.S. business schools.
time_period: Roughly 1990-2017.
units: Professor-year observations of business school professors and associate dean role transitions.
n_sample: Final cleaned sample of 1,639 professors for 14,651 professor-years.
authors: Dyer, J.; Kryscynski, D.; Law, C.; Morris, S.
theories: equity theory (Adams, 1963); firm-specific human capital theory (Becker, 1964; Wang & Barney, 2006); strategic human capital theory
keywords: associate dean; business academia; compensation increases; firm-specific human capital dilemma; firm-specific investments; individual performance; professional service firms; research productivity
research_question: The paper asks how individual research performance affects a business school professor's likelihood of taking on a firm-specific administrative role as associate dean and the compensation increase attached to that role. More broadly, it asks whether individual performance intensifies the firm-specific human capital dilemma by increasing both firm desire for high performers and high performers' resistance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that universities often prefer research-productive faculty for firm-specific administrative roles because performance signals ability, credibility, and capacity to help others. At the same time, high performers face higher opportunity costs and mobility risks because research productivity is portable and externally valued. The authors therefore predict a lower probability of becoming an associate dean as research productivity increases, while also expecting stronger inducements for high performers. The first prediction is supported; the compensation prediction is reversed, with lower-performing associate deans receiving larger salary increases.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends firm-specific human capital theory by making individual performance a moderator of the classic firm-specific human capital dilemma rather than treating employee resistance as uniform. It shows that the dilemma can intensify for high performers because firm demand and employee resistance move in opposite directions as performance rises. The exploratory evidence further refines the theory by showing how salary bands and equity concerns can constrain financial inducements, producing a zone of misaligned incentives and possible boundary conditions around star performers.
practical_implication: For business schools, associate dean selection involves a trade-off: high-performing faculty may bring credibility and capability but sacrifice more research productivity and may resist the role more strongly. Lower-performing faculty may gain more financially from the role and may be easier to attract, but schools need to assess whether they can perform the administrative work effectively. Compensation systems based on salary bands or internal equity may unintentionally make high performers less willing to accept firm-specific administrative roles.
limitations: The setting is business academia, where tenure, visible publication metrics, nonprofit missions, and public salary information may make the human capital dilemma different from other professional service firms. The authors also cannot directly observe resistance in the archival data and therefore use exploratory interviews and supplemental analyses to support that mechanism. Generalizability depends on whether other contexts have similar job security, performance transparency, relative value of general versus firm-specific investments, and organizational mission.
future_research: Future research could test whether the proposed performance-based dilemma appears in consulting, financial services, legal services, health care, and other professional service settings. The authors also call for work on star performers, where firms may stop wanting the highest performers to take firm-specific roles because their continued general human capital production is too valuable. Additional research should examine other factors that moderate individual resistance to firm-specific investments and the conditions under which firms compensate, undercompensate, or avoid assigning such roles.
abstract: The "firm-specific human capital dilemma" suggests that firms generally want employees to make firm-specific investments but that employees prefer not to make them. We suggest that individual performance may moderate this dilemma such that the dilemma increases as individual performance increases—that is, firms may prefer high performers in firm-specific roles while high performers may resist these roles more than their lowerperforming counterparts. We examine our extended firm-specific human capital theory in a context in which the classic firm-specific human capital dilemma likely exists: business academia. Using a unique data set of 4,164 business school professors from 39 of the top 100 U.S. business schools, we examine how research performance affects propensity to become an associate dean and their compensation increases when taking on these roles. Even though associate dean roles come with a significant pay increase, we find that higherperformingindividualsare lesslikelytobecomeassociatedeans. Surprisingly,wefind that lower performers receive higher pay increases when taking on these roles. We conduct exploratory interviews to understand this surprising finding, and discuss implications and opportunities for future research.

title: From the Editors—Achieving Fit and Avoiding Misfit in Qualitative Research
methods: Editorial essay; the editors develop guidance for qualitative manuscripts by examining fit as internal coherence among research question and motivation, data collection, data analysis, findings, theory development, and contribution.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Howard-Grenville, J.; Nelson, A.; Vough, H.; Zilber, T. B.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: data analysis; data collection; fit; internal coherence; qualitative research; research question; theory development
research_question: The editorial asks how authors of qualitative research can achieve fit understood as internal coherence in AMJ manuscripts. It focuses on how research question and motivation, data collection, data analysis, findings, and theory development should align with one another and with the assumptions of the research approach.
mechanism_summary:
- Core concern: Qualitative manuscripts are often rejected when the research project or written paper lacks internal coherence.
- Research question and motivation: Authors should ensure that the question can be addressed by the data and connects to a theoretical conversation with appropriate scope.
- Data collection and analysis: Data sources, analytical approach, data quantity, data quality, and reporting of analytical moves should fit one another.
- Findings and theory development: Findings should be traceable to the analysis, use labels consistently, and ground theoretical claims in the empirical material.
- Contribution and practical relevance: The discussion should return to the motivating question and show implications for theory, practice, and understanding organizations.

The editorial's process logic is developmental rather than causal. It argues that qualitative papers become stronger when authors repeatedly test the fit among the major elements of a research project and manuscript, especially as inductive work evolves through data collection, analysis, writing, and revision. Internal coherence is presented as a way to preserve methodological variety and authenticity while still giving readers confidence in the paper's authority, transparency, and trustworthiness.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes to management-methods discourse by reframing fit in qualitative research as internal coherence rather than compliance with a single methodological template. It clarifies that good qualitative research depends on alignment among research questions, data, analysis, findings, and theoretical contribution, while still allowing different paradigmatic stances and analytical approaches.
practical_implication: Prospective AMJ authors should ask whether their data can answer the research question, whether the question is theoretically motivated and properly scoped, and whether the analysis authentically explains how insights emerged. They should also check whether findings, models, labels, and discussion claims can be traced back to the data and analysis.
limitations: Not reported in paper

title: Navigating Space for Personal Agency: Auxiliary Routines as Adaptations in Toxic Organizations
methods: Qualitative, inductive single-organization case study using grounded-theory analysis of interviews, observations, contact summary forms, research memos, and triangulated coding of diminishment dynamics and auxiliary routines.
industry: Consulting firm
time_period: One-year data collection period, including two interview waves separated by six months
units: Organization members, middle leaders, senior leaders, business areas, interviews, and observed meetings
n_sample: 34 organization members; 57 interviews; 14.5 hours of observed meetings
authors: Kahn, William A.; Rouse, Elizabeth D.
theories: conservation of resources theory (Hobfoll, 1989, 2001, 2011); emotional capability (Huy, 1999); organizational routines (Feldman, 2000; Feldman & Pentland, 2003; Sonenshein, 2016); toxic organizations and destructive leadership (Frost, 2003; Lipman-Blumen, 2006; Padilla et al., 2007)
keywords: auxiliary routines; emotional capability; organization dysfunction; organizational routines; personal agency; toxic organizations
research_question: How do organization members work with and around toxic conditions that narrow personal agency while still accomplishing necessary work? The paper asks how recurring patterns of coordinated behavior allow managers and subordinates to navigate role and psychological diminishment originating from senior leadership.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: organizational toxicity, CEO centrality, CEO aggression, role diminishment, psychological diminishment, personal agency, focal routines, and auxiliary routines.
- Process / routines: absorption, dissemination, and differentiation.
- Triggering conditions: persistent diminishment by senior leaders, collusion by other Alpha members, and hierarchical boundaries that varied in permeability.
- Emergent outcomes: held, narrowed, or expanded space for personal agency; maintenance, amplification, or separation from diminishment; and reduced organizational growth.
- Boundary conditions: the routines depended on middle leaders' positions between senior leaders and group members, and differentiation depended on a distinct client base and external network.

The process begins with toxic organizational conditions that reduce members' role authority and psychological space. Middle leaders respond by initiating auxiliary routines: absorption buffers subordinates and holds limited space for agency, dissemination aligns middle leaders upward and amplifies diminishment downward, and differentiation creates more separate group space that expands agency. These routines help work continue, but they also stabilize the toxic system and limit firm-wide integration and growth.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends routine theory by theorizing auxiliary routines as emergent, coordinated adaptations to socioemotional complexity, not only as supports for focal task routines. It also contributes to research on toxic organizations by shifting attention from individual coping choices to system-level patterns through which members collectively manage and perpetuate toxicity. Finally, it links auxiliary routines to emotional capability by showing how routines can regulate collective emotional energy, either supporting or handicapping members' availability for work.
practical_implication: The study suggests that organization members facing toxic conditions may develop recurring pathways for protecting themselves and others while still doing their work, but these pathways have costs. Middle leaders need to attend to whether their boundary-management routines buffer others, transmit toxicity, or create healthier independent bases of agency. Leaders and consultants should examine how structures, decision processes, and collusion authorize some people while deauthorizing others, because those patterns shape both personal agency and actual work.
limitations: The authors state that the theorizing is limited by one specific organization with idiosyncratic personality, political, hierarchical, structural, and cultural dynamics. AMP involved a particular form of toxicity centered on CEO centrality and aggression, so other organizations with peer-, partner-, or customer-generated toxicity may develop different auxiliary routines. The small case setting also leaves open whether a larger cohort of middle leaders would produce variations on these routines or different mechanisms for managing collective emotional energy.
future_research: Future research could chart the range, frequency, triggers, and implications of other auxiliary routines across different toxic organizational contexts. Studies could examine whether routines focus on boundary negotiation, coalition building, dissent, or other responses when toxicity has different sources. Additional empirical work could also investigate how auxiliary routines relate to emotional capability in settings marked by emotional exhaustion, emotional labor, dysfunctional decision-making, or unacknowledged organizational disturbance.
abstract: Many workers experience organization dysfunction stemming from leaders. Yet organization members have limited responses; they can directly or indirectly confront senior leaders, engage individual stress coping strategies, or leave the organization. We offer another response by theorizing auxiliary routines as behavioral sequences through which multiple actors coordinate responses to complex and enduring socioemotional dynamics that threaten to undermine the enactment of standard operating task routines. Through a qualitative, inductive study of a consulting firm, we delimit three auxiliary routines—absorption, dissemination, and differentiation—through which people navigate between the destructiveness of organizational toxicity and the need to perform given roles and tasks. We illustrate how these routines emerged in response to role and psychological diminishment originating from senior leaders, how the routines helped manage and sometimes perpetuate diminishment, and the consequences for individuals’ personal agency and the organization as a whole. In doing so, we contribute to knowledge about coping with toxic organizational conditions and on routines as a facet of emotional capability in organizations.
apa_citation: Kahn, W. A., & Rouse, E. D. (2021). Navigating space for personal agency: Auxiliary routines as adaptations in toxic organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1419-1444. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2019.0880

title: Clustering and Connectedness: How Inventor Network Configurations within Incumbent Firms Influence Their Assimilation and Absorption of New Venture Technologies
methods: Longitudinal patent-citation analysis using logistic regression with robust standard errors clustered by incumbent firm, new venture patent, and incumbent firm-new venture patent dyad.
industry: Information technology subsectors: computer hardware, communications equipment, electronic components, and telecommunications.
time_period: 1990 to 2006 for incumbent inventor networks; new ventures founded between 1990 and 2002.
units: Incumbent firm-new venture patent dyads.
n_sample: 549,219 observations.
authors: Kim, J. Y.; Steensma, H. K.; Heidl, R. A.
theories: absorptive capacity; social capital theory
keywords: absorptive capacity; corporate venture capital investments; internal inventor network configuration; network clustering; network connectedness; new venture technologies
research_question: How do incumbent firms' internal inventor network configurations influence their ability to assimilate and absorb new venture technologies? The paper also asks whether network clustering and connectedness condition the relationship between corporate venture capital investment and absorption of investee technologies.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that clustered inventor networks create localized structural, relational, and cognitive social capital that helps inventors translate externally derived insights, trust cluster members, and use external technologies in internal competition with other clusters. Highly connected inventor networks instead make in-house expertise broadly accessible, strengthen network-level identity, and reduce internal competition, which can reinforce insularity and crowd out external technologies. Empirically, CVC investment, clustering, and absorption are positively associated; connectedness is negatively associated with absorption and weakens the advantage of CVC investment, while the predicted clustering x CVC interaction is not supported.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to absorptive capacity research by showing that identifying external technologies through CVC investment is insufficient unless internal inventor networks support assimilation. It contributes to social network research by distinguishing clustering from connectedness at the complete-network level and showing that social capital can facilitate in-house knowledge flow while impeding external technology absorption.
practical_implication: Incumbent firms should monitor inventor network configuration rather than assuming that more internal connectedness is always beneficial. Relatively autonomous inventor clusters may improve absorption of external technologies, while excessive connectedness may reduce the value of costly CVC investments. New ventures considering incumbent investors face a tradeoff because clustered incumbent investors may offer more useful support but may also be more capable of absorbing or misappropriating venture technologies.
limitations: The study does not directly observe the proposed mechanisms linking network configuration to social identity, trust, internal competition, knowledge sharing, or absorption. Patent coauthorship captures only part of inventor relationships, and patent citations capture only patentable technology absorption. The sample is limited to CVC-active U.S. public IT incumbents and patent-holding new ventures, so generalizability beyond that setting is uncertain.
future_research: Future research could use qualitative data to verify how inventor network configurations shape trust, social identity, internal competition, and technology sharing. Broader samples could test whether the findings hold for non-patenting ventures, non-CVC-active incumbents, other industries, and other types of knowledge such as external market knowledge. Additional work could examine tradeoffs between network configurations that support external technology absorption and those that support invention rates or product development.
abstract: We explore how an incumbent firm’s internal inventor network configuration influences its ability to assimilate and absorb new venture technologies. We find that incumbents that have internal inventor network configurations in which inventors are heavily clustered into cohesive subgroups of interconnected inventors are more likely to build on new venture technologies. We suggest that such networks engender specific social capital in terms of information conduits, trust, and common vernaculars that is ideal for inventors to translate and share with their cluster members the technological insights that they have derived from outside sources. Moreover, any insularity that may result from having cohesive clusters is mitigated by internal competition between clusters. In contrast, having a highly connected inventor network engenders social capital that impedes incumbents’ absorption of new venture technologies. Broadly distributed access to internal technology, combined with a strong social identity that results from high levels of connectedness, can lead to insularity and a “not invented here” syndrome. We also find that highly connected internal inventor networks diminish any advantage that incumbent firms gain from having corporate venture capital investments in new ventures in terms of absorbing their technologies.

Clustering and connectedness: How inventor network configurations within incumbent firms influence their assimilation and absorption of new venture technologies. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1527-1552. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0225

title: The Dynamics of Framing: Image, Emotion, and the European Migration Crisis
methods: Qualitative, process-oriented study combining historical contextualization, qualitative frame analysis, content analysis of U.K. newspaper coverage, emotion coding, visual analysis of the Alan Kurdi photograph, and semi-structured interviews with editors and journalists.
industry: U.K. national newspapers and media organizations.
time_period: May 8 to September 2, 2015, and September 3, 2015, to September 2, 2016; 118 days before and 366 days after publication of the Alan Kurdi photograph.
units: Newspaper articles, frame-coded article subset, emotion-coded passages, and editors/journalists involved with newspapers during the European migration crisis.
n_sample: 4,858 newspaper articles; qualitative subset of 1,955 articles from The Guardian and The Daily Telegraph; 17 semi-structured interviews.
authors: Klein, Janina; Amis, John M.
theories: framing theory (Goffman, 1974; Entman, 1993; Benford & Snow, 2000); media framing and legitimacy (Bail, 2012; Bitekine & Haack, 2015; Roulet & Clemente, 2018); sociological theory of emotions (Collins, 2004; Jasper & Polletta, 2019; Zietsma et al., 2019)
keywords: Alan Kurdi; European migration crisis; emotional array; framing; iconic images; media organizations
research_question: The paper asks how and why the framing of a contentious societal issue changes over time, with particular attention to emotions in media organizations. Empirically, it examines how the publication of the Alan Kurdi photograph altered U.K. newspaper framing of the European migration crisis.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / frames: migrant frame, refugee frame, frame prominence, framing bricolage, emotional array, iconic photograph, receptive ideology, non-receptive ideology, emotional fatigue.
- Process / phases: pre-image framing of displaced people, publication and circulation of the Alan Kurdi photograph, rapid frame-emphasis shift, emotional-array amplification/degradation, newsroom behavior change, and temporal diminishing of the image effect.
- Practices / analytic moves: historical contextualization, frame identification, frame-prominence coding, emotional-intensity coding, visual analysis, and interview-based reconstruction of newsroom mechanisms.
- Emergent outcomes: the refugee frame gained prominence, the migrant frame lost dehumanizing emotional force, resource allocation and campaigning changed in some newspapers, and the duration of change varied by ideology and emotional fatigue.
- Boundary conditions: the process depends on an emotionally powerful image, media organizations as framing agents, audience expectations, organizational ideology, and the continuing salience of the issue.

The process begins with two historically available frames: migrants as economic or social threat and refugees as vulnerable people needing protection. The Alan Kurdi photograph carried emotional cues that aligned with the refugee frame, intensifying compassion, solidarity, anger, and shame while weakening disgust, fear, anger, and dehumanizing language in the migrant frame. In receptive newspapers, emotional energy and moral justification supported longer-lasting reframing and action; in non-receptive newspapers, perceived reader expectations produced a more instrumental and shorter-lived shift. Emotional fatigue and competing news issues then reduced attention, although the emotional arrays remained altered.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends framing theory by showing that macro-level frames are more plastic and temporally dynamic than static accounts imply. It introduces emotional arrays as the combination of emotions, emotional intensity, and associated language through which frames gain meaning, legitimacy, and behavioral force. It also theorizes distinct mechanisms of framing change in media organizations with receptive versus non-receptive ideologies, showing how iconic images can reshape frame emphasis even when ideology would otherwise resist change.
practical_implication: For actors trying to influence public policy or social debate, the study suggests that iconic photographs can create a window for reframing, but the mechanism and duration of that window vary across media organizations. Advocacy and policy actors should attend not only to message content, but also to the emotional array attached to competing frames and to whether target media organizations are ideologically receptive. The findings also caution that emotional fatigue and new events can quickly redirect media resources even after a powerful reframing moment.
limitations: The authors identify scope conditions around the focal organizations, the medium of the photograph, and the extreme nature of the case. The empirical setting is U.K. newspapers, so the theorizing needs testing in other framing organizations such as social media platforms, television companies, governments, and nongovernmental organizations. The Alan Kurdi photograph was unusually powerful, so less extreme images or other forms of text may not generate the same cross-ideological effect.
future_research: Future research could test the theory across other media, organizational, and policy settings, including social media and multimodal technologies. The authors call for work on how frame plasticity varies over time, whether hybrid frames emerge from conflicting frames, and how different emotional arrays produce different social outcomes. They also highlight emotional fatigue as a promising area for studying why reframing effects decay or persist.
abstract: an inherently dynamic process.
apa_citation: Klein, J., & Amis, J. M. (2021). The dynamics of framing: Image, emotion, and the European migration crisis. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1324-1354. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0510

title: High Risk, Low Return (and Vice Versa): The Effect of Product Innovation on Firm Performance in a Transition Economy
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study with a quantitative core: multiplicative heteroskedasticity models estimate effects on firm return on sales and performance variance, with 2SLS, matching, longitudinal, IPR, corruption, and media-attention robustness or post hoc analyses; qualitative evidence comes from 33 retrospective interviews and archival pharmaceutical-industry articles.
industry: Domestic manufacturers of chemical drugs in the Chinese pharmaceutical industry.
units: Domestic pharmaceutical firms and firm-year observations.
n_sample: 2,343 firms in the final quantitative sample; 10,841 firm-year observations in the main models; 33 retrospective interviews.
authors: Li, X.; Vermeulen, F.
theories: Bowman's paradox; institutional theory (North, 1990, 1993); performance landscape theory (Levinthal, 1997)
keywords: firm performance; institutional transition; product innovation; risk-return relationship; transition economy
research_question: The paper asks when a specific strategic action can generate a Bowman-type effect by increasing risk while decreasing expected return. It studies whether product innovation in China's transitioning pharmaceutical industry lowered average firm profitability while increasing variance in firm performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that long product-development lead times expose innovating firms to unpredictable shifts in institutional rules, drug approval, pricing, and appropriability conditions. In this setting, new products could occasionally create large upside gains, but more often the targeted performance peak had diminished by commercialization, producing lower average returns and higher variance. The authors argue that firms may still innovate because they focus on upside potential and visible top innovators rather than expected value.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts Bowman-paradox research from population-level correlations between firm risk and return to the level of a particular strategic action. It shows that product innovation can be high risk and low return when lengthy lead times meet institutional transition and uncertain value appropriability. It also argues that variance in performance should be studied as a dependent variable in its own right, not only as noise around mean performance.
practical_implication: Managers in turbulent transition economies should not infer that a strategy is generally profitable merely because it is common among top performers. For long-cycle innovation projects, they need to evaluate both expected value and performance variance, especially where pricing, approval, IPR, and corruption risks affect appropriability. Policymakers seeking indigenous innovation should recognize that unstable institutions may make innovation privately unattractive even when the upside cases are visible.
limitations: The authors state that they do not observe the pre-transition period, so they cannot directly test whether product innovation would avoid a Bowman effect without institutional change. They also observe new products that emerge from the invention pipeline and seek production permission, but not abandoned development processes, products withheld from permission requests, R&D expenditures, or each product's inherent promise. The sample consists mostly of small and medium-sized firms, making the influence of a single new product especially salient.
future_research: Future research could examine how other strategic actions, such as mergers and acquisitions, international expansion, top management turnover, or adoption of management techniques, affect both mean performance and variance. Studies could also test whether similar mechanisms arise from market or technological uncertainty rather than institutional transition. Additional work observing aborted product-development processes and complementary-resource arrangements could clarify how firms generate and trade off risk and return.
abstract: Common wisdom suggests that high-risk strategies will be associated with high expected returns and vice versa. Focusing on the effect of new product development on firm performance, in this paper we argue that this relationship may reverse in a market undergoing substantial institutional transition. We examine domestic pharmaceutical firms in China during the 1990s and find that in this context, introducing new products was associated with lower average firm profitability but higher variance. In conformity with our predictions, these relationships were stronger in areas where the rate of institutional change was higher and for product types that took longer to develop. Thus, we explain why, for particular strategic actions, high risk may be associated with low returns. A key conceptual corollary of these findings—and for strategic management research in general—is that firms may sometimes be more focused on the potential upside of their actions than on the expected value of those actions.
apa_citation: Li, X., & Vermeulen, F. (2021). High risk, low return (and vice versa): The effect of product innovation on firm performance in a transition economy. *Academy of Management Journal*, 64(5), 1383-1418. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1311

title: Office Chitchat as a Social Ritual: The Uplifting Yet Distracting Effects of Daily Small Talk at Work
methods: Experience sampling study of employed adults over 15 workdays, with scale validation samples and multilevel path analysis of within-person mediation and cross-level moderation.
industry: Full-time employees working outside the home; no single industry reported.
country: United States; participants were recruited through a Northeastern U.S. university alumni network and LinkedIn.
time_period: Three-week period, operationalized as 15 consecutive workdays with morning, afternoon, and evening surveys.
units: Employee-days nested within employees.
n_sample: 100 employees and 978 Level 1 data points in the primary ESM study; three independent samples totaling 455 participants for scale validation.
authors: Methot, J. R.; Rosado-Solomon, E. H.; Downes, P. E.; Gabriel, A. S.
theories: interaction ritual theory; microrole transitions perspective
keywords: cognitive work engagement; interaction rituals; microrole transitions; organizational citizenship behavior; positive social emotions; self-monitoring; small talk; well-being
research_question: The paper asks how and why daily small talk at work affects employees' end-of-day well-being and organizational citizenship behavior. It examines whether these effects operate through positive social emotions and cognitive work engagement, and whether self-monitoring changes the strength of these pathways.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is dual-sided. Drawing on interaction ritual theory and microrole transitions, small talk works as a polite social ritual that generates positive social emotions, which support well-being and OCB. At the same time, small talk can distract employees from cognitively engaging in work, reducing OCB through a resource and attention pathway. Higher self-monitoring weakens the negative small-talk-to-engagement pathway, suggesting that employees who navigate social cues more fluidly experience less disruption.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces small talk as a distinct management construct rather than treating it as trivial background communication. It extends interaction ritual theory and microrole transition theory by showing that brief, scripted, seemingly inconsequential exchanges can shape daily emotions, engagement, well-being, and citizenship behavior. It also adds an individual-difference boundary condition by showing that self-monitoring matters for the distracting side of small talk.
practical_implication: Organizations should recognize that casual workday interaction can support well-being and citizenship by creating social connection, especially in settings where remote, gig, or flexible work reduces informal contact. At the same time, office and workday design should preserve both opportunities for spontaneous small talk and conditions for focused work, because small talk can also interrupt cognitive engagement. Managers can use small talk carefully in onboarding and cross-cultural integration because it may help create belonging without requiring deep personal disclosure.
limitations: The primary study did not measure alternative daily communication episodes such as gossip, incivility, or task-focused exchanges, so the paper cannot fully position small talk among all daily interpersonal interactions. The ESM design used global self-reports of small talk and did not capture the qualitative content, partner, initiator, or recipient of each interaction. Small talk, positive social emotions, and cognitive work engagement were measured at the same time point, which leaves some concern about reverse causality despite supplemental analyses.
future_research: Future studies could compare different forms and motives of small talk, including weather talk, personal-hobby talk, networking, affiliative talk, and talk used simply to pass time. Research could examine whether morning and afternoon small talk have different effects, and whether small talk initiated by the focal employee differs from small talk received as an interruption. Dyad-level and cross-cultural studies could clarify how relationship closeness, partner identity, expatriate adjustment, and culturally specific small-talk norms shape the effects found here.
abstract: Small talk—trivial communication not core to task completion—is normative and ubiquitous in organizations. Although small talk comprises up to one-third of adults’ speech, its effects in the workplace have been largely discounted. Yet, research has suggested that small talk may have important consequences for employees. Integrating theories of interaction rituals and microrole transitions, we explore how and why seemingly inconsequential workday conversations meaningfully impact employees’ experiences. In a sample of employed adults, we used an experience sampling method to capture within-individual variationinsmalltalkoverathree-weekperiod.Giventhatweare thefirsttoexaminesmall talk as an episodic phenomenon, we also conducted a validation of our daily small talk measure with master’s students and two samples of employed adults. Using multilevel path analysis, results show that small talk enhanced employees’ daily positive social emotions atwork,whichheightened organizational citizenshipbehaviors(OCB) and enhanced well-being at the end of the workday; furthermore, small talk disrupted employees’ ability to cognitively engage in their work, which compromised their OCB. Additionally, higher levels of trait-level self-monitoring mitigated negative effects of small talk on work engagement. Combined, results suggest that the polite, ritualistic, and formulaic nature of small talk is uplifting yet also distracting.

title: The Effects of Racial Diversity Congruence between Upper Management and Lower Management on Firm Productivity
methods: Empirical quantitative longitudinal panel study using EEO-1 racial-demography data, Compustat productivity data, random-effects multilevel mixed-effects linear regression, polynomial regression, and response surface analyses, with a Fortune 500 replication sample.
industry: Primary sample of U.S.-based computer hardware and computer software firms; supplemental Fortune 500 replication sample.
time_period: Racial-demography data from 2007 to 2011, with productivity measured at time t + 1.
units: Firm-year observations of upper-management and lower-management racial diversity and firm productivity.
n_sample: Primary high-tech sample: 168 firms and 594 firm-year observations; supplemental Fortune 500 sample: 417 firms and 1,992 firm-year observations.
authors: Richard, O. C.; Triana, M. del C.; Li, M.
theories: absorptive capacity; knowledge-based view; upper echelons theory
keywords: absorptive capacity; firm productivity; knowledge-based view; lower management; racial diversity congruence; upper management
research_question: The paper asks whether congruence between racial diversity in upper management and lower management is associated with higher firm productivity. It further asks whether high–high racial diversity congruence outperforms low–low congruence, and whether high upper-management/low lower-management incongruence differs from the reverse pattern.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that racial diversity functions as a knowledge-based resource, but its productivity value depends on how diversity-based knowledge and absorptive capacity are distributed across managerial tiers. Congruence between upper and lower management supports knowledge symmetry and strategy implementation, while incongruence creates knowledge asymmetry. High–high congruence is theorized to generate the strongest productivity because both strategy formulation and strategy implementation benefit from racial diversity-based knowledge.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends upper echelons theory by arguing that lower management should be incorporated into explanations of firm outcomes, because lower managers implement strategy and transmit knowledge upward. It also contributes to knowledge-based view and diversity research by showing that racial diversity effects depend on cross-tier alignment rather than on diversity within a single managerial group alone.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that firms should avoid large racial-diversity disparities between lower and upper management if they want to convert diversity-based knowledge into productivity gains. Organizations with racially diverse lower management may especially need to improve racial diversity in upper management so that ideas, knowledge, and absorptive capacity are not concentrated in lower tiers with less strategic influence.
limitations: The authors state that the study does not directly measure the mechanisms explaining the relationship between racial diversity congruence and firm productivity. They also do not measure the knowledge of every upper- and lower-level manager, and the EEOC data do not allow them to distinguish subgroups within broad racial categories or identify whether diversity came from internal promotion or external hiring.
future_research: Future research could directly measure the mechanisms linking managerial racial diversity to productivity, including promotion versus external hiring, leadership, empowerment culture, and knowledge exchange across tiers. The authors also call for studies of racial diversity congruence in other industries, nationality congruence across management tiers, and faultline approaches that consider multiple demographic characteristics simultaneously.
abstract: We examine whether matching levels of racial diversity in upper management and lower management (i.e., racial diversity congruence) impact firm productivity. In a sample of high-tech firms, we found that congruence between upper-management racial diversity and lower-management racial diversity positively impacts firm productivity, supporting knowledge-based view perspectives. Furthermore, organizations with high levels of racial diversity in both upper and lower management (i.e., high–high racial diversity congruence) realized superior productivity compared to organizations with low levels of racial diversity in both upper and lower management (i.e., low–low racial diversity congruence). Results also revealed differences across levels of racial diversity incongruence between upper management and lower management (i.e., asymmetry effects) whereby firmswith amore racially diverse uppermanagement thanlowermanagement outproduced firms with a more racially diverse lower management than upper management. A supplemental sample of Fortune 500 firms enhanced generalizability, as the pattern of findings was very similar to that of the high-tech sample. We discuss the study’s implications and make a call for future research that simultaneously considers the upper echelons and the lower echelons.

title: Balancing the Yin and Yang: TMT Gender Diversity, Psychological Safety, and Firm Ambidextrous Strategic Orientation in Chinese High-Tech SMEs
methods: Empirical quantitative study using multiwave TMT survey data from Chinese high-tech SMEs, OLS hierarchical regressions, bootstrapping-based mediation and moderated-mediation tests, supplemental endogeneity checks, and semistructured interviews to interpret key results.
industry: Privately held high-tech small and medium-sized enterprises.
country: China; firms were located in Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, and Chengdu.
time_period: Three survey waves: demographics, slack, and controls at t1; TMT psychological safety two weeks later at t2; ASO about one year later at t3.
units: Top management teams and TMT members nested in firms.
n_sample: 373 TMT members from 120 firms in the final main-study sample; supplemental interviews with 23 top managers from 17 Chinese high-tech SMEs.
authors: Tang, S.; Nadkarni, S.; Wei, L.; Zhang, S. X.
theories: social role theory; upper echelons perspective
keywords: TMT gender diversity; TMT psychological safety; firm ambidextrous strategic orientation; firm slack; social role theory; upper echelons
research_question: The paper asks why and when TMT gender diversity generates strategic advantage for firms. Specifically, it examines whether TMT psychological safety explains the effect of TMT gender diversity on firm ambidextrous strategic orientation and whether firm slack changes the strength of this mediated relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that gender-diverse TMTs combine women's communal, socially sensitive proclivities with men's agentic, voice-raising proclivities. This complementarity fosters psychological safety, understood as both mutual trust and support and the ability to speak up and challenge others. TMT psychological safety then helps members differentiate and integrate exploration and exploitation, supporting ASO. The mediated effect is stronger when firm slack is lower, because resource scarcity makes constructive TMT dynamics more important.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the generic cognitive-variety explanation for TMT demographic diversity by arguing that the strategic value of TMT gender diversity is interpersonal and gender-specific. It contributes to upper echelons research by showing that TMT psychological safety transmits the relationship between gender diversity and ASO. It also shifts theorizing away from a female-centered "more women is better" account toward a gender-balance account that treats men and women as complementary participants in TMT dynamics.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that firms should treat TMT gender balance as relevant to the interpersonal quality of strategic decision-making, not only as a representation or cognitive-diversity issue. Managers seeking ambidextrous strategy should pay attention to whether TMT members can both support one another and openly challenge ideas. The results also imply that gender-diverse TMTs may be especially valuable when firms face resource scarcity.
limitations: The authors state that the SME setting may limit generalizability to large and established firms. They also note that the Chinese context may limit generalizability to other countries, including countries with different levels of gender egalitarianism. The study focuses on ASO and firm slack, leaving other strategic outcomes and other external environmental moderators for future work.
future_research: Future research could test the interpersonal benefits of TMT gender balance in large firms and in countries with different cultural gender norms. Studies could examine other outcomes shaped by TMT psychological safety, such as entrepreneurial orientation or other strategic orientations. Additional work could also test whether munificence, dynamism, uncertainty, or other external conditions moderate the mediated effect of TMT gender diversity.
abstract: This paper offers a novel theoretical account of why and when top management team (TMT) gender diversity lends strategic advantage. Building on social role theory, we develop a moderated-mediation model showing: (a) TMT psychological safety mediates the effect of TMT gender diversity on firm ambidextrous strategic orientation (ASO) (why), and (b) firm slack moderates this mediated effect (when). We tested our model in the context of Chinese high-tech smalland medium-sized enterprises. After confirming gender differences in social role–based proclivities at the TMT level, a multiwave survey study of 373 members from 120 TMTs showed that TMT gender diversity positively affects ASO via TMT psychological safety, and this mediated effect is stronger when firm slack is lower than higher.We further interviewed 23 top managers to supplement key quantitative results. Our study advances upper echelons researchon TMTgenderdiversity in two ways. First, ithighlights the gender-specific interpersonal benefit of TMT gender diversity, which is markedly distinct from the cognitive-variety argument associated generically with TMT demographic diversity. Second, it considers both men and women in TMTs in a more balanced manner, thereby offering an alternative account to the female-focused theorization of the positive strategic implications of TMT gender diversity.

title: Customer Concentration, Executive Attention, and Firm Search Behavior
methods: Longitudinal archival study of U.S. publicly listed manufacturing firms using patent data, customer-supplier data, industry segment data, financial statement data, and textual measures of executive attention from shareholder letters and earnings conference calls. The paper estimates OLS regressions with industry and year fixed effects, mediation tests using Monte Carlo and bootstrapping, moderation tests, instrumental-variable analyses, difference-in-differences checks, and robustness checks with alternative measures.
industry: Manufacturing firms, SIC 2000-3999.
time_period: 1976 to 2005 for the main sample; 1996 to 2005 for tests using the TNIC product-market-competition measure.
units: Supplier firm-year observations.
n_sample: 19,101 supplier firm-year observations in the main sample; 2,783 observations for executive-attention analyses using public statements; 7,084 observations for product-market-competition tests.
authors: Zhong, W.; Ma, Z.; Tong, T. W.; Zhang, Y.; Xie, L.
theories: attention-based view; demand-based view; organizational search
keywords: attention-based view; customer concentration; demand-side factors; executive attention; firm search behavior; search breadth; search depth
research_question: The paper asks whether and how a demand-side structural factor, customer concentration, affects firm search behavior. It specifically examines whether major customers shape executives' existing-oriented attention and thereby increase search depth while reducing search breadth.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that dependence on a few major customers directs executives' attention toward the existing competitive environment, existing resources and capabilities, and established management practices. This existing-oriented attention encourages firms to deepen search within familiar knowledge domains and to limit broader exploration into new fields. The paper finds partial mediation through existing-oriented attention, and it shows that social performance feedback above aspirations and high product market competition strengthen the customer-concentration relationship with deeper and narrower search.
theoretical_contribution: The paper adds a demand-side explanation to organizational search research by showing that customer structure can help explain why firms persist in myopic search. It extends the attention-based and cognition literatures by positioning customers, not only technologies, capabilities, or competitors, as sources of executive attention. It also integrates demand-side and supply-side accounts by showing that social performance feedback and product market competition condition the effect of customer concentration.
practical_implication: The findings imply that firms highly dependent on a few major customers should monitor whether customer demands are narrowing executive attention and search behavior. The results also suggest that positive performance relative to peers and high product market competition can reinforce customer-driven search myopia rather than automatically encouraging broader exploration.
limitations: The authors note that patent data may not capture all forms of search because patenting propensity varies across industries and some firms may avoid patenting critical knowledge. They also state that executive attention measures based on public statements may be affected by social desirability bias and emotional elements. The paper further acknowledges that it does not explain the determinants of customer concentration and focuses on customer structure rather than the content of heterogeneous customer demands.
future_research: Future research could use alternative indicators of search behavior beyond patents and improve executive-attention measurement through field experiments, video coding, or other designs. Scholars could examine why customer concentration emerges, especially in smaller, younger, less profitable, and more R&D-intensive firms. Additional work could also study how different customer-demand characteristics, not just the concentration structure of customers, affect firm search behavior.
abstract: It is unclear why, despite the increasing emphasis on innovation in modern business, firms are still myopic in their search efforts. Although prior studies have examined the role of supply-side factors such as technologies, capabilities, and managerial cognition, they rarely explore how demand-side factors such as customers can shape managerial cognition and firm search behavior. Extending the attention-based view to the demand side, we argue that major customers channel the attention of executives to the existing competitive environment, resources and capabilities, and management practices (i.e., existing-oriented attention), resulting in firms’ increased emphasis on deep search within familiar domains and limiting their search in new fields. Through an empirical examination of the patenting behavior of U.S. publicly listed firms, we show that customer concentration increases search depth and decreases search breadth via executives’ existing-oriented orientation. We also find that both performance feedback above social aspiration levels and product market competition amplify the effects of customer concentration. Our study contributes to the organizational search literature by adding a demand-side explanation. It also extends the cognition view by foregrounding the role of customers in shaping executive attention. Moreover, it explores the interaction between supplyand demandside factors in driving firm search behavior.

title: Distinct but Not Apart? Stigma Reduction and Cross-Industry Evaluative Spillovers: The Case of Medical Marijuana Legalization
methods: State-level quantitative panel study using medical marijuana legalization laws as staggered policy shocks. The authors estimate difference-in-differences models with state and year fixed effects, PPML regressions for alcohol and tobacco sales, OLS models for marijuana consumption, and supplementary analyses of media discourse, binge drinking, gambling sales, pretrends, and robustness specifications.
industry: U.S. vice industries, focusing on alcohol and tobacco sales as recipient industries affected by medical marijuana legalization.
country: United States, covering all 50 states plus Washington, DC.
units: State-year observations.
n_sample: Balanced panel with 816 state-level observations for the main alcohol and tobacco sales analyses.
authors: Aranda, A. M.; Conti, R.; Wezel, F. C.
theories: evaluative spillovers; organizational stigma; procedural legitimacy; stigma as label; stigma as moral evaluation
keywords: cross-industry evaluative spillovers; health safety attribute; medical marijuana legalization; patient registration system; stigma reduction
research_question: The paper asks whether stigma reduction in one industry can generate positive evaluative spillovers across industry boundaries. It examines when medical marijuana legalization changes customer behavior toward other vice industries, especially alcohol and tobacco, and whether formal patient registration systems strengthen those spillovers.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism begins when legitimate but incongruent information from medical marijuana legalization challenges taken-for-granted vice stigma and shifts audiences from label-based judgment to attribute-based evaluation. Alcohol, unlike tobacco, is theorized to share the health safety attribute with medical marijuana when consumed responsibly, so evaluative spillovers should increase alcohol sales more than tobacco sales. The paper argues that patient registration systems make the health safety claim more procedurally legitimate, which is why the positive spillover to alcohol appears mainly when legalization is paired with such systems.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to stigma research by showing that stigma reduction need not remain confined to the focal industry where reevaluation begins. It reconciles stigma as a vilifying label with stigma as moral evaluation by arguing that legitimate incongruent information can move audiences into an attribute-centered reassessment mode. It also adds counterfactual quantitative evidence that formal rules and procedures shape the credibility and cross-industry reach of stigma reduction.
practical_implication: The findings imply that policymakers should consider how regulations in one stigmatized industry can alter evaluations and behavior in adjacent industries. Medical marijuana rules accompanied by patient registration systems changed alcohol sales patterns, suggesting that formal procedures can make a stigma-reducing health-safety claim more credible. The paper cautions against assuming that customer preferences remain fixed when new laws redefine the moral meaning of stigmatized products.
limitations: The authors note that their theory accounts for multiple audiences but their empirical analysis focuses mainly on customers and, secondarily, media discourse. They also acknowledge that they infer micro-level reassessment processes from aggregate behavior rather than testing individual-level mechanisms directly. The boundary conditions are limited to settings where industries share a vilifying label and differ in whether they possess the morally approved attribute made salient by a legitimate source.
future_research: Future research could examine other audiences such as social movements, watchdog groups, religious organizations, social media, banks, insurers, and corporations. Studies could test the individual-level mechanisms directly, for example through laboratory experiments. Further work could also generalize the argument beyond vice industries to other contexts where a legitimate source makes a morally approved attribute salient across stigmatized categories.
abstract: Previous research on stigma reduction has been primarily confined to single industries. However, industry boundaries are porous in the eyes of audience members and can hardly act as artificial confines to moral reevaluations. We contend that evaluative spillovers induced by stigma reduction in a focal industry diffuse to other industries that share the same vilifying label when (a) they possess the morally approved attribute that underlies the reduction of stigma, and (b) the morally approved attribute is embedded in formal rules and procedures that ensure the desired purposes. Empirically, we focus our tests on the legalization of marijuana as a medicine in several U.S. states during the period 2000–2015, which has reduced the “vice” stigma around marijuana by highlighting the “health safety” attribute of marijuana, namely its safe consumption and potential health benefits. We show that legalization generated evaluative spillovers to other “vice” industries sharing the same health safety attribute as marijuana (i.e., alcohol), but not to those that did not share it (i.e., tobacco). Those spillovers were primarily observed when the law was accompanied by a patient registration system that highlighted the health safety attribute of marijuana by limiting its use to medical purposes.
