title: Examining the “I” in Team: A Longitudinal Investigation of the Influence of Team Narcissism Composition on Team Outcomes in the NBA
methods: Longitudinal quantitative analysis of 2013-2014 NBA game-level team data using generalized estimating equations in SPSS, Monte Carlo indirect-effect tests, and robustness checks with alternative coordination and familiarity measures.
industry: National Basketball Association professional basketball teams.
time_period: 2013-2014 regular season.
units: Team-game performance episodes for 30 NBA teams.
n_sample: 2,460 performance episodes; hypothesis tests used 2,430 observations after excluding the first game for each team.
authors: Grijalva, Emily; Maynes, Timothy D.; Badura, Katie L.; Whiting, Steven W.
theories: agency model of narcissism (Campbell, Brunell, & Finkel, 2006; Campbell & Foster, 2007); social exchange theory (Blau, 1964; Gergen, 1969); strategic core theory (Humphrey, Morgeson, & Mannor, 2009)
keywords: National Basketball Association; agency model of narcissism; narcissism; social exchange theory; team coordination; team familiarity; team narcissism composition; team performance
research_question: The paper asks whether the composition of narcissism within teams undermines coordination and, through coordination, team performance. It further asks whether these effects differ across mean, maximum, and core-role operationalizations of team narcissism and whether team familiarity amplifies the effects over time.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines the agency model of narcissism with social exchange theory. Because narcissists are high in agency and low in communion, their self-interested behavior is expected to trigger reciprocal selfishness and weaken the exchange relationships needed for coordination. In high-familiarity teams, lower-narcissism teams gain coordination as members learn to work together, whereas higher-narcissism teams fail to capture these normative coordination gains.
theoretical_contribution:
The article shifts narcissism research from individual job performance to team-level outcomes, showing that narcissism can matter for organizational performance through interdependent team processes even when individual-level performance relationships are weak. It also clarifies team personality composition by comparing mean, maximum, and core-role narcissism rather than assuming one aggregation approach.

The paper contributes a temporal perspective by showing that team familiarity changes the observed narcissism-coordination relationship. Its surprising result is that narcissism does not mainly make coordination deteriorate over time; rather, higher narcissism prevents the improvements in coordination that lower-narcissism teams realize as familiarity accumulates.
practical_implication:
Organizations should consider narcissism when forming teams, especially for highly interdependent teams that must coordinate over extended periods. The findings suggest avoiding highly narcissistic members in central or influential team roles when those roles shape workflow and interpersonal norms.

The paper also implies that managers should not rely only on individual talent when composing teams. When narcissistic team members cannot be avoided, compensation and incentives that tie rewards to team performance may help align narcissists' goals with collective outcomes.
limitations:
The narcissism measure uses unobtrusive Twitter indicators rather than direct questionnaire measures, although the authors report validation evidence for the composite measure. The NBA context may limit generalizability because it is a visible, competitive, highly interdependent action-team setting with immediate performance feedback and strong individual incentives.

The authors also note that NBA teams have rotating membership and a seasonal fresh-start structure that may affect how familiarity accumulates. The study does not specify a precise time frame for when familiarity should become more negative in narcissistic teams, and core-role findings apply most directly to teams with differentiated central roles.
future_research:
Future research could test more fine-grained mechanisms, such as norms, trust, and selfish behavior, to explain how team narcissism affects coordination. Studies could also examine whether core-role and high-status narcissism operate similarly across other forms of team structure.

The authors encourage research in other industries, countries, and team types to test the boundary conditions of the findings. Additional longitudinal work could examine the timing of familiarity effects across contexts where team members do or do not experience a clear seasonal reset.
abstract: Previous research has shown that narcissism is unrelated to job performance, yet this individual-level effect may be underestimating narcissism’s wider influence on organizational performance. To assess this possibility, we draw on social exchange theory and the agency model of narcissism to investigate how team narcissism composition affects team coordination and performance. Our model was tested using game-level longitudinal data from National Basketball Association teams. Teams with higher mean and maximum levels of narcissism as well as higher narcissism members in core roles (i.e., central and influential roles) had poorer coordination and in turn performance than teams with lower levels. In addition, having higher team familiarity amplified the effects of narcissism for team mean and core role narcissism. The nature of the observed interaction, however, was surprising. Originally, we hypothesized that narcissism would lead to greater decrements in coordination as familiarity increased. Instead, we found that teams with higher mean and core role narcissism maintained the same levels of coordination over time, whereas teams with lower narcissism experienced improvements in coordination. Thus, team-level narcissism appears to prevent teams from capitalizing on normative coordination gains that occur as familiarity increases. These results underscore the importance of considering narcissism when forming teams.

title: “God at Work”: Engaging Central and Incompatible Institutional Logics through Elastic Hybridity
methods: A 24-month ethnographic case study of KT Bank, using ethnographic observations, semi-structured interviews, documentary evidence, and iterative qualitative coding.
industry: Islamic banking.
time_period: 24-month fieldwork period ending with the bank opening in July 2015.
units: KT Bank, the first Islamic bank in Germany and the Eurozone, plus internal staff and field-level actors involved in its founding.
n_sample: 60 days of ethnographic observation, 73 semi-structured interviews, and 1,350 documents.
authors: Gümüsay, A. A.; Smets, M.; Morris, T.
theories: institutional logics; institutional theory; paradox theory
keywords: Islamic banking; elastic hybridity; hybrid organizations; institutional logics; polyphony; polysemy
research_question: The paper asks how contested hybrid organizations can constructively engage central and incompatible logics to reduce conflict and increase organizational resilience. It focuses on the opening of KT Bank, where religion and market logics were both core to the organization and deeply implicated in employees' personal convictions.
mechanism_summary:
- Key tensions: Central and incompatible religion and market logics in a nascent Islamic bank operating in Germany.
- Organizational mechanism: Polysemy, through conceptual and presentational ambiguity, makes space for multiple meanings around Islamic banking, Sharia compliance, purpose, symbols, and presentation.
- Individual mechanism: Polyphony, through spatial, temporal, and multilingual separation, lets employees take space to enact different balances of religion and market.
- Emergent state: Elastic hybridity, formed through the recursive interplay of polysemy and polyphony, supports inclusiveness and optionality without forcing a fixed organizational compromise.
- Boundary conditions: The case is especially revelatory because it involves a nascent organization, a Western market context, and religion as a demanding institutional logic.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. KT Bank reduced conflict by keeping organizational meanings sufficiently open while allowing individuals to enact different balances of religion and market across places, times, and languages. This made competing logics temporarily more compatible or less central without permanently separating, blending, or resolving them.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by theorizing polysemy and polyphony as multilevel mechanisms for engaging conflicting institutional logics. It develops elastic hybridity as a state in which a hybrid organization maintains unity in diversity and remains resilient despite central, incompatible logics. It also extends paradox theory by showing how frontline staff, not only managers or formal structures, participate in dynamic balancing.
practical_implication: For leaders of contested hybrids, the study suggests that prescribing one permanent balance of competing values can intensify conflict when those values are personally consequential. A more workable approach may be to create interpretive and practical spaces that allow members to enact different balances while retaining a shared organizational umbrella.
limitations: The authors identify three boundary conditions: the case concerns a nascent organization trying to reach the starting line, it is located in a specific sociocultural context combining market and religious logics from different institutional systems, and religion is a particularly demanding logic. These features make the case theoretically revealing; the authors nevertheless argue that the implications are likely applicable in more established settings and less conflictual contexts, while they also identify weaker forms of normative logics as an area for future study.
future_research: Future research could examine whether elastic hybridity operates similarly in established organizations and in settings where competing logics come from the same institutional system. The authors also point to other normative logics, such as community, family, and profession, as contexts where similar dynamics may appear in weaker forms. Further work could also study inclusive organizations that accommodate religious variety, freedom, and broader pluralities of values and beliefs.
abstract: Based on a 24-month ethnographic case study of the opening of the first Islamic bank in Germany, we make three contributions to the institutional theory literature. First, we outline “polysemy” and “polyphony” as mechanisms that dynamically engage conflicting logics through an organizational–individual interplay. Borrowing from paradox theory, we explain how hybrids can empower individuals to fluidly separate and integrate logics when neither structural compartmentalizing nor organizational blending is feasible because management cannot prescribe a specific balance of logics. Second, we explain the state of “elastic hybridity,” constituted through the recursive, multilevel relationship between polysemy and polyphony. Elastic hybrids maintain unity in diversity. They are capable of institutionally bending without organizationally breaking and thus enable individuals to practice more of their personal convictions at work while still experiencing a sense of shared organizational purpose. Third, we show how contested hybrids can be made to last. By dynamically making logics either less central or more compatible, elastic hybrids become less conflict prone and more resilient without permanently becoming more aligned or estranged.

title: Toward a Process Theory of Making Sustainability Strategies Legitimate in Action
methods: Longitudinal qualitative case study and ethnography of TechPro from 2012 to 2015, with follow-up visits in 2016, combining field observations, 90 open-ended interviews with 83 informants, documentary data, first-order coding, tension coding, and process analysis of recurrent action cycles.
industry: Premium, technologically advanced consumer goods manufacturing
time_period: 2012-2015, with follow-up visits in 2016
units: One anonymized global manufacturer, TechPro; managers, functions, organizational sites, tasks, meetings, documents, and strategy implementation episodes
n_sample: 80 days of field observation, 90 open-ended interviews with 83 informants, and 80 documents
authors: Hengst, Iris-Ariane; Jarzabkowski, Paula; Hoegl, Martin; Muethel, Miriam
theories: integrative view of sustainability; paradox perspective on corporate sustainability; strategy implementation as a process of legitimation
keywords: action cycles; co-enactment; decoupling; integration; legitimacy making; mainstream competitive strategy; qualitative case study; sustainability strategy
research_question: How do organizational actors implement a sustainability strategy alongside an existing mainstream competitive strategy, and what does this imply for the legitimate coexistence of the two strategies? The paper studies how actors work through action-level tensions that arise even when the sustainability strategy is legitimate at the organizational level.
mechanism_summary:
- Key tensions: Tensions between product features, tensions between organizational values, and tensions between strategic goals.
- Process / action cycles: Compromising-reinterpreting or splitting; sacrificing-valorizing; procedural embracing-synergizing.
- Emergent outcomes: Co-enactment of the sustainability strategy with the mainstream competitive strategy in specific tasks and reinforcement of the sustainability strategy's organizational legitimacy.
- Boundary conditions: Strong organizational and actor-level moral legitimacy of the new strategy, and tasks where actors must enact it alongside an already legitimate existing strategy.

The process starts with a sustainability strategy that is legitimate as an organizational purpose but difficult to enact within mainstream competitive tasks. Product-feature tensions trigger mutual adjustment through compromise, reinterpretation, or splitting; value tensions trigger prioritization through sacrifice and valorization; and strategic-goal tensions trigger combination through procedural embracing and synergizing. Across repeated tasks, these action cycles legitimate the sustainability strategy in action, making co-enactment possible and cumulatively reinforcing its organizational-level integration with the mainstream strategy.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the integrative view of sustainability by theorizing co-enactment of dual strategies as a process that can avert decoupling without eliminating tensions. It contributes an action-level account of how organizations respond to sustainability tensions, showing that repeated task-level action cycles can recursively reinforce organizational-level legitimacy. It also extends strategy implementation as a legitimation process by showing that legitimacy is constructed relationally between multiple strategies rather than only gained or lost by a single strategy.
practical_implication: The study suggests that sustainability strategies become substantively integrated when managers work through concrete implementation tensions in everyday tasks, not only when leaders announce sustainability as a legitimate organizational purpose. Managers should attend to the specific action cycles through which employees mutually adjust, prioritize, or combine sustainability and competitive demands, because these local resolutions can accumulate into broader strategic integration.
limitations: The study examines one anonymized company implementing a sustainability strategy in a context where sustainability already had strong moral legitimacy. The authors present this as a boundary condition: the framework should be especially relevant where the new strategy appeals to organizational participants' value systems, but it may not transfer directly to settings where actors do not see the new strategy as desirable or right.
future_research: Future research could examine how other strongly legitimate strategies, such as innovation or digitalization strategies, become integrated with existing strategies through action-level legitimation. The authors also call for more work on multiple, potentially competing strategies that have different legitimacy appeals to stakeholders and create implementation struggles across pluralistic organizations.
abstract: We draw on a three-year qualitative study of the processual dynamics of implementing a sustainability strategy alongside an existing mainstream competitive strategy. We show that, despite the legitimacy of the sustainability strategy at the organizational level, actors experience tensions with its implementation at the action level vis-à-vis the mainstream strategy, thus creating the potential for decoupling. Our findings show that working through these tensions on specific tasks enables actors to legitimate the sustainability strategy in action and to co-enact it with the mainstream strategy within those tasks. Cumulatively, multiple instances of such co-enactment at the action level reinforce the organizational-level legitimacy of the sustainability strategy and its integration with the mainstream strategy. We draw these findings together into a dynamic process model that contributes to the literature on integration of dual strategies at the action and organizational levels as a process of legitimacy making.
apa_citation: Hengst, I.-A., Jarzabkowski, P., Hoegl, M., & Muethel, M. (2020). Toward a process theory of making sustainability strategies legitimate in action. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(1), 246-271. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0960

title: Fostering Positive Relational Dynamics: The Power of Spaces and Interaction Scripts
methods: Empirical qualitative intervention study of a global distributed technology consulting team, using meeting observations, weekly and end-of-intervention interviews, facilitator field notes, meeting transcripts, emails, analytic memos, open coding, grounded theory building, and iterative process theorizing.
industry: Technology consulting team working in the health care industry within TaxCo, a large professional services firm.
time_period: Twelve weeks of data collection: two weeks before the intervention plus a 10-week intervention.
units: One global distributed team and its interactions in collaborative work time calls and pulse check meetings.
n_sample: One team; 13 intervention participants in weekly pulse checks; 127 interviews; 15 observed meetings.
authors: Lee, Michael Y.; Mazmanian, Melissa; Perlow, Leslie
theories: organizational scripts; positive relationships at work; spaces / bounded social settings for organizational change
keywords: connectedness; global distributed teams; interaction scripts; interpersonal sharing; openness; positive relational dynamics; respect; spaces
research_question: How can teams cultivate positive relational dynamics characterized by respect, openness, and connectedness? The paper asks how a global distributed team moved from mistrust, minimal communication, and disconnection toward more positive relational dynamics during an intervention built around spaces and interaction scripts.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: positive relational dynamics; respect, openness, and connectedness; spaces; interaction scripts; counter-normative interpersonal sharing; uncertainty, social risk, and collective action problems.
- Intervention elements: collaborative work time calls created dyadic spaces for personal and work-related sharing, while pulse check meetings created whole-team spaces for discussing work challenges.
- Process / phases: early weeks involved "trying on" new personal and work-related sharing; later weeks involved deeper enactment and team adaptation of the scripts.
- Enabling conditions: leadership support and external facilitation legitimated the spaces and scripts and helped team members manage the risk of new interaction patterns.
- Emergent outcomes: sharing interactions generated positive responses, energy, script adaptation, and a feedback cycle of greater respect, openness, and connectedness.

The process model is that bounded spaces opened a temporary setting where everyday team norms were less dominant, but spaces alone did not tell team members how to behave. Interaction scripts supplied content parameters and participation rules that made risky forms of sharing more specific, legitimate, and collectively enactable. As team members shared personal lives and work challenges and received positive responses, the team built energy and adapted the scripts, which helped the new relational dynamics become more accepted.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on positive relationships at work by showing an empirical process through which respect, openness, and connectedness can be fostered rather than only treated as beneficial relational states. It extends organizational change research by theorizing interaction scripts as a complement to spaces: spaces create openings for change, while scripts guide what interaction patterns can emerge within those openings. It also contributes to global team research by showing how relational closeness can be developed in a distributed team without the whole team meeting face to face.
practical_implication: Managers seeking to improve team relational dynamics should not rely only on informal appeals for openness or connection. The study suggests designing bounded meeting spaces with explicit content parameters, participation rules, leadership support, and facilitation so team members can safely practice new ways of sharing personal information and work challenges.
limitations: The study is limited by temporal scope: the authors observed a two-week assessment plus a 10-week intervention, so they likely captured unfreezing and changing but not the full refreezing of new team norms. The evidence comes from one global distributed technology consulting team and an intervention supported by leaders and facilitators, which limits certainty about whether similar dynamics would occur in other teams or without those enabling conditions.
future_research: Future research could examine how team relational dynamics evolve over longer timeframes and whether spaces and interaction scripts remain necessary after new patterns are established. The authors also call for research on which content parameters and participation rules make scripts more or less effective, whether bounded spaces can sometimes be sufficient without scripts, whether scripts can work outside bounded spaces, whether external facilitation is necessary, and how interaction scripts matter for other forms of organizational change.
abstract: Despite well-accepted understanding that relational dynamics characterized by respect, openness, and connectedness are critical for healthy team functioning, we know little about how to foster such dynamics. Drawing on observation and interview data from an intervention that fostered positive change in the relational dynamics of a global distributed team, this paper theorizes the mechanisms that enabled a move toward positive relational dynamics. We find that the intervention brought about relational changes by not only creating spaces where the team could experiment with new forms of interaction, but also by utilizing "interaction scripts"—concrete guidelines for interaction that specify content parameters and participation rules. We establish that the combination of spaces and interaction scripts was critical for helping the team enact counternormative forms of interpersonal sharing that led to the emergence of positive relational dynamics. While existing research has highlighted the importance of spaces for enabling positive relational change, this paper theorizes the complementary role that interaction scripts can play in the change process. These findings have implications for research on positive relationships at work, organizational change, and global and geographically dispersed teams.

title: Founder CEO Succession: The Role of CEO Organizational Identification
methods: Event history analysis using Cox semiparametric proportional hazards models on a hand-collected panel of founder CEO-managed U.S. IPO firms, with robust standard errors clustered at the firm level and multiple robustness checks.
industry: Newly listed IPO firms; the paper does not restrict the sample to a single industry.
time_period: IPO firms newly listed from 2000 to 2013, observed through the sample period for founder CEO succession.
units: Founder CEO-managed firms and firm-year observations.
n_sample: 448 founder CEO-managed firms with 2,073 firm-year observations.
authors: Lee, J. M.; Yoon, D.; Boivie, S.
theories: organizational identification theory (Ashforth & Mael, 1989; Dukerich et al., 2002); unfolding model of turnover / organizational shock (Lee & Mitchell, 1994; Lee et al., 1996)
keywords: core founder status; founder CEO succession; initial public offering; organizational identification; voluntary succession
research_question: The paper asks how founder CEOs’ organizational identification with their firms affects the timing of voluntary founder CEO succession after an IPO. It specifically examines whether prior entrepreneurial experience, number of cofounders, core founder status, and time as a private firm predict faster or slower voluntary departure from the CEO role.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that IPOs disrupt founders’ ownership, control, and identification with the organization, making post-IPO founder CEO succession a setting where differences in organizational identification should matter. Prior entrepreneurial experience and more cofounders are expected to weaken the founder CEO’s identification with the focal firm, increasing the hazard of voluntary succession. Core founder status and a longer private-firm period are expected to strengthen identification, decreasing the hazard of voluntary succession.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends organizational identification theory by applying it to founder CEOs, a group expected to have unusually strong baseline identification with the organizations they created. It contributes to founder CEO succession research by shifting attention from shareholder control, performance, and human capital toward founders’ psychological attachment to the firm. It also adds to corporate governance and upper echelons research by showing that CEO organizational identification can shape leadership-transition outcomes, not only agency costs or firm performance.
practical_implication: Boards and investors should treat founder CEO succession as partly shaped by the founder’s psychological attachment to the firm, not only by performance or governance constraints. The findings imply that succession planning may need to account for heterogeneity among founder CEOs, because strong identification can help reduce agency problems but may also make leadership transitions more politically difficult.
limitations: The sample is limited to U.S. IPO firms whose founder CEOs survived until the IPO, so the findings may not generalize to less successful ventures or other corporate life-cycle stages. The study uses archival proxies for organizational identification rather than direct measures, which limits the ability to test the proposed mechanism explicitly. The authors also acknowledge possible measurement error in classifying voluntary succession and cannot fully rule out alternative explanations.
future_research: Future research could compare the role of organizational identification in CEO succession across different stages of the corporate life cycle, such as venture-capital investment, first product development, IPO, and mature-stage operations. Studies using simulations, experiments, surveys, or other methods could directly test whether the proposed archival indicators accurately capture founder CEO organizational identification. Future work could also examine whether similar identification mechanisms apply to hired managers and other organizational actors in different contexts.
abstract: Drawing from the organizational identification literature, we theorize that founder CEO succession decisions are dependent on the strength of these CEOs’ organizational identification with their firms. Our theoretical premise is that factors that decrease founder CEOs’ organizational identification—namely, prior entrepreneurial experience and the number of cofounders—will positively affect their voluntary succession. Conversely, factors that increase founder CEOs’ organizational identification—specifically, the length of time that their organization was a private firm and core founder status— will negatively affect their voluntary succession. We find strong support for our arguments in the context of firms that undertook an initial public offering during the period from 2000 to 2013. Our findings enable us to illustrate that founder CEOs’ succession decisions may be better understood by considering factors that might influence their psychological traits rather than focusing only on their performance and control.

title: How Long Does It Take to Get to the Learning Curve?
methods: Quantitative analysis of a global remittances firm's franchisee selection decisions, using multilevel regression analysis with random effects to model accumulated experience, pace, performance variance, and daily transaction volume across remittance markets.
industry: Money transfer and remittances franchises
country: 13 European host nations and 64 home nations represented in host-home remittance markets
units: Franchisee-approving decisions nested in remittance markets
n_sample: 3,620 selection decisions in 165 markets
authors: Musaji, Serghei; Schulze, William S.; De Castro, Julio O.
theories: learning curve model; learning from failure; organizational learning theory; strategic learning
keywords: franchisee selection; learning curve; organizational learning; pace; performance variance; strategic decision making; strategic learning
research_question: How much accumulated experience is needed before strategic decision outcomes trend reliably positive, and how do the pace and variance of those experiences shape the journey to the learning curve? The paper examines these questions in franchisee selection decisions made by a global remittances firm across remittance markets.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that strategic learning differs from continuous learning-by-doing because early strategic decisions are episodic, ambiguous, and costly to reverse. When accumulated experience is low, spurious success and failure, weak causal understanding, and limited feedback can initially make the experience-performance relationship negative. As more decisions accumulate, decision makers gain enough information to identify better franchisees and markets, producing a U-shaped relationship that eventually resembles a traditional learning curve. Slower pace gives the organization more time to process feedback and lowers the number and cost of decisions needed to reach the positive portion of the curve, while higher variance improves information content and lowers cost without materially reducing the required number of decisions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational learning and strategic learning theory by showing that the positive learning curve may not begin immediately in strategic decision contexts. It identifies an initial negative phase of learning and estimates the experience threshold needed before performance trends positive. It also extends learning-curve theory by showing that attributes of the learning experience matter differently: slower decision pace shortens the journey and reduces its cost, while higher outcome variance reduces cost without materially hastening the journey.
practical_implication: For strategic decision makers, the study cautions that learning from a few strategic decisions may be unreliable, even when the decisions are repeated and relatively homogeneous. Managers should avoid assuming that faster decision pace automatically accelerates learning; allowing time between decisions can improve feedback processing and reduce long-run opportunity costs. The findings also support early codification of performance information so decision makers can distinguish real patterns from noisy early outcomes.
limitations: The authors measure franchisee performance only once, on a date distal from the original selection decisions, which constrains inference despite helping identify long-run franchisee success. They infer learning from performance patterns rather than directly measuring decision makers' learning processes. They also note limited information about individual decision makers, peer-level learning, and the representativeness of franchisee selection relative to more complex strategic decisions such as mergers and acquisitions.
future_research: Future research should examine which attributes of strategic decisions facilitate or impair learning when experience is limited. The paper also calls for more attention to the quality of strategic decision outcomes, rather than only binary success or failure. Additional work could test whether the number of experiences needed to reach the learning curve changes in more complex or heterogeneous strategic-decision contexts.
abstract: The learning curve describes learning from experience, even in its earliest phases, as an iterative process in which the ratio of positive to negative outcomes rises sharply with experience before becoming subject to diminishing returns. In contrast, the organizational learning literature has suggested that learning when experience is limited is difficult, and unfavorable outcomes are common. Resolution of these competing claims is especially important in the context of strategic decision making, where the costs of unreliable learning are significant. We develop theory and draw on a unique dataset of strategic decisions—the selection of franchisee applicants by a large global remittances firm over a 14-year period—to test competing predictions about how long it takes to get to the learning curve; that is, to the point after which performance trends reliably positive. Results from 3,620 selection decisions in 165 markets indicate that it took about 19 decisions per market to reach the learning curve. Further, we identify factors that reduce the cost of reaching the learning curve, as well as the number of decisions required to reach it. Implications for organizational learning theory in general, and strategic decision making in particular, are explored.

title: Unintended Consequences: Information Releases and CEO Stock Option Grants
methods: Empirical quantitative event-study and panel analysis of CEO option grants at large U.S. publicly traded companies from 2009-2013. The authors combine Thompson-Reuters insider filings, Execucomp, ISS director data, Compustat, Eventus abnormal returns, and LexisNexis press releases; they use event-study CARs, LIWC press-release tenor measures, generalized estimating equations, OLS with firm-clustered robust standard errors, and structural equation modeling.
industry: Large U.S. publicly traded companies across GICS industries.
units: CEO option grant dates, CEOs, firms, and firm press releases.
n_sample: 1,753 option grant dates representing 659 CEOs across 627 firms; 49,436 press releases.
authors: Quigley, Timothy J.; Hubbard, Timothy D.; Ward, Andrew; Graffin, Scott D.
theories: agency theory (Eisenhardt, 1989; Jensen & Meckling, 1976); equity theory (Adams, 1963); impression management (Elsbach, Sutton, & Principe, 1998); managerial discretion (Hambrick & Finkelstein, 1987)
keywords: CEO underpayment; agency theory; cumulative abnormal returns; impression management; information asymmetry; managerial discretion; negative press releases; option grants; stock options
research_question: How do CEOs use their informational advantage before stock option grant dates, and can the timing and tenor of firm information releases reduce stock prices in ways that personally benefit CEOs? The paper asks whether stock options, intended by agency theory to align interests, can create pregrant incentives for CEOs to use impression management against shareholders' interests.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that stock options align CEO and shareholder interests after grants but create a temporary pregrant incentive to lower the firm's share price and strike price. Because information asymmetry persists, CEOs can influence when information is released and how it is framed. More negatively valenced press releases before option grants are theorized and found to depress cumulative abnormal returns, while underpaid CEOs and CEOs in high-discretion settings release more negative information before grants. Supplemental analyses add nuance: mandatory negative releases carry the stronger price effect, while discretionary releases are less important for the stock-price response.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to agency theory by showing a loophole in a core governance prescription: stock options can be manipulated when information asymmetry remains unresolved. It also extends impression management research by showing that CEOs may use impression management to create negative, not only positive, stakeholder impressions. More broadly, it argues that outcome-based contracts do not remove the informational advantage that allows self-serving executive action.
practical_implication: Boards and regulators should recognize that CEO control over information timing and tenor can affect option strike prices even after SOX curtailed backdating. The authors recommend smaller and more frequent option or stock grants, closer review or auditing of firm information releases around grant dates, and stronger information pathways between outside directors and managers beyond the CEO.
limitations: The study examines CEOs of large publicly traded U.S. firms, so governance systems in other countries and smaller or less complex firms may differ. It does not directly observe whether stock price depression is conscious CEO behavior rather than a natural tendency. The study also does not test whether more negative firm releases subsequently shape media coverage.
future_research: Future research could extend the analysis to countries with different regulatory environments and governance practices. Scholars could examine whether firm size and complexity change the information-asymmetry mechanism, whether the tactic spreads through board interlocks or other networks, and whether press-release tenor affects media coverage as the next step in the proposed causal chain.
abstract: Scholars, regulators, and practitioners have long struggled with challenges emanating from the separation of ownership and control of modern corporations. Agency theory typically prescribes the use of stock options, or other outcome-based contractual arrangements, to overcome the critical issue of information asymmetry. We theorize that this arrangement, which leaves information asymmetry in place, provides CEOs an informational advantage that can be used, via impression management techniques, to circumvent some of the intended benefits of option grants. Specifically, we argue that the period leading up to an option grant creates a scenario where CEOs are incentivized to reduce the stock price of their firm for personal gain. Our results suggest that CEOs respond to this incentive by adjusting the tenor of releases from the firm during the pregrant period, providing CEOs a substantial economic gain. We also show that underpaid CEOs and CEOs with higher discretion pursue this activity more frequently. Our findings highlight a critical challenge of agency theory: if information asymmetry remains, a motivated CEO can often circumvent the contractual arrangements intended to mitigate that very problem. We offer future research paths and practical recommendations to address this issue.
apa_citation: Quigley, T. J., Hubbard, T. D., Ward, A., & Graffin, S. D. (2020). Unintended consequences: Information releases and CEO stock option grants. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(1), 155-180. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0455

title: Revisiting the Portability of Performance Paradox: Employee Mobility and the Utilization of Human and Social Capital Resources
methods: Panel OLS regressions on lobbyist-semiannual periods with lobbyist fixed effects, year fixed effects, Huber-White robust standard errors clustered by lobbyist and firm, plus robustness checks and post hoc firm-level regressions.
industry: U.S. federal lobbying industry
time_period: Registered U.S. federal lobbyists between 1998 and 2008; analysis drops 1998 observations and uses 18 semiannual periods.
units: Lobbyist-semiannual periods, with supplemental firm-semiannual analyses.
n_sample: 125,657 lobbyist-period observations from 16,255 unique lobbyists; supplemental firm-level sample of 22,836 observations from 3,137 lobbying firms.
authors: Raffiee, Joseph; Byun, Heejung
theories: labor market matching; person-organization fit literature; social capital literature; strategic human capital
keywords: U.S. lobbying industry; employee mobility; employee utilization; human capital resource complementarity; human capital resource fit; human capital resource similarity; portability of performance paradox; social capital resources
research_question: The paper asks when external hires can be integrated and utilized in a new firm's value-creating activities despite the portability of performance paradox. It examines whether human capital resource similarity, human capital resource complementarity, retained internal social capital, and retained external social capital weaken the post-mobility decline in employee utilization.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that external mobility creates integration frictions because hiring firms may have difficulty using the employee's human and social capital in current value-creating work. Human capital complementarity lowers these frictions when the employee's issue expertise fills a need in the hiring firm, while retained internal or external social capital preserves coworker coordination or client work after the move. The results support a descriptive pattern: utilization falls after mobility, complementarity and client transfer attenuate that decline, similarity does not consistently do so, and complementarity appears to substitute for transferred social capital.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper reframes the portability paradox around employee utilization rather than treating performance portability as mainly a firm-specific human capital problem. It contributes to strategic human capital and P-O fit research by distinguishing human capital resource similarity from complementarity and showing that complementarity, not similarity, is the more consistent moderator of post-mobility utilization decline.

It also contributes to social capital and employee mobility research by separating internal social capital transfer from external client transfer and examining their interactions with human capital fit. The paper is careful that its evidence is descriptive rather than causal, but it offers a cross-level account linking individual post-mobility utilization with supplemental hiring-firm revenue patterns.
practical_implication:
Managers should expect adjustment costs when hiring externally and should not infer that a strong prior performer will be immediately usable in the same way at the new firm. The findings suggest prioritizing hires whose human capital complements the hiring firm's work and considering whether hires can retain valuable coworker or client relationships.

The paper also warns that recruiting for both human capital fit and social capital transfer may have diminishing returns because these resources can partly substitute for each other. For professional service firms, this implies a more selective external hiring logic than simply hiring workers with high prior revenue.
limitations:
The authors state that lobbying has idiosyncrasies, so the findings may generalize most directly to professional and business service contexts rather than all employment settings. They also state that employee mobility is endogenous and that human capital fit and social capital transfer are not randomly assigned, so the results should not be read causally despite matching and robustness checks.

The study measures utilization through lobbying revenue rather than directly observing individual contributions or individual performance. It also cannot observe other dimensions of human capital fit or managerial and HR practices that may affect employee integration and turnover.
future_research:
Future research could test mobility and employee utilization in nonservice contexts and use research designs that randomly manipulate or more strongly identify human capital fit and social capital transfer. The authors also encourage work on other dimensions of human capital fit, cross-level interactions with psychological and attitudinal fit, and the HR practices that moderate employee utilization after mobility.

Further work could examine heterogeneity in where employees move, because competing firms differ in their resource endowments and ability to use external hires. This would help clarify when individual-level post-mobility utilization declines coexist with positive hiring-firm revenue effects.
abstract: This study revisits the portability of performance paradox—the common finding that external hires fail to replicate prior performance after switching firms—by examining how the nature of an employee’s human capital and social capital resources relate to the ease with which external hires can be utilized in an organization’s value creating activities. Drawing theoretically from the person–organization fit and social capital literatures, we theorize that the integration and utilization of external hires will correlate with two types of human capital resource fit: similarity and complementarity, and two dimensions of retained social capital resources: internal and external. Using data from the U.S. lobbying industry and novel empirical estimates of worker–firm fit, we provide descriptive evidence that employee utilization (performance) decreases post-mobility, consistent with the portability paradox. However, this relationship attenuates—in magnitude and duration—when there is human capital resource complementarity (but not similarity) between the employee and hiring firm or when the employee transfers social capital resources (internal or external). We also find some evidence that human capital and social capital function as substitutes, and post hoc analyses suggest the characteristics of human and social capital which facilitate the utilization of external hires also correlate with hiring firm performance.

title: Product Innovation and Educational Diversity in Top and Middle Management Teams
methods: Linked employer-employee panel study using Swedish CIS, LISA, and registered firm-characteristics data; the paper estimates probit and ordered probit models with clustered standard errors.
industry: Firms with 10 or more employees across manufacturing, construction, and services sectors.
units: Firm-year observations with identified top management teams and middle management teams.
n_sample: 486 firms and 1,873 observations for innovation engagement models; 414 firms and 1,233 observations for product innovation outcome models.
authors: Schubert, T.; Tavassoli, S.
theories: informational variety perspective; problem-based view of the firm (Baer, Dirks, & Nickerson, 2013; Felin & Zenger, 2015; Nickerson & Zenger, 2004); social identity theory; upper echelons theory (Hambrick & Mason, 1984; Hambrick, 2007)
keywords: diversity in management teams; educational diversity; firm innovation; middle management teams; product innovations; top management teams
research_question: The paper asks how educational diversity in top management teams and middle management teams differently affects firms' innovation engagement and product innovation outcomes. It specifically examines whether TMT diversity is tied to the decision to innovate, while MMT diversity is tied to realized innovation outcomes and market novelty.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that TMTs and MMTs occupy different organizational roles in the innovation process. TMT educational diversity broadens the knowledge pools and cognitive frames used for strategic problem formulation, making firms more likely to engage in innovation activities. MMT educational diversity affects problem solving and implementation because middle managers allocate resources, select and manage innovation projects, and coordinate functions. Because educational diversity is expected to raise creativity, its outcome effect is strongest for new-to-market product innovation rather than imitative new-to-firm innovation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the informational variety perspective by showing that diversity effects depend on the organizational level and task responsibilities of the management team. It challenges TMT-centered upper echelons explanations by showing that some innovation effects attributed to top managers may actually stem from diversity in lower-level MMTs. It also conceptualizes innovation as a process with separable engagement and outcome stages.
practical_implication: Firms should align diversity interventions with the innovation problem they face. If the issue is whether the firm engages in innovation at all, increasing educational diversity in the TMT may help strategic problem formulation. If the issue is converting innovation resources into successful and novel products, increasing educational diversity in the MMT may be more relevant.
limitations: The paper notes that it does not explicitly examine how TMTs and MMTs interact across organizational levels. It also cautions that the main hypotheses should not be treated as universally true, because firm size and other contingencies may condition the diversity-innovation relationship. The authors also state that they cannot assert context-independence, although robustness checks support the results across alternative methodological choices.
future_research: Future research could examine the social processes linking TMTs and MMTs, including trust, debate, and conflict across levels. Scholars could also refine the theory by studying moderators such as firm size and other organizational contingencies and by developing the proposed theory around the organizational level of the team.
abstract: The effects of diversity in management teams on firm innovation have become an important topic in strategic management. With a few exceptions, however, the literature has focused on diversity in top management teams (TMTs), while the role of diversity in lower management levels, particularly middle management teams (MMTs), has usually been neglected. In this paper, we intend to fill this gap by explicitly differentiating between the effects of diversity in TMTs and MMTs. By matching various firm-level and individual-level datasets, we compile a linked employer–employee panel dataset for Sweden for the period 2004–2012. Focusing on measures of educational diversity, we find that the effects differ considerably between MMTs and TMTs. TMTs’ diversity determines whether firms engage in innovation activities at all, while MMTs’ diversity affects the actual outcome of innovation processes, in particular successful product innovations and their degree of market novelty.

title: Investment Ties Gone Awry
methods: Empirical quantitative study of U.S. VC-backed ventures using SDC Platinum data from 1980-2014; Heckman treatment effects models estimate the effect of VC withdrawal on valuation and round size, with 2SLS, propensity-score matching, difference-in-differences, selection-model, mediation, and long-term exit robustness checks.
industry: VC-backed ventures across SDC Platinum industry classifications, including biotechnology, communications, computer hardware, computer software, consumer-related, industrial/energy, internet-specific, medical/health, semiconductors, and other.
time_period: 1980-2014, with second-round investments after 1985 and first-round investments before 2007 for exit-observation coverage.
units: VC-backed ventures and their second financing rounds; valuation analyses use the subset with complete valuation data.
n_sample: 2,181 ventures in the final sample; 535 ventures with complete valuation data for the valuation analysis.
authors: Shafi, Kourosh; Mohammadi, Ali; Johan, Sofia A.
theories: adverse selection and information asymmetry; behavioral decision-making theory; signaling theory (Spence, 1974; Connelly et al., 2011)
keywords: VC withdrawal; adverse selection; follow-on round of financing; new joining investors; reputation; signaling theory; status; venture valuation
research_question: What are the financial and partner-selection costs to entrepreneurial ventures when an existing venture capitalist does not repeat its investment tie in a follow-on financing round? The paper asks whether VC withdrawal lowers venture valuation by creating adverse-selection perceptions and deterring new, high-status, and high-reputation investors from joining the syndicate.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that withdrawal by an insider VC can be read by prospective investors as negative private information or as a signal of adverse-selection risk, even when the withdrawal is unrelated to underlying venture quality. Because new investors cannot fully observe the withdrawing VC's private information or motives, they may treat the venture as riskier and exclude it from consideration. This reduces the chance of attracting new investors, especially high-status and high-reputation VCs, which weakens the venture's bargaining position and depresses valuation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends research on interorganizational relationship discontinuation by shifting attention from why ties dissolve to the performance consequences for entrepreneurial ventures after investment ties are not repeated. It contributes to signaling theory by showing that signals affect not only valuation directly but also the quality of exchange partners a venture can attract. It also connects partner selection and entrepreneurial resource mobilization by showing how disrupted preexisting social ties impede search, access, and transfer of financial resources.
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs should not treat early investment from prestigious VCs as unambiguously beneficial, because a later decision not to continue investing can damage valuation and deter other investors. The paper suggests that entrepreneurs should evaluate whether seed and early-stage investors are committed partners rather than treating early investment as a cheap option. VCs should also be careful in syndicate partner selection because withdrawal by one investor can put the venture and the syndicate's shared investment at risk.
limitations: The study is set in VC syndicate networks, so generalization to other interorganizational relationships depends on whether potential partners face adverse-selection risk and whether existing partners are expected to continue their ties. The authors also acknowledge limitations from econometric identification assumptions, including the possibility that private information and adverse-selection mechanisms interact. VentureXpert data did not allow the authors to distinguish cases in which discontinuing investors retained diluted equity from cases in which they privately sold their stake.
future_research: Future research could examine whether similar negative signals from relationship termination operate in client relationships, alliances, or other settings with uncertainty about organizational quality. Studies using different methodologies, including field experiments, could better rule out confounding processes and distinguish private-information from adverse-selection mechanisms. Further work could test whether alternative signals, such as patenting or prestigious board members, weaken the effects of VC withdrawal on subsequent collaboration formation.
abstract: Forming early relationships increases entrepreneurial ventures' chances of survival and success by allowing access to critical resources from partners. However, since not all ventures achieve their desired goals through collaboration due to uncertainty, such relationships are sometimes abandoned. This paper investigates the costs of ties that have gone awry in the context of venture capital investments. We conjecture that the adverse perceptions of signals associated with tie discontinuation reduce an investee venture's valuation in the follow-on round of financing by partially deterring prospective investors, particularly higher-quality ones, from joining the syndicate. By examining large-sample evidence that supports our theory, we suggest that early entrepreneurial ties to venture capitalists may be a double-edged sword, especially in light of the costs of tie discontinuation.

title: Should I Stay or Should I Go? Founder Power and Exit via Initial Public Offering
methods: Mixed-methods design combining an observational archival study of U.K. entrepreneurial IPOs with two randomized lab experiments. Study 1 uses binary and multinomial regression on 313 founders from 177 first-time LSE and AIM entrepreneurial listings between 2002 and 2010; Study 2 experimentally manipulates high versus low power among entrepreneurial decision makers and managers taking an entrepreneurship course.
industry: Entrepreneurial IPOs and entrepreneurial firms listed on the London Stock Exchange main market or AIM.
time_period: 2002-2010 for the archival IPO sample; experiments conducted after Study 1 with entrepreneurial decision makers and managers taking an entrepreneurship course.
units: Founders at risk of full or partial exit at IPO, plus experimental decision makers.
n_sample: 313 founders from 177 entrepreneurial IPOs; two experiments with 181 entrepreneurial decision makers and 190 managers taking an entrepreneurship course.
authors: Souitaris, Vangelis; Zerbinati, Stefania; Peng, Bo (Grace); Shepherd, Dean
theories: frustration theory (Fox & Spector, 1999; Spector, 2002; Storms & Spector, 1987); power theory (Child, 1972; Finkelstein, 1992; Finkelstein & Hambrick, 1996; Nakauchi & Wiersema, 2015)
keywords: founder exit; founder power; frustration; full exit; initial public offerings; partial exit
research_question: How and why does founders' power influence their decision to exit from their ventures via IPO? The paper asks whether low founder power predicts full exit, whether frustration explains that relationship, and whether power matters differently for full versus managerial or financial partial exits.
mechanism_summary:
- Archival IV(s): Founder power at IPO, measured through structural, ownership, expertise, and prestige dimensions.
- Experimental IV(s): Assigned high- versus low-power condition at the time of IPO.

The mechanism starts from power theory: IPOs create uncertainty, negotiation, and political turmoil, making founders' capacity to influence venture decisions consequential. When founders lack power over ventures they created, they experience frustration because their goals are blocked. Full exit is theorized as a vigorous withdrawal response to that frustration, whereas managerial and financial partial exits can reflect other career, ownership, or financial motives and are therefore less tightly tied to low power.
theoretical_contribution: The article extends founder-exit research by explaining why founders may voluntarily leave high-potential ventures through IPOs, rather than focusing only on forced CEO replacement or failure-related exit. It distinguishes full exit from managerial and financial partial exits, showing that exit is not an all-or-nothing outcome. It also contributes to power and entrepreneurship theory by identifying frustration as an emotional mechanism linking low power to founder exit and by specifying that this mechanism is stronger for full exits than for partial exits.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that founders should clarify whether they value continued influence or wealth realization before accepting power-reducing investment and IPO arrangements. If remaining influential is central to their goals, reduced power may generate frustration and increase the likelihood of full exit. Investors should also recognize that reducing founder power can push founders out; when continued founder involvement is valuable, investors may need to negotiate partial-exit arrangements rather than unintentionally prompting full exit.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 relies on secondary data, which makes it difficult to identify the exact mechanisms underlying founder exit and to rule out all alternative explanations such as founders' health, marital status, or involuntary managerial partial exits. They also focus on IPOs on the LSE, so generalization to other geographies and IPO markets requires replication or theoretical extension.
future_research: Future research could examine how different dimensions and configurations of founder power interact to shape frustration and exit. The authors also call for closer study of how financial upside or gain might interact with frustration in founders' decisions to exit or stay after IPO.
abstract: Founders can voluntarily exit their ventures via initial public offerings (IPOs). This study builds on power theory to develop and test a model of founder exit using a dataset of 313 founders from 177 entrepreneurial IPOs between 2002 and 2010. We largely find support for the model—a negative relationship between founder power and full exit. To capture the underlying mechanism of the power–exit relationship, we conducted two experiments in which we randomly assigned decision makers to either a highor lowpower condition. We find that decision makers in the low-power condition are more likely to use a full exit via IPO than those in the high-power condition, and that frustration mediates this relationship. However, founders can also engage in partial exits, including a managerial partial exit in which the founder leaves management but keeps ownership, and a financial partial exit in which the founder divests ownership but remains in management. We find that the negative relationship between founder power and exit is more negative for full exits than for partial exits. With this paper, we contribute to the literature on exit by identifying a novel mechanism—frustration— underlying power’s influence on the likelihood and type of founder exit.

title: Academy of Management Journal in 2020 and Beyond
methods: Editorial essay outlining AMJ's 22nd editorial team's composition, journal priorities, credibility initiatives, inclusiveness goals, and planned author- and reviewer-facing practices.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Tihanyi, Laszlo
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: editorial team; global and inclusive journal; journal mission; methodological transparency; paper development workshops; societal relevance
research_question: The editorial asks how AMJ's 22nd editorial team will serve the journal from 2020 through 2022. It focuses on the team's priorities for maintaining AMJ's mission while increasing relevance, credibility, global reach, and inclusiveness.
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial continuity: The new team frames its work as continuing AMJ's mission to publish empirical research that tests, extends, or builds management theory and contributes to practice.
- Team structure: The editorial describes a larger and more diverse editorial team, including deputy editors, associate editors across micro, macro, and qualitative areas, and an expanded editorial review board.

The process logic is editorial rather than causal: AMJ's standing is presented as depending on a capable and diverse editorial infrastructure, rigorous and transparent empirical standards, and broader engagement with authors and scholarly communities across countries and methods. The proposed initiatives aim to make the journal more relevant to societal conversations while preserving high theoretical and empirical standards.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a new theory. Its contribution is to articulate how AMJ's incoming editorial team interprets the journal's mission: publish original empirical research with strong theoretical and practical contributions while strengthening societal relevance, methodological credibility, and global inclusiveness.
practical_implication: Prospective AMJ authors should expect continued emphasis on strong empirical and theoretical contributions, transparent methods, data integrity, and fit with AMJ's mission. Reviewers and editors are asked to support timely, constructive, and methodologically attentive evaluation, while the journal plans outreach and mentorship for authors in underrepresented locations and institutions.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editorial encourages empirical management research that joins societal conversations, addresses contemporary managerial and organizational problems, and introduces externally important but understudied topics to AMJ readers. It also calls for future editorial guidance on strengthening theoretical arguments across micro, macro, qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods traditions.

title: It Takes Three: Relational Boundary Work, Resilience, and Commitment among Navy Couples
methods: Empirical qualitative study using paired interviews with U.S. Navy couples, additional interviews with high-level officers and IT professionals, archival material on Navy policies, and iterative NVivo coding.
industry: U.S. Navy and military work-family context.
country: United States, centered on the U.S. Navy.
time_period: Couple interviews were conducted in 2003, 2004, and 2010; additional officer and IT professional interviews were conducted in 2013.
units: Navy couples, with Navy members and spouses as paired informants, plus high-level officers and IT professionals for organizational context.
n_sample: 58 interviews with 29 couples, plus 14 additional interviews, for 72 total interviews.
authors: Beckman, C. M.; Stanko, T. L.
theories: border theory; boundary theory; family systems theory
keywords: adjustability; cohesion; family systems theory; organizational commitment; relational boundary work; resilience; work-nonwork boundary
research_question: The paper asks how employees, spouses, and organizations jointly construct work-nonwork boundaries, and how those relational boundary-work patterns are associated with couple resilience and organizational commitment. It studies this question in the U.S. Navy, where long deployment separation and organizational rules create strong pressures toward both segmentation and integration.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: Relational boundary work, cohesion, adjustability, couple resilience, and organizational commitment.
- Relational system: Boundary work is coconstructed by the Navy employee, the spouse, and organizational expectations rather than by the employee alone.
- Process dimensions: Cohesion captures separateness versus togetherness; adjustability captures stability versus change in how couples enact shared roles.
- Boundary configurations: The observed configurations are balanced, chaotic, rigid, enmeshed, and insecure couples.
- Emergent outcomes: Moderate adjustability is associated with couple resilience, while moderate cohesion is associated with organizational commitment in this Navy context.

The process is not a variable-based causal test. The authors theorize from qualitative evidence that the same individual integration or segmentation behavior can have different consequences depending on the spouse's response and the Navy's expectations. Couples with moderate cohesion and moderate adjustability can maintain both connection and role flexibility during deployment, whereas extreme adjustability weakens resilience and extreme cohesion or separation weakens commitment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to boundary-work research by moving the level of analysis from individual boundary management to a relational system involving employees, spouses, and organizations. It develops relational boundary work as a construct and uses family systems theory to specify cohesion and adjustability as two dimensions that explain why individual integration and segmentation behaviors are insufficient on their own. It also links relational boundary configurations to both couple-level resilience and organization-level commitment.
practical_implication: The study suggests that organizations should understand employees' work-nonwork boundary management as embedded in partner relationships, not merely as an individual preference or policy-compliance issue. In settings with intense work demands, separation, or technology-mediated communication, organizations should attend to how policies and expectations shape couples' cohesion and adjustability rather than assuming that individual integration or segmentation behaviors are sufficient on their own.
limitations: The authors note that they could not directly link each couple's relational boundary work to specific organizational policies in real time. The study is also cross-sectional, so it cannot establish causality or track how couples move among configurations over time. The Navy context is extreme, with long separations and strong organizational identity, which makes the setting theoretically useful but also limits direct generalization.
future_research: Future research should examine relational boundary work in other organizational contexts with different levels of boundary permeability and flexibility. The authors also call for longitudinal work to study whether couples shift toward more balanced patterns with experience, and for research on gender because Navy-spouse identities and gendered expectations may shape relational boundary work.
abstract: Although scholars have generally focused on how individuals manage their work and home demands, employees, outsiders, and organizations coconstruct work–nonwork boundaries. Using interviews with couples from the U.S. Navy, an organizational context that encourages a mix of segmentation and integration behaviors, we develop the construct of relational boundary work to describe the joint behaviors of multiple parties in a relational system to manage the work–home interface. Drawing on family systems theory, we delineate five couple configurations using two dimensions to describe how couples promote togetherness or separateness (cohesion) and how couples balance stability and change in enacting roles (adjustability). Extreme adjustability (very high or very low) is problematic for resilience; this describes both chaotic (low cohesion, high adjustability) and rigid (low cohesion, low adjustability) couples. Extreme cohesion (very high or very low), in contrast, undermines organizational commitment; this describes enmeshed (high cohesion, moderate adjustability), chaotic, and rigid couples. In contrast, balanced couples (moderate cohesion, moderate adjustability) are both resilient and committed in this organization. An examination of relational boundary work reveals that understanding employees’ behaviors alone may not illuminate outcomes, and underscores the importance of conceptualizing boundaries as cocreated by employees, outsiders, and organizations within a relational system.

title: Problem-Solving or Self-Enhancement? A Power Perspective on How CEOs Affect R&D Search in the Face of Inconsistent Feedback
methods: Empirical quantitative study of S&P 500 firm-year observations from 2002 to 2014. The authors construct measures of positive performance feedback, negative performance prospects, four sources of CEO power, and R&D search, then estimate Arellano-Bond dynamic panel models with firm, CEO, board, industry, and time controls plus robustness checks using alternative samples and dependent-variable operationalizations.
industry: S&P 500 firms across four-digit SIC industries with at least five competitors, excluding financial services, utilities, unidentified industries, and firms whose R&D expenditures exceeded sales.
country: Not separately reported in paper; sample consists of S&P 500 firms.
units: Firm-year observations.
n_sample: 241 firms and 1,887 firm-year observations.
authors: Blagoeva, Radina R.; Mom, Tom J. M.; Jansen, Justin J. P.; George, Gerard
theories: CEO power (Finkelstein, 1992); behavioral theory of the firm; self-enhancement theory
keywords: CEO power; R&D search; behavioral theory of the firm; inconsistent feedback; performance feedback; self-enhancement
research_question: When firms face inconsistent feedback, why do some decision makers respond through problem solving and increased R&D search while others respond through self-enhancement and reduced R&D search? The paper asks how four sources of CEO power shape the firm's response to positive backward-looking performance feedback combined with negative forward-looking prospects.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism contrasts problem solving with self-enhancement. Positive past feedback paired with negative prospects creates ambiguity about whether the firm should treat the situation as a problem requiring search or as a threat to be reframed. Structural and ownership power give CEOs more ability and incentive to protect their position by emphasizing the positive signal and reducing R&D search; expert power unexpectedly works similarly in the main models. Prestige power instead gives CEOs confidence, stakeholder support, and access to information, making problem-solving responses and increased R&D search more likely.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper advances research on inconsistent performance feedback by specifying when problem-solving versus self-enhancement logics are likely to dominate. It shows that the source of CEO power matters: structural and ownership power support self-enhancing assessment, prestige power supports problem solving, and broad expert power does not operate as predicted.

The study also contributes to behavioral theory of the firm research by integrating backward-looking performance feedback with forward-looking performance prospects. It argues that decision makers attend differently to inconsistent past and future signals, and that CEO-stakeholder power dynamics condition whether firms increase or decrease R&D search.
practical_implication:
The findings imply that external monitoring bodies should pay close attention to R&D search decisions when CEOs have high structural or ownership power, because these power bases are associated with lower search under inconsistent feedback. Firms seeking stronger R&D responses to inconsistent feedback may benefit from CEOs with prestige-based power, and boards can support less prestigious CEOs or assist CEOs who lack sales and marketing expertise when inconsistent signals require search.

The post hoc results also suggest caution around broad assumptions about CEO expertise. Expertise rooted in sales and marketing appears different from general firm-specific expertise, so boards may need to distinguish functional backgrounds rather than treating all expert power as equivalent.
limitations: The authors note that multiple sources of CEO power over the same stakeholder may coexist, but their models do not examine combinations of power sources. They also note that expert power has a negative association with problem solving in their main results even though prior work often treats expert power as a beneficial persuasive power source. The paper further notes that the four CEO power sources may operate as substitutes or complements, and that its findings are based on two configurations of inconsistent feedback.
future_research:
Future research could examine how different sources of power combine as substitutes or complements, including configurational approaches such as qualitative comparative case analysis. The authors also call for work on which soft-power sources can negatively affect decision making and under what circumstances.

Additional research could investigate how self-enhancement can be offset when firms face inconsistent feedback. The conclusion also points to governance research on how TMT members, boards, and other stakeholders interact with and influence one another after inconsistent feedback.
abstract: Firms consider multiple reference points simultaneously to assess performance; however, these referents may be inconsistent in signaling success or failure. Consequently, decision makers use one of two contrasting decision rules when responding to inconsistent feedback: problem solving or self-enhancement. So far, disparate theoretical logics and mixed evidence has limited our understanding about when decision makers shift their attention from positive to negative aspects of inconsistent feedback, or vice versa, and increase or decrease their research and development (R&D) search. We examine how different types of chief executive officer (CEO) power explain why some firms may respond to inconsistent feedback—that is, positive performance feedback and negative prospects—in distinct ways. We find that firms engage in less R&D search as a response to inconsistent feedback when CEOs have high levels of structural, ownership or expert power. In contrast, when CEOs have high levels of prestige power, firms undertake more R&D search as a response to inconsistent feedback. Our findings provide new insights and contribute to conversations about CEO power and performance feedback within the context of the behavioral theory of the firm.
