title: The Art of the Pivot: How New Ventures Manage Identification Relationships with Stakeholders as They Change Direction
methods: An inductive qualitative process study of the Impossible Project, using interviews, archival data, participant observation, open coding, temporal bracketing, visual mapping, and triangulation.
industry: Analog instant photography.
country: Not reported as a single national sample; the case includes Impossible's Berlin head office and its user community.
time_period: 2013-2016 focal period, with follow-up context into 2017.
units: The Impossible Project, its staff and retailers, and members of its user community.
n_sample: 40 interviews with Impossible staff and retailers, 34 interviews with community members, archival materials, and eight weeks of participant observation.
authors: Hampel, C. E.; Tracey, P.; Weber, K.
theories: identification management; lean start-up; organizational identification
keywords: identification reset work; lean start-up; new ventures; pivot; stakeholder identification; user community
research_question: The paper asks what consequences pivoting has for new ventures that rely on stakeholders who identify with them, and how such ventures can manage relations with these stakeholders during pivots. It studies this question through Impossible's shift from an analog instant-film venture serving a niche user community to an analog-digital photography company seeking mass-market customers.
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: A new venture enacts a live pivot that changes its identity, strategy, products, operations, and community interactions.
- Stakeholder reactions: Community-based supporters feel personally betrayed and attack the venture; product-based supporters feel anxious and doubt the venture's new focus.
- Identification reset work: The venture seeks empathy for its technical and commercial challenges and mythologizes both the technology and its commitment to the product.
- Transition paths: Some attackers and doubters disengage, while many doubters resume support after developing reverence for the venture's film progress and understanding its struggles.
- Boundary condition: A small group of attackers remains hostile despite the reset work.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. Impossible reduced stakeholder hostility by exposing its vulnerabilities and reframing the pivot as a shared struggle to keep analog instant photography alive. This moved many stakeholders away from an "us versus them" relationship and toward either detached acceptance or renewed support, allowing the venture to continue its pivot.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to identification management by theorizing identification reset work as a way new ventures can repair threatened relationships with external stakeholders over whom they have limited control. It extends user community research by showing that intense community identification can become a liability during radical change. It also contributes to lean start-up scholarship by distinguishing early conceptual pivots from later live pivots, where the central challenge is managing existing stakeholder identification relationships.
practical_implication: For new ventures, pivoting is not a cost-free strategic correction when loyal stakeholders identify with the venture's prior direction. Founders and managers may need to communicate the necessity, vulnerability, and product commitment behind the pivot, while avoiding claims that make stakeholders expect a return to the old relationship.
limitations: The authors note that they study one venture and one user community, so the internal dynamics of the community and competitors' attempts to shape those dynamics remain underexplored. They also emphasize that timing may matter: Impossible's pivot occurred when concern about the survival of instant film was especially high, which may have intensified stakeholder reactions.
future_research: Future research could examine the internal dynamics of user communities during venture pivots and how competitors influence those dynamics. It could also study how ventures use temporal work to defuse identification threats, how they manage the benefits and risks of stakeholder anthropomorphism, and how identification reset work operates when stakeholder reactions are polarized rather than mainly hostile.
abstract: Many new ventures have to “pivot”—radically transform what they are about—because their original approach has failed. However, pivoting risks disrupting relationships with key stakeholders, such as user communities, who identify with ventures. Stakeholders may respond by withdrawing support and starving ventures of the resources needed to thrive. This can pose an existential threat to ventures, yet it is unclear how they might manage this problem. To explore this important phenomenon, we conduct a qualitative process study of the Impossible Project, a photography venture that encountered significant resistance from its user community as it pivoted from an analog focus to an analog–digital positioning. We develop a process model of stakeholder identification management that reveals how ventures can use identification reset work to defuse tensions with stakeholders whose identification with the venture is threatened. A core finding is that ventures can remove the affective hostility of stakeholders and rebuild connections with many of them by exposing their struggles, thus creating a bond focused around these shared experiences. Through this study and its findings, we offer contributions to scholarship on identification management, user community identification, and the lean start-up.

title: Fall from Grace: The Role of Dominance and Prestige in the Punishment of High-Status Actors
methods: Empirical quantitative multi-study design combining archival NHL player-season analysis with random coefficient multilevel regressions, a controlled lab experiment with a confederate group leader, and an MTurk scenario experiment using ANOVA and bootstrapped structural equation mediation.
industry: Professional ice hockey/NHL, behavioral-lab work groups, and Fortune 500 executive transgression scenarios.
country: United States and Canada for the NHL teams; a European business school behavioral lab; Amazon Mechanical Turk online participants.
time_period: Study 1 uses NHL player-season data from 2014-2016; collection dates for Studies 2 and 3 are not reported in paper.
units: NHL player-season observations, lab participants nested in work groups, and MTurk participants evaluating CEO or senior VP scenarios.
n_sample: Study 1: 1,294 player-season observations with 756 unique NHL players; Study 2: 152 participants in 38 work groups; Study 3: 491 MTurk participants.
authors: Kakkar, Hemant; Sivanathan, Niro; Gobel, Matthias S.
theories: evolutionary theory of dominance and prestige (Henrich & Gil-White, 2001; Maner & Case, 2016); moral credentials (Miller & Effron, 2010; Monin & Miller, 2001); third-party attribution theories (Malle & Knobe, 1997; Skarlicki & Kulik, 2004)
keywords: ambiguous transgressions; dominance; intentionality; moral credentials; prestige; punishment; social status; third-party judgments
research_question: Why are some high-status actors punished harshly for ambiguous norm violations while others receive leniency for comparable misconduct? The paper asks whether the basis of status, dominance versus prestige, explains third-party punishment judgments toward high-status transgressors.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that observers infer different motives from different forms of high status. Dominance-based status signals assertiveness, control, self-interest, and agency, so ambiguous transgressions by dominant high-status actors are judged as more intentional and less morally credentialed. Prestige-based status signals expertise, helpfulness, respect, and prior other-oriented behavior, so observers grant more benefit of the doubt and punish less severely. Across the studies, intentionality and lack of moral credentials explain the harsher punishment of dominant versus prestigious high-status actors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reconciles contradictory findings on whether high status protects or harms transgressors by separating dominance-based from prestige-based status. It contributes to status theory by showing that the type of status, not merely rank, shapes third-party judgments after ambiguous wrongdoing. It also links status research to retributive justice and organizational misconduct literatures by identifying intentionality and moral credentials as parallel mechanisms behind punishment judgments.
practical_implication: Organizations should recognize that dominant and prestigious leaders may face different public and stakeholder reactions during crises or misconduct allegations. When a dominant leader is implicated, timely explanation, apology, and distancing may be especially important because observers are more likely to infer intentionality and lower moral credentials. The findings also caution policymakers, juries, and organizational decision makers that status type can bias punishment judgments for similar ambiguous acts.
limitations: The authors note that contingency factors such as the nature of the transgression and observer identification with the high-status actor may moderate the effect. Study 1 cannot fully rule out endogeneity or unobserved confounds, and it cannot measure the psychological mediators directly. The paper also leaves open whether prestigious actors would be punished more harshly when their transgression violates the specific identity or principles on which their prestige is based.
future_research: Future research could examine when prestige becomes a liability, especially for transgressions that contradict the source of a prestigious actor's standing. Scholars could test whether competence-based versus integrity-based trust violations change the dominance/prestige pattern. Additional work could examine observer identity, in-group leniency, black-sheep effects, and whether leaders' awareness of prestige creates incentives to conceal wrongdoing.
abstract: When actors transgress social norms, their social status colors the severity with which they are punished. While some argue that high-status transgressors attract severe punishment when accused of ambiguous transgressions, others contend the opposite. In this paper, we attempt to reconcile this theoretical inconsistency. We propose that the capacity for social status to color third-party judgments of transgressions may depend on the status type of high-status actors. Drawing on the evolutionary theory of dominance and prestige as two alternate forms of status within social hierarchies, we suggest that actors associated with dominance-based status will be penalized more harshly than actors whose status is based on prestige. Across multiple studies employing archival field data, controlled lab experiments, and different instantiations of dominance, prestige, and misconduct, we consistently demonstrate that high-status dominant actors are punished more harshly than their prestigious counterparts. Further, we find that attributions of intentionality and lack of moral credentials explain the harsher punishments meted out to dominant (vs. prestigious) high-status actors. In this way, we provide both a parsimonious reconciliation of the inconsistency in the extant literature and a theoretical explanation of how status type of high-status actors differentially impacts the judgment, decisions, and behaviors of third parties.

title: Does Negative Feedback Benefit (or Harm) Recipient Creativity? The Role of the Direction of Feedback Flow
methods: Two-study empirical design combining a quasi-field experiment in a Korean health food company with a randomized laboratory experiment at a large North American university; analyses used regression, simple slopes, and moderated mediation with conditional indirect effects.
industry: Study 1: creative jobs in product development, R&D, and marketing at a Korean health food company; Study 2: undergraduate laboratory participants
country: Korea in Study 1; North American university context in Study 2
time_period: Study 1 used March and June quarterly evaluations with creativity measured two months later; Study 2 timing not reported in paper
units: Feedback recipients: employees in Study 1 and undergraduate students in Study 2
n_sample: 225 employees in Study 1; 356 undergraduate students in Study 2
authors: Kim, Yeun Joon; Kim, Junha
theories: feedback intervention theory; peer competition; social power theory
keywords: direction of feedback flow; feedback intervention theory; meta-processes; negative feedback; recipient creativity; task processes
research_question: How does negative feedback influence recipient creativity, and why have prior studies found positive, negative, and null relationships? The paper asks whether the direction of feedback flow explains when negative feedback improves creativity through task processes and when it harms creativity through meta-processes.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that negative feedback makes recipients aware of a creativity-standard gap, but the recipient's social relationship to the sender channels attention differently. In bottom-up feedback, supervisors have social power and are more likely to treat negative feedback from followers as task-relevant information, increasing task processes and creativity. In top-down feedback, followers are vulnerable to supervisors' resource control, so negative feedback shifts attention toward threat and social evaluation. In lateral feedback, peer competition similarly makes negative feedback threatening, reducing task focus and creativity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates conflicting theories of negative feedback and creativity by organizing them around feedback intervention theory's two pathways: task processes and meta-processes. It extends feedback intervention theory by introducing direction of feedback flow as a boundary condition that determines which pathway is activated. It also argues that feedback should be conceptualized as a social flow between actors, not merely as a valenced message.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that negative feedback has a uniform effect on creativity. Bottom-up negative feedback can be useful when formal systems allow followers to give thoughtful criticism to supervisors for developmental purposes. For top-down and lateral feedback, managers should avoid interrupting active creativity tasks with negative feedback and should consider timing, follow-up sessions, and feedback forms that reduce threat and competition.
limitations: Study 1 was conducted in Korea, so national culture, shame, and power distance may have influenced responses to negative feedback, although Study 2 replicated the pattern in a North American laboratory context. Study 2 relied on undergraduate students, limiting external validity relative to employee samples. The paper also focuses on unsought negative feedback and creativity, not sought feedback, positive feedback, or routine performance.
future_research: Future research should test the model with employee samples in additional cultural contexts and examine when bottom-up negative feedback may threaten supervisors, such as when power is unstable or illegitimate. The authors also call for research on positive feedback, routine performance, and negative feedback that follows feedback seeking, because these may operate through different mechanisms from task processes and meta-processes in the present model.
abstract: Negative feedback alerts recipients to a creativity–standard gap, and thus may offer an opportunity to improve creativity. However, existing theories and empirical evidence are contradictory, with the literature containing evidence of positive, negative, and null relationships between negative feedback and recipient creativity. The goal of our research is twofold: first, to organize the contradictory theories under a comprehensive theoretical framework, and, second, to resolve the inconsistency between negative feedback and recipient creativity. Across two studies—a quasi-field experiment and a laboratory experiment—we find that the direction of feedback flow determines the nature of the relationship between negative feedback and recipient creativity, via two distinct mechanisms: task processes and meta-processes. Negative feedback increases recipient creativity in the bottom-up feedback flow (from followers to supervisors), because it heightens the recipients’ focus on task processes, whereby the recipients focus on the generation of better task strategies to close the creativity–standard gap. In contrast, in the top-down (from supervisors to followers) or lateral (between peers) feedback flows, negative feedback heightens the recipients’ focus on meta-processes—a psychological state in which recipients feel threatened by negative feedback—and thus hinders recipient creativity.

title: The Boon and Bane of Creative “Stars”: A Social Network Exploration of How and When Team Creativity Is (and Is Not) Driven by a Star Teammate
methods: Empirical quantitative study using two multiwave, multisource field samples of Chinese R&D and sales teams; the authors model direct, indirect, moderated, and moderated-mediation paths using regression analyses in Mplus with a sandwich estimator for nested teams.
industry: R&D teams from aerospace, chemicals, hydropower, manufacturing, metallurgy, and transportation firms; sales teams from two customer service firms.
time_period: R&D sample collected in two waves six months apart; sales sample collected in two waves about two months apart.
units: Teams, team members, team leaders, R&D executives, and regional sales managers.
n_sample: 84 R&D teams with 676 employees; 94 sales teams with 457 team members.
authors: Li, Yuan; Li, Ning; Li, Chuanjia; Li, Jingyu
theories: social model of team creativity (Perry-Smith & Shalley, 2003; Perry-Smith & Mannucci, 2017); star performers research (Aguinis & O'Boyle, 2014; Call, Nyberg, & Thatcher, 2015); team microdynamics perspective (Humphrey & Aime, 2014)
keywords: nonstars' learning; social model of team creativity; star centrality; team coordination; team creative stars; team creativity; workflow network
research_question: The paper asks how a team creative star's centrality in the workflow network affects team creativity. It specifically examines whether star centrality has simultaneous positive direct effects and negative indirect effects through nonstars' learning, and whether team coordination changes these effects.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is dualistic. Centrally located creative stars can improve team creativity directly because they access diverse inputs, understand team workflow, and can spread novel ideas through the team. At the same time, teammates' reliance on a central star can reduce nonstars' own exploratory and exploitative learning, which indirectly weakens team creativity. Team coordination buffers the negative learning pathway by helping members integrate actions and maintain participation rather than overdepending on the star.
theoretical_contribution:
The article extends the social model of team creativity by showing that team creativity depends on interaction patterns between creative stars and nonstars, not simply on aggregating individual creativity. It also complicates star-performer theory by showing that a central star can be both a boon and a bane for team-level creative outcomes.

The paper further contributes to team microdynamics research by placing star centrality and team coordination in the same model. Its evidence shows that team coordination weakens the negative star-centrality effect on nonstars' learning, while the predicted strengthening of the direct positive effect on creativity is unsupported and, in the R&D sample, reversed.
practical_implication:
Managers should avoid assuming that placing creative stars in central workflow positions is unambiguously beneficial. The study suggests that central creative stars can lift team creativity directly but can also suppress the learning behavior of other members.

The paper recommends supporting nonstars and promoting effective team coordination. Coordination can reduce overreliance on stars, create shared language and common goals, and encourage broader participation in the team's creative process.
limitations:
The authors note that star identification differs across the two samples and that the R&D sample's highest-rated member may not always be meaningfully superior to other members. They also caution that the China context may limit generalizability because collectivism and power distance could accentuate dependence on central creative stars.

The study focuses on how star network position affects nonstars' learning, but nonstars may also shape star performance and contribution. The direct beneficial effect of star centrality may also depend on contextual factors such as team size and network density.
future_research:
Future research could test other measures of creative stars, including objective indicators such as patents or awards, and replicate the model in other cultural contexts. Studies could also examine how network connections between stars and nonstars influence the stars' own performance.

The authors encourage work on contextual factors that shape team creative processes and on how stars and nonstars contribute differently to exploration, exploitation, radical creativity, incremental creativity, and different phases from creativity to innovation.
abstract: Although previous research has highlighted the disproportional contributions of star employees to their teams, an emerging line of research has begun to examine the potentially negative consequences of team stars. Drawing on a social model of team creativity, we develop a dualistic model of the influences of team creative stars on team creativity. Specifically, we explore the roles of two types of team members—star and nonstar employees—in driving team creativity. Across two multiwave and multisource field samples, we find that a creative star who occupies a central position in the team workflow network has both a positive direct effect on team creativity and a negative indirect effect on team creativity via reducing nonstars’ learning (i.e., exploratory and exploitative activities). Our study also reveals that team coordination can mitigate the detrimental effect of a star’s centrality on nonstars’ learning behavior, and subsequently buffer the indirect effect on team creativity.
apa_citation: Li, Y., Li, N., Li, C., & Li, J. (2020). The boon and bane of creative “stars”: A social network exploration of how and when team creativity is (and is not) driven by a star teammate. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(2), 613-635. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0283

title: Relational Reconciliation: Socializing Others across Demographic Differences
methods: Empirical qualitative, theory-building study based primarily on semi-structured interviews with tutors in an urban charter high school, supplemented by administrator interviews, observations of training and leadership sessions, internal documents, and iterative inductive coding.
industry: Urban charter high school / educational socialization context.
time_period: Data collection included administrator interviews and meetings over a three-year period; tutor interviews covered two cohorts.
units: Tutors as socialization agents, with administrators, students, training practices, and documents providing context.
n_sample: 58 individuals: six administrators and 52 tutors.
authors: Ramarajan, L.; Reid, E.
theories: identity work; relational identity negotiation; social identity threat; socialization theory
keywords: demographic differences; diversity; elaborated socialization; identity; relational reconciliation; social identity threat; socialization agents
research_question: The paper asks how socialization agents in demographically diverse work contexts navigate the tension between organizational demands to assimilate members into a collective and socializees' demands for recognition of race, class, and other identity differences. It studies tutors in an urban charter school where largely White, middle- and upper-class educators socialized largely racial-ethnic minority and lower-income students into a dominant professional culture.
mechanism_summary:
- Competing demands: The organization demands assimilation into middle- and professional-class norms, while students demand recognition of demographic identity differences and inequalities.
- Identity threat: Tutors fear being seen through negative race and class stereotypes, such as privileged oppressors, saviors, or betrayers.
- Relational approaches: Tutors use multifaceted disclosure and empathic inquiry to engage students rather than avoid identity difference.
- Moments: These approaches produce moments of closeness and moments of estrangement, both of which reshape how tutors understand themselves in relation to students.
- Self-constructions: Tutors learn to hold connected and distant selves at the same time.
- Emergent practices: This bridging enables elaborated socialization: personalized practices and personal rules combined with expected organizational practices.

The process is recursive rather than linear. When tutors anchor only on connection, they risk abandoning the school's expected practices; when they anchor only on distance, they risk implementing impersonal prescribed practices that amplify students' recognition demands. Relational reconciliation allows them to keep both facets in view, reducing identity threat and supporting more responsive socialization across demographic divides.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to socialization research by repositioning socialization agents as active parties whose identities are threatened and transformed through socialization, rather than as passive transmitters of organizational tactics. It contributes to identity and diversity scholarship by theorizing relational reconciliation as an interpersonal way of engaging social identity threat. It also shows that socialization practices can vary because agents experience misalignment with organizational assimilation demands, not only because socializees react differently.
practical_implication: The study suggests that employees and leaders working across race and class divides should treat the work as self-transformation, not only as learning about the other. Organizations that seek to reduce inequality should make room for employees to experiment, stumble, and develop inclusive practices rather than simply enforcing uniform socialization systems. Leaders should also examine whether expected practices reproduce assimilation pressures and should surface effective alternative practices already emerging in local work.
limitations: The authors note that the setting had strong institutionalized socialization practices and strong norms of colorblindness and professionalism, so future work should test whether the process operates similarly in weaker or more individualized socialization contexts. Tutors occupied a one-year role, and their transience may have made it easier to construct distance from students. The study also examined minors being socialized into societal professional norms, giving tutors more authority than agents may have when socializing adults into internal organizational roles.
future_research: Future research should examine relational reconciliation in other organizational settings, including contexts with weaker assimilation norms and less prosocial missions. The authors call for work on how role transience, authority differences, social class, and intersections of gender, race, and class shape the process. They also encourage large-sample studies of whether relational reconciliation differs across identities and studies of how elaborated socialization affects socializees' performance and well-being.
abstract: In demographically diverse organizations, employees charged with socializing others— socialization agents—must navigate a deep tension between the organization’s needs to integrate individuals into a collective and individuals’ needs for recognition of their unique identities. Through a qualitative study of employees in an urban charter high school where race and class inequalities are salient, we find that socialization agents experience this tension as identity threatening. We develop a theoretical model of relational reconciliation that traces how agents engage with this identity threat in an ongoing, stumbling process. Through relational reconciliation, agents come to redefine their selves in relation to their “socializees,” which enables them to engage in elaborated socialization practices that aim to meet the needs of both the organization and the socializee. Our work repositions socialization agents as active parties in socialization, explores the tensions of socializing members of marginalized groups into a dominant culture, and reveals the importance of engaging with one’s own identities to reconcile these tensions.

title: How Formal and Informal Hierarchies Shape Conflict within Cooperatives: A Field Experiment in Ghana
methods: Empirical mixed-method field experiment in newly formed cooperatives in rural Ghana. The quantitative analysis randomly assigned cooperatives to flat or formal hierarchical control structures and used ANOVA, OLS, bootstrapped mediation, and moderated mediation; follow-up qualitative interviews illustrated the proposed mechanisms.
industry: Income-generating cooperative microenterprises producing shea butter, soap, or baskets.
country: Ghana, focused on the rural northern and upper east regions around Tamale and Bolgatanga.
time_period: Fieldwork spanned six trips between 2014 and 2017; training occurred in September 2015, the quantitative survey in September 2016, and follow-up interviews after final data collection.
units: Newly formed income-generating cooperative groups, with member survey responses aggregated to the group level.
n_sample: 40 cooperative groups in the final quantitative sample: 22 in the hierarchy condition and 18 in the flat condition.
authors: Slade Shantz, A. F.; Kistruck, G. M.; Pacheco, D. F.; Webb, J. W.
theories: collective psychological ownership; cooperative ownership and control-structure fit; formal and informal hierarchy
keywords: Ghana; collective psychological ownership; cooperatives; field experiment; formal hierarchy; informal hierarchy; intragroup conflict
research_question: The paper asks whether formal hierarchy reduces or exacerbates conflict within cooperatives, and whether informal hierarchy changes that relationship. It studies newly formed cooperatives in rural Ghana to test whether formal hierarchical control structures weaken collective psychological ownership and thereby increase intragroup conflict relative to flat structures.
mechanism_summary:
- Qualitative process evidence: Follow-up interviews with selected cooperatives illustrated how hierarchy shaped role confusion, shirking, learning, knowledge sharing, and deference to elders.

The proposed mechanism is that pairing equal cooperative ownership with unequal formal control differentiates roles and authority, shifting members from a collective "we" orientation toward a more individualistic "me" orientation. That lower collective psychological ownership reduces shared responsibility and makes conflict more likely. Informal hierarchy, especially age-based authority in the Ghanaian context, attenuates this effect because elder authority can clarify roles and provide socially legitimate conflict-avoidance guidance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to cooperative theory by explaining why formal hierarchy may increase, rather than reduce, conflict when it conflicts with equal ownership. It identifies collective psychological ownership as a mechanism linking formal structure to conflict and shows that informal hierarchy conditions this relationship. It also extends hierarchy research by showing that formal and informal hierarchies can coexist and interact, rather than simply substitute for one another.
practical_implication: For development organizations and other actors forming cooperatives, the study cautions against assuming that formal hierarchy will solve coordination and conflict problems. In early-stage cooperatives, formal hierarchy may damage members' shared sense of ownership enough to outweigh coordination benefits. Flat structures may be especially useful when organizations need members to develop broad responsibility, shared learning, and mutual support.
limitations: The authors note that the study was conducted in a context where informal hierarchy was highly salient, so the boundary conditions may differ where informal hierarchy is weaker. The cooperative members were almost exclusively women, raising the possibility that gendered preferences for flat structures or shared decision making partly shaped the results. The cooperatives were small and resource-constrained, and the study did not measure whether elected formal leaders overlapped with informal hierarchy status.
future_research: Future research should examine formal and informal hierarchy in contexts where informal hierarchy is less salient, in larger cooperatives, and in settings where flat structures may create territoriality rather than redundancy. The authors also call for work on whether formal and informal hierarchy become more congruent in more educated or resource-rich contexts, whether rotating hierarchy positions changes collective psychological ownership, and whether longer-term data reveal benefits of hierarchy beyond conflict reduction.
abstract: As an organizational form, cooperatives are increasingly being used throughout the world across different industries and sectors. While it has been suggested that various benefits can be derived from shared ownership, cooperatives are often characterized by conflict among members that, in turn, can lead to eventual failure of the cooperatives. Existing theory has suggested that the choice of formal control structure can play an important role in mitigating conflict, but a longstanding debate exists as to whether flat versus hierarchical control structures are more effective. To add further insight into this theoretical discussion, we conducted a field experiment involving 40 newly formed cooperatives in rural Ghana, which were randomly assigned to either a flat or hierarchical control structure. The quantitative results of our field experiment and subsequent qualitative data suggest that formal hierarchical control structures lead to lower levels of collective psychological ownership, which in turn result in higher levels of conflict compared to flat control structures within cooperatives. However, our results also suggest that the extent to which the choice of formal control structures influences conflict among cooperative members can be highly dependent on the absence or presence of an informal hierarchy.

title: Cocreating Rigorous and Relevant Knowledge
methods: An empirical qualitative process study of NBS cocreation projects, combining real-time observations of two projects, interviews with prior project participants, focus groups, workshops, documents, memos, and iterative qualitative analysis.
industry: Business sustainability research-practice collaboration.
time_period: Project 1 meetings ran from January 2014 to September 2014; Project 2 meetings ran from February 2015 to August 2015.
units: Two NBS cocreation projects involving researchers, managers, NBS staff, and academic advisors, plus participants in similar previous projects.
n_sample: Two observed projects; 67 interviews with 47 individuals; 20 meetings and focus groups.
authors: Sharma, G.; Bansal, P.
theories: process ontology; research-practice knowledge cocreation; temporality in organizational studies
keywords: business sustainability; cocreation; incomplete objects; process ontology; research-practice gap; rigor and relevance; temporal connections
research_question: The paper asks how researchers and managers imbricate rigorous and relevant knowledge, given the challenges inherent in the cocreation process. It focuses on how researcher and practitioner knowledge systems become connected over time rather than only within discrete collaboration events.
mechanism_summary:
- Research-practice tension: Researchers seek generalizable and defensible rigor, while managers seek relevant, context-specific, prescriptive knowledge.
- Process lens: Cocreation is treated as continuous becoming, not as a bounded event with a simple success or failure outcome.
- Temporal device: Participants make connections between past, present, and future joint events, keeping apparently weak events in the context of the whole project.
- Object device: Participants recognize objects such as frameworks, slides, diagrams, and reports as incomplete, which invites contribution and shows that inputs can change the project.
- Emergent outcome: Rigor and relevance become imbricated over time as researchers and managers work together, retreat to their own knowledge systems, and revise objects across events.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. Sharma and Bansal show that researcher-manager cocreation advances when actors can see the ongoing process and can see objects changing through their contributions. Temporal connections sustain participation across disappointing or non-dialogic events, while incomplete objects create openings for managers and researchers to contribute without either knowledge system being collapsed into the other.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on the research-practice gap by shifting the analysis of cocreation from event-based or synoptic accounts to a process ontology. It theorizes temporal connections and incomplete objects as devices that make the process visible to participants and help explain how rigor and relevance can be imbricated rather than traded off. It also extends work on engaged scholarship and knowledge cocreation by showing that cocreation occurs between events as well as within dialogic encounters.
practical_implication: For facilitators of researcher-practitioner collaboration, the study suggests designing projects so participants can see continuity across meetings and can work with objects that are visibly unfinished. Failed or non-dialogic interactions need not derail a project if participants can connect them to prior progress, future possibilities, and evolving outputs. Researchers should preserve rigor, but also show how practitioner input has been considered, incorporated, revised, or rejected.
limitations: The authors identify boundary conditions around the type of knowledge, the structure of the NBS process, and empirical generalizability. Some domains, such as climate change policy debates, may require expert knowledge transfer rather than cocreation because treating settled science as open to cocreation could stall action. The study is also grounded in NBS's structured series of meetings with a clear beginning and end, so other cocreation processes may reveal additional devices.
future_research: Future research could examine other forms of cross-boundary knowledge work, including interdisciplinary research and sustainability institutes. Scholars could study whether temporal connections and incomplete objects operate similarly in less structured collaborations or in contexts without a clear project endpoint. Further work could also identify additional devices that make cocreation processes visible to participants.
abstract: The communities of research and practice are embedded in different knowledge systems; research favors rigor, while practice favors relevance. Many management scholars have concluded that cocreating knowledge with these two knowledge systems is difficult and rare, with such criticisms or reservations often being based on an event-based account of cocreation in which the cocreation activities occur over a distinct period of time with a clear beginning and end. However, event-based accounts bring the challenges of cocreation into focus. In the present research, we have assumed a process ontology, which brings the dynamics into focus and recognizes that cocreation is continuous. We observed two projects in which researchers and managers collaborated to generate knowledge related to business sustainability, and conducted 67 interviews with 47 participants in similar projects. We found that, by making the process explicit, participants were better able to cocreate knowledge. Furthermore, we identified two devices that helped to make the process explicit: (1) making temporal connections between events and (2) recognizing the incompleteness of the objects. Our study contributes to prior research on cocreation by showing that cocreation occurs not just within events but also between events, so that rigor and relevance are imbricated over time.

title: The Genesis and Metamorphosis of Novelty Imprints: How Business Model Innovation Emerges in Young Ventures
methods: Empirical qualitative longitudinal multiple-case study using interviews, real-time observation, internal documents, archival data, temporal bracketing, replication logic, member checks, and iterative coding.
industry: Young ventures in health care information systems, mobile applications, online vacation rentals, social networks, online fashion, and travel services.
country: One European country; the specific country is anonymized in the article.
time_period: Ventures were founded between 2008 and 2009, data collection began in 2011, and business models were tracked from founding until 2017.
units: Six new ventures, with founders, employees, investors, board members, customers, meetings, internal documents, and archival sources.
n_sample: Six ventures; 53 interviews, 16 observed meetings, and 1,270 pages of internal documents.
authors: Snihur, Y.; Zott, C.
theories: business model innovation as a boundary-spanning activity system; imprinting theory
keywords: business model innovation; cognitive imprinting; founder novelty orientation; imprinting theory; novelty imprinting; structural imprinting
research_question: The paper asks how, if at all, founders imprint business model novelty in young ventures. It examines how business model innovation can emerge and persist despite imprinting theory's usual emphasis on stability and inertia.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: Business model innovation, novelty imprinting, founder novelty orientation, structural imprinting, cognitive imprinting, and high versus low BMI.
- High-BMI founder practices: Industry-spanning search, complex system thinking style, and powerful centralized decision making.
- Low-BMI founder practices: Industry-focused search, internal efficiency thinking style, and organic decentralized decision making.
- Imprinting pathways: Structural imprinting directly shapes business model content, governance, and structure; cognitive imprinting transmits founder practices to venture members.
- Enablers: Employee selection, memorable early mentoring, and role modeling help founder practices become cognitive imprints.
- Reinforcement: Venture members' cognitive imprints reinforce structural imprints, sustaining either high novelty or low novelty over time.

The process is not a variable-based causal test. The authors theorize that founders imprint business model novelty through two linked pathways: founders directly shape early business model structures, and they also shape employees' cognition so that employees later enact and reproduce founder-oriented practices. In high-BMI ventures, the founder practices orient members toward distant search, system-level thinking, and decisive implementation; in low-BMI ventures, the corresponding practices orient members toward industry imitation, efficiency, and consensus-bound incrementalism.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to imprinting theory by developing the concept of novelty imprinting, showing that imprinting can produce and sustain novel structural imprints rather than only organizational inertia. It also specifies cognitive imprinting as a cross-level process through which employees assimilate founder practices and reinforce structural imprints. For business model innovation research, the paper identifies founder novelty orientation as a mechanism linking founder practices to the emergence and persistence of BMI.
practical_implication: The study suggests that founders have substantial influence over early business model structures and over the cognitive practices that later become institutionalized in ventures. It implies that founders should be deliberate about search boundaries, system-level thinking, decision authority, hiring, mentoring, and role modeling because these practices may become difficult to change after the early imprinting period.
limitations: The authors note that the study sampled new ventures in a few industries in one country and followed them for about 10 years, which limits generalizability across industries and national environments. The study focuses on business models, so it does not establish whether similar imprinting mechanisms explain other venture features such as resources or culture. It also does not test whether early high-BMI ventures perform better or worse than ventures that pivot toward more novel business models later.
future_research: Future research could study different industries and countries to examine environmental variation in novelty imprinting. The authors also call for work on whether and how other venture features, such as resources or culture, are imprinted, and for closer examination of founder power in BMI design and implementation. Additional research could compare the performance of ventures that introduce high BMI early with ventures that shift from incremental to more novel business models later.
abstract: In this research, we ask whether and how founders bring about business model innovation. Grounded in an in-depth longitudinal multiple-case study, our analysis reveals three practices that help explain how founders' thinking patterns and behaviors shape business model innovation in their ventures: industry-spanning search, complex system thinking style, and powerful centralized decision making. Three corresponding yet opposing founder practices are present in cases with low business model innovation. When interpreted through the lens of imprinting theory, our findings reveal how founders achieve novelty imprinting, which we conceive as imprinting processes that result in novel imprints. Our emergent theoretical framework affirms the possibility of novelty imprinting, and thus explains a puzzle regarding the coexistence of imprint stability and novel structure. It also delineates the nature of cognitive imprinting and explains how cognitive imprints reinforce structural imprints in the context of business model innovation, thereby expanding the scope of imprinting and business model research.

title: The Legitimacy Threshold Revisited: How Prior Successes and Failures Spill Over to Other Endeavors on Kickstarter
methods: Large-scale longitudinal study of Kickstarter campaigns using generalized least squares models, with robustness checks, difference-in-differences analysis, propensity score matching, and qualitative content analysis of Kickstarter Campus discussions.
industry: Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns across 15 basic categories and 165 subordinate categories.
country: Campaigns launched in 194 countries, with the United States as the omitted referent in country controls.
time_period: April 2009 through December 2014.
units: Crowdfunding campaigns / entrepreneurial endeavors.
n_sample: 182,358 entrepreneurial endeavors from 156,028 entrepreneurs; 7,026,260 unique backers; 17,440,089 pledges.
authors: Soublière, J.-F.; Gehman, J.
theories: institutional theory of legitimacy; legitimacy threshold (Zimmerman & Zeitz, 2002); recursive model of legitimacy
keywords: Kickstarter; crowdfunding; entrepreneurial endeavors; legitimacy spillovers; legitimacy threshold
research_question: How does the legitimacy bestowed upon prior entrepreneurial endeavors affect the legitimacy of subsequent related endeavors? The paper asks whether the magnitude and type of prior success or failure on Kickstarter change how audiences support later campaigns in the same category.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that prior campaign outcomes prime audiences' legitimacy assessments of related later campaigns. Blockbuster successes and path breaking failures expand the carrying capacity for subsequent campaigns by encouraging audience support, whereas unsung successes and broken path failures reduce later support. The mechanism is recursive because individual legitimation outcomes collectively flow back into the category and shape later resource acquisition.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to legitimacy theory by showing that legitimacy is not only a threshold crossed by individual endeavors but also a recursive category-level process. It qualifies the usual positive view of legitimacy by showing that prior successes can be detrimental and prior failures can be beneficial, depending on their magnitude. It also reframes entrepreneurial categories as simultaneously cooperative and competitive spaces rather than as moving cleanly from cooperation to competition as they mature.
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs using crowdfunding platforms should attend to recent outcomes in their category because those outcomes can alter audience receptivity before a focal campaign launches. The findings also imply that entrepreneurs need to cultivate new audiences rather than rely only on established category backers, since established backers are especially exposed to spillover effects from prior successes and failures.
limitations: The analysis is observational and uses resource acquisition as a proxy for legitimacy, so related social evaluation constructs such as reputation, celebrity, certification, or authenticity may partly overlap with the measured effects. The empirical setting is a transparent crowdfunding platform, which may amplify spillovers relative to settings where successes and failures are less visible. The paper also focuses on campaigns at an early conception-stage legitimacy threshold, leaving later market performance outside the analysis.
future_research: Future research could examine backers' decision-making processes more directly and separate legitimacy from other social evaluations. Scholars could test whether similar success and failure spillovers appear in other settings, such as record labels, studio pitches, academic publishing, or other entrepreneurial platforms. The authors also call for work on transparency and secrecy, cross-platform spillovers, later marketplace outcomes, and textual or visual cultural spillovers in crowdfunding pitches.
abstract: How does the legitimacy conferred on entrepreneurial endeavors affect the legitimacy of subsequent ones? We extend the notion of a “legitimacy threshold” to develop and test a recursive model of legitimacy. Whereas extant research has focused on whether entrepreneurial endeavors garner sufficient support from key audiences to cross this threshold, we argue that the order of magnitude by which they succeed or fail is also consequential for later entrants. Distinguishing “blockbuster” from “unsung” successes, and “path breaking” from “broken path” failures, we contend that recent successes and failures affect related subsequent endeavors in predictable, though sometimes counterintuitive ways. We test our hypotheses by examining 182,358 entrepreneurial endeavors pitched within 165 categories over a six-year period on Kickstarter, one of the most important crowdfunding platforms. We show that individual outcomes, taken collectively, generate legitimacy spillovers, either by encouraging audiences to repeatedly support other related endeavors or by discouraging them from doing so. Our research contributes to understanding the recursive nature of legitimacy, the competitive dynamics of entrepreneurial efforts, and crowdfunding platforms.

title: From “That’s Interesting” to “That’s Important”
methods: Editorial essay contrasting interestingness with important, problem-driven management research and discussing implications for AMJ authors, reviewers, and evaluators.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Tihanyi, Laszlo
theories: Davis's theory of interestingness; problem-driven research
keywords: important management research; interestingness; practical implications; problem-driven research; societal problems; theoretical contributions
research_question: The editorial asks why management research should move beyond merely interesting findings toward important problems with societal relevance. It focuses on the trade-offs created when AMJ submissions prioritize counterintuitive interestingness over research that can improve organizations, managerial behavior, and society.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: The pursuit of interestingness can encourage catchy titles, counterintuitive propositions, complex post hoc models, and thin practical implications.
- Field-level concern: Easy access to large data sets and analytical tools can make unusual or surprising effects easier to find while weakening attention to meaningful relationships and societal problems.
- Alternative standard: Important management research should address problems involving organizations and management that affect individuals, communities, stakeholders, and societies.
- Editorial implication: AMJ should recognize problem-driven, societally relevant work without treating theoretical contribution and practical importance as substitutes.
- Evaluation system: Schools, journals, citations, media incentives, and reviewer patience shape whether scholars are rewarded for important research or for attention-grabbing findings.

The process logic is editorial rather than causal. Tihanyi argues that an overemphasis on interestingness can shift scholarly effort toward surprising findings and away from questions that matter for workplace abuse, dishonest communication, state-owned enterprises, ethical leadership, inclusion, international trade, and societal crises. The essay positions problem-driven research as a way to develop stronger theory while helping managers and organizations address consequential problems.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a new theory. Its contribution is to sharpen the distinction between interestingness and importance as evaluative standards for management scholarship, arguing that problem-driven research can be both theoretically meaningful and socially consequential.
practical_implication: Authors should frame AMJ submissions around important managerial and organizational problems rather than relying mainly on surprising associations, rare settings, or counterintuitive effects. Editors, reviewers, and schools should reward research that has societal relevance, practical implications beyond short-term profit motives, and potential value for stakeholders and communities.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editorial calls for more research on questions such as how corporate innovations can improve or save lives, when international trade benefits countries and people, how managers can improve working conditions, how organizations can become more inclusive, and how business and government can address societal problems and crises. It also encourages theory development that helps improve managerial behavior and organizational action in response to major societal challenges.

title: Dissonant Ties in Intraorganizational Networks: Why Individuals Seek Problem-Solving Assistance from Difficult Colleagues
methods: Empirical mixed-method study using whole-network survey data from engineers in one large manufacturing firm's engineering department, logistic and negative binomial regressions for performance consequences, multiplex ERGM for tie-formation drivers, and semi-structured interviews analyzed with NVivo to interpret mechanisms.
industry: Aerospace engineering in the engineering department of a large manufacturing firm.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Engineers, directed problem-solving ties, difficult working relationships, and dissonant ties.
n_sample: 239 engineers invited to the survey, 171 completed questionnaires, and 18 semi-structured interviews.
authors: Brennecke, Julia
theories: cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1957); cognitive-consequentialist instrumental networking and cost-benefit theorizing (Borgatti & Cross, 2003; Nebus, 2006); network multiplexity perspective (Kilduff & Brass, 2010); social ledger theory (Labianca & Brass, 2006)
keywords: difficult colleagues; dissonant ties; instrumental networking behavior; intraorganizational networks; organizational architecture; problem-solving assistance
research_question: The paper asks why employees seek problem-solving assistance from colleagues with whom they have difficult working relationships. It examines whether these dissonant ties improve individual performance and how formal hierarchical rank, tenure, and unit membership shape employees' willingness to form them.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cost-benefit account of instrumental networking under cognitive inconsistency. Employees may approach difficult colleagues when the expected work benefits of unique knowledge, assumption-challenging interaction, and improved problem solving outweigh the unpleasantness and risks of the tie. The evidence suggests that dissonant ties are associated with higher effectiveness evaluations, while shorter-tenured egos, longer-tenured alters, tenure similarity, and cross-unit boundaries make dissonant tie formation more likely; high-ranking difficult alters are avoided because they carry disproportionate risk.
theoretical_contribution:
The article introduces dissonant ties as a cognition-based positive-negative network multiplexity construct and shows that positive and negative workplace ties need not be mutually exclusive or neutralize each other. It extends social ledger theory by showing that overlapping positive and negative ties can generate distinct instrumental benefits rather than simply offsetting benefits and liabilities.

The study also contributes to intraorganizational network research by connecting the performance consequences and formation drivers of a new tie type. By linking dissonant tie formation to formal hierarchical rank, tenure, and unit membership, it explains why employees sometimes seek assistance from difficult colleagues despite prior evidence that people avoid disliked or difficult others.
practical_implication:
For knowledge-intensive work, difficult colleagues should not be treated only as relational liabilities. The study suggests that some difficult colleagues provide valuable problem-solving resources, especially when their expertise or tenure makes their knowledge useful.

At the same time, the usefulness of these ties depends on organizational context. Managers should recognize that high-ranking difficult colleagues may be avoided because of perceived career risk, while cross-unit distance may make difficult but useful interactions easier to sustain.
limitations:
The cross-sectional design does not allow causal testing of the relationship between dissonant ties and performance or of the interplay between positive and negative networks. The author notes that performance may also influence dissonant tie formation, and that longitudinal or experimental research is needed to confirm the causal direction.

The performance measure is limited to effectiveness, so the study does not test whether dissonant ties similarly affect efficiency or innovativeness. The paper also does not quantitatively test the proposed mediating mechanisms, and its conceptualization focuses on the simultaneity of positive and negative cognition-based ties rather than their strength or differentiated content.
future_research:
Future research could use longitudinal, experimental, or dynamic network designs to study causal direction, coevolution of positive and negative ties, and the short-term fluctuation or long-term stability of dissonant ties. It could also test mediators of the dissonant tie-performance relationship to compare the relative roles of unique resources, challenged assumptions, diverse perspectives, and cognitive activity.

The author encourages refinement of the construct by examining the strength of positive and negative tie components and by differentiating the qualities that make a colleague difficult, such as arrogance, different priorities, or hindering work. Further work could also extend the analysis beyond ego, alter, and dyad effects to triads and balance theory in positive-negative multiplex networks.
abstract: This paper investigates employees seeking problem-solving assistance from colleagues with whom they find it difficult to work. In so doing, the paper introduces the construct of “dissonant ties”: network ties to colleagues that are simultaneously positive and negative. The study builds on the assumption that individuals in knowledge-intensive workplaces employ dissonant ties to access distinct work-related benefits, and establishes a link between dissonant ties and performance. Subsequently, it provides an in-depth analysis of employees’ willingness to rely on this potentially unpleasant but instrumental networking behavior, and suggests that formal hierarchical rank, tenure, and unit membership, as critical elements of the organizational architecture, drive dissonant tie formation. In the empirical analysis, the study utilizes survey and interview data collected from engineers in a large manufacturing firm. The findings confirm that seeking problem-solving assistance from difficult colleagues entails performance benefits. Moreover, the embeddedness of individuals in the organizational architecture shapes the employment of dissonant ties. Dissonant ties are, hence, context driven. By simultaneously addressing the consequences and the drivers of employees’ networking behavior, the study presents a comprehensive theory of dissonant ties that challenges and refines previous research on the interplay between positive and negative networks.

title: Constructing and Sustaining Counter-Institutional Identities
methods: Qualitative multiple case study of four Assertive Community Treatment teams, using semi-structured interviews, nonparticipant meeting observations, documents, within-case analysis, and cross-case analysis.
industry: Mental health care; Assertive Community Treatment teams serving clients with severe and persistent mental illness.
time_period: 2010-2013, with team-specific data collection periods reported in Table 2.
units: Four ACT teams and their members.
n_sample: 51 team members; 55 interviews totaling 1,362 pages; 17 observed meetings totaling 122 pages.
authors: Chreim, S.; Langley, A.; Reay, T.; Comeau-Vallée, M.; Huq, J.-L.
theories: authoritative texts; counter-institutional identity construction; identity foil; identity regulation; identity work
keywords: Assertive Community Treatment; authoritative texts; counter-institutional identity; identity foil; identity work
research_question: How do individuals and collectives construct and sustain counter-institutional identities? The paper examines this question in ACT teams whose values, roles, and practices are positioned against the dominant hospital-based medical model of mental health care.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: counter-institutional identity, identity foil, authoritative texts, oppositional identity work, relational identity work, and encapsulation.
- Setting / contrast: ACT teams are defined against the dominant hospital-based medical model through recovery-oriented values, generalist roles, and pride in work with stigmatized clients.
- Process / practices: leaders model and filter; groups regulate and bond; individual members reframe and self-select.
- Cross-level dynamics: mutually reinforcing leader, group, and member identity work strengthens boundaries around "who we are" while preserving the foil of "who we are not."
- Boundary variation: Alpha exemplifies strong encapsulation; Gamma and Delta are becoming ACT; Omega approximates ACT with more permeable boundaries and internalized tensions.

The process is not a variable-based causal mechanism but a cross-level identity construction process. Authoritative ACT Standards provide identity prescriptions and legitimate roles; leaders, groups, and members then enact identity work that excludes elements of the dominant institution while elevating counter-institutional values, roles, and practices as superior. Strong counter-institutional identity depends on both oppositional identity work against the foil and relational identity work that supports members inside the group.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops counter-institutional identity construction as a distinctive identity phenomenon in which individuals and groups define "who we are" through direct opposition to dominant institutional values, roles, and practices. It contributes a cross-level model showing how authoritative texts, leader identity work, group identity work, and member identity work interact to construct and sustain such identities. It also theorizes encapsulation and the identity foil as central to explaining why some counter-institutional identities become coherent and durable while others remain fragmented.
practical_implication: For groups or organizations grounded in counter-institutional principles, leaders need to recognize that members must do identity work to define themselves against the dominant institution and to see difference as a source of pride. Authoritative texts such as standards, charters, founding documents, or legislation can guide modeling, filtering, regulating, bonding, reframing, and self-selection. Managers can use these texts to sustain counter-institutional identity in established arrangements or in novel organizational forms that depart from institutionalized models.
limitations: The study is grounded in four ACT teams in Canadian mental health care, so transferability depends on whether other settings share similar authoritative texts, social goals, work-group forms, and relationships to a dominant institutional model. The authors identify boundary conditions around whether a counter-institutional setting is localized or part of a wider movement, whether it is oriented toward social and other-oriented goals, and whether it is a work group, organization, or voluntary collective. They also note that encapsulation can have a darker side in less laudable counter-institutional settings.
future_research: Future research could examine how counter-institutional pockets seed deeper institutional change as they become partly institutionalized themselves. It could also study whether other-oriented goals affect the sustainability of counter-institutional identities and how organizational form changes the relative importance of leader filtering, group regulation, member self-selection, and authoritative texts. The authors also call for more attention to the darker side of counter-institutional identity dynamics.
abstract: How do individuals and collectives construct and sustain identities that run counter to dominant institutions? We develop the notion of counter-institutional identity as involving individual and collective constructions of “who we are” that are in strong opposition to dominant values and principles in the field, diverge from roles that are established through socialization and training, and involve practices that are proudly construed in direct contrast to field norms. We draw on findings from a comparative case study of Assertive Community Treatment teams to theorize about the identity work of groups and individuals that enables and constrains counter-institutional identity constructions. We develop a cross-level process model of encapsulation in which authoritative texts (or prescriptive documents) play a role in sanctioning and enhancing counter-institutional identities. The model shows how rigorous positioning against “who we are not” (an “identity foil”) through practices of oppositional identity work are combined with practices of relational identity work that reinforce counter-institutional identities by positively valuing “who we are” as superior to the foil. These practices are crucial to understanding how and why counter-institutional identities are created and sustained.

title: Across the Great Divides: Gender Dynamics Influence How Intercultural Conflict Helps or Hurts Creative Collaboration
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design: Study 1 used a laboratory collaboration task with business-student dyads, video-coded conflict and information elaboration, and expert-rated poster creativity; Study 2 used a matched field survey of U.S. employee-colleague intercultural dyads, regression models, simple slopes, and bootstrapped mediation tests.
industry: Study 1: business students in a laboratory collaboration task; Study 2: employees across accounting, banking and finance, higher education, health care, media, fashion, information technology, and other industries.
country: Study 1: a large Asian university; Study 2: United States.
time_period: Study 1 involved a short laboratory collaboration; Study 2 dyads had known each other for an average of 6.19 years. Calendar data-collection dates are not reported in paper.
units: Collaborating dyads: student dyads in Study 1 and matched employee-colleague intercultural dyads in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1 recruited 450 business students and analyzed 197 complete videos for coded measures; Study 2's final sample consisted of 139 matched intercultural employee-colleague dyads.
authors: Chua, Roy; Jin, Mengzi
theories: categorization-elaboration model; conflict-outcome moderated model; gender-in-context perspective; social role theory
keywords: creativity; dyad gender; information elaboration; intercultural conflict; intercultural creative collaboration; relationship conflict; task conflict
research_question: How does dyad gender shape whether intercultural task conflict and relationship conflict help or hurt creative collaboration effectiveness? The paper asks whether women and men dyads manage intercultural conflict differently, and whether information elaboration explains the resulting effects on creativity.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that gender is a salient social cue in intercultural same-gender collaboration, so collaborators enact gendered conflict-management expectations when cultural differences generate disagreement. Women dyads are expected to handle task conflict more cooperatively, which supports exchange, discussion, and integration of task-relevant information and helps turn task conflict into creative collaboration benefits. Men dyads are expected to handle task conflict more competitively, reducing information elaboration and lowering creativity. Relationship conflict generally disrupts collaboration, but it is especially damaging for women dyads because attention to relational repair diverts effort from task-relevant information elaboration.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a gender-and-conflict contingency model explaining why intercultural collaboration does not always produce creativity benefits despite access to nonredundant ideas. It integrates conflict-outcome and categorization-elaboration perspectives by specifying information elaboration as the process through which intercultural task and relationship conflict affect creative collaboration under different dyad-gender conditions. It also extends gender-and-creativity research from individual creativity and group gender diversity to same-gender intercultural dyadic collaboration.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat intercultural creative dyads as uniformly beneficial or uniformly risky. Women dyads may be especially able to use task conflict productively, but they may also need stronger relational foundations before creative work when relationship conflict is likely. Men dyads may be less derailed by relationship conflict, but the paper suggests they need more cooperative conflict-management approaches to use intercultural task conflict for creativity.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 offered less concrete evidence about how relationship conflict was managed because the short laboratory interactions did not allow relationship conflict to meaningfully arise. They also acknowledge that dyad gender could affect conflict emergence as well as conflict handling, although their research focuses on what happens after intercultural conflict exists. Study 2 collected variables at the same time point, raising common-method concerns, although responses came from both members of each dyad and were aggregated.
future_research: Future research should measure how women and men handle relationship conflict in more realistic organizational settings. The authors also call for work on how conflict-management behaviors feed back into later conflict formation, whether trust is an alternative mechanism linking intercultural conflict and creative collaboration, and whether relationship-conflict effects also appear in same-culture collaborations.
abstract: Collaborating across cultures can potentially increase creativity owing to access to diverse ideas and perspectives, but this benefit is not always realized. One reason for this is that the conflict that arises in intercultural creative collaboration is a double-edged sword, and so how it is managed matters. In this research, we examine how the gender of collaborating dyads influences the link between intercultural conflict (task and relationship) and creative collaboration effectiveness. Through two studies (a laboratory study and a field survey), we found that intercultural task conflict has a negative effect on creative collaboration in men dyads but a positive effect on creative collaboration in women dyads. Conversely, intercultural relationship conflict has a negative impact on creative collaboration in general, but this effect is stronger for women dyads than for men dyads. These effects can be traced to how men versus women dyads handled intercultural conflict. There is also evidence that information elaboration (exchange, discussion, and integration of task-relevant information and ideas) mediates the effects of dyad gender and intercultural conflict on creative collaboration. These findings extend current understanding of when and how intercultural collaborations can result in creativity benefits from a gender and conflict management perspective.
