title: Token Female Voice Enactment in Traditionally Male-Dominated Teams: Facilitating Conditions and Consequences for Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative field experiment in a controlled U.S. Marine Corps training facility; participants were randomly assigned to all-male or female-token teams, rotated through leadership roles, completed four counterbalanced tasks varying in complexity, and were observed in real time, with hierarchical linear modeling used for task episodes nested within teams.
industry: Military training and combat-related team tasks
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Active-duty enlisted personnel in 39 all-male or female-token teams, generating 156 team-task observations
n_sample: 173 enlisted personnel
authors: Farh, Crystal I. C.; Oh, Jo K.; Hollenbeck, John R.; Yu, Andrew; Lee, Stephanie M.; King, Danielle D.
theories: gender stereotypes; minority influence; tokenism
keywords: leader's gender beliefs; minority influence; task complexity; team performance; token female voice enactment; traditionally male-dominated teams
research_question: When is a token female's voice incorporated into the actions of a traditionally male-dominated team, and with what consequences for team performance? The paper asks what conditions facilitate token female voice enactment and when acting on that voice helps or harms team performance.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that tokenism and gender stereotypes can make a token female's suggestions less likely to be enacted, but minority influence mechanisms can make a demographically distinct member's suggestions more carefully processed. Leaders with more favorable beliefs about women's military capabilities legitimize the token female's competence and help the team consider her suggestions. When the task is complex, enacting token female voice contributes divergent ideas and deeper processing that improve performance; when the task is low in complexity, the same divergence can slow efficient execution and hurt performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends voice research by shifting attention from voice frequency to voice enactment, or whether expressed suggestions are incorporated into team action. It reconciles tokenism, gender stereotype, and minority influence perspectives by showing that leader gender beliefs condition whether token female voice is enacted. It also contributes to team diversity and minority influence research by identifying token female voice enactment as a micro-dynamic through which diversity shapes team performance under task-complexity boundary conditions.
practical_implication: Managers of female-token teams should attend not only to whether token women speak up, but also to whether their suggestions are enacted. For complex tasks, the paper suggests that managers should facilitate token female voice enactment because it can help teams generate innovative performance strategies. For low-complexity tasks requiring rapid execution, managers should be cautious about enacting divergent suggestions that may delay an otherwise workable solution.
limitations: The sample included only 12 women, and those women came from gender-integrated combat support functions while men came from all-male direct combat specialties, so functional diversity cannot be fully ruled out as an alternative explanation. The study did not measure voice content, voice quality, or how suggestions were presented, limiting the ability to determine whether enacted female voice differed in substance or style. The military setting involved high authority differentiation and physically demanding tasks, which may limit generalization to lower-authority or nonphysical team contexts.
future_research: Future research should replicate the study with more female participants, control for occupational function, and assess individual differences in competence, cognitive ability, specialized training, and voice presentation. Researchers should track specific voice episodes and suggestion quality to explain how particular enacted suggestions affect team outcomes. The authors also call for work on why leader gender beliefs matter, whether leaders solicit token female voice, and how voice enactment operates in teams marked by other forms of diversity.
abstract: When is a token female's voice incorporated into the actions of a traditionally male-dominated team, and to what ends? Drawing from the tokenism, gender stereotypes, and minority influence literatures, we advance a model that specifies the conditions that facilitate token female voice enactment and when enacting the female's voice enhances team performance. Using a sample of active-duty military men and women, we employed live observation techniques to study voice enactment in all-male teams versus female-token teams (i.e., teams with a token female member) throughout a series of complex and physically demanding tasks. Our findings revealed that (a) token female voice enactment was higher when team leaders possessed more favorable beliefs about women's capabilities in the military, and (b) token female voice enactment enhanced team performance in more complex tasks but harmed team performance in less complex tasks. Additionally, our supplementary analyses revealed that female-token teams were more reflective before engaging in action relative to all-male teams, as the latter tended to engage in agentic, "action-first" strategies. Theoretical and practical implications for facilitating female voice enactment in traditionally male-dominated contexts are discussed.

title: Rivals’ Negative Earnings Surprises, Language Signals, and Firms’ Competitive Actions
methods: Empirical quantitative study using quarterly competitor-dyad data on publicly listed U.S. firms from 2003 to 2014, combining RavenPack competitive action data, Thomson Reuters StreetEvent conference-call transcripts, I/B/E/S earnings forecasts, and Compustat controls; hypotheses are tested with random-effects negative binomial regressions, year-quarter and industry fixed effects, and dyad-clustered robust standard errors.
industry: Dominant-business firms in oligopolistic four-digit SIC industries.
time_period: 2003 to 2014, inclusive.
units: Firm-rival-quarter observations for competitor dyads in oligopolistic industries.
n_sample: 130 competitor-dyads in 38 industries, corresponding to 3,202 firm-rival-quarter observations with complete information.
authors: Guo, Wei; Sengul, Metin; Yu, Tieying
theories: awareness–motivation–capability (AMC) perspective (Chen, 1996; Smith et al., 2001); communication literature on plain language, complex language, and vague language (Eagleson et al., 1990; Li, 2008; Miller, 2010)
keywords: awareness–motivation–capability (AMC) perspective; competitive action intensity; competitive dynamics; complex language; earnings conference call; negative earnings surprises; vague language
research_question: Why and how do firms take competitive action in response to critical events that affect rivals, even when the focal firm has not been directly attacked? The paper asks whether rivals’ negative earnings surprises increase focal firms’ competitive action intensity and whether complex or vague language in rivals’ earnings conference calls strengthens that relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism follows the awareness-motivation-capability logic. A rival’s negative earnings surprise is public and salient, signals vulnerability, and may reduce the rival’s willingness or ability to respond because short-term financial-market pressure, management instability, internal coordination problems, reduced market value, and higher capital costs shift its priorities. This changes the focal firm’s perceived opportunity and relative capability, motivating more tactical competitive actions. Complex and vague language in the rival’s post-surprise conference call further signals possible obfuscation and deeper vulnerability, strengthening the positive association between the negative surprise and focal action intensity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends competitive dynamics research beyond direct attack-response dyads by showing that critical events befalling rivals can trigger focal firms’ competitive actions. It contributes to language and competition research by showing that complex and vague language can increase, rather than dampen, rivals’ competitive actions when it reveals vulnerability after a negative earnings surprise. It also contributes to research on capital markets and firm behavior by shifting attention from how missing earnings targets affects a firm’s own strategy to how such surprises shape rivals’ strategies.
practical_implication: Firms experiencing negative earnings surprises should recognize that rivals may treat the event as a window of opportunity for tactical attacks. The findings imply that complex or vague conference-call language after a negative surprise can invite more competitive action by making vulnerability more detectable. Managers may therefore need to communicate simply and clearly after negative earnings surprises if they want to reduce rivals’ incentives to attack.
limitations: The sample is restricted to dominant-business firms in oligopolistic industries, where strategic interdependence makes the proposed competitive-dynamics story especially observable. Data restrictions prevent the authors from fully unpacking attributes of competitive actions, including announcements versus execution, intended responses versus planned actions, action repertoire complexity, and differences across action types. The study also focuses on conference calls and tactical actions, leaving other communication channels and strategic actions less directly examined.
future_research: Future research could examine how top management team characteristics shape the relationship between negative earnings surprises and competitive action intensity. Additional work could distinguish among action announcements, executions, planned actions, action repertoire complexity, and specific action types such as pricing, marketing, and legal actions. Scholars could also test the model in other firms and industries, examine other communication channels such as annual reports or investor presentations, and study other vulnerability-generating events such as CEO death, media attacks, production interruptions, or lawsuits.
abstract: Research in competitive dynamics has primarily analyzed how characteristics of observable attacks influence firms’ competitive responses. Why and how firms take action in response to critical events that affect their rivals, without being attacked themselves, is less well understood. Focusing on negative earnings surprises, we argue that a focal firm is likely to view a rival’s negative earnings surprise as an opportunity to exploit its vulnerability. Therefore, such surprises are positively associated with the intensity of competitive actions initiated by a focal firm. Furthermore, the complexity and vagueness of a rival’s language in an earnings conference call strengthens the positive relationship between the negative earnings surprise and the focal firm’s intensity of competitive actions. We tested our arguments using data from 3,202 earnings releases and conferences calls of publicly listed firms between 2003 and 2014 in the United States. The results and robustness checks support our predictions.

title: CFO Gender and Financial Statement Irregularities
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study using merged Execucomp, Compustat, ISS, CRSP, IBES, and Thomson Reuters data; the authors estimate panel regressions with firm-clustered standard errors, industry and year fixed effects, quasi-experimental SOX and global-financial-crisis analyses, random-effects, firm fixed-effects and hybrid models, probit restatement models, propensity score matching, and a treatment-effects model.
industry: U.S.-based public firms covered by the merged databases, excluding utilities and financial firms.
units: Firm-year observations.
n_sample: 18,659 firm-year observations covering 2,186 unique U.S.-based firms; 1,550 female-CFO firm-year observations and 339 unique female-CFO firms.
authors: Gupta, Vishal K.; Mortal, Sandra; Chakrabarty, Bidisha; Guo, Xiaohu; Turban, Daniel B.
theories: managerial discretion theory (Hambrick, 2007; Wangrow et al., 2015); upper echelons theory (Hambrick & Mason, 1984)
keywords: CFO gender; FSD Score; analyst coverage; financial misreporting; financial statement irregularities; institutional ownership
research_question: Does CFO gender influence the likelihood of corporate financial misreporting, and is this relationship contingent on external governance mechanisms? The paper asks whether firms with female CFOs have lower financial statement irregularities than comparable firms with male CFOs, especially when institutional ownership and analyst coverage are weak.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level: CFO gender is treated as a senior-executive attribute that can shape firm-level financial reporting because CFOs have direct responsibility for financial statements. Drawing on upper echelons theory and literatures on gender differences in ethics and risk taking, the authors argue that female CFOs are less likely than male CFOs to engage in financial misreporting. Managerial discretion theory supplies the contingency: when monitoring from institutional owners or analysts is weak, CFO attributes should matter more; when monitoring is strong, external governance constrains discretion and reduces male-female CFO differences.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends upper echelons theory by showing that gender, an executive characteristic often overlooked in strategic-leadership research, is associated with a firm-level misconduct outcome. It also extends managerial discretion theory by treating institutional ownership and analyst coverage as governance mechanisms that condition the effect of a specific executive attribute on corporate behavior. Methodologically, it contributes evidence on the Financial Statement Deviation Score as a tool for studying financial misreporting beyond detected fraud cases.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that regulators, investors, boards, and other stakeholders should pay attention to CFO characteristics when assessing financial reporting risk, while recognizing that governance monitoring can constrain managerial discretion. The results also imply that institutional owners and securities analysts may be especially important safeguards in settings where executives have greater opportunity to influence reporting choices.
limitations: The authors do not directly measure CFO ethical attitudes or risk-taking behaviors, so the psychological and social processes connecting gender to reporting choices remain a black box. The FSD Score is an indicator of the likelihood of financial misreporting rather than direct proof of fraudulent accounting, and it cannot clearly separate fraud from erroneous misreporting. The study examines institutional owners and securities analysts, so whether the moderation pattern generalizes to other governance mechanisms such as media or employees is not established.
future_research: Future research should directly examine the mechanisms through which male and female CFOs may differ, including ethics, risk taking, overconfidence, gender roles, and biological attributes. Scholars could test whether other stakeholders or governance mechanisms shape the relationship between executive gender and financial misreporting. Additional work could examine other corporate decisions and sociocultural contexts beyond large public firms in the United States.
abstract: The increasing presence of women in upper echelon positions draws attention to the possible effects of executive gender on corporate decisions and actions. In this study, we formulate theory about the impact of chief financial officer (CFO) gender on financial misreporting to generate two key insights. First, we hypothesize that firms with female CFOs will have a lower likelihood of financial misreporting than comparable firms with male CFOs. Second, we argue that the relation between CFO gender and financial misreporting will be contingent on governance mechanisms (e.g., institutional ownership and analyst coverage), such that misreporting of firms with male CFOs will differ more compared to that of firms with female CFOs when governance is weak. Our results, based on a novel leading indicator of the likelihood of financial misreporting, provide support for our predictions. Various alternative econometric specifications, including (but not limited to) exogenous shocks, propensity score matching, and modeling treatment effects, random effects, firm fixed effects, and hybrid effects provide general support for our theory and hypotheses. Implications and directions for future research are discussed.

title: Organizations, Risk Translation, and the Ecology of Risks: The Discursive Construction of a Novel Risk
methods: Empirical qualitative process study of BPA between 1993 and 2013, using systematic text searches, archival documents, media and organizational texts, semi-structured interviews, descriptive/analytical/pattern coding, and iterative process analysis of risk translations and their interactions.
industry: Chemicals management around bisphenol A, including regulators, scientists, chemical manufacturers, retailers, and NGOs.
time_period: 1993-2013, with interviews conducted in 2011 and 2012.
units: Organizations and actor groups involved in BPA risk construction: scientists, chemical manufacturers, regulators, retailers, and NGOs.
n_sample: 50 interviews reported in Table 1, plus systematic searches of BPA-related texts and documents.
authors: Hardy, Cynthia; Maguire, Steve
theories: discursive approach to risk; ecology of risks; risk translation
keywords: bisphenol A; discursive construction; ecology of risks; grand challenges; novel risks; risk objects; risk translation
research_question: How are risk objects constructed in the case of novel risks? The paper also asks what role risk translation plays when organizations face equivocal risks that prevailing scientific risk-assessment techniques cannot settle.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: novel risks; equivocal meaning in relation to risk; risk objects; translated organizational risks; the body of risk knowledge; the ecology of risks.
- Risk translations: actors translated BPA's equivocality into professional risk for scientists, regulatory risk for chemical manufacturers, reputational risk for retailers and NGOs, and operational risk for Canadian and Australian regulators.
- Risk-management actions: actors managed translated risks by defending or challenging scientific methods, funding or publishing research, lobbying regulators, withdrawing BPA-containing products, promoting BPA-free alternatives, and revising or preserving chemicals-management processes.
- Process / phases: early equivocality around BPA became contestation as translated risks interacted; later, a strengthening chain connected endocrinologists, Canadian regulators, Canadian NGOs, Canadian retailers, Australian NGOs, and Australian retailers.
- Emergent outcome: the ecology of risks evolved until synergistic strengthening actions outweighed weakening actions by toxicologists, manufacturers, and Australian regulators, helping BPA become constructed as a risk object.

The process model is that novel risks become actionable for organizations through translation into familiar organizational risks. These translations are local and not necessarily coordinated, but actions taken to manage one translated risk heighten or dampen other actors' translated risks. Over time, the interaction of translated risks forms an ecology that can reproduce equivocality, generate contestation, and eventually stabilize a risk object's meaning when risk knowledge and organizational practices are revised.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizing and risk research by theorizing how organizations respond when the dominant body of risk knowledge cannot determine whether an object poses a risk. It extends risk translation research by showing that organizations translate equivocal novel risks into familiar categories of organizational risk, rather than merely shifting responsibility for already established risks. It also develops the concept of an ecology of risks to explain how uncoordinated organizational actions cumulatively construct novel risk objects and shape societal responses to grand challenges.
practical_implication: The paper implies that organizations facing novel risks may act more effectively by recognizing which familiar risk category they have translated the equivocal object into, and by anticipating how their risk-management actions can heighten other actors' translated risks. For grand challenges such as climate change, the authors suggest that proponents of action should attend to, and influence, the risks different organizations translate rather than treating opposition as a simple split between supporters and deniers.
limitations: The authors state that they could not systematically collect BPA data from all jurisdictions, so the mapped ecology is only part of a larger global ecology. They also note that interviews were conducted toward the end of the study period and include retrospective accounts, although they addressed this by analyzing contemporaneous textual data. A third limitation is that the study follows the successful construction of a risk object rather than a case where a novel risk is not eventually constructed.
future_research: Future research could use the model to study other novel risks and cases where objects become less risky over time rather than being constructed as risk objects. The authors also point to wicked problems and grand challenges, including climate change, as settings where researchers can examine how organizations translate equivocality into familiar organizational risks and how ecologies of risks shape collective responses.
abstract: The contemporary “risk society” is associated with the emergence of a wide range of risks characterized by uncertainty and unfamiliarity. These “novel” risks pose a major challenge for organizations: their negative effects may be significant, but prevailing riskassessment techniques are limited in their ability to identify these effects. Building on our prior work on the chemical bisphenol A (BPA), this study examines how organizations deal with novel risks. It finds that organizations engage in “risk translation” by translating equivocality associated with the novel risk into more familiar risks, providing them with a clearer basis and guide for action. As multiple organizations take actions to manage these translated risks, the interactive effects result in an “ecology of risks” that evolves over time, allowing for the construction of a novel risk. The study contributes to research on organizing and risk by theorizing how organizations respond to novel risks, as well as by highlighting the role of translated organizational risks in constructing novel risks and shaping societal responses to grand challenges.

title: My Coworkers are Treated More Fairly than Me! A Self-Regulatory Perspective on Justice Social Comparisons
methods: Two daily experience-sampling studies of employees, testing a within-person moderated serial mediation model. Study 1 surveyed full-time employees at the beginning and end of each workday for 15 workdays and analyzed 680 daily cases from 96 individuals. Study 2 surveyed staff members and nominated coworkers at midday and end of day for 15 workdays and analyzed 853 daily cases from 100 individuals. Analyses used multilevel path analysis in Mplus, group-mean centering, random slopes for hypothesized paths, controls for alternative mechanisms, and parametric bootstrapping with 20,000 resamples for mediation and moderated mediation.
industry: Study 1: full-time employees in various positions; Study 2: staff members from a large U.S. Southern university, with coworker reports for helping behavior.
time_period: Each study collected daily surveys over 15 workdays.
units: Employees' daily within-person observations; Study 2 also used nominated coworker reports for helping behavior.
n_sample: Study 1: 96 individuals and 680 daily cases; Study 2: 100 individuals and 853 daily cases.
authors: Koopman, Joel; Lin, Szu-Han (Joanna); Lennard, Anna C.; Matta, Fadel K.; Johnson, Russell E.
theories: equity theory (Adams, 1965); group engagement model (Blader & Tyler, 2009); organizational justice theory; referent cognitions theory (Folger, 1986); self-regulation theory (Carver & Scheier, 1990; Johnson, Chang, & Lord, 2006); social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954); social exchange theory
keywords: discrepancy awareness; envy; experience sampling; helping behavior; instigated incivility; justice perceptions; justice social comparison perceptions; organizational justice; self-regulation; self-regulatory resource depletion
research_question: Why, when, and for whom do justice social comparison perceptions influence employee behavior? The paper asks whether low justice social comparisons reduce helping and increase instigated incivility through envy and self-regulatory resource depletion, especially when employees' own justice perceptions are low.
mechanism_summary:
- Alternative mechanisms: Psychological contract breach or psychological tension for equity theory, group identification for the group engagement model, felt obligation for social exchange theory, and overall fairness for referent cognitions theory.

The authors theorize that low justice social comparisons create discrepancy awareness: employees see their own treatment as falling below the reference standard implied by coworkers' treatment. This discrepancy elicits envy, which is costly to suppress and therefore depletes self-regulatory resources. Depleted employees then have fewer resources to enact helping and inhibit low-intensity deviant behavior such as instigated incivility. Low justice perceptions intensify the first stage because the comparison occurs in a more threatening, resource-poor justice context.
theoretical_contribution: The paper revitalizes social comparison as a foundational but underdeveloped element of organizational justice theory by specifying why, when, and for whom justice social comparisons matter. Its central contribution is integrating social comparison with self-regulation to identify envy and resource depletion as a mechanism that predicts behavior beyond equity theory, the group engagement model, social exchange theory, and referent cognitions theory. It also shifts justice social comparison research toward a daily within-person perspective, showing that much of the variance in justice social comparisons occurs within individuals rather than only between them.
practical_implication: The findings imply that supervisors should attend not only to whether employees are treated fairly in absolute terms, but also to whether their treatment varies across employees or across days in ways employees can compare. Differential or inconsistent justice can trigger envy and resource depletion, reducing helping and increasing incivility. The paper cautions that even when supervisors have reasons for uneven treatment, employees are observing those differences.
limitations: Most focal variables were collected from the same source, creating common-method-variance concerns, although Study 2 used coworker reports for helping and the authors used time separation, different scale anchors, and group-mean centering. The justice social comparison measure asked participants to report perceived discrepancy directly, which has known limitations because respondents may combine self and comparison information differently. The authors also note that the effect sizes are small, which they attribute partly to within-person modeling and the three-stage indirect path.
future_research: Future research could examine downward justice social comparisons and whether emotions such as sympathy, pity, or pride operate through mechanisms other than resource depletion. The authors also call for work on additional emotional responses such as anger, resentment, anxiety, depression, and rumination, as well as person-level moderators such as social comparison orientation and justice orientation. They further suggest integrating justice social comparison operationalization with person-environment fit logic, including atomistic versus molecular fit approaches.
abstract: Social comparison processes were integral to the origins of the organizational justice literature, and are incorporated within several justice-based constructs and theories. Yet, despite this, the justice social comparison literature is theoretically underdeveloped; while the extant literature affirms that justice social comparisons influence employee outcomes, it does not explain why, when, or for whom these effects occur. We build new theory on why justice social comparison perceptions influence employee behavior (specifically, helping and instigated incivility) by viewing the phenomenon through a self-regulatory lens. Doing so enables us to identify a novel explanatory mechanism and boundary condition for these effects. In two experience sampling studies, each conducted over multiple weeks, we test our proposed mechanism—envy and self-regulatory resource depletion—against four alternative justice-based mechanisms derived from equity theory, the group engagement model, social exchange theory, and referent cognitions theory. Findings were consistent with our theorizing, verifying that our integration of self-regulation with social comparison processes offers new insights to the justice literature. Overall, our scholarship has the potential to change the conversation about social comparisons in the justice literature by revitalizing a foundational aspect of justice rarely considered in contemporary research.

title: Last to Come and Last to Go? The Complex Role of Gender and Ethnicity in the Reputational Penalties for Directors Linked to Corporate Fraud
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a proprietary data set on financial misconduct and directors' demographic characteristics. The authors test Hypotheses 1 and 2 with OLS models of fraud-tainted directors' net loss of outside directorships, using Huber-White heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors clustered by firm, and test Hypothesis 3 with a logit model of whether a fraud-tainted minority director loses a specific outside directorship at a nonfraudulent firm.
industry: Director labor market and corporate governance context involving firms accused of financial fraud.
time_period: Fraud cases from 1996 to 2012, with director labor-market outcomes measured over the three years after the fraud was initially revealed.
units: Fraud-tainted directors for Hypotheses 1 and 2; fraud-tainted minority director by nonfraudulent-firm board pairings for Hypothesis 3.
n_sample: 2,030 fraud-tainted directors at 197 firms with financial fraud for Hypotheses 1 and 2; 356 unique combinations of fraud-tainted minority directors serving at nonfraudulent firms for Hypothesis 3.
authors: Naumovska, Ivana; Wernicke, Georg; Zajac, Edward J.
theories: agency theory; resource-provisioning role of directors; social embeddedness of markets; social identity theory
keywords: board diversity; corporate fraud; corporate misconduct; director labor market; ex post settling-up; minority directors; reputational immunity; resource-provisioning role
research_question: How does a director's demographic minority status affect the ex post settling-up process in the director labor market after corporate fraud? The paper asks whether socioeconomic pressures for board diversity can lessen or reverse the reputational penalties usually imposed on fraud-tainted directors, and whether media discourse and the diversity level of nonfraudulent boards amplify or attenuate that effect.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cross-level reputational calculus in which director labor-market evaluators weigh fraud-tainted directors' apparent monitoring failure against their resource-provisioning and legitimacy-conferring value. Because women and ethnic minority directors are underrepresented and increasingly sought after, socioeconomic pressures for board diversity can counterbalance penalties attached to corporate fraud. This reputational immunity is stronger when media discourse heightens the value of board diversity and weaker when a nonfraudulent firm already has more minority directors, reducing the focal director's marginal diversity contribution.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends ex post settling-up research by showing that director labor-market penalties are not only agency-theoretic assessments of directors as monitors. They also reflect the socially embedded value of directors as resource providers and conferrers of legitimacy under evolving norms for board diversity.

It contributes to corporate governance, corporate misconduct, and labor-market discrimination research by theorizing and testing how minority status can produce reputational immunity in a specific upper-echelons market. The contribution is bounded: the authors do not claim broad advantage for women or ethnic minority directors, but identify conditions under which demand and perceived scarcity can partially reverse expected penalties.
practical_implication:
For boards and nominating committees, the findings imply that diversity pressures can shape retention and appointment decisions even after serious corporate misconduct. Firms may keep or appoint fraud-tainted minority directors because those directors contribute legitimacy and diversity value, especially on less diverse boards.

The authors also imply that expanding the supply of minority directors through broader search processes and less traditional routes could reduce uneven ex post settling-up across demographic groups. As the minority-director pipeline deepens, the imbalance in reputational penalties may diminish.
limitations:
The study is limited to boards of directors in the United States, where diversity quotas are implicit; the authors explicitly ask whether similar or stronger results would appear in countries with explicit quotas for women directors. The design also interprets director labor-market outcomes as reputational penalties, while acknowledging that some directors may voluntarily exit the director labor market after misconduct.

The paper addresses but cannot exhaust all alternative explanations. Supplementary analyses test perceived lower influence, benevolent sexism, firm status, audit-committee accountability, busyness, and separate female versus ethnic-minority effects, but the authors call for more direct research on perceptions of directors' influence and ethical dispositions.
future_research:
Future research could examine how reputational immunity decays as boards move from historically low to more moderate diversity levels. The authors also call for work on whether fraud-tainted minority directors who retain seats become more isolated or less influential in boardroom processes, and on backlash, tokenism, and perceptions that minorities are tokens.

Additional research could compare implicit-quota contexts such as the United States with explicit quota regimes, examine voluntary director exit after misconduct, and compare legal sanctions with reputational penalties after regulatory changes such as Sarbanes-Oxley. The paper also encourages more integrative work across economics, sociology, social psychology, organizational studies, and legal studies on corporate misconduct.
abstract: Scholars have found consistent evidence that directors who served on boards of firms accused of misconduct face reputational penalties in the director labor market. While commonly interpreted in terms of an “ex post settling-up” process that penalizes directors for failing in their role as monitors of management, the fundamentally social basis of the director labor market suggests that the ex post settling-up process may also incorporate a resource-provisioning role for directors as conferrers of legitimacy. We analyze how growing socioeconomic pressures that aim to redress the longstanding underrepresentation of female and ethnic minority directors may lessen, for these sought-after directors, the penalties typically imposed by the labor market in the aftermath of corporate misconduct. Using a rich proprietary data set on financial misconduct and directors’ demographic characteristics, we find strong support for our hypotheses regarding a possible “reputational immunity” effect. We also provide supplementary analyses demonstrating the specific mechanisms underlying our predictions, and establishing the robustness of the results to a variety of alternative explanations. We discuss the implications of our theoretical perspective and empirical findings for future research on corporate governance, corporate misconduct, and the duality of minority status as it relates to discriminatory outcomes in modern labor markets.

title: Being Different, Being Absent? A Dynamic Perspective on Demographic Dissimilarity and Absenteeism in Blue-Collar Teams
methods: Empirical quantitative longitudinal archival HR study of blue-collar newcomers nested in teams; the authors model yearly absenteeism as count data using negative binomial generalized linear mixed growth models, with repeated measures nested within individuals and time-varying team demographic composition.
industry: Blue-collar sorting and delivery work in a large public service business unit.
time_period: Seven annual time points between 2010 and 2016.
units: Individual newcomers in blue-collar teams, with yearly absenteeism observations.
n_sample: 2,711 newcomers from 820 blue-collar teams with 10,304 members; 13,830 observations in the negative binomial growth-curve models.
authors: Reinwald, Max; Kunze, Florian
theories: anchoring events theory; self-categorization theory; social identity theory; status characteristics; tokenism
keywords: absenteeism behavior; anchoring events; blue-collar teams; demographic dissimilarity; relational demography; social identity theory
research_question: How does individual-level demographic dissimilarity in teams unfold over time, and how does this affect individual absenteeism? The paper asks whether gender and age dissimilarity produce dynamic absenteeism trajectories, and whether those trajectories are asymmetric for women and older employees in blue-collar teams.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is dynamic and cross-level. Drawing on the social identity approach, the authors argue that dissimilar newcomers are likely to be categorized as out-group members and to perceive discrimination, social exclusion, or alienation. Anchoring events theory adds the temporal logic: early negative exchanges can be stored in autobiographical memory and bias later interpretations of team interactions, so absenteeism does not necessarily rise immediately but increases over time. The effect should be strongest for women and older employees because tokenism, status characteristics, and blue-collar job prototypes make them more likely to perceive negative anchoring events in predominantly male and younger teams.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends relational demography by replacing a static account of dissimilarity effects with a temporal model of how those effects intensify across team membership. It integrates the social identity approach with anchoring events theory to explain why dissimilarity may have little initial association with absenteeism but stronger effects later. It also refines asymmetric relational-demography theory by showing that low-status demographic groups, especially women and older employees in the study context, are most likely to exhibit steeper absenteeism trajectories.
practical_implication: The findings caution against relying only on diversity-friendly recruitment and assuming that repeated contact across demographic differences will naturally lead to acceptance. Organizations should attend to newcomer socialization, structured transfer and recruitment processes, formal mentoring, inclusive climates, and supervisor relationships that may reduce early negative anchoring events for demographically dissimilar workers. The cost estimates in the paper also imply that rising absenteeism among dissimilar women and older employees can be financially material for blue-collar employers.
limitations: The authors cannot directly test the proposed psychological mechanism because the archival HR data do not measure individual perceptions of anchoring events, discrimination, or social exclusion. Generalizability is limited because the sample consists of blue-collar workers in one Swiss organization, a setting where gender and age job prototypes may be especially strong. The study focuses on surface-level demographic attributes and does not test whether deep-level diversity, intersectional dissimilarity, or better multidimensional dissimilarity measures alter the observed trajectories.
future_research: Future research should directly measure individual perceptions of anchoring events, for example through diary studies of newcomers. Replication in white-collar settings, different firms, industries, and countries would clarify whether the dynamics depend on strong job prototypes and informal staffing procedures. Additional work could examine performance, creativity, turnover, lateness, deep-level diversity, and multidimensional or intersectional dissimilarity as part of longer withdrawal trajectories.
abstract: This study offers a new theoretical and empirical perspective on the dynamic effect of demographic dissimilarity on absenteeism behavior by team members over time. Integrating social identity theory with the theory of anchoring events (i.e., key social interactions), we propose that individual absenteeism behavior depends on the relational dissimilarity to the team age and gender. Using a sample of 2,711 individual newcomers in 820 blue-collar teams tracked over seven years, we show that gender and age dissimilarity effects are not constant over time; rather, dissimilar individuals increase their absences more strongly over the years. Particularly, women and older employees in predominantly male and younger teams show a steeper increase in absenteeism over time and, accordingly, higher absolute absenteeism at later stages of team membership than do their less dissimilar counterparts. We discuss the implications for relational demography and diversity theory, as well as for diversity management.

title: Dare to Be Different? Conformity Versus Differentiation in Corporate Social Activities of Chinese Firms and Market Responses
methods: Panel study of Chinese listed firm-years using CSR activity data, analyst coverage and recommendation data, and CSMAR firm-level data; the main models are firm fixed-effects regressions, with robustness checks using instrumental variables, first-difference regressions, dose-response functions, and an alternative multidimensional-scaling measure of emphasis differentiation.
industry: Chinese listed firms reporting CSR activities across multiple issue fields; no single industry is specified.
units: Firm-year observations for Chinese listed firms that reported CSR activities.
n_sample: 3,230 firm-year observations.
authors: Zhang, Y.; Wang, H.; Zhou, X.
theories: institutional perspective on CSR; optimal distinctiveness; strategic balance perspective; strategic perspective on CSR
keywords: Chinese listed firms; analyst coverage; analysts' investment recommendations; corporate social responsibility (CSR); emphasis differentiation; market value; optimal distinctiveness; scope conformity
research_question: How can firms achieve optimal distinctiveness in CSR by conforming in one dimension of a complex practice while differentiating in another, and how do analysts and financial markets respond to those CSR strategies? The paper asks whether CSR scope conformity increases analyst coverage, whether CSR emphasis differentiation improves analyst recommendations and market value, and whether state ownership, firm visibility, high-status house coverage, and earnings pressure condition these relationships.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: CEO and governance characteristics, socially contested industries, ownership concentration, list age, firm size, ROA, financial leverage, share price, overall level of CSR, and related firm-level factors.

The mechanism is compensatory orchestration within a complex CSR practice. CSR scope is the more material and salient dimension, so conformity to established reporting guidelines helps firms appear legitimate to analysts and increases coverage. CSR emphasis is more abstract and allows firms to align CSR attention with idiosyncratic stakeholder and strategic needs, so differentiation in emphasis can signal value and produce more favorable analyst recommendations and higher market value. The effects depend on legitimacy pressure and audience evaluation capacity: state-owned and highly visible firms benefit more from scope conformity, while emphasis differentiation is valued more when firms are covered by high-status houses and less when firms face high earnings pressure.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends optimal distinctiveness theory by showing that firms need not locate a single balance point between conformity and differentiation; they can orchestrate the two within different dimensions of one complex practice. It theorizes this as compensatory orchestration, where legitimacy in one dimension can support differentiation in another. It also contextualizes optimal distinctiveness by showing that legitimacy pressures and audience status shape the effectiveness of conformity and differentiation strategies.
practical_implication: For executives designing social programs, the findings suggest that investors and analysts attend to nonfinancial metrics as well as financial metrics. Firms may gain basic legitimacy by covering important CSR fields consistent with reporting frameworks, but they also need CSR emphasis that fits their competitive positioning and stakeholder context. Managers should therefore avoid treating CSR rankings or broad coverage alone as sufficient, and should orchestrate overt scope conformity with substantive emphasis differentiation.
limitations: The paper notes that its differentiation measure captures the number of social activities in CSR fields but not the qualitative uniqueness of each activity. It also acknowledges that the Chinese listed-firm CSR setting is especially useful because scope guidelines and open-ended emphasis make the conformity-differentiation contrast salient, but this context may not generalize without nuance. Finally, the paper finds only scant supplementary evidence on learning over time by firms and analysts, leaving that process underexplored.
future_research: Future research could develop more comprehensive measures of CSR differentiation that capture qualitative differences in specific activities within each CSR field. Studies could also examine whether firms and analysts learn over time to balance, orchestrate, and evaluate CSR conformity and differentiation. The authors suggest applying the framework to other complex management practices, including total quality management and diversity programs, and to CSR contexts outside China.
abstract: Building on the literature on optimal distinctiveness, this study explores the effects of conformity versus differentiation in corporate social responsibility (CSR) practices on evaluations by security analysts and responses of the financial market in general. We develop the argument that while conformity in CSR scope enhances analyst coverage, differentiation in CSR emphasis leads to more-favorable analyst recommendations and higher market value. This suggests that firms may be able to simultaneously conform in CSR scope and differentiate in CSR emphasis to achieve optimal distinctiveness. To further enhance our understanding of the variation in the relationship between conformity and differentiation and the response of analysts and the market, we investigate how some firmand analyst-level factors moderate this relationship. Using the case of corporate social activities of Chinese listed firms during the period from 2008 to 2014, we show that scope conformity has a stronger effect on analyst coverage for state-owned firms and firms with higher visibility; on the other hand, the relationship between emphasis differentiation, and analyst recommendation and market value strengthens for firms covered by high-status brokerage houses but weakens for those experiencing high earnings pressure.
apa_citation: Zhang, Y., Wang, H., & Zhou, X. (2020). Dare to be different? Conformity versus differentiation in corporate social activities of Chinese firms and market responses. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(3), 717-742. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0412

title: Not in My Pay Grade: The Relational Benefit of Pay Grade Dissimilarity
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a three-part survey and company records from employees nested in work teams, with multilevel path analysis in Mplus 7 and bootstrapped moderated indirect effects.
industry: Marketing teams in a telecommunications company.
time_period: Three waves: Time 1 company records and leader ratings, Time 2 one month later member relational uncertainty, and Time 3 one month after Time 2 member identification and turnover intention plus leader-rated task performance.
units: Individual team members nested in work teams.
n_sample: 203 members from 33 work teams.
authors: Zhang, Lida L.; George, Elizabeth; Chattopadhyay, Prithviraj
theories: pay dispersion; relational demography; social identity perspective; uncertainty reduction
keywords: pay grade dissimilarity; relational demography; relational uncertainty; social identity; task performance; team identification; turnover intention
research_question: The paper asks how individual team members respond to pay grade differences within their teams. Specifically, it examines whether pay grade dissimilarity reduces relational uncertainty, whether this effect is stronger for lower pay grade members, and whether lower relational uncertainty is associated with team identification, task performance, and turnover intention.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an uncertainty-reduction account grounded in relational demography and the social identity perspective. Pay grade differences create a legitimate and stable status hierarchy that gives team members cues about expected interaction patterns, reducing relational uncertainty about how to behave with teammates. Because lower pay grade members are theorized to be more attentive to social influence, pay grade dissimilarity reduces their relational uncertainty more strongly. Lower relational uncertainty is then associated with stronger identification with the team, better leader-rated task performance, and lower intention to leave the team.
theoretical_contribution:
The article contributes to pay dispersion research by shifting attention from collective-level pay dispersion to individual pay grade dissimilarity and by specifying a social identity-related process through which pay differences matter. It shows that relative pay can have relational benefits for lower paid team members when pay grade differences are perceived as legitimate.

The paper also extends relational demography theory by identifying a positive effect of dissimilarity on identification-related outcomes. Instead of treating demographic dissimilarity mainly as a source of self-enhancement threats or in-group bias, it shows that dissimilarity on a legitimate and stable status dimension can reduce uncertainty about team interactions.
practical_implication:
For managers, the findings suggest that pay differences within teams are not uniformly harmful; when a pay grade system is transparent, stable, and perceived as legitimate, pay grade dissimilarity may clarify interaction expectations and support team attachment and performance. The implication is not simply to widen pay differences, but to attend to whether employees understand and accept the status basis of pay grades.

The results also imply that lower pay grade employees may be especially sensitive to the relational information embedded in pay grade structures. Managers should therefore treat the legitimacy and communication of pay grade differences as part of the social architecture of teams, not only as a compensation issue.
limitations:
The authors note that the observed effect sizes are small, explaining about 3-5% of variance, although they argue that restricted variance in pay grade dissimilarity may have attenuated effects and that individual-level effects can accumulate across larger units. The study is also conducted in China, a context with lower uncertainty avoidance and higher power distance, so cultural scope conditions may matter.

The mediator and two dependent variables, team identification and turnover intention, are self-reported, although they were measured at different waves to reduce common method variance. The design is time-lagged but not experimental, so the authors call for stronger causal evidence.
future_research:
Future research could extend the argument into a multilevel framework by examining whether aggregated uncertainty reduction links pay differences to performance and turnover at group or organizational levels. It could also examine higher-level moderators, especially cultural uncertainty avoidance and power distance, that may condition the individual-level process.

The authors also suggest that future work could replicate the study experimentally to strengthen causal inference. More broadly, additional research could test whether the positive uncertainty-reduction effects of status differences hold only when status hierarchies are perceived as legitimate and stable.
abstract: We draw upon relational demography and social identity perspectives to argue that working with teammates who are dissimilar in pay grade can help individual team members reduce social uncertainty in their work relationships within the team, subsequently influencing their identification with the team, performance, and turnover intention. This effect is more pronounced for team members in a lower pay grade because they are more sensitive to social influence owing to their lower status in the team. We test these arguments through a three-part survey of 203 employees from 33 work teams of a telecommunication company in China. Our data show that pay grade dissimilarity is associated with lower relational uncertainty, more for individuals with a lower pay grade, and that lower relational uncertainty, in turn, is associated with higher task performance, higher identification with the team, and lower intent to leave the team. This paper contributes to the literature on pay dispersion by highlighting the importance of relative pay, especially for individuals who are lower paid than others, and uncovering the social identity-related process underlying its effects. Post hoc analysis suggests that these effects are present especially when the pay system is perceived to be legitimate.
apa_citation: Zhang, L. L., George, E., & Chattopadhyay, P. (2020). Not in my pay grade: The relational benefit of pay grade dissimilarity. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(3), 779-801. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1344

title: The Roles of Material Artifacts in Managing the Learning–Performance Paradox: The Kaizen Case
methods: Qualitative process study of two kaizen transformation projects in two manufacturing plants of a Chinese electronics parts maker, using archival artifacts, videos, pictures, around 80 hours of on-site observations, and 32 semi-structured interviews with 20 informants; analysis was iterative and abductive, using chronological case stories, coding of artifact-mediated interactions, and process-model development.
industry: Electronics parts manufacturing
time_period: December 2014-June 2016
units: Two transformation projects in the M&A and die-casting plants of C-Maker
n_sample: Two projects; 32 semi-structured interviews with 20 informants; around 80 hours of on-site observations
authors: Aoki, Katsuki
theories: epistemic objects (Knorr-Cetina, 1997, 2001; Rheinberger, 1997); paradox perspective (Smith & Lewis, 2011; Lewis & Smith, 2014); practice lens (Lê & Bednarek, 2017)
keywords: connecting; continuous improvement; disconnecting; epistemic objects; kaizen; learning–performance paradox; material artifacts; supporting; triggering
research_question: How do material artifacts contribute to transforming organizations in ways that effectively manage the learning–performance paradox? The paper asks this in the setting of kaizen implementation, where frontline employees are expected to maintain efficient performance while also experimenting, learning, and improving standardized procedures.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Learning–performance paradox; material artifacts; social interaction; epistemic objects; kaizen; 4S/5S; performance orientation and learning orientation.
- Process / phases: Sociomaterial stimulation; competing or interrelating epistemic objects; frontline employees' responses to paradox.
- Artifact roles: Triggering, supporting, disconnecting, and connecting.
- Contrasting pathways: In the M&A project, triggering and supporting artifacts interacted with disconnecting artifacts, producing competing epistemic objects and regression to performance-only work. In the Die-Casting project, triggering and supporting artifacts interacted with connecting artifacts, producing interrelating epistemic objects and persistent acceptance of the paradox.
- Boundary conditions: The theorized process is especially relevant to formal, hierarchical organizations where frontline employees have limited authority and depend on managerial support for kaizen.

The process begins when artifacts such as red tags, pictures, videos, painted lines, problem follow-up sheets, SOPs, tables, and graphs become part of everyday interaction. These artifacts can render the learning–performance paradox salient by directing attention to both fixing operational problems and learning new ways to improve procedures. Whether this salience is sustained depends on the interplay among artifact roles: disconnecting artifacts such as customer KPIs and 5S scores can split managerial and frontline understandings, whereas connecting artifacts can link local 4S activities to broader TPS-JIT or kaizen objectives and create support for continued learning.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends paradox research by showing that material artifacts do more than cue attention to paradox; their interplay creates organizational contexts that shape whether actors respond defensively or proactively. It moves beyond discourse-centered accounts by theorizing how artifact-mediated micro interactions become durable cognitive and relational conditions for managing paradox.

The paper also extends the epistemic-objects literature by distinguishing competing epistemic objects from interrelating epistemic objects. This framework explains how the same kind of lean or visual-management artifact can support kaizen in one context while becoming part of disciplinary control in another.
practical_implication:
Managers implementing kaizen or lean systems should not assume that visual tools, 4S/5S routines, kanban cards, SOPs, or problem sheets automatically promote learning. The study warns that these artifacts can narrow attention to customer demands, cleanliness, and short-term performance unless managers actively connect them to broader improvement objectives.

The paper also cautions against using consultants or managers mainly to solve problems quickly for frontline employees. Sustaining kaizen requires interaction that lets frontline employees investigate causes, propose ideas, revise artifacts, and see how their local improvements connect to organizational objectives.
limitations:
The study is based on two transformation projects in one Chinese manufacturing company, so its process model is bounded by this setting. The author explicitly notes that the theory may be most salient for formal, hierarchical organizations and may travel differently to organic, knowledge-intensive organizations where frontline employees have more authority and independence.

The research setting also limits geographic and political generalizability. The paper calls attention to China as the empirical setting and notes that Western countries may involve stronger either-or thinking, labor-union politics, and conflict around using frontline employees as a force for incremental innovation.
future_research:
Future research should examine whether the competing and interrelating epistemic-objects framework applies beyond manufacturing, including service industries that have introduced lean tools and artifacts. Studies could test whether large logistics firms, general merchandise stores, hospitals, or other bureaucratic service organizations show similar dynamics.

The paper also calls for research in countries other than China, especially Western settings where tradeoff approaches, labor unions, power politics, and conflict may shape responses to the learning–performance paradox. Another path is to analyze how competing epistemic objects can become generative rather than purely defensive, including when conflict becomes a source of innovation.
abstract: This paper aims to uncover the roles of material artifacts in managing the learning– performance paradox. It analyzes qualitative data on two transformation projects to implement kaizen (continuous improvement) collected from two manufacturing plants in a Chinese company. In both projects, material artifacts triggered social interaction, through which frontline employees were stimulated to focus on both performance and learning. However, in one project, the interplay of material artifacts that play multiple roles led to competing understandings of organizational objectives between managerial staff and frontline employees, which resulted in regression to the previous state where frontline employees focused exclusively on performance. In the other project, by contrast, the interplay of artifacts led to interrelating understandings of organizational objectives between these actor groups, which resulted in frontline employees’ constant acceptance of the learning–performance paradox. This paper contributes to extant literature by showing how the interplay of material artifacts that play multiple roles, such as triggering, supporting, disconnecting, and connecting, contributes to rendering paradox salient, as well as to creating organizational contexts for actors’ responses to it.
apa_citation: Aoki, K. (2020). The roles of material artifacts in managing the learning–performance paradox: The kaizen case. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1266-1299. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0967

title: “And Who Are You?”: A Performative Perspective on Authority in Organizations
methods: Analytic autoethnography of a six-month consulting assignment, using observations, field notes, field documents, informal conversations, follow-up meetings, and grounded-theory coding of empirical episodes.
industry: Management consulting in a French energy-sector restructuring assignment.
time_period: 2011, over a six-month EnergyCorp assignment.
units: One focal consultant, one restructuring assignment, human allies, material artifacts, abstract entities, and episodes in which authority was on trial.
n_sample: 13 empirical episodes selected from a six-month autoethnography, supported by field notes, documents, 124 reported informal conversations, and nine follow-up meetings.
authors: Bourgoin, A.; Bencherki, N.; Faraj, S.
theories: actor-network theory; communicative constitution of organizations; performativity; relational authority
keywords: activation; actor-network theory; authority; autoethnography; communicative constitution of organizations; passivation; performativity; post-bureaucratic organizing
research_question: How does an actor effectuate authority when they lack the traditional endowments of expertise and hierarchy? The paper examines this question through the work of a management consultant whose authority was repeatedly on trial during a high-stakes restructuring assignment.
mechanism_summary:
- Core process: the performance of authority through relational shaping of the situation.
- Key actants: human allies, material artifacts, and abstract entities.
- Activation movements: mobilizing human allies, equipping with material artifacts, and invoking abstract entities to foreground relations with other actants.
- Passivation movements: distancing from human allies, gearing down from material artifacts, and revoking abstract entities to background relations with other actants.
- Situational adjustment: activation and passivation are not fixed alternatives; the consultant adjusted between them as situations changed and as prior attempts succeeded or failed.
- Emergent outcome: collective action proceeds when actants align with the demand of the situation and remains impeded when they do not.

The process is not a variable-based causal mechanism. Authority is performed when a focal actor shapes a situation by distributing authorship of collective action across relations with people, tools, documents, methods, and principles. Activation gives weight to an action by foregrounding other actants, while passivation foregrounds the focal actor by downplaying those relations; authority depends on balancing these micro processes in context.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends relational authority research by specifying micro processes through which relations become authoritative, rather than treating authority as a stable property of position, expertise, or acceptance. It also grounds actor-network theory and communicative constitution of organizations research at the interactional level by showing how human, material, and semiotic actants are woven into situated performances of authority. The broader contribution is a performative perspective suited to post-bureaucratic organizing, where authority is fluid, contested, and accomplished through the shaping of situations.
practical_implication: For consultants, managers, and other actors working without clear hierarchical authority, the paper implies that authority depends on how they bring people, artifacts, methods, and principles into or out of the situation. Actors should not assume that credentials, rank, expertise, or a mandate will automatically orient collective action; these resources must be made to count in specific encounters. The findings also warn that downplaying others' contributions may help in one audience but damage relations or legitimacy with another.
limitations: The study is based on an autoethnographic account of one consultant in one restructuring assignment, so its claims depend on the authors' reflexive reconstruction of episodes rather than external observation or comparative cases. The authors also note that presenting data as episodes can make authority appear segmented even though they understand it as a continuous performance. Because the focal narrative is told from Thomas's point of view, other actants' agencies are analyzed through that situated account rather than through symmetrical firsthand accounts.
future_research: Future research could use the performative lens to examine power dynamics in increasingly nonhierarchical work settings. It could also test how authority performances unfold for actors with different statuses, professions, or organizational positions, and how stable networks of people, artifacts, and abstract entities make some authority performances more durable across situations. Further work could compare activation and passivation across settings where authority is contested by different audiences.
abstract: As work and organizational realities become increasingly “post-bureaucratic,” the conventional and stable bases of a person’s authority—their position, their expertise, or the acquiescence of a subordinate—are eroding. This evolution calls us to revise our understanding of authority, and to consider more deeply how it is achieved in contexts that are both fluid and fragmented. Building on a six-month autoethnography of a consulting assignment, we show that authority is a practical, relational, and situated performance. It exists in a tension between two mirroring processes—activation and passivation—through which relations are either leveraged or downplayed to shape the situation and steer collective action. Our study also reveals that the performance of authority involves not just people, but also a broader range of actants, including artifacts and abstract entities. In line with current research on performativity in organizations, our findings contribute to the relational program on authority and the revelation of its sociomaterial dimension. Thus, we provide an action-based understanding of authority that is better suited for the study of post-bureaucratic organizing.
apa_citation: Bourgoin, A., Bencherki, N., & Faraj, S. (2020). “And who are you?”: A performative perspective on authority in organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1134-1165. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1335

title: When is it Good to be Bad? Contrasting Effects of Multiple Reputations for Bad Behavior on Media Coverage of Serious Organizational Errors
methods: Event-level quantitative study using cross-sectional probit models, with robustness checks using logit, generalized estimating equations, negative binomial, OLS, Tobit, winsorized outlier specifications, and alternative media coverage measures.
industry: Oil and gas industry.
units: Major oil spills matched to publicly traded oil and gas firms.
n_sample: 113 major oil spills committed by 23 distinct oil and gas firms.
authors: Chandler, D.; Polidoro, F., Jr.; Yang, W.
theories: capability reputation; character reputation; expectancy confirmation; media newsworthiness; organizational reputation
keywords: bad behavior; media coverage; oil spills; organizational reputation; serious organizational errors
research_question: When does a firm's reputation for bad behavior increase or decrease media coverage of a subsequent serious organizational error? The paper asks whether character reputation and capability reputation for bad behavior have contrasting effects on the likelihood that the media covers major oil spills.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism rests on the media's need for news to be new under uncertainty about a serious error's severity and culpability. A character reputation for bad behavior makes a subsequent oil spill seem like new corroborating evidence of a broader pattern, increasing newsworthiness. A capability reputation for bad behavior makes a subsequent oil spill seem redundant, reducing newsworthiness; larger spills strengthen both effects, so repeat offenders with larger spills can be even less likely to receive coverage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational reputation research by showing that reputations for bad behavior are not uniformly liabilities and that character and capability reputations can have opposing consequences. It extends work on serious organizational errors by showing that media response is not proportional only to error magnitude or culpability, but is shaped by firm-specific reputational cues. It also contributes to research on organizational misconduct by showing how media coverage helps socially construct which harmful actions become public misconduct.
practical_implication: The findings imply that media scrutiny of serious errors is selective and can under-cover firms with repeated task-specific failures. Firms with broad character reputations for bad behavior may face more attention when a related but different error occurs, while repeat offenders may escape coverage because their actions appear less novel. Media coverage should therefore be interpreted as a socially constructed and selective signal rather than as a neutral reflection of error severity or public harm.
limitations: The study is limited to major oil spills by oil and gas firms in the United States from 1985 to 2016, so generalizability to other industries, countries, monitors, and forms of firm behavior remains uncertain. The authors also note that the stronger capability reputation effect may reflect the direct match between the dependent variable and the specific capability reputation studied. Because most major oil spills received no media coverage, the paper cannot fully explain whether outlets were unaware of the events, deliberately ignored them, or selected other competing stories.
future_research: Future research could test whether the same mechanisms apply to media coverage of good behavior and whether good and bad reputations combine differently across audiences. The authors also call for studies of other capability reputations and monitors, such as financial analysts responding to firms with reputations for missing earnings estimates. Additional work could examine how journalists choose among competing events and whether information overload reduces public and media attention to serious firm errors.
abstract: We have long known that organizational reputation is consequential. While highlighting the effects of a reputation for good behavior, however, prior work has largely overlooked the possibility that a reputation for bad behavior is qualitatively distinct. In addition, we know that organizational reputation is multidimensional. Although this is conceptually intriguing only if different types of reputation produce different effects, concurrent tests of such differences are rare. In response, we study the effects of multiple reputations for bad behavior on the media coverage of a serious error by a firm. Due to the need for the news to be new, we predict the media is more likely to cover errors that supplement a firm’s general character reputation, but will likely ignore errors that are redundant given a firm’s specific capability reputation. We test this theory in the context of 113 major oil spills in the United States, from 1985 to 2016. Results confirm the theorized contrasting effects. Counterintuitively, we also find the media is even less likely to cover repeat offenders that cause larger spills. We conclude that, at least for media coverage of oil spills, being bad can have its benefits for firms.
apa_citation: Chandler, D., Polidoro, F., Jr., & Yang, W. (2020). When is it good to be bad? Contrasting effects of multiple reputations for bad behavior on media coverage of serious organizational errors. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1236-1265. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1248
