title: Making Change from Behind a Mask: How Organizations Challenge Guarded Institutions by Sparking Grassroots Activism
methods: Longitudinal qualitative case study of ICO's campaign against child marriage in Indonesia, using interviews, observation, archival documents, visual material, Google Trends, and iterative process analysis.
industry: International children's rights and nongovernmental advocacy around child marriage.
time_period: Archival, interview, and observational data span 1974-2019, with the core campaign data concentrated from late 2013 until after the June 2015 Constitutional Court verdict.
units: ICO, ICO Indonesia, local NGOs, lawyers, student activists, politicians, Islamic scholars or Imams, child brides and husbands, coalition meetings, campaign documents, media coverage, and public events.
n_sample: 105 interviews, 90 observation hours, 7,027 pages of archival documents, and 23 hours of archival visuals.
authors: Claus, L.; Tracey, P.
theories: astroturfing and grassroots mobilization; institutional theory; nongovernmental organization and advocacy organization research; social movement theory
keywords: alter ego; astroturfing; child marriage; grassroots activism; guarded institutions; high-stakes event; institutional change; public dissent
research_question: The paper asks how organizations can challenge guarded institutions when they are unable or unwilling to advocate publicly against them. It examines this question through ICO's covert campaign against child marriage in Indonesia.
mechanism_summary:
- Contextual problem: Child marriage in Indonesia operated as a guarded institution, morally reinforced and coercively protected by religious and political elites.
- Organizational constraint: ICO wanted to challenge child marriage but depended on government and religious relationships for other child-welfare work, making open dissent risky.
- Strategy 1, crafting an alter ego: ICO and partners built a secretive coalition and feigned a grassroots social movement through StopChildMarriage, with students and local actors as the public face.
- Strategy 2, incubating public dissent: The coalition used the alter ego to create and exploit a high-stakes judicial-review event, provoking public outrage and fueling broader grassroots activism.
- Emergent outcome: Public contestation moved beyond ICO's control as independent activists, organizations, media actors, and local initiatives took up the anti-child-marriage cause.

The process centers on covert institutional disruption rather than direct public advocacy. ICO masked its organizational role, mimicked grassroots mobilization, and used a high-stakes event to shift child marriage from a repressed issue to one that could be publicly contested. The paper argues that what began as strategically organized, quasi-astroturfed activism became increasingly independent grassroots activism.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a process model explaining how organizations can challenge guarded institutions when open advocacy is too risky. It contributes two strategies--crafting an alter ego and incubating public dissent--and specifies their tactics, including secretive coalition building, feigning a social movement, provoking public outrage, and fueling grassroots activism. It also challenges a sharp distinction between astroturfing and grassroots mobilization by showing how organization-led mobilization can stimulate activism that later becomes more organic and bottom-up.
practical_implication: Organizations facing coercively protected social problems may need to assess whether open contestation would endanger their mission or beneficiaries. The study suggests that indirect coalition work, careful protection of local partners, and event-based mobilization can create space for public dissent when direct advocacy is unavailable. It also raises ethical risks because covert mobilization and organizational disguise can be used for emancipatory or oppressive purposes.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the theory is built from a single-case study and cannot capture the full range and complexity of the dynamics involved. They also note that structuring the analysis around ICO may privilege ICO's perspective and make the change effort appear more strategically choreographed than it was. The case depends partly on digital communication, Indonesia's political and religious context, and guardians who were political and religious leaders, so the model may not transfer unchanged to more tightly surveilled settings or institutions guarded by corporate or military actors.
future_research: Future research could test whether crafting an alter ego and incubating public dissent operate similarly in other guarded institutions, including those protected by corporate, military, or state actors. Scholars could also examine functional equivalents to high-stakes events, such as photographs, books, documentaries, or sustained social-media work. The paper further invites deeper study of the ethical implications of foreign organizations covertly mobilizing local activism around contested moral issues.
abstract: We examine how organizations can challenge institutions that are coercively protected by powerful elites—guarded institutions—when they are unable or unwilling to advocate publicly against them. To do so, we draw on an in-depth qualitative study of efforts to combat child marriage in Indonesia. We explore how an international children’s rights organization worked alongside local nongovernmental organizations and activists to disrupt the institution of child marriage through two discrete strategies: the crafting of an alter ego that takes the appearance of a social movement that has emanated from the grassroots but is actually highly organized, and the use of this alter ego to support the incubation of public dissent by means of a high-stakes event. We contribute to the literature by developing a theorized account of how organizations can challenge guarded institutions when they cannot speak out—an important organizational problem that has received limited attention. We also challenge the theoretical distinction that has been drawn between the organizational mobilization of activists, often referred to as astroturfing, and seemingly organic mobilization that is said to emerge at the grassroots level.
apa_citation: Claus, L., & Tracey, P. (2020). Making change from behind a mask: How organizations challenge guarded institutions by sparking grassroots activism. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 965-996. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0507

title: Identity Trajectories: Explaining Long-Term Patterns of Continuity and Change in Organizational Identities
methods: Longitudinal qualitative multiple-case study of four Canadian nonprofit organizations, using interviews with organizational members and funders, archival documents, observations, longitudinal reconstruction, open coding, cross-case comparison, and grounded-theory building.
industry: Nonprofit organizations.
time_period: From each organization's founding to the time of the study, with data collection waves in 2005-2007, 2011-2012, and 2014-2015.
units: Four nonprofit organizations: Earth, Just, Meals, and Kids.
n_sample: 41 interviews with organizational members.
authors: Cloutier, C.; Ravasi, D.
theories: identity work; organizational categories; organizational identity theory; social psychological theories of identity
keywords: identity enrichment; identity refinement; identity trajectories; identity work; means-ends structure; organizational identities
research_question: In the absence of major external events, how do organizational identity claims evolve over time, and why do they evolve the way they do? The paper examines this question by tracking long-term continuity and change in the organizational identities of four nonprofit organizations.
mechanism_summary:
- Core contrast: identity refinement versus identity enrichment.
- Structural condition: whether claims defining organizational ends are category-based or relationship-based.
- Identity work processes: identity reflection, identity enactment, and identity enforcement.
- Refinement trajectory: category-based ends and attribute-based means produce planned reflection, structured enactment, rigorous enforcement, and gradual clarification of a core identity.
- Enrichment trajectory: relationship-based ends and category-based means produce ad hoc reflection, emergent enactment, flexible enforcement, and ongoing reinterpretation or addition of identity claims.
- Mechanisms: relative compulsion to conform to categorical expectations and latitude in the pursuit of opportunities.

The paper theorizes identity change as a process shaped by the means-ends structure of identity claims. When organizations define their ends through category-based claims, members are more likely to preserve categorical fit, enact identity through formal structures, reject identity-inconsistent opportunities, and refine a stable position. When organizations define their ends through relationship-based claims, members are more likely to treat categories as flexible means for serving focal constituents, pursue opportunities across categorical boundaries, and enrich or reinterpret identity over time.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational identity theory by explaining long-term identity continuity and change outside disruptive events. It shows that identity claims are not equally consequential: claims defining organizational ends shape trajectories more strongly than claims defining means. It also challenges content-based hierarchy assumptions by arguing that category-based claims do not always precede relationship-based or attribute-based claims; their importance depends on whether members use them to define ends or means.
practical_implication: For nonprofit organizations, the findings suggest that managing mission drift is not only about staying the course but also about maintaining coherence between organizational means and ends. Managers can use the structure of identity claims to guide reflection, enactment, enforcement, activity choices, performance measures, and external messages. The paper also suggests that founders and managers should consider whether defining purpose in categorical or relational terms best fits their aims, because this early structure shapes future strategic options and identity work.
limitations: The authors note that the study is based on nonprofit organizations, though they argue that the theoretical logic may transfer to organizations operating within institutionalized classification systems and relationships with constituencies. They also consider sector differences as a possible alternative explanation because the four organizations operated in different nonprofit sectors, but report that their analysis did not support this explanation. Transferability therefore depends on whether other settings share comparable classification systems, constituency relationships, and opportunities to define organizational ends in categorical or relational terms.
future_research: Future research could examine alternative configurations of identity claims beyond the two observed here, such as attribute-based claims defining means with relationship-based ends, or relationship-based claims defining means with category-based ends. It could also investigate how the means-ends structure of identity claims shapes identity work and strategic change in for-profit firms, professional service organizations, or other settings where category membership and focal-constituency relationships both matter.
abstract: In this study, we track long-term patterns of continuity and change in the organizational identities of four nonprofits. Our findings reveal two trajectories, explained by the different means–ends structure of identity claims at each organization’s founding and the different pattern of identity work that they subsequently carry out. Our observations suggest that not all the attributes members use to make and give sense of “who we are” as an organization are equally consequential for members’ decisions. Claims used to define organizational ends are more likely to shape long-term patterns of identity change and continuity than are claims used to define the means used to pursue these ends, because they affect members’ relative compulsion to conform to categorical expectations as well as the latitude of their pursuit of opportunities for growth.
apa_citation: Cloutier, C., & Ravasi, D. (2020). Identity trajectories: Explaining long-term patterns of continuity and change in organizational identities. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1196-1235. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1051

title: Perception Is Reality: How CEOs’ Observed Personality Influences Market Perceptions of Firm Risk and Shareholder Returns
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of S&P 1500 CEOs and firms from 1993 to 2015, using the Open Language Chief Executive Personality Tool to estimate CEOs' observed five-factor personality traits from earnings-call Q&A language; hypotheses are tested with random-effects panel regression, serial-correlation correction in Stata, and robustness checks using multilevel longitudinal models.
industry: S&P 1500 firms across primary industries; specific industries are not enumerated.
units: CEO-firm-year observations for S&P 1500 firms.
n_sample: 18,748 observations consisting of 2,880 CEOs of 2,008 unique S&P 1500 firms.
authors: Harrison, Joseph S.; Thurgood, Gary R.; Boivie, Steven; Pfarrer, Michael D.
theories: financial economic theory of risk and returns; five-factor model of personality; upper echelons perspective
keywords: firm stock risk; market perceptions; observable personality traits; risk-return relationship; shareholder returns; upper echelons
research_question: How do CEOs' observed personality traits influence market perceptions of firm risk and shareholder returns? The paper asks whether observed conscientiousness, neuroticism, and extraversion shape firm stock risk and condition the relationship between stock risk and returns.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that CEOs' observable verbal and behavioral cues lead market actors to extend judgments about the CEO to the firm. More conscientious CEOs are expected to make the firm appear less risky and more capable of translating risk into returns because they signal deliberation, dependability, and careful management. More neurotic CEOs are expected to make firms appear riskier and less able to convert risk into returns because their cues suggest instability, anxiety, and less predictable leadership. More extraverted CEOs are expected to raise perceived risk and weaken the risk-return relationship because boldness, dominance, and excitement seeking may be read as aggressive risk taking rather than disciplined value creation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends upper echelons research by shifting attention from CEOs' effects on internal strategic choices to CEOs' effects on external market perceptions of firm risk and value creation. It contributes to CEO personality research by distinguishing observed personality from self-reported or underlying personality and showing that externally visible traits have firm-level capital-market consequences. It also contributes to risk-return theory by showing that the risk-return relationship is contingent on how market actors view the CEO.
practical_implication: Boards should consider that CEO personality can affect not only internal leadership but also external perceptions of risk and shareholder value. The findings imply that high conscientiousness and low neuroticism may be desirable from a market-perception standpoint. The authors especially caution boards against equating high extraversion with leader effectiveness when selecting or elevating CEOs.
limitations: The study relies on publicly available CEO language from earnings-call Q&A sessions, and CEOs may manage impressions or receive coaching before these calls. The open-language personality tool improves prediction but remains partly opaque from a face-validity standpoint. The study also cannot directly observe the deeper cognitive processes by which investors translate CEO cues into investment judgments, and it focuses on CEOs rather than broader executive coalitions.
future_research: Future research could triangulate CEO personality using open-language, closed-language, and videometric approaches to clarify which aspects of observed traits drive firm outcomes. Scholars could unpack the investor cognition and causal mechanisms connecting visible CEO cues to market perceptions of risk and returns. Additional work could examine how the observable traits of other executives, or combinations of CEO and top management team traits, shape market judgments across different situations and outcomes.
abstract: We develop theory to explain how CEOs’ observable personality traits influence market perceptions of firm risk and shareholder returns. Using a linguistic tool to measure nearly 3,000 CEOs’ personality traits, we find that CEOs’ observed levels of conscientiousness, neuroticism, and extraversion have important consequences for the perceived riskiness of the firm, as reflected in stock volatility. We also find that these traits alter the relationship between stock risk and returns. Whereas financial economic theory generally posits a positive relationship between risk and returns, on average, we find that this relationship may be either positive or negative for a specific firm depending upon the observed personality of its CEO. Our theory and findings extend upper echelons research by showing that CEOs’ personality traits not only affect market perceptions of the firm but also how those perceptions translate into value creation.
apa_citation: Harrison, J. S., Thurgood, G. R., Boivie, S., & Pfarrer, M. D. (2020). Perception is reality: How CEOs' observed personality influences market perceptions of firm risk and shareholder returns. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1166-1195. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0626

title: Take a Stand or Keep Your Seat: Board Turnover after Social Movement Boycotts
methods: Empirical quantitative archival study of social movement boycotts and director turnover. The paper constructs a hand-collected boycott dataset, validates boycotts as turnover-inducing crises using difference-in-differences with matched controls and fractional logit models, and tests director-level exit using two-stage Heckman selection logic and logit models with standard errors clustered by boycott.
industry: Publicly listed firms targeted by social movement boycotts, matched to Compustat and ISS/RiskMetrics; the sample spans multiple industries rather than one named sector.
country: United States context; boycotts were identified from major U.S. media outlets and director ideology was measured from U.S. Federal Election Commission records, but the paper does not state that all firms were U.S.-headquartered.
time_period: Boycotts occurring between 2000 and 2014.
units: Firm-boycott observations and directors serving on targeted firms' boards.
n_sample: 120 firm-boycott observations for the main boycott sample; director-level models use 102 firm-boycott events and 1,137 observations after missing controls.
authors: McDonnell, Mary-Hunter; Cobb, J. Adam
theories: identity threat; rigidity of the right hypothesis; self-determination theory; social identity and organizational identification
keywords: board turnover; contentious crises; corporate social responsibility; director ideology; social movement boycotts; values alignment
research_question: How do directors' personal values affect their decision to exit the board or remain loyal amid contentious crises? The paper examines this question by studying whether ideological alignment between directors and social movement activists predicts director turnover after boycotts.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that boycotts operate as contentious cues of corporate character. When directors are ideologically aligned with activist challengers, activists' claims reveal a conflict between the firm's perceived values and the directors' own values, producing identity threat and making exit more likely. When directors are ideologically opposed to the challengers, the same boycott can strengthen identification with the firm and reduce exit, especially for conservative directors. The market reaction matters because a more negative stock response increases the salience of the boycott for directors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends board-turnover research by showing that directors' loyalty during crises is shaped not only by performance or reputational risk, but also by perceived values alignment. It contributes to CSR and member-motivation research by showing that social performance is not interpreted uniformly: the same boycott can increase exit among sympathetic directors while entrenching directors who oppose the activists. It also adds to social movement research by showing that contentious activism can alter the loyalty of corporate insiders, not only external stakeholders.
practical_implication: Boards facing contentious social challenges should expect director retention risks to vary by directors' own values and by the ideological valence of the challenge. The findings imply that polarized social issues can produce both exit and entrenchment inside the boardroom, complicating assumptions that social activism has uniform governance effects. Activists and firms should also recognize that boycotts may unintentionally demotivate sympathetic insiders while strengthening opponents' attachment to the firm.
limitations: The authors could not directly observe directors' reasons for leaving, because firms usually do not disclose detailed rationales for board departures and directors may be constrained from discussing exits publicly. Political contributions are also a coarse proxy for ideological alignment, and they may miss within-issue salience, party inconsistency, and differences between social and fiscal conservatism. Finally, identity threat and identification are inferred from patterns in archival data rather than directly measured.
future_research: Future research could examine how activism shapes employee attrition, recruitment, and insider willingness to champion reform after contentious challenges. The authors call for finer-grained measures of ideological alignment, including survey approaches that can capture issue-level values more directly. They also suggest direct tests of identification and identity threat in lower-level employee contexts, potentially using surveys or field experimental designs.
abstract: While prior work has shown that a firm’s market performance affects the loyalty of its board, little is known about how corporate social responsibility affects directors’ willingness to serve. In this project, we shed light on this question by exploring how social movement boycotts that challenge a firm’s social responsibility affect board turnover. We find that boycotts provoke a significant increase in turnover at targeted firms, and that directors are especially likely to leave after boycotts that signal that the firm’s social values conflict with their personal values. Specifically, we find that an ideological match between a board member and the activist challengers predicts exit: liberals are more likely to leave after liberal challenges and conservatives are more likely to leave after conservative challenges. Moreover, we show that turnover is consistent with the rigidity of the right hypothesis in political psychology: conservatives, as compared to liberals, are more prone to entrenchment when their firms face challenges from the opposition. Our study offers strong evidence that corporate social performance matters to corporate directors, and provides insights into the manner in which contentious crises affect the motivation of corporate insiders.
apa_citation: McDonnell, M.-H., & Cobb, J. A. (2020). Take a stand or keep your seat: Board turnover after social movement boycotts. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1028-1053. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0890

title: The Underdog Effect: When Low Expectations Increase Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative multimethod design with one multisource field study of newly hired employees, two online mouse-target experiments, and one laboratory negotiation experiment; analyses include regression, logistic regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderated mediation tests of underdog expectations, desire to prove others wrong, perceived credibility, and performance.
industry: Study 1 uses newly hired employees at a multibillion-dollar consumer packaged goods company; Studies 2 and 4 use online participant samples, and Study 3 uses students in an introductory management course.
country: Study 1 company is headquartered in the United States; broader country restrictions for the experimental samples are not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 measured underdog expectations during training and supervisor-rated performance approximately seven weeks later; experiment dates are not reported in paper.
units: Newly hired employees, online participants, and negotiation dyads.
n_sample: Four studies: Study 1 final sample of 371 employees, Study 2 n = 327 participants, Study 3 n = 78 dyads, and Study 4 n = 589 participants.
authors: Nurmohamed, Samir
theories: Golem effect; psychological reactance theory; self-enhancement theory; self-fulfilling prophecy
keywords: desire to prove others wrong; perceived credibility; performance; psychological reactance; self-enhancement; self-fulfilling prophecy; underdog expectations
research_question: When do underdog expectations increase rather than inhibit individual performance? The paper asks whether individuals' perceptions that others view them as unlikely to succeed can motivate performance through the desire to prove others wrong, and whether this effect depends on observers' perceived credibility.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that underdog expectations can activate self-enhancement and psychological reactance motives: individuals discount less credible low expectations, seek to protect positive self-appraisals, and work harder to show observers that their judgments are wrong. This desire to prove others wrong explains the performance benefit in Study 3 and partly explains the conditional effect in Study 4. When observers are credible, the same underdog expectations are more likely to be internalized or to make proving others wrong performance-disruptive, aligning the findings with the Golem effect and self-fulfilling prophecy.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the assumption that low expectations from others are uniformly detrimental by showing that underdog expectations can motivate performance. It contributes a relational mechanism, the desire to prove others wrong, to expectations and motivation research, moving beyond self-efficacy as the dominant explanation for expectation effects. It also identifies perceived observer credibility as a boundary condition that reconciles the underdog effect with self-fulfilling prophecy theory.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that leaders and organizations may help employees reframe low expectations as an opportunity to prove others wrong. It also implies that managers can reduce the force of low expectations by highlighting why doubting observers may lack credibility. At the same time, organizations should be cautious when people who hold low expectations also have direct authority over employees, because their lack of support may outweigh any motivational benefit.
limitations: The paper notes that its full theoretical model is tested only in the final study, and the mechanisms are measured only in Studies 3 and 4. The conditional indirect effects through proving others wrong are not strongly supported in all analyses, including some low-credibility analyses. Task self-efficacy receives little support as a mechanism, leaving open whether relative inexperience, overconfidence, goal-setting conditions, or boundary-condition effects explain its limited role.
future_research: Future research should examine other mechanisms that may explain the effects of underdog expectations, including proving oneself right, sense of challenge, pride, and feeling that one has nothing to lose. Scholars should also examine settings where credibility and status diverge, and test whether high-status observers produce different responses than low-status observers. Additional research could study how proving others wrong operates in stereotype threat and reactance contexts, including whether it creates performance benefits or costly overexertion.
abstract: Existing theory and research has documented the benefits of facing high expectations and the perils of encountering low expectations. This paper examines the performance effects of underdog expectations, defined as individuals’ perceptions that others view them as unlikely to succeed. Integrating theory and research on self-enhancement with psychological reactance, I predict that underdog expectations have the potential to boost performance through the desire to prove others wrong when others’ credibility is in question. Studies 1 and 2 provide support for the positive relationship between underdog expectations and performance. Study 3 reveals support for the positive effect of underdog expectations on performance through the desire to prove others wrong. Study 4 demonstrates that these effects depend on the perceived credibility of observers: when observers’ expectations are seen as more credible, underdog expectations undermine performance (consistent with the Golem effect and self-fulfilling prophecy), but when observers’ expectations are viewed as less credible, underdog expectations boost performance (demonstrating the underdog effect). My theory and results challenge the assumption that perceiving low expectations from others is always detrimental, and offer meaningful insights into why and when underdog expectations increase versus inhibit performance.

title: Reinventing the State-Owned Enterprise? Negotiating Change during Profound Environmental Upheaval
methods: Inductive qualitative longitudinal single-case study of Turbo Company, a Chinese state-owned power equipment manufacturer, using official government documents, archival organizational documents, semi-structured interviews, participant observation, MAXQDA-assisted coding, chronological case reports, member checks, and iterative movement from empirical themes to conceptual categories and aggregate dimensions.
industry: Power equipment manufacturing
units: Turbo Company, a state-owned enterprise undergoing transformation during China's transition away from a centrally planned economy
n_sample: Single case; more than 770 archival organizational documents, more than 300 official government documents, 31 interviews, and 11 executive meetings observed
authors: Raynard, Mia; Lu, Fangmei; Jing, Runtian
theories: institutional upheaval and transition economies (Hoskisson et al., 2000; Newman, 2000; Peng, 2003); organizational values and change (Amis et al., 2002; Perkmann & Spicer, 2014); values work (Gehman et al., 2013)
keywords: institutional upheaval; mitigating risks of nonconformity; negotiated obsolescence; organizational change; reconditioning; state-owned enterprise; transition economies; values work
research_question: How can an organization purposefully encode practices and structures that appear antithetical to its underpinning values during profound environmental upheaval? The paper examines this question through Turbo Company, a Chinese state-owned enterprise that had to reconcile market-oriented change with socialist roots, employee welfare commitments, and state-enterprise expectations.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Organizational values and change; values work; archetypal socialist organizing template; institutional upheaval; value system discrepancies; appropriateness; continuity and radical change.
- Context / triggering condition: China's transition away from a centrally planned economy eroded the relevance of Turbo's prior organizing template and created pressure to adopt market-oriented structures, incentives, and governance arrangements.
- Process / strategies: Priming for change; reconditioning through coercive embedding, targeted persuasion, and normalizing paradoxes; negotiated obsolescence through indifferent substitution and objectifying and replacing; mitigating risks of nonconformity through external entrainment, grassroots monitoring and feedback, and signifying consent.
- Emergent outcome: Turbo reconfigured its organizing template by introducing new value commitments while removing or replacing institutionalized elements tied to old commitments, without fully abandoning the coherence of its socialist value system.
- Boundary conditions: The model is developed from a single, highly embedded state-owned enterprise in China's transition economy, where government mandates, Party authority, employee welfare expectations, and risks of nonconformity were especially salient.

The process starts when environmental upheaval makes the old organizing template less useful but does not automatically dissolve the organization's inherited values. Turbo's leaders first anchored change narratives to legitimate state mandates, then used values work to make controversial changes implementable: they reconditioned members toward market-oriented commitments, negotiated replacements for valued socialist-era arrangements, and continually aligned scope, timing, and pressure with external policy shifts and internal acceptability. The mechanism is therefore not a clean break from the past, but a negotiated reconfiguration in which continuity in implementation helps make value-incongruent change more acceptable.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to organizational change research by showing that values do not only channel what change options are considered or get upended during radical change. In Turbo's case, values regulated how change was implemented, providing procedural continuity while the organization altered its mission, structures, incentives, and employee-enterprise relationships.

The paper also contributes to research on transition economies by theorizing how organizations manage the risks of divergent change when external rules, political expectations, and internal norms are unsettled. Its model of values work explains how managers balance risk taking and risk minimization through external entrainment, grassroots monitoring, and signifying consent.
practical_implication:
For managers facing controversial or value-incongruent change, the study suggests that implementation processes matter as much as change content. Change is more likely to gain traction when managers connect new practices to familiar values, negotiate replacements for valued arrangements, and monitor what internal and external audiences consider appropriate.

The paper also cautions that coercive pressure must be selective and calibrated. Turbo's leaders used top-down pressure to move reforms forward, but they also delayed, modified, or abandoned initiatives when employee resistance, policy ambiguity, or risks of nonconformity made the change too dangerous.
limitations:
The study draws on a single qualitative case of Turbo Company, so the model is bounded by a state-owned enterprise in China's transition economy. The authors explicitly note that the setting involves unusually high political ambiguity, strong state authority, socialist legacies, and risks such as sanctions, imprisonment, labor unrest, and retrospective accountability.

The paper's evidence is also weighted toward leaders, managers, archival documents, and executive meetings. The authors address this limitation by using staff appeals, meeting minutes, and other documents to understand lower-level experiences, but the account remains more top-down than a study centered on ordinary employees' lived experience.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether changes in normative expectations are more or less likely than technological disruption or regulatory change to dislodge organizational values. The paper also invites comparative work on how different contextual conditions and different levels of commitment to an archetypal template shape the mutability of organizing templates.

Further studies could examine how values work evolves as transition economies mature and how prospective alignment strategies help managers anticipate future shifts in the boundaries of appropriateness. These questions would extend the model beyond Turbo's specific Chinese SOE context and test how organizations manage value-incongruent change in other turbulent environments.
abstract: This study builds theory on organizational change through a qualitative study investigating how a small state-run factory in China transformed into a global leader in power equipment manufacturing. Drawing on cross-level longitudinal data from the company’s founding in 1966 to 2016, we unpack a process of organizational change that unfolded during China’s transition away from a centrally planned economy. Our findings draw attention to the role of “values work” in facilitating and mitigating the risks of implementing highly controversial and seemingly immoral changes, which, in the case of the present study, were necessitated when the relevance of prior experience and organizing templates eroded. We present a model illustrating three strategies that, in combination, animate this values work: reconditioning, negotiated obsolescence, and mitigating risks of nonconformity. The model contributes to an understanding of how organizations reconcile the need for radical change with pressures for continuity and coherence. It also shows how managers find a balance between taking risks and minimizing them through efforts to time and align ongoing changes with shifting conceptualizations of appropriateness—both inside and outside the organization.

title: Making Space for Art: A Spatial Perspective of Disruptive and Defensive Institutional Work in Venezuela’s Art World
methods: In-depth longitudinal qualitative case study of Venezuela’s art world after the Bolivarian Revolution, using two rounds of semi-structured interviews, nonparticipant observation in public and private art spaces, secondary policy/media/government material, visual data, and inductive coding informed by Lefebvre’s spatial theory.
industry: Venezuela’s art world, including museums, galleries, art fairs, salons, cultural foundations, and public and private art venues
country: Venezuela, with fieldwork in Caracas and international art-scene sites connected to Venezuelan art
time_period: Data collected in 2009-2012 and 2016-2017, with analysis of changes in Venezuela’s art world since the late 1990s
units: Venezuelan art-world actors, state-run and private art spaces, public museums, alternative venues, art salons, secondary cultural-policy events, and visual/material spatial artifacts
n_sample: 40 semi-structured interviews; just over 800 pages of interview transcripts; just under 100 secondary sources; approximately 200 photographs; nonparticipant observation across art settings
authors: Rodner, Victoria; Roulet, Thomas J.; Kerrigan, Finola; vom Lehn, Dirk
theories: Henri Lefebvre’s theory of the production of space (Lefebvre, 1974/1991); institutional work (Lawrence & Suddaby, 2006; Lawrence, Suddaby, & Leca, 2009); space and place in institutional work (Lawrence & Dover, 2015; Weinfurtner & Seidl, 2019)
keywords: Henri Lefebvre; Venezuela’s art world; bubble of freedom; defensive institutional work; disruptive institutional work; material dimensions; social dimensions; space; symbolic dimensions
research_question: The paper asks what role space plays in the disruption and defense of institutions, and how the dimensions of space interact in that disruption and defense. It examines these questions in Venezuela’s art world after the Bolivarian Revolution, where government actors and displaced art professionals used different spatial tactics to contest what art should be and who could legitimate it.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Space; disruptive institutional work; defensive institutional work; material, social, and symbolic dimensions of space; government appropriation of official art venues; displaced art actors’ alternative “bubble of freedom.”
- Process / phases: Government centralization and reclamation of official art spaces; exclusion and displacement of established art professionals; clustering of private galleries and alternative venues; social and symbolic reconstruction of value-granting practices.
- Spatial dimensions: Material positioning through proximity, distance, boundaries, and isolation; social embodiment and enactment of space through actors’ practices and networks; symbolic expressiveness through curatorial discourse, rebranding, and value conferral.
- Emergent outcomes: Coexistence of competing institutional prescriptions in different spaces rather than a simple replacement of one institution by another; partial defense of art-world values in a spatially isolated but symbolically meaningful private-sector cluster.
- Boundary conditions: The process is theorized in a mature field marked by a strong power imbalance, where government actors controlled publicly financed cultural spaces and displaced actors retained social and symbolic links to the global art world.

The process begins when the Chávez administration appropriates and reorganizes museums, galleries, art salons, and cultural agencies to align official art space with Bolivarian ideology. Established art professionals respond by distancing themselves from state-run venues and clustering private galleries, foundations, and alternative venues into a “bubble of freedom” where they can continue curatorial and value-conferring practices. Material demarcation enables new social interactions, and those interactions reinforce symbolic legitimacy; at the same time, the bubble protects defensive work while also narrowing access to wider audiences and material resources.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to institutional work by showing that space is not merely a background location for institutional struggle but a strategic lever through which actors disrupt and defend institutions. It extends research on place and materiality by distinguishing material positioning, social embodiment/enactment, and symbolic expressiveness, and by showing how these dimensions mutually reinforce one another during institutional conflict.

The study also refines accounts of institutional change by showing coexistence between competing institutional prescriptions rather than straightforward deinstitutionalization or replacement. Controlling official places such as museums does not automatically produce control over the institution, because displaced actors may retain social and symbolic resources in alternative spaces.
practical_implication:
For cultural-sector leaders and policymakers, the study cautions that physical control of museums, galleries, or public venues does not by itself confer legitimacy over artistic practices or audiences. Spatial redesign, rebranding, and centralized governance may disrupt existing institutional roles, but they can also isolate official venues from the social networks and symbolic resources that make those venues meaningful.

For displaced professionals and field actors, the study shows the defensive value of clustering, alternative venues, and international connections. It also warns that protective spatial isolation can become a double-edged strategy when alternative spaces preserve professional practices but reduce public accessibility and dependence on scarce private resources.
limitations:
The authors identify the scope of the case across time and space as a limitation, since the model is grounded in the disrupted Venezuelan art sector. The setting involves a mature field, a strong power imbalance, and government control over publicly financed cultural spaces, so the findings may travel most directly to fields where established actors can be forcefully excluded from institutional spaces.

The study also does not observe radical spatial destruction as institutional work. Its account therefore speaks more directly to appropriation, displacement, demarcation, isolation, and symbolic reconfiguration than to cases where actors destroy places or remove all spatial supports for institutional practice.
future_research:
The paper calls for research on the interaction of time and space in institutional struggles, especially because spatial support for institutions can develop over decades or centuries. Future studies could examine how temporal organizing and spatial organizing jointly challenge, maintain, or sediment institutional practices.

The authors also encourage research on power, space, and resources from an institutional perspective, including cases where actors destroy places or deprive others of spatial supports for institutional practice. They further suggest multimodal research on how spatial artifacts such as galleries, museums, biennales, and fairs constrain and enable meaning-making, discourse, and institutionalization.
abstract: The physical and material aspects of space, such as geographical distance or boundaries, have social and symbolic consequences that impact how people influence and are influenced by institutions. Social actors can, however, contest how space is conceived, perceived, and lived, thus making space a crucial lever in the disruption and defense of institutions. However, we lack understanding of the spatial aspects of such institutional struggles. In exploring how space is leveraged in institutional work, our study foregrounds the sociopolitical nature of space, building on and expanding the theorization of Henri Lefebvre. We draw on an in-depth longitudinal analysis of the material, social, and symbolic aspects of the spatial dimensions of disruptive and defensive institutional work over the past 20 years in Venezuela’s art world. Following the start of the Bolivarian Revolution in the late 1990s, the incoming government transformed the organization of the national cultural landscape, resulting in a prolonged period of institutional disruption and defense. Analyzing data relating to Venezuela’s art world during this time, we demonstrate that actors use the material, social, and symbolic dimensions of space to challenge and maintain their key values and practices—and that these three dimensions are intertwined.
apa_citation: Rodner, V., Roulet, T. J., Kerrigan, F., & vom Lehn, D. (2020). Making space for art: A spatial perspective of disruptive and defensive institutional work in Venezuela’s art world. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 1054-1081. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1030

title: Signal Strength, Media Attention, and Resource Mobilization: Evidence from New Private Equity Firms
methods: Longitudinal panel analysis of first-time private equity firms using Preqin fundraising and performance data, ProQuest Global Newsstream media-attention data, and linear probability models with PE firm fixed effects and heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors clustered at the PE firm level.
industry: Independent private equity firms, specifically venture capital and buyout funds.
country: Global private equity sample, with geographical investment focus and GP location categorized as United States, Europe, and rest of world; the majority of first-time PE funds focused on the United States.
time_period: First funds raised between 1999 and 2007, with firm-year data collected up to December 2017.
units: First-time PE firm-years at risk of raising a follow-on fund.
n_sample: 205 new PE firms and 1,057 firm-year observations.
authors: Vanacker, T.; Forbes, D. P.; Knockaert, M.; Manigart, S.
theories: bounded rationality; information intermediaries; signaling theory; sociocognitive perspective
keywords: follow-on fund; media attention; private equity firms; realized performance; resource mobilization; signal strength; signaling theory; unrealized performance
research_question: How do multiple simultaneous signals of different strengths influence resource provision decisions for new firms, and when does media attention alter the effectiveness of weak versus strong signals? The paper examines whether unrealized performance and realized performance help first-time private equity firms raise follow-on funds, and whether media attention strengthens these relationships differently.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Fund age, fund age squared, called capital, S&P 500 return, PE raised on GDP, calendar-year dummies, and PE firm fixed effects; descriptive and robustness models also account for fund size, stage focus, geography, GP location, industry focus, and vintage year.

The mechanism combines signaling theory with a sociocognitive account of attention and evaluation. Unrealized performance is a weaker signal because it is based on estimated, not yet exited portfolio value, but it can still draw prospective capital providers into considering a new PE firm and can anchor their evaluation. Realized performance is a stronger signal because it reflects realized distributions from exits. Media attention makes weak performance signals more observable and may legitimize the signal source, so it strengthens the fundraising effect of unrealized performance more than the effect of realized performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances signaling theory by showing that new firms can convey multiple performance signals that differ in strength, and that a weak signal can still mobilize resources. It also integrates signaling theory with a sociocognitive perspective by showing that signal effectiveness depends on the information environment, specifically media attention as an information intermediary. The study contributes empirical evidence that realized performance is more strongly correlated with eventual realized returns than unrealized performance, while also showing that media attention makes the weaker signal more effective for fundraising.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that new firms should not rely only on strong but hard-to-obtain signals such as realized outcomes or prominent affiliations. When strong signals are unavailable, weaker but credible signals of future performance may still help attract resource providers, especially if the firm has enough media attention to be noticed and evaluated. For PE firms, communicating unrealized performance can support fundraising, but its effectiveness is contingent and should not be treated as automatic.
limitations: The paper notes that the private equity setting involves sophisticated capital providers, so the magnitude and dynamics of weak-signal effects may differ for less sophisticated resource providers or other resource markets. It also acknowledges that the study cannot separately observe attention-set formation and evaluation, even though the theory distinguishes these phases. Finally, the analysis assumes that new PE firms generally want to raise a follow-on fund, while exceptional situations such as partner conflicts or departures may lead some firms not to seek one.
future_research: Future research could test whether weak signals and media attention operate similarly in entrepreneurial contexts outside private equity. The paper also calls for work on other types of weak signals, such as announcements about future actions, and on whether different resource providers attend differently to weak and strong signals. Additional studies could directly examine consideration-set formation and evaluation processes, and investigate why some PE firms may decide not to raise follow-on funds.
abstract: Past research has shown that new firms can facilitate resource mobilization by signaling their unobservable quality to prospective resource providers. However, we know less about situations in which firms convey multiple signals of different strengths—that is, signals that are moreor less-correlated with unobservable firm quality. Building on a sociocognitive perspective, we propose that prospective resource providers respond differently to signals of different strengths and that the effectiveness of signals, especially weak signals, will be contingent on the media attention new firms receive. Empirically, we conduct a longitudinal analysis examining the ability of new private equity firms to raise a follow-on fund. Consistent with our theory, we find that unrealized performance, a relatively weak signal, positively influences fundraising. However, we fail to find statistical evidence that its effect is weaker than that of realized performance, a relatively strong signal. Further, media attention strengthens the relationship between unrealized performance and fundraising, but media attention exerts less impact on the relationship between realized performance and fundraising. Taken together, our findings deepen our understanding of how new firms can mobilize resources with signals of different strengths and of how the media—as a key information intermediary— differently impacts their effectiveness.

title: Beyond the Pyramid: Alternative Formal Hierarchical Structures and Team Performance
methods: Multi-method quantitative study combining an agent-based computational model of six formal hierarchical structures with a survey-based field study of clinical nursing shifts; Study 1 simulated a 6 x 2 between-team design, and Study 2 used archival hierarchy data, two online surveys, and linear mixed models to predict patient care.
industry: Clinical nursing shifts in hospitals
time_period: Two survey waves administered three to four months apart; no calendar dates reported.
units: Study 1 simulated teams; Study 2 clinical nursing shifts
n_sample: Study 2 final sample of 68 shifts; Study 1 simulated 500 teams in each cell of the model design.
authors: Wellman, Ned; Applegate, J. M.; Harlow, John; Johnston, Erik W.
theories: formal hierarchy and power; group engagement model and social identification; perspective taking; team-level theory of formal hierarchical differentiation
keywords: agent-based computational model; clinical nursing shifts; formal hierarchical differentiation; formal hierarchy skewness; patient care; perspective-taking accuracy; perspective-taking motivation; social identification; task variety; team performance
research_question: How do alternative formal hierarchical structures beyond the pyramid and leaderless team affect team performance? The paper asks how formal hierarchy shape and skewness influence team members' perspective-taking motivation, social identification, team-optimal behavior, and performance under different levels of perspective-taking accuracy.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that formal hierarchical differentiation creates power imbalances that shape whose perspectives team members try to incorporate. Positively skewed pyramids contain more low-authority members, increasing perspective-taking motivation; this helps when members can accurately infer one another's task preferences but hurts when task variety makes such inference unreliable. Negatively skewed inverse pyramids contain more high-authority members, reducing misplaced perspective taking and improving performance when perspective-taking accuracy is low. The field study tests this model by showing that inverse-pyramid-like nursing shifts provide better patient care than pyramid-like shifts when task variety is high, but not when task variety is low.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends hierarchy research by identifying a taxonomy of six formal hierarchical structures and showing that alternatives to the pyramid and leaderless team can matter for team performance. It challenges functional accounts that treat pyramid-shaped hierarchy as generally superior by showing that the inverse pyramid can outperform the pyramid when task conditions reduce perspective-taking accuracy.

It also contributes a team-level account of power and hierarchy by linking formal hierarchy skewness to perspective-taking motivation, social identification, and team-optimal behavior. This reframes prior task-contingency findings around whether team tasks make others' preferences easier or harder to infer.
practical_implication:
Organizations should not default to pyramid-shaped team structures when task work is ambiguous, novel, or high in variety. For such teams, a negatively skewed hierarchy or a more evenly distributed formal authority structure may be more appropriate than a traditional pyramid.

Managers evaluating team structures should also avoid overreacting to early performance variation. The modeling results suggest that some structures fluctuate early and then stabilize, so structure-performance patterns may need to be assessed over repeated decisions rather than a single episode.
limitations:
The agent-based model is intentionally parsimonious and assumes that the ideal team outcome is the option that best satisfies collective member utilities. The authors note that other teams may value other effectiveness criteria, so the model's conclusions may not generalize to every type of team outcome.

Study 2 has a modest shift-level sample size, uses clinical nursing shifts primarily composed of Caucasian females, and measures task variety and patient care from the same source at different times. The study also does not directly test the theorized mediators, such as perspective-taking motivation and accuracy.
future_research:
Future research could test the taxonomy across other team contexts and effectiveness criteria, including outcomes where the best solution is not simply the team-optimal aggregation of member preferences. Studies could also examine other bases of hierarchy, especially status hierarchies, and how they interact with formal authority structures.

The authors call for designs that directly manipulate formal hierarchical structure and measure perspective-taking motivation and accuracy. Laboratory or field experiments could compare multiple explanatory mechanisms, including internal rivalries, power struggles, demographic subgroups, and individual differences in perspective taking.
abstract: Formal hierarchical differentiation is a cornerstone of the organizing process. Prior research has focused primarily on pyramid-shaped formal hierarchies, despite documented limitations of the pyramid structure. We adopt a multi-method approach to consider the utility of alternative hierarchical shapes. First, we identify six “pure type” formal hierarchies that teams might employ. Next, we develop three propositions explaining the effects of hierarchy on team members’ cognition and behavior. We use the propositions to parameterize an agent-based computational model in which formal hierarchical differentiation influences team performance by creating power imbalances that affect team members’ perspective-taking motivation, and by influencing members’ social identification with the team. The modeling results reveal how the effects of the six hierarchies are contingent upon task characteristics that influence team members’ perspective-taking accuracy (e.g., task variety), and enable us to craft an expanded, team-level theory of the association between formal hierarchical differentiation and team performance. A field study of 68 clinical nursing shifts in five mid-sized hospitals supports a key theoretical prediction. Specifically, we find that a negatively skewed (inverse pyramid–shaped) formal hierarchy enhances team performance relatively to a positively skewed (pyramidshaped) hierarchy when task variety is high, but not when task variety is low.
apa_citation: Wellman, N., Applegate, J. M., Harlow, J., & Johnston, E. W. (2020). Beyond the pyramid: Alternative formal hierarchical structures and team performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(4), 997-1027. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1475

title: Interorganizational Relationships as Political Battlefields: How Fragmentation within Organizations Shapes Relational Dynamics between Organizations
methods: Longitudinal inductive case study of a dyadic strategic alliance between Alpha and Beta, using interviews, archival documents, e-mails, event analysis, visual mapping, and second-order theorizing.
industry: Strategic alliance between Alpha, a multinational manufacturer of heavy vehicles, and Beta, a developer and manufacturer of motion control systems.
country: Specific country not reported; both organizations had sales and R&D activities in Asia, Europe, and the Americas.
time_period: Alliance history and data covered 2010-2016, with longitudinal follow-up until March 2016.
units: One dyadic, multi-project strategic alliance involving Alpha, Beta, the Knight and Queen R&D projects, Alpha directors, Alpha technology managers, and Beta representatives.
n_sample: 33 Alpha interviews with 24 informants, six Beta interviews with six informants, 160 archival documents, 1,064 e-mails, and a 396-event database.
authors: Brattström, A.; Faems, D.
theories: competing logics; interorganizational relational dynamics; organizational politics; trust dynamics
keywords: commitment; competing partnership logics; dual relational dynamics; internal fragmentation; interorganizational relationships; organizational politics; relational dynamics; strategic alliance; trust
research_question: How does internal fragmentation within one partner organization influence relational dynamics between organizations? The paper examines this question by studying how competing coalitions inside Alpha shaped trust and commitment dynamics in its strategic alliance with Beta.
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering context: Alpha's technological transition created a need to collaborate differently with suppliers.
- Competing partnership logics: Alpha directors held an embedded partnership logic, while Alpha technology managers held a transactional partnership logic.
- Divergent framing-action sequences: directors interpreted events through cooperative framings and took nurturing actions toward Beta; technology managers interpreted events through competitive framings and took destabilizing actions.
- Mixed emotional states: Alpha and Beta directors experienced disappointment in the current relationship while retaining hope for a better future relationship.
- Relational outcome: negative trust dynamics coexisted with renewed formal commitments, producing dual relational dynamics.
- Feedback process: the dual relational dynamics sustained the competing partnership logics inside Alpha.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. Internal coalitions used the interorganizational relationship as a political battlefield for broader supplier-management logics. Directors' nurturing actions regenerated hope and formal commitments, while technology managers' destabilizing actions produced disappointment and mistrust, preventing the reinforcing trust-commitment spiral assumed in much prior interorganizational research.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a political perspective on interorganizational relationships by showing that partner organizations should not be treated as monolithic actors. It specifies how within-partner coalitions can frame and act on the same interorganizational events differently, and how those politically charged sequences can generate dual relational dynamics rather than positive or negative reinforcing spirals. It also shows that interorganizational relationships can feed back into internal fragmentation by giving coalitions evidence for their competing partnership logics.
practical_implication: For managers of strategic alliances, the paper implies that trust and commitment problems may originate inside a partner organization rather than only between partners. Alliance governance therefore requires attention to internal coalitions, supplier-management logics, and the way internal groups frame external events. Dedicated alliance functions or routines may help manage the internal implications of interorganizational relationships, not only the formal relationship between firms.
limitations: The study is based on one dyadic strategic alliance between a buyer and supplier, with unusually rich longitudinal access to Alpha but more limited access to Beta. The authors acknowledge that the six Beta interviews allowed them to understand Beta's reactions and trust perceptions but did not permit a deep examination of internal dynamics within Beta. The case's strategic, high-investment supplier-alliance setting may also make internal fragmentation especially salient.
future_research: Future research could examine whether other types of interorganizational relationships, including competitor partnerships, multiparty constellations, and innovation ecosystems, generate similar or different forms of coalition building. It could also study coalition building across organizational boundaries and investigate how a political perspective changes theories of interorganizational governance, outsourcing decisions, and alliance design. Further work could compare contexts in which interorganizational relationships amplify internal fragmentation with contexts in which external conflict strengthens internal unity.
abstract: Whereas extant theorizing on interorganizational relational dynamics has highlighted the importance of between-partner differences, we shift attention to within-partner differences. We explore how internal fragmentation—that is, the existence of multiple coalitions within a partner organization, each with different interests and perspectives— influences the evolution of relational characteristics in interorganizational relationships. Based on a longitudinal case study of a dyadic strategic alliance, we develop a process model, describing how internal fragmentation within one of the partner organizations can lead to a counterintuitive relational pattern—namely, “dual relational dynamics”—where decision makers of both partners continue renewing their formal commitments, while simultaneously experiencing negative trust dynamics. We show that the existence of different belief systems within one partner organization can lead to a politically charged process, wherein different coalitions within this organization frame and act upon interorganizational events in different ways. This politically charged process can fuel both hope and disappointment among decision makers of both partner organizations, leading to dual relational dynamics. Our findings contribute by advocating a political perspective on interorganizational relationships. We also demonstrate the relevance of this political perspective by showing how it challenges the dominant notion of interorganizational relational dynamics as reinforcing spirals.
apa_citation: Brattström, A., & Faems, D. (2020). Interorganizational relationships as political battlefields: How fragmentation within organizations shapes relational dynamics between organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1591-1620. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0038

title: Catching the Big Fish: The Role of Scandals in Making Status a Liability
methods: Archival quantitative study of U.S. publicly traded firms accused of securities fraud through securities class action lawsuits; Cox proportional hazard regression models estimate the likelihood and timing of SEC enforcement action, with robustness checks using binary dependent-variable models, alternative status measures, sample exclusions, and scandal-specific analyses.
industry: Publicly traded firms from multiple industries accused of securities fraud through securities class action lawsuits.
time_period: Class action lawsuits filed from 2006-2011, covering the options backdating scandal of 2006-2007 and the subprime mortgage scandal of 2007-2009; SEC enforcement searches followed each lawsuit for up to seven years.
units: Securities class action lawsuits against publicly traded firms, modeled as firm-year risk observations for SEC enforcement action.
n_sample: 806 lawsuits against 737 publicly traded firms; 3,786 observations; 112 SEC enforcement actions.
authors: Dewan, Yasir; Jensen, Michael
theories: labeling perspective (Becker, 1963; Erikson, 1962; Kitsuse & Cicourel, 1963; Greve et al., 2010); organizational status and status hierarchy (Gould, 2002; Jensen, Kim, & Kim, 2011); social-control-agent perspective on organizational misconduct (Greve et al., 2010)
keywords: SEC enforcement action; labeling of misconduct; multiple-actor scandal; organizational misconduct; organizational status; social control agents; social status
research_question: When do social control agents label alleged organizational violations of rules and norms as misconduct, and how does a multiple-actor scandal change whether high organizational status is an asset or a liability? The paper asks whether high-status firms accused of securities fraud are more likely to face SEC enforcement action when their alleged violation is part of a widespread scandal rather than a standalone violation.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is sociopolitical rather than purely psychological. In standalone allegations, high status can protect firms by generating trust, legitimacy, power, and benefit of the doubt. During a multiple-actor scandal, public attention, audience-provided evidence, reputational contamination, vengeance, and deterrence incentives weaken those protections while increasing the hazards of visibility and high expectations, so status becomes associated with a greater likelihood of formal labeling by the SEC.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to organizational misconduct research by explaining when status shifts from protection to liability in social-control-agent labeling decisions. It extends prior work that emphasized psychological mechanisms such as violated expectations and status anxiety by specifying sociopolitical mechanisms through which multiple-actor scandals reduce status protections and heighten status hazards. It also advances labeling research by showing that regulatory labeling is not merely a direct implication of law or norms, but is shaped by organizational status and scandal context.
practical_implication: For high-status firms, the study implies that status should not be treated as a stable shield in misconduct contexts: during a multiple-actor scandal, visibility and symbolic value may make them more attractive enforcement targets. For regulators and other social control agents, the findings clarify how scandal can alter the political and evidentiary environment in which enforcement discretion is exercised.
limitations: The authors note that SEC enforcement action is only the final observable outcome of a longer enforcement process that begins with informal inquiry and may include formal investigation and Wells notices, so the study cannot test the theory at earlier stages of enforcement. They also treat two scandals, options backdating and subprime mortgage, as the empirical scandal contexts; because scandals are rare events, this constrains the breadth of direct empirical comparison even though the authors discuss corroborating evidence from other scandals.
future_research: The authors call for in-depth case studies to establish which specific sociopolitical mechanisms, or combinations of mechanisms, account for the status-liability effect during scandals. They also encourage research on the perceptions, motivations, and behavior of firms, social control agents, and news media as scandals unfold, and on whether scandals produce influential social movements, regulatory change, and longer-term social order or disorder.
abstract: This study focuses on how scandal shapes the effect of social status in labeling of an alleged violation of rules and norms as misconduct by social control agents. It suggests that organizational status is more likely to be a liability than an asset when alleged violation is part of a multiple-actor scandal. Specifically, an alleged violation by a high-status organization is more likely to be labeled as misconduct when that violation is part of a multiple-actor scandal compared to when it is a standalone violation. This is because multiple-actor scandal triggers sociopolitical mechanisms that decrease the protective benefits of status and augment the potential hazards of status, making status a liability during a multiple-actor scandal. Focusing empirically on the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as the focal social control agent and on the SEC enforcement action as labeling of misconduct, we find that status in itself neither protects nor exposes organizations to the enforcement action, but that status increases the likelihood of the enforcement action when misconduct is part of a multiple-actor scandal.
apa_citation: Dewan, Y., & Jensen, M. (2020). Catching the big fish: The role of scandals in making status a liability. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1652-1678. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0685

title: What Drives Exploration? Convergence and Divergence of Exploration Tendencies among Alliance Partners and Competitors
methods: Panel-data quantitative study of publicly traded U.S. electronics firms, using patent-class diversity to measure focal-firm, alliance-partner, and competitor exploration; two-stage panel models with fixed effects, AR(1) correction, and selection controls test linear, quadratic, and moderated associations.
industry: Electronics industry sectors: electronic devices, semiconductor components, computer hardware, industrial and commercial machinery and computer equipment, electronic and electrical equipment and components, and measurement, analysis, and control instruments
time_period: 1990-2006, with patent and alliance histories measured from 1985
units: Firm-year observations for publicly traded electronics firms and their alliance partners and primary competitors
n_sample: 180 firms and 2,337 firm-year observations for competitor exploration; 153 firms and 1,474 firm-year observations for partner exploration
authors: Duysters, Geert; Lavie, Dovev; Sabidussi, Anna; Stettner, Uriel
theories: exploration-exploitation framework; imitation and legitimation; organizational learning; vicarious learning
keywords: alliance partners; competitors; exploitation; exploration; firm-specific uncertainty; imitation; legitimation; technological proximity; vicarious learning
research_question: What drives a firm's tendency to explore in its knowledge domains, and how do the exploration levels of its alliance partners and primary competitors shape convergence or divergence in that tendency? The paper asks whether firms adjust exploration interdependently through reference-group learning rather than only through industry conditions or firm-specific traits.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that firms use alliance partners and primary competitors as reference groups when deciding how much to explore. At lower alter-exploration levels, imitation and legitimacy-seeking pull the focal firm toward convergence with partners and competitors. At excessive alter-exploration levels, perceived risk and specialization pressures push the focal firm toward exploitation, producing an inverted U-shaped association. Firm-specific uncertainty strengthens convergence, incoherence in partners' or competitors' exploration weakens it, and technological proximity to competitors unexpectedly weakens convergence because differentiation from close rivals becomes more salient.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on antecedents of exploration by showing that firm exploration tendencies are interdependent and shaped by unique cooperation and competition networks, not only by industry-level conditions or internal organizational characteristics. It extends vicarious learning theory by identifying when reference-group behavior leads to convergence and when perceived risk, specialization, incoherence, and proximity lead to divergence. It also refines exploration-exploitation research by distinguishing learning from partners' and competitors' knowledge from learning from their exploratory behavior.
practical_implication: Managers should not infer desirable exploration levels only from broad industry trends; they should consider the exploratory behavior of their specific alliance partners and primary competitors. Under uncertainty, reference groups may provide useful cues, but managers should avoid blindly matching excessive or incoherent exploration patterns. The findings also suggest that firms may need to diverge from close competitors' exploration when differentiation and specialization are strategically valuable.
limitations: The authors note that they do not directly observe the proposed mechanisms of imitation, legitimacy, perceived risk, balance across modes, and differentiation. The study focuses on exploration in the knowledge domain and measures it through patent-class diversity, which may not capture novelty to the world or other forms of exploration. Generalizability is also bounded by the focus on the electronics industry and by competitor definitions based on knowledge similarity.
future_research: Future research should study the performance implications of converging with partners' and competitors' exploration levels. Additional work could examine other reference groups, such as corporate venture capital investors, customers, and suppliers, and identify which partners or competitors firms follow when reference-group exploration is incoherent. The authors also call for direct tests of the mechanisms and for extensions to domains such as diversification, internationalization, alternative competitor definitions, more complex exploration measures, and other industries.
abstract: Management research has alluded to organizational and environmental conditions that drive firms’ tendencies to explore versus exploit. We complement this research by developing theory on vicarious learning to explain how a firm adjusts its own exploration level based on the exploration levels of its alliance partners and competitors. Using panel data on 180 electronics firms publicly traded in the United States, we reveal an inverted U-shaped association between a firm’s exploration tendency and the exploration levels of its partners and competitors. Convergence is explained by imitation and legitimation, while divergence is associated with risk perception and specialization in the knowledge domain. We further show how the convergence of the exploration tendency becomes stronger under firm-specific uncertainty but weaker when the exploration patterns exhibited by the firm’s partners and competitors are incoherent. Finally, counter to expectations, we show that this convergence is weakened by the technological proximity of the firm’s competitors. Our findings inform research on vicarious learning and the antecedents of exploration by underscoring the role of interdependence in firms’ exploration tendencies.
apa_citation: Duysters, G., Lavie, D., Sabidussi, A., & Stettner, U. (2020). What drives exploration? Convergence and divergence of exploration tendencies among alliance partners and competitors. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1425-1454. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1409
