title: When Work and Family Blend Together: Examining the Daily Experiences of Breastfeeding Mothers at Work
methods: Mixed-method multistudy design: Study 1 used semi-structured interviews and content analysis with breastfeeding women working full-time; Study 2 used a 15-day experience sampling design with multilevel path analysis in Mplus 7.4.
industry: Multiple industries represented in Study 1, including medical, education, government, insurance, and transportation; Study 2 was not restricted to a particular industry.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Breastfeeding women working full-time; Study 2 day-level observations
n_sample: 38 women in Study 1; 106 women and 1,206 days of data in Study 2
authors: Gabriel, Allison S.; Volpone, Sabrina D.; MacGowan, Rebecca L.; Butts, Marcus M.; Moran, Christina M.
theories: role transition and boundary theory (Ashforth et al., 2000); work–family border theory (Clark, 2000); work–family interference and enrichment theory (Greenhaus & Beutell, 1985; Greenhaus & Powell, 2006)
keywords: blended work–family experiences; breastfeeding at work; breastfeeding compassion; breastfeeding enrichment; breastfeeding interference; breastfeeding stigma; negative affect; positive affect; quality of the breastfeeding space; work–family balance satisfaction
research_question: How do breastfeeding women working full-time experience breastfeeding at work as a blended work–family experience, and how do those daily experiences affect breastfeeding, work, and family outcomes? The paper asks whether breastfeeding at work operates only as interference or can also generate enrichment when work and family roles are fully blended during the workday.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that breastfeeding at work creates a borderland in which a family role is physically, temporally, and psychologically brought into work. When women appraise that blended experience as interference, negative affect increases and positive affect decreases, which undermines breastfeeding goal progress and work goal progress through negative affect and lowers work–family balance satisfaction through reduced positive affect. When women appraise breastfeeding at work as enriching, negative affect decreases and positive affect increases, producing the opposite pattern for breastfeeding and work goal progress through lower negative affect and improving balance satisfaction through higher positive affect. Contextual features shape these affective experiences, with stigma and breastfeeding-space quality having direct affective effects and compassion strengthening the interference-positive affect relationship in the tested model.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends work–family theory by showing that some experiences are not transfers between separate work and family domains but fully blended states in which role boundaries are thin or absent. It demonstrates that the same blended experience, breastfeeding at work, can generate both interference and enrichment rather than fitting only the traditional family-demand model. It also adds contextual detail to work–family border theory by examining stigma, compassion, and the physical breastfeeding space as features that influence daily affect in the borderland.
practical_implication: Organizations should treat breastfeeding at work as a normal work–family accommodation issue, not as time off or a private inconvenience. The paper points to practical value in sufficient pumping time, supportive supervisor and coworker responses, and high-quality breastfeeding spaces that are private, quiet, spacious, comfortable, and equipped for pumping. It also suggests that reducing stigma and increasing compassion can improve breastfeeding mothers' affective experiences at work.
limitations: The samples were recruited partly through online breastfeeding support groups, which may bias participation toward women more willing to discuss breastfeeding. The paper did not restrict the studies to a particular industry, so industry- or occupation-specific norms around breastfeeding at work remain unresolved. The Study 2 outcomes were self-reported by the women themselves, including breast milk production, work goal progress, and work–family balance satisfaction.
future_research: Future research should examine more racially, culturally, economically, and occupationally diverse samples of breastfeeding women at work. The authors call for work on industry and occupation differences, supervisor or coworker ratings of productivity, partner or childcare-provider reports of family outcomes, and additional daily experiences such as incivility, ostracism, guilt, pride, and identity coactivation. They also suggest studying other fully blended work–nonwork experiences, including family business work and telecommuting.
abstract: Although several work–family theories describe complexities associated with fulfilling work and family roles, extant research has not fully explained blended work–family experiences, such as women working full-time and breastfeeding at work. To address this shortcoming, we conducted a multistudy investigation. In Study 1, we interviewed 38 women about their daily experiences surrounding breastfeeding at work. We then developed a theoretical model to examine possible challenges and benefits associated with this blended work–family experience and tested it with an experience sampling investigation assessing 106 women over 15 workdays in Study 2. Results suggested that breastfeeding interference increased negative affect and decreased positive affect daily, with negative affect hindering breastfeeding goal progress (i.e., ounces of breast milk produced at work) and work goal progress. However, positive experiences tied to breastfeeding enrichment decreased negative affect and increased positive affect, with positive affect increasing work–family balance satisfaction. Beyond these relationships, we explored effects associated with contextual features of breastfeeding at work—breastfeeding stigma, breastfeeding compassion, and quality of the breastfeeding space. Combined, our work enhances theoretical understanding of blended work–family experiences, highlighting that blending work and family roles daily can yield both positive and negative consequences across domains.
apa_citation: Gabriel, A. S., Volpone, S. D., MacGowan, R. L., Butts, M. M., & Moran, C. M. (2020). When work and family blend together: Examining the daily experiences of breastfeeding mothers at work. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1337-1369. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1241

title: Ups and Downs: The Role of Legitimacy Judgment Cues in Practice Implementation
methods: Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis of 195 subunit-practice observations, combining two-wave manager surveys, ASSET4 country and industry CSR ratings, parent-firm communication data, and calibrated set-theoretic conditions.
industry: Gas and power production and services MNE implementing health and safety, gender diversity in management, and biodiversity CSR practices.
country: ENERGREEN subunits in 24 countries, including Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Chile, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Mexico, the Netherlands, Pakistan, Peru, Romania, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Spain, Switzerland, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
time_period: Practice implementation was observed from 2012 to 2014; parent authorization was measured from 2009-2013 magazine issues and country/industry endorsement used 2011 ASSET4 scores.
units: Subunit-practice observations across 65 subunits and three CSR practices.
n_sample: 195 observations from 65 subunits and three practices, based on 490 distinct survey respondents across two waves.
authors: Jacqueminet, A.; Durand, R.
theories: institutional theory; legitimacy judgment theory; validity and propriety in legitimacy judgments
keywords: corporate social responsibility practices; institutional demands; legitimacy judgments; organizational conformity and decoupling; practice implementation; set-theoretic approach; validity and propriety cues
research_question: The paper asks what sets of validity cues and propriety conditions lead organizational subunits to increase or decrease their implementation of a practice over time. It studies this question in the context of three CSR practices implemented by subunits of a multinational enterprise.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is configurational rather than additive. Subunits form legitimacy judgments by weighing validity cues from industry peers, country peers, and the parent firm alongside propriety evaluations of strategic importance and value compatibility. Consonant high propriety and some validity support implementation increases, while inconsistent validity cues or dissonance between strategic importance and value compatibility can make implementation fragile and lead subunits to scale practices down.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by explaining within-firm practice implementation as a dynamic legitimacy judgment process rather than as direct conformity to external pressure. It specifies how validity cues and propriety evaluations combine in nonsymmetrical configurations that explain both increases and decreases in implementation. It also extends work on conformity and decoupling by showing that authorization from the parent firm may help initiate implementation, whereas country and industry endorsement become more important for durable or high implementation.
practical_implication: Managers should not assume that corporate adoption, performance metrics, or internal authorization will sustain CSR practice implementation across subunits. The study suggests that firms need to monitor actual implementation status at the subunit level and reinforce both strategic importance and value compatibility. It also implies that external country and industry endorsement matters for durable implementation, so policymakers, industry associations, and MNEs need aligned signals if sustainability commitments are to become practices inside firms.
limitations: The authors identify the single-firm design as a constraint on generalizability and note that CSR practices may be especially easy to decouple from corporate commitments compared with accounting or quality-management practices. The two-year observation window may not capture longer implementation dynamics or changes in validity and propriety cues. The analysis also infers legitimacy judgment formation from available cues and implementation patterns rather than directly observing the judgment process at a micro level.
future_research: Future research could test the explanation in other organizational settings and with practices less prone to decoupling than CSR. Longer-period studies could observe how validity and propriety cues, and their relative weights, change after implementation begins. More fine-grained research could examine specific practices within broad CSR domains and observe legitimacy judgment formation more directly.
abstract: We explore the way validity and propriety cues contribute to legitimacy judgments about a practice and to explaining whether the subunit of a large firm increases or decreases the implementation of this practice. Empirically, we examine the extent to which 65 subsidiaries of a multinational enterprise implemented three corporate social responsibility practices. Adopting a set-theoretic approach, we find that both validity and propriety cues are extremely relevant to the understanding of subunits' implementation of practices over time. The endorsement of a practice in a subunit's environment plays a particularly crucial role in the extent to which it is implemented, relative to authorization by the parent firm. Furthermore, subunits strongly rely on the active evaluation of the practice's propriety, such that the consonance between the two propriety dimensions (strategic importance and value compatibility) is central to implementation increase, while dissonance between them can favor implementation decrease. By advancing our understanding of legitimacy judgment formation and practice implementation patterns, our study enriches explanations of organizational conformity and decoupling, and contributes to our understanding of how firms respond to multiple institutional demands.

title: Identity Asymmetries: An Experimental Investigation of Social Identity and Information Exchange in Multiteam Systems
methods: Three quantitative studies: a laboratory experiment with four-team multiteam systems using a computer-based strategy simulation and generalized linear mixed models with probit links; a vignette experiment testing instrumental motives and reciprocity-oriented sharing; and a computational simulation extrapolating Study 1 estimates to alternative identity configurations.
industry: Not reported in paper.
country: Study 1 recruited participants from a large Midwestern university in the United States; Study 2 recruited participants in the UK and USA through Prolific Academic; Study 3 used simulated multiteam systems.
time_period: Not reported in paper.
units: Study 1 participants, five-member teams, directed team dyads, and four-team multiteam systems; Study 2 employed online participants; Study 3 simulated four-team multiteam systems.
n_sample: Study 1 main analyses used 420 participants nested in 21 multiteam systems; Study 2 analyzed 258 individuals; Study 3 generated 10,000 systems for each identity configuration.
authors: Mell, J. N.; DeChurch, L. A.; Leenders, R. Th. A. J.; Contractor, N.
theories: self-categorization theory; social identity theory
keywords: identity asymmetries; information sharing; interteam performance; multiteam systems; self-categorization; social identity
research_question: How do identity asymmetries between component teams in a multiteam system affect interteam information sharing and interteam performance? The paper examines whether team-focused and system-focused teams approach interteam interaction with different motives, and whether those motives make some identity configurations more disruptive than others.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that team-focused teams treat interteam relations more instrumentally, sharing proactively when they expect direct reciprocal value from another team. System-focused teams treat other component teams as part of the same in-group and therefore share more benevolently and less conditionally. Identity asymmetry is most harmful when a team-focused source interacts with a system-focused seeker, because the source has less reason to invest in proactive anticipatory sharing while the seeker depends on that sharing for interteam performance; the reactive-sharing pathway was theorized but did not provide a supported indirect effect in Study 1. The simulation extends this dyadic mechanism to show that system-level performance is nonlinear: partial shifts toward system focus can create asymmetric dyads before the benefits of broad system focus dominate.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes causal evidence that social identity affects interteam coordination and performance in multiteam systems, but not through a simple linear benefit of superordinate identification. It introduces identity asymmetry as a dyadic and configural property, showing that the effect of one team's identity focus depends on the identity focus of its partner team. It also extends social identity and self-categorization theory by linking identity foci to instrumental versus benevolent motives for interteam information exchange.
practical_implication: Organizations managing multiteam systems should watch for arrangements that make some teams system-focused while others remain team-focused, such as workflow centrality, physical or social isolation, or inconsistent leader rhetoric. Interventions to build system identification may need to be broad and simultaneous, because a staggered or partial shift can temporarily increase identity asymmetries and weaken information sharing. The paper especially emphasizes proactive information sharing as a managerial target, because source teams may know who needs information better than seeking teams know where to request it.
limitations: The authors note several boundary conditions: the theory assumes reciprocal informational dependence between teams, alignment between team goals and system goals, and tasks in which source teams can anticipate who needs what information. They also acknowledge that low variability in reactive information sharing may have underpowered the test of Hypothesis 1b. The laboratory setting simplified field realities such as long-standing relationships, power and status differences, organizational politics, and stronger naturally occurring identities.
future_research: Future research could examine temporal sequences of proactive and reactive information sharing rather than aggregated information-sharing totals. It could also study identity asymmetries in field multiteam systems where identities evolve over longer periods and where status, power, politics, and goal misalignment interact with social identity. The authors further suggest research on the dynamic nature of identity asymmetries, including how initial asymmetries and interaction patterns may shift component teams' identity foci over time.
abstract: Many complex organizational tasks are performed by networks of teams, or "multiteam systems." A critical challenge in multiteam systems is how to promote information exchange across teams. In three studies, we investigate how identity "asymmetries"— differences between teams in terms of whether the team or overarching system constitutes their primary focus of identification—affect interteam information sharing and performance. In Study 1, we manipulate teams' foci of identification (team vs. system focused) in a sample of 84 five-member teams working in one of 21 four-team multiteam systems performing a computer strategy simulation. We find that, while system-focused teams shared information equally with all teams, team-focused teams shared less information with system-focused teams than they did with other team-focused teams. Interteam information sharing positively predicted interteam performance. In Study 2, we test the assumptions underlying our theory in a vignette experiment, demonstrating that team-focused individuals adopt instrumental motives toward interteam interaction. Finally, in Study 3, we investigate the implications of system composition in terms of team identity foci by means of a simulation study based on the empirical results of Study 1. The results of the simulation yield novel propositions about the nonlinear effects of social identity in multiteam systems.

title: Water Wars in Detroit: Custodianship and the Work of Institutional Renewal
methods: Longitudinal qualitative study of Detroit public water services and the water shutoff crisis, using formal and informal interviews, nonparticipant observation, archival materials, insider e-mail journals, investigator journals, meeting minutes, and iterative grounded-theory analysis.
industry: Public water services in Detroit, Michigan, centered on the Detroit Water and Sewerage Department and related government, community, union, activist, water-expert, corporate, and NGO actors.
time_period: The study began prior to the 2014 Detroit household water shutoffs and followed the ongoing crisis through 2017; data sources span roughly 2012-2017.
units: Custodians of public water services, including operatives, warriors, converts, and agnostics, plus archival, observational, journal, meeting-minute, media, government, NGO, and proprietary water-system data.
n_sample: 42 formal one-on-one interviews, 48 informal interviews, 120+ hours of observation across 32 events, and extensive archival, journal, meeting-minute, media, government, NGO, and water-system datasets.
authors: Montgomery, A. W.; Dacin, M. T.
theories: institutional custodianship; institutional renewal; institutional theory; institutional work
keywords: affordability; custodianship; grand challenges; institutional custodians; institutional entropy; institutional renewal; public water services; resource access; water crisis
research_question: Who are institutional custodians, and what evokes custodianship when a neglected societal institution faces entropy? The paper examines this question through Detroiters' defense and renewal of public water services before, during, and after the 2014 water shutoffs.
mechanism_summary:
- Context / institutional problem: public water services in Detroit had become taken for granted and neglected, creating institutional entropy around access, affordability, infrastructure, and public ownership.
- Custodian forms: operatives, warriors, converts, and agnostics emerged at different moments with different social positions, motivations, and understandings of institutional rules.
- Energizing roles: defenders, reinforcers, and reifiers restored attention to the value, publicness, rights basis, and lived consequences of water services.
- Resourcing roles: replenishers, retoolers, and exalters brought new coalitions, policy options, emotional commitment, and symbolic connection to water.
- Intersections: public ownership, the human right to water, and clean water access linked otherwise heterogeneous custodians and helped catalyze later custodial action.
- Renewal outcome: custodianship was distributed and heterogeneous; different actors renewed different dimensions of the institution rather than acting as one homogeneous group.

The paper develops a process account rather than a variable-based causal model. As different aspects of public water services became threatened, different custodians were catalyzed to act, and their framing and roles sometimes intersected across public ownership, rights, and health-and-safety concerns. Institutional renewal occurs through the restoration of energy and resources to a neglected institution, but the authors do not claim that renewal guarantees long-term institutional stability.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by showing that custodians are not only homogeneous insiders with formal roles; they can be heterogeneous, distributed, morally motivated, and variably connected to the institution. It extends institutional work and custodianship research by identifying four forms of custodians, their energizing and resourcing roles, and the intersections through which their actions can renew a neglected institution. It also conceptualizes institutional renewal as a necessary response to institutional entropy, distinct from routine maintenance and from outright institutional entrepreneurship.
practical_implication: For leaders and communities dealing with neglected public institutions, the paper implies that renewal may require engaging heterogeneous custodians rather than relying only on formal insiders or technical fixes. Public institutions such as water services, healthcare, education, and democracy may gain renewed energy when different actors connect around shared institutional remnants, rights claims, public ownership, and access concerns. The Detroit case also warns that water access and affordability crises can deepen inequality and disproportionately affect economically vulnerable communities and communities of color.
limitations: The authors identify the single-case design as a limitation because the boundaries of the theory are not fully defined. Water may be especially likely to attract cultural, emotional, spiritual, and religious attachments, so other institutions may not evoke the same forms or intensity of custodianship. The authors also note that social movement theory is closely related, but their custodianship lens deliberately focuses on actors' institutional loyalties and roles, including actors who would not define themselves as movement participants.
future_research: Future research could test whether other institutions, such as public healthcare, education, religions, democracy, or legal institutions, inspire similar forms of heterogeneous custodianship. The authors call for work on how many custodians are required, which custodian types are needed in different contexts, and how custodians interact over time. They also suggest studying the intersections between movements, activists, and custodians, including how custodians frame institutional challenges and how movements use institutional loyalties and frames.
abstract: We examine the role of custodianship in the renewal of the institution of public water services in Detroit, Michigan. Our longitudinal qualitative study begins prior to the 33,000 household water shutoffs of 2014 and follows this ongoing crisis through 2017. It reveals the complexity of the task of renewing neglected societal institutions suffering institutional entropy. We provide an in-depth study of the characteristics, motivations, and actions of institutional custodians—actors who maintain and enhance institutionalized practices. We inductively identify four groups of custodians (“operatives,” “warriors,” “converts,” and “agnostics”) who are catalyzed to act at different times, take on unique roles, and have distinct understandings of institutional rules. In doing so, we establish that custodianship is both distributed and heterogeneous, rather than static and homogeneous, and highlight key intersections across custodians. Our study also offers timely insights into resource access and affordability in marginalized communities, and the role of institutions in addressing grand challenges such as the emerging global water crisis.
apa_citation: Montgomery, A. W., & Dacin, M. T. (2020). Water wars in Detroit: Custodianship and the work of institutional renewal. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1455-1484. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1098

title: Who is Punished Most for Challenging the Status Quo?
methods: Mixed-methods CONVEX design combining qualitative fieldwork, an industry-wide panel analysis, and a subsequent interpretivist study. The quantitative phase uses longitudinal data on Champagne houses from 1998 to 2007, estimating random-effects, instrumental-variable, and Mundlak specifications to test whether traditionality weakens price penalties for vertical integration, foreign diversification, and vertical disintegration. The qualitative phase analyzes 78 interviews with grape sellers, buyers, and industry insiders through open coding, theme development, and process analysis to explain sellers' sense-making and attribution processes.
industry: Champagne grape market between Champagne houses and independent grape growers.
time_period: Quantitative panel: 1998-2007; fieldwork and interviews: October 2008 to October 2016.
units: Champagne houses as buyers in the quantitative panel; grape sellers, grape buyers, and industry insiders in the interview sample.
n_sample: Complete quantitative data for 64 of 66 Champagne houses; 78 interviews with 17 industry experts, 14 grape buyers, and 47 grape sellers.
authors: Ody-Brasier, Amandine; Vermeulen, Freek
theories: attribution theory; institutional theory; norm enforcement; role theory
keywords: Champagne grape market; attribution; role digressions; sanctioning; status quo; traditionality
research_question: Why are some firms punished more than others when they challenge established industry roles? The paper asks whether Champagne houses that appear more traditional are penalized less by grape sellers than less traditional houses for the same role digressions, and how sellers interpret those violations.
mechanism_summary:
- Quantitative IV(s): Buyer role digressions through vineyard acquisition, foreign winemaking subsidiaries, and supplying supermarket brands.
- Quantitative DV(s): Average price paid by Champagne houses for grape inputs.
- Qualitative process elements: Sellers' commitment to the institutionalized status quo; buyer traditionality as a signal of commitment; attribution of violations to situational constraints versus volition and bad faith; penalizing actions through price, allocation, quality sorting, and stigmatization.

The process begins with an institutionalized role division in which growers supply grapes and houses make, brand, sell, and distribute Champagne. When houses cross role boundaries, sellers interpret the same behavior differently depending on whether the buyer carries traditional characteristics. Less traditional buyers' deviations confirm suspicion and are attributed to disposition and volition, whereas traditional buyers' deviations are treated as out of character and attributed to external constraints, reducing sellers' willingness to punish them.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on norm enforcement and market structuration by showing that punishment for role transgressions varies with the violator's perceived traditionality, not only with the violation itself. It identifies sellers' interpretation of motives as the mechanism linking buyer identity characteristics to sanctioning, extending institutional and role-theoretic accounts of how market role systems are maintained. It also reframes field-level inertia as partly contextual: exchange partners' sanctions can make less traditional firms especially constrained when they try to initiate structural change.
practical_implication: Firms seeking to change established role systems should recognize that exchange partners may judge their motives through preexisting identity cues. In this setting, less traditional Champagne houses faced stronger price and relational penalties for the same deviations than traditional houses, so strategic moves that challenge a status quo may require careful management of how commitment to the field is interpreted. The findings also suggest that firms controlling scarce resources can protect established role systems through everyday exchange decisions, not only formal regulation.
limitations: The paper does not present a standalone limitations section. Its scope is anchored in the Champagne grape market, where growers control a legally constrained scarce resource and can price, allocate, sort, or stigmatize buyers; generalization depends on whether exchange partners in other settings have comparable sanctioning capacity and value the status quo. The quantitative evidence is observational panel evidence strengthened by instrumental-variable and Mundlak analyses, while the qualitative phase explains the attribution process in this specific institutional context.
future_research: The paper does not provide an explicit future research agenda. Its discussion implies opportunities to examine whether traditionality moderates sanctioning in other mature industries, how emotions shape norm enforcement, and when contextual inertia prevents less traditional firms from initiating field-level change.
abstract: Over time, markets evolve into particular structures, with clearly defined roles in terms of who does what in the industry. When a firm ventures beyond these established roles, it often gets punished by its exchange partners. Our interviews in the Champagne grape market, however, suggest that some buyers are penalized more than others in such circumstances. Quantitative analysis confirms that nontraditional buyers receive price penalties for role deviations—through diversification, vertical integration, or disintegration— whereas traditional firms are treated more leniently. A subsequent interpretivist study, using interview data from 78 market participants to explore the exact mechanisms underlying this effect, reveals that sellers blame less traditional buyers when they cross the boundaries of their usual roles because they are thought to act out of volition and bad faith, whereas the same transgressions by more traditional firms are believed to have been necessitated by external circumstances. We conclude that the sanctioning behavior of actors in response to role transgressions by their exchange partners is driven by their interpretation of the motives underlying these transgressions, rather than by the actions themselves. As a result, nontraditional firms may find it difficult to deviate from the traditional roles in their industry.
apa_citation: Ody-Brasier, A., & Vermeulen, F. (2020). Who is punished most for challenging the status quo? *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1621-1651. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0683

title: Virtually (In)separable: The Centrality of Relational Cadence in the Formation of Virtual Multiplex Relationships
methods: Longitudinal inductive grounded theory study using open-ended semistructured interviews, observation, archival materials, memoing, open coding, focused coding, axial coding, and NVivo 10 analysis.
industry: Sales and customer service divisions of Cloudly, a pseudonymous global Fortune 500 technology corporation with a largely remote workforce.
country: United States; the study focused on Cloudly's Midwest field division, and the firm was headquartered in the Northeast United States.
time_period: Calendar dates not reported; Figure 1 reports longitudinal interview waves at 3-6, 4.5-7.5, and 9-12 months post-hire.
units: Virtual coworker relationships among new hires, internal role transitioners, and experienced hires.
n_sample: 64 individuals; 114 interviews; more than 75 hours of observation; and archival materials.
authors: Schinoff, B. S.; Ashforth, B. E.; Corley, K. G.
theories: coworker friendship formation; multiplex relationships; relational cadence; virtual work
keywords: coworker friendship; coworker multiplex relationships; friendship-related cadence; grounded theory; relational cadence; virtual work; work-related cadence
research_question: How do virtual coworkers become friends and thus form multiplex relationships? The paper asks how employees who interact primarily through communication technologies establish coworker friendships when geographic proximity and routine face-to-face shared experiences are weakened.
mechanism_summary:
- Virtual work barrier: Remote work makes coworkers' availability, responsiveness, and social context harder to read, creating a breakdown in cadence.
- Work-related cadence: Coworkers assess accessibility, skill relevance, rapport, and instrumentality, then cultivate cadence through scheduled contact, medium choice, face-to-face contact when possible, imagining coworkers, self-disclosure, and alternative information sources.
- Friendship-related cadence: Coworkers assess availability for friendship, desire, chemistry, trust, and instrumentality, then cultivate cadence through spontaneous interaction and relational expanding.
- Multiplex cadence: Work-related and friendship-related cadences become distinct but codependent patterns that support a virtual work-friendship relationship.
- Contextual support: Managerial stage setting can create conditions for work-related and friendship-related cadence, while its absence can stunt friendship-related cadence.

The process is interpretive rather than variable-based. Virtual coworkers first evaluate whether interaction patterns can converge around temporal rhythm and relational particulars. When convergence seems possible, they intentionally cultivate work-related and friendship-related cadence; when both cadences reinforce one another, the relationship can become multiplex.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a cadence-based theory of virtual coworker multiplex relationships by identifying relational cadence as a mechanism through which virtual employees establish and grow coworker friendships. It extends coworker friendship and multiplexity research by showing that work-related and friendship-related cadences are deeply intertwined in virtual settings rather than separable relationship streams. It also theorizes virtual friendship formation as more intentional and potentially more laborious than collocated friendship formation because employees must deliberately create temporal rhythm and relational familiarity.
practical_implication: For managers of remote or hybrid employees, the study implies that relationship formation should not be left entirely to spontaneous interaction. Managers can support relational cadence by creating regular touchpoints, encouraging appropriate personal connection, helping employees understand one another's roles and availability, and using stage-setting practices that make virtual colleagues more socially legible. For virtual employees, the findings suggest that reliable responsiveness, thoughtful medium choice, and modest relational expanding can help turn work contact into more durable relational connection.
limitations: The study is based on one pseudonymous Fortune 500 technology firm and focused on sales and customer service divisions that HR identified as geographically dispersed and friendly. The authors note that the IT context was male-dominated, that most informants still had some possibility of face-to-face contact, and that Cloudly's culture made videoconferencing counternormative. The method also relied on one partner's account of a friendship relationship, which limits evidence about dyadic reciprocity.
future_research: Future research could test how relational cadence operates in fully virtual contexts where face-to-face contact is impossible, in organizations that routinely use videoconferencing, and in more gender-balanced samples. Studies could collect dyadic interaction data such as instant-message transcripts, e-mail chains, paired interviews, or journals to examine how both partners experience cadence. The authors also point to extensions into remote leader emergence, newcomer socialization, and the effects of virtual work on nonwork friendships and family relationships.
abstract: The increasing use of technology and rise of virtual work has fundamentally changed how employees interact with each other. No longer can employees reliably predict when and where their coworkers will work, transforming the very ways in which coworker relationships unfold over time. This is perhaps especially true for coworker multiplex relationships, which fuse a coworker relationship with a friendship relationship and strongly affect job satisfaction and turnover intentions. Through a qualitative study of a Fortune 500 technology firm with a largely remote workforce, we build theory on how virtual coworkers form friendships with each other on the path to multiplexity. Our emergent theory reveals the centrality of “relational cadence”—perceived convergence in the patterns of interaction between oneself and a particular coworker—to the establishment and growth of these relationships. It also differentiates work-related from friendship-related cadence, stresses the symbiosis of these cadences in multiplexity, and emphasizes the importance of temporal rhythm and understanding relational particulars (the nature of the specific coworker relationship) in the development of each form of cadence. These findings highlight how virtualization affects the experience of relating at work, and thereby make important contributions to literatures on relationships at work, coworker friendships, and virtual relationships.
apa_citation: Schinoff, B. S., Ashforth, B. E., & Corley, K. G. (2020). Virtually (in)separable: The centrality of relational cadence in the formation of virtual multiplex relationships. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1395-1424. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0466

title: Stakeholder Preservation or Appropriation? The Influence of Target CSR on Market Reactions to Acquisition Announcements
methods: Quantitative event-study and regression analysis of U.S. public-firm acquisition deals, using SDC, KLD, CRSP, Compustat, ExecuComp, patent, and occupational data; acquirer announcement returns are estimated with Eventus and tested with Heckman two-stage models with robust standard errors clustered by acquirer.
industry: Acquisition, merger, and majority-interest acquisition deals across industries; no single focal industry reported
time_period: Deals from 2000-2012, with lagged KLD, ExecuComp, Compustat, and moderator variables from 1999-2011
units: Acquisition deals involving U.S. public firms
n_sample: 237 deals
authors: Tong, Li; Wang, Heli; Xia, Jun
theories: implicit contracts; stakeholder appropriation perspective; stakeholder preservation perspective
keywords: acquisition announcement; business similarity; implicit contracts; market reaction; stakeholder appropriation; stakeholder preservation; stakeholder value congruence; target corporate social responsibility
research_question: How does a target firm's CSR affect market reactions to acquisition announcements, and do the observed contingencies align more with stakeholder preservation or stakeholder appropriation? The paper asks whether acquirer gains from high-CSR targets are better explained by honoring target stakeholders' implicit contracts and building trust, or by defaulting on those contracts and transferring wealth to acquirers.
mechanism_summary: The paper develops two competing explanations for why target CSR may be associated with positive acquirer announcement returns. The stakeholder preservation perspective argues that preserving implicit contracts with stakeholders of high-CSR targets can help acquirers elicit trust, cooperation, and reciprocal support, creating expected acquisition value. The stakeholder appropriation perspective argues that high-CSR targets offer larger opportunities for wealth transfer because their stakeholders hold more favorable implicit contracts that acquirers may later alter or default on. The empirical tests favor the preservation account: target CSR is positively associated with acquirer abnormal returns, stakeholder value congruence strengthens that relationship, and business similarity weakens it.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to acquisition research by directly comparing stakeholder preservation and stakeholder appropriation as alternative explanations for acquirer value gains from target stakeholders. It extends CSR and market-response research by shifting attention from acquirer CSR to target CSR in acquisition announcements. It also complicates the usual positive view of similarity in mergers and acquisitions by showing that stakeholder value congruence and business similarity have different implications depending on whether stakeholder preservation or appropriation is expected.
practical_implication: For acquirer managers, the study suggests that target stakeholders should be considered a source of acquisition value, not merely a cost or redundancy to be removed. The authors advise managers to pay attention to preserving target stakeholders' implicit contracts and eliciting their cooperation, while avoiding blind protection of ineffective or unhelpful stakeholder arrangements. The findings also caution managers not to assume that all forms of similarity between merging firms are beneficial, because business similarity may undermine value creation from target CSR.
limitations: The authors could not directly measure how target stakeholders behaved or reacted during acquisition integration, so the mechanism is inferred from announcement returns and contingency patterns. Their business similarity measure incorporates multiple resource and strategy dimensions but may not fully capture all strategic similarities between acquirer and target. The sample is limited to large U.S. public firms covered by KLD, and the study relies on net CSR scores from KLD data, which the authors acknowledge have measurement limitations.
future_research: Future research could directly measure stakeholder preservation and appropriation during acquisition integration using qualitative, survey, or value-creation-and-distribution approaches. Additional studies could examine contexts in which appropriation may matter more, such as labor-intensive industries or later stages of integration. Future work could also distinguish primary from secondary stakeholders, internal from external stakeholders, smaller firms, non-U.S. settings, and alternative CSR data sources or measures.
abstract: This study examines how target corporate social responsibility affects the economic gains for acquirers, as reflected in market reaction to an acquisition announcement, from two distinct perspectives: stakeholder preservation versus stakeholder appropriation. The stakeholder preservation perspective suggests that positive market reaction to an acquisition stems from potential new value creation by honoring implicit contracts and maintaining good relationships with target stakeholders. By contrast, the stakeholder appropriation perspective posits that positive market reaction is primarily derived through wealth transfer to acquirers by defaulting on implicit contracts with target stakeholders. Using a data set of acquisitions in the United States, we find that target corporate social responsibility is positively associated with acquirer abnormal returns upon an acquisition announcement. Moreover, stakeholder value congruence between the merging firms strengthens this positive relationship, whereas business similarity between them weakens it. These findings align with the stakeholder preservation perspective and challenge the stakeholder appropriation perspective.
apa_citation: Tong, L., Wang, H., & Xia, J. (2020). Stakeholder preservation or appropriation? The influence of target CSR on market reactions to acquisition announcements. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1535-1560. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0229

title: Four More Years: Presidential Elections, Comparative Mindset, and Managerial Decisions
methods: Four-study empirical quantitative design: Study 1 uses a quasi-experiment with fixed-effects autoregressive panel forecasting on firm advertising spending; Study 2 uses a quasi-experimental StratSim panel with random-effects models; Studies 3 and 4 use between-subjects experiments with practicing HR and marketing managers, ANOVA/logistic models, and mediated moderation analysis.
industry: Cross-industry firms and managerial decision contexts: public firms' advertising spending, business simulation teams, HR managers, and marketing professionals
country: United States-focused studies, with non-U.S. firms as a Study 1 control group
time_period: Study 1 firm data from 1950-2011; Study 2 StratSim data from 2002-2004; Study 3 Tennessee Senate-election setting in fall 2018; Study 4 Ohio state-level political stimuli with survey timing not reported
units: Firms, industry-firm-product-period observations, MBA/EMBA teams, HR managers, and marketing professionals
n_sample: Study 1: 27,535 observations; Study 2: 15,524 advertising observations and 13,008 training observations; Study 3: 103 participants; Study 4: 221 participants
authors: Xu, Alison Jing; Moorman, Christine; Qin, Vivian Yue; Rao, Akshay R.
theories: comparative mindset theory / mindset effects; negativity bias; sequential whether-to-buy / which-to-buy purchase decision process
keywords: comparative mindset; comparative political information; decision frame; managerial decisions; managerial spending; negative information; presidential elections
research_question: Does exposure to comparative political information during elections activate a comparative mindset that changes managerial spending decisions in nonpolitical domains? The paper also asks whether reduced importance of negative information explains this effect and whether a rejection rather than selection decision frame attenuates it.
mechanism_summary: The authors argue that elections expose managers, as citizens, to repeated comparative political information, making comparison procedures more accessible. This comparative mindset short-circuits the usual sequence of deciding whether to buy, which to buy, and how much to spend, moving managers directly toward which-to-buy comparisons. Because negative information is less diagnostic in that comparative stage than in the whether-to-buy stage, managers attach less weight to negative attributes, evaluate options more favorably, and spend more. A rejection frame restores attention to negative attributes and attenuates the spending effect.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends managerial decision-bias research by identifying presidential elections and associated comparative political information as a societal-level environmental factor that can influence nonpolitical managerial decisions. It also extends comparative mindset theory from consumer choice to managerial decision making and spending levels, specifying reduced importance of negative information as a process mechanism and rejection framing as a boundary condition.
practical_implication: Managers should treat presidential elections and other large-scale political elections with high levels of comparative political information as possible sources of decision bias, especially for discretionary spending decisions. The paper suggests that organizations can reduce inflated choice likelihood and spending by using debiasing procedures such as counterfactual reasoning, feature-based analysis, accountability, forcing a revisit of the whether-to-buy step, and framing decisions around rejection as well as selection.
limitations: The authors note that additional boundary conditions are likely beyond the rejection-frame condition tested in Study 4. They specifically identify decision scrutiny, macroeconomic context, firm-specific performance, and risk orientation as factors that may moderate the comparative mindset effect, so the findings should not be read as universal across all spending contexts.
future_research: Future research should examine when decision scrutiny amplifies or attenuates comparative mindset effects by shifting attention toward benefits or costs. The authors also call for work on how macroeconomic conditions, firm performance, risk seeking, and additional debiasing procedures shape whether comparative mindsets inflate managerial spending.
abstract: Presidential elections reflect societal-level events that expose citizens to large amounts of comparative political information. We suggest that this exposure activates a "comparative mindset" that changes managers' business decisions in nonpolitical domains. In this state, managers are more likely to select from available options and increase their spending level. Four studies demonstrate this effect. Study 1 uses a quasi-experiment to show that U.S. firms, but not non-U.S. firms, spend more on advertising in U.S. presidential election years versus nonelection years. In a controlled business simulation, Study 2 shows that participants spend more on advertising and training in presidential election years versus nonelection years. Two experiments involving practicing managers follow. Study 3 exposes managers to comparative political information featuring a U.S. Senate election; we observe an increase in spending on training and development programs. Study 4 exposes managers to comparative political information for state-level political races, finding that doing so reduces the importance of negative information in the subsequent managerial decision process and leads to increased marketing spending. Moreover, shifting the decision frame from selecting to rejecting options restores the focus on negative information and attenuates the effect. We conclude with a discussion of the research's theoretical and practical contributions.
apa_citation: Xu, A. J., Moorman, C., Qin, V. Y., & Rao, A. R. (2020). Four more years: Presidential elections, comparative mindset, and managerial decisions. *Academy of Management Journal, 63*(5), 1370-1394. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0602

title: You Are Great and I Am Great (Too): Examining New CEOs’ Social Influence Behaviors during Leadership Transition
methods: Event history analysis using Cox proportional hazards regression models on CEO-year observations, with computer-aided content analysis of new CEOs' earnings conference-call opening remarks and Heckman two-stage corrections for selection into predecessor-chair retention and negative stock market reactions.
industry: Publicly listed S&P 500 companies, excluding financial firms and utilities.
country: United States public companies inferred from the S&P 500 sampling frame; the paper does not state country directly.
time_period: CEO succession events from 2001 to 2012, followed through each new CEO's first three years or until departure.
units: CEO succession events, new CEOs, predecessor CEOs, boards, and CEO-year observations.
n_sample: 440 CEO succession events after exclusions, including 28 early dismissals and 1,688 event-history observations.
authors: Yi, X.; Zhang, Y. A.; Windsor, D.
theories: CEO succession; social influence theory; upper echelons research
keywords: CEO succession; early dismissal; ingratiation; leadership transition; new CEOs; self-promotion; social influence behaviors; stock market reactions
research_question: How do new CEOs' social influence behaviors during leadership transition alter the relationship between two vulnerability conditions and their likelihood of early dismissal? The paper focuses on predecessor CEOs remaining as board chairs and negative stock market reactions to new CEO appointments.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is audience-specific social influence during early CEO tenure. Ingratiation toward a retained predecessor CEO can elicit liking-based approval and reduce the adverse effect of predecessor-chair retention on new CEO survival. Self-promotion can elicit competence-based approval from shareholders and boards and reduce the adverse effect of a negative stock market reaction. The same behaviors can also backfire with nontarget audiences: commitment to strategic continuity can amplify the adverse effect of negative market reaction, and self-centered expression can amplify the adverse effect of predecessor-chair retention.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to CEO succession research by shifting attention from succession as an event to the leadership transition period and showing how new CEOs' own social influence behaviors shape early survival prospects. It also extends social influence theory by documenting both beneficial and adverse consequences of ingratiation and self-promotion, depending on whether the relevant audience is the target or a nontarget audience. Methodologically, it develops unobtrusive proxies for upper-echelon social influence using public conference-call language.
practical_implication: The paper implies that new CEOs should consider which audience a social influence behavior is likely to affect. Ingratiating a retained predecessor may be useful when that predecessor remains powerful, and self-promotion may help when investors initially react negatively, but each tactic can create negative impressions among other stakeholders. Boards evaluating new CEOs should also recognize that public transition-period language can shape perceptions and early dismissal risk.
limitations: The study infers social influence behaviors from public earnings conference-call opening remarks rather than directly observing private interactions between new CEOs, predecessors, boards, and shareholders. The sample is limited to publicly listed S&P 500 companies and excludes financial firms and utilities, so the findings may not generalize to private firms, regulated industries, or non-U.S. governance settings. The authors address selection concerns with two-stage corrections and robustness checks, but the design remains observational.
future_research: Future research could apply similar language-based measures to other upper-echelon social interactions and to other issues involving social interaction processes among upper echelons. The paper also points to further work on social influence behaviors in leadership transitions, including how self-promotion and ingratiation can help with target audiences while backfiring with nontarget audiences.
abstract: In this study, we examine new CEOs’ social influence behaviors in leadership transition periods. Taking charge is challenging for new CEOs, particularly when (a) predecessor CEOs stay on as board chairs, or (b) the stock market reacts negatively to new CEO appointments. We propose that new CEOs’ social influence behaviors may alter the adverse impacts of these factors on their early survival prospects. We examine two types of social influence behaviors displayed by new CEOs: (1) ingratiation toward predecessor CEOs and (2) self-promotion. We create proxies for such behaviors using a computer-aided content analysis of transcripts of new CEOs’ conference calls with securities analysts. We find that ingratiation toward predecessors reduces the adverse impact of predecessors’ remaining as board chairs while self-promotion mitigates the negative impact of negative stock market reactions. However, we also find evidence demonstrating that new CEOs’ social influence behaviors can backfire. Accordingly, our study makes important contributions to both the CEO succession literature and the social influence literature.
apa_citation: Yi, X., Zhang, Y. A., & Windsor, D. (2020). You are great and I am great (too): Examining new CEOs' social influence behaviors during leadership transition. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(5), 1508-1534. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0365

title: Geographical Dissimilarity and Team Member Influence: Do Emotions Experienced in the Initial Team Meeting Matter?
methods: Two-study quantitative survey design with MBA project teams; peer-rated perceived influence was analyzed with multilevel models using PROC MIXED in SAS to test interactions between geographical dissimilarity and emotion categories over time.
industry: MBA student project teams in management education settings.
country: Study 1 used MBA students at a university in Hong Kong; Study 2 used MBA students at an Indian business school.
time_period: Study 1 followed teams over about two months; Study 2 followed a first-term project lasting three months.
units: Individual MBA students nested in project teams.
n_sample: 192 complete Study 1 responses in 48 teams; 338 complete Study 2 responses in 75 teams.
authors: Chattopadhyay, Prithviraj; George, Elizabeth; Li, Jiping; Gupta, Vishal
theories: emotions and decision-making research; self-categorization theory (Turner, 1987); social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1986)
keywords: MBA project teams; emotions; geographical dissimilarity; initial team meeting; perceived influence; self-categorization theory; social identity theory
research_question: How does a team member's geographical dissimilarity from teammates shape perceived influence in team decisions over time, and do emotions experienced in the initial team meeting determine whether the relationship is positive or negative? The paper asks this question by contrasting social identity theory arguments about out-group categorization with self-categorization theory arguments about the value of dissimilar members' skills and perspectives.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a moderation process in which initial emotions shape how geographically dissimilar teammates are categorized and how they interact with the team over time. Pleasant high-activation emotions are theorized to promote inclusiveness, cognitive flexibility, social engagement, and creativity, making dissimilar members more influential early in the project. Unpleasant low-activation emotions are theorized to encourage systematic and persistent problem solving, so their positive influence effect develops later. Unpleasant high-activation emotions are theorized to create early social engagement and creativity but also later abrasiveness and cognitive depletion, making the authors' evidence for this category more tentative.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to relational demography research by showing that geographical dissimilarity need not have a uniformly negative relationship with individual influence in teams. It uses emotions experienced in the initial team meeting to reconcile social identity theory's negative prediction about dissimilarity with self-categorization theory's positive prediction about valued dissimilarity. It also adds an affective mechanism to a literature that the authors argue has emphasized cognitive categorization processes.
practical_implication: Managers of geographically diverse teams should treat initial team meetings as consequential moments for later influence patterns. The paper suggests designing early activities that elicit pleasant high-activation emotions among highly dissimilar members, helping low-activation members gain earlier access to decision making, and tempering the later abrasiveness of members experiencing unpleasant high-activation emotions. It also points to emotional awareness and management training as useful supports for diverse project teams.
limitations: The evidence comes from MBA student project teams rather than organizational teams, and the authors note that the projects were relatively short. Study 1 could not rule out whether the observed effects came from repeated later emotions, which is why Study 2 added trait-emotion controls and later emotion checks. The conclusions about unpleasant high-activation emotions are explicitly more tentative because the full predicted pattern could not be tested symmetrically across both studies.
future_research: Future research should test whether the findings replicate in longer organizational projects and in settings beyond MBA teams. The authors also call for work on whether transient emotions have long-term consequences in other team processes, such as creativity. They suggest examining other forms of dissimilarity, such as gender or race, when both positive and negative aspects of dissimilarity are salient.
abstract: It is both important and challenging to gain influence within geographically diverse teams. We argue that the emotions team members experience in their initial team meetings moderate the effect of geographical dissimilarity on their perceived influence on team decisions over time. Specifically, we contrast social identity theory–based arguments that geographical dissimilarity negatively influences perceived influence with self-categorization theory–based arguments that there is a positive relationship between geographical dissimilarity and perceived influence. We argue that the emotions team members experience in their initial meeting determine which of these relationships eventuate over time. Across two studies, our data support our arguments. We find that for individuals experiencing pleasant high-activation emotions, their geographic dissimilarity was more positively related with perceived influence in the initial stage of a project; for those experiencing unpleasant low-activation emotions, their geographic dissimilarity was positively related with perceived influence in the later stage; for those experiencing unpleasant high-activation emotions, their geographic dissimilarity was initially positively and later negatively related with perceived influence.
apa_citation: Chattopadhyay, P., George, E., Li, J., & Gupta, V. (2020). Geographical dissimilarity and team member influence: Do emotions experienced in the initial team meeting matter? *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(6), 1807-1839. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0744

title: Motivation Purity Bias: Expression of Extrinsic Motivation Undermines Perceived Intrinsic Motivation and Engenders Bias in Selection Decisions
methods: Four-study empirical quantitative design using hiring simulations, cover letters, interview scripts, video and transcript stimuli, business-school student samples, online participant samples, and hiring-manager samples; analyses include logistic and OLS regressions, clustered standard errors, bootstrapped indirect effects, and an internal random-effects meta-analysis.
industry: Organizational selection for salaried employment; Study 2 used a project finance consultant hiring simulation and Studies 3a/3b used a general project manager selection context. Participants included business school students, online respondents, and hiring managers.
country: Partly not reported in paper; Studies 3a and 3b recruited hiring managers through a U.S.-based market research organization.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual job candidates or candidate profiles evaluated by individual decision makers in hiring simulations.
n_sample: Four main studies plus supporting pilots/pretests; main study samples included 256 candidate-perspective business students and 310 decision-maker students in Study 1, 302 online participants in Study 2, 239 hiring managers in Study 3a, and 247 hiring managers in Study 3b.
authors: Derfler-Rozin, R.; Pitesa, M.
theories: impression management; motivation purity bias; popular management myths; self-determination theory
keywords: extrinsic motivation; hiring managers; intrinsic motivation; management myths; motivation purity bias; selection decisions
research_question: The paper asks whether decision makers penalize job candidates who express extrinsic motivation because they infer that such candidates are less intrinsically motivated. It focuses on whether this "motivation purity bias" affects selection decisions even though the authors argue that expressed extrinsic motivation should not be treated as a negative signal in salaried employment contexts.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that decision makers draw on a management myth that treats extrinsic and intrinsic motivation as antagonistic. When a candidate signals interest in salary, benefits, flexibility, or similar extrinsic job features, decision makers infer lower intrinsic motivation, and lower perceived intrinsic motivation then reduces candidate evaluations and selection likelihood. The paper tests this process across naturally written cover letters, experimental interview scripts, and hiring-manager evaluations of video or transcript stimuli.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces motivation purity bias as a selection-bias mechanism rooted in naive beliefs about motivation rather than stereotypes about social categories. It integrates motivation research with organizational decision-making bias research by showing that decision makers' beliefs about candidates' motives can shape consequential hiring judgments. It also contributes to research on the science-practice gap by arguing that outdated or simplified management ideas can persist in managerial judgment even when later evidence points in a different direction.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that organizations should reduce opportunities for decision makers to penalize benign discussion of extrinsic job features, for example by making salary, benefits, and flexibility information available early and limiting unnecessary motive-based interpretation during selection. It also implies that training or selection-process design should correct the assumption that extrinsic interest necessarily signals low intrinsic motivation. For candidates, the authors note the uncomfortable implication that openly volunteering high extrinsic motivation may trigger bias rather than provide useful information to employers.
limitations: The authors describe the investigation as the first test of the phenomenon and state that more research is needed on generalizability, robustness, and actionable boundary conditions. They used multiple methods and samples, but the research was largely experimental and did not include access to real hiring notes or naturally occurring interview records. The paper also leaves open whether motivation purity bias harms some candidates more than others, especially those with stronger needs for money, time flexibility, or other extrinsic job features.
future_research: Future research should test motivation purity bias with real hiring notes, real interviews, and other consequential organizational decisions. The authors call for work on whether the bias disproportionately harms candidates who need or must discuss extrinsic job features, and whether it is stronger for particular candidate groups such as women. They also encourage broader research on naive views of motivation and the possibility that people undervalue extrinsic motivation in domains beyond selection.
abstract: Organizational selection decisions often involve an exchange of information between candidates and decision makers as to why candidates are motivated to work in the given position. Drawing on popular management myths as our overarching framework, we theorize that candidates' expressions of extrinsic motivation lead decision makers to infer that the candidate is less intrinsically motivated, in turn engendering bias against such candidates. We term this effect motivation purity bias, and argue that it emerges despite ample evidence, which we review, that penalizing expressed extrinsic motivation is not only unfair to candidates but also counterproductive from the standpoint of maximizing future employee performance. Four studies conducted among hiring managers and business school students yield support for our theory. We discuss implications for fairness and efficiency of organizational selection decisions, as well as for prospects of developing a more balanced view of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in management research and practice.
apa_citation: Derfler-Rozin, R., & Pitesa, M. (2020). Motivation purity bias: Expression of extrinsic motivation undermines perceived intrinsic motivation and engenders bias in selection decisions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(6), 1840-1864. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0617

title: Political Risk and Alliance Diversity: A Two-Stage Model of Partner Selection in Multipartner Alliances
methods: Two-stage quantitative study of infrastructure project-finance banking syndicates. The first stage estimates lead-firm selection with hierarchical binomial multivariable logistic regression and project fixed effects; the second stage compares realized syndicates with simulated counterfactual syndicates using hierarchical GLM models with logistic links, random effects, and robustness checks on sampling, specification, and construct measurement.
industry: Infrastructure project finance banking syndicates financing large-scale infrastructure projects.
units: Projects, potential lead firms, realized syndicates, and unrealized counterfactual syndicates.
n_sample: 1,044 projects; 96,521 potential lead-firm observations; 1,044 realized syndicates and 33,460 counterfactual syndicates.
authors: Dorobantu, S.; Lindner, T.; Müllner, J.
theories: institutional theory; interorganizational diversity and coordination costs; multipartner alliance partner selection
keywords: alliance diversity; country knowledge; multipartner alliances; partner selection; political influence; political risk; project finance
research_question: How does political risk in the project country influence partner selection in multipartner alliances, and how does that selection process shape alliance diversity? The paper asks this at two levels: which firm is selected as the lead firm, and which group of other partners the lead firm selects.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a two-stage partner-selection process shaped by institutional context. In politically risky countries, project sponsors are more likely to select lead firms with host-country knowledge and political influence, and those lead firms are more likely to select partner groups with extensive host-country knowledge; the paper did not find the same supported political-risk interaction for syndicate political influence. Because politically useful knowledge may be distributed across dissimilar banks, the search for country knowledge leads lead firms to accept more diverse multipartner alliances despite higher coordination costs.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to multipartner alliance research by theorizing partner selection as a sequential process: first a lead firm is selected, then the lead firm selects a group of other partners. It also links alliance research to institutional context by showing that host-country political risk changes how firms weigh context-specific resources against coordination costs. Finally, it reframes alliance diversity as a by-product of resource search under political risk rather than as a goal in itself.
practical_implication: For lead firms and project sponsors in politically risky infrastructure settings, the findings imply that partner selection should account for the alliance's collective country knowledge and political influence, not only dyadic fit or low coordination costs. The paper also suggests that more diverse syndicates may be strategically useful when political risk makes host-country resources especially valuable. Managers should therefore treat diversity-related coordination costs as part of a tradeoff against political-risk management needs.
limitations: The study focuses on regulatory or political institutions, so it does not test how cognitive, normative, or other institutional pillars shape partner selection. Its empirical setting is infrastructure project finance, where political interference is salient and banking syndicates have observable lead-firm and partner-selection structures. The authors also note that institutional context may shape the pool of potential partners itself, even though their empirical approach accounts for this possibility.
future_research: Future research could examine regulatory uncertainty and other pillars of institutional theory in partner selection and alliance diversity. It could also test whether the findings generalize to other regulated settings such as energy, mining, transportation, agriculture, banking, biotech, pharmaceuticals, education, health care, and real estate. Additional work could examine how political risk affects alliance size and whether firms respond to rising political risk by reaching beyond prior alliance partners.
abstract: We examine how political risk influences partner selection in multipartner alliances, and consequently their diversity. We propose a two-stage theoretical model—first, a lead firm is selected to lead the alliance; second, the lead firm selects other partners— and we argue that political risk affects both stages. In the first stage, firms with knowledge of and influence in the project country are selected to lead projects in countries with high political risk. In the second stage, the lead firm selects a group of partners with knowledge and influence to ensure that the alliance—as a whole—has the resources needed in such countries. We also show, as a corollary, that the imperative to find these resources drives the lead firm to work with more-diverse multipartner alliances despite the higher coordination costs involved. We test our hypotheses by analyzing, first, the selection of the lead firm in 1,044 multipartner banking syndicates that financed some of the world’s largest infrastructure projects in 68 countries between 2003 and 2012. Controlling for the lead firm, we then examine how political risk affects the selection of other partners in the multipartner alliance by comparing the realized syndicates with over 33,000 counterfactual (unrealized) multipartner syndicates.
apa_citation: Dorobantu, S., Lindner, T., & Müllner, J. (2020). Political risk and alliance diversity: A two-stage model of partner selection in multipartner alliances. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(6), 1775-1806. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0265
