title: Kin Ties and the Performance of New Firms: A Structural Approach
methods: Quantitative registry-data study of newly founded firms in greater Stockholm. The authors classify kin ties among initial members into horizontal founder, horizontal employee, and vertical founder-employee structures; estimate competing-risk survival models with successful exits separated from failures; use log sales as an additional performance outcome; and use two-stage residual inclusion with founders' and spouses' siblings as an instrument for kin-tie prevalence.
industry: New organizations/firms founded in the greater Stockholm area; not restricted to one industry, with industry fixed effects in the models.
time_period: Firms founded between 1998 and 2003; founder and employee attributes observed back to 1990.
units: New firms and their initial members, including founders and first-year salaried employees.
n_sample: 4,967 new firms; more than 50,000 founders and salaried employees.
authors: Ertug, Gokhan; Kotha, Reddi; Hedström, Peter
theories: family-embedded perspective on entrepreneurship (Aldrich & Cliff, 2003); informal organizational structures and social ties in organizations (Barnard, 1938; Coleman, 1988); structural contingency approach to kin ties in new firms
keywords: horizontal employee kin ties; kin ties; new firms; performance; structural contingency approach; vertical founder-employee kin ties
research_question: How do kin ties influence the performance of new firms when those ties occupy different structural locations in the organization? The paper asks whether kin ties between founders, between founders and employees, or between employees have different implications for survival and sales.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a structural contingency argument. Kin ties can improve coordination, cooperation, and private information about member capabilities, but they can also reduce information diversity and trigger nepotism concerns. The paper predicts that horizontal employee kin ties should be performance-enhancing because they provide coordination benefits without strong founder-level nepotism concerns, while vertical founder-employee kin ties should be detrimental because they make favoritism concerns more salient. Horizontal founder kin ties are treated as theoretically ambiguous because positive and negative mechanisms may offset one another.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to entrepreneurship research by moving beyond whether kin ties are good or bad for new firms and specifying when different kin-tie structures are likely to enhance, impair, or have no clear relation to performance. It adds granularity to the family-embedded perspective on entrepreneurship by showing that the family effect depends on where family members are located in the new firm's hierarchy. It also contributes to contingency/configuration research by showing how multiple mechanisms can be amplified or suppressed by structural conditions.
practical_implication: The findings caution against blanket advice that entrepreneurs should avoid kin in new firms. The results suggest that kin ties between founders are not negatively related to performance, kin ties between employees are positively related to performance, and kin ties between founders and employees are the more concerning configuration. Mentors and investors should therefore distinguish between hiring founders' kin as employees and hiring employees' kin, rather than treating all kin involvement as equivalent.
limitations: The study is based on one national setting, Sweden, and the authors note that new firms there survive longer than in some other developed-country samples. The structural approach does not directly isolate or test the individual mechanisms it theorizes, such as information asymmetry, cooperation, diversity, and nepotism concerns. The authors also do not model the dynamic process by which members join a new firm or bring kin into the organization over time.
future_research: Future research could examine the framework across multiple geographic locations to assess generalizability. Studies could also test whether religious, institutional, or political affiliations complement or substitute for kin ties in shaping coordination and cooperation. Process studies could trace how different kin-tie structures emerge during member recruitment and how those dynamics affect new firm performance.
abstract: Kin ties are all but ubiquitous in new firms. However, their effects on performance are not straightforward, as they can provide new firms with advantages (enhanced coordination and cooperation) as well as disadvantages (reduced diversity, nepotism concerns, and the possible spillover of personal conflict). As kin ties may have both positive and negative implications for performance, a contingency approach to the performance of new firms is valuable. We develop such an approach by relating different structural configurations of kin ties—whether they are between founders, between founders and employees, or between employees—to the performance of new firms. We test our predictions using data on 4,967 new firms founded in Stockholm between 1998 and 2003. Our theory deepens our understanding of why kin ties have heterogeneous effects on the performance of new firms.
apa_citation: Ertug, G., Kotha, R., & Hedström, P. (2020). Kin ties and the performance of new firms: A structural approach. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(6), 1893-1922. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1218

title: Discovery as an Abductive Mechanism for Reorienting Habits within Organizational Change
methods: Qualitative field study of a DeltaCare organizational change initiative, using formal and conversational interviews, field observations, internal and external archival materials, field notes, inductive coding, abductive analysis, data-rich vignettes, and abduction sequences as the analytic unit.
industry: Horizontally integrated, medium-sized, nonprofit health system delivering inpatient medical care.
country: Central region of the United States.
time_period: Data were collected over a 30-month period in 2007-2009, with periodic telephone updates through 2011 and document collection through 2013.
units: DeltaCare clinicians, managers, staff members, senior leaders, patients, volunteers, and board members involved in creating and implementing a new inpatient care delivery model.
n_sample: 25 in-depth semistructured formal interviews, five semistructured follow-up interviews, conversational interviews, approximately 900 pages of interview transcripts, 100 pages of field notes, 275 pages of internal documents, and 150 pages of external documents.
authors: Golden-Biddle, K.
theories: pragmatism and abductive reasoning; process studies of organizational change; reorientation of habits
keywords: abduction sequences; discovery; doubt; inquiry; organizational change; pragmatism; reorienting habits; surprise
research_question: How did discovery unfold within the organizational change process? The paper studies how DeltaCare participants reoriented prevailing habits of belief and action while creating a new inpatient care delivery model.
mechanism_summary:
- Indeterminate situation: Participants first encountered surprising difficulty mapping and walking care flows, which exposed fragmented care delivery and patient hardship.
- Abduction sequences: Discovery unfolded through five interdependent sequences: engaging the indeterminate situation, deepening its significance, constructing an imagined configuration, trying on new habits, and negotiating new habits.
- Motors of discovery: Surprise, doubt, and inquiry moved participants from interrupted prevailing beliefs toward new actionable beliefs.
- Constructively oriented responses: Participants sustained discovery by halting activity, reflecting on what they did not yet know, involving patients and clinicians, experimenting with Trio and tollgates, and revising contested practices.
- Habit reorientation: Discovery helped participants move away from independent professional habits toward collaborative bedside care and negotiated interdependence.

The process is abductive rather than a linear implementation mechanism. Surprises disrupted settled beliefs about care delivery; doubt made those beliefs problematic; inquiry enabled participants to imagine, test, and negotiate new ways of working. Across the five sequences, discovery operated continuously through organizational change rather than only at the outset.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational change theory by explaining discovery as an abductive mechanism through which participants reorient prevailing habits of belief and action. It theorizes abduction sequences as loosely connected and overlapping episodes of creative social activity driven by surprise, doubt, and inquiry. It also contributes a methodology for future process research by proposing abduction sequences as an analytic means for examining discovery in change, innovation, learning, and other inquiry processes.
practical_implication: For managers and change participants, the study implies that surprise and doubt should not be treated only as obstacles to implementation. Change work can benefit when participants pause to examine puzzling situations, involve those affected by the work, and use constructive inquiry to test and negotiate new practices. The DeltaCare case also suggests that leaders, OD support, and lean tools may help discovery when they are used to surface and explore problems rather than merely enforce predetermined solutions.
limitations: The study is based on a single medium-sized health system and a system-level change initiative in an organization that did not face immediate survival pressure. DeltaCare also had a credible OD function, senior leadership involvement, and recently introduced lean management, all of which may have shaped members' ability to sustain discovery. The author notes that these contextual features may limit transferability to more time-pressured settings or organizations without similar support for inquiry.
future_research: Future research could examine discovery in time-pressured environments, including crisis or urgent radical-change settings. The paper also calls for research on leaders who are disposed to foster rather than derail discovery, and on whether intentionally incorporating discovery into lean management or other prescriptive methods changes their effects. Additional studies could analyze how political, cultural, and emotional dynamics foster or derail discovery processes within change.
abstract: Process studies of organizational and strategic change have drawn attention to the dynamics that generate such change, but we still know little about how discovery unfolds within change. A field study of efforts to create a new system for delivering inpatient medical care revealed that surprises and discoveries, and constructively oriented responses to them, occurred continuously throughout organizational change, not merely at the outset. Seeking to understand this empirical puzzle, I drew on the concept of abduction from pragmatism and organizational studies. This study makes two contributions to theory about the relation between discovery and change. First, I develop a framework that explicates the central role of discovery as an abductive mechanism that enables participants to reorient prevailing habits. Analyses reveal discovery to operate through what I call “abduction sequences,” or loosely connected and overlapping episodes of creative social activity. Three key motors and their attendant feelings drive discovery via abduction sequences: surprise, doubt, and inquiry. Second, I provide a methodology for use in future research on discovery. Specifically, I propose abduction sequences as a useful analytic means for examining discovery within change and other inquiry processes, such as innovation and learning, that generate fundamentally new ways of working.

title: From the Editors: Publishing Practical and Responsible Research in AMJ
methods: Editorial (From the Editors essay): the authors develop normative editorial guidance on publishing practical and responsible AMJ research, organized around harmful practical implications, rigorous methodology, careful interpretation, and collective field responsibility.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Hideg, Ivona; DeCelles, Katherine A.; Tihanyi, Laszlo
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: counterintuitive findings; diversity of scholars; methodological rigor; open science; practical implications; responsible research
research_question: How should AMJ authors, reviewers, editors, and readers produce and evaluate management research so that its practical implications are rigorous, ethical, and socially responsible rather than harmful or easily misused?
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Management research should help make organizations and society better, so practical implications need to be treated as an essential part of the manuscript rather than as a final technical hurdle.
- Harm-risk focus: Research on sensitive topics can unintentionally reinforce victim blaming, stereotypes, insensitive practices, or harmful organizational decisions if its implications are shallow, sensationalized, or ethically underdeveloped.
- Methodological responsibility: Counterintuitive and controversial findings require especially strong empirical evidence, transparency, replication, preregistration where appropriate, and caution against HARKing, p-hacking, false positives, small effects, and unsupported causal language.
- Collective responsibility: Authors, reviewers, editors, mentors, and audience members should scrutinize methodology, interpretation, and practical implications, while broadening participation by diverse scholars and viewpoints.
- Field-development practices: The editorial recommends presenting work to diverse and interdisciplinary audiences and integrating responsible-management-research discussions into doctoral seminars.

The process logic is normative rather than causal: practical responsibility begins when researchers formulate questions, continues through methodological design and interpretation, and extends into review, publication, and wider communication. Hideg, DeCelles, and Tihanyi argue that sensitive or counterintuitive findings can create social harm when methodological limits and ethical implications are not made explicit. They therefore call for a field-wide practice of coupling theoretical contribution with credible evidence, careful language, and attention to the consequences of research for organizational members and external stakeholders.
theoretical_contribution: The essay is not a theory-building article; it contributes editorial guidance about how AMJ should understand the relation between theoretical contribution, practical implication, and responsible scholarship. It reframes practical implications as ethically consequential claims that must be supported by rigorous methods and careful interpretation, especially when research concerns vulnerable groups, sensitive workplace issues, CSR, discrimination, corruption, harassment, or other socially consequential topics.
practical_implication: Authors should consider potential misuse and unintended consequences from the beginning of the research process, avoid sensationalized framing, and spell out implications concretely and comprehensively. They should also use stronger methodological safeguards for controversial or counterintuitive findings, report results transparently, avoid causal language when causality is not warranted, and present findings to diverse or interdisciplinary audiences before submission. Reviewers and editors should scrutinize practical implications, replicability, transparency, and interpretations of sensitive findings more actively.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editorial encourages research that seeks genuine solutions to organizational and societal challenges while being mindful of ethical and social consequences. It also calls for more research done with, rather than merely on, marginalized groups, more attention to developing economies and nontraditional professions, and more doctoral training on responsible and practical management research.

title: A Dual-Agency Model of Firm CSR in Response to Institutional Pressure: Evidence from Chinese Publicly Listed Firms
methods: Panel study of Chinese publicly listed firms around the Twelfth Five-Year Plan. The authors use RKS CSR ratings, a post-policy indicator for 2011-2014, firm fixed-effect OLS models with robust standard errors clustered by province, robustness checks for CSR-reporting selection and lagged provincial CSR, and mechanism tests split by corruption levels and state ownership.
industry: Publicly listed firms on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges.
units: Firm-year observations for Chinese listed firms.
n_sample: 746 firms and 3,075 observations in the main analyses.
authors: Li, Shuping; Lu, Jane Wenzhen
theories: dual-agency model of public CSR agents and private CSR agents; institutional theory (Campbell, 2007; North, 1991); upper echelon theory (Carpenter, Geletkanycz, & Sanders, 2004; Hambrick & Mason, 1984)
keywords: Chinese listed firms; Twelfth Five-Year Plan; corporate social responsibility; dual-agency model; institutional pressure; legitimacy concerns; private CSR agents; public CSR agents
research_question: How do political institutions and human agents jointly influence firms' CSR performance? The paper asks when Chinese firms respond to a national CSR initiative, the Twelfth Five-Year Plan, by increasing CSR, and how that response varies with provincial officials' promotion incentives and CEOs' legitimacy concerns.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a dual-agency process in which institutional pressure is expected to affect firm CSR only when relevant public and private agents have incentives to act on that pressure. Public CSR agents, namely provincial officials, are theorized to press firms toward CSR when CSR helps their promotion prospects, especially when they are politically contestable or have moderate career horizons. Private CSR agents, namely CEOs, are theorized to increase CSR when they need legitimacy, especially when they are politically connected to the central government or are early enough in their tenure to face stronger legitimacy concerns. The estimates show a positive post-plan CSR shift and stronger responses under those public- and private-agent conditions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to CSR research by explaining why a homogeneous national CSR initiative can produce heterogeneous firm responses. It extends institutional theory by bringing individual agents back into the institution-CSR relationship and by distinguishing public agents' career concerns from private agents' legitimacy concerns. It also provides a cross-level account of CSR implementation in which national policy, provincial officials, CEOs, and firms jointly shape CSR performance.
practical_implication: For public policy, the findings suggest that target-based evaluation systems for social and environmental initiatives can motivate local officials to promote CSR when those targets matter for officials' careers. For firms, the paper suggests that CEO selection and CEO-government embeddedness can affect alignment with CSR-related institutional pressure. The broader implication is that government CSR initiatives depend not only on policy design but also on the incentives of the agents expected to implement them.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that politician qualities are not fully observed, so contestability and career horizon could partly reflect effectiveness rather than only career incentives. They also note that the dependent variable is firm-level CSR, which does not directly measure province-level environmental or social outcomes. Generalizability may be constrained in countries with highly centralized political power, little political mobility, or settings where social criteria are not important for officials' promotion.
future_research: Future research could examine how politicians' individual talents alter the relationship between national policy and firm responses. The authors also suggest studying outcomes more directly tied to dual agents, including officials' career movements and province-level environmental changes. Further work could examine when officials implement national policy because of self-interest versus alternative mechanisms that do not depend on self-interest.
abstract: Findings from prior studies regarding the relationship between government corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives and firm CSR performance have been mixed. To address this research gap, we developed a dual-agency model incorporating both public agents (government officials) and private agents (corporate CEOs) to investigate when firms respond to government initiatives by increasing their CSR. We tested our model in a sample of 746 Chinese listed firms during the period 2009–2014 when a national CSR initiative, the Twelfth Five-Year Plan, took place. Our results show that firms responded positively to the plan by increasing their CSR performance, but their response varied according to the incentives of both public and private CSR agents. Firms were more likely to increase CSR when public agents were more motivated to seek promotion to the central government or when private agents had greater concerns for legitimacy. Our examination of the role of two different types of CSR agents within institutions contributes to the institutional view of CSR by highlighting the interplay of institutions and human agents in promoting firm CSR. It also advances public policy and managerial practices regarding the development and selection of CSR agents inside and outside firms in a given institutional environment.

title: Too Hot to Handle and Too Valuable to Drop: An Expanded Conceptualization of Firms’ Reactions to Exchange Partner Misconduct
methods: Quantitative archival study of publicly traded firms' campaign contributions to U.S. congresspersons accused of misconduct, using simultaneous seemingly unrelated regression models for ending, commitment-level, and hedging outcomes and generalized linear models for boomerang behavior.
industry: Publicly traded firms in Compustat with campaign-contribution relationships to U.S. congressional politicians accused of misconduct.
time_period: Biennial election cycles from 1992 to 2018, using politician misconduct events identified from 1970 to 2010 as part of the event search.
units: Firm-misconduct politician observations and firm-misconduct politician cycles.
n_sample: 3,797 firm-misconduct politician observations for commitment hypotheses; 3,483 firm-misconduct politician cycles for altering commitment and hedging; 812 firm-misconduct politician cycles for boomerang tests.
authors: Nalick, Michael; Kuban, Scott; Hill, Aaron D.; Ridge, Jason W.
theories: mixed gambles theorizing; negative spillover theorizing; relational embeddedness; relational uncertainty
keywords: boomerang; exchange partner misconduct; hedging; mixed gambles; negative spillover; politicians; relational embeddedness; relational uncertainty
research_question: How do firms react to exchange partner misconduct when maintaining the relationship creates association risks but ending it creates detachment risks? The paper asks whether firms' reactions extend beyond a binary maintain-or-end choice to include altering commitment levels, hedging by adding partners, and boomeranging back to a partner after temporarily ending commitment.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a mixed-gamble response to exchange partner misconduct. Relational embeddedness increases the upside of preserving a valuable relationship, while relational uncertainty increases concern that the partner may not be able or willing to deliver future benefits and may expose the firm to negative spillover. Firms therefore manage the trade-off by changing contribution levels, adding a competitor relationship while maintaining the original one, or temporarily ending and later restarting the relationship. The evidence supports positive effects of embeddedness on partner commitment and boomerang behavior and a negative effect of uncertainty on partner commitment; it also supports uncertainty increasing hedging, while several hypothesized moderation effects are not supported.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends negative spillover research by moving beyond the dominant maintain-or-end framing of reactions to exchange partner misconduct. It integrates mixed gambles with negative spillover, relational embeddedness, and relational uncertainty to theorize a broader set of strategic options: altering commitments, hedging, and boomeranging. It also adds temporality to misconduct-response theory by showing that ending a relationship need not be permanent.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that firms facing exchange partner misconduct should consider a broader menu of responses than simply staying or exiting. Managers can reduce exposure while preserving potential value by decreasing commitment, maintaining a relationship while adding alternatives, or temporarily pausing and later restarting exchange when conditions change. The authors' post-hoc evidence also suggests that political-relationship portfolios may shape firms' exposure to spillover from any single misconduct event.
limitations: The empirical context is corporate political activity, so the authors note that generalizability should be tested in other exchange settings such as buyer-supplier relationships or industry supply chains. The study observes publicly visible campaign-contribution relationships, which may miss covert or less observable exchange relationships. The theory focuses on relational uncertainty and does not theorize stigma anxiety, partly because of measurement difficulties.
future_research: Future research could examine other strategies firms use to manage negative spillover, including partner substitution and impression-management responses after associations with transgressors become public. It could test the model in other misconduct contexts, such as supplier misconduct in petroleum or automotive supply chains. The authors also call for research on when relational uncertainty is more influential than relational embeddedness, why hedging behaves differently from other responses, and how stigma anxiety relates to alternative risk-management strategies.
abstract: Multiple theories addressing firms’ reactions to exchange partner misconduct coalesce to depict a trade-off. On the one hand, maintaining commitments to transgressors poses negative spillover risks, so theories posit firms are more likely to avoid such risks by ending commitments as negative spillover rises. On the other hand, exchange relationships often create embedded value, so theorizing also posits firms are more likely to avoid risking loss by maintaining commitments as relationships are more embedded. We argue this “maintain or end” choice oversimplifies a complex situation in which there are mixed gambles (i.e., choices offering both positive and negative outcomes). We integrate theorizing on mixed gambles and negative spillover to develop a broader conceptualization of alternative strategies for firms to reconcile these risk trade-offs beyond a binary “maintain or end” reaction, theorizing firms may: (a) increase or decrease commitments to transgressors, (b) hedge against risks by adding new partners while maintaining existing ones, or (c) “boomerang” by restarting exchange after previously ending commitments. Using firms’ relationships with politicians accused of misconduct to test our arguments, findings support our theorizing. Collectively, we offer a more complete understanding of firms’ reactions to exchange partner misconduct, extending theory and practical knowledge in multiple ways.

title: Historical Origins of Firm Ownership Structure: The Persistent Effects of the African Slave Trade
methods: Empirical quantitative cross-national firm-level study combining historical country-level African slave-trade data with World Bank Enterprise Survey establishment data from African countries. The authors estimate linear probability models with firm- and country-level controls, robustness checks with multilevel, logit/probit, and instrumental-variable models, cross-industry interaction tests for manufacturing, and 2SLS models for institutions and social capital as historically persistent mechanisms.
industry: Broad cross-industry sample of business establishments in Africa, with a specific cross-industry test contrasting manufacturing firms with other sectors.
country: 41 sub-Saharan African countries with historical slave export data and World Bank Enterprise Survey coverage.
time_period: Firm-level World Bank Enterprise Survey data from 2006-2016; historical slave-trade export data between A.D. 1400 and 1900.
units: Business establishments/firms nested in countries, plus country-level slave exports, institutional measures, and social-capital measures.
n_sample: Over 30,000 firms; main dependent-variable models use 30,004 firm observations for sole proprietorship and 29,754 for majority ownership.
authors: Pierce, L.; Snyder, J. A.
theories: historical persistence of traumatic shocks; institutional economics; path dependence; social capital
keywords: concentrated ownership; firm ownership structure; historical African slave trade; institutions; social capital; traumatic shocks
research_question: How do historical traumatic shocks help explain present-day firm ownership structure? The paper asks whether African countries more exposed to the historical slave trade have higher modern ownership concentration, and whether weakened institutions and low social capital partly explain that relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a historical-persistence argument. The authors theorize that severe traumatic shocks can weaken institutions and social capital, and that these weakened conditions persist long enough to restrict modern firms' access to diffuse ownership. In countries with higher historical slave extraction, firms are therefore more likely to remain sole proprietorships or majority-owned firms, especially in manufacturing where capital needs make diffuse ownership more valuable. The paper is careful that its IV and 2SLS evidence raises confidence and supports plausible channels, but does not definitively establish a causal path from the slave trade through institutions and social capital to ownership concentration.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends management and strategy research on ownership structure by moving the explanation for weak institutions and low social capital backward into history. It recasts institutions and social capital not only as predictors of ownership concentration but also as historically persistent mechanisms through which traumatic shocks can shape modern firms. It also contributes to calls for more historically grounded management research and more research on African firms by using the African slave trade as a quantifiable historical origin of firm structure.
practical_implication: The findings imply that managers, investors, and policy actors in high slave-trade African countries may face ownership-concentration patterns rooted partly in historically persistent contracting and trust constraints. Efforts to expand firms' access to equity-based capital therefore need to address institutional weakness and social-capital deficits rather than treating concentrated ownership only as a contemporary owner preference. The manufacturing results suggest that these constraints may be especially consequential where capital investment is central to productivity and scale.
limitations: The authors caution that, like most studies of shocks from centuries past, the paper cannot strongly establish the causal link between the slave trade and modern ownership concentration. They also state that the mechanisms cannot be definitively isolated because history is complex, country-level mechanism measures leave only 35-41 observations, and SEM mediation assumptions are violated in this cross-national setting. The World Bank Enterprise Survey also lacks detailed ethnicity, trust, and network measures that would allow more direct tests of social capital mechanisms.
future_research: Future research could examine whether other traumatic shocks, including climate change, conflict, natural disaster, epidemic disease, nuclear events, and forced migration, reshape institutions, social capital, and firm ownership structure. The authors also call for more management and strategy research on African firms and for richer cross-national firm-level data on ethnicity, trust, and networks. They suggest that new global event and location data may create opportunities to study African firms and build broader knowledge about doing business in Africa.
abstract: This paper uses evidence from the historical African slave trade to extend prior theory linking modern firm ownership structure to institutions and social capital. We argue that institutions and social capital are not simply predictors of ownership structure but can also be historically persistent mechanisms through which past traumatic shocks to society shape modern businesses. Using data from over 30,000 firms across 41 sub-Saharan countries, we show that firms in areas that suffered high historical slave extraction are today more likely to have concentrated ownership. High slave export countries have more sole proprietorships and majority ownership, with our model implying a difference of 43 percentage points between the lowest and highest export countries. This difference is particularly pronounced in the manufacturing sector, where high capital needs can necessitate diffuse ownership when credit markets are weak. Finally, we present modest evidence that weakened institutions and social capital are among the mechanisms through which the historical slave trade increases modern ownership concentration. Our paper answers recent calls to bring both Africa and history back into management research through our theoretical extension into distinct and quantifiable historical origins of firm structure.
apa_citation: Pierce, L., & Snyder, J. A. (2020). Historical origins of firm ownership structure: The persistent effects of the African slave trade. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(6), 1687-1713. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0597

title: “Tapping” into Goodwill: Enhancing Corporate Reputation through Customer Volunteering
methods: Sequential mixed-method field study at a local microbrewery: Study 1 used observation, informal interviews, and 48 semi-structured customer interviews with open, axial, and selective coding; Study 2 used multisource, three-wave survey data from volunteering customers and friends, analyzed with structural equation modeling in Mplus using bias-corrected bootstrapping and FIML.
industry: Local microbrewery corporate community engagement program involving customer volunteering.
time_period: Five-month weekly volunteering program; quantitative customer and friend surveys included Time 1, Time 2 one month later, and Time 3 two years later.
units: Customer volunteers and recruited friends of customer volunteers.
n_sample: Study 1 included 48 formal semi-structured interviews; Study 2 included 140 volunteering customers at Time 1, 113 usable customer responses at Time 2, 65 usable customer responses at Time 3, 93 usable friend responses at Time 2, and 35 usable friend responses at Time 3.
authors: Rodell, Jessica B.; Sabey, Tyler B.; Rogers, Kristie M.
theories: corporate reputation and sensemaking theory; emotional contagion theory
keywords: corporate community engagement; corporate reputation; customer patronage; customer volunteering; emotional contagion; product purchases; sensemaking
research_question: How do customers perceive corporate volunteering initiatives that invite their own participation, and what are the implications for customer attitudes and behaviors toward the company? The paper refines this into two Study 2 questions: what impact volunteering engagement has on stakeholder attitudes and behaviors toward the company, and how customers' volunteering experiences and attitudes spread to others.
mechanism_summary: The authors first use qualitative data to identify customer engagement, enriching experience, enhanced company reputation, customer loyalty, and contagion as central themes. In Study 2, they theorize a sensemaking process in which engaged customer volunteering provides reputation-relevant information that customers attach to the company. They also theorize an emotional contagion process in which customers' positive reactions to volunteering spread through conversations with friends, shaping friends' evaluations and support behaviors. The quantitative results support positive indirect relationships for customer patronage and purchases through corporate reputation, support an indirect relationship to friends' reputation perceptions through emotional contagion, and support the serial indirect relationship for friends' product purchases but not friends' patronage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends corporate volunteering research beyond employee volunteers by examining customers as participating stakeholders. It introduces corporate reputation and emotional contagion as mechanisms through which customer volunteering can be associated with goodwill toward a firm, including among people who did not directly attend the event. It also contributes to reputation research by showing how reputation can be shaped through micro-level, first-hand and second-hand stakeholder experiences rather than only through macro-level media or analyst channels.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that firms with community engagement programs may benefit from involving customers, especially when the volunteering experience helps customers engage directly with a prosocial activity and with the firm. For managers, the paper frames customer volunteering as a possible win-win: the company may build reputation and financially supportive behaviors while broadening community participation. The authors are careful that this implication is most directly supported for settings resembling their field context: an on-site, customer-facing, local volunteering program.
limitations: The study is constrained by recruitment from an existing volunteering initiative at one local microbrewery, with a relatively low response rate and smaller two-year follow-up samples. The behavioral outcomes are self-reported rather than objectively observed attendance or purchase records. The authors also note that serial mediation effects have low explanatory power and that generalizability may depend on industry, program structure, customer-facing physical presence, local image, and company size or novelty.
future_research: Future research should examine customer volunteering in different industries and program structures, including activities held at nonprofits and activities with direct beneficiary interaction. The authors call for work on how customer involvement fits into broader system-level dynamics of corporate community engagement and business strategy. They also encourage a more macro approach to studying how volunteering programs should be structured and how they connect to a company's larger strategy.
abstract: Companies often engage in prosocial initiatives—such as employee volunteering programs—as a way to balance their economic goals with a set of social goals. In an attempt to expand the impact of such programs, some companies have begun soliciting help from their customers as well. Given the significant investment these programs represent, it is important that companies understand whether they offer the anticipated social and economic returns. Using multimethod data from a local microbrewery, we develop and test theory about the reputational implications of customers’ involvement in a corporate community engagement initiative. Our results suggest that customers’ engagement in such initiatives is related to positive views of the organization (i.e., corporate reputation), as well as positive customer behaviors—brewery patronage and purchases—two years later. Moreover, it appears that customers spread this sentiment to others—creating the potential for an even broader audience to see the company as reputable and, in turn, provide support.

title: Portfolio Spillover of Institutional Investor Activism: An Awareness–Motivation–Capability Perspective
methods: Longitudinal archival quantitative study of S&P 1500 firms from 2000 to 2013. The authors identify activist ownership from Schedule 13D/13D/A filings, measure restructuring and growth announcements using Capital IQ Key Development data, and estimate firm fixed-effects Poisson models with Heckman selection controls, subgroup and interaction tests for moderators, and supplementary quasi-natural-experiment and dynamic panel analyses.
industry: S&P 1500 public companies across industries.
units: Firm-year observations for non-targeted firms exposed to activist investor ownership, plus comparison firms not in activist investors' portfolios.
n_sample: The paper reports 1,861 non-targeted firms in activist investors' portfolios plus 45 additional firms; focal action counts include 10,331 restructuring announcements and 80,526 growth-action announcements.
authors: Shi, Wei; Connelly, Brian L.; Hoskisson, Robert E.; Ketchen, David J., Jr.
theories: awareness–motivation–capability framework (Chen, 1996; Chen, Su, & Tsai, 2007); shareholder activism and corporate governance research
keywords: awareness–motivation–capability framework; constitutional constraints; corporate restructuring; growth activity; institutional investor activism; portfolio spillover; shareholder activism; transactional ownership
research_question: Do institutional investors' activist campaigns spill over to firms in the same investors' portfolios that have not been targeted for activism? The paper asks whether non-targeted firms restructure more and reduce growth activity when activist investors own larger stakes, and whether those responses depend on activist capability and focal-firm motivation.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an awareness–motivation–capability argument applied to corporate governance rather than competitive dynamics. As activist ownership rises, executives of non-targeted firms become more aware that activists may target them next, which makes preemptive restructuring more likely and growth initiatives less likely. The response is stronger when activists have more capability to launch a credible campaign and when firms have more motivation to respond, reflected in weaker constitutional constraints and higher transactional ownership.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the awareness–motivation–capability framework from competitive threats to governance threats, showing how firms may respond to an implicit rather than explicit external threat. It develops the concept of portfolio spillover to explain how activism aimed at one portfolio firm can shape strategic actions at other firms owned by the same activist investors. It also contributes to corporate governance research by showing that activist influence depends not only on how much activists own but also on governance protections and the presence of transactional investors.
practical_implication: Boards and executives of non-targeted firms should recognize that activist ownership can create pressure for preemptive restructuring and reduced growth even before any direct activist demand appears. The findings suggest that such defensive actions may not always improve performance, so boards should scrutinize whether responses to implicit activist threat are strategically justified. Activist investors and other shareholders may also use the findings to understand how activism at one firm can affect other portfolio firms.
limitations: The authors note that they do not directly measure whether executives feel threatened by activist investors. Because the evidence is archival, they also cannot directly observe how constitutional constraints or transactional ownership shape activist capability and firm motivation. The sample focuses on large S&P 1500 firms, which may limit generalizability to smaller firms or other governance settings.
future_research: Future research could use primary data such as interviews or participant observation to examine how executives perceive and respond to activist threat. The authors suggest studying portfolio spillover from corporate investors and new corporate entrants, as well as contingencies beyond constitutional constraints and transactional ownership. They also call for broader samples to test boundary conditions outside large S&P 1500 firms.
abstract: Scholars have investigated how shareholder activism by institutional investors— organizations that manage money on behalf of clients—directly shapes the actions of firms that are targeted for activism. We shift attention to an indirect process we call “portfolio spillover”—the extent to which activist behavior targeted toward a firm in an investor’s portfolio of holdings influences actions by other firms that are not presently targeted for activism. We examine portfolio spillover by extending the awareness– motivation–capability framework from its traditional domain of competitive dynamics to the governance arena. We theorize that firms will be more likely to respond to investors targeting other portfolio members to the extent that those firms become aware of the implicit threat of activism. We also develop and test theory about how the capability of activists to launch a successful campaign and the motivation of firms to react can moderate this relationship. Using data from a sample of S&P 1500 companies from 2000–2013, we find that firms restructure and reduce growth in response to portfolio spillover. These relationships are stronger when activist investors have capability to attack and firms have motivation to respond.

title: Once in Orange Always in Orange? Identity Paralysis and the Enduring Influence of Institutional Logics on Identity
methods: Qualitative study using archival documents and interviews at institutional and individual levels; the author analyzed Canadian corrections logics and then coded interviews with previously incarcerated men to compare unsuccessful de-identification and successful de-identification patterns.
industry: Canadian corrections and prison reintegration, accessed through a nonprofit community organization supporting recently released people.
time_period: Fieldwork at the NCO was conducted from July-September 2011 and then one day per week in February, March, and May 2012; interviewees had been released within one year, mostly in the first six months after release.
units: Previously incarcerated men transitioning from prison back into society, plus Canadian corrections field actors and archival records used to identify institutional logics.
n_sample: 43 previously incarcerated men used in the study; total data included 4,439 pages of archival data and 57 interviews.
authors: Toubiana, Madeline
theories: identity and de-identification theory; institutional logics perspective; total institutions
keywords: Canadian corrections; de-identification; identity material; identity paralysis; institutional logics; total institutions
research_question: How and why can individuals' efforts to de-identify with institutional logics fail during transition out of a total institution? The paper examines previously incarcerated men's efforts to disentangle themselves from prison-associated logics as they move back into society.
mechanism_summary:
- Institutional logics in prison: Public safety, jailhouse, and rehabilitative logics provide rules, identity prescriptions, and narratives for understanding self and action.
- Identity paralysis pattern: Some men remain identified with prison logics after release when they lack identity targets and material, feel labeled, resign themselves to existing identifications, and rely on jailhouse or rehabilitative narratives to justify self.
- De-identification pattern: Other men target family or religious logics, access identity material, craft turning points that make new logic content meaningful, and engage in emotion work to manage anger tied to past identifications.
- Process outcome: Identity paralysis is the freezing of identification with an undesirable or no longer appropriate target.

The process is not a simple switch from one cognitively accessible logic to another. De-identification breaks down when men are aware of alternatives but cannot materially claim them and simultaneously experience negative social evaluations. Under those conditions, the content of jailhouse and rehabilitative logics remains useful for explaining the self, but that usefulness can keep men attached to identities they want to leave behind.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional logics theory by showing that logics are not merely cognitive toolkits that actors can switch among when a new logic becomes accessible. Identity material and the content of logics shape whether a logic can become a viable source of identification or de-identification. It also contributes to identity-transition research by theorizing identity paralysis as failed de-identification driven by resignation, material constraint, labeling, and reliance on existing logic narratives rather than by a simple desire to hold on to a lost identity.
practical_implication: For prison reintegration and other exits from total institutions, the paper suggests that wanting to change is insufficient without material, symbolic, and emotional support for new identities. Transition support should help people access identity material, develop narratives that connect past and present selves, and manage emotions attached to prior institutional identifications. The paper also cautions that rehabilitative narratives can support dignity during incarceration yet still contribute to identity paralysis after release if they reinforce victimhood without enabling new self-definitions.
limitations: The study focuses on the exit period between release and reintegration, which enabled detailed analysis of transition but did not directly observe identity change over a longer time period. The author also notes that the model is developed from an extreme case: exit from a total institution. The findings are likely most relevant where individuals leave highly institutionalized domains with dominant logics that have strongly shaped identity.
future_research: Future research could study individuals before, during, and after transition to examine how de-identification unfolds over time. The paper encourages testing the model in other highly institutionalized settings, such as refugee camps, the military, professions, or organizations with totalizing features. It also calls for work on what governing logic or combination of logics best supports transition out of total institutions.
abstract: We know that individuals' identities can become intertwined with institutions through processes of identification. But what happens when individuals need or desire to disentangle their identities from institutions after identification has taken place? In this paper, I examine previously incarcerated men's efforts to de-identify with the institutional logics associated with prison as they transition back into society. While past work has tended to characterize de-identification efforts as ultimately successful, I reveal how individuals can remain stuck in their identifications and experience identity paralysis. In doing so I add nuance to our understanding of de-identification by revealing the factors that can contribute to its breakdown and failure. I highlight specifically the importance of identity material and the content of institutional logics in influencing de-identification processes, and thus extend the existing focus on the cognitive accessibility of logics. Importantly, I reveal that challenges to de-identification result not merely from the individuals "holding on" to old targets but rather from their becoming stuck and resigning themselves to existing targets when they simultaneously feel they lack identity material to realize new identities and face negative social evaluations. Indeed my findings point to the powerful and durable ways in which institutions shape our identities even when we desire to change them.
apa_citation: Toubiana, M. (2020). Once in orange always in orange? Identity paralysis and the enduring influence of institutional logics on identity. *Academy of Management Journal*, 63(6), 1739-1774. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0826

title: Playing It Safe for My Family: Exploring the Dual Effects of Family Motivation on Employee Productivity and Creativity
methods: Empirical mixed-method design dominated by two quantitative SEM studies: a two-wave survey and archival productivity study of low-wage blue-collar textile workers, a survey study of higher-income white-collar employees nested in teams, and a qualitative interview study analyzed thematically to probe mechanisms.
industry: Sample 1 used textile manufacturing workers; Sample 2 used white-collar employees from finance, information technology, nonprofit organizations, and other industries; the qualitative study interviewed employees from a wide variety of organizations.
time_period: Quantitative data were collected in 2015 and 2017; qualitative interviews were conducted in 2018.
units: Individual employees, supervisors, team peers, and qualitative interviewees.
n_sample: 187 blue-collar workers with supervisor data, 439 white-collar employees in 84 teams, and 40 qualitative interviewees.
authors: Zhang, Xin-an; Liao, Huiyao; Li, Ning; Colbert, Amy E.
theories: gender role theory; hard work versus smart work framework (Bracha & Fershtman, 2013); self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 2010)
keywords: employee creativity; employee productivity; family financial pressure; family motivation; gender; job instrumentality; self-determination theory
research_question: When does family motivation energize employee performance, and when does it undermine creativity? The paper asks whether family motivation is associated with productivity through work effort, with lower creativity through job instrumentality, and whether family financial pressure and gender help explain when family motivation is activated.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a double-edged motivational process. Drawing on self-determination theory, the authors argue that family motivation can make employees work harder because work helps them support family members, producing higher productivity through work effort. At the same time, family motivation can make employees see work mainly as a financial instrument, which heightens job instrumentality and is associated with lower creativity because creative work is uncertain and may not yield immediate economic returns. The qualitative study extends this account by describing meaningfulness detachment, uncertainty avoidance, short-term orientation, conformity, conservative career choices, and possible unethical behavior as related processes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to family motivation theory by challenging the view that family motivation primarily energizes employees and by showing that its effects differ across performance criteria. It links self-determination theory with the hard work versus smart work framework to explain why the same motive can support productivity while reducing creativity. It also extends the nomological network of family motivation by identifying family financial pressure as an antecedent and gender as a boundary condition.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers should not treat family motivation as uniformly beneficial for performance. If organizations want family-motivated employees to engage in creativity, they should reduce uncertainty around creative work, create psychological safety, solicit ideas actively, and recognize creative attempts even when they fail. The authors also suggest protecting short-term financial rewards when employees are asked to pursue longer-term creative projects.
limitations: The authors state that all samples were collected in China, which may limit generalizability because Chinese family obligations and gender relations may shape how family motivation is experienced. They also note that the quantitative design was time-lagged but still cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. In addition, their quantitative model did not capture either mechanism used to explain why job instrumentality reduces creativity: reduced willingness to accept uncertainty and focus on immediate returns.
future_research: Future research could use longitudinal or experimental designs to strengthen causal inference and test whether family motivation operates differently outside China. The authors call for work on when family motivation is experienced as more autonomous, such as when it is tied to being a role model or an equal breadwinner. They also suggest extending the nomological network by examining creativity contingencies, conservative career choices, and possible links between family motivation and unethical behavior.
abstract: Research has shown that family motivation exerts an energizing effect on employee performance. Challenging this, we argue that family motivation is a double-edged sword with both an energizing and a debilitating effect on employee performance, depending on the performance criterion in question. Specifically, drawing upon self-determination theory and the “hard work versus smart work” framework, we hypothesize that family motivation is positively related to employee productivity via enhanced work effort (i.e., energizing effect). However, family motivation also stimulates employees to see their jobs as a means to gain financial support for their family, rather than an end in itself, which is associated with lower levels of creativity (i.e., debilitating effect). We further propose that employees’ family motivation is higher when they experience higher levels of family financial pressure, and that financial pressure is more strongly related to family motivation for women than for men. We find support for our hypotheses in a sample of 187 low-wage, blue-collar workers and a sample of 439 relatively high-income, whitecollar employees. We also conduct a qualitative study with 40 high-income employees; results provide a more nuanced understanding of the ways in which family motivation shapes perceptions of the job and subsequent behaviors and outcomes.

title: Gender, Brokerage, and Performance: A Construal Approach
methods: Three-study empirical quantitative design: two field studies using perceived and actual friendship-network brokerage measures with student performance outcomes, plus a between-participants experiment testing anxiety as a moderated mediator.
industry: Business-school MBA/management education settings in Studies 1 and 2; employed online participants in a workplace-problem experiment in Study 3.
country: England/United Kingdom in Studies 1 and 2; United States and Canada in Study 3.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals: MBA, EMBA, master's, exchange students, and employed online participants.
n_sample: Study 1: 160 MBA students; Study 2: 164 Executive MBA, MBA, master's, and exchange students; Study 3: 232 employed U.S. and Canadian residents.
authors: Brands, R. A.; Mehra, A.
theories: construal perspective; stereotype threat (Spencer, Logel, & Davies, 2016); structural hole theory of social capital (Burt, 1992)
keywords: brokerage; construal; friendship network brokers; performance; stereotype threat
research_question: The paper asks why women and men obtain different performance returns from friendship network brokerage. It specifically examines whether the difference comes from brokers' own construal of brokerage, rather than only from audience reactions to brokers.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that brokerage in friendship networks carries masculine associations and a negative stereotype about women's broker performance. When women perceive themselves as friendship network brokers, this activates stereotype threat, increasing anxiety about performance and negative social evaluation. That anxiety reduces their ability to capitalize on informational advantages from brokerage, lowering performance relative to comparable men or women in closed networks.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a construal approach to brokerage that shifts attention from network structure alone to how individuals perceive and interpret the network positions they occupy. It contributes to research on gender and social networks by showing that women brokers may be disadvantaged not only because others penalize them, but also because gendered stereotypes alter their own experience of brokerage. It also extends network cognition research by showing that social identity and stereotype threat shape how network structures affect performance.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that encouraging brokerage will generate equal returns for all employees. The authors suggest raising awareness of stereotype threat, explicitly challenging the legitimacy of gendered broker stereotypes, and helping women reappraise threat in brokerage roles as part of career training and professional education.
limitations: The authors identify the business-school and business-context setting as a possible boundary condition because gender stereotypes about competence and leadership are especially salient in business. The studies focus on friendship relations, so the argument may not apply in the same way to instrumental or mandated workflow networks. The paper also notes that ego-centric construal may interact with others' reactions, but it does not directly test that combined process.
future_research: Future research could examine whether stereotype threat is weaker when brokerage occurs in instrumental rather than friendship networks. Scholars could also test how contextual factors such as gender composition, cultural artifacts, nationality, ethnicity, rank, or role affect the salience of gender in brokerage construal. The authors further call for research on whether prior brokerage success, women in formal authority positions, withdrawal, turnover, and network change alter or follow from network-based stereotype threat.
abstract: We present a new theory that seeks to explain differences in the performance of men and women friendship network brokers—individuals who bridge disconnected friends. In contrast to previous audience-centered explanations, our phenomenological theory emphasizes how brokers construe (i.e., perceive and interpret) their networks. We contend that when women perceive themselves as brokers in friendship networks they experience threat, rooted in negative stereotypes about women brokers, which undermines their performance. Using data from a cohort of MBA students, Study 1 finds that women (but not men) exhibit lower performance when they perceive themselves as brokers in small-group friendship networks. Using data from a larger group of MBA students, Study 2 replicates this finding and rules out the possibility that underlying differences in the propensity to connect those whom one bridges may explain the observed gender-based difference in broker performance. Using an experimental design, Study 3 finds that elevated anxiety about task performance and negative social evaluations mediate the relationship between brokerage and performance for women but not for men. Women and men differ in how they psychologically construe brokerage in friendship networks, and this difference helps to account for gender differences in the performance of network brokers.
apa_citation: Brands, R. A., & Mehra, A. (2019). Gender, brokerage, and performance: A construal approach. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 196-219. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0860

title: Diversity Thresholds: How Social Norms, Visibility, and Scrutiny Relate to Group Composition
methods: Field analysis of S&P 1500 corporate board composition using Monte Carlo simulations and OLS regressions, plus four randomized experiments manipulating social norms, scrutiny, and visibility.
industry: U.S. corporate boards, conference panels, and hypothetical work teams.
time_period: Archival board data from 2002-2013; board additions from 2004-2013; experiments with U.S. participants and MBA students.
units: Corporate boards, board additions, and individual experimental participants making selection decisions.
n_sample: Field analyses include 1,441 S&P 1500 companies and 9,989 board member additions; experiments include 479 MTurk participants, 556 MBA students, 200 MTurk participants, and 603 MTurk participants.
authors: Chang, E. H.; Milkman, K. L.; Chugh, D.; Akinola, M.
theories: descriptive social norms; goal-setting theory; impression management
keywords: descriptive social norms; group diversity; scrutiny; visibility; women and minorities in organizations
research_question: The paper asks how social norms and scrutiny affect decisions about adding members of underrepresented populations to groups. It specifically examines whether decision makers use descriptive social norms as diversity thresholds and whether visibility and scrutiny strengthen this tendency.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that decision makers facing scrutiny seek safety in numbers by matching the diversity levels observed in peer groups. Once the descriptive social norm is reached, they relax efforts to add additional underrepresented members, producing clustering at salient thresholds such as two women on a board. Visibility increases the expected scrutiny of group composition, making conformity to descriptive social norms more likely.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a threshold-based account of persistent underrepresentation by showing how descriptive social norms can limit, rather than simply encourage, diversity gains. It links social norm theory, impression management, and goal-setting logic to explain why scrutinized groups may cluster at minimally acceptable levels of representation.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that scrutiny can increase diversity, but only up to the descriptive norm that decision makers perceive as sufficient. Policymakers and advocates may need to shift salient norms toward more ambitious standards, such as population parity or explicitly endorsed ideals, rather than allowing peer averages to define adequacy.
limitations: The authors note that Studies 1A and 1B are correlational and cannot fully rule out reverse causality or omitted confounds such as firm performance. They also acknowledge that the experiments examine individual decisions in simplified settings, while real group-member selection processes are more complex and often involve multiple decision makers.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how descriptive social norms around diversity shift, including whether interventions can make more ambitious norms salient. It also recommends examining other organizational contexts, group sizes, and psychological mechanisms through which descriptive social norms and scrutiny create diversity-threshold effects.
abstract: Across a field study and four experiments, we examine how social norms and scrutiny affect decisions about adding members of underrepresented populations (e.g., women, racial minorities) to groups. When groups are scrutinized, we theorize that decision makers strive to match the diversity observed in peer groups due to impression management concerns, thereby conforming to the descriptive social norm. We examine this first in the context of U.S. corporate boards, where firms face pressure to increase gender diversity. Analyses of S&P 1500 boards reveal that significantly more boards include exactly two women (the descriptive social norm) than would be expected by chance. This overrepresentation of two-women boards—a phenomenon we call “twokenism”—is more pronounced among more visible companies, consistent with our theorizing around impression management and scrutiny. Experimental data corroborate these findings and provide support for our theoretical mechanism: decision makers are discontinuously less likely to add a woman to a board once it includes two women (the social norm), and decision makers’ likelihood of adding a woman or minority to a group is influenced by the descriptive social norms and scrutiny faced. Together, these findings provide a new perspective on the persistent underrepresentation of women and minorities in organizations.
apa_citation: Chang, E. H., Milkman, K. L., Chugh, D., & Akinola, M. (2019). Diversity thresholds: How social norms, visibility, and scrutiny relate to group composition. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 144-171. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0440

title: Something in Common: Competitive Dissimilarity and Performance of Rivals with Common Shareholders
methods: Empirical quantitative panel/network study of firm-dyads using RavenPack competitive action data, Thomson Reuters institutional holdings, L-MR-QAP, and instrumental two-stage least squares models.
industry: S&P 500 firms; rival dyads defined within the same four-digit Standard Industrial Classification industry.
units: Firm-dyads among S&P 500 firms; 68,227 intra-industry rival dyads from 1,984 firms.
n_sample: 1,984 firms; 68,227 intra-industry rival dyads; 2,727 unique institutional investors.
authors: Connelly, B. L.; Lee, K. B.; Tihanyi, L.; Certo, S. T.; Johnson, J. L.
theories: agency theory; competitive dynamics
keywords: agency theory; common institutional ownership; competitive action repertoires; competitive aggressiveness; joint performance; performance disparity
research_question: The paper asks how common institutional ownership shapes competition between rival firms and whether rival firms with common owners achieve better joint performance and lower performance disparity when they compete with dissimilar competitive action repertoires.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that common institutional owners function as shared principals across rival firms. Instead of simply reducing competition, these owners can pressure managers to avoid direct rivalry by competing in different action spheres. When rivals are both competitively aggressive and dissimilar in their action repertoires, they can increase joint performance while keeping performance disparity low.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to competitive dynamics by identifying common institutional ownership as an antecedent of competitive action repertoire dissimilarity in rival dyads. It also extends agency theory from a within-firm principal-agent framing to an interfirm governance mechanism in which common principals influence multiple managerial agents across rival firms.
practical_implication: Managers should attend not only to who owns their firm but also to where those owners are invested among rivals. The findings also caution regulators against assuming that common ownership necessarily suppresses competition, because the study finds that common ownership can be associated with more competitive actions when those actions are differentiated across rivals.
limitations: The study measures whether rivals use different action types but does not observe whether different actions are used to pursue the same underlying strategic objective. It also does not distinguish among types of shareholders, shareholder time horizons, or the magnitude and nature of specific competitive moves.
future_research: Future research could unpack finer-grained action types, the pace at which firms move into dissimilar action repertoires, and boundary conditions that prevent firms from reaching the optimal competitive solution. Additional work could examine industry-level common ownership, more complex rivalry sets beyond dyads, and survey evidence on how common owners motivate managers to take or refrain from competitive actions.
abstract: Economists have long held that bringing firms under the umbrella of a common ownership structure creates monopolistic conditions that reduce competition. We challenge this view by investigating competition between firms in a nuanced manner. We examine the competitive and performance implications of “common institutional ownership,” which occurs when an institutional investor owns a sizeable number of shares in two publicly traded firms. We argue that rival firms with common ownership structures will engage in dissimilar competitive action repertoires to avoid direct competition with each other. Competing aggressively, but with dissimilar action repertoires, allows rivals to maintain high levels of performance. Competing with dissimilar action repertoires also helps ensure that performance disparity between the two firms remains low. In other words, competitive aggressiveness with dissimilar action repertoires yields an optimal competitive solution for rival firms and their common owners.
apa_citation: Connelly, B. L., Lee, K. B., Tihanyi, L., Certo, S. T., & Johnson, J. L. (2019). Something in common: Competitive dissimilarity and performance of rivals with common shareholders. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 1-21. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0515
