title: Toward a Model of Organizational Mourning: The Case of Former Lehman Brothers Bankers
methods: Inductive grounded theory case study based primarily on semi-structured interviews with former Lehman Brothers bankers, supplemented by archival documents for contextual background.
industry: Investment banking and finance; former Lehman Brothers bankers.
time_period: Interviews conducted between May 2013 and September 2014, several years after Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 in September 2008.
units: Former Lehman Brothers bankers who were at the firm when it filed for Chapter 11.
n_sample: 45 former Lehman bankers; 72 additional semi-structured interviews after four exploratory interviews.
authors: Crosina, E.; Pratt, M. G.
theories: continuing bonds theory; job loss; organizational death; personal mourning
keywords: continuing bonds; job loss; organizational death; organizational mourning; personal mourning; post-death organizing
research_question: The paper asks how organizational mourning unfolds for former members after organizational death and what effects mourning has on those members. It also examines why different expressions of mourning emerge among individuals mourning the same organization and how those expressions relate to subsequent career paths.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / phases: Experiencing the death event, remembering the organization, assessing loss, salvaging through evaluation and restoration, and creating continuity and detaching.
- Pathways: Recreators mourn by salvaging relationships and recreating Lehman-like teams in similar finance work; Repurposers mourn by salvaging entrepreneurial culture and skills for new entrepreneurial ventures.
- Triggering conditions: The unexpected bankruptcy and organizational death of Lehman Brothers created shock, sadness, uncertainty, and perceived loss among former members.
- Emergent outcomes: Former bankers created continuing bonds with Lehman in different ways, shaping whether they stayed in similar jobs with former colleagues or moved into entrepreneurial careers.
- Boundary conditions: The authors present an inductive model from former Lehman Brothers bankers and do not claim statistical generalizability to all organizational deaths.

The process begins with the shock and sadness of Lehman's sudden death, then moves through remembering what Lehman was, assessing what was lost, and salvaging what could still be kept alive. Recreators' familial memories made the loss feel like losing a dear person, so they restored continuity through former colleagues and similar banking work. Repurposers' learning-oriented memories made the loss feel like losing a valued job, so they restored continuity through entrepreneurial skills and ventures. Organizational mourning therefore involves both holding on and letting go, with different forms of continuity shaping later detachment and career trajectories.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a theoretical model of organizational mourning as a post-death process linking organizational attachment, loss, salvaging, continuity, detachment, and career action. It extends research on organizational death and post-death organizing by explaining what happens between organizational closure and later responses, rather than focusing only on death announcements or legacy organizations. It also contributes to personal mourning research by showing how the quality of remembering a lost entity can shape what continuing bonds people seek to preserve.
practical_implication: Dying organizations and those supporting displaced employees should attend to what former members believe they have lost and what they may want to carry forward. Employees who mainly miss colleagues may benefit from alumni clubs, team-based hiring, or other ways to preserve relationships, whereas those who miss the work or skills may benefit from support in recombining those skills into new career paths. The paper also warns that spreading former members into new organizations can transfer both valuable skills and potentially problematic practices.
limitations: The study is an inductive single-case analysis of former Lehman Brothers bankers, so the authors claim analytic rather than statistical generalizability. The authors captured mourning at one point in time several years after Lehman's organizational death; while they defend retrospective inquiry as legitimate for mourning, they note mourning may look different closer to or further from the death event and call for other-timepoint or longitudinal designs. The sample also includes informants who landed in new jobs or ventures, so it may not capture more dysfunctional mourning trajectories among those who could not move on.
future_research: Future research should test the model across multiple cases of organizational death and examine whether similar mourning processes occur after mergers, acquisitions, or broad organizational change. Scholars could study whether different attachments to organizations predict different mourning paths and whether attributions for organizational death affect the quality of mourning. Longitudinal work could also examine mourning closer to the death event, later after the event, and among individuals whose mourning trajectories are less functional.
abstract: Focusing on the post-bankruptcy reactions of former Lehman Brothers’ bankers, we build a model of organizational mourning that depicts the thoughts, feelings, and actions of individual members dealing with the loss of their organization. We argue that organizational mourning is a process comprised of five interrelated phases, namely: (1) “experiencing the death event,” (2) “remembering the organization,” (3) “assessing loss,” (4) “salvaging: evaluate and restore,” and (5) “creating continuity and detaching.” Our empirical case suggests that at its core, organizational mourning involves both holding on and letting go of a defunct organization. Understanding how former members mourn is crucial to appreciate how they may ultimately find continuity after an organizational death, including how they enact their subsequent career paths. We conclude by discussing implications for theory of our research—notably, for literatures on post-death organizing, and personal mourning—as well as implications for practice.
apa_citation: Crosina, E., & Pratt, M. G. (2019). Toward a model of organizational mourning: The case of former Lehman Brothers bankers. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 66-98. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0140

title: Relational Attachment at Work: A Complementary Fit Perspective on the Role of Relationships in Organizational Life
methods: Three field studies using multi-wave survey data, scale validation, confirmatory factor analysis, polynomial regression with response surface analysis, logistic regression for turnover, Poisson regression for absenteeism, and mediation tests.
industry: Employees from varied occupations and organizations; Study 2 sampled non-faculty university employees, and Study 3 drew from alumni, a health care company, and small colleges.
time_period: Study 1 collected three waves of data, with Time 2 four weeks after Time 1 and Time 3 one year after Time 2; Studies 2 and 3 collected two waves four weeks apart.
units: Individual employees
n_sample: Main studies: Study 1 n = 312, Study 2 n = 173, Study 3 n = 210; scale-validation samples n = 182 and n = 147.
authors: Ehrhardt, K.; Ragins, B. R.
theories: Kahn's needs-based model of meaningful connections; person-environment fit theory; privacy regulation theory
keywords: complementary fit; relational attachment; relational needs fit; social support; work relationships
research_question: The paper asks why and how employees become attached to others at work, and how this relational attachment affects organizational attachment, desirable work attitudes, positive psychological states, turnover, absenteeism, and privacy-boundary reactions. It specifically examines whether relational needs fit, rather than general social support, explains when work relationships produce attachment and when too much personal support becomes intrusive.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that employees become attached to others at work when their work relationships meet their instrumental and personal support needs. This relational attachment then generalizes into stronger organizational commitment and other positive work and well-being outcomes. The model also specifies a threshold process: when personal support exceeds what employees want or need, it can violate privacy boundaries, increase perceived intrusion, and reduce relational attachment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends Kahn's needs-based model of meaningful connections by integrating a person-environment complementary fit perspective, shifting attention from whether support is available to whether received support fits individual relational needs. It contributes to positive relationships at work by theorizing and testing relational attachment as a cumulative attachment to one's constellation of work relationships. It also brings the social support paradox into organizational research by showing that personal support can become "too close for comfort" when it exceeds employees' desired level.
practical_implication: Managers should treat work relationships as a source of organizational attachment and well-being, but should not assume that more support is always better. Support needs to be tailored to individual preferences, especially when support concerns personal matters. The findings also imply that communication and relationship-building training should help employees and managers recognize needs, boundaries, and nonverbal cues of privacy violation.
limitations: The authors note that the studies used self-report data, creating potential same-source bias, although they used multiple time points, behavioral outcomes in Study 1, and common-method checks to reduce this concern. They also note limits to generalizability because samples were more educated and more non-Hispanic White than the U.S. working-adult population, all respondents were employed in the United States, and women were overrepresented in Studies 2 and 3.
future_research: Future research could extend the complementary fit model to career needs, developmental relationships, relationships outside the workplace, and outcomes such as career efficacy and satisfaction. The authors also call for work on privacy thresholds, including how relationship roles, power, cultural norms, social media, generation, diversity, and changing needs affect when closeness becomes intrusive. Longitudinal studies could examine how privacy thresholds and work relationships evolve over time.
abstract: Organizational scholars concur that supportive work relationships can attach employees to their workplace and improve the quality of organizational life, but they lack insights into how or why this occurs. Moreover, models of social support focus on what relationships provide without considering the fit between what people need and receive from their work relationships. Addressing these limitations, we developed and tested a theoretical model of relational attachment at work using a complementary fit perspective. After validating measures, we tested, extended, and replicated our model in three field studies. Results revealed that employees became more attached to their organization and experienced more beneficial outcomes when they had stronger psychological attachment to others at work. This relational attachment was not driven by general social support, but, rather, by “relational needs fit,” which reflects employees’ experience of having their needs met by their work relationships. However, receiving more personal support than what was wanted or needed intruded into employees’ privacy boundaries and created a “too close for comfort” reaction whereby they pulled back from their work relationships. This “too much of a good thing” finding indicates that, while positive relationships at work are effective, social support should be tailored to individuals’ needs.
apa_citation: Ehrhardt, K., & Ragins, B. R. (2019). Relational attachment at work: A complementary fit perspective on the role of relationships in organizational life. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 248-282. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0245

title: Public Governance, Corporate Governance, and Firm Innovation: An Examination of State-Owned Enterprises
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a quasi-experimental Chinese innovation procurement policy. The authors use propensity score matching, difference-in-differences estimation, fixed-effects Poisson models for patent counts, and firm fixed-effects Tobit models for the proportion of novel patents.
industry: Publicly listed Chinese state-owned enterprises in industrial categories connected to the 2006 government procurement catalogs, with matched control SOEs outside designated categories.
time_period: 2000-2012, with 2007 onward treated as the post-policy period.
units: SOE-year observations and invention patents filed with and granted by the State Intellectual Property Office.
n_sample: Full-sample preferred models report 3,676 observations for number of patents and 6,622 observations for proportion of novel patents; treatment-only models report 2,539 and 3,324 observations, respectively.
authors: Jia, Nan; Huang, Kenneth G.; Zhang, Cyndi Man
theories: Weberian theory of government quality (Weber, 1968); agency theory (Eisenhardt, 1989); multitasking model (Holmstrom & Milgrom, 1991)
keywords: agency risk; corporate governance; difference-in-differences; firm innovation; innovation procurement policy; patent novelty; public governance; state-owned enterprises
research_question: The paper asks how agency risk affects the allocation of effort across innovation activities when principals rely heavily on quantifiable innovation metrics. It examines whether corporate governance and public governance reduce SOE agents' tendency to pursue patent quantity at the expense of patent novelty.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in agency theory and the multitasking model: when principals evaluate innovation through patent counts, agents can satisfy measurable targets by producing more general patents while underinvesting in more novel patents whose value is harder to measure. Better incentive alignment and stronger monitoring reduce this moral hazard by making agents more attentive to firm value rather than only to quantifiable policy targets. Higher-quality public governance makes state principals more accountable and better able to collect information, which strengthens the effect of corporate governance on innovation novelty.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends agency research on innovation by shifting attention from underinvestment in innovation to inefficient deployment of innovation resources. Its core contribution is to distinguish innovation quantity from innovation novelty and show that agency risk can increase observable innovation while reducing the proportion of more novel innovation.

It also links corporate governance to public governance in state capitalism. The study argues that the accountability and quality of state principals shape whether conventional governance tools, such as incentive alignment and monitoring, reduce agency risk in SOEs.
practical_implication:
The findings imply that patent-count targets can increase visible innovation output while still weakening the novelty mix of firm innovation if governance is weak. For SOEs and policymakers, promoting innovation requires governance systems that reward novelty and value creation, not only measurable patent volume.

The paper also suggests that corporate governance reforms work better when public governance is stronger. State owners seeking innovation should therefore attend both to firm-level governance tools and to the quality of the public governance environment in which SOE principals operate.
limitations:
The authors use granted invention patents only, which is a conservative choice and may underestimate a broader post-policy increase in lower-quality patenting. They also acknowledge that they cannot entirely rule out the alternative explanation that the Chinese state intentionally prioritized patent quantity, although the interaction results are more consistent with the agency-based explanation.

The empirical context is Chinese SOEs responding to a specific state innovation procurement policy, so the findings may not generalize directly to privately owned firms or to other political and institutional settings. The paper also notes that it lacks a theory for why corporate governance appears to function differently in low-quality public governance environments.
future_research:
The authors identify privately owned enterprises as a fruitful setting for future work on the same moral hazard because incentive alignment and monitoring also address agency risk outside SOEs. Future research could examine how the governance of principals in private firms, including different ownership types, shapes innovation outcomes.

They also suggest connecting innovation research to work on financial control and multidivisional firms. Future studies could test whether financial control affects not only the overall amount of R&D or innovation but also the composition of innovation between incremental and novel outputs.
abstract: Innovation activities create substantial firm value, but they are difficult to manage owing to agency risk, which is commonly thought to result in shirking, and hence underinvestment in innovation. However, agency risk can also create inefficient allocation of resources among innovation activities, on which the literature has provided limited understanding. We examine an important outcome created by agency risk—that agents pursue quantity of innovation at the expense of novelty—and investigate how it is influenced by corporate and public governance. We theorize that improved corporate governance tools, including better alignment of agents’ private incentives and stronger monitoring, and high-quality public governance reduce such agency risk in state-owned enterprises (SOEs). Furthermore, higher-quality public governance enhances the functioning of corporate governance tools in further reducing such agency risk in innovation. We test our theory by examining SOEs in China that responded to the state’s pro-innovation policies relying disproportionately on quantifiable outcomes (e.g., patent counts) for assessing innovation performance. Our difference-in-differences estimates provide overall support for our hypotheses. These findings provide new insights on how agency risk affects innovation by distinguishing the consequences for quantity and novelty of innovation and for how conventional corporate governance tools shaping innovation depend on public governance.

title: The Coercive Isomorphism Ripple Effect: An Investigation of Nonprofit Interlocks on Corporate Boards
methods: Fixed-effects linear regression of firm-year panel data, supplemented by robustness checks, post-hoc mediation analysis, alternative dependent-variable tests, and qualitative post-hoc interviews with corporate directors.
industry: Large publicly traded U.S. firms; specific industries are not reported as a bounded sector.
units: Firm-year observations from large publicly traded U.S. firms
n_sample: 984 observations from 209 firms
authors: Krause, R.; Wu, Z.; Bruton, G. D.; Carter, S. M.
theories: forced compliance literature from social psychology; institutional theory
keywords: board interlocks; coercive isomorphism; forced compliance; intangible assets; nonprofit interlocks
research_question: The paper asks whether coercive isomorphism can spread indirectly through board interlocks rather than only through direct pressure inside the organizational field where the pressure originates. It examines whether nonprofit board interlocks transmit overhead aversion to corporate boards and thereby reduce corporate investment in intangible assets.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that directors who acquiesce to nonprofit-sector coercive pressures to minimize overhead internalize overhead aversion and carry that attitude to corporate boards on which they also serve. When those directors influence corporate board decision making, especially if they are powerful, the firm reduces investment in intangible assets such as R&D and advertising. The ripple effect is stronger when industry mimetic pressures favor high intangible asset investment because the imported overhead aversion runs against the receiving field's prevailing norm.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends institutional theory by arguing that coercive isomorphism can ripple across organizational fields through interlocking directors, not only through direct dependence or pressure. It contributes to board interlock research by treating directors as psychologically affected actors rather than impersonal information conduits. It also identifies director power and conflicting mimetic pressure as contingencies that shape when the coercive isomorphism ripple effect is most consequential.
practical_implication: The authors argue that CEOs and boards should evaluate nonprofit interlocks carefully because such ties may bring legitimacy benefits while also importing overhead aversion. For large public firms, the risk is that directors' nonprofit-board experience may unintentionally discourage investment in intangible assets that support future growth and firm value.
limitations: The authors state that their measured variables are distal from the proposed psychological mechanisms, so the evidence depends on assumptions about directors' exposure to coercive isomorphism and internalization of overhead aversion. They also note that the study does not empirically distinguish attitude-congruent from attitude-discrepant forced compliance. The sample is limited to the largest U.S. firms, and the firm-value analysis using Tobin's Q is post hoc rather than a formal test of theory.
future_research: The authors call for finer-grained measurement of the psychological assumptions linking nonprofit board exposure to corporate board behavior. They encourage research on attitude-congruent versus attitude-discrepant forced compliance, other types of cross-field linkages beyond board interlocks, distinctions among nonprofit organizations, other contexts such as healthcare administration or social enterprises, and a wider array of performance outcomes.
abstract: Institutional theorists have long recognized that board interlocks serve as conduits of information, which can facilitate mimetic isomorphism under conditions of uncertainty. In contrast, the potential for coercive isomorphism—which is a response to direct coercion rather than uncertainty—to spread through board interlocks remains unknown. Drawing on the forced compliance literature from social psychology, we propose that coercive isomorphism exhibits a ripple effect, whereby conforming to coercive pressures leads directors to internalize their acquiescence and apply it to the other boards on which they sit. We test this relationship in the context of nonprofit interlocks on the boards of 209 publicly traded U.S. firms between 2010 and 2014, predicting that coercive pressure to minimize overhead in the nonprofit sphere—a phenomenon known as the nonprofit starvation cycle—spreads to corporate boards through nonprofit interlocks, leading the corporate boards to reduce firm investment in intangible assets. We find that this relationship manifests across our sample, but is strongest via interlocks held by powerful directors and in industries characterized by high investment in intangible assets. Finally, we also find that the coercive isomorphism ripple effect ultimately decreases firm value.

title: When Do Ethnic Communities Affect Foreign Location Choice? Dual Entry Strategies of Korean Banks in China
methods: Empirical quantitative study of South Korean banks' province-level investments in China using conditional logit models, split-sample comparisons by institutional reliability, and robustness tests using initial entries and Chaoxian ratio measures.
industry: Banking and foreign direct investment by South Korean banks in Chinese provinces.
units: Korean bank-province-year location choices across 16 Chinese province options.
n_sample: 82 unique investments by 11 Korean banks; conditional logit sample size is 976 province alternatives across 61 firm-investment years.
authors: Li, Yong; Hernandez, Exequiel; Gwon, Sunhwan
theories: formal institutions; informal institutions; institutional theory
keywords: Chaoxian; Korean banks in China; dual entry strategies; ethnic communities; foreign location choice; formal institutions
research_question: The paper asks when ethnic communities affect foreign location choice by coethnic firms. It examines why the same foreign firm may rely on a coethnic community in one location but not in another, focusing on the reliability of formal institutions as the boundary condition.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that coethnic communities act as informal institutions that reduce exchange hazards through shared language, norms, solidarity, and social enforcement. These community-based mechanisms help foreign banks transact with borrowers, workers, and information providers when formal institutions are weak or unstable. Because interpersonal exchange within an ethnic community is not scalable beyond the community's social sphere, the community's effect on location choice weakens when formal institutions are reliable enough to support broader impersonal exchange.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to research on ethnic communities and international expansion by explaining heterogeneity in firms' use of coethnic communities across locations. It reframes ethnic communities as informal institutions and identifies formal institutional reliability as a boundary condition for their influence on foreign location choice.

It also contributes to institutional theory by shifting attention from whether formal and informal institutions substitute or complement each other to the scalability of governance mechanisms. The argument is that formal institutions are "first best" for growth-oriented foreign entry because they can support more numerous and broader transactions than community-based informal governance.
practical_implication:
Foreign firms should not treat the presence of coethnic communities as uniformly valuable across all locations. The value of such communities is higher where property rights are weak or uncertainty makes formal governance less reliable.

For banks and other growth-oriented entrants, the findings imply that coethnic communities can help manage demand, labor, and information hazards, but they may also limit market scale if firms rely on them as the primary exchange infrastructure. Location strategy should therefore weigh both ethnic community size and the reliability of formal institutions.
limitations:
The authors could not examine performance consequences because nearly all Korean bank subsidiaries established in China since 1992 survived through 2016, making survival uninformative. Subsidiary-level financial and operational performance data were unavailable.

The study also does not separately observe the demand, supply, and knowledge benefits of ethnic community reliance. Instead, it relies on prior research for those mechanisms and tests institutional reliability as the boundary condition for the community-location choice relationship.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether ethnic communities matter differently for foreign investments motivated by goals other than growth, such as research and development. Scholars could also compare similar dual entry strategies in developed markets where institutional quality varies across regions within a country.

The authors call for more work from the ethnic community's perspective, including whether the entry of coethnic firms affects jobs, wages, and entrepreneurship for ethnic individuals. Future studies could also investigate whether formal versus informal institutional arrangements shape the complexity of acquisitions, alliances, and other cross-border exchanges.
abstract: Research has shown that firms typically expand into foreign locations with sizeable coethnic communities. However, in many cases the ethnic community influences the investment choice of the same firm in one location but not another. We offer an institutional lens to explain this heterogeneity. Ethnic groups function like informal institutions that facilitate transactions between foreign firms and customers, suppliers, and information providers through interpersonal exchange. Relying on ethnic communities to mediate transactions in foreign markets is valuable but limited by the relatively small scale of these communities. In contrast, relying on formal institutions allows firms to expand more broadly into foreign markets because the impersonal exchange inherent in formal governance is more scalable. This is manifested in “dual entry strategies” wherein ethnic communities have a significantly stronger influence on location choice in places with unreliable (weak and unstable) formal institutions than in places with reliable formal institutions. We found support for these ideas using a unique dataset of South Korean banks’ investments in Chinese provinces during 1992–2013. To mitigate endogeneity concerns, we exploited a historical migration that created a quasirandom distribution of ethnic Koreans across provinces. Our work contributes to research on international expansion, ethnic communities, and institutional theory.
apa_citation: Li, Y., Hernandez, E., & Gwon, S. (2019). When do ethnic communities affect foreign location choice? Dual entry strategies of Korean banks in China. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 172-195. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0275

title: Only Timeline Will Tell: Temporal Framing of Competitive Announcements and Rivals’ Responses
methods: Empirical quantitative study of competitive action announcements in duopoly industries. The authors identify action-response dyads from press releases and media reports, measure temporal framing through customized automated content analysis, and estimate rivals' response speed using stratified Cox proportional hazard event-history models with robustness checks for endogeneity, action characteristics, alternative vagueness measures, and firm fixed effects.
industry: Duopoly firms from 14 four-digit SIC industries.
units: Competitive action announcements, focal firm-rival response dyads, and day-level event-history observations.
n_sample: 2,130 competitive action press releases from 28 duopoly firms in 14 industries; Cox models report 47,688 observations.
authors: Nadkarni, Sucheta; Pan, Lingling; Chen, Tianxu
theories: action-based view of competitive dynamics; framing theory (Benford & Snow, 2000; Entman, 1993; Scheufele, 1999); intertemporal choice theory (Loewenstein, 1988; Loewenstein & Prelec, 1992)
keywords: competitive action announcements; competitive interactions; intertemporal choice theory; rivals' response speed; temporal distance; temporal framing; temporal frequency; temporal vagueness
research_question: The paper asks whether variation in focal firms' temporal framing of competitive action announcements influences rivals' response speed. It examines whether temporal vagueness, temporal distance, and the frequency of these cues shape how quickly rivals retaliate.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that rivals rely on focal firms' press-release timelines because they lack access to the focal firms' actual action timelines. Vague timelines increase uncertainty about when and how the action will unfold, encouraging rivals to discount the action and delay response. Distal timelines reduce perceived imminence, and repeated vagueness or distance cues increase salience, further slowing rivals' response speed.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends competitive dynamics research by adding linguistic temporal framing to action-based explanations of rivalry. It shows that rivals respond not only to observable action characteristics, announcement timing, and competitive context, but also to how firms linguistically present action timelines.

The paper also contributes to organizational communication research by showing a competitive downside of language that may be favorable to constituents. Clear and proximal framing can please shareholders or other constituents but also invite faster rival retaliation, creating a trade-off in how firms communicate competitive actions.
practical_implication:
Managers communicating competitive actions face a trade-off between mobilizing constituents and deterring rivals. Clear, proximal timelines may generate favorable reactions from shareholders, suppliers, and complementors, but they can also accelerate competitor retaliation.

For firms in intense rivalry, vague or distal temporal framing can delay rival responses, but it may weaken constituent confidence. Communication strategy should therefore consider both public-relations audiences and competitors that monitor the same announcements.
limitations:
The sample is restricted to duopoly industries, where rivalry is unusually intense and the top two firms have explicit competitive interdependence. The authors caution that the framing effects may not generalize to less concentrated industries with more varied rivals and competitive positions.

The study focuses only on temporal framing of competitive action announcements and on competitors' responses. It does not test other forms of framing, such as positive versus negative framing or attribution framing, and it does not directly examine reactions from other audiences such as shareholders.
future_research:
Future research could examine temporal framing in less concentrated industries and test whether the effects differ when firms face many rivals with heterogeneous stakes. Studies could also investigate other framing forms, including valence framing and attribution framing, to clarify how language more broadly shapes interfirm rivalry.

The authors also point to research on other audiences, especially shareholders. Future studies could examine how firms balance constituent reactions against competitive deterrence when deciding whether to frame action timelines clearly, vaguely, proximally, or distally.
abstract: Research has focused predominantly on the influence of the language firms use in their announcements on the reactions of constituents such as shareholders and the media. We extend this research by examining a new form of linguistic construction––temporal framing—in the context of competitive interactions. Building on intertemporal choice theory, we theorized and tested how a focal firm’s temporal framing of its competitive action announcements affects rivals’ response speed. We examined three dimensions of temporal framing: temporal vagueness (lack of clarity and completeness regarding timelines), temporal distance (length of the action timeline: proximal versus distal), and frequency (repetition of vagueness and distance cues). Based on analysis of 2,130 competitive action press releases of 28 duopoly firms from 14 industries, we found that the temporal framing dimensions, both individually and interactively, were related to the response speed of rivals. Specifically, temporally vague and distally framed timelines in action announcements delayed rivals’ response speed, and increased frequency of vagueness and distance cues strengthened these effects. This study explicates the linguistic underpinnings of competitive interactions and highlights the importance of temporal framing in the competitive context.

title: The Coevolution of Social Networks and Thoughts of Quitting
methods: Longitudinal network study using SIENA stochastic actor-based modeling to estimate coevolution between thoughts of quitting and advice and friendship ties across three survey waves.
industry: Healthcare organizations: veterinarian, physiotherapist, acupuncture practice, pharmacies, and dental practices.
time_period: Three survey time points approximately four months apart.
units: Employees nested in eight healthcare organizations; outgoing advice and friendship ties.
n_sample: 121 employees; 1,932 network relations across two networks and three time points.
authors: Tröster, C.; Parker, A.; van Knippenberg, D.; Sahlmüller, B.
theories: coevolution perspective; conservation of resources theory (Hobfoll, 1989, 2001)
keywords: advice ties; conservation of resources theory; friendship ties; network churn; network stasis; thoughts of quitting
research_question: The paper asks whether employees’ thoughts of quitting are a precursor to, a consequence of, or mutually intertwined with changes in their workplace social networks. It examines this question at the tie level by distinguishing advice ties from friendship ties and by separating tie creation, retention, and dissolution.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on conservation of resources theory, the paper argues that workplace ties provide valued resources and that employees seek to protect existing resources while selectively acquiring new ones. The authors expected newly created ties to reduce thoughts of quitting and dissolved ties to increase them, but found no support for network changes predicting thoughts of quitting. In the reverse direction, thoughts of quitting increased advice network churn by making employees more likely to drop old advice ties and create new ones, while increasing friendship tie retention as employees protected valued affective resources.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances a dynamic coevolution perspective on turnover cognitions and social networks by showing that thoughts of quitting can shape network change rather than merely result from network embeddedness. It contributes to social network theory by demonstrating that aggregate network size can miss tie-level dynamics, especially the different patterns of advice network churn and friendship network stasis. It also extends conservation of resources theory by treating social ties as resources whose perceived loss and gain structure employees’ network behavior.
practical_implication: The paper cautions managers against assuming that larger networks or network expansion will directly reduce employees’ thoughts of quitting. Instead, shifts in networking behavior, especially greater churn in advice ties and greater retention of friendship ties, may signal that employees are considering leaving and could prompt timely retention interventions.
limitations: The authors state that, despite the longitudinal design, simulation-based analysis, and covariates, the study cannot establish causality. The study examines thoughts of quitting rather than actual turnover, so its findings speak directly to withdrawal cognitions rather than exits. The sample is located in Dutch healthcare organizations, and the authors note that cultural context, within-organization friendship only, unmeasured advice content, omitted personality variables, and unmeasured relationship age or intensity limit the scope of inference.
future_research: The paper calls for constructive replication and stronger designs, ideally including experimental data, to increase confidence in the observed network effects. Future work should examine tie quality, tie duration, incoming or reciprocated ties, external friendships, and different kinds of advice relationships. The authors also encourage research that moves beyond network size to model how fit, sacrifice, and other job embeddedness elements interact with social network dynamics.
abstract: Research has shown that employees who occupy more central positions in their organization’s network have lower turnover. As a result, scholars commonly interpret turnover as the consequence of social networks. Based on conservation of resources theory, we propose an alternative coevolution perspective that recognizes the influence of changes in individuals’ social network position on their thoughts of quitting (the consideration of turnover), and which also posits that thoughts of quitting shape individuals’ agency in maintaining and changing their social network. Extending previous research, we predict that creation (dissolution) of both friendship ties and advice ties are negatively (positively) related to subsequent thoughts of quitting. We then develop and test the novel hypotheses that for friendship ties, thoughts of quitting are positively related to tie retention and negatively related to tie creation (leading to network stasis), whereas for advice ties thoughts of quitting are negatively related to tie retention and positively related to tie creation (leading to network churn). In a longitudinal network analysis that assessed 121 employees across three time points, we find support for our hypotheses that thoughts of quitting affect network changes, but do not find that network changes affect thoughts of quitting.
apa_citation: Tröster, C., Parker, A., van Knippenberg, D., & Sahlmüller, B. (2019). The coevolution of social networks and thoughts of quitting. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 22-43. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0914

title: Human Capital Acquisition and Organizational Innovation: A Temporal Perspective
methods: Empirical quantitative study using 2003-2006 Workplace and Employee Survey data. The authors model organizational innovation with ordinal logistic regressions, using 2003-2005 hiring patterns for managers and professionals, collaborative work practices, and controls to predict 2006 product and process innovation.
industry: Large multi-industry sample of business organizations, excluding nonprofit enterprises and organizations with fewer than 10 employees.
time_period: 2003-2006, with 2003-2005 hiring-pattern measures and 2006 innovation outcomes.
units: Organizations/workplaces in the Workplace and Employee Survey.
n_sample: 1,006 organizations that hired during at least one year of the newcomer observation window.
authors: Wang, Taiyuan; Zatzick, Christopher D.
theories: context-emergent turnover (CET) theory (Nyberg & Ployhart, 2013); learning-by-hiring; strategic human capital
keywords: collaborative work practices; context-emergent turnover; hiring rate; hiring rate change; hiring rate dispersion; human capital acquisition; learning-by-hiring; organizational innovation
research_question: The paper asks how temporal patterns of managerial and professional hiring influence organizational innovation. It specifically examines whether hiring rate, hiring rate change, and hiring rate dispersion affect product and process innovation, and whether collaborative work practices condition those relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that managerial and professional newcomers bring novel knowledge, skills, abilities, and perspectives that can support product and process innovation. Higher hiring rates and more time-dispersed hiring increase the flow of new ideas while also shaping how easily newcomers and incumbents collaborate. Collaborative work practices support communication, participation, information sharing, and trust, which can help organizations integrate newcomers when hiring increases, but can also substitute partly for the integration benefits of evenly dispersed hiring.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper advances strategic human capital and learning-by-hiring research by shifting attention from who organizations hire to when they hire. It separates hiring rate, hiring rate change, and hiring rate dispersion to show that temporal hiring patterns have distinct implications for organizational innovation.

It also extends human capital research by treating hiring as more than replacement for employee turnover. The study argues that hiring has strategic value because continuous or increasing inflows of managerial and professional newcomers shape both new knowledge acquisition and the development of collaborative human capital.
practical_implication:
The findings imply that organizations seeking innovation should manage hiring as a temporal process, not only as a headcount or talent-quality decision. Regular hiring of managers and professionals can maintain a continuous inflow of new knowledge and perspectives.

The study also suggests that collaborative work practices are especially useful when hiring rates increase or fluctuate, because they help integrate newcomers with incumbents. Organizations with fewer such practices may need more continuous and even hiring to reduce integration problems.
limitations:
The authors note that the WES data do not include specific measures of knowledge combination and exchange, so the proposed mechanisms are inferred rather than directly tested. The data also focus on managerial and professional newcomers and lack finer-grained measures of newcomer quality, exact within-year hiring timing, and whether new hires are returnees.

The innovation outcome is an additive self-reported index of improved and new products and processes, without information on ultimate economic benefits. The authors also note that industry contexts may differ because some organizations hire specifically for innovation tasks while service and retail businesses may hire mainly to meet operational demand.
future_research:
Future research could directly measure how different kinds of knowledge, skills, abilities, and other characteristics diffuse after hiring and how long that diffusion takes. Researchers could also examine finer-grained hiring timing, returnees, newcomer quality, and other strategic or cultural conditions that shape whether new hires contribute to innovation.

The authors also call for research using alternative innovation measures, such as sales and profits from new products and services, to test the economic consequences of hiring patterns. Additional studies could examine whether temporal hiring patterns influence broader outcomes beyond innovation, including productivity and profitability, across industries with different hiring motives.
abstract: Newcomers contribute to organizational innovation by bringing in new knowledge and ideas, on the one hand, and by collaborating and exchanging with incumbents, on the other. We propose that an organization’s ability to use these contributions is influenced by hiring rate, hiring rate change, and hiring rate dispersion, which affect both the flow of new ideas into the organization and the level of collaboration between newcomers and incumbents. Using four years of data from a large, multi-industry sample, we find that hiring rate and hiring rate dispersion increase organizational innovation. We also find that increases in hiring rates from year to year are positively related to innovation for organizations with more collaborative work practices, while the relationship between hiring rate dispersion and innovation is less positive when organizations have more collaborative work practices. This study highlights how temporal patterns of hiring influence human capital acquisition and development.
apa_citation: Wang, T., & Zatzick, C. D. (2019). Human capital acquisition and organizational innovation: A temporal perspective. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(1), 99-116. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0114

title: Dominant Coalitions Directing Acquisitions: Different Decision Makers, Different Decisions
methods: Empirical quantitative study of Chinese listed firms from 2000-2012 using CSMAR and WIND data, sequential event-history and ordered logit models for acquisition choices, logit models for state-bank loans, and new potential state coalition measures based on factor analysis, faultlines, and heuristic board stateness.
industry: Listed firms in China making acquisitions or loan applications.
units: Chinese listed firms, acquisition events, acquisition target choices, and loan-source choices.
n_sample: 2,337 firms and 28,847 firm-year observations; 31,442 acquisitions of equity or assets; 16,823 loan observations.
authors: Zhang, Cyndi Man; Greve, Henrich R.
theories: behavioral theory of the firm; dominant coalition theory; faultline theory; problemistic search; upper echelons theory
keywords: acquisitions; board of directors; dominant coalitions; performance relative to aspiration levels; problemistic search; upper echelons theory
research_question: The paper asks how potential dominant coalitions are built within boards and how those coalitions shape acquisition decisions when firm performance differs from aspiration levels. It focuses on whether board members' state versus market experience changes the type of acquisition target, and whether similar coalition logic appears in state-bank loan choices.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that board members use prior state or market experience to evaluate which strategic actions feel familiar, feasible, and proximate. Performance below or above aspiration levels triggers a decision occasion, after which experience-based subgroups try to assemble dominant coalitions by relying on member number, commitment, status, and recruitable allies. In the acquisition tests, stronger state coalitions reduce responsiveness toward market-oriented acquisitions, whereas weaker state coalitions leave more scope for market-oriented acquisition choices. The separate state-bank loan analysis is treated more cautiously: its results run contrary to Hypothesis 2 and suggest a boundary condition because loan-source decisions mix firm and bank decision making.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to dominant coalition theory by turning coalition building into measurable potential coalitions based on board members' experience, commitment, status, and recruitable allies. It also extends upper echelons theory by replacing simple average-composition logic with a coalition-based account of how decision-making groups reach strategic choices.

It contributes to performance feedback theory by making upper-echelons effects contingent on performance relative to aspiration levels. The resulting account links the trigger for organizational change with the content of the decision selected by the board.
practical_implication:
The findings imply that boards' experience composition can shape consequential acquisition choices, not merely the propensity to change. For Chinese listed firms, state-experienced boards may be more likely to favor internal or state-bridged actions, while market-experienced coalitions support more market-oriented acquisitions when performance feedback creates a problem or opportunity.

The paper also implies that governance reform does not erase legacy decision logics simply by formalizing board structures. Directors' prior state and market experience remain relevant to how boards interpret performance feedback and choose strategic responses.
limitations:
The study predicts potential rather than realized coalitions, so the authors cannot observe the actual bargaining, persuasion, agenda control, or alliance recruitment inside each board decision. They also note that features of each specific choice could make the realized coalition differ from the potential coalition inferred from board composition.

The state-bank loan test is a boundary condition because loan-source choices mix firm and bank decision making: banks assess loan risk using profitability relative to other firms, and high-stateness firms do not respond to performance by changing loan source in the same way the acquisition theory predicts.
future_research:
Future research could apply the coalition-building approach to other kinds of decision-maker experience, decision-making groups, organizational behaviors, and high-stakes decisions. The authors specifically suggest studying financial, technological, and market affiliations in top management teams and boards.

Further work could also examine the actual processes of coalition influence, including agenda control, information release, order of speech, and other procedural interventions. Such studies would extend the paper's potential-coalition measures toward more direct evidence on how coalitions are built and retained across decisions.
abstract: Coalitions are important in organizational decision making, but the question of how coalitions are built and make decisions in response to firm performance is still not sufficiently explored. In this study, we develop and test theory on how potential coalitions are built through shared experience and recruitment of allies. When organizations respond to performance relative to aspiration levels, either as problemistic search following low performance or opportunity exploration following high performance, members form coalitions to influence decisions. We develop theory of coalition formation that builds on upper echelons theory and the theory of dominant coalitions to predict how past experience of decision makers leads to preferred actions by each member and subsequent coalition formation. We use this theory to make new measures of potential coalitions and apply it to acquisitions made by firms in China. We find evidence that the experience of members of the key decision-making group—the board of directors—affects the potential coalition building, and hence the type of acquisition target, as predicted.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: How Figurative Language and Gesturing in Entrepreneurial Pitches Influences Investment Judgments
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study. Study 1 inductively codes 17 videotaped technology-entrepreneur pitches for figurative language and gesture, developing a typology of literal, rhetorical, demonstrative, and integrative pitching strategies. Study 2 uses a 2 x 2 between-subjects video experiment manipulating figurative language and gesture, tested with professional investors and business students, with mediation and moderated-mediation analyses of mental imagery, passion, and propensity to invest.
industry: Study 1 examines independent technology entrepreneurs across sectors including biomedical innovations, inkjet printing, and tidal energy. Study 2 uses a digital temperature-controlled compression-device venture pitch evaluated by investors and business students.
country: United Kingdom: Study 1 is based on a regional investment forum in the North of England; Study 2 recruits investors through UK investor events and a Manchester investment hub, plus business students at a large U.K. university.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Entrepreneurial pitches, pitching entrepreneurs, professional investors, business students, and manipulation-check working adults.
n_sample: Study 1: 17 technology entrepreneurs. Study 2: 124 professional investors and 180 business students. Manipulation check: 128 working adults.
authors: Clarke, Jean S.; Cornelissen, Joep P.; Healey, Mark P.
theories: cognitive science on gesture and mental imagery; entrepreneurial passion and expressive behavior; rhetoric and framing in entrepreneurship
keywords: entrepreneurial pitches; figurative language; gesturing; investment judgments; mental imagery; nonverbal expressions; propensity to invest; verbal tactics
research_question: The paper asks how entrepreneurs combine verbal tactics and expressive nonverbal behaviors when pitching to investors, and how those channels separately and jointly influence potential investors' judgments. It specifically examines whether figurative language, gesturing, and mental imagery shape investors' propensity to invest.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / pitching strategies: Literal, rhetorical, demonstrative, and integrative pitching approaches, distinguished by high or low use of figurative language and high or low use of gesturing.
- Study 1 process: Inductive coding of naturalistic technology-entrepreneur pitches identifies variation in literal versus figurative language and beat, iconic, deictic, and metaphoric gestures.
- Study 2 experimental factors: High versus low figurative language and high versus low gesturing in video pitches.
- Outcome: Propensity to invest, measured through investment intentions and investment likelihood.
- Boundary condition: The indirect effect of gesture through mental imagery is stronger when gestures are coupled with figurative language.

The central process is that ideational gestures do more than signal passion: they help viewers mentally simulate the product, venture, and market. Figurative language alone has limited direct impact, but gestures that depict and symbolize the business idea increase propensity to invest by evoking mental imagery. The integrative value of figurative language appears mainly in strengthening the gesture-to-imagery pathway rather than directly persuading investors.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends entrepreneurship research on pitching by shifting attention from generic passion displays to the communicative functions of specific verbal and nonverbal behaviors. It shows that gestures can carry meaning, not only affect, and that beat and ideational gestures should not be collapsed into a simple frequency-based indicator of passion.

It also qualifies rhetoric-and-framing arguments in entrepreneurship. Figurative language does not directly persuade investors in this setting, but it matters when aligned with gestures that enable mental imagery, thereby offering a more integrated account of entrepreneurial communication.
practical_implication:
For entrepreneurs, the findings imply that effective pitching depends not only on what is said but on how product and venture ideas are embodied through gestures. Entrepreneurs should use gestures to depict concrete product features and abstract venture trajectories, rather than relying only on metaphors, anecdotes, or enthusiastic delivery.

For investors, the study suggests that nonverbal cues can shape investment judgments through cognitive imagery as well as emotional impressions. The authors argue that distinguishing meaningful gestural depiction from generalized energetic body language can support more evidence-based recommendations for entrepreneurs and investors in practice.
limitations:
The experimental materials used a male actor, so the authors note that future work should test whether the effects hold for female entrepreneurs. The experiment jointly manipulated beat and ideational gestures, which means the separate effects of these gesture types remain unresolved.

The experimental venture involved a basic technological product that experienced and novice investors could understand, so the findings may differ for more technically or conceptually complex ventures. The mediators and dependent variable were also measured contemporaneously, which may inflate observed relationships.
future_research:
Future research should examine other nonverbal modalities in entrepreneurial communication, including intonation, pitch, prosody, posture, facial expressions, gaze, and the development of entrepreneur-investor relationships over time. It should also compare interpersonal pitching with mediated forms of entrepreneurial communication such as business plans and IPO prospectuses.

The authors also call for research separating beat gestures from ideational gestures and testing whether the same mechanisms operate across entrepreneur gender and venture complexity. Additional studies could measure mediators and investment judgments at different times to strengthen causal evidence about the communication process.
abstract: A key challenge for entrepreneurs is to convince investors of their business ideas via a pitch. While scholars have started to explore how entrepreneurs convey their passion and preparedness in a pitch, they have overlooked the possible variation that exists in entrepreneurs’ verbal and nonverbal expressions. We build on research in cognitive science and entrepreneurship to examine the nature and influence of specific forms of speech and gesturing used by entrepreneurs when pitching. In an initial qualitative field study we identify distinct pitching strategies entrepreneurs use, involving different combinations of verbal tactics (i.e., using literal and figurative language to frame a venture) and gesture (i.e., using different types of hand gestures to emphasize parts of their pitch and convey product and venture ideas). In a subsequent experimental study, we examine the impact of these strategies on investors’ propensity to invest. We find that, although variation in the type of language used by an entrepreneur has limited effects, using gestures to depict and symbolize business ideas has strong positive effects. Our findings indicate that the skilled use of gestures by entrepreneurs helps potential investors imagine aspects of a new venture for themselves, thereby enhancing perception of its investment potential.
apa_citation: Clarke, J. S., Cornelissen, J. P., & Healey, M. P. (2019). Actions speak louder than words: How figurative language and gesturing in entrepreneurial pitches influences investment judgments. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(2), 335-360. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1008

title: Experience and Behavior: How Negative Feedback in New Versus Experienced Domains Affects Firm Action and Subsequent Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative study of U.S. mutual fund companies using firm-year and fund-level panel analyses. The authors estimate firm and year fixed-effects OLS models, a lagged-dependent-variable specification, an Arellano-Bond model, negative binomial models for new fund counts, and fund fixed-effects OLS models for spillover performance.
industry: U.S. mutual fund industry, including open-end equity, bond, and money market funds.
units: Mutual fund firms, new funds, existing funds, firm-year observations, and fund-year observations.
n_sample: The main firm-level analysis uses 810 firms and 8,817 firm-year observations; fund-level models use 14,064 new-fund observations and 58,168 existing fund-year observations.
authors: Eggers, J. P.; Suh, Jung-Hyun
theories: behavioral theory of the firm (Cyert & March, 1963; March & Simon, 1958); organizational learning from performance feedback; problem-driven search
keywords: distant search; domain-specific experience; firm performance; local search; mutual fund companies; negative feedback; new product development; retreat
research_question: The paper asks when and why negative feedback improves versus harms subsequent organizational performance. It specifically examines how domain-specific experience shapes firms' interpretation of poor performance on new products and their subsequent choices among retreat, local search, and distant search.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in the behavioral theory of the firm. Negative feedback in a new domain is interpreted as evidence that the unfamiliar domain itself is risky, leading firms to retreat toward familiar domains and thereby incur opportunity costs and cannibalization. Negative feedback in an experienced domain is interpreted as a fixable product-level problem, leading firms to allocate resources locally and, when needed, search more distantly for new opportunities.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends behavioral theory of the firm research by showing that negative feedback does not have uniform performance implications. Domain-specific experience determines whether poor performance triggers damaging retreat from exploration or productive problem-driven search.

It also moves beyond a simple change-versus-persistence account of performance feedback. By distinguishing retreat, local search, and distant search, the study provides a mechanism-level explanation of how firms choose among different behavioral responses to failure and how those responses aggregate into firm performance.
practical_implication:
The findings imply that managers should not treat failure in unfamiliar domains as straightforward evidence that exploration is unattractive. Premature retreat from new domains can leave growth opportunities unpursued and redirect resources into familiar domains where new products cannibalize existing ones.

For failures in experienced domains, the study suggests that firms can benefit from allocating resources to correct the problem because relevant experience makes the feedback more interpretable and actionable. The practical lesson is to diagnose whether poor performance reflects a fixable product-level issue or uncertainty in a genuinely new domain before reallocating resources.
limitations:
The authors note that they directly test only a subset of the full theoretical model, leaving some mechanisms supported indirectly rather than through direct empirical tests. The mutual fund industry is also a relatively stable context in which retreat to familiar domains is viable, so the performance implications may differ in high-technology industries where continued exploration is necessary for survival.

The study treats experience as binary, distinguishing whether the firm has any prior experience in a domain. The authors acknowledge that depth of experience may further shape how managers interpret feedback, but incorporating continuous experience would add conceptual and empirical complexity.
future_research:
Future research could test the behavioral mechanisms in other industries, especially high-technology contexts where firms cannot easily retreat from new domains. Such work would clarify whether negative feedback in new domains is always damaging or only damaging when retreat is strategically feasible.

Future studies could also examine how the depth of prior experience changes feedback interpretation. More direct evidence on when local search is judged to have failed would help explain the timing of shifts from local problem solving to distant search.
abstract: How organizations respond to failure (negative feedback) has important implications for subsequent organizational performance. This study focuses on theoretical and empirical distinctions between the different potential organizational reactions to failure (in this case around new product development) and how those feedback-driven choices aggregate to affect firm performance. To understand when and why negative feedback is organizationally beneficial, we focus on how possession of domain-specific experience affects the way in which firms interpret and respond to negative feedback, offering both organizationand mechanism-level theories. In particular, we distinguish between conditions that should lead to different behavioral responses to negative feedback: retreat, local search, or distant search. We find support for our theory using data on all U.S. mutual fund companies from 1962 to 2002, and testing both aggregated and mechanism-level theories. Our results show that negative feedback on new funds launched in new domains is particularly damaging to subsequent organizational performance, as firms retreat from the unknown in favor of already exploited domains. In contrast, negative feedback in experienced domains can produce positive outcomes by encouraging action to search for both local solutions to correct the problem and distant solutions to expand the firm's opportunities.
apa_citation: Eggers, J. P., & Suh, J.-H. (2019). Experience and behavior: How negative feedback in new versus experienced domains affects firm action and subsequent performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(2), 309-334. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0046

title: Boards as a Source of Inertia: Examining the Internal Challenges and Dynamics of Boards of Directors in Times of Environmental Discontinuities
methods: Inductive comparative case study of 10 large Swiss electric utility companies during the Swiss energy transition, using archival data, event timelines, cross-case analysis, and semi-structured interviews with board members, CEOs, and top managers.
industry: Electric utility companies.
units: Boards and executives of 10 large Swiss electric utility companies.
n_sample: 10 firms; 52 semi-structured interviews with 41 directors and top-level executives.
authors: Hoppmann, J.; Naegele, F.; Girod, B.
theories: agency theory; corporate governance; micro-perspective on boards; organizational inertia
keywords: agency theory; boards of directors; corporate governance; environmental discontinuities; organizational inertia; self-evaluation; self-reconfiguration
research_question: The paper asks how boards of directors contribute to organizational inertia during environmental discontinuities. More specifically, it examines how environmental and strategic change affect boards' ability to govern strategic change, how boards renew that ability, and what board-internal factors explain variation in board adjustment.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / challenges: Environmental discontinuity, strategic change, board ability to judge strategic issues, strategy evaluation, strategy reconfiguration, self-evaluation, self-reconfiguration, board members' self-interest, and board chair actions and experience.
- Process / phases: Environmental discontinuities and strategic change reduce boards' ability to judge strategic issues; boards must identify this gap through self-evaluation and renew the ability through self-reconfiguration.
- Board activities: Strategy evaluation monitors the environment and reviews strategy; strategy reconfiguration approves, stimulates, or limits strategic change initiatives.
- Renewal activities: Self-reconfiguration occurs through adaptation of composition, adaptation of size, learning and education, and adjustment of decision-making.
- Boundary conditions: The empirical setting is 10 large Swiss electric utilities exposed to the energy transition between 2009 and 2015.

The process begins when environmental discontinuities make existing board knowledge, routines, and ties less useful for judging strategic issues. If a board recognizes this loss of ability through self-evaluation, it can renew itself by changing composition, reducing size, improving learning, or changing decision-making routines. If board members' self-interest blocks self-evaluation and self-reconfiguration, the board may limit or rubber-stamp strategic change in ways that prolong organizational inertia. Experienced board chairs can partly overcome this barrier by initiating board renewal in a top-down manner.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to agency theory by showing that board members themselves may face conflicts of interest that harm firm performance, rather than only acting as monitors of managerial self-interest. It extends strategic management work on organizational inertia by identifying boards as a potential source of inertia when they fail to renew their ability to judge strategic issues. It also contributes to corporate governance research by developing a dynamic view of board capital, board evolution, and the role of the board chair in sustaining board power vis-a-vis management.
practical_implication: Firms facing environmental discontinuities should not assume that existing board expertise and routines remain adequate as strategic conditions change. Boards need explicit self-evaluation and self-reconfiguration practices, including competency reviews, education, size adjustment, and decision-making reforms. The findings also imply that board chairs are critical governance actors because they can initiate renewal when ordinary board members have incentives to avoid exposing weaknesses or losing valued mandates.
limitations: The study focuses on the Swiss electricity industry, a highly regulated setting with country-specific board responsibilities, so the authors call for caution in generalizing to other sectors or national governance systems. The study relies on retrospective interviews rather than direct real-time observation of boardroom processes, although the authors triangulate interviews with multiple archival and informant sources. The paper also provides initial evidence on antecedents of self-evaluation and self-reconfiguration rather than a complete account of why some boards engage in these practices more than others.
future_research: Future research should examine board mechanisms during environmental change in other national and industrial contexts. The authors call for ethnographic studies of boardroom processes over extended periods and for micro-level work on how board members' motivations and interests shape board dynamics and organizational outcomes. They also suggest studying how board chairs are selected or changed and how board self-evaluation and self-reconfiguration relate to firm history, board member backgrounds, ownership structures, and the relative power of owners, management, and the board.
abstract: The literature on corporate governance indicates that, by engaging in strategy-related activities, boards of directors can help firms adapt to environmental discontinuities. So far, however, studies shed limited light on board-internal challenges and dynamics in such difficult times, thus providing few insights into the conditions under which boards may contribute to organizational inertia. We use a comparative case study of 10 major Swiss electric utility companies during the energy transition to show in detail how environmental and strategic change impair boards' ability to judge strategic issues, and how boards use self-evaluation and self-reconfiguration to renew this ability. Moreover, we offer original insights into the board-internal antecedents of board renewal, and show that environmental discontinuities pose a dilemma for boards, since self-evaluation and self-reconfiguration are critical for preventing organizational inertia yet may run counter to board members' self-interest. By showing that board members, like managers, experience conflicts of interest that can harm firm performance, our study contributes to agency theory and an emerging micro-perspective on boards. Moreover, by highlighting boards as a source of organizational inertia, our study challenges existing findings in the field of strategic management and makes several more specific contributions to important debates in the corporate governance literature.
apa_citation: Hoppmann, J., Naegele, F., & Girod, B. (2019). Boards as a source of inertia: Examining the internal challenges and dynamics of boards of directors in times of environmental discontinuities. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(2), 437-468. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1091
