title: Responding to Bad Press: How CEO Temporal Focus Influences the Sensitivity to Negative Media Coverage of Acquisitions
methods: Empirical quantitative archival study of S&P 500 firms' large acquisition announcements. The authors measure media reactions around acquisition announcements using Factiva sources and LIWC, measure CEO past and future temporal focus from annual-report shareholder letters, and estimate Tobit regressions predicting subsequent acquisition spending with extensive CEO-, acquisition-, firm-, industry-, media-, and stock-market controls.
industry: Large acquisitions above $100 million by firms listed in the S&P 500; the study is not restricted to a single industry.
country: United States, represented by firms listed on the S&P 500; the paper reports the sampling frame as the S&P 500 rather than a separate country field.
time_period: Acquisition announcements from 2006 through 2011, with subsequent acquisition spending measured over the 365 days after the focal acquisition.
units: Large acquisition announcements by S&P 500 firms with media coverage and available CEO, annual-report, acquisition, firm, and industry data.
n_sample: 747 acquisitions.
authors: Gamache, D. L.; McNamara, G.
theories: negativity effect; reciprocal effects model of media influence; temporal focus perspective; upper echelons theory
keywords: CEO temporal focus; negative media reactions; soft external performance feedback; subsequent acquisition activity
research_question: The paper asks whether soft external performance feedback from the media influences subsequent strategic action after a major acquisition announcement. It also asks whether CEO temporal focus shapes how strongly negative media reactions affect later acquisition spending.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that negative media coverage acts as soft external performance feedback that can make CEOs more cautious about repeating acquisition activity. CEOs high in past focus are expected to attend more to negative prior feedback and carry it into later decisions, strengthening the negative media reaction-subsequent acquisition spending relationship. CEOs high in future focus are expected to emphasize future opportunities and long-term possibilities, weakening the influence of negative media reactions on later acquisition spending.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends upper echelons theory by showing that CEOs respond not only to hard, quantifiable external feedback such as stock market reactions, but also to softer stakeholder evaluations in media coverage. It specifies CEO temporal focus as a cognitive attribute that shapes which executives attend to and act on negative media feedback.

It also contributes to acquisition research by showing that subsequent acquisition behavior is influenced by subjective media evaluations of prior acquisitions, not only by economic indicators. The supplemental analyses further distinguish media reactions from stock market reactions because temporal focus moderates the former but not the latter.
practical_implication: The findings imply that CEOs' responses to media evaluations can shape subsequent strategic action, not only reactions to stock-market feedback. Negative media coverage is associated with lower subsequent acquisition activity, especially when the CEO is strongly past focused, whereas CEOs high in future focus appear less influenced by negative media reactions.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that an omitted variable could influence both negative media reaction and subsequent acquisition spending, although their confounding-threshold analysis suggests this would need to be a relatively strong omitted correlate. The study also does not show whether CEOs' responsiveness to negative media coverage benefits the firm or moves it away from better strategic actions.
future_research:
Future research could examine other forms of soft performance feedback and whether they fit within an aspirational framework of CEO decision making. The authors also call for more research on CEO temporal focus as a moderator of stakeholder feedback, including feedback from institutional investors and market analysts.

Future studies could extend the acquisition logic beyond subsequent deal activity to post-acquisition integration, such as whether negative media reactions lead CEOs to invest more effort in proving the acquisition successful or to pursue faster cost reductions. They also call for work on whether attending to media coverage improves firms' future actions or distracts CEOs from the best strategic course.
abstract: Management scholars have demonstrated that CEOs look to cues provided from external stakeholders when determining the direction and timing of strategic action. Research has focused on “hard” forms of external performance feedback, primarily in the form of stock market reactions. To understand both whether and to what degree “soft” external performance feedback of strategic actions influences the subsequent strategic decisions of firms, we build our arguments from and contribute to upper echelons theory. We argue that negative media reactions to the announcement of a major acquisition will shape the degree to which the firm will engage in subsequent acquisition activity. However, our theory suggests that an important individual attribute, CEO temporal focus, will influence how sensitive CEOs are to media coverage. Using a sample of 747 large acquisitions made between 2006 and 2011, we find strong support for our hypotheses. Additionally, our supplemental analysis demonstrates an important difference between the influence of stock market and media reactions following an acquisition. While CEO temporal focus shapes which CEOs will be influenced by media reactions, it appears that CEOs’ propensity to be influenced by stock market reactions is not moderated by their temporal focus.

title: It’s Not Just What is Said, but When it’s Said: A Temporal Account of Verbal Behaviors and Emergent Leadership in Self-Managed Teams
methods: Longitudinal empirical quantitative study of self-managed project teams, using videotaped meeting interaction coding, round-robin emergent leadership ratings, and multilevel modeling across first, midterm, and final meetings.
industry: Self-managed consulting project teams working on a real problem for a large automobile manufacturer.
country: International university setting in Germany, with participants from 30 nationalities.
time_period: Eight-week consulting project, with meetings videotaped in weeks 1, 5, and 7 before a week-8 final presentation.
units: Team members nested in self-managed project teams, with verbal behaviors coded from meetings and emergent leadership rated by fellow team members.
n_sample: 42 self-managed project teams; 136 students signed up for the project work.
authors: Gerpott, F. H.; Lehmann-Willenbrock, N.; Voelpel, S. C.; van Vugt, M.
theories: discursive perspective on leadership; functional leadership theory; team lifecycle theory
keywords: change-oriented communication; emergent leadership; interaction coding; relations-oriented communication; self-managed teams; task-oriented communication; temporal account; verbal behaviors
research_question: The paper asks when changes in task-, change-, and relations-oriented verbal behaviors predict emergent leadership at different points in a self-managed team’s lifecycle. It focuses on whether the behavioral antecedents of informal leadership vary across the first, midterm, and final project meetings.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is temporal fit between a member's communication and the team's changing functional needs. Task-oriented statements help teams accomplish work and remain positively associated with emergent leadership throughout the lifecycle. Change-oriented communication signals direction and initiative early, when the team is establishing its project approach, but loses relevance later. Relations-oriented communication becomes more important near project completion, when social cohesion and support help teams manage final task pressure.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends emergent leadership research by shifting behavioral antecedents from a static account to a time-sensitive account of social influence in self-managed teams. It links functional leadership theory, discursive leadership, team development, and interaction coding to show that leadership ascription depends not only on what members say but also on when they say it. The findings refine prior debates by showing that task-oriented behavior remains consistently relevant, change-oriented behavior matters early, and relations-oriented behavior matters most at the end.
practical_implication: Organizations and leadership-development programs should train members of self-managed teams to read the temporal context of team interaction and adapt their verbal behavior flexibly. The authors caution against teaching employees to use one behavior mechanically at one point in time; instead, they emphasize situational awareness, behavioral flexibility, feedback from videotaped meetings, coaching, and reflective practice.
limitations: The conceptual model assumes a particular lifecycle pattern in which teams align goals early, focus on task execution, and concentrate on goal attainment near the final meeting; other group-development perspectives could imply different timing. The study used consulting project teams embedded in a university setting, so the findings may not generalize to other organizational contexts where relational communication is more central from the start. The a priori coding scheme also captures each statement's primary function but cannot fully represent the simultaneous relational meanings of communication.
future_research: Future research could experimentally vary team activities, goal clarity, social conflict, or time pressure across lifecycle phases to test whether different temporal demands change which behaviors predict emergent leadership. Scholars could examine project teams in other settings, such as caregiving work, where relations-oriented communication may matter earlier. Future work could also use finer-grained within-meeting analyses or relational-control coding to capture both content and interpersonal meaning in ongoing communication.
abstract: “Emergent leadership”—the ascription of informal leadership responsibilities among team members—is a dynamic phenomenon that comes into place through social interactions. Yet, theory remains sparse about the importance of verbal behaviors for emergent leadership in self-managed teams over a team’s lifecycle. Adopting a functional perspective on leadership, we develop a temporal account that links changes in task-, change-, and relations-oriented communication to emergent leadership in early, middle, and late team phases. We test the hypothesized relationships in 42 teams that provided round-robin emergent leadership ratings and videotapes of their first, midterm, and final meetings. Team members’ verbal behaviors were captured using finegrained empirical interaction coding. Multilevel modeling showed that task-oriented communication was a stable positive predictor of emergent leadership at all time points. Change-oriented communication predicted emergent leadership at the start of a project and diminished in relevance at the midterm and final meetings. Relations-oriented communication gained importance, such that an increase in relations-oriented behaviors toward the project end predicted emergent leadership. We discuss theoretical implications for conceptualizing the behavioral antecedents of emergent leadership from a timeand context-sensitive perspective.
apa_citation: Gerpott, F. H., Lehmann-Willenbrock, N., Voelpel, S. C., & van Vugt, M. (2019). It’s not just what is said, but when it’s said: A temporal account of verbal behaviors and emergent leadership in self-managed teams. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 717-738. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0149

title: Crossed Wires: Endorsement Signals and the Effects of IPO Firm Delistings on Venture Capitalists’ Reputations
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of VC-backed IPOs using Arellano-Bond dynamic panel GMM models with robust standard errors clustered at the VC level. The analysis models lead VC reputation at t+1 as a function of portfolio-firm delisting and moderators including underpricing, post-IPO performance, and survival duration.
industry: VC-backed newly public firms across SIC-coded industries, with delistings for negative reasons rather than acquisitions.
time_period: VC investment data from 1990 to 2010, with IPO firms followed from the IPO year through up to the fifth post-IPO year.
units: Lead VC-firm-year observations.
n_sample: 151 unique lead VCs and 1,587 VC-firm-year observations; the final firm sample includes 370 IPO firms, 31 of which delisted for negative reasons.
authors: Gomulya, David; Jin, Kyuho; Lee, Peggy M.; Pollock, Timothy G.
theories: attribution theory (Heider, 1958; Kelley, 1973; Weiner, 1986); expectancy violation theory (Burgoon, 1978; Burgoon & Le Poire, 1993); signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al., 2011)
keywords: IPO firm delistings; attribution theory; endorsement signals; negative feedback loops; scapegoating; signaling theory; venture capital firms' reputations
research_question: The paper asks whether endorsers suffer reputational penalties when the firms they endorsed later fail to meet expectations. Specifically, it examines whether negative delistings by newly public VC-backed firms damage lead VCs' subsequent reputations, and whether IPO underpricing, post-IPO performance, and post-IPO survival duration change the size of that penalty.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines signaling and attribution logics. Reputable lead VCs endorse startups by financing and taking them public, which raises stakeholder expectations about the startups' quality and prospects. When those firms later delist for negative reasons, stakeholders search for a blameworthy actor and attribute part of the failure back to the salient lead VC, damaging its reputation. The penalty is attenuated when post-IPO market performance is stronger and when the firm survives longer after IPO, because these conditions cognitively decouple the portfolio firm from its VC; IPO underpricing does not significantly strengthen the penalty.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends signaling theory by empirically testing the often-assumed penalty cost of inaccurate endorsement signals. It shows that negative feedback can travel from a failed signal recipient back to the signal sender, even when the sender has limited ongoing control over the recipient.

It also contributes to research on organizational reputation by showing that reputation can be damaged by distant events involving affiliated firms, not only by a focal firm's own misconduct or proximal crises. The robustness tests further refine endorsement theory by showing that lead VCs, rather than non-lead syndicate members, bear the reputational penalty.
practical_implication:
For venture capital firms and other professional service firms, the findings imply that endorsements create long-tail reputational exposure. Firms that raise client or portfolio-company expectations can be penalized later if those expectations are violated, even when the subsequent failure is only partly under their control.

The study also suggests that endorsers should manage expectations and attend to portfolio firms' post-endorsement viability, not only the short-term gains from successful IPO exits. Stronger post-IPO market performance and longer survival help reduce, but do not eliminate, reputational damage from later failure.
limitations:
The study is limited to delistings of VC-backed firms in the United States, so institutional, regulatory, and VC-market differences may affect generalizability to other countries. The reputation measure is objective and formative rather than a direct longitudinal measure of stakeholder perceptions, making the test conservative but leaving the perceptual process indirectly observed.

The design also cannot fully determine whether particular delistings were caused by inadequate VC due diligence, premature VC exit pressure, or external forces beyond both the VC's and portfolio firm's control. The authors note that such distinctions could matter for whether stakeholder punishment is reasonable.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether and how VCs repair reputational damage after portfolio-firm delistings, including which repair mechanisms work and how long recovery takes. Studies could also test whether current successes offset past failures in stakeholders' evaluations.

The authors also call for research on the nature of negative events behind delistings. Future work could distinguish failures attributable to VC actions from failures driven by external shocks, and test whether stakeholders respond differently across these causal conditions and national contexts.
abstract: Signaling theorists have paid a great deal of attention to the costs of acquiring characteristics that can serve as signals, such as endorsements from reputable third parties. However, limited attention has been devoted to the penalty costs associated with providing inaccurate signals and the factors that can exacerbate or attenuate the penalties. We examine the effect of negative feedback loops on venture capital (VC) firms’ reputations that result from the failures (delistings) of the newly public firms they once endorsed. Drawing on signaling and attribution theories, we argue that endorsements by reputable VC firms create high expectations that, when violated, cause stakeholders to look for scapegoats, resulting in reputational damage to the endorsing VCs. We find empirical support for this argument, and for the attenuating effect of both post-IPO market performance and survival. Our study contributes to the conversation about endorsements as signals, and empirically tests the implicit assumption that endorsements place the reputation of the endorser at risk.
apa_citation: Gomulya, D., Jin, K., Lee, P. M., & Pollock, T. G. (2019). Crossed wires: Endorsement signals and the effects of IPO firm delistings on venture capitalists’ reputations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 641-666. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0796

title: The Voice Bystander Effect: How Information Redundancy Inhibits Employee Voice
methods: Three-study empirical quantitative design: a correlational multi-source field study of employees, peers, and managers in teams; a laboratory experiment manipulating information redundancy; and a scenario experiment manipulating information redundancy and average peer-LMX. Analyses use regression models, cluster-robust standard errors in Study 1, and mediation or moderated-mediation tests with bootstrapped indirect effects in Studies 2 and 3.
industry: Study 1 uses the India branch of a Fortune 500 electronics company servicing consumer and business markets; Study 2 uses undergraduate students in a university Student Affairs Committee scenario; Study 3 uses U.S.-based workers in a mobile game development company scenario.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual employees, undergraduate participants, and U.S.-based worker participants.
n_sample: Study 1: 132 employees and 25 managers from 25 teams; Study 2: 163 undergraduate students; Study 3: 440 U.S.-based workers.
authors: Hussain, Insiya; Shu, Rui; Tangirala, Subrahmaniam; Ekkirala, Srinivas
theories: leader-member exchange theory (Graen & Uhl-Bien, 1995); theories of the bystander effect and the volunteer's dilemma (Darley & Latane, 1968; Diekmann, 1985)
keywords: average peer-LMX; bystander effects; diffusion of responsibility; employee voice; information redundancy; leader-member exchange
research_question: The paper asks why employees may remain silent about work-related ideas, concerns, and opinions that are widely known among peers. Specifically, it examines whether information redundancy reduces employee voice by diffusing responsibility, and whether this effect is stronger when peers have high-quality relationships with the manager.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a voice bystander effect. When employees believe peers possess the same work-related information, they feel less personally responsible for raising that information to managers. This diffusion of responsibility lowers voice, especially when those peers appear capable of speaking up because they have strong relational access to the manager. Across the three studies, the authors distinguish this account from psychological safety, efficacy, and instrumentality explanations.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends employee voice research by showing that shared information can inhibit, rather than enable, speaking up. It challenges the assumption that common knowledge creates safety or confidence in numbers, arguing instead that information redundancy can create diffusion of responsibility.

It also extends bystander-effect theory by moving the phenomenon into workgroups with ongoing relationships. The paper shows that the relational capacity of other observers, captured through average peer-LMX, shapes whether a focal employee passes responsibility for action to peers.
practical_implication:
Managers should not assume that widely shared awareness of a problem makes voice more likely. Practices that spread information broadly and build strong manager-employee ties can still leave each employee waiting for someone else to speak up.

The authors suggest that managers reduce this risk by emphasizing each employee's unique contribution and making individual voice feel important rather than redundant. This is especially relevant for issues that many employees know about but no one escalates.
limitations:
The authors note that Study 1 did not measure diffusion of responsibility directly, even though Studies 2 and 3 supported that mechanism experimentally. Study 1 also used a relatively small field sample of 132 employees nested in 25 teams and lacked gender diversity because all participants were male.

The paper further limits its tested moderator to average peer-LMX. The authors identify other possible moderators, including personality traits such as conscientiousness, peers' voice-relevant competencies, and whether the issue involves challenging voice or a clear and unambiguous threat to the team.
future_research:
Future research should test the mediation process in field settings and examine the model in larger and more gender-diverse team samples. Such work would clarify whether diffusion of responsibility operates similarly in naturally occurring organizational contexts.

The authors also call for research on additional boundary conditions of the voice bystander phenomenon. Future studies could examine personality, peer competence, and issue type to determine when shared information decreases voice and when employees remain personally responsible for speaking up.
abstract: Employees often remain silent rather than speak up to managers with work-related ideas, concerns, and opinions. As a result, managers can remain in the dark about issues that are otherwise well known to, or universally understood by, frontline employees. We propose a previously unexplored explanation for this phenomenon: Voice is prone to "bystander effects," such that, the more certain information is shared among employees, the less any particular employee feels individually responsible for bringing up that information with managers. We theorize that such bystander effects are especially likely to occur when peers of focal employees, on average, enjoy high-quality relationships with managers and thereby have adequate relational access to voice up the hierarchy. Using a correlational study involving managers and employees working in teams in a Fortune 500 company, as well as two experimental studies (a laboratory study involving undergraduate students working in a hierarchical setting, and a scenario study with a sample of U.S.-based workers), we provide evidence for our conceptual model. We also discuss the theoretical and managerial implications of our findings.

title: The Social Practice of Coevolving Strategy and Structure to Realize Mandated Radical Change
methods: Longitudinal, real-time interpretive qualitative case study of Telco, using meeting observations, interviews, work shadowing, documents, chronological case analysis, process analysis, and iterative movement between data and theory.
industry: Telecommunications / communications provider.
time_period: 28 months, from inception of the mandated change to the regulator's strategic review.
units: Telco, its corporate center and divisions, senior and middle managers, frontline employees, implementation meetings, work shadowing episodes, and documents related to the mandated change.
n_sample: 254 audio-recorded meeting observations, 130 audiotaped interviews, 16 days of work shadowing, and more than 1,500 documents.
authors: Jarzabkowski, P.; Lê, J.; Balogun, J.
theories: practice breakdowns; practice theory; strategy as practice; structuration theory
keywords: action cycles; breakdowns; espoused strategy and structure; mandated radical change; practice approach; reflecting action cycles; strategy and structure
research_question: The paper asks how people's actions bring about a mandated radical change of strategy and structure. It focuses on how senior, middle, and frontline actors at Telco enacted, reinforced, reflected on, and modified an espoused strategy and structure under a legally binding regulatory mandate.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Mandated radical change, espoused strategy and structure, realized radical change, performing action cycles, reinforcing action cycles, reflecting action cycles, unintended consequences, breakdowns, and the "spirit" of the mandate.
- Process / cycles: Actors perform the initial espoused strategy and structure; unintended consequences emerge; actors reinforce existing actions because the mandate is legally binding; unintended consequences escalate into breakdowns; actors shift into reflecting action cycles; modified strategy and structure are enacted through new performing cycles.
- Strategic and structural elements: Independence, industry supplier, equivalence, and products, each carrying intertwined strategic objectives and structural arrangements.
- Managerial levels: Frontline employees, middle managers, and top managers all participate in action cycles, with problems escalating upward and revised understandings cascading back through the organization.
- Boundary conditions: The process is theorized for a detailed, externally imposed, legally binding mandate where failure carries financial penalties and possible breakup.

The central process is cumulative rather than linear. Under mandated change, actors initially treat unintended consequences as signs that they should work harder to enact the espoused strategy and structure, not as permission to reinterpret the change. Only when these reinforced actions produce breakdowns do actors step back from everyday performance, reflect on the mandate's intent, and modify the espoused strategy and structure in ways that still comply with the mandate. Strategy and structure therefore coevolve through situated action across organizational levels.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends process theories of radical change by showing that breakdowns can be necessary triggers for reflective action under mandated change. It contributes to practice-based strategy and organization theory by explaining how performing, reinforcing, and reflecting action cycles produce the coevolution of strategy and structure. It also expands accounts of top managers in change processes by showing them not only as designers of change but also as active participants in working out how the mandate should be realized.
practical_implication: The study implies that managers implementing mandated change should treat breakdowns as diagnostic moments for examining whether current actions realize the intent of the mandate, not only as execution failures. It also suggests that top managers need to stay actively engaged with middle managers, frontline employees, and regulators, because the meaning of compliance may need to be worked out through practice. For organizations under regulatory mandates, faithful implementation may require modifying the espoused strategy and structure while preserving the mandate's underlying intent.
limitations: The authors present Telco as an extreme case of externally imposed, detailed, legally binding mandated change, so the process may differ when mandates are weaker, less specific, internally imposed, or easier to abandon. The study is a qualitative single-case process analysis, designed for theory development rather than statistical generalization. The paper also notes that the case involved top managers who had helped negotiate the mandate, which may shape the reflecting cycles observed.
future_research: Future research could examine whether less detailed or less binding mandates generate the same reinforcing action cycles and breakdowns, or whether actors adapt more flexibly before breakdown occurs. Studies could also compare externally imposed mandates with internally imposed mandates from powerful corporate actors or parent companies. The authors further suggest examining how different degrees of constraint, legal consequence, and top-manager responsibility shape managerial engagement with radical change.
abstract: This paper draws on a longitudinal interpretive case study to develop a theoretical model of how actions by people across an organization coevolve strategy and structure in order to realize a mandated radical change. Mandated change, imposed by a powerful external actor, extends understanding of the dynamics of radical change. While other studies have examined how unintended consequences shape the way radical change is realized, under mandated change, actors focus on bringing about the change in ways that will be, collectively, considered to realize the intended mandate. Our study, grounded in a practice approach concerning how actions bring about radical change, identifies three different action cycles: performing action cycles, reinforcing action cycles, and reflecting action cycles. Shifts in cycles are triggered by unintended consequences that escalate into breakdowns. Cumulative cycles, arising from the escalation of unintended consequences that lead to breakdowns, are necessary for bringing about a mandated change in strategy and structure. Following breakdown, actors switch to reflecting actions in which they consider the underlying intent of the mandate and how to modify the espoused strategy and structure to bring about that intent.
apa_citation: Jarzabkowski, P., Lê, J., & Balogun, J. (2019). The social practice of coevolving strategy and structure to realize mandated radical change. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 850-882. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0689

title: Stuck in the Past? The Influence of a Leader’s Past Cultural Experience on Group Culture and Positive and Negative Group Deviance
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design. Study 1 uses a three-wave, multisource field survey of sales groups in a South Korean manufacturing company, analyzed with hierarchical regressions and PROCESS mediation/moderated-mediation models. Study 2 uses a two-wave laboratory experiment with three-person groups to manipulate leader and follower past experience with cultural tightness and information about countercultures, analyzed with ANOVA and hierarchical regressions.
industry: Study 1 examines sales groups in a manufacturing company; Study 2 uses student laboratory groups performing HR-related group ideation tasks.
country: Study 1 is set in South Korea; Study 2 is conducted at a large North American university.
time_period: Study 1 has three waves of data collection; Study 2 has two waves approximately 10 days apart.
units: Sales employees, group leaders, division heads, archival voice records, undergraduate participants, and three-person laboratory groups.
n_sample: Study 1: 404 employees in 91 sales groups. Study 2: 527 participants in 176 three-person groups.
authors: Kim, Yeun Joon; Toh, Soo Min
theories: bounded rationality; career history and career imprinting; cultural tightness-looseness; functionality perspective of culture formation; group identification theory; leader-trait perspective of culture formation
keywords: bounded rationality; career history; counterproductive work behavior; cultural tightness; group culture; leader’s past cultural experience; prohibitive voice; promotive voice
research_question: The paper asks where group cultures come from and whether leaders transfer cultural tightness from groups in which they previously participated as followers to groups they later lead. It also asks when this transfer is stronger and whether transferred cultural tightness reduces both negative group deviance and constructive forms of voice.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is cultural transfer under bounded rationality and career-history imprinting. Leaders responsible for group functioning do not simply optimize culture from current contingencies; they rely on familiar cultural solutions learned in prior groups, especially when those prior cultures are internalized through identification or tenure. Transferred tightness then creates strong norms and conformity pressure, reducing counterproductive work behavior but also suppressing promotive and prohibitive voice.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends culture-formation theory by introducing leaders’ past cultural experience as an antecedent distinct from both functionality and leader-trait explanations. It argues that leaders shape cultures through remembered cultural solutions, not only through current environmental adaptation or stable personal values and traits.

It also contributes to cultural tightness-looseness research by moving the construct to the group level in organizational settings and linking it to both antecedents and consequences. The evidence frames cultural tightness as a double-edged sword: it can reduce harmful deviance while also discouraging constructive challenge and voice.
practical_implication:
Organizations hiring or assigning group leaders should consider the cultures those leaders may import from prior groups, especially when leaders strongly identified with or spent longer time in those groups. Explicit cultural expectations and incentives may be needed when the desired culture differs from the leader’s prior cultural template.

The findings also imply that tight and loose cultures should be matched to task demands. Tight cultures may fit work requiring protocol compliance and stability, whereas looser cultures may be better for work that depends on constructive deviance, dissent, and new ideas.
limitations:
The authors focus on cultural tightness rather than cultural values such as individualism, collectivism, or power distance, so it remains unclear whether the same transfer logic applies to other cultural dimensions. Study 1 and Study 2 also examine newly formed groups, leaving open how cultural transfer operates in ongoing groups where past and present cultural experience are harder to separate.

The laboratory study uses students and brief group interaction, so it cannot capture the full complexity of workplace culture formation over time. The counterculture manipulation in Study 2 also gives participants indirect information about effectiveness rather than repeated direct experience with cultural success or failure.
future_research:
Future research should test whether cultural values interact with cultural tightness and whether voice norms can make tight cultures increase, rather than suppress, employee voice. The authors also call for work on cultural transfer in ongoing groups, particularly the role of early-career cultural experience and career imprinting.

Additional studies should examine culture formation in self-managing groups, where no formal leader holds disproportionate authority. Future work could also test whether groups adjust transferred cultures after repeated direct feedback that an imported cultural solution is ineffective.
abstract: Extant research on the antecedents of cultures has posited that cultures result from the internal and external changes experienced by the group (the functionality perspective) and from a group leader’s personal values and personality traits (the leader–trait perspective). The current study proposes another important but neglected antecedent of cultures: a leader’s past cultural experience. Specifically, we theorize that group leaders enact cultures based on their past cultural experiences, essentially transferring cultures from their former groups to their current groups. Two studies, one in the field (Study 1) and another in the laboratory (Study 2), reveal that the levels of cultural tightness in current groups are predicted by group leaders’ past experience with cultural tightness in their former groups in which they were followers. This relationship becomes stronger when the group leaders identified with or had longer tenure in their former groups. In addition, the cultural tightness that leaders transferred from their former groups to their current groups influences negative (counterproductive work behavior) and positive (promotive and prohibitive voice) forms of group deviance. The theoretical and managerial implications of our findings for leadership and culture are discussed.
apa_citation: Kim, Y. J., & Toh, S. M. (2019). Stuck in the past? The influence of a leader’s past cultural experience on group culture and positive and negative group deviance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 944-969. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1322

title: Ego-Network Stability and Innovation in Alliances
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of U.S. pharmaceutical firms' alliance ego networks. The authors construct annual alliance-network measures, measure innovation with citation-weighted patent counts net of self-citations, and estimate Poisson fixed-effects unconditional quasi-maximum likelihood models with firm and year fixed effects plus robustness tests.
industry: Pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical firms, restricted to pharmaceutical-domain alliances and pharmaceutical patents.
time_period: 1985-2005 for alliance/network observations, with patent data observed through 2010 to reduce right-censoring.
units: U.S. pharmaceutical firm-year observations for firms with at least two direct alliance ties.
n_sample: 198 U.S. pharmaceutical firms and 1,236 firm-year observations.
authors: Kumar, Pankaj; Zaheer, Akbar
theories: network closure (Coleman, 1990); network resource theory (Gulati, 2007); social resource theory (Lin, 1982, 1990); structural holes theory (Burt, 1992)
keywords: alliance portfolios; biopharmaceutical firms; ego network configurations; ego-network stability; geographic concentration; innovation; network closure; structural holes
research_question: The paper asks how stability in a firm's alliance ego-network composition affects the focal firm's innovation performance. It also asks whether spanning structural holes mitigates the innovation penalty of stability and whether geographic concentration of inventive activities aggravates that penalty.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that repeated alliance partners initially provide useful social resources, but over time the knowledge accessible through the same partners becomes less diverse, more redundant, and more prone to lock-in. Because R&D alliances in fast-moving pharmaceutical contexts rely on changing knowledge requirements, stable partner composition can reduce the focal firm's exposure to novel recombinations. Structural holes soften this negative effect by giving the focal firm access to more diverse and less redundant partner information, whereas geographically concentrated inventive activity worsens it by limiting the firm's access to dispersed knowledge sources.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper adds a compositional lens to network research by showing that ego-network stability matters beyond the usual configuration lens of structural holes versus closure. It argues that network structures cannot be evaluated only by their degree of openness because the continuity or churn of the partner set can independently shape innovation outcomes.

It also extends social resource and network resource perspectives by emphasizing that the value of network resources depends on whether partners continue to provide nonredundant knowledge over time. The study therefore reframes stability, often treated as a foundation for social capital, as potentially detrimental in innovation-intensive alliance settings.
practical_implication:
Managers using alliances for innovation should monitor not only the number and structure of alliance ties but also whether the partner portfolio is becoming stale. The results imply that refreshing partners, spanning structural holes, and maintaining geographically dispersed inventive activity may help reduce the innovation costs of excessive network stability.

The paper also suggests that persistent open-ended alliances are not automatically beneficial for innovation. When alliance persistence is difficult to avoid, managers may be able to limit its negative consequences through more open ego-network structures and broader geographic access to knowledge.
limitations:
The empirical setting is the biopharmaceutical industry, so the authors expect the findings to generalize most clearly to industries where innovation is salient and alliances are used for innovation-related purposes. In industries where innovation is less critical or alliances serve other goals, network stability may not produce the same negative effects.

The authors also exclude isolates and pendants because stability and structural holes are not meaningfully defined for firms with zero or one alliance tie. In addition, the analysis treats relevant innovation knowledge as potentially coming from any alliance type, even though future work could distinguish upstream research alliances from downstream commercialization alliances.
future_research:
Future research could examine how ego-network stability affects innovation at other levels, including individual scientists, and could study the antecedents of ego-network stability itself. The authors also call for work on how local ego-network stability shapes global network properties such as small-worldliness, connectivity, and centrality.

Another opportunity is to classify alliance networks by value-chain activity and test whether stability has different innovation effects in upstream versus downstream relationships. Future studies could also examine the trade-off between the cost of changing network partners and the declining innovation value of stable partner portfolios.
abstract: Much research has shown that firms’ ego network configurations—i.e., structural holes or network closure—help them achieve superior innovation outcomes. However, little is known about how the stability of the firm’s ego-network composition affects the firm’s innovation. In this paper, we investigate the outcomes of ego-network stability in an alliance context, arguing that stability actually reduces innovation for the focal firm. We further investigate two contingencies—namely, the structural holes the focal firm spans and the geographic concentration of its inventive activities—that moderate the detrimental innovation effects of ego network stability. Focal firms can limit the negative effects of ego-network stability on innovation by spanning structural holes in their alliance portfolios, whereas the negative effects are worsened when the focal firms’ inventive activities are geographically concentrated in a single country. We empirically test our hypotheses using 198 biopharmaceutical firms headquartered in the United States over a 21-year period from 1985 to 2005. Our results support our predictions.
apa_citation: Kumar, P., & Zaheer, A. (2019). Ego-network stability and innovation in alliances. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 691-716. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0819

title: Visions of Change as Visions of Continuity
methods: Two quantitative studies: a multilevel field survey of leader-follower dyads during planned organizational change, followed by a laboratory experiment manipulating vision of continuity and uncertainty with behavioral support measures.
industry: Organizations undergoing planned change, plus a Dutch business school education-program change experiment; no single industry focus.
country: Study 2 used a Dutch business school; Study 1 country or region is not reported in paper.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employees nested within leaders in Study 1; student participants in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1: 209 completed leader-follower matched surveys representing 74 leaders; Study 2: 199 analyzed student participants.
authors: Venus, M.; Stam, D.; van Knippenberg, D.
theories: social identity theory; uncertainty-identity theory; visionary leadership theory
keywords: collective continuity; leader vision; organizational change; social identity; support for change; work-related uncertainty
research_question: The paper asks what characterizes an effective leader vision of organizational change. It examines whether visions that assure followers of organizational identity continuity generate greater support for change, especially when followers experience high work-related uncertainty.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that change can threaten employees' subjective continuity of organizational identity. A vision of continuity frames the future as preserving the organization's defining features, increasing perceived collective continuity; this matters most under uncertainty because social identity provides an uncertainty-reduction function.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to visionary leadership research by specifying a content feature of effective change visions: assuring continuity rather than only emphasizing dissatisfaction with the status quo or an attractive future. It also contributes to organizational change and social identity research by showing that leader vision communication can shape perceived collective continuity, which helps explain support for change under uncertainty.
practical_implication: Managers leading change should not only rationalize why change is needed or portray the future positively. They should also identify what employees understand as central to the organization's identity and frame planned change as preserving, reaffirming, or continuing those defining features.
limitations: Study 1 raises possible common method and common source concerns for the self-reported antecedent and mediator, although the authors argue these concerns are offset by Study 2 and by supervisor-rated support in Study 1. The paper also calls for tests of whether the findings generalize to other change outcomes, such as satisfaction, trust in management, and turnover intentions, and to other change contexts.
future_research: Future research could examine the framing strategies leaders use to create perceived continuity, including linking past and future, framing change as preserving identity, and using organizational symbols or work design. The authors also suggest examining leader-member exchange, value congruence, change size perceptions, industry turbulence, and cases where change itself targets identity.
abstract: Despite wide consensus that leader vision is a key vehicle for leaders to motivate followers to support organizational change, it remains far from clear what characterizes an effective vision of change. Research on organizational change that has used a social identity perspective has asserted that one important reason why followers resist change is because change may pose a threat to their subjective sense of continuity of organizational identity. Accordingly, we hypothesize that leaders that communicate visions of change can address this resistance by assuring followers that the essence of the organizational identity will remain unchanged—making their vision of change also a vision of continuity. In line with our proposition that collective continuity is valued because it serves an uncertainty-reduction function, such visions should be more predictive of vision effectiveness the higher follower work-related uncertainty. Across a field study and an experimental study we find support for these predictions.
apa_citation: Venus, M., Stam, D., & van Knippenberg, D. (2019). Visions of change as visions of continuity. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 667-690. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1196

title: “Matter Battles”: Cognitive Representations, Boundary Objects, and the Failure of Collaboration in Two Smart Cities
methods: Longitudinal inductive qualitative field study of two smart city projects, using interviews, observation, document review, comparative field data, thick descriptions, narrative analysis, NVivo open coding, and iterative process theorizing.
industry: Smart city and sustainable urban development projects.
time_period: SmartTown late 2009-mid-2012; SmartBlock early 2011-mid-2012.
units: Two large-scale smart city projects, SmartTown and SmartBlock, plus industry-level data on the smart city industry.
n_sample: 104 project interviews with 59 individuals; 14 industry stakeholder interviews; nine field visits; observations; and archival documents.
authors: Zuzul, T. W.
theories: boundary objects; cognitive representations; collaboration across boundaries; intractable conflict
keywords: ambiguity; boundary objects; cognitive representations; collaboration across boundaries; materiality; matter battles; smart cities
research_question: The paper asks why and how attempts to develop boundary objects, usually treated as tools of integration, can become divisive conflicts that derail collaboration. It examines this question in two smart city projects where actors from different knowledge domains tried to transform ambiguous ideas into material urban-development outcomes.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Extreme novelty, concept ambiguity, process ambiguity, divergent cognitive representations, boundary objects, materiality, matter battles, negative emotions, stereotyping, and collaboration failure.
- Process / phases: Extreme novelty creates ambiguity; actors form divergent smart and city representations; boundary object development forces concrete choices; choices reify some representations while violating others; repeated matter battles produce negative emotional and cognitive dynamics; actors withdraw from collaboration.
- Boundary objects: SmartBlock contract, SmartBlock master plan, SmartBlock pro forma, SmartTown financial deck, and SmartTown master plan.
- Emergent outcomes: Conflict over material decisions, simplified us-versus-them stereotypes, reduced interaction, disengagement, project withdrawal, and abandonment of collaboration.
- Boundary conditions: The process is theorized for extremely novel, cross-boundary innovation projects that require diverse experts to create material outcomes without settled templates or accepted authority structures.

The process begins when novelty leaves actors without shared definitions of what smart cities are or how they should be built. Actors from technology, design, urban engineering, architecture, real estate, and consulting domains develop different cognitive representations of the same projects. When boundary objects require concrete decisions about materials, financial assumptions, or development plans, those choices become consequential because the resulting city is physical, durable, and difficult to reverse. The conflicts therefore become matter battles: high-stakes disputes over material outcomes that intensify emotions, stereotyping, and withdrawal rather than integration.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on cross-boundary collaboration by showing that boundary objects can become weapons of division, not only tools of integration. It links cognitive representations and boundary objects by explaining how ambiguous settings allow divergent mental maps to form and then become reified through material choices. It also develops the construct of matter battles as a form of intractable conflict that can emerge in novel organizational projects even without long-standing group divisions.
practical_implication: The study implies that leaders of novel cross-boundary innovation projects should not assume that boundary objects will automatically integrate diverse expertise. They need to surface and compare actors’ cognitive representations before object development forces irreversible choices. The paper suggests that pre-prototypes or other low-stakes draft objects may help reveal divergent representations before decisions become embedded in high-stakes material outcomes.
limitations: The study was designed to generate rather than test theory, so the process model should be treated as analytically grounded but not statistically tested. The evidence comes from two deviant smart city projects that both failed, which supports process theorizing but limits claims about prevalence or comparative success conditions. The author also notes that the cases did not allow systematic comparison of which kinds of boundary objects are more or less likely to generate matter battles.
future_research: Future research can test whether the matter-battle process appears in settings with clearer leadership, more established power dynamics, or less expert collaborators. Studies can also examine which kinds of boundary objects are especially likely to produce matter battles, including whether flexibility, reversibility, or optionality reduce conflict. The paper further calls for work on interventions, such as practices that reveal or integrate cognitive representations before ambiguity is transformed into materiality.
abstract: In this paper, I present a longitudinal study of two smart city projects that brought together experts from diverse knowledge domains. Both projects structured collaboration around the development of boundary objects that could integrate actors’ expertise. In both projects, however, the objects sparked conflicts that exacerbated rather than attenuated differences. I develop a process model exploring how and why the development of boundary objects can manifest as divisive conflict that derails collaboration. In both projects, extreme novelty gave rise to concept ambiguity, a lack of shared ideas about what smart cities were, and process ambiguity, a lack of shared ideas about how smart cities should be developed. Ambiguity led actors from diverse domains to form divergent cognitive representations about smart cities. As they developed boundary objects, actors made decisions that violated some cognitive representations, while reifying others into material outcomes. Their efforts to develop the objects manifest as matter battles: high-stakes conflicts about material outcomes that, over time, set the stage for collaboration failure. In advancing these ideas, I provide an alternative perspective to the literature on collaboration across boundaries, which has primarily treated boundary objects as tools of integration rather than weapons of division.
apa_citation: Zuzul, T. W. (2019). “Matter battles”: Cognitive representations, boundary objects, and the failure of collaboration in two smart cities. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(3), 739-764. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0625

title: Born to Take Risk? The Effect of CEO Birth Order on Strategic Risk Taking
methods: Archival empirical-quantitative panel study of South Korean Chaebol-affiliated public firms using generalized estimating equations, robust standard errors, year and industry fixed effects, lagged predictors, and a Heckman two-stage correction for family-CEO sample selection. Strategic risk taking is measured as the logged sum of capital expenditures, R&D spending, and acquisitions.
industry: Publicly traded firms affiliated with South Korean family-controlled business groups, or Chaebols.
country: South Korea, with supplemental analysis using a smaller U.S. public-firm CEO sample.
time_period: 1999-2015 for the primary South Korean CEO-year panel.
units: CEO-year observations for family CEOs of publicly traded Chaebol-affiliated firms.
n_sample: 71 CEOs across 67 firms; final sample size of 503 CEO-years.
authors: Campbell, R. J.; Jeong, S.-H.; Graffin, S. D.
theories: birth order theory; evolutionary theory; sibling rivalry; upper echelons theory
keywords: CEO birth order; Chaebols; evolutionary theory; family-controlled business groups; sibling rivalry; strategic risk taking; upper echelons theory
research_question: The paper asks whether CEO birth order is associated with strategic risk taking, and whether this relationship is strengthened or weakened by conditions tied to sibling rivalry. It specifically examines whether closest-sibling age gap, CEO age, and the presence of a sibling CEO condition the birth order-risk taking relationship.
mechanism_summary: The theorized mechanism is that birth order shapes childhood sibling rivalry and niche differentiation, which in turn forms durable risk-taking tendencies that later carry into CEO strategic decision making. Later-born CEOs are expected to take more strategic risk because later-born siblings historically faced stronger incentives to use riskier behavior to attract parental investment. The results support the main positive association, show stronger effects when sibling age gaps are smaller and when a sibling is also a CEO, and do not support CEO age as a weakening moderator.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends upper echelons research by shifting attention from work-related executive experiences to early-life family-domain experiences. It contributes to family science and birth order research by theorizing boundary conditions around sibling rivalry, and it advances strategic risk-taking research by identifying CEO birth order as an observable ex ante correlate of strategic risk preferences.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that CEO birth order may be one observable input when organizations think about CEO strategic risk-taking tendencies. In family business groups, the presence of sibling CEOs may make sibling rivalry especially salient, so early-life family-domain experience can be relevant when interpreting executives' risk preferences.
limitations: The authors note endogeneity and sample-selection concerns, although they use a Heckman two-stage correction and lagged predictors to mitigate them. The sibling rivalry mechanism is not directly measured, the primary sample is male CEOs in South Korean Chaebols, and the U.S. supplemental sample is small and constrained by historical census data. They also could not control for other executives' birth order or CEO personality traits such as the Big Five.
future_research: Future research could examine whether CEO birth order influences other strategic decisions and could test more directly how family experiences shape executive psychological properties such as risk-taking propensity. The authors also call for studies in other countries, larger datasets using sources such as census and Ancestry.com records, samples with enough female CEOs to test gender differences, and designs that can control for other top-management-team and personality factors.
abstract: The importance of birth order has been the subject of debate for centuries, and has captured the attention of the general public and researchers alike. Despite this interest, scholars have little understanding of the impact birth order has on CEOs and their strategic decisions. With this in mind, we develop theory that explains how CEO birth order may be associated with strategic risk taking. Drawing from evolutionary theory arguments related to birth order, we theorize that CEO birth order is positively associated with strategic risk taking; that is, earlier-born CEOs will take less risk than later-born CEOs. As evolutionary theory proposes that birth order effects are driven by sibling rivalry, we also argue that this relationship is moderated by three factors related to sibling rivalry: age gap between a CEO and the closest born sibling, CEO age, and the presence of a sibling CEO. Our results provide support for our theorizing and suggest that birth order may have important implications for organizations. We believe this study helps advance strategic management research, the broader multidisciplinary “family science” literature, and the much-needed cross-pollination of ideas between the two.
apa_citation: Campbell, R. J., Jeong, S.-H., & Graffin, S. D. (2019). Born to take risk? The effect of CEO birth order on strategic risk taking. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(4), 1278-1306. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0790

title: Identity Affirmation as Threat? Time-Bending Sensemaking and the Career and Family Identity Patterns of Early Achievers
methods: Qualitative inductive grounded theory study using two waves of semi-structured interviews, open and axial coding, first-order concepts, second-order themes, aggregate dimensions, and iterative comparison with identity and work-family literatures.
industry: Professionals across academic, corporate executive, entrepreneurial, attorney, nonprofit, and community-oriented career settings.
time_period: Wave 2 sampled recipients of 40 Under 40 awards from 1994-2015; Wave 1 provided preliminary interview data.
units: Professionals with salient career and family identities, especially recipients of 40 Under 40 awards who had experienced early career success.
n_sample: 20 Wave 1 interviews and 45 Wave 2 semi-structured interviews with 40 Under 40 award recipients.
authors: Dahm, P. C.; Kim, Y. (S.); Glomb, T. M.; Harrison, S. H.
theories: identity threat theory; identity work; sensemaking; temporal self-understandings; work-family balance
keywords: career identity affirmation; dual identity affirmation; family identity threat; identity bursts; identity projecting; identity residue; time-bending sensemaking; work-family balance
research_question: The paper asks how career identity affirmation from external recognition can create identity threat for individuals with salient career and family identities. It also asks how those individuals construe time to make sense of career and family identities, mitigate threat, and achieve internal dual identity affirmation.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Career identity affirmation, dual identity affirmation, career identity threat, family identity threat, and the difficulty of enacting valued career and family identities simultaneously.
- Triggering condition: Early career success recognized through 40 Under 40 awards affirmed participants' career identities but also made future career expectations and family sacrifices more salient.
- Time-bending sensemaking strategies: Identity residue links present self-concepts to past identity enactment; identity projecting links present self-concepts to imagined future enactment; identity bursts provide brief, intense enactments of a threatened identity.
- Identity patterns: Chronic accelerating relies heavily on family identity projecting and bursts while maintaining high career focus; lane switching uses accumulated career residue to shift into more family-focused cruising; seasonalizing alternates career and family focus across shorter or longer seasons.
- Emergent outcomes: Participants sought dual identity affirmation by redefining balance over time rather than only in the present moment.

The process is temporal and interpretive rather than a variable-based causal model. External recognition can affirm career identity while simultaneously threatening both career and family identities. Early achievers respond by stretching the time horizon of identity enactment into the past, present, and future, allowing them to feel connected to identities that cannot always be enacted at the same time.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to identity and work-family theory by showing that identity affirmation can be an instigator of identity work, not only a stabilizing outcome. It develops the time-bending sensemaking concepts of identity residue, identity projecting, and identity bursts, and links them to three career-family identity patterns: chronic accelerating, lane switching, and seasonalizing. It also reframes work-family balance as something individuals may construct across time through past and future selves, not only through present-time role allocation.
practical_implication: The study suggests that organizations should not assume early achievers always want a straight career ladder to the top. Flexible work, vacation time, sabbaticals, and career systems that allow acceleration, cruising, and renewed acceleration may help professionals sustain both career and family identities. Awards and other public recognition may also require coaching, peer discussion, or mentoring support because affirmation can create new identity pressure.
limitations: The authors note that the study relies on retrospective interview accounts rather than repeated interviews with the same informants over time. Generalizability is also limited because the focal sample consists of early achievers who received public external recognition at a young age, so the same patterns may differ among less publicly affirmed professionals or among people whose career identities are less central.
future_research: The authors call for panel data or experience sampling research to track how time-related sensemaking strategies shape identity management over time. They also suggest future work on typologies of identity affirmation, the emergence of additional patterns such as chronic cruising, and gender differences in how men and women enact time-bending identity strategies.
abstract: We develop a model of dual identity affirmation through which professionals make sense of their career and family identities by incorporating past and future identity enactment into present self-concepts, and by enacting suspended career or family identities in fleeting momentary ways. The model emerged from a qualitative inductive study of professionals whose career identities had been affirmed by achieving early career success recognized by a 40 Under 40 Award. Identity affirmation often sparked career and family identity threat that individuals resolved through time-bending sensemaking. During times of family focus, early achievers attained a sense of dual identity affirmation by believing that they had in the past (identity residue), or would again in the future (identity projection), focus on the career role, mitigating career identity threat. During periods of career focus, they similarly projected future or remembered past family involvement to mitigate family identity threat. Early achievers also found more fleeting ways to maintain their identities in identity bursts that helped them resolve threat to their career or family identity while the other was taking precedence. Three identity patterns emerged: identity bursts anchored chronic accelerating, while residue was key to lane switching; seasonalizing was anchored by both residue and projecting.
apa_citation: Dahm, P. C., Kim, Y. (S.), Glomb, T. M., & Harrison, S. H. (2019). Identity affirmation as threat? Time-bending sensemaking and the career and family identity patterns of early achievers. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(4), 1194-1225. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0699

title: Does Losing Temporary Workers Matter? The Effects of Planned Turnover on Replacements and Unit Performance
methods: Longitudinal monthly matched unit-employee and performance data analyzed with store fixed effects, month and year fixed effects, manager fixed effects, clustered standard errors, quadratic and two-part spline specifications, and supplemental interviews.
industry: Food and beverage services for travelers.
time_period: Monthly data from 2007 to 2014, excluding September observations in the final analyses.
units: Store-month-year observations for basic operators in 255 stores.
n_sample: 13,280 store-month-year observations.
authors: De Stefano, F.; Bonet, R.; Camuffo, A.
theories: capacity theory of collective turnover; context-emergent turnover (CET) theory
keywords: firm-specific human capital; numerical flexibility; operational disruption; planned turnover; replacements; temporary workers; unit performance
research_question: The paper asks whether the planned departure of temporary workers due to contract expiration improves unit performance through numerical flexibility or impairs performance through operational disruption. It also asks how the proportion of replacements and replacements' firm-specific experience shape that planned turnover-performance relationship.
mechanism_summary: Planned temporary worker turnover can initially improve performance by reducing slack and labor costs when units adjust staffing to demand. Beyond an optimal level, exits deplete collective human capital and disrupt routines, so the performance effect turns negative. Replacements can restore productive capacity at low levels of planned turnover, but high replacement intensity, especially with novice replacements, increases disruption when turnover is already high.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reconciles collective turnover research and contingent work research by showing that planned temporary worker turnover is neither uniformly harmful nor costless. It develops and tests an inverted U-shaped account in which numerical flexibility benefits coexist with operational disruption costs. It also extends context-emergent turnover and capacity theory by distinguishing the quantity of replacements from their firm-specific human capital.
practical_implication: Managers should treat temporary workers as resources that can accumulate firm-specific human capital rather than as disposable plug-in labor. The paper suggests that staffing flexibility has hidden costs when high planned turnover forces remaining workers to absorb departures and train replacements. Managers can reduce disruption by avoiding excessive waves of novice replacements after high temporary-worker turnover.
limitations: The evidence comes from one company in Italy, a context with high employment protection for permanent workers and unusually low non-temporary turnover. The jobs studied are low-skill food and beverage service roles, so generalizability to more complex knowledge work remains uncertain. The archival design does not directly measure operational disruption or remaining workers' reactions, and the study is not experimental.
future_research: Future research should examine settings with less employment protection, more simultaneous forms of turnover, and different uses of temporary work. Studies could test whether unit-level HR practices, climate, and managerial discretion moderate the effects of planned temporary worker turnover. Additional work could directly measure disruption, overwork, training burdens, and replacement learning after specific turnover events.
abstract: This study examines the performance consequences of planned turnover. In particular, we investigate the departure of temporary workers due to the expiration of their contracts. We reconcile the contradictory predictions of collective turnover research—that any type of worker’s exit impairs organizational performance—and of contingent work research—that temporary workers’ exits improve organizational performance because they provide flexibility. We argue that the planned turnover of temporary workers has an inverted U-shaped relationship with unit performance because it combines flexibility benefits and disruption costs. We also argue that the costs of planned temporary worker turnover are moderated by the proportion and the firm-specific experience of their replacements. We test these arguments using longitudinal monthly data from a leading multinational company in the food and beverage industry, and find support for our hypotheses. The study suggests that managers hiring temporary workers should consider the cost of losing them and challenges the widespread scholarly and managerial assumption that temporary workers are disposable resources.
apa_citation: De Stefano, F., Bonet, R., & Camuffo, A. (2019). Does losing temporary workers matter? The effects of planned turnover on replacements and unit performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(4), 979-1002. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0291

title: Bringing the Firms (and Forms) Back In: Organizational Form Identity and Individual Turnover
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study dominated by quantitative panel analysis: guided open-ended industry interviews inform theory and measure validation, while GEE logit models and event-history robustness checks estimate managerial turnover in Korean TV advertising.
industry: Korean TV advertising industry.
units: Managerial employees observed as person-year spells in advertising agencies, with external mobility between firms as the focal turnover event.
n_sample: 17,810 person-year spells and 1,449 turnover events in the main GEE tables.
authors: Dobrev, S. D.; Kim, T.-Y.
theories: career mobility and turnover theory; organizational form identity; resource partitioning theory
keywords: Korean TV advertising industry; career mobility; generalist organizations; individual turnover; organizational form identity; specialist organizations
research_question: The paper asks how organizational form identity, especially the distinction between specialist and generalist firms, shapes individual voluntary turnover beyond the structural effect of firm size. It examines whether specialist employment increases turnover through perceived weak internal career prospects while also reducing turnover for employees whose experience, rank, or educational prestige makes specialist work more appealing.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level: employees interpret their own career experience through the social identity attached to the employing organizational form. Specialist firms create a push toward turnover because employees expect weaker internal labor markets and slower advancement; long promotion waiting times intensify that push. At the same time, specialists have identity-based appeal because they are viewed as flexible, less bureaucratic, and more meaningful workplaces, so experienced, high-ranking, or high-status employees are less likely to leave specialists than employees without those career buffers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to turnover research by bringing organizational form identity into models that usually emphasize individual-level psychological, demographic, or career variables. It extends resource partitioning and organizational form theory by showing how macro-level distinctions between specialist and generalist firms shape individual career mobility. It also clarifies why firm size alone is theoretically underspecified: size becomes consequential partly because it is encoded in categorical identities that employees use to interpret work and career prospects.
practical_implication: The findings imply that retention practices should be tailored by organizational form. Specialist firms may retain employees more effectively by clarifying promotion schedules while emphasizing autonomy, creativity, purpose, flexibility, and intrinsic rewards. They may also gain more from disproportionate investment in higher-echelon, experienced, or high-status employees, who are most likely to fit specialist employment.
limitations: The authors caution that the single-industry Korean advertising context limits generalizability, even though similar patterns may occur in professional service industries such as investment banking or management consulting. They also note that the data lack fine-grained information on formal and informal organizational structures and employment policies inside each agency. The study lacks gender data, which could meaningfully affect observed career patterns.
future_research: Future research should test whether the observed specialist-generalist turnover dynamics generalize to other industries, countries, and cultural settings. The paper also points to work that can directly observe organizational employment policies, internal structures, and individual perceptions of organizational form identities. More broadly, future turnover models should examine how organizational forms shape attachment, commitment, satisfaction, and other psychological mechanisms usually studied at the individual level.
abstract: Ideas about the role of the organization in models of voluntary turnover remain scant. We posit that the social audience in general, and people working in organizations in particular, sort organizations into categories (“organizational forms”) and rely on knowledge of the taken-for-granted external identities of firms in these categories to interpret their experience as employees. Although many of these interpretations revolve around size, categorical distinctions between “small” and “large” firms pack concepts and ideas that extend significantly beyond a simple distinction based on size, and would be better understood as an organizational form distinction between specialist and generalist firms. Focusing on the organizational form of a specialist, we claim that two features of its form identity work against each other to influence turnover: employees of specialists realize that it is hard to develop careers internally (a push factor) but value the more relaxed environment, meaningful work, and flexibility of their jobs (a pull effect). We propose a theory to parse out the two effects, find empirical support for it in analyses of managerial turnover in the Korean TV advertising industry, and conclude that the construct of organizational form offers an opportunity to extend models of career mobility and individual turnover.
