title: The Spawning of Ecosystems: How Cohort Effects Benefit New Ventures
methods: Empirical quantitative longitudinal study of VC-backed U.S. biotech ventures using dyad-year and firm-year panel data; models include panel OLS, rare-events logistic regression, panel negative binomial regression, firm fixed effects for knowledge-quality tests, and robustness checks using instrumental variables, propensity-score matching, and stochastic actor-oriented models.
industry: Biotech new ventures.
time_period: Ventures founded from 1990 to 2000 and tracked until 2013.
units: Dyad-year observations among new biotech ventures for overlap, alliances, and inventor migration; firm-year observations for knowledge quality.
n_sample: 658 VC-backed biotech ventures; more than 1.6 million dyad-year observations; 5,167 firm-year observations in the knowledge-quality models.
authors: Howard, M. D.; Boeker, W.; Andrus, J. L.
theories: entrepreneurial migration; knowledge management perspective; migration cohort effects; organizational spawning; social capital
keywords: cohort effect; entrepreneurial migration; inventor migration; knowledge quality; migration cohort ecosystem; shared migration ties
research_question: The paper asks how the spawning of knowledge from incumbent firms, represented by inventors moving from incumbents to new ventures, creates a cohort-based ecosystem of firms that can share knowledge, engage in direct exchange, and create higher-quality knowledge. It focuses on whether shared migration cohort ties shape knowledge overlap, market overlap, alliances, inventor hiring, and knowledge quality among new biotech ventures.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that inventors who share contemporaneous experience at the same incumbent carry similar knowledge management practices, technological understandings, and social connections into different new ventures. These shared migration cohort ties make ventures more likely to recognize similar technologies and markets, form alliances, and hire from one another. Cohort ecosystem membership also broadens a new venture's knowledge search by making other ecosystem firms' knowledge developments more observable and usable. However, prior direct collaboration among the migrating inventors can reduce novelty because firms may be building from overly similar prior knowledge.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes the concept of a migration cohort effect: inventors with shared contemporaneous incumbent experience create unique relationships between the new ventures they join. It extends employee migration and organizational spawning research beyond dyadic parent-to-progeny knowledge transfer by showing that multiple progeny firms can form an intermediate ecosystem structure within an industry. It also contributes to innovation research by linking migration-based affiliations to knowledge overlap, market overlap, direct exchange, and knowledge quality.
practical_implication: The findings imply that entrepreneurial ventures may benefit not only from hiring knowledge workers from successful incumbents, but also from understanding the broader cohort ecosystem created by those workers' shared histories. For managers in technology-intensive fields, migration cohort ties can identify likely alliance partners, talent pools, and firms pursuing related knowledge trajectories. For policymakers, the results suggest that regulations governing hiring practices and labor mobility can affect interorganizational knowledge flows and innovation dynamics, not just individual employment moves.
limitations: The authors note that founders and migrating knowledge workers may leave incumbents precisely to pursue different technologies, products, or markets, which could limit or negate shared incumbent imprinting. They also acknowledge that larger incumbents may expose employees to only partly overlapping knowledge management practices, and that cohort ecosystem effects may diminish as ventures grow, diversify, hire new personnel, change alliance portfolios, or move into other technological areas. The robustness tests address several alternatives, but the instrumental-variable analysis could not fully rule out endogeneity for direct inventor migration.
future_research: Future research could examine how migration cohort ecosystems affect the evolution and pace of technological advancement across industries, including whether strong early incumbents eventually create societal benefits or stifle field-level development. Scholars could study technological complexity, modularity, coordinated action among ecosystem firms, comparisons across parent-firm ecosystems, and parent-level conditions that make some incumbents better spawners of successful generational spin-offs. The authors also call for work on additional outcomes such as survival, growth, overall performance, product launches, successful IPOs, firm characteristics, capabilities, and power imbalances between firms.
abstract: Research has examined the process of “entrepreneurial migration,” whereby employees from successful industry incumbents move to new ventures. This phenomenon has been linked to direct benefits to entrepreneurial firms, offering valuable knowledge and routines obtained by employees during their tenure at incumbent firms. We propose a theoretical framework in which shared experience—a common background in beneficial knowledge management practices—creates a “cohort effect,” facilitating direct ties and innovation benefits to new ventures receiving inventors from the same incumbent firms. Analyzing longitudinal data on inventor migration to 658 new biotech ventures tracked from 1990 to 2013, we find shared migration ties increase knowledge and market overlap between firms, enhancing their likelihood of direct engagement through alliances and employee hiring as well as the quality of knowledge they develop. Our core theoretical contribution is the identification of a migration cohort effect, in which inventors who share contemporaneous experiences at incumbent firms and migrate to new ventures create unique relationships between those ventures. Where prior research on spawning and migration has focused primarily on the direct benefit of human capital transfer from incumbents to new ventures, we explore the broader network implications of similarities and interactions between firms receiving this human capital.

title: A Functional Model of Workplace Envy and Job Performance: When do Employees Capitalize on Envy by Learning from Envied Targets?
methods: Empirical quantitative study using two round-robin survey data sets from South Korean cosmetic and financial industry employees; the authors use social relations modeling for dyadic envy, learning, friendship, and undermining relationships, and multilevel analyses for job performance outcomes.
industry: Cosmetic sales employees in Study 1; bank tellers and insurance salespersons in Study 2.
time_period: Two survey waves separated by approximately one month; Study 2 also uses insurance sales performance for the three months after the Time 2 survey.
units: Employee dyads nested in teams, plus individual job performance ratings and insurance sales performance.
n_sample: Study 1 main analysis: 52 employees in 11 teams, producing 267 directed dyadic ratings. Study 2 main analysis: 215 employees in 30 teams, producing 1,688 directed dyadic ratings; sales performance was available for 134 employees.
authors: Lee, K.; Duffy, M. K.
theories: core self-evaluations; peer-based learning; social functional view of emotions; workplace envy research
keywords: advice seeking; core self-evaluations; friendship; job performance; observational learning; social functional view of emotions; social undermining; workplace envy
research_question: The paper asks how and when workplace envy can improve job performance rather than only producing destructive behavior. It specifically examines whether envious employees learn from envied targets through observational learning and advice seeking, and whether core self-evaluations and workplace friendship make constructive responses more likely than social undermining.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that envy signals an unfavorable status comparison and creates pressure to reduce the gap between the envier and the envied target. Employees may respond destructively by undermining the target, but they may also use the target as a source of performance-relevant information. Higher core self-evaluations and friendship make it more likely that envy is handled through advice seeking, and friendship also helps in Study 2 for observational learning. Advice seeking is the more robust learning channel and remains a stronger predictor of performance when observational learning is considered at the same time.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a functional model of workplace envy that treats envy as capable of both destructive and constructive transmutation. It extends workplace envy research by identifying peer-based learning, especially advice seeking from the envied target, as a mechanism through which envy can improve performance. It also refines social functional emotion theory by showing that personal and relational resources shape whether envy serves competitive and coordinating functions or turns into social undermining.
practical_implication: Organizations should not treat envy only as a toxic emotion to suppress. Managers can help employees convert upward comparisons into development by encouraging learning from high performers and by using appraisal conversations to identify relative weaknesses constructively. The findings also imply that building positive self-regard and workplace friendships can make advice seeking from envied colleagues more likely.
limitations: The authors did not test whether learning and performance benefits eventually reduce envy, so the feedback loop from constructive action back to emotional experience remains unclear. Several non-performance constructs were self-reported, although the authors used temporal separation, supervisor ratings, archival sales data, and marker-variable checks to reduce common-method concerns. Study 1 also relied on single-item roster measures, and both studies were conducted in South Korea, which may limit generalizability to more individualistic cultural settings.
future_research: Future research could examine whether successful learning from envied targets reduces envy over longer repeated episodes, or whether persistent comparison gaps shift envy toward admiration or other targets. Scholars could also test curvilinear envy effects, since very high envy may stop increasing constructive advice seeking or undermining. Further studies should examine whether the model generalizes across cultures, especially individualistic cultural settings.
abstract: We integrate the social functional view of emotions with recent developments in workplace envy research to develop and test a novel theoretical framework showing that envious employees can use their envy to promote self-enhancing actions rather than other-diminishing behaviors. We theorize that enviers’ core self-evaluations and friendship ties will attenuate the extent to which enviers undermine envied targets and promote the extent to which enviers actively learn from their envied targets through observational learning and advice seeking. Using two data sets from round-robin surveys of employees in the cosmetic (Study 1) and the financial (Study 2) industries, we show that, while enviers undermine envied targets, they also capitalize on their envy by seeking advice from the envied targets, and enviers who have higher core self-evaluations and friendship with the envied targets are more likely to seek advice from those targets; higher core self-evaluation also decreases the likelihood of undermining the envied targets. We found limited support for the role of envy in triggering enviers’ observational learning. Furthermore, enviers who learn from envied targets perform better and advice seeking is more influential for enviers’ performance than observational learning.
apa_citation: Lee, K., & Duffy, M. K. (2019). A functional model of workplace envy and job performance: When do employees capitalize on envy by learning from envied targets? *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(4), 1085-1110. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1202

title: Career Resourcing and the Process of Professional Emergence
methods: Historical qualitative analytical case study using archived oral-history interviews, career-history interviews, archival and secondary sources, inductive coding, narrative analysis, and resourcing-informed process theorizing.
industry: Health services research and the American health-care system.
time_period: Emergence and institutionalization of health services research between the 1930s and the 1990s, with broader historical analysis from the 1930s to the present day.
units: Early health services researchers, their career histories, professional organizations, research centers, funding bodies, and archival accounts of the emergence of HSR.
n_sample: Core data set of 24 interviews with 23 people, supplemented by AHSR interviews and panel material, first-hand accounts, Institute of Medicine reports, secondary histories, CVs, biographies, obituaries, and related sources.
authors: Nigam, A.; Dokko, G.
theories: career resourcing; institutional theory; professional emergence; resourcing perspective; structuration theory
keywords: career actions; career resourcing; health services research; institutional change; professional emergence; resourcing perspective
research_question: The paper asks what process links individuals' career actions to the emergence of a new profession. Empirically, it examines how early health services researchers' job moves, research projects, mentoring, funding work, and institution-building actions helped create and institutionalize health services research.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / process elements: Career resourcing, career actions, assets, resources, personal career schemas, profession-building schemas, accretion, institutional work, professional community, professional infrastructure, and professional emergence.
- Career actions: Individuals moved into jobs, produced knowledge, mentored students and colleagues, obtained funding, created research centers, formed professional associations, and built tools or programs that later supported further career and profession-building actions.
- Assets / resources: Career actions generated stature, knowledge, material support, and community ties; these assets became resources when actors used them to enable subsequent actions for themselves and others.
- Schemas: Personal career schemas motivated actors to pursue interesting, fulfilling, or impactful work, while profession-building schemas oriented some later actions toward deliberately creating HSR infrastructure and community.
- Emergence pathways: Professional emergence occurred through accretion across individuals and generations, and through deliberate institutional work that built the professional community and infrastructure.

The process is recursive and temporal. Career actions generated assets that actors later converted into resources, and those resources enabled further career actions, including actions by other people. Over time, dispersed career-motivated actions accumulated into a professional community, body of knowledge, and infrastructure; in some cases, those accumulated resources also made deliberate profession-building institutional work possible.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional change and professional emergence theory by explaining a bottom-up process through which individual careers can shape institutions. It extends institutional work theory by showing that institutional consequences can arise not only from purposive institution-building but also from dispersed, personally motivated career actions that accumulate over time. It also brings resourcing theory into a multilevel institutional setting, showing how assets become resources across careers, generations, and professional fields.
practical_implication: The study implies that new professions can be built by supporting career pathways, research infrastructure, mentoring relationships, funding opportunities, and jobs that allow dispersed actors to generate and reuse resources. For actors trying to develop an emerging profession, the findings suggest that personal career moves and institution-building actions are not separate domains: career development can gradually create the stature, knowledge, material support, and community needed for professional infrastructure.
limitations: The authors note that the retrospective interviews at the heart of the data create limitations because respondents may imperfectly recall their career actions and may present themselves as more heroic or coherent than they were at the time.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how career resourcing interacts with other professional-emergence mechanisms, including ethos, identity, discourse, work practices, and institutional work. It also suggests examining the coevolution of new professions, careers, jobs, and work in organizations, and comparing career resourcing processes across existing professions, different institutional events, and complex multilevel systems.
abstract: We theorize a career resourcing process that explains how individuals can create a new profession. Using historical archives, we trace the emergence of health services research as a new research profession through the career actions of early practitioners. We find that career resourcing can lead to the institutionalization of a new profession by (a) a process of accretion, wherein people pursuing fulfilling careers generate resources that contribute to institutionalization, or (b) institutional work to deliberately build the professional community and infrastructure. We contribute to research on institutional change by specifying career actions that can lead to the institutionalization of a new profession, and by developing theory that accounts for the motivations and the means of individuals to act in ways that result in the institutionalization of a new profession.

title: Social Identification in Multiteam Systems: The Role of Depletion and Task Complexity
methods: Laboratory simulation study with repeated multiteam-system performance episodes, a manipulated task-complexity condition, aggregated survey measures, multilevel path analysis in Mplus 7, and bootstrapped moderated mediation tests.
industry: University business-college teamwork program using the Leadership Development Exercise simulation.
time_period: Two program years, with each multiteam system participating in three performance episodes after prior team training.
units: Undergraduate students nested in component teams, multiteam systems, and performance episodes.
n_sample: 289 students, 66 component teams, 22 multiteam systems, and 66 performance episodes.
authors: Porck, J. P.; Matta, F. K.; Hollenbeck, J. R.; Oh, J. K.; Lanaj, K.; Lee, S. M.
theories: depletion research; self-regulation theory; social identity theory; uncertainty management theory
keywords: depletion; multiteam system performance; multiteam systems; social identification; social identity theory; task complexity; uncertainty perspective
research_question: The paper asks how identification with a component team versus identification with the larger multiteam system affects multiteam system performance. It further asks whether depletion mediates those effects and whether task complexity strengthens the indirect relationships.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that multiteam system identification directs members toward an abstract higher-order identity that increases uncertainty about norms, interdependencies, and appropriate action, thereby depleting cognitive resources and reducing performance. Component team identification instead gives members a more concrete identity prototype tied to specialized team tasks, reducing uncertainty and depletion. Task complexity intensifies both pathways because complex multiteam-system tasks make information cues, interdependence, and environmental change harder to manage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the assumption that higher-order system identification should always improve performance in multiteam systems. It extends social identity theory by showing that nested identities can have opposite performance implications when the higher-order target is abstract and uncertainty-inducing. It also links multiteam-system theory with depletion and task-complexity research by specifying depletion as the resource mechanism connecting identification to system performance.
practical_implication: Managers of complex multiteam systems should not assume that cultivating identification with the largest collective is always beneficial. When task complexity is high, the paper suggests that performance may improve when members identify strongly with their component teams and trust leadership teams to coordinate the broader system. Leaders should reduce uncertainty by clarifying component-team roles, interdependencies, and the system-level coordination picture.
limitations: The study uses undergraduate students in a laboratory simulation, so generalizability to experienced employees and field multiteam systems remains uncertain. The level-1 sample of 66 performance episodes is relatively small, although the authors note that this is sizable for multiteam-system research and use a within-subject design to improve precision. The laboratory task offers psychological realism, but the authors note that how its goal hierarchy maps to real-world goal hierarchies is debatable.
future_research: Future research should test whether the findings generalize to field settings, older and more experienced working adults, larger samples, and multiteam systems with different levels of task complexity. Additional studies could examine how different component-team roles, especially boundary-spanning leadership teams, alter the costs and benefits of social identification. The paper also points to future work on how multiple identities combine, conflict, overlap, or shift over time in multiteam systems.
abstract: Organizations construct multiteam systems to address complex challenges that require the joint efforts of multiple teams. Taking an uncertainty perspective and integrating social identity theory with depletion research, we theoretically and empirically examine the role of social identification in multiteam system performance. In contrast to general assumptions in the literature regarding the need to develop identity at the highest level of a system, we argue that within a multiteam system, identification with that system negatively relates to multiteam system performance, whereas identification with the component team positively relates to multiteam system performance. Our uncertainty perspective suggests that identification with the multiteam system introduces uncertainty regarding the appropriate norms and interdependencies in the system, which leads to more depletion, and consequently lower system performance. Conversely, identification with the component team offers less uncertainty, resulting in less depletion and higher multiteam system performance. Thus, our integrated theoretical framework suggests that depletion mediates the negative effects of multiteam system identification and the positive effects of component team identification on multiteam system performance. Moreover, consistent with our uncertainty perspective, the indirect effect of identification on multiteam system performance via depletion is stronger when task complexity is high and weaker when task complexity is low.

title: Middle-Status Conformity Revisited: The Interplay between Achieved and Ascribed Status
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study using OLS models with conductor and decade fixed effects, robust standard errors, curvilinear interaction terms, split-sample tests, and hybrid between-within robustness models.
industry: U.S. symphony orchestras and orchestral classical music repertoire.
units: Conductor-year observations for principal conductors of major U.S. symphony orchestras.
n_sample: 1,031 conductor-year observations; 100 principal conductors; 27 major U.S. symphony orchestras.
authors: Prato, M.; Kypraios, E.; Ertug, G.; Lee, Y. G.
theories: ascribed and achieved status; middle-status conformity theory (Phillips & Zuckerman, 2001); status inconsistency
keywords: U.S. symphony orchestras; achieved status; ascribed status; conformity; middle-status conformity
research_question: The paper asks when middle-status conformity applies and when the opposite pattern, middle-status deviance, should be expected. It examines whether actors' conformity based on achieved status depends on the ascribed status inherited from their social group.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that ascribed status changes how actors interpret their achieved-status position. High ascribed status gives low- and high-achieved-status actors security or aspiration pressure that encourages deviance, leaving middle-status actors most conformist. Low ascribed status instead makes low-achieved-status actors focus on survival and high-achieved-status actors protect a precarious standing, producing greater conformity at the low and high ends of achieved status.
theoretical_contribution: The paper revisits the scope conditions of middle-status conformity and argues that the classic inverted U-shaped pattern is a special case rather than a universal default. It contributes a more general status theory by distinguishing malleable achieved status from less malleable ascribed status and showing that their interplay can generate either middle-status conformity or middle-status deviance. It also extends research on multiple status hierarchies by emphasizing hierarchy malleability as a condition shaping behavior under status inconsistency.
practical_implication: The findings imply that audiences and organizations should not expect status-based conformity pressures to operate uniformly across actors. In fields where inherited group status is salient, similarly achieved individuals may make different conformity or deviance choices because they face different risks of exclusion, scrutiny, or legitimacy loss. The framework can inform analysis of leaders' strategic decisions when diffuse characteristics such as gender, race, or country of origin interact with individually achieved status.
limitations: The authors state that the theory applies to contexts with variation on salient status characteristics and with a clear distinction between high- and low-ascribed-status groups. They note that the study treats ascribed status as fixed, even though nominal characteristics can sometimes change or be reinterpreted. They also acknowledge that the empirical test focuses on individual actors, although they argue the logic may extend to organizations.
future_research: Future research could examine settings where ascribed status is more variegated than a high-versus-low distinction. Scholars could study how changes in nominal status characteristics, scandals, institutional changes, or sudden status gains and losses affect conformity through other status lenses. The authors also call for research on how achieved organizational status interacts with less malleable status transferred by country, industry, or category affiliation.
abstract: Decisions about conforming to or deviating from conventional practices in a field are an important concern of organization and management theory. The position that actors occupy in the status hierarchy has been shown to be an important determinant of these decisions. The dominant hypothesis, known as “middle-status conformity,” posits that middle-status actors are more likely to conform to conventional practices than highand low-status actors do. We challenge this hypothesis by revisiting its fundamental assumptions and developing a theory according to which actors’ propensity to conform based on their achieved status further depends on the ascribed status that they inherit from their social group. Specifically, we propose that middle-status conformity applies only to actors who have a sense of security, based on their high ascribed status. Regarding actors with low ascribed status, we propose that highand low-status actors show greater conformity than middle-status actors. We test our hypotheses using data from the U.S. symphony orchestras from 1918 to 1969.

title: New Ways of Seeing Big Data
methods: Editorial essay (From the Editors). The authors develop a programmatic argument about big data as a research perspective, methodology, and organizational phenomenon, then outline publication barriers and guidance for management scholars.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Simsek, Zeki; Vaara, Eero; Paruchuri, Srikanth; Nadkarni, Sucheta; Shaw, Jason D.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: big data; ethics; machine learning; management scholarship; methodology; privacy; theory
research_question: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Big data should not be treated as the end of theory or as a purely data-driven substitute for conventional management research. The editors argue for a two-way dialogue in which management scholarship both learns from and actively shapes big data research.
- Perspective: The paper challenges pure empiricism, emphasizes the continued importance of causal adequacy and context, and suggests that big data inquiry may need abductive combinations of deductive and inductive logic.
- Concept: The editors define big data around the generation, organization, storage, retrieval, analysis, and visualization of large and varied data sets, while noting the methodological, epistemological, and politico-ethical questions attached to such data.
- Methodology: The editorial highlights data access, cleaning, integration, storage, computational skill, machine learning, visualization, transparency, and theory-guided data construction as central methodological concerns.
- Phenomenon: The paper frames big data as an organizational and societal phenomenon involving strategy, decision-making, data teams, infrastructure, power shifts, ethics, privacy, access, and inequality.
- Publishing barriers: Authors need to justify why big data fits the research question, make data creation and analysis transparent, validate constructs, avoid computational black boxes, and show the importance of predictive findings rather than relying on massive sample size alone.

The process logic is editorial and programmatic rather than causal. Simsek and colleagues argue that management scholars can enrich big data research by bringing attention to theory, context, construct clarity, research design, ethics, and organizational phenomena. At the same time, big data can expand management scholarship by enabling new empirical approaches, new questions about organizations and decision-making, and new forms of theory building and testing when used carefully.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes a management-oriented agenda for studying big data as concept, methodology, and phenomenon. Its theoretical contribution is not a new formal theory but a positioning argument: management research should resist claims that data volume replaces theory and should instead use theory, context, and construct clarity to make big data research more meaningful and managerially relevant.
practical_implication: Management scholars pursuing big data studies should explain why big data is appropriate for the research question, document data access, integration, analysis, and visualization choices, and justify analytical techniques in relation to the claims being made. They should also address transparency, construct validity, ethical and privacy risks, and the interpretability of machine-learning or predictive results.
limitations: The editorial does not provide empirical evidence, test propositions, or evaluate specific big data studies. Its guidance is necessarily broad because it addresses an emergent research area with rapidly changing technologies, techniques, access conditions, and publication expectations.
future_research: The editors encourage future management research on when big data provides actionable insight better than smaller high-quality data, how theory can guide data cleaning and construction, and how conventional and big data methods can complement each other. They also call for research on organizational big data teams, decision-making, infrastructure, ethics, privacy, unequal access, and the possibility of a big data divide.

title: Holier than Thou? Identity Buffers and Adoption of Controversial Practices in the Islamic Banking Category
methods: Empirical mixed-methods design: random-effects logistic regression on a panel of Islamic banks, with country and year fixed effects, bank-group clustered robust standard errors, and qualitative interviews/documents for industry context.
industry: Islamic banking
units: Full-fledged Islamic banks observed by bank-year, with CB-owned Islamic banks used to construct outsider code-violation and code-preservation measures
n_sample: Main quantitative sample: 66 full-fledged Islamic banks and 42 CB-owned Islamic banks in 12 countries; 536 bank-year observations in the main models; qualitative supplement: 21 open-ended interviews
authors: Syakhroza, M. A.; Paolella, L.; Munir, K.
theories: organizational categories; organizational identity; social identity theory
keywords: Islamic banking; code preservation; code violation; derivatives; identity buffer; zakat
research_question: The paper asks how the relative difference between a code violator's identity and an insider's identity affects the focal insider's decision to adopt a new code-violating practice. Empirically, it asks when full-fledged Islamic banks adopt derivatives, and whether that likelihood differs when derivatives are first adopted by peer insiders versus CB-owned outsider banks.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an identity-buffer process. When a peer insider violates a code, other insiders avoid imitation because endorsing a fellow insider's deviance threatens the collective insider identity. When an outsider violates a code, insiders can adopt the profitable controversial practice while retaining their relative identity advantage over outsiders. When outsiders simultaneously preserve another salient code through zakat payment, that advantage narrows, so insiders become less willing to follow the outsider's code violation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational category research by showing that insiders' responses to code violation depend on relative identity differences between the violator and potential adopter, not simply on whether a practice violates a category code. It develops the concept of an identity buffer to explain why outsider-initiated violations can diffuse to insiders while insider-initiated violations are resisted. It also extends social identity theory by showing that in-group loyalty can make insiders stricter toward in-group deviants rather than uniformly favoring them.
practical_implication: For organizations in identity-sensitive categories, controversial practice adoption depends on who introduces the practice and whether identity differences remain visible to audiences. Incumbents may have more room to copy outsider practices when their insider identity remains distinct, but that room narrows when outsiders credibly display code-preserving behavior. Outsider entrants can therefore shape insider behavior not only by violating codes but also by selectively preserving other salient codes.
limitations: The authors note that their measures of code violation and code preservation are binary, even though identity and code adoption are multidimensional. They were also unable to fully examine how outsiders' social position in their original conventional banking category shaped their entry into Islamic banking. A further boundary condition is that derivatives are profitable financial products, so the findings may differ for code violations whose economic payoff is neutral or uncertain.
future_research: Future work could measure gradations in code violation and preservation, including how a firm's grade of category membership affects the type and extent of code violation it can undertake. Researchers could also examine how outsiders' prior-category identities shape whether they enter a new category as code violators, code preservers, or both. Another avenue is to study code violations with uncertain economic value, such as emerging technological standards, to see whether identity-buffer dynamics operate similarly when adoption is risky rather than clearly profitable.
abstract: Existing scholarship on categories has frequently highlighted how some category members violate codes that others diligently abide by. In this paper, we consider differences in identity across category members, and ask how these relative differences determine their response to a code-violating change. Taking a case where category members are identified as “insiders” and “outsiders,” we argue that insiders’ reaction to a code violation depends upon the extent to which they believe their identity is distinct from the code violator’s, who might be an insider or an outsider. We suggest that it is the presence or absence of an “identity buffer”—i.e., a relative identity advantage—that determines insiders’ reaction. We hypothesize that when a fellow category insider introduces a code violation, the focal insider will be more likely to refrain from the practice. When an outsider introduces the violation, insiders will be more likely to adopt the violation provided they can retain an identity buffer. We posit that when outsiders adopt code-preserving behavior, thus narrowing the identity buffer between insiders and outsiders, it will mitigate insiders’ likelihood of code violation adoption. We find support for our hypotheses using data on the Islamic banking industry in 12 countries (2003–2014).

title: Defending Mao’s Dream: How Politicians’ Ideological Imprinting Affects Firms’ Political Appointment in China
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of Chinese city-year observations using ordinary least squares regressions with city fixed effects, year dummies, interaction tests, instrumental-variable robustness checks, alternative dependent variables, and firm-level robustness models.
industry: Privately held publicly listed firms on the Shenzhen and Shanghai Stock Exchanges; no single industry focus is reported.
units: City-year observations matched to incumbent mayors and the political appointments of private listed firms headquartered in those cities.
n_sample: 2,402 city-year observations; 760 city mayors; 242 Chinese cities.
authors: Wang, Danqing; Du, Fei; Marquis, Christopher
theories: imprinting theory (Marquis & Tilcsik, 2013); political exchange view of corporate political strategy; political ideology
keywords: China; corporate political strategies; ideological imprinting; political ideology; private firms' political appointments
research_question: The paper asks how city mayors' imprinted political ideologies affect the likelihood that private firms in their jurisdictions receive political appointments in China. It further examines when that ideological imprint is intensified by prior Cultural Revolution exposure and when it persists or decays depending on communist legacy and economic development in the mayor's working environment.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that joining the Communist Party during the Mao era imprints mayors with orthodox communist ideology and party identity that make private entrepreneurs appear less legitimate as political insiders. Mayors with stronger imprints therefore endorse fewer private-firm executives for PC or PPCC deputyship. The imprint is stronger when mayors experienced the Cultural Revolution at a young age, persists or strengthens in provinces with stronger communist legacies, and attenuates in economically developed cities where market-oriented demands make the old ideology less compatible with current governance tasks.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to corporate political strategy research by shifting attention from firms' demand for political ties to politicians' receptivity to those ties. It shows that politicians' ideological values are antecedents of firms' political participation, not merely background context for instrumental exchange.

It also contributes to individual-level imprinting theory by showing that imprint strength and persistence vary with prior ideological experiences and later imprint-environment fit. The paper extends political ideology research beyond the U.S. liberal-conservative framing by examining Chinese communist ideology and party affiliation as both a value system and an in-group identity.
practical_implication:
For firms, political appointment depends not only on their own resources, contribution, or willingness to pursue political ties, but also on the ideological background of local political decision makers. Private firms operating in authoritarian or transitional settings may face different political-access prospects across jurisdictions because officials interpret the legitimacy of business participation differently.

For policymakers and analysts, the findings imply that state-firm interactions should be evaluated through the attributes of state agents, not only through formal institutions or aggregate state interests. The same political appointment channel can carry different consequences depending on the decision maker's ideological imprint.
limitations:
The authors state that the study remains theoretically silent on firm-level dynamics, even though supplementary analyses suggest firms benefit less from appointments when mayors have strong communist ideology. They also note that the paper does not theorize interaction patterns between mayors and party secretaries in China's dual power structure.

The study's China setting is powerful for examining communist ideological imprinting, but the authors caution that its institutional arrangements limit generalizability. The communist ideology imprint is most applicable to transitional economies such as those in Eastern Europe, Russia, and Asia.
future_research:
Future research could theorize how firms respond strategically to politicians' biased attitudes and how different types of firms are affected by politicians' ideology. Further work could examine power sharing between mayors and party secretaries and how leader experience or discretion changes firms' political participation.

The authors also encourage research on how city-level economic and institutional conditions shape mayor turnover and the antecedents of mayor ideology. Comparative work could examine other political ideologies and how they affect firms' strategies in different institutional contexts.
abstract: Prior studies on corporate political strategies have taken an exchange view to examine these strategies’ benefits and costs for firms and politicians, but have paid less attention to how politicians’ political values shape their perceptions of, and willingness to engage in, these exchanges. We investigate how politicians’ imprinted political ideologies affect the likelihood of firms’ political appointments. Examining 760 city mayors across 242 Chinese cities from 2001 to 2013, we find that cities have fewer private firms appointed to local councils if the mayor—the key decision maker for such appointments—is more strongly imprinted with an orthodox communist ideology that opposes capitalism. The intensity and evolution of such an ideological imprint are influenced by contextual factors. The imprint’s strength is shaped by the mayors’ prior exposure to intense ideological experiences, such as experiencing the Cultural Revolution at a young age. Working in an environment consistent with the ideology (e.g., a province with a greater communist legacy) sustains and even strengthens the imprint, whereas working in an environment inconsistent with the ideology (e.g., a city with greater economic development) attenuates it. We discuss the implications of these findings for political strategy research, imprinting theory, and nascent research on political ideology.

title: Deviant versus Aspirational Risk Taking: The Effects of Performance Feedback on Bribery Expenditure and R&D Intensity
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of Chinese listed firms using spline models for performance below and above social and historical aspirations, industry-clustered standard errors, year, industry, and city fixed effects, and multiple robustness tests.
industry: Chinese listed companies outside the financial sector.
units: Firm-year observations for listed companies.
n_sample: 9,633 firm-year observations covering 2,224 listed companies.
authors: Xu, D.; Zhou, K. Z.; Du, F.
theories: behavioral theory of the firm; problemistic search; slack search
keywords: R&D intensity; behavioral theory of the firm; bribery expenditure; performance feedback; risk-taking behavior
research_question: The paper asks whether low- and high-performing firms differ in their risk-taking behavior when performance feedback places them below or above aspiration levels. It examines whether negative feedback motivates deviant risk taking through bribery expenditure while positive feedback motivates aspirational risk taking through R&D intensity, and whether legal development and industry competition condition those relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that performance below aspirations creates pressure for quick remedies, making low-performing firms more willing to use myopic and deviant actions such as bribery. Performance above aspirations reduces immediate strain and directs firms toward future-oriented capability building, making high-performing firms more likely to invest in R&D. Strong legal development weakens the bribery path and strengthens the R&D path, while high competition intensifies both the bribery response among low performers and the R&D response among high performers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the behavioral theory of the firm by using a consistent motivation-based logic for both below- and above-aspiration performance rather than combining problemistic search for poor performance with slack-capacity logic for strong performance. It distinguishes deviant risk taking from aspirational risk taking and shows that firms at different points relative to aspirations are not simply more or less risk seeking, but tend toward different types of risky action. It also extends BTOF by theorizing legal development and industry competition as environmental boundary conditions.
practical_implication: The findings imply that regulators and investors should watch low-performing firms more closely for bribery risk, especially where legal development is weak or industry competition is high. They also suggest that strong legal institutions can both deter corruption among troubled firms and encourage R&D among high-performing firms. Competition is more ambiguous as a policy lever because it may stimulate innovation among strong performers while also increasing bribery pressure among weak performers.
limitations: The authors note that the bribery expenditure measure is a proxy based on abnormal entertainment and travel expenses, and that it cannot perfectly separate bribes from conventional lobbying or relationship-building expenses. They also state that the study cannot concurrently examine morality or ethics as a moderator of deviant risk taking. The China setting provides useful institutional variation, but the authors caution that bribery, guanxi, and gift-giving may operate differently from developed-economy contexts.
future_research: Future research should develop more objective and accurate measures of bribery. It should examine moral and ethical factors as additional boundary conditions for the relationship between performance feedback and bribery. The authors also call for studies across wider national contexts, including both developed and emerging economies, to test whether the same contrasting risk-taking patterns generalize beyond China.
abstract: Combining the theses of “problemistic search” and “slack search,” past research in the behavioral theory of the firm suggests that both lowand high-performing firms may engage in the same type of risk-taking activity. We counter this view with a consistent, motivation-based logic in the theory: low-performing firms are fixated on finding shortterm solutions to immediate problems, so they have an increased probability of exhibiting deviant risk-taking behavior such as bribery, whereas high-performing firms are concerned about sustaining their competitive advantage in the long run and will more likely engage in aspirational risk taking such as research and development (R&D). Using a sample of 9,633 firm-year observations covering 2,224 listed companies in China, we find that, as a firm’s performance falls further below its aspiration level, it has larger abnormal entertainment spending, an implicit measure of bribery expenditure, but not higher R&D intensity. However, as a firm’s performance rises further above its aspiration level, it has greater R&D intensity, but not more bribery expenses. Legal development and industry competition moderate the relationship between performance feedback and risk-taking behavior.

title: Structuring Reality Through the Faultlines Lens: The Effects of Structure, Fairness, and Status Conflict on the Activated Faultlines–Performance Relationship
methods: Multi-source, multi-wave cross-lagged survey design using four waves, team member surveys, supervisor ratings, confirmatory factor analyses, and bootstrapped mediation and moderated mediation analyses.
industry: Social health care services.
time_period: Four data-collection waves at six-week intervals; calendar dates not reported in paper.
units: Teams in a Spanish health care organization.
n_sample: 271 employees and 41 leaders in 41 teams.
authors: Antino, M.; Rico, R.; Thatcher, S. M. B.
theories: faultlines theory; justice theories; social identity approach; status conflict
keywords: activated team faultlines; social identity approach; status conflict; team justice climate; team performance; team structure clarity
research_question: The paper asks how activated team faultlines affect team performance when team members use faultline-based subgroups to interpret their social reality. It specifically examines whether activated faultlines reduce team performance through lower team justice climate and higher status conflict, and whether team structure clarity weakens this process.
mechanism_summary: The argument is that activated faultlines operate as an informal sensemaking structure that makes intersubgroup status relations ambiguous or illegitimate. Those perceptions reduce team justice climate, which increases status conflict as subgroups defend or elevate perceived status. Status conflict then draws attention away from common team tasks and impairs team performance. Clear team structures provide an alternative, legitimating structure around roles, procedures, and priorities, reducing the negative effect of activated faultlines on team justice climate.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reconceptualizes activated faultlines as a sensemaking structure rather than only as a more refined diversity measure. It extends faultlines research by identifying team justice climate and status conflict as mechanisms linking activated faultlines to performance, and by showing how team structure clarity can attenuate that pathway. It also contributes a measurement approach that combines dormant faultline strength with perceived faultline activation.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat all possible demographic splits as equally threatening; the study suggests diagnosing whether team members actually perceive dormant faultlines as activated. For teams with activated faultlines, managers can reduce ambiguity and perceived illegitimacy by clarifying roles, procedures, priorities, and authority relations. The paper also suggests that leaders should attend to status expectations in diverse teams and use structure to support fairness perceptions before status conflict undermines performance.
limitations: The authors note that most measures were perceptual, except demographic information used in the activated faultline measure. The field design did not manipulate independent variables, so the cross-lagged and multisource design does not establish causality. The results come from a specific organizational and cultural context, a Spanish health care organization, which limits generalizability.
future_research: Future research could use nonobtrusive process measures and objective performance indicators to test activated faultlines and status conflict. The authors call for research designs that can test causal relationships and for replication across cultures. They also suggest longitudinal work on how activated faultlines change over time, how different diversity attributes become weighted, whether activated faultlines affect psychological safety, and whether leadership styles provide the clarity that helps manage faultline-based teams.
abstract: We investigate how activated team faultlines represent an informal sensemaking structure through which teammates interpret their social reality. Constructed from intersubgroup comparisons, activated team faultlines likely result in ambiguous or illegitimate status perceptions. Thus, activated faultlines threaten team justice climate, which drives status conflict, impairing team performance. We explore the effects of team structure clarity in providing certainty or legitimacy around status and structure, ameliorating the negative effect of activated faultlines on team justice climate. We test our model using a multi-source (three sources), multi-wave cross-lagged design (four waves) on a sample of 271 employees and 41 leaders in 41 teams. We find that the negative relationship between activated faultlines and team performance is mediated by the team justice climate–status conflict causal chain. We also find that team structure clarity reduces activated faultlines’ negative effect on team justice climate. Results highlight the value of using team faultlines, the social identity approach, and justice theories to understand how diverse teams interpret their social reality, which influences their performance. Furthermore, our research provides practical guidance to managers in building clear structures that minimize harmful effects of activated faultlines on justice perceptions and team performance.
apa_citation: Antino, M., Rico, R., & Thatcher, S. M. B. (2019). Structuring reality through the faultlines lens: The effects of structure, fairness, and status conflict on the activated faultlines-performance relationship. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(5), 1444-1470. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0054

title: The Ideator’s Bias: How Identity-Induced Self-Efficacy Drives Overestimation in Employee-Driven Process Innovation
methods: Empirical mixed-method study combining Tobit and OLS analyses of a proprietary corporate process-innovation dataset, post hoc semi-structured interviews, and four scenario-based online experiments to test whether role and social identities affect idea overvaluation through self-efficacy.
industry: Process innovation in a product division of a European-based automotive supplier, covering manufacturing processes such as injection molding, electroplating, painting, cabling, final assembly, and testing.
country: European-based firm for the corporate dataset; U.S. online panel participants for the scenario experiments.
time_period: The core corporate dataset covers process innovation ideas submitted or completed in 2009.
units: Employee-generated process innovation ideas and scenario-experiment participants.
n_sample: 944 ideas in the main corporate analysis, after missing-value exclusions; experiments report n = 153, n = 152, n = 141, and n = 298.
authors: Fuchs, C.; Sting, F. J.; Schlickel, M.; Alexy, O.
theories: identity theory; overconfidence; self-efficacy theory; social identity theory
keywords: collaborative ideation; employee-driven process innovation; ideator’s bias; organizational position; overconfidence; self-efficacy
research_question: The paper asks when and why employees overestimate the economic value of their own process innovation ideas. It focuses on whether organizational position and collaborative ideation activate role and social identities that increase self-efficacy and, in turn, intensify the ideator’s bias.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that salient role identities and social identities shape situation-specific self-efficacy. Higher-level employees draw more optimistic self-efficacy from managerial role identity, while lower-level employees gain additional collective self-efficacy when ideating in groups. The field data support higher overvaluation among higher-level and collaborative ideators, and the interaction shows that collaboration mainly raises overvaluation among lower-level employees rather than adding to already elevated higher-level self-efficacy. The interviews and experiments triangulate the identity-induced self-efficacy account and help rule out alternative explanations such as power, endowment effects, groupthink, and shared mental models.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes an organizationally embedded, situational micro-account of ideator’s bias based on identity-induced self-efficacy, moving beyond trait-like accounts of overconfidence. It also cautions innovation research against treating team-generated ideas as inherently higher potential without accounting for team members’ overvaluation. Finally, it links self-efficacy and overconfidence by showing how personal and collective self-efficacy can become a source of biased idea valuation in organizational settings.
practical_implication: The authors suggest separating idea generation from idea evaluation so ideators can gain distance from identities salient during ideation. When ideator input is necessary, managers should apply additional scrutiny to valuations from groups and higher-level employees because those contexts are especially prone to overvaluation. The paper also suggests priming accurate forecasting during evaluation rather than only encouraging inventive confidence.
limitations: The authors acknowledge the peculiarities of a process-innovation setting where accounting provides standardized evaluations and decision makers rely comparatively little on ideators’ own estimates. They also note that employees in the focal setting are encouraged to generate ideas, so overestimation could operate differently in organizations with greater inertia. Cultural orientation and organizational socialization may also affect whether role identity, group identity, or hybrid identities become salient.
future_research: Future research should test whether the findings generalize to non-Western countries, more hierarchical or more egalitarian societies, and organizations with different cultures or onboarding practices. The authors also call for work on when collective self-efficacy contributes to groupthink or escalation of commitment, and on whether identity cues can sometimes evoke moderate self-efficacy that reduces biased forecasts.
abstract: Grasping the true value of ideas is essential for corporate innovation success. When it comes to forecasting the value of one’s own innovation ideas, however, people may err systematically. In this paper, we shed light on this ideator’s bias, and examine when and why certain ideas are more prone to biased evaluations. Specifically, we argue that biased idea evaluations depend on the self-efficacy that ideators may derive from their specific role and social identity in the firm when generating a specific idea. We test our theoretical predictions of such a situation-specific perspective on overconfidence by using a corporate dataset on process innovations and their valuations. Furthermore, we triangulate our predicted mechanism and rule out alternative explanations through a series of additional interviews and four scenario-based experiments. Consistent with our situation-specific, identity-based account, we find that ideas from employees at a higher (vs. lower) organizational level, and from employees generating ideas in groups (vs. individually) are more prone to an ideator’s bias. In doing so, our study helps explain when the ideator’s bias prevails in a real-life organizational context, raises caution about some current proxies to identify high-potential ideas, and provides fresh insights to established theories around overconfidence and self-efficacy.

title: Impression Offsetting as an Early Warning Signal of Low CEO Confidence in Acquisitions
methods: Archival empirical-quantitative event-level study of large U.S. acquisitions using Tobit regression, robust standard errors clustered by firm, and controls at the CEO, board, firm, industry, and acquisition levels. The dependent variable is subsequent CEO stock option exercises; impression offsetting is measured as positive, unrelated firm-authored press releases in the three-day window centered on the acquisition announcement.
industry: Large completed majority acquisitions by S&P 500 acquirers where both acquirer and target were public U.S.-based firms.
time_period: Acquisitions announced between 1995 and 2009.
units: Acquisition events by S&P 500 firms, with CEO, board, firm, industry, press-release, stock-market, and insider-filing data.
n_sample: 491 acquisitions after missing-data exclusions from an initial 770 acquisitions.
authors: Gamache, D. L.; McNamara, G.; Graffin, S. D.; Kiley, J. T.; Haleblian, J.; Devers, C. E.
theories: agency theory; anticipatory impression management; behavioral theory; signaling theory
keywords: CEO confidence; CEO option exercises; acquisitions; anticipatory impression management; downside risk; impression offsetting
research_question: The paper asks whether investors can gauge a CEO's confidence in an acquisition when it is announced. It also asks why CEOs use anticipatory impression management, theorizing that impression offsetting around acquisition announcements is an ex ante signal that CEOs have low confidence in the acquisition's long-term value-creation potential.
mechanism_summary: The theorized mechanism is that CEOs with low acquisition-related confidence release unrelated positive information around the acquisition announcement to reduce scrutiny and buffer negative market reactions. If the acquisition later appears unlikely to create value, the CEO can protect accumulated equity value by exercising options after the announcement. The positive impression-offsetting-to-option-exercise relationship is expected to be stronger when downside risk is more salient: for older CEOs, CEOs of high-reputation firms, and CEOs operating in more dynamic industries.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to impression management research by identifying low action-specific CEO confidence as a motivation for anticipatory impression offsetting. It extends signaling theory by showing that impression offsetting can function as an unintended signal, rather than only an intentional signal, of executive confidence. It also contributes to behavioral and governance research by offering an observable way to study CEO confidence in strategic actions that may be driven by self-interest or social pressures.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that investors should treat unrelated positive announcements surrounding an acquisition as a warning signal that the CEO may lack confidence in the deal's value-creation potential. When an acquisition is accompanied by impression offsetting, investors should scrutinize the acquisition's value logic rather than interpreting the additional positive announcements in isolation.
limitations: The authors cannot directly observe CEO confidence and rely on subsequent stock option exercises as an established behavioral proxy. The design is observational and cannot fully rule out omitted-variable explanations, although the authors use extensive controls, two-stage residual inclusion Tobit models, and impact-threshold analysis. The sample is limited to large completed acquisitions by public U.S.-based S&P 500 firms with public U.S.-based targets.
future_research: The authors call for future research to examine alternative unobtrusive measures of CEO confidence and compare them with option-exercise signals. They also suggest extending impression offsetting research beyond acquisitions to other strategic and governance actions, and examining additional CEO-level moderators such as narcissism, prevention focus, or construal level.
abstract: Researchers have long been interested in understanding the motives behind CEOs’ actions. On the one hand, CEOs may pursue strategic actions because they are confident they will enhance firm value. Alternatively, CEOs may take actions even when they have low confidence in the value of those actions, perhaps driven by self-interest or social pressures. Although research suggests that CEO option exercises following an acquisition announcement are an ex post behavioral outcome of low CEO confidence in the acquisition’s value-creation potential, prior research has not identified any ex ante signals shareholders can look for to assess acquiring CEOs’ confidence when the acquisition is announced. We address this concern by exploring a potential early warning signal of low CEO confidence: impression offsetting. We theorize that impression offsetting—measured as other unrelated positive announcements made by the firm in the days immediately surrounding the acquisition announcement—may serve as an ex ante signal of low CEO confidence in the acquisition’s value-creation potential, and, as such, will be positively associated with CEO option exercises, an ex post behavioral outcome of low confidence. We test our theory with a sample of 491 large acquisitions and find consistent support for our hypotheses.

title: The Goldilocks Effect of Strategic Human Resource Management? Optimizing the Benefits of a High-Performance Work System Through the Dual Alignment of Vertical and Horizontal Fit
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study using Workplace Panel Survey data and matched financial information; the authors estimate fixed-effects models with establishment and year effects, test HPWS by market-entry-timing and HPWS-internal-consistency interactions, and use bootstrapping to test indirect effects through product sales.
industry: Business establishments across 17 industry sectors, with manufacturing the predominant sector.
time_period: Four WPS waves from 2005 to 2011, with subsequent financial performance data.
units: Business establishments observed at the establishment-year level.
n_sample: 1,416 business establishments and 3,456 establishment-year observations.
authors: Han, J. H.; Kang, S.; Oh, I.-S.; Kehoe, R. R.; Lepak, D. P.
theories: AMO framework; absorptive capacity; knowledge-based view; market entry timing research; strategic human resource management
keywords: AMO framework; financial performance; high-performance work system; horizontal fit; internal consistency; market entry timing; product sales; strategic human resource management; vertical fit
research_question: The paper asks how vertical fit and horizontal fit jointly shape the relationship between a high-performance work system and organizational performance. Specifically, it examines whether HPWS effects differ across first-mover, fast-follower, and fence-sitter market entry timing modes, and whether those effects are strengthened when HPWS practices are internally consistent across ability, motivation, and opportunity domains.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: Current product sales or financial performance, establishment size, total assets, capital-to-labor ratio, other entry timing, establishment fixed effects, and year fixed effects.

The mechanism is a dual-alignment argument. Vertical fit occurs when an HPWS supports the knowledge requirements of a firm's market entry timing mode; the authors argue that this fit is strongest for fast followers, weaker for first movers, and weakest for fence sitters. Horizontal fit occurs when the ability-, motivation-, and opportunity-enhancing domains of the HPWS are implemented with similar intensity, reducing bottlenecks in employees' knowledge search, sharing, and application. Product sales then transmits the dual-alignment effect to financial performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to SHRM by theorizing and testing the interplay between vertical and horizontal fit rather than treating them as separate fit concepts. It sharpens vertical-fit theory by focusing on market entry timing as a specific element of strategy instead of broad strategic types. It also contributes to horizontal-fit research by operationalizing internal consistency across AMO domains and showing that consistent implementation conditions when HPWS practices produce stronger performance benefits.
practical_implication: The findings imply that managers should not treat HPWS investments as universally beneficial. An HPWS is most useful when the knowledge needed for strategy execution is within employees' reach for absorption and leveraging, as in a fast-follower strategy, and less useful when knowledge requirements demand broad external experimentation or are already routine. The paper also implies that managers should balance investments across ability-, motivation-, and opportunity-enhancing HR practices rather than overemphasizing one domain.
limitations: The authors note that the HPWS-entry-timing relationship may depend on contextual factors such as technological and market change that were not directly examined. They also did not observe the intervening knowledge-based mechanisms, leaving absorptive capacity and knowledge behaviors theoretically supported but not directly measured. Additional limitations include single-rater measurement for HPWS and entry timing, many binary HR-practice measures, and the focus on one HR system type.
future_research: Future research should test the dual-alignment argument under different environmental conditions, especially where first-mover advantages vary by technological and market change. The authors call for studies that directly measure knowledge-based mechanisms and organizational flexibility as pathways linking HR systems to entry timing requirements. They also suggest examining more objective HR and strategy measures, richer response scales, and alternative HR systems that may fit other market entry timing modes.
abstract: Although vertical and horizontal fit in strategic human resource management are foundational to the links between a high-performance work system (HPWS) and organizational performance, little is known about how these two fits interact to affect organizational performance. We address this shortcoming while also advancing knowledge on each type of fit. We offer a more nuanced examination of vertical fit (which has typically been assessed with respect to organizations’ broad strategic types) by focusing on the alignment of an HPWS with an organization’s market entry timing mode—a key element of strategy. We propose that among organizations pursuing new product development, the effect of an HPWS on organizational performance is most positive under a fast-follower entry timing, followed by a first-mover and finally a fence-sitter entry timing. We then hypothesize that the benefit of vertical fit is magnified when the complementary human resources practices comprising an HPWS are implemented with greater internal consistency (or with similar intensities) across the ability, motivation, and opportunity domains—reflecting a positive interaction between vertical and horizontal fit in predicting the effectiveness of an HPWS. Analyses of four-wave nationally representative panel data yield strong support for our dual-alignment model of SHRM.
apa_citation: Han, J. H., Kang, S., Oh, I.-S., Kehoe, R. R., & Lepak, D. P. (2019). The goldilocks effect of strategic human resource management? Optimizing the benefits of a high-performance work system through the dual alignment of vertical and horizontal fit. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(5), 1388-1412. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1187

title: Where the Heart Functions Best: Reactive–Affective Conflict and the Disruptive Work of Animal Rights Organizations
methods: Inductive qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with ARO advocates, textual archival data from six large U.S. animal rights organizations, and visual archival data. The authors used grounded thematic analysis, constant comparison, NVivo coding of interview/text/video/image materials, and semiotic analysis of visuals.
industry: U.S. animal rights organizations working to disrupt industrial practices in modern factory farming operations.
time_period: Interviews were conducted between February and August 2015; archival data were collected from ARO websites.
units: ARO advocates, textual archival items, videos, and still images.
n_sample: 29 semi-structured interviews with 30 ARO advocates; textual data from six large U.S. AROs comprising 852 items; 211 videos and several hundred still images.
authors: Jarvis, L. C.; Goodrick, E.; Hudson, B. A.
theories: emotion in institutional work; institutional work; reactive–affective conflict
keywords: animal rights organizations; emotion; emotional suppression; factory farming operations; institutional work; reactive–affective conflict; visuals
research_question: The paper asks what motivates actors to suppress their emotions in support of institutional work, and how strategies of institutional work can incorporate emotional suppression while still eliciting emotion in potential supporters. It studies this problem through the disruptive institutional work of U.S. animal rights organizations seeking to challenge factory farming practices.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Reactive emotions of moral shock, anger, and sorrow; affective commitment to animal wellbeing and AROs' disruptive work; reactive–affective conflict.
- Triggering conditions: Potential supporters' cognitive and emotional investment in the status quo, and emotive norms governing the settings where institutional work is performed.
- Process / tactics: Suppressing emotion to plant seeds in face-to-face advocacy, eliciting emotion through visuals, and suppressing emotion to gather evidence in undercover investigations.
- Emergent outcomes: ARO advocates decouple emotion elicitation from their own emotional display, reducing the risk that potential supporters dismiss them as irrational or fanatical.
- Boundary conditions: The process is developed in a setting where the target practices are highly institutionalized, negative externalities are often hidden, and change agents work from the margins.

The process centers on reactive–affective conflict: advocates' reactive emotional displays may undermine the affective commitment that motivates their disruptive work. In street-side advocacy, suppressing emotion helps advocates appear calm enough to make potential supporters receptive to seeds of information, while visuals carry the emotional force. In undercover investigations, suppressing emotion allows advocates to maintain cover long enough to gather visual evidence of factory farming practices.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional work research by showing that emotion matters not only through workers' emotional displays but also through their strategic suppression of emotion. It theorizes reactive–affective conflict as an experiential mechanism linking workers' reactive emotions, affective commitments, audience characteristics, and emotive norms. It also extends research on visuality in organizations by showing how visuals can elicit emotion while decoupling that elicitation from stigmatized human advocates.
practical_implication: The paper implies that organizations trying to mobilize support for disruptive institutional projects may need to manage advocates' emotional displays as carefully as their messages. For AROs, the findings suggest that calm interpersonal engagement, emotionally resonant visuals, and disciplined evidence-gathering can be mutually reinforcing tactics when audiences are defensive or heavily invested in the status quo.
limitations: The authors state that their data collection focused on AROs and their advocates, which produces a single-sided view of the moral worth of factory farming operations and their practices. They also note that the study was not designed to test the success or failure of different emotive tactics, and that gender differences in the perception of emotional display were not the primary purpose of the research.
future_research: Future research could examine both sides of institutional battles, including how targets of disruption counter advocates' emotive tactics. Researchers could also study audience reception of emotional displays and visuals, gendered perceptions of emotion in institutional work, and how victims' emotional experiences are marshaled by third parties in work on societal grand challenges.
abstract: We study the emotive aspect of institutional work performed by U.S. animal rights organizations (AROs) attempting to disrupt industrial practices in modern factory farming operations perceived to be abusive to animals. Drawing on an inductive, qualitative analysis of interviews with ARO advocates, as well as textual and visual archival data collected from AROs’ websites, we argue that the suppression of emotion plays a critical role in AROs’ disruptive work. We find that advocates are motivated to suppress their emotions by a perceived incompatibility between their reactive emotional displays and their affective commitment to institutional work, or what we label reactive–affective conflict. We show how two triggers of reactive–affective conflict—potential supporters’ investment in the status quo and emotive norms governing institutional work—encourage ARO advocates to suppress their emotions in face-to-face interactions with audiences while attempting to elicit emotions via visuals as their strategy of disruptive work. We contribute to the literature on the strategic use of emotion in institutional work by highlighting important relationships between the characteristics of potential supporters, the nature of institutional work, and institutional workers’ management of their own emotions to further their institutional projects. In doing so, we add needed nuance to extant conceptualizations of how emotion is strategically deployed as part of purposeful efforts to create, maintain, and disrupt institutions.
apa_citation: Jarvis, L. C., Goodrick, E., & Hudson, B. A. (2019). Where the heart functions best: Reactive–affective conflict and the disruptive work of animal rights organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(5), 1358-1387. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0342
