title: Between Legitimacy and Efficiency: An Institutional Theory of Corporate Giving
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of publicly listed nonfinancial firms on the KOSPI market using generalized estimating equations with an exchangeable correlation structure, robust standard errors, industry and year dummies, lagged corporate giving, firm controls, media-content measures, and robustness checks for reverse causality.
industry: Publicly listed nonfinancial firms on the KOSPI market.
units: Firm-year observations for publicly listed nonfinancial companies.
n_sample: 5,778 firm-year observations for 747 publicly listed companies.
authors: Jeong, Y.-C.; Kim, T.-Y.
theories: institutional theory; legitimacy theory; slack resources perspective
keywords: corporate giving; economic efficiency; firm performance; institutional theory; legitimacy management cost; negative media coverage; positive media coverage
research_question: The paper asks how much organizations spend to manage external legitimacy in the context of corporate giving. It examines how positive media coverage of giving, negative media coverage of lawsuits against family owners, and firm performance jointly shape the ratio of corporate giving to sales.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a tension between social legitimacy and economic efficiency. Positive media attention raises external audience expectations, so firms spend more on corporate giving to maintain legitimacy; this effect is stronger among high-performing firms because they have more room to bear the cost. Negative media attention to lawsuits against family owners creates legitimacy pressure, but it also creates immediate efficiency pressure; firms therefore reduce giving, and the reduction is unexpectedly stronger among high performers, suggesting that they rely more heavily on economic efficiency logic under severe conflict.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends institutional theory by treating legitimacy management cost as a variable rather than an assumed or negligible condition. It argues that conformity to institutional expectations should be analyzed not only through legitimacy benefits and illegitimacy penalties, but also through the costs organizations pay to manage external legitimacy.

It also contributes to research on external audiences by showing that positive and negative media evaluations have different dynamics in corporate giving. Positive media feedback reinforces giving, whereas negative media attention to family-owner lawsuits is associated with less giving, especially under high firm performance.
practical_implication:
The findings suggest that managers should treat corporate giving as a recurring legitimacy-management decision under resource constraints, not simply as an ad hoc philanthropic act. Positive media attention can raise future audience expectations, while legal conflicts involving central owners can shift attention and resources toward immediate efficiency concerns.

For external audiences, the study implies that visibility and evaluation matter: media coverage helps shape how much firms spend on corporate giving. For firms in governance contexts where family owners are central to organizational identity, legal disputes involving those owners may materially affect social spending decisions.
limitations:
The authors caution that not all institutional conformity is costly, because some organizations may symbolically adopt practices without full implementation. The study's Korean KOSPI context and the prevalence of family-controlled firms also limit generalizability to other countries and unlisted private firms.

The data measure aggregate annual corporate giving and do not observe the portfolio of charitable activities or how spending is distributed across causes and stakeholders. The study also does not jointly observe legitimacy management costs, illegitimacy penalties, and legitimacy benefits in one integrated empirical design.
future_research:
Future research could examine how legitimacy management cost shapes not only adoption of institutionalized practices but also the scope and degree of implementation. Studies in other countries, markets, and unlisted private firms could test whether the same legitimacy-efficiency dynamics hold outside the Korean listed-firm context.

Future work could also collect portfolio-level corporate giving data and integrate legitimacy management costs, illegitimacy penalties, and legitimacy benefits in the same design. Such research would clarify how organizations decide whether legitimacy management improves performance or survival.
abstract: This study explores the cost of legitimacy management in the context of corporate giving. Specifically, how much does an organization spend in order to manage external legitimacy? We view corporate giving as a means by which firms may seek external legitimacy, and propose that, in response to evaluations of external audiences, organizations strategically manage such costs under a tension between legitimacy and efficiency concerns. We examine this argument by developing an institutional theory of corporate giving and testing our hypotheses using the corporate giving behaviors of publicly listed Korean companies from 2003 to 2011. Consistent with our proposition concerning the role of external audiences in shaping legitimacy management costs, we show that strategic decisions regarding how much a firm spends on corporate giving are related to the extent that the firm receives positive or negative media attention. Furthermore, we find that the relationship between media evaluations and corporate giving varies with a firm’s performance, which suggests that its internal efficiency condition can be an important contingency factor in determining its legitimacy management cost. We discuss the implications of these findings for the study of legitimacy management processes and the role of external audiences in such processes.

title: Dynamics and Implications of Distress Organizing
methods: Qualitative, theory-generating single-organization study of a child welfare agency, using document and website analysis, large and small group meetings, 85 semi-structured interviews, grounded theory analysis, and focused analysis of 87 child removal events.
industry: Child welfare agency responsible for child care and protection
time_period: Second year of a three-year project focused on distress and coping practices
units: Agency members across offices, including social workers, supervisors, program managers, office directors, senior administrators, and attorneys; child removal events
n_sample: 85 semi-structured individual interviews; 22 all-staff meetings; 22 office manager/director meetings; 87 child removal events described by 34 social workers
authors: Kahn, William A.
theories: compassion in organizations; organizing and sensemaking theory; social construction theory; social defenses in organizations
keywords: child welfare agency; collective avoidance mechanisms; compassion; dispassionate responding; distress organizing; grounded theory; interpersonal avoidance patterns; psychological distress
research_question: How do organization members who are regularly exposed to psychological distress socially construct ways of navigating the paradoxical demands to both extend themselves toward others and protect themselves from distressing emotional experience? The study asks how individual, interpersonal, and organizational dynamics in a child welfare agency shape members' approaches to distress, dispassionate responding, and moments of compassion.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Psychological distress, the simultaneous need to work effectively with distressed others and protect the self, and the tension between emotional availability and self-protective disengagement.
- Collective avoidance mechanisms: Intent task focus, clinical review structures, and constricting narratives that reduce the time, space, and impetus for members to experience distressing emotion.
- Interpersonal avoidance patterns: Detachment, deflection, and suppression in relationships with coworkers, clients, and supervisors.
- Emergent outcomes: A culture of disengagement, dispassionate responses to others' distress, emotional isolation, emotional exhaustion, and further avoidance.
- Counter-process: Momentary compassion when members notice, empathize with, and act to alleviate a distressed coworker's suffering, and when the distressed worker is available to receive support.

The process begins with recurring distress episodes in child welfare work, including loss, traumatic stress, and public assaults on agency members' identities. Agency members collectively organize around task completion, clinical case review, and toughness narratives while also avoiding distress interpersonally through detachment, deflection, and suppression. These mutually reinforcing patterns create distress organizing: a socially constructed process that reduces emotional availability and legitimates dispassionate responding. Distress is therefore amplified rather than alleviated, except in brief moments when caring relationships, principles of care, or identification with another's suffering support compassion.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to theory on emotional distress in organizations by shifting attention from individual coping to the social contexts that members enact together. It theorizes distress organizing as a collective-level process through which avoidance mechanisms and interpersonal patterns maintain and amplify distress. It also extends work on compassion and organizing by showing that organizations can contain prevailing cultures of disengagement alongside temporary counter-prevailing moments of compassion.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that psychological distress in emotionally intense work is not inevitable even in under-resourced settings, because avoidance mechanisms can be bounded or interrupted. Leaders and members can reduce distress amplification by legitimizing help-seeking, embedding other-focused support in role expectations, and treating emotional pain as central rather than peripheral to the work. These practices matter because narrow task focus and dispassionate case review can unintentionally leave workers isolated with distress that later affects clients and coworkers.
limitations: The study is a theory-generating case study of one child welfare agency, an organization especially likely to be compromised by distress because of child protection work, overwhelming demands, compassion fatigue, necessary evils, emotion labor, and dirty work. The author notes that this overdetermination may limit generalizability, and that distress organizing may appear differently in less emotionally saturated task environments.
future_research: Future research could examine other forms of distress organizing in which avoidance is not the central organizing response. The paper also calls for research on how leaders at different organizational levels collude with or interrupt cultures of disengagement, and on how individual tendencies, existing relationship qualities, and situational factors enable compassion to temporarily supersede dispassionate responding.
abstract: This study offers a theory-generating examination of the social construction processes through which members regularly exposed to psychological distress navigate paradoxical demands to both extend and protect the self in their work with others. A qualitative study of a child welfare agency found that members organized themselves to avoid the conscious experience of psychological distress. Distress organizing involved, first, the use of collective avoidance mechanisms that constrained the time, space, and impetus for members to experience the distress of their work; and, second, patterns of interpersonal avoidance that prevented relationships in which such experiencing could occur. The mutually reinforcing, cumulative effect of distress organizing sharply reduced members' emotional availability to clients and coworkers, which manifested as largely dispassionate responses to others' distress. Dispassionate responding led to emotional isolation and emotional exhaustion, with which members coped by further avoidance of others. Distress organizing thus amplified rather than ameliorated distress. Amplification processes were temporarily suspended when agency members momentarily created conditions for providing and receiving compassion. These findings contribute to theory about social contexts of psychological distress in organizations, the alleviation of such distress, and the bases of organizing processes.

title: The Dark Side of Transformational Leader Behaviors for Leaders Themselves: A Conservation of Resources Perspective
methods: Two experience-sampling studies using weekly leader and follower surveys over six weeks, analyzed with multilevel path analysis in Mplus. Study 1 used leader-follower dyads; Study 2 used leaders with multiple followers.
industry: Variety of industries, including banking, communications, education, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail.
time_period: Six weekly survey waves; calendar dates not reported in paper.
units: Leaders, followers, and weekly leader-follower observations.
n_sample: Study 1: 130 leader-follower dyads and 591 weekly matched surveys. Study 2: 77 leaders, 211 followers, and 378 weekly matched surveys after removing questionable observations.
authors: Lin, S.-H.; Scott, B. A.; Matta, F. K.
theories: conservation of resources theory; transformational leadership
keywords: conservation of resources theory; emotional exhaustion; experience-sampling; follower competence; follower conscientiousness; transformational leader behaviors; turnover intentions
research_question: The paper asks whether transformational leader behaviors have detrimental intrapersonal consequences for leaders even while producing follower and leader benefits. It also asks when those detriments are more likely to emerge, focusing on follower conscientiousness and follower competence as boundary conditions.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on conservation of resources theory, the paper argues that transformational leader behaviors require leaders to expend time, energy, emotion regulation, and attention. In the short term, those resource expenditures increase leader emotional exhaustion, and emotional exhaustion increases leader turnover intentions as leaders seek to protect remaining resources. The boundary-condition evidence differs across studies: follower conscientiousness moderated the indirect effect in Study 1, while follower competence, rather than broad conscientiousness, emerged as the significant moderator in Study 2.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts transformational leadership research from its predominant follower-centered focus to an actor-centric account of consequences for leaders themselves. It uses conservation of resources theory to challenge the assumption that transformational leadership is uniformly positive by showing that the same behaviors can create leader benefits and leader resource losses. It also extends within-person leadership theory by showing that follower characteristics shape the intrapersonal consequences of leader behavior.
practical_implication: The findings suggest caution in encouraging managers to display transformational leader behaviors consistently without attention to recovery and context. Leaders may need breaks, recovery activities, and more strategic deployment of transformational behaviors when they are depleted or when followers are less likely to benefit from those efforts. Organizations should recognize that behaviors often treated as desirable can still carry resource costs for leaders.
limitations: The authors note that the studies measured focal variables at the same time, so the experience-sampling and lagged controls do not establish causality. Study 1 relied on one follower report, raising concerns about selection bias and representativeness, although Study 2 included multiple followers. The paper also focuses on short-term proximal outcomes, transformational leader behaviors only, and follower characteristics rather than directly measuring whether followers waste leaders' transformational efforts.
future_research: Future research could use designs that better establish causality and test long-term consequences of transformational leader behaviors for burnout, turnover, and career mobility. The authors also call for work on other positive and negative leader behaviors, leader characteristics as moderators, and direct assessment of whether followers actually waste leaders' transformational efforts or whether leaders merely perceive those efforts as wasted.
abstract: The vast majority of theory and research to date on transformational leadership has focused on how transformational leader behaviors influence followers, portraying those behaviors as unequivocally beneficial. We pivot from this predominant focus to a focus on the detriments of transformational leader behaviors for leaders themselves. Drawing from conservation of resources theory, we propose that although transformational leader behaviors produce gains for both leaders and followers, those behaviors also trigger losses for leaders themselves. The results of two experience-sampling studies, whereby leaders and their followers completed weekly surveys for six weeks, revealed that transformational leader behaviors were associated with increases in leader emotional exhaustion and subsequent leader turnover intentions, and these detrimental consequences occurred over and above benefits to followers (Study 1) and benefits to leaders themselves (Study 2). Furthermore, the extent to which transformational leader behaviors were associated with increases in emotional exhaustion depended upon attributes of followers, such that leaders experienced greater increases in emotional exhaustion when their transformational leader behaviors were directed toward followers low in conscientiousness (Study 1) and competence (Study 2). Overall, our work provides answers to both why and under what conditions the dark side of transformational leader behaviors is likely to appear.

title: The Stuff of Legend: History, Memory, and the Temporality of Organizational Identity Construction
methods: Inductive qualitative theory-building study of four corporate museums at Alessi, Alfa Romeo, Ducati, and Piaggio, using semi-structured interviews, museum observations, archival sources, grounded-theory coding, comparative case analysis, and process theorizing.
industry: Corporate museums and archives connected to design, automotive, motorcycle, and light-vehicle organizations.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Four corporate museums at Alessi, Alfa Romeo, Ducati, and Piaggio; organizational members and external participants using those museums and archives.
n_sample: 59 in-depth semi-structured interviews with 47 informants, supplemented by museum observations and archival documents.
authors: Ravasi, D.; Rindova, V. P.; Stigliani, I.
theories: material memory; organizational identity; organizational memory; social memory studies
keywords: corporate museums; cross-temporal sensemaking; history; material memory; mnemonic communities; organizational identity; organizational memory
research_question: The paper asks how organizational members systematically engage with history and material memory to construct task-relevant understandings of organizational identity. It focuses on how the past is brought to bear on present identity understandings and future-oriented organizational action.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / modes: Identity stewardship, identity evangelizing, heritage mining, material memory, historicized identity understandings, mnemonic communities, and cross-temporal sensemaking.
- Process / phases: Members use corporate museums and archives as material memory, prioritize different identity definitional standards according to task audiences, construct historicized identity understandings, and translate those understandings into action.
- Identity stewardship: Members prioritize enduringness, treat artifacts as identity markers, search for intertemporal patterns, and use the past to maintain legitimacy with core members of the mnemonic community.
- Identity evangelizing: Members prioritize centrality, treat artifacts as organizational relics, abstract essential qualities, and use the past to stimulate identification among new or potential members.
- Heritage mining: Members prioritize distinctiveness, treat artifacts as symbolic resources, recontextualize historical cues, and use the past to enhance the meaning and appeal of new offerings.
- Boundary conditions: The empirical setting consists of four corporate museums with rich historical artifacts and audiences that vary in knowledge of and attachment to the organizations' histories.

The process begins when members face identity-related tasks, such as product innovation, brand communication, HR induction, or merchandising, that require them to explain what distinguishes the organization. Depending on whether their primary audience consists of core, new, or peripheral members of the mnemonic community, they emphasize enduringness, centrality, or distinctiveness. These priorities shape how they interpret artifacts and connect past, present, and future. The result is not a single organizational identity narrative, but situated, task-relevant identity understandings that guide action in different domains.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational identity research by showing how material memory supports the construction of situated, task-relevant identity understandings rather than only broad, shared narratives of "who we are." It specifies three cross-temporal sensemaking processes through which members use the past: searching for intertemporal patterns, holistic abstraction of essential features, and intuitive recontextualization. It also contributes to research on organizational history and memory by theorizing mnemonic communities and historical imperatives as conditions that constrain and enable how organizations use history.
practical_implication: The findings imply that corporate museums and archives can shape action when members use them as interpretive resources, not simply as repositories of historical information. Organizations with meaningful historical artifacts can support innovation, brand work, training, and communication by helping different role holders connect the past to present tasks in audience-sensitive ways. The study also suggests that managers should recognize tensions between historically precise continuity for core audiences and more flexible symbolic reuse for broader audiences.
limitations: The authors identify mnemonic communities as an important boundary condition and note that the four cases involve organizations with iconic products, celebrated brands, and rich historical artifacts. They also state that the inductive interview protocol was not designed to measure antecedents of engagement modes because these constructs emerged later in the analysis. The transferability of the model to less glamorous organizations, mundane objects, or settings without museum facilities remains an empirical question.
future_research: Future research could examine whether similar processes unfold in less celebrated organizations and around historical objects outside formal museum facilities. The authors also point to opportunities to study how professional training, tenure, identification, and career-related factors influence members' modes of engagement with history and identity. They further encourage research on the compatibility of different situated identity understandings and on how these understandings affect coordination across functions and audiences.
abstract: A growing body of research on how organizations engage with their histories has shown that organizational members revisit history in the light of present-day concerns to inspire or legitimize future courses of action. Studies of the processes through which organizational history is brought to bear on the present and future, however, remain rare. To uncover the processes and practices through which organizational members systematically engage with history, we investigate uses of material memory in four corporate museums. Our analysis uncovers three distinct modes of engagement, reflecting different temporal perspectives on organizational identity, involving different cross-temporal interpretative processes, and influencing action in different ways. Our theoretical insights have significant implications not only for understanding the use of history in organizations, but also for research on organizational identity and organizational memory.

title: Bringing “Together”: Emotions and Power in Organizational Responses to Institutional Complexity
methods: Inductive organizational ethnography using 15 months of participant observation in Together, semi-structured interviews, informal interactions, field notes, archival documents, and staged qualitative analysis of institutional logics, emotions, nationality, time, events, and power relations.
industry: Jewish-Palestinian community-service and peace-building organization operating cultural, educational, youth, dialogue, sports, restaurant, and hotel activities.
time_period: Data were gathered between March 2012 and June 2013 during fieldwork covering routine periods and national, political, religious, and violent events.
units: Organizational members, departments, formal meetings, organizational events, ongoing observations, interviews, informal interactions, and written and visual materials.
n_sample: 72 interviewees, 117 interviews, 59 formal meetings, 21 team meetings, 9 organizational events, and 93 sporadic days of ongoing observations.
authors: Sadeh, L. J.; Zilber, T. B.
theories: emotion rules; emotions and institutions; institutional complexity; institutional logics; systemic power
keywords: emotion rules; emotions; ethno-nationalism; ethnography; institutional complexity; institutional logics; systemic power; universalism
research_question: The paper asks what role emotions play in stabilizing or destabilizing constellations of logics inside organizations facing institutional complexity. It also asks how systemic power shapes the emotional generation of institutional stability and change.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Universalistic logic, ethno-national logic, emotional control, emotional eruption, emotion rules, emotion work, and systemic power.
- Process / routine stabilization: Material objects, texts, and interactions generate emotion rules that cultivate hope, closeness, care, love, safety, and avoidance, helping Together sustain universalism during routine periods.
- Triggering conditions: External political or violent events, especially Memorial and Independence Days and the 2012 Israel-Gaza War, activate ethno-national emotions such as fear, suspicion, anger, tension, and splitting.
- Emergent outcomes: Emotional eruptions temporarily make ethno-nationalism more salient inside the organization, even though the universalistic constellation is restored after events pass.
- Power dynamics / boundary conditions: Jewish and Palestinian members face unequal emotion work; Palestinian members must work harder to bracket discrimination and movement restrictions, while emotional eruption is more organizationally available around events salient to Jewish society.

The process is not a simple causal variable model. Together maintains a desired constellation of logics by controlling emotional content and emotional process through material, textual, and interactional arrangements. When external events pierce this routine control, unbidden emotions make the rejected ethno-national logic salient. Systemic power mediates both sides of the process by shaping which events count as disruptive and how much emotion work privileged and underprivileged members must perform.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional complexity research by moving beyond cognitive mechanisms such as sensemaking and negotiation to show how emotions and power constitute the lived experience of logics. It theorizes emotional control as a mechanism through which organizations stabilize a desired constellation of logics, and emotional eruption as a mechanism through which rejected logics re-enter organizational life. It also extends institutional theory by showing that emotion rules are not neutral: systemic power differentiates members' experience of logics and the organizational consequences of emotional eruption.
practical_implication: The paper implies that organizations pursuing social change against dominant societal logics cannot rely only on formal goals, inclusive symbols, or avoidance of conflict. They need to recognize that emotional control may preserve cooperation in routine periods while also suppressing the sensemaking needed when disruptive events occur. Leaders in conflict-laden or hybrid organizations should attend to unequal emotional burdens across groups, because apparently shared emotion rules can require much heavier work from underprivileged members.
limitations: The authors state that the ethnographic design provides depth but is based on one organization, so analytic generalization is bound by the study context. The case involves an organization committed to a logic that challenges a dominant societal logic, and it involves highly incompatible logics, which may limit transferability to organizations where logics are more compatible or where emotion rules align with dominant institutions. The authors also discuss limits linked to the first author's Jewish identity and limited Arabic, which constrained access to some Palestinian members' experiences.
future_research: Future research should examine how emotional dynamics influence organizational responses to institutional complexity under different degrees of dominance between logics and in contexts where logics are more compatible. The paper also calls for work on when collective sensemaking moderates the effect of emotional eruptions on constellations of logics. More broadly, future studies should connect affective, political, and cognitive processes in institutional complexity.
abstract: The theoretical puzzle of how organizations deal with contradicting logics has been extensively investigated during the past two decades. This stream of research has focused on the cognitive, but has overlooked emotions and power, which are fundamental to the lived experience of logics, and to their constitution. Drawing on a 15-month ethnography of “Together,” a Jewish–Palestinian organization in a mixed city in Israel, we explore how the organization succeeds in challenging societal dominant notions of ethno-nationalism by stimulating universalistic notions, and how it occasionally fails to do so, as ethno-nationalism creeps in. Our findings indicate that emotional control allows organizations to deal with contradictory logics and achieve their desired constellation, while unbidden emotions disrupt local efforts and enable changes in desired constellations of logics. Further, systemic power mediates the very experience of logics and the prospects of changing their constellation: Social asymmetry necessitates harder emotion work on behalf of the underprivileged, differentiating their experience of logics, and limiting the extent to which emotional eruption is a viable option. Thus, our study highlights the intersection of logics, emotions, and power, and how logics are managed and failed to be managed.

title: From Montagues to Capulets: Analyzing the Systemic Nature of Rivalry in Career Mobility
methods: Empirical mixed-method study combining fieldwork, interviews, archival historical data, dyad-year panel fixed-effects logit models, robustness checks, and stochastic actor-oriented network models.
industry: Palio di Siena horse-racing labor market and the city-neighborhood contrade that hire jockeys.
time_period: 1743-2011 for jockey career mobility; field visits and interviews occurred between 2013 and 2018, with additional journalist interviews from 2012-2014.
units: Neighborhood-dyad years, jockey career moves between contrade, and qualitative informants.
n_sample: 480 jockeys, 3,072 career moves, 44,196 dyad-year observations, 36 study interviews, and 75 journalist interviews.
authors: Sgourev, S. V.; Operti, E.
theories: balanced triads; network constraint; professionalization; systemic theory of rivalry
keywords: Palio di Siena; career mobility; professionalization; relational constraints; relational gaps; systemic theory of rivalry
research_question: The paper asks how rivalry operates as a systemic form of relational constraint rather than only as a dyadic psychological relationship. It examines whether rivalries among Siena's contrade constrain jockey career mobility not only between direct rivals, but also through allies of rivals, rivals of allies, and increasingly professionalized market conditions.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / relational structures: Rivalry, alliances, allies of rivals, rivals of allies, professionalization, and relational gaps in mobility networks.
- Process / mechanisms: Rivalry creates expectations of loyalty and purity of affiliation; jockeys who move to a rival or adjacent rival camp risk stigmatization, damaged relationships, and possible retaliation.
- Empirical outcomes: Career moves between contrade, modeled as dyad-year mobility ties.
- Boundary / system conditions: The constraining effect is tested in a competitive labor market for Palio jockeys and examined as the market professionalizes over time.

The paper's process argument is that rivalry organizes social structure by creating categorical boundaries around friend and foe. Those boundaries make some otherwise plausible career moves socially costly, even when competitive labor-market logic would predict mobility toward attractive employers. Alliances extend the effect beyond direct rival dyads, so jockeys avoid not only rivals but also allies of rivals and rivals of allies. Professionalization does not erase these relational constraints; in the authors' account, it reinforces adherence to informal norms because reputation and professional standing depend on respecting the rivalry system.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to rivalry scholarship by shifting attention from dyadic rivalry effects to the extended relational system in which rivalry is embedded. It links rivalry, alliance networks, and career mobility by identifying relational gaps: expected but unrealized mobility ties that arise from antagonistic network structure. It also contributes to network and mobility research by theorizing missing ties as the product of systemic relational constraints rather than only lack of opportunity, information, or economic interest.
practical_implication: The authors argue that rivalry can spill across groups and domains, so managers should not assume rivalry remains confined to direct competitors or symbolic conflict. In organizational settings, rivalry may constrain information exchange, staffing, collaboration, or mobility through adjacent relationships as well as direct rival ties. The paper suggests managerial attention is needed to prevent rivalry from diffusing into work-related tasks and adjacent social relationships.
limitations: The authors identify the lack of direct data on jockey remuneration as the main limitation, because contracts between captains and jockeys are secret. They use proxies, dyad fixed effects, and year fixed effects to address resource-endowment and market-opportunity differences, but the paper cannot directly observe compensation incentives. They also note that the study's bounded historical setting raises scope conditions for contexts where crossing organizational boundaries does not carry comparable identity or professional implications.
future_research: Future research should examine the interplay between relational constraints and market incentives in labor markets with more direct compensation data. The authors also call for work on individual-level factors explaining why some actors move to rivals while others do not, other forms of market exchange beyond mobility, and relational gaps in email exchanges, casual talk, co-attendance at third-party events, and other business contexts. Additional work could test whether the consequences of rivalry extend beyond direct rivals through collaborative ties.
abstract: The paper proposes a systemic theory of rivalry that addresses a key limitation of past research by articulating how rivalry spreads across levels of analysis and between social domains. Shifting the perspective from what rivalry does to what it prevents from doing, we conceptualize rivalry as a system of relational constraints that extends beyond the level of direct rivals. Using qualitative and quantitative data on the mobility of jockeys in the Palio di Siena (1743–2011), the famous horse race in Siena, Italy, we document relational gaps in the mobility network—career moves that do not occur, even if expected on economic grounds. The analysis shows that rivalry constrains not only the moves to rivals but also to allies of rivals and rivals of allies. The effect becomes stronger over time, attesting that relational constraints persist in developed markets. Our fieldwork reveals that the constraining ability of rivalry is based on conformity to expectations of loyalty and adherence to group identities. The observed relational gaps are pertinent not only to scholarship on rivalry but also to mobility and network research.

title: Microfoundations of Corporate Social Responsibility and Irresponsibility
methods: Three empirical experiments: Study 1 used an online vignette experiment manipulating CSR, CSI, and control conditions; Study 2 used an online vignette experiment manipulating CSR/CSI/control and country-of-origin warmth and competence; Study 3 used a laboratory product-evaluation experiment with behavioral helping and purchase-price measures.
industry: Experimental contexts involved electronics/calculator and pen manufacturing scenarios; the authors describe the study as tested in technology and manufacturing industries.
country: Participants in Studies 1 and 2 were based in the United States; Studies 2 and 3 manipulated firm country-of-origin cues for the United States or Sweden, Germany, Portugal, and Pakistan.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual participants evaluating fictitious firms or pen manufacturers, with outcomes including warmth, competence, reputation, purchase intentions, subjective quality, helping behavior, and purchase price.
n_sample: 774 participants across three experiments: 102 in Study 1, 572 in Study 2, and 100 recruited in Study 3 before exclusions.
authors: Shea, C. T.; Hawn, O. V.
theories: BIAS map; microfoundations of corporate social responsibility; social perception and stereotypes; stereotype content model
keywords: competence; corporate social irresponsibility; corporate social responsibility; country of origin; purchase intentions; reputation; social perception; stereotype content model; warmth
research_question: The paper asks how individuals perceive CSR and CSI, and whether warmth and competence explain when these practices translate into outcomes such as reputation, purchase intentions, subjective quality, helping behavior, and purchase price. It also asks whether country-of-origin stereotypes change CSR rewards and CSI penalties by providing independent cues about organizational warmth and competence.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that CSR acts as a warmth signal and CSI as a negative warmth signal in initial social judgments of organizations. Warmth perceptions mediate the effects of CSR and CSI on immediate evaluations such as reputation and purchase intentions, while country-of-origin stereotypes create assimilation or contrast effects. Low-warmth firms can receive larger relative CSR rewards because CSR violates expectations positively, whereas high-warmth firms can face harsher CSI penalties because irresponsibility violates expectations negatively; competence sometimes buffers or amplifies these effects.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a microfoundational account of CSR and CSI by linking corporate social strategy to individual-level social perception. It extends CSR research beyond macro-level performance links by showing warmth and competence as psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions for CSR/CSI effects. It also connects the stereotype content model and BIAS map to strategy and international management by showing how country-of-origin stereotypes shape evaluations of firms' social behavior.
practical_implication: Managers should account for how stakeholders perceive both the firm's CSR/CSI behavior and other warmth-competence cues, including country of origin. CSR may be especially useful for firms initially perceived as low in warmth, including new multinationals or firms from low-warmth country contexts, because it can improve warmth and competence perceptions. The paper also warns that high-warmth firms may be penalized more sharply for CSI because irresponsibility conflicts with the warmth expectations attached to them.
limitations: The authors note that controlled experiments provide causal leverage but limit ecological scope; future work should test other scenarios, industries, stakeholders, CSR/CSI activities, outcomes, and methods. The country manipulations use actual countries, which improves realism but reduces experimental precision and limits the number of warmth-competence combinations. The study was tested in technology and manufacturing contexts, and it could not directly address decoupling or greenwashing dynamics.
future_research: Future research could examine stakeholder-specific judgments, organizational-level outcomes, and additional firm or country attributes such as size, status, and industry stereotypes. The authors suggest testing these ideas with real-world data, including country-level social evaluations and cross-border mergers and acquisitions. They also call for work on how different CSR actions generate warmth or competence perceptions and how stakeholders interpret symbolic versus substantive CSR.
abstract: This study examines the importance of social perception of corporate social responsibility (CSR) and irresponsibility (CSI). Drawing from social psychology literature on stereotypes, we argue that two fundamental dimensions of social perception—warmth and competence—help explain the underlying processes and conditions under which CSR leads to specific outcomes. We propose that firms engaging in CSR are perceived as higher in warmth and, by default, competence; moreover, different perceptions of the organization’s warmth and competence can moderate CSR rewards and CSI penalties. To demonstrate this, we conduct three experiments. Experiment 1 links CSR with perceptions of warmth and competence, showing that warmth perceptions mediate the relationship between CSR and important outcomes, such as purchase intentions and reputation. Experiment 2 adds information on firms’ countries of origin, revealing that CSR rewards and CSI penalties differ depending on the (mis)alignment of CSR strategy with country stereotypes. Experiment 3 replicates these findings using behavioral paradigms. We find that firms from high-warmth countries (the United States, Sweden, Portugal) receive lower CSR rewards and pay higher CSI penalties than firms from low-warmth countries (Germany, Pakistan) but this effect is moderated by competence. Our micro–macro study advances social evaluation, strategic CSR, and international management literatures.

title: Constructing a Distant Future: Imaginaries in Geoengineering
methods: Empirical qualitative longitudinal case study of geoengineering discourse using a multi-step abductive analysis, coding of imaginaries, temporal mapping, co-occurrence analysis, actor attribution, and dialectic mapping.
industry: Geoengineering and climate-change discourse across scientific, policy, media, NGO, activist, journalistic, and business spaces.
country: Cross-regional discourse; the news corpus includes Europe, North America, Australia, and other regions.
time_period: Geoengineering discourse through 2016, organized into phases from pre-1990 to 2010-2016.
units: Scientific articles, popular press books, governmental reports and hearings, speeches and debates, press releases, websites, conference reports, newspaper articles, and coded imaginary instances.
n_sample: Over 2,500 documents totaling more than 12,000 pages of text and 23 hours of video, plus 647 coded instances of imaginaries.
authors: Augustine, G.; Soderstrom, S.; Milner, D.; Weber, K.
theories: as-if reality; construal-level theory; dialectical analysis; distant future; imaginaries
keywords: as-if reality; climate change; dialectic process; distant future; geoengineering; imaginaries
research_question: The paper asks how the distant future of geoengineering was conceived and how it came to be treated as if it were real. More broadly, it asks how distant futures acquire enough concreteness and credibility to orient collective efforts despite ambiguity, controversy, and the absence of implementation.
mechanism_summary:
- Empirical setting: Geoengineering as a hypothetical set of planetary-scale climate technologies.
- Key constructs: Distant future, near future, imaginaries, as-if reality, concreteness, and credibility.
- Imaginaries / dialectic positions: Technofix, Human Hubris, Plan B, Governance First, and Conspiracy of Elite Control.
- Analytic process: Abductive analysis, coding of imaginary dimensions, temporal mapping, actor attribution, co-occurrence analysis, and dialectic mapping.
- Emergent outcome: Increasing as-if reality for geoengineering without substantial implementation.

The analysis identifies Technofix as an initial imaginary that imports a societal-level belief in scientific progress and human mastery of nature into climate change discourse. Human Hubris contests this imaginary, while Plan B and Governance First attempt partial syntheses that make geoengineering more concrete while leaving core oppositions unresolved. The dialectic attracts more actors and more differentiated debate, so controversy increases rather than decreases the as-if reality of geoengineering.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes the concept of the distant future as a way to distinguish futures that are distant from experience and convention from near futures organized around uncertainty, probability, and practical expectations. It theorizes imaginaries as moral and cosmological structures that allow actors to imagine discontinuous future possibilities. It also contributes to research on future-oriented action by showing that opposition and dialectic debate can make a distant future more concrete and credible without implementation or consensus.
practical_implication: The paper implies that actors working on grand challenges should not treat controversy only as a barrier to action. For distant futures, debate can draw in more participants, elaborate alternative possibilities, and build the discursive material needed for robust action. The implication is not that geoengineering should be implemented, but that radical alternatives become consequential partly through how they are contested.
limitations: The paper does not present a separate limitations section. Its research agenda indicates boundary issues that remain unresolved, including how distant futures transition into near futures, what accelerates or blocks as-if reality, and whether the geoengineering pattern generalizes to other settings. The authors therefore leave the conditions under which distant futures gain as-if reality as a question for further empirical work.
future_research: Future research should examine the interplay between near and distant futures, including cases where forecasts, models, or crises prompt more radical imagined alternatives. The authors call for work on the pace, roadblocks, and attempted syntheses through which distant futures gain or fail to gain as-if reality. They also encourage comparative studies in other settings, such as artificial intelligence, bionic enhancement, space exploration, and other grand-challenge or radical-innovation domains.
abstract: We develop the concept of the distant future as a new way of seeing the future in collective efforts. While a near future is represented in practical terms and concerned with forming expectations and goals under conditions of uncertainty, a distant future is represented in stylized terms and concerned with imagining possibilities under conditions of ambiguity. Management research on future-oriented action has developed around problems of the near future. To explore distant futures, we analyze the case of geoengineering, a set of planetary-scale technologies that have been proposed as solutions to the threat of climate change. Geoengineering has increasingly been treated as if it were a reality, despite continued controversy and the absence of any implementation. We find that societal-level imaginaries that were built on deeply held moral bases and cosmologies underpinned the conception of geoengineering, and that a dialectic process of discursive attempts to reconcile oppositional imaginaries increased the concreteness and credibility of geoengineering so that it has increasingly been treated as an “as-if” reality. We suggest that distant futures orient collective efforts in distinctive ways, not as concrete guides for action but by expressing critiques and alternatives, that can become treated as as-if realities.

title: Energizing through Visuals: How Social Entrepreneurs Use Emotion-Symbolic Work for Social Change
methods: Inductive qualitative longitudinal study using semi-structured interviews, naturalistic observations, archival data, and online/social media data; analysis used open coding, axial coding, and inductive theory generation.
industry: Anti-plastic pollution movement and nonprofit social entrepreneurship
country: United States, with California-based observation and online/social media interactions
time_period: August 2010 to September 2018 for interviews; broader study materials span 2009 to 2018
units: NPO founders, staff, advisors, movement leaders, target actors, events, archival materials, and social media exchanges
n_sample: 50 semi-structured interviews; 1,789 transcribed minutes; seven NPO events; 578 Facebook posts and 2,504 comments in the systematic Facebook data; 4,517 tweets reviewed; 33 Instagram exchanges analyzed
authors: Barberá-Tomás, D.; Castelló, I.; de Bakker, F. G. A.; Zietsma, C.
theories: emotion work (Hochschild, 1979); emotional energy (Quinn & Dutton, 2005; Collins, 2004); moral shock (Jasper, 2011); symbolic work (Phillips & Lawrence, 2012)
keywords: emotion-symbolic work; emotional energy; enactment of a cause; moral shock; multimodal interactions; social entrepreneurs; visual images
research_question: The paper asks how social entrepreneurs use visual images and textual interactions to influence targets to enact a difficult cause. Empirically, it examines how anti-plastic pollution social entrepreneurs used the Midway albatross visual and related multimodal interactions to move targets toward refusing, rather than merely recycling, plastic.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: visual images, textual interactions, moral shock, emotional energy, and enactment of a difficult cause.
- Process / phases: symbol production and diffusion; connecting target actors to the cause, an emerging collective identity, and the social entrepreneurs; emotional transformation; enactment.
- Triggering conditions: a difficult cause that requires target actors to acknowledge responsibility for plastic pollution and change convenient, taken-for-granted behavior.
- Emergent outcomes: energetic arousal, identification, and moral emotions that support pledging to act, performing the cause, and evangelizing.
- Boundary conditions: the authors argue that powerful visuals alone are insufficient; multimodal emotion-symbolic work is needed to transform shock into sustained enactment.

The process begins when social entrepreneurs produce and diffuse a morally shocking visual symbol. They then use verbal and visual interactions to anchor the symbol to the cause, responsibilize target actors, promote solidarity and hope, and establish the legitimacy and influence of the NPO. In this account, negative emotions such as sadness, rage, despair, and guilt are transformed into emotional energy that supports enactment of the anti-plastic cause.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces emotion-symbolic work as the deliberate production and use of symbols, often multimodally, to manage target actors' emotions and emotional energy in order to influence action. It contributes to social entrepreneurship research by shifting attention from entrepreneurs' own emotions to how entrepreneurs evoke and transform others' emotions. It also contributes to research on visuals and multimodality by showing how visual symbols and text can work together to transform moral shock into emotional energy and enactment.
practical_implication: For social entrepreneurs and other change leaders, the implication is that emotionally powerful visuals should not be treated as self-sufficient persuasion devices. The case suggests that leaders need to connect the visual to a concrete cause, a collective identity, and credible actors if they want targets to move from shock to action. The paper also implies that discipline and responsibilization can be used, but they must be paired with solidarity and hope to reduce alienation.
limitations: The authors identify social media data as a limitation because brief online exchanges lack nonverbal cues, although they also note that images, emoticons, slang, memes, and digital traces help convey emotion. The study is bounded by a challenging environmental cause that required actors to acknowledge guilt and take difficult actions in a plastic-saturated world. The authors also call for more research on how emotional energy is maintained over time and how emotion-symbolic work unfolds across other causes and audiences.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how social entrepreneurs maintain control over social influence processes, direct emotional energy over time, handle competition among entrepreneurs working on similar causes, and manage possible dark sides of emotion-symbolic work. It also suggests studying which types of visuals are most powerful, how audiences' epistemologies and cultural codes shape visual influence, and how combinations of emotions affect enactment.
abstract: Little is known about how social entrepreneurs try to induce enactment of their cause, especially when this cause is difficult to embrace. Through a longitudinal study, we analyze how anti-plastic pollution social entrepreneurs use multimodal (visual and verbal) interactions to influence their targets and promote their cause. Our findings reveal that these social entrepreneurs use what we call “emotion-symbolic work,” which involves using visuals and words to elicit negative emotions through moral shock, and then transforming those emotions into emotional energy for enactment. The emotional transformation process entails connecting target actors to a cause, a collective identity, and the social entrepreneurs themselves. Our exploration of emotion-symbolic work offers new ways of seeing by emphasizing the use of multimodal interactions to affect emotions in efforts to influence target actors to enact a cause.

title: Why Do Extreme Work Hours Persist? Temporal Uncoupling as a New Way of Seeing
methods: Historical qualitative case study of Consult, combining archival materials, retrospective semi-structured interviews, and abductive process analysis.
industry: Elite strategy consulting and the German consulting industry.
country: Germany, with additional interviews from United Kingdom, United States, and Netherlands subsidiaries.
time_period: Historical evolution over more than 40 years; data collected between 2013 and 2017.
units: Consult, its consultants, managers, partners, HR representatives, executives, clients, and comparison consultants at other firms.
n_sample: 88 semi-structured interviews, including 52 at Consult, plus archival materials and 257 press articles.
authors: Blagoev, B.; Schreyögg, G.
theories: modern social systems theory (Luhmann, 1995, 2012a, 2018); positive feedback; temporal uncoupling
keywords: extreme work hours; positive feedback; temporal lock-in; temporal structuring; temporal uncoupling
research_question: The paper asks why and how extreme work hours persist in a state of asynchrony relative to dominant societal work time rhythms. It investigates this puzzle through the historical emergence, reinforcement, and maintenance of extreme work hours at an elite strategy consulting firm called Consult.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: temporal structuring, temporal uncoupling, synchrony with clients, asynchrony from societal work time rhythms, positive feedback, temporal lock-in.
- Process / phases: outcome-oriented temporal structuring in office projects; process-oriented temporal structuring in presence projects; temporal lock-in after hiring and retention pressures made extreme work hours increasingly problematic.
- Reinforcing processes: daytime synchronization with clients increased client expectations for presence, speed, and availability; desynchronization from societal work time norms aligned hiring, rewards, scheduling, and project calculation around long hours.
- Emergent outcomes: extreme work hours became embedded in Consult's internal activity system and in client-consultant expectations, making later work-life initiatives difficult to sustain.
- Boundary conditions: the explanation is grounded in an elite consulting context where client visibility, implementation-oriented projects, and price competition made availability and speed central to perceived value.

The process begins with a shift from weekly alternation between client interaction and desk work to presence projects in which consultants worked on-site with clients during the day. This increased synchrony with clients, but pushed desk work into evenings and weekends, thereby increasing asynchrony from regular work time. Positive feedback then made both sides of the pattern self-reinforcing: clients came to expect continuous availability, while Consult reorganized internal practices around extreme hours. Over time, this produced temporal lock-in, where the firm maintained the temporal structure despite employee burnout, attrition, and repeated change efforts.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes temporal uncoupling as an alternative to the dominant entrainment lens in organizational temporality research. Rather than treating organizations as time takers that adapt to external Zeitgebers, the authors theorize organizations as time makers that select which rhythms to synchronize with and which to desynchronize from.

The paper also explains the persistence of extreme work hours as temporal lock-in. This shifts attention from only cultural, technological, or power-based pressures toward endogenous temporal dynamics in which small temporal shifts become reinforced through positive feedback and eventually hard to reverse.
practical_implication:
The paper argues that piecemeal HR initiatives, work-life rules, and cultural change programs are unlikely to change extreme work hours when the underlying temporal arrangement remains intact. Sustainable change would require a systemic redesign of the business model, value proposition, project scoping, staffing, scheduling, and client expectations that currently make extreme availability valuable.

For consulting firms, this may require experimenting with business units or service models that are not premised on extreme speed and 24-7 availability. It may also require collective field-level action if single firms face competitive penalties for reducing extreme work hours alone.
limitations:
The authors identify retrospective data as a limitation, even though it was useful for studying long-term organizational dynamics. They also note that the analysis foregrounds synchronization with clients and societal work time rhythms while backgrounding broader industry-level dynamics.

The paper's focus on temporality also leaves other relevant factors, such as digital technologies, organizational control, and power, outside the main analysis. These factors may interact with temporal uncoupling and lock-in but are not fully examined in this study.
future_research:
Future research could use ethnographic, time-use, or digital trace data to examine the micro-dynamics of temporal uncoupling and temporal lock-in. Studies could also analyze how multiple temporalities across families, professional organizations, universities, government agencies, competitors, and industries interact.

The authors also call for research on how digital technologies shape synchronization, desynchronization, and temporal uncoupling. Further work could link temporal lock-in to organizational control and power, and investigate innovative temporal arrangements that help organizations manage extreme work hours more sustainably.
abstract: This paper develops temporal uncoupling as a new way of seeing the puzzling persistence of extreme work hours, as well as the temporal relations of organizations and their environments. Drawing on a historical case study, we trace and analyze the genesis, reinforcement, and maintenance of extreme work hours in an elite consulting firm over a period of 40 years. We find that a small shift in temporal structuring mobilized two positive feedback processes. These processes consolidated a temporal order that increasingly uncoupled from the traditional workweek. Grounded in these findings, we make two contributions. First, we challenge the orthodox view of entrainment as an ideal synchronous relation between organizations and their environments. Instead, we offer temporal uncoupling as an alternative lens. It enables us to see how both synchrony and asynchrony are potentially viable options, which coexist and sometimes coconstitute each other. Second, we shed new light on temporality as a constitutive force that underpins extreme work hours and offer a novel explanation of their persistence as a case of systemic temporal lock-in. We develop positive feedback as a mechanism that explains how small temporal shifts can become consolidated into hardly reversible temporal lock-ins.

title: Reconceptualizing What and How Women Negotiate for Career Advancement
methods: Empirical mixed-methods, multi-study research combining literature review, interviews, surveys, written negotiation accounts, grounded-theory coding, confirmatory factor analysis, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, ordered logistic regression, chi-square tests, and comparative analysis across six studies.
industry: Public, private, and nonprofit sectors, including government, professional services, corporate, entrepreneurial, nonprofit, military, law enforcement, and political contexts
country: Six world regions, including North America, the Middle East and North Africa, Africa, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and South America across the study samples
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Senior executives, partners, civil servants, nonexecutive managers, and early- or mid-career professionals recounting career negotiations
n_sample: More than 450 male and female professionals across six studies
authors: Bowles, Hannah Riley; Thomason, Bobbi; Bear, Julia B.
theories: gender roles and stereotypes; idiosyncratic work arrangements / i-deals (Rousseau, 2005; Rousseau et al., 2006); lack of fit model (Heilman, 1983); leadership claiming (Derue & Ashford, 2010)
keywords: asking; bending; career advancement; gender in career negotiations; leadership claiming; shaping
research_question: How can research on gender in career negotiations move beyond a pay-negotiation deficit account to explain what women negotiate for career advancement and how they negotiate role development, work–family conflicts, compensation, and leadership claims in organizational contexts?
mechanism_summary:
- Focal phenomenon: Gendered career negotiation as agency in organizational context.
- Negotiation subjects: Role development, workload or work–family flexibility, and compensation or job offers.
- Negotiating strategies: Asking, bending, and shaping.
- Career gains: Enhanced leadership or authority, increased compensation, and greater work–life balance.
- Contextual conditions: Gender roles and stereotypes, organizational norms, policies, practices, and demographics shape the decision to negotiate, the choice of strategy, and negotiation outcomes.

The process starts from broad career ambitions and specific role, pay, or workload goals. Asking involves routine negotiations in line with organizational norms; bending seeks individual exceptions when standard paths do not fit; shaping advances an individual proposal that would also change organizational practices or structures. Across the studies, bending helps explain how women navigate work–family conflicts and nontraditional career paths, while shaping is developed as a process of leadership claiming through multiparty support for organizational change.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the dominant account that women’s career-negotiation problem is mainly a lack of assertiveness in pay bargaining. It broadens the construct of career negotiation by integrating role, workload, and compensation negotiations and by proposing asking, bending, and shaping as distinct strategies with different career implications. It also positions negotiation as a micro-mechanism of gender inequality and leadership advancement that operates through individual agency embedded in organizational norms and contexts.
practical_implication: The paper argues that training and advising should not focus narrowly on job-offer or pay-asking simulations. Students and executives should also learn how to negotiate role advancements and workloads through the multiparty processes of bending and shaping. Organizations and public-sector leaders should create policies and cultures that allow women and men to negotiate mutually beneficial work arrangements that support continued employment, career growth, and professional contribution.
limitations: The authors state that the analyses rely on narrative accounts, which may be affected by retrospective sensemaking or social desirability. They also note that moving from the conceptual framework to predictive models would require longitudinal research on what and how men and women negotiate for career advancement. Although the samples span diverse organizational contexts, they are biased toward high-achieving professionals, limiting what can be inferred about less elite workers.
future_research: Future research should test longitudinal effects of workload negotiations on women’s career trajectories and continued employment. The paper calls for more targeted research on contextual factors that inhibit or facilitate men’s and women’s career negotiations. It also recommends deeper study of early-stage and mid-level career negotiation processes, opportunities and barriers for less elite workers, and the possibility that less educated workers may benefit more from collective than individual negotiations.
abstract: We propose a conceptual framework for expanding the scope of future research on the role of gender in career negotiations. Extant research on gender in career negotiations emphasizes women’s disadvantages relative to men in compensation negotiations. We present an inductive study of what and how women negotiate for career advancement and the attainment of leadership positions in organizations, drawing on data from diverse samples of negotiation accounts by senior executive, mid-level, and early career professionals from the public, private, and nonprofit sectors and six world regions. Integrating insights from six studies, we propose a more comprehensive perspective on what men and women negotiate for career advancement, including their role development and work–family conflicts, as well as compensation. We also identify three distinct negotiating strategies—asking, bending, and shaping—that vary in the extent to which the negotiator conforms to, deviates from, or attempts to redefine organizational norms. Our analyses suggest that the choice of negotiating strategy has implications for men’s and women’s career progression, particularly for women’s navigation of nontraditional career paths and men’s and women’s leadership claiming. We suggest new directions for research on the role of negotiation in career advancement and in promoting and mitigating gender inequality in organizations.
apa_citation: Bowles, H. R., Thomason, B., & Bear, J. B. (2019). Reconceptualizing what and how women negotiate for career advancement. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(6), 1645-1671. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1497

title: Sensemaking from the Body: An Enactive Ethnography of Rowing the Amazon
methods: Enactive ethnography of the first-ever attempt to scull the navigable Amazon, combining video-based analysis, post-journey interviews, audio journal entries, fieldnotes, and first-person carnal-sociology analysis.
industry: Not reported in paper
country: Nauta (Peru), with the voyage oriented toward Macapa, Brazil, along the navigable Amazon.
time_period: The journey began on September 13, 2013, after eight months of preparation.
units: Rowers' embodied sensemaking during the Amazon row, analyzed through video segments, audio journals, fieldnotes, interviews, and first-person experience.
n_sample: 755 video segments, 62 audio journal entries, fieldnotes, interviews, and the rowers' experiences.
authors: de Rond, M.; Holeman, I.; Howard-Grenville, J.
theories: carnal sociology; embodied sensemaking; enactive ethnography; organizational sensemaking
keywords: audio journal; carnal sociology; embodied organizational sensemaking; enactive ethnography; real-time video; sensemaking from the body
research_question: The paper asks how the body is involved in organizational sensemaking, and what is learned by studying sensemaking both "of the body" and "from the body." It uses the Amazon rowing journey to examine how carnal sociology can extend embodied sensemaking beyond observable sensorimotor behavior to the lived, suffering, situated body.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / vantage points: Embodied organizational sensemaking, carnal sociology, enactive ethnography, "of the body" analysis, and "from the body" analysis.
- Process / data logic: The video-based account identifies bodily sensing, movement, gesture, discomfort, and coordination as visible aspects of sensemaking; the enactive account uses audio journals, fieldnotes, recollection, and first-person experience to recover what the body felt from the inside.
- Embodied process: The body provides cues, registers pain, fear, exhaustion, skill, and relational tension, and shapes whether sensemakers speak, stay silent, act, or fail to act.
- Boundary conditions: The empirical setting is an extreme, temporary, high-risk rowing journey, but the paper argues that carnal sociology can also inform more conventional organizational settings.

The process account contrasts what can be seen from outside the body with what can be known by performing the phenomenon. Video made visible how rowers sensed currents, adjusted action, and coordinated with little talk. The enactive ethnography showed that sensemaking also depended on hunger, fatigue, fear, injury, social history, skill, and the relational position of the sensemaker. The central process is therefore not simply noticing, interpreting, and acting, but sensemaking that unfolds through a body that is sentient, suffering, skilled, sedimented, and situated.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational sensemaking by shifting attention from cognition and discourse toward embodied experience as a constitutive part of sensemaking. It develops a complementary "from the body" approach that foregrounds the holistic body and argues that the "who" of sensemaking matters alongside the "how." It also contributes methodologically by showing how enactive ethnography and carnal sociology can help researchers access forms of organizational experience that video, interviews, and retrospective accounts may leave under-specified.
practical_implication: For researchers and organizational analysts, the implication is to treat bodies, skills, histories, exhaustion, emotion, and relational positioning as consequential to how people make sense of uncertain situations. The paper suggests that organizational settings such as coordination, routines, socialization, identity work, change, and temporary organizing may be better understood when researchers attend to how sensemaking unfolds from embodied participation rather than only from discourse or observation.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the case is extreme and foregrounds physical and emotional suffering more strongly than many ordinary organizational settings. They also identify methodological challenges: researchers cannot always perform the phenomenon they study, enactive access may require special skills or permissions, and representing "being a lived body" in scholarly text is difficult. The paper therefore presents carnal sociology as promising but methodologically demanding rather than as a simple replacement for existing sensemaking methods.
future_research: The paper encourages scholars to use carnal sociology in longitudinal organizational settings where bodily, emotional, and relational change can be traced over time. It also points to opportunities in everyday immanent sensemaking, coordination, routines, strategizing, temporary organizations, socialization, identity, and organizational change. Future work can further test how video, audio diaries, fieldnotes, photographs, first-person participation, and alternative writing styles can communicate embodied organizational phenomena.
abstract: Drawing on real-time video, an audio journal, interviews, and field notes from the first-ever attempt to scull the navigable Amazon, we explore the promise of carnal sociology to enrich our understanding of embodied organizational sensemaking. We investigate the body’s role in sensemaking from two vantage points: “of the body” and “from the body.” Using methodological and conceptual anchors provided in carnal sociology, we contrast what each approach tells us about the nature and process of sensemaking. Doing so helps us outline a complementary approach to embodied sensemaking that attends to (1) how a “new way of seeing” the body as sentient, sedimented, situated, and capable of suffering enables a more holistic understanding of the role of embodiment in sensemaking; (2) the importance this then places on the “who” of sensemaking; and (3) carnal sociology’s broader methodological implications for organizational sensemaking.
apa_citation: de Rond, M., Holeman, I., & Howard-Grenville, J. (2019). Sensemaking from the body: An enactive ethnography of rowing the Amazon. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(6), 1961-1988. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1417
