title: What You Don’t See Can Hurt You: Awareness Cues to Profile Indirect Competitors
methods: Temporal exponential random graph models using longitudinal competition-network data; maximum pseudo-likelihood estimation with bootstrapped confidence intervals; robustness checks across additional focal-firm networks and alternative specifications.
industry: Customer experience management (CEM) arena.
units: Dyad-year observations of competitive encounters among focal firms, direct rivals, and indirect competitors.
n_sample: 15,824,693 observations, including 142,446 competitive encounters across 25 focal firms and 2,920 unique firms.
authors: Downing, S. T.; Kang, J.-S.; Markman, G. D.
theories: awareness–motivation–capability (AMC) framework; competitive dynamics research; network architecture models
keywords: awareness–motivation–capability framework; competitive encounters; degree of separation; hostility profile; indirect competitors
research_question: The paper asks how the awareness construct in the awareness–motivation–capability framework can become more predictive for identifying indirect competitors before they become direct rivals. It specifically examines which firm-, dyad-, and network-level awareness cues define a hostility profile for competitive encounters.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that diversified firms move across markets, asymmetric competitive pressure makes some dyads more vulnerable to competitive encounters, and network convergence brings indirect competitors into direct rivalry. Degree of separation bounds this process: second- and third-degree indirect competitors can become competitive threats, while more distant firms generally fall outside the hostility profile. The paper models these cues jointly across firm, dyad, and network levels rather than treating competitor identification as a single-industry or single-dyad problem.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends competitive dynamics and the awareness–motivation–capability framework by shifting awareness from a reactive focus on known direct rivals to a predictive profile of current and potential rivals. It argues that an arena view, rather than an industry-bound view, better captures cross-industry competition and multisided rivalry. Methodologically, it introduces temporal exponential random graph modeling as a way to model interdependent competitive encounters across multiple levels.
practical_implication: Managers can use the hostility profile to prioritize attention toward direct rivals and second- and third-degree indirect competitors, rather than monitoring every possible firm in a competitive landscape. The paper suggests that applying diversification, asymmetric pressure, convergence, and degree-of-separation cues can help firms preempt, ally with, defend against, retreat from, or ignore would-be rivals more deliberately.
limitations: The findings are based on one competitive arena, customer experience management, so the authors call for research on whether the hostility profile generalizes to other arenas. The paper also notes that the AMC framework would still struggle to time exactly when an indirect competitor becomes a direct rival. Although robustness checks are extensive, the authors state that more research is needed before the hostility profile is deemed empirically generalizable and theoretically robust.
future_research: Future research could test whether different arenas and nonmarket players require different hostility profiles. The authors also call for work on the timing of competitive engagements and on whether similar profiling principles can predict collaborative ties such as alliances, buyer–supplier partnerships, and joint ventures. More broadly, they encourage profiling studies that define boundary conditions and make management theories more predictive.
abstract: The awareness–motivation–capability (AMC) framework instructs firms to be aware of rivals, yet it offers limited guidance on how to profile those who are not yet rivals but stand to become so. Because rivals are embedded in dyads, triads, tetrads, etc., a multilevel view can unearth awareness cues that specify a hostility profile and make the awareness construct prescient. Studying thousands of competitive encounters over 10 years, we show that, at the firm and dyad levels, diversification and asymmetric pressure (differential exposure to competitive pressure) are reliable cues predicting competitive encounters. At the network level, convergence drives triadic encounters (competition with a rival’s rival), and the degree of separation among indirect competitors defines the outer bounds of the hostility profile. Specifically, direct rivals and secondand third-degree indirect competitors merit awareness—more distal players do not. Together, the awareness cues and hostility profile delineate the conceptual bound within which awareness is prescient and beyond which it is misplaced. Challenging several assumptions, our study shows that an arena view assists in predicting cross-industry competition; applying firm, dyad, and network levels of analysis is advisable to better foresee competition; and indirect competitors are “profilable,” allowing us to “see” rivals even before they strike.

title: From Actions to Paths to Patterning: Toward a Dynamic Theory of Patterning in Routines
methods: Longitudinal field study of ProjectBQ, a video game development project team, combining scrum-sheet archival task data, observations, interviews, narrative network construction in ThreadNet, network property computation, project narrative, and causal loop diagramming.
industry: Video game development.
time_period: Data collected over 15 months; scrum sheets downloaded between May 2011 and February 2012; first-author observation from May 2011 to August 2012.
units: ProjectBQ routine/action paths, 2,428 coded tasks/events, 159 coded sequences, 11 sprints, observations, interviews, and archival materials.
n_sample: Final list of 2,428 tasks from 122 daily scrum-sheet versions; observations of 39 team meetings, 7 client meetings, 4 play test sessions, 11 informal interviews, and 4 formal interviews.
authors: Goh, K. T.; Pentland, B. T.
theories: narrative networks; patterning; routine dynamics; strong process theory
keywords: narrative network; organizational routines; paths; patterning; patterns of action; routine dynamics
research_question: The paper asks what drives a pattern of action to become more or less varied over time. It studies how paths, understood as time-ordered sequences of actions or events, link situated actions to broader patterns in organizational routines.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: Paths, situated actions, patterns of action, narrative networks, routine dynamics, and patterning.
- Empirical setting: ProjectBQ, a video game development project team at GameSG, studied through scrum sheets, observations, interviews, and archival materials.
- Patterning phases: The project moved through increasing complexity during concepting and experimentation, decreasing complexity around a prototype deliverable, a surge in complexity during building and revisions, and declining complexity after feature lock.
- Mechanisms: Reinforcement loop, performance loop, revision loop, delay loop, cut-back loop, and motivation loop.
- Analytic logic: Narrative networks made sequences of actions visible as paths, and changes in nodes, handoffs, and estimated paths allowed the authors to theorize how routines become more or less varied.

In the authors' account, each situated action can enact, reinforce, add, or dissolve paths in a narrative network. Performance demands and revisions can increase the number of actions and handoffs, while repetition, cut-backs, deadlines, and declining motivation can reduce path variety. The paper therefore treats patterning itself as a process through which routine dynamics unfold, rather than only as an outcome of other motors of change.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to routine dynamics by making the link between specific actions, paths, and patterns of action empirically visible. It extends strong process theory by operationalizing paths in narrative networks and showing how action patterns change over time. It also argues that patterning can be understood as a motor of routine dynamics alongside, and sometimes more naturally than, lifecycle, teleological, dialectical, or evolutionary explanations.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers and process analysts should look beyond compliance with prescribed paths and attend to the space of possible paths in work processes. In uncertain or emergent work, encouraging path creation may be more useful than enforcing one best path, because it can reveal opportunities and sustain variety. The path-based perspective may help managers think about expanding or contracting the space of possibilities in innovation, dynamic team processes, and other complex emergent phenomena.
limitations: The authors note that a path-based perspective depends on the availability of meaningful longitudinal traces of action; ProjectBQ's scrum sheets made this unusually feasible. They also caution that the choice of time window matters, because three-week sprint snapshots provide a storyboard rather than a continuous movie. The method assumes sequential task performance and may understate complexity when concurrent activities are interdependent, and the complexity metric may overstate or understate actual paths because it abstracts from differences in handoff difficulty.
future_research: The paper points to future work on routine dynamics as network dynamics, especially through repetitive reinforcement and morphogenesis. Future studies could examine how degrees of freedom and stringency of constraints shape whether paths are reinforced, elaborated, or newly created. The authors also suggest further research on how exploration and innovation are encouraged by conditions or efforts that sustain variety in pathways.
abstract: This paper demonstrates a new way of seeing and theorizing about the dynamics of organizational routines through the concept of paths—time-ordered sequences of actions or events in performing work. Empirically and conceptually, paths provide the missing link between specific actions and patterns of action. When routines are represented as a narrative network, tracing the formation and dissolution of action paths can generate new insights about the dynamic patterning of actions in routine performances. We traced action paths using longitudinal field data from a videogame development project, and found that action patterns change dramatically over time based on the needs of the project. We explain these changes in terms of generic mechanisms that lead to the enactment of more (or fewer) paths in the narrative network. We propose that patterning can be seen as a new motor of routine dynamics and discuss generic mechanisms through which patterning can influence narrative network structure.
apa_citation: Goh, K. T., & Pentland, B. T. (2019). From actions to paths to patterning: Toward a dynamic theory of patterning in routines. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(6), 1901-1929. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0042

title: The Assembly of a Field Ideology: An Idea-Centric Perspective on Systemic Power in Impact Investing
methods: Empirical qualitative inside-out research on impact investing in Europe, combining insider and outsider data collection, public and hidden transcripts, observations, documents, and dichotomy-based coding of ideas in opposition.
industry: Impact investing in Europe, examined through EVPA, GECES, and GSG as interaction sites.
units: Field-level ideas, interactions, public transcripts, hidden transcripts, observations, emails, conference calls, interview transcripts, strategy documents, and publications.
n_sample: Almost 800 hours of observations and over 3,000 pages of documentation.
authors: Hehenberger, Lisa; Mair, Johanna; Metz, Ashley
theories: field ideology; institutional theory of organizations; micro-sociology tradition on ideology; systemic power
keywords: field ideology; idea-centric perspective; impact investing; inside-out research; suppression; systemic power
research_question: The paper asks how some ideas become dominant and form part of what shapes thinking, reasoning, and acting in a field. It studies this question in the European impact investing field by examining idea-level contestation before dominant ideas consolidated into a widely shared field ideology.
mechanism_summary:
- Empirical context / sites: Impact investing in Europe, with EVPA, GECES, and GSG as interaction sites where field participants negotiated ideas.
- Ideas in opposition: Dichotomies such as standardized versus customized, self-sufficiency versus dependency, scaling versus going native, measuring impact versus telling stories, and tool first versus need first.
- Organizing themes: Field ambition, focus of investment, and anchor for decision making.
- Dominant field ideology: Standardized ambition, self-sufficiency, scaling, rational/head-based decision making, measuring impact, and tool-first approaches.
- Suppression modes: Devaluing, prioritizing means over ends, and simplifying.
- Alternative paths: Customized, participatory, beneficiary-centered, ecosystem-nurturing, narrative, and need-first ideas persisted as paths not taken and possible futures.

The process starts as ideas from philanthropy, finance, social economy, policy, and adjacent fields enter impact investing and are negotiated in repeated interactions. Dichotomy-based analysis makes latent conflict visible at the level of ideas, showing how some ideas become patterned into an emerging field ideology while others are abandoned, sidelined, or left unstructured. Suppression operates through devaluing alternative ideas, prioritizing tools and practices over social ends, and simplifying complex social problems into investable, measurable, scalable forms. These modes reinforce systemic power by restricting options and shaping what becomes valued and taken for granted in the field.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes an idea-centric perspective for studying institutional life in fields and introduces field ideology as a coherent system of ideas and beliefs that orders a field. It specifies suppression as a mechanism through which systemic power arises and is perpetuated in field formation. It also shows how attention to sidelined ideas can reveal alternative pasts and possible futures, thereby linking institutional durability and transformation.
practical_implication: The paper gives practitioners and policy makers a way to reflect on how their language, tools, standards, and investment practices shape a field in intended and unintended ways. For impact investing, it cautions that emphasis on scale, measurement, financial tools, and self-sufficiency can suppress local, participatory, beneficiary-centered, and need-first approaches. It therefore suggests that field participants should attend not only to dominant practices but also to the ideas that those practices devalue, bypass, or simplify.
limitations: The authors state that their approach addresses how ideas become dominant but does not allow them to predict when or why some ideas are suppressed. The study is based on one field, and its findings are shaped by the specificities of impact investing, including high uncertainty and the difficulty of establishing causal links between funded interventions and social impact. The paper also acknowledges opportunity costs from not foregrounding actor-centric, strategic field, or social network explanations.
future_research: Future research should combine the idea-centric perspective with actor-centric traditions to link suppression modes to field participants' tactical and strategic toolkits. The authors call for work that specifies the conditions under which devaluing, prioritizing means over ends, and simplifying affect systemic power in fields. They also encourage studies in a more diverse set of fields to clarify how field features shape the assembly of field ideology and power-laden idea dynamics.
abstract: We advance a novel idea-centric perspective to study power-laden aspects of institutional life in fields. Our study includes data from the field of impact investing in Europe from 2006–2018, collected from the inside and analyzed collaboratively by inside and outside researchers. We develop an analytical tool based on dichotomies to detect latent forms of conflict that easily remain unnoticed and to see how some ideas become dominant while others are abandoned or sidelined. We display the assembly of a field ideology—a coherent system of ideas that shapes thinking, reasoning and acting in a field. Furthermore, we specify suppression as a mechanism that gives rise to and perpetuates systemic power in fields, restricting options and shaping what is valued. Our study provides insights into the dynamic nature of institutional life in fields, including alternative paths not taken and possible futures.

title: Can Joy Buy You Money? The Impact of the Strength, Duration, and Phases of an Entrepreneur’s Peak Displayed Joy on Funding Performance
methods: Quantitative analysis of Kickstarter crowdfunding pitch videos using FaceReader facial expression analysis and STATA OLS regressions predicting logged funding amount and logged number of backers.
industry: Kickstarter crowdfunding projects across categories
time_period: Projects listed for funding on October 7, 2015
units: Entrepreneurial projects with pitch videos showing visible facial expressions for more than 7.55 seconds
n_sample: 1,460 entrepreneurial projects
authors: Jiang, L.; Yin, D.; Liu, D.
theories: emotional contagion; event system theory; gestalt characteristics theory; primacy and recency effects
keywords: crowdfunding; emotion temporal dynamics; entrepreneurs’ displayed joy; facial expression analysis; funding performance; peak displayed joy
research_question: The paper asks whether displaying positive emotion, specifically joy, during an entrepreneur’s funding pitch helps gain financial support. It focuses on whether the strength, duration, and beginning/ending phases of peak displayed joy are associated with crowdfunding performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that a stronger peak display of joy becomes especially salient and memorable to pitch viewers, making viewers more likely to experience positive affect and infer favorable qualities about the entrepreneur. Event system theory adds that duration and phase matter: brief peak joy can intensify attention and support, but prolonged peak joy can backfire by appearing excessive, unprofessional, or overly optimistic. The empirical results support positive associations for peak displayed joy, especially in the beginning and ending phases, and an inverted U-shaped association for peak duration in the full pitch and beginning phase.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper connects emotion temporal dynamics research with the interpersonal influence of displayed emotions. It contributes by showing that displayed emotion should not be treated only as a static average level; peak strength, duration, and phase can matter for observers’ decisions in an entrepreneurial funding context.

It also contributes methodologically by using automated facial expression analysis to measure dynamic displayed emotion frame by frame in pitch videos. This provides a scalable visual method for studying fine-grained emotional displays in management research.
practical_implication:
The paper suggests that entrepreneurs using crowdfunding pitch videos should attend not only to whether they display joy, but also to when and how long they display peak joy. Higher peak displayed joy is associated with better funding outcomes, but extended time at peak joy can harm funding performance.

Entrepreneurs should pay particular attention to the beginning and ending phases of pitches, where peak displayed joy is especially consequential. The authors caution that entrepreneurs should avoid prolonged peak joy, including in the beginning phase.
limitations:
The study focuses on peak states of displayed joy while controlling for other temporal characteristics such as ending states, trend, and average. The authors note that other temporal properties, including emotion covariation, inertia, and the ordering of positive and negative emotions, remain open for future work.

The research examines joy and controls for average negative emotions, but it does not analyze the temporal characteristics of negative emotions or subtler positive emotions such as gratitude, passion, and contentment. The crowdfunding setting also did not allow the authors to collect granular individual-backer data on motivations or support decisions.
future_research:
Future research could examine other temporal dynamics of displayed emotions, including covariation, inertia, and the ordering of positive and negative emotional moments. Studies could also analyze negative emotions or subtler positive emotions in contexts where those emotions are more prominent.

The authors also encourage future work in traditional pitching contexts where individual investors can be observed or interviewed. Such designs could test the affective and cognitive mechanisms linking entrepreneurs’ peak displayed joy to each viewer’s funding decision.
abstract: Does displaying positive emotions (e.g., joy) during a funding pitch help an entrepreneur gain more financial support? Past research has approached this question mostly by treating emotional displays as static and focusing on the overall or average levels of displayed emotions. However, emotional displays are temporally dynamic and more salient in some moments or phases than others. Drawing from gestalt characteristics and event system theories, we take a dynamic approach to examine the “peak” moments of entrepreneurs’ displayed joy—specifically, the strength and duration of peak displayed joy during different phases of a pitch. We analyzed data from over eight million frames in 1,460 pitch videos, using the latest facial expression analysis technology. The findings unveil the benefit of pitching with a greater level of peak displayed joy, especially during the beginning and ending phases of a pitch. Moreover, the amount of time an entrepreneur spends at the peak level of his or her displayed joy has an inverted U-shaped relationship with funding performance. This research highlights not only the importance of investigating emotion temporal dynamics in the interpersonal context, but also the unique research opportunities provided by facial expression analyses in understanding complex management phenomena.

title: Eyes Wide Open: Perceived Exploitation and Its Consequences
methods: Empirical mixed-methods, five-study design: mixed-methods scale item generation and content validity assessment, a validation study using MTurk survey data, and two field studies testing the model with structural equation modeling and bootstrap indirect effects.
industry: Construction and medicine in the two focal field studies; scale development and validation also included working professionals, MTurk respondents, and student sorters.
country: United Kingdom, United States, and Israel in the focal field studies; validation respondents were mostly in the United States.
time_period: Study 2 used two survey waves separated by a three-month lag; dates for data collection were not reported.
units: Employees and workers evaluating perceived exploitative employee-organization relationships, emotions, attitudes, and behavioral intentions.
n_sample: Main field studies: Study 1 n = 219 and Study 2 n = 139; validation and scale-development samples were used for scale construction and construct validity.
authors: Livne-Ofer, Ephrat; Coyle-Shapiro, Jacqueline A-M.; Pearce, Jone L.
theories: affective events theory (Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996); causal reasoning framework (Martinko et al., 2002); employee-organization relationship literature; exploitation theory in political economy and sociology
keywords: anger and hostility; burnout; employee engagement; employee silence; perceived exploitation; perceived exploitative employee-organization relationships; psychological withdrawal; shame and guilt; turnover intentions
research_question: How can organizational behavior theorize and measure employees' perceptions that their organizations exploit them, and what emotional, attitudinal, and behavioral consequences follow from those perceived exploitative employee-organization relationships?
mechanism_summary:
- Focal construct: Employees' perceived exploitative employee-organization relationships.

The paper argues that perceived exploitation is an overall appraisal of an employee-organization relationship in which the employee sees the organization as purposefully taking advantage of them for organizational benefit. That appraisal can trigger outward-focused anger and hostility toward the organization, which helps explain revenge, lower engagement, higher turnover intentions, and lower organizational commitment. It can also trigger inward-focused shame and guilt, which helps explain burnout, silence, and psychological withdrawal. The two field studies support most of the predicted partial mediation paths, with revenge nonsignificant in Study 1 but supported in Study 2.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces and validates perceived exploitative employee-organization relationships as a distinct construct in organizational behavior, differentiating it from psychological contract breach, low perceived organizational support, distributive injustice, perceived organizational obstruction, and organizational cruelty. It extends exploitation research beyond structural accounts in sociology and industrial relations by focusing on individual-level perceptions and consequences. It also contributes to workplace emotions research by showing that outward-focused and inward-focused negative emotions explain different employee responses to negative organization relationships.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that employees simply leave when they experience the employment relationship as exploitative. The paper argues that organizations need to ascertain whether employees hold such perceptions, understand why those perceptions arise, and address the underlying practices or attributions. It also suggests that perceived exploitation can affect outcomes relevant to both employee well-being and organizational performance, including turnover intentions, commitment, burnout, silence, and withdrawal.
limitations: The authors identify common method bias as a primary limitation, although they attempted to mitigate it through counterbalancing, time separation in Study 2, cross-over tests, and common latent factor checks. They also note limits to generalizability despite using distinct studies across different occupations and industries. A further limitation is the three-month separation in Study 2, which was chosen to manage attrition among residents likely to move from residencies to fellowships or permanent posts.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how perceived exploitative relationships develop, including whether they emerge gradually or through abrupt threshold events. It encourages studies of contractors, gig-economy workers, temporary workers, and migrant workers, as well as supervisor roles in shaping perceptions of organizational exploitation. It also suggests examining buffers such as calling or attraction to the work, alternative mechanisms such as resource depletion and thwarted psychological needs, actual behavior beyond intentions, adverse health outcomes, and links to mobilization, social movements, and collective action.
abstract: Drawing on the array of literature on exploitation from several social science disciplines, we propose a new way of seeing employer–employee relationships by introducing the concept of perceived exploitative employee–organization relationships, distinguish it from related concepts, and conduct five studies to develop a scale and test our theoretical model of the effects of such employee perceptions. Contributing to the employee– organization relationships and workplace emotions literatures, perceived exploitation is defined as employees’ perceptions that they have been purposefully taken advantage of in their relationship with the organization, to the benefit of the organization itself. We propose and find that such perceptions are associated with both outward-focused emotions of anger and hostility toward the organization and inward-focused ones of shame and guilt at remaining in an exploitative job. In two studies including construction workers and a time-lagged study of medical residents, we find that the emotions of anger and hostility partially mediate the effects of perceived exploitation on employee engagement, revenge against the organization, organizational commitment, and turnover intentions, whereas the emotions of shame and guilt partially mediate the effects of perceived exploitation on employee burnout, silence, and psychological withdrawal.
apa_citation: Livne-Ofer, E., Coyle-Shapiro, J. A.-M., & Pearce, J. L. (2019). Eyes wide open: Perceived exploitation and its consequences. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(6), 1989-2018. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1421

title: Ecological Rationality: Fast-and-Frugal Heuristics for Managerial Decision Making under Uncertainty
methods: Three-study quantitative design comparing D-inference and logistic regression: cross-validation on actual applicant data in Study 1, simulations across task environments in Study 2, and a within-subject experiment with comparative model testing in Study 3.
industry: Personnel selection; Study 1 used actual applicants at an airline company, Study 2 used simulated personnel-selection task environments, and Study 3 used recruiting decisions for receptionist and lead data analyst positions.
country: Southeast Asia for Study 3 participants; Study 1 country not reported in paper.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Job applicants, simulated paired-comparison selection task environments, and individual participants making paired-comparison recruiting decisions.
n_sample: Study 1 used data from 236 applicants; Study 2 examined 1,728 simulated task environments; Study 3 analyzed a final sample of 143 participants.
authors: Luan, S.; Reb, J.; Gigerenzer, G.
theories: bias-variance analysis of prediction error; bounded rationality; ecological rationality; fast-and-frugal heuristics
keywords: D-inference; ecological rationality; fast-and-frugal heuristics; logistic regression; managerial decisions; personnel selection; uncertainty
research_question: The paper asks whether a fast-and-frugal heuristic can make personnel-selection predictions that are as good as, or better than, logistic regression under uncertainty. It also asks under which ecological conditions D-inference outperforms logistic regression and whether decision makers adapt their strategy use to task characteristics.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is ecological fit between a decision strategy and a task environment. D-inference searches cues sequentially, stops when the difference on a cue exceeds a threshold, and decides noncompensatorily; this can reduce variance and cue-search costs when uncertainty is high, learning opportunities are limited, and one cue is substantially more informative than others. Logistic regression can perform relatively better when sample size is large and the task is more linearly predictable. Study 3 extends the prescriptive analysis by showing that many participants used D-inference and that experienced participants were more likely to vary strategy use across conditions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces ecological rationality as an alternative way to evaluate managerial heuristics, shifting the benchmark from universal economic or logical rationality to fit between strategy and environment. It challenges the common view that heuristics are necessarily inferior to more information-intensive strategies and advances a contingency view of managerial decision making. It also contributes to personnel selection by modeling cue integration processes rather than only cue validities.
practical_implication: The paper implies that managers should not be trained only to avoid heuristics or to default to analytical strategies. Training and decision aids should help managers build a repertoire of heuristic and analytical strategies and choose among them based on task environment, objectives, and information costs. In personnel selection, the findings suggest that transparent heuristic rules may sometimes be more accurate, faster, and less costly than compensatory weighting strategies.
limitations: The authors caution that the studies primarily compare D-inference and logistic regression, so the findings should not be generalized automatically to all decision strategies. They also note that Studies 1 and 2 assume efficient parameter learning, whereas managers may make learning errors in practice. The evidence is further bounded by paired-comparison personnel-selection decisions, a single decision criterion of future job performance, one real-world dataset, scenario-based experimental tasks, and a personnel-selection context.
future_research: Future research should test additional strategies such as take-the-best, the recognition heuristic, the 1/N heuristic, and machine-learning algorithms. The authors call for work on how managers learn decision strategies, how D-inference extends to multistage selection systems, and how simple heuristics perform in multi-criteria selection decisions. They also encourage research on heuristics in other managerial domains such as strategy, finance, and marketing.
abstract: Heuristics are often viewed as inferior to “rational” strategies that exhaustively search and process information. Introducing the theoretical perspective of ecological rationality, we challenge this view and argue that, under conditions of uncertainty common to managerial decision making, managers can actually make better decisions using fast-and-frugal heuristics. Within the context of personnel selection, we show that a heuristic called D-inference can more accurately predict which of two job applicants would perform better in the future than can logistic regression, a prototypical rational strategy. Using data from 236 applicants at an airline company, we demonstrate, in Study 1, that, despite searching less than half of the cues, D-inference leads to more accurate selection decisions than logistic regression. After this existence proof, we examine, in Study 2, the ecological conditions under which the heuristic predicts more accurately than logistic regression using 1,728 simulated task environments. Finally, in Study 3, we show in an experiment that participants adapted their strategies to the characteristics of a task—and increasingly so the greater their previous experience in selection decisions. The aim of this article is to propose ecological rationality as an alternative to current views about the nature of heuristics in managerial decisions.
apa_citation: Luan, S., Reb, J., & Gigerenzer, G. (2019). Ecological rationality: Fast-and-frugal heuristics for managerial decision making under uncertainty. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(6), 1735-1759. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2018.0172

title: Dynamic Systems Theory and Dual Change Score Models: Seeing Teams through the Lens of Developmental Psychology
methods: Four-wave longitudinal study of student teams moving from standalone teams into multiteam systems; survey measures were aggregated to the team level and analyzed with nested intercept-only, linear, and dual change score models.
industry: Undergraduate student teams in entry-level courses using the leadership development exercise simulation.
time_period: One school year, with waves approximately three to four weeks apart.
units: Teams nested in multiteam systems.
n_sample: 139 teams nested in 47 multiteam systems.
authors: Matusik, J. G.; Hollenbeck, J. R.; Matta, F. K.; Oh, J. K.
theories: dynamic systems theory; event system theory; structural adaptation theory
keywords: dual change score models; dynamic systems theory; multiteam systems; team development
research_question: The paper asks how team properties change when formerly standalone teams are restructured into interdependent multiteam systems. It also asks whether those changes are linear and non-past-dependent or nonlinear and past-dependent, depending on whether the team property is informed by observable behavioral evidence.
mechanism_summary:
- Dynamic property terms: Observability of the evidence associated with the team property; prior levels of the same team property in the dual change score models.

Drawing on event system theory, structural adaptation theory, and dynamic systems theory, the paper argues that moving into a multiteam system disrupts formerly independent teams by imposing interdependence and reducing autonomy. Observable properties such as goal commitment, backup behavior, and relationship conflict should change gradually and linearly because team members can monitor and conform to visible behaviors. Less observable motivational, cognitive, and affective properties should be more past-dependent and reactive because members compare current internal states with prior states. The results support linear change for the observable properties, dual-change-score dynamics for psychological empowerment and team identification, and a nonmonotonic pattern for cohesion that did not fit the three main model classes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends dynamic systems theory from developmental psychology to team development and integrates it with event system theory and structural adaptation theory. Its central contribution is a within-construct account of team dynamics in which a property is dynamic only when its prior level predicts subsequent change in that same property. It also argues that calling all team properties dynamic is too broad because observable behavioral properties may change linearly without past-dependent proportional change.
practical_implication: Managers should pay close attention to the early transition from standalone teams to multiteam systems because less observable states such as psychological empowerment and team identification may decline steeply at first. Observable behavioral changes may look small initially but can accumulate linearly over time. The paper also suggests that teams that begin with high empowerment or identification may need particular support because they experienced larger declines after restructuring.
limitations: The authors note that they tested a relatively abstract theoretical framework with a concrete empirical setting: one transition from standalone teams to multiteam systems. They also used comparatively simple univariate models, which were appropriate for introducing the method but do not test more complex reciprocal dynamics among constructs. Cohesion required post hoc exploratory modeling because its pattern was nonmonotonic.
future_research: Future research should test whether the same dynamic principles hold for other events, such as team membership changes. The authors also call for multivariate and bivariate dual change score models that add predictors of intercepts, slopes, and interval-specific latent change. More broadly, they encourage researchers to use within-construct longitudinal logic to study different forms of change rather than relying on simple pre-post designs.
abstract: Empirical research examining team development has long lagged behind purely conceptual work. Moreover, traditional designs and logics frequently employed in the organizational sciences generally preclude the possibility of studying the trajectories of various team properties. This is problematic as continuity, nonlinearity, and within-construct feedback are implicit in many eminent conceptualizations of teams. Hence, the present investigation integrates dynamic logic, theory, and methodology from the discipline of developmental psychology—wherein the nature of the topic has necessitated a more careful examination of change over time—into the organizational literature. As a product of this integration, we propose and test a novel theoretical perspective that provides several contributions to teams research. First, we extend theory that has thus far been primarily used to explain intraindividual development in children to detail three testable principles of dynamism in team properties. Second, and utilizing a within-construct logic, we demonstrate that teams are indeed dynamic systems, but that the extent to which any particular team property may be considered dynamic is contingent upon characteristics of the property itself. Finally, we illustrate how teams’ unique pasts may be leveraged to predict their asymmetric reactions to disruptive events in the future by employing a contemporary modeling technique.

title: Making the Invisible Visible: Paradoxical Effects of Intersectional Invisibility on the Career Experiences of Executive Black Women
methods: Qualitative grounded theory study using two waves of semi-structured interviews and cross-case analysis of senior-level executive Black women interviewed around 2007 and 2014.
industry: Diverse industries among senior-level executive Black women, with common representation from financial services, consumer products, and health care or pharmaceuticals.
time_period: Two interview waves, approximately 2007 and 2014.
units: Executive Black women in senior-level roles; interviews and career trajectories.
n_sample: 59 participants who completed both interviews.
authors: Smith, A. N.; Watkins, M. B.; Ladge, J. J.; Carlton, P.
theories: dual stigma; intersectional invisibility; intersectionality framework; outsider within status
keywords: Black women; agentic visibility tactics; credible visibility; intersectional invisibility; outsider within
research_question: How do executive Black women experience and manage intersectional invisibility as they navigate senior-level careers? The paper asks how benign and hostile forms of intersectional invisibility shape these women's credible visibility and career trajectories.
mechanism_summary:
- Contexts: Intersectional dual stigma, professional investment and support, and personal support and self-assurance produce executive Black women's outsider within status.
- Paradox: Benign intersectional invisibility creates a license for authenticity, while hostile intersectional invisibility creates a need to reduce perceived threat.
- Agentic visibility tactics: Executive Black women lean into risk, use bold autonomy, strategically deploy invisibility, and consciously craft cross-race and cross-gender relationships.
- Career trajectories: These tactics help create credible visibility, but trajectories still vary across credible ascent, reinvention, plateau, and hypervisibility.

The process is not a simple disadvantage story. The authors argue that the same intersectional position can both loosen stereotypical constraints and intensify scrutiny, so executive Black women must continually balance authenticity, threat reduction, risk-taking, relationship work, and strategic visibility.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances a theory of the paradoxical effects of intersectional invisibility by showing that it operates through both benign and hostile dimensions rather than being wholly positive or wholly negative. It also extends social identity management research by identifying agentic visibility tactics through which intersectionally invisible actors seek credible visibility while managing the tension between fitting in and standing out.
practical_implication: The paper cautions against one-size-fits-all advice for advancing women because executive Black women's career experiences are shaped by the intersection of race, gender, and executive status. It suggests that sponsors, mentors, and organizations should recognize the longer career runways and distinct visibility burdens facing Black women rather than assuming that generic confidence, risk-taking, or relationship-building advice is sufficient.
limitations: The authors note that the study focuses only on senior-level executive Black women, so the findings may not generalize to Black women at lower organizational levels or to other intersectional groups. They also acknowledge limitations from retrospective self-reports, reliance on the women's own perspectives rather than others' perceptions, two waves of data, and the inability to make definitive claims about the causal effects of specific tactics on career outcomes.
future_research: Future research should examine whether benign and hostile intersectional invisibility operate similarly for other groups with multiple subordinate identities and at different organizational levels. The authors also call for empirical work that tests how specific agentic visibility tactics relate to career outcomes and for more longitudinal research on the experiences and outcomes associated with intersectional invisibility.
abstract: The unique and complex experiences of and challenges for Black women, which are tied to their intersecting marginalized identities, have largely been overlooked in management research. Although Black women are physically visible in that they are different from most of their colleagues, intersectional invisibility research suggests that they can be simultaneously invisible—easily overlooked or disregarded—because they are nonprototypical members of their gender and racial identity groups. To shed new light on the role that intersectional invisibility plays in Black women’s perceptions and experiences, we conducted two waves of in-depth interviews across seven years with 59 Black women who occupy senior-level positions in organizations. We develop a theoretical model to explain the paradoxical effects of executive Black women’s “outsider within” status in which they simultaneously experience opportunities and constraints associated with two forms of intersectional invisibility: benign and hostile. To manage both forms of intersectional invisibility, executive Black Women adopt a number of critical strategies to gain credible visibility needed to ascend in their careers.

Making the invisible visible: Paradoxical effects of intersectional invisibility on the career experiences of executive Black women. *Academy of Management Journal*, 62(6), 1705-1734. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.1513

title: The Other Side: Occupational Interactional Requirements and Work–Home Enrichment
methods: Three empirical quantitative studies: a cross-sectional ATUS/O*NET time-use analysis, a two-wave survey of full-time employees in Singapore, and a U.S. experience-sampling study; analyses include simultaneous regression models, path analysis, bootstrapped mediation, and multilevel path analysis.
industry: Full-time workers across occupational clusters rather than a single industry.
time_period: Study 1 uses ATUS data from 2003 to 2015; Study 2 uses two waves one week apart; Study 3 uses two consecutive workweeks.
units: Full-time employees/workers living with a family member.
n_sample: Study 1: 17,490 respondents; Study 2: 274 participants with complete responses; Study 3: 79 participants and 610 matched survey pairs.
authors: Bhave, D. P.; Lefter, A. M.
theories: conservation of resources theory; self-determination theory
keywords: emotional labor; occupational interactional requirements; time allocation; vitality; work–home enrichment
research_question: The paper asks whether occupational interactional requirements enrich employees' lives at home, and through which facets of the home domain this enrichment appears. It tests whether workplace interactions operate as restorative job properties that generate vitality and transfer resources from work to home.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is resource transfer. The authors integrate conservation of resources theory and self-determination theory to argue that workplace interactions can satisfy relatedness needs, spark vitality, and make employees more able to invest effort in the home domain. In Study 1, this appears as more time spent caring for family and less time spent in leisure; in Studies 2 and 3, vitality mediates the relationship between occupational interactional requirements and work–home enrichment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the dominant emotional-labor assumption that occupational interactional requirements are primarily depleting. It reframes interactive work as a contextual social resource that can replenish vitality and generate benefits across the work–home interface. It also contributes to work–family research by linking occupational attributes to both objective time-allocation indicators and employees' perceived work–home enrichment.
practical_implication: Organizations can treat workplace interactions as a possible source of recovery rather than only as a demand to be minimized. The authors suggest practices that increase the meaningfulness of interactions, sequence positive interactions after resource-draining work, and encourage reflection on positive interactions before employees leave work.
limitations: The studies focus on employees who are employed full-time and live with family members, so the findings may not generalize to other family structures. The analysis is primarily individual-level and relies mainly on employees' own reports of work–home enrichment rather than reports from spouses, partners, or other family members. The authors also note that they could not identify employees' motives behind allocating time to different home activities.
future_research: Future research could examine couple-level and workgroup-level processes, significant-other reports, and variation across different family structures. It could also test whether occupational values such as altruism or status strengthen the vitality benefits of interactional requirements. Further work could use more granular measures of housework and study other nonwork activities such as volunteering.
abstract: We examine how occupational interactional requirements influence work–home enrichment. We conceptualize “occupational interactional requirements” as restorative properties of jobs that provide employees with resources that they transfer to the home domain. We identify two manifestations of work–home enrichment: (1) through objective indicators of how employees allocate their time at home, and (2) through employees’ perceptual reflections of their work–home enrichment. In terms of objective indicators, our results indicate that employees transfer these resources by spending more time in resource-draining activities such as caring for family, and less time in resource-replenishing activities such as socializing and relaxing. This suggests that occupational interactional requirements facilitate a reallocation of time in the home domain. In terms of perceptual reflections, we observe that occupational interactional requirements spark employees’ vitality, which, in turn, enriches their life at home. Our results attest to considering workplace interactions as resource-replenishing features of jobs that provide benefits across the work– home interface.

title: Collaborative Stakeholder Engagement: An Integration between Theories of Organizational Legitimacy and Learning
methods: Longitudinal panel analysis of U.S. local law enforcement agencies using LEMAS survey data and FBI Uniform Crime Reporting crime rates. The study estimates random-effects Tobit models for calls for service and random-effects ordered logistic models for community policing practices, with lagged predictors, year effects, and robustness checks using generalized ordered logistic regression.
industry: Local law enforcement agencies
time_period: 1997, 2000, 2003, and 2007 reporting periods, with 1993 observations used to construct initial lagged variables
units: Agency-year observations
n_sample: 2,380 agency-year observations in the full estimation sample; model Ns vary across analyses because of missing variables and restricted use-of-force complaint data
authors: Desai, V. M.
theories: organizational learning theory; theories of organizational legitimacy; theories of organizational search and exploration
keywords: collaborative stakeholder engagement; community policing; organizational learning; organizational legitimacy; organizational search
research_question: How do organizations balance the search benefits of collaborative stakeholder engagement against the legitimacy risks created when collaboration exposes internal practices to external scrutiny? In the law enforcement setting, the paper asks when agencies use community policing as a search tool and when stakeholder power or controversial practices suppress that response.
mechanism_summary: Collaborative engagement gives organizations access to external information that may help them solve problems, so agencies facing higher crime rates should be more likely to use community policing practices. The same engagement also makes organizational practices more transparent to stakeholders, so agencies should temper collaboration when powerful stakeholders can hold them accountable or when controversial practices have already threatened legitimacy. The results generally support this logic most clearly for more substantive combinations of community policing practices rather than isolated or superficial adoption.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates organizational search and learning theories with organizational legitimacy theory by treating collaborative stakeholder engagement as both an information-search mechanism and a legitimacy-exposure mechanism. It contributes to learning theory by showing that organizations may abstain from reciprocal search activities when those activities risk revealing practices to stakeholders. It also contributes to legitimacy research by showing that legitimacy concerns can indirectly shape organizational search and learning, not only direct reputation-management tactics.
practical_implication: Organizations using stakeholder collaboration to solve problems should recognize that the same openness that improves information access can increase scrutiny of internal practices. For law enforcement agencies, community policing may generate more outside information, but agencies with powerful oversight bodies or visible force-related complaints may avoid substantive engagement unless they can manage the associated legitimacy risks.
limitations: The empirical context is local law enforcement, where agencies are not exposed to the same competitive pressures as market-oriented organizations, so collaborative engagement may operate differently in other settings. The data are coarse because many measures are observed only every three to four years in the LEMAS survey, leaving possible intervening issues unobserved. Some measures, especially use-of-force complaints, are available only for restricted periods and may underreport the underlying incidents they proxy.
future_research: Future research should test the framework in other collaborative contexts such as crowdsourcing, open source software development, and telemedicine. The paper also calls for research on how outside parties modify their interactions with organizations as they learn about them, how power disparities shape collaboration, and how fragmented stakeholder communities and organizations iteratively influence one another over time.
abstract: Organizations often collaborate with stakeholders such as customers, communities, and other groups to pursue shared goals, and these partnerships are known to affect an organization’s legitimacy with those groups as well as its access to information from them. While these concerns could be examined within each of their own independent literatures, existing theories are ill equipped to handle this process in tandem. Thus, studying these collaborations provides an opportunity to more broadly explore how organizations balance knowledge search or exploration efforts with their needs to manage organizational legitimacy. Accordingly, I suggest that collaboration facilitates access to external information, and that organizations pursue it when the information is needed to solve related problems. However, I also argue that collaborations reciprocally allow stakeholders to more directly scrutinize organizational practices. Thus, I predict that organizations suppress their use of collaborations to solve problems when their legitimacy is potentially or already at risk, such as when powerful stakeholders can hold an organization accountable for inappropriate acts or when some organizational actions have already been deemed as controversial. I test related predictions on the community policing efforts of a law enforcement agency panel, finding general support for several of the study’s predictions.
apa_citation: Desai, V. M. (2018). Collaborative stakeholder engagement: An integration between theories of organizational legitimacy and learning. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 220-244. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0315

title: Emerging Intentionality in Routine Dynamics: A Pragmatist View
methods: Yearlong ethnographic study of CellCo, an anonymized pharmaceutical company, using nonparticipant observation, audio recordings, semi-structured interviews, informal discussions, document collection, iterative qualitative analysis, and thickly descriptive narratives of routine performances.
industry: Pharmaceutical company producing cell tissues and proprietary plates.
time_period: Main fieldwork from February 2011 to February 2012.
units: Routine performances at CellCo, especially assembling, shipping, newsletter, and sales routines.
n_sample: CellCo had 18 employees; the fieldwork included 30 semi-structured interviews, more than 80 assembling-routine performances, more than 100 shipping-routine repetitions, nearly 1,000 pages of field notes, 3,000 pages of transcripts, and approximately 8,000 internal documents.
authors: Dittrich, K.; Seidl, D.
theories: practice-theoretical approaches to routines; pragmatist theory of action; routine dynamics
keywords: emerging intentionality; ends-in-view; foregrounding means; intentionality; pragmatist theory of action; routine change; routine dynamics
research_question: The paper asks how the enactment of means influences actors' ends, and how this influence contributes to routine change. It investigates this question by studying how CellCo participants performed and patterned routines when new means in concrete situations generated new ends-in-view.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / distinctions: Ends-in-view in specific performances, general goals for a routine, means, unfolding situations, purposeful action, purposive action, and emerging intentionality.
- Empirical routines: Assembling plates, shipping, newsletter, and sales routines at CellCo.
- Process / phases: Unfamiliar situations generate questions; participants foreground available means; new ends-in-view emerge; participants may update routine goals and associated action patterns; progressive means-ends cycles can extend across routines.
- Boundary conditions: The authors emphasize CellCo's young age, simple and predictable routines, and entrepreneurial openness to experimentation as conditions that made foregrounding means especially visible.
- Emergent outcomes: Routine change arises not only from actors pursuing pre-established goals, but also from situated action in which new means generate new purposes.

The process centers on foregrounding means. When existing goals are less salient or the situation is unfamiliar, participants probe available material, relational, and socio-material means; this engagement can generate new ends-in-view, such as preserving lab space, organizing assembling as a student part-time job, creating predictable plate supply, or using a regional shipping hub to provide a better customer deal. Some emergent ends remain temporary exceptions, while others become new routine goals and stabilize as revised action patterns.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to routine dynamics by expanding intentionality beyond purposeful action guided by pre-existing goals. It theorizes purposive action as a form of intentional action in which ends-in-view emerge through engagement with means in situated routine performances. It also revises assumptions that intentionality is rooted in individual actors or prior cognition, arguing instead that intentionality is dynamically constituted through action.
practical_implication: The paper implies that managers seeking routine change should attend to situated action and the means people engage, not only to actors' stated goals or mental intentions. For practice, the authors argue that changing routines may require intervening in actions and material or relational means rather than trying only to change cognition.
limitations: The authors identify important boundary conditions rather than a formal limitations section. Because CellCo was young, entrepreneurial, and organized around relatively simple routines with predictable outcomes, foregrounding means may have been more prevalent and easier to observe than in established, high-reliability, or highly complex organizations.
future_research: The authors call for research on how power shapes which ends-in-view are enacted and which patterns dominate over time, including reconsideration of the routine truce under a relational view of intentionality. They also suggest studying how actors emerge as particular selves through ends-in-view in routine performances, and how action in routines displays varying degrees of social autonomy.
abstract: This paper responds to recent interest in the role of intentionality in the internal dynamics of routines. Previous research has focused on how routine participants bring particular intentions to the performance of a routine and choose the means for accomplishing the pre-defined ends accordingly. Drawing on the pragmatist theory of action and a yearlong ethnographic study of a pharmaceutical company, we uncover “emerging intentionality” in routine performances. We show how the foregrounding of means within the concrete situation at hand might lead to the emergence of new ends to pursue. Moreover, we find that the emergence of new ends in routine performances might result in updating the goals for the routine and its associated patterns. With these findings, we contribute to a better understanding of the full spectrum of intentional action in routine dynamics, ranging from purposeful action (foregrounding ends) to purposive action (foregrounding means). This expanded perspective on intentionality in routine dynamics suggests a greater potential for continuous routine change than previous research has acknowledged.
apa_citation: Dittrich, K., & Seidl, D. (2018). Emerging intentionality in routine dynamics: A pragmatist view. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 111-138. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0010

title: Motivation and Ability? A Behavioral Perspective on the Pursuit of Radical Invention in Multi-Technology Incumbents
methods: Empirical quantitative patent study using USPTO/NBER patent data and Compustat. The authors estimate panel logit models with firm-level random effects for pursuit of potentially radical patents, OLS firm fixed-effects models with selection correction for logged forward citations, and probit firm fixed-effects models for breakthrough patents.
industry: Cross-industry sample of USPTO patents filed by for-profit firms, with financial-data analyses for publicly traded firms.
units: Patents, firms, firm-technology-class observations, and technology domains.
n_sample: 785,490 usable patents from 16,455 firms in the all-firm sample; 315,494 patents from 1,755 publicly traded firms in the public-firm subsample.
authors: Eggers, J. P.; Kaul, Aseem
theories: aspiration-level performance feedback; behavioral theory of the firm (Cyert & March, 1963; Greve, 2003); capability-based perspective
keywords: behavioral theory; incumbent firms; patent data; performance aspirations; radical invention; radical technologies; technological diversity
research_question: The paper asks when and why incumbent firms pursue potentially radical inventions and whether their motivation to pursue radical invention aligns with their ability to develop successful radical technologies. It focuses on variation within established, multi-technology firms rather than the standard entrant-versus-incumbent framing of radical technological change.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines behavioral theory and a capability-based account of invention. Firms are most motivated to pursue radical invention when technology-area performance is moderately below aspirations because underperformance encourages riskier search, but this motivation falls when performance is far below aspirations or substantially above aspirations. Ability moves differently: stronger prior performance in a technology area indicates stronger capabilities and therefore higher expected success for potentially radical inventions. This creates a mismatch in which firms may overinvest in radical invention when moderately below aspirations and underinvest when substantially above aspirations.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends behavioral theory of the firm by linking performance feedback not only to the choice to search radically but also to the likely success of that search. It shows that the same performance conditions that motivate distant search may not be the conditions under which firms are most capable of succeeding.

It also contributes to radical innovation research by recentering incumbent firms as sources of competence-enhancing radical inventions. The paper separates motivation from ability and demonstrates that incumbents' difficulty is not simply lack of willingness or capability, but a systematic mismatch between where they are motivated and where they are able.
practical_implication: Not reported in paper.
limitations:
The study relies on patent data, so it observes patented invention rather than all inventive effort and does not directly observe commercialization outcomes. Patent citations and breakthrough status are useful measures of technological success, but they do not fully capture market value or strategic value to the firm.

The empirical design requires prior performance in a technology class, which limits the main analysis to existing firms and technology areas where firms already have patenting experience. The authors also note that they examine the development of radical inventions rather than the later decision to commercialize them.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether the motivation-ability mismatch also appears in commercialization decisions after radical inventions have been developed. This would clarify whether performance relative to aspirations shapes a firm's motivation and ability to commercialize successful radical inventions.

Additional work could use alternate measures of technological invention, such as scientific publications, and could examine radical invention by established firms outside technology areas in which they are already active.
abstract: We examine the role of incumbent firms in developing radical technologies, distinguishing between their motivation and ability to develop radical inventions. We argue that the motivation to pursue radical invention will be strongest when performance is moderately below aspiration, and will weaken as performance either falls substantially below aspiration or rises substantially above aspiration. At the same time, ability will increase with performance, resulting in a behavioral mismatch between ability and motivation—firms overinvest in radical invention when performance is moderately below aspiration and underinvest when performance is substantially above aspiration, with these effects being stronger for broad, multi-technology firms. We show empirical support for our arguments using patent data, using an empirical approach that distinguishes the potential radicalness of an invention from its eventual success. Our study highlights the role of established firms as a source of radical technologies, and examines the behavioral biases that may limit firms from pursuing competenceenhancing radical technologies.
apa_citation: Eggers, J. P., & Kaul, A. (2018). Motivation and ability? A behavioral perspective on the pursuit of radical invention in multi-technology incumbents. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 67-93. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1123

title: Rewards for Patents and Inventor Behaviors in Industrial Research and Development
methods: Survey of inventors linked to European Patent Office patent applications; firm-level false positives and false negatives are modeled against inventor behaviors using OLS regressions with robust standard errors clustered by firm, plus robustness checks.
industry: For-profit corporations' formal R&D patenting projects
country: 23 countries surveyed, including 20 European countries, Israel, the United States, and Japan
time_period: Patent priority dates between 2003 and 2005
units: Patent-inventor observations among inventors whose regular job is inventing in an R&D department
n_sample: 3,955 patent-inventor observations
authors: Giarratana, M. S.; Mariani, M.; Weller, I.
theories: signaling theory; social identity theory
keywords: Pay for performance (PFP); corporate scientists; false negatives; false positives; patented inventions; social identity theory
research_question: The paper asks how pay for performance for patents creates false positives and false negatives, and how these false rewards differ in their association with inventor behaviors. It focuses on whether corporate scientists react differently from other inventors when firms reward low-quality patents or fail to reward high-quality patents.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that false positives are tangible signals that a firm's patent reward system violates the scientific community's priority-based, winner-take-all norms. Corporate scientists, whose identity is tied to scientific prestige, peer recognition, and intellectual challenge, respond by withdrawing effort from R&D tasks and reducing interactions with close R&D peers. False negatives are theorized to be noisier and less threatening because they may reflect uncertainty or selective reward practices consistent with scientific norms.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends the informational perspective on pay for performance by distinguishing false positives from false negatives rather than treating all reward errors as equivalent. It adds social identity theory to agency-based accounts, showing that employee reactions to compensation systems depend on group-based identities and the meaning employees attach to reward signals.
practical_implication: Managers should not assume that broadening patent rewards will uniformly motivate inventors. Increasing reward breadth can create more false positives, and corporate scientists may respond negatively when rewards appear insufficiently selective. Firms should monitor dissatisfaction and behavioral withdrawal after compensation-system changes and improve patent appraisal processes where reward decisions are noisy or politically biased.
limitations: The study relies on cross-sectional survey data and cannot prove causality or fully exclude unobserved confounds. The authors also note potential aggregation and measurement issues, including common method bias and recall bias, although they report several checks designed to reduce these concerns.
future_research: Future work could test the proposed mechanism through laboratory experiments or scenario studies. Research could also examine other settings where employees identify with external communities whose norms conflict with organizational reward practices, and further study how performance assessment reliability shapes future behavior through compensation systems.
abstract: This study investigates the effects of rewards in a research and development (R&D) setting in which employees’ inventive efforts lead to patented inventions. Pay for performance (PFP) for inventions is associated with two challenges: Low-quality inventions may be rewarded (false positives), and high-quality inventions may be overlooked (false negatives). Building on previous findings regarding the motivational and informational effects of rewards, we use social identity theory to predict that different types of inventors react differently to such false positive and false negative information. Specifically, we hypothesize that PFP that produces false positives has detrimental effects on corporate inventors with a taste for science, who are motivated by scientific prestige, reputation, and intellectual curiosity. The empirical results from survey data related to 3,995 inventor–patent pairs show that, for this particular group of inventors, false positives are associated with reduced effort in research activities and fewer interactions with peers in the R&D department. In addition, these effects are stronger when firms have many patents and thus provide less noisy information to corporate inventors.

title: The Strategic Value of Selection Practices: Antecedents and Consequences of Firm-level Selection Practice Usage
methods: Random coefficient modeling of Human Capital Corporate Panel survey data matched to Korean Information Service financial data, with firms nested within industries and controls for firm age, firm size, unionization, HPWS, labor costs, prior firm performance, industry growth, and industry dynamism.
industry: Manufacturing, finance, and non-finance service firms across 28 Korean SIC-based subindustries
time_period: Selection-practice data for 2004; firm performance and industry sales data for 2000-2007
units: Firms nested within industries
n_sample: 413 firms
authors: Kim, Youngsang; Ployhart, Robert E.
theories: contingency theory
keywords: collective turnover; contingency theory; firm performance; selection practices; strategic human resource management
research_question: Why do firms differ in their use of selection practices, and when do selection practices relate to subsequent firm performance? The paper asks whether external industry conditions and internal firm conditions shape both selection-practice usage and the selection-performance relationship.
mechanism_summary: The core mechanism is contingent fit between a firm's selection system and its competitive environment. Contingency theory implies that firms choose more or fewer selection practices in response to external industry conditions and internal human-capital conditions. More selection practices can build higher-quality generic human capital and raise productivity, but their value depends on context: dynamic industries and low collective turnover strengthen the performance benefits, while stable industries can make the costs or rigidity of more selection practices outweigh their benefits.
theoretical_contribution: The paper brings contingency theory into personnel selection research, challenging the assumption that selection practices have uniformly positive firm-level value. It extends strategic HRM by showing that choices inside a specific HR practice, not only broad HPWS bundles, can be strategically consequential. It also reframes validity generalization: selection practices may generalize at the individual level while their firm-level performance value remains contingent on industry and organizational conditions.
practical_implication: Managers should not reduce selection rigor automatically when growing or dynamic industries create pressure to hire quickly. Selection practices are most valuable when they provide appropriate and nonredundant coverage of job-relevant attributes, when turnover is low enough to retain selected human capital, and when managers forecast staffing returns in relation to competitive context. The paper cautions that selection investments in stable industries may not pay off in the same way as in dynamic industries.
limitations: The authors note that the findings may be shaped by South Korean culture, the specific firms studied, the timing of the data, and the study context. The selection measure is based on one HR manager's report of firm-level hiring, does not distinguish jobs or employee types, and captures the number rather than the validity or quality of practices. The design uses multiple time periods but does not eliminate endogeneity, causality, omitted-variable, or reverse-causality concerns.
future_research: Future research should replicate the findings in other cultural and institutional settings and examine specific selection practices of known validity. The authors call for studies with multiple respondents per firm, direct measures of human capital resources as mediators, and longer longitudinal designs that observe changes in selection practices over time. Further work should test when selection practices create, weaken, or even harm firm-level performance under different environmental conditions.
abstract: The expectation that selection practices contribute to organizational performance has been long assumed; however, research on personnel selection has neglected to consider why firms differ in their use of selection practices and whether selection practices relate to organizational performance under different competitive environments. Based on strategic human resource management research, we introduce contingency theory to examine whether external (industry characteristics) and internal (prior firm performance and collective turnover) environments affect the use of selection practices, how the adoption of selection practices relates to subsequent firm performance, and whether the external (industry) and internal (selection stages and collective turnover) environments moderate the selection–performance relationship. Using a sample of 413 firms, we found that firms use more selection practices when there is less collective turnover and when firms are within low-growth and stable industries. The results also show that firms employing more selection practices generated greater productivity but not profit. Positive effects occur when firms have less collective turnover and are within dynamic industries but, surprisingly, the effects of selection on performance can actually be negative in stable industries. These findings provide new insights about the strategic value of personnel selection; one that is sensitive to and contingent upon competitive environments.
