title: Organizational Affective Tone: A Meso Perspective on the Origins and Effects of Consistent Affect in Organizations
methods: Survey-based empirical quantitative study of German firms using multi-source firm-level survey data, OLS regression models, mediation tests, path analysis, and post-hoc interaction analyses.
industry: Firms operating across a range of industries, including service, retail, wholesale trade, finance, insurance, real estate, production, and manufacturing.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Firms and their human resource managers, top management team members, and employees.
n_sample: 24,015 individuals from 161 firms.
authors: Knight, A. P.; Menges, J. I.; Bruch, H.
theories: job demands-resources model; open systems perspective
keywords: consumer-centric industries; organizational affective tone; organizational structure; personnel policies; workforce strain
research_question: The paper asks why some organizations develop a more positive or negative affective tone and whether that tone matters for workforce strain. It examines whether consumer-centric activity shapes organizational affective tone through personnel practices and organizational design.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is a meso open-systems process. Organizations whose domains include more consumer-centric activity place greater value on positive affect and lower negative affect, and this logic is embedded through emotion-focused personnel practices and lower centralization. Formalization was hypothesized as part of the structural pathway but was not supported in the results. Organizational affective tone then functions as a contextual resource or demand: positive tone is expected to reduce workforce strain, while negative tone is expected to increase it.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a meso explanation for collective affect by linking organizational affective tone to the macro domain in which an organization creates value. It extends affect research beyond small-group emotional contagion by showing how organizational design and personnel practices can embed consistent affect across a whole firm. It also connects organizational affective tone to workforce strain as a contextual demand or resource.
practical_implication: The findings imply that leaders can shape organizational affective tone through choices about personnel practices and organizational design, especially centralization. Firms moving toward more consumer-centric activity may need to cultivate affective capacity slowly through selection, promotion, structure, leader behavior, and training. The results also suggest that affective tone is relevant to employee exhaustion and sickness absence, although the strain effects vary across contexts.
limitations: The study uses cross-sectional data, so causal conclusions remain tentative, especially for the relationship between affective tone and workforce strain. The sample is limited to medium-sized German firms, which restricts generalizability to other countries and larger multinational organizations. The split-sample design supports multi-source measurement but prevents tests of individual-level and cross-level mechanisms such as trait affectivity.
future_research: Future research could examine other macro factors, such as economic conditions, that may shape organizational affective tone. Studies could compare firms within the same industry to explain strategic deviations from the average affective tendency of consumer-centric organizations. Longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs are also needed to test causal ordering and cross-level interactions between organizational affective tone and individual strain.
abstract: Grounded in an open systems perspective, we build and test new theory about how the kinds of industries in which an organization participates influence organizational affective tone and connect to workforce strain. We propose that the more an organization’s activities lie in consumer-centric industries (e.g., service, retail), the more positive and less negative the organization’s affective tone. We connect consumer-centric industry participation and affective tone by explaining how personnel policies and organizational structure generate and sustain consistent positive and negative affect throughout an organization. Additionally, we examine the effects of organizational affective tone on workforce strain. The results of a survey-based study of 24,015 human resource managers, top management team members, and employees of 161 firms largely support our predictions. We discuss the implications of considering macro contextual factors for understanding affect in organizations.
apa_citation: Knight, A. P., Menges, J. I., & Bruch, H. (2018). Organizational affective tone: A meso perspective on the origins and effects of consistent affect in organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 191-219. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0671

title: Does Proactive Personality Matter in Leadership Transitions? Effects of Proactive Personality on New Leader Identification and Responses to New Leaders and their Change Agendas
methods: Four-wave before-and-after transition survey using three sources: team members, former leaders, and new leaders. The analysis uses polynomial regression, response surface modeling, and bootstrapping-based moderated mediation tests to examine proactive personality congruence and former-new leader contrast.
industry: Hospitality industry; employees and low- to middle-level managers in a large private upscale hotel group in mainland China.
time_period: January, March, May, and July 2015, with two-month intervals across the leadership transition.
units: Hotel employees nested in work teams, newly encountered direct low- to middle-level managers, and former leaders.
n_sample: Final sample of 155 employees from 51 work teams, with new leaders and former leaders also surveyed.
authors: Lam, Wing; Lee, Cynthia; Taylor, M. Susan; Zhao, Helen H.
theories: congruence effects; contrast effects; leader identification perspective
keywords: change agenda; congruence; contrast effects; engagement; leader identification; leadership transitions; proactive personality; voice behavior
research_question: Why and how do teams develop identification with a new leader during leadership transitions, and how does that identification shape teams' receptiveness to the new leader's change agenda? The paper asks whether congruence between team and new-leader proactive personalities, conditioned by the contrast between former and new leaders' proactive personalities, predicts new leader identification, change-agenda identification, engagement, and voice.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an identification process activated by leadership transition. When a proactive new leader is paired with a proactive team, the leader and team are more likely to share norms, values, and a sense of oneness, which strengthens identification with the new leader and the leader's change agenda. This congruence effect is stronger when the new leader's proactive personality positively contrasts with the former leader's proactive personality, because team members evaluate the new leader against the former leader as a salient reference point. Stronger identification then carries through to more engagement with, and voice about, the change agenda.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends leadership-transition research beyond CEO and top-management succession by explaining middle- and lower-level leader transitions through team-level identification mechanisms. It shows that reactions to a new leader depend not only on new leader-team congruence but also on the contrast between the former and new leader.

The paper also extends proactivity research by integrating proactive personality congruence with leader identification, rather than treating proactive personality as only an individual-level predictor of proactive behavior. It adds a before-and-after transition design with former-leader, new-leader, and team-member data, improving on designs that rely only on posttransition perceptions.
practical_implication:
Organizations should consider both fit with the team and contrast with the former leader when appointing new leaders during transitions. A proactive new leader may be especially effective when the team is also proactive and the former leader was less proactive.

The findings also imply that newly appointed leaders can benefit from visibly demonstrating their positive proactive characteristics early in the transition. Training and onboarding can help new leaders establish identification with teams and build receptiveness to change agendas.
limitations:
The study's data were collected only in China, so the authors caution that the findings may not generalize to cultures with different power-distance, relationship-orientation, or communication patterns. The research context is also a hospitality setting undergoing leadership transitions, which may differ from more routine or less dynamic work contexts.

The study focuses on proactive personality and therefore cannot rule out alternative trait-based explanations such as psychological resilience, openness to change, perspective taking, or political skill. It also measures proactivity primarily as proactive personality, leaving room for future work on different forms and meanings of proactive behavior, including potentially harmful proactivity.
future_research:
Future research could compare high- and low-context cultures to test whether new leader-team proactive personality congruence operates similarly across cultural settings. Additional studies could examine whether congruence in other traits, such as resilience or openness to change, affects leadership transitions.

The authors also call for work on routine work contexts and on different forms of proactivity. Future studies could investigate whether proactive leader-team congruence remains beneficial when tasks are structured and repetitive, or when proactive behavior is viewed as disruptive rather than constructive.
abstract: Despite the growing frequency of leadership transitions and their significant impact on team and organizational performance, little research has examined why and how teams develop identification with a new leader, or their subsequent receptiveness to the new leader’s change initiatives. Drawing from the contrast and congruence effects and the theoretical perspectives of leader identification, this study empirically tests a model in which the congruence of new leaders’ and their teams’ proactive personalities foster new leader identification, as well as the team’s behavioral responses to the new leader’s change agenda. This effect is strongest when the new leader’s proactive personality is higher than that of the former leader’s proactive personality (positive contrast). Our findings of a four-wave “before-and-after” transition survey of 155 hotel employees and 51 new leaders, achieved through polynomial regression analyses, proved very insightful. We found that the congruence between a new leader’s and his or her team’s proactive personalities, and the positive contrast between a former leader’s and the new leader’s proactive personalities, enhanced new leader identification and the team’s shared identification with the new leader’s change agenda, and thereby led the team to exhibit more behavioral engagement with, and voice behavior about, the new leader’s change agenda.
apa_citation: Lam, W., Lee, C., Taylor, M. S., & Zhao, H. H. (2018). Does proactive personality matter in leadership transitions? Effects of proactive personality on new leader identification and responses to new leaders and their change agendas. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 245-263. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0503

title: Microfoundations of Organizational Paradox: The Problem Is How We Think about the Problem
methods: Multi-study scale development and validation, followed by a quantitative field test using employee surveys, supervisor-rated outcomes, qualitative coding of open-ended tension examples, CFA, regression, and PROCESS moderated mediation.
industry: Large consumer products company with electronic, industrial, pharmaceutical, medical, and fabric departments; additional scale-development samples included employees and students.
country: Study 1 samples from the U.S., UK, Israel, and China; Study 2 tested the model in a large firm in the U.S.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals: employees, students, product specialists, and supervisor-rated product specialists.
n_sample: Study 1 used eight samples ranging from 80 to 300 participants; Study 2 surveyed 135 product specialists, with supervisor ratings for 91.
authors: Miron-Spektor, E.; Ingram, A.; Keller, J.; Smith, W. K.; Lewis, M. W.
theories: organizational paradox theory; paradox mindset
keywords: experiencing tensions; in-role job performance; innovation; organizational paradox; paradox mindset; resource scarcity
research_question: The paper asks why some individuals thrive with organizational tensions while others struggle, and what conditions intensify employees' experience of tensions. It examines whether resource scarcity surfaces tensions and whether paradox mindset changes the effects of those tensions on in-role job performance and innovation.
mechanism_summary: Resource scarcity makes competing demands more salient by forcing individuals to compare goals and allocate limited time and funding. Experiencing tensions can deplete or energize employees depending on whether they approach contradictions as dilemmas to resolve or paradoxes to accept and engage. A paradox mindset helps individuals value, accept, and feel comfortable with tensions, making them more likely to search for both/and responses that support performance and innovation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the microfoundations of organizational paradox by theorizing individual variation in how employees experience and respond to tensions. It develops and validates measures of experiencing tensions and paradox mindset across multiple samples, then shows that paradox mindset helps explain when tensions undermine or improve job outcomes.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that recognizing tensions is not enough; employees and leaders also need a mindset that enables acceptance, comfort, and productive engagement with contradictions. The paradox mindset scale offers a way for leaders and practitioners to assess their approaches to tensions and begin building awareness around how those approaches affect job outcomes.
limitations: The model test is cross-sectional, so longitudinal or experimental designs would provide stronger evidence of causality and reduce common-method concerns. The outcomes rely on supervisors' evaluations, the field test focuses on product specialists in one U.S. firm, and the study examines limited time and finances as the main sources of learning and performing tensions.
future_research: Future work should test the model across cultures, contexts, and other kinds of tensions, including organizing and identity tensions. The paper also calls for research on cognitive, behavioral, organizational, cultural, developmental, and training-related factors that may strengthen or weaken paradox mindset.
abstract: Competing tensions and demands pervade our work lives. Accumulating research examines organizational and leadership approaches to leveraging these tensions. But what about individuals within firms? Although early paradox theory built upon micro-level insights from psychology and philosophy to understand the nature and management of varied competing demands, corresponding empirical studies are rare, offering scarce insights into why some individuals thrive with tensions while others struggle. In response, we contribute to the microfoundations of organizational paradox with a theoretical model and robust measures that help unpack individuals’ varied approaches to tensions. Following rigorous scale development in Study 1, including samples from the U.S., UK, Israel, and China, we test our model in a large firm in the U.S. using quantitative and qualitative methods. We identify resource scarcity (i.e., limited time and funding) as a source of tensions. We also demonstrate that a paradox mindset—the extent to which one is accepting of and energized by tensions—can help individuals leverage them to improve in-role job performance and innovation. Our results highlight paradox mindset as a key to unlocking the potential of everyday tensions.

title: Reframing the Decision-Makers’ Dilemma: Towards a Social Context Model of Creative Idea Recognition
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design: a 2 x 2 laboratory experiment with undergraduate participants and a quasi-experimental organizational survey of employees, using PROCESS moderated mediation tests and coded role-description measures of economic mindset.
industry: Not reported in paper.
country: United States for Study 1; Study 2 country not reported.
time_period: Not reported in paper.
units: Undergraduate participants and employees evaluating creative product ideas under manipulated or observed decision-maker roles.
n_sample: Study 1: 154 undergraduates; Study 2: 84 employees.
authors: Mueller, J.; Melwani, S.; Loewenstein, J.; Deal, J. J.
theories: economic mindset; implicit theories of creative ideas; role theory; social context model of creative idea recognition
keywords: creative idea recognition; creativity assessments; decision-maker roles; economic mindset; implicit theories; social approval cues
research_question: The paper asks whether decision-maker roles shape which ideas people recognize as creative. It specifically examines whether those roles evoke an economic mindset that makes low social approval cues reduce creativity assessments, even when usefulness ratings are unaffected.
mechanism_summary: Decision-maker roles involve responsibility for allocating resources, so they can activate concerns with accuracy, rationality, and economic consequences. This economic mindset makes social approval cues salient when people judge creative ideas. When an otherwise creative idea has low social approval, people in decision-maker roles treat that cue as evidence that the idea is less creative; when social approval is high, the downgrading pattern does not appear.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a social context model of creative idea recognition that links organizational roles, economic mindsets, implicit theories, and creativity assessments. It reframes the decision-makers' dilemma by arguing that decision-makers may not experience a tradeoff between creative ideas and socially approved ideas because low social approval can make them see the idea as less creative in the first place. It also extends creativity research beyond idea attributes by showing how role-induced mindsets shape what people count as evidence of creativity.
practical_implication: Organizations that ask decision-makers to select creative ideas may still reject creative ideas if those ideas lack social approval. The paper suggests using a two-step process in which people with little decision-making responsibility first rate idea creativity, giving decision-makers a separate creativity signal before resource-allocation decisions. It also implies that idea sellers may benefit from credible evidence of social approval when presenting creative ideas to decision-makers.
limitations: The studies held the ideas constant and manipulated or measured decision-making roles, but did not examine cases where decision-makers had domain expertise about the focal idea. The paper focused on one role and one conflicting cue, low social approval, leaving open whether other organizational roles and other cues produce similar mindset-cue mismatches. Study 2 was quasi-experimental, so the organizational evidence extends but does not fully replicate the causal leverage of Study 1.
future_research: Future research could examine actual field decision-makers with domain expertise and separate the effects of expertise from decision-making responsibility. Scholars could test other roles in the innovation process, including idea-generator roles, and other cues such as feasibility, efficiency, or technical difficulty. Further work could also study whether less creative ideas with high social approval are misrecognized as creative by decision-makers with stronger economic mindsets.
abstract: Can decision-maker roles—roles with responsibility for allocating resources toward ideas—shape which ideas people in those roles view as creative? Prior theory suggests that expertise should influence creativity assessments, yet examples abound of experts in different roles disagreeing about whether the same idea is creative. We build and test a social context model of creative idea recognition to show how decision-maker roles can shift creativity assessments. In an experimental study, we show that relative to nondecision-making roles, decision-making roles inculcate an economic mindset and so lead to downgrading otherwise creative ideas with cues of low social approval. A quasiexperimental study triangulates and extends this finding showing that organizational decision-making roles can habitually evoke an economic mindset that shapes creativity assessments. In both studies, decision-maker role, economic mindset, and social approval levels were unrelated to idea usefulness ratings. By integrating work on organizational roles, economic mindsets, and implicit theories of creative ideas, we provide a broadly applicable theoretical framework to describe how social context shapes creativity assessments. This work has important implications for the creativity and innovation literatures, and suggests a new interpretation of the longstanding puzzle of why organizations desire but often reject creative ideas.

title: When the Dust Settles: The Consequences of Scandals for Organizational Competition
methods: Empirical quantitative study using county-level church membership data, Catholic sex-abuse scandal publicity, and denomination strictness/similarity measures; the authors estimate Arellano-Bond dynamic panel models for Catholic membership and generalized estimating equation models for non-Catholic denomination-county dyads, with robustness checks using survey and alternative similarity/strictness measures.
industry: Christian denominations, including the Catholic Church and 16 other Christian denominations.
units: Counties and denomination-county dyads observed across church membership waves.
n_sample: Main reported models include 5,660 Catholic county observations and 169,390 non-Catholic denomination-county observations, with 50,149 denomination-county dyads in the full GEE model.
authors: Piazza, A.; Jourdan, J.
theories: church-sect strictness theory; scandal theory; social identity theory; substitution effect
keywords: organizational competition; organizational membership; scandal publicity; scandals; strictness
research_question: The paper asks how scandals durably affect competition among organizations within a field after the immediate fallout subsides. It focuses on whether scandal publicity harms the implicated organization while creating relative membership advantages for competitors that offer close substitutes and are perceived as enforcing stricter conduct norms.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines identity threat, substitution, and evaluative shift. Publicized misconduct threatens members' identification with the implicated organization, making exit more likely and recruitment harder. Competitor organizations can gain when they offer a comparable experience without the tainted category association. Scandals also make conduct standards more salient, so stricter denominations should benefit more than less strict alternatives when members and potential members reassess organizational options.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends scandal research beyond contamination and short-term investor reactions by theorizing scandals as events that reshape competition within organizational fields. It distinguishes penalties for the implicated organization from substitution benefits for competitors, and argues that scandals can create durable evaluative shifts that favor organizations perceived as enforcing stricter norms. The study also contributes to organizational competition research by showing how moralized events redistribute membership resources across organizations.
practical_implication: Scandal-stricken organizations should treat member or customer loss as a competitive risk, not only a reputational problem, and should act to reduce identity threat and leakage of key constituencies. Competitors can benefit by credibly emphasizing close substitute offerings, categorical distance from the scandal-stricken actor, and stricter standards of conduct.
limitations: The setting links similarity and strictness through a unidimensional church-sect continuum, which may not hold in other industries or fields. Churches also differ from market-based organizations because members often have deep identity ties and because norm enforcement may be especially salient in religious organizations. The data are aggregate, so the authors cannot directly observe individual coping, exit, or switching mechanisms.
future_research: Future research could test whether the competitive effects of scandals vary by organization type, constituency type, and category structure. It could also examine the durability of contamination versus substitution effects, whether stricter organizations sustain advantages after scandals, and when field-level scandals produce broader evaluative backlash. Additional work could investigate scope conditions such as information asymmetry, internal control, network closure, emotional solidarity, and collective liability.
abstract: Recent works have documented the dark side of scandals, revealing how they spread, contaminate associated organizations, and taint the perception of entire fields. We complement this line of work by exploring how scandals durably affect competition within a field, translating into relative advantages for certain organizations over others. First, scandals may benefit organizations that provide a close substitute to the offerings of the implicated organization. Second, scandals pave the way for moralizing discourses and practices, shake taken-for-granted assumptions about the conduct of organizations, and result in a shift in criteria used to evaluate organizations within the field. Our arguments suggest that organizations whose offerings are most similar to those of the implicated organization, yet are perceived as enforcing stricter standards of conduct, are likely to benefit the most from a scandal. We find support for these arguments in a county-level study of membership in the Catholic Church and 16 other Christian denominations in the United States in the wake of a series of sex abuse cases perpetrated by Catholic clergy between 1971 and 2000. This study contributes to our understanding of the competitive effects of scandals on organizations, and carries important implications for the management of organizations in scandal-stricken fields.
apa_citation: Piazza, A., & Jourdan, J. (2018). When the dust settles: The consequences of scandals for organizational competition. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 165-190. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1325

title: Disasters and Community Resilience: Spanish Flu and the Formation of Retail Cooperatives in Norway
methods: Empirical quantitative historical study of Norwegian municipalities. The authors analyze cooperative founding with complementary log-logistic discrete-time hazard models, using Spanish Flu mortality as the focal contagious-disease shock, spring frost as a contrast weather shock, and controls for prior organizational diversity, community characteristics, and pre-flu founding history.
industry: Retail cooperatives and other nonprofit community organizations in Norway.
time_period: Cooperative founding data from 1905 to 1955, with hypothesis tests focused on post-Spanish-Flu intervals through 1949.
units: Norwegian municipalities and municipality-year founding spells.
n_sample: 630 municipalities reduced to 597 usable municipalities because of boundary, coastal-access, and medical-district matching issues.
authors: Rao, H.; Greve, H. R.
theories: civic capacity; community resilience; disaster framing; institutional legacies
keywords: Spanish Flu; civic capacity; community resilience; disaster frames; institutional legacies; retail cooperatives; spring frost
research_question: The paper asks why some communities recover organizationally after disasters while others lose the capacity to form new community organizations. It specifically examines whether disasters framed as harm caused by other community members, such as contagious disease, weaken cooperative founding differently from hardships attributed to nature, such as spring frost.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a disaster-framing account of community resilience. When a contagious disease is attributed to infected community members, the disaster frame fosters suspicion, fear of others, and reduced willingness to cooperate, making collective action to found retail cooperatives harder. In contrast, spring frost is framed as an act of nature and can create a sense of shared fate that supports cooperation. The estimated negative effect of Spanish Flu mortality persists for decades but weakens over time as trust and organizational capacity recover.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends disaster and community-resilience research by shifting attention from disaster occurrence or magnitude to the causal framing through which community members interpret the event. It shows that disasters are socially constructed as well as physical events, and that attribution to other people can generate a durable cooperation deficit.

It also contributes to institutional-legacies research by showing that contagious disease can erode, not only create, long-term community organizing capacity. The study links historical shocks to later rates of organizational founding and specifies civic capacity as a community resource that shapes resilience.
practical_implication:
Policy responses to pandemics should not stop at immediate isolation, treatment, school closure, and meeting bans. The paper implies that planners should also consider long-term support for rebuilding community organizations and social infrastructure after contagious-disease outbreaks.

For communities, the findings suggest that nonprofit diversity and civic capacity matter because they provide routines, experienced founders, and venues for collective action. Investments in local associational capacity may help communities recover from cooperation-damaging shocks.
limitations: Not reported in paper.
future_research:
Future research could compare settings in which contagious diseases, infectious diseases that do not spread person to person, and climate shocks receive different causal attributions. Such work would clarify when disasters produce shared fate, blame, stigma, or cooperation deficits.

The authors also call for studies of whether exogenous shocks affect organizational death rates as well as birth rates. Future work could examine whether organizations founded during shocks survive longer or shorter lives than organizations founded under more munificent conditions.
abstract: Why are some communities resilient in the face of disasters, and why are others unable to recover? We suggest that two mechanisms matter: the framing of the cause of the disaster, and the community civic capacity to form diverse non-profits. We propose that disasters that are attributed to other community members weaken cooperation and reduce the formation of new cooperatives that serve the community, unlike disasters attributed to chance or to nature, which strengthen cooperation and increase the creation of cooperatives. We analyze the Spanish Flu, a contagious disease that was attributed to infected individuals, and compare it with spring frost, which damaged crops and was attributed to nature. Our measure of resilience is whether the community members could form retail cooperatives—non-profit community organizations. We find that communities hit by the Spanish Flu during the period 1918–1919 were unable to form new retail cooperatives in the short and long run after the epidemic, but this effect was reduced over time and countered by civic capacity. Implications for research on disasters and institutional legacies are outlined.

title: New Ways of Seeing: Theory Integration across Disciplines
methods: Editorial guidance essay that draws on prior commentary, reviews, how-to articles, and exemplar AMJ articles to articulate motivations, best practices, and caveats for cross-disciplinary theory integration.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Shaw, Jason D.; Tangirala, Subrahmaniam; Vissa, Balagopal; Rodell, Jessica B.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: communication clarity; cross-disciplinary theory integration; disciplined integration; reciprocal integration; theory development
research_question: The editorial asks what motivates management scholars to integrate theory across disciplines and what effective cross-disciplinary integration should look like. It focuses on when such integration can solve management puzzles, explain recurring findings, or offer new ways of seeing existing phenomena.
mechanism_summary:
- Motivations: Cross-disciplinary theory integration can help solve puzzles in the management literature, explain recurring patterns of findings or stylized facts, and offer a new way of seeing an existing issue or phenomenon.
- Best practices: Effective integration requires disciplined integration, work at theoretical intersections, and reciprocal integration that contributes back to the borrowed-from disciplines where possible.
- Danger zones: Authors should attend to compatibility across epistemology, human-nature assumptions, and levels of analysis, and should maintain communication clarity around constructs and definitions.
- Editorial stance: The article presents cross-disciplinary integration as one possible route to novelty and insight, not as a universal standard for theoretical contribution.

The process logic is editorial and developmental rather than empirical. Shaw, Tangirala, Vissa, and Rodell argue that cross-disciplinary theory integration is useful when management theory faces unresolved puzzles, recurring unexplained findings, or opportunities for a new perspective, but only when authors reconcile assumptions, clarify constructs, and integrate theories in a disciplined and reciprocal way.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes guidance for theory development by clarifying when cross-disciplinary theory integration is likely to advance management scholarship. It identifies disciplined integration, integration at theoretical intersections, and reciprocal integration as characteristics of stronger theory-building efforts, while warning against incompatibility and communication ambiguity.
practical_implication: For AMJ authors, the editorial implies that borrowing from outside disciplines should be theoretically necessary, clearly motivated, and carefully integrated rather than merely imported.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editorial encourages future management research to use cross-disciplinary theory integration under conditions of flux, mystery, or unexplained empirical patterns. It also suggests that future work should study exemplar contributions and follow best practices so that new ways of seeing can appear in AMJ.

title: When and Why People Engage in Different Forms of Proactive Behavior: Interactive Effects of Self-construals and Work Characteristics
methods: Two-study quantitative design: Study 1 is a between-subjects experiment using self-construal priming, work-characteristics manipulation, situational judgment outcomes, ANOVA, ordinal regression, and sensitivity checks; Study 2 is a time-lagged subordinate-supervisor field survey analyzed with confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, latent moderated structural equations, and conditional indirect-effect tests.
industry: Study 1 used U.S. working adults recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk; Study 2 used employees from two large manufacturing companies in a southern province of China.
time_period: Study 1 was an online experiment; Study 2 used three survey waves, with employee follow-up after two months and supervisor ratings two months later.
units: Working adults, employees, and subordinate-supervisor pairs.
n_sample: Study 1 retained 61 participants for final analysis; Study 2 included 205 matched subordinate-supervisor pairs.
authors: Wu, C.-H.; Parker, S. K.; Wu, L.-Z.; Lee, C.
theories: self-construal theory (Markus & Kitayama, 1991); trait activation theory (Tett & Guterman, 2000)
keywords: career commitment; job autonomy; job interdependence; proactive behavior; self-construals; trait activation theory; work unit commitment
research_question: When and why do employees engage in different forms of proactive behavior at work? The paper asks whether employees' independent and interdependent self-construals lead to career-oriented versus work unit-oriented proactive behavior when job autonomy or job interdependence activates the relevant self-construal.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is trait activation through goal regulation. Independent self-construal should direct attention toward personal career goals, but it translates into career-oriented proactive behavior mainly when job autonomy gives employees discretion to act on those goals. Interdependent self-construal should direct attention toward collective and relational goals, but it translates into work unit-oriented proactive behavior mainly when job interdependence makes collective contribution salient. Study 1 experimentally supports the interdependent self-construal by job interdependence path; Study 2 supports both proposed interaction paths and the corresponding commitment mediators.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances a differential approach to proactivity by explaining why employees pursue different proactive targets rather than treating proactivity as one general tendency. It integrates self-construal theory and trait activation theory to show that person-situation fit shapes the form of proactive behavior. It also specifies commitment as a goal-regulation mechanism linking self-construals and work design to proactive action.
practical_implication: Managers should align work design with the form of proactive behavior they want to promote. Work requiring collective improvement can be supported by interdependent work structures and by making team interconnections salient. Work requiring personal career initiative can be supported by autonomy, discretion, and job designs that allow employees with independent self-construals to pursue career-relevant goals.
limitations: Study 1 used a stringent exclusion rule for the self-construal priming task, leaving a relatively small final sample. In Study 2, predictors and mediators were self-reported, so common method bias remains a concern even though the design was time-lagged and supervisor-rated outcomes were used. The Study 2 sample came from technical and administrative employees in two Chinese manufacturing companies, limiting certainty about generalizability to other organizations, jobs, and cultural contexts.
future_research: Future studies should cross-validate the experimental findings with larger samples and test the field model in additional organizational, occupational, and cultural contexts. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify whether self-construals shape work environments, whether work designs reinforce self-construals over time, and how different forms of proactive behavior may feed back into employees' identities and work contexts. Future work could also measure motives directly to distinguish self-expression motives from instrumental success motives.
abstract: When and why do people engage in different forms of proactive behavior at work? We propose that as a result of a process of trait activation, employees with different types of self-construal engage in distinct forms of proactive behavior if they work in environments consistent with their self-construals. In an experimental Study 1 (n 5 61), we examined the effect of self-construals on proactivity and found that people primed with interdependent self-construals engaged in more work unit–oriented proactive behavior when job interdependence was also manipulated. Priming independent self-construals did not enhance career-oriented proactive behavior, even when we manipulated job autonomy. In a field Study 2 (n 5 205), we found that employees with interdependent self-construals working in jobs with high interdependence reported higher work unit commitment and higher work unit–oriented proactive behavior compared to employees in low interdependent jobs. Employees with independent self-construals working in jobs with high autonomy also exhibited stronger career commitment and more careeroriented proactive behavior than did those in jobs with low autonomy. This research offers a theoretical framework to explain how dispositional and situational factors interactively shape people’s engagement in different forms of proactive behavior.

title: The Mixed Blessing of Leader Sense of Humor: Examining Costs and Benefits
methods: Two empirical quantitative three-wave field studies, one with part-time MBA students working full-time in China and one with full-time employees recruited through Qualtrics in the United States; analyses use confirmatory factor analysis, ordinary least squares regression, PROCESS bootstrapped mediation, and moderated mediation.
industry: Study 1 participants came from varied industries, especially banking, finance, manufacture, and government; Study 2 participants most often worked in sales, banking and financial services, and engineering.
time_period: Three survey waves in each study; the text reports roughly two weeks between Study 1 waves and roughly 10 days between Study 2 waves.
units: Full-time employees rating their leaders and self-reporting follower outcomes.
n_sample: Study 1: 215 participants completing all three waves; Study 2: 200 participants completing all three waves.
authors: Yam, K. C.; Christian, M. S.; Wei, W.; Liao, Z.; Nai, J.
theories: benign violation theory; leader-member exchange theory; social information processing theory
keywords: benign violation theory; follower deviance; leader aggressive humor; leader sense of humor; leader2member exchange; social information processing theory; work engagement
research_question: The paper asks how and when a leader's sense of humor affects follower behavior in both beneficial and harmful ways. It specifically tests whether leader humor increases follower deviance through perceived acceptability of norm violations while also increasing work engagement through leader-member exchange.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is social signaling. Drawing on benign violation theory, the authors argue that humor often involves benign norm violations; integrating social information processing theory, they argue that followers treat leader humor as information about what kinds of conduct are acceptable. This creates a mixed process: leader humor can make norm violation seem acceptable and thereby relate to deviance, but it can also signal openness and relational permissiveness, improving LMX and work engagement. Aggressive humor changes the signal by making the norm violation more hostile, amplifying the negative path and attenuating the positive path.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces benign violation theory into organizational humor research and integrates it with social information processing theory to explain why leader humor can have both positive and negative follower outcomes. It challenges the assumption that leader humor is uniformly beneficial by showing that the same broad behavior can relate to deviance and engagement through different mediators. It also advances humor research by distinguishing general leader sense of humor from aggressive humor style as a boundary condition.
practical_implication: The authors caution leaders and organizations against treating humor as an unqualified leadership asset. Leaders can use humor to support relational quality and engagement, but should minimize aggressive humor because it can damage relationships and communicate tolerance for norm violations. Organizations can also reduce the deviance risk by clarifying conduct norms and socializing employees into shared organizational values.
limitations: The authors note that their leader sense-of-humor measure may not be fully valence-free, even though supplemental evidence and Study 2 correlations reduce this concern. The studies examine only one boundary condition, leader aggressive humor, and rely on self-reported deviance. The field designs are correlational, so the evidence supports the proposed direction more strongly than alternative models but does not definitively establish causality.
future_research: Future research should develop stronger organizational measures of humor and test other leader humor styles, such as self-deprecating humor. It could examine follower characteristics, additional outcomes such as creativity or group conflict, and other mediating mechanisms. Experimental studies and research in industries where humor is explicitly expected would help clarify causality and boundary conditions.
abstract: Workplace humor is ubiquitous, yet scholars know little about how it affects employees’ behaviors in organizations. We draw on an emerging psychological theory of humor— benign violation theory—to suggest that a leader’s sense of humor often conveys counternormative social information in organizations. We integrate this theory with social information processing theory to develop hypotheses about the effects of a leader’s sense of humor on follower behavior. We suggest that although a leader’s sense of humor is positively associated with leader2member exchange and ultimately work engagement, it can also signal to followers the acceptability of norm violation at work. These perceptions in turn are positively associated with followers’ deviance. Furthermore, we propose that these indirect effects are moderated by leader aggressive humor. Data from two three-wave field studies in China and the United States provide support for our hypotheses. Taken together, our results suggest that a leader’s sense of humor can be a mixed blessing and elicit unforeseen negative behaviors from their followers.

title: Introducing Team Mindfulness and Considering its Safeguard Role Against Conflict Transformation and Social Undermining
methods: Three multi-wave quantitative field studies: Study 1 develops and validates a team mindfulness scale; Studies 2 and 3 use survey data from teams and multilevel structural equation modeling to test moderated mediation in team conflict processes.
industry: MBA project teams and healthcare organization teams.
time_period: Multi-wave survey designs; Study 2 follows MBA teams across a semester, and Study 3 uses two-month lags between survey waves.
units: Teams and individual team members.
n_sample: Study 2: 198 individuals in 44 teams; Study 3: 292 individuals in 48 teams.
authors: Yu, L.; Zellmer-Bruhn, M.
theories: conflict expression theory; mindfulness theory; team conflict theory
keywords: multilevel team conflict processes; relationship conflict; social undermining; team conflict; team mindfulness
research_question: The paper asks whether team mindfulness can be conceptualized and measured as a team-level shared property, and whether it safeguards teams against dysfunctional multilevel conflict processes. Specifically, it examines whether team mindfulness reduces relationship conflict, weakens the task conflict-to-relationship conflict link, and limits spillover from team relationship conflict to individual social undermining.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that team mindfulness provides attentional stability, present-focused awareness, and experiential, nonjudgmental processing during conflict. These qualities reduce personalization, oppositional intensity, negative emotionality, and reactive escalation, making task conflict less likely to transform into relationship conflict and relationship conflict less likely to spill over into individual social undermining.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces team mindfulness as a collective-level construct that is distinct from individual mindfulness and from aggregate individual mindfulness. It contributes to mindfulness research by validating a team mindfulness measure and showing that mindfulness can operate as a team-level safeguard in interpersonal processes. It also extends team conflict and social undermining research by theorizing and testing conflict transformation as a multilevel process in which team relationship conflict predicts individual social undermining.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that managers and team leaders may benefit from team-level mindfulness training, meditation, or activities designed to support present-focused attention and nonjudgmental processing in team interactions. Such interventions may help teams prevent task disagreements from becoming relationship conflict and reduce the interpersonal costs of conflict.
limitations: The authors note that the studies use single-source data and correlational designs, so causal ordering should be interpreted cautiously. They also caution that team mindfulness and relationship conflict were measured at the same time in the field studies, and that future research should directly measure conflict expression, oppositional intensity, and negative emotions rather than infer these mechanisms from conflict measures.
future_research: Future research should use experimental or stronger longitudinal designs to test causal order and the development of team mindfulness. The authors also call for work on how team mindfulness relates to performance, how individual and team mindfulness jointly shape outcomes, and how team mindfulness relates to affective emergent states such as cohesion or psychological safety.
abstract: The authors introduce the concept of team mindfulness, defined as a shared belief among team members that their interactions are characterized by awareness and attention to present events, and experiential, nonjudgmental processing of within-team experiences. Team mindfulness is examined as a safeguard against multilevel team conflict transformation processes. Results from three multi-wave field studies validate a team mindfulness instrument and indicate that team mindfulness (1) negatively relates to team relationship conflict, (2) reduces the connection between task conflict and relationship conflict at the team level, (3) and reduces the cross-level spillover of team relationship conflict to individual social undermining. The research contributes to the growing workplace mindfulness literature by conceptualizing mindfulness at the team level and demonstrating its positive effects for team functioning. Results also contribute to research on team conflict and social undermining, showing that team mindfulness is a promising intervention to reduce team conflict and its ill effects.
apa_citation: Yu, L., & Zellmer-Bruhn, M. (2018). Introducing team mindfulness and considering its safeguard role against conflict transformation and social undermining. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(1), 324-347. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0094

title: Coordinating Service Provision in Dynamic Service Settings: A Position-practice Relations Perspective
methods: Longitudinal qualitative field study of UK child and adolescent mental health service provision, using interviews, observations across physical and virtual sites, service and patient documents, online interaction records, grounded coding, and iterative theorizing with role-based interaction and position-practice relations literatures.
industry: Child and adolescent mental health care service provision.
time_period: November 2009 to March 2011.
units: CAMHS workers, current and past CAMHS patients, workers in other service organizations, carers, parents, siblings, friends, interaction episodes, breakdowns, documents, and online-site records.
n_sample: 58 interviews, including 38 formal and 20 ethnographic interviews; observations in CAMHS physical sites, other service organizations, virtual sites, and service improvement initiatives; archival and contemporary documents.
authors: Aristidou, Angela; Barrett, Michael
theories: position-practice relations (Giddens, 1984; Stones, 2005); practice theory; relational coordination theory; role theory
keywords: continuity of service provision; dynamic service settings; position-practice relations; practice theory; role-based interaction; technology-enabled interaction
research_question: The paper asks how diverse interaction among dispersed actors contributes to coordinating and supporting continuous service provision in dynamic service settings. The empirical puzzle is how continuity can be maintained when interaction spans physical and virtual space, unfolds over time, involves technology, and includes actors outside formal organizational role sets.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / lens: Position-practices and position-practice relations (PPR) webs around the task of maintaining service provision for a specific patient.
- Setting / phenomenon: UK child and adolescent mental health care as a dynamic service setting where patient needs evolve and interaction crosses organizational, non-organizational, physical, and virtual spaces.
- Process / phases: Existing PPR webs are unsettled by breakdowns; actors then mobilize agency through spanning time and stretching space; the PPR web is reconfigured, reaffirmed, or rebalanced for future service provision.
- Actors / relations: Current patients, CAMHS workers, past patients, parents, siblings, friends, social-service workers, educational-service workers, voluntary-sector workers, and online participants.
- Emergent outcomes: Continuity of service provision is supported through extraorganizational interaction, trust carried from past interactions, and technology-enabled connections that may be invisible to formal service organizations.

The process account shows service continuity as an evolving PPR web rather than as coordination within a fixed role set. When breakdowns occur, actors draw on histories of interaction and imagined future care arrangements, while also mobilizing interaction across physical and virtual spaces. These actions can introduce, remove, or rekindle position-practices, making service provision depend on distributed agency rather than only formal organizational roles.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a position-practice relations perspective to role-based interaction and coordination research in dynamic service settings. It extends role-based accounts by showing that service provision may be extraorganizational and may involve current customers, past customers, friends, carers, and other actors who are not located within formal intra- or inter-organizational role sets. It also bridges role theory and practice theory by theorizing how agency, temporality, spatiality, technology, and histories of trust reconfigure PPR webs over time.
practical_implication: The paper implies that service provision in dynamic service settings cannot be understood only through formal workers, customers, and organizational partners. Its PPR lens makes visible how carers, friends, past customers, online communities, and other extraorganizational actors can participate in maintaining continuity. The findings also show that technology-enabled interaction and histories of trust can affect coordination even when they sit outside formal organizational role sets.
limitations: The article does not present a standalone limitations section. The main scope boundary visible in the design is that the evidence comes from one 1.5-year qualitative study of UK child and adolescent mental health services, using observations, interviews, documentation, and online-site records. The account supports theory development about coordination in dynamic service settings, but it does not estimate how frequently particular PPR reconfigurations occur or their comparative performance effects. The discussion argues that the PPR lens can transfer beyond the studied context, but that transferability remains a theoretical proposition for later research.
future_research: The authors call for future research on the transition from position-practices into formal organizational roles, using the observed emergence of the Peer Support Worker role as an example. Future work could examine how such transitions affect interaction within PPR webs and within official intra- and inter-organizational role sets. Additional research could also test how PPR webs operate in other dynamic service settings and how technology-enabled spaces alter coordination, substitution, trust building, and practice breakdowns.
abstract: How is continuity of service provision supported in dynamic service settings (DSS) when interactions span space and time, and are being increasingly infused by technology? We explored this question through our 18-month qualitative study of the DSS of UK mental health. We found that the pattern of interaction that emerges is constantly reconfigured through processes of spanning time, stretching space, and through distributed agency. Further, we found that service provision does not only occur among work roles with clear (cross)organizational links but also through diverse interaction among current customers and their friends, as well as customer-to-customer interactions. We characterize such service provision which is not anchored to any service organization as being extraorganizational. Further, we highlight the importance of the history of interactions and how trust built through diverse interactions in the past may influence trust building in current interactions. To explain our findings we introduce the concepts of “positionpractices” and position-practice relations (PPR) to theorize how diverse interactions among dispersed actors contribute to service provision continuity in DSS. We develop a conceptual process model which identifies processes of spanning time, and the stretching of space by which the PPR web of service provision is dynamically reconfigured, and identify consequences for both our case as well as other dynamic service settings.
apa_citation: Aristidou, A., & Barrett, M. (2018). Coordinating service provision in dynamic service settings: A position-practice relations perspective. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 685-714. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0310

title: A Role–resource Approach–avoidance Model of Job Crafting: A Multimethod Integration and Extension of Job Crafting Theory
methods: Empirical mixed-methods research using semistructured employee and supervisor interviews, qualitative domain and taxonomic coding, O*NET-linked job design controls, supervisor and employee outcome measures, a second survey sample, confirmatory factor analysis, OLS regression, and hierarchical linear modeling.
industry: Study 1 covered workers in five organizations, six industries, and 58 jobs, including manufacturing, service, agriculture, education, artistic, and technology sectors; Study 2 sampled working adults across managerial, professional, craft, health, clerical, skilled, semiskilled, and labor occupations.
country: Study 2 sampled working adults from the U.S.; Study 1 country was not reported in paper.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employees, supervisors, employee-described job crafting activities, and working adults responding to an online survey.
n_sample: Study 1 included 246 interviews with 50 supervisors and 196 employees, 433 job-crafting descriptions, and a final matched sample of 158 employees working for 35 supervisors; Study 2 included 323 working adults.
authors: Bruning, Patrick F.; Campion, Michael A.
theories: approach and avoidance motivation; job crafting theory; resource-based perspective of job crafting; role-based perspective of job crafting
keywords: approach crafting; avoidance crafting; job crafting; resource crafting; role crafting; work withdrawal
research_question: The paper asks how job crafting can be organized into a more comprehensive taxonomy that integrates role-based and resource-based perspectives with approach and avoidance themes. It also asks how specific forms of job crafting relate to enrichment, engagement, strain, performance, and work withdrawal.
mechanism_summary:
- Focal construct: Job crafting as worker-initiated changes to structural, social, and cognitive aspects of work intended to improve the job for the worker.
- Taxonomic dimensions: Role crafting versus resource crafting, crossed with approach crafting versus avoidance crafting.
- Specific forms: Work role expansion, social expansion, work role reduction, work organization, adoption, metacognition, and withdrawal crafting.
- Outcomes: Enrichment, engagement, strain, performance, work-home conflict, process improvement, bored behavior, neglect, and turnover intentions.
- Evidence structure: Study 1 develops and tests the taxonomy using interviews, coding, and matched outcome data; Study 2 cross-validates the dimensional structure and tests additional outcomes with survey data.

The process account distinguishes changes to role boundaries from changes to resources and demands. Approach role crafting expands tasks or social relationships to increase fit and enrichment, whereas avoidance role crafting reduces work roles and can connect to withdrawal. Approach resource crafting organizes, imports, or cognitively manages resources to improve engagement and performance, whereas avoidance resource crafting removes the worker mentally or physically from aversive stimuli and shows fewer positive relationships.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates two previously parallel job crafting perspectives by showing that role-based and resource-based crafting each contain approach and avoidance forms. It extends job crafting theory by identifying seven specific job crafting types, including clearer distinctions between work role reduction and withdrawal crafting and between work organization, adoption, and metacognition. It also links the taxonomy to differentiated outcomes, showing that approach crafting is generally more consistently related to positive outcomes than avoidance crafting.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that employees and organizations should distinguish between job crafting strategies rather than treating job crafting as uniformly beneficial. Workers seeking enrichment may benefit more from expanding work roles and social relationships than from reducing roles, while workers seeking engagement or performance gains may benefit from work organization, adoption, and metacognition. Avoidance strategies may sometimes reduce demands or improve efficiency, but they are also associated with work withdrawal and should be used cautiously.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 asked specifically for examples intended to increase efficiency/effectiveness and decrease stress, which may have shaped the kinds of job crafting examples elicited. Study 2 relied on employee self-reports, although it replicated Study 1 patterns and controlled for personal characteristics and social desirability. The studies sampled varied jobs, so occupation-specific research is needed to reduce error linked to different work requirements and conditions.
future_research: Future research should examine specific occupations and work contexts to test whether different job crafting forms operate differently under more homogeneous job requirements. The paper also calls for future quantitative measures of withdrawal crafting that include systematic reductions of cognitive demands. Additional research could use more comprehensive scales and multiple data sources to clarify the longer-term consequences of avoidance crafting.
abstract: Job crafting refers to changes to a job that workers make with the intention of improving the job for themselves. It may include structural (i.e., physical and procedural), social, and cognitive forms. We draw on two studies to develop a role–resource approach– avoidance taxonomy that integrates and extends the dominant roleand resource-based perspectives of job crafting according to characteristics of approach and avoidance. Study 1 used both qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze job crafting activities described during employee interviews to understand the nature and outcomes of specific job crafting activities. Study 2 provides quantitative support for the specific job crafting types emerging from Study 1, and further explores job crafting outcomes. Approach role crafting includes role expansion and social expansion, while avoidance role crafting includes work-role reduction. Role crafting outcomes include: increased enrichment, increased engagement, and decreased strain through changes in work role boundaries. Approach resource crafting includes work organization, adoption, and metacognition, while avoidance resource crafting includes withdrawal crafting. Resource crafting outcomes include: increased performance, increased engagement, and reduced strain through the development, acquisition, and conservation of resources. Avoidance crafting positively relates to work withdrawal and tends to have fewer relationships with positive outcomes compared to approach crafting.

title: Leader Humor as an Interpersonal Resource: Integrating Three Theoretical Perspectives
methods: Two empirical quantitative dyadic survey studies using multilevel modeling in HLM 7.0, confirmatory factor analysis, and Monte Carlo mediation tests; Study 2 used a two-wave, time-lagged design.
industry: Study 1 sampled three U.S. organizations in interior design/refurbishing, banking, and health care; Study 2 sampled a statewide nonprofit providing adoption, foster care, and counseling services.
time_period: Study 2 collected survey data at two points in time about four weeks apart; calendar dates were not reported.
units: Leader-subordinate dyads nested within leaders.
n_sample: Study 1 final sample was 250 subordinate responses from 77 leaders; Study 2 sent 545 subordinate surveys, retained 240 Time 2 subordinate responses, and reported maximum model samples of 363 Level-1 observations and 87 Level-2 leaders.
authors: Cooper, Cecily D.; Kong, Dejun Tony; Crossley, Craig D.
theories: broaden-and-build theory; conservation of resources theory; social exchange theory
keywords: burnout; leader humor; leader-member exchange; organizational citizenship behaviors; positive emotion; social exchange
research_question: The paper asks whether social exchange, stress relief, and positive emotion mechanisms translate leader humor into subordinate organizational citizenship behaviors. It specifically tests whether leader-triggered positive emotion acts as a proximal mediator between leader humor and later LMX and burnout, and whether LMX and burnout mediate the leader humor-OCB relationship.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism treats leader humor as an interpersonal, socioemotional resource. Leader humor is expected to trigger subordinate positive emotion, which should build high-quality social exchange with the leader through LMX and potentially reduce burnout. The supported pathway is leader humor to positive emotion to LMX to OCBs; the stress relief pathway through burnout was not supported.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to humor research by integrating social exchange theory, conservation of resources theory, and broaden-and-build theory into a single model of leader humor. It shows that leader humor is linked to subordinate OCBs primarily through positive emotion and LMX rather than through burnout reduction.

It also contributes to LMX research by identifying leader humor as a socioemotional leader behavior and antecedent of high-quality leader-member exchange. Empirically, it validates a concise three-item leader humor measure and tests multiple proposed humor mechanisms concurrently.
practical_implication:
Managers can use humor as a low-cost socioemotional resource to enrich subordinates' emotional experience and strengthen leader-subordinate relationships. The findings suggest that humor may help motivate subordinates to go beyond formal job requirements through stronger LMX.

The paper cautions against assuming that leader humor directly relieves subordinate burnout. Its practical value is more clearly relational and emotional than stress-reducing in the tested samples.
limitations:
Study 1 was cross-sectional, and Study 2 measured LMX, burnout, and OCBs at the same second time point. The paper also studied leader humor directed toward subordinates but did not observe reciprocal humor exchanges between leaders and subordinates.

The authors used generalized OCB measures and dyadic data, leaving leader-focused OCBs, full workgroup dynamics, and event-level humor episodes outside the empirical design. The unsupported burnout pathway may also depend on measuring humor exposure rather than humor expression or sense of humor.
future_research:
Future research could assess subordinate humor toward leaders and examine leader and subordinate humor expressions simultaneously. Studies with three or more waves could separate independent variables, mediators, and outcomes across different periods.

The authors call for work on boundary conditions such as cultural differences, industry humor norms, and both parties' sense of humor. They also suggest examining full workgroups, relative LMX, group-level LMX differentiation, leader outcomes, employee engagement, thriving at work, and event-level humor episodes.
abstract: We integrate theoretical perspectives on humor to test the processes through which leader humor (LH) facilitates subordinate organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs). In doing so, we argue that humor is a key interpersonal resource for leaders and derive our comprehensive model with logic from three individual-resource-related theories— social exchange theory, conservation of resources theory, and broaden-and-build theory. Leader-triggered positive emotion and subsequent social exchange, operationalized as leader–member exchange (LMX), functioned as key sequential mechanisms mediating the relationship between LH and subordinate OCBs. LH induced positive emotion in subordinates, which fostered high-quality LMX and, in turn, OCBs. Contrary to expectations, the stress relief explanation of LH was not supported. This research contributes to knowledge of humor in organizations, and particularly LH, as it is the first to establish a link between LH and OCBs and also represents the first integration and concurrent examination of three functions of humor. We additionally offer empirical contributions to the humor literature by providing a comprehensive test of prior conceptual arguments regarding mechanisms of LH and validating a measure of LH that can be used in future research. For LMX research, we draw attention to LH as an overlooked but important socioemotional resource for social exchange.

title: Maneuvering in Poor Visibility: How Firms Play the Ecosystem Game when Uncertainty is High
methods: Inductive embedded multiple-case qualitative process research on two multinational technology firms, each attempting to create two innovation ecosystems, using interviews, research workshops, case narratives, and extensive secondary archival data.
industry: Information technology and telecommunications.
time_period: Exploratory engagement began in mid-2008; the in-depth phase lasted from late 2008 to mid-2010, followed by research workshops from mid to late 2010.
units: Two anonymized multinational technology firms, Red and Green; four embedded ecosystem-creation cases: Jade, Emerald, Ruby, and Coral.
n_sample: 48 interviews from Red and Green, plus 25 exploratory interviews across 10 technology-based multinationals, three final research workshops, and over 1,500 pages of secondary data.
authors: Dattée, B.; Alexy, O.; Autio, E.
theories: generative technologies; innovation ecosystems; strategic entrepreneurship; systems dynamics perspective on ecosystems
keywords: control points; dynamic control; ecosystem creation; generative technological innovations; innovation ecosystems; value propositions
research_question: The paper asks how an ecosystem champion can compel others to commit to a de novo ecosystem creation effort when uncertainty is too high to create a meaningful ex ante blueprint. It also asks how firms can position themselves for value appropriation when they lack enough visibility to know what the eventual ecosystem will look like.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Generative technological innovations, protovision, envisioned blueprint, enacted resonance, ecosystem drift, sliding control points, and dynamic control.
- Process / phases: Firms narrow the future by probing external applications, switch to and keep up with ecosystem dynamics after external pull, roadmap and preempt future control points, and enact resonance between internal and external commitments.
- Control practices: Influencing, monitoring, and updating help firms amplify reinforcing loops and counteract balancing loops that dissolve the emerging blueprint.
- Emergent outcomes: Ecosystem creation becomes a collective discovery process in which firms delay irreversible commitment while steering value creation and value capture.
- Boundary conditions: The model is developed from large technology firms in multilayered IT and telecommunications settings where generative technologies create high uncertainty and heterogeneous future applications.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. The paper theorizes ecosystem creation as coupled feedback loops through which firms try to move from broad protovisions toward clearer ecosystem blueprints. Dynamic control matters because ownership of particular assets is insufficient when external actors' creative agency can make the ecosystem drift away from the focal firm's anticipated value creation and make intended control points slide away from future value capture.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to innovation ecosystem research by extending blueprint-based views to contexts where no clear value proposition can be planned ex ante. It introduces a systems-dynamics account of de novo ecosystem creation, showing how firms use dynamic control to influence, monitor, and update an emerging collective process. It also contributes to strategic entrepreneurship by combining goal-oriented and process-oriented views of opportunity creation under uncertainty.
practical_implication: The paper implies that managers should not treat high-uncertainty ecosystem creation as a one-time design problem. They need to build external pull, use partners' exploration to narrow possible futures, and delay irreversible commitments while still preempting undesirable ecosystem directions. Managers also need capabilities for business development, technology marketing, partner vetting, roadmapping, and ongoing monitoring rather than relying only on ownership of current resources.
limitations: The authors state that the purposive case selection is biased toward large firms with the market power and resources to engage credibly in de novo ecosystem creation. The empirical setting is multilayered IT and telecommunications, a context where generative technologies and ecosystem approaches are especially salient. The model therefore needs replication in less layered and less modular industry architectures.
future_research: The authors call for research on how ecosystems get out of control when initiating firms lose the ability to steer evolution or become ostracized. They also suggest studying abductive search and strategizing, the origination and defense of control points, competitive dynamics in ecosystem feedback control, and the role of enacted resonance across different ecosystem types. Future work could use simulation, design structure matrices, or qualitative comparative analysis to examine clarity, momentum, and ecosystem configurations.
abstract: Innovation ecosystems are increasingly regarded as important vehicles to create and capture value from complex value propositions. While current literature assumes these value propositions can be known ex ante and an appropriate ecosystem design derived from them, we focus on generative technological innovations that enable an unbounded range of potential value propositions, hence offering no clear guidance to firms. To illustrate our arguments, we inductively study two organizations, each attempting to create two novel ecosystems around new technological enablers deep in their industry architecture. We highlight how ecosystem creation in such conditions is a systemic process driven by coupled feedback loops, which organizations must try to control dynamically: firms first make the switch to creating the ecosystem, following an external pull to narrow down the range of potential applications; then need to learn to keep up with ecosystem dynamics by roadmapping and preempting, while simultaneously enacting resonance. Dynamic control further entails counteracting the drifting away of the nascent ecosystem from the firm’s idea of future value creation and the sliding of its intended control points for value capture. Our findings shed new light on strategy and control in emerging ecosystems, and provide guidance to managers on playing the ecosystem game.
