title: Compromised Ethics in Hiring Processes? How Referrers’ Power Affects Employees’ Reactions to Referral Practices
methods: Multi-study quantitative design with one experimental vignette study, one online live-chat experiment, one field survey, and one two-wave time-lagged scenario study; analyses use ANOVA, regression, and PROCESS mediation models.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Students and U.S. employees evaluating or recalling referral-based hiring decisions.
n_sample: Study 1 recruited 148 participants; Study 2 recruited 88 employees and excluded 10 unusable cases; Study 3a analyzed 164 employees; Study 3b recruited 190 employees.
authors: Derfler-Rozin, R.; Baker, B.; Gino, F.
theories: attribution of motives; relational power; social exchange and reciprocity
keywords: hiring manager motives; moral judgments; referral-based hiring practices; referrer power; support for hiring decision
research_question: When are organizational members more likely to perceive referral-based hiring decisions as immoral, and how does the referrer's power relative to the hiring manager shape employees' support for the hiring decision? The paper asks whether observers infer self-interested and counter-organizational motives when a hiring manager accepts a referral from a higher-power referrer.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is serial: a higher-power referrer makes observers more likely to infer that the hiring manager is trying to gain future benefits or power through reciprocity with the referrer. These perceived self-interested and counter-organizational motives make the hiring manager's action seem less moral, and harsher moral judgment then reduces employees' support for the hiring decision. The studies also test lack of agency and referrer legitimacy as alternative mechanisms, but these do not account for the core relationship.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on referral-based hiring by treating employee referrals as an ethically evaluated organizational practice rather than only an efficiency-enhancing selection tool. It extends power and attribution theory by showing that observers judge a focal actor's motives partly from the power relationship between that actor and another organizational member. It also contributes to behavioral ethics by linking inferred motives, moral judgment, and support for a managerial hiring decision.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that employees evaluate referral-based hiring decisions through perceived power dynamics, not only through the referred candidate's qualifications. Organizations may reduce perceived ethical costs by increasing transparency about why a referred candidate is selected or by limiting early visibility of referrer identity when possible. High-power employees should be especially cautious and selective in making referrals because their recommendations may trigger suspicion about the hiring manager's motives.
limitations: The paper does not observe downstream consequences such as mentoring of the referred hire, respect for the manager, or later workplace engagement. Some field evidence relies on self-reported employee perceptions, and the authors note that common method bias remains a concern. The mid-power condition also behaved differently across studies, partly because power was operationalized differently.
future_research: Future research could examine downstream consequences of support for referral-based hiring decisions, such as mentoring of the referral hire, respect for the hiring manager, and workplace engagement. Studies could observe how employees and managers react to the same referral practice in a specific organizational context, including whether reactions differ when employees observe referral practices in their own organization versus another organization. Additional work could also test the model in cultural contexts where business relationships are more strongly rooted in interpersonal ties.
abstract: In this paper, we explore referral-based hiring practices and show how a referrer’s power (relative to the hiring manager) influences other organizational members’ support (or lack thereof) for who is hired, through perceptions of the hiring manager’s motives and morality. We apply principles derived from the literature on attribution of motives to research on relational power to delineate a model that explains employees’ moral evaluations of and reactions to referral practices based on the power relationship between a referrer and a hiring manager. Specifically, we predict that employees are more likely to see the acceptance of a referral from a higher- (as opposed to a lower-) power referrer as a way for the hiring manager to gain more power in the relationship with the referrer, thereby attributing more self-interested motives and more counterorganizational motives to the hiring manager in such situations. These motives are then associated with harsher moral judgments of the hiring manager, which in turn lead to less support for the hiring decision. We find support for our model in two experimental studies and two field studies. We discuss implications for the literature on referral practices, ethics, and observers’ reactions to power dynamics.
apa_citation: Derfler-Rozin, R., Baker, B., & Gino, F. (2018). Compromised ethics in hiring processes? How referrers’ power affects employees’ reactions to referral practices. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 615-636. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1355

title: Gender-inclusive Gatekeeping: How (Mostly Male) Predecessors Influence the Success of Female CEOs
methods: Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis of archival CEO succession data, calibrated predecessor, successor, governance, and performance conditions, contingency, necessity, robustness, and matched male-succession analyses, plus qualitative case interpretation of sufficient configurations.
industry: Large U.S. corporations in the S&P 1500 and Fortune 500.
time_period: Female CEO succession events between 1989 and 2009; complete-data cases span 1992-2009.
units: CEO succession events involving female successors, with firm post-succession performance as the outcome.
n_sample: 84 complete-data female CEO succession cases, from an initial search of 98 female CEO succession events.
authors: Dwivedi, Priyanka; Joshi, Aparna; Misangyi, Vilmos F.
theories: executive succession theory; gatekeeping theory; organizational imprinting and role blueprints; role congruity theory
keywords: CEO succession; female CEOs; gender-inclusive gatekeeping; male-typed leadership schemas; qualitative comparative analysis
research_question: The paper asks how predecessor CEOs and local succession contexts shape whether incoming women CEOs overcome male-typed leadership schemas and achieve high post-succession firm performance. It focuses on why some female CEO successors succeed while others do not, rather than treating CEO gender as a uniform performance effect.
mechanism_summary:
- Core conditions: predecessor legacy, successor insider origin, governance structure, inherited performance, and embedding context.
- Success recipes: handing over the legacy, partnering the legacy, and turning around the legacy.
- Agentic mechanisms: predecessor mentoring, sponsorship, endorsement, and post-succession partnering.
- Structural mechanisms: local role and power imprints, inclusive organizational practices, and governance arrangements that alter local leadership expectations.
- Comparative boundary: the sufficient configurations for women CEOs do not map cleanly onto matched male CEO successions.

The process account is configurational: women CEOs' success emerges when predecessor legacy and successor insider origin combine with governance and context to make gender-inclusive gatekeeping possible. Long-tenured or founder predecessors can sponsor, endorse, and partner with insider female successors while local role imprints and inclusive practices reduce the salience of global male-typed leadership schemas. The three recipes differ in whether power is fully handed over, shared through partnership, or retained by the predecessor to support a turnaround.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances a midrange theory of gender-inclusive gatekeeping in which mostly male predecessors can help alter local leadership schemas for women entering CEO roles. It shifts research on women executives away from sex-difference comparisons and toward within-gender variability shaped by local organizational agents, governance structures, and succession histories. It also extends executive succession and gatekeeping research by showing that predecessor influence can be inclusive rather than only constraining or exclusionary.
practical_implication: Boards and incumbent CEOs should treat CEO succession as a local context in which predecessor behavior, governance design, and inclusion practices can materially affect women successors' chances of success. Long-tenured predecessors can support women successors through visible sponsorship, careful handoff or partnering, and role-specific development before succession. Firms in male-dominated contexts may need structural inclusion practices and clear power transfer to counteract male-typed leadership expectations.
limitations: The authors caution that generalizing fsQCA findings requires care, and the empirical setting is restricted to rare female CEO successions in large U.S. firms. The analysis captures observable predecessor, successor, governance, and performance conditions, but other predecessor attributes such as prestige, openness, empathy, or leadership style remain unexamined. The matched male comparison is informative but does not exhaust the gendered dynamics of executive succession.
future_research: Future research should test whether predecessor legacy and successor insider origin also enable gender-inclusive gatekeeping in lower-level leadership transitions and other professions. Scholars could examine additional predecessor attributes, successor characteristics, professional-network relationships, internal labor markets, and other local governance or institutional conditions. The paper also calls for more work on men in leadership roles, including whether masculine role expectations shape why similar succession conditions work differently for male successors.
abstract: Male-typed leadership schemas have been widely acknowledged as barriers to women’s success in leadership roles. We explore how local organizational agents and contexts enable women leaders to overcome these barriers and achieve success at the highest levels in firms. Specifically, we focus on chief executive officer (CEO) succession events and study how several facets of predecessor CEOs and the succession context combine to influence incoming women’s post-succession performance. We conduct a qualitative comparative case study of all CEO successions that involved female successors between 1989 and 2009 across the largest corporations in the United States. Our findings suggest that women’s success occurred when a confluence of local firm-level factors and attributes of the (mostly) male predecessors promoted genderinclusive gatekeeping during succession. Our qualitative comparative analysis approach reveal three recipes for female success: “handing over the legacy,” “partnering the legacy,” and “turning around the legacy.” Moreover, a comparison to a matchedsample of men CEO succession events shows that these three recipes for success are unique to women. Based upon our findings, we propose that male predecessors’ gender-inclusive gatekeeping facilitates female leaders’ success and occurs when local enabling conditions and the embedded context enact agentic and structural mechanisms to alter leadership schemas.
apa_citation: Dwivedi, P., Joshi, A., & Misangyi, V. F. (2018). Gender-inclusive gatekeeping: How (mostly male) predecessors influence the success of female CEOs. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 379-404. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1238

title: Resolution, Relief, and Resignation: A Qualitative Study of Responses to Misfit at Work
methods: Two-phase qualitative interview design using a grounded theory approach, open coding, follow-up interviews, and NVivo-supported analysis.
industry: Diverse industries and occupations, including manufacturing, retail, local government, consultancy, university, finance, insurance, real estate, services, consulting, technology, science, healthcare, education, nonprofit management, government, and military.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employees who described experiences of fit and misfit at work.
n_sample: 81 interviewees across Phase 1 and Phase 2.
authors: Follmer, E. H.; Talbot, D. L.; Kristof-Brown, A. L.; Astrove, S. L.; Billsberry, J.
theories: attraction–selection–attrition model; person–environment fit theory; stress and coping theory
keywords: misfit; person–environment fit; relief; resignation; resolution; stress and coping; turnover
research_question: The paper asks how people become aware of and experience misfit at work, and what people do in response to misfit. It focuses on employees' own descriptions of misfit rather than treating misfit only as low scores on person–environment fit measures or as a simple antecedent of dissatisfaction and turnover.
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering conditions: Misfit may follow organizational change, role change, new supervisors or coworkers, gradual disillusionment with values in use, or social signals from others.
- Core experience: Employees describe misfit as painful, stressful, isolating, and salient even when they fit other parts of the work environment.
- Response approaches: Resolution seeks to reduce the source of misfit through exit, internal transfer, changing the environment, or changing the self.
- Relief-seeking: Surface-level behavior change, buffering misfit with areas of fit, and temporal framing reduce the pain of misfit without removing the underlying incompatibility.
- Resignation: When resolution and relief-seeking fail, employees may distance themselves from work or take pride in misfit while continuing to experience strain.

The process begins when employees reassess fit after change, disillusionment, or social cues and experience misfit as a problem requiring action. Employees often first consider leaving but frequently defer exit because of limited mobility, embeddedness, career investment, or concern about job-hopping. They then combine resolution and relief-seeking strategies over time; if these do not work, resignation strategies allow them to endure misfit until exit becomes possible or the condition remains tolerable.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends person–environment fit theory by showing that fit is not only a selection or attraction outcome but an active, effortful, and dynamic process of maintaining compatibility at work. It develops a qualitative model of misfit responses that goes beyond dissatisfaction and turnover by distinguishing resolution, relief-seeking, and resignation. It also links misfit to stress and coping processes, showing how employees appraise whether to leave, change the environment, change themselves, or manage the strain of unresolved incompatibility.
practical_implication: Managers can retain and develop employees by recognizing when employees are trying to resolve misfit and supporting personal change, mentoring, internal transfer, or environmental reform. Because misfit is multidimensional, managers should look for areas of fit that can buffer misfit elsewhere while also addressing the source of incompatibility. The paper cautions that asking employees to change values, ethics, or authenticity may create proud misfits who resent the organization rather than employees who genuinely fit better.
limitations: The authors state that their sampling strategy limits generalizability: Phase 1 participants self-selected into a study about fit and misfit, and Phase 2 purposively sampled people who had recently experienced work changes and already identified themselves as misfits. The study did not deliberately model national culture, even though data collection began in the United Kingdom and ended in the United States. The qualitative design develops propositions and process insight rather than testing causal effects or estimating population prevalence.
future_research: Future research should test the propositions on broader samples and examine whether the model extends beyond the United Kingdom and United States, especially in Eastern cultural contexts where fit may be viewed differently. Additional work could study individual differences and contextual factors that shape whether employees choose personal change, environmental change, buffering, internal transfer, or pride in misfit. The authors also call for research connecting workplace and nonwork responses to misfit and for work on the long-term consequences of surface-level behavior change and taking pride in misfit.
abstract: Research has portrayed person–environment (PE) fit as a pleasant condition resulting from people being attracted to and selected into compatible work environments; yet, our study reveals that creating and maintaining a sense of fit frequently involves an effortful, dynamic set of strategies. We used a two-phase, qualitative design to allow employees to report how they become aware of and experience misfit, and what they do in response. To address these questions, we conducted interviews with 81 individuals sampled from diverse industries and occupations. Through their descriptions, we identified three broad responses to the experience of misfit: resolution, relief, and resignation. Within these approaches, we identified distinct strategies for responding to misfit. We present a model of how participants used these strategies, often in combination, and develop propositions regarding their effectiveness at reducing strain associated with misfit. These results expand PE fit theory by providing new insight into how individuals experience and react to misfit—portraying them as active, motivated creators of their own fit experience at work.
apa_citation: Follmer, E. H., Talbot, D. L., Kristof-Brown, A. L., Astrove, S. L., & Billsberry, J. (2018). Resolution, relief, and resignation: A qualitative study of responses to misfit at work. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 440-465. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0566

title: Heavy Is the Head that Wears the Crown: An Actor-centric Approach to Daily Psychological Power, Abusive Leader Behavior, and Perceived Incivility
methods: Experimental experience sampling study of professional and managerial employees, with a one-time background survey and three daily surveys across 10 consecutive workdays; psychological power was manipulated daily, and hypotheses were tested with multilevel path analyses in Mplus 7.3.
industry: Professional and managerial employees across varied industries, including medicine, engineering, education, and banking.
time_period: Three-workweek study period, including 10 consecutive workdays of daily surveys.
units: Professional and managerial employees enrolled in executive MBA courses; day-level observations nested within individuals.
n_sample: 108 participants and 832 day-level data points.
authors: Foulk, Trevor A.; Lanaj, Klodiana; Tu, Min-Hsuan; Erez, Amir; Archambeau, Lindy
theories: consent-based theories of power (Hindess, 1996; Overbeck, 2010); self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000); social distance theory of power (Magee & Smith, 2013)
keywords: abusive leader behavior; agreeableness; experience sampling; leader well-being; perceived incivility; psychological power
research_question: The paper asks how daily psychological power affects leaders' own abusive behavior, perceived incivility from others, and subsequent well-being. It examines whether agreeableness weakens these power effects and whether abusive behavior and perceived incivility help explain reduced daily need fulfillment and relaxation.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism integrates social distance theory with consent-based theories of power. Psychological power increases leaders' social distance from others, making abusive behavior and negative perceptions of others more likely. Because leaders operate in interdependent work contexts, those power-induced behaviors and perceptions then feed back onto leaders: abusive behavior predicts lower relaxation and need fulfillment, while perceived incivility predicts lower need fulfillment. Agreeableness partly buffers the abusive-behavior pathway.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes an actor-centric account of psychological power by showing that power does not only harm followers or powerless actors; it can also harm powerholders through their own negative behavior and perceptions. It extends abusive leadership and workplace incivility research by identifying daily psychological power as a dynamic predictor of enacted abuse and perceived incivility. It also adds agreeableness as an individual-difference boundary condition in power research.
practical_implication: The findings imply that organizations should treat psychological power as a fluctuating daily state rather than only a formal role attribute. Accountability structures, honest upward feedback, and leader awareness of power's corrupting effects may help reduce abusive behavior. The paper also suggests that placing more agreeable people in powerful roles and providing relaxation or mindfulness opportunities may reduce harm to both followers and leaders.
limitations: The study relies on self-reported mediators and outcomes, which raises common method and source-bias concerns even though the independent variable was manipulated and measures were time separated. The power manipulation may also have activated competitiveness, so its effects may not generalize to every form of psychological power. The authors note that abusive leadership had a low base rate in the sample and that they did not measure follower reactions to leaders' power, incivility perceptions, or abusive behavior.
future_research: Future research should replicate the findings with multiple data sources and examine whether power also affects negative or positive behaviors at home. The authors call for work disentangling psychological power from competitiveness and comparing psychological with structural power. They also encourage studies of follower reactions, power loss, longer time spans, and other moderators such as prosocial motivation, self-monitoring, narcissism, and self-concern.
abstract: Recognizing that powerholders operate in dynamic relational and interdependent work contexts, we posit that the effects of psychological power on powerholders are more complex than currently depicted in the literature. Although psychological power prompts behaviors and perceptions that harm the powerless, these reactions are not without consequence for the actor. We integrate the social distance theory of power with consent-based theories of power to posit that, although psychological power elicits negative behaviors and perceptions, these same reactions hurt leaders’ subsequent well-being. To explore this possibility, we conducted an experimental experience sampling study with a sample of managerial employees whom we surveyed for 10 consecutive workdays. We find that leaders enact more abusive behavior and perceive more incivility from others on days when they are exposed to psychological power compared to days when they are not. Leaders higher in agreeableness are less affected by psychological power. In turn, abusive behavior and perceived incivility harm leaders’ subsequent well-being as indicated by their reduced need fulfillment and ability to relax at home. We discuss theoretical implications for research on psychological power, abusive leadership, perceived incivility, and leader well-being, as well as practical implications for employees and their organizations.
apa_citation: Foulk, T. A., Lanaj, K., Tu, M.-H., Erez, A., & Archambeau, L. (2018). Heavy is the head that wears the crown: An actor-centric approach to daily psychological power, abusive leader behavior, and perceived incivility. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 661-684. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1061

title: We Ask Men to Win and Women Not to Lose: Closing the Gender Gap in Startup Funding
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design: a field study of TechCrunch Disrupt New York City Q&A transcripts from 2010 through 2016 using LIWC frequency counts, blind manual coding, t-tests, mixed-effects models, regressions, mediation analysis, and robustness checks; followed by a within-subjects, counterbalanced experiment with angel investors and potential seed investors allocating hypothetical startup funding across manipulated question and answer regulatory-focus conditions.
industry: Early-stage startup venture funding, centered on TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield companies and seed/pre-seed startup investing.
country: United States: Study 1 used TechCrunch Disrupt New York City, and Study 2 used Mid-Atlantic angel investors plus U.S.-based potential seed investors from Amazon Mechanical Turk.
time_period: Study 1 covered TechCrunch Disrupt New York City from 2010 through 2016; Study 2 data collection timing was not reported in paper.
units: Startup companies, founder/CEO presenters, VC investor questions, entrepreneur responses, angel investors, potential seed investors, and funding allocations.
n_sample: Study 1 analyzed 189 companies, 1,857 investor questions, 1,718 entrepreneur responses, and 140 investors; Study 2 included 194 angel investors and 106 potential seed investors.
authors: Kanze, Dana; Huang, Laura; Conley, Mark A.; Higgins, E. Tory
theories: linguistic style matching; regulatory fit; regulatory focus theory (Higgins, 1997, 1998); representativeness heuristic
keywords: entrepreneurship; gender bias; prevention-focused questions; promotion-focused questions; regulatory focus theory; startup funding; venture capital
research_question: The paper asks whether gender-based differences in investor questions during startup funding Q&A interactions help explain why male entrepreneurs raise more venture funding than female entrepreneurs seeking comparable capital. It further asks whether entrepreneurs can reduce this disadvantage by switching from prevention-focused to promotion-focused answers.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that gender stereotypes lead investors to ask male entrepreneurs promotion-focused questions about gains, growth, and opportunity, while asking female entrepreneurs prevention-focused questions about risk, losses, and defensibility. Entrepreneurs tend to match the regulatory focus of the questions they receive, so female entrepreneurs are induced to position their ventures as avoiding losses rather than pursuing gains. This Q&A dynamic lowers funding outcomes, while switching prevention-focused questions into promotion-focused answers can improve allocations.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on gender inequality in venture funding by shifting attention from direct investor preferences and entrepreneur demand to the processual Q&A interaction through which bias is enacted. It extends regulatory focus theory to venture funding and introduces motivational matching as a mechanism connecting question framing, entrepreneur positioning, and capital allocation. The paper also bridges micro-level social psychology and macro-level startup funding outcomes by showing how individual interaction patterns can reproduce gendered resource disparities.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that entrepreneurs, especially women, can improve funding outcomes by answering prevention-focused questions with promotion-focused responses that redirect attention to growth, market opportunity, and upside potential. The paper also implies that venture capitalists should monitor and balance the regulatory focus of their questions so they do not systematically ask women to prove they will avoid losses while asking men to describe how they will win.
limitations: The field study is correlational, even though it controls for startup age, quality, capital needs, past experience, and related factors. The setting is TechCrunch Disrupt New York City, a public pitch-competition context with 23 female entrepreneurs among 189 ventures, so the pattern needs testing in other funding contexts. The experiment improves causal identification but uses scripted vignettes and immediate hypothetical funding allocations rather than real investment decisions over time.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether the regulatory focus of investor questions varies by gender in online settings such as crowdfunding platforms, where face-to-face gender cues may be less vivid. They also suggest studying contexts where women are not a minority or where startup uncertainty is reduced by stronger track records. Future work could examine specialized domains such as social entrepreneurship or corporate social responsibility, where prevention-oriented framing may be more positively valued, and test whether the effect changes after temporal delay.
abstract: Male entrepreneurs are known to raise higher levels of funding than their female counterparts, but the underlying mechanism for this funding disparity remains contested. Drawing upon regulatory focus theory, we propose that the gap originates with a gender bias in the questions that investors pose to entrepreneurs. A field study conducted on question-and-answer interactions at TechCrunch Disrupt New York City during 2010 through 2016 reveals that investors tend to ask male entrepreneurs promotion-focused questions and female entrepreneurs prevention-focused questions, and that entrepreneurs tend to respond with matching regulatory focus. This distinction in the regulatory focus of investor questions and entrepreneur responses results in divergent funding outcomes for entrepreneurs whereby those asked promotion-focused questions raise significantly higher amounts of funding than those asked prevention-focused questions. We demonstrate that every additional prevention-focused question significantly hinders the entrepreneur's ability to raise capital, fully mediating gender's effect on funding. By experimentally testing an intervention, we find that entrepreneurs can significantly increase funding for their startups when responding to prevention-focused questions with promotion-focused answers. As we offer evidence regarding tactics that can be employed to diminish the gender disadvantage in funding outcomes, this study has practical as well as theoretical implications for entrepreneurship.
apa_citation: Kanze, D., Huang, L., Conley, M. A., & Higgins, E. T. (2018). We ask men to win and women not to lose: Closing the gender gap in startup funding. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 586-614. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1215

title: One Step Forward, One Step Back: White Male Top Manager Organizational Identification and Helping Behavior toward Other Executives Following the Appointment of a Female or Racial Minority CEO
methods: Longitudinal survey and archival study of CEO succession events at large and mid-sized public U.S. companies, using OLS regression for organizational identification, logit regression for board recommendations, robust clustered standard errors, Sobel and bootstrapped mediation tests, and supplemental Heckman selection models.
industry: Large and mid-sized public companies with more than $50 million in sales.
time_period: Survey questions about organizational identification, mentoring, task-related help, and board recommendations covered 2006 to 2011; analyses were restricted to periods with CEO succession.
units: CEO succession events, focal top executives, executive-subordinate dyads, and executive-peer dyads.
n_sample: 589 CEO succession events; organizational-identification models used 1,025 focal executives; helping-behavior models used 2,101 executive-subordinate dyads and 1,889 executive-peer dyads.
authors: McDonald, Michael L.; Keeves, Gareth D.; Westphal, James D.
theories: common ingroup identity model; intergroup relations theory; organizational identification; social identity theory
keywords: helping behavior; intergroup relations; minority-status CEO; organizational identification; white male top managers
research_question: The paper asks how white male top managers respond intrapsychically and behaviorally when their firm appoints a female or racial minority CEO. It specifically examines whether such appointments reduce white male top managers' organizational identification and, through that reduction, decrease the help they provide to other executives, especially female and racial minority colleagues.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a moderated mediation account. Drawing on intergroup relations and organizational identification literatures, the paper argues that white male top managers hold less favorable views of the organization and feel less valued by a minority-status CEO, which weakens their organizational identification. Lower identification then reduces attraction, empathy, and self-other overlap with colleagues, lowering work-related help. Because weaker organizational identification makes race and gender more salient bases for out-group categorization, the reduction in help is especially strong for female and racial minority executives.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on women and racial minorities in corporate leadership by shifting attention from external stakeholder reactions to internal executive reactions. It theorizes a "reverse generalized Matthew effect": appointing a minority-status CEO can indirectly disadvantage other minority-status executives by triggering reduced helping from white male top managers. It also extends organizational identification and CEO succession research by showing how demographic differences between an incumbent top manager and a new CEO can shape executive identification and discretionary helping behavior.
practical_implication: The findings imply that appointing a female or racial minority CEO may not automatically improve the internal support available to other female and racial minority executives. Boards and senior teams should recognize that white male executives may withdraw support in subtle but consequential ways after such succession events. The authors argue that compensatory measures that bolster organizational identification may help mitigate these effects.
limitations: The study focuses on large and mid-sized public U.S. companies, so the findings may not transfer directly to private firms, smaller organizations, nonprofits, or non-U.S. settings. The empirical design uses longitudinal survey and archival data around CEO succession events, which supports temporal ordering but remains observational. The sample included no CEOs who were both racial minority and female, and racial minority women were too rare among top managers to support statistically meaningful intersectional comparisons.
future_research: Future research could examine other outcomes of reduced organizational identification after minority-status CEO appointments, including extra-role behavior, strategic decision quality, strategy execution, and top manager turnover. Studies could also examine whether reduced help compromises executive careers or whether compensatory measures can mitigate the negative effects of minority-status CEO appointments on white male top managers' organizational identification. As racial minority women become more represented in top management and CEO roles, future work should examine whether effects are stronger or different for dual-minority CEOs and colleagues.
abstract: In this paper, we examine white male managers' intrapsychic and behavioral responses to the appointment of a female or a racial minority CEO at their firm. Drawing from intergroup relations literatures, we theorize how and why the appointment of a minority-status CEO is likely to impact the amount of help that white male top managers provide to their fellow executives. We first explain how white male managers' negatively biased perceptions of racial minority and female CEOs lead them to experience a diminished sense of organizational identification following the appointment of a minority-status CEO. We then examine how this diminished sense of organizational identification is likely to reduce white male managers' general propensities to provide help to other executives at the firm. We finally consider how reduced identification might have especially strong negative implications for the amount of help that white male managers provide to colleagues who are racial minorities or women. Our results consistently support our theoretical expectations that, following the appointment of a female or racial minority CEO, white male top managers tend to experience a diminished sense of organizational identification, and, in turn, provide less help to colleagues, with this reduction particularly pronounced for help provided to minority-status colleagues.
apa_citation: McDonald, M. L., Keeves, G. D., & Westphal, J. D. (2018). One step forward, one step back: White male top manager organizational identification and helping behavior toward other executives following the appointment of a female or racial minority CEO. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 405-439. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0358

title: New Ways of Seeing: Radical Theorizing
methods: Editorial guidance essay that draws on philosophy of science, innovation and organizational learning research, and examples of prominent management theorists to explain approaches to radical theorizing and offer practical advice for scholars.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Nadkarni, Sucheta; Gruber, Marc; DeCelles, Katy; Connelly, Brian; Baer, Markus
theories: innovation and organizational learning; philosophy of science
keywords: distant search; innovation portfolio; radical theorizing; scientific progress; theory development
research_question: The editorial asks how management scholars can engage in radical theorizing that generates new ways of seeing and advances theory beyond incremental extension. It focuses on why radical theorizing matters for scientific progress, what forms it can take, and how researchers can cultivate it in their own work.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Radical theorizing produces completely new theoretical insights that may substantially depart from existing paradigms and open future research directions.
- Approaches: The editorial identifies inductive theory generation, evocative theoretical boundary spanning, theoretical consensus shifting, and diverse theoretical integration as broad routes to radical theorizing.
- Exemplars: The discussion uses prior management theorists, including Denise Rousseau, Barry Staw, and Ken Smith, to illustrate openness to anomalies, broad knowledge, boundary spanning, and diverse collaboration.
- Practical guidance: Scholars are encouraged to read beyond their immediate domain, embrace disagreement and anomalies, see work through others' eyes, spend time inside organizations, and manage a portfolio that includes radical projects.

The process logic is editorial and developmental rather than causal. Nadkarni and colleagues argue that radical theory emerges when scholars move beyond local search, notice anomalies or inadequacies in existing explanations, borrow or integrate distant ideas carefully, and devote part of their research portfolio to transformational questions rather than only incremental extensions.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes a typology of radical theorizing approaches based on the kind of phenomenon being investigated and the state of existing theory. It also frames radical theorizing as a disciplined route to scientific progress, connecting management theory development to philosophy of science and innovation search.
practical_implication: For management scholars, the editorial implies that producing bolder theory requires intentional exposure to distant knowledge, openness to disagreement, attention to practical anomalies, and portfolio-level allocation of time to radical projects. It also suggests that AMJ authors should ask how their manuscripts challenge, change, or advance theoretical understanding before submission.
limitations: The editorial does not test propositions, evaluate systematic evidence, or provide empirical validation of the proposed typology. Its recommendations are broad guidance for theory development rather than a method with guaranteed outcomes.
future_research: The editorial encourages future management research that pursues radical theorizing through new phenomena, distal theories, consensus-challenging explanations, and integration of competing perspectives. It also points to opportunities for scholars to study anomalies and underexplored organizational problems that existing theories do not yet explain well.

title: Are Family Firms Good Employers?
methods: Longitudinal quantitative study of private Belgian firms using Bureau van Dijk data, social balance accounts, propensity-score matched pair designs, and robustness checks with random-effects maximum likelihood regressions.
industry: Belgian nonfinancial firms that employ staff.
time_period: 1996 to 2014 for most hypotheses; 2008 to 2014 for off-site training because training reporting began in 2008.
units: Private firm-year observations comparing family and nonfamily firms.
n_sample: 102,094 firm-years from 14,961 private firms; matched analyses used 39,600 firm-years for most outcomes and 14,382 firm-years for off-site training.
authors: Neckebrouck, Jeroen; Schulze, William; Zellweger, Thomas
theories: agency theory (Eisenhardt, 1989; Jensen & Meckling, 1976); stewardship theory (Davis et al., 1997; Donaldson & Davis, 1991)
keywords: agency theory; employment practices; family firms; financial stewardship; labor productivity; organizational stewardship; stewardship theory
research_question: The paper asks whether family firms are good employers when compared with nonfamily firms. It tests whether family control is associated with financial stewardship and organizational stewardship, especially compensation, off-site training, dismissals, voluntary turnover, and labor productivity.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism contrasts stewardship and agency accounts of family control. Stewardship theory predicts that family identification, long-term orientation, and concern for stakeholders should support investment in the firm and its workforce. Agency theory predicts that controlling families may protect family welfare and control while shifting costs onto nonfamily employees. The findings separate these dimensions: family firms appear to be better financial stewards but worse organizational stewards, and the negative employment-practice pattern strengthens with age and family involvement.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes by distinguishing financial stewardship from organizational stewardship rather than treating either dimension as a proxy for the whole construct. It extends agency and stewardship theory from governance and performance to workforce-wide employment practices in private firms. It also adds evidence that family control can support long-term financial investment while still producing poorer employee-facing practices.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that Belgian employees should be cautious about assuming family firms offer better employment conditions, because the study finds lower pay, less training, higher voluntary turnover, and lower productivity in family firms. Family business owners should attend to how family control may weaken workforce commitment and human capital development. Policymakers concerned with job quality may need to consider family-firm employment practices because family firms employ a large share of the workforce.
limitations: The study examines a restricted set of employment practices and does not observe climate, job satisfaction, commitment, citizenship behavior, teamwork, or performance appraisal. Its Belgian setting provides strong administrative data but limits direct generalization to countries with different labor regulations, unionization, or employee involvement institutions. Endogeneity remains a general concern, although the authors argue that propensity-score matching, longitudinal data, and robustness tests reduce this risk.
future_research: The authors call for fresh theorizing on firm governance, strategic human resource management, and cooperation in closely held firms. Future research should examine whether stewardship is better captured through organizational climate and employee experiences, and should study how private family firms can address human capital and employee motivation problems. Additional work could test whether similar family-firm employment patterns appear under different national labor-market institutions.
abstract: Family firms employ about 60% of the global workforce. While it is widely assumed that they are good employers, data about their conduct are mixed. In this study, we extend stewardship and agency theories to test competing propositions about the impact of family on employment practices using data from 14,961 private Belgian firms over a 19year period. Higher investments, lower dividend payout, and higher risk tolerance indicate that family firms are better financial stewards of their companies than nonfamily firms. However, family firms are worse organizational stewards than nonfamily firms: they offer lower compensation, invest less in employee training, and exhibit higher voluntary turnover and lower labor productivity. Further, and contrary to earlier research, we find that financial practices in private family firms do not change over time, and that the deleterious influence of family on employment practices rises with both firm age and with heightened family involvement. Together, our findings suggest that a more nuanced understanding of stewardship and agency theory is needed to understand the impact of family on the governance of private firms.
apa_citation: Neckebrouck, J., Schulze, W., & Zellweger, T. (2018). Are family firms good employers? *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 553-585. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0765

title: Planning for Future Leadership: Procedural Rationality, Formalized Succession Processes, and CEO Influence in CEO Succession Planning
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study that used qualitative interviews and meetings to develop theory, then tested hypotheses with CHRO surveys, archival financial and governance data, random coefficient models, logistic random coefficient models, and supplemental endogeneity analyses.
industry: Large U.S.-based public companies across six SIC-based industry categories, with 71% belonging to the Fortune 500.
time_period: Survey administrations occurred between April and June in 2013, 2014, and 2015; archival financial and governance data came from the year preceding each survey.
units: Firm-year observations, companies, CHRO survey respondents, qualitative CHRO interviews and meetings, CEOs, board members, and directors involved in CEO succession planning.
n_sample: 355 firm-year observations from 218 companies; qualitative grounding from nine CHRO interviews, meetings with 40 CHROs, one retired CEO, one current CEO, one board member, and interviews with 22 directors.
authors: Schepker, Donald J.; Nyberg, Anthony J.; Ulrich, Michael D.; Wright, Patrick M.
theories: agency and power theories; boards as information-processing groups; procedural rationality in decision-making theory
keywords: CEO influence; CEO succession candidates; boards as information-processing groups; executive succession planning processes; formalized succession processes; procedural rationality
research_question: The paper asks how boards overcome informational barriers in CEO succession planning and whether procedurally rational, formalized succession processes improve succession planning outcomes. It also asks whether CEO influence directly affects those outcomes and weakens the benefits of formalized board processes.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that procedurally rational board processes create systematic information gathering and analysis around CEO role requirements, candidate identification, and candidate development. These formalized processes should reduce adverse selection and decision biases by giving boards more objective information about succession candidates. CEO influence was expected to impede this information processing by shaping candidate access and information flow, but the empirical tests supported formalized process effects more consistently than CEO influence or its moderating role.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to corporate governance and CEO succession research by theorizing boards as information-processing groups that can use procedural rationality to overcome information deficits. It shifts CEO succession planning research from event-centered succession outcomes toward ongoing board processes, showing that formalized processes are associated with more candidate options, stronger internal-succession readiness, faster expected succession, and greater use of external help. It also refines CEO-influence arguments by showing limited support for CEO influence as a direct or moderating constraint in this setting.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that boards should actively institutionalize CEO succession processes rather than relying on informal CEO-centered knowledge. Directors can improve succession readiness by defining future CEO role requirements, identifying candidates against those requirements, and developing candidates before a transition becomes urgent. The study also implies that boards and CEOs still need collaboration, because boards remain dependent on management for candid information about internal talent.
limitations: The study uses data from large U.S.-based organizations, so succession planning may operate differently in smaller firms or in other national governance systems. The results concern ongoing, friendly succession planning rather than unexpected, contested, or forced CEO transitions. The measures also do not assess the quality of the formalized processes, and common-method concerns and reciprocal causation remain possible despite the authors' robustness checks.
future_research: Future research could examine when CEO influence operates as stewardship rather than agency-driven interference, and how CEOs positively help boards interpret succession information. The paper also calls for work on CHROs, external consultants, board committees, and the distinct phases of succession planning, from defining roles through transition. Additional research should study how processes change for unexpected succession events, known succession timelines, smaller firms, and non-U.S. governance settings.
abstract: Despite substantive organizational ramifications, surprisingly little theory explains executive succession planning processes. A firm’s board of directors has the fiduciary responsibility to select CEOs, but, historically, boards have failed to exercise this authority. Increasing focus on corporate governance has prompted directors to become more engaged in organizational management, but boards face significant barriers to gathering and processing information. However, there is a dearth of research examining how boards overcome informational barriers to enhance decision-making effectiveness. Accordingly, the current study integrates procedural rationality in decision-making with research on boards as information-processing groups to explore how and why boards conduct succession planning processes. Procedural rationality results in formalized processes designed to collect essential information about CEO succession candidates; these processes, in turn, lead to a greater quantity and quality of CEO succession candidates. We also illustrate how CEOs can influence the effectiveness of board information gathering and processing. The tests of the theoretically generated hypotheses rely on in-depth qualitative interviews, coupled with unique survey and archival data from 355 firm-year observations of 218 large organizations, collected over three years.
apa_citation: Schepker, D. J., Nyberg, A. J., Ulrich, M. D., & Wright, P. M. (2018). Planning for future leadership: Procedural rationality, formalized succession processes, and CEO influence in CEO succession planning. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 523-552. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0071

title: Ripping off the Band-Aid: Scrutiny Bundling in the Wake of Social Disapproval
methods: Panel quantitative study using Canadian upstream petroleum firm-year data, negative and positive media coverage coded with LIWC, fixed-effects regressions with robust standard errors, and Heckman, 2SLS, GEE, and GMM robustness checks; the authors also used executive color casting to interpret the phenomenon.
industry: Upstream petroleum firms, with resource development and resource access as core activities.
time_period: 2003-2010, with media variables lagged one year.
units: Firm-year observations for publicly reported upstream petroleum firms.
n_sample: 326 firm-year observations from 102 firms after missing data; fixed-effects tables report 311 observations from 100 firms after outlier exclusions.
authors: Titus Jr., Varkey K.; Parker, Owen; Bass, A. Erin
theories: event strength (Morgeson, Mitchell, & Liu, 2015); scrutiny-bundling perspective; social approval (Bundy & Pfarrer, 2015); stakeholder attention (Barnett, 2014; Madsen & Rodgers, 2015)
keywords: aspiration-relative performance; firm size; negative media coverage; scrutiny bundling; scrutiny-hazarding action; social disapproval; upstream petroleum industry
research_question: The paper asks when managers engage in scrutiny-hazarding action: core operational activity that is strategically necessary but likely to attract burdensome stakeholder attention. It examines whether social disapproval, measured through negative media coverage, leads upstream petroleum firms to shift more strongly toward resource development relative to resource access.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is scrutiny bundling: managers facing social disapproval may cluster necessary scrutiny-hazarding actions into an already negative period to reduce prolonged attention over time. The paper argues that stakeholder attention is bounded, so additional scrutiny attached to related actions may be less damaging when bundled with existing disapproval. The full model does not fully support the main social-disapproval effect or the media-focus interaction, but it supports the buffering logic: strong aspiration-relative performance and larger firm size weaken the social disapproval-scrutiny-hazarding action relationship.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a scrutiny-bundling perspective to social evaluation and strategic decision-making research. It shifts attention from avoidance, distraction, problem resolution, or status quo deviation to the timing of unavoidable core actions that may attract scrutiny. It also extends buffering arguments by showing that firm size and aspiration-relative performance can reduce managers' sensitivity to social disapproval.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that managers should treat media disapproval as a signal that may shape rivals' timing of scrutiny-hazarding actions, especially among smaller or lower-performing firms. Firms may use this insight to anticipate competitors' development moves, partnership needs, or asset transactions when those competitors are under social disapproval. The paper does not prescribe scrutiny bundling as normatively appropriate or effective, and managers should not read the evidence as proof that bundling reduces long-term scrutiny.
limitations: The authors note that the relationship may reverse at extreme levels of organizational vulnerability that their data cannot capture. They also acknowledge that, despite controls and robustness tests, they cannot account for every issue shaping investment decision-making. The empirical setting is Canadian upstream petroleum, so the study theorizes scrutiny-hazarding action through a context where resource-development activity is strategically central and likely to attract scrutiny.
future_research: Future research could examine scrutiny bundling at extreme levels of firm vulnerability, where very fragile firms may avoid concentrated scrutiny and very robust firms may invite it. Additional studies could test whether scrutiny bundling appears in other industries, other kinds of social evaluation, and other forms of core but controversial activity. Further work could also examine whether scrutiny bundling actually reduces long-term scrutiny or merely changes its timing.
abstract: Activities that hazard the possibility of increased scrutiny are an unavoidable reality for many firms. While managers may face the need to engage in these activities, there is little research on when managers decide to do so. Existing theoretical perspectives on status quo deviations have not sufficiently addressed how managers order the firm’s essential activities that differ primarily in terms of the scrutiny those activities engender. Drawing from concepts in the accounting and political science literatures, we advance a “scrutiny-bundling” perspective that suggests that firms engage in scrutiny-hazarding action in the wake of social disapproval, assessed in this study via negative media coverage. We further theorize that a strong linkage between the focus of media coverage and the specific scrutiny-hazarding action exacerbates this relationship. We then contend that managers at firms that are either large in size or that perform well relative to their aspirations are less sensitive to social disapproval, and are therefore less likely to engage in scrutiny bundling. We test our hypotheses on a sample of 100 firms in the upstream petroleum industry and find general support for our theories.
apa_citation: Titus, V. K., Jr., Parker, O., & Bass, A. E. (2018). Ripping off the Band-Aid: Scrutiny bundling in the wake of social disapproval. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 637-660. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0435

title: A Competence-Based View of Industry Evolution: The Impact of Submarket Convergence on Incumbent−Entrant Dynamics
methods: Panel event-history analysis of semiconductor fab closure using Cox proportional hazards models with submarket, country, firm, fab, and industry controls.
industry: Global semiconductor manufacturing industry; five submarkets: analog, discrete, MEMS, logic, and memory.
units: Fab-year observations for semiconductor manufacturing production facilities, linked to firm and submarket characteristics.
n_sample: Main Cox models use 15,559 observations, 1,128 failures, and 1,565 subjects; the broader cleaned data include 17,806 fab-year observations.
authors: Uzunca, B.
theories: competence-based view of industry evolution; disruptive innovation; industry life cycle theory
keywords: customer competences; incumbent-entrant dynamics; industry evolution; submarket convergence; technological competences
research_question: The paper asks how convergence in the technological and customer competences required by submarkets affects the relative success of industry incumbents and entrants. It examines whether convergence in both competence dimensions protects incumbents, while non-convergence in either dimension gives entrants space to gain a foothold.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that submarket convergence changes which competences can be leveraged across the industry. When both technological and customer competences converge, incumbents can apply accumulated competences and slack resources across submarkets, while entrants face head-on competition and have fewer ways to differentiate. When only one competence dimension converges, the remaining non-convergent dimension preserves room for entrants to avoid direct incumbent competition and survive long enough to potentially disrupt incumbents.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a competence-based view of industry evolution that defines intra-industry boundaries by the technological and customer competences needed to compete in submarkets. It extends industry evolution, disruption, and competitive dynamics research by showing that incumbent dominance, entrant disruption, and continued submarket separation can coexist within the same industry depending on the pattern of competence convergence. It also reframes disruption as incumbents' lack of the competences needed to produce or sell in different submarkets, rather than only as incumbent myopia.
practical_implication: Managers should assess industry threats at the submarket level rather than relying on broad industry categories. Incumbents need to identify whether their advantage rests on technological or customer competences and monitor whether adjacent submarkets are converging in ways that remove or preserve entrants' room to differentiate. Entrants can gain a foothold by locating submarkets where at least one competence dimension remains sufficiently distinct from incumbent-dominated areas.
limitations: The empirical evidence comes from the semiconductor manufacturing industry, so the tests are strongest for a setting with observable submarkets, production facilities, and technology/product profiles. The outcome is fab closure, which captures entrant exit or incumbent repositioning in a submarket but does not directly measure all firm-level strategic responses or industry-level survival. The competence-distance measures use technology- and product-category data, so the results should be interpreted through those observed proxies for technological and customer competence.
future_research: Future research could convert the paper's two-submarket theoretical illustration into a formal mathematical model or simulation. Scholars could further improve the framework to reconcile Klepper's account of incumbent dominance through shakeouts with Christensen's account of entrant disruption. The paper also calls for more work on incumbent repositioning as a strategic response to disruption, beyond treating survival and failure as the only outcomes.
abstract: Understanding intra-industry boundaries is important because it offers insight into firms’ strategic options based on their competences. Defining intra-industry heterogeneity in terms of the technological and customer competences that are required to produce and sell different products in each submarket, this paper explores whether the convergence of these competences, i.e., an increase in the degree to which competences can be leveraged across submarkets, exerts differential effects on the success of industry incumbents versus entrants. Empirical evidence from the global semiconductor manufacturing industry shows that convergence in both technological and customer competences decreases entrants’ survival chances, whereas a lack of convergence in any one of the two types of competence—that is, in one set of competences or another but not in both—gives entrants sufficient room to gain a foothold in the industry and to potentially disrupt incumbents. As a strategic response to disruption, multiplant industry incumbents can reposition themselves by changing their focus across submarkets while not necessarily exiting the industry entirely. The paper contributes to the literature on industry evolution, disruption, and competitive dynamics and has implications for future research and practice.
apa_citation: Uzunca, B. (2018). A competence-based view of industry evolution: The impact of submarket convergence on incumbent−entrant dynamics. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(2), 738-768. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1080

title: Misery Loves Company: An Investigation of Couples’ Interrole Conflict Congruence
methods: Survey-based dyadic quantitative study of employee and romantic partner pairs, analyzed with polynomial regression, response surface methodology, and bootstrapped mediation tests linking employee and significant-other FWC/WFC congruence to balance satisfaction, employee job satisfaction, and significant-other relationship satisfaction.
industry: Government employees working for a Midwestern state in the United States, with jobs in varied professions including information technology, public relations, and social services.
time_period: Calendar data-collection dates not reported; focal employees completed an initial online survey, then a mailed survey, and significant others received a separate survey approximately one week after the focal employee completed the initial survey.
units: Employee and romantic partner dyads; focal employees worked full-time and lived with a spouse or significant other.
n_sample: 141 employee and romantic partner dyads.
authors: Wilson, Kelly Schwind; Baumann, Heidi M.; Matta, Fadel K.; Ilies, Remus; Kossek, Ellen Ernst
theories: balance theory (Heider, 1958); family systems theory (Hammer et al., 2003)
keywords: balance satisfaction; dyadic interrole conflict congruence; family-to-work conflict; interrole conflict; job satisfaction; relationship satisfaction; work-to-family conflict
research_question: The paper asks how congruence or incongruence between an employee's and romantic partner's interrole conflict shapes the employee's balance satisfaction and downstream satisfaction outcomes. It specifically tests whether family-to-work conflict and work-to-family conflict congruence operate differently when both partners' own conflict experiences are considered jointly.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in balance theory: partners experience congruent levels of interrole conflict as a more balanced and validating state, while incongruence creates tension around work and family role sacrifices. The supported effect is strongest for family-to-work conflict because the family domain is shared by both partners. When both partners experience similar levels of FWC, the employee reports higher balance satisfaction than when only one partner carries high FWC, and this balance satisfaction helps explain employee job satisfaction and partner relationship satisfaction.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces dyadic interrole conflict congruence as a work-family construct and shows that partner conflict is not merely background context but a boundary condition for interpreting an employee's own interrole conflict. It challenges the individual-level assumption that less conflict is always better by showing that high FWC can be less harmful when the partner experiences similarly high FWC. The study also contributes to work-family balance research by linking balance satisfaction to dyadic fit between partners' conflict experiences.
practical_implication: The findings imply that organizations and supervisors should pay attention to employees' family systems rather than treating work-family conflict as a purely individual issue. Benefits that reduce family demands for both partners, such as reliable childcare support or household-service assistance, may be especially relevant for lowering FWC in dual-earner couples. Supervisors may also need to identify employees whose FWC is higher than their partner's and provide family-supportive emotional and instrumental support.
limitations: The authors state that the research design was mostly cross-sectional, so the study cannot establish causal ordering among interrole conflict congruence, balance satisfaction, job satisfaction, and relationship satisfaction. The study included SO relationship satisfaction as one crossover outcome but did not test a full crossover model with both partners' balance satisfaction and downstream outcomes. The authors call for future work using different and more heterogeneous samples to assess whether the same patterns hold beyond the sampled employees and significant others.
future_research: The authors call for longitudinal research that examines interrole conflict congruence across multiple time periods and tests whether changes in congruence precede changes in job and relationship satisfaction. They also encourage fuller crossover models that include both partners' outcomes, additional outcomes such as performance, health, and general well-being, and international samples across different industries. Future work could examine antecedents of congruence, including shared values and provider-role attitudes, and could compare partner-reported conflict with focal employees' perceptions of both partners' conflict.
abstract: Previous research on interrole (family-to-work and work-to-family) conflict has demonstrated that such conflict is detrimental for outcomes in the work and home domains for employees and their family members. Although research has begun to integrate multiple parties into the interrole conflict literature, studies have overlooked how employee interrole conflict and partner interrole conflict can jointly influence employee outcomes. We advance work–family research by integrating balance theory with the interrole conflict literature to investigate dyadic interrole conflict congruence and challenge the implicit assumption that less interrole conflict always results in superior outcomes. Using a polynomial regression analysis of 141 employee and romantic partner dyads, we demonstrate that congruence between couples’ experiences of family-to-work (but not work-to-family) conflict is positively associated with balance satisfaction, and ultimately employee job satisfaction and partner relationship satisfaction. Thus, when it comes to balance satisfaction and its downstream correlates, the harmful effects of high family-to-work conflict (FWC) are largely mitigated if an employee’s partner shares a similarly high level of FWC, and the beneficial effects of low FWC are largely eliminated if an employee’s partner does not share a similarly low level of FWC.

title: An Examination of the Firm-level Performance Impact of Cluster Hiring in Knowledge-intensive Firms
methods: Archival empirical quantitative study of large domestic U.S. law firms using OLS regression for main effects and moderated hierarchical regression for interaction effects.
industry: Large domestic U.S. law firms from The American Lawyer top 200 list that hired two or more lateral partners in 2010.
time_period: Cluster-hire and firm data for 2010, with change in profit per partner measured between 2010 and 2011 and prior-year change measured between 2009 and 2010.
units: Law firms; cluster hires of lateral partners.
n_sample: 112 law firms.
authors: Eckardt, R.; Skaggs, B. C.; Lepak, D. P.
theories: group dynamics; signaling theory; strategic human capital
keywords: cluster hiring; co-mobility; expertise overlap; knowledge-intensive firms; strategic human capital
research_question: The paper asks how cluster hiring as an approach to acquiring strategic human capital affects firm-level performance in knowledge-intensive firms. It focuses on whether the performance impact depends on the cluster hire's expertise overlap, co-mobility, and fit with the hiring firm's existing strategic human capital depth.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that cluster hiring can create economic value when expertise overlap adds novel and legitimate strategic human capital to areas where the hiring firm has little existing depth. Co-mobility can reduce firm-level performance by creating integration problems and appropriation concerns, even if it may help individual movers. The results support a negative main effect of co-mobility, a positive expertise-overlap effect only under low co-mobility, and a positive expertise-overlap effect only when existing strategic human capital depth is low.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends strategic human capital research by moving cluster hiring from an individual-mobility question to a firm-level performance question. It clarifies cluster hiring as a strategic human capital acquisition tactic whose value depends on composition and fit, not merely on moving multiple employees together. It also shows that positive individual-level arguments about co-mobility do not necessarily scale to firm-level profitability.
practical_implication: Knowledge-intensive firms should not treat cluster hiring as uniformly beneficial. The findings imply that cluster hires are more likely to improve profitability when they add concentrated expertise in areas where the firm has little existing strategic human capital and when they involve low co-mobility. Firms should be cautious about acqui-hiring or team lift-outs that bring high co-mobility because these moves may create integration and appropriation costs.
limitations: The authors identify the single-industry context as a limitation: the study uses law firms, which are a prototypical knowledge-intensive setting but may have industry-specific features. They also note the cross-sectional nature of the data, which limits insight into whether the relationships change over time. The study therefore cannot show the longer-term temporal dynamics of cluster hiring or interventions that might reduce the negative effects of co-mobility.
future_research: The authors call for research that tests the findings in other industry contexts and examines contextual moderators of cluster hiring's value-generating ability. They suggest that network perspectives could examine novelty and integration, group-dynamics work could identify ways to reduce intergroup bias, and human capital complementarities could explain how firms capture more value from cluster hires. They also encourage longitudinal designs that can assess longer-term effects and interventions around co-mobility.
abstract: This research investigates the firm-level performance impact of cluster hiring approaches to the acquisition of strategic human capital in knowledge-intensive firms. We theorize that factors such as novelty and legitimacy, appropriation, and integration impact the ability of cluster hires to generate economic value. In turn, we hypothesize that the composition of the cluster hire (degree of expertise overlap and degree of comobility) and its fit with the strategic human capital at the hiring firm are likely to influence these factors to affect firm performance. The results from an archival study of cluster hires in 112 domestic U.S. law firms lend credence to the overarching perspective put forth in this paper, and demonstrate that the performance impact of cluster hiring is contingent on its composition and fit with the existing strategic human capital at the hiring firm. Specifically, we find that while the co-mobility dimension has a negative impact on firm performance, the degree of expertise overlap is positively related to firm performance when it adds strategic human capital to an area where the hiring firm has little or no presence. Additionally, we find that expertise overlap positively impacts firm performance when the cluster hire involves low levels of co-mobility.
