title: Does “Could” Lead to Good? On the Road to Moral Insight
methods: Four-study empirical quantitative design using randomized mindset manipulations in online and laboratory experiments, plus background pilot and executive-survey evidence. The focal studies used written ethical-dilemma responses, speeches, dyadic chat discussions, independent blind coding and judging, ANOVA, t-tests, mediation analysis, and mediated moderation analysis to test whether a could mindset increases divergent thinking and moral insight.
industry: Not reported in paper as a single industry sample; the studies used online participants, full-time employees, university lab dyads, students, and scenario-based ethical dilemmas.
country: United States where reported: Study 3 used a university in the northeastern United States, and Study 4 used full-time and part-time students in the United States; Study 1 and Study 2 online participant countries were not reported.
time_period: Not reported in paper for the four focal experiments.
units: Individual participants, full-time employees, dyads, student participants, written responses, speeches, chat discussions, and independent judge ratings.
n_sample: Study 1 analyzed 205 participants; Study 2 analyzed 310 full-time employees plus 258 independent judges; Study 3 analyzed 202 individuals forming 101 dyads plus 100 independent raters; Study 4 analyzed 572 students plus 272 independent judges.
authors: Zhang, Ting; Gino, Francesca; Margolis, Joshua D.
theories: behavioral ethics and moral decision-making; conflict resolution and negotiation research; insight and creativity research
keywords: behavioral ethics; could mindset; creativity; divergent thinking; ethical decision-making; moral dilemmas; moral insight; should mindset
research_question: The paper asks when individuals facing right-versus-right moral dilemmas find moral insight solutions rather than simply choosing one moral imperative over another. It specifically tests whether prompting people to ask what they could do, rather than what they should do, increases divergent thinking and thereby helps them generate solutions that honor or reconcile competing moral imperatives.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that a should mindset narrows attention toward weighing competing obligations and choosing among salient options, while a could mindset makes additional possibilities cognitively available. This broader mindset increases divergent thinking, which helps individuals formulate responses that move beyond forced tradeoffs and preserve multiple moral imperatives. Across the focal studies, this process increased moral insight in hypothetical, incentive-compatible, dyadic, and enacted right-versus-right contexts, but the could mindset did not add moral insight in hybrid dilemmas where self-gain was also present.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to behavioral ethics by shifting attention from misconduct and right-versus-wrong temptation to the problem of resolving right-versus-right moral dilemmas. It introduces moral insight as a distinct ethical problem-solving outcome and theorizes it as an application of creative cognition to moral conflicts. It also qualifies prior work linking creativity to unethical behavior by showing that creative, divergent thinking can support ethical resolution when the task is to reconcile competing moral imperatives rather than justify self-serving wrongdoing.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that managers, ethics representatives, counselors, and employees can improve moral-dilemma problem solving by beginning with the question “What could I do?” before adjudicating what they should do. This prompt can move conversations away from the two most salient options and toward a broader set of responses that preserve competing obligations. The paper cautions, however, that the evidence does not imply replacing should-based moral reasoning; rather, could-based exploration can precede and enrich subsequent ethical evaluation.
limitations: The authors note that Studies 1 to 3 measured what participants said they would do in scenarios rather than directly observing decisions that affected key constituents. They also note that the experiments were conducted in labs or online panels, which limits external validity even though several dilemmas were adapted from real employee situations. A further limitation is possible demand effects from explicitly asking participants to adopt either a could or should mindset.
future_research: The authors call for research on when expansive could mindsets lead to moral insight versus unethical creative justification, especially as self-gain becomes more tempting. They also propose field research on whether instilling a could mindset helps employees generate moral insight in real workplace ethical challenges. Additional work is needed on how observers evaluate the ethicality of moral insight decisions, because resolving the focal tension may reduce the salience of ethical sacrifice.
abstract: Dilemmas featuring competing moral imperatives are prevalent in organizations and are difficult to resolve. Whereas prior research has focused on how individuals adjudicate among these moral imperatives, we study the factors that influence when individuals find solutions that fall outside of the salient options presented. In particular, we study moral insight, or the discovery of solutions, other than selecting one of the competing moral imperatives over another, that honor both competing imperatives or resolve the tension among them. Although individuals intuitively consider the question “What should I do?” when contemplating moral dilemmas, we find that prompting people to consider “What could I do?” helps them generate moral insight. Together, these studies point toward the conditions that enable moral insight and important practical implications.
apa_citation: Zhang, T., Gino, F., & Margolis, J. D. (2018). Does “could” lead to good? On the road to moral insight. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(3), 857-895. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0839

title: To Delegate or Not to Delegate: Gender Differences in Affective Associations and Behavioral Responses to Delegation
methods: Five-study empirical quantitative design using MBA surveys, MTurk scenario and manager surveys, a controlled behavioral laboratory delegation experiment with a confederate subordinate, and an MBA role-play framing experiment. Analyses included LIWC text analysis, ANOVA, binary logistic regression, independent coder and confederate ratings, task-performance scoring, and PROCESS mediation tests.
industry: Not reported in paper
country: United States where reported; the paper reports U.S.-resident MTurk participants and East Coast private-university samples, while Study 1 also included international MBA students.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals in leadership, manager, subordinate, or participant roles; free-response texts; delegation decisions; confederate and coder ratings; and task-performance outcomes.
n_sample: Five studies: Study 1 final sample of 97 MBA participants; Study 2 final sample of 171 MTurk participants; Study 3 final sample of 130 managers; Study 4 final sample of 137 behavioral-lab participants; Study 5 recruited 135 MBA students.
authors: Akinola, Modupe; Martin, Ashley E.; Phillips, Katherine W.
theories: backlash theory; gender-role incongruence; social role theory
keywords: affective associations; backlash theories; delegation; fear of backlash; gender-role incongruence; guilt; leadership behavior; social role theory
research_question: The paper asks whether women and men differ in how they perceive, emotionally associate with, and behaviorally enact delegation. It specifically tests whether delegation’s agentic and communal properties create gender-role incongruence for women, leading to more negative affective associations, less delegation, lower-quality subordinate interactions, and whether communal framing can attenuate these responses.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that delegation is both communal and agentic, but the agentic element is more salient and costly for women because social role and backlash expectations penalize women’s agency more than they reward women’s communality. This produces more negative affective associations with delegation, including anxiety, guilt, and fear of backlash. Those associations can reduce women’s willingness to delegate and degrade the quality of interactions when women do delegate. Reframing delegation as a way to help subordinates develop makes the communal element more salient and reduces women’s negative affective responses.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to gender and leadership research by showing that leadership behaviors can be gender-role paradoxical rather than simply agentic or communal. It provides empirical evidence that women and men differ in delegation behavior and identifies affective associations as a process through which gender-role incongruence shapes delegation. It also extends backlash and social role theory by showing that communal reframing can change women’s responses to a seemingly agentic leadership behavior.
practical_implication: The findings imply that organizations should not assume that delegation is experienced similarly by male and female leaders, even when delegation is formally encouraged as a developmental practice. Framing delegation as mentoring, developing, and empowering subordinates may help women view delegation as more communal and selfless, reducing negative affect and potentially increasing delegation. The paper also suggests that failure to address these affective barriers may hinder women’s time management, subordinate development, and leadership effectiveness.
limitations: The authors note that Study 3 did not find gender differences in self-reported delegation among managers, while Study 4 found behavioral differences in a student laboratory sample, leaving open whether behavioral gender differences generalize across organizations, experience levels, and hierarchy. They also note that Study 4 involved participants with no ongoing subordinate relationship, which may suppress or exaggerate delegation behavior compared with real work relationships. A further limitation is that Studies 2 and 4 operationalized delegation in a time-scarce, agentic way, which may have minimized delegation’s communal aspects.
future_research: The authors call for behavioral studies of delegation across men and women in organizations with varied work experience and hierarchical levels. They recommend longitudinal work on how familiarity and relationship length with subordinates affect women’s likelihood of and comfort with delegation. They also call for research that distinguishes associated, prospective, and retrospective anxiety; tests broader negative affective mechanisms such as anticipatory guilt; and compares communal with noncommunal or agentic-legitimating reframings of delegation.
abstract: Effectively delegating work to others is considered critical to managerial success, as it frees up managers’ time and develops subordinates’ skills. We propose that female leaders are less likely than male leaders to capitalize on these benefits of delegating. Although delegation has communal (e.g., relational) and agentic (e.g., assertive) properties, we argue that female leaders, as compared to male leaders, find it more difficult to delegate tasks due to gender-role incongruence. In five studies, we draw upon social role and backlash theories to show that women imbue delegation with more agentic traits, have more negative associations with delegating, and feel greater guilt about delegating than men. These associations result in women delegating less than men and, when they do delegate, having lower-quality interactions with subordinates. We further show that reframing delegation as communal attenuates women’s negative associations with delegation. These findings reveal that even when a given behavior has both agentic and communal elements, perceptions of agency can undermine women’s engagement in them. However, emphasizing the communal nature of seemingly agentic acts may encourage women’s engagement in such critical leadership behaviors. These findings have theoretical and practical implications for research on gender differences and leadership behavior in the workplace.

title: New Ways of Seeing through Qualitative Research
methods: Editorial guidance essay that argues for methodological diversity in qualitative research, describes qualitative methods as genres with distinct assumptions, and offers principles for writing, reviewing, and reading qualitative papers.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Bansal, Pratima; Smith, Wendy K.; Vaara, Eero
theories: inductive theorizing; qualitative research genres
keywords: inductive theorizing; methodological diversity; new ways of seeing; qualitative genres; qualitative research
research_question: The editorial asks how qualitative research can help management scholars develop "new ways of seeing" and why AMJ authors should use a broader range of qualitative genres. It focuses on how methodological diversity, genre-specific assumptions, and internal coherence can strengthen inductive theory building.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Qualitative research can surface new theoretical insights by building theory inductively from data, especially in complex or understudied empirical contexts.
- Genre diversity: The editorial presents variance-based case studies, process studies, engaged scholarship, historical studies, and discourse studies as different qualitative genres with distinct assumptions and forms of insight.
- Quality principles: Authors and reviewers should know the epistemology of the genre, align research questions, data, and analysis, write authentically and clearly, and use exemplars without forcing their work into rigid templates.
- Editorial stance: The essay treats methodological diversity as necessary for qualitative research to avoid premature institutionalization around a narrow set of norms.

The process logic is editorial and methodological rather than empirical. Bansal, Smith, and Vaara argue that qualitative research advances theory when scholars deliberately match research questions, data, analysis, and onto-epistemological assumptions to the qualitative genre they are using. Their central warning is that templates can help establish rigor but can also narrow what qualitative research is able to reveal.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes to management-methods discourse by framing qualitative methods as genres rather than as a single method category. This framing helps distinguish the assumptions and analytic logics of variance-based cases, process studies, engaged scholarship, historical work, and discourse analysis while preserving the shared goal of inductive theorizing.
practical_implication: For AMJ authors, the editorial implies that qualitative papers should make their epistemological assumptions visible, align questions, data, and analysis, and defend methodological choices in relation to the chosen genre. For reviewers, it cautions against evaluating all qualitative manuscripts against one dominant case-study template.
limitations: The editorial presents examples of qualitative genres rather than an exhaustive taxonomy. Its guidance should therefore be read as an editorial orientation toward methodological variety, not as a complete classification of qualitative research.
future_research: The editorial encourages future management research to use a broader range of qualitative genres and to keep developing qualitative methods rather than allowing the field to settle too quickly around a few norms. It also invites scholars to juxtapose methodological approaches to stimulate innovation within and across genres.

title: The Paradox of Family Structure and Plans after Work: Why Single Childless Employees May Be the Least Absorbed at Work
methods: Three-study quantitative design: Study 1 uses a cross-sectional survey of business school alumni with ordinary least squares regression; Study 2 uses a five-workday diary survey of university employees with multilevel structural equation modeling; the Study 2 supplement uses a two-wave Qualtrics panel survey with mixed models and PROCESS mediation analyses.
industry: Business school alumni, university administrative/professional staff, and full-time online panel employees; exact industries for the panel sample are not reported in paper.
country: Study 1 sampled alumni of a private U.S. university; country is not fully reported for every sample.
time_period: Study 2 covered five consecutive workdays; exact calendar dates are not reported in paper.
units: Individual workers, their family structures, anticipated after-work activities, construals of those activities, and work absorption.
n_sample: Study 1 final sample size was 353; Study 2 included 97 daily-survey participants and 354 matched morning-afternoon responses; the Study 2 supplement final sample included 196 participants.
authors: Dumas, T. L.; Perry-Smith, J. E.
theories: anticipatory boundary transitions; boundary theory; current concerns theory
keywords: after-work activities; boundary theory; current concerns theory; family structure; work absorption
research_question: How does family structure affect employees' work absorption, and do anticipated after-work domestic or leisure activities explain why single, childless employees may be less absorbed at work than employees with other family structures? The paper asks whether family responsibilities can enhance work absorption even when the relevant family experience is not explicitly positive.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is anticipatory rather than affect-transfer based. Because domestic responsibilities are obligatory and goal directed, anticipating them can reinforce a work-like mindset and keep employees psychologically immersed in work. Single, childless employees anticipate fewer domestic activities, which reduces this reinforcing process and helps explain their lower work absorption; anticipated leisure activities are associated with lower absorption but do not mediate the family-structure effect.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends work-family enrichment research by showing that family can benefit work through anticipated responsibilities, not only through positive affect, skill transfer, or prosocial motivation. It contributes to boundary theory by linking anticipatory boundary transitions to current work absorption rather than only to after-work recovery or role conflict. It also broadens ideal-worker theorizing by directly examining single, childless workers and showing that being less encumbered by family responsibilities does not necessarily translate into greater work absorption.
practical_implication: Managers should not assume that single, childless employees are naturally more available, focused, or work-absorbed because they lack spouse or child responsibilities. Organizations may need broader work-life policies that respect nonfamily commitments and support diverse forms of nonwork life. Employees and managers can also use reminders or planning around goal-directed domestic or nonwork tasks selectively, because anticipated activities can shape absorption before the workday ends.
limitations: The studies rely partly on self-reported survey behavior, creating potential common method variance, although Study 2 uses multiple survey points and family structure is not an attitude measure. The Study 2 and supplement samples are predominantly female, and the authors note that spousal employment status, gender, and unstudied cohabitating heterosexual couples require further exploration. The paper studies absorption rather than time spent at work or productivity, so the findings do not establish effects on objective performance.
future_research: Future research should examine how spousal employment status, gender, parental status, marital status, and cohabitation jointly shape the family-structure effects documented here. Additional work should compare the anticipatory effects of after-work activities with their following-day recovery effects, including moderators such as how active, passive, challenging, goal directed, or routine the activities are. Researchers should also examine whether work absorption, rather than face time or constant accessibility, predicts valued outcomes in professional knowledge work.
abstract: Existing research has shown that positive family experiences can affect work positively. In this article, however, we consider how family may enhance work even when family experiences are not explicitly positive. We draw on boundary theory and cognitive psychology’s current concerns theory to evaluate how employees’ family structures and associated after-work activities affect their work absorption. A survey of business school alumni (Study 1) revealed that single, childless workers reported lower absorption than workers with other family structures. Further, a daily diary study of university employees (Study 2) showed that employees’ planned after-work activities explained the relationship between family structure and work absorption. Specifically, single, childless workers anticipated fewer domestic after-work activities, resulting in lower work absorption. Due to similarities between domestic responsibilities and work tasks—for example, their obligatory and goal-directed nature—anticipating domestic responsibilities after work reinforces, rather than distracts from, the work mindset, thus keeping employees more immersed psychologically in their work. This finding suggests that having a spouse and/or children can affect employees’ work absorption positively through the anticipation of domestic duties after work. Thus, our study contributes to a more comprehensive view of how employees’ work and nonwork lives are connected.

title: Deep Help in Complex Project Work: Guiding and Path-Clearing Across Difficult Terrain
methods: Inductive, multimethod qualitative field study at GlowDesign, a pseudonymous design consultancy. The authors combined onsite observation, informal interviews, SMS daily diaries, weekly interviews with project team members and repeat help givers, critical-incident interviews, open coding, temporal sequencing, case memos, and iterative theorizing around 27 deep-help cases.
industry: Design consultancy conducting complex knowledge-intensive project work, including product design, brand development, and strategy consulting.
country: Not reported in paper as a single-country sample; Glow had offices in North America, Europe, and Asia, roughly half headquartered in California, and Round 1 observation occurred at a large U.S. East Coast office.
time_period: Not reported in paper as calendar data-collection dates; the paper reports that Glow projects typically lasted 5-22 weeks and that the four Round 2 projects lasted 6-12 weeks.
units: Project teams, help givers, help receivers, deep-help cases, diary entries, weekly interviews, critical-incident interviews, and observed project interactions.
n_sample: The focal analysis used 27 deep-help cases. The broader data included 36 hours of onsite observation over 21 visits, 11 informal interviews, 401 daily diary entries from four project teams, 84 weekly project-team interviews with 13 core team members, 25 weekly help-giver interviews with eight repeat givers, and 30 critical-incident interviews including pilots.
authors: Fisher, Colin M.; Pillemer, Julianna; Amabile, Teresa M.
theories: external team leadership; helping in organizations; process perspective; social construction and social interactionist perspectives; temporality in organizations
keywords: complex project work; deep help; external leadership; guiding; helping frame; knowledge-intensive project work; path clearing; temporal rhythm
research_question: The paper asks how the deep-help process unfolds in complex project work. More specifically, it examines how project teams at a design consultancy receive extensive external help when they face ambiguous, difficult project problems that cannot be handled through brief favors, quick advice, or single feedback encounters.
mechanism_summary:
- Key phenomenon: Deep help, defined as intensive, repeated assistance in which high-status external leaders devote substantial time to helping project teams with especially difficult problems.
- Initial phase: Surveying, in which givers and receivers identify issues through prior knowledge, observation of project artifacts, receiver requests, and receiver distress.
- Guiding process: A critical juncture leads giver and receivers to adopt prolonged, tightly clustered sessions, establish and reinforce a helping frame, map the project by steeping in it, range by introducing a new work process, and end when time expires or receivers reassert autonomy.
- Path-clearing process: A persistent deficiency leads the giver to make a generalized offer, wait for a specific request, adopt short and scattered interactions, iteratively map and range by looking ahead and filling holes, reinforce the helping frame through availability or menial tasks, and continue until a phase or project ends.
- Process deviations: Guiding can become a takeover when high-status givers fail to preserve receivers' autonomy; path clearing can become a swoop-and-poop when givers offer shallow criticism or monitoring without removing obstacles.

The process model is not a variable-based causal model but an inductive explanation of how helping becomes socially constructed over time. The same high-status involvement can be interpreted as support, leadership, monitoring, or implied criticism depending on whether parties establish and maintain a helping frame. Temporal rhythm matters because clustered time helps guides understand and work through critical junctures, while intermittent time lets path clearers remain available without becoming enmeshed in the team's work.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends helping theory beyond the initiation of brief, one-time helping episodes by showing that help can unfold across multiple interactions and through distinct processes. It contributes to external team leadership theory by conceptualizing deep help as a form of hands-on external leadership whose social meaning must be negotiated rather than assumed. It also contributes to temporality research by theorizing interaction rhythm, not just clock time or total time spent, as both a resource-allocation decision and a signal that shapes whether help is experienced as autonomy-supporting or autonomy-threatening.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that teams and external leaders should recognize guiding and path clearing as legitimate responses to serious problems in complex projects rather than equating deep involvement with micromanagement. Organizations can support productive deep help by giving senior employees schedule flexibility, making helping norms explicit, and encouraging leaders to treat as-needed deep help as part of their responsibilities. Givers should make their helping intention explicit through questions, listening, availability, and, in path clearing, menial tasks; teams should communicate emergent problems even when they cannot yet specify the exact help needed.
limitations: The authors identify Glow as an extreme setting because its culture strongly valued helping, its structure was relatively nonhierarchical with loose role definitions, and its projects were creative and ambiguous. They also report limited information about interpersonal relationships between givers and receivers, limited ability to study how multiple deep-help cases within a project interrelate, and limited direct observation of the deep-help interactions themselves. The data therefore support theory building about deep help in complex knowledge work but do not establish how common the processes are in more hierarchical, less creative, or less help-oriented organizations.
future_research: The authors call for research beyond Glow's boundary conditions to examine how helping norms, flat structure, and project complexity interact to shape responses to critical junctures and persistent deficiencies. They also propose work on how giver-receiver relationship quality, leader-member exchange, and trust shape deep help; how multiple deep-help episodes within the same project influence each other; and how direct observation could reveal physical, emotional, cognitive, and microprocessual aspects of deep-help interactions. Additional research should examine the possible role of clients and other outsiders, because the study focused primarily on interactions among Glow employees.
abstract: How do teams working on complex projects get the help they need? Our qualitative investigation of the help provided to project teams at a prominent design firm revealed two distinct helping processes, both characterized by deep, sustained engagement that far exceeds the brief interactions described in the helping literature. Such deep help consisted of (1) guiding a team through a difficult juncture by working with its members in several prolonged, tightly clustered sessions, or (2) path clearing by helping a team address a persistent deficit via briefer, intermittent sessions throughout a project’s life. We present a model theorizing these processes, which has two noteworthy features. First, it emphasizes the socially constructed nature of helping behavior. That is, the parties must establish and maintain a helping frame for their interaction, especially when help givers are high-status external leaders. Second, the model specifies that the rhythms of deep help—the duration and temporal patterns of giver–receiver interactions— are resource-allocation decisions that also contribute to the social meaning of help. These findings illuminate the theoretical and practical overlap between helping and external leadership in knowledge-intensive project work, and the role of temporality in the helping process.

title: Open-System Orchestration as a Relational Source of Sensing Capabilities: Evidence from a Venture Association
methods: Empirical qualitative field study of a venture association and its annual B2BMatch initiative, using semi-structured interviews, observation, archival material, abductive analysis, open coding, axial coding, and grounded model building.
industry: Cross-sector nonprofit venture association and business matchmaking initiative involving mostly SMEs.
country: Italy, with Working Together headquartered in Italy and operating local branches in Italy and abroad.
time_period: Initial data collection covered 22 months beginning in January 2011, with additional evidence collected in 2013 and 2014.
units: Working Together, B2BMatch, participant firms, local branches, local advisors, buyers, interviews, observations, and archival materials.
n_sample: 81 interviews, including 50 informants from participant firms, four buyers from multinational enterprises, and 27 Working Together informants; the 2011 event had approximately 2,400 corporate participants.
authors: Giudici, Alessandro; Reinmoeller, Patrick; Ravasi, Davide
theories: dynamic capability perspective (Teece, 2007; Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997); network orchestration (Dhanaraj & Parkhe, 2006); relational ontology of social phenomena (Crossley, 2011; Emirbayer, 1997)
keywords: business matchmaking; closed-system orchestration; dynamic capabilities; open-system orchestration; sensing capabilities; venture associations
research_question: How do open-system orchestrators support the dispersed entrepreneurial efforts and sensing capabilities of network members? The paper asks how this form of orchestration differs from closed-system orchestration by hub firms and how it helps firms recognize new opportunities and form new business relationships.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: open-system orchestration, closed-system orchestration, sensing capabilities, mutual trustworthiness, organizational self-awareness, positive emotional experience, experiential learning, and dispersed collaboration.
- Orchestration processes: building collaborative engagement, facilitating members' introspection, encouraging members' exploration of complementarities, and fostering dispersed collaboration.
- Cognitive and emotional micro-foundations: assumptions of mutual trustworthiness lowered relational barriers, enhanced organizational self-awareness clarified search purposes, and positive emotional experience energized interaction.
- Emergent outcomes: recognition of new entrepreneurial opportunities and formation of new business relationships.
- Boundary conditions: the case was a highly successful, larger-than-average matchmaking initiative, mostly involving SMEs, and WT predominantly engaged in open-system orchestration.

The process model begins with a venture association creating a collaborative context around B2BMatch rather than directing members toward a centrally controlled innovation goal. Through preparatory activities, referrals, event design, and interaction monitoring, WT helped firms reflect on their own resources and identify complementarities with other members. These interactions supported members' sensing capabilities as relationally co-created capacities, while repeated participation also helped some firms internalize search routines beyond the event.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends network orchestration research by theorizing open-system orchestration as a distinct form used by organizations such as incubators, regional agencies, and venture associations to support decentralized entrepreneurial search. It contributes to dynamic capability theory by showing how sensing capabilities can be co-created relationally rather than residing exclusively inside firms. It also elaborates the cognitive and emotional micro-foundations through which trust, self-awareness, and positive affect support opportunity search in innovation networks.
practical_implication: The study suggests that venture associations, incubators, and similar intermediaries can improve members' opportunity search by designing collaborative norms, reflection spaces, high-quality referrals, and interaction settings that lower barriers among participants. It also implies that member firms need to engage thoughtfully and systematically; the benefits of open-system orchestration depend on their preparation, willingness to collaborate, and repeated learning from participation.
limitations: The authors state two boundary conditions. First, most B2BMatch participants were SMEs, where strategic decisions about business development, purchasing, and sales were concentrated in a small team, often including owner-managers. Second, WT engaged predominantly in open-system orchestration, so settings that combine open- and closed-system orchestration may show different or interfering processes.
future_research: Future research could examine open-system orchestration in larger organizations where responsibility for search and business development is more dispersed. The authors also call for research on how open-system orchestration affects new business models, leadership development, and tensions among different classes of dynamic capabilities. Additional work could compare orchestrators that combine open- and closed-system processes to test whether the mechanisms are compatible.
abstract: Research on innovation networks has highlighted the pivotal role that actors with more prominence and power, such as hub firms, may play in orchestrating the activities of other network members along a collective innovation effort. Our study examined the under-theorized, but no less important, type of orchestration that characterizes other organizations, such as business incubators and venture associations, who seek to support the dispersed entrepreneurial efforts of network members. We refer to this type as “open-system” orchestration, as opposed to the commonly studied “closed-system” type performed by hub firms. Our findings reveal how the processes of open-system orchestration differ markedly from those of closed-system orchestration, and detail how these processes influence the micro-foundations of network members’ sensing capabilities. By doing so, we also offer empirical substantiation and theoretical elaboration to the idea that dynamic capabilities might not reside exclusively inside firms, but could be co-created relationally with other parties in the business ecosystem.
apa_citation: Giudici, A., Reinmoeller, P., & Ravasi, D. (2018). Open-system orchestration as a relational source of sensing capabilities: Evidence from a venture association. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(4), 1369-1402. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0573

title: Silver Bullet or Ricochet? CEOs’ Use of Metaphorical Communication and Infomediaries’ Evaluations
methods: Empirical-quantitative panel study using manually coded CEO metaphorical communication in 937 quarterly earnings calls from U.S. pharmaceutical, hardware, and software firms from 2002 to 2011. Analysis I estimates changes in journalists' reporting favorability using 25,415 hand-coded New York Times and Wall Street Journal statements and robust firm fixed-effects panel models. Analysis II estimates changes in analysts' evaluations using 6,969 EPS forecast before-after pairs and 393 buy-hold-sell recommendation before-after pairs from I/B/E/S, again using robust firm fixed-effects models and interaction tests with negative and positive earnings surprises.
industry: U.S. pharmaceutical, computer hardware, and software industries
time_period: 2002 to 2011, with the methods section specifying firms operating between January 1, 2002, and July 31, 2011
units: Firm-quarter earnings conference calls, CEOs, firms, journalists' firm-related statements, analysts' EPS forecasts, and analysts' buy-hold-sell recommendations
n_sample: 937 hand-coded quarterly earnings conference calls; Analysis I: 43 firms, 98 CEOs, 449 before-after comparisons, and 25,415 journalist statements; Analysis II: 47 firms, 101 CEOs, 624 EPS forecast comparisons from 6,969 analyst forecast pairs, plus 270 recommendation comparisons from 393 analyst recommendation pairs
authors: König, A.; Mammen, J.; Luger, J.; Fehn, A. S.; Enders, A.
theories: discursive framing (Cornelissen & Werner, 2014); negativity bias; rhetoric and classical rhetorical devices; social cognition and cognitive shortcuts; socially situated constituent-minded sensemaking (Wiesenfeld, Wurthmann, & Hambrick, 2008)
keywords: discursive framing; earnings surprises; executive communication; impression management; infomediaries; journalists; metaphorical communication; securities analysts; socially situated sensemaking
research_question: How does the degree to which a CEO uses metaphorical communication affect the favorability of different infomediaries' assessments of the CEO's firm? The paper focuses on whether journalists and securities analysts respond differently to the same CEO rhetorical device because their sensemaking is socially situated in different professional thought worlds.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is audience-specific. Metaphorical communication provides broad, familiar, engaging frames that reduce journalists' effort in translating firm information for a mainstream audience, so journalists evaluate firms more favorably when CEOs use more metaphorical communication. Analysts, by contrast, work in a fact-oriented thought world and need precise, unambiguous information for investor audiences, so metaphorical communication becomes distracting or suspect and leads to less favorable evaluations. Negative earnings surprises intensify both effects because poor performance increases reliance on cognitive shortcuts under uncertainty.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on executive communication and CEO-infomediary relations by showing that the rhetorical form of CEO communication, not only the amount or content of information, shapes firm evaluations by critical audiences. It also complicates the common view of metaphor as a rhetorical asset by showing that metaphorical communication can be beneficial with journalists and harmful with analysts, creating a rhetorical dilemma when CEOs address multiple audiences simultaneously. More broadly, it links organizational reputation, executive communication, and impression management through the lens of socially situated sensemaking.
practical_implication: Corporate leaders, coaches, and speechwriters should treat metaphorical communication as an equivocal lever rather than a universal persuasive tool. When communicating with infomediaries, CEOs may need to decide which audience matters most at a given time and adjust rhetorical style accordingly, especially when firm performance disappoints market expectations. More metaphor may help journalists produce favorable coverage but can reduce analysts' favorability; less metaphor may preserve analyst confidence while forfeiting some journalistic appeal.
limitations: The authors note that they use only preliminary measures for whether CEOs' metaphors were aligned with the message being conveyed, leaving open whether metaphor quality, fit, or source-domain choice changes the effects. The design analyzes conference calls and cannot fully rule out endogeneity in CEOs' use of metaphorical communication, although the paper reports extensive robustness checks, simultaneity tests, and residualized models. The setting is limited to U.S. pharmaceutical, hardware, and software firms and to two types of infomediaries, so effects may differ for other industries, cultures, communication channels, or audiences.
future_research: Future research could examine characteristics of metaphorical communication, including whether specific source domains such as sports, journeys, or violence have different effects and whether automated methods can classify such domains reliably. Scholars could also study other CEO communication vehicles, such as interviews, public speeches, presentations, and roadshows, as well as nonverbal delivery cues such as facial expressions, gestures, and tone of voice. The paper further calls for work on other audiences, including customer-advocacy groups, rating agents, shareholder groups, and internal organizational members, where metaphorical communication may produce additional rhetorical dilemmas.
abstract: We combine literature on rhetoric and socially situated sensemaking to illuminate the challenges that emerge when chief executive officers (CEOs) try to influence infomediaries by using metaphorical communication—figurative linguistic expressions that convey thoughts and feelings by describing one domain, A, through another domain, B. Specifically, we theorize that because different infomediaries are situated in different thought worlds, CEOs’ use of metaphorical communication has contradictory effects on journalists’ and securities analysts’ evaluations: while it triggers more favorable statements from journalists, it prompts more unfavorable assessments from analysts. Moreover, we integrate findings from cognitive psychology to argue that these contradictory effects increase the more a firm’s performance falls behind market expectations. Our hypotheses find support in an extensive analysis of 937 quarterly earnings calls in the U.S. pharmaceutical, hardware, and software industries, and of journalists’ statements and analysts’ earnings forecasts and recommendations. Our novel theorizing and findings suggest that the use of discursive frames, especially in the form of metaphorical communication, in firms’ interactions with critical audiences creates thought-provoking and thus-far neglected dilemmas. In developing and testing these thoughts, we contribute to and link ongoing conversations in management science, especially discussions of organizational reputation, executive communication, and impression management.
apa_citation: König, A., Mammen, J., Luger, J., Fehn, A. S., & Enders, A. (2018). Silver bullet or ricochet? CEOs’ use of metaphorical communication and infomediaries’ evaluations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(4), 1196-1230. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0626

title: Experience and Signaling Value in Technology Licensing Contract Payment Structures
methods: Empirical-quantitative study of university technology licensing contracts from a prominent U.S. university technology transfer office. The authors use OLS to predict commercial success, measured as licensing revenue earned by the TTO from an invention, and seemingly unrelated regression with licensing-manager fixed effects and sample-selection correction to jointly predict upfront fixed-fee payments and royalty rates in the patented-contract sample.
industry: University technology licensing and academic invention commercialization
units: Invention-contract pairs, inventions, licensing contracts, licensing managers, inventors, and licensee firms
n_sample: 964 invention-contract pairs: 527 patented and 437 non-patented contracts; 427 inventions licensed through 472 contracts; main SUR analyses use 527 patented contracts
authors: Kotha, R.; Crama, P.; Kim, P. H.
theories: academic entrepreneurship; bargaining perspective; information asymmetry; signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al., 2011)
keywords: academic entrepreneurship; collaborative innovations; contract payment structure; licensing manager experience; royalty payments; signaling theory; technology licensing; upfront payments
research_question: How does licensing manager experience shape technology licensing contract payment structures, and when do experienced managers use lower upfront fixed fees and higher royalty rates as a signal of value rather than bargain for maximum immediate payments? The paper examines whether signaling ability and signaling need jointly explain contract terms in university technology licensing.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a signaling tradeoff in contract design. Experienced licensing managers are better able to select promising inventions and match them with capable licensees, so they can credibly give up guaranteed upfront payments in exchange for higher, performance-contingent royalties. This lower-upfront, higher-royalty structure signals confidence in the invention-licensee match to skeptical licensee firms. The signal becomes stronger when information asymmetry is higher or when signal need changes, including science-intensive inventions, more experienced inventors, and broader patent scope.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends signaling theory by integrating the sender's ability to signal with the receiver-side need for a signal, rather than assuming superior information and signal need are fixed. It shows that contract payment structures can function as intentional, recipient-specific signals whose strength varies with licensing manager experience and invention conditions. It also contributes to academic entrepreneurship by linking opportunity selection, partner matching, and licensing contract design as mechanisms through which experience shapes commercialization outcomes.
practical_implication: Technology transfer offices and other organizations involved in licensing should treat experience as a capability for selecting inventions, matching them with appropriate partners, and crafting credible contract signals. The findings imply that inexperienced licensing managers may benefit from mentoring, pairing with senior managers, and repeated exposure to licensing deals. Experienced managers should not standardize every contract; they can adjust upfront fees and royalty rates to the uncertainty and information asymmetry in each agreement.
limitations: The authors note that although post-hoc analyses isolate selection and matching mechanisms, future work should verify their relative magnitude more directly. The study is based on one technology transfer office, which offers advantages for isolating licensing capabilities but limits direct generalization to other TTOs, corporate licensors, or non-academic licensing contexts. The data also do not provide comprehensive information on unsuccessful licensing attempts, although the analyses control for unlicensed inventions in licensing managers' portfolios.
future_research: Future research should examine how initial negotiation reference points influence contract structure and should distinguish contract experience from prior interactions with multiple inventors more carefully. Studies using licensing data from multiple TTOs and non-academic corporate licensors could test whether the framework generalizes beyond the focal university context. The authors also suggest applying the framework to other settings where intermediaries help buyers and sellers agree on uncertain quality and value, such as artistic and cultural products or professional athletics.
abstract: When commercializing technology, the lack of proven results and a reluctance to invest upfront in resources hamper efforts by firms to work jointly with inventors to bring new discoveries to market. An effective contract payment structure—a mix of upfront and royalty payments—can help overcome these hurdles. We conduct our research in university technology licensing, where licensing managers act as intermediaries to unite inventors and licensee firms. Rather than leveraging their experience to bargain for maximum payments, highly experienced managers offer contractual payment structures that trade lower upfront payments for higher royalty payments in order to signal value. The signal instills confidence in the value of the partnership for skeptical licensee firms, and experienced licensing managers can amplify signals as needed to overcome the uncertainties inherent in technology commercialization. By explicitly addressing these variations in signal strength, we develop new theory that builds on classical signaling principles. We test and confirm these predictions in a sample of over 950 invention-licensing contracts. In addition to advancing signaling theory, our work has implications for academic entrepreneurship, and for how experience shapes valuesharing agreements in collaborative innovations.
apa_citation: Kotha, R., Crama, P., & Kim, P. H. (2018). Experience and signaling value in technology licensing contract payment structures. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(4), 1307-1342. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1233

title: The Benefits of Not Seeing Eye to Eye with Leadership: Divergence in Risk Preferences Impacts Multiteam System Behavior and Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative study of 92 14-person United States Air Force multiteam systems in a ten-round Leadership Development Simulation. The authors measured leadership-team and component-team risk preferences from planning worksheets, objective performance from the simulation score, aspirational behavior from well-vetted northern missions, and unwarranted risk behavior from unescorted missions to unexplored areas. Analyses used polynomial regression with response surface modeling, block-variable mediation in Mplus, and multilevel latent growth curve models.
industry: Military leadership training / United States Air Force simulation context.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Fourteen-person multiteam systems composed of leadership and component teams, with round-level simulation behavior and objective performance outcomes.
n_sample: 92 multiteam systems composed of 1,288 United States Air Force officers.
authors: Lanaj, Klodiana; Foulk, Trevor A.; Hollenbeck, John R.
theories: multiteam systems theory; risk preference theory; team diversity and information/decision-making perspective; team learning perspective
keywords: aspirational behavior; component teams; divergence; leadership teams; multiteam systems; risk preferences; system performance; team learning; unwarranted risk behavior
research_question: The paper asks how convergence versus divergence in risk preferences between leadership and component teams during planning affects multiteam system behavior and performance during execution. It further asks whether divergent risk preferences facilitate multiteam system learning over time.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that divergent risk preferences prevent premature consensus during planning and stimulate consideration of broader information, contingencies, and alternative plans. In these authority-differentiated multiteam systems, vertical divergence between leadership and component teams helps the system pursue well-vetted, high-reward aspirational behavior, which in turn improves objective performance. Convergence suppresses this aspirational behavior and is associated with weaker performance. The growth-curve results suggest that divergence becomes more beneficial over time for performance and aspirational behavior, consistent with the authors' learning interpretation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the prevailing multiteam systems argument that goal and plan convergence is generally preferable for system performance. It shows that, for risk preferences in divisional, authority-differentiated multiteam systems, divergence between leadership and component teams can improve performance rather than undermine it. It also contributes to team learning, risk, and diversity research by showing that deep-level divergence can be beneficial in a specific meso-level structure and that its effects strengthen over time.
practical_implication: The findings imply that leaders of multiteam systems should not treat early disagreement about risk as evidence that the system is failing. During planning for complex, high-stakes work, leadership teams may need to create room for component teams to express divergent risk preferences and avoid rapid agreement for its own sake. The paper also suggests that leaders can deliberately elicit component-team perspectives before stating their own risk preferences, while recognizing that the benefits of divergence may emerge during execution rather than immediately.
limitations: The authors note that the design did not collect survey data on members' attitudes or affective processes, such as psychological safety, team identification, satisfaction, or conflict. They also did not observe individual team-member risk preferences or the decision process through which teams formed a shared risk preference. Additional limitations include the simulation-specific operationalization of aspirational and unwarranted risk behavior, inability to record the full communication process, wide confidence intervals around principal-axis tests, and the fact that authority differentiation was a context rather than an experimentally varied construct.
future_research: The authors call for research on how individual risk preferences become team-level risk preferences and how within-team divergence interacts with multiteam-system-level divergence. They also recommend studying aspirational and unwarranted risk behavior in other contexts, such as medical, disaster relief, or new product launch multiteam systems. Future work should test other strategic goals beyond risk, examine systems with different coordination structures and boundary-spanning arrangements, and distinguish system-level from component-team-level outcomes.
abstract: Multiteam systems are large structures of interdependent teams that coordinate via planning before embarking on important projects. Although rarely studied, theory suggests that expression of convergent versus divergent goals and preferences during planning by leadership and component teams matters for multiteam system performance. Addressing this important issue, in a sample of multiteam systems consisting of Air Force officers, we examine how convergent versus divergent preferences for risk expressed during planning by the leadership and component teams impact multiteam system behavior and performance during the performance episode. Drawing from literatures on multiteam systems, diversity, and risk we posit and show that divergent (vs. convergent) preferences for risk have positive implications for multiteam system behavior and performance. Specifically, when the leadership and component teams hold divergent risk preferences, multiteam systems engage in more aspirational behavior and perform better. Alternatively, when the leadership and component teams hold convergent risk preferences, multiteam systems perform worse, partially because they display lower aspirational behavior. Consistent with a learning perspective, the beneficial effects of divergent preferences for risk increase over time. We discuss the implications of our findings for research and practice.
apa_citation: Lanaj, K., Foulk, T. A., & Hollenbeck, J. R. (2018). The benefits of not seeing eye to eye with leadership: Divergence in risk preferences impacts multiteam system behavior and performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(4), 1554-1582. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0946

title: Shared Team Experiences and Team Effectiveness: Unpacking the Contingent Effects of Entrained Rhythms and Task Characteristics
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study combining archival quantitative analysis of operating-room and billing records with semi-structured interviews. The quantitative phase uses multilevel hierarchical linear models of surgeries nested in procedure types, testing linear, curvilinear, and interaction terms for shared team task-specific experience, task frequency, and task difficulty; the qualitative phase analyzes interview transcripts and notes for patterns in team composition, task characteristics, team dynamics, and team effectiveness.
industry: Healthcare; perioperative surgical suite in a large general medical and surgical community hospital.
time_period: Archival data cover surgeries from January 1, 2012 to December 31, 2013; 2013 is the focal outcome year, with 2012 used to compute shared experience.
units: Surgical crew-based teams, surgeries, procedure types, operating-room personnel interviews, team efficiency, and patient post-surgery recovery rate.
n_sample: 8,236 focal surgeries performed in 2013; 6,799 surgeries from 2012 used to compute prior shared experience; 30 semi-structured interviews with operating-room personnel.
authors: Luciano, Margaret M.; Bartels, Amy L.; D’Innocenzo, Lauren; Maynard, M. Travis; Mathieu, John E.
theories: learning and knowledge acquisition models; social entrainment theory; task characteristic theories
keywords: complacency; entrained rhythms; shared team task-specific experience; social entrainment theory; surgical teams; task difficulty; task frequency; team effectiveness
research_question: The paper asks when shared team task-specific experience improves or harms team effectiveness in crew-based teams. It specifically examines whether task frequency and task difficulty shape whether entrained rhythms produce synchronization benefits or complacency detriments for surgical team efficiency and patient post-surgery recovery.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that prior shared experience with the same team members on the same type of task creates shared knowledge and entrained rhythms that can help crew members coordinate efficiently. For infrequent tasks, the paper argues that these synchronization benefits are less likely to be offset by complacency, producing a positive relationship between STTS experience and efficiency, especially on difficult tasks. For frequent tasks, deeply familiar procedure rhythms can reduce vigilance and system monitoring, so high STTS experience can become inefficient through complacency; task difficulty amplifies these negative consequences because difficult cases have less room for error.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends social entrainment theory by treating entrained rhythms as a dual-edged process that can generate both synchronization benefits and complacency detriments. It contributes to team effectiveness research by showing that shared experience is not uniformly beneficial and that task frequency and task difficulty are important boundary conditions in crew-based arrangements. It also integrates archival and interview evidence to connect shared team experience, task characteristics, efficiency, and patient recovery in a field setting rather than a laboratory context.
practical_implication: The findings imply that crew staffing decisions should consider both task frequency and task difficulty rather than simply maximizing repeated team membership. For infrequent and more difficult procedures, managers may benefit from building higher levels of shared team task-specific experience; for frequent procedures, especially difficult ones, managers should watch for complacency and use interventions such as briefing, teamwork training, and debriefing to maintain vigilance without destroying useful rhythms. In hospitals, the paper frames these staffing and intervention choices as consequential for operating-room efficiency, patient recovery, and cost.
limitations: The authors note that complacency is difficult to examine outside the laboratory because interviews and observations are vulnerable to evaluation apprehension and Hawthorne effects. The archival data cannot directly measure the strength or dynamics of entrained rhythms during each surgery, so the study infers those processes from records and interview evidence. The empirical setting is a single U.S. hospital and one type of crew-based team, which limits comparison across hospitals, procedure-volume profiles, and team structures.
future_research: The authors call for richer measures of entrained rhythms, including experience-sampling designs that track rhythm dynamics over time and distinguish why surgeries become faster or slower. They also recommend studying additional task characteristics, unanticipated events, attention, and situational cues that may shape complacency and synchronization. Further work should compare hospitals with different procedure volumes, examine other team structures such as intact teams, ad hoc teams, and multiteam systems, and assess individual differences, composition, strategic staffing, and caregiver well-being implications.
abstract: This study explores the conditions under which shared team task-specific (STTS) experiences in crew-based arrangements may negatively influence team effectiveness. We suggest that the entrained rhythms featured in social entrainment theory act as a dual-edged sword with the potential to generate complacency detriments in addition to the commonly cited synchronization benefits. We argue that the manifestation and influence of the countervailing forces (i.e., synchronization and complacency) on the STTS experience—team effectiveness relationship will depend on salient task characteristics (i.e., frequency and difficulty). More specifically, frequently performed tasks create conditions for complacency to manifest (generating an inverted-U shaped relationship between STTS experience—team efficiency), whereas infrequently performed tasks do not (generating a positive, linear relationship). We further this distinction by layering on task difficulty that, we posit, acts to amplify the respective negative and positive consequences. Analyses of archival data from 8,236 surgeries performed over one year at a large hospital located in the southwestern region of the United States were consistent with our hypotheses and 30 semi-structured interviews with operating room personnel added richness and precision to our theory. Ancillary analyses on patient post-surgery recovery rate yielded additional insights. Implications and future directions are discussed.

title: A Micro-institutional Inquiry into Resistance to Environmental Pressures
methods: Three quantitative experiments: a laboratory experiment manipulating weak versus strong organizational identification, a laboratory experiment manipulating utilitarian versus normative identity content, and an online MTurk experiment using a normative-pressure ISO 31000 task; analyses use ANOVA and PROCESS mediation models.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Participants acting as organizational decision-makers in laboratory or online flower-shop scenarios.
n_sample: Study 1 usable n=169; Study 2 usable n=173; Study 3 usable n=506.
authors: Schilke, O.
theories: institutional theory; organizational identity; social identity theory
keywords: environmental pressures; micro-institutional research; organizational identification; organizational identity; resistance to environmental pressures
research_question: The paper asks why organizational decision-makers facing the same environmental pressures vary in whether they resist those pressures or give in to them. More specifically, it asks whether organizational identification affects resistance, whether certainty and attention explain that effect, and whether normative versus utilitarian identity content changes resistance.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is cognitive and identity-based. Strong organizational identification increases resistance because it bolsters the decision-maker's certainty and reduces attention to environmental stimuli. Normative identity further strengthens resistance relative to utilitarian identity because it turns attention inward toward organizational ideals rather than outward toward competitive or institutional comparison.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by adding microfoundations to explanations of organizational responses to environmental pressures. It shows that organizational decision-makers' identification and identity content help explain within-field heterogeneity rather than treating organizations as passively conforming to macro-level pressures. It also integrates organizational identity research with institutional theory and demonstrates how experiments can be used to test micro-level institutional mechanisms.
practical_implication: The paper suggests, with explicit caution, that organizations may manage environmental conformity versus resistance partly through identity salience and identity content. When organizations seek to implement practices that challenge established field templates, leaders who strongly identify with the organization may be more willing to resist environmental pressure. The implication is not that resistance is always beneficial, but that identity processes can shape whether organizations automatically conform or maintain agency under pressure.
limitations: The paper largely brackets how organizational identity is constructed and instead focuses on its consequences for resistance. It also treats individual decision-makers as representatives of organizational actors, while acknowledging that organization-level outcomes may emerge through more complex aggregation, interaction, and interdependence. Finally, the experimental findings generalize through theory rather than direct one-to-one correspondence with large organizations in field settings.
future_research: Future research could examine how organizational identity develops and is negotiated in organizations, especially through qualitative, practitioner, field-replication, and mixed-method designs. Further work could study how social interaction and collective aggregation translate individual-level responses into organization-level action. The paper also calls for research on competing institutional logics, non-binary responses to institutional pressure, institutional work strategies such as challenging or manipulating institutions, and legitimacy judgments by external audiences.
abstract: This article contributes to the emerging stream of micro-institutional research, which zooms in on the internal organizational processes that are responsible for organizations’ differential responses to the external environment. Specifically, the investigation offers new knowledge of how organizational identity processes can shape whether decisionmakers will resist versus give in to environmental pressures. Building on the notion that organizational identity acts as a filter through which decision-makers relate to the external environment, I develop the theoretical argument that strong organizational identification increases resistance to environmental pressures due to two mechanisms: (1) it bolsters the decision-maker’s certainty and (2) it deflects the decision-maker’s attention from the environment. A series of laboratory experiments not only test the mediated relationship between organizational identification and resistance to environmental pressures but also contrast different types of organizational identity. The empirical results support the hypothesized positive link between organizational identification and resistance, which becomes particularly strong when the organizational identity is normative (vs. utilitarian). The findings reported here enrich institutional theory by adding microfoundations to organizational practice adoption decisions and shedding new light on relevant enabling conditions for agency and within-field heterogeneity.

title: Examining Follower Responses to Transformational Leadership from a Dynamic, Person–Environment Fit Perspective
methods: Two experience sampling method studies. Study 1 used end-of-workday surveys over 15 workdays and tested response-surface and mediation hypotheses with first-order autoregressive HLM, polynomial regression, confirmatory factor analysis, and block-variable mediation. Study 2 used three surveys per day over 15 consecutive workdays, broader transformational-leadership measures, OCB outcomes, daily predictors of transformational leadership needed, and the same HLM, polynomial, CFA, and mediation logic.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Study 1 used 15 online daily surveys at the end of each workday, Monday through Friday for three weeks. Study 2 used three daily surveys for 15 consecutive workdays. Calendar dates are not reported in paper.
units: Employees' daily observations of transformational leadership needed and received, affect, work attitudes, OCBs, and daily predictors of leadership need.
n_sample: Study 1 analyzed 65 individuals who provided 846 daily responses, with 747 daily observations after lagged controls. Study 2 analyzed 93 individuals who provided 913 day-level observations.
authors: Tepper, Bennett J.; Dimotakis, Nikolaos; Lambert, Lisa Schurer; Koopman, Joel; Matta, Fadel K.; Park, Hee Man; Goo, Wongun
theories: affective events theory; metafit; person–environment fit theory; transformational leadership theory
keywords: challenge stressors; meaningful work; organizational citizenship behaviors; person–environment fit; positive affect; transformational leadership needed; transformational leadership received; uncertainty; work attitudes
research_question: The paper asks how followers respond on a daily basis when the transformational leadership they receive fits, falls short of, or exceeds the transformational leadership they need. It also asks whether positive affect explains the within-person links from transformational leadership needed and received to daily work attitudes and organizational citizenship behaviors, and which daily conditions predict stronger need for transformational leadership.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines person–environment fit theory with affective events theory. Transformational leadership is treated as an environmental supply, while followers' daily need for such leadership varies with activated psychological needs and work conditions. Fit between needed and received transformational leadership should raise positive affect; deficiency and excess should reduce it. Positive affect then carries the daily fit experience into work attitudes and discretionary citizenship behavior, while challenge stressors, uncertainty, and meaningful work help explain when followers need more transformational leadership.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to transformational leadership theory by challenging the assumption that more transformational leadership is always better. It theorizes and tests transformational leadership as a dynamic, episodic phenomenon whose effects depend on day-level fit with follower needs. It also extends P–E fit theory by showing the value of modeling need fulfillment within persons over time rather than treating within-person variation as error.
practical_implication: The authors argue that transformational leadership training should help leaders diagnose followers' dynamic needs and calibrate the amount of transformational behavior they provide. Leaders should avoid both under-supplying and over-supplying transformational leadership, because excess can be less favorable than fit. They should also pay attention to the type of stressors followers face, because challenge stressors and uncertainty evoke need for transformational leadership whereas hindrance stressors may call for a more transactional response.
limitations: The authors note that their conceptualization relies on Bass' model of transformational leadership, despite criticisms of that model and unresolved questions about whether its between-person structure is isomorphic at the within-person level. They also did not examine fit for other forms of leadership needed and received, such as transactional leadership. Finally, the studies focused on a limited set of outcomes and did not test why some leaders are better than others at tailoring transformational behavior to follower needs.
future_research: The authors call for more focused tests of the Bass model at within- and between-person levels, and for dynamic P–E fit research that embeds transformational leadership within broader models of leadership needed and received. They encourage future ESM work on additional outcomes such as justice, stress, intrinsic motivation, creativity, trust, empowerment, and organizational commitment. They also recommend research on leader-side predictors of fit, including depletion, personality, trait empathy, and political skill.
abstract: We invoke the person–environment fit paradigm to examine on a daily basis follower affective, attitudinal, and behavioral responses to transformational leadership needed and received. Results from two experience sampling method (ESM) studies suggested that positive affect was higher on days when transformational leadership received fit follower needs (compared to days when the amount received was deficient or in excess of follower needs) and on days when absolute levels of fit was higher. We also found that positive affect mediated the within-person effects of transformational leadership needed and received on subordinates’ daily work attitudes (Studies 1 and 2) and organizational citizenship behaviors (Study 2). Supplemental analyses in Study 2 revealed that subordinates need more transformational leadership when they experience more challenge stressors, face greater uncertainty at work, and perform more meaningful work.
apa_citation: Tepper, B. J., Dimotakis, N., Lambert, L. S., Koopman, J., Matta, F. K., Park, H. M., & Goo, W. (2018). Examining follower responses to transformational leadership from a dynamic, person–environment fit perspective. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(4), 1343-1368. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0163
