title: The Differential Impact of Knowledge Depth and Knowledge Breadth on Creativity over Individual Careers
methods: Empirical quantitative longitudinal panel study of core creators in the Hollywood animation industry, using awards and nominations as creativity outcomes, genre-based measures of knowledge depth and breadth, career age as moderator, controls for creator, team, movie, studio, year, and role characteristics, and panel negative binomial regression estimated with GEE.
industry: Hollywood animation industry; feature-length animated movies released in United States movie theaters.
time_period: Animated movies produced and released from 1978 through 2013.
units: Core crew members, movie-creator dyad observations, feature-length animated movies, genres, awards, nominations, studios, roles, and years.
n_sample: 3,409 observations for 2,070 creators across 231 feature-length animated movies.
authors: Mannucci, P. V.; Yong, K.
theories: career age and creativity (Lehman, 1953; Simonton, 1997, 2000); cognitive entrenchment (Audia & Goncalo, 2007; Dane, 2010); knowledge structures and creative cognition (Amabile, 1983; Campbell, 1960; Dane, 2010; Mednick, 1962)
keywords: Hollywood animation industry; career age; creativity; knowledge breadth; knowledge depth; knowledge structures
research_question: The paper asks when knowledge depth and knowledge breadth are more or less conducive to individual creativity over the course of a career. It examines whether career age changes the creativity effects of depth and breadth because individual knowledge structures become increasingly rigid over time.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is temporal and cognitive. Early-career creators have relatively flexible but less complex knowledge structures, so depth helps them build richer domain schemas and generate creative outcomes. As career age increases, linkages within and between knowledge domains become more rigid; depth then becomes less beneficial and can intensify entrenchment, whereas breadth helps loosen knowledge structures by exposing creators to different domains.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reconciles mixed findings about knowledge depth, knowledge breadth, and creativity by showing that their effects depend on career age. It contributes to research on career age and creativity by specifying why different knowledge configurations are useful at different career stages. It also adds a temporal microfoundation to creativity theory by connecting changes in knowledge structures to variation in creative output over individual careers.
practical_implication: The findings imply that learning and development programs should vary by career stage. Newer employees may benefit more from deepening domain knowledge and learning the rules, norms, and procedures of their field. Later-career employees may need exposure to diverse domains and tasks that broaden their knowledge base and help refresh creative cognition.
limitations: The archival design does not directly observe the cognitive mechanisms by which career age changes knowledge structures, so alternative mechanisms such as skill-building dynamics, intrinsic motivation, or job stability cannot be fully ruled out. The setting is a creative, project-based industry, which may limit generalizability to tasks or industries where creativity is less central. Some robustness checks, including the analysis of job stability among permanent hires, had limited sample size.
future_research: The authors call for future research that directly studies intra-individual creative cognition and the joint role of knowledge and cognition in shaping creativity. They also suggest examining linkages between knowledge domains, not only within-domain schemas, and testing whether other creativity antecedents vary in effect across career stages. Further studies should examine the knowledge-depth, knowledge-breadth, and career-age relationship in settings beyond the animation industry.
abstract: While usually argued to be fostering creativity, the effect of knowledge depth and breadth on creativity is actually mixed. We take a dynamic approach to the knowledge–creativity relationship and argue that the effect of knowledge depth and knowledge breadth is likely to be contingent on career age. We propose that individuals’ knowledge structures become increasingly rigid as career age grows and that, because of this, knowledge depth and breadth have different effects on creativity at different points of the career. More specifically, we hypothesize that knowledge depth is more beneficial for creativity in earlier stages of one’s career, when creators need to increase the complexity of knowledge structures, while knowledge breadth is more beneficial in later stages, when flexibility is most needed. We test and find support for our hypotheses in a longitudinal study set in the context of the Hollywood animation industry, a setting characterized by the presence of a variety of creators involved in knowledge-intensive activities. Theoretical and practical implications of the results are discussed.
apa_citation: Mannucci, P. V., & Yong, K. (2018). The differential impact of knowledge depth and knowledge breadth on creativity over individual careers. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(5), 1741-1763. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0529

title: The Social Consequences of Voice: An Examination of Voice Type and Gender on Status and Subsequent Leader Emergence
methods: Two-study quantitative design: Study 1 uses a three-wave lagged field survey of USMA Sandhurst competition teams with regression, relative-importance, mediation, and moderated-mediation analyses; Study 2 uses a 2 x 2 between-subjects randomized vignette experiment with bootstrap mediation.
industry: Study 1: United States Military Academy Sandhurst competition teams; Study 2: adults across a variety of industries evaluating an insurance sales team scenario.
country: Study 1: United States; Study 2: Not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 surveys were administered three months before the competition, 10 days before the competition, and immediately following the competition; Study 2: Not reported in paper.
units: Study 1: individual USMA cadets nested in Sandhurst teams; Study 2: individual MTurk participants evaluating a hypothetical peer.
n_sample: Study 1: 174 of 324 eligible competing USMA cadets; Study 2: 196 adults.
authors: McClean, E. J.; Martin, S. R.; Emich, K. J.; Woodruff, T.
theories: expectation states theory
keywords: expectation states theory; gender; leader emergence; prohibitive voice; promotive voice; status; voice
research_question: The paper asks how peers respond to promotive versus prohibitive voice and whether these voice types shape peer-rated status and subsequent leader emergence. It further asks whether the social consequences of voice differ by speaker gender.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that voice can function as a status-claiming behavior, but peers grant status only when the behavior is seen as valuable and legitimate. Promotive voice is theorized to be more status-enhancing than prohibitive voice because it emphasizes future-oriented improvement and positive movement toward an ideal state, whereas prohibitive voice highlights problems and potential harm. Expectation states theory further implies that gender shapes legitimacy judgments, so men receive greater status and leader-emergence benefits from promotive voice than women do.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends voice research by shifting attention from managers' reactions to peers' social evaluations of speakers. It links voice, status, and leader emergence by showing that promotive voice can increase peer-granted status and leadership emergence, while also showing that these benefits depend on gender. It also contributes to expectation states theory by distinguishing between types of assertive behavior rather than treating speaking up as uniformly status-enhancing.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that employees may gain respect and influence by speaking up in ways that focus on ideas for moving the group toward an ideal state. It also warns that these benefits are not evenly distributed: women may speak up without receiving the same status and leadership credit as men. The authors recommend managerial practices such as documenting, recognizing, and amplifying women's voice to counter unequal status-conferral processes.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 took place in a male-dominated and distinctive military academy competition setting, even though Study 2 used a more gender-balanced context. They also note that Study 1 relied on self-ratings of voice and that the two studies used different measures of leader emergence. The paper did not directly examine the substantive content of specific voice episodes or the role of formal leaders in shaping the voice-status-emergence process.
future_research: The paper calls for research in settings with different gender compositions, including teams with mostly women, and for more objective measures of employee voice such as direct observation. It also calls for work on how the content of discrete voice events affects peer perceptions of respect and influence. Additional future research should examine other change-oriented behaviors, clarify leader-emergence measurement, and investigate how formal leaders affect whether voice accrues status.
abstract: This paper explores the impact of two types of voice and gender on peer-rated social status and subsequent leader emergence. Across two studies—a three-wave field study and an experiment—we find that speaking up promotively, but not prohibitively, is positively and indirectly related to leader emergence via status, and that this relationship is conditional on the gender of the speaker. Specifically, men who spoke up promotively benefited the most in terms of status and leader emergence, not only compared to men who spoke up prohibitively, but also compared to women who spoke up promotively. This research extends our understanding of the outcomes of voice by articulating how it impacts one’s place in his or her group’s social structure, and ultimately whether he or she is seen as a leader. We also add to our understanding of leader emergence by suggesting that talking a lot or participating at a high level in a group may not be enough to emerge as a leader—it also depends how you do it and who you are.
apa_citation: McClean, E. J., Martin, S. R., Emich, K. J., & Woodruff, T. (2018). The social consequences of voice: An examination of voice type and gender on status and subsequent leader emergence. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(5), 1869-1891. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0148

title: Playing Cat and Mouse: Contests over Regulatory Categorization of Dietary Supplements in the United States
methods: Inductive qualitative single-case study of the U.S. dietary supplement industry using extensive archival documents, interviews, congressional hearings, FDA oral histories, books, NVivo-supported coding, iterative theory-data comparison, and process theorizing.
industry: U.S. dietary supplement industry and the regulatory category contest involving supplement makers, the FDA, Congress, consumers, health stores, and incumbent food and pharmaceutical actors.
time_period: Historical context starts in the 1940s, with the main categorization process focused on 1973-1994; data sources also span 1968-2013 FDA oral histories, 1977-1994 trade journals, 1988-1994 newspapers, and 1972-2006 law journals.
units: Regulatory categories, category changes, supplement makers, regulators, legislators, consumers, value-chain actors, archival documents, interviews, hearings, and public claims.
n_sample: 375 specialized news-journal articles; 138 newspaper articles; 80 law-journal articles; 10 trade-journal executive interviews; 2 retrospective interviews; 35 relevant FDA oral-history transcripts from 238 reviewed; 6 congressional hearings; and 11 books.
authors: Ozcan, Pinar; Gurses, Kerem
theories: categorization theory; corporate political strategy; hard and soft power; institutional work
keywords: advocacy work; category audiences; category work; dietary supplements; hard power; institutional work; regulatory categorization; soft power
research_question: The paper asks how regulatory categories are determined through the strategies and interaction of firms, regulators, and other category audiences. Empirically, it examines how U.S. dietary supplement makers moved first from the drug category to the food category in 1976 and then into a newly created dietary supplement category in 1994.
mechanism_summary:
- Key actors / audiences: supplement makers, the FDA, Congress and other state actors, consumers, health stores, pharmaceutical companies, food corporations, public-interest groups, and category incumbents.
- Process / phases: movement between extant categories through the Proxmire Amendment of 1976, followed by creation of a new dietary supplement category through DSHEA in 1994.
- Firms' category work: dissociation from unfavorable categories and category evaluators, association with target categories, and selective representation through less controversial labels such as vitamins.
- Firms' advocacy work: lobbying legislators directly, hooking consumers through cultural meta-narratives, activating them through dramatization and urgency, and coordinating action through health stores and the value chain.
- Regulator work: FDA category work associated supplements with drug or food-additive categories, while maintenance work relied on educating, policing, deterrence, raids, product seizures, labeling restrictions, and scientific authority.
- Emergent outcome: firms used soft power over consumers to activate hard power from Congress, thereby overpowering FDA categorization decisions and changing the legal category governing the industry.

The process is a multi-actor political contest rather than a purely cognitive categorization process. Supplement makers first cognitively prepared audiences for category change by reframing what supplements were and who should evaluate them. They then mobilized consumers and legislators so that Congress could impose legal changes on the FDA. The regulator, by contrast, relied heavily on scientific expertise, education, and coercive enforcement, which made it vulnerable to firms' freedom-of-choice framing and public mobilization.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional work by showing how advocacy work can combine soft power and hard power to produce regulatory change, especially when less powerful firms mobilize other audiences that have leverage over state actors. It contributes to categorization research by defining category work as efforts to influence category attributes, boundaries, and membership, and by distinguishing movement between extant regulatory categories from new regulatory category creation. It also links institutional work and corporate political strategy by treating regulatory categorization as a multi-player contest among firms, regulators, legislators, consumers, value-chain actors, and incumbents.
practical_implication: For firms in regulated markets, the study implies that changing regulation may require more than direct lobbying: firms may need to cognitively prepare audiences for category change and mobilize actors who can influence legislators. For regulators, the case shows the limits of relying only on scientific authority, education, and enforcement when firms can frame regulation as a threat to public values. For entrants facing powerful regulators, the paper suggests that category incumbents' divisions and value-chain access to consumers can create openings for regulatory change.
limitations: The authors state that the study is set in a single industry, where the broader political and cultural climate may have contributed to the outcome. They also note that the alternative medicine movement in the 1970s and 1980s may have widened political support for the dietary supplement movement. A further boundary condition is that the setting involved individuals' health and well-being, making the public especially susceptible to heightened emotions.
future_research: The authors call for studies of regulatory categorization in other markets, such as energy or broadcasting, where the issues may have less dramatic implications for society at large. They also suggest examining newer settings such as peer-to-peer platforms and e-cigarettes to understand when firms can or cannot mobilize public support for favorable categorization. Future work should further investigate hard versus soft power tactics and how power is distributed among different category audiences across regulatory settings.
abstract: Regulatory categorization can be a matter of life and death to firms, as it sets legal limitations on the production and sales of their product. In this paper we set out to uncover this critical process, for which there is only anecdotal information in extant literature, by asking how regulatory categories are determined through the strategies and interaction of firms, regulators, and other category audiences. We use extensive archival data to examine how U.S. dietary supplement makers first moved from the drug to the food category in 1976, and, when faced with resistance from the Food and Drug Administration, created an entirely new category in 1994, which then fueled their explosive market growth. Our findings show that regulatory categorization is a contest between firms and the regulator, where firms try to disrupt unfavorable regulation by overpowering the regulator through hard power imposed by other state actors, which is achieved through pressure from another category audience—consumers—who are themselves won over through soft power.
apa_citation: Ozcan, P., & Gurses, K. (2018). Playing cat and mouse: Contests over regulatory categorization of dietary supplements in the United States. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(5), 1789-1820. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1221

title: The Short-lived Benefits of Abusive Supervisory Behavior for Actors: An Investigation of Recovery and Work Engagement
methods: Three-study quantitative design: two randomized experiments testing the effect of abusive supervisory behavior on recovery, followed by a multi-wave daily diary field study using HLM, RMediation, and moderated path analysis to test recovery, work engagement, empathic concern, and job demands.
industry: Study 1a used students in China; Study 1b used U.S. supervisors across manufacturing, service, and other industries; Study 2 used Chinese supervisors across manufacturing, service, education and public management, and other industries.
time_period: Study 2 collected data over four weeks, including twice-daily surveys across 10 consecutive workdays; the experiments were single-session studies.
units: Supervisors or supervisor-role participants and supervisor-day observations.
n_sample: Study 1a: 64 undergraduate and graduate students; Study 1b: 100 U.S. supervisors; Study 2: 72 supervisors and 565 complete daily observations.
authors: Qin, X.; Huang, M.; Johnson, R. E.; Hu, Q.; Ju, D.
theories: conservation of resources theory (Halbesleben et al., 2014; Hobfoll, 1989, 2001)
keywords: abusive supervision; abusive supervisory behavior; conservation of resources theory; empathic concern; job demands; recovery level; work engagement
research_question: The paper asks whether, why, and when engaging in abusive supervisory behavior has proximal benefits for supervisors themselves. It focuses on whether abusive supervisory behavior can improve supervisors' recovery level and work engagement, and whether empathic concern and job demands condition those effects.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is resource-based. The authors argue that abusive supervisory behavior can conserve supervisors' resources by releasing them from the effortful inhibition of aggressive impulses and can generate resources by increasing a sense of control. This resource recovery then supports same-day work engagement. The benefits are bounded: high empathic concern creates additional stress after abuse, low job demands make resource gains less salient, and cumulative abuse becomes detrimental over longer time windows.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends abusive supervision research by shifting the focal actor from subordinates as recipients to supervisors as perpetrators, showing that abusive behavior can have short-term benefits for actors even while remaining harmful overall. It contributes to conservation of resources theory by treating a "bad" behavior as a possible short-term resource-conservation and resource-generation event, while showing that the same behavior becomes resource-consuming over longer time periods. It also identifies empathic concern and job demands as personal and contextual boundary conditions on actor-centric abusive supervision effects.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that organizations should not treat abusive supervision only as irrational or purely destructive from the supervisor's perspective; short-term recovery and engagement benefits may reinforce the behavior. The authors point to less harmful recovery alternatives, including workday breaks, coworker communication, cultivating empathic concern, and reducing or managing supervisors' job demands. Interventions should target the resource pressures and perceived control deficits that make abusive behavior temporarily rewarding.
limitations: The authors note that Study 2 relies on supervisor self-reports of daily abusive behavior, recovery, and engagement, creating potential common method variance despite temporal separation, controls, and supporting experiments. The tested outcomes are limited mainly to recovery and engagement, and the moderators focus on empathic concern and job demands rather than other organizational or subordinate factors. The same-day design captures proximal effects, while longer-term consequences are explored through supplementary analyses rather than a dedicated long-horizon longitudinal design.
future_research: The authors call for research on broader actor-based outcomes of abusive supervision, including negative affect, burnout, productivity, promotion potential, and social sanctions from subordinates. They suggest examining additional moderators such as organizational context and subordinate status, and testing whether supervisors are affected differently depending on whom they abuse. They also recommend longitudinal studies with different time frames and further investigation of cultural contingencies in the consequences of abusive supervisory behavior for actors.
abstract: Although empirical evidence has accumulated showing that abusive supervision has devastating effects on subordinates’ work attitudes and outcomes, knowledge about how such behavior impacts supervisors who exhibit it is limited. Drawing upon conservation of resources theory, we develop and test a model that specifies how and when engaging in abusive supervisory behavior has immediate benefits for supervisors. Via two experiments and a multi-wave diary study across 10 consecutive workdays, we found that engaging in abusive supervisory behavior was associated with improved recovery level. Moreover, abusive supervisory behavior had a positive indirect effect on work engagement through recovery level. Interestingly, supplemental analyses suggested that these beneficial effects were short-lived because, over longer periods of time (i.e., one week and beyond), abusive supervisory behavior was negatively related to supervisors’ recovery level and engagement. The strength of these short-lived beneficial effects was also bound by personal and contextual factors. Empathic concern––a personal factor––and job demands––a contextual factor––moderated the observed effects. Specifically, supervisors with high empathic concern or low job demands experienced fewer benefits after engaging in abusive supervisory behavior. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of these findings, and propose future research directions.
apa_citation: Qin, X., Huang, M., Johnson, R. E., Hu, Q., & Ju, D. (2018). The short-lived benefits of abusive supervisory behavior for actors: An investigation of recovery and work engagement. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(5), 1951-1975. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1325

title: Short Seller Influence on Firm Growth: A Threat Rigidity Perspective
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of S&P 1500 firms from 2000 to 2014, using firm fixed-effects OLS regressions as the primary tests, fixed-effects Poisson checks, instrumental-variable regressions, a Regulation SHO natural experiment, supplementary analyses, and dynamic GMM robustness checks.
industry: Cross-industry publicly traded firms listed in the Standard & Poor's 1500 Index; no single industry restriction is reported.
country: North American publicly traded firms; exact country distribution is not separately reported.
units: Firm-years and firm growth-action announcements.
n_sample: Primary Table 3 models report 23,509 observations; the growth-action data include 126,273 growth actions.
authors: Shi, Wei; Connelly, Brian L.; Cirik, Kubilay
theories: threat rigidity theory
keywords: board centrality; financial slack; firm growth; growth actions; news sentiment; short interest; short sellers; threat rigidity theory
research_question: The paper asks how high levels of short interest influence firm growth decisions. Specifically, it examines whether short sellers, treated as an indirect external threat, lead managers to undertake fewer growth actions and to use a less diverse mix of growth modes.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is threat rigidity. The authors argue that short sellers threaten managers by publicly betting against and denigrating the firm, even though they do not directly control it. Under high short interest, managers restrict information processing and narrow their span of control, which makes risky and cognitively demanding growth actions less attractive. Absorptive capacity, board centrality, financial slack, and positive media sentiment are expected to dampen this response because they improve information processing, control, resources, or external support.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends threat rigidity theory by applying it to an indirect threat: short sellers who cannot directly impose organizational harm but can unsettle managers through capital-market pressure and public criticism. It also contributes to investor-influence research by studying short sellers as a hostile investor type rather than as monitors or activists seeking firm improvement. Finally, it adds to managerial risk-taking research by showing that capital-market signals about a firm's prospects can shape growth decisions.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that managers should recognize how short-seller pressure may bias them toward defensive, internally focused decisions. Awareness of threat-rigidity tendencies may help managers develop more reasoned responses to short sellers rather than automatically reducing growth activity. The findings also matter for policy makers because short selling may have organizational consequences beyond market-price effects.
limitations: The authors state that they do not directly measure the psychological mechanism of threat rigidity and instead infer it through moderator analyses. They also examine managerial actions rather than managers' public statements or counter-campaigns. In addition, the sample focuses on S&P 1500 companies, so the effects may differ for smaller and younger firms.
future_research: Future research could directly measure the psychological and cognitive processes triggered by short-interest pressure, for example through survey instruments. It could also study how managers publicly respond to short sellers and whether those responses affect strategic decision-making. The authors further suggest expanding samples to smaller and younger firms and parsing competitive actions and competitor countermoves in more detail.
abstract: Whereas most investors seek to maximize their investment, there are some who profit from downward stock price movement. Engaging in such behavior is called “short selling,” and it has increased considerably among publicly traded North American firms in recent years. This study builds on threat rigidity theory to develop arguments about the behavioral consequences of short sellers. We theorize that, when firms have a high level of short interest, managers adopt a defensive stance by halting new growth initiatives and limiting the range of growth modes in which they participate. We also suggest that managers’ ability to process information and exercise control moderate these main effects. Specifically, we argue that managers will be less reactionary when firms have high absorptive capacity, possess high board centrality, maintain sufficient financial slack, and are well regarded by the media. Results largely support our theory, as we show that short sellers can have a profoundly deleterious effect on firm growth prospects.
apa_citation: Shi, W., Connelly, B. L., & Cirik, K. (2018). Short seller influence on firm growth: A threat rigidity perspective. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(5), 1892-1919. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.1010

title: Fish out of Water: Translation, Legitimation, and New Venture Creation
methods: Qualitative, in-depth single-case study of H-Farm using semi-structured interviews, archival data, field notes, historical case analysis, open coding, constant comparison, axial coding, and grounded theory model building.
industry: Digital, web, and new media entrepreneurship; specifically an Italian business incubator/accelerator and its venture-capital and entrepreneurship ecosystem.
country: Italy, with the focal venture located in Veneto and category-level comparisons to Silicon Valley, the United States, and European accelerator networks.
time_period: H-Farm's development from 2005 to 2017.
units: H-Farm as the focal organization, plus founders, partners, managers, startuppers, local stakeholders, investors, accelerators, archival items, and field observations.
n_sample: 53 semi-structured interviews, 1,316 archival items, and six field-note observations.
authors: Tracey, Paul; Dalpiaz, Elena; Phillips, Nelson
theories: institutional theory; optimal distinctiveness; organizational legitimacy; translation
keywords: category authentication work; dual optimal distinctiveness work; institutional theory; legitimacy pressures; local authentication work; misaligned translation; new venture creation
research_question: The paper asks how entrepreneurs create and legitimate a new venture by translating an existing organizational form from a different and misaligned institutional context. Empirically, it examines how H-Farm translated the business incubator/accelerator form from Silicon Valley and other U.S. technology regions into Veneto, Italy.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / pressures: local-level legitimacy, category-level legitimacy, optimal distinctiveness, misaligned translation, and target-form evolution.
- Process / phases: improvising, converging, and optimizing.
- Entrepreneurial work: local-level authentication work, category-level authentication work, and dual optimal distinctiveness work.
- Triggering conditions: perceived shifts in the target organizational form and reflection on the limits of H-Farm's current model.
- Emergent outcomes: a model of entrepreneurship through misaligned translation in which legitimacy pressures vary over time rather than being resolved at a single threshold.
- Boundary conditions: stakeholder diversity and the rapid evolution of the organizational form may shape whether the process is generative or creates muddled meaning.

The process begins with improvising, where entrepreneurs loosely emulate a poorly aligned target form and work to make the venture locally understandable. It then shifts to converging, where entrepreneurs seek category-level acceptance from stakeholders associated with the target form while continuing local authentication. In the optimizing phase, growing local and international competition makes the venture pursue dual optimal distinctiveness: what once authenticated the venture locally helps it stand out at the category level, while category-level authentication helps distinguish it locally.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional entrepreneurship research by identifying the distinct legitimacy pressures faced by ventures created through misaligned translation: local-level legitimacy, category-level legitimacy, and later a dual optimal-distinctiveness challenge. It also theorizes legitimation as gradated and temporal rather than as crossing a single legitimacy threshold. Finally, it extends translation theory by showing that entrepreneurial translation involves a moving target being transposed by a moving object, making translation iterative, dynamic, and ongoing rather than a one-off act of faithful emulation.
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs translating an organizational form into a misaligned context should not treat faithful imitation as sufficient. The H-Farm case suggests that they need to build local resonance first, then seek category-level acceptance when growth requires resources outside the local context, and later manage similarity and differentiation at both levels. The paper also cautions that if dual optimal distinctiveness work backfires, entrepreneurs may create muddled meaning for local and category-level stakeholders.
limitations: The authors note that their case involved local and category-level stakeholders who were mainly entrepreneurs and investors, and that these pressures were sufficiently homogeneous for H-Farm to harness them productively. They caution that translating forms with more diverse stakeholders, such as social enterprises moving between the global north and global south, may create more incompatible legitimacy pressures. They also indicate that the dynamics of dual optimal distinctiveness may differ when the target organizational form is more static and has crisper boundaries.
future_research: Future research could examine whether the differences between local-level and category-level legitimacy pressures remain or erode as a translated organizational form matures. It could also study misaligned translation in settings with more diverse stakeholder expectations, where local and category-level pressures may become competing tensions. The conclusion further invites work that builds on, extends, and refines the model for other digital ventures and other forms of new venture creation through misaligned translation.
abstract: We draw on institutional theory to study a common type of new venture creation that has been neglected in the literature: the translation of an existing organizational form from a different—and misaligned—institutional context. To do so, we conducted an indepth case study of H-Farm, an Italian venture that was founded as a business incubator, a type of organization that first emerged in Silicon Valley and other U.S. technology regions. Our study illuminates the specific configuration of legitimacy pressures inherent in this type of entrepreneurship, and theorizes the strategies that entrepreneurs can enact to address them: local authentication work, category authentication work, and dual optimal distinctiveness work. We also show that the legitimacy pressures experienced by entrepreneurs may vary significantly as ventures mature, and challenge the notion of a specific “legitimacy threshold” that new ventures are required to reach. Finally, our model conceptualizes translation as an iterative, dynamic, and ongoing accomplishment rather than a “one off” activity with clear beginning and end points.
apa_citation: Tracey, P., Dalpiaz, E., & Phillips, N. (2018). Fish out of water: Translation, legitimation, and new venture creation. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(5), 1627-1666. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0264

title: Ideological Misfit? Political Affiliation and Employee Departure in the Private-equity Industry
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study dominated by archival quantitative analysis: the authors track U.S. private-equity investment professionals from 1999 to 2008, measure political ideology from Federal Election Commission contributions, estimate polynomial random-effects discrete-time logistic regression models of departure, and supplement the analysis with semistructured interviews, destination-firm analysis, simulation, and Glassdoor robustness checks.
industry: U.S. private equity industry.
units: Investment professionals, private equity firms, individual-year observations, and supplemental interview informants.
n_sample: Over 40,000 investment professionals; primary archival data include 40,733 individuals, 4,641 private equity firms, 143,455 individual-year observations, and 25 interview informants.
authors: Bermiss, Y. S.; McDonald, R.
theories: attraction–selection–attrition (ASA); person–organization (PO) fit theory; political psychology; self-categorization theory
keywords: employee departure; ideological misfit; person–organization fit; political ideology; polynomial regression; private equity
research_question: The paper asks how ideological misfit between an employee's political ideology and the prevailing political ideology of the employing organization affects departure. It also asks whether the departure effect differs for conservative misfit versus liberal misfit.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is that political ideology functions as a person–organization fit dimension. When employees' political ideology diverges from the organization's prevailing ideology, the paper theorizes that they experience discomfort, hostile climate, detachment, and weaker identification, making departure more likely. The evidence is asymmetric: conservative misfits are more likely to depart, whereas liberal misfits are less likely to depart in some conditions, which the authors interpret through conservative sensitivity to misfit and through possible misfit strategies such as missionary action or discreet dissent.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to employee mobility research by theorizing departure as a sociocultural process shaped by political ideology rather than only as an economic or vacancy-driven process. It extends person–organization fit theory by introducing political ideology as a fit dimension and showing that misfit effects need not be symmetrical or uniformly detrimental. It also broadens research on political ideology in organizations beyond senior executives by studying rank-and-file professionals.
practical_implication: The paper implies that managers should treat political ideology as a potentially consequential but difficult-to-observe dimension of fit. It cautions against assuming that ideological homogeneity is always desirable, because some ideological misfits may become sources of productive dissent or learning if the organization provides enough security for minority viewpoints. Managers in small, human-capital-intensive firms should pay attention to whether political discourse creates silence, alienation, or avoidable departures.
limitations: The authors note that political contributions are an imperfect measure of political ideology and that the archival data cannot fully distinguish voluntary from involuntary departure. They also acknowledge that the study does not account for all turnover antecedents, including compensation, leadership, group cohesion, stress, and other demographic predictors. The empirical context is U.S. private equity, so the pattern may not generalize to other industries or to other salient ideologies.
future_research: The authors call for future research integrating ideology with other antecedents of turnover, including job dissatisfaction, job search, and quit intentions. They also suggest studying whether misfit works similarly for other salient workplace ideologies, such as religious or philosophical ideologies. Further work could test the causal mechanisms behind the conservative-versus-liberal asymmetry and examine whether the findings replicate in other industry contexts.
abstract: Though organizations are increasingly active participants in the political realm, little research has investigated how an organization’s heightened focus on political ideology impacts employees. We address this gap by exploring how an individual’s political ideological misfit with an organization’s prevailing ideology impacts departure. By tracking the movements of over 40,000 investment professionals in the U.S. private equity industry over 10 years, we investigate the consequences of the ideological misfit that arises when individuals’ political ideologies diverge substantially from the prevailing ideology of their firms. We hypothesize that ideological misfit increases the likelihood of departure, though the effects vary with liberal or conservative ideological orientation. Polynomial regression analyses reveal that the fit relationship between individual and organizational political ideology deviates from the idealized congruence relationship that underlies prevailing theory. Specifically, we find that departure is more likely for employees experiencing conservative misfit (a personal ideology more conservative than the firm’s) versus liberal misfit (a personal ideology more liberal than the firm’s). Conservatives are more likely to depart than liberals regardless of fit, and departing misfits tend to join new organizations that are closer to their own ideology.
apa_citation: Bermiss, Y. S., & McDonald, R. (2018). Ideological misfit? Political affiliation and employee departure in the private-equity industry. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2182-2209. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0817

title: Becoming Who We Serve: A Model of Multi-Layered Employee–Customer Identification
methods: Inductive qualitative study using grounded-theory analysis of semi-structured interviews, member-check interviews, and company documents in a focal police-officer credit union, with a comparison postal-worker credit union.
industry: Credit unions providing financial services to defined occupational customer groups.
country: United States; the focal and comparison credit unions were located in the same large U.S. city.
time_period: Calendar dates for interview data collection are not reported in paper; COP-CU interview data were collected in three rounds, POST-CU data in two rounds, and COP-CU documents covered five years of quarterly newsletters.
units: Employees and customers at COP-CU, plus employees at POST-CU.
n_sample: 41 COP-CU employees, five COP-CU customers for member checks, and 12 POST-CU employees.
authors: Cardador, M. T.; Pratt, M. G.
theories: identity theory; relational identification; relational job design; self-expansion; social identity theory
keywords: employee identification with customers; employee–customer identification; meaningful work; multilayered employee–customer identification; organizational identification; self-expansion; service effectiveness
research_question: The paper asks what the nature of employee–customer identification is, what role organizations may have in cultivating such bonds, and what perceived implications employee–customer identification has for employees and the employing organization. It specifically examines an alternative to the assumption that ECID is anchored in customers becoming "like us" through shared organizational values.
mechanism_summary:
- Organizational practices: Bridging practices helped COP-CU employees understand, appreciate, and become involved with police-officer customers; valuing practices clarified and reinforced why serving police officers mattered.
- Identity process: These practices supported collective-level and role-level self-expansion, producing multilayered employee–customer identification.
- Collective-level expressions: Employees came to see themselves and police officers as part of the same family and as part of the police social collective.
- Role-level expressions: Employees came to see their work as familial emotional support and as sharing elements of policing, especially protecting and serving.
- Perceived implications: Occupational self-expansion contributed to work meaningfulness, familial self-expansion contributed to perceived service effectiveness, and these were linked to organizational identification, growth, and profitability.
- Comparison case: POST-CU showed little evidence of bridging and valuing practices, self-expansion, meaningful work, or distinctive service effectiveness, weakening alternative explanations based only on credit-union form, small size, defined membership, service mission, or personal ties to the customer occupation.

The process is not presented as a statistical causal test; the authors use an inductive comparative design to build a model. COP-CU's bridging practices blurred boundaries between bankers and police officers, while valuing practices promoted social agency by motivating employees to form strong reciprocal connections with police officers. Those connections enabled employees to become more like the customers they served rather than only seeing customers as sharing organizational values. The resulting M-LECID operated through multiple identity layers and was associated with perceived task significance, organizational instrumentality, and identification-based trust.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to workplace identification research by challenging the assumption that employee identification is necessarily anchored in the organization. It shows that employee–customer identification can involve employees taking on customer-linked identity content, so part of "who we are" as organizational employees becomes anchored in customers. It also extends identification and self-expansion theory by showing that identification can be multilayered, with collective and role-level self-expansion occurring in the same employee–customer relationship.
practical_implication: Organizations that rely on repeated service relationships may foster productive ECID by creating bridging practices that help employees understand and interact with the service group, and valuing practices that make the mission of serving that group clear and rewarded. The paper also warns that closeness to customers may create risks: employees may become too customer-anchored, organizational flexibility may be constrained, and practices that encourage closeness may frustrate employees or customers if the organization does not enable or reward the connection.
limitations: The study is inductive, so it supports analytical and naturalistic generalizability rather than population-level statistical generalizability. The comparison design does not directly replicate two credit unions serving the same customer population, so police-officer customer characteristics may still have influenced the identity dynamics observed at COP-CU. The authors also note that they did not collect longitudinal data, leaving the temporal ordering between organizational practices, self-expansion, and identification open to further testing.
future_research: Future research should test multilayered employee–customer identification in other service contexts, including organizations with different customer groups, more heterogeneous customer bases, or other stakeholder targets. Studies could examine when customer categorization and organizational practices foster self-expansion, whether multilayered identifications differ from unidimensional identifications in resilience or behavioral consequences, and how employees respond when the customer group becomes threatened or morally contested. Longitudinal designs could also examine how bridging and valuing practices contribute to self-expansion and M-LECID over time.
abstract: Though employee identification with customers has received little explicit attention in organizational scholarship, and has only recently emerged as an area of focus in marketing, research suggests that customers should play a central role in the identity dynamics of employees. What makes employee–customer identification different from other forms of identification (e.g., employee–organization and customer–organization identification) is that although the organization may be the conduit for identification to occur, it may not be the focus of identification. Indeed, in the organization we explore here, organizational practices lead employees to identify with customers, but to do so in such a way that employees become—at least in part—more like “who they served” than vice versa. Moreover, the bonds we find between employees and customers are multilayered, incorporating nonwork identities, as well as identities at different levels of inclusiveness (e.g., collective and role). This paper explores and models the development and consequences of multilayered employee–customer identification, argues for its theoretical and practical implications, and suggests avenues for future research.
apa_citation: Cardador, M. T., & Pratt, M. G. (2018). Becoming who we serve: A model of multi-layered employee–customer identification. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2053-2080. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1201

title: How Can Leaders Overcome the Blurry Vision Bias? Identifying an Antidote to the Paradox of Vision Communication
methods: Empirical quantitative article using three experiments. Study 1 was a Brexit-day experiment with British government officials; Study 2 was a preregistered high-powered online experiment with full-time employees; Study 3 was a preregistered experiment with senior corporate executives and coworker ratings. The paper uses between-subjects experimental conditions, a within-subjects control in Study 3, Coh-Metrix and human-coded imagery measures, ANCOVA, OLS regression, PROCESS moderated-mediation tests with truncated regression checks, tobit robustness checks, and linear mixed models.
industry: Study 1: British government/public-sector roles. Study 2: participants crafted visions for financial services or health services. Study 3: senior executives at major firms; exact industries not reported in paper.
country: Study 1: United Kingdom. Study 2: participants came from various countries. Study 3: country not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 launched on June 24, 2016. Study 3 recruited participants over a five-month period. Study 2 data-collection dates not reported in paper.
units: Leaders, full-time employees, senior corporate executives, coworker raters, crafted vision statements, image-based rhetoric scores, mental imagery, cognitive style, and employee inspiration ratings.
n_sample: Three experiments: Study 1 n = 166 government officials; Study 2 final n = 652 full-time employees; Study 3 n = 123 senior corporate executives, with coworker inspiration ratings for n = 100.
authors: Carton, A. M.; Lucas, B. J.
theories: cognitive style as analytical versus efficient thinking (Epstein et al., 1996); dual cognitive processing (Allen, Kaut, & Lord, 2008; Epstein, Pacini, Denes-Raj, & Heier, 1996); mental time travel and temporal projection (Suddendorf, Addis, & Corballis, 2009); vision communication and leadership theory (Bass, 1990; Nanus, 1992; Stam et al., 2014)
keywords: blurry vision bias; cognitive style; dual cognitive processing; image-based rhetoric; mental imagery; mental time travel; temporal projection; vision communication
research_question: The paper asks why leaders continue to communicate abstract, hard-to-visualize visions even though image-based rhetoric is more inspiring, and whether temporal projection can help them overcome this "blurry vision bias." It also asks when this intervention works best, focusing on whether efficient versus analytical cognitive style changes the effect of mental imagery on image-laden vision communication.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in dual cognitive processing. A direct focus on word selection keeps leaders in the meaning-based system, where they process abstract concepts and therefore continue to craft abstract visions. Temporal projection instead asks leaders to imagine a future scenario as if they were observing it firsthand; this activates the experience-based system, creates mental imagery, and makes image-based rhetoric the natural language for communicating what they have imagined. The effect is stronger for efficient thinkers because they are less likely than analytical thinkers to override imagery with abstract semantic processing.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to leadership and vision communication theory by explaining the descriptive-prescriptive gap in which leaders are advised to choose better words but still produce blurry, abstract visions. It integrates leadership, linguistics, and dual cognitive processing to specify why temporal projection improves vision rhetoric, how mental imagery mediates the effect, and when cognitive style constrains it. It also redirects theory from wordsmithing toward the cognitive system leaders activate before choosing words.
practical_implication: The paper implies that leaders should not rely only on advice to use vivid words. A more useful intervention is to mentally project themselves to a future moment when the organization's vision has been realized, imagine what people would see and experience, and then translate that scene into words. The findings also imply that analytically oriented leaders may need additional support or pairing with more intuitive visionary communicators when crafting inspiring visions.
limitations: The authors caution that the moderated mediation evidence should be interpreted carefully because the mediator and moderator were nonnormally distributed and the conditional indirect effects were driven partly by a very strong independent-variable-to-mediator relationship. They also note that the word "company" in the mental time travel manipulation may have been less appropriate for some Brexit-study participants who worked in agencies. A further limitation is that some Brexit-study participants did not occupy high-ranking roles, even though Studies 2 and 3 included leaders with larger spans of control and senior executives.
future_research: The authors suggest examining whether temporal projection generalizes to team leaders, including evidence from a supplementary MBA-team experiment. They also call for research on delivery, cadence, follower characteristics, and whether leaders can sustain high-quality vision communication after temporal projection. Future work could also study how leaders refine visions after converting mental imagery into words.
abstract: Evidence suggests that organizational leaders can inspire employees by communicating a vision of the future with image-based rhetoric—words and phrases that are readily envisioned in the mind's eye (e.g., "our vision is to make moviegoers laugh"). Yet research has demonstrated that most leaders do not craft visions with image-based rhetoric, instead favoring abstract language that cannot easily be visualized. We integrate theory on leadership and dual cognitive processing to argue that this problem is exacerbated when leaders focus on word selection when crafting visions because they overemphasize the meaning-based cognitive system (in which they consider the abstract meaning of words) and underemphasize the experience-based cognitive system (in which they can generate vivid mental images of what the future could look like). We introduce a novel tactic to help leaders activate the experience-based system and, in turn, generate and communicate more impactful visions. We also investigate boundary conditions. We test our predictions with three experiments featuring three distinct samples, including one with senior corporate executives and one in which members of the British government crafted visions on the day Britain announced it would exit the European Union ("Brexit").
apa_citation: Carton, A. M., & Lucas, B. J. (2018). How can leaders overcome the blurry vision bias? Identifying an antidote to the paradox of vision communication. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2106-2129. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0375

title: Managing Technological Transitions by Building Bridges
methods: Longitudinal quantitative study using firm, product, and patent data on photography incumbents; models estimate digital inventive performance with conditional fixed effects Poisson quasi-maximum likelihood and Huber-White robust standard errors.
industry: Research-active photography firms transitioning from analog to digital technologies.
time_period: The broader focal-firm patent observation period runs from 1974 through 2010; regression analysis stops at 2004 to allow forward citations to accumulate.
units: Photography firms, firm-year patent portfolios, individual inventors, digital and analog photography patents, APS cameras, and digital cameras.
n_sample: 293 firm-year observations for 14 firms; final patent sample included 84,861 patents and 32,585 individual inventors.
authors: Cohen, S. L.; Tripsas, M.
theories: absorptive capacity (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990); knowledge recombination (Fleming, 2001; Kogut & Zander, 1992); real options logic (McGrath, 1997); theories of inertia
keywords: hybrid product bridges; intergenerational knowledge bridges; inventive performance; inventor bridges; radical technological transitions; technology bridges
research_question: Which factors explain variation in incumbents' inventive performance as they transition from an old technological generation to a new one? The paper asks whether and how firms' use of intergenerational knowledge bridges between analog and digital photography affects digital inventive performance, and whether old-technology inventive performance changes the value of those bridges.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls: percent analog patents, digital exploration, number of digital patents, firm size, digital camera models, new digital inventors, firm fixed effects, and year fixed effects.

The paper theorizes intergenerational knowledge bridges as recombination across old and new technological generations. Inventor bridges can carry old capabilities, routines, and cognitive frames into the new domain, lowering inventive performance on average. Technology and hybrid product bridges can also reinforce old knowledge, but when a firm has strong analog inventive performance, old-technology knowledge becomes a usable foundation for learning digital technology rather than only an inertial constraint.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends research on technological transitions by shifting attention from incumbent-versus-entrant comparisons to heterogeneity among incumbents' inventive performance in the new technology. It qualifies inertia-based accounts by showing that old-technology knowledge can be harmful on average but useful when paired with strong old-technology R&D capability. It also links absorptive capacity, recombination, and real options reasoning to explain why technology and hybrid product bridges can function as temporary stepping-stones during transitions.
practical_implication: The findings imply that firms should not assume all old-technology knowledge is either obsolete or valuable during a transition. Redeploying old-technology inventors into new-technology work may hurt inventive performance, while technology bridges and hybrid products are more likely to help firms with strong existing R&D capability. Managers designing transition units should therefore consider both staffing choices and whether the organization has the capability to identify and leverage relevant old knowledge.
limitations: The authors note that patent data do not directly measure inventors' beliefs or behaviors. The study is also limited to one technological domain, digital photography, in which the new technology ultimately overcame the old. The results should be interpreted as correlational rather than necessarily causal.
future_research: The authors call for research in settings with multiple competing new technologies or where the new technology does not fully displace the old. They also call for work on when bridges are useful, when firms should stop bridging and disengage from old technology, how firms redeploy old expertise into new markets, and how organization design for new-technology development affects inventive performance.
abstract: While much research has demonstrated that radical technological transitions challenge incumbents, surprisingly little empirical work has examined which factors drive variation in their ability to invent in the new domain. Through a longitudinal study of photography firms transitioning from analog to digital technologies, we examine a key source of heterogeneity: whether and how incumbents integrate knowledge related to both old and new technologies to bridge generations. Specifically, we explore how the use of three types of intergenerational knowledge bridges—(1) inventor bridges, (2) technology bridges, and (3) hybrid product bridges—influences inventive performance in the new generation. Consistent with theories of inertia, we find that, on average, inventor and technology bridges are associated with lower performance in the new generation. However, the strength of a firm’s inventive performance in the old generation positively moderates this effect. When performance in the old technology is strong, both technology and hybrid product bridges are associated with higher inventive performance in the new generation. This finding suggests that, when combined with a strong R&D program, old-technology knowledge forms a foundation that incumbents can leverage to learn new technologies as they navigate transitions.

title: Social Valuation Across Multiple Audiences: The Interplay of Ability and Identity Judgments
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study dominated by quantitative panel analysis: Poisson GMM models with continuous endogenous covariates, selection correction, coarsened exact matching, robustness checks, and 10 semi-structured interviews with grant reviewers for interpretation.
industry: Academic science and research funding at Minerva, a pseudonymous large U.K. research university, including grant applications, awarded grants, and industry contracts.
units: Academic scientists, scientist-year observations, grant applications, awarded grants, and industry contracts.
n_sample: 9,502 academics; 34,647 scientist-year observations; 28,579 grant applications; 7,427 awarded grants; 1,817 industry contracts; 10 grant-reviewer interviews.
authors: Fini, Riccardo; Jourdan, Julien; Perkmann, Markus
theories: identity conformity; institutional logics; social valuation; socially endogenous inferences
keywords: academic scientists; endogenous indices; exogenous indices; industry evaluation; multiple audiences; peer evaluation; social valuation
research_question: How is the peer evaluation of a candidate influenced by earlier evaluations made by external, nonpeer audiences? The paper studies this question in academic science, where scientists seek grants from peer evaluators while also receiving industry contracts from an external audience.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a countervailing valuation process. External audience evaluations provide peer evaluators with positive information about a candidate's unobservable ability, so moderate industry evaluation can improve peer valuation. At higher levels, the same industry evaluation can signal deviation from the expected peer identity of an academic scientist, producing an inverted U-shaped relationship. This curvilinear effect is weaker where the academic discipline is closer to industry and where strong or regular publication records provide endogenous evidence of academic quality and identity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to social valuation research by separating endogenous indices from exogenous indices and showing why prior positive evaluations do not always reinforce later valuation. It argues that evaluations by external audiences carry both ability information and identity information, making social approval from another audience potentially valuable up to a point and damaging beyond it. It also connects audience-based valuation to institutional logics by showing how peer audiences judge candidates partly through identity expectations embedded in their own valuation framework.
practical_implication: For universities, the findings imply that faculty engagement with external audiences can help scientists obtain peer-valued resources, but excessive industry recognition may create an identity penalty, especially for junior researchers or those without strong publication records. University managers may reduce this penalty by strengthening alternative endogenous indices that reassure peer audiences about academic quality and identity. More broadly, organizations entering new audience domains should manage the trade-off between external audience appreciation and standing with their core audience.
limitations: The authors note that the study is situated in public science, raising questions about generalizability to settings where peer and external audiences use more orthogonal valuation criteria. They also state that their empirical approach relies on panel and matched-sample analyses rather than private reviewer scores or randomized assignment, because such scores and experimental designs are unavailable in their setting. External audience evaluations may also reflect unobserved reputation and status attributes beyond the measured industry contracts.
future_research: Future research could examine how intangible attributes such as reputation and status shape the relationship between external audience valuation and peer audience valuation. The paper also suggests studying settings where peer and external audiences differ more dramatically, including cases in which external audience appreciation may cease to function as an ability signal. Additional work could test the framework in organizations and markets where candidates are simultaneously evaluated by consumers, business customers, shareholders, clients, regulators, or other audiences.
abstract: How is an evaluating audience influenced by previous evaluations made by another audience? This question is critical to individuals and organizations reaching out to multiple audiences for key resources. While extant work has suggested evaluators are influenced by previous evaluations made by their peers, we develop theory about how evaluators' assessment of a candidate is shaped by previous evaluations made by an external (nonpeer) audience. We argue that the latter represent exogenous indices that affect evaluators in two opposing ways: they positively influence peer valuation by pointing to candidates' unobservable abilities, yet, since they are conferred by an external audience, they are also indicative of candidates' deviation from an expected peer identity. The combination of the two opposite effects suggests an inverted U-shaped relationship between exogenous indices and peer valuation. Further, this effect is moderated by the identity proximity between audiences, and the availability of previous peer evaluations (endogenous indices). We test and find support for our arguments using unique data on the peer valuation of 9,502 academic scientists applying for research grants at a research university. Our work contributes to the understanding of valuation and socially endogenous inferences, and has implications for the management of organizations in multi-audience environments.
apa_citation: Fini, R., Jourdan, J., & Perkmann, M. (2018). Social valuation across multiple audiences: The interplay of ability and identity judgments. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2230-2264. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0661

title: Different Strokes for Different Teams: The Contingent Effects of Positive and Negative Feedback on the Creativity of Informationally Homogeneous and Diverse Teams
methods: Empirical quantitative laboratory experiment with a 2 x 2 between-group design manipulating informational diversity (homogeneous vs. diverse) and feedback valence (positive vs. negative). The study used ANOVAs, planned contrasts, video-coded measures of information elaboration and generative processing, and Hayes moderated mediation analysis with bootstrapped confidence intervals.
industry: Laboratory creativity task about a theater action plan; participants were university students.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Three-person teams; team plans, video-coded team processes, and participant surveys.
n_sample: 78 three-person teams were analyzed for team creativity; analyses involving video-coded measures used 77 teams.
authors: Hoever, Inga J.; Zhou, Jing; van Knippenberg, Daan
theories: information elaboration and generative processing routes to team creativity; team-information-processing perspective on team creativity; teams-as-information-processors lens (Hinsz et al., 1997)
keywords: feedback valence; generative processing; information elaboration; informational diversity; team creativity; teams-as-information-processors
research_question: How do positive and negative feedback affect team creativity, and when does each form of feedback work better for informationally homogeneous versus informationally diverse teams? The paper specifically asks whether feedback valence interacts with informational diversity to promote team creativity through two team information-processing routes: information elaboration and generative processing.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a fit between feedback valence and the team's informational foundation. Negative feedback prompts systematic effort, attention to novel external information, and review of unused informational resources; this benefits informationally diverse teams because members hold different information and perspectives that can be elaborated and integrated. Positive feedback encourages flexible use of existing information and divergent insights; this benefits informationally homogeneous teams because shared knowledge makes members' ideas more likely to trigger one another's generative processing. The experiment supports the interaction on creativity and shows conditional indirect effects through elaboration and generative processing.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to team creativity theory by integrating two previously separate information-processing routes: information elaboration from the team performance and decision-making tradition, and generative processing from the brainstorming tradition. It shows that both routes can enhance team creativity, but they depend on different combinations of feedback valence and informational diversity.

It also shifts feedback-valence theory from an individual-level main-effect account to a team-specific contingency account. Rather than assuming positive feedback is generally better for creativity, the study identifies informational diversity as a team-level moderator with no direct individual-level counterpart.
practical_implication:
Managers should match feedback valence to the informational composition of the team when the goal is creativity. Negative feedback can help informationally diverse teams by pushing members to search, discuss, and integrate their distinct informational resources, while positive feedback can help informationally homogeneous teams by encouraging flexible and mutually stimulating use of shared knowledge.

When managers must give feedback that does not fit the team's informational diversity, the paper suggests compensating through process support. Diverse teams receiving positive feedback may need prompts to share and integrate unshared information, while homogeneous teams receiving negative feedback may need novel information or support for generative processing.
limitations:
The study is a laboratory experiment with student teams, so the authors caution that follow-up work is needed to test generalizability to field settings. The feedback was randomly assigned and bogus rather than based on teams' actual creativity, although the authors argue this supports internal validity and may make the effects conservative if credibility was doubted.

The feedback occurred during an ongoing task, so its effects may differ from feedback on completed tasks or repeated feedback across future work. The teams were low in authority differentiation and temporal stability, and the informational-diversity manipulation may not capture demographic diversity or diversity that triggers social categorization.
future_research:
Future studies could test the model in field settings, with actual performance-based feedback, repeated feedback, and teams that vary in authority differentiation, skill differentiation, and temporal stability. Research could also examine whether external informational resources, such as leaders, knowledge-management systems, or boundary spanning, can substitute for the internal informational resources of diverse teams.

The paper also points to future work on how elaboration and generative processing interact over time, especially whether elaboration can trigger generative processing in diverse teams. Additional research should examine how team affective and motivational states interact dynamically with team information processing, and whether the feedback-diversity fit extends to other team tasks beyond creativity.
abstract: Feedback is a ubiquitous management tool. Employing it to enhance team creativity raises an important question of whether positive or negative feedback is more effective. Unfortunately, prior research on feedback valence and creativity is limited to the individual level, neglecting team creativity’s interdependent and knowledge-intensive nature. We address this issue and advance the team-information-processing perspective on team creativity by integrating two heretofore separate research streams to develop a team-specific model about how negative and positive feedback enhance creativity via two alternative information processing routes, contingent on teams’ informational diversity. Negative feedback fuels teams’ systematic effort and attention to external, novel information. In informationally diverse teams, in which members hold different information and perspectives, these efforts promote team creativity through information elaboration. Conversely, positive feedback propels members to flexibly use their information and contribute the resultant divergent insights to the team. In informationally homogeneous teams, wherein these insights relate to others’ information and perspectives, these divergent insights trigger teams’ generative processing and in turn creativity. Results from a team experiment support the predicted feedback valence by informational diversity interaction on team creativity through elaboration and generative processing.

Different strokes for different teams: The contingent effects of positive and negative feedback on the creativity of informationally homogeneous and diverse teams. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2159-2181. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0642
