title: Entrepreneurial Imaginativeness in New Venture Ideation
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a quasi-experimental design. Participants from a Qualtrics online panel generated new venture ideas from a common facial-recognition technology scenario, selected their best idea, and completed measures of creative, social, and practical imaginativeness, motivation, knowledge, experience, and controls. Two expert raters scored idea quantity and idea quality; the authors used hierarchical linear regression, Baron and Kenny mediation tests, a Sobel test, and relative weight analysis.
industry: General working population across 20 industry classifications; specific industries are not reported in paper.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals from the general working population, new venture ideas, selected best ideas, and expert-rated idea quality.
n_sample: 506 completed responses.
authors: Kier, A. S.; McMullen, J. S.
theories: creative problem-solving; entrepreneurial action; imagination and mental simulation
keywords: creative imaginativeness; creative problem-solving; entrepreneurial imaginativeness; idea quality; idea quantity; new venture ideation; practical imaginativeness; social imaginativeness
research_question: The paper asks whether entrepreneurial imaginativeness can be conceptualized and measured as distinct creative, social, and practical cognitive skills, and whether those skills explain new venture idea quantity and quality. It also asks whether idea quantity mediates the relationship between imaginativeness and idea quality.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that imaginativeness combines the cognitive ability of imagination with task-relevant entrepreneurial knowledge. Creative imaginativeness helps individuals form novel means-ends connections, social imaginativeness helps them understand others' needs and perspectives, and practical imaginativeness helps them identify problems and evaluate feasible solutions. The study finds that all three forms predict idea quantity, that idea quantity fully mediates the creative imaginativeness-idea quality link, and that idea quantity partially mediates the practical imaginativeness-idea quality link.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to entrepreneurship theory by moving imagination from an assumed latent ability to a measurable set of entrepreneurial imaginativeness skills. It extends creative problem-solving theory by showing that creative, social, and practical imaginativeness explain new venture ideation beyond motivation, knowledge, and experience. It also suggests that opportunity recognition, effectuation, bricolage, narrative/storytelling, and analogical reasoning may depend on unevenly distributed forms of imaginativeness rather than on a uniform imaginative capacity.
practical_implication: The paper implies that venture teams should not assume that all founders possess the same form of imagination. New venture ideation may benefit from diagnosing or developing creative, social, and practical imaginativeness separately, or from composing teams whose members compensate for one another's imaginative strengths and weaknesses. It also implies that tools such as effectuation, bricolage, design thinking, and lean startup may work differently depending on the imaginativeness of the individuals using them.
limitations: The authors note that the study uses a mechanistic, post-positivistic approach that measures imaginativeness as a cognitive skill rather than examining imagination more directly through alternative philosophical worldviews. They also state that the study uses a cross-sectional design, which may be limited because entrepreneurship unfolds over time. The common facial-recognition scenario improves comparability but leaves open whether the findings generalize across phases of entrepreneurship, teams, existing organizations, and other venture contexts.
future_research: The authors call for research on how entrepreneurial imaginativeness affects other models of entrepreneurial action, including effectuation, bricolage, design thinking, lean startup, improvisation, and analogical or metaphorical reasoning. They suggest work across levels of analysis, especially how individual imaginativeness combines into team-level entrepreneurial imaginativeness. They also recommend longitudinal and interpretive research on the antecedents, development, unconscious, embodied, and sensory aspects of imagination.
abstract: Although theories of entrepreneurial action regularly acknowledge the importance of imagination, the ability is rarely defined or measured, and thus effectively treated as uniform in degree and type. Using a creative problem-solving lens, we identify and measure three different cognitive skills—creative, social, and practical imaginativeness—that vary across individuals. Each skill combines the ability of imagination with the knowledge needed to mentally simulate various task-related scenarios used in generating and selecting ideas for new value creation. We then conduct a quasi-experiment to examine each skill’s relative effect on new venture ideation. We find that the three imaginativeness skills vary across individuals and that they predict new venture idea quantity and quality differently over and above the effects of motivation, knowledge, and experience. We conclude with implications for theory development in entrepreneurship and creative problem-solving.
apa_citation: Kier, A. S., & McMullen, J. S. (2018). Entrepreneurial imaginativeness in new venture ideation. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2265-2295. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2017.0395

title: From Protest to Product: Strategic Frame Brokerage in a Commercial Social Movement Organization
methods: Inductive longitudinal qualitative case study of Addiopizzo Travel, using interviews, naturalistic observation, archival data, frame analysis, open coding, abductive analysis, and grounded-theory-style process-model development.
industry: Responsible tourism industry and Sicilian anti-racket movement.
country: Italy; the empirical setting is Sicily, especially Palermo.
time_period: 2009 to September 2016.
units: Addiopizzo Travel, AT entrepreneurs, responsible tourism actors, tourists, tourism service providers, anti-racket activists, anti-racket movement documents, AT documents, media coverage, tourist reports, and observed events.
n_sample: 73 semi-structured interviews, 41 days of naturalistic observation, 224 AT documents, 443 anti-racket movement documents, 15 prior scholarly accounts, and 42 tourist reports.
authors: Lee, M.; Ramus, T.; Vaccaro, A.
theories: interactional framing; social enterprise and hybrid organizations; social movement framing; strategic framing
keywords: commercial social movement organizations; dual mobilization; frame development; mobilizing technology; social enterprise; strategic frame brokerage; strategic framing
research_question: The paper asks how a social movement organization entering an existing industry can frame its commercial activities so that they mobilize industry actors while retaining support from the social movement whose goals it shares. Empirically, it examines how Addiopizzo Travel reconciled anti-racket movement frames with responsible tourism industry frames while asking how to meet market demands without betraying the anti-racket movement.
mechanism_summary:
- Initial frame transposition: AT transposed anti-racket movement frames of community, security, dignity, and denunciation into commercial tourism offerings.
- Validation with multiple audiences: AT tested whether these frames resonated with tourists and tourism service providers and whether they remained consistent with anti-racket movement ideology.
- Search through interaction: When some frames failed to resonate, AT interacted with tourists, tourism service providers, and activists to surface alternative interpretations of its activities.
- Strategic lamination and transformation: AT transformed security into sustainability and dignity into beauty by layering newly keyed industry and activist interpretations onto original movement frames.
- Retention and selective referral: AT retained community because it resonated with both audiences, while denunciation was selectively referred to other parts of the anti-racket movement rather than used to frame AT's commercial activities directly.
- Operationalization: Validated frames guided new tours, partnerships, booking services, and referrals that mobilized commercial actors without severing ideological ties to the movement.

The process is strategic frame brokerage: leaders of a commercial social movement organization broker between movement activists and commercial actors by repeatedly validating, revising, retaining, transforming, or selectively referring movement frames. The mechanism is not a statistical causal model; it is an inductive process model showing how interaction supplies distributed interpretations that leaders incorporate into frames capable of dual mobilization. The core tension is that frames strong enough to preserve movement ideology may be confusing or threatening to market actors, while market-resonant frames may be judged by activists as mission drift.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on frame development by integrating strategic framing and interactional framing. It shows that social movement leaders do not only impose frames top-down or wait for frames to emerge bottom-up; they can strategically elicit, broker, and laminate interpretations from multiple supporter groups. It also contributes to social enterprise and hybrid organization research by showing how mission drift concerns can be managed through framing, and to social movement research by theorizing commercialization as a mobilizing technology that can attract supporters who are not already ideological adherents.
practical_implication: For commercial social movement organizations and social enterprises, the paper implies that market entry requires active frame work with both commercial audiences and movement constituencies. Managers should validate whether frames are narratively credible to customers and partners while also checking whether activists see them as ideologically consistent. When a movement frame is too central to transform, selective referral may preserve the movement connection without forcing the commercial activity to carry a frame that undermines market resonance.
limitations: The authors identify as a boundary condition the existence of established interpretive frames in both the social movement and the commercial industry. In settings with nascent market categories or less established movements, a social movement organization may shape the category or the movement rather than merely broker between existing frames. They also note that some movements may not be amenable to commercial transactions, that frame brokerage may not always find common ground, and that the process is costly in time and attention.
future_research: The paper calls for research on strategic frame brokerage in nascent market categories, newer social movements, and contexts where common ground between activists and industry actors is harder to find. It also suggests studying the limits of multivalent frames, delaminating processes through which frame meanings decay or become more specific, and the skills needed to transition from collective action to commerce. Future work could also examine how commercial social movement organizations coordinate with other movement organizations and whether commercial participation complements or substitutes for traditional activism.
abstract: Social movement organizations that engage directly in commercial activities face the particular challenge of mobilizing movement activists and commercial actors simultaneously. In a seven-year case study of a Sicilian anti-racket social movement organization that uses commercial activities to combat Mafia racketeering, we show how strategic framing enables such dual mobilization. Our findings show that original antiracket social movement frames were modified through a process of strategic frame brokerage that incorporated, through interaction, the distributed interpretations of tourists, tourism service providers, and anti-racket activists. As a result of this process, original social movement frames were retained, transformed, or managed through selective referral. We discuss the implications of our findings for research on processes of frame development, social enterprise, and commercialization as a “mobilizing technology” for social movements.
apa_citation: Lee, M., Ramus, T., & Vaccaro, A. (2018). From protest to product: Strategic frame brokerage in a commercial social movement organization. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2130-2158. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0223

title: A Network View of Advice-giving and Individual Creativity in Teams: A Brokerage-driven, Socially Perpetuated Phenomenon
methods: Empirical mixed-methods article. Study 1 uses a three-wave field survey of R&D teams in Chinese manufacturing firms, network betweenness centrality for advice brokerage, leader ratings of individual creativity, latent change score modeling, Mplus regression models, moderated path analysis, and robustness checks. Study 2 uses face-to-face interviews with nominated advice-giving brokers and recipients, followed by inductive thematic analysis and independent quote classification.
industry: Study 1: research and development teams from manufacturing firms whose products served manufacturing, transportation, hydropower, metallurgy, chemicals, and aerospace. Study 2: manufacturing firms whose products served manufacturing, electric power, and chemicals.
time_period: Study 1 used three survey waves: Time 1, Time 2 approximately six months later, and Time 3 six months after Time 2; exact calendar dates are Not reported in paper. Study 2 interview dates are Not reported in paper.
units: Individual team members, advice givers, advice recipients, team leaders, advice-giving ties, creativity ratings, psychological safety perceptions, and interview themes.
n_sample: Study 1 Time 1 survey included 278 employees from 43 teams, with 247 usable responses from 40 teams; Time 2 produced 233 creativity ratings; Time 3 produced 207 ratings from 38 team leaders. Study 2 interviewed 92 employees in 21 teams, including 51 advice recipients and 41 advice givers.
authors: Li, Y.; Li, N.; Guo, J.; Li, J.; Harris, T. B.
theories: componential model of creativity (Amabile, 1983); network brokerage theory (Burt, 2004; Freeman, 1979); psychological safety theory (Edmondson, 1999); social view of creativity (Perry-Smith & Shalley, 2003)
keywords: advice brokerage; advice-giving; brokerage; individual creativity; latent change score modeling; psychological safety; social networks; teams; thematic analysis
research_question: The paper asks when advice-giving in teams improves creativity for advice recipients and advice givers, rather than simply consuming the giver's time or reinforcing existing ideas. It focuses on whether a giver's brokerage position in the team's advice-giving network makes advice more creatively useful, whether recipients' creativity gains socially perpetuate gains for givers, and whether recipients' psychological safety strengthens these effects.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that brokers give advice from positions that connect otherwise unconnected teammates, so their advice is more likely to carry nonredundant knowledge, perspectives, and integrative ideas. Recipients who feel psychologically safe are more willing to use this brokered advice in creative problem solving, increasing their own creativity. Those recipient gains then feed back into the team context and the giver's subsequent creativity. The qualitative study extends the model by showing additional processes: idea integration, perspective taking, knowledge accumulation, reflection, collective creativity, and creative feedback.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to social views of creativity by showing that advice-giving is not uniformly helpful; its creative value depends on the giver's brokerage position in the team advice network. It extends brokerage theory into within-team networks by showing that brokers can act as catalysts for others' creativity rather than hoarding information for private advantage. It also connects network structure with psychological safety and dynamic creativity change, showing that creativity in teams can be socially perpetuated across givers and recipients over time.
practical_implication: The paper implies that managers should encourage employees to provide novel and helpful advice across relatively separate camps or subgroups within teams. It also implies that managers can strengthen creativity by creating psychologically safe environments, publicly supporting creative behavior, discouraging ridicule of failed attempts, and making members' areas of expertise more visible so that cross-subgroup advice exchange becomes easier.
limitations: The authors state that Study 1 could not capture the specific underlying processes linking brokered advice to creativity, which motivated the qualitative follow-up. They also note that the indirect effect through recipients' creativity was relatively small and that other mediators, such as creative feedback and knowledge reflection, may explain why giving advice enhances givers' creativity. Additional limitations are that Study 2 focused only on brokers rather than comparing brokers and nonbrokers, several qualitative processes overlapped, psychological safety had a counterintuitive negative correlation with recipient creativity, and both studies were conducted in China despite some theory being developed in Western contexts.
future_research: The authors call for research on other mediators of the advice brokerage-creativity relationship, especially creative feedback and knowledge reflection. They also encourage broker versus nonbroker comparisons, replication and extension of the qualitative themes, and work on when psychological safety becomes an asset or liability for creativity. Because the empirical setting was China, they further call for validation in other cultures.
abstract: One potential benefit of team contexts is that members can share knowledge and ideas to help one another solve problems (e.g., advice-giving), thereby enhancing members’ creative potential. However, individuals’ advice-giving actions do not guarantee increases in recipients’ creativity and, in some cases, may even be a creative liability for the giver’s own subsequent creativity. We argue that considering advice givers’ brokerage in the team’s advice-giving network (i.e., advice brokerage) may clarify this phenomenon. Specifically, we posit that advice given from a brokerage position contains more nonredundant content that boosts recipients’ creativity. Further, we expect advice brokerage to positively influence a giver’s own creativity, though this effect is at least partially explained via recipients’ proximal creativity gains (e.g., recipients’ creativity change mediates the relationship). Recipients’ perceptions of psychological safety accentuate these relationships. Longitudinal field data support the main hypotheses, but also suggest that advice brokerage has more immediate proximal effects on givers’ creativity; an additional qualitative study elucidates several mechanisms by which brokered advice boosts creativity, including two associated with generating diverse ideas (idea integration, perspective-taking), two associated with domain-specific knowledge accumulation (knowledge accumulation, reflection), collective creativity, and creative feedback. The study yields several important implications.
apa_citation: Li, Y., Li, N., Guo, J., Li, J., & Harris, T. B. (2018). A network view of advice-giving and individual creativity in teams: A brokerage-driven, socially perpetuated phenomenon. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2210-2229. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0212

title: No Employee an Island: Workplace Loneliness and Job Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative field study using a multirater, multilevel, time-lagged design. Employees self-reported workplace loneliness, controls, and emotional culture at Time 1; six weeks later supervisors rated job performance, employees reported affective commitment, and coworkers rated approachability. The authors used mixed-effects models, hierarchical linear modeling, multilevel structural equation modeling, and bootstrapping to test mediation, moderation, and moderated mediation.
industry: Two organizations: a public municipality and a private service and manufacturing outsourcer.
time_period: Time 1 and Time 2 were six weeks apart; exact calendar dates: Not reported in paper.
units: Employees nested in work groups, their coworkers, and supervisors.
n_sample: 672 employees across 143 work groups and 114 supervisors.
authors: Ozcelik, H.; Barsade, S. G.
theories: affect theory of social exchange (Lawler, 2001, 2006; Lawler & Thye, 2007); regulatory loop model of loneliness (Cacioppo & Hawkley, 2009)
keywords: affect theory of social exchange; affective commitment; affiliation; approachability; emotional culture; job performance; regulatory loop model of loneliness; workplace loneliness
research_question: The paper asks how workplace loneliness relates to employee job performance and why that relationship occurs through affiliation at work. It also asks whether the affective affiliative context of the work group, including emotional cultures of companionate love and anger and coworker loneliness, moderates loneliness' effects on affiliative outcomes.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is that workplace loneliness weakens affiliation. Drawing on the regulatory loop model of loneliness, the paper argues that lonelier employees become more socially vigilant, defensive, and withdrawn, which makes them appear less approachable to coworkers. Drawing on affect theory of social exchange, it argues that negative social exchanges are attributed beyond immediate coworkers to the organization, reducing affective commitment. Lower approachability and lower affective commitment then relate to poorer supervisor-rated job performance, with the broader affective affiliative context shaping some of the loneliness-affiliation links.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends loneliness research into the workplace by showing that loneliness is not only an individual psychological state but also a relational workplace phenomenon associated with job performance. It contributes to organizational affect research by examining a discrete affective experience rather than generalized positive or negative affect. It also integrates the regulatory loop model of loneliness with affect theory of social exchange to explain both the psychological withdrawal of lonely employees and the interpersonal/contextual dynamics through which coworkers and organizations become implicated.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers should treat workplace loneliness as an organizational problem rather than merely as a private employee issue. Organizations can reduce the performance costs of loneliness by providing timely support, improving opportunities for social connection, and addressing maladaptive social cognitions rather than only bringing lonely employees together. The authors also caution that interventions require sustained effort because loneliness itself can inhibit employees' motivation and skill in reaching out.
limitations: The authors state that the time-lagged design and theory suggest the modeled direction, but the study cannot confirm causality. They note that poorer performance could isolate employees and increase loneliness, and that reciprocal cycles may operate. They also identify limitations from using managerial performance ratings rather than objective performance measures and from studying workplace loneliness only within the United States.
future_research: The authors call for research on how organizations and employees can alleviate workplace loneliness, how often and how quickly workplace loneliness changes, and which antecedents prevent loneliness from arising. They also suggest examining cognitive attributions, other moderators of approachability, objective performance outcomes such as sales volume or output, and cross-cultural variation in workplace loneliness.
abstract: This research investigates the link between workplace loneliness and job performance. Integrating the regulatory loop model of loneliness and the affect theory of social exchange, we develop a model of workplace loneliness. We focus on the central role of affiliation in explaining the loneliness–performance relationship, predicting that despite lonelier employees’ desire to connect with others, being lonelier is associated with lower job performance because of a lack of affiliation at work. Through a time-lagged field study of 672 employees and their 114 supervisors in two organizations, we find support that greater workplace loneliness is related to lower job performance; the mediators of this relationship are lonelier employees’ lower approachability and lesser affective commitment to their organizations. We also examine the moderating roles of the emotional cultures of companionate love and anger, as well as of the loneliness of other coworkers in the work group. Features of this affective affiliative context moderate some of the relationships between loneliness and the mediating variables; we also find support for the full moderated mediation model. This study highlights the importance of recognizing the pernicious power of workplace loneliness over both lonelier employees and their organizations. We offer implications for future research and practice.
apa_citation: Ozcelik, H., & Barsade, S. G. (2018). No employee an island: Workplace loneliness and job performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2343-2366. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1066

title: Not Too Tired to be Proactive: Daily Empowering Leadership Spurs Next-morning Employee Proactivity as Moderated by Nightly Sleep Quality
methods: Empirical quantitative time-lagged experience sampling study using twice-daily online surveys over a two-week period. The authors tested a moderated mediation model with multilevel structural equation modeling in Mplus 8, modeling days nested within employees and separating empowering leadership, proactive goals, sleep quality, and proactive behaviors across daily time points.
industry: Employed university alumni working across a wide range of industries including banking, healthcare, education, and technology.
time_period: Two-week survey period; exact calendar dates not reported.
units: Employee-day observations from employed university alumni.
n_sample: 98 employees and 609 data points in the final analytic sample.
authors: Schilpzand, Pauline; Houston, Lawrence; Cho, Jeewon
theories: Model of Proactive Motivation; self-regulatory resource perspective
keywords: employee proactivity; empowering leadership; experience sampling methodology; proactive goal setting; risk-taking behavior; sleep quality; voice behavior
research_question: How do daily empowering leadership behaviors shape employees' next-morning proactive goal setting and next-day proactive goal-striving behaviors? The paper asks whether nightly sleep quality qualifies employees' ability to convert daily empowerment opportunities into proactive goals, risk-taking, and voice behavior.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a daily carryover process. Empowering leadership creates accountability, ambiguity, and autonomy, which motivate employees to set proactive goals the next morning. Those proactive goals then guide goal-striving behaviors during the workday, expressed as informed risk-taking to improve one's own work and voice behavior to improve work situations. The self-regulatory resource argument is that high-quality sleep restores the resources employees need to set and enact those proactive goals, whereas poor sleep weakens both the goal-setting response to empowerment and the translation of goals into risk-taking and voice.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to workplace proactivity theory by showing that proactivity is not only a stable individual difference but also a within-person, goal-driven process that fluctuates across days. It extends Parker et al.'s Model of Proactive Motivation by integrating a self-regulatory resource perspective and identifying sleep quality as a daily resource condition that strengthens or weakens proactive goal setting and goal striving.

The paper also contributes to empowering leadership research by treating empowering leadership as a daily behavior rather than only as a stable leadership style. This dynamic view explains why the same employee may respond differently to empowerment opportunities across days depending on nightly recovery.
practical_implication:
Managers can promote daily risk-taking and voice by sharing power and creating daily empowerment opportunities, but those opportunities are more likely to translate into proactivity when employees are well rested. The authors suggest assigning well-rested employees to novel and challenging work requiring initiative, while assigning employees with poorer sleep to more routine tasks that are less vulnerable to sleep-related cognitive deficits.

The paper also implies that organizations should treat sleep quality as relevant to proactive performance rather than as a purely private issue. The authors suggest that allowing naps may help employees capitalize on empowerment opportunities.
limitations:
All study variables were self-reported by participants, so common method concerns remain despite temporal separation of morning and afternoon surveys, interaction tests, and structural equation modeling. The study also measured sleep subjectively rather than with objective sleep measures such as actigraphy.

The authors note that the study did not examine possible negative consequences of employee proactivity, such as proactive goals being viewed as self-serving or ineffective by others. They also did not include a lengthy list of daily or stable control variables, including chronic sleep deprivation.
future_research:
Future research could use nonself-report measures, such as supervisor ratings of daily risk-taking and voice, and objective sleep measures such as actigraphy. It could also study the possible costs of proactivity to provide a more balanced account of employee proactive behavior at work.

The paper encourages future studies to incorporate theoretically relevant controls such as chronic sleep deprivation. It also points to nutrition as another resource-restorative influence that could be integrated into models of proactive and overall employee performance.
abstract: Building on the Model of Proactive Motivation, we hypothesize that a leader’s daily empowering leadership behaviors function as a motivator for employees to display a greater amount of proactive goal-striving behavior, by means of enhanced daily proactive goal setting. Expanding the Model of Proactive Motivation, we incorporate the largely neglected self-regulatory resource perspective and hypothesize that employee sleep quality operates as a qualifying influence on employees’ ability to set and strive for proactive goals that allow employees to take advantage of empowerment opportunities. Using a time-lagged experience sampling methodology, our hypotheses were tested in a sample of 98 professionals who completed twice-daily surveys over a two-week period. Study results confirm our hypotheses that experiencing daily empowering leadership enhances employees’ next morning proactive behaviors of risk-taking and voice behavior due to more proactive goal setting at the start of the workday. Finally, employee next-day goal-setting and goal-striving behavior is especially enhanced for those employees who experienced higher levels of sleep quality. Theoretical and practical implications derived from our research are discussed.
apa_citation: Schilpzand, P., Houston, L., & Cho, J. (2018). Not too tired to be proactive: Daily empowering leadership spurs next-morning employee proactivity as moderated by nightly sleep quality. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2367-2387. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0936

title: From the Editors—Seeing Practice Impact in New Ways
methods: Editorial essay that reframes management research practice impact through three pathways: trailing, leading, and concurrent impact.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Simsek, Zeki; Bansal, Pratima (Tima); Shaw, Jason D.; Heugens, Pursey; Smith, Wendy K.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: collective body of knowledge; concurrent; leading; practice impact; research pathways; research-practice gap; trailing
research_question: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial problem: The essay asks whether management research influences how practitioners think, talk, or perform their work, but argues that the field has framed practice impact too narrowly around ex post evaluations of individual studies.
- Trailing pathway: Research affects practice after a study is completed, often through translated findings, articles, slide decks, teaching cases, books, meta-analyses, and cumulative bodies of knowledge.
- Leading pathway: Practice affects research before and during design, as practitioners help researchers formulate questions, identify data sources, understand context, and shape meaningful representations of findings.
- Concurrent pathway: Researchers and practitioners jointly create impact during the research process through engaged scholarship, relational scholarship, action research, participant observation, and other reciprocal forms of inquiry.
- Reframed unit of impact: The editors argue that research streams, collective knowledge, teaching, and co-creative research processes are better frames for practice impact than a single article's immediate managerial implications.

The process logic is editorial and programmatic rather than causal. Simsek, Bansal, Shaw, Heugens, and Smith argue that practice impact emerges through multiple pathways over time: research can trail practice through cumulative evidence, lead research through practitioner involvement in question and design formation, or occur concurrently when researchers and practitioners jointly produce knowledge. The editorial's core move is to replace a narrow, article-level impact frame with a broader portfolio view of complementary academic and experiential knowledge systems.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes a three-pathway framework for thinking about management research practice impact: trailing, leading, and concurrent. Its main conceptual contribution is to shift the level of reasoning from individual studies and immediate practical implications to research streams, collective bodies of knowledge, researcher-practitioner dialogue, teaching, and co-created inquiry processes. It also argues that academic and practitioner knowledge systems should be treated as complementary and mutually dependent rather than as substitutes.
practical_implication: For authors and editors, the essay implies that practice impact should be evaluated through a portfolio of research activities rather than only through direct implications attached to a single article. It encourages researchers to consider when practitioner engagement should shape research questions, design, data collection, interpretation, and dissemination. It also highlights management education as a major route through which research-informed frameworks, cases, and evidence can influence future managerial practice.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editors call for studies of different impact pathways that can strengthen the field's impact balance sheet. They suggest that different concepts, tools, and techniques are needed to probe and understand that balance sheet, and that the trailing, leading, and concurrent pathways provide one framework for systematic development.
abstract: Not reported in paper

title: When Equity Seems Unfair: The Role of Justice Enforceability in Temporary Team Coordination
methods: Inductive comparative field study of temporary teams in four hospital emergency departments, using observations, semi-structured interviews, archival materials, and electronic medical record staffing data; qualitative analysis used within-site memos, line-by-line open coding, and focused coding around assignment processes.
industry: Hospital emergency departments using pod-based temporary doctor-nurse teams.
time_period: Fieldwork over a two-year period; electronic medical record staffing data covering one year at each ED.
units: Temporary teams of doctors and nurses in four EDs: Alpine, Belleview, Carter, and Dyer.
n_sample: 30 interviews at Alpine, 43 at Belleview, 45 at Carter, and 54 at Dyer; one year of electronic medical record case data at each site.
authors: Valentine, M.
theories: organizational justice; role-based coordination; temporary group coordination
keywords: extra-role behaviors; justice enforceability; organizational justice; team coordination; temporary teams; work distribution
research_question: The paper asks under what conditions members of temporary groups engage in the extra-role behaviors that are core to effective group coordination. It examines why temporary teams with similar pod structures in emergency departments varied in whether they developed tightly coupled coordination.
mechanism_summary:
- Key context: Temporary ED teams had shared role structures and tightly interdependent patient-care work, but team membership was fluid and short-lived.
- Assignment processes: Alpine and Belleview used exactly equal round-robin patient assignment, while Carter and Dyer used Charge Nurse judgments of pod capacity.
- Justice enforceability: Equal assignment made cheating difficult and supported perceptions that fair work distribution was enforceable; equitable assignment was more flexible but gameable.
- Team response: High justice enforceability fostered solidarity, updating, monitoring, helping, and synchrony; low justice enforceability fostered self-protection, individual focus, limited helping, and weak team coordination.

The process centers on whether temporary team members believe authorities can enforce fair work distribution when others may cheat. When fairness is enforceable, members see themselves as "in it together" and invest in extra-role behaviors that knit together their interdependent responsibilities. When fairness is unenforceable, members fear becoming suckers for others' slack effort and retreat into individual responsibilities, which weakens team coordination.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on temporary group coordination by showing that the same formal role structure can be enacted either as coordinated collective work or as individually bounded role performance. It introduces justice enforceability as an organizational justice construct: perceptions that authorities can act fairly given the possibility that others may cheat decisions or procedures. This extends justice theory beyond whether authorities follow justice rules to whether fair treatment can be protected in high-turnover, gameable settings.
practical_implication: Organizations using temporary teams should attend to whether work assignment systems make fair contribution enforceable, not only whether leaders intend to allocate work equitably. The ED comparison suggests that team members may accept stressful equal assignment when it provides visible assurance that others cannot cheat workload distribution. Leaders should therefore examine whether accountability and assignment safeguards give temporary team members reason to trust that extra-role effort will not simply let others free ride.
limitations: The study is based on four hospital emergency departments matched on several characteristics and centered on pod-based doctor-nurse teams, so the findings may depend on contexts where work is countable and roles are relatively clear. The paper notes that the ED setting is distinctive because patients can be counted and physician and nurse roles are clearly defined. It does not claim that exactly equal assignment is universally preferable; it shows a tradeoff between stressful enforceability and flexible but gameable equity.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how temporary teams interface with larger systems, including boundary-spanning relationships beyond the immediate team. It also suggests studying change and learning in temporary teams, where constant membership change may alter expectations about "the way it's done here." Future work should examine justice enforceability when tasks are less divisible, roles are more ambiguous, or the dynamics of justice and coordination differ from emergency departments.
abstract: Temporary teams can accomplish tightly coupled complex work even without the shared experience that enables coordination in longstanding teams. To advance understanding of this process, I conducted an inductive study of temporary teams in four hospital emergency departments (EDs), and found that the teams in two EDs coordinated effectively, but the teams in the other two EDs did not. To theorize an explanation, I draw on the organizational justice literature and introduce the idea of justice enforceability, defined as the perception that authorities can act fairly, given the potential for other people to cheat. The team members' perceptions of justice enforceability were focused on whether the distribution of work within and between teams was fair or could be cheated. When team members perceived that justice was enforceable, they were willing to engage in the extrarole behaviors that wove together their individual responsibilities. But when they perceived that cheating was possible, they avoided the extra-role behaviors that would have made them suckers for working hard while others cheated. Justice enforceability thus resolves a common tension in temporary teams, namely that the potential for uneven effort can undermine team coordination. In these ED teams, members only trusted that authorities could act fairly when the distribution of work was exactly equal; then team members felt they were all "in it together," and each put in the work to coordinate as a team.

title: Knowing Me, Knowing You: Inventor Mobility and the Formation of Technology-oriented Alliances
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study dominated by quantitative dyad-year analysis: the authors combine alliance data, patent-based inventor mobility measures, firm financial controls, probit regressions with three-way clustered standard errors, instrumental-variable probit checks, and exploratory interviews with managers and scientists in the biopharmaceutical field.
industry: Global pharmaceutical industry.
country: Global sample; no single country reported.
time_period: 1990 to 2005 for the main alliance-formation analyses, using lagged mobility measures from prior five-year windows.
units: Firm dyad-years among large global pharmaceutical firms; inventor moves, technology-development and technology-transfer alliances, patents, firm controls, and exploratory interview respondents.
n_sample: 42 global pharmaceutical firms over 16 years; descriptive analyses report 11,502 dyad-year observations, with regression samples varying by alliance outcome; 15 exploratory interviews with R&D managers and scientists.
authors: Wagner, S.; Goossen, M. C.
theories: embeddedness perspective; learning-by-hiring and inventor mobility; organizational decision frames and frame alignment (Cornelissen & Werner, 2014; Corner et al., 1994; Kaplan, 2008)
keywords: alliance formation; decision frames; firm-specific knowledge; frame alignment; inventor mobility; pharmaceutical industry; technological familiarity; technology-oriented alliances
research_question: The paper asks whether hiring R&D scientists from a competitor increases the likelihood that the hiring firm later forms a technology-oriented alliance with that competitor. It further asks when this mobility-alliance relationship is strengthened or weakened by inventor firm-specific knowledge, the hiring firm's familiarity with the competitor's technology, and the distinction between technology-development and technology-transfer alliances.
mechanism_summary:
- Controls / identification checks: Prior alliances, technological convergence, technological distance, geographical distance, firm patents, patent citations, R&D intensity, employees, year dummies, three-way clustered standard errors, lagged mobility windows, and instrumental-variable probit regressions.

The mechanism is cross-level: mobile inventors carry technological knowledge and cognitive elements from a prior employer into the hiring firm, helping the hiring firm understand the competitor and align decision frames during alliance formation. This makes collaboration more likely for technology-development alliances, where uncertainty, joint coordination, and interpretive alignment are more important than in technology-transfer agreements. The effect is stronger when inventors know more about the prior firm and weaker when the hiring firm is already technologically familiar with the potential partner.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to alliance formation research by showing how nonexecutive mobile inventors can shape interfirm collaboration, not only CEOs, board ties, prior alliances, or resource complementarities. It extends employee mobility and learning-by-hiring research by arguing that mobility transfers cognitive elements and decision frames, not only technical knowledge, and that mobility and alliances can be complementary rather than substitutes. It also brings an organizational-frames lens into technology-oriented alliance formation by specifying how frame alignment helps reduce interpretive uncertainty between potential partners.
practical_implication: The paper implies that managers should involve R&D scientists in identifying and evaluating collaboration partners rather than treating them only as implementation resources after alliances are formed. It also reframes employee mobility as more than a threat of knowledge leakage: mobile inventors may create contact points, reduce uncertainty, and enable future R&D collaboration with competitors. For firms managing mobility restrictions, the findings suggest that limiting inventor movement may also reduce indirect knowledge spillovers through alliances.
limitations: The authors note that the study is rooted in a knowledge-intensive pharmaceutical context and relies heavily on patent data, so the conclusions may not generalize to industries where knowledge is more explicit or embedded in organizational routines, objects, or procedures rather than individuals. They also acknowledge that patents are imperfect for identifying employee mobility, despite their manual verification of mobility events. Finally, without a natural experiment, the analysis cannot fully rule out remaining unobserved heterogeneity, and the authors cannot observe which firm initiates alliance negotiations.
future_research: The authors call for future research that identifies exogenous changes in mobility or alliance formation to examine the relationship more causally. They suggest studying whether alliances related to prior inventor mobility are more effective or less likely to fail because organizational frames are bridged by mobile employees. They also propose case studies or ethnographies of frame alignment processes, and research on directional events such as acquisitions or reverse mobility from the focal firm to competitors.
abstract: We link the hiring of research and development scientists from industry competitors to the subsequent formation of collaborative agreements, namely technology-oriented alliances. By transferring technological knowledge as well as cognitive elements to the hiring firm, mobile inventors foster the alignment of decision frames applied by potential alliance partners in the process of alliance formation, thereby making collaboration more likely. Using data on inventor mobility and alliance formation among 42 global pharmaceutical firms over 16 years, we show that inventor mobility is positively associated with the likelihood of alliance formation in periods following inventor movements. This relationship becomes more pronounced if mobile employees bring additional knowledge about their prior firm’s technological capabilities and for alliances aimed at technology development rather than for agreements related to technology transfer. It is weakened, however, if a firm is already familiar with the competitor’s technological capabilities. By revealing these relationships, our study contributes to research on alliance formation, employee mobility, and organizational frames.

title: Consequences of Downward Envy: A Model of Self-esteem Threat, Abusive Supervision, and Supervisory Leader Self-improvement
methods: Two empirical quantitative, multi-source, multi-wave field studies of supervisor-subordinate dyads in China. The paper uses supervisor and subordinate surveys, organizational records, confirmatory factor analysis, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation tests, RMediation confidence intervals, and moderated indirect-effect tests for warmth and competence.
industry: Study 1: human resources management-consulting company. Study 2: natural gas service company.
time_period: Study 1 collected data in four waves over six months. Study 2 collected data in three waves with one-month and two-month lags; calendar dates not reported in paper.
units: Supervisor-subordinate dyads, supervisors' downward envy and self-esteem threat, subordinate-rated abusive supervision, supervisor-reported or archival self-improvement indicators, and supervisors' perceptions of subordinates' warmth and competence.
n_sample: Study 1: 216 independent supervisor-subordinate dyads. Study 2: 225 independent supervisor-subordinate dyads.
authors: Yu, L.; Duffy, M. K.; Tepper, B. J.
theories: abusive supervision as strategic leveling-down behavior (Tepper, 2000; Tepper et al., 2012); social functional view of envy and emotions (Hill & Buss, 2006; Keltner & Haidt, 1999; Smith & Kim, 2007); universal dimensions of social cognition: warmth and competence (Cuddy et al., 2011; Fiske et al., 2002)
keywords: abusive supervision; competence; downward envy; self-esteem threat; social functional view of envy; supervisor-subordinate dyads; supervisory self-improvement; warmth
research_question: The paper asks how supervisory leaders express and manage envy of direct reports, and whether downward envy leads to either abusive supervision or supervisory leader self-improvement through self-esteem threat. It also asks when supervisors choose each response, focusing on supervisors' perceptions of subordinates' warmth and competence.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism begins with downward envy as a painful feeling of inferiority toward a subordinate who possesses something the supervisor desires but lacks. From the social functional view of envy, this emotion threatens the supervisor's self-esteem and motivates gap-reduction behavior. When the envied subordinate is perceived as cold and competent, self-esteem threat is more likely to translate into abusive supervision as a leveling-down response. When the envied subordinate is perceived as warm and competent, self-esteem threat is more likely to translate into supervisory self-improvement as a leveling-up response.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends leadership theory by showing that supervisory leaders can experience downward envy toward direct reports, despite the formal privileges of leadership roles. It contributes to envy theory by specifying self-esteem threat as the mediator linking downward envy to two different adaptive responses, and by using warmth and competence from social cognition theory to explain why one response becomes abusive while the other becomes developmental. It also reframes abusive supervision as potentially strategic and goal-directed, not only as an impulsive hostile reaction to frustration.
practical_implication: The paper implies that organizations should treat downward envy as a possible risk factor for abusive supervision, while recognizing that abuse is not inevitable. Training can help supervisors recognize envy and abusive triggers, manage those reactions, and channel envy into formal or informal self-improvement. The authors also suggest that employees should not hide competence, but that pairing competence with warmth may reduce the likelihood that supervisory envy turns into abuse.
limitations: The authors note that they did not test whether abusive supervision or self-improvement actually reduced the perceived gap and self-esteem threat that motivated those behaviors. They also did not examine the precursors of downward envy, how direct reports respond to being envied, or fully rule out common method bias for the relationship between downward envy and self-esteem threat because both were measured from supervisors at the same time.
future_research: Future research should examine whether leveling-down through abusive supervision or leveling-up through self-improvement repairs envy-induced self-esteem threat, and whether abusive responses may worsen rather than repair supervisors' emotional states. The authors also call for work on antecedents of downward envy, including supervisors' relative standing on warmth and competence compared with direct reports. Additional research should study how envied subordinates respond to downward envy and which reactions are more or less effective.
abstract: We invoke theory and research on the social functional view of envy to propose a novel theoretical framework of supervisory leader envy of direct reports. Findings from two multi-source, multi-wave studies of supervisor–subordinate dyads provide support for the theses that (1) downward envy of subordinates threatens supervisors’ self-esteem and triggers adaptive strategies in the form of abusive supervision and supervisory self-improvement; and (2) supervisors are more likely to respond to downward envy induced self-esteem threat with abuse when they perceive envied subordinates to be cold and competent and they are more likely to respond with self-improvement when they perceive envied subordinates to be warm and competent.
apa_citation: Yu, L., Duffy, M. K., & Tepper, B. J. (2018). Consequences of downward envy: A model of self-esteem threat, abusive supervision, and supervisory leader self-improvement. *Academy of Management Journal*, 61(6), 2296-2318. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0183

title: Pay Formalization Revisited: Considering the Effects of Manager Gender and Discretion on Closing the Gender Wage Gap
methods: Longitudinal quantitative study using personnel records from FinServ's U.S. retail branches, comparing less formalized base salary with highly formalized bonus pay through cross-sectional time-series generalized estimating equation models with employee-, manager-, branch-, position-, and state-level controls.
industry: Retail branches of a globally diversified financial services firm offering consumer financial products and services
country: United States, across eight U.S. states
time_period: January 1996 through May 1999
units: Full-time non-managerial employees and branch managers in retail branches; employee-year observations nested in branches
n_sample: The abstract reports 857 employees in 120 retail branches; the methods report 897 unique full-time non-managerial employees, 2,139 non-managerial person-years, and 156 full-time branch managers.
authors: Abraham, Mabel
theories: social identity theory; status characteristics theory
keywords: formalization of pay systems; gender pay inequality; gender wage gap; less formalized pay systems; manager gender; social identity theory
research_question: Under what conditions do less formalized pay systems reduce, rather than perpetuate, gender pay inequality? The paper asks whether male and female managers use discretion differently in pay decisions and whether those differences depend on the organizational position of the employees being evaluated.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that formalized pay constrains managerial discretion, whereas less formalized pay allows manager identity and status dynamics to shape compensation decisions. Drawing on social identity theory, the paper argues that male and female managers may differ in their gender-based in-group preferences when they have discretion. Because women are a lower-status gender group and managerial roles are higher-status positions, female managers are expected to favor female subordinates most clearly in lower-status jobs, where support for women is less status-threatening. Empirically, female managers close the base-salary gap among tellers by paying female tellers more and male tellers less than male managers do; the same pattern does not appear for formalized bonus pay or for higher-status positions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts the formalization debate from whether formalized pay systems reduce inequality on average to when discretion can reduce inequality. It shows that the effects of pay formalization depend on who exercises discretion and on the local status ordering of the employees being evaluated. The contribution is a more conditional account of gender pay inequality that connects pay-system formalization, manager gender, social identity theory, and hierarchical position.
practical_implication: The paper warns organizations against assuming that either more formalized pay systems or more women in management will automatically reduce gender pay inequality. Pay formalization may be more useful when women are absent from management or when managers oversee higher-status jobs. Less formalized systems may support both discretion and equity when women are in management and oversee lower-level employees.
limitations: The study is based on one Fortune 500 retail bank, so the author treats generalizability as a limitation even though the branches provide parallel subunits across eight U.S. states. The personnel records did not provide usable controls for employee education or direct job tenure, so the models rely on age and organizational tenure as proxies. The data also do not isolate the precise behavioral mechanism explaining why female managers compensate lower-level male and female employees more equally.
future_research: Future research should replicate the empirical strategy across firms to assess generalizability. The paper calls for studies of other manager characteristics, such as race, that may structure in-group and out-group categorizations under less formalized reward systems. It also recommends research that simultaneously considers manager characteristics and context-specific status ordering, and research that unpacks whether female managers reduce inequality by paying women more, men less, or both.
abstract: While most studies of the formalization of pay systems suggest that it helps reduce inequality, some recent studies suggest the opposite. The present study draws on social identity theory to shift this debate from whether formalization reduces inequality to when, or under what conditions, less formalized pay systems may also serve to reduce inequality. Specifically, I consider both the gender of the decision maker and the job of the employee being evaluated. The goal of this study is to determine whether male and female managers differ in how they use the discretion afforded by less formalized pay systems, and to identify the implications for pay among employees at different levels of the organizational hierarchy. Among 857 employees in 120 retail branches of a financial services firm, I find evidence of less gender pay inequality in terms of less formalized components of pay for employees reporting to a female manager. However, this effect is only among employees in the lowest organizational ranks. These findings demonstrate that it is critical to take manager gender and the organizational position of the employees being evaluated into account when assessing the relationship between the formalization of pay and gender pay inequality.
apa_citation: Abraham, M. (2017). Pay formalization revisited: Considering the effects of manager gender and discretion on closing the gender wage gap. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(1), 29-54. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1060

title: Pull the Plug or Take the Plunge: Multiple Opportunities and the Speed of Venturing Decisions in the Australian Mining Industry
methods: Empirical quantitative study of Australian mineral exploration ventures using Register of Australian Mining data, mineral price data, and Cox competing-risks event-history regressions in Stata 13 with time-varying covariates and robust standard errors clustered by mineral identifier.
industry: Australian mineral mining industry.
units: Mining ventures at the prospecting and developing stages, observed as venture-year observations.
n_sample: 3,269 mining ventures over a 9-year period, yielding 6,563 venture-year observations; 83 advanced from prospecting to developing, 1,526 terminated while prospecting, 74 advanced from developing to exploiting, and 132 terminated while developing.
authors: Bakker, R. M.; Shepherd, D. A.
theories: attentional orientation and attention-based view (Ocasio, 1997; Cho & Hambrick, 2006); behavioral decision-making literature (Cyert & March, 1963; Levitt & March, 1988; March & Shapira, 1987); organizational learning and exploration-exploitation (March, 1991; Levitt & March, 1988)
keywords: Australian mining industry; attentional orientation; decision speed; environmental dynamism; opportunity-evaluation decisions; project portfolio; venture advancement; venture termination
research_question: The paper asks what determines the speed at which firms make opportunity-evaluation decisions when they are pursuing multiple potential opportunities at the same time. It focuses on whether a firm's attentional orientation toward earlier-stage exploration makes it faster or slower to terminate or advance ventures at prospecting and developing stages, and whether environmental dynamism changes those relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is stage- and decision-specific. Firms that focus attention on earlier-stage exploration develop experience, routines, and confidence for early fault detection, so they terminate prospecting ventures faster. The same orientation makes advancement decisions slower because advancement requires assessing upside potential, feasibility, scaling, and later-stage exploitation issues for which exploration-focused firms have weaker domain-specific routines and confidence. Environmental dynamism weakens or intensifies these effects at the initial prospecting stage because dynamic markets make existing knowledge and information less reliable, but the paper does not find significant moderation at the developing stage.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper extends opportunity-evaluation research by moving beyond the assumption that firms evaluate one opportunity at a time. It shows that a firm's internal portfolio of active potential opportunities shapes how quickly it evaluates a focal venture, and it highlights prospecting, developing, and exploiting as analytically distinct stages.

The paper also contributes to decision-speed research by challenging the idea that firms are generally fast or slow decision makers. Decision speed is presented as domain-specific: attention determines where firms develop experience, standard operating procedures, and confidence, so the same firm can be quick for one kind of venturing decision and slow for another.
practical_implication:
Managers should not assume that general decisiveness transfers automatically across all opportunity decisions. By focusing attention on the decision domains most relevant to the firm's future, managers can build experience, routines, and confidence for faster "pull the plug" or "take the plunge" decisions in those domains.

The findings also imply a tradeoff: a portfolio orientation that helps a firm rapidly terminate weak early-stage prospects may slow advancement decisions and later-stage termination decisions. Managers therefore need to align attention with the kinds of venture decisions where speed matters most.
limitations:
The study investigates one industry, mineral mining, so the authors cannot determine how far the findings generalize to other industries, especially creative R&D settings or ventures focused primarily on learning. Few ventures progressed all the way from initial prospect to operational mine during the observation period, which prevented analysis of sequences of multiple decisions across the full opportunity process.

The dependent variable uses yearly duration data, so finer-grained monthly data might reveal more precise decision-speed patterns. The authors also did not analyze decisions to start new exploration ventures, had relatively small advancement-event subsamples, lacked location novelty measures, and did not test whether faster decisions improved firm performance.
future_research:
Future research could test the framework in industries with faster venture progression or more dynamic portfolios, and could examine whether earlier decision speed affects later advancement or termination decisions. Studies using finer-grained duration data could clarify the timing of opportunity-evaluation decisions more precisely.

Additional work could examine decisions to start exploration ventures, distinguish new-to-firm from new-to-industry locations, and connect decision speed to performance. The authors specifically suggest examining whether speed itself matters or whether better fit between timing, the venture, and the environment is more important.
abstract: Effectively capturing opportunities requires rapid decision making. We investigate the speed of opportunity-evaluation decisions by focusing on firms’ venture termination and venture advancement decisions. Experience, standard operating procedures, and confidence allow firms to make opportunity-evaluation decisions faster; we propose that a firm’s attentional orientation, as reflected in its project portfolio, limits the number of domains in which these speed-enhancing mechanisms can be developed. Hence, firms’ decision speed is likely to vary between different types of decisions. Using unique data on 3,269 mineral exploration ventures in the Australian mining industry, we find that firms with a higher degree of attention toward earlier-stage exploration activities are quicker to abandon potential opportunities in early development but slower to do so later, and that such firms are also slower to advance on potential opportunities at all stages compared to firms that focus their attention differently. Market dynamism moderates these relationships, but only with regard to initial evaluation decisions. Our study extends research on decision speed by showing that firms are not necessarily fast or slow regarding all the decisions they make, and by offering an opportunity-evaluation framework that recognizes that decision makers can—in fact, often do—pursue multiple potential opportunities simultaneously.

title: Moral Symbols: A Necklace of Garlic against Unethical Requests
methods: Six-study empirical design: five laboratory experiments using deception, prisoner-dilemma, and in-basket simulation tasks, plus an organizational survey of subordinate-supervisor dyads in India; analyses include chi-square tests, regression, and bootstrapped mediation tests.
industry: Laboratory studies used student, MTurk, and nationwide participant samples; the field survey drew from varied professions including IT, accounting, and sales.
country: United States for the laboratory and online studies; India for the organizational dyad survey.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Participants acting as leaders or superiors in experiments; subordinate-supervisor dyads in the field survey.
n_sample: Six-study program: five laboratory samples plus a field sample of 104 subordinate-supervisor dyads.
authors: Desai, Sreedhari D.; Kouchaki, Maryam
theories: dual-system or synthetic framework for morality (Cushman et al., 2006; Greene et al., 2004; Haidt, 2001; Moore & Gino, 2015); social learning theory of ethical leadership (Brown et al., 2005; Brown & Trevino, 2006); two-stage signaling-processing model of ethical decision making (Tenbrunsel & Messick, 1999)
keywords: moral awareness; moral symbols; perceived moral character; social influence; unethical behavior; unethical requests
research_question: The paper asks whether subordinates can reduce superiors' unethical behavior and unethical requests by exposing them to moral symbols. It specifically examines whether moral symbols work through increased moral awareness in the superior and through inferences that the symbol-displaying subordinate has high moral character.
mechanism_summary: Moral symbols operate as subtle social influence cues. They make morality more cognitively accessible and increase superiors' moral awareness, which lowers unethical behavior in general. In interpersonal contexts, they also lead superiors to infer that the displayer has high moral character; this makes superiors less willing to direct unethical requests toward that particular subordinate. The studies distinguish this protective effect from simple avoidance by showing that moral symbols did not reduce requests in a no-dilemma condition.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts behavioral ethics and ethical leadership research from a primarily top-down account toward a bottom-up account of how followers can shape leaders' ethical behavior. It contributes a dual-process explanation of moral symbols by separating a general moral-awareness pathway from a displayer-specific perceived-moral-character pathway. It also extends moral identity and social influence research by showing that moral displays can regulate others' ethical behavior, not only the displayer's own behavior.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that employees may have a low-conflict, preemptive way to reduce unethical requests from superiors by displaying morally meaningful symbols. For organizations, subtle moral cues may complement formal ethics programs and codes of conduct. The studies also suggest that such displays did not produce detectable backlash in the tested settings, although the authors caution that broader workplace consequences require further study.
limitations: Several studies were laboratory experiments using controlled scenarios, and the field evidence came from subordinate-supervisor dyads in India, so generalizability to Western field settings remains open. The experimental unethical behaviors were largely pecuniary forms of deception or fraudulent reporting, leaving uncertainty about whether moral symbols would reduce discrimination, harassment, or other workplace misconduct. The authors also note possible collateral damage, because unethical superiors who avoid the moral-symbol displayer might redirect unethical requests toward other employees.
future_research: Future research should test moral symbols in additional field settings, especially Western organizational contexts, and examine a wider range of unethical behaviors. The authors call for work on other forms of moral symbols, morality-related personality moderators, and why perceived subordinate morality deters unethical requests. They also encourage study of authenticity and impression management in moral-symbol displays, including whether strategic or inauthentic displays work differently from naturally occurring ones.
abstract: This paper investigates whether, by exposing superiors to moral symbols, subordinates can discourage their superiors from asking them to perform unethical acts. Findings from five laboratory studies and one organizational survey study demonstrated that exposure to moral symbols displayed by the subordinates dissuades superiors from both engaging in unethical behaviors themselves and asking their subordinates to engage in unethical behavior. This paper shows that the display of moral symbols leads to two main consequences: (1) the activation of the concept of morality and increases in individuals’ moral awareness to decrease unethical behavior, and (2) eliciting inferences about the moral character of the displayer to lower the likelihood of that person being subjected to unethical directives. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that moral symbols influence ethical decisions without provoking hidden backlash effects against those who display them. In sum, our findings show that followers can serve as a form of social influence to guide their leader’s behavior and reduce the occurrence of unethical acts in the workplace.
apa_citation: Desai, S. D., & Kouchaki, M. (2017). Moral symbols: A necklace of garlic against unethical requests. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(1), 7-28. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0008

title: Green by Comparison: Deviant and Normative Transmutations of Job Search Envy in a Temporal Context
methods: Two quantitative field studies using survey data and moderated regression analyses: Study 1 surveyed unemployed job seekers at different search lengths, and Study 2 followed graduate human-resources students across internship and post-graduation job-search events.
industry: Job-search context; unemployed job seekers and graduate human-resources students, not an industry-specific firm sample.
time_period: Study 1 measured search length at one survey point; Study 2 followed participants across a two-year internship and post-graduation job-search process.
units: Individual job seekers.
n_sample: Study 1 final analysis n=334; Study 2 analysis-wise n=35-45 depending on outcome and event.
authors: Dineen, B. R.; Duffy, M. K.; Henle, C. A.; Lee, K.
theories: envy theory; social comparison theory; temporal pressure and appraisal theory
keywords: employment opportunities; job search effort; job search envy; resume fraud; social comparison; temporal pressure
research_question: How does job search envy translate into deviant or normative job-search behavior as temporal pressure and perceived employment opportunities change? The paper asks whether envy leads job seekers toward resume fraud or greater search effort under different clock-based, event-based, and market-based search pressures.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that upward social comparison during job search produces envy, and the pressure context shapes whether that envy is appraised as a challenge or a threat. Under higher temporal pressure, search situations seem less changeable or more critical, making resume fraud a more likely response. Under lower temporal pressure, especially when opportunities appear plentiful, envy is more likely to be channeled into increased search effort.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces job search envy as a socio-emotional link between social comparisons and job-search behavior. It extends envy and job-search theory by showing that envy can transmute into both deviant and normative behaviors, and that this transmutation depends on clock-based time, event criticality, and perceived employment opportunities. It also adds a temporal lens to social comparison theory by showing that the same comparative emotion can have different behavioral associations at different stages of a search.
practical_implication: Recruiters should recognize that job seekers may be more prone to resume fraud when envy coincides with longer searches or more critical search events, even when job markets appear favorable. Career counselors and placement offices can use this insight to help job seekers acknowledge envy, maintain self-worth, and redirect comparative pressure into legitimate search effort rather than resume embellishment. The supplementary findings also suggest that internship resume screening may require particular care.
limitations: The resume fraud measures are self-reported, so fraud may be underreported or shaped by willingness to disclose unethical behavior. Study 2 had a smaller-than-planned sample and missing data across the five survey waves, making its search-effort findings less robust than the replicated resume-fraud pattern. The paper also theorizes changeability, criticality, and challenge-versus-threat appraisals but does not directly measure these mediating processes in the main studies.
future_research: Future work should directly test the proposed mediating processes, including perceived changeability, event criticality, and challenge-versus-threat appraisal. Researchers should examine objective or detected resume fraud alongside self-reports, while recognizing that detected fraud may miss successful deception. The authors also call for extending the temporal model to other pressured goal-striving contexts and for qualitative work on how job seekers choose, change, or avoid social comparison referents.
abstract: We propose a novel temporal-based theory of how a painful social comparative emotion—job search envy—transmutes as deviant or normative job search behaviors (resume fraud or search effort). We theorize that as job searches progress across time or discrete events, temporal-based pressure increases via perceptions that situations are less changeable or more critical, propelling envious job seekers toward deviant rather than normative search behavior. We propose that market-based pressure, deriving from employment opportunity perceptions, further moderates these effects. In a first study of unemployed job seekers, after more search time passes, job search envy relates to deviant search behavior. Market pressure further qualifies this relationship, although contrary to our prediction, lower market pressure exacerbates rather than attenuates the relationship. Study 2, a two-year study of graduate students engaged in internship and full-time job searches, focuses on event-based temporal pressure and mostly replicates the Study 1 findings. It also indicates that under lower event and market pressures, job seekers expend more effort but do not commit resume fraud in response to job search envy. Overall, we conclude that job search envy transmutes differently depending on temporaland market-based contingencies and discuss future research possibilities.
apa_citation: Dineen, B. R., Duffy, M. K., Henle, C. A., & Lee, K. (2017). Green by comparison: Deviant and normative transmutations of job search envy in a temporal context. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(1), 295-320. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0767
