title: Imprinting through Inheritance: A Multi-Genealogical Study of Entrepreneurial Proclivity
methods: Empirical quantitative multi-genealogical study of the Israeli information technology and communication industry. The authors build organizational genealogies from IVC Research Center records, LinkedIn, firm websites, newspaper archives, and interviews, then estimate negative binomial panel time-varying models and a Logit panel first stage with Huber-White clustered standard errors.
industry: Israeli information technology and communication industry.
time_period: Industry evolution from its inception in the 1950s through 2005; ancestral-era indicators distinguish the cooperative era up to 1977 from the competitive era between 1977 and 1985.
units: Genealogy-year observations of first-, second-, and third-generation founders' start-up creation within 14 organizational genealogies.
n_sample: 14 genealogies including 443 start-ups; 492 observations for first- and second-generation analyses and 181 observations for the third-generation analysis.
authors: Ellis, Shmuel; Aharonson, Barak S.; Drori, Israel; Shapira, Zur
theories: agency-based transmission; lineage inheritance; mental models; organizational imprinting theory; tacit knowledge transfer
keywords: entrepreneurial proclivity; entrepreneurial tenure gap; era-based imprinting; genealogical approach; heredity processes; imprinting effects; lineage-based transmissions; organizational lineage inheritance
research_question: The paper asks how era-based imprinting effects on entrepreneurial proclivity persist across time, organizations, and generations of founders. It examines whether competitive versus cooperative founding eras shape ancestral founders' entrepreneurial proclivity, whether that proclivity is inherited by later generations, and when transmission weakens because founders' and prospective founders' mental models diverge.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an agency-based lineage inheritance process. Competitive founding eras imprint entrepreneurial proclivity onto ancestral founders, who then transmit tacit entrepreneurial knowledge to organization members through direct work interaction. Employees who leave to found new ventures reproduce and modify that inherited knowledge in the next generation, but transmission weakens when the founder's accumulated entrepreneurial experience creates a mental-model gap with novice prospective entrepreneurs.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to organizational imprinting theory by showing that imprinting longevity need not depend only on inertia, institutionalization, or path dependence within a single organization. It theorizes and tests a lineage inheritance process in which imprinted entrepreneurial knowledge travels across organizational boundaries through employees-turned-founders.

It also contributes to entrepreneurship and industry-evolution research by linking national-era conditions to multi-generational patterns of start-up formation. The study shows that ancestral founders can have a ripple effect on the evolution of an industrial sector, but only when agency-based tacit knowledge transmission remains effective.
practical_implication:
For entrepreneurial ecosystems, the findings imply that founding-era conditions and early entrepreneurial role models can shape later venture creation through work-based learning and founder-employee interaction. The study also suggests that such transmission depends on the fit between founders' entrepreneurial experience and prospective entrepreneurs' own founding challenges, because large tenure gaps can weaken inherited entrepreneurial knowledge.

For founders and managers, the study suggests that entrepreneurial knowledge is not transmitted automatically through organizational membership. As founders become more experienced, their knowledge may become less useful to novice employees unless they bridge the mental-model gap that separates expert and novice entrepreneurial practice.
limitations:
The authors note that the study focuses on entrepreneurial knowledge in the Israeli ITC industry, so other industries may have different evolutionary speeds, generation structures, and inheritance dynamics. They also acknowledge that the Israeli case is one national setting and call for examination in other institutional environments, including Western Europe, the United States, emerging economies, and socially oriented economies such as China.

The data do not directly observe the content of tacit entrepreneurial knowledge or founders' and employees' mental models. The authors use entrepreneurial tenure gap as an indicator of mental-model misalignment, and they cannot rule out the possibility that founders hired employees similar to themselves rather than transmitting entrepreneurial proclivity through interaction.
future_research:
Future research could examine whether technological knowledge, not only entrepreneurial knowledge, is inherited across organizational generations and whether progeny ventures remain in the parent's technological domain. It could also study factors that inhibit or facilitate transmission of different forms of tacit knowledge across generations.

The authors call for deeper research on entrepreneurs' mental models, including what differentiates expert from novice entrepreneurs and why particular mental-model compositions interfere with knowledge transmission. They also suggest extending genealogical approaches to explain where new industries come from and how industry trajectories emerge.
abstract: We offer an organizational lineage inheritance theoretical framework for understanding the longevity of imprinting effects of two consecutive eras with distinct environmental conditions, values, and norms. Adopting a genealogical approach, we find that era-based imprinting is contingent on lineage-based transmissions. Era-based initial conditions strongly influence the entrepreneurial proclivity of the first generation of firms but have no influence on subsequent generations, and each generation is influenced by the entrepreneurial proclivity of the former. We show two mediation effects and one moderation effect, supporting our theoretical argument that the longevity of imprinting effects is due to heredity processes. First, the effect of era-based initial conditions on the entrepreneurial proclivity of the second generation is mediated by the entrepreneurial proclivity of the first generation. The effect of the entrepreneurial proclivity of the first generation on the third-generation's entrepreneurial proclivity is mediated by the entrepreneurial proclivity of the second generation. Second, a mismatch between the mental models of the knowledge-transmitting agents (the founders) and the knowledge-receiving agents (organization members—prospective entrepreneurs) moderates the effect of the entrepreneurial proclivity of one generation on the entrepreneurial proclivity of the next.
apa_citation: Ellis, S., Aharonson, B. S., Drori, I., & Shapira, Z. (2017). Imprinting through inheritance: A multi-genealogical study of entrepreneurial proclivity. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 500-522. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0150

title: Signaler Credibility, Signal Susceptibility, and Relative Reliance on Signals: How Stakeholders Change their Evaluative Processes After Violation of Expectations and Rehabilitative Efforts
methods: Empirical quantitative study using U.S. financial earnings restatement data from the GAO, matched nonrestating firms, Compustat financial measures, OLS value-relevance models, three-way interactions, clustered robust standard errors, simple slope tests, and robustness checks.
industry: U.S. public firms across industries, with each restating firm matched to a nonrestating firm from the same four-digit SIC code, time period, and similar asset size
time_period: Restatements from 2003 through 2006, with financial data spanning five years before to three years after the restatement year
units: Restating firms, matched nonrestating firms, firm-year observations, and CEO replacement events
n_sample: 7,498 firm-years before list-wise deletion; the restatement sample includes 352 downward and 99 upward earnings restatement firms plus matched firms
authors: Gomulya, David; Mishina, Yuri
theories: organizational impression management and rehabilitative actions; screening theory (Sanders & Boivie, 2004); signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al., 2011)
keywords: CEO replacement; book value; earnings; financial restatements; signaling and screening theory; stakeholder evaluation; violation of expectations
research_question: Do stakeholders change the process by which they evaluate a firm after the firm violates expectations, and are those process changes reversed after credible rehabilitative efforts? The paper examines this question in the context of investors' reliance on earnings and book value after financial restatements and subsequent CEO replacement.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that financial restatements reduce the credibility of the firm as signaler, making investors more skeptical of signals that are more susceptible to errors or manipulation. Earnings are treated as a stronger but more susceptible flow signal, while book value is treated as a weaker but more resistant stock signal. After restatements, investors shift toward book value; after CEO replacement, a visible and costly rehabilitative action, they partially shift back toward earnings. The shifts are stronger after downward restatements because more severe violations make signaler credibility more salient.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends research on violation of expectations by showing that stakeholders' reactions are not limited to more or less favorable evaluations; the underlying evaluative process itself can change. It contributes to signaling and screening theory by distinguishing noise from the signal itself from noise attributable to the signaler's behavior, and by showing that compromised signaler credibility can alter the relative usefulness of otherwise familiar signals. It also shows that rehabilitative actions can reverse these shifts, making evaluative reliance historically contingent rather than fixed.
practical_implication: For firms that have violated stakeholder expectations, the paper implies that simply producing favorable financial signals may not restore investor evaluations if those signals depend on compromised credibility. Credible rehabilitative actions, such as replacing the incumbent CEO after a restatement, can help restore investor reliance on signals that had become less trusted. Managers and boards should recognize that recovery involves repairing the evaluative process stakeholders use, not only improving the level of observable performance indicators.
limitations: The authors limit the empirical setting to financial restatements, so they cannot establish whether similar shifts in signal reliance occur after other forms of expectation violation. They examine investors in aggregate rather than individual investors or other stakeholder categories. The focal signal contrast is between earnings and book value, which differ as flow and stock signals; other bases of signal susceptibility, such as third-party reporting, verifiability, or consistency of measurement rules, remain untested.
future_research: Future research should examine other types of expectation violations to assess whether stakeholders similarly change their evaluative processes outside financial restatements. Studies could compare different stakeholder groups or individual investor categories rather than treating investors as a whole. The authors also call for research on other reasons signals become more or less manipulable and on cases where signals are redundant enough that stakeholders may switch completely to the less noisy signal instead of merely changing relative reliance.
abstract: Prior studies have shown that a firm’s violation of expectations might lead to less favorable evaluations of that firm by stakeholders. However, the literature has been silent on whether and how the process by which stakeholders evaluate a firm could change subsequent to the violation. Drawing from signaling and screening theory, we examine how evaluative processes might change in the context of financial restatements. We find that investors appear to shift their relative reliance on particular signals in determining a firm’s stock price following an earnings restatement. These changes are at least partly reversed following the replacement of an incumbent CEO. We further find that these evaluative changes vary depending on the severity of the violation.
apa_citation: Gomulya, D., & Mishina, Y. (2017). Signaler credibility, signal susceptibility, and relative reliance on signals: How stakeholders change their evaluative processes after violation of expectations and rehabilitative efforts. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 554-583. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.1041

title: Institutional Logics and Power Sources: Merger and Acquisition Decisions
methods: Cox proportional hazards models of market-oriented M&A announcements and event-study regressions of cumulative abnormal returns, using CSMAR and WIND data on Chinese listed firms with ownership, board, financial, industry, and region controls; interviews and press/web review provide contextual support.
industry: Nearly all listed Chinese firms across 84 CSRC 3-digit industries.
units: Listed Chinese firms and firm-year spells
n_sample: 2,337 firms and 24,151 firm-year spells
authors: Greve, H. R.; Zhang, C. M.
theories: institutional logics; theory of organizational coalitions and power
keywords: institutional logics; market capitalism logic; mergers and acquisitions; organizational coalitions and power; state socialism logic
research_question: How do firms choose among strategic actions backed by competing institutional logics? The paper studies this question by examining how state socialism and market capitalism coalitions shaped Chinese listed firms' market-oriented M&A decisions during economic transition.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism links competing institutional logics to strategic decisions through coalitions and power sources. State ownership and directors with state experience proxy the power of a state socialism coalition, which is expected to discourage market-oriented M&As. Legal-person ownership and stockholding directors proxy the power of a market capitalism coalition, which is expected to encourage M&As. As market capitalism became more established, the positive effect of market-capitalism coalition power increased, while investors reacted skeptically to M&As by firms with high state ownership.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends institutional logics research by shifting attention from field-level dominance to firm-level choices among actions backed by competing logics. It connects institutional logics with coalition and power theory, showing that external ownership power and internal board representation jointly shape strategic decisions.
practical_implication: The findings imply that contested strategic actions depend on coalition building within boards and on the ownership groups that empower those coalitions. Managers and directors should expect ownership configurations and board members' prior experience to affect whether market-oriented strategies gain support, especially in transitional institutional environments.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: Future research could examine boards as decision-making bodies where owner configurations and personal experience shape coalitions across different institutional contexts. The paper also calls for deeper study of compromises across agenda items and relationships among managerial careers, participation, and power in decision making.
abstract: Institutional theory has explained the greater prevalence of many strategic actions by increases in their legitimacy over time, but it has not explained how firms choose among actions backed by competing institutional logics. We address this topic by linking institutional logics with the theory of organizational coalitions and power to predict how such choices are affected both by external influence (through ownership) and by internal influence (through shared decision making). In particular, we analyze how the old state socialism logic and the new market capitalism logic competed to influence Chinese firms’ mergers and acquisitions (M&As). We find that these institutional logics affected M&A decisions via the coalitions committed to each logic—coalitions whose balance of power reflected the external power source of ownership and the internal power source of board representation. We also find that each coalition’s strength changed as the market capitalism logic became more established during China’s economic transition, and that investors viewed M&As by firms with high state ownership skeptically.
apa_citation: Greve, H. R., & Zhang, C. M. (2017). Institutional logics and power sources: Merger and acquisition decisions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 671-694. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0698

title: “Dancing on Hot Coals”: How Emotion Work Facilitates Collective Sensemaking
methods: Empirical qualitative, multi-method process study of patient advocates in teaching and U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals, using interviews, shadowing, documents, conference observation, and iterative inductive coding of mediating episodes, sensemaking and sensegiving activities, and emotions.
industry: Healthcare / hospital patient advocacy.
time_period: Data collection proceeded over an eighteen-month period.
units: Patient advocates and their mediating episodes involving patients, families, and hospital staff.
n_sample: Phase 2 included 20 patient advocates at 10 teaching hospitals and 11 patient advocates at 7 VA hospitals, plus shadowing of 5 teaching-hospital advocates and 3 VA-hospital advocates; Phase 1 included 18 key informants and documents for context.
authors: Heaphy, E. D.
theories: emotion work; emotional labor; sensegiving; sensemaking
keywords: client conflicts; collective sensemaking; emotion dynamics; emotion work; empathetic account; mediating work; patient advocates; sensegiving
research_question: The paper asks how mediators engage in emotion work to intervene in collective sensemaking around client conflicts. It studies patient advocates as hospital employees who mediate conflicts among patients, families, and staff without direct authority over the parties.
mechanism_summary:
- Tabula rasa interactions: Mediators encourage emotion-rich accounts from clients while maintaining emotional neutrality, listening, asking questions, taking notes, and ending interactions before negative emotions amplify.
- Emotional inference: Mediators use clients' expressed emotions and their own felt emotions as cues for understanding what clients care about and how the conflict is evolving.
- Exclaiming interactions: When mediators experience unpleasant or highly activated emotions, they turn to peers to discuss emotion-rich accounts, elaborate provisional understandings, and mitigate their own emotions.
- Empathetic accounts: Mediators cycle through tabula rasa and exclaiming interactions until they develop accounts that make multiple perspectives cognitively and emotionally understandable.
- Directing interactions: Mediators selectively deploy abridged accounts to influence clients' or staff members' sensemaking while mitigating others' emotions.
- Re-narrating interactions: When clients resist sensegiving, mediators tell empathetic accounts from another party's perspective to provoke updating.
- Inflaming interactions: Subtle emotion triggers, dissatisfaction with responses, or clients who persistently push can amplify negative emotions and derail sensemaking or sensegiving.

The process is not a variable-based causal model but a qualitative process model of interaction sequences. Mediators first generate and interpret emotional and discursive cues across multiple parties, then pivot from sensemaking to sensegiving once the account is empathetic enough to support action. Emotion work matters because it shapes whether interactions produce provisional accounts, elaborated accounts, updating, or derailment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on organizational responsiveness to client conflicts by showing how employees can respond through sensemaking-intensive mediation rather than routinized control. It extends sensemaking theory by identifying how emotion work and emotion dynamics shape the creation, plausibility, and deployment of accounts. It also contributes to emotion and compassion research by showing that empathy can become embedded in accounts and used selectively as a sensegiving resource.
practical_implication: The study suggests that employees who mediate conflicts need skills in emotion work, not only procedures for complaint handling. Organizations can improve responsiveness by institutionalizing mediating capacity that helps constituents express emotion-rich accounts, develop shared understanding, and update interpretations. The findings also imply that ignoring or minimizing emotion may undermine conflict handling in settings where sensemaking is needed.
limitations: The author notes that patient advocacy in hospitals is a highly emotional setting where advocates expect to handle conflict and emotion as part of their role, so the process may differ in lower-emotion contexts. The study focuses mainly on the patient advocates' perspective, supplemented by observation of clients, leaving less direct evidence on how clients themselves experience and shape the dyadic process.
future_research: Future research could examine how the process transfers to other organizational contexts, especially lower-emotion settings where mediators may need to create rather than contain emotional activation. Scholars could study how clients actively shape collective sensemaking as individuals or through extra-organizational forums. Additional work could examine which emotions become embedded in plausible accounts across roles and settings, and how those emotional qualities affect later sensegiving.
abstract: While organizations and researchers have traditionally conceptualized customers as consumers of their services and products, there is a growing recognition that organizations need to develop more collaborative relationships with clients. In this research, I explore one implication of this shift—how employees respond to client conflicts. In a multi-method qualitative study, I studied patient advocates, hospital employees who mediate conflicts between patients, families, and staff. I develop a process model that shows how mediators construct a web of discrete social interactions that, over time, enables them to develop an empathetic account of the conflict. They then selectively deploy the account to engage in sensegiving. The process model integrates research on emotions and sensemaking in novel ways. I identify how emotion work triggers emotion dynamics in interactions that facilitate or disrupt sensemaking and sensegiving. I show how plausible accounts are developed over the course of social interactions and that mediators pivoted from sensemaking to sensegiving when the account was characterized by empathy. Overall, this research shows how mediators actively generate, interpret, and influence their own and others’ emotions, and that mediators’ emotion work contributes to the success of collective sensemaking.
apa_citation: Heaphy, E. D. (2017). “Dancing on hot coals”: How emotion work facilitates collective sensemaking. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 642-670. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0101

title: Does Diversity-Valuing Behavior Result in Diminished Performance Ratings for Non-White and Female Leaders?
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design. Study 1 uses a field sample of executives with peer-rated diversity-valuing behavior and boss-rated competence and performance, analyzed through hierarchical moderated regression and moderated mediation tests. Study 2 uses a between-subjects experiment manipulating hiring manager sex, race, and diversity-valuing behavior, analyzed with ANOVA and bootstrapped moderated mediation.
industry: Study 1 spans executives across multiple industries, organizations, and functions; Study 2 uses employed adults evaluating an executive hiring scenario.
country: United States for Study 1 executives and Study 2 employed adults; Study 2 participants were sampled from a North America online database.
time_period: Study 1 uses an entire calendar-year cohort; Study 2 time period is not reported.
units: Executives in Study 1 and employed adult evaluators rating a hiring manager in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1 reports 362 executives with a usable sample of 350; Study 2 reports 307 adults.
authors: Hekman, David R.; Johnson, Stefanie K.; Foo, Maw-Der; Yang, Wei
theories: attribution theory; glass ceiling literature; social mobility and social competition; stereotype content model; tokenism
keywords: competence judgments; diversity-valuing behavior; glass ceiling; performance ratings; tokenism; workplace discrimination
research_question: Does leader diversity-valuing behavior produce lower performance ratings for non-White and female leaders than for White and male leaders, and is this penalty explained by lower perceived competence?
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that diversity-valuing behavior makes non-White and female leaders' low-status demographic categories salient. Observers may interpret the same behavior as nepotistic, socially competitive, or warm in ways that activate competence stereotypes for low-status leaders. Those lower competence judgments then translate into worse performance ratings for non-White and female leaders, while White and male leaders are not penalized in the same way.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends glass ceiling research by identifying a mechanism through which the ceiling can be maintained even when organizations promote diversity initiatives. It formally introduces and tests the diversity-valuing behavior construct and shows that its consequences depend on leader demographics. The paper also contributes to tokenism and workplace discrimination research by explaining why non-White and female leaders may avoid advocating for demographically similar others: doing so can damage their perceived competence and performance evaluations.
practical_implication: The paper cautions organizations against making diversity advocacy appear to be the special responsibility of non-White and female leaders. It suggests that organizations may reduce penalties by rewarding demographic unselfishness in hiring and promotion rather than singling out leaders' diversity-valuing behavior. The authors also imply that visible White male support for diversity initiatives may carry legitimacy advantages because White and male leaders are less likely to be penalized for the same behavior.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1's diversity-valuing behavior measure partly captures an underlying value of diversity rather than only observed behavior, although Study 2 addresses this concern through an experimental manipulation. They also acknowledge that Study 2 measures competence and performance at the same time and from the same source, while Study 1 uses different sources. They further discuss possible social desirability in Study 2, where participants may overrate non-White and female leaders to avoid appearing biased.
future_research: Future research could examine whether the same model holds when non-White or female leaders engage in diversity-valuing behavior without making that behavior highly visible. The authors also call for research comparing leaders' value of diversity with actual diversity-valuing behavior as predictors of competence and performance judgments. Additional work could examine whether different measures of perceived competence mediate the interaction between leader race or sex and diversity-valuing behavior in different ways.
abstract: We seek to help solve the puzzle of why top-level leaders are disproportionately White men. We suggest that this raceand sex-based status and power gap persists, in part, because ethnic minority and female leaders are discouraged from engaging in diversityvaluing behavior. We hypothesize, and test in both field and laboratory samples, that ethnic minority or female leaders who engage in diversity-valuing behavior are penalized with worse performance ratings, whereas White or male leaders who engage in diversity-valuing behavior are not penalized for doing so. We find that this divergent effect results from traditional negative race and sex stereotypes (i.e., lower competence judgments) placed upon diversity-valuing ethnic minority and female leaders. We discuss how our findings extend and enrich the vast literatures on the glass ceiling, tokenism, and workplace discrimination.
apa_citation: Hekman, D. R., Johnson, S. K., Foo, M.-D., & Yang, W. (2017). Does diversity-valuing behavior result in diminished performance ratings for non-white and female leaders? *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 771-797. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0538

title: Health Systems in Transition: Professional Identity Work in the Context of Shifting Institutional Logics
methods: Empirical qualitative inductive study using 113 semi-structured interviews with primary-care physicians, unstructured naturalistic observations, field notes, and documentary and archival sources, analyzed through open coding, axial coding, and aggregate theoretical dimensions.
industry: Primary health care and family medicine in health systems undergoing transition from narrow specialism to generalism.
country: Estonia, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and Slovenia.
time_period: Interviews were conducted during 2004-2008, with field observations and archival material used to contextualize health-system reforms.
units: Primary-care physicians, including family medicine academics/educators, family medicine physicians, and narrow specialists.
n_sample: 113 physicians: 18 family medicine academics/educators, 60 family medicine physicians, and 35 narrow specialists.
authors: Kyratsis, Y.; Atun, R.; Phillips, N.; Tracey, P.; George, G.
theories: identity work; institutional logics; professional identity; social identity theory
keywords: generalism; identity work; institutional logics; narrow specialism; professional identity; professional identity threats; professional logic
research_question: The paper asks how professionals manage their professional identities when a contested shift in the professional logic of their field threatens an established professional identity. It studies this question among physicians in five European transition countries where primary health care moved from Soviet-era narrow specialism toward Western-style generalism and family medicine.
mechanism_summary:
- Field-level trigger: A professional logic shift from narrow specialism to generalism changed expectations about expertise, patient relationships, clinical tasks, and the organization of primary care.
- Identity threats: Physicians experienced professional values conflict, status loss, and social identity conflict as the new logic challenged their existing professional selves.
- Identity work: Physicians who reconstructed their identities engaged in authenticating, reframing, and cultural repositioning.
- Identity outcome: When these forms of identity work were performed effectively, physicians adopted a new professional identity aligned with generalism; others remained rooted in the old logic.
- Boundary conditions: The process was shaped by physicians' tenure, professional status concerns, national and ethnic identities, and political associations with Soviet, European, and Western models of health care.

The process is cross-level rather than a variable-based causal test. A macro-level change in professional logic created micro-level threats to physicians' sense of who they were, what counted as legitimate medical expertise, and how they should relate to patients and society. Authenticating connected family medicine to enduring medical values, reframing rebuilt the status content of the family physician role, and cultural repositioning linked the new professional identity to valued national or Western cultural narratives.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to professional identity research by explaining how established professionals, not only entrants to a profession, reconstruct identities when field-level logics shift. It also contributes to institutional theory by showing how local enactment of a new institutional logic depends on micro-level identity work, especially when the new logic is contested and incompletely supported. The model links professional values conflict, status loss, and social identity conflict to authenticating, reframing, and cultural repositioning as distinct identity-work responses.
practical_implication: The study suggests that health-system reformers and other change agents should treat professional identity change as part of large-scale institutional change, not as a secondary communication problem. They can support professionals by supplying identity narratives, rhetorical strategies, role models, and resources that help professionals manage status loss, perceived incompetence, and conflicts between professional and social identities.
limitations: The authors identify the study as qualitative theory elaboration rather than theory testing, so its propositions require larger-scale quantitative examination. The setting is also unusual because professional logic change occurred alongside broad post-Communist societal and economic transformation, which may limit direct generalization. The study focuses on physicians and mainly on those who successfully reconfigured their professional identities, leaving other professions and unsuccessful or hybrid identity responses less fully examined.
future_research: Future research should test the proposed dynamics in larger-scale studies and in settings where the professional logic shifts without simultaneous societal transformation. The authors also call for research on other professions and on professionals who do not successfully transition, including those who retain old identities or develop hybrid identities spanning old and new logics.
abstract: We investigate how established professionals manage their identities in the face of identity threats from a contested shift in the professional logic that characterizes their field. To do so, we draw on interviews with 113 physicians from five European transition countries who faced pressure for change in their professional identities due to a shift in the logic of health care from a “narrow specialism” in primary care, which characterized the Soviet health system, to “generalism,” which characterizes primary care in the West. We found three important forms of professional identity threats experienced by physicians during this period—professional values conflict, status loss, and social identity conflict. In addition, we identified three forms of identity work—authenticating, reframing, and cultural repositioning—that professionals who successfully transitioned to the new identity performed in order to reconstruct their professional identities so that they were aligned with the new logic. Based on these findings, we present a model of how established professionals change their professional identities as a result of a contested shift in the professional logic of their field, and discuss the underlying mechanisms through which this occurs.
apa_citation: Kyratsis, Y., Atun, R., Phillips, N., Tracey, P., & George, G. (2017). Health systems in transition: Professional identity work in the context of shifting institutional logics. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 610-641. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0684

title: Why and When Does the Gender Gap Reverse? Diversity Goals and the Pay Premium for High Potential Women
methods: Four empirical quantitative studies: a field study of employees in a Fortune 500 organization, a laboratory experiment with graduate business students, a field study of top executives in S&P 1500 organizations, and a laboratory experiment with working adults. Analyses use hierarchical regression, clustered standard errors, median regression, experimental manipulation checks, and moderated mediation tests.
industry: Study 1 examined employees at the corporate headquarters of a Fortune 500 organization; Studies 2 and 4 used a simulated consumer products company; Study 3 examined S&P 1500 organizations in consumer goods, consumer services, and manufacturing.
country: The paper does not report one common sample country across all four studies.
time_period: Study 1 conducted a survey over three weeks; Study 3 used executive pay data from 1992 through 2006; Studies 2 and 4 do not report calendar dates.
units: Individual employees, graduate business students evaluating a target employee, top executives, and working adults evaluating a target employee.
n_sample: Study 1: 1,311 employees; Study 2: 270 graduate business students; Study 3: 35,602 observations for 8,968 executives in 2,320 organizations; Study 4: 303 Mechanical Turk participants.
authors: Leslie, Lisa M.; Manchester, Colleen Flaherty; Dahm, Patricia C.
theories: meso paradigm in organizational research; strategic human resource management theory; supply and demand
keywords: diversity goals; diversity value perceptions; female premium; gender pay gap; high-potential women; strategic human resource management
research_question: The paper asks why a female pay premium emerges against the backdrop of an overall gender pay penalty and when the gender gap reverses. It tests whether organizational diversity goals create demand for high-potential women, whether perceived diversity value explains pay rewards, and whether the premium grows stronger when diversity goals are stronger.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level. Organizational diversity goals and the scarcity of women in upper echelons increase perceived demand for high-potential women. Managers and evaluators therefore see high-potential women as more valuable for achieving diversity goals, infer stronger retention expectations, and allocate higher pay or rewards. The premium is bounded: it appears for high-potential women, not low-potential women, and is larger where diversity goals are stronger.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the assumption that the gender pay gap uniformly disadvantages women by showing that a female penalty can reverse for high-potential women. It contributes a mechanism, perceived diversity value, that explains why a premium can arise, and a boundary condition, high potential, that explains when it arises. It also develops a meso-level account linking macro organizational diversity goals to micro evaluator perceptions and pay decisions.
practical_implication: The findings imply that pay-equity audits should not only compare men and women overall, because an aggregate female penalty can mask a high-potential female premium. Organizations should examine pay by potential rating and job level, and should clarify whether diversity value is an appropriate factor in reward decisions. The paper also warns that diversity goals may generate legal, fairness, or backlash concerns if they unintentionally produce gender-based pay disparities.
limitations: The authors note that the field studies have strong external validity but do not permit causal inference or direct tests of all individual-level mechanisms. The laboratory studies provide internal validity and all-else-equal comparisons but rely on simulated tasks and include only some participants with management experience. Study 3 uses industry as a proxy for diversity-goal strength, so other industry differences may also contribute to the observed premium.
future_research: Future research could examine other sources of contextual variation, including whether legal, social, moral, or business-case motives for diversity goals change the size of the female premium. The authors also suggest extending the theory to other groups targeted by diversity initiatives, including racial minorities.
abstract: Abundant research has documented a gender pay gap; women earn less than men, all else being equal. Against the backdrop of an overall female penalty, we propose that the widespread adoption of diversity goals in organizations creates a female premium for certain women. We integrate the economic principle of supply and demand with theory from the field of strategic human resource management and theorize that individuals perceive high-potential women—who have the abilities needed to reach the upper echelons of organizations, where women remain underrepresented—as more valuable for achieving organizational diversity goals than high-potential men and, in turn, reward them with higher pay. Two field studies (Studies 1 and 3) and two laboratory experiments (Studies 2 and 4) reveal a female premium that is unique to high-potential women (Studies 1 and 2), driven by perceptions that high-potential women have more diversity value than high-potential men (Studies 2 and 4), and larger in contexts where diversity goals are stronger (Studies 3 and 4). Our theory and findings challenge the assumption that the gender pay gap uniformly disadvantages women and offer new insight into why and when the female penalty reverses and becomes a female premium.
apa_citation: Leslie, L. M., Manchester, C. F., & Dahm, P. C. (2017). Why and when does the gender gap reverse? Diversity goals and the pay premium for high potential women. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 402-432. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0195

title: Emotions Uncorked: Inspiring Evangelism for the Emerging Practice of Cool-Climate Winemaking in Ontario
methods: Longitudinal, inductive qualitative study of Ontario cool-climate wineries and external audience members, combining semi-structured interviews, in situ observations of winery interactions and rituals, archival texts, social media and media materials, iterative coding, and process-model development.
industry: Ontario cool-climate winemaking and fine wine wineries.
time_period: Figure 1 covers VQA dissemination and evangelist activities from 1980 to 2014; primary interview and observation dates are not reported.
units: Ontario wineries and members of six external audience groups, including restaurant operators, wine media, regulators, viticultural institutions, consumers/connoisseurs, and wine society representatives.
n_sample: 86 semi-structured interviews, more than 250 hours of winery-based observations, and archival, media, website, newsletter, blog, review, and social-media materials.
authors: Massa, F. G.; Helms, W. S.; Voronov, M.; Wang, L.
theories: identity and emotion in institutional work; institutional perspective on evangelism; ritual theory
keywords: emerging practices; emotional experiences; institutional evangelism; institutionalized templates; organizational rituals; organizing; proselytizing; receptive identities
research_question: The paper asks how organizational actors engender institutional evangelism among audience members. It examines how Ontario wineries converted some external audience members from spectators into advocates for the emerging practice of cool-climate winemaking.
mechanism_summary:
- Institutionalized templates: Wineries drew on provenance, hedonic, and glory templates to interpret and present cool-climate winemaking.
- Organizational rituals: Wineries translated those templates into ceremonies, artifacts, and accounts during tastings, tours, dinners, events, and other interactions.
- Receptive identities: Gourmand and regional identities made some audience members more open to emotional resonance with the rituals.
- Inspiring emotional experiences: Provenance rituals elicited reverence, hedonic rituals elicited elation, and glory rituals elicited awe.
- Non-receptive identities: Professional or consumer identities could keep audience members at arm's length, leading to failed conversion.
- Evangelistic behaviors: Converted audience members proselytized by retelling stories and recreating experiences, and organized by founding events, societies, campaigns, and support structures.

The process model is qualitative and multilevel rather than a variable-based causal test. Organizational actors craft ritualized interactions from institutionalized templates; audience members' salient identities shape whether those interactions become inspiring emotional experiences; and those experiences motivate proselytizing and organizing that disseminate the emerging practice. The paper emphasizes that evangelism can spread through a recursive cycle in which converted audience members recreate rituals and convert others.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a process model of institutional evangelism that explains how external audience members become devoted advocates for an emerging practice. It extends work on audiences, institutional change, and evangelism by showing that organizational rituals can convert outsiders, not only reinforce insiders' commitment. It also advances emotion and identity research by specifying reverence, elation, and awe as emotional experiences whose effects depend on receptive gourmand and regional identities.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that organizations trying to build support for unfamiliar practices should attend to ritualized experiences, not only messages or formal claims. Effective audience engagement requires ceremonies, artifacts, and accounts that translate the practice into emotionally resonant experiences for audience members whose identities make them receptive. The study also cautions that the same rituals may fail with audiences whose professional or consumer identities make them interpret the interaction as marketing or salesmanship.
limitations: The study is based on a single context: Ontario cool-climate winemaking and its audiences. The authors note that the context involved an emerging practice with a negative reputation, limited resources, and audience members who could become emotionally attached to regional and gourmand meanings.
future_research: Future research could examine how evangelistic behaviors differ across audience types such as regulators, media, connoisseurs, and critics, especially because each audience is governed by different professional norms. Scholars could also study evangelism for more contested, stigmatized, technological, artisanal, human-rights, or environmental practices, where different rituals and emotions may be involved. Cross-sector studies of tours, dinners, social events, and other ritualized encounters could test how organizations outside wine use rituals to create or fail to create audience engagement.
abstract: This paper examines how organizations create evangelists, members of key audiences who build a critical mass of support for new ways of doing things. We conduct a longitudinal, inductive study of Ontario’s cool-climate wineries and members of six external audience groups who evangelized on behalf of their emerging winemaking practice. We found that wineries drew from three institutionalized vinicultural templates— “provenance,” “hedonic,” and “glory”—to craft rituals designed to convert these audience members. These rituals led to inspiring emotional experiences among audience members with receptive gourmand and regional identities, driving them to engage in evangelistic behaviors. While a growing body of work on evangelists has emphasized their individual characteristics, the role of emotions in driving their activities, as well as how they advocate for organizations, our study demonstrates how evangelism can be built through ritualized interactions with organizations. Specifically, we reveal how organizations develop rituals that translate emerging practices into inspiring emotional experiences for particular members of audiences. This suggests that rituals can be used not only to incite dedication within organizational boundaries, but to inspire members of external audiences to act as social conduits through which emerging practices spread.
apa_citation: Massa, F. G., Helms, W. S., Voronov, M., & Wang, L. (2017). Emotions uncorked: Inspiring evangelism for the emerging practice of cool-climate winemaking in Ontario. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 461-499. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0092

title: Is Consistently Unfair Better than Sporadically Fair? An Investigation of Justice Variability and Stress
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design. Study 1 is a randomized laboratory experiment manipulating consistently fair, consistently unfair, and variably fair supervisor feedback during a stock-price simulation, with heart rate as a physiological stress indicator and ANOVA/planned comparisons. Study 2 is a multilevel experience-sampling field study of employee-supervisor dyads over three weeks, analyzed with multilevel path analysis in Mplus and bootstrapped indirect effects.
industry: Study 1 uses junior- and senior-level undergraduate management students in a stock-price simulation. Study 2 includes full-time working adults from tourism, education, real estate/construction, government, health care, technology, retail/distribution, financial, and manufacturing industries.
time_period: Study 1 is a single laboratory session; Study 2 collects one daily survey each working day over a three-week period.
units: Study 1 participants and Study 2 employee-supervisor dyads with daily observations nested within employees.
n_sample: Study 1 reports an effective sample of 161 participants after quality checks; Study 2 includes 97 employees providing 995 daily surveys.
authors: Matta, Fadel K.; Scott, Brent A.; Colquitt, Jason A.; Koopman, Joel; Passantino, Liana G.
theories: fairness heuristic theory; organizational justice theory; uncertainty management theory
keywords: experience-sampling; fair treatment; justice variability; organizational justice; stress; supervisor self-control; uncertainty management theory
research_question: Does variability in fair treatment over time create employee stress beyond the effects of average fairness, and can consistently unfair treatment be less stressful than unpredictably fair treatment? The paper also asks whether justice variability strengthens the daily uncertainty-stress relationship, transmits effects to job dissatisfaction and emotional exhaustion, and reflects supervisor self-control.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in uncertainty management theory: employees use fairness to manage uncertainty, but variable fair treatment makes fairness itself uncertain. When fair treatment fluctuates, employees lose predictability about how they will be treated, so variability becomes stressful even when average fairness is not low. That daily stress carries justice variability into job dissatisfaction and emotional exhaustion, although the hypothesized CWB mediation is not supported. Supervisor self-control matters because supervisors with more self-discipline and impulse control are better able to provide stable fair treatment over time.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces justice variability as a distinct construct that captures between-person differences in the stability of fairness over time. It challenges the dominant justice assumption that more fairness is always better by showing that variably fair treatment can be more stressful than consistently unfair treatment. It also extends uncertainty management theory by showing that uncertainty about justice can intensify, rather than buffer, the effects of general workplace uncertainty.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that organizations should focus not only on increasing average fairness but also on helping supervisors deliver fair treatment consistently. Justice training that produces short-term spikes followed by decline may introduce harmful variability unless embedded in longer-term leadership development and feedback systems. The supervisor self-control findings also imply that selection and promotion systems may benefit from assessing traits linked to consistent, disciplined treatment of employees.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 measured physiological stress but not perceptual stress, while Study 2 measured perceptual stress but not physiological stress. Study 1 manipulated interpersonal justice rules even though the theory centers on overall fairness, and its design did not fully cross average justice and justice variability. Study 2 relied on self-reported Level 1 variables and used overall fairness rather than dimension-specific justice measures.
future_research: Future research could examine which employees are most affected by justice variability, such as those low in trust propensity. The authors also call for work on whether justice variability matters differently at high versus low average justice, how temporal factors such as self-control depletion across the day shape variability, and how justice variability differs from other within-person variability constructs that have a more internal locus.
abstract: Research on organizational justice has predominantly focused on between-individual differences in average levels of fair treatment experienced by employees. Recently, researchers have also demonstrated the importance of considering dynamic, withinindividual fluctuations in fair treatment experienced by employees over time. Drawing on uncertainty management theory, we merge these two streams of research and introduce the concept of "justice variability," which captures between-person differences in the stability of fairness over time. Contrary to the intuitive notion that more fairness is always better, our work shows that being treated consistently unfairly can be better for employees than being treated fairly sometimes and unfairly at other times. Specifically, in a lab study, variably fair treatment resulted in greater physiological stress than both consistently fair and consistently unfair treatment. In a multilevel, experience-sampling field study, we replicated the positive association between justice variability and stress, and we also showed that justice variability exacerbated the positive, daily relationship between general workplace uncertainty and stress. Moreover, daily stress mediated the effects of justice variability on daily job dissatisfaction and emotional exhaustion. Finally, we showed that supervisors with more self-control tended to be less variable in their fair treatment over time.

title: When Job Performance is All Relative: How Family Motivation Energizes Effort and Compensates for Intrinsic Motivation
methods: Empirical quantitative field study using survey measures of family, intrinsic, and external motivation; ten working days of morning diary measures of energy and stress; objective daily job performance scores; and multilevel moderated mediation analysis with multilevel structural equation modeling in Mplus.
industry: Coupon-processing maquiladora work.
time_period: A two-week diary and objective-performance measurement period; the calendar dates are not reported in the paper.
units: Female employees nested within daily diary and objective performance observations.
n_sample: 97 employees with complete survey data and at least 3 diary entries; 791 daily ratings.
authors: Menges, J. I.; Tussing, D. V.; Wihler, A.; Grant, A. M.
theories: action identification theory (Vallacher & Wegner, 1987, 1989); prosocial motivation (Grant, 2007, 2008a); self-determination theory (Gagne & Deci, 2005; Ryan & Deci, 2000)
keywords: action identification; energy; family motivation; intrinsic motivation; job performance; prosocial motivation; stress; work-family dynamics
research_question: The paper asks whether family motivation, defined as the desire to expend effort to benefit one’s family, improves job performance and whether it is especially important when intrinsic motivation is low. It further asks whether energy and stress explain how family motivation compensates for low intrinsic motivation.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that family motivation reframes monotonous work as serving the meaningful purpose of supporting family members. This higher-level action identification supplies energy when intrinsic enjoyment of the task is weak, which helps employees sustain effort and performance. The evidence supports the energy pathway: family motivation predicted performance when intrinsic motivation was low, and the conditional indirect effect through energy was significant. The stress pathway was not supported; stress did not predict performance, and family motivation increased stress when intrinsic motivation was high.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces family motivation as a distinct and potent form of prosocial motivation whose beneficiaries are outside the workplace but are affected by employment itself. It challenges the assumption that prosocial and intrinsic motivations mainly operate synergistically, showing instead a compensatory pattern in which family motivation can substitute for low intrinsic motivation. It also extends work-family research by identifying family as a source of work energy and objective performance, not only as a source of conflict or enrichment.
practical_implication: Managers can help employees connect work to valued family outcomes, especially in routine jobs with limited intrinsic motivation. Family-salient practices or benefits may strengthen performance by making work feel meaningful, but the paper cautions against exploiting family dependence because family motivation did not reduce stress and may intensify pressure. The implication is to support family motivation through humane job design and benefits, not through threats or insecurity.
limitations: The study was conducted in one Mexican maquiladora with an all-women sample, limiting generalizability across genders, cultures, occupations, and income strata. It did not directly measure family financial need, family structure, or antecedents of family motivation, and the external motivation control had limited reliability. The design uses strong temporal separation and objective performance data, but the field evidence remains observational rather than experimentally causal.
future_research: Future research could examine antecedents of family motivation, including family benefits, organizational culture, family structure, life stage, and financial pressure. Studies could test whether family motivation predicts outcomes beyond job performance, such as turnover, commitment, voice, citizenship, counterproductive behavior, or unethical behavior. Additional work could compare men and women, investigate different cultural contexts, and model within-person fluctuations in task-level intrinsic and family motivation.
abstract: Supporting one’s family is a major reason why many people work, yet surprisingly little research has examined the implications of family motivation. Drawing on theories of prosocial motivation and action identification, we propose that family motivation increases job performance by enhancing energy and reducing stress, and it is especially important when intrinsic motivation is lacking. Survey and diary data collected across multiple time points in a Mexican maquiladora generally support our model. Specifically, we find that family motivation enhances job performance when intrinsic motivation is low—in part by providing energy, but not by reducing stress. We conclude that supporting a family provides a powerful source of motivation that can boost performance in the workplace, offering meaningful implications for research on motivation and the dynamics of work and family engagement.
apa_citation: Menges, J. I., Tussing, D. V., Wihler, A., & Grant, A. M. (2017). When job performance is all relative: How family motivation energizes effort and compensates for intrinsic motivation. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 695-719. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0898

title: Forgone, but not Forgotten: Toward a Theory of Forgone Professional Identities
methods: Inductive qualitative grounded-theory study combining open-ended survey responses and semi-structured interviews, with iterative coding and a data-structure approach.
industry: Wide range of occupations including academia, accounting, administration, consulting, HR, IT, marketing, psychotherapy, and other work roles.
country: Survey respondents were United States-based; interviewees varied by nationality, including American, Brazilian, British, Dutch, Indian, Iranian, Irish, Romanian, South African, and Spanish.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals describing alternative selves and forgone professional identities.
n_sample: 380 individuals, based on 347 open-ended survey responses and 33 in-depth semi-structured interviews.
authors: Obodaru, O.
theories: Schwartz's theory of universal values; alternative selves; identity theory; self-expansion theory; simulation theory
keywords: alternative selves; forgone professional identities; imagined enactment; professional identity; real enactment; unfulfilled values; vicarious enactment
research_question: The paper asks whether forgone professional identities can remain part of the self-concept, why people would want to retain them, and how people can hold on to a professional identity without occupying the associated work role. It examines how people deal with the professional "roads not taken" in contemporary careers.
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering condition: A career fork-in-the-road leads a person to take one work role and forgo another.
- Core construct: A forgone professional identity is retained when it is tied to values that remain unfulfilled in the person's actual professional identity.
- Process elements: People enact the forgone identity through real enactment, imagined enactment, and vicarious enactment.
- Strategy contingencies: The use of these enactment strategies varies with characteristics of the forgone identity, individual differences such as segmenting versus integrating work and nonwork, and situational constraints.

The process model argues that people do not necessarily forget professional identities attached to forgone work roles. When the forgone identity embodies an unfulfilled value, people experience negative emotions around letting it go and seek ways to make it feel real and self-descriptive. Real, imagined, and vicarious enactment let people retain the identity even when the formal work role is absent.
theoretical_contribution: The paper expands professional identity theory by showing that people may define themselves not only through work roles they formally hold, but also through professional identities they have forgone. It also expands identity enactment beyond real activities and social interactions by theorizing imagined enactment and vicarious enactment as routes through which identities can become self-descriptive. These constructs reposition alternative selves as potential self-definitions, not only self-comparisons.
practical_implication: For managers, the paper suggests that understanding employees' forgone identities can reveal unfulfilled values, unrealized potential, and possible routes for job or leisure crafting. For individuals, the paper suggests that giving up a career option does not necessarily require abandoning the corresponding identity or values; imagined and vicarious enactment may help people retain meaningful aspects of who they might have become.
limitations: The author notes that the process model is based on retrospective accounts and that a longitudinal design would better capture how enactment strategies evolve after a career fork-in-the-road. The sample is diverse by age, gender, occupation, and nationality, but the paper does not fully theorize subgroup variation across these dimensions.
future_research: Future research could examine how gender, occupation, personality traits such as fantasy-proneness, and situational constraints shape the use of real, imagined, and vicarious enactment. The paper also calls for research on whether the identified strategies are exhaustive, whether virtual enactment is another form, how people who never forgo a professional identity experience identity development, and what outcomes follow from retaining forgone professional identities.
abstract: Through an inductive, qualitative study, I developed a process model of how people deal with professional identities they have forgone by choice or constraint. I show that, when forgone professional identities are linked to unfulfilled values, people look for ways to enact them and retain them in the self-concept. I further identify three strategies that people use to enact foregone professional identities: (1) real enactment (i.e., enacting the forgone identity through real activities and social interactions either at work or during leisure time), (2) imagined enactment (i.e., enacting the forgone identity through imagined activities and interactions, either in an alternate present or in the future), and (3) vicarious enactment (i.e., enacting the forgone identity by observing and imagining close others enacting it and internalizing these experiences). These findings expand our conceptualization of professional identity beyond identities enacted through activities and interactions that are part of formal work roles, and illuminate the key role of imagination and vicarious experiences in identity construction and maintenance.
apa_citation: Obodaru, O. (2017). Forgone, but not forgotten: Toward a theory of forgone professional identities. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(2), 523-553. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0432

title: Artful and Contorted Coordinating: The Ramifications of Imposing Formal Logics of Task Jurisdiction on Situated Practice
methods: Empirical qualitative field study using 16 months of ethnographic observation in one hospital labor and delivery unit, semi-structured interviews, informal ethnographic conversations, grounded-theory coding, narrative maps of ordering work, and triangulation of observational and interview data.
industry: Hospital obstetric care; specifically a labor and delivery unit implementing an electronic health records system.
time_period: The main fieldwork ran for 16 months around an EHR implementation, with observations beginning in February 2010 and ending in June 2011; key-informant follow-ups continued semiannually between 2011 and 2015.
units: Ordering practices and coordinating interactions among nurses, physicians, and other caregivers in the H1 labor and delivery unit.
n_sample: 55 separate L&D observations; 32 semi-structured interviews with caregivers in the L&D unit; and 28 additional interviews outside H1 before observation began.
authors: Pine, Kathleen H.; Mazmanian, Melissa
theories: coordination theory; formal logics of action; occupational task jurisdiction; situated practice
keywords: artful coordinating; contorted coordinating; coordination; electronic health records; formal logics of action; situated practice; task jurisdiction
research_question: The paper asks how the introduction of a digital work process system affects the way integrating conditions for ongoing coordinating are realized in practice and the form of coordinating that emerges. It also asks how work-system design, especially design that assumes alignment between formal delineations of action and situated practice, affects organizational outcomes.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: formal logics of task jurisdiction; situated practice; common understanding; predictability; formal and informal accountability.
- Process / forms: pre-EHR artful coordinating, where formal logics remained resources for situated action, and post-EHR contorted coordinating, where EHR permissions imposed formal accountability directly on everyday work.
- Triggering condition: implementation of the Voyage EHR shifted ordering from a more flexible paper/TDS-supported practice to a permission-bound digital workflow.
- Emergent outcomes: nurses and physicians spent effort working around the EHR, social norms around task jurisdiction weakened, predictability declined, and patient-care work became slower and more cumbersome.
- Boundary conditions: the argument is developed in complex, time-sensitive, uncertain work where formal work systems cannot fully anticipate local contingencies.

The process is that pre-EHR clinicians used formal rules, local context, and situated contingencies together to coordinate ordering work. Because nurses could flexibly alter, manage, or support orders under tacit norms, common understanding also generated informal accountability and predictability. After the EHR embedded strict permissions, clinicians had to coordinate both the patient-care task and the system workaround; this made formal accountability more visible but undermined the local negotiations that had previously made work predictable.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends coordination research by showing that Okhuysen and Bechky's integrating conditions can combine in different ways and produce different forms of coordinating. It distinguishes formal accountability from informal accountability and argues that formal accountability can undermine, rather than support, predictability when it is imposed through a heavy-handed work system. It also reframes workarounds as an integral feature of contorted coordinating, not merely a temporary implementation problem.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that digitized workflow systems improve coordination simply because they make formal accountability more visible. In complex and time-sensitive work, work systems need enough flexibility for specialists to adapt, migrate discretion, and preserve common understanding around the work itself. Otherwise, employees may spend scarce time pacifying the system while patient care, responsiveness, social relations, and record accuracy suffer.
limitations: The study is based on one labor and delivery unit in one hospital, so the empirical setting is narrow and shaped by teaching-hospital norms around nurses, residents, and attending physicians. The pre-EHR emergency vignette relies on interviews and participant descriptions rather than direct observation of an equivalent pre-EHR event. The paper also focuses on ordering work within a digital work process system that coordinates action and creates formal records.
future_research: Future work could examine how work process systems can be designed to accommodate multiple logics of action and accountability while supporting common understanding. Research could also investigate how formal and informal accountability interact across other complex, uncertain workplaces beyond medicine. The authors further call for attention to technologies that both coordinate action and create official accounts of work, especially where incentives for "perfect" records may distort situated practice.
abstract: Ongoing coordination is the backbone of work process and organizational effectiveness. Coordinating requires that interdependent specialists achieve integrating conditions for coordination—including understanding who is accountable for carrying out a given task, how a sequence of actions should proceed, and how one’s work fits into the whole on an ongoing basis. Navigating the inevitable disconnect between formal logics of action and the specifics of the local context and situation at hand is a hallmark of effective coordinating. Nevertheless, as work systems designed to direct action with a heavy hand are increasingly implemented in organizations, the disconnect between formal delineations and situated practice is transformed with large negative consequences for organizations. Through 16 months of empirical research using ethnographic methods surrounding implementation of an electronic health records (EHR) system in a hospital obstetric unit, we find that the EHR rendered what was once a productive disconnect between formal logics and situated practice into an unproductive disconnect. Further, this shift engendered a new form of ongoing coordinating. What was once “artful coordinating”—in which clinicians across occupations drew upon formal logics, local context, and situated contingencies as resources to action and, in so doing, created conditions of predictability and informal accountability—became “contorted coordinating,” characterized by working around formal logics of the EHR while struggling to meet the demands of local context and situated contingencies, thus undermining predictability.

title: Negotiating the Challenges of a Calling: Emotion and Enacted Sensemaking in Animal Shelter Work
methods: Inductive qualitative study using narrative interviews, open coding, constant comparative analysis, Gioia-style data structuring, and temporal bracketing.
industry: Animal welfare and animal shelters
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Animal shelter workers
n_sample: 50 animal shelter workers
authors: Schabram, K.; Maitlis, S.
theories: callings literature; emotion and enacted sensemaking; performance and learning frames; sensemaking theory
keywords: animal shelter work; burnout; callings; emotion; enacted sensemaking; thriving; workplace challenges
research_question: The study asks how the ways individuals negotiate the challenges of a calling vary across individuals and over time. It focuses on animal shelter workers because this setting makes the emotional, identity, and sensemaking dynamics of pursuing a prosocial calling transparently observable.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: challenges of animal shelter work, accounts of self and purpose, emotional responses, enacted sensemaking, calling paths, burnout, thriving.
- Process / phases: workers enter with passion and purpose, encounter similar challenges, interpret those challenges through accounts of self and purpose, respond through cycles of emotion and enacted sensemaking, and gradually enact divergent work environments and outcomes.
- Calling paths: identity-oriented workers preserve a sense of special gifts for animals; contribution-oriented workers seek to apply valuable skills for broader impact; practice-oriented workers treat challenges as opportunities for learning and mastery.
- Emergent outcomes: identity and contribution paths tend toward broken or defeated burnout and exit from shelter work, while the practice path tends toward learning, growth, continued animal welfare work, and community building.

The process is recursive rather than linear. Initial accounts of self and purpose frame how workers interpret challenges; emotional responses then energize enacted sensemaking, including experimenting with tasks, relationships, roles, and boundaries. These actions change the work environment and generate new cues, so small early differences in framing and enactment accumulate into distinct calling paths.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends callings research by showing that a calling is not a unitary work orientation with uniform consequences. It identifies three calling paths and explains how people pursuing the same calling can end up thriving, leaving in a defeated state, or leaving with a broken sense of fit. It also contributes to research on workplace challenges by theorizing how emotion and enacted sensemaking recursively shape burnout and thriving trajectories over time.
practical_implication: Organizations that employ people with callings should not assume passion and dedication are self-sustaining resources. The study suggests that called employees may work unpaid hours, take on difficult tasks, bring work home, and become exhausted unless organizations help them negotiate challenges constructively. Support should be tailored to the path: calibrating identity expectations, giving realistic previews of contribution limits, and supporting learning and growth for practice-oriented workers.
limitations: The sample was designed for theory development and consisted mostly of women in North American animal welfare organizations, so transferability to other gender compositions, cultures, and calling domains remains uncertain. The study also relies on one-time narrative interviews with current and former employees rather than real-time longitudinal observation, so retrospective accounts may reflect participants’ current energy, satisfaction, and distance from shelter work.
future_research: Future research could test whether similar identity-, contribution-, and practice-oriented calling paths appear in other occupations, especially in different cultural and gendered contexts. Longitudinal studies could observe how accounts of self and purpose, emotional responses, and enacted work environments change in real time.
abstract: An important and underexamined issue in the study of callings concerns the challenges people face in pursuing a calling and how they negotiate those challenges. This process may be especially intense and consequential because callings involve work that is rooted in people’s values and that matters a great deal to them. Drawing on narrative interviews with 50 animal shelter workers, we identify three different “calling paths” that evolve as employees respond to the challenges they encounter. While all individuals in our study entered animal shelter work with similar passion and purpose, and faced similar kinds of challenges, those on different paths interpreted challenges differently, had different emotional responses to them, engaged in different kinds of enacted sensemaking, and developed different accounts of themselves and their guiding purpose, through which they interpreted subsequent challenges. The result was the emergence of three increasingly divergent calling paths over time, culminating in different emotional, psychological, and behavioral outcomes. Based on these findings, we develop a model of the recursive process through which individuals negotiate the challenges of a calling, contributing to the literatures on callings and employee responses to workplace challenges.
