title: Multinational Enterprises within Cultural Space and Place: Integrating Cultural Distance and Tightness–Looseness
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study using the Toyo Keizai Japanese Overseas Investments by Country dataset. The analysis uses GLS random-effects models with robust estimates, mean-centered continuous predictors, residual-centered interaction terms, robustness checks with alternative cultural values measures and stricter ownership thresholds, and latent growth curve modeling for longitudinal checks.
industry: Foreign subsidiaries of Japanese MNEs across sectors; the paper controls for sector similarity but does not restrict the sample to one industry.
country: Japanese MNE foreign subsidiaries in 28 host countries with cultural distance and tightness–looseness scores.
time_period: 1990-2013 observation period; final GLS models report 17,658 observations from 3,022 subsidiaries.
units: Subsidiary-year observations for wholly owned foreign subsidiaries of Japanese MNEs.
n_sample: Final GLS models report 17,658 observations and 3,022 subsidiaries; the preanalysis sample was 63,627 observations representing 8,538 subsidiaries in 28 countries.
authors: Shin, D.; Hasse, V. C.; Schotter, A. P. J.
theories: cultural distance (Kogut & Singh, 1988); tightness–looseness (Gelfand et al., 2011; Pelto, 1968); transaction cost economics (Williamson, 1985)
keywords: Japanese MNEs; cultural distance; expatriate parent-country nationals; tightness–looseness; transaction cost economics
research_question: The paper asks why, when, and in which direction cultural distance between an MNE's home and host country affects the proportion of expatriate parent-country nationals in foreign subsidiaries. It also asks whether host-country tightness–looseness amplifies the curvilinear cultural distance-staffing relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in transaction cost economics. At low to medium cultural distance, rising ex ante costs of expatriate deployment make local staffing more attractive, reducing the expatriate PCN proportion. At medium to high cultural distance, rising ex post costs from monitoring and opportunism make expatriate PCNs more valuable for coordination and control, increasing their proportion. Tight host-country norms amplify this pattern because they make expatriate adjustment costlier at lower distance levels and make control concerns more salient at higher distance levels.
theoretical_contribution:
The paper contributes to cross-cultural management theory by replacing a simple linear cultural distance prediction with a transaction-cost account of a convex, partly U-shaped relationship between cultural distance and expatriate PCN staffing. It reconciles prior positive, negative, and mixed findings by distinguishing ex ante and ex post cost logics across the cultural-distance continuum.

It also integrates values-based cultural distance with norms-based tightness–looseness. By treating cultural distance as cultural space and tightness–looseness as location-bound cultural place, the paper shows that country-level norm strength moderates how cultural distance affects MNE staffing decisions.
practical_implication:
Managers should not make expatriate-versus-local staffing decisions from cultural distance alone. The paper recommends a more deliberate cost analysis that includes both ex ante costs of expatriate deployment and ex post costs of monitoring and control in culturally distant subsidiaries.

The findings also imply that expatriate preparation should address both cognitive cultural differences and place-bound normative pressures. Cross-cultural training may help with values-based distance, but tight local norms may require additional mechanisms such as mentoring, local relationships, scenario-based preparation, and safeguards against opportunistic behavior.
limitations:
The study does not directly measure ex ante and ex post transaction costs, so the cost mechanism is inferred from the staffing pattern rather than observed directly. The dataset has substantial advantages but is limited by the common denominator of Japanese ownership, and Japanese MNEs are known to rely heavily on long-term expatriate PCNs.

The study also depends on available tightness–looseness scores, limiting country coverage. It does not examine different managerial assignee types, alternative expatriate assignment forms, or individual-level variance such as managerial status, cultural background, personality, spousal adjustment, and career goals.
future_research:
Future research could replicate the model in other home-country settings and extend tightness–looseness scores to a larger set of countries. The paper also points to the value of studying Quadrant 4 in its cultural-space/place framework and examining the qualitative specificity of local norms rather than treating tightness–looseness as a distance measure.

Additional work could directly measure ex ante and ex post transaction costs, incorporate transaction benefits, and study alternative assignee forms such as inpatriates, third-country nationals, short-term assignments, commuter assignments, and virtual assignments. The authors also suggest multilevel research on individual differences, organizational structures, job characteristics, and polycultural abilities.
abstract: Prior research into the effects of cultural differences between multinational enterprises’ (MNEs’) home and host countries on expatriate staffing decisions in foreign subsidiaries has produced a large number of conflicting findings. We address some of these conflicting findings and aim to advance theory in two ways. First, we draw on transaction cost economics to explain why and how the effects of cultural distance on the proportion of expatriate parent-country nationals form a curvilinear relationship, instead of a linear one as commonly proposed. Second, we integrate the values-based cultural distance concept with the norms-based tightness–looseness concept. This allows us to simultaneously account for cultural differences between countries and location-bound normative cultural effects within countries, which cannot be overcome solely through expatriate learning and adaptation. Using a large global dataset of Japanese MNEs, we find support for a convex relationship between cultural distance and the proportion of expatriate parent-country nationals. We also find a moderating (steepening) effect of tightness–looseness on this relationship. The results reconcile some of the tensions between the subjectivists’ values-based approach, which positions culture in the shared cognitions realm, and the structuralists’ approach, which places culture in a normative situational environment.

title: The Message is on the Wall? Emotions, Social Media and the Dynamics of Institutional Complexity
methods: Empirical qualitative process study of a Canadian nonprofit federation, using Facebook comments and likes, media stories, interviews with leaders, organizational documents, web materials, press releases, and staged qualitative coding of logic activation, organizational response, member emotions, and influence activities.
industry: Nonprofit health advocacy and support organization serving individuals with a degenerative disease.
time_period: October 2009 to October 2011.
units: One anonymized Canadian nonprofit federation, its members, leaders, Facebook page activity, media coverage, and organizational communications.
n_sample: 1,849 unique Facebook comments by 472 unique members, 11,293 likes, 116 media stories, 13 interviews, and organizational documents and communications.
authors: Toubiana, M.; Zietsma, C.
theories: emotional registers of logics; emotions in institutional processes; institutional complexity; institutional logics
keywords: Facebook; emotional register; emotions; institutional complexity; institutional logics; shaming; shunning; social media
research_question: How are organizations that face institutional complexity affected by emotions when they confront disruptive events? The paper examines this question through the conflict between the DDF, an anonymized Canadian nonprofit federation, and members whose expectations were violated when the organization prioritized a research logic over a care logic after a controversial treatment emerged.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Institutional complexity between research and care logics; different emotional registers attached to those logics; members' expectations of care-based advocacy; leaders' research-based, nonemotive response.
- Process / phases: Activation of different logics and investment of hope; members' betrayal and shaming while leaders justified authority; members' anger and shunning; DDF regret and mollification.
- Influence activities: Members moved from hope to betrayal, shaming, anger, and shunning, amplified through Facebook and media attention.
- Organizational response: The DDF initially defended its research-logic position, then expressed regret, reintroduced care-logic communication, and adapted through more personal local engagement.
- Boundary conditions: The case involves serious illness, a nonprofit advocacy setting, high emotional investment, and social media activity that may not represent all members.

The process is cross-level. A disruptive treatment activated members' care logic and their hope that the DDF would advocate for access; the DDF instead enacted a research logic grounded in evidence, safety, and professional expertise. Facebook amplified members' betrayal and anger, turning emotion into shaming and then shunning that destabilized the organization through lost support, legitimacy pressure, and public conflict. Resettlement began when DDF leaders expressed regret and communicated in ways that acknowledged members' care logic and emotions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by showing that institutional logics differ not only in goals, means, and sources of legitimacy, but also in emotional registers that prescribe legitimate emotional expression and reasoning. It extends research on institutional complexity by explaining how disruptive events can surface emotional incompatibilities between logics and destabilize an organizational settlement. It also theorizes social media as an emotional echo chamber that amplifies discrete emotions and converts them into influence activities such as shaming and shunning.
practical_implication: Organizations facing emotionally invested constituents should not treat social media communication as one-way transmission of official positions. The study suggests that justifying a rational or expert position may intensify conflict when the audience is embedded in a different logic with a different emotional register. Managers should communicate in the audience's logic, acknowledge emotions after perceived breaches, and respond early before online amplification pushes supporters away and escalates negative affect.
limitations: The authors note that the study focuses predominantly on members posting on Facebook, even though these members may differ from stakeholders who did not engage online. They also state that their data do not conclusively show whether emotive media coverage itself activated the care logic.
future_research: Future research should examine whether stakeholders who engage online differ significantly from those who do not and how such differences affect organizational response. The authors also call for research on whether disruptive triggers with particular emotional content activate logics with matching emotional registers. More work is needed on social media, emotional amplification, and advocacy for uncertain ideas in other institutionally complex contexts.
abstract: In this paper, we explore how emotions influence organizations in situations of institutional complexity. In particular, we study members’ and leaders’ emotive responses and influence activities in response to a disruptive event that led to a violation of expectations. Our findings show that when people’s expectations of an organization’s actions are violated it can trigger a process of emotional escalation that leads to destabilization of the organization through the emotion-laden influence activities of shaming and shunning. The violation in our case resulted in strong negative emotions expressed on Facebook. Facebook acted as an emotional echo chamber where negative emotions were amplified and led to members’ emotion-driven influence activities, eventually triggering regret and adaptation by the organization. We discuss implications for the study of emotions in institutional dynamics.
apa_citation: Toubiana, M., & Zietsma, C. (2017). The message is on the wall? Emotions, social media and the dynamics of institutional complexity. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(3), 922-953. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0208

title: The Emergence of Change in Unexpected Places: Resourcing across Organizational Practices in Strategic Change
methods: Longitudinal, in-depth qualitative case study of strategic change in health care contract management within the National Health Service in England. The authors compare three contract-management practices using observation, interviews, shadowing, archival documents, event-history construction, coding in NVivo, and process analysis.
industry: Public health care services and health care contract management.
time_period: The focal analysis covers July 2009 to March 2013; interviews extended from July 2010 to October 2014.
units: MgmtAgency contract-management practices, MgmtAgency managers, health care provider representatives, GP representatives, and related public health care organizations.
n_sample: More than 700 hours of observation, 66 semi-structured interviews, and over 20 GB of archival data.
authors: Wiedner, Rene; Barrett, Michael; Oborn, Eivor
theories: Bourdieu's relational framework; practice-based theories; resource dependence theory; resourcing perspective
keywords: organizational practices; resources; resourcing; resourcing space; strategic change
research_question: The paper asks how strategic change initiatives shape the use of resources across multiple organizational practices, and why change can emerge in practices that were not prioritized by senior managers. Empirically, it examines divergent developments in hospital, mental health, and community care contract management following strategic change at MgmtAgency in the English NHS.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Potential resources, valued resources, resource revaluations, resource redistributions, agents' interests, coordination costs, scrutiny, willingness to challenge, and resourcing space.
- Process / phases: Strategic change initiators redirect valued resources and attention toward designated change agents and prioritized practices; this redistributes interests across practices; those interests shape coordination costs and scrutiny; change emerges where willing agents can use available resources with low interference.
- Practice-level comparison: Hospital contract management received substantial resources and attention but remained hard to change because GP representatives were reluctant to challenge hospital doctors and faced high coordination costs. Community care contract management drew strong GP and manager interest, creating willingness to challenge but also high scrutiny and negotiation costs. Mental health contract management was deprioritized and lightly resourced, but this lack of interest created space for Kate, GP representatives, and mental health clinicians to coordinate changes quickly.
- Emergent outcome: The most substantial change emerged in mental health contract management, the practice least expected to become the strategic change showpiece.

The process account argues that strategic change initiatives do more than allocate resources to targeted practices. They also revalue and redistribute resources across a field of practices, pulling attention toward some sites and away from others. Where low interest reduces scrutiny and coordination costs, skilled agents may gain resourcing space that allows mutual adjustment and practical change, even without large budgets, staffing, or formal priority.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to strategic change research by shifting attention from whether resources enable change to how strategic change initiatives shape what counts as valuable and where resources, attention, and power become concentrated. It extends resourcing theory by showing that resource use is conditioned by cross-practice redistributions of value, interest, coordination costs, and scrutiny, not only by local skillful use within a single practice. The concept of resourcing space explains how favorable conditions for change can arise in neglected practices because limited attention can reduce interference.
practical_implication: For managers, the study cautions that allocating more resources and formal authority to a priority area does not guarantee change if coordination costs, scrutiny, or deference to powerful incumbents block action. It also suggests that apparently neglected areas may contain usable space for experimentation when actors can recognize and use the lower-interference conditions. Change leaders should therefore monitor unintended cross-practice effects rather than evaluating only the formally targeted practice.
limitations: The authors state that, despite multiple data sources, they cannot rule out all alternative explanations for the dynamics identified. Some parts of the analysis rely on data not captured in real time. The single-case design and intra-case comparisons limit generalization beyond the English NHS setting.
future_research: The paper calls for more research on dynamics across practices, including practices that do not feature prominently on the executive agenda. Future work could examine how strategic change initiatives generate resource revaluations and resourcing space in settings with different occupations, power relations, and degrees of participation. Comparative studies could also investigate when neglected practices become sites of experimentation versus sites of stagnation.
abstract: In our longitudinal, in-depth case study of strategic change within the National Health Service in England, we compare three practices related to contracting health care services. Contrary to what we would have believed from the extant literature, we found that the most profound change did not emerge in practices that witnessed the greatest increase in the quantity of resources or in which change agents were given the highest degree of control. Instead, change emerged in a practice that was not treated as a priority and that subsequently attracted interest from a very limited number of individuals. Our findings contribute to the resourcing literature by showing that the ability to use resources is shaped by how they are valued and distributed, and that strategic change initiatives can act as triggers for resource revaluations and redistributions. Specifically, we demonstrate that strategic change initiatives may contribute to the emergence of favorable conditions for change in practices that do not become associated with valued resources. This is because a lack of valued resources attracts limited interest from stakeholders, thereby allowing changes to emerge as powerful agents face minimal coordination costs and scrutiny when attempting to align arrangements with their own interests. Our study thereby shows how and why change initiatives can trigger divergent developments across multiple practices and lead to change emergence in unexpected places. It also highlights the role of what we call “resourcing space” in contributing to emergent change.

title: Newcomer Identification: Trends, Antecedents, Moderators, and Consequences
methods: Five-wave longitudinal quantitative study using random coefficient modeling, multilevel mediation tests, and proportional hazard models with repeated-measures covariates to examine changes in perceived prestige, psychological contract fulfillment, organizational identification, and voluntary turnover.
industry: IT services organization.
time_period: Survey waves during newcomers' first year, with voluntary turnover tracked over three years of employment.
units: Newcomers to one Indian IT services organization.
n_sample: 1,346 newcomers.
authors: Zhu, J.; Tatachari, S.; Chattopadhyay, P.
theories: psychological contract theory; social identity approach; uncertainty reduction
keywords: newcomer socialization; organizational identification; perceived organizational prestige; personal prestige; psychological contract fulfillment; voluntary turnover
research_question: How does organizational identification change across newcomers' entry, institutionalized socialization, informal socialization, and first assignment, and how do perceived organizational prestige and psychological contract fulfillment explain these changes? The paper also asks how personal prestige markers shape these trajectories and whether the trajectories predict voluntary turnover.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that newcomers use organizational prestige to build positive and clear social identities, while psychological contract fulfillment translates changes in perceived prestige into changes in identification. Formal socialization temporarily raises perceived prestige, contract fulfillment, and identification by reducing uncertainty and emphasizing positive organizational information; informal socialization and first assignment then expose newcomers to more ambiguous organizational realities. Higher personal prestige markers alter how newcomers benchmark the firm's prestige, producing different trajectories and downstream turnover risk.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends social identity research by theorizing organizational identification as a dynamic construct that rises, falls, and partially recovers across newcomer milestones rather than as a stable attitude. It contributes to psychological contract theory by showing how a diffuse organizational attribute, perceived prestige, can be interpreted through contract fulfillment and then linked to identification and turnover. It also connects newcomer socialization milestones to longitudinal changes in prestige, contract fulfillment, and identification.
practical_implication: Managers should treat the period between formal socialization and first assignment as a high-risk point for declines in contract fulfillment and identification. The findings suggest reinforcing positive organizational features, reducing uncertainty, increasing veteran support, grouping newcomers with similar qualifications or regional backgrounds where appropriate, and respecting preferred-location assignments when possible.
limitations: The study is based on one Indian IT services firm, so generalizability depends on whether other firms use comparable institutionalized socialization and first-assignment timing. The authors also note possible reciprocal relationships among prestige, psychological contract fulfillment, and identification, and acknowledge that psychological contract violation emotions could further mediate the process. The perceived prestige measure was shortened, although a separate validation sample supported it.
future_research: Future studies should examine how different temporal distributions, durations, and intensities of socialization milestones affect identification and turnover trajectories. Research could also test reciprocal dynamics among perceived prestige, contract fulfillment, and identification, include psychological contract violation as a finer-grained mediator, and examine other pre-entry organizational information that shapes newcomer identification and retention.
abstract: We examine changes in organizational identification among 1,346 newcomers at critical milestones during their first year. Integrating the social identity approach with the literature on psychological contracts, we argue that changes in newcomer perceptions of organizational prestige influence changes in their organizational identification over time, mediated by changes in their perceptions of the extent to which their psychological contract has been fulfilled. Our five-wave results reveal that perceived prestige, psychological contract fulfillment, and organizational identification rise during institutionalized socialization, then fall immediately after this period, and finally recover and stabilize as employees settle into their first assignment. Newcomers’ personal prestige markers, including academic qualifications, the proportion of in-group members in the incoming cohort, and organizational preferential treatment moderate these change patterns, which subsequently predict the speed and occurrence of newcomers’ voluntary turnover over three years of employment.
apa_citation: Zhu, J., Tatachari, S., & Chattopadhyay, P. (2017). Newcomer identification: Trends, antecedents, moderators, and consequences. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(3), 855-879. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0466

title: Falling in Love Again with What We Do: Academic Craftsmanship in the Management Sciences
methods: Editorial (From the Editors) essay using the analogy of sushi craftsmanship to argue for academic craftsmanship in management research.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Baer, Markus; Shaw, Jason D.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: academic craftsmanship; clear, honest, and direct communication; pride and perfection; research question; societal welfare
research_question: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Craftsmanship framing: Baer and Shaw define academic craftsmanship as the noble and socially responsible pursuit of perfection in creating new understandings about organizations.
- Falling in love with the question: They argue that scholars should craft research questions that need answering, are worth answering, and are personally meaningful.
- Pride and perfection: They connect academic craftsmanship to care in study design, data analysis, manuscript preparation, and psychological ownership of ideas.
- Societal welfare: They argue that management research should contribute to scholarly, student, business, and public communities through rigor, relevance, and accessible communication.
- Anti-shortcut norm: They warn against opportunistic projects, hasty execution, and novelty-through-terminology that obstruct knowledge accumulation.

The process is editorial and normative rather than empirical. Baer and Shaw use Jiro Ono's sushi craftsmanship as an analogy for scholarly work, then translate craftsmanship into three expectations for management researchers: intimate commitment to worthwhile questions, pride and care in execution, and responsibility to the communities served by research.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a formal theory. Its contribution is to articulate "academic craftsmanship" as a standard for management scholarship that integrates intrinsic motivation, careful research design, clear communication, rigor, relevance, and responsibility to the wider community.
practical_implication: For authors, the editorial implies that research projects should begin with carefully crafted questions rather than available data, opportunistic collaborations, or momentary novelty. It also advises scholars to treat design, analysis, writing, and accessibility as craft responsibilities rather than as secondary steps after publication goals.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The editorial encourages future management research to formulate questions that address important problems, contribute to community or societal welfare, and are personally meaningful enough to sustain long-term scholarly commitment. It also implies a need for work that combines well-crafted theory, carefully designed empirical studies, rigorous analysis, and clear communication for audiences inside and outside academia.
abstract: Not reported in paper

title: Bringing the Boss’s Politics In: Supervisor Political Ideology and the Gender Gap in Earnings
methods: Longitudinal archival quantitative study of associate lawyers and supervising partners in a large U.S. law firm, combining internal personnel records, client billings, performance-based bonus data, and public political donation records; analyses use mixed effects regression models with worker and supervisor random intercepts plus robustness checks with fixed effects and alternative relationship thresholds.
industry: Legal services; one large, full-service law firm.
time_period: Worker-year data cover 2002 to 2007 inclusive; supervisor political donations are measured over 1990 to 2014.
units: Worker-supervisor-year ties between standard associate lawyers and supervising partners.
n_sample: 908 worker-supervisor-year observations on 359 distinct workers tied to 119 distinct supervisors over six years; regression models report N=906.
authors: Briscoe, F.; Joshi, A.
theories: male-typed schemas of success; managerial discretion; motivated cognition; perceptual filtering; political ideology
keywords: conservatism; gender gap in earnings; gender inequality; law firms; managerial discretion; motivated cognition; perceptual filtering; performance-based pay; political liberalism; supervisor political ideology
research_question: To what extent do supervisors' personal political values shape performance evaluation and reward allocation decisions for male and female professional workers? The paper asks whether supervisor liberalism versus conservatism reduces or enlarges the gender gap in performance-based pay, and whether that effect changes with worker seniority and work-unit ideology.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that political ideology shapes how supervisors interpret ambiguous performance information when objective criteria are weak. Liberal supervisors are theorized to reject inequality and social-status-quo explanations, making them more likely to give female workers the benefit of the doubt in male-typed professional settings. Conservative supervisors are theorized to accept existing outcome differences as reflecting individual human capital or motivation, which preserves a larger gender gap in rewards. This ideological difference becomes more consequential as workers gain seniority because senior work is more complex, subjective, and tied to entry into the firm's leadership ranks.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on gender inequality by shifting attention from supervisor demographic similarity and formal organizational practices to supervisors' personal political beliefs as a source of bias in reward allocation. It shows how ostensibly gender-neutral values about inequality and social change can enter everyday managerial decisions through perceptual filtering. It also extends political ideology research from senior executives and firm-level outcomes to proximal supervisory decisions affecting individual workers.
practical_implication: The paper cautions against assuming that more discretion or more female supervisors will automatically reduce gender inequality in professional workplaces. It suggests that organizations should track gender gaps at the supervisor level and create incentives or peer-observation mechanisms that reward equitable allocation of bonuses, projects, and learning opportunities. The authors also note that client advocacy and professional association pressure may help because some sources of gender inequality originate outside formal organizational policy.
limitations: The study uses one large law firm, so the authors state that the results need replication in other settings to assess generalizability. The design relies on political donations as an unobtrusive proxy for ideology and cannot directly observe the psychological process of perceptual filtering or all possible subjective information supervisors may use. The authors also acknowledge that their opportunity-provision measures are limited, so they cannot entirely rule out access to valuable work as a pathway.
future_research: Future research should test whether supervisor ideology affects other historically disadvantaged groups, including racial minorities, LGBT workers, immigrants, and religious minorities. The authors call for work on whether subordinates perceive supervisor ideological leanings and adjust mobility or career behavior in response. They also suggest studying parenting, other dispositional measures related to inequality and social change, and the consequences of outsourcing or automating routine work for bias in subjective evaluation.
abstract: The gender gap in earnings and rewards remains persistent across many professional and managerial work contexts. In these settings, where there are few objective criteria for performance and organizational mechanisms are weak, we propose that personal political values can serve as a powerful influence on whether supervisors reduce or enhance inequalities in performance-based rewards. We develop theory about how political liberalism versus conservatism affects supervisors’ perceptions and allocative decision-making. Combining internal personnel and billings data with publicly available political donation records in a large law firm, we test the effect of political ideology among supervising law firm partners on the performance-based bonuses awarded to male and female subordinate lawyers. We find the male–female gender gap in performance-based pay is reduced for professional workers tied to liberal supervisors, relative to conservative supervisors. We further find this political ideology effect increases for workers with greater seniority in the organization. Our findings contribute to an understanding of the determinants of the gender earnings gap, suggesting that, in settings where managers have leeway over rewards and careers, their personal political beliefs have an important influence on outcomes for male and female workers.
apa_citation: Briscoe, F., & Joshi, A. (2017). Bringing the boss’s politics in: Supervisor political ideology and the gender gap in earnings. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(4), 1415-1441. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2016.0179

title: Ideology and the Micro-foundations of CSR: Why Executives Believe in the Business Case for CSR and how this Affects their CSR Engagements
methods: Four empirical quantitative studies using executive, MBA/EMBA, and student samples. The studies combine an incentivized prediction game measuring belief in the CSP-CFP link, a fair market ideology scale, an experimental salience manipulation, mediation analysis, and a multiple-mediator model linking fair market ideology, moral outrage, and tendency for CSR engagement.
industry: Executive education and student participant samples; the prediction-game company information used social and financial performance data for large companies from the Dow Jones Sector Titans Index rather than one focal industry.
country: Studies 1-3 recruited participants from a large Swiss university; Study 4 recruited from Swiss and Dutch MBA/EMBA settings.
time_period: Participant data collection dates are not reported in paper. The prediction-game company data used Covalence EthicalQuote and COMPUSTAT information for 2002-2006.
units: Individual executives, MBA/EMBA participants, and students; company-level CSP/CFP data were used as stimuli in the prediction games.
n_sample: Study 1: 47 executives; Study 2: 75 business and economics students; Study 3: 102 students; Study 4: 96 managers and executives.
authors: Hafenbrädl, Sebastian; Waeger, Daniel
theories: micro-foundations of CSR; system justification theory; upper echelons theory
keywords: CSR engagement; business case for CSR; fair market ideology; micro-foundations of CSR; moral outrage; system justification theory
research_question: The paper asks why executives believe in the business case for CSR and whether that belief actually makes them more inclined to engage in CSR. It examines whether fair market ideology explains executives' belief in a positive CSP-CFP link while also weakening moral outrage toward ethical problems, thereby offsetting the expected positive effect of business-case belief on CSR engagement.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that fair market ideology motivates managers to justify and idealize the market economy system. This makes them more likely to believe that CSR must have economic value because firms already engage in CSR, but it also dampens moral outrage when they confront ethical problems in the market system. In Study 4, the positive indirect path from fair market ideology to CSR engagement through belief in the CSP-CFP link is neutralized by the negative indirect path through weaker moral outrage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to micro-foundations research on CSR by showing that executives' CSR-related beliefs and moral emotions are not independent drivers but can originate in the same ideology. It cautions against the assumption that belief in the business case for CSR is enough to motivate CSR engagement, because the same fair market ideology that produces business-case belief also reduces moral responsiveness to ethical problems. It also advances upper echelons research by directly measuring belief in the CSP-CFP link through a prediction game rather than relying only on distant biographical proxies.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that persuading executives about the financial merits of CSR may be insufficient if those executives also have weaker moral outrage toward social, environmental, or ethical problems. CSR engagement may require attention not only to instrumental business-case arguments but also to the moral sensitivity that makes executives perceive problems as requiring action. Organizations should be cautious about treating business, economics, or law educational backgrounds as simple proxies for higher CSR orientation.
limitations: The authors note that the studies took place in controlled classroom settings, which supported clean measurement and causal inference but may limit external validity. Their measure of business-case belief represents the CSP-CFP relationship as one linear coefficient, even though executives may believe in more complex or nonlinear returns to CSR. The analysis is also at the individual-executive level, while real CSR decisions are often made in teams.
future_research: Future research could test the framework with field data on actual CSR engagement and follow executives over time to examine whether changes in fair market ideology affect business-case beliefs, moral outrage, and firm CSR behavior. Researchers could also test whether executives perceive nonlinear returns to CSR and whether executive-team diversity in ideology, education, and moral outrage changes CSR decisions. The authors also suggest extending the framework to consumers, investors, regulators, and other evaluators of corporate activity.
abstract: Existing research on executives’ belief in the business case for corporate social responsibility (CSR) is built on two premises. The first is that, in order to believe in the business case, executives need factual evidence that this business case indeed exists. The second premise is that those executives who do believe in the business case will readily invest in CSR-related activities. The results from our four studies tell a different story. We show that managers, rather than focusing on factual evidence, believe in the business case because they espouse a fair market ideology—the tendency to justify and idealize the market economy system. At the same time, even though managers espousing a fair market ideology believe in the business case for CSR, they are not more inclined to engage in CSR than managers who do not hold such an ideology, because they also experience weaker moral emotions when confronted with ethical problems. By drawing on system justification theory, we simultaneously explore antecedents and consequences of executives’ belief in the business case for CSR and of their moral emotions. In doing so, we help advance knowledge about the micro-foundations of CSR.

title: Unequal Bedfellows: Gender Role-based Deference in Multiplex Ties between Korean Business Groups
methods: Event-study analysis of Korean chaebol dyad-market-year observations around marriage ties, combining difference-in-differences logic, coarsened exact matching, probit models with clustered standard errors, endogeneity checks, and supplementary performance regressions; qualitative executive interviews provide contextual evidence.
industry: Korean chaebols across 4-digit industry markets
units: Chaebol dyad-market-year observations around intermarriage events
n_sample: 60 Korean chaebols; 23 marriages; four event-study datasets
authors: Han, JungYun; Shipilov, Andrew V.; Greve, Henrich R.
theories: Confucian gender-role norms; competitive positioning; multiplex relationships; status and deference theory
keywords: Korean business groups; competitive positioning; deference; gender-based status differences; market entries or exits; multiplex relationships
research_question: The paper asks whether deference in the personal domain of a multiplex tie can spill over into the business domain and shape strategic market entry and exit. It examines this question through marriages between owner-families of Korean business groups, where Confucian gender-role norms create asymmetric deference between the husband's and wife's families.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is cross-level: culturally prescribed gender-role deference between families alters strategic behavior by the business groups those families own. Marriage creates a trusted communication channel, but the husband's chaebol is expected to actively reconfigure market positions while the wife's chaebol accommodates and restrains its own entry or exit. The quantitative results support this asymmetry: after marriage, husbands' chaebols become more likely to enter and exit wives' markets, whereas wives' chaebols become less likely to enter or exit husbands' markets.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to multiplexity research by identifying deference spillover as a mechanism through which one relational domain can shape behavior in another. It also contributes to competitive positioning by showing that market entry and exit are not only responses to economic overlap, market munificence, or multimarket contact, but can also be shaped by personal ties and culturally grounded status asymmetries.
practical_implication: The study implies that personal-family ties can influence market strategy even without formal alliances or ownership links. Apparently economic market-positioning decisions may reflect embedded family obligations, gendered status hierarchies, and informal coordination between business groups.
limitations: The study is set in Korean chaebols, where owner-family control and Confucian kinship norms make the mechanism especially visible. The authors argue that the implications go beyond Korea and other Confucian cultures because deference in one relational domain can spill into another, but the empirical evidence is drawn from this specific Korean business-group context.
future_research: Future research could examine other multiplex ties in which deference in one domain conflicts with or reinforces deference in another. It could more directly study the conditions under which a deference pattern in one domain dominates another and identify additional sources of multiplexity effects on interorganizational networks and interpersonal behavior in organizations.
abstract: Deference within a dyad occurs when one partner acknowledges that the other is entitled to some privileges. Although deference is a well-known consequence of relationships between partners of unequal status, little is known on whether deference in one domain can affect interactions between the same actors in other domains. This can happen within multiplex relationships, especially when they involve firms that have both business and personal interactions between their key decision makers. We combine insights from the literatures on status, multiplex relationships, and competitive positioning to examine how actors’ behaviors in a business domain of a multiplex relationship are shaped by the deference norms in a personal domain of the same relationship. We argue that marriages between owner-families of Korean business groups cause deferential behaviors between these families as a function of gender-based status differences within kinship ties. We show empirically that the inter-personal deference resulting from marriage affects business group market entries or exits, and in turn the group’s performance. Thus, we shed light on how deference spillovers represent a novel mechanism through which one partner can extract advantage over another within a multiplex relationship.

title: Glass Breaking, Strategy Making, and Value Creating: Meta-Analytic Outcomes of Women as CEOs and TMT members
methods: Meta-analysis of 146 primary studies using random-effects meta-analytic effect-size estimation, random-effects meta-regression for moderators, and meta-analytic structural path analysis for mediation.
industry: Firm-level primary studies across multiple organizational contexts; no single industry restriction is reported.
time_period: Primary data collection in the included studies ranged from 1983 through 2014.
units: Primary studies and effect sizes concerning female CEOs, female TMT membership, strategic risk-taking, long-term financial performance, and short-term stock market returns.
n_sample: 146 primary studies, including 90 published and 56 unpublished studies.
authors: Jeong, Seung-Hwan; Harrison, David A.
theories: group polarization; managerial discretion; role incongruity theory; upper echelons perspective
keywords: decision latitude; female representation in the upper echelons; firm performance; long-term financial performance; role incongruity theory; short-term stock market returns; strategic risk-taking
research_question: The paper asks what firm-performance consequences follow from female representation in upper echelons roles, specifically female CEOs and female TMT members. It also asks why those consequences occur and under what country-level and organizational conditions they become stronger or weaker.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that female CEOs and female TMT members influence strategy making through unique resource portfolios and TMT decision-process changes that reduce strategic risk-taking. Reduced risk-taking helps explain why female representation is associated with stronger long-term financial performance. At the same time, role incongruity perceptions among investors produce negative short-term market reactions to female CEO appointments, even though the longer-term financial association is positive.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates upper echelons theory, gender differences in strategic risk-taking, team information elaboration, managerial discretion, and role incongruity theory into one meta-analytic framework. It clarifies that the accumulated evidence does not support a long-term financial performance penalty for women in CEO or TMT roles; instead, the main financial effects are small and positive. It also separates long-term value creation from short-term investor reactions, showing that stakeholder perceptions and realized firm outcomes can diverge.
practical_implication: The findings offer no empirical basis for avoiding female executive appointments on expected financial-performance grounds. Boards and investors should be cautious about interpreting immediate negative stock-market reactions to female CEO appointments as evidence of weaker leadership effectiveness. The results also imply that women executives may have greater impact where country and organizational contexts give executives more decision latitude.
limitations: The authors note that meta-analysis of firm-level summary data permits only indirect inference about the behavioral mechanisms inside CEOs and TMTs. They cannot fully rule out omitted variables or endogeneity, and the available primary studies constrain how precisely female TMT membership, strategic risk-taking, and industry contexts can be measured. The observed effects are also small, even though small financial-performance correlations may still be practically meaningful.
future_research: Future research should examine finer-grained mechanisms, including female executives' risk-taking tendencies, TMT information elaboration, and possible marginalization processes inside male-dominated executive groups. The authors call for longitudinal, multinational, and multi-year primary studies that can connect CEO and TMT changes to later strategic choices and subsequent firm performance. They also encourage studies of additional moderators, broader stakeholder reactions, and corporate social performance outcomes.
abstract: We conduct a comprehensive synthesis of the research on how female representation in the upper echelons (i.e., top management teams and chief executive officer positions) might affect firm performance. To help resolve longstanding theoretical, empirical, and substantive debates, we present an integrative conceptual framework based on the overarching concepts of unique resource portfolios, team decision-processes, and role incongruence perceptions. We test predictions from this framework using meta-analytic techniques on a sample of 146 primary studies conducted in 33 different countries. We find that female representation in the upper echelons in general is positively and weakly related to forms of long-term financial performance, but negatively and weakly related to short-term stock market returns. We observe that reduced strategic risk-taking is a mediating mechanism that explains why financial performance is improved. We also show that financial performance improvements are accentuated in environmental and organizational contexts that provide greater decision latitude to executives. Finally, we discuss and provide preliminary tests for extending these effects to other stakeholders (corporate social performance) and different time intervals for performance.

title: Symbiont Practices in Boundary Spanning: Bridging the Cognitive and Political Divides in Interdisciplinary Research
methods: Nine-month field study of a U.S. NSF-funded nanotechnology research center, combining observations, 22 semi-structured interviews, documentary evidence, publication/coauthorship data, citation analysis, and student career data.
industry: University-based nanotechnology and interdisciplinary science research.
time_period: Fieldwork from September 2008 to May 2009; archival publication and career data spanning the NSF grant period and through 2013.
units: Nano Center faculty, PhD students, postdoctoral fellows, meetings, collaborations, instruments, publications, and career paths.
n_sample: 242 Nano Center participants in Table 1; 22 interviewees; 2,355 publications; 68 Nano Center PhD graduates compared with 65 materials science PhD students.
authors: Kaplan, S.; Milde, J.; Cowan, R. S.
theories: Knorr-Cetina's symbiont concept; boundary objects; boundary spanning theory; sociomaterial perspective on boundary spanning
keywords: boundary spanning; interdisciplinary research; scientific instruments; sociomaterial perspective; symbiont practices
research_question: The paper asks how interdisciplinary collaborations take place when cognitive structures and political economies remain anchored in disciplines. More specifically, it asks how cognitive and political boundaries are spanned simultaneously in interdisciplinary research.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: cognitive incommensurability across disciplines; political economy of research rewards; costly scientific instruments; student capacities; symbiont practices.
- Process / practices: matching disciplinary language and methods with instrument possibilities; developing cospecialization between students and instruments; engaging disciplinary actors to design experiments using specific instruments.
- Emergent outcomes: interdisciplinary collaborations become possible when students translate across disciplines, master instruments, absorb some risk, and make instruments legible and useful to faculty in different domains.
- Boundary conditions: the prominence of the student-instrument relationship is tied to an instrument-intensive scientific context and the uncertainty of nanotechnology as an emerging field.

The central process is sociomaterial rather than purely interpersonal. Instruments create incipient possibilities for new questions, funding, and collaboration, but these possibilities remain unrealized until students develop specialized competence and use that competence to connect faculty, methods, and disciplinary interests. Students also need the instruments because instrument expertise helps classify them, staff them on projects, and support their career prospects, producing a reciprocal symbiosis.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a sociomaterial perspective on boundary spanning by showing that boundary work can occur through symbiont practices rather than through people or objects alone. It extends boundary-spanning and boundary-object research by arguing that instruments do more than convey information across domains: they become subjects of boundary-spanning practices whose possibilities are actualized through student-instrument symbiosis. It also explains why lower-status actors, not only high-status brokers, may do critical boundary-spanning work when the required investments are costly and uncertain.
practical_implication: From a policy standpoint, the authors argue that their framework can help evaluate university practices designed to facilitate interdisciplinary work. The study highlights the need to enable student-instrument symbiosis on both cognitive and political dimensions and suggests that targeted interventions may address interdisciplinary barriers without physically separating interdisciplinary units from departments.
limitations: The authors identify boundary conditions rather than a formal limitations section. The instrument-laden nature of nanotechnology research and uncertainty around new instruments in the emerging nanotechnology field may explain why the student-instrument relationship was so visible in this case.
future_research: The paper does not present a formal future-research agenda.
abstract: Organizing for interdisciplinary research must overcome two challenges to collaboration: the cognitive incommensurability of knowledge and the political economy of research based in the disciplines. Researchers may not engage in interdisciplinarity because they would have to invest in new knowledge unrelated to their discipline or risk losing career-related rewards. Our field study of a university interdisciplinary research center shows that boundary spanning occurred as students interacted with scientific instruments in a symbiotic relationship through what we call symbiont practices: matching disciplinary language and methods with the experimental possibilities of instruments, developing cospecialization between students and instruments, and engaging disciplinary actors to design experiments using instruments. Instruments engendered incipient interdisciplinary possibilities, but they required the students—engaging in symbiont practices—to actualize that potential. Simultaneously, students required instruments in order to be classified, staffed on projects, and placed in jobs. These practices resolved both the cognitive and economic challenges of boundary spanning by mobilizing material resources that were costly (cognitively and politically) for actors on either side of the disciplinary divide to engage. In conceptualizing interdisciplinary research as occurring through symbiont practices, we develop a sociomaterial perspective on boundary spanning.

title: The Face of the Firm: The Influence of CEOs on Corporate Reputation
methods: Panel study of large U.S. firms using Fortune reputation ratings, ExecuComp CEO data, CEO and firm media coverage from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, Financial World CEO awards, COMPUSTAT financial controls, generalized propensity score analysis, and fixed-effects robustness models.
industry: Large industrial and service firms covered by Fortune's Most Admired Company survey.
units: Firm-years for large U.S. firms and their CEOs
n_sample: 372 firms; 1,599 firm-years
authors: Love, E. G.; Lim, J.; Bednar, M. K.
theories: certification contests; information availability; uncertainty reduction; upper echelon perspective
keywords: CEOs; corporate reputation; industry awards; leader prominence; leader quality; media coverage; outsider standing
research_question: The paper asks to what degree CEOs independently matter for firm reputation and which CEOs affect their firms' reputations. It focuses on whether CEO media coverage, media tenor, industry awards, and outsider status shape Fortune reputation ratings after accounting for firm financial performance and firm-level media coverage.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that evaluators use CEOs as signals of the firm's underlying capabilities and propensities, especially because leadership quality is difficult to observe directly. Media coverage can make CEOs salient and provide positive or negative evaluations of CEO quality, while industry awards act as certification contests that reduce uncertainty about leadership quality. The findings support quality-signal effects: positive CEO media tenor and CEO awards are associated with stronger firm reputations, negative CEO media tenor is associated with weaker firm reputation, and prominence alone and outsider status are not supported.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends upper-echelons and CEO celebrity research by showing that CEOs can influence not only firm actions and performance but also corporate reputation as a consequential intangible outcome. It also contributes to corporate reputation research by positioning leadership as an integral determinant of reputational judgments, distinct from the firm behaviors, outcomes, and capabilities emphasized in prior work. More broadly, it develops the idea that social evaluations can transfer between internal actors and organizations whose reputations co-evolve.
practical_implication: The findings imply that boards and executives should not assume that CEO visibility itself improves corporate reputation; reputational effects depend more on signals of CEO quality than on prominence alone. Firms may gain reputational benefits when CEOs receive credible positive evaluations such as industry awards or favorable coverage, but negative CEO coverage can damage firm reputation.
limitations: The paper notes that the study covers a relatively short and historically specific period, uses large U.S. public firms, and does not capture all relevant CEO characteristics. It also cautions that CEO information was less available for smaller firms, so the findings may not apply to small or less well-known firms.
future_research: Future research could examine whether leader-quality signals affect non-U.S. firms differently, given evidence that CEO effects vary across national contexts. The paper also calls for studies of private and family firms, more nuanced work on outsider CEO succession, and closer examination of the processes through which leaders enter reputational evaluations and produce enduring rather than transitory effects.
abstract: It is widely assumed that CEOs shape how people view firms, but the question of how these leaders influence corporate reputations has received little theoretical or empirical attention. This study addresses two core questions in this vein: to what degree do leaders really matter for firm reputation, and which leaders affect their firm’s reputation? We develop theory to explain how and why leaders should enter into evaluations of the firms that they lead. Specifically, we propose that CEOs’ effects on corporate reputation will depend on leader prominence and on perceptions of leader quality. We thus test hypotheses that examine how CEOs’ media coverage, industry awards, and outsider standing affect the reputations of their firms. Our findings indicate that highly regarded CEOs enhance their firms’ reputations, sometimes substantially, and CEOs who receive negative press coverage damage their firms’ reputations. However, CEO prominence alone is not associated with higher firm reputation. We discuss implications for research on top leaders and corporate reputations.

title: I Just Can’t Control Myself: A Self-Regulation Perspective on the Abuse of Deviant Employees
methods: Two multisource field studies: Study 1 uses a time-lagged supervisor-subordinate dyad design with hierarchical regression and bootstrapped moderated mediation; Study 2 uses four-wave longitudinal cross-lagged mediation models with multilevel modeling and Monte Carlo confidence intervals.
industry: Study 1: a variety of organizations; Study 2: a property management company
time_period: Study 1: two survey waves separated by two weeks; Study 2: weekly surveys across four weeks
units: Supervisor-subordinate dyads
n_sample: Study 1: 165 matched dyads; Study 2: 169 unique supervisor-subordinate dyads
authors: Mawritz, Mary B.; Greenbaum, Rebecca L.; Butts, Marcus M.; Graham, Katrina A.
theories: self-regulation theory; social exchange theory
keywords: abusive supervision; bottom-line mentality; social exchange; subordinate deviance; subordinate performance; supervisor self-regulation impairment
research_question: The paper asks why and when subordinate deviance leads supervisors to engage in abusive supervision. It tests whether supervisor self-regulation impairment explains this relationship more strongly than social exchange, and whether subordinate performance and supervisor bottom-line mentality intensify the impairment process.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that deviant subordinate behavior consumes supervisors' limited self-regulatory resources because supervisors must process, interpret, and manage the aversive behavior. Once impaired, supervisors are less able to constrain abusive urges, making abusive supervision more likely. The effect is stronger when the deviant employee is also a high performer, because the supervisor receives inconsistent performance information, and when the supervisor has a high bottom-line mentality, because deviance conflicts with a salient goal of bottom-line attainment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to abusive supervision research by shifting attention from deliberate retaliation toward a self-regulation explanation of how supervisors may abuse deviant employees without careful forethought. It also compares self-regulation theory with social exchange theory and finds that self-regulation impairment is the stronger mediator in the tested model. The study further extends work on subordinate performance and bottom-line mentality by showing that normally valued performance-related conditions can make deviance more draining for supervisors.
practical_implication: The findings imply that organizations should treat subordinate deviance as a trigger that can escalate into abusive supervision through supervisor resource depletion. Organizations can reduce this risk by setting clear norms against destructive behavior, rewarding conduct aligned with normative standards, training supervisors to conserve self-regulatory resources, and making clear that abusive responses to deviance or bottom-line threats are not tolerated.
limitations: Study 1 is time-lagged but cannot rule out reverse causality for some relationships; Study 2 was designed to address this with a more controlled four-wave design and social exchange comparison. Across both studies, the authors note that the sample sizes were relatively small, so larger replications are warranted.
future_research: Future research could examine other employee behaviors that may provoke abuse, such as domineering or threatening behavior, and whether supervisors sometimes use abusive supervision coercively to change employee conduct. The authors also call for more work on bottom-line mentality, including moderators that explain when a narrow bottom-line focus drains or conserves self-regulatory resources.
abstract: Drawing on self-regulation theory, we contribute to the abusive supervision literature by testing supervisors’ self-regulation impairment as a key mediator of the relationship between subordinate deviance and abusive supervision. Further, given that the process underlying the relationship between subordinate deviance and abusive supervision may be explained by social exchange theory, we examine the differential strength of supervisor self-regulation impairment versus social exchange as mediating mechanisms. We also explore the moderating effects of subordinate performance and supervisor bottom-line mentality (i.e., a one-dimensional frame of mind that revolves around securing bottom-line outcomes to the neglect of competing priorities) on the relationship between subordinate deviance and supervisor self-regulation impairment. We found that supervisor self-regulation impairment mediated the relationship between subordinate deviance and abusive supervision, and the indirect effect was stronger in the presence of high subordinate performance and high supervisor bottom-line mentality. We then replicated these findings in a longitudinal field study across four time periods, and demonstrated that self-regulation impairment provides a stronger explanation for the relationship between subordinate deviance and abusive supervision than social exchange. The theoretical and practical implications of our research are discussed.
apa_citation: Mawritz, M. B., Greenbaum, R. L., Butts, M. M., & Graham, K. A. (2017). I just can’t control myself: A self-regulation perspective on the abuse of deviant employees. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(4), 1482-1503. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0409

title: Risk Aversion and Guanxi Activities: A Behavioral Analysis of CEOs in China
methods: Empirical quantitative study combining a manager and firm survey with incentivized behavioral tasks using multiple price list formats for risk elicitation. The analysis uses OLS regression models, split-sample contingency tests by firm age and market orientation, and interaction models linking guanxi, risk aversion, and firm performance.
industry: Private manufacturing companies in textiles, ordinary machinery, automobile and vehicle parts, pharmaceuticals, and electronic and communication appliances.
time_period: The focal analysis uses the 2009 CEO survey; the broader panel survey was first conducted in 2006 and repeated at three-year intervals, with 2012 data used for robustness checks.
units: CEOs and private manufacturing firms in seven municipalities of China's extended Yangzi Delta region.
n_sample: 345 valid CEOs in the risk-aversion task analysis.
authors: Opper, Sonja; Nee, Victor; Holm, Håkan J.
theories: behavioral strategy; guanxi theory; investment theory; upper echelon theories
keywords: CEO preferences; China; behavioral strategy; guanxi activities; investment theory; risk aversion
research_question: The paper asks whether CEO risk aversion helps explain between-firm differences in strategic reliance on guanxi activities after organizational resources and institutional conditions are considered. It also asks whether firm age and market orientation condition this association, and whether risk-averse CEOs obtain stronger financial returns when they do use guanxi.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an investment logic of relational strategy. Guanxi activities require costly investments of CEO time and firm resources, while future returns are uncertain because ties may fail, political or market conditions may change, and partners may move or defect. More risk-averse CEOs are therefore less inclined to invest heavily in guanxi at the margin, especially for established firms and nonlocal government ties where risk-return tradeoffs are more salient. When risk-averse CEOs do use guanxi, the paper argues that their caution may lead them to select and manage ties more carefully, which is associated with stronger ROA effects.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends guanxi research by shifting attention from organizational and institutional antecedents to CEO dispositional preferences. It develops a behaviorally grounded investment theory of guanxi strategy, arguing that personal risk preferences shape relational strategic choices and their performance consequences. It also contributes to behavioral strategy and upper-echelons research by using incentivized risk-elicitation tasks with a stratified random sample of CEOs rather than relying only on demographic proxies or convenience samples.
practical_implication: Executives should not treat guanxi investment as an unavoidable cultural requirement for doing business in China. The findings suggest that guanxi's financial value is limited and contingent on behavior-strategy fit, especially the CEO's risk preferences and the firm's age and market orientation. For policymakers, the weak direct performance effects of guanxi support efforts to separate business and government spheres as markets become more institutionalized.
limitations: The authors caution that the sample is relatively homogeneous: private manufacturing firms in one of China's most developed and liberalized regions, with many owner-managed and medium-scale firms. This setting may make CEO preferences especially visible in firm strategy and limits generalization to other ownership forms, regions, or institutional environments. The analysis is association-based, and the authors note that causal inference from the sample requires caution despite robustness checks and intertemporal stability.
future_research: Future research could test similar behavioral mechanisms in less developed Chinese regions, rural areas, and more institutionally varied settings. The authors also call for research on whether risk-averse CEOs select exchange partners more carefully and monitor guanxi more closely. Broader applications could examine whether CEO risk aversion affects other long-horizon relational strategies such as R&D partnerships, internationalization, lobbying, alliances, and mergers and acquisitions.
abstract: In China, the strategic use of personal relationships is pervasive in transactions with government authorities as well as in interfirm relations. Explanations as to when and why firms rely on guanxi emphasize a close link between organizational resources, environment, and corporate strategic choices. Our study shifts attention to the importance of CEO preferences, specifically risk aversion, and suggests an investment theory of strategic reliance on personal relations to achieve organizational goals. To explore the association between CEO risk aversion and reliance on guanxi activities, we combine incentivized behavioral tasks using multiple price list formats for risk elicitation with a manager and firm survey. Our analysis focuses on 345 randomly sampled CEOs of private manufacturing companies in the Yangzi Delta region in China. The results confirm the importance of risk preferences in explaining strategic choices and performance effects: there is a negative association between risk aversion and reliance on guanxi activities, although company age and market orientation moderate the behavioral effect of risk preferences. However, when risk-averse CEOs utilize guanxi, they tend to be more successful, as measured by the firm’s financial performance. More generally, our results underscore the importance of personal preferences as determinants of corporate strategy and performance.

title: Institutional Complexity in Turbulent Times: Formalization, Collaboration, and the Emergence of Blended Logics
methods: Inductive, longitudinal multiple case study using grounded-theory coding of interviews and archival data from four Italian work integration social enterprises.
industry: Work integration social enterprises in cleaning services, carpentry, and waste management.
time_period: Organizational processes from mid-2008 to the end of 2012; data gathered between early 2009 and late 2013.
units: Four mature work integration social enterprises: Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta.
n_sample: Four mature WISEs.
authors: Ramus, Tommaso; Vaccaro, Antonino; Brusoni, Stefano
theories: hybrid organizations; institutional complexity; institutional logics perspective
keywords: blended logics; collaboration; environmental turbulence; formalization; institutional complexity; social enterprises
research_question: The paper asks how organizations originally guided by a central institutional logic change when environmental turbulence amplifies a previously peripheral competing logic. Empirically, it examines how Italian work integration social enterprises responded when the financial crisis made both social and commercial logics central to organizational survival.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Institutional complexity, environmental turbulence, internal tensions, social logic, commercial logic, collaboration, formalization, blended logics.
- Process / phases: Collaboration without formalizing the peripheral logic; simultaneous collaboration and formalization; sequential formalization, formalized collaboration, and collaborative formalization.
- Practices: Meetings, shared information, conjoint hiring and contract-management work, written rules, role clarification, and revised procedures for social and commercial tasks.
- Emergent outcomes: Dominant-logics relapse at Alpha and Beta, unresolved conflict at Gamma, and blended-logics integration at Delta.
- Boundary conditions: The process is observed in mature Italian WISEs facing crisis-driven pressure to satisfy both social and commercial demands.

The process argument is that collaboration alone does not resolve institutional complexity because existing formalized practices pull interaction back toward the historically dominant logic. Simultaneous formalization and collaboration can also intensify conflict when carriers of each logic lack flexibility in applying new procedures. Delta succeeded because an initial period of separated formalization helped members understand which rules were essential and which could be flexibly negotiated; later collaboration then enabled formalized collaboration and collaborative formalization, producing practices that blended social and commercial logics.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends research on institutional complexity and hybrid organizations by showing how organizations can move among Besharov and Smith's logic-multiplicity types after an external shock. It contributes a process model in which the timing and sequencing of formalization and collaboration, not either mechanism alone, explains whether organizations relapse into a dominant logic, remain contested, or develop blended logics. It also connects institutional complexity to organizational design by showing how organizations can alternate differentiation and integration rather than search for one stable structural balance.
practical_implication: Managers of hybrid organizations should not assume that cross-functional collaboration will integrate competing logics by itself. The findings suggest that members first need clear, formalized understandings of their own logic-specific priorities and procedures before collaboration can support flexible exception handling. Practically, managers can use formal rules to clarify responsibilities and then use structured collaboration to revise those rules into integrated practices.
limitations: The authors note that the study is based on four Italian WISEs, so the timing and sequencing model needs testing in other hybrid contexts and other combinations of logics. The comparative design also prevents strong conclusions about the microprocesses through which members decide when to shift from compartmentalization to integration. The paper further notes that reciprocal identification appears important but cannot be established conclusively from the available data.
future_research: Future research could use event-history or ethnographic longitudinal designs to examine how much time organizations should allocate to logic compartmentalization and integration. Studies could investigate the signals through which members recognize that a strategy shift is needed, as well as the role of reciprocal identification in resolving tensions. The authors also call for larger-sample research on how perceived time horizons and pressure intensity shape whether organizations sequence or immediately combine formalization and collaboration.
abstract: This paper explores how organizations dealing with institutional complexity manage internal tensions triggered by environmental turbulence. Based on a longitudinal, comparative study, we extend previous research that has identified collaboration and formalization as possible mechanisms to reconcile organizational tensions in such situations. We show that neither of these mechanisms is sufficient in itself to resolve tensions. Rather, it is the structured interaction between collaboration and formalization that allows organizations to successfully blend logics and reconcile their conflicting demands. On the basis of our findings, we develop a process model that explains how organizations change in response to environmental turbulence.
