title: High-Stakes Institutional Translation: Establishing North America’s First Government-sanctioned Supervised Injection Site
methods: Empirical qualitative process study of the establishment of Insite in Vancouver, using interviews, observation, documentary analysis, secondary sources, historical timeline construction, constant comparative analysis, temporal bracketing, and NVivo coding.
industry: Drug use, addiction, harm reduction, and supervised injection-site organizing in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside.
country: Canada; the case is set in Vancouver.
time_period: Interviews were conducted between June 2004 and June 2007; the historical narrative covers the events leading to Insite's September 2003 opening.
units: Translations, actors, organizations, documents, public events, and material sites involved in establishing Insite.
n_sample: 36 interviews with 25 individuals.
authors: Lawrence, T. B.
theories: emotions and institutions; institutional change; institutional translation
keywords: discursive translations; emotion; high-stakes institutional translation; institutional translation; material translations; supervised injection site
research_question: The paper asks how actors import contentious responses to serious social problems into communities that initially reject those responses. It examines this question through the establishment of Insite, North America's first government-sanctioned supervised injection site for users of illegal drugs.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: High-stakes institutional translation; contested concepts and objects; discursive and material translations; pain, protest, anger, empathy, and collective reflexivity.
- Process / phases: Energizing through public expressions of pain and protest and a new interpretive scheme; exploring through discursive and material translations; integrating through translations that connect the contentious concept to local ideas, routines, and relationships.
- Practices: Government reports, conferences, newspaper accounts, public protests, demonstration sites, illegal sites, Four Pillars framing, mayoral politics, and the final sanctioned Insite facility.
- Emergent outcomes: A contested foreign practice becomes a locally embedded practice supported by health authorities, city officials, nonprofit actors, police cooperation, researchers, and drug-user advocates.
- Boundary conditions: The process concerns practices with serious material consequences and profound moral or ethical challenges for the target community.

The process begins when public pain and protest disrupt established assumptions about drug use and addiction and create energy for translation work. Actors then repeatedly construct the supervised injection-site concept in discursive and material forms, first making it visible and contested, then connecting it to locally legitimate routines and relationships. Over time, the translations and translators co-evolve: early isolated actors and advocacy groups give way to more connected networks capable of embedding the practice institutionally. Emotion is not incidental to this process; anger helps trigger disruption, while empathy sustains later translation work and connects actors across social worlds.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends institutional translation theory by theorizing how communities import practices that are politically, culturally, or morally problematic but potentially effective responses to serious social problems. It contributes a process model of high-stakes institutional translation and distinguishes exploratory versus integrative and discursive versus material translations. It also contributes to research on emotions and institutions by showing how anger and empathy energize, sustain, and connect distributed agency in institutional change.
practical_implication: For communities facing serious social problems, the paper implies that importing a contentious response may depend on many smaller translations rather than one decisive intervention. Practitioners should engage in translations of the idea and also enable others to translate it through different texts, spaces, demonstrations, routines, and relationships. The study also suggests that collective emotionality and collective reflexivity can help actors who do not usually collaborate tie their work together around a common cause.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: The paper identifies several issues for further scholarly development rather than presenting a standalone future-research section. It points to the conditions under which collective reflexivity can integrate distributed agency, the value of adding translation concepts to social movement research, and the potential role of empathy in connecting social enterprise organizations to broader social change processes.
abstract: Around the world, potentially effective responses to serious social problems are left untried because those responses are politically, culturally, or morally problematic in affected communities. I describe the process through which communities import such practices as “high-stakes institutional translation.” Drawing on a study of North America’s first supervised injection site for users of illegal drugs, I propose a process model of highstakes institutional translation that involves a triggering period of public expressions of intense emotion, followed by waves of translations in which the controversial practice is constructed in discursive and material terms many times over.
apa_citation: Lawrence, T. B. (2017). High-stakes institutional translation: Establishing North America’s first government-sanctioned supervised injection site. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(5), 1771-1800. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0714

title: Male Immorality: An Evolutionary Account of Sex Differences in Unethical Negotiation Behavior
methods: Three-study empirical quantitative design: a two-wave survey of employed adults using OLS regression, followed by two controlled laboratory experiments using between-subjects manipulations of mating motivation, opponent sex or attractiveness, and unethical negotiation behavior severity, analyzed with logistic regression.
industry: Study 1 sampled employed adults from different industries who negotiated as part of their work; Studies 2 and 3 used behavioral-lab participant pools in simulated seller-buyer negotiations.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual employed adults and laboratory participants making negotiation-behavior choices.
n_sample: Study 1: 138 employed adults; Study 2: 317 recruited participants and 305 analyzed negotiation responses; Study 3: 375 recruited participants, with 189 analyzed in the deception condition and 189 analyzed in the dodging condition.
authors: Lee, M.; Pitesa, M.; Pillutla, M. M.; Thau, S.
theories: evolutionary psychology; parental investment theory; socialization-based perspectives
keywords: evolutionary psychology; intrasexual competition; mating motivation; norm violation severity; opponent attractiveness; parental investment theory; sex differences; unethical negotiation behavior
research_question: The paper asks when sex differences in unethical negotiation behavior are more versus less pronounced, and whether men's greater unethical negotiation behavior can be explained by mating motivation and intrasexual competition. It also asks whether opponent sex, opponent attractiveness, and the severity of the unethical tactic condition this pattern.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in evolutionary psychology and parental investment theory. The authors argue that men's evolved tendency toward intrasexual competition makes mating motivation more likely to increase unethical negotiation behavior among men, especially when the opponent is an attractive same-sex rival. Because social sanctions for severe norm violations are theorized to have been more costly for women, the sex difference should be strongest for outright deception and attenuated for less severe tactics such as dodging a question.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends socialization-based accounts of sex differences in unethical behavior by integrating them with evolutionary theory and specifying when sex differences should appear. It contributes to unethical work behavior and negotiation research by showing that mating motivation, same-sex competition, opponent attractiveness, and norm violation severity jointly shape unethical negotiation behavior. It also qualifies the assumption that physical attractiveness generally benefits negotiators by showing that attractive male opponents can elicit more unethical behavior from mating-motivated men.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that managers should be attentive to conditions under which male negotiators may be more likely to behave unethically, particularly when mating motivation and same-sex competition are salient and the opponent is an attractive man. They also suggest that negotiator assignment, team composition, timing, stress reduction, and organizational cultures that amplify male competitiveness may matter for reducing unethical negotiation behavior.
limitations: The authors state that they did not model participants' own attractiveness, even though unattractive males may face different mating competition pressures. They also limit the empirical setting to distributive negotiations and note that integrative, mixed-motive, coalition, and face-to-face negotiations may produce different dynamics. The paper further notes that relationship status and sexual orientation were only explored, and that the small number of participants reporting predominantly homosexual orientation limited power for that moderation test.
future_research: The paper calls for future research on participant attractiveness, hormonal mechanisms involving testosterone and cortisol, and extensions to integrative, mixed-issue, coalition, and face-to-face negotiations. It also encourages research on conditions under which women negotiate equally or more unethically than men, including female-biased sex ratios and other organizational contexts that may increase women's intrasexual competition.
abstract: Past research has found that men negotiate more unethically than women, although many studies report comparable rates of unethical negotiation behaviors. Based on evolutionary psychology, we predict conditions under which sex differences in unethical negotiation behavior are more versus less pronounced. We theorize that greater levels of unethical behavior among men occur because of greater male intrasexual competition for mates. This suggests that more male unethical negotiation behavior should primarily emerge in situations associated with intrasexual competition. Using a two-wave survey design, Study 1 found a positive relationship between mating motivation and unethical negotiation behavior for male, but not female, employees. Study 2 was a controlled experiment, replicating this effect and showing that the gender difference was most pronounced when negotiating with same-sex, attractive opponents. Study 3 used a similar experimental design and found support for another implication of evolutionary theory—that mating motivation would prompt unethical behavior in both men and women when the behavior constitutes a less severe norm violation. We discuss contributions to the literature on unethical behavior at work, negotiations, and the role of attractiveness in organizations.
apa_citation: Lee, M., Pitesa, M., Pillutla, M. M., & Thau, S. (2017). Male immorality: An evolutionary account of sex differences in unethical negotiation behavior. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(5), 2014-2044. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0461

title: The Danger of Not Listening to Firms: Government Responsiveness and the Goal of Regulatory Compliance
methods: Empirical quantitative analysis of the 2013 Vietnam Provincial Competitiveness Index survey of domestic private firms, using entropy balancing to address selection into commenting, OLS models for the share of workers with formal contracts, ordered probit models for a compliance scale, robustness tests with trade union and recruitment-budget outcomes, size-disaggregated models, and structural-equation mediation analysis of government legitimacy.
industry: Domestic private firms across industries in Vietnam; the PCI survey is stratified by province, industry, age, and legal form.
time_period: 2013 PCI survey, tied to the 2012 Labor Code that went into effect on May 1, 2013, with attention to the October 31, 2013 implementation-period cutoff.
units: Domestic private firms, firm participation in regulatory commenting, government responses to comments, and firm-level labor-law compliance.
n_sample: The main analyses use 5,633 firms from a final PCI sample of 7,500 firms.
authors: Malesky, E.; Taussig, M.
theories: deliberative democracy; institutional theory; organizational legitimacy; procedural justice
keywords: Vietnam; corporate political activity; corporate social responsibility; deliberative democracy; emerging economies; government legitimacy; government responsiveness; procedural justice; regulatory compliance; self-regulation
research_question: The paper asks whether firm participation in the design of government regulations increases subsequent regulatory compliance in emerging economies, and whether this relationship depends on firms seeing government as responsive to their input. It examines this question in Vietnam by linking firms' comments on draft regulations, government responses to those comments, perceptions of government legitimacy, and compliance with the Labor Code.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that participation can make firms view the rule-making process as fair and government as a legitimate regulatory authority, which makes compliance with the resulting regulation more likely. However, participation has this constructive effect only when government is seen as responsive to firm input. If firms comment but receive no response, the process can look symbolic or unfair, lowering perceived legitimacy and making compliance less likely than among firms that did not participate.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a firm-level theory of regulatory compliance built from individual-level procedural justice and deliberative democracy arguments. It qualifies participation-based accounts by showing that responsiveness is not a procedural detail but a contingency that determines whether participation increases compliance or produces backlash. It also contributes to nonmarket strategy, CSR, self-regulation, corporate political activity, and institutional theory by foregrounding SMEs and by showing how direct firm-government interactions shape legitimacy assessments in emerging economies.
practical_implication: The paper warns governments that broader firm consultation alone is unlikely to improve regulatory compliance if agencies do not genuinely listen and respond. For resource-constrained emerging-economy governments, the practical lesson is to build modest, representative, and credible participation systems that make firms feel heard rather than launching large pro forma consultation exercises. The authors also caution that governments should consult all types of firms, not only large or politically connected firms.
limitations: The authors state that empirical research on firm regulatory compliance is difficult because firms resist revealing illegal behavior, and the study examines a relatively simple, low-cost form of labor-law compliance. They also note that the data are observational and cross-sectional, so causal identification is limited and the analysis cannot fully rule out unobserved heterogeneity or determine whether participation increased legitimacy or more positive government views made participation more likely. The theoretical argument focuses on legitimacy as the mechanism and does not empirically examine alternative mechanisms such as participation changing the substance of regulations.
future_research: The paper calls for research on environmental regulations and other forms of compliance where externalities are higher and internal firm costs differ from labor-contract compliance. It also identifies future work on optimal government policy, indirect participation, low-cost participation platforms such as online comment systems and workshops, and conditions under which participation improves or weakens the substance of regulation. The authors further propose research on whether the participation-legitimacy-compliance mechanism applies in global value chains involving multinational buyers and emerging-economy suppliers.
abstract: Firms in emerging economies exhibit dangerously low rates of compliance with government regulations aimed at protecting society from the negative externalities of their operations. This study builds on individual-level theories from organizational behavior (procedural justice) and political science (deliberative democracy) to develop new firm-level theory on the mechanism by which a firm is more likely to comply with a regulation after participating in its design by government. We hypothesize and find supporting evidence that such participation increases the likelihood of compliance by positively shaping the firm’s view of government legitimacy, but only if the firm views government as responsive to its input. Without this responsiveness, regulatory compliance is even less likely than if the firm did not participate at all. Our empirical work is novel in its focus on the political activities of firms not only within the authoritarian-ruled emerging economy context of Vietnam, but also through study of a highly representative sample dominated by small and medium sized enterprises. We discuss how our work contributes to nonmarket strategy literatures on corporate social responsibility, self-regulation, and corporate political activity, as well as its implications for public policy.
apa_citation: Malesky, E., & Taussig, M. (2017). The danger of not listening to firms: Government responsiveness and the goal of regulatory compliance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(5), 1741-1770. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0722

title: When Can Humble Top Executives Retain Middle Managers? The Moderating Role of Top Management Team Faultlines
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a multisource, multiphase dataset from private companies in China. The authors model middle managers nested in companies, use hierarchical linear modeling for job satisfaction, hierarchical generalized linear modeling for voluntary turnover, and test cross-level moderation by TMT faultlines.
industry: Private companies in manufacturing, service, and trading sectors.
time_period: Three waves: Time 1 survey, Time 2 roughly two weeks later, and Time 3 one year after Time 2.
units: Top management teams, top executives, and middle managers.
n_sample: 43 TMTs, 313 top executives, and 502 middle managers.
authors: Ou, Amy Y.; Seo, Jungmin (Jamie); Choi, Dongwon; Hom, Peter W.
theories: leader humility theory; multilevel leadership theory; top management team faultline theory; voluntary turnover theory
keywords: executive humility; job satisfaction; middle managers; multilevel inquiry; top management team faultlines; voluntary turnover
research_question: The paper asks when humble top executives can retain middle managers, given that top executives are both immediate leaders of MMs and members of the TMT that shapes the broader organizational context. It specifically examines whether TMT faultlines weaken the positive relationship between top executive humility and MM job satisfaction and weaken the negative relationship between MM job satisfaction and voluntary turnover.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level. Humble top executives should increase MM job satisfaction by valuing subordinates, soliciting their input, and supporting needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness. TMT faultlines create a demanding context marked by coordination problems, subgroup divisions, and uncertainty, which diverts MMs' attention from humble leader behavior and can make humility appear less useful or less credible. Faultlines also reduce the retention power of job satisfaction because MMs attend to TMT conflict and future career uncertainty rather than relying on current job satisfaction as a reason to stay.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a multilevel theory of middle manager voluntary turnover by integrating micro-level leader humility and job satisfaction mechanisms with macro-level TMT faultline context. It identifies TMT faultlines as a boundary condition for leader humility effects, showing that humility does not always translate into subordinate satisfaction and retention. It also extends the TMT faultline literature by showing that faultlines can spill over beyond the top team and shape lower-level managers' responses to their leaders and jobs.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that employee retention is a collective leadership responsibility, not only a matter of the immediate supervisor's behavior. HR managers and top executives should monitor leadership-team faultlines because they can undermine otherwise retention-supportive leadership and job satisfaction. TMTs with strong faultlines should pay attention to coordination across executive subgroups and middle-manager units, promote shared organizational identity, and improve communication and consensus around strategic implementation.
limitations: The authors note that the data come mainly from functionally structured companies in China, so the findings may not generalize to divisionally structured firms or culturally different societies. The sample includes 43 TMTs, which may limit statistical power for detecting more complex relationships such as curvilinear effects of leader humility. The study tests TMT faultlines as a moderator of one leader characteristic and two subordinate outcomes, leaving other leadership characteristics and outcomes untested.
future_research: Future research could test whether TMT faultlines moderate other leader characteristics, such as servant leadership, and other subordinate outcomes, such as job performance. Studies could examine whether similar cross-level faultline effects occur in lower-level leadership teams, plants, or multiteam systems. The authors also suggest examining faultlines formed by deep-level differences in personality traits and values, not only surface-level demographic attributes.
abstract: Top management in organizations must effectively retain middle managers (MMs)— who are central linking pins in strategy processes—as loss of their human and social capital can threaten strategy implementation. While long envisioning how leaders motivate subordinates to stay, management scholars have largely neglected how teams in which leaders belong (e.g., top management teams [TMT]) constitute an organizational context that moderates their ability to retain subordinates. Building on recent theory and research that a leader’s humility discourages subordinates from voluntarily departing by increasing their job satisfaction, we propose that faultlines in TMTs can exert cross-level effects attenuating how humble executives sustain MMs’ job satisfaction, and how MMs’ job dissatisfaction drives their voluntary turnover. We verify these effects with a multisource, multiphase dataset of 43 TMTs, 313 top executives, and 502 MMs. Our study thus bridges the macro and micro divide to offer a multilevel inquiry into contextual influences on voluntary turnover, identifies a boundary condition for leader humility effects, and clarifies how TMT faultlines represent a contextual constraint on how top executives induce MM subordinates to stay.
apa_citation: Ou, A. Y., Seo, J., Choi, D., & Hom, P. W. (2017). When can humble top executives retain middle managers? The moderating role of top management team faultlines. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(5), 1915-1931. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1072

title: Corporate Volunteering Climate: Mobilizing Employee Passion for Societal Causes and Inspiring Future Charitable Action
methods: Empirical quantitative multilevel survey study of companies affiliated with United Way Worldwide, using two-wave employee surveys, company liaison surveys, aggregation of climate measures, multilevel structural equation modeling in MPlus, FIML, and bias-corrected bootstrapping for moderated indirect effects.
industry: Fifty companies affiliated with United Way Worldwide across utilities, retail, financial, education and health, and other industries.
time_period: Two employee survey waves approximately four weeks apart; calendar dates are not reported.
units: Company liaisons, employees nested within companies, volunteers and non-volunteers in corporate volunteering programs.
n_sample: Final sample included 50 companies and 229 employee participants, including 160 corporate volunteers and 69 non-volunteers.
authors: Rodell, J. B.; Booth, J. E.; Lynch, J. W.; Zipay, K. P.
theories: collective pride; intergroup emotions theory; sensemaking process; work climate literature; work-nonwork spillover
keywords: United Way Worldwide; affective commitment; collective pride; company-provided resources; corporate volunteering climate; corporate volunteering intentions; employee belief in the cause; personal volunteering intentions; sensemaking
research_question: The paper asks what conditions foster a corporate volunteering climate and what implications such a climate has for employees inside and outside the workplace. It compares company-driven resources with employee-driven belief in the volunteering cause, then examines whether corporate volunteering climate relates to affective commitment and future corporate and personal volunteering intentions through collective pride.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level and sensemaking-based. Employees infer a corporate volunteering climate from company policies and from peers' passion for the volunteering cause; these two sources act as substitutes, so either top-down support or bottom-up belief can foster the climate when the other is weaker. The climate then creates collective pride, which is associated with higher affective commitment for both volunteers and non-volunteers and with personal volunteering intentions overall. For corporate volunteering intentions, the indirect relationship through collective pride is significant for non-volunteers but not for volunteers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces corporate volunteering climate as a group-level perception, shifting corporate volunteering research beyond individual volunteers and individual volunteer experiences. It contributes to work climate and corporate volunteering research by showing how top-down company resources and bottom-up employee belief can jointly shape a volunteering climate, and by showing that this climate can matter for both volunteers and non-volunteers. It also extends the volunteering literature by distinguishing corporate volunteering intentions from personal volunteering intentions, showing how a work-domain climate may be associated with nonwork charitable intentions.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that companies can cultivate a corporate volunteering climate either by providing resources and formal support or by supporting employee passion for causes that employees already value. For firms with limited existing volunteering activity, a formal program may help make volunteering salient; for firms with an existing volunteer base, allowing employees to pursue causes they care about may organically strengthen the climate. Managers should also recognize that corporate volunteering climate may influence non-volunteers, not only employees already participating in company programs.
limitations: The authors note several limitations: the study relies on self-reports, although focal antecedents and outcomes were separated in time and modeled at different levels where possible. The sample includes 50 companies but relatively few respondents per company, raising concerns about whether climate perceptions fully represent the broader organizations. The companies were recruited through existing United Way Worldwide partnerships, which may limit between-company variance and introduce selection bias. The study also uses volunteering intentions rather than subsequent volunteering behavior and does not observe direct beneficiaries or societal impact.
future_research: The paper calls for research with broader company samples, including organizations with strong volunteering programs and organizations without existing programs, as well as more representative employee samples within each organization. Future work could examine other employee motives, such as socializing or skill development, and whether perceived sincerity of colleagues' motives shapes non-volunteer reactions to corporate volunteering climate. The authors also suggest examining how communication and attributions for company-provided resources affect employee reactions to corporate volunteering programs.
abstract: Today’s corporations are increasingly engaging in efforts to address societal concerns ranging from hunger and poverty to education and financial stability, predominantly through corporate volunteering. Yet, because research has been focused on the individual volunteer we still know relatively little about how corporate volunteering can help address grand challenges. In this study, we introduce the concept of “corporate volunteering climate” in order to examine the broader, more systemlevel functioning of corporate volunteering in workplaces. Drawing on the sensemaking process, we theorize about how this climate develops—to what extent is it driven by company-level policies versus employee convictions for a cause? We also explore the potential influence of corporate volunteering climate for volunteers and non-volunteers, in terms of the workplace (through employee affective commitment) and the community (through employee intentions to volunteer, whether through corporate opportunities or personally). The results of a study conducted with United Way Worldwide suggest that corporate volunteering climate arises through both employee belief in the cause and corporate policies, and that these forces act as substitutes for each other. Moreover, by fostering a sense of collective pride among employees, this climate is related to affective commitment, and corporate and personal volunteering intentions.

title: Self-reliance: A Gender Perspective on its Relationship to Communality and Leadership Evaluations
methods: Four-study quantitative design combining 360-degree leadership evaluations of young managers with three experiments manipulating or varying leader gender and agentic trait, analyzed with hierarchical linear regression, between-subjects ANOVA, and moderated mediation.
industry: Study 1 involved young managers across a range of industries; Studies 2-4 used political, financial-services, and Silicon Valley technology leader contexts rather than an industry sample.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Young managers or MBA students, MTurk participants, and evaluated male or female political and executive leaders.
n_sample: Study 1 regression analyses report N = 234; Study 2 reports 123 participants; Study 3 reports 521 participants; Study 4 reports 533 participants after exclusions and listwise deletion.
authors: Schaumberg, R. L.; Flynn, F. J.
theories: expectancy violation theory; prescriptive and proscriptive gender stereotypes; role congruity theory
keywords: communality; expectancy violation theory; gender stereotypes; leadership evaluations; role congruity theory; self-reliance
research_question: The paper asks whether self-reliance, as a discrete agentic trait, is more positively associated with leadership evaluations for women than for men. It also asks whether perceived communality explains this female advantage relative to self-reliant male leaders and to leaders described as dominant or only generally positive.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in expectancy violation theory. Self-reliance signals agency for both men and women, but the authors argue that observers assimilate women's self-reliance to feminine stereotypes of communality rather than treating it as evidence of low communality. As a result, self-reliant women are seen as similarly competent but more communal than self-reliant men, which improves their leadership evaluations.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the undifferentiated treatment of agency in role congruity accounts of gender and leadership evaluation. It shows that a desirable masculine trait can operate as a positive expectancy violation for female leaders, so gender stereotypes can sometimes buffer rather than penalize women's displays of agency. It also brings self-reliance into trait theories of leadership by showing that its evaluative meaning depends on both leader gender and perceived communality.
practical_implication: The findings imply that female leaders' displays of agency are not uniformly penalized and that self-reliance can improve evaluations when it is not read as low communality. For evaluators and organizations, the results suggest that leadership assessments may depend on trait-specific gender inferences rather than on agency as a single broad category.
limitations: The authors note that the experimental effects in Studies 2-4 may not fully generalize to evaluations of one's own leader, especially in longstanding relationships where beliefs about a leader's communality may diverge from gender stereotypes. They also state that the paper focuses on broad leadership evaluations, which may mask more specific judgments about leadership styles or behaviors. The evidence for a male advantage in dominance was weaker than role congruity theory and expectancy violation theory would predict, possibly because the experiments focused on high-status leaders.
future_research: The paper calls for research on whether self-reliance shapes evaluations of one's own leader differently from evaluations of unfamiliar or vignette-based leaders. It suggests examining more specific evaluations of self-reliant men and women, such as perceived transformational, transactional, or servant leadership styles. It also proposes studying whether other prescriptive masculine traits, such as being analytical, rational, or logical, can produce similar female advantages and whether knowledge of such advantages affects women's efficacy in pursuing leadership roles.
abstract: We posit a female advantage in the relationship between self-reliance and leadership evaluations. We test this prediction in four studies. First, using multi-rater evaluations of young managers, we find that self-reliance relates positively to leadership evaluations for women, but not for men. Next, in each of three experiments, we manipulate the gender of a leader and the agentic trait he or she displays (e.g., self-reliance, dominance, no discrete agentic trait). We find that self-reliant female leaders are evaluated as better leaders than self-reliant male leaders are. In contrast, we find a male advantage or no gender advantage for dominant leaders or leaders who are described positively, but not in terms of any discrete agentic trait. Consistent with expectancy violation theory, the female advantage in the relationship between self-reliance and leadership evaluations emerges because self-reliant female leaders are seen as similarly competent, but more communal, than self-reliant male leaders are. We discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the effects of self-reliance, gender stereotypes, and stereotype violations on leadership evaluations.

title: Shady Characters: The Implications of Illicit Organizational Roles for Resilient Team Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative study using longitudinal game-, player-, and team-level NHL data from the 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 seasons. The authors use OLS regressions with injury and opponent fixed effects, robust standard errors, injury-event windows, enforcer indicators, replacement proxied by post-injury penalty concentration, and team-experience interactions.
industry: Professional National Hockey League hockey teams.
time_period: 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 NHL seasons.
units: Injury-game observations around player injuries, including enforcer and formal-role injuries.
n_sample: 1,473 injury events; main Hypothesis 1 analyses use 12,493 injury-game observations, and replacement analyses use 15,067 game observations.
authors: Stuart, H. C.; Moore, C.
theories: organizational misconduct; role theory; team familiarity; team resilience
keywords: enforcer; illicit roles; organizational misconduct; organizational roles; professional hockey teams; resilient team performance; team experience
research_question: The paper asks how illicit organizational roles affect resilient team performance when their occupants depart. It specifically examines whether losing an NHL enforcer disrupts team performance more than losing formal role occupants, whether replacement attempts slow recovery, and whether the enforcer's team experience magnifies the disruption.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that illicit role occupants specialize in work that cannot be formally codified, openly trained, or transparently replaced because the activities are forbidden but believed to support organizational goals. When an enforcer leaves, the team loses a role occupant whose effectiveness depends on trust, local social context, and context-specific knowledge. Attempts to substitute another player into that role slow recovery because replacements lack the same credibility and embedded experience, while longer team tenure makes the departed enforcer more locally valuable and therefore more disruptive to lose.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to role theory by theorizing illicit organizational roles: roles that specialize in prohibited activity and operate outside formal organizational structures. It extends research on teams by showing that non-core, informal, and illicit roles can affect resilient performance even though they are marginal to formal workflow. It also contributes to organizational misconduct research by showing that teams may organize prohibited activity through a role-based allocation of labor.
practical_implication: The paper explicitly cautions that the findings do not imply teams should create illicit roles; instead, such roles create vulnerability for resilient performance. For managers and regulators, the findings imply that identifying people who specialize in illicit activity may help organizations and enforcement bodies detect and discourage misconduct. The authors also suggest that rotating personnel in ethically risky areas may hinder illicit activity because competence in these roles depends on time and local relationships.
limitations: The authors note that the injury-based design can speak only to teams that already have an enforcer, not to whether having an enforcer improves performance. They observe only short-run performance immediately after the player's exit, so longer-term implications of not replacing illicit role occupants remain uncertain. They also study one illicit role in professional hockey, which raises generalizability concerns for other illicit roles, less specialized teams, and settings where informal role requirements are more ambiguous.
future_research: The paper calls for research that replicates the findings across other illicit roles and organizational contexts, such as rogue traders or convicted insider traders. It also suggests studying how illicit roles emerge, why some organizations resist adopting them, why they spread or persist across industries, and what incentives help make them obsolete. Future work could also directly test micro mechanisms such as coordination loss, lack of trust in replacements, and the conditions under which teams can avoid replacing illicit role occupants while sustaining performance.
abstract: In this paper we theorize about illicit roles and explore their effects on resilient team performance. We define an illicit role as one whose occupants specialize in activity forbidden by the law, regulatory bodies, or professional societies, in the belief that doing so provides a competitive advantage. Using longitudinal data on professional hockey teams, we examine the enforcer—a player who specializes in the prohibited activity of fighting. We find that team performance is more disrupted by the injury of an enforcer than by the injury of occupants of other formal roles on the team. In addition, team performance recovers more slowly after this setback to the extent the team tries to replace an enforcer, and the performance disruptions associated with his exit are magnified as a function of his experience with his team. We use these findings to develop new theory about organizational roles that operate outside official channels and formal structures. We suggest that such role occupants are more difficult to replace than their formal counterparts, in part because to enact these roles effectively requires experience in the local social context.

title: Networks, Technology, and Entrepreneurship: A Field Quasi-experiment among Women in Rural India
methods: Seven-year field quasi-experiment in 20 rural Indian villages. Ten villages received staffed Internet-enabled ICT kiosks and ten geographically proximal villages served as controls. The study used annual structured interviews, kiosk-use logs, government filings where available, social-network centrality measures, and generalized estimating equations with repeated person-year observations to predict ICT use, entrepreneurial activity, and entrepreneurial profit.
industry: Rural village entrepreneurship and microbusiness activity, including restaurants, handicrafts, farming support, food delivery, and milk delivery.
time_period: Seven annual waves over a seven-year field quasi-experiment.
units: Adult women in 20 rural villages; person-year observations for longitudinal models; women-founded businesses for profit analyses.
n_sample: Sampling frames covered 8,330 adult women in intervention villages and 8,600 adult women in control villages, with reported sample sizes of 6,662 intervention and 6,801 control respondents across annual waves. The main tables report n = 94,241 for most person-year analyses and n = 1,400 for profit.
authors: Venkatesh, Viswanath; Shaw, Jason D.; Sykes, Tracy Ann; Wamba, Samuel Fosso; Macharia, Mary
theories: social networks theory; socio-structural view of ICT use; temporal theory
keywords: ICT use; entrepreneurial activity; entrepreneurial profit; field quasi-experiment; rural India; social networks; women's entrepreneurship
research_question: The paper asks how women's social networks, ICT use, and time jointly relate to the initiation and success of women's entrepreneurial ventures in rural India. It specifically examines whether family centrality, community centrality, and ties to men in power shape ICT use, entrepreneurial activity, and entrepreneurial profit, and whether ICT use and time change these relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is socio-structural and temporal. Family and community ties can provide support, information, and resources that encourage ICT use and entrepreneurial activity, while ties to men in power can reinforce patriarchal constraints and pressure women toward the status quo. ICT use supplies information, access to programs, communication channels, and e-government resources that complement supportive family and community networks. For ties to men in power, the interaction pattern is more constrained: ICT use is associated with increased entrepreneurial activity over time only when those ties are low, and the interaction does not emerge for profit. Over time, the benefits of combining supportive network positions with ICT use become stronger for entrepreneurial activity and, for family and community centrality, for profit.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on grand challenges, women's entrepreneurship, social networks, and ICT interventions by showing how social structure and technology operate jointly rather than independently in a rural developing-country context. It qualifies the generally positive view of network centrality by distinguishing supportive ties to family and community from constraining ties to men in local power. It also extends entrepreneurship research by modeling time explicitly and showing that ICT-enabled network effects unfold dynamically across a seven-year intervention.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that relatively modest ICT access, when staffed and made accessible to women, can support entrepreneurial activity and profit in rural India. Policy makers and development organizations should not treat ICT infrastructure as sufficient by itself; staffed kiosks, women-accessible locations, women-only training, and local facilitation matter because literacy, mobility, and gender norms shape whether women can use ICT resources. The results also imply that interventions should account for social networks, because family and community ties can amplify ICT benefits whereas ties to male local officials may constrain women's entrepreneurial activity.
limitations: The authors state that they are unable to disentangle the complex mechanisms underlying the cultural constraints associated with women's ties to men in power. They also treat the design of the ICT intervention as a black box, so the study does not identify which specific design features of the kiosks drive the observed effects. Generalizability is bounded by the rural Indian setting; the authors note that other countries and contexts may involve similar and different constraints, such as different governmental regulations or gender-related institutions.
future_research: The paper calls for detailed qualitative work on how women with ties to men in power can overcome sociocultural barriers to new business initiation. It also recommends studying other interventions and complementary investments, including government programs, NGO initiatives, media activities, mobile technologies, and scalable ICT designs. Future research should examine other network types such as advice, friendship, and hindrance networks, multiplex ties across family and power networks, and cross-context studies of women's empowerment and grand challenges in settings beyond rural India.
abstract: We address a grand economic challenge faced by women in rural India. We consider the interplay of women’s social networks (ties to family, to community, and to men in power), information and communication technology (ICT) use, and time in relating to the initiation and success of women’s entrepreneurial ventures. Results from a sevenyear field quasi-experiment in 20 rural villages in India support the model. Ties to family and community positively, and to men in power negatively, relate to ICT use, entrepreneurial activity, and entrepreneurial profit. ICT intervention also strongly impacts entrepreneurship, with 160 new businesses in the 10 intervention villages compared to 40 in the controls. Results also demonstrate the dynamic interplay of social networks and ICT use. For ties to family and community, the amplification effect is such that the highest levels of entrepreneurial activity and success are observed among women with high centrality and ICT use—effects that increase over time. For ties to men in power, ICT use is associated with increased entrepreneurial activity only when these ties are low, but these interactive temporary temporal patterns do not emerge for profit. We address implications for the grand challenges of empowering women in less developed countries.

title: An Inconvenient Truth: How Organizations Translate Climate Change into Business as Usual
methods: Longitudinal, comparative qualitative case study of five major Australian corporations, using interviews, corporate documents, media releases, case histories, timelines, open coding, axial coding, and NVivo matrix coding to build a grounded process model.
industry: Five major Australian corporations from electricity and gas, banking, manufacturing, insurance, and media and communications.
units: Corporate case studies, manager interviews, corporate documents, sustainability reports, policy documents, presentations, and media releases.
n_sample: Five case studies; 70 interviews; 1,629 pages of transcript; 377 documents; 1,819 pages of documents.
authors: Wright, C.; Nyberg, D.
theories: business and the natural environment literature; grand challenges; new corporate environmentalism; translation perspective (Czarniawska & Joerges, 1996; Callon, 1986)
keywords: business as usual; climate change; corporate environmentalism; critique; grand challenges; translation
research_question: The paper asks how firms engage over time with competing market and social/environmental demands when translating complex challenges such as climate change into practice. It examines why initially strong corporate climate commitments in proactive firms are narrowed, diluted, or redirected toward business-as-usual concerns.
mechanism_summary:
- Empirical setting: Five proactive Australian corporations facing climate-change pressure across electricity and gas, banking, manufacturing, insurance, and media and communications.
- Triggering tension: External and internal critique makes climate change salient while exposing conflict between business growth and environmental demands.
- Framing: Senior managers associate climate change with business-compatible meanings such as risk, opportunity, innovation, leadership, and win-win outcomes, while disassociating it from sacrifice, regulation, or threats to growth.
- Localizing: Managers make those framings operational through incorporation, commensuration, and proselytization, creating roles, products, metrics, advocacy, and eco-efficiency practices that temporarily align business and environmental concerns.
- Normalizing: Market evaluation later reasserts shareholder-value tests, leading firms to purify climate initiatives back toward core business or dilute them into broader sustainability language.
- Emergent outcome: The revolutionary implications of climate change are translated into familiar corporate routines and less threatening business-as-usual formulations.

The process is dialectical rather than a variable-based causal test. Critique repeatedly reveals tensions between climate demands and business imperatives: initial social/environmental critique prompts framing, dissonance between framing and practice prompts localization, and later market evaluation prompts normalization. The model explains deterioration over time by showing how corporate climate initiatives are continually judged against dominant market discourses, especially under financial stress, leadership change, and shifting political conditions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to business and the natural environment research by explaining how corporate environmental initiatives deteriorate over time rather than only how they are initially framed or implemented. It develops a grounded model of grand-challenge translation that links framing, localizing, and normalizing through continuous critique. It also qualifies both optimistic win-win accounts and purely cynical greenwashing accounts by showing that managers may be authentically concerned while still constrained by short-term profitability and shareholder-value pressures.
practical_implication: The paper argues that relying primarily on corporate leadership, market mechanisms, or business innovation is insufficient for climate-change response because corporations tend to translate grand challenges into terms compatible with value creation. For policy and practice debates, this implies a need for regulatory guidance, limits on short-term corporate political influence, and incentives for longer-term planning.
limitations: The authors note that the study uses five organizational case studies of proactive Australian firms, so care is needed in generalizing to firms that ignore, reject, or dismiss climate change. They also note that climate change is politically contentious, which may limit direct transfer of the model to less polarized issues. Because the analysis focuses on internal organizational translation, it is partially blind to broader societal and global processes of climate-change translation and to how the process might differ across political regimes.
future_research: The paper calls for future research on organizational dynamics in businesses that reject or dismiss climate change, particularly as the physical and political ramifications of climate change worsen. It also points to research comparing the model across other social and environmental challenges, less contentious issues, less polarized societies, and different political regimes. Further work could examine the explanatory power of globally dominant market discourses and the societal-level translation processes that shape corporate climate action.
abstract: Climate change represents the grandest of challenges facing humanity. In the space of two centuries of industrial development, human civilization has changed the chemistry of the atmosphere and oceans, with devastating consequences. Business organizations are central to this challenge, in that they support the production of escalating greenhouse gas emissions but also offer innovative ways to decarbonize our economies. In this paper, we examine how businesses respond to climate change. Based on five in-depth case studies of major Australian corporations over a 10-year period (2005–2015), we identify three key stages in the corporate translation of climate change: framing, localizing, and normalizing. We develop a grounded model that explains how the revolutionary import of grand challenges is converted into the mundane and comfortable concerns of “business as usual.” We find that critique is the major driver of this process by continuously revealing the tensions between the demands of the grand challenge and business imperatives. Our paper contributes to the literature on business and the natural environment by identifying how and why corporate environmental initiatives deteriorate over time. More specifically, we highlight the policy limitations of a reliance on business and market responses to the climate crisis.

title: The Value of Voice to Managers: Employee Identification and the Content of Voice
methods: Empirical mixed-methods design with three studies: an inductive qualitative field study of emergency department employees, a two-wave employee-manager survey study analyzed with multilevel models and bootstrap mediation tests, and a scenario experiment with full-time managers randomly assigned to high or low voice-content dimensions.
industry: Study 1 was an emergency department in a large hospital; Study 2 used a commercial real estate development firm and a national defense contractor; Study 3 used full-time managers recruited through MTurk.
country: Study 1 was in the southern United States; Study 2 and Study 3 country coverage is not fully reported in paper.
time_period: Study 2 surveys were administered in two waves approximately two months apart; calendar dates for the three studies are not reported.
units: Employees, managers, and manager evaluations of voiced ideas.
n_sample: Study 1 included 35 informants; Study 2 included 97 employees and 27 managers; Study 3 included 396 full-time manager respondents.
authors: Burris, E. R.; Rockmann, K. W.; Kimmons, Y. S.
theories: Hirschman's voice and exit framework; multiple identifications; organizational identification; self-categorization theory; social identity theory
keywords: employee identification; employee voice; importance; interdependencies; managerial value of voice; professional identification; resources; voice content; work unit identification
research_question: The paper asks how the target of employee identification shapes the content of employee voice and how that content affects managers' valuation of voiced ideas. It examines whether work unit and professional identification lead employees to speak up about different issues, and whether dimensions of voice content such as importance, required resources, and interdependencies explain why managers value some voice more than other voice.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: Work unit identification, professional identification, voice content, work-unit-related voice, profession-related voice, and managerial value or endorsement of voice.
- Process / mediating pathway: Identification with the work unit or profession shapes what employees notice as worth voicing; the resulting voice content then influences how managers evaluate the value of the employee's ideas.
- Voice-content dimensions: Importance of implementation, resources required to implement the change, and interdependencies involved in implementation.
- Empirical tests: Study 1 inductively identifies the dimensions and links them to work unit versus professional identification; Study 2 tests mediation between identification targets, domain-specific voice, and managerial value; Study 3 experimentally manipulates importance, resources, and interdependencies to assess managerial endorsement.

The process is identity-based: employees speak up about issues connected to the part of work that is self-defining for them. Work unit identification tends to produce voice that is more locally relevant and easier for managers to act on, whereas professional identification can produce voice tied to broader professional standards but requiring more resources or coordination. Managers then value voice partly according to whether the content appears important, feasible, and implementable within their constraints.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts voice research from the frequency of speaking up to the content of what is voiced and the implementation implications of that content. It contributes to employee voice theory by identifying importance, resources, and interdependencies as dimensions that matter for managerial evaluation. It also extends identification theory by showing that different targets of identification can shape not only whether employees speak up, but what they speak up about and how managers respond to those ideas.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that employees should be cautious about repeatedly voicing issues that require substantial resources or interdependencies from an immediate supervisor, because such voice may be valued less even when the issue is important. Employees may benefit from directing some issues to more appropriate organizational targets or crafting suggestions in ways that account for local constraints. Managers should recognize that they may overlook important ideas when those ideas are difficult to implement, and should separate evaluation of the problem from development of feasible solutions.
limitations: The authors state that causal and generalizability claims require caution because the first two studies are cross-sectional and the designs do not fully rule out reverse causality. They also note that the studies did not manipulate identification targets directly, did not fully demonstrate all proposed mechanisms, and focused on only two identification targets: the local work unit and the profession. The paper further limits its outcome to direct supervisors' judgments of value, leaving open whether other managers or higher-level leaders would evaluate the same voice differently.
future_research: The authors call for field studies over time and experiments that manipulate employee identification targets to test the causal links more directly. They suggest construct development work to formalize measures of the voice-content dimensions and research on when particular subdimensions, such as financial resources versus time and effort, matter most for managerial value. They also recommend studying how voice should be directed to different targets who may vary in receptivity to particular content.
abstract: Previous research on employee voice has aimed to understand the antecedents and outcomes of the frequency of speaking up. Yet, how these antecedents translate into outcomes may depend on what employees speak up about and its implications for implementation. We engage in three studies to explore what individuals speak up about, why they speak up about those things, and the consequences of voicing such content. First, through a qualitative field study, we find evidence for three dimensions of voice content: the importance of initiating change, the required resources to enact the desired change, and the interdependencies involved in implementing the desired change. Further, specific targets of identification—either one’s local work unit or one’s broader profession—shape whether the issues individuals raise take into account barriers related to resources and interdependencies. Next, in a quantitative field study, we find that voicing on issues related to one’s work unit or profession mediates the relationship between employee identification and managers’ valuation of voice. Finally, in an experiment, we manipulate importance, resources, and interdependencies of implementation and find these dimensions of voice content influence managerial value of voice. These results offer meaningful theoretical implications for the literatures on employee voice and identification.
apa_citation: Burris, E. R., Rockmann, K. W., & Kimmons, Y. S. (2017). The value of voice to managers: Employee identification and the content of voice. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2099-2125. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0320

title: Constructing a Shared Governance Logic: The Role of Emotions in Enabling Dually Embedded Agency
methods: Longitudinal qualitative study of the Okanagan Water Stewardship Council using naturalist observations, semi-structured interviews, archival data, temporal bracketing, visual mapping, open coding, member checks, and peer debriefing.
industry: Water stewardship and water management in the Okanagan watershed, British Columbia.
time_period: The case context spans the OBWB and Council from 2003 to 2014, with naturalist observations from September 2012 to March 2014, interviews from October 2012 to June 2014, and archival materials covering 2003 to 2014.
units: Council members, OBWB directors and staff, water experts, government representatives, First Nations, agricultural groups, water suppliers, meeting observations, interviews, and archives.
n_sample: Table 1 reports 32 monthly OBWB and Council meetings, 45 interviews, 46 archived presentations, over 2,500 OBWB meeting-minute pages, and over 2,000 Council meeting-minute pages; the methods narrative elsewhere states 46 interviews.
authors: Fan, G. H.; Zietsma, C.
theories: commons logic; embedded agency; institutional complexity; institutional logics; sociology of emotions
keywords: dually embedded agency; emotional energy; emotions; institutional complexity; institutional logics; moral emotions; shared governance logic; social emotions; water sustainability
research_question: The paper asks how actors embedded in disparate institutional logics can construct a new logic that builds shared understandings and governs interactions across multiple fields. Empirically, it examines how members of the Okanagan Water Stewardship Council built and later weakened a shared governance logic for water sustainability.
mechanism_summary:
- Empirical setting: The Okanagan Water Stewardship Council, a voluntary technical advisory body working on basin-wide water sustainability in British Columbia.
- Key tension: Council members remained attached to home logics from agriculture, fisheries, water supply, government, First Nations, science, conservation, and other fields while trying to govern a shared resource collectively.
- Emotional facilitators: Social emotions, moral emotions, and emotional energy shaped members' capacity to work across their home logics.
- Agentic mechanisms: Openness and reflexivity, commitment, and engagement linked emotions to the construction or weakening of the new logic.
- Logic-construction cycles: Agreeing on values, shared learning, and enacting shared values built the shared governance logic during 2006-2008.
- Logic-weakening cycles: Reduced shared learning, violated shared values, and limited enactment weakened the shared governance logic during 2009-2013.

The process is recursive rather than a one-time settlement. Positive emotions helped members become more open about their home logics, more committed to basin-wide values, and more engaged in collective action, which strengthened shared values, common language, and concrete projects. When trust, moral clarity, and emotional energy declined, the same interaction cycles turned negative and weakened the shared governance logic without fully dissolving it.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a multilevel process model of new logic construction in bridging issue fields, showing how microlevel interactions can produce mesolevel shared values and practices with macrolevel consequences for governance. It extends institutional-logics theory by foregrounding emotions as mechanisms that enable dually embedded actors to loosen the constraints of home logics while becoming committed to a new shared logic. It also contributes to embedded-agency research by distinguishing social emotions linked to openness and reflexivity, moral emotions linked to commitment, and emotional energy linked to engagement.
practical_implication: The paper argues that practitioners and policymakers working on water sustainability and multi-field shared governance should not treat collaboration as only a cognitive or structural design problem. Agenda setting, decision making, consultation, and accountability contain emotional elements that affect participation, momentum, conflict, and adherence to shared values. For voluntary collaborative arrangements, maintaining trust, respect, moral commitment, and emotional energy is especially important because formal sanctions are limited.
limitations: The authors present boundary conditions rather than a separate limitations section. The model is developed from a watershed organization in which actors were dually embedded in home logics and a new shared governance logic, so it may apply most directly to settings where actors remain attached to their home fields while sharing a common issue. The authors also state that governing across multiple fields requires common interests and ongoing negotiation, which limits transfer to settings where no common moral purpose or convergent interest can be constructed.
future_research: The authors call for future research on other combinations of positive and negative emotions that enable or constrain agency. They also identify values, emotions, and logics, and the dynamics among them, as promising topics for future theoretical and empirical inquiry.
abstract: In a longitudinal qualitative study of a water stewardship council, we build theory about how and why actors embedded in disparate logics across multiple fields can overcome the constraints of their home logics to construct a new, shared governance logic together. Our findings suggest a recursive model of new logic construction in which council members mobilize three emotional facilitators (social emotions, moral emotions, and emotional energy) to affect three logic-construction cycles (agreeing on values, shared learning, and enacting shared values). Emotional facilitators work through three agentic mechanisms: enabling actors to become open and reflexive about their home logics and simultaneously increase their commitment to and engagement in constructing a shared governance logic. Ongoing interactions involving emotional facilitators, agentic mechanisms, and logic-construction cycles are essential in sustaining the new logic. The process model foregrounds the role of emotions in enabling dually embedded agency, thereby extending extant theory that has tended to focus narrowly on cognitive dynamics. We discuss implications for our understanding of institutional agency, the role of emotions in new logic construction, and the role of microlevel interactions in the formation of macrolevel structures.
apa_citation: Fan, G. H., & Zietsma, C. (2017). Constructing a shared governance logic: The role of emotions in enabling dually embedded agency. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2321-2351. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0402

title: Hidden Badge of Honor: How Contextual Distinctiveness Affects Category Promotion among Certified B Corporations
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study combining web-scraped textual and graphical measures of B Corp category promotion, MSCI ESG KLD STATS measures of regional and industry contextual distinctiveness, hurdle models estimated in R, robustness checks, and semistructured interviews with B Corp entrepreneurs and executives.
industry: Certified B Corporations across different industries and geographies, with industry measured using SIC divisions.
time_period: B Corps certified as of December 2013 and still certified as of November 2015; promotion data were collected in late October and early November 2015; interviews were conducted between July and October 2015 plus published secondary interviews.
units: Certified B Corporation websites, B Corp firms, regional and industry contexts, and interviewees.
n_sample: Initial quantitative sample of 526 U.S. B Corps; 507 websites were successfully gathered; reported hurdle models use n = 465; qualitative supplement includes 49 interviews with entrepreneurs and executives from 44 companies.
authors: Gehman, J.; Grimes, M.
theories: category hierarchy theory; contextual distinctiveness; organizational category theory; subordinate category peer groups
keywords: B Corporations; Certified B Corporation; category peers; category promotion; contextual distinctiveness; corporate sustainability; promotional forbearance; social entrepreneurship; subordinate categories
research_question: The paper asks why organizations pursue membership in an organizational category, such as Certified B Corporation status, but then vary in how much they promote that membership. It examines whether category promotion is driven by the contextual distinctiveness of a subordinate category within firms' regional and industry basic categories, and whether larger subordinate category peer groups amplify that effect.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a distinctiveness process rather than a membership-claiming process. B Corp membership can provide a firm with symbolic and practical resources for standing out from non-certified firms in the same region or industry, but this benefit is weaker when similar ESG practices are already common among non-members in that context. Larger B Corp peer groups make the subordinate category more familiar and credible, which increases members' willingness to use the category as a promotional signal. The interviews support this interpretation by showing that firms became B Corps largely for identity enactment and validation, while they promoted the certification when it helped differentiate them from non-certified companies.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to category research by separating category membership from category promotion and showing that the two are driven by different logics. It extends work on promotional forbearance beyond stigma by showing that even a celebrated category can be hidden when it offers limited contextual distinctiveness. It also develops a relational view of category distinctiveness, arguing that subordinate categories must be assessed against the basic regional and industry categories in which members are embedded.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that B Corp and similar certifications may not generate equal promotional value across contexts. Certification providers may find it easier to recruit members in contexts that already share the certification's values, but those members may be less likely to promote the label because it offers less distinctiveness. The authors therefore suggest that certification providers may need to support members in regions and industries where the label has greater cultural value as a tool for differentiation.
limitations: The authors note that their data provide limited panel structure, so they could not directly test the dynamics between collective and contextual category legitimation over time. They also focus on firms' decisions to promote certification rather than audience evaluations of the value or reputation produced by promotion. The empirical setting is Certified B Corporations, a value-laden certification, which leaves open whether the same contextual distinctiveness process operates similarly for less normative categories defined more by technical or material differences.
future_research: The paper calls for research on audience evaluations of subordinate category promotion and on whether promotion creates value in contexts where distinctiveness may also carry negative valence. It suggests longitudinal work on how diffusion, isomorphic pressure, contextual familiarity, and contextual distinctiveness jointly shape category promotion over time. It also identifies social media as a promising context for studying how organizations promote category membership through multiple information channels.
abstract: Why would an organization pursue membership in an organizational category, yet forego opportunities to subsequently promote that membership? Drawing on prior research, we develop a theoretical model that distinguishes between basic and subordinate categories and highlights how organizations may differ in their promotion of the same subordinate category. We hypothesize that a subordinate category’s contextual distinctiveness within different basic categories increases promotion, and that these effects are amplified in relatively larger subordinate category peer groups. To test our hypotheses, we developed a proprietary web-based software toolset and gathered textual and graphical data regarding B Corporations’ web-based promotion of their certification. We supplemented our statistical analysis with interviews of Certified B Corporation entrepreneurs and executives. Our findings challenge prior assumptions about the causes of promotional forbearance, while extending our understanding of category distinctiveness within contexts as well as sources of intra-category variation.
apa_citation: Gehman, J., & Grimes, M. (2017). Hidden badge of honor: How contextual distinctiveness affects category promotion among Certified B Corporations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2294-2320. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0416
