title: Design Performances: How Organizations Inscribe Artifacts to Change Routines
methods: Inductive ethnographic single-case study of a law enforcement agency and an external game-theory research organization designing a game-theoretic software artifact, using participant observation, interviews, archival materials, temporal mapping, and iterative coding.
industry: Law enforcement and transit-security patrolling routines.
time_period: February 2013 to September 2013, with project events from July 2012 through August 2013.
units: Design performances, project events, actors, artifacts, theories, and practices in the Metropol and Algo-Security pilot project.
n_sample: 31 events during the author's field work.
authors: Glaser, V. L.
theories: performativity; practice perspective; routine dynamics; sociomaterial assemblages
keywords: design performances; game-theoretic artifact; patrolling routines; performativity; routine dynamics; sociomaterial assemblages; strategy tools
research_question: The paper asks how organizational actors design artifacts to change routines. It studies how Metropol and Algo-Security created a game-theoretic software artifact intended to modify counterterrorism and fare-evasion patrolling routines.
mechanism_summary:
- Key construct: Design performances, defined as organizational actions to create an artifact in order to intentionally change or influence a routine.
- Process elements: Abstracting grammars of action, exposing assumptions, distributing agency, and appraising outcomes.
- Sociomaterial assemblage: Actors, artifacts, theories, and practices are iteratively recombined as the artifact is designed.
- Empirical setting: A pilot project in which a law enforcement organization and game-theory experts designed software for randomized patrol scheduling.
- Emergent outcomes: The design performances changed the artifact, altered understandings of patrolling routines, and created assemblages that could shape future routine performances.

The process begins when an intention to change a routine is informed by existing routine experience and external communities, here Metropol's patrolling routines and Algo-Security's game-theoretic expertise. Through design performances, actors translate routine activity into abstract action grammars, make assumptions about criminal behavior and patrol coordination explicit, decide how agency should be distributed between humans and the algorithm, and develop ways to appraise outcomes. These mechanisms inscribe the artifact and produce a sociomaterial assemblage that can influence subsequent routine dynamics.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to routine dynamics by shifting attention from ongoing routine performance to the design activities through which artifacts are created to intentionally change routines. It contributes to performativity by showing how game theory was locally translated into an artifact and assemblage that shaped organizational practice. It also contributes to strategy-tool research by theorizing how organizational actors design or redesign tools through design performances rather than only using already-formed tools.
practical_implication: The paper implies that organizations designing artifacts for routine change should attend to more than the technical object itself. Managers and external experts need to surface assumptions, specify how much agency the artifact should hold relative to human actors, and decide how outcomes will be evaluated. The study also suggests that strategy tools may become more adaptive when their design process explicitly works through actors, artifacts, theories, and practices in the local context.
limitations: The author states that the theory is based on a single extreme case involving a software artifact based on a mathematical algorithm. The setting was a pilot project rather than an artifact design process tightly embedded in ongoing routine performance. The paper also notes that the designers and users communicated closely and that confrontational political dynamics were muted between Metropol and Algo-Security.
future_research: The author calls for research on whether other types of artifacts have different inscribing practices and different implications for routine dynamics. Future studies should examine design performances that are more tightly connected to ongoing routine performance, settings where designers are more distant from users, and contexts where political dynamics are more confrontational. The paper also suggests examining whether the composition of the project team structurally influences the design process.
abstract: Organizations often create and employ artifacts in order to change their routines, but little is known about how artifacts can be designed to intentionally influence routine dynamics. In this paper, I present findings from an inductive, ethnographic study of how a law enforcement agency fabricated a game-theoretic artifact to modify its patrolling routine. Based on my in-depth analysis of the actions associated with creating this gametheoretic artifact, I develop a theoretical model that shows how organizational actors iteratively engage in a series of design performances to envision new sociomaterial assemblages of actors, artifacts, theories, and practices. These design performances influence routine dynamics by both eliciting mechanisms of abstracting grammars of action, exposing assumptions, distributing agency, and appraising outcomes, and by creating new assemblages that can be deployed in future routine performances. By revealing the generativity of design performances and sociomaterial assemblages, this empirical study contributes to our understanding of routine dynamics, performativity, and strategy tools.

title: Language and Competition: Communication Vagueness, Interpretation Difficulties, and Market Entry
methods: Empirical quantitative study of the U.S. domestic airline industry using computerized content analysis of incumbent firms' annual reports, OLS regression for firm-year antecedent models, and Cox proportional hazards survival models for entrant-market-quarter market-entry models.
industry: U.S. domestic airline industry.
time_period: 1995-2001, with potential entrants observed until June 30, 2001.
units: Incumbent airline firm-years, city-pair markets, potential entrants, and entrant-market-quarter observations.
n_sample: Final sample of 18 domestic airlines, 5,156 markets, and 8,095 realized new market entries; antecedent models used 91 firm-year observations.
authors: Guo, W.; Yu, T.; Gimeno, J.
theories: awareness-motivation-capability framework; competitive dynamics; competitive signaling theory; interfirm rivalry; strategic communication
keywords: annual reports; competitive dynamics; corporate communications; interpretation; market entry; strategic communication; vague language
research_question: The paper asks when managers of incumbent firms are more likely to use vague language in corporate communication and how rivals react to such vagueness. It specifically examines whether market-entry threats increase incumbents' communication vagueness and whether that vagueness is associated with fewer entries by potential entrants.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that incumbents facing stronger entry threats tilt corporate communication toward vaguer language, making their strategies and actions harder for rivals to interpret. For potential entrants, vague information can lengthen decision-making and increase the perceived risk of entry, reducing the likelihood of entering a market. The effect is expected to be stronger when entrants pay more attention to incumbents, as in markets with larger incumbents or higher concentration.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to competitive dynamics by separating attention to rivals from interpretation of rivals' information, arguing that awareness requires more than noticing competitive signals. It extends competitive signaling theory by showing that vague and equivocal communication, not only explicit aggressive signaling, can shape competitive interaction. It also adds a competitive-rivalry setting to research on language as a strategic tool in organizations.
practical_implication: The authors argue that communication and competitive intelligence are important managerial skills. For managers analyzing rivals, the findings imply attention to both what competitors communicate and what they leave unclear. For managers whose firms are being watched, the paper suggests that public communication can be interpreted by competitors as a strategic signal, especially when multiple audiences have divergent interests.
limitations: The authors state that the findings are based on firms in a single industry over a specific time period, which may limit generalizability. They also note that environmental uncertainty is controlled through proxies and that interpretation difficulty is assumed from vague language rather than directly observed. The study relies primarily on annual reports and automated text analysis, limiting attention to other communication channels and within-document variation.
future_research: The paper calls for direct measures of interpretation difficulty, such as surveys or cognitive maps, to unpack links between language use, interpretation, and interfirm behavior. It also suggests studying vagueness across communication channels and developing more fine-grained qualitative measures of language use. Future work could examine other language characteristics, resource diversion stratagems, rival-specific characteristics, mental maps, cognitive frameworks, identity domains, sensemaking processes, and issue framing in competitive dynamics.
abstract: Firms have a lot to lose from the entry of competitors into their markets. Grounded in the research on interfirm rivalry and strategic communication, we proposed and tested hypotheses suggesting that, when the managers of incumbent firms perceive a high threat of entry, they are more likely to use vagueness in their corporate communications to make their strategies and actions harder to discern. This lessened interpretation results in fewer competitive entries by potential entrants. We used computerized content analysis to quantify the use of vague language in incumbent firms' annual reports and empirically tested our hypotheses through data from the U.S. domestic airline industry. We found robust support for our hypotheses. By revealing that strategic use of language shapes competitive interactions, our research sheds new light on the process through which information is delivered, received, and interpreted by rivals. This process is at the heart of competitive dynamics and strategy research.

title: How Organizations Move from Stigma to Legitimacy: The Case of Cook’s Travel Agency in Victorian Britain
methods: In-depth historical, inductive qualitative case study of Thomas Cook’s travel agency in Victorian Britain, using historical records, Cook archival material, establishment press articles, scholarly sources, interviews with archivists and period historians, grounded theory coding, temporal bracketing, and member checks.
industry: Victorian travel agency and early tourism in Britain, centered on Thomas Cook’s travel agency.
time_period: The main transition examined is between 1861 and 1877.
units: Thomas Cook’s travel agency, the establishment press, the British elite, and archival records of travel-agency stigmatization and legitimation.
n_sample: 369 press articles, 155 Cook’s Excursionist Magazine items, 18 Thomas Cook documents, 26 competitor documents and magazine items, 26 books, 20 scholarly articles, and 9 interviews.
authors: Hampel, C. E.; Tracey, P.
theories: moral legitimacy; organizational stigma and legitimacy literatures; social class
keywords: Victorian Britain; moral legitimacy; organizational destigmatization; organizational stigma; social class; stigma elimination work; stigma reduction work
research_question: The paper asks how stigmatized organizations can destigmatize among hostile audiences and why audiences come to accept stigmatized organizations as legitimate. It examines these questions through the case of Thomas Cook’s travel agency moving from elite stigmatization to normative approval in Victorian Britain.
mechanism_summary:
- Initial audience evaluation: The Victorian elite stigmatized Cook’s travel agency because it feared that conducted tours threatened social status, travel exclusivity, and the moral order of class hierarchy.
- Phase 1, stigma reduction work: Cook deflected attention from stigma, isolated stigmatizers as a misguided minority, and demonstrated a narrow service to society.
- Intermediate audience reaction: Establishment hostility softened, but the stigma had not yet disappeared.
- Phase 2, stigma elimination work: Cook allied with former stigmatizers and demonstrated a broader service to society through education, national welfare, and international goodwill.
- End audience evaluation: Former stigmatizers came to view the travel agency as socially valuable and conferred normative approval.
- Boundary conditions: The model is framed for organizations that can plausibly challenge claims of harm and for cases where leaders are willing to endure public scrutiny.

The process is dialogical rather than a one-sided organizational tactic: Cook’s actions mattered because they interacted with audience fears and changing audience evaluations. Destigmatization occurred first by reducing elite fear that the organization threatened them, and then by persuading the same audience that the organization served a positive social role. The paper does not claim a variable-based causal test; it develops an inductive process model from historical evidence.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a process model of organizational destigmatization that explains how an organization can purge stigma rather than merely cope with it. It extends stigma-management research by distinguishing destigmatization from shielding, straddling, and co-opting, and it extends legitimacy research by showing how audiences can confer moral legitimacy on an organization that maintains practices once viewed as deviant. It also contributes to work on social class by showing how organizations may simultaneously challenge and reinforce class structures to gain approval.
practical_implication: The study suggests that stigmatized organizations may need to address the fear behind audience condemnation rather than simply hide, dilute, or exploit the stigma. In this case, Cook’s travel agency reduced hostility by presenting itself as nonthreatening and later gained support by linking its work to education, national welfare, and international goodwill. The implication is bounded: the authors do not present this route as applicable to organizations that clearly cause harm.
limitations: The authors identify the single historical case and its distinctive Victorian class context as important boundary conditions for transferability. They also note that their archival evidence mainly captures public interactions between Cook and the press, and that surviving documents may omit destroyed records or informal interactions that affected stigmatizers’ views.
future_research: The paper suggests studying how social media intermediaries may alter processes of stigmatization and destigmatization because contemporary organizations can communicate through channels beyond mainstream media. It also points to future work on private lobbying by marked organizations and on contexts that share the key characteristics of the Cook case, especially organizations that can contest perceived harm.
abstract: Based on an in-depth historical study of how Thomas Cook’s travel agency moved from stigmatization to legitimacy among the elite of Victorian Britain, we develop a model of organizational destigmatization. We find that audiences stigmatize an organization because they fear that it threatens a particular moral order, which leads them to mount sustained attacks designed to weaken or eradicate the organization. Our model suggests that an organization that experiences this form of profound disapproval can nonetheless purge its stigma and become legitimate through a two-step process: first the organization engages in stigma reduction work designed to minimize overt hostility among audiences by showing that it does not pose a risk to them. Second it engages in stigma elimination work designed to gain support from stigmatizers by showing that it plays a positive role in society. Our study therefore reorients organizational stigma research from a focus on how organizations can cope with the effects of stigma, and considers instead how they can eradicate the stigma altogether. We also shed light on much neglected audiencelevel dynamics by examining the process through which audiences construct stigma and why these constructions may change.
apa_citation: Hampel, C. E., & Tracey, P. (2017). How organizations move from stigma to legitimacy: The case of Cook’s travel agency in Victorian Britain. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2175-2207. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0365

title: Pliable Guidance: A Multilevel Model of Curiosity, Feedback Seeking, and Feedback Giving in Creative Work
methods: Field study of T-shirt designers in an online community, combining designer surveys, archival forum data, LIWC-based text analysis of feedback comments, coded design changes, two-level HGLM with overdispersed Poisson regression, and three-level HGLM with a Bernoulli logit link.
industry: Graphic designers participating in an online T-shirt design workshop and weekly T-shirt competitions.
time_period: Survey recruitment invitation was posted for approximately one month; calendar dates for the archival workshop data are not reported.
units: Designers, designs, shirt drafts, feedback comments, feedback-seeking questions, and coded design changes.
n_sample: 39 designers and 39 designs, 274 shirt drafts, and 1,662 feedback responses; the main design-change models used 1,656 feedback comments, 234 drafts, and 39 individuals.
authors: Harrison, S. H.; Dossinger, K.
theories: componential model of creativity; feedback theory; pliable guidance; social nature of creativity
keywords: ambivalent feedback; creative work; design revision; feedback giving; feedback seeking; open questions; pliable guidance; trait curiosity
research_question: The paper asks how trait curiosity shapes feedback seeking and feedback acceptance during the revision and evaluation stages of creative work. It examines whether curious designers ask more open questions, whether open questions attract more feedback, whether emotionally ambivalent feedback predicts later design revision, and whether curiosity strengthens that response to ambivalent feedback.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a multilevel feedback process organized around pliable guidance. Curious creative workers seek feedback in open ways that give feedback providers latitude to respond, which increases the amount of feedback they receive. Feedback providers' ambivalent language gives designers both direction and room for interpretation, making feedback more likely to be accepted and translated into revisions. Curiosity also makes designers more responsive to that ambivalent feedback, so individual differences shape how social feedback becomes part of creative revision.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to creativity theory by showing that curiosity matters not only at idea generation, but also in later stages when creative workers evaluate and revise provisional ideas. It develops pliable guidance as a theoretical umbrella for feedback seeking and feedback giving in creative work, arguing that useful feedback balances direction with interpretive freedom. It also extends multilevel creativity theorizing by showing that comments nest within drafts and drafts nest within individuals, making individual traits a context for social influence.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that creative workers and managers should attend to the language of feedback rather than treating feedback only as quantity or valence. For creative tasks, feedback providers may be more useful when they express ambivalence that signals both promise and problems, and feedback-seeking systems can prompt such responses. The paper also suggests that organizations may benefit from understanding how curiosity supports revision and from giving creative workers time to prototype, receive feedback, and revise.
limitations: The authors note that the study has a small individual-level sample and a nonrandom selection process because participants had already used feedback from the design community. They also caution that T-shirt designers in an online community may differ from workers in more traditional organizational settings, especially because the activity may be hobby-like and computer mediated. The study did not control for intrinsic motivation, which the authors identify as a related construct that future work should compare with curiosity.
future_research: The authors call for research on states of curiosity and antecedents that could encourage feedback seeking and accepting feedback. They suggest examining additional signals of pliability, including tone of voice, facial expressions, posture, and organizational conditions such as time pressure, hierarchy, and group interdependence. They also recommend testing whether feedback prompts that make ambivalence salient improve feedback interactions and clarifying how time for revision affects creative outcomes.
abstract: We propose and test a multilevel model that positions trait curiosity as a key individual difference during the revision and evaluation stages of the creative process. Using a sample of T-shirt designers, their creative drafts, and the questions and comments that feedback seekers and providers posted to an online workshop, we find curiosity acts as a bridge connecting creative workers with their feedback providers in novel ways. We advance pliable guidance as a theoretical umbrella to describe how feedback seekers and providers in creative work find a balance between the direction that makes feedback informative and the freedom to explore that infuses new ideas in their work. Our findings show that more curious individuals seek feedback by asking more open questions, which allows them to obtain more feedback. We also find that ambivalent feedback is more likely to lead to feedback acceptance and design revision. Finally, our results suggest that curiosity is an important moderator of how creative workers respond to ambivalent feedback. Our research highlights the pivotal role curiosity plays in drawing individuals into a collaborative process when developing their creative ideas, one that is guided and inspired by the social environment.
apa_citation: Harrison, S. H., & Dossinger, K. (2017). Pliable guidance: A multilevel model of curiosity, feedback seeking, and feedback giving in creative work. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2051-2072. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0247

title: Is There a Doctor in the House? Expert Product Users, Organizational Roles, and Innovation
methods: Empirical mixed-methods study of young U.S. surgical instrument ventures, combining a customized longitudinal firm-year panel with in-depth qualitative fieldwork. The quantitative tests use fixed-effects negative binomial models for product approvals, QML Poisson robustness checks, instrumental variables, inverse probability of treatment weighting, and additional sensitivity analyses.
industry: U.S. investor-backed surgical instrument ventures.
units: Young surgical instrument ventures and firm-year observations.
n_sample: 231 ventures and 1,864 firm-years.
authors: Katila, R.; Thatchenkery, S.; Christensen, M. Q.; Zenios, S.
theories: evolutionary perspective on innovation; organizational roles research; user innovation; variation-selection view of innovation
keywords: expert users; organizational roles; physician-users; product innovation; professional users; surgical instrument ventures; variation-selection; young firms
research_question: The paper asks how professional users in different organizational roles are related to product innovation in young firms. It examines whether physician-users help or hinder innovation when they occupy inventor, executive, CEO, and board-member roles in surgical instrument ventures.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is role activation of expert-user knowledge. User-inventors and user-board members are theorized to improve innovation because their tasks emphasize variation or combine variation and selection, allowing physician-users to broaden product ideas and improve relevance. User-executives, especially user-CEOs, are less beneficial because executive roles emphasize selection, and the paper argues that expert users may then rely too narrowly on prior domain knowledge and familiar solutions. The empirical results support positive curvilinear effects for user-inventors and user-board members, no overall support for user-executives, and a negative relationship for user-CEOs.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the evolutionary perspective on innovation by showing that variation and selection effects depend on the organizational role through which expert users participate. It extends user innovation research by moving beyond whether professional users are present to how their expertise is activated or constrained by specific internal roles in young firms. It also contributes to organizational roles research by showing that role tasks can change the innovation consequences of the same domain expertise.
practical_implication: Young ventures should not treat professional user expertise as uniformly beneficial. The findings suggest involving physician-users in technical and governance roles, especially in moderation and together with non-users, while being cautious about placing users in CEO or heavily selection-oriented executive roles. The policy implication is also role-specific: broad restrictions on physician involvement in medical-device firms may reduce conflicts of interest, but may also weaken innovation when they block useful technical or governance contributions.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the design cannot completely rule out reverse causality or selection into roles, so they use fixed effects, rich controls, lagged variables, instrumental variables, IPTW regressions, and robustness tests to address alternative explanations. The setting is surgical instrument ventures, where user influence is especially salient, so the findings may be weaker in other medical-device segments or industries. The paper also notes limited data on founders and on users' medical practice experience.
future_research: The authors call for research on the specific roles that user-founders take after founding and how those paths affect innovation. They also suggest examining how differences in users' capabilities and backgrounds, including educational, professional, and medical practice experience, moderate the relationships between user roles and innovation.
abstract: We explore the impact on innovation that domain experts, i.e., professional end users of a product have as inventors, executives, and board members in a young organization. Using a dataset of 231 surgical instrument ventures spanning a 25-year period alongside in-depth qualitative fieldwork, we find that professional physician–users (surgeons) strengthen innovation in some roles but block it in others. These experts are related to an increase in a firm’s innovation when they take a technology role as inventors, and particularly when they take a governance role on a fledgling firm’s board. However, despite their frequent involvement in executive roles, surgeon– executives are less likely to be helpful, and especially likely to block innovation, as chief executives. Our results emphasize expert users as a critical external dependency for a young firm’s innovation, but show that expertise can backfire when there is a mismatch with a particular organizational role. A key finding is that expert users are more helpful in suggesting a broad variety of solutions to a firm’s innovation problems but less helpful in selecting the best ones for the organization to pursue. Our findings have implications for research on the evolutionary perspective of innovation, user experts and their organizational roles in young firms, and entrepreneurial policy.
apa_citation: Katila, R., Thatchenkery, S., Christensen, M. Q., & Zenios, S. (2017). Is there a doctor in the house? Expert product users, organizational roles, and innovation. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2415-2437. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.1112

title: Compromise on the Board: Investigating the Antecedents and Consequences of Lead Independent Director Appointment
methods: Empirical quantitative study of S&P 1500 firms with combined CEO-board chair positions as of 2002. The paper uses BoardEx, Institutional Shareholder Services/RiskMetrics, company proxy statements, Compustat, Thomson Reuters Institutional Holdings, ExecuComp, CRSP, IBES, FactSet, SEC 10-Ks, and ExecuNet data; analyses include GLLAMM multinomial logit, conditional fixed-effects logistic regression, fixed-effects regressions, and Cox proportional hazard models.
industry: S&P 1500 publicly traded firms; no single industry restriction reported.
time_period: 2002-2012, with independent and control variables lagged by one year.
units: Firms, firm-years, boards, and independent directors.
n_sample: Final sample of 522 firms; reported model samples include 2,008 firm-years for board-leadership outcomes, 3,130 director observations for lead-director selection, 5,681 firm-years for performance descriptives, and 2,885 firm-years for future CEO-board chair separation.
authors: Krause, R.; Withers, M. C.; Semadeni, M.
theories: agency theory; bargaining and negotiations; classical organization theory; political view of boards; power circulation; power institutionalization
keywords: CEO duality; CEO power; agency theory; board leadership; classical organization theory; firm performance; lead independent director
research_question: The paper asks when boards appoint a lead independent director, which independent director is chosen, how the appointment relates to firm performance, and whether the structure becomes permanent or leads to later CEO-board chair separation.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that board leadership choices reflect the balance of power between the CEO and the board. High CEO power favors no change from CEO duality, low CEO power favors CEO-board chair separation, and moderate CEO power favors the compromise of appointing a lead independent director. The same compromise logic extends to director selection, where a director with moderate power is most likely to be chosen. Performance benefits depend on whether the lead independent director can provide oversight without sacrificing unity of command; this is more likely when CEO power is low.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces the lead independent director as a compromise board leadership structure that sits between agency theory's prescription of independent monitoring and classical organization theory's prescription of unity of command. It extends the political view of board decision-making by showing that balanced power can generate a compromise outcome rather than a winner-take-all outcome. It also contributes to board leadership theory by showing that the appointment can be symbolic for analysts but substantively beneficial for stock performance, analyst ratings, and ROI when CEO power is low.
practical_implication: The authors argue that balancing power between the CEO and board need not produce a governance impasse. Boards and CEOs can use lead independent director appointment as a meaningful compromise that preserves CEO duality's unity of command while adding independent oversight. The findings also caution that the structure is most beneficial when the CEO is not very powerful; otherwise it may function more as symbolic governance.
limitations: The authors identify limitations in their conceptualization of CEO and board power, noting that other forms of power exist beyond the measures captured. They also focus on two governance changes from CEO duality: appointment of a lead independent director and separation of CEO and board chair roles. Finally, the theory assumes that independent directors are motivated to restrict CEO power, but the study does not explain why boards vary in this motivation.
future_research: The paper encourages examination of other governance outcomes, including movement from an independent chair to combined CEO-chair roles with or without a lead independent director. It also calls for research on factors that shape boards' motivation to restrict CEO power, such as stock ownership, external responsibilities, and social pressures. The authors further suggest studying more proximal consequences of lead independent director appointment, such as CEO compensation, CEO retaliation against directors, and continuing board discord after compromise.
abstract: Board leadership has always been conceptualized as a tradeoff between two desirable yet mutually exclusive organizational attributes. Classical organization theory prescribes unity of command, achieved by combining the chief executive officer (CEO) and board chair positions; in contrast, agency theory prescribes independent monitoring, achieved by separating the CEO and board chair positions. Extant theory does not acknowledge the possibility that a compromise might exist between these competing theoretical prescriptions, one which might reduce their mutual exclusivity. Such a compromise has emerged in practice, however: the lead independent director. In the present research, we initiate theoretical exploration of this compromise between the prescriptions of agency theory and classical organization theory, addressing the questions of when a board will choose to appoint a lead independent director, who among the independent directors will serve in the position, how lead independent director appointment will impact firm performance, and whether this compromise is a permanent solution or a stepping stone to a more extreme outcome. Analysis of S&P 1500 firms from 2002 to 2012 reveals that lead independent director appointment reflects balanced power on the board, impacts firm performance positively under the right conditions, and generally becomes institutionalized as a permanent governance structure.

title: Pay-for-performance, Sometimes: An Interdisciplinary Approach to Integrating Economic Rationality with Psychological Emotion to Predict Individual Performance
methods: Empirical quantitative longitudinal field study using monthly compensation, performance, indebtedness, and PFP exception data from a for-profit healthcare provider; the authors analyze observations nested within individuals and business units using mixed effects models, lagged analyses, and a post hoc three-way interaction.
industry: For-profit healthcare provider using a revenue-based commission system with monthly draws for medical practitioners.
time_period: January 2006 to August 2009.
units: Monthly practitioner observations nested within individuals and business units.
n_sample: 33,581 observations of 1,573 individuals in 404 units.
authors: Maltarich, M. A.; Nyberg, A. J.; Reilly, G.; Abdulsalam, D.; Martin, M.
theories: economics-based incentive-intensity principle (Milgrom & Roberts, 1992); expectancy theory (Vroom, 1964); psychological contract theory (Rousseau, 1988, 1995)
keywords: PFP exceptions; PFP indebtedness; expectancy theory; individual performance; pay-for-performance; psychological contract theory
research_question: The paper asks how employees respond to pay-for-performance systems when they underperform and whether economic rationality alone is sufficient to predict those responses. It tests how PFP, PFP indebtedness, and PFP exceptions jointly shape future individual performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism integrates economic incentive logic, expectancy theory, and psychological contract theory. PFP should raise performance when employees can see a stronger link between performance and pay, but accumulated indebtedness weakens expectancy because employees have lower perceived achievability and a harder path to additional pay. PFP exceptions remove indebtedness and can create a positive psychological-contract response, improving performance immediately. The paper finds that this exception effect is short-lived, which qualifies both stable economic-incentive expectations and purely affective explanations.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to PFP theory by identifying underperformance and indebtedness as boundary conditions for the PFP-performance relationship. It integrates economics-based incentive-intensity logic with expectancy theory and psychological contract theory to explain why underperforming employees may not respond as economic rationality alone predicts. It also adds a temporal contribution by showing that performance gains from PFP exceptions dissipate after roughly two months.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that accumulated indebtedness can damage the motivational link between PFP and performance, so system design should avoid letting employees fall too far into debt. PFP exceptions can improve the benefiting employee's performance, but the paper cautions that this benefit appears short run and may carry unseen costs. The results therefore support careful, context-sensitive use of exceptions rather than treating them as a durable fix.
limitations: The authors note that the data come from one organization in the health care industry, which limits generalizability if the organization or industry is unusual in handling indebtedness or PFP exceptions. The study is also limited to U.S. units and to one type of draw-against-commission PFP system. The authors further note that they could not observe employee selection into this pay system and that individual-level effects do not establish what is best for the overall unit or organization.
future_research: The paper calls for additional work on the optimal draw level because draws may affect both employee indebtedness and recruitment quality. It also calls for research integrating additional affective and economic-rationality components, including justice and agency, into broader PFP theory. Future studies should examine the organizational-level impact of PFP policies and whether the findings generalize to other PFP systems.
abstract: This interdisciplinary study integrates economicsand psychology-based explanations to promote a clearer understanding of how employees respond to the pay-for-performance (PFP) system. By examining the combined performance predictions in the common, but rarely studied, situation in which employees do not meet expectations, we can more clearly view how economic rationality and psychological factors combine to explain employee behaviors in response to PFP. We test our hypotheses using unique longitudinal data from the health care industry. The theoretical insights contribute to a PFP theory that explains how and why PFP functions, and in doing so reconciles prior research inconsistencies.

Pay-for-performance, sometimes: An interdisciplinary approach to integrating economic rationality with psychological emotion to predict individual performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2155-2174. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0737

title: In The Beginning: Identity Processes and Organizing in Multi-Founder Nascent Ventures
methods: Longitudinal qualitative field study of nine nascent ventures across three municipalities, using grounded theory, iterative cross-case analysis, direct and participant observation, interviews, field notes, and archival documents.
industry: Nascent ventures focused on textile and apparel entrepreneurship and local economic and social revitalization.
time_period: Cases were followed for up to 28 months, with some later follow-up for archival records.
units: Multi-founder nascent ventures, founding groups, and individual founders involved in organizing efforts.
n_sample: Nine nascent ventures that began as four groups and expanded through mergers, disbandings, and new organizing efforts; the authors coded 30 founders.
authors: Powell, E. E.; Baker, T.
theories: collective identity prototypes; founder identity theory; identity theory; role identities; social identity theory
keywords: collective identity prototype; founder identity; grounded theory; identity homophily; identity processes; multi-founder nascent ventures; role identities; social identities
research_question: The paper asks how and why identity processes shape organizing efforts in multi-founder nascent ventures. It examines how founders' social and role identities affect early structuring, collective identity prototype construction and enforcement, consensus, and continued engagement in joint organizing.
mechanism_summary:
- Key identity foundations: Founders bring communitarian, missionary, or hybrid social identity profiles, along with role identities, into early organizing.
- Prototype construction: Founders first emphasize commonalities and show pragmatic deference, but their enactment of the community as connected or separate shapes recruitment, roles, and authority.
- Prototype enforcement: Early structuring choices become value-laden elements of a collective identity prototype; in-groups then enforce the prototype through adjustment, exclusion, or, when competing in-groups persist, disbanding and reforming.
- Emergent outcomes: The process shapes whether founders reach working consensus and whether they remain engaged in the nascent venture.

The process begins with multiple founders who share a desire to help the community but differ in how they understand that community and their relationship to it. Those differences initially surface through practical organizing choices, especially whether to recruit community members or skill holders, whether roles remain fluid or stable, and whether authority is shared or positional. These choices then become part of "who we are" for the emerging in-group, so disagreements about organizing become identity-laden rather than merely task-based. Communitarian in-groups tend to develop warmer ties and small-win signals that sustain engagement, whereas missionary in-groups in the observed cases reach consensus without continued engagement; contested cases disband when neither in-group can dominate.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends founder identity theory from individual founders to multi-founder organizing by showing how individual social identities become incorporated into collective identity prototypes and in-groups. It also extends founder identity theory from operational ventures to nascent ventures, showing that identity processes shape basic organizing questions before a venture becomes operational. The study integrates social identity theory and identity theory by linking founders' social identities, role construction, prototype enforcement, and early venture consensus or disbanding.
practical_implication: The authors state that hidden identity dynamics may affect nascent venture processes and outcomes before they appear as interpersonal conflicts. They suggest that founders may benefit from attending to these dynamics, and that tools for measuring founder social identities or serial entrepreneurs' tacit skills in assessing identity issues may prove useful in forming new venture teams. They also caution against treating either communitarian or missionary organizing as generally superior for nascent venture survival or instrumental effectiveness.
limitations: The authors state that the specific details of the findings are unlikely to be broadly empirically generalizable because the study is grounded in a particular context. The sample included communitarian and missionary founders but not Darwinian founders, limiting what the study can say about self-oriented founder identities. They also note that relationships between connected or separate enactments of community and specific structuring patterns may vary across venture contexts, institutional pressures, prior founder ties, paid work arrangements, and large organizing wins.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how founders' identities shape and are shaped by organizing, including how identity homophily develops during venture nascence. Future studies should examine contexts that include self-oriented Darwinian founders, different institutional pressures on roles and authority, and contingencies that affect whether founders remain engaged. The authors also call for work on demographic features as possible value-infused identity prototype elements, sources of continued engagement, team entrepreneurial passion, and how identity dynamics operate across broader types of ventures.
abstract: We conducted a longitudinal field study of nine nascent ventures attempting to revitalize local municipalities to understand how and why identity processes shape organizing in multi-founder nascent ventures. We develop grounded theory and a process model showing how the patterning of founders’ social and role identities shapes early structuring processes, how this in turn influences the construction of a collective identity prototype and its attempted enforcement by an in-group, and how the overall process influences whether or not founders remain engaged in their joint organizing efforts. In some cases, founders’ identities adjust as they experience periods of pragmatic deference, contestation, and domination by an in-group that moves increasingly toward identity homophily. Our contributions extend the growing entrepreneurship literature on founder identity from an individual focus toward understanding how founding teams work through organizing issues, and from a focus on established organizations to exploring why and whether teams move forward in nascent ventures. We open up a series of important questions for future research about how founders become “who we are.”
apa_citation: Powell, E. E., & Baker, T. (2017). In the beginning: Identity processes and organizing in multi-founder nascent ventures. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2381-2414. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0175

title: Discordant vs. Harmonious Selves: The Effects of Identity Conflict and Enhancement on Sales Performance in Employee–Customer Interactions
methods: Three-study empirical quantitative design: a longitudinal field study matching employee survey data with archival sales and HR records, analyzed with multilevel models and multilevel SEM, followed by two 2 x 2 between-subjects MTurk experiments using moderation-of-process tests, ANOVA, and planned comparisons.
industry: Study 1 sampled call center customer service employees at a large company managing credit-card customer service for retail and financial-services brands; Studies 2a and 2b used MTurk adults in simulated call-center selling scenarios.
country: Studies 2a and 2b used participants located in the United States; Study 1 country was not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 matched survey responses to sales performance in each of the four months after survey completion; dates for the survey and experiments were not reported in paper.
units: Customer service representatives and monthly sales observations in Study 1; individual MTurk participants reporting selling intentions in Studies 2a and 2b.
n_sample: Study 1: 763 final participants; Study 2a: 1002 adults; Study 2b: 795 adults.
authors: Ramarajan, L.; Rothbard, N. P.; Wilk, S. L.
theories: identity theory; symbolic interactionism
keywords: employee-customer interactions; identity conflict; identity enhancement; intrinsic motivation; multiple work-role identities; perspective-taking; role-immersion; role-taking; sales performance
research_question: The paper asks how employees' experience of multiple work identities as conflicting or enhancing affects performance in tasks that require interpersonal interaction, especially employee-customer sales interactions. It also asks whether role-immersion, operationalized as intrinsic motivation, and role-taking, operationalized as perspective-taking, explain those relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is grounded in identity theory and symbolic interactionism. The authors argue that identity conflict drains motivational and cognitive resources, reducing role-immersion and role-taking, whereas identity enhancement creates complementarity and energy across work-role identities. In the field study, intrinsic motivation mediates the relationships in the predicted direction; perspective-taking is related to the focal identity variables but does not mediate in the expected direction because it has a negative relationship with sales. The experiments strengthen causal inference by manipulating identity conflict or enhancement jointly with intrinsic motivation or perspective-taking.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on multiple identities by showing that relationships among identities, not only the strength or salience of individual identities, predict organizationally relevant performance. It treats identity conflict and identity enhancement as distinct constructs rather than opposite ends of one continuum and shows that each has independent effects. It also extends identity theory to interdependent work by connecting multiple work-role identities to role-immersion, role-taking, and employee-customer performance.
practical_implication: The authors argue that managers should pay attention to the psychological experience of asking employees to hold multiple work-role identities because these experiences shape customer interaction and performance. They suggest two managerial levers: decreasing identity conflict and increasing identity enhancement by helping employees understand synergies among their work roles. They also caution that perspective-taking can hinder performance in some people-work contexts when it sensitizes employees too much to customers' needs.
limitations: Study 1 does not provide causal evidence for the relationships between the independent variables and mediators, and it may be subject to omitted variable bias. The Study 1 measures of identity conflict and enhancement may not reflect the underlying values associated with particular identities. The paper is also limited to brand-based work-role identities in a sales context, and the experimental dependent variable is intention to sell rather than objective sales behavior.
future_research: The authors call for research on when people prioritize, compartmentalize, or integrate identities in response to identity conflict, and on when identity conflict has positive versus negative effects. They also suggest examining mechanisms beyond role-immersion and role-taking, such as integrative complexity and learning, and studying more than two identities at once. Future work could examine interaction dynamics, dyadic employee-customer identity effects, relational identification, group-level patterns of identity conflict and enhancement, and extensions beyond sales and brand identities.
abstract: Across multiple studies, we examine how identity conflict and enhancement within people affect performance in tasks that involve interactions between people. We also examine two mechanisms: role-immersion, operationalized as intrinsic motivation, and role-taking, operationalized as perspective-taking. In Study 1, a longitudinal field study of customer service representatives (n 5 763) who simultaneously identify with multiple brands they represent to customers, we examine the relationships between identity conflict and enhancement, on the one hand, and objective sales performance, on the other. We find independent effects for identity conflict and enhancement on intrinsic motivation, perspective-taking and performance, such that identity conflict negatively and enhancement positively affects all three variables above and beyond average identification. Intrinsic motivation further mediates the relationships between identity conflict and enhancement on sales in a direction consistent with our theorizing. However, while significant, perspective-taking does not mediate these relationships in the expected direction, because it has a negative effect on sales. In Studies 2a and 2b, we strengthen causal inference using an experimental moderation-of-process approach to constructively replicate and extend our findings. The paper demonstrates how multiple identities within people can have consequences for performance in tasks that involve interactions between people.
apa_citation: Ramarajan, L., Rothbard, N. P., & Wilk, S. L. (2017). Discordant vs. harmonious selves: The effects of identity conflict and enhancement on sales performance in employee-customer interactions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2208-2238. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.1142

title: The Suitability of Simulations and Meta-Analyses for Submissions to Academy of Management Journal
methods: Editorial (From the Editors) methods-guidance essay explaining when simulation-based and meta-analytic approaches fit AMJ's mission and when they are unlikely to be appropriate as standalone submissions.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Shaw, Jason D.; Ertug, Gokhan
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: empirical designs; meta-analysis; meta-analytic path modeling; simulations; theory testing
research_question: The editorial asks when simulations and meta-analysis may be successfully used in submissions to AMJ and when their use may not be appropriate for full review. It frames the issue as one of mission fit rather than categorical acceptance or rejection of either method.
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial premise: AMJ's mission requires theoretical and empirical contributions while remaining open to different theoretical approaches, empirical designs, levels of analysis, and regions of origin.
- Simulation guidance: Simulations can contribute when they complement or enhance empirical designs, especially by evaluating alternative models, triangulating findings, exploring inductive theory, or assessing robustness.
- Meta-analysis guidance: Standard meta-analytic summaries can fall outside AMJ's mission when they only estimate bivariate population-level associations, but meta-analytic techniques can fit when used for theory testing, theory building, or settings where primary or secondary data are difficult to obtain.
- Boundary conditions: The editorial presents guidelines with fuzzy boundaries, not formal policy, and emphasizes accessibility and current methodological standards.

The process logic is editorial and methodological rather than empirical. Shaw and Ertug argue that simulations and meta-analyses can be valuable for AMJ when they help test, extend, or build management theory and contribute to practice, but that standalone computational representations or standard empirical summaries often need additional empirical or theoretical leverage to fit the journal's mission.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a new theory. Its contribution is to clarify how two increasingly influential methodological approaches can be aligned with AMJ's theory-and-empirical-contribution mission, distinguishing acceptable uses from weaker standalone uses.
practical_implication: For prospective AMJ authors, the editorial implies that simulation-based and meta-analytic submissions should be designed around theory testing, theory building, triangulation, robustness, or empirically difficult questions rather than method novelty alone. It also signals that authors should write these designs accessibly for AMJ's broad audience and conform to current standards for the chosen approach.
limitations: The authors state that the suggestions are guidelines with fuzzy boundaries rather than black-and-white policy statements. They also note that they cannot anticipate every possible use of these techniques and do not aim to provide a tutorial on best practices.
future_research: The editorial encourages researchers to use simulations and meta-analytic designs creatively in ways that align with AMJ's mission. It points toward future work that uses these approaches to generate novel insights into management-relevant theory and phenomena while maintaining accessibility and methodological rigor.
abstract: Not reported in paper

title: Those with the Most Find It Hardest to Share: Exploring Leader Resistance to the Implementation of Team-based Empowerment
methods: Convergent parallel mixed methods study combining a longitudinal quasi-experimental analysis of same-day appointment access for VHA primary care teams with qualitative analysis of semistructured interviews conducted during and after early implementation of team-based empowerment.
industry: Veterans Health Administration primary care teams implementing Patient Aligned Care Teams.
time_period: Quantitative performance data cover 7 months before and 37 months after the adoption of team-based empowerment; qualitative interviews were conducted during initial implementation and one year later.
units: Health care team providers and primary care team members.
n_sample: Quantitative sample of 224 providers, including 142 physician providers and 82 nonphysician providers; qualitative data include 30 initial interviews and 14 follow-up interviews.
authors: Stewart, Greg L.; Astrove, Stacy L.; Reeves, Cody J.; Crawford, Eean R.; Solimeo, Samantha L.
theories: expectations states theory (Berger et al., 1974; Berger & Zelditch, 1998); identity work (Dutton et al., 2010; Ibarra, 1999); team-based empowerment and shared leadership
keywords: Veterans Health Administration; leader delegation; leader identity work; leader resistance; leader status; shared leadership; team-based empowerment
research_question: The paper asks why leaders resist the implementation of team-based empowerment even when sharing tasks and leadership could improve personal and organizational outcomes. It specifically examines whether teams led by higher-status physician providers are less effective in implementing team-based empowerment than teams led by lower-status nonphysician providers, and what identity and delegation processes explain that difference.
mechanism_summary:
- Focal intervention: Team-based empowerment through the VHA's Patient Aligned Care Teams.
- Status condition: Higher-status physician providers versus lower-status nonphysician providers as team leaders.
- Quantitative outcome: Team effectiveness measured as same-day appointment access.
- Qualitative process: Leader identity work, with leaders either embracing an empowering identity or protecting a hierarchical identity.
- Delegation patterns: Balanced delegation, insufficient delegation, and overabundant delegation.

The process begins when team-based empowerment asks leaders to shift from hierarchical control toward shared task and leadership responsibility. For higher-status physician leaders, this shift can create status threat because the new role weakens the distinct physician-in-charge identity. Leaders who protect the old hierarchical identity tend to delegate improperly, either by withholding tasks and control or by pushing too much responsibility onto team members without coordination. Leaders who embrace the empowering identity are more likely to use balanced delegation that recognizes team member expertise and supports team effectiveness.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to research on team-based empowerment and shared leadership by showing that leader status shapes whether a move from bureaucracy to team structure succeeds. It adds an identity-work explanation for leader resistance, arguing that high-status leaders may need to change who they perceive themselves to be before changing what they do. It also extends delegation research by distinguishing balanced delegation from both insufficient and overabundant delegation.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that organizations implementing team-based empowerment should not treat structural redesign alone as sufficient. High-status leaders may need help developing an empowering leader identity that is compatible with their professional identity, including role models, training, cross-training, altered incentives, and coaching. Effective empowerment also requires leaders to stay involved while using team member strengths, involving others in planning and decision making, and avoiding the simple dumping of tasks.
limitations: The authors note that the convergent parallel mixed methods design did not allow them to empirically test the mediating mechanisms discovered through qualitative analysis. They also state that same-day appointment access is an indirect measure of team effectiveness and that other factors may influence access to appointments. The interviews were designed broadly to elicit barriers and facilitators of team-based empowerment rather than to directly assess identity work and delegation.
future_research: The paper calls for quantitative tests of the full model in which team-based empowerment triggers different identity-work responses among high- and low-status leaders, which then shape delegation patterns and team effectiveness. It also recommends studying additional obstacles such as failure to recognize expertise, lack of trust among team members, and whether patient complexity or team member specialization limits delegation. Future research should examine how balanced delegation varies across task types and whether teams with less specialization require the same acknowledged leader role.
abstract: We use a convergent parallel mixed methods approach to explore barriers to the successful implementation of a team-based empowerment initiative within the Veterans Health Administration. Although previous research has suggested that leaders often actively obstruct empowerment initiatives, little is known about the reasons behind and effects of such hindering. Using a longitudinal quasi-experimental design, we support a hypothesis that higher-status physician leaders are less successful than lower-status nonphysician leaders in implementing team-based empowerment. In parallel, we analyze qualitative data obtained through interviews conducted during early months of the team-based empowerment initiative to identify common themes for why and how leaders facilitated or obstructed implementation. Leader identity work and leader delegation were identified as themes explaining (1) why higher-status leaders struggled with the new empowering role and (2) how specific leader actions either facilitated or inhibited sharing of tasks and leadership. Results suggest that team-based empowerment creates a status threat for high-status leaders who then struggle to protect their old identity as someone with distinct professional capabilities, which in turn leads to improper delegation behavior. Therefore, in order for team-based empowerment to succeed, leaders may need to change their perceptions of who they are before they will change what they do.
apa_citation: Stewart, G. L., Astrove, S. L., Reeves, C. J., Crawford, E. R., & Solimeo, S. L. (2017). Those with the most find it hardest to share: Exploring leader resistance to the implementation of team-based empowerment. *Academy of Management Journal*, 60(6), 2266-2293. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.1173

title: Moving from Abuse to Reconciliation: A Power-Dependence Perspective on When and How a Follower Can Break the Spiral of Abuse
methods: Scale development for balancing operations followed by two empirical field studies using time-lagged three-wave panel designs; Study 1 used multi-source matched leader-follower-coworker data from a real estate firm and Study 2 replicated the model in a commercial bank, with polynomial regressions, response surface modeling, moderated regressions, and mediated moderation tests.
industry: Real estate in Study 1 and banking in Study 2.
time_period: Three-wave panel designs; Study 1 used four-week lags between waves and Study 2 used six-week intervals, with exact calendar dates not reported.
units: Leader-follower dyads and matched leader, follower, and coworker responses.
n_sample: Scale development used 286 MTurk participants; Study 1 obtained 219 matched and completed responses; Study 2 obtained 363 matched and completed responses.
authors: Wee, E. X. M.; Liao, H.; Liu, D.; Liu, J.
theories: approach and avoidance motivation; coping theory; followership; power-dependence theory
keywords: abusive supervision; approach balancing operations; balancing operations; followership; leader dependence; leader reconciliation; power-dependence theory
research_question: The paper asks which state of power dependence in a leader-follower dyad predicts abusive supervision and how followers can change that dyadic power imbalance over time. It further asks whether followers' approach balancing operations can reduce future abusive supervision and increase leaders' reconciliatory behavior after abuse.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is power-dependence based. When the follower is asymmetrically dependent on the leader, the leader has greater power in the dyad and is more likely to abuse the follower. Approach balancing operations, especially coalition formation and value enhancement, increase the leader's dependence on the follower by making the follower more instrumental to the leader's goals and resources. As the leader becomes more dependent on the follower, abusive supervision is less likely to persist and the leader is more likely to engage in reconciliation after abuse; avoidance balancing operations do not produce the same relational change.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to abusive supervision research by specifying follower asymmetric dependence on the leader as the dyadic power state most likely to produce abuse, rather than treating leader power as a static hierarchical fact. It contributes to followership by presenting followers as agentic actors who can use approach balancing operations to alter power dependence, reduce abuse over time, and prompt leader reconciliation. It also develops and validates a balancing operations scale organized around approach and avoidance motivation.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that followers may have coping strategies beyond leaving the organization or managing the personal consequences of abuse. Approach balancing operations can help followers change their relationship with the leader by increasing their instrumental value or collective leverage. The authors also suggest that leaders, followers, and organizations should monitor relational power dependence and encourage mutual high dependence, such as through shared performance goals, before dyadic power imbalance becomes too polarized.
limitations: The authors state that they did not study leaders' strategies to counter followers' balancing operations, including possible power conflict when leaders feel threatened. The research focused on dyadic relations rather than power dependence within teams with multiple followers under one leader. The two empirical studies were based in China, so cultural setting may condition the strength or form of the effects.
future_research: The authors call for research on leaders' counter-strategies when followers use balancing operations and on power-dependence patterns in teams rather than only dyads. They also recommend studying antecedents and contingencies of followers' use of balancing operations, including legitimacy perceptions, self-efficacy, locus of control, and organizational events. Future research should further investigate moral licensing and cleansing in abusive supervision and examine balancing operations in other cultural settings.
abstract: Despite the burgeoning research on abusive supervision, the literature lacks an in-depth understanding of how followers can successfully break the spiral of abusive supervision over time and influence their leaders to engage in reconciliatory behaviors following abusive supervision. Using power-dependence theory as our framework, we first examine the specific state of power dependence that predicts abusive supervision. We then theorize balancing operations as coping strategies that the follower can use to address the persistence of abusive supervision over time by changing the power imbalance within the dyad. We hypothesize that through the follower’s approach balancing operations, the leader is more likely to regard the abused follower as someone who is instrumental to his or her pursuit of goals and resources, resulting in a reduction in future abuse and an increase in the leader’s future reconciliation. After developing and validating measures of balancing operations, we test the hypotheses using a three-wave panel design with field data from a real estate company (Study 1). In addition, we strengthen our conclusions by replicating our results through a different field sample in a commercial bank (Study 2). The findings’ theoretical and practical implications for abusive supervision and followership are discussed.

title: Understanding the Direction, Magnitude, and Joint Effects of Reputation When Multiple Actors’ Reputations Collide
methods: Empirical quantitative event-study design using IBES analyst recommendation changes from 1996 to 2008. The study estimates OLS regressions of downgrade and upgrade cumulative abnormal returns, with robust standard errors clustered over firms and controls for analyst, firm, management, industry, year, and fiscal-quarter factors.
industry: U.S. publicly traded firms covered by IBES analyst recommendation data across global industry-classification-system sectors.
units: Individual analyst recommendation-change events modeled as CEO-by-analyst dyads at covered firms.
n_sample: 36,878 recommendation-change observations: 19,512 downgrades and 17,358 upgrades.
authors: Boivie, Steven; Graffin, Scott D.; Gentry, Richard J.
theories: attribute-specific and audience-specific reputation; reputation as collective social judgment; social evaluations
keywords: CEO reputation; analyst recommendations; analyst reputation; cumulative abnormal returns; firm reputation; reputation
research_question: The paper asks how the reputations of analysts, CEOs, and firms individually and jointly affect shareholder reactions to changes in analysts’ stock recommendations. It focuses on whether multiple actor reputations have distinct, relative, and interactive effects on the cumulative abnormal returns associated with recommendation upgrades and downgrades.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that investors use reputation as social information under uncertainty, but they weight each reputation according to its attribute specificity and relevance to the audience’s expectations. Analyst reputation is built around forecast accuracy and is directly relevant to stock recommendations, so it amplifies market reactions to upgrades and downgrades. CEO reputation buffers recommendation changes when analysts are not stars, but star analyst reputation can dominate CEO reputation when the two reputations collide.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends reputation research by shifting from single-actor reputation effects to simultaneous and joint effects among multiple reputations in one market context. It develops a framework in which the direction and magnitude of a reputation’s effect depend on attribute specificity and audience relevance. Empirically, it shows that analyst reputation has the strongest effect on shareholder reactions and can reduce the influence of CEO reputation, while firm reputation is less consistent in this setting.
practical_implication: The findings imply that star analysts can move markets more strongly than non-star analysts when they issue recommendation changes. Investors should interpret analyst research with attention to the reputations of both the analyst and the CEO, because CEO reputation buffers only some recommendation changes and does not offset star analyst downgrades. Firms and market participants should also recognize that the practical value of a reputation depends on the audience and decision context, not only on whether the reputation is favorable.
limitations: The authors identify the U.S.-specific sample as a limitation, noting that generalizability to other equity-market contexts is unclear. They also treat recommendation changes in isolation, even though clustered downgrades or upgrades may reinforce or damage CEO reputation nonlinearly. A further limitation is that reputations come from different certification sources, and the CAR models explain limited incremental variance despite practically meaningful valuation effects.
future_research: Future research could test whether the findings generalize outside U.S. equity markets and to other settings where multiple actor reputations overlap. Studies could examine nonlinear effects when multiple analysts target the same firm around the same time. The authors also suggest comparing reputational overlap in settings where the same body provides certification, such as relay CEO successions.
abstract: Despite extensive research efforts into the effects of reputation, virtually all of it has examined the effect of one type of reputation on one or more specific outcomes. But, how, for example, might the reputations of analysts, CEOs, and firms individually and jointly affect firm outcomes? To answer this question, the present study focuses on a context in which reputations are particularly relevant: changes in analyst recommendations and the effect of those changes on stock market reactions. Our study contributes to the increasing reputation literature by being one of the first to recognize and measure how the market accounts for multiple reputations. Further, we argue and find that the reputations of different actors interact with each other when determining particular firm outcomes. We also find that different actor’s reputations influence the reactions of observers.
apa_citation: Boivie, S., Graffin, S. D., & Gentry, R. J. (2016). Understanding the direction, magnitude, and joint effects of reputation when multiple actors’ reputations collide. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 188-206. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0521
