title: Fuzzy Logic and the Market: A Configurational Approach to Investor Perceptions of Acquisition Announcements
methods: Event-study design using three-day cumulative abnormal returns around acquisition announcements, combined with fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of nine calibrated acquirer- and deal-level conditions.
industry: All major industry sectors, including manufacturing, services, trade, financial, and natural resources.
time_period: 1990 through 2004.
units: Completed acquisitions that resulted in full ownership of the target firm.
n_sample: 2,403 deals.
authors: Campbell, Joanna Tochman; Sirmon, David G.; Schijven, Mario
theories: bounded rationality (Cyert & March, 1963; Simon, 1945); fuzzy set theory (Zadeh, 1965); signaling theory (Spence, 1973)
keywords: abnormal stock returns; asymmetric causality; equifinality; fuzzy set methodology; investor perceptions; mergers and acquisitions
research_question: The paper asks which configurations of acquirer- and deal-specific factors elicit positive investor reactions to M&A announcements and which configurations fail to elicit positive reactions. It examines investor judgment as holistic, configurational sensemaking rather than as the additive evaluation of independent deal attributes.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is configurational: investors facing bounded rationality, information asymmetry, and high-velocity decision contexts use salient signals about opportunity, motivation, and ability to form holistic perceptions of an announced acquisition. Fuzzy set analysis shows equifinality, with multiple configurations producing positive reactions, and asymmetric causality, with poorly received deals differing qualitatively from well-received deals rather than simply reversing the same factors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a mid-range configurational theory of M&A stock market performance by treating acquisition announcements as complex signals evaluated as gestalts. It contributes to M&A research by showing that individual deal factors such as relatedness, financing, premium, leverage, and experience have contingent meanings within configurations, and it contributes to behavioral strategy by theorizing investors as boundedly rational market participants rather than purely reductionist evaluators.
practical_implication: The findings imply that managers should consider how acquisition attributes will be read together before announcing a deal. Cash financing is especially consequential because investors reacted positively to configurations with cash financing and negatively to configurations combining high premiums with no cash financing, particularly when other factors suggested integration difficulty, hubris, turnaround risk, or overextension.
limitations: The study explains only part of the variation in positive and negative M&A announcement reactions, and the authors note that the overall solution coverage is limited. The design uses short-term cumulative abnormal returns, so it captures investors' perceived value of strategy formulation rather than long-term acquisition implementation performance. The sample is limited to acquisitions by North American acquirers in developed financial and regulatory settings.
future_research: Future research should refine the configurational framework by identifying additional deal prototypes, examining finer time periods, and testing boundary conditions such as changing credit-market environments. The authors also call for work on whether these configurations generalize to emerging-market contexts, whether deal communication wording and tone shape investor reactions, and how stock-financed deals can elicit positive reactions when cash financing is absent.
abstract: Prior research on mergers and acquisitions (M&As) has substantially advanced our understanding of how isolated acquirerand deal-specific factors affect abnormal stock returns. However, investors are likely to perceive and evaluate M&As holistically—that is, as complex configurations (i.e., gestalts) of characteristics, rather than as a list of independent factors. And, yet, extant M&A literature has not addressed why and how configurations of factors elicit positive or negative reactions. Overlooking the interdependent nature of factors known to influence acquisition success has limited our understanding of both M&As and investor judgment. Taking an inductive approach to addressing this important issue, the present study relies on fuzzy set methodology. Our results provide compelling evidence that investor perceptions of M&A announcements are not only configurational in nature but also characterized by equifinality (or the presence of multiple paths to success) and asymmetric causality (i.e., configurations that represent bad deals are not simply a mirror image of good deals, but differ fundamentally). By constructing a typology of “good” and “bad” deals as perceived by market participants, we develop a mid-range theory of M&A stock market performance. As such, this study offers novel theoretical and empirical insights to scholars as well as implications for practitioners.

title: Third Party Employment Branding: Human Capital Inflows and Outflows Following “Best Places to Work” Certifications
methods: Empirical quantitative archival and survey study of BPTW competition participants from 2011-2013. The authors use regression models with lagged dependent variables, HR-practice controls, moderators for company size and industry job openings, and effects-coded contrasts to test certification effects on turnover and applicant pool quality.
industry: Companies from 16 BPTW competitions across multiple BLS industry categories, concentrated in professional and business services and education and health services.
units: Company-level BPTW competition participants.
n_sample: 624 cases used in at least one analysis; 617 in the turnover regression and 466 in the applicant pool quality regression.
authors: Dineen, Brian R.; Allen, David G.
theories: celebrity firms perspective; identity perspective; signaling theory; strategic human resource management theory
keywords: Best Places to Work; applicant pool quality; collective turnover; employment branding; signaling theory; third party employment branding
research_question: How do single and repeated third party employment branding signals, specifically BPTW certifications, relate to firm-level human capital outflows and inflows? The paper asks whether certification lowers collective turnover, whether repeated certification follows a crystallization or celebrity pattern, and whether company size and industry job openings condition applicant pool quality effects.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that third party certifications provide credible and comparable employment-branding signals. For incumbents, certification strengthens identification and makes leaving seem less attractive relative to uncertified alternatives, lowering collective turnover. For job seekers, certification affects applicant pool quality through competing heuristic and sorting logics, with the observed effects stronger for smaller firms and when job openings are scarcer.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends signaling theory by treating third parties as signal transmitters whose certifications add credibility and comparability to employment-branding claims. It broadens employment branding research beyond applicant attraction by showing that external branding signals can also matter for incumbent retention and collective turnover. It also develops the crystallization-versus-celebrity distinction for repeated signals, finding evidence more consistent with diminishing marginal turnover benefits after the initial certification.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that firms may gain retention benefits from BPTW certification, but that repeated certification may have diminishing marginal value for turnover. Smaller firms and firms operating when job openings are scarce may gain particular applicant-quality benefits from certification. The paper cautions that competition entry has costs and possible employee-reaction risks, so managers should weigh certification strategy against expected retention, applicant quality, and feedback-report benefits.
limitations: The authors note that organization mortality limits generalizability because firms that stopped competing no longer supplied outcome data. The archival design prevents direct testing of the individual-level processes the theory invokes, including identification, embeddedness, reputation perceptions, and emotional reactions to novel signals. They also state that the design strengthens confidence through lagged outcomes and HR-practice controls but cannot directly establish that BPTW certifications caused the observed differences.
future_research: Future research could manipulate third party employment branding signals in controlled settings to test whether they change individual perceptions and emerge as firm-level outcomes. Longer-period studies could examine whether applicant pool quality mediates long-run turnover effects and whether certification effects replicate in stronger labor markets or among larger firms. The authors also encourage research on certification rankings, signal contagion among employees, attribution processes, customer spillovers, and whether turnover involves stronger or weaker performers.
abstract: “Best Places to Work” (BPTW) and similar competitions are a proliferating form of third party employment branding. Little is known, however, about how single or repeated third party employment branding occurrences relate to key human capital outcomes. Extending signaling theory by considering signal credibility and comparability, we use archival and survey data from 624 BPTW participants in 16 competitions across a three-year period to develop and test hypotheses linking BPTW certifications to collective turnover rates and key informant perceptions of applicant pool quality. We find that certifications are associated with lower turnover rates, and in addition, propose competing crystallization and celebrity hypotheses that model turnover trajectories with repeated certifications, finding diminishing marginal turnover reductions across multiple certifications. We also examine company size and industry job opening moderators, finding that as certifications increase, applicant pool quality is: (1) higher in smaller companies, and (2) higher when job openings are scarcer. Finally, beyond being certified or not, we find supplemental evidence for effects of the specific certification level achieved (e.g., 2nd versus 15th). This investigation advances theory related to collective turnover, applicant pool quality, and employment branding, and is relevant to company decisions about seeking or re-seeking third party certifications.

title: Classical Deviation: Organizational and Individual Status as Antecedents of Conformity
methods: Quantitative historical panel analysis of U.S. symphony-orchestra programming, using linear models with orchestra, musical director, and decade fixed effects; predictors are lagged one year, with lagged dependent-variable and random-effects robustness checks.
industry: Major U.S. symphony orchestras
units: Orchestra-years, orchestras, and musical directors
n_sample: 1,090 orchestra-years, 27 orchestras, and 154 musical directors
authors: Durand, Rodolphe; Kremp, Pierre-Antoine
theories: middle-status conformity theory (Phillips & Zuckerman, 2001); organizational conformity and legitimacy; status theory
keywords: alignment; conventionality; distinctiveness; middle-status organizations; musical directors; organizational conformity; status effects
research_question: The paper asks how organizational and individual status shape two distinct forms of organizational conformity: alignment with peer repertoires and conventionality through emphasis on salient canonical attributes. It examines whether middle-status organizations and middle-status individual leaders conform differently because they face different exposure to penalties and rewards.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism separates penalty avoidance from quality-comparison rewards. Alignment lets organizations blend in with peers and reduce sanctions for misalignment, so middle-status organizations have the strongest incentive to align. Conventionality lets individual leaders stand out on salient, comparable repertoire choices and claim quality recognition, so middle-status musical directors have the strongest incentive to adopt conventional programming; this effect is stronger when orchestra status or low alignment creates more room for reward capture.
theoretical_contribution: The paper decomposes conformity into alignment and conventionality, showing that organizations can conform by blending in or by standing out on highly salient field attributes. It refines middle-status conformity theory by linking organizational status more strongly to alignment and individual leader status more strongly to conventionality, thereby integrating status effects across organizational and individual levels. It also challenges the assumption that misalignment necessarily equals deviance, because misaligned actors may still be conventional.
practical_implication: For organizations and leaders in status-ordered fields, conformity pressure is not a single strategic constraint. The study shows that organizations may reduce penalties by maintaining broad alignment with peer norms, while individual leaders may seek recognition by concentrating effort on salient, quality-comparable choices. Interpreting conformity therefore requires distinguishing between blending in with peers and emphasizing canonical features that invite quality comparison.
limitations: The study is based on major U.S. symphony orchestras between 1879 and 1969, a setting with strong programming norms, elite cultural audiences, and unusually visible individual artistic leaders. The authors note that their analysis does not explain norm dynamics and considers conformity only with a contemporaneous norm. Generalization should be tested in fields with different audience structures, technological change, or competing institutional logics.
future_research: Future research should test whether audience heterogeneity changes the relationship between status, alignment, and conventionality. Other individual or organizational characteristics besides status may also shape responses to negative sanctions and positive rewards. Research on faster-changing normative environments could examine discrepancies between historical norms and contemporary imperatives for conformity.
abstract: Beside making organizations look like their peers through the adoption of similar attributes ("alignment"), this paper highlights the fact that conformity also enables organizations to stand out by exhibiting highly salient attributes key to their field or industry ("conventionality"). Building on the conformity and status literatures, and using the case of major U.S. symphony orchestras and the changes in their concert programming between 1879 and 1969, we hypothesize and find that middle-status organizations are more aligned and middle-status individual leaders make more conventional choices than their lowand high-status peers. In addition, the extent to which middle-status leaders adopt conventional programming is shown to be moderated by the status of the organization and by its level of alignment. Thus, this paper offers a novel theory and operationalization of organizational conformity, and contributes to the literature on status effects, and, more broadly, to the understanding of the key issues of distinctiveness and conformity.

title: Status Matters: The Asymmetric Effects of Supervisor–Subordinate Disability Incongruence and Climate for Inclusion
methods: Multilevel field survey of employees nested in work units in a German federal agency, using hierarchical linear modeling to test dyadic disability congruence effects on LMX and performance and unit-level climate for inclusion as a cross-level moderator.
industry: Public service / federal agency
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employees nested in work units; supervisor-subordinate disability congruence scenarios
n_sample: 1,253 employees from 54 work units
authors: Dwertmann, David J. G.; Boehm, Stephan A.
theories: climate for inclusion; leader-member exchange theory; relational demography; similarity-attraction paradigm; social identity and self-categorization; status mechanisms; stigma-by-association
keywords: climate for inclusion; disability incongruence; employee performance; leader-member exchange; status mechanisms; workforce diversity
research_question: How does supervisor-subordinate disability incongruence affect leader-member exchange quality and subsequent subordinate performance? Does unit-level climate for inclusion buffer the negative LMX effects of disability incongruence, and does this buffering differ depending on whether the supervisor or subordinate has the disability?
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that disability incongruence weakens LMX through relational demography, similarity-attraction, social identity, stigma, and status mechanisms. Incongruence is expected to be especially damaging when the supervisor has a disability because subordinates may experience stigma-by-association and a status-based discrepancy between the supervisory role and disability stereotypes. Climate for inclusion operates as a unit-level norm that can reduce stereotyping and social categorization, but the paper finds this buffer only when the supervisor, not the subordinate, has a disability.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends relational demography and disability research by showing that disability incongruence matters in both directions and that the supervisor-with-disability scenario is especially consequential for LMX. It contributes to LMX and organizational climate research by demonstrating a cross-level moderation effect: inclusive unit climates can partially buffer negative dyadic effects, but asymmetrically. The study also foregrounds status as a mechanism that shapes when demographic incongruence is especially damaging.
practical_implication: Organizations should treat positive LMX relationships across disability-status differences as a central inclusion and performance concern. The findings suggest that inclusive climates, equitable HR practices, disability-supportive leadership, and manager accountability for developing diverse subordinates can reduce the relational costs of disability incongruence. The practical emphasis is strongest for contexts in which supervisors with disabilities may otherwise face stigma-by-association dynamics from subordinates.
limitations: The data come from one German federal agency with strong disability rights norms and unusually high representation of employees with disabilities, which may limit generalizability across countries, sectors, and more competitive organizational cultures. Disability congruence was reported by subordinates, so the measure captures perceived rather than independently verified supervisor disability status. The study also uses subjective performance ratings, although the authors justify them as aligned with the organization's promotion and benefit system.
future_research: Future studies should test whether combining higher hierarchical status with membership in a devalued demographic group consistently produces negative relational outcomes or whether status sometimes buffers them. Research should examine disability type and severity, because physical, intellectual, and mental or psychological disabilities may generate different stereotypes and LMX patterns. Further work should also investigate why climate for inclusion affects supervisors and subordinates asymmetrically and identify antecedents of inclusive climates.
abstract: Growing workforce diversity increases the likelihood that supervisors and subordinates will differ along demographic lines, a situation that has important implications for their relationship quality and individual outcomes. In a sample of 1,253 employees from 54 work units, we investigate the effects of differences in disability status between supervisors and subordinates on leader–member exchange (LMX) quality and subsequent performance ratings, and find that incongruence in general is related to lower LMX quality and lower performance. In addition, we propose and find an asymmetrical effect of disability incongruence, such that LMX quality is worse in dyads in which the supervisor has a disability than in dyads in which the subordinate has a disability. Furthermore, we investigate the moderating role of unit-level climate for inclusion on this relationship and find support for a buffering effect of inclusive climates on the negative incongruence-LMX relationship for scenarios in which the supervisor, but not the subordinate, has a disability. We build relevant theory for the relational demography, disability, LMX, and organizational climate literatures by predicting these effects on the basis of status mechanisms. These findings have important practical implications, as they provide companies with a feasible way to manage their diverse workforce.
apa_citation: Dwertmann, D. J. G., & Boehm, S. A. (2016). Status matters: The asymmetric effects of supervisor–subordinate disability incongruence and climate for inclusion. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 44-64. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0093

title: The Art of Representation: How Audience-specific Reputations Affect Success in the Contemporary Art Field
methods: Artist-year panel study using ArtFacts.Net exhibition data, conditional logit models with artist fixed effects, year fixed effects, artist-clustered standard errors, and SUEST/Wald tests for cross-model comparisons.
industry: Contemporary art field; museum and gallery exhibitions.
units: Artist-year observations for newly emerging artists.
n_sample: 311,839 artist-year observations on 58,014 newly emerging artists; estimation samples are 116,590 museum observations and 154,098 gallery observations.
authors: Ertug, G.; Yogev, T.; Lee, Y. G.; Hedström, P.
theories: accountability research; audience-specific reputation; signaling theory; status theory
keywords: accountability; audience-specific reputations; contemporary art field; status
research_question: How do actors' audience-specific reputations affect their success with different audiences in the same field, and how do status, cross-audience interaction, and audience accountability condition these effects?
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that reputation is valuable when it reduces uncertainty for a focal audience whose concerns match the attribute signaled by that reputation. Museums are more accountable to diverse stakeholders and care more about artistic quality, so a reputation for artistic quality is more valuable for museum success and is more strongly reinforced by high-status museum affiliations. Interaction with a non-focal audience can signal lack of fit, especially for high-status museums, reducing the value of an artist's audience-specific reputation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances reputation theory by showing that reputation effects are audience-specific rather than uniformly actor-level. It also contributes to research on reputation-status interplay and inter-audience spillovers by identifying audience accountability as a boundary condition that shapes whether other signals enhance or discount the value of reputation.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that people working across multiple client or audience groups should not assume that a positive reputation with one audience will transfer equally to another. They may need to build separate reputations around the attributes valued by each audience and attend to whether the focal audience must justify its decisions to diverse stakeholders.
limitations: The paper reports no statistical support for the differential effect of magazine-cover appearances on gallery versus museum success, which the authors attribute to noise in measuring commercial viability. It also examines only two additional signals, status and interaction with other audiences, and focuses on the contemporary art field, limiting generalizability to other settings.
future_research: Future research could use better measures of commercial viability, such as auction appearances or sales ratios, where systematic data are available. It could also examine additional signals or intangible assets and test the framework in other multi-audience settings, including academic careers, biotechnology scientists, doctor-managers, and contexts with clearer audience hierarchies.
abstract: We study the effects of actors’ audience-specific reputations on their levels of success with different audiences in the same field. Extending recent work that has emphasized the presence of multiple audiences with different concerns, we demonstrate that considering audience specificity leads to an improved understanding of reputation effects. Using data on emerging artists in the field of contemporary art from 2001 to 2010, we investigate the manner in which artists’ audience-specific reputations affect their subsequent success with two distinct audiences: museums and galleries. Our findings suggest that audience-specific reputations have systematically different effects with respect to success with museums and galleries. Our findings also illuminate the extent to which audience-specific reputations are relevant for emerging research on the contingent effects of reputation. In particular, our findings support our predictions that audiences differ from one another in terms of the extent to which other signals (specifically, status and interaction with other audiences) enhance or reduce the value of audience-specific reputations. Our study thus advances theory by providing empirical evidence for the value of incorporating audience-specific reputations into the general study of reputation.

title: Reputation and Status: Expanding the Role of Social Evaluations in Management Research
methods: Editorial thematic-issue introduction and narrative review of AMJ research on reputation, status, and related social evaluations, using counts and illustrative studies to map theoretical lenses, units of analysis, outcomes, and future research directions.
industry: Management research / Academy of Management Journal
units: AMJ articles on reputation, status, and related social evaluations; articles curated in the thematic issue
n_sample: 121 prior AMJ articles plus 15 articles in the thematic issue
authors: George, Gerard; Dahlander, Linus; Graffin, Scott D.; Sim, Samantha
theories: impression management; organizational identity; signaling theory; social identity theory; social network theory; sociocognitive theories
keywords: future research directions; reputation; social approval assets; social evaluations; status
research_question: How has AMJ research examined reputation, status, and related social evaluations, and what unresolved questions should guide future work? The editorial asks how organizations and individuals seek, leverage, lose, repair, create, avoid, and respond to social evaluations across levels, domains, and audiences.
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial purpose: The article introduces an AMJ thematic issue on reputation and status and takes stock of social evaluation research in the journal.
- Review focus: It maps constructs such as reputation, status, image, network centrality, and publicity/public relations across units of analysis and theoretical lenses.
- Thematic issue synthesis: It summarizes 15 articles to show how social evaluations operate for individuals, organizations, stakeholders, audiences, investors, consumers, analysts, journalists, and relational partners.
- Future directions: It identifies unresolved problems around multiple levels and domains, actors outside the public eye, stability and loss of social evaluations, creation and consumption of social evaluations, and the benefits and burdens of high status or reputation.

The process logic is editorial and agenda-setting rather than causal hypothesis testing. George, Dahlander, Graffin, and Sim argue that social evaluations shape organizational life through stakeholder perceptions of quality, standing, legitimacy, trust, and accountability. Their synthesis emphasizes that the field has focused heavily on positive effects and high-status or high-reputation actors, leaving open questions about negative fallout, repair, under-the-radar actors, cross-level mechanisms, multiple audiences, and the conditions under which reputation and status become burdens rather than assets.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes by positioning reputation, status, and adjacent constructs as a broader social evaluations literature with substantial theoretical plurality. It clarifies that AMJ research has used lenses such as signaling theory, social identity theory, social network theory, impression management, organizational identity, and sociocognitive theories across individual, dyadic, team, firm, and organizational contexts. Its main contribution is not new theory but a research agenda that broadens the field beyond positive effects, single domains, static hierarchies, and highly visible actors.
practical_implication: For organizational leaders, the editorial implies that reputation and status are strategic but risky social approval assets: they can help attract resources, talent, audiences, and favorable interpretations, yet also raise expectations, scrutiny, and exposure to sudden loss. For researchers and editors, it encourages designs that examine multiple audiences, levels, and domains, including how organizations respond to negative evaluations and how actors manage or avoid visibility.
limitations: The editorial is bounded by its focus on AMJ research trends and the 15 papers assembled in the thematic issue, so it should be read as an agenda-setting synthesis rather than a comprehensive review of all reputation and status research. Because it is an editorial, it does not test the proposed future directions empirically.
future_research: The editorial calls for research linking micro-level mechanisms to macro-level outcomes, comparing status and reputation across multiple domains and audiences, and studying actors that lack high reputation or fly under the radar. It also encourages work on status loss, reputation repair, the creation and consumption of social evaluations, and the conditions under which high status or reputation becomes a burden. Future studies should use varied methods, including lab, field, archival, mixed-method, and longer-panel designs, to examine these dynamics more directly.

title: Ready, AIM, Acquire: Impression Offsetting and Acquisitions
methods: Empirical quantitative study of public-company acquisition announcements using press-release coding, event-study cumulative abnormal returns, paired t-tests, OLS regression with robust standard errors, and negative binomial regression with robust standard errors.
industry: Public-company acquisition deals across industries; both acquirers and targets were public companies.
time_period: Acquisitions announced between 1995 and 2009.
units: Acquisition announcements by publicly traded acquirers of publicly traded targets.
n_sample: 770 acquisition announcements; missing data reduced the impression-offsetting models to 758 observations and the cumulative-abnormal-return models to 701 observations.
authors: Graffin, Scott D.; Haleblian, Jerayr (John); Kiley, Jason T.
theories: anticipatory impression management; expectancy violation theory; impression management
keywords: acquisition announcements; anticipatory impression management; cumulative abnormal returns; expectancy violation theory; impression offsetting
research_question: The paper asks whether acquiring firms use anticipatory impression management to offset the negative expectancy violations associated with acquisition announcements. It also asks whether impression offsetting is more frequent when acquirer or target characteristics make an acquisition more likely to be viewed negatively, and whether offsetting improves shareholder reactions.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that managers anticipate that acquisitions may violate investors' expectations that firms should enhance shareholder value. They therefore release positive but unrelated information contemporaneously with the acquisition announcement, forcing investors to process multiple pieces of news at once and reducing the perceived negativity of the acquisition event. The authors further argue that riskier acquisitions, serial acquirers, and high-reputation acquirers create stronger predictive expectancy violations, increasing the likelihood of offsetting.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces impression offsetting as a distinct anticipatory impression management tactic, separate from strategic noise and big bath accounting. It extends expectancy violation theory to explain when firms proactively manage stakeholder perceptions before or during potentially negative events. It also contributes by quantifying the market benefits of an impression management tactic in the acquisition context.
practical_implication: The findings imply that managers can reduce negative market reactions to acquisition announcements by timing positive unrelated disclosures around the focal event. For investors and analysts, the results suggest that press releases near acquisition announcements should be interpreted cautiously because contemporaneous positive news may bias the observed market reaction. Acquisition researchers should also account for confounding positive announcements when estimating market reactions.
limitations: The authors could not directly observe managerial intent, so they infer agency from deviations between event-window press releases and baseline press-release behavior. The study focuses on public-company acquisitions with available press-release and market data, limiting direct generalization to private deals or nonmarket stakeholder reactions. The authors also note that the tactic is inexpensive and effective, but the study does not explain why many firms still do not use it.
future_research: Future research could examine CEO characteristics, reputation, or tenure as predictors of impression offsetting. Researchers could also study positive expectancy violations, the interaction between anticipatory and reactive impression management, and the timing of negative announcements. Additional work could re-examine acquisition market reactions after accounting for systematic positive-news offsets.
abstract: Drawing on expectancy violation theory, we explore the effects of anticipatory impression management in the context of acquisitions. We introduce impression offsetting, an anticipatory impression management technique organizational leaders employ when they expect a focal event will negatively violate the expectations of external stakeholders. Accordingly, in these situations, organizational leaders will announce the focal event contemporaneously with positive, but unrelated information. We predict impression offsetting will generally occur in the context of acquisitions, but also more frequently for specific acquiring firms and acquisitions that are more likely to lead to an expectancy violation. We also posit that offsetting will effectively inhibit observers' perceptions of events as negative expectancy violations by positively influencing shareholder reactions to acquisition announcements. Consistent with our hypotheses, in a sample of publicly traded acquisition targets, we find evidence for impression offsetting, in which characteristics of both acquirers and their announced acquisitions predict its frequency of use. We also find evidence that impression offsetting is efficacious; on average, it reduces the negative market reaction to acquisition announcements by over 40%, which translates into approximately $246 million in market capitalization.

title: Magnification and Correction of the Acolyte Effect: Initial Benefits and Ex Post Settling up in NFL Coaching Careers
methods: Empirical quantitative archival career-history study of NFL coaches using random-effects logistic regression, interaction models for evaluative certainty, Wald tests for knowledge-match comparisons, Heckman two-stage selection correction, and chi-square/Fisher tests for post-promotion outcomes.
industry: National Football League coaching careers.
units: Coach-year observations for NFL coaches entering the league during the sample period.
n_sample: 1,298 coaches and 10,269 coach-years.
authors: Kilduff, M.; Crossland, C.; Tsai, W.; Bowers, M. T.
theories: basking in reflected glory; quasi-random careers; signaling theory; social capital theory; social network theory
keywords: NFL coaching careers; acolyte effect; career advancement; high-reputation workplace ties; signaling theory; social networks
research_question: What are the long-term career consequences of initially beneficial high-reputation workplace ties? The paper asks which acolytes benefit most from high-reputation leader ties, whether the mechanism is knowledge transfer, intrinsic quality, or unreliable signaling, and whether acolytes continue to outperform after promotion.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that acolyte ties operate as social signals when evaluators lack other information about a coach's quality. These ties initially magnify promotion chances, especially for less central and less experienced coaches, but the evidence does not support a knowledge-transfer or intrinsic-quality explanation. Instead, acolyte status appears to be an unreliable signal that later produces settling-up effects as promoted acolytes experience fewer favorable post-promotion outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends social network and signaling theory by theorizing both the initial benefits and later penalties of high-reputation third-party ties. It challenges rich-get-richer accounts of reputational endorsement by showing that, in a highly competitive labor market, misleading social signals can be corrected over time. It also introduces the acolyte as a theoretical construct for explaining how actors and evaluators simplify complex social-network information in career markets.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that organizations should not treat high-reputation leader ties as straightforward evidence of candidate quality. For individuals, ties to prestigious leaders can help open promotion opportunities but may also create inflated expectations and later career risk if the signal is not backed by observable performance.
limitations: The authors note that the NFL is an unusually competitive, interlinked industry with quantitative performance indicators and stochastic season outcomes, which may limit generalizability. They also could not link coaches to specific performance outcomes as directly as sports studies of players can, and the archival design cannot directly observe the cognitive and emotional processes behind evaluator reactions, envy, or halo effects.
future_research: Future research could test acolyte effects in other settings, including academia and entertainment, where high-reputation endorsements may matter but performance is harder to observe. It could also examine alternatives to ex post settling up, such as acolytes resting on their laurels, losing aspiration after proximity to stars ends, or being punished by others' envy. Experimental work could isolate the halo effects and boundary conditions of network endorsements more directly.
abstract: What are the long-term consequences of initially beneficial high-reputation workplace ties? Under uncertainty, acolytes (i.e., subordinates with work connections to high-reputation industry leaders) are likely to benefit in terms of signaling fitness for promotion in the external job market. Analysis of promotion outcomes of coaches in the National Football League over 31 years showed that the acolyte effect was reduced for individuals for whom uncertainty was lowest (acolytes with considerable industry experience or high centrality in the co-worker industry network). There was no support for either a knowledge-transfer or an intrinsic-quality explanation for why acolytes initially gained advantage. Rather, evidence supported the idea that ties to high-reputation leaders were somewhat randomly distributed so that acolytes faced ex post settling-up consequences after their promotions: i.e., fewer further promotions or lateral moves, and more demotions. Thus, acolytes initially benefited from loose linkages between their unobservable quality and signals offered by their industry-leader ties, but also suffered as the unreliability of social network signals became evident. The results suggest that a competitive job market may exhibit selfcorrection over time. We offer countervailing theory and evidence to the prevailing view that high-reputation third-party endorsements perpetuate a rich-get-richer social structure that is resistant to performance outcomes.

title: The Online Shadow of Offline Signals: Which Sellers Get Contacted in Online B2B Marketplaces?
methods: Rare-events logistic regression of buyer-seller dyads in an Italian online B2B marketplace, modeling whether a buyer requested a quotation from a seller while controlling for buyer, seller, region, industry, distance, prior contact, and fixed-effect factors.
industry: Italian online B2B marketplace covering a multitude of industries; sampled sellers represented nine major industry divisions.
time_period: Fourth quarter of 1999 to July 2001
units: Buyer-seller dyads at risk of a request for quotation
n_sample: 116,417 buyer-seller dyads, 438 realized requests for quotation, 34 unique buyers, 301 contacted sellers, and 4,557 sampled sellers
authors: Lanzolla, G.; Frankort, H. T. W.
theories: institutional perspective (Shapiro, 1987; Zucker, 1986); reference points in behavioral decision theory (Helson, 1948; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981); signaling theory (Spence, 1974)
keywords: geographic location; legal status; local institutional quality; offline seller characteristics; online B2B marketplaces; requests for quotation
research_question: The paper asks what impels buyers to contact particular sellers in online B2B marketplaces when social structures are sparse and buyers have limited social cues. It specifically examines whether visible offline seller characteristics, especially geographic location and legal status, shape buyer-seller contact initiation online.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that visible offline characteristics signal seller reliability in an anonymous online marketplace. Geographic location signals local institutional quality, especially judicial efficiency and the absence of corruption or organized crime, while legal status signals the strength of institutionally induced obligations and controls. Buyers use these signals to infer trading and value appropriation risks, and the effectiveness of institutional-quality signals depends partly on the buyer's own local institutional quality as a reference point.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates an institutional perspective with signaling theory to show how offline institution-based signals can shape online buyer-seller contact dynamics. It extends signaling research by showing that signal effectiveness can vary across signal recipients because buyers interpret seller institutional quality relative to buyer-specific reference points. It also contributes to research on online market segmentation by showing that sellers can become differentiated before pricing information is disclosed.
practical_implication: For sellers in online B2B marketplaces, offline characteristics that are visible online may affect whether buyers even initiate contact. Sellers located in higher-quality institutional environments or operating under stronger legal-status obligations may enjoy advantages in attracting requests for quotation. Marketplace operators and sellers should recognize that online profile fields such as location and legal form may function as substantive signals, not merely descriptive metadata.
limitations: The authors note that data limitations prevent complete coverage of company size and order types, although supplementary analyses did not suggest seller size confounded the main results. The study focuses on an Italian marketplace from 1999-2001, so formal institutional variation is largely ruled out by design, but this also limits direct evidence about cross-national or state-level formal institutional signals. The relative legal status test is limited by coarse categorical measurement.
future_research: Future research could examine how transaction-specific characteristics such as order quantity moderate institution-based signaling effects. Studies could also test formal institutional signals in online B2B markets that cross regional, state, or national borders, and examine other offline seller characteristics such as industry association membership or prominent partner affiliations. The authors also encourage research on how buyers combine multiple signals, including brand, reputation, certification, price, geographic location, and legal status.
abstract: This article extends the understanding of what impels buyers to contact particular sellers in online business-to-business (B2B) marketplaces, which are typically characterized by sparse social structures and concomitant limitations in observing social cues. Integrating an institutional perspective with signaling theory, our core argument is that offline seller characteristics that are visible online—in particular, geographic location and legal status—convey credible signals of seller behavior because they provide buyers with information on sellers’ local institutional quality and the institutionally induced obligations and controls acting on sellers. Using unique data from a large, Italian, online B2B marketplace between the fourth quarter of 1999 and July 2001, we find that both sellers’ local institutional quality and their legal statuses affect a buyer’s likelihood of contacting a seller. Moreover, consistent with the idea that a buyer’s own local institutional quality generates a relevant reference point against which sellers are evaluated, we find that a buyer is progressively more likely to contact sellers the higher their local institutional quality relative to the buyer. Jointly, our findings imply that, in online B2B marketplaces, signals conveyed by sellers’ geographic locations and legal statuses may constitute substantive sources of competitive heterogeneity and market segmentation.
apa_citation: Lanzolla, G., & Frankort, H. T. W. (2016). The online shadow of offline signals: Which sellers get contacted in online B2B marketplaces? *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 207-231. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0051

title: Unearned Status Gain: Evidence from a Global Language Mandate
methods: Inductive qualitative field study using semi-structured interviews with U.S.-based native English-speaking employees of a Japanese high-tech organization after an English language mandate, supplemented by Japanese employee and executive interviews and triangulated with organizational artifacts and observations.
industry: High-tech e-commerce / Internet marketplace organization
country: United States subsidiaries of a Japanese organization, with supplemental Japanese informants
time_period: 15-month interview period, approximately one year after the English mandate
units: U.S.-based native English-speaking employees, with supplemental Japanese executives, expatriates, and headquarters employees
n_sample: 90 primary U.S.-based native English-speaking American employees; 66 supplemental Japanese interviews
authors: Neeley, Tsedal B.; Dumas, Tracy L.
theories: attribution theory; equity theory; organizational identification; perspective taking; status characteristics theory
keywords: intergroup contact; language mandate; lingua franca; status dynamics; status rationalization; status stability appraisal; unearned status gain
research_question: How do people experience and respond to unearned status gain? The paper examines this question through native English speakers' responses to an organizational English mandate that elevated English fluency as a valued status characteristic without requiring effort or achievement from them.
mechanism_summary:
- Organizational trigger: GlobalMoves designated English as the company-wide business language, making native English fluency a newly valued organizational characteristic.
- Unearned status gain experience: Native English-speaking employees attributed their elevated standing to chance, felt greater belonging, anticipated career advancement, and gained access to expanded information and people networks.
- Contact condition: Employees with limited Japanese contact mainly reported optimistic benefits, while those with regular Japanese contact also observed nonnative speakers' hardship.
- Response processes: Regular contact produced perspective taking, status rationalization, and status stability appraisal.
- Supplemental context: Japanese informants generally saw English as strategically necessary but reported career anxiety, productivity loss, and communication stress under the mandate.

The process begins with organizational action that selects and elevates a characteristic outside employees' control. Native English speakers interpret the resulting status gain as lucky and beneficial, but regular contact with Japanese coworkers makes the unequal distribution of costs salient. This salience produces sympathy and counterfactual awareness, rationalization that Japanese employees can earn benefits through effort, and recurring appraisal of whether the English-based status advantage will endure.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces unearned status gain as a dynamic status phenomenon distinct from earned status and from stable privilege. It extends status theory by showing that the origin of status gain matters: gains produced by organizational action can generate both positive outcomes and discomfort because recipients know the gain was not earned. It also links status dynamics to intergroup contact, arguing that contact with those disadvantaged by the same organizational action shapes perspective taking, rationalization, and stability concerns.
practical_implication: Organizations should recognize that strategic changes such as language mandates alter status hierarchies, not only communication routines. Leaders need to support both disfavored employees and those favored by the change, because beneficiaries may experience uncertainty and unease alongside new opportunity. The paper suggests replacing a sense of luck with responsibility, using training, facilitation, and integration into core activities to help employees work across language and status differences.
limitations: The study centers on U.S.-based workers in one Japanese company, where meritocratic assumptions about earned status are important to how unearned gain is interpreted. The authors note that the model may not apply in societies where status ascription is more normative or where status mobility through achievement is less expected. The qualitative design supports theory building but does not test causal mechanisms, and the long-term status dynamics remain uncertain as Japanese employees' English proficiency changes.
future_research: Future research should examine unearned status gain across other countries, organizations, and types of organizational change beyond language mandates. Longitudinal studies could test how these dynamics evolve as disadvantaged employees acquire the newly valued characteristic or as organizational priorities shift again. Quantitative field and laboratory studies could test the proposed mechanisms linking organizational action, attribution to chance, perspective taking, status rationalization, and status stability appraisal.
abstract: Theories of status rarely address “unearned status gain,” defined as an unexpected and unsolicited increase in relative standing, prestige, or worth attained not through individual effort or achievement but from a shift in organizationally valued characteristics. We build theory about unearned status gain drawing from a qualitative study of 90 U.S.-based employees of a Japanese organization following a company-wide English language mandate. These native English-speaking employees believed that the mandate elevated their worth in the organization, a status gain they attributed to chance, hence deeming it unearned. They also reported a heightened sense of belonging, optimism about career advancement, and access to expanded networks. Yet, among those who interacted regularly with Japanese counterparts, narratives also revealed discomfort, which was manifested in at least two ways. These informants engaged in “status rationalization,” emphasizing the benefits that Japanese employees might obtain by learning English, and prevaricated on whether the change was temporary or durable, a process we call “status stability appraisal.” The fact that these narratives were present only among those working closely with Japanese employees highlights intergroup contact as a factor in shaping the unearned status gain experience. Supplemental analysis of data gathered from 66 Japanese employees of the organization provided the broader organizational context and the nonnative speakers’ perspective of the language shift. This study’s findings expand our overall understanding of status dynamics in organizations, and show how status gains can yield both positive and negative outcomes.

title: Category Spanning, Evaluation, and Performance: Revised Theory and Test on the Corporate Law Market
methods: Quantitative longitudinal panel study of corporate law firm-location dyads in London, New York City, and Paris, using random-effects GLS estimations with clustered-robust standard errors and mediation tests.
industry: Corporate legal services
country: United Kingdom, United States, and France, represented by London, New York City, and Paris
units: Law firm-location dyads and yearly observations
n_sample: 377 firm-location dyads and 2,180 observations
authors: Paolella, Lionel; Durand, Rodolphe
theories: audiences’ theory of value; category-spanning theory; goal-based view of categorization
keywords: category spanning; clients’ theory of value; corporate legal services; evaluation; goal-based view; inclusive category combination; performance
research_question: The paper asks when category spanning harms or helps organizational evaluation and performance. It examines whether clients’ theory of value in complex corporate legal-service markets makes category-spanning law firms more positively evaluated, especially when their category combinations are more inclusive, and whether evaluation mediates the category spanning-performance relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that complex, high-stakes, nonrecurrent client problems shift valuation from a prototype-based view toward a goal-based view. Under this theory of value, clients evaluate category-spanning producers as more capable of handling complex legal requirements rather than as confusing departures from a single category. More inclusive category combinations make the span more salient and coherent, increasing evaluation; higher evaluation then transfers partly into revenue performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper revises category-spanning theory by showing that audience penalties are contingent on the audience’s theory of value rather than inherent to category spanning. It links category spanning, evaluation, and performance in one model and shows that evaluation mediates part of the effect of spanning on performance. It also adds category-combination inclusiveness to category research, arguing that audiences assess configurations within a whole category system rather than isolated category distances alone.
practical_implication: For professional service firms, spanning categories can be valuable when clients face complex problems and need coherent multi-practice capability. Producers should consider both how many categories they span and whether the combination is recognizable and inclusive within the market’s category system, because this affects evaluation and revenue.
limitations: The authors note that they lacked details on contracts and deals, which required treating clients as homogeneous even though clients may vary in their theories of value. They also lacked branch-office profit data, so they could not weight spanning by the value of each practice in a firm’s portfolio and had to rely on revenue-per-lawyer estimates. The setting does not test prototype-based and goal-based valuation concurrently or isolate the emergence of new categories in firms’ portfolios.
future_research: Future research should test audiences’ theories of value in settings that include both standard and complex requirements, so the strength of evaluation mediation can be compared across theory-of-value conditions. Research could also examine how audiences’ theories of value change over time and how cultural, social, and institutional factors shape both category systems and conformity behavior.
abstract: Studies suggest that category-spanning organizations receive lower evaluation and perform worse than organizations focused on a single category. We propose that (a) these effects are contingent on clients’ theory of value, and that, as clients expect more sophisticated services, they tend to value category spanners more positively, and (b) the evaluation of producers mediates the relationship between category spanning and performance. We test our hypotheses using original data on corporate legal services in three markets (London, New York City, and Paris) over the decade 2000–2010. We find that (a) category spanners receive a better evaluation, and more so when their categorical combination is more inclusive, and (b) evaluation mediates significantly the relationship between category spanning and performance. This study enriches our understanding of how audiences apprehend a whole market category system and why organizations span categories.
apa_citation: Paolella, L., & Durand, R. (2016). Category spanning, evaluation, and performance: Revised theory and test on the corporate law market. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 330-351. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0651

title: Persona Non Grata? Determinants and Consequences of Social Distancing from Journalists Who Engage in Negative Coverage of Firm Leadership
methods: Panel empirical study combining CEO and journalist surveys with archival content analysis of media coverage. The paper estimates GLS random-effects models of CEO social distancing in CEO-journalist-alter CEO triads and random-effects negative binomial models of subsequent journalist coverage valence.
industry: Large public U.S. companies with more than $200 million in sales; focal and alter CEOs are in broadly defined same industries, including competitors, buyers, and suppliers.
time_period: CEO and journalist surveys from 2009 to 2012, with journalist reporting measured in prior and subsequent 12-month windows.
units: CEO-journalist-alter CEO triads for social distancing models and journalist reporting observations for coverage-valence models.
n_sample: 800 focal CEOs in the initial frame; 367 initially agreed; 311 participated throughout; random sample of 550 journalists; main models report N = 22,563 triads and N = 1,752 coverage observations.
authors: Shani, Guy; Westphal, James D.
theories: professional careers theory; social identification and self-categorization; social psychological theory of social distancing
keywords: CEOs; career stage; firm leadership; journalists; negative coverage; social distancing
research_question: The paper asks when CEOs socially distance themselves from journalists who have written negative coverage of other firms' leadership and strategy, and how that distancing affects the valence of journalists' later coverage. It also asks whether journalists' career stage changes their vulnerability to this social influence.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that CEOs socially identify with friends, demographically similar CEOs, and fellow members of the corporate elite, so negative coverage of those leaders elicits negative affect and distrust toward the journalist. Distancing withholds access, information, and status from journalists, creating negative reinforcement that encourages more positive and less negative subsequent coverage of firm leadership. The effect is strongest for middle-career journalists, who are theorized to be less protected by early-career idealism or late-career return to professional ideals.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends corporate governance and strategic leadership research by theorizing social distancing as a collective form of negative social influence over information intermediaries. It shifts attention from individual CEO influence tactics to elite-level patterns in which multiple CEOs' social and psychological connections jointly shape journalists' behavior toward corporate leaders as a group. It also adds a career-stage account of why information intermediaries vary in their susceptibility to elite social influence.
practical_implication: The findings imply that journalists' access to CEOs can be socially conditioned by prior critical reporting about other leaders, which may reduce the objectivity and negativity of subsequent coverage. For stakeholders who rely on media as a governance mechanism, social distancing can weaken external pressure for needed changes in leadership, governance, and strategy. The authors suggest that greater awareness and publicity around distancing behavior could deter CEOs from using this form of influence.
limitations: The study focuses on large public U.S. companies and journalists at major U.S. news and business publications, so the findings may not generalize to other national media systems, private firms, or other information-intermediary contexts. The design uses panel surveys and archival content analysis, but the core distancing construct depends on reported willingness and responsiveness in CEO-journalist interactions. The evidence concerns social distancing around coverage of firm leadership and strategy, not all forms of media criticism or stakeholder influence.
future_research: Future research could test whether the theory generalizes to other information intermediaries, such as sell-side security analysts, or to auditor-client relationships. Studies could examine whether similar patterns of distancing arise in other elite communities where group members are affected by a third party's behavior. Further work could also investigate how other journalist attributes shape vulnerability to CEO influence and whether distancing affects coverage of less-connected or minority leaders differently.
abstract: We consider how social and psychological connections among CEOs explain the propensity for corporate leaders to distance themselves socially from journalists who engage in negative reporting about firm leadership at other companies, and we examine the consequences for the valence of journalists’ subsequent coverage. Our theoretical framework suggests that journalists who have engaged in negative coverage of a firm’s leadership and strategy are especially likely to experience distancing from other leaders who (a) have friendship ties to the firm’s CEO, (b) are demographically similar to the CEO on salient dimensions, or (c) are socially identified with the CEO as a fellow member of the corporate elite. Our theory and findings ultimately suggest that, due to the multiple sources of social identification between CEOs, journalists who engage in negative coverage of firm leadership tend to experience social distancing from multiple CEOs, and that such distancing has a powerful influence on the valence of journalists’ subsequent reporting about firm leadership and strategy across all the firms they cover. We also extend our theoretical framework to suggest how the effect of social distancing on the valence of journalists’ coverage is moderated by the early and late stages of the journalists’ career.
apa_citation: Shani, G., & Westphal, J. D. (2016). Persona non grata? Determinants and consequences of social distancing from journalists who engage in negative coverage of firm leadership. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 302-329. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1162

title: Protecting Market Identity: When and How Do Organizations Respond to Consumers’ Devaluations?
methods: Empirical-quantitative study of TripAdvisor hotel reviews, using review-level logit models for public response occurrence and OLS models with Heckman correction for LIWC-coded justification in responses.
industry: Hotels and hospitality
country: United Kingdom, focused on London hotels
units: TripAdvisor reviews, hotel-reviewer pairs, and public responses by London hoteliers
n_sample: 209,950 reviews
authors: Wang, Tao; Wezel, Filippo Carlo; Forgues, Bernard
theories: evaluation literature; identity literature; market identity literature; organizational reputation
keywords: consumer devaluations; expert evaluations; justification; market identity; organizational reputation; public responses
research_question: The paper asks when organizations publicly respond to consumer devaluations that challenge their market identity and how they craft those public responses. It examines whether the severity of devaluation and organizational reputation shape both the likelihood of response and the degree of justification used in the response.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that expert evaluations certify market identity and set consumers’ expectations, so consumer ratings below expert ratings create an identity threat. As devaluation becomes more severe, the benefit of publicly defending the organization’s market identity outweighs the risks of drawing attention to complaints or appearing defensive. Reputation amplifies this sensitivity because highly ranked organizations have more to lose from devaluations, although the evidence for reputation’s effect on response style is limited and varies across justification measures.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts identity-threat research from internal-external mismatches toward consumer challenges to expert-certified market identities. It contributes to market identity research by treating organizations as active defenders of market identity after evaluations occur, not only as passive subjects of third-party evaluations. It also extends research on ratings, rankings, and performativity by showing that public evaluations elicit organizational responses under specific conditions rather than automatically.
practical_implication: Managers in service industries should monitor whether consumer evaluations devalue the organization relative to expert benchmarks, not only whether reviews are negative in absolute terms. When responding publicly, they should craft responses that credibly justify actions and address would-be customers’ interpretations, because response style can shape subsequent evaluations.
limitations: The authors limit the conceptual development to consumer evaluations that are lower than expert evaluations, leaving over-evaluations and changes in expert ratings outside the scope. They also note that market identity may include persistent and malleable characteristics, but the study does not distinguish how responses differ across those characteristics. The study does not isolate the sources of disagreement between experts and consumers and focuses on one public-response channel without analyzing the full qualitative content of consumer reviews.
future_research: Future research could examine what happens when consumers rate organizations more highly than experts or when expert ratings change without corresponding consumer updates. It could also distinguish responses to persistent versus malleable identity characteristics and analyze the qualitative content of consumer reviews to better understand why expert-consumer disagreements arise. Additional work combining online data, archival data, and interviews could test whether the findings generalize across response channels.
abstract: This article examines the conditions under which organizations publicly respond to unfavorable consumer evaluations that challenge their market identity. Because organizations’ market identities are certified by expert evaluations, consumers’ devaluations that challenge these expert evaluations represent an identity threat. However, organizations do not always react to consumers’ devaluations because of the risks associated with public responses. Hence, we first predict that organizations are more likely to respond to severe devaluations than to weaker ones; second, we propose that organizations, when faced with severe devaluations, are more likely to craft responses that justify their actions and behaviors. We further contend that, for any market identity under consideration, an organization’s reputation amplifies these relationships. Analyses of a dataset of London hoteliers’ responses to online reviews posted on TripAdvisor during the period 2002–2012 lend substantial support to our hypotheses.
apa_citation: Wang, T., Wezel, F. C., & Forgues, B. (2016). Protecting market identity: When and how do organizations respond to consumers’ devaluations? *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 135-162. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0205

title: Reputation as a Benefit and a Burden? How Stakeholders’ Organizational Identification Affects the Role of Reputation Following a Negative Event
methods: Empirical quantitative study using multilevel linear regressions on longitudinal university-stakeholder group-year data, with year fixed effects, random intercepts for university and stakeholder group, maximum likelihood estimation, and university-clustered standard errors.
industry: Four-year, degree-granting U.S. colleges and universities that were NCAA members.
units: University-stakeholder group-year observations distinguishing non-alumni and undergraduate alumni donations.
n_sample: 7,368 university-stakeholder group-year observations; 1,118 university-stakeholder groups; 658 universities.
authors: Zavyalova, Anastasiya; Pfarrer, Michael D.; Reger, Rhonda K.; Hubbard, Timothy D.
theories: organizational identification; organizational reputation; social capital and goodwill; stakeholder attention and violation of expectations
keywords: legislative references; negative event; organizational identification; organizational reputation; stakeholder support
research_question: The paper asks why prior studies find high organizational reputation to be either a benefit or a burden after a negative event. It examines whether stakeholders' level of organizational identification explains when reputation buffers organizations from withdrawal of support and when it amplifies negative reactions.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that high reputation activates competing forces after wrongdoing. For low-identification stakeholders, greater attention and violation of expectations dominate because their cognitive and emotional connection to the organization is weak, making withdrawal less costly. For high-identification stakeholders, social capital and a reservoir of goodwill dominate at lower levels of wrongdoing because the organization is tied to their self-concept, although exploratory results suggest this benefit declines once wrongdoing becomes more severe.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends reputation research by showing that high reputation can be both a benefit and a burden after a negative event, depending on stakeholder identification. It specifies which mechanisms dominate for low- versus high-identification stakeholders: attention and violated expectations for the former, and social capital and goodwill for the latter. It also adds a boundary condition by showing that support from high-identification stakeholders may decline when the volume of wrongdoing becomes too high.
practical_implication: The findings imply that managers should segment reputation-repair responses by stakeholder identification rather than assuming one audience reaction. For low-identification stakeholders, the paper suggests reducing the perceived volume of wrongdoing by explaining corrective action. For high-identification stakeholders, managers may benefit from invoking stakeholders' connection to the organization, while recognizing that severe wrongdoing can deplete goodwill.
limitations: The authors study NCAA major infractions among U.S. universities, a context where stakeholder identification may be unusually strong. They also do not measure organizational identification directly, instead using non-alumni and undergraduate alumni donations as proxies for low and high identification. The authors note that they cannot rule out all alternative explanations or make definitive causal claims, although robustness checks support the reported relationships.
future_research: Future research could test the model in other industries where identification varies, such as automotive companies, high-tech firms, or organizations with salient religious or political identities. Studies could measure organizational identification directly and examine whether negative events become stigmatizing for some stakeholders while prompting others to defend the organization. The authors also encourage research on how different types of negative events and specific reputation dimensions shape whether reputation becomes a benefit or a burden.
abstract: Research about the effects of an organization’s general reputation following a negative event remains equivocal: Some studies have found that high reputation is a benefit because of the stock of social capital and goodwill it generates; others have found it to be a burden because of the greater stakeholder attention and violation of expectations associated with a negative event. We theorize that stakeholders’ level of organizational identification helps explain which mechanisms are more dominant. We test our hypotheses on a sample of legislative references associated with National Collegiate Athletic Association major infractions from 1999–2009. Our results indicate that high reputation is a burden for an organization when considering low-identification stakeholder support: As the number of legislative references increases, a high-reputation university will receive fewer donations from non-alumni donors compared to universities without this asset. In contrast, high reputation is a benefit when considering high-identification stakeholder support: As the number of legislative references increases, a high-reputation university will receive more donations from alumni donors compared to universities without this asset. However, an exploratory investigation reveals that alumni donations to high-reputation universities decline as the number of legislative references increases, suggesting that the benefit of a high reputation has a limit.
apa_citation: Zavyalova, A., Pfarrer, M. D., Reger, R. K., & Hubbard, T. D. (2016). Reputation as a benefit and a burden? How stakeholders' organizational identification affects the role of reputation following a negative event. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(1), 253-276. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0611
