title: After the Break-Up: The Relational and Reputational Consequences of Withdrawals from Venture Capital Syndicates
methods: Empirical quantitative study of U.S. VC-firm dyad-years using Thomson Reuters VentureXpert data, rare-events logit models, multiway-clustered standard errors, year fixed effects, dyadic network measures, robustness tests with alternative measures and firm fixed effects, and interview evidence used to refine mechanisms.
industry: Dedicated venture capital firms and VC syndication relationships.
time_period: Syndication dyad-years from 1985 to 2008, with 1980-1984 data used to initialize network measures.
units: Potential and realized active VC-firm dyad-years.
n_sample: 250,730 dyad-year observations in the final sampled dataset.
authors: Zhelyazkov, Pavel I.; Gulati, Ranjay
theories: enforceable trust; network dynamics; organizational reputation; relational embeddedness
keywords: network dynamics; reputation; syndication; tie dissolution; venture capital syndicates; withdrawals
research_question: The paper asks how a VC firm's withdrawals from prior syndicates shape its likelihood of forming subsequent syndication ties. It distinguishes relational consequences for abandoned coinvestors, global reputational consequences from public withdrawal histories, and local reputational consequences transmitted through abandoned coinvestors' network contacts.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that withdrawal can make abandoned coinvestors reassess a VC firm's reliability and damage interpersonal and interorganizational relationships, reducing repeat syndication. Public withdrawal histories can signal unreliability to the broader VC market, while abandoned coinvestors can transmit negative private information to their own contacts. Contrary to the authors' amplification hypothesis, global and local negative information attenuate each other, suggesting redundancy in the information available to prospective partners.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to network dynamics research by showing that past ties do not always cast a positive shadow over future tie formation; withdrawals can disrupt repeat ties and relationships with structurally proximate actors. It extends reputation research by distinguishing global public reputation from local private reputational information and by showing that social ties shape audience reactions to the same behavioral record. It also provides evidence for network-based ex post punishment of behavior perceived as violating collaboration norms.
practical_implication: For VC firms, withdrawal decisions can carry future syndication costs beyond the abandoned deal, especially through damaged relationships and negative information flows. The findings imply that prospective syndication partners attend not only to technical resources and network position but also to a partner's reliability record. Firms facing liquidity-driven withdrawals may suffer less reputational damage, suggesting that audiences interpret withdrawals partly through attribution processes.
limitations: The authors note that withdrawal decisions are not randomly assigned and may be driven by unobserved factors that also affect future syndication. Archival data cannot fully distinguish deliberate, pre-negotiated, forced, liquidity-driven, or relationship-breakdown withdrawals. The VC setting also involves small, cohesive firms, so private information transmission may be stronger than in large, divisionalized organizations.
future_research: Future research could use qualitative or survey evidence to examine withdrawal circumstances, attribution processes, and relationship dynamics before and after syndicate exits. Additional work could test whether the theory generalizes to strategic alliances, investment banking syndicates, or institutional contexts where collaborators can be forcibly removed rather than voluntarily withdraw. Research could also examine how internal cohesion within organizations affects their ability to transmit reputational information.
abstract: Organizational theorists are increasingly interested in the antecedents of terminating interorganizational relationships, but have paid little attention to the disruptive consequences of such terminations on future tie formations. To redress this imbalance, the present study focuses on how venture capital (VC) firms' withdrawals from VC syndicates are associated with their subsequent syndication in the period from 1985 to 2008. We argue that withdrawals disrupt the relationships of the withdrawing VC firms with the coinvestors and reduce the likelihood of them entering into subsequent exchange (relational consequences). Furthermore, public information on the withdrawals can undermine the withdrawing VC firm's reputation for reliability, making it a less desirable exchange partner overall (global reputational consequences). Finally, we find that abandoned coinvestors can spread negative private information about the withdrawing firm, reducing its chances of syndication with their other network contacts (local reputational consequences). We also show that the global and local reputational consequences attenuate each other, due to redundancy in the content of the information each provides. We discuss the implications of our theory for the research on network dynamics and reputation.

title: The Grammar of Decoupling: A Cognitive-Linguistic Perspective on Firms’ Sustainability Claims and Stakeholders’ Interpretation
methods: Mixed-method matched-pair field study of 12 multinational corporations, combining grammatical/textual analysis of executive interviews and sustainability-report CEO letters with OLS and ordered probit models of stakeholder evaluations, followed by qualitative analysis of stakeholder accounts.
industry: Six industry settings: chemicals, mining/natural resources, banking, energy, high-tech, and food/beverages.
country: Matched headquarters regions including Northern Europe, Anglo-Saxon countries, and Southern Europe.
time_period: Data collection occurred from 2005 to 2007, with Innovest scores from 2005 and 2006.
units: Stakeholder-firm dyads, executives, sustainability reports, and stakeholder interviewees for 12 multinational corporations.
n_sample: 261 interviews in total: 119 executive interviews and 142 stakeholder interviews; 108 numerical stakeholder evaluations were analyzed.
authors: Crilly, D.; Hansen, M.; Zollo, M.
theories: cognitive-linguistic perspective; institutional theory of decoupling; stakeholder interpretation
keywords: cognitive-linguistic perspective; decoupling; grammar; stakeholders; sustainability claims
research_question: Can stakeholders detect firms that espouse sustainability policies but do not consistently implement them, and which stakeholders are persuaded by these decoupled claims? The paper asks why stakeholders are sometimes misled despite access to firm communications and external metrics.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Implementor firms versus decoupler firms; sustainability claims; grammatical complexity; stakeholder specialism; resource relations and conflicts of interest.
- Firm communication process: Implementors use more exclusive language and past-oriented empirical claims, while decouplers make broader inclusive and future-oriented claims despite communicating similar content.
- Stakeholder interpretation process: Specialist stakeholders use non-negotiable standards and past empirical evidence; generalist and resource-receiving stakeholders rely more on peripheral cues, shared identity, and future-oriented confidence.
- Emergent outcomes: Stakeholders generally rate implementors more highly, but resource-receiving stakeholders evaluate firms positively regardless of implementation, whereas specialists are better able to distinguish decouplers.

The central process is interpretive rather than simply informational. Decoupling is difficult to detect because truthful and less truthful firms communicate similar content, but differ in grammatical structure. Stakeholders' own cognitive and motivational positions shape whether they attend to those linguistic cues and whether they evaluate sustainability performance from observed implementation or from relationship-based confidence.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends decoupling theory by arguing that the problem is not only information asymmetry between firms and stakeholders. It shows that grammatical structure can reveal differences in managers' cognitive construal of sustainability commitments and in stakeholders' interpretive work. It also adds a stakeholder-heterogeneity account, distinguishing perceptive specialist stakeholders from resource-dependent or generalist stakeholders who may miss or discount evidence of decoupling.
practical_implication: Stakeholders should not rely only on the content of sustainability claims or the availability of metrics, because firms with different implementation records may cover similar topics in their reports. Specialist stakeholders and evaluators may be better positioned to assess implementation when they define non-negotiable standards and compare firms using concrete past evidence. Firms and monitors should also recognize that resource relationships can make stakeholder evaluations more favorable without necessarily improving implementation.
limitations: The study is based on a small number of firms, and the authors encourage replication with larger samples and different contexts. The authors do not claim that executives in decoupler firms are deliberately deceptive; their language may reflect confusion about how to achieve sustainability commitments.
future_research: Future research could apply cognitive-linguistic analysis to other corporate communications, such as executives' communications with financial markets or stock repurchase announcements. Additional work could examine how stakeholders interpret sustainability metrics and how rhetoric shapes the presentation and sensemaking of data. The authors also call for research on stakeholder heterogeneity, especially how potent stakeholders and perceptive stakeholders share information and coordinate influence.
abstract: Can firms deceive their stakeholders, by failing to deliver on their commitments to undertake sustainability practices without being detected? Extant theory posits that, due to information asymmetry, stakeholders struggle to comprehend the actual change in firms’ practices. In contrast, we advance a cognitive-linguistic perspective to explain why stakeholders are sometimes misled. Accordingly, we propose that firms’ deception does not appear in the content of their communication, but in its linguistic properties, which derive from how managers cognitively construe the sustainability challenge. Thus, firms cover the same points of content in their reports, but firms that practice what they preach use more complex styles of language than do firms that decouple their action from their statements. Moreover, we theorize that generalist stakeholders and stakeholders with conflicts of interest are unable to detect these linguistic nuances, whereas specialist stakeholders can. We find evidence for this cognitive-linguistic perspective in a textual analysis of grammatical structure in 261 interviews conducted in a large field study of 12 multinational corporations and their stakeholders. This lens advances our understanding of how firms deceive and how stakeholders can detect such deception and opens a new and promising avenue for research on firm–stakeholder relations.

title: Under the Radar: Regulatory Collaborations and their Selective Use to Facilitate Organizational Compliance
methods: Panel study of U.S. natural gas-transmission pipeline operators from 2010 to 2013. The analysis uses feasible generalized least squares regression for accident-rate outcomes, random-effects Tobit regression for pipeline assessments, and random-effects logistic regression for regulatory conference participation.
industry: U.S. natural gas-transmission pipeline operators
units: operator-year observations
n_sample: 2,961 operator-year observations
authors: Desai, Vinit M.
theories: information asymmetry between regulators and regulated organizations; organizational search and learning under uncertainty; regulatory compliance literature
keywords: organizational compliance; organizational search and learning; organizational visibility; regulatory collaborations; regulatory mandates
research_question: The paper asks why organizations vary in complying with regulatory mandates when managers may intend to comply but face uncertainty about what to change or how to change it. It specifically examines whether organizations use voluntary collaborations with regulators as a learning tool after enforcement actions, and which organizations select into or avoid those collaborations.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a reciprocal search-and-learning process under regulatory uncertainty. Regulatory collaborations reduce information asymmetry by giving organizations richer knowledge about mandates and regulators better visibility into organizational practices, which should increase compliance investments and reduce performance problems after enforcement. However, firms with less visible practices may avoid these collaborations because sharing private information with regulators could raise future enforcement risk.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates organizational search and learning theory with the literature on regulatory compliance, showing that compliance can depend on whether organizations search for information through regulators after enforcement pressure. It also contributes to organizational learning theory by distinguishing reciprocal learning from more familiar unidirectional search, because collaboration exposes both regulators and firms to new private information. The study identifies a selection effect: firms that may need to learn the most may avoid the learning channel because of disclosure risk.
practical_implication: For regulators, the findings imply that voluntary knowledge-sharing forums can improve compliance after enforcement actions, but may disproportionately attract already visible firms. Regulatory agencies may need additional strategies to reach less visible or more opaque operators that avoid collaboration despite potentially greater compliance needs.
limitations: The paper notes that regulatory collaboration is a relatively new construct and that the study cannot directly observe managers' motives for participating in conferences. It also cannot directly observe the specific content, quality, or richness of knowledge exchanges during those conferences. The empirical window is short, and the natural gas-transmission setting has fixed infrastructure and technological features that may limit direct generalization.
future_research: Future research could study settings with richer qualitative or narrative data on the actual exchanges between organizations and regulators. The paper also points to work on reciprocal learning, peer-to-peer learning in regulator-involved settings, and how organizations protect against disclosure risks when learning from powerful external agents.
abstract: Why do organizations vary in complying with regulatory mandates? While some may resist these pressures, what to change or how to change it may be unclear even when managers do intend to fully comply. Though scarce in the literature, theories regarding how organizations search for and learn from information under uncertainty provide an ideal window through which to examine organizational responses to regulatory mandates and other external pressures. In this study, I adapt these theories to posit that organizations establish close collaborative relationships with regulatory agents to overcome uncertainty following enforcement actions, and I ascertain that such collaborations can enhance organizational compliance with enforced mandates. However, I also find that organizations with the least visible practices will go “under the radar,” foregoing such collaborations because of the risks associated with disclosing private information to regulators. Thus, paradoxically, those organizations that could arguably learn or change the most through these exchanges in fact eschew them. This study and its findings deepen our understanding regarding organizational compliance with external pressures, emphasize the role of organizational visibility in interactions with outside agents, and contribute to the literatures on organizational search and learning by examining a reciprocal learning process.

title: Bringing Africa In: Promising Directions for Management Research
methods: From the Editors essay and literature overview of management scholarship on Africa, using Social Sciences Citation Index searches and thematic coding of articles on business management in Africa to identify challenges and future research directions.
industry: Business and economics scholarship on business management in Africa.
units: Peer-reviewed articles on Africa, with a subset focused on business management in Africa.
n_sample: 552 peer-reviewed articles on Africa; 154 articles on business management in Africa; roughly 41 in top management journals.
authors: George, Gerard; Corbishley, Christopher; Khayesi, Jane N. O.; Haas, Martine R.; Tihanyi, Laszlo
theories: agency theory; institutional logics; institutional theory; resource-based view; social capital theory; transaction cost economics
keywords: Africa; building capabilities; enabling opportunities; institutional voids; leadership and governance; management scholarship; natural resources; organizational and social resilience
research_question: The editorial asks why Africa should be brought into mainstream management research and theories. It aims to show how African contexts can both influence existing theories and generate new theory in management research.
mechanism_summary:
- Contextual premise: Africa combines fast growth, demographic change, institutional voids, resource constraints, weak infrastructure, informal markets, and sociopolitical heterogeneity.
- Literature overview: The authors review management scholarship on Africa and group the existing literature into navigating institutional voids, developing capabilities, and enabling opportunities.
- Theory-extension logic: African contexts expose boundary conditions in theories developed mainly in resource-abundant Western and Eastern developed economies.
- Theory-generation logic: Underresearched African phenomena can generate new frameworks for leadership and governance, natural-resource management, resilience, entrepreneurship, labor mobility, and managing across cultures and countries.
- Audience and purpose: The editorial invites management scholars to adopt Africa as a research context and to produce evidence useful to business executives and policy makers.

The process is editorial and agenda-setting rather than causal. George and colleagues use Africa's institutional, economic, demographic, cultural, and ecological diversity to argue that management research can learn from contexts where firms must design around voids, build capabilities under resource constraints, and operate in informal or fragile institutions. The article turns a thematic overview of prior work into a research agenda for extending existing theory and building new theory from African phenomena.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes by reframing Africa as a theoretically generative context rather than only a setting for social-development concerns. It identifies how management theories about institutions, resources, governance, entrepreneurship, leadership, CSR, informal markets, and cross-cultural management can be tested, extended, or reworked through African evidence. It also organizes the existing literature into three broad categories and links them to future research domains.
practical_implication: For researchers, the editorial recommends studying Africa not as a peripheral application site but as a context where management problems are pressing, varied, and theoretically revealing. For business executives and policy makers, it points to questions about navigating weak institutions, building managerial and employee capabilities, improving governance, managing natural resources, strengthening resilience, supporting entrepreneurship, and adapting across cultural and national boundaries.
limitations: The editorial is a narrative and thematic overview rather than an empirical study that tests propositions or adjudicates among competing explanations. Its review is limited to the Social Sciences Citation Index search strategy, articles published between 1990 and 2015, and a January 16, 2016 search date.
future_research: The authors call for research on leadership and governance in African contexts, including how organizations can respond to fragile state governance and conflict. They also call for research on managing human and natural resources, organizational and social resilience, institutional capacity, labor mobility, entrepreneurship, and managing across cultures and countries. Across these areas, they urge scholars to examine both how African phenomena modify existing management theories and how they can generate new theories.

title: Coming Back to Edmonton: Competing with Former Employers and Colleagues
methods: Negative binomial regression models with joint time on ice as an exposure parameter, player-level clustered standard errors, and position and team dummies; supplementary analyses use draft-team splits, move-circumstance indicators, hybrid random-effects negative binomial models, and time interactions.
industry: Professional ice hockey / National Hockey League
time_period: 2011/12 NHL regular season
units: Ordered player-player-game observations among opposing field players who had moved teams
n_sample: 429,667 observations from a constructed 690,873 player-player-game dataset after retaining movers
authors: Grohsjean, Thorsten; Kober, Pascal; Zucchini, Leon
theories: human capital theory; social capital theory; social identity theory; theories of identity and identification
keywords: National Hockey League; collective and relational identity; competitive behavior; employee mobility; former colleagues; former employer; human and social capital theory
research_question: The paper asks how individuals behave when they have to compete against their former employer and former colleagues. It reframes employee mobility by asking not only what mobile employees can do through transferred human and social capital, but also what they are willing to do when prior collective and relational identities remain salient.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is cross-level. At the collective level, competing against a former organization creates identity conflict because the individual identifies with both organizations but can increase the welfare of only one; more competitive behavior toward the former organization helps strengthen identification with the new organization and deidentify with the former one. At the relational level, former coworker or friend relationships can remain inclusive, so individuals can support the new organization while sparing former colleagues by directing competitive behavior toward non-former colleagues. The NHL analyses support this contrast: players check former teams more, but check former teammates less.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to human capital theory and employee mobility research by adding willingness and identity-based motivation to the usual focus on transferable human and social capital. It also contributes to theories of identity and identification by showing that collective and relational identities need not converge after mobility; leaving an organization may instead trigger divergence, producing different behavior toward former organizations and former colleagues.
practical_implication: The study implies that firms hiring from competitors may gain not only human and social capital but also heightened effort when new employees compete against former employers. It also warns that employees may be less competitive toward former colleagues, which makes team hiring, employee bonding, staffing timing, and non-compete clauses relevant to how firms manage mobility from rivals.
limitations: The empirical setting is a single professional sports industry where head-to-head competition is visible, decisions are fast, and behavior is constrained by explicit rules. The authors also note that identification is continuous but their independent variables are not continuous measures of identification, and that focusing on competitive behavior captures only part of how movers may change their behavior.
future_research: Future research could measure identification more continuously and examine whether identity transitions change helpful behavior as well as competitive behavior. It could also test the framework in broader managerial settings, such as sales, professional services, advertising, or product competition, where former employers and former colleagues remain salient but behavior is less rule-bound than in ice hockey.
abstract: Drawing on human and social capital theory, research on employee mobility has discussed the benefits and drawbacks of hiring employees from rival firms. To explain the performance implications of employee mobility, the literature has focused on what moving individuals can do, but has ignored what they are willing to do. However, to fully understand what individuals will actually do at the new firm, we need to understand both. We argue that what individuals are willing to do depends on their collective and relational identity. When competing against a former employer, individuals experience a conflict in their collective identity as they identify with both organizations but can only increase the welfare of one. To reduce this conflict, individuals strengthen their identification with the new organization and deidentify with the former by competing harder against the former organization. At the relational level, individuals can still identify with their ex-colleagues without harming the welfare of the new organization by competing harder with non-former colleagues but behaving less competitively toward former colleagues. We analyze data from the National Hockey League and find strong support for our hypotheses.
apa_citation: Grohsjean, T., Kober, P., & Zucchini, L. (2016). Coming back to Edmonton: Competing with former employers and colleagues. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(2), 394-413. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0200

title: Friends and Profits Don’t Mix: The Performance Implications of Repeated Partnerships
methods: Project-level quantitative analysis of Oregon bridge-construction bid data. The study uses an ordered probit first-stage self-selection correction for level of outsourcing, logit estimation clustered by prime contractor for winning bids, Tobit estimation clustered by prime contractor for percent margin, and an overbid robustness model.
industry: Bridge construction projects requiring onsite construction from raw materials.
units: Prime contractors, subcontractor partner systems, bid proposals, and bridge construction projects.
n_sample: 580 prime-contractor/partner bid-proposal sets across 144 bridge projects; profitability models use the 144 winning bids.
authors: Holloway, S. S.; Parmigiani, A.
theories: relational governance / relational contracting (Macauley, 1963; MacNeil, 1978, 1980; Ring & Van de Ven, 1992); relational view of interorganizational advantage (Dyer & Singh, 1998); transaction cost economics (Williamson, 1985, 1996)
keywords: bridge construction; partner selection; profitability; relational governance; repeated partnerships; revenue
research_question: For a given level of outsourcing, how do repeated partnerships affect prime contractors' revenue and profitability? The paper asks whether the proportion of repeated partners and the depth of those repeated relationships have distinct implications for winning bids versus earning margins.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that repeated partnerships create shared routines, richer collaboration, and better adaptation under uncertainty, which help prime contractors configure partner systems that win bids. The same relational depth can reduce profitability because known partners may have bargaining power, weaker efficiency incentives, and may crowd out cheaper or technically superior alternatives. The results support the depth-based predictions: deep repeated relationships increase the likelihood of winning bids but reduce percent margin, while the simple proportion of repeated partners is not significant in the main revenue or profitability models.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to research on repeated partnerships by separating revenue from profitability and showing that relational benefits can improve one performance dimension while harming another. It adds nuance to relational governance research by distinguishing the system-level proportion of repeated partners from dyadic relationship depth, showing that depth matters more than mere familiarity. It also extends transaction cost economics by demonstrating that partner identity affects performance after the outsourcing choice has been made.
practical_implication: Prime contractors should not treat repeated partners as uniformly beneficial. Deep repeated relationships may help win new business by reducing coordination and adaptation costs, but they can also lower margins if partners appropriate more value, slack on efficiency, or prevent consideration of better alternatives. Managers therefore need to balance trusted partners with newer or cheaper partners when configuring project teams.
limitations: The authors identify the mature bridge-construction setting as a boundary condition: the industry has established firms, stable technology, a single low-cost performance criterion, and one public customer. The project-level data identify prime contractor profitability but not each partner's profit share, and the data do not provide richer dyadic details about how each repeated relationship was governed. Outsourcing is also highly correlated with the number of partners in this setting, which may not hold elsewhere.
future_research: Future research could test whether the revenue-profitability trade-off appears in rapidly changing industries where innovativeness and speed matter more than low cost. Scholars could examine settings with specific investments or uniquely skilled suppliers, study how the product or service being transacted affects repeated partnerships, and trace how the advantages and disadvantages of repeated partnerships develop over time. Further work could also investigate the specific governance mechanisms used in repeated partner relationships.
abstract: Firms use repeated partnerships to gain benefits of shared experience such as improved coordination, collaboration, and adaptation. However, there are downsides to partnering repeatedly, including vulnerability to opportunistic partners upon whom the firm becomes dependent, muted efficiency incentives, and overlooking better options. This paper unpacks the effects of repeated partnerships by investigating their impact on two distinct types of performance: revenue and profitability. To understand repeated partnerships, we analyze a unique dataset of 580 partnerships that completed 144 bridge construction projects. Controlling for project attributes that affect the level of outsourcing, we posit that a greater proportion of repeated partners and deeper relationships with these partners will result in greater revenue through winning bids, but that the prime contractor will not necessarily garner higher profits. We find support for these predictions, highlighting the trade-offs of repeated partnerships.

title: The Operational and Signaling Benefits of Voluntary Labor Code Adoption: Reconceptualizing the Scope of Human Resource Management in Emerging Economies
methods: Longitudinal empirical-quantitative study of Sri Lankan apparel manufacturing plants using plant-year data from 2007 to 2012, generalized estimating equations, and mediation tests to assess employee, operational, and financial outcomes of voluntary labor code adoption.
industry: Apparel manufacturing plants
units: Plant-years for apparel manufacturing plants
n_sample: 122 apparel manufacturing plants; maximum possible 732 plant-year observations, with actual observations varying by model because of missing data.
authors: Jayasinghe, Mevan
theories: certified management standards; contingency theory; corporate social responsibility; human capital investment theory; instrumental stakeholder perspective
keywords: apparel manufacturing plants; emerging economies; employee outcomes; financial performance; human resource management; operational performance; signaling; voluntary labor code adoption
research_question: The paper asks whether voluntary labor code adoption can be understood as an effective human resource investment for emerging-economy manufacturers and whether it improves employee outcomes, operational performance, and financial performance. It further asks whether financial gains arise through internal operational improvements, external signaling, or both.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that voluntary labor code adoption improves basic labor standards through changes in work practices, amenities, and certification, which can reduce employee withdrawal and improve operational performance. The paper also theorizes a signaling pathway: certification makes otherwise unobservable labor standards visible to retailers and end-consumers, allowing adopters to differentiate themselves and increase sales volume. Empirically, GwG adoption is associated with lower absenteeism, higher productivity, higher on-time delivery through reduced absenteeism, and higher sales volume, with signaling providing the clearest explanation for sales-volume gains.
theoretical_contribution: The paper expands strategic HRM theory by arguing that, in emerging economies, effective HR investments may begin with meeting core labor standards rather than with resource-intensive systems aimed at discretionary employee contributions. It integrates contingency and human capital investment perspectives with certified management standards and CSR arguments to show that HR investments can affect performance through both internal employee-operational processes and external signaling. The contribution is a contextualized account of HRM in emerging-economy manufacturing that broadens the relevant set of HR investments beyond high-performance work systems.
practical_implication: For emerging-economy manufacturers, voluntary labor code adoption may be a commercially valuable HR investment rather than merely a compliance or social-responsibility cost. The findings suggest that improving basic labor standards can reduce absenteeism, support on-time delivery and productivity, and help firms win higher sales volume through credible signaling to external stakeholders. Managers should treat labor-code adoption as potentially complementary to, and possibly foundational for, more resource-intensive HR systems.
limitations: The paper notes that signaling is inferred from the direct effect of code adoption on sales volume rather than measured through retailers' redistribution of orders from non-adopters to adopters. The study is based on one industry and one country, so the results may depend on apparel manufacturing, Sri Lankan institutions, retailer composition, and local labor regulation. The analysis also does not fully account for adoption costs, potential endogeneity from managerial discretion in adopting the code, or the dynamic relationship between labor-code adoption and resource-intensive HR systems.
future_research: Future research should measure signaling mechanisms more directly, including whether retailers shift orders from non-adopters to adopters. The paper calls for longitudinal, multi-industry and multi-country studies to test whether labor-code effectiveness varies with labor regulation, culture, and retailer composition. It also recommends research on the antecedents of voluntary labor code adoption, its costs, and its complementarity with resource-intensive HR systems.
abstract: Labor codes have been voluntarily adopted and used by manufacturers in emerging economies for the past two decades as a means of ensuring minimally acceptable or core labor standards for workers. However, far too little is known of the potential benefits from the voluntary adoption of labor codes to the manufacturer, and prior human resource management research has been virtually silent on the business implications of their use for emerging economy manufacturers participating in global supply chains. Drawing on previous work across multiple disciplines and proposing a framework that extends human resource management theory more explicitly and rigorously to the context of emerging economy manufacturing, I theorize and demonstrate that the voluntary adoption of a labor code can constitute an effective human resource investment in emerging economies in improving establishment-level employee outcomes and operational and financial performance. The hypotheses are tested using longitudinal data on a sample of apparel manufacturing plants in Sri Lanka. Implications of this study include providing insight into how to expand the scope and relevance of human resource management theory to better understand research and practice in emerging economies.
apa_citation: Jayasinghe, M. (2016). The operational and signaling benefits of voluntary labor code adoption: Reconceptualizing the scope of human resource management in emerging economies. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(2), 658-677. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0478

title: Fail Often, Fail Big, and Fail Fast? Learning from Small Failures and R&D Performance in the Pharmaceutical Industry
methods: Dynamic panel analysis of pharmaceutical firms' patent expirations and R&D performance using Arellano-Bond estimation, supplemented by exploratory interviews with patent attorneys and pharmaceutical scientists to interpret the output-quality pattern.
industry: Pharmaceutical industry.
country: USPTO patent data; firm-headquarters country distribution is not reported in paper.
time_period: Firm patenting and expiration variables tracked from 1980 to 2002, with expired patents observed from 1985 to 2002.
units: Firm-year observations for pharmaceutical firms' patent portfolios.
n_sample: 97 pharmaceutical firms; final panel contains 2,015 firm-year observations.
authors: Khanna, R.; Guler, I.; Nerkar, A.
theories: intelligent failures; learning from failure; organizational learning literature; performance feedback theory
keywords: R&D output; R&D output quality; experimentation; organizational learning; small failures
research_question: The paper asks whether firms learn from failed innovation attempts and under what conditions small failures in experimentation affect subsequent R&D performance. It focuses on whether the number, importance, and timing of voluntary patent expirations shape firms' later R&D output and R&D output quality.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a multilevel learning process in pharmaceutical R&D. Patent non-renewals give firms negative feedback about the value of prior R&D bets, allowing IP offices to adapt portfolio-selection filters and improve the quality of selected patents. Idea generation adapts more slowly because individual scientists receive limited direct feedback, search is path dependent, and personal incentives may make negative feedback difficult to absorb; this produces fewer patents in the short run but higher-quality patent output.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends organizational learning research by separating small failures in experimentation from catastrophic or operational failures. It shows that learning from failure can have opposite effects on different dimensions of innovation performance, decreasing patent output while increasing patent quality. It also contributes a multilevel account in which firm-level selection mechanisms respond faster to failure feedback than individual-level idea-generation mechanisms.
practical_implication: For R&D managers, the findings imply that failed exploratory projects should be evaluated early and consciously rather than ignored or treated only as waste. The paper suggests that firms can improve the quality of their R&D portfolio by learning from patent non-renewals and by removing subpar projects early, while recognizing that such feedback may temporarily reduce patent output.
limitations: The authors could not observe the underlying reasons for patent failures or distinguish among different causes of patent expiration. They also could not directly observe the process through which failures improve R&D performance, including whether improvements come from ongoing projects, R&D resource reallocation, or both. Patent expirations are a distinct type of failure in pharmaceutical R&D, so generalization to other industries depends on similar uncertainty, long development cycles, and separate idea-generation and selection processes.
future_research: Future studies could distinguish among different reasons for patent expirations and examine how each reason shapes subsequent learning outcomes. Additional research could directly test the multilevel model of idea generation and selection, including how feedback moves from IP offices to scientists. The authors also call for work comparing patent-stage failures with ideas that fail before patenting and for tests in other R&D-intensive settings such as venture capital, corporate venturing, and film production.
abstract: Do firms learn from their failed innovation attempts? Answering this question is important because failure is an integral part of exploratory learning. In this study, we consider whether and under what circumstances firms learn from their small failures in experimentation. Building on organizational learning literature, we examine the conditions under which prior failures influence firms’ R&D output, in terms of amount and quality. Our empirical analysis of voluntary patent expirations (i.e., patents that firms give up by not paying renewal fees) in 97 pharmaceutical firms between 1980 and 2002 shows that the number, importance, and timing of small failures are associated with a decrease in R&D output (patent count) but an increase in the quality of the R&D output (forward citations to patents). Exploratory interviews further suggest that the results are driven by a multilevel learning process from failures in pharmaceutical R&D. Our findings contribute to the organizational learning literature by providing a nuanced view of learning from failures in experimentation.

title: Integrating the Bright and Dark Sides of OCB: A Daily Investigation of the Benefits and Costs of Helping Others
methods: Experience sampling study of employees surveyed three times per workday for ten workdays, analyzed with multilevel path analysis in Mplus 7.11 to test daily within-person mediation and cross-level moderation by trait promotion and prevention focus.
industry: Mixed administrative, service, clerical, and technical roles across a university and other organizations; no single industry sector is specified.
time_period: Ten workdays; specific calendar dates are not reported in paper.
units: Employees and employee-day observations.
n_sample: 82 employees providing 748 day-level data points.
authors: Koopman, Joel; Lanaj, Klodiana; Scott, Brent A.
theories: cognitive-affective processing system framework; conservation of resources theory; regulatory focus theory
keywords: cognitive-affective processing system; conservation of resources theory; employee well-being; organizational citizenship behavior; positive affect; regulatory focus; work goal progress
research_question: The paper asks whether daily organizational citizenship behavior is good or bad for the actors who perform it, and more precisely for whom it is beneficial or detrimental and why. It examines whether daily OCB has positive and negative implications for emotional exhaustion, job satisfaction, and affective commitment through two paths: positive affect for job satisfaction and affective commitment, and work goal progress for all three well-being indicators, with promotion and prevention focus shaping these daily relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is dual rather than uniformly positive or negative. Drawing on CAPS and COR, the authors argue that helping others can generate psychological resources and positive affect, improving job satisfaction and affective commitment, while also consuming scarce work time and reducing perceived progress toward work goals, thereby increasing exhaustion and lowering satisfaction and commitment. Promotion-focused employees are more attuned to resource gains from OCB, whereas prevention-focused employees are more sensitive to the resource losses and goal-progress costs of OCB.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the OCB literature by integrating the bright-side and dark-side streams in one daily, actor-focused model. It extends COR by modeling resource generation and resource consumption simultaneously in a dynamic within-person design, and extends CAPS by specifying how daily helping episodes activate affective and goal-progress processes. It also positions regulatory focus as a cross-level boundary condition explaining why the same helping behavior can have different well-being implications for different employees.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that encouraging high levels of citizenship behavior may improve mood and commitment but can also drain actors by interfering with goal progress. Organizations that depend on helping should monitor exhaustion, avoid treating OCB as costless, and support practices that replenish resources, such as reflection on the prosocial impact of helping. The findings also suggest that employees' regulatory focus matters: promotion focus may amplify the benefits of OCB, while prevention focus may make the costs more salient.
limitations: The authors note that the study relies on self-reports, although they separated measures across time, controlled for related constructs, and centered daily variables within individuals. They also did not disentangle all possible mediators, such as recipient gratitude, pride, contentment, guilt, or recipient indifference, and the lagged next-day analyses were underpowered. The study examined interpersonally focused OCB only, with relatively mild helping items, and did not test whether organizationally focused or change-focused OCB would operate similarly.
future_research: Future research could collect observer ratings of daily OCB and use designs better able to capture next-day spirals in OCB, well-being, and subsequent helping. The authors call for work on specific OCB event features, including complexity, novelty, routine character, and time or resource intensity. They also encourage research on additional individual boundary conditions, broader well-being outcomes such as physiological and behavioral consequences, and downstream effects such as home helping, workplace reciprocation, or deviant behavior after OCB.
abstract: Although the general picture in the organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) literature is that OCB has positive consequences for employees and organizations, an emerging stream of work has begun to examine the potential negative consequences of OCB for actors. Drawing from the cognitive-affective processing system framework and conservation of resources theory, we present an integrative model that simultaneously examines the benefits and costs of daily OCB for actors. Utilizing an experience sampling methodology through which 82 employees were surveyed for 10 workdays, we find that daily OCB is associated with positive affect, but it also interferes with perceptions of work goal progress. Positive affect and work goal progress in turn mediate the effects of OCB on daily well-being. Moreover, employees’ trait regulatory focus influences the strength of the daily relationships between OCB and its positive and negative outcomes. We conclude by discussing theoretical and practical implications of our multilevel model.

title: Mechanisms of Hybrid Governance: Administrative Committees in Non-Equity Alliances
methods: Empirical quantitative study of non-equity alliances in the biopharmaceuticals industry. The paper uses probit models to estimate whether alliance contracts establish steering committees, with controls for partner experience, knowledge stocks, deal size, contract length, incentive payments, prior ties, deal type, cross-border status, phase, therapeutic area, technology area, and year.
industry: Biopharmaceutical alliances.
country: Domestic and cross-border alliances; individual countries are not listed.
time_period: Alliances formed during the 1990-2010 timeframe.
units: Non-equity alliance contracts between firms.
n_sample: 524 non-equity alliances.
authors: Reuer, Jeffrey J.; Devarakonda, Shivaram V.
theories: Williamson's theory of governance structures; hybrid governance; transaction cost theory
keywords: administrative committees; coordinated adaptation; hybrid governance; interdependence; non-equity alliances; steering committees; technological uncertainty; technology overlap
research_question: The paper asks how frequently steering committees appear in contracts for non-equity alliances and how alliance transactional attributes affect their inclusion. It focuses on whether technological uncertainty, partner interdependence, and technology overlap explain when partners delegate authority to an administrative committee.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that non-equity alliances face adaptive limits because contracts cannot fully anticipate future contingencies and lack the administrative fiat of hierarchies. Steering committees create a dedicated interface for information processing, joint decision making, coordination, and dispute prevention. Partners are therefore more likely to contract for such committees when technological uncertainty increases sequential adaptation needs, when interdependence raises coordination costs, and when technology overlap increases concerns about managing know-how access and leakage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends research on interorganizational contracts by showing that partners can create administrative controls in non-equity alliances through contractually delegated steering committees, not only through equity-based governance. It contributes to the theory of hybrid governance by separating administrative control from incentive alignment and by identifying conditions under which non-equity alliances can incorporate more hierarchical governance features. It also adds a structural-planning mechanism to work on contractual contingency planning and decision-right allocation.
practical_implication: For executives designing alliance contracts, the findings suggest that steering committees are most useful when partners anticipate substantial coordinated adaptation needs. Managers should consider these committees when alliances involve uncertain technologies, reciprocal or otherwise interdependent activities, and overlapping technological resources. The paper also implies that firms should weigh the committee's contracting and governance costs against whether a non-equity alliance can cope with disturbances without moving to a more hierarchical form.
limitations: The analysis is limited to biopharmaceutical alliances, a context with complex collaboration and potentially distinctive contracting conditions. The study examines alliance structuring decisions at inception rather than how committees evolve during implementation. It also studies antecedents of steering committees rather than their consequences for alliance performance, conflict resolution, new products, or knowledge transfer.
future_research: Future research could test whether the antecedents of steering committees generalize to other industries and collaborative contexts. Studies could examine longitudinal changes in committee existence, structure, responsibilities, and relationships with other control rights as alliances unfold. Additional work could investigate committee composition, attorney involvement, behavioral consequences, and whether administrative committees complement or substitute for relational governance mechanisms such as trust.
abstract: Recent research on the governance of hybrid organizational forms has investigated the contractual foundations of collaborations by examining how firms craft complex contracts, as well as plan for changing circumstances during contract execution. We build upon and extend this research by considering the contractual delegation of authority to a dedicated structural interface for a collaboration. In particular, our theory suggests that partners are more likely to employ steering committees to help partners guide their interactions, address unanticipated contingencies that materialize, and mitigate incipient conflicts when partners have substantial needs for coordinated adaptation. An analysis of alliances in the biopharmaceuticals industry explicates the formal governance mechanisms that support high-tech partnerships and identifies determinants of the administrative structures firms utilize in contractual agreements to enhance their adaptive limits.
apa_citation: Reuer, J. J., & Devarakonda, S. V. (2016). Mechanisms of hybrid governance: Administrative committees in non-equity alliances. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(2), 510-533. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0098

title: Perceptions of Employee Volunteering: Is It “Credited” or “Stigmatized” by Colleagues?
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design: Study 1 used a field survey of employee volunteers and colleagues, analyzed with structural equation modeling and bootstrapped moderated mediation; Study 2 used a laboratory experiment with manipulated volunteering, citizenship behavior, and attributed motives, analyzed with between-subjects ANOVAs.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Study 1 used a four-week lag between employee and colleague surveys; Study 2 used a two-week lag between participant survey waves. Calendar dates are not reported.
units: Employee volunteers paired with supervisors or coworkers in Study 1; undergraduate business students evaluating fictitious profiles in Study 2
n_sample: Study 1: 260 employee volunteers; Study 2: 305 students completing Time 2
authors: Rodell, Jessica B.; Lynch, John W.
theories: reputation perspective; theories of person perception and attribution
keywords: credits; employee volunteering; impression management attributions; intrinsic attributions; stigmas; supportive reactions; volunteering reputation
research_question: The paper asks how colleagues perceive employee volunteering and whether those perceptions affect how supervisors and coworkers treat employees who volunteer more often. It focuses on whether volunteering is credited, stigmatized, or both, and on how attributed motives shape those reputational evaluations.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is reputational. Colleagues observe employee volunteering, infer motives, and translate those inferences into positive credits or negative stigmas. Intrinsic attributions amplify the positive volunteering-credit relationship, while impression management attributions amplify stigmatization. Credits then increase supportive reactions, but their benefits are weaker when stigmas are also high.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to employee volunteering research by shifting attention from the volunteer's attitudes and behavior to colleagues' interpretations and treatment of the volunteer. It also extends reputation research by treating reputation as attribute-specific and potentially ambivalent: the same non-work behavior can produce both credits and stigmas depending on perceived motives.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that employee volunteering can affect interpersonal treatment at work, not only volunteer wellbeing or organizational image. Volunteer programs may be more beneficial when employees' participation is perceived as intrinsically motivated and less beneficial when it appears impression-management oriented, because stigma can weaken the rewards associated with positive credits.
limitations: The field study contains some same-source, same-time colleague reports for credits, stigmas, attributions, and supportive reactions, leaving possible common method and causal-order concerns despite temporal and source separation where possible. The paper studies volunteering frequency rather than the initial decision to volunteer, persistence of volunteering, specific volunteer causes, or the timing of volunteering during versus outside work hours.
future_research: Future research could examine how different company supports for volunteering shape colleague attributions and whether formal volunteer programs reduce or intensify reputational evaluations. It could also study how intrinsic and impression-management attributions coexist, how specific volunteer causes or schedules affect stigma, and whether volunteering direction and persistence produce different workplace reactions than volunteering frequency.
abstract: As research begins to accumulate on employee volunteering, it appears that this behavior is largely beneficial to employee performance and commitment. It is less clear, however, how employee volunteering is perceived by others in the workplace. Do colleagues award volunteering “credit” (e.g., associating it with being concerned about others) or do they “stigmatize” it (e.g., associating it with being distracted from work)? Moreover, do those evaluations predict how colleagues actually treat employees who volunteer more often? Adopting a reputation perspective, we draw from theories of person perception and attribution to explore these research questions. The results of a field study reveal that colleagues gave credit to employee volunteering when they attributed it to intrinsic reasons and stigmatized employee volunteering when they attributed it to impression management reasons. Ultimately, through the awarded credits, volunteering was rewarded by supervisors (with the allocation of more resources) and coworkers (with the provision of more helping behavior) when it was attributed to intrinsic motives—a relationship that was amplified when stigmas were low and mitigated when stigmas were high. The results of a laboratory experiment further confirmed that volunteering was both credited and stigmatized, distinguishing it from citizenship behavior, which was credited but not stigmatized.

title: There’s No Beer without a Smoke: Community Cohesion and Neighboring Communities’ Effects on Organizational Resistance to Antismoking Regulations in the Dutch Hospitality Industry
methods: Mixed-methods study combining newspaper articles, telephone interviews with small bar owners, and negative binomial spatial-lag models of resistance across Dutch municipalities.
industry: Dutch hospitality industry, focused on small bars and pubs.
time_period: Resistance measured using SSB membership at the end of 2008, with fines data for 2008-2009 and community covariates primarily from 2007-2008.
units: Dutch municipalities and small bars or pubs.
n_sample: 427 municipalities in the statistical analyses; 19 telephone interviews with small bar owners.
authors: Simons, T.; Vermeulen, P. A. M.; Knoben, J.
theories: community cohesion; institutional theory; mimetic processes
keywords: community cohesion; institutional pressures; neighboring communities; organizational resistance; smoking regulations
research_question: How do community cohesion and resistance in neighboring communities shape small bars’ active resistance to institutional pressure from a powerful state actor? The paper asks why resistance to the Dutch smoking ban varied across municipalities even though small bars faced the same national regulation.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism links community embeddedness to organizational resistance. Residential stability creates a latent relational infrastructure that can be mobilized when the smoking ban threatens valued local bars, while kinship generates belonging, mutual obligation, and willingness to defend the community’s social function. Resistance in neighboring communities supplies signals, information, and coordination opportunities, but cohesive communities have less permeable boundaries and are therefore less influenced by neighboring resistance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional theory by showing that community-level social cohesion helps explain heterogeneous organizational resistance to the same institutional pressure. It brings community back into the study of institutional processes by showing that resistance is socially embedded rather than only a narrow strategic response by individual organizations. It also develops a spatial account of resistance by showing that neighboring communities matter, but that their influence depends on the focal community’s cohesion.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that regulators and managers should attend to local community characteristics when anticipating organizational responses to new rules. Even small and resource-constrained organizations may resist powerful actors when they serve an important community function and can draw on cohesive local support.
limitations: The authors note that the theory mainly applies to small and relatively powerless organizations facing pressure from a powerful and legitimate actor. They also note that the arguments are most applicable when the institutional pressure threatens the normative framework of the community. Although the time structure and qualitative evidence make reverse causality unlikely, the study cannot fully rule out omitted historical community factors that influence both cohesion and resistance.
future_research: Future research could examine longer time periods to capture the dynamics of organizational resistance to regulatory pressures at the community level. The authors also call for more fine-grained measures of local social endowments, including histories of community activism, and for studies of other communities such as virtual or open-source communities that share collective identity and may face powerful adversaries.
abstract: This study highlights the importance of communities in explaining organizational resistance to institutional pressures. Examining the active resistance of small bars to smoking regulations in 427 Dutch municipalities (communities), we argue that the likelihood of organizational resistance to institutional pressure from a powerful actor is affected by the social cohesion of the focal community. In addition, we propose a contiguity effect that emphasizes the broader social context of the community—its neighboring communities—as a source for support or information about appropriate ways to resist such pressures. By incorporating community attributes to account for organizations’ heterogeneous responses to institutional pressure, the study advances current institutional scholarship and demonstrates empirically how such a theory can help explain the success of relatively weak organizational actors’ resistance in the face of strong institutional pressures by the state—that is, as a result of their embeddedness in a community.

There’s no beer without a smoke: Community cohesion and neighboring communities’ effects on organizational resistance to antismoking regulations in the Dutch hospitality industry. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(2), 545-578. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0379

title: Corporate Social Responsibility: An Overview and New Research Directions
methods: From the Editors editorial and narrative overview of CSR research published in AMJ from 1958 through 2015, using content analysis to classify prior articles by antecedent, outcome, and process focus, outcome type, CSR measure, and country setting.
industry: CSR research published in AMJ.
country: U.S. and non-U.S. CSR research contexts, with examples including Canada, France, Germany, India, Japan, Russia, Spain, the United Kingdom, and China.
units: AMJ articles on CSR, excluding the current thematic issue.
n_sample: 87 articles on CSR published in AMJ between 1958 and 2015.
authors: Wang, Heli; Tong, Li; Takeuchi, Riki; George, Gerard
theories: institutional logics; stakeholder theory
keywords: CSR research; corporate social responsibility; employee engagement; institutional environments; multinational enterprises; organizational purpose; stakeholder claims
research_question: The editorial asks how CSR research in AMJ has evolved and what new research directions can better capture the complexity of corporate social responsibility. It aims to move attention from whether firms should engage in CSR toward how firms conceptualize, organize, implement, and evaluate their societal obligations across stakeholders and institutional contexts.
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial purpose: The authors introduce a thematic issue on CSR and position its seven studies as exemplars of broader shifts in CSR scholarship.
- Literature overview: They classify AMJ CSR articles from 1958 through 2015 by antecedent, outcome, and process focus, and by shifts in outcomes, CSR dimensions, and country settings.
- Field-level shift: CSR research is described as moving from shareholder-value debates and aggregate CSR measures toward process, nonfinancial outcomes, specific CSR dimensions, and global contexts.
- Research agenda: The editorial highlights stakeholder interdependencies, CSR motives and tradeoffs, institutional environments, multinational CSR, and individual roles in CSR as priority directions.
- Practical problem: Managers face difficulties measuring CSR impact, balancing stakeholder claims, allocating scarce resources, and adapting CSR across national institutional environments.

The process is agenda-setting rather than hypothesis-testing. Wang and colleagues synthesize prior AMJ CSR research and the thematic issue to argue that CSR scholarship should study the organization and implementation of CSR, not only its antecedents or financial consequences. Their central logic is that CSR operates across firms, stakeholders, communities, institutions, multinational structures, and employees, so future research needs multi-level accounts of tradeoffs, motives, and context.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes by organizing AMJ's CSR literature into historical research trends and by reframing CSR as a multi-level phenomenon involving stakeholder claims, institutional variation, organizational purpose, and individual engagement. It pushes CSR scholarship beyond aggregate CSR-performance questions toward richer theorizing about processes, mechanisms, interdependencies, and boundary conditions. It also links the thematic issue's articles to broader opportunities for theory building in stakeholder, institutional, hybrid-organization, and employee-level CSR research.
practical_implication: For managers, the editorial emphasizes that CSR is no longer mainly a question of whether to act but of how to plan, prioritize, measure, and communicate CSR effectively. It points to practical challenges in balancing shareholder and non-shareholder claims, preventing CSR mandates from becoming symbolic or corrupt, managing global CSR across diverse institutions, and aligning employee engagement with corporate responsibility missions. For multinational firms, it stresses the difficulty of responding to diverse stakeholder pressures without shifting irresponsible practices across borders.
limitations: The editorial is a narrative overview and thematic introduction focused on CSR research in AMJ rather than the full CSR literature across journals. Its trend analysis is limited to AMJ articles on CSR through 2015. Because it is an editorial, it proposes research directions rather than testing theoretical claims or estimating empirical relationships.
future_research: The authors call for research on interdependencies among stakeholder claims, conflicts among non-shareholder groups, and how firms prioritize competing CSR demands. They encourage work on compliance, commitment, motives, and competing priorities in CSR implementation, especially under mandates or institutional pressure. They also call for more research on CSR in emerging economies, multinational enterprises, individual employees, stakeholder perceptions, and the cognitive and motivational conditions that shape evaluations of corporate social activities.

title: Competition, Regulatory Policy, and Firms’ Resource Investments: The Case of Renewable Energy Technologies
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study using annual data on U.S. electricity-generation firms from 1999 to 2010. The authors estimate random-effects Tobit models for the percentage of renewable electricity generation, random-effects Probit models for waste-to-energy, wind, and solar investment, split-sample tests by RPS presence, two-sample t-tests, and post-hoc two-stage random-effects Probit models for RPS policy likelihood.
industry: U.S. electricity generation segment, including private energy firms, investor-owned utilities, and government utilities
units: Firm-state-year observations for firms with operational electricity generation facilities
n_sample: 1,542 firms and 10,518 firm-year observations
authors: Weigelt, Carmen; Shittu, Ekundayo
theories: institutional theory; resource-based view (RBV)
keywords: clean technologies; competition; new resource investments; regulatory mandates; renewable energy investments; resource-based view
research_question: How does the presence and strength of regulatory mandates alter the effect of competitors’ new resource investments on a focal firm’s own renewable energy investments? The paper asks whether regulatory policy substitutes for or complements competitive signals when firms reconfigure resource portfolios toward clean technologies.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that competitors’ investments reduce uncertainty about the value, functioning, and strategic need for new renewable resources, prompting focal firms to invest. Regulatory mandates also reduce uncertainty, but because they are codified, enforceable, and apply to the focal firm and competitors alike, firms attend more to mandates than to competitive signals when mandates are present. This dampening effect is stronger for technologically distant resources such as wind and solar and, for some resource types, when RPS mandates are more established.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the resource-based view by showing that resource portfolio reconfiguration is shaped by external regulatory and competitive forces, not only by internal resource endowments and capabilities. It specifies a substitution relationship between regulatory mandates and competitors’ resource investments and shows that this relationship varies across resource types by technological distance from incumbents’ existing resource base. The study also links RBV reasoning to institutional theory by showing how mandates can redirect managerial attention and resource redeployment.
practical_implication: For policy makers, the findings imply that renewable energy mandates are especially influential when few competitors have already invested and when the targeted resource is technologically distant from incumbents’ existing resource base. The paper also suggests that stable, established mandates can make firms less reliant on competitors’ behavior as a guide for new clean technology investments. For managers, the findings indicate that resource investment decisions should account for how regulatory pressure can supersede competitive imitation as an external signal.
limitations: The authors state that they control for electricity demand and retail market deregulation but do not explicitly study customer demand in deregulated markets where customers can choose electricity providers. They also note that the dichotomous RPS measure is crude, although they partially address policy variation with yearly RPS goals. The study is limited to the U.S. electricity industry, so the same policy-competition interaction may not generalize to other industries.
future_research: The authors call for more fine-grained research on the structure of regulatory policies across states. They suggest testing the interplay between competition and regulatory policy in other industry contexts. They also identify opportunities to study organizational decision making, resource identities, value networks, vertical integration, transmission agreements, and firms’ nonmarket strategies in resource portfolio configuration.
abstract: We study the interplay between regulatory mandates and competition on a focal firm’s new resource investments. While prior literature has separately pointed to the influence of competition and regulatory policy on a focal firm’s resource decisions, less is known about how the policy effect interacts with the competitive effect. Studying how regulatory mandates moderate the effect of competition on a focal firm’s new resource investments, we show that resource redeployment is not simply a function of internal firm decisions but a response to external forces. We find that regulatory mandates dampen the effect of competitors’ new resource investments on a focal firm’s new resource investments. Distinguishing between different clean technology types, we show that this dampening effect is the stronger, the more distant the new resource is from incumbents’ old resource base, and the more established the mandate is. We test our hypotheses in the context of renewable energy investments in waste-to-energy, wind, and solar in the U.S. electricity industry. Our data comprise 1542 utilities and private energy firms and their renewable investments from 1999 to 2010.
apa_citation: Weigelt, C., & Shittu, E. (2016). Competition, regulatory policy, and firms’ resource investments: The case of renewable energy technologies. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(2), 678-704. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0661
