title: Psyched-up to Suck-up: Self-regulated Cognition, Interpersonal Influence, and Recommendations for Board Appointments in the Corporate Elite
methods: Longitudinal survey and archival study of corporate director dyads. The study uses repeated surveys around director meetings, negative binomial random-effects models for director cognitions, logit models for board recommendations, clustered robust variance estimators, ordered logit and negative binomial robustness checks, and Heckman selection models.
industry: Corporate directors at large and mid-sized public U.S. companies with more than $100 million in sales.
time_period: A six-month survey period around director interactions and nominating committee meetings; the population frame was listed in Reference USA in 2005.
units: Corporate directors, director dyads, director-meeting survey observations, and board-appointment recommendations.
n_sample: 434 participating directors; 374 complete dyads; 4,002 observations for cognition models; 248 complete dyads for recommendation models.
authors: Westphal, James D.; Shani, Guy
theories: ingratiation; self-regulation theory; similarity-attraction principle; social influence theory
keywords: board appointments; corporate elite; demographic dissimilarity; ingratiator's dilemma; interpersonal influence; self-regulated cognition; social status
research_question: How can corporate directors overcome the ingratiator's dilemma when trying to influence relatively high-status colleagues? The paper asks whether anticipating interaction with a high-status alter leads directors to reflect on shared characteristics and avoid reflection on nonshared characteristics, and whether this self-regulated cognition makes expressions of liking and admiration more effective in securing board-appointment recommendations.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that anticipating interaction with a high-status colleague prompts directors to focus cognitively on shared personal and social characteristics while avoiding nonshared characteristics. This pattern induces more genuine positive affect and admiration, making later expressions of liking and admiration appear less like strategic flattery. The influence benefit is especially pronounced when the target is both high-status and demographically dissimilar, because such targets are attractive sources of opportunity but also more vigilant for insincere ingratiation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to social influence research by identifying a cognitive route through which actors can resolve the ingratiator's dilemma rather than merely using more subtle influence tactics. It extends self-regulation research by theorizing self-regulated social cognition: cognition about another person that regulates feelings or attitudes before interaction. It also contributes to corporate governance research by showing how micro-level interpersonal psychology helps directors convert elite ties into recommendations for board appointments.
practical_implication: The findings imply that directors' interpersonal influence depends not only on what they say or do in meetings but also on how they prepare cognitively before interacting with powerful colleagues. For leaders in demographically diverse elite settings, reflecting on shared characteristics may increase sincere liking and reduce the risk that compliments or admiration are read as opportunistic. The study also suggests that influence behaviors can shape access to board seats and other elite opportunities beyond formal governance performance.
limitations: The paper does not present a formal limitations section, but the empirical setting bounds the claims to corporate directors at large and mid-sized public U.S. firms. The design relies heavily on survey reports around director interactions, although the authors use inter-rater checks, archival controls, selection models, and robustness analyses. The theory focuses on self-regulated cognition about shared personal and social characteristics, leaving other forms of anticipatory cognition less directly tested.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether the mechanism generalizes to firm leaders beyond corporate directors, lower-level managers, and professionals outside the corporate sphere. Future work could examine whether influence-target characteristics such as personality traits moderate the effects of self-regulated cognition. The paper also suggests studying other kinds of anticipatory cognition, such as reflection on organizational characteristics or strategy, before interactions with important constituents.
abstract: This study reveals how self-regulated cognition in advance of social interaction can resolve the so-called “ingratiator’s dilemma,” which is that the most attractive targets of social influence—those who have relatively high social status—tend to be the most difficult to ingratiate successfully. Our theoretical argument suggests that in anticipation of social interaction with a relatively high-status colleague, corporate directors tend to reflect on characteristics shared with that colleague, while avoiding thoughts about characteristics not shared. We explain how this pattern of cognition induces genuine positive feelings and admiration for the colleague, such that their interpersonal behaviors are less likely to appear as insincere attempts to curry favor, and thus more likely to engender influence. We further suggest that this pattern of cognition is especially valuable when interacting with relatively high-status colleagues who are demographically dissimilar from the focal actor. Finally, our theoretical framework indicates how this self-regulated cognition facilitates advancement in the corporate elite by positively moderating the effects of one’s interpersonal behavior on the likelihood that colleagues will recommend him or her for a board appointment. We test our hypotheses with a unique dataset that includes survey data from a large sample of directors collected before and after meetings.
apa_citation: Westphal, J. D., & Shani, G. (2016). Psyched-up to suck-up: Self-regulated cognition, interpersonal influence, and recommendations for board appointments in the corporate elite. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(2), 479-509. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0010

title: Converging Winds: Logic Hybridization in the Colorado Wind Energy Field
methods: Inductive historical case study of the Colorado wind energy field, using semi-structured interviews, naturalistic observation, newspaper articles, CPUC releases, utility archives, resource plans, archival reports, and video footage to build a process model of field-level logic hybridization.
industry: Colorado wind energy field.
time_period: The case period is 1999-2008; supplementary data collection and archival coverage extend beyond that period.
units: Field actors including environmental SMOs, clean energy SMOs, wind energy firms, electric utilities, policy makers, regulators, researchers, attorneys, and related stakeholders.
n_sample: 34 interviews with 30 participants, 546 Denver Post articles, 58 CPUC press-release pages, 31 archived utility press releases, 10 resource plans, 1,781 pages of archival documents, and 12 videos.
authors: York, J. G.; Hargrave, T. J.; Pacheco, D. F.
theories: hybrid organizing; institutional logics; logic hybridization; social movement framing
keywords: ecologizing logic; economizing logic; field-level logics; hybrid organizations; logic hybridization; social movement organizations; wind energy
research_question: How can organizational responses to logic incompatibility and evolving field conditions lead to field-level logic hybridization? The paper asks how hybrid organizations contribute to that process and what distinguishes hybridization from blending, assimilation, and replacement.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Incompatibility between economizing and ecologizing logics; dominant and subordinate field logics; field centralization; social movement organizations; hybrid organizations; wind energy practices and governance arrangements.
- Process / phases: Compromise through the Windsource program elaborated the dominant economizing logic; reframing around the Lamar wind farm assimilated wind energy into least-cost economizing criteria; contestation through Amendment 37 reduced power concentration; clean energy SMOs and wind firms legitimated hybrid frames and practices; utilities and policy makers embedded the hybridized logic through strategy and governance.
- Triggering conditions: High field centralization around Xcel and the CPUC, persistent logic incompatibility, and SMO frustration with compromise and assimilation.
- Emergent outcomes: A hybridized clean energy logic that constructed wind energy as simultaneously economically valuable and environmentally beneficial.
- Boundary conditions: The process is most applicable to centralized fields with a dominant logic and high perceived incompatibility between logics.

The process is recursive: organizational responses alter field-level conditions, and those altered conditions enable later responses. Compromise and assimilation do not end conflict because they preserve the dominant logic's goals, but they give subordinate actors legitimacy, learning, and broader public reach. Once contestation decentralizes the field, hybrid organizations can instantiate new frames, practices, and governance arrangements that make previously incompatible goals appear jointly achievable.
theoretical_contribution: The paper defines field-level logic hybridization as the emergence of rules of action, interaction, and interpretation that integrate the goals of previously incompatible logics through material forms, practices, and governance arrangements. It distinguishes hybridization from blending, where elements coexist, and assimilation, where subordinate means serve dominant goals. It also extends institutional logics and hybrid organizing research by showing how compromise, reframing, contestation, legitimation, and embedding unfold as a field-level process rather than only as organizational responses.
practical_implication: For advocates of environmentally relevant sectors, compromise with incumbents may build legitimacy and learning but may also reinforce the incumbent logic if the subordinate logic's goals remain unacknowledged. Contestation can become necessary when compromise and economic reframing fail to shift the field's power structure. Hybrid organizations are especially important because they can connect technical, market, policy, and movement work around a frame that makes economic and environmental goals mutually reinforcing.
limitations: The authors note that all themes were triangulated from multiple data sources, but the study comes from a unique Colorado wind energy context. They frame the findings as most relevant to fields marked by high centralization and high perceived logic incompatibility; fields with more compatible logics may not require hybridization and may instead accommodate multiple logics through assimilation or blending.
future_research: Future research could compare hybridization with blending and assimilation in other fields where practices are reconstructed to support previously incompatible goals. Additional studies could examine when developmental changes such as assimilation are necessary intermediary steps toward hybridization. The authors also call for further work on the internal tensions of hybrid organizations and on how those tensions affect field-level logic hybridization.
abstract: This study explores the hybridization of field-level logics, a process that integrates previously incompatible logics within an organizational field. Through an inductive study of the wind energy field in Colorado, we find that logic hybridization resulted when social movement organizations (SMOs), electric utility firms, hybrid organizations, and policy makers variously responded to incompatibility between economizing and ecologizing logics. After compromise with electric utilities and efforts to justify wind power in economic terms failed to reduce the dominance of the economizing logic, SMOs switched tactics to promote the ecologizing logic. Once SMOs succeeded in altering the balance of power in the field, hybrid organizations then emerged to legitimize a new set of frames, practices, and arrangements that integrated the previously incompatible logics. Electric utility firms and policy makers then formalized and embedded the new hybridized logic in the field. Our findings suggest that the hybridization of field-level logics is a complex process in which organizational actions and field-level conditions recursively influence each other over time. This process is critical to understanding how entrepreneurs, firms, policy makers, and SMOs each contribute to the emergence of environmentally relevant sectors.

title: What Do I Take With Me? The Mediating Effect of Spin-out Team Size and Tenure on the Founder–Firm Performance Relationship
methods: Large-scale quantitative study using linked employer-employee U.S. Census LEHD data from legal services, with parent-firm panel regressions, spin-out survival models, Sobel mediation tests, and Monte Carlo confidence intervals.
industry: Legal services.
time_period: Ten years in ten large U.S. states.
units: Parent firm-years and spin-out firm-years.
n_sample: 11,822 parent firm-year observations and 42,624 spin-out firm-year observations spanning approximately 10,000 spin-outs.
authors: Agarwal, Rajshree; Campbell, Benjamin A.; Franco, April Mitchell; Ganco, Martin
theories: employee entrepreneurship; knowledge-based entrepreneurship; knowledge-based view
keywords: co-mobility; employee entrepreneurship; firm performance; knowledge-based view; legal services; spin-out founder; team size; team tenure
research_question: The paper asks how spin-out founders affect knowledge transfer and firm performance by mobilizing teams, rather than only by carrying their own human capital into a new venture. It examines whether founder performance shapes spin-out team size and tenure, and whether those team characteristics mediate the effects of founder performance on parent firm performance and spin-out survival.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a founder-as-catalyst process within the knowledge-based view. Higher-performing founders have better access to coworkers, stronger information about complementary skills, and a more credible signal for persuading others to leave secure employment. Larger teams transfer more distributed and complementary knowledge from the parent to the spin-out, while longer-tenured teams carry routines and organizational experience that especially benefit the new venture. The results support team size as a mediator for both parent and spin-out outcomes, and team tenure as a mediator for spin-out survival but not for parent firm performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper refines the knowledge-based view by showing that team-based knowledge is not always an isolating mechanism when the rival is a spin-out founded by an informed insider. It contributes to employee entrepreneurship research by linking founder characteristics and founding-team characteristics as interdependent rather than independent sources of parent and spin-out performance. It also advances microfoundational theorizing by connecting individual founder performance, team mobilization, and firm-level outcomes in one mediation model.
practical_implication: For established firms, the findings suggest that reducing the harm from employee entrepreneurship may require attention to potential followers, not only to the high-performing founder. Retention efforts aimed at team members may be more cost effective than trying only to deter founders. For potential founders, the ability to attract a larger and more experienced team is an important validation of both the opportunity and the founder’s capacity to exploit it.
limitations: The authors note generalizability concerns because the empirical setting is legal services, where human capital and client relationships are central and physical capital is less important. They cannot directly measure competitive interactions, the specialties or knowledge bases of team members, or the size of the opportunity pursued by the spin-out founder. They also cannot distinguish voluntary from involuntary mobility and cannot completely rule out reverse mediation, although they argue this pathway is logically unlikely in the empirical context.
future_research: Future research could test whether the relationships extend to manufacturing and other settings where complementary assets include physical capital and intellectual property. The authors call for work that measures direct parent-spin-out competition, compares parent and spin-out knowledge bases, and examines opportunity quality more directly. They also identify demographic homophily and skill or task diversity within founding teams as important directions for decomposing how team composition affects firm performance.
abstract: We extend the knowledge-based perspective to consider the impact of spin-out founders on knowledge transfer to new ventures. We argue that existing theory largely ignores the founder’s role as a team catalyst who mobilizes a team and transmits the team’s knowledge to a new venture. We address this gap by building theory on the role of a spin-out founder as a facilitator of co-mobility and whose impact on firm outcomes is mediated by the size and organizational experience of the recruited team. The support for our hypotheses, through use of linked employee–employer U.S. Census data from the legal services industry, has theoretical and practical implications for the knowledge-based view and human resource strategies for both existing and entrepreneurial firms.

title: Partners in Crime: The Effects of Diversity on the Longevity of Cartels
methods: Archival quantitative study of prosecuted cartels using Cox proportional hazard survival models with robust standard errors clustered by cartel. The study models cartel termination hazard as a function of variety of age-based experience, separation in uncertainty avoidance, and power disparity, with firm-, cartel-, industry-, country-, and regulatory controls.
industry: Primary, manufacturing, transportation, and retailing industries, with manufacturing industries containing the majority of cartels
country: European Union cartels with participating firms primarily located in European countries, plus some firms outside Europe
time_period: Cartels prosecuted between 2001 and 2011
units: cartel-year observations
n_sample: 41 cartels involving 463 firms, split into 195 cartel-year observations
authors: Bertrand, Olivier; Lumineau, Fabrice
theories: collective organizational misconduct; diversity theory; self-enforcing interfirm governance
keywords: cartels; diversity theory; longevity of cartels; organizational misconduct; power disparity; uncertainty avoidance
research_question: The paper asks how different facets of diversity between firms participating in a cartel influence cartel longevity. It focuses on whether the profile of cartel partners helps explain how collective organizational misconduct is maintained in secret over time.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism links interfirm diversity to the information exchange, coordination, and control needed to sustain secret collective misconduct. Variety of age-based experience gives cartel members different pools of knowledge and experience that can help organize concealed activity. Separation in uncertainty avoidance makes coordination harder because partners differ in tolerance for risk and formalization, while power disparity can create a leader capable of enforcing the agreement, limiting opportunism, and stabilizing the group.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends organizational misconduct research by shifting attention from individual or intraorganizational wrongdoing to coordinated misconduct among independent firms. It also refines diversity theory by showing that distinct dimensions of diversity can have different effects in the same empirical setting: age-based variety and power disparity increase cartel longevity, while separation in uncertainty avoidance decreases it.
practical_implication: The paper implies that antitrust authorities and other stakeholders should pay attention not only to whether firms collude, but also to the composition of the colluding group. Understanding which diversity profiles make secret collective misconduct more sustainable may help stakeholders identify cartels that are especially likely to persist.
limitations: The authors identify endogeneity and selection issues as the main limitations. The sample includes only detected cartels prosecuted by European antitrust authorities, so it excludes cartels that escaped detection and cartels that dissolved without being caught.
future_research: Future research could test the framework in other forms of collective misconduct, such as mafias or drug cartels. The authors also encourage research on internal managerial diversity within firms involved in collective misconduct and on multilevel diversity across individual, firm, and network levels.
abstract: Despite the importance of organizational misconduct, still not much is known about coordinated misconduct between firms. In this study, we seek a better understanding of how the profile of the partners involved in cartels affects the longevity of their joint misconduct activities. Drawing upon diversity theory, we leverage a distinction between three types of diversity—variety of age-based experience, separation in uncertainty avoidance, and power disparity—in collective organizational misconduct between firms, and study their respective influence on the longevity of cartels. Our empirical analysis gives support to our main arguments: the longevity of cartels tends to be increased by the level of variety of age-based experience and power disparity between partners but reduced by their level of separation in uncertainty avoidance. Implications for the literature on organizational misconduct are discussed.
apa_citation: Bertrand, O., & Lumineau, F. (2016). Partners in crime: The effects of diversity on the longevity of cartels. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(3), 983-1008. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1209

title: The Digital Workforce and the Workplace of the Future
methods: Editorial agenda-setting essay that synthesizes prior research and examples to identify how digital technologies and digitally fluent workers may reshape competencies, identity, communication, work design, and virtual collaboration.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Colbert, Amy; Yee, Nick; George, Gerard
theories: digital fluency; identity development; motivation theory; technology-mediated communication
keywords: digital fluency; digital natives; digital workforce; gamification; technology usage; virtual collaboration; work redesign
research_question: The editorial asks how the increasing prevalence of technology and the entrance of digital natives into the workforce may change how people approach work, relate to others, and collaborate in organizations. It also asks how jobs and organizations might be redesigned to leverage digital workforce competencies while limiting the downsides of constant connectivity and technologically mediated interaction.
mechanism_summary:
- Core phenomenon: The emergence of a digital workforce whose members develop digital fluency, technology-mediated communication habits, and experience with online games, virtual worlds, and social media.
- Potential benefits: Digital fluency, virtual collaboration skills, comfort with technology-based instruction, risk taking through trial-and-error learning, and familiarity with gamified motivation systems.
- Potential risks: Reduced self-awareness, weaker face-to-face interaction, lower empathy, overload from email and communication technologies, blurred work-nonwork boundaries, and constant connectivity.
- Work-redesign agenda: Organizations can redesign jobs, communication norms, meeting practices, technology policies, gamification systems, and virtual collaboration tools to use technology more mindfully and effectively.

The process argument is that technology changes both worker competencies and the conditions under which work is coordinated. Digital fluency and online-world experience can help organizations train, collaborate, innovate, and motivate, but the same technologies can fragment attention, weaken relational quality, and extend work into nonwork time. The editorial therefore frames future work design as a balancing problem: organizations need to leverage digital capabilities while creating norms and systems that preserve focused work, recovery, face-to-face connection, and effective collaboration.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes by setting a research agenda on the digital workforce as an emerging management topic, linking individual-level technology experiences to organizational-level work design and collaboration challenges. It highlights digital fluency, online identity development, technology-mediated communication, gamification, mindful technology use, and immersive virtual collaboration as areas where management scholars can develop stronger theory. The article also extends prior AMJ editorials on digital platforms, information and attention, and design by focusing on the individual worker and the future workplace.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat digital technology only as an efficiency tool; they also need to manage its effects on motivation, communication, attention, recovery, identity, and collaboration. Organizations may benefit from technology-based training, virtual collaboration tools, gamified work systems, and social media competencies, but they should also experiment with technology-free meetings, reduced reliance on email, smartphone-free recovery periods, and locally negotiated communication norms. The practical implication is to design work so that technology serves organizational goals rather than creating automatic expectations of constant connectivity.
limitations: The editorial is agenda-setting rather than empirical, so it does not test its claims or provide a single bounded sample, design, or causal estimate. It relies on examples and prior studies from multiple domains, including technology use, gaming, empathy, email overload, work-nonwork boundaries, and virtual teams. The authors also note that digital natives are only beginning to enter the workforce and that technology itself is constantly shifting, so the implications for work remain incomplete and provisional.
future_research: Future research should examine how digital fluency influences job performance, career progression, conflict, and collaboration across occupations and age-diverse groups. Scholars should study how technology use shapes identity development, authenticity, empathy, communication styles, relationship quality, work-family conflict, recovery, and mindful usage norms. The editorial also calls for research on gamification, immersive virtual collaboration, virtual reality, avatars, and other technological advances that may reshape how teams coordinate and experience presence.

title: The Behavioral Theory of the (Governed) Firm: Corporate Board Influences on Organizations’ Responses to Performance Shortfalls
methods: Longitudinal panel study of for-profit hospitals in California from 2005 to 2011. The paper models annual service line divestitures with conditional fixed-effects poisson regression and robust standard errors.
industry: For-profit hospitals.
units: Hospital-year observations.
n_sample: 607 hospital-year observations.
authors: Desai, Vinit M.
theories: Behavioral Theory of the Firm; corporate governance and board influence; performance feedback theory
keywords: Behavioral Theory of the Firm; corporate boards; corporate governance; organizational change; performance feedback
research_question: The paper asks what board characteristics moderate the relationship between performance feedback and organizational change, and through what processes those moderating influences occur. It focuses on whether board size, board turnover, and board equity ownership shape how organizations respond when performance falls below aspiration levels.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that performance shortfalls increase both managerial search for change and board monitoring, advising, and resource-provision influence. Boards with divergent interests can force compromises, provide conflicting advice, compel reconsideration, or withhold resources, limiting the extent of organizational change. The results support moderation by board size and board equity ownership, but not by board turnover.
theoretical_contribution: The paper connects the Behavioral Theory of the Firm with corporate governance research by showing that responses to performance feedback may depend on interactions between managerial and board coalitions rather than a single dominant coalition. It contributes to performance feedback theory by offering board structure as a reason why the direct relationship between poor performance and change can appear mixed or non-significant. It also contributes to board research by showing how boards may limit, rather than promote, aggressive change during performance shortfalls.
practical_implication: For managers and directors, the paper implies that governance structure can materially shape whether performance shortfalls lead to major organizational change. Larger boards or boards with higher equity ownership may require managers to negotiate more extensively over proposed changes, which can reduce or reverse the usual momentum toward problemistic search and change.
limitations: The paper notes that hospital boards may be more involved in operational decisions than boards in many other contexts, so board characteristics may have stronger effects in this setting. The healthcare industry is also highly institutionalized, which may constrain service line divestitures differently from change in other industries. The study cannot directly observe board decision making, so it infers governance processes from archival panel data.
future_research: Future research could replicate the theory in other settings where boards influence different forms of strategic or operational change. Studies could directly observe governance practices to clarify how directors and managers negotiate specific change proposals under performance shortfalls. Further work could distinguish among alternative mechanisms that explain why high board size or equity ownership reverses, rather than only weakens, the expected performance feedback effect.
abstract:
The Behavioral Theory of the Firm provides a well-evidenced perspective on organizational decision making that has influenced a wide array of literatures, including the

title: How Open System Intermediaries Address Institutional Failures: The Case of Business Incubators in Emerging-Market Countries
methods: Mixed-method empirical study combining semi-structured interviews with incubators and incubatees in multiple emerging markets, a World Bank infoDev survey dataset of incubators, confirmatory factor analysis to construct MID and BCD measures, and Tobit regressions with robustness checks using OLS and generalized linear models.
industry: Business incubators and entrepreneurial support services in emerging-market countries.
country: 68 emerging-market countries across Asia-Pacific, Eastern and Central Europe, Middle East, sub-Saharan and North Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean.
time_period: infoDev data gathered from 2008 through 2010, with collection reported as starting in 2006; market-development covariates from 2004-2006.
units: Business incubators, with country-level commercial institution measures and sponsor-type classifications.
n_sample: 133 incubators in 68 countries.
authors: Dutt, N.; Hawn, O.; Vidal, E.; Chatterji, A.; McGahan, A.; Mitchell, W.
theories: institutional entrepreneurship; institutional theory; institutional voids literature; sponsorship literature
keywords: business capability development; business incubators; emerging-market countries; institutional failures; market infrastructure development; open system intermediaries
research_question: How do open system intermediaries remedy institutional failures in emerging-market countries, and how do country-level commercial institutions and incubator sponsors shape their relative emphasis on market infrastructure development versus business capability development? The empirical setting is business incubators in emerging markets.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that open system intermediaries respond to institutional voids by balancing services that build broader market infrastructure with services that develop specific firms. When commercial institutions are weaker, incubators have stronger reasons to provide MID services that make entrepreneurship feasible; when institutions are more developed, incubators can place relatively more emphasis on BCD services because client firms have a better chance of succeeding. Sponsor identity shapes this service mix because private, academic, government, and NGO sponsors carry different motivations, skills, and resource endowments.
theoretical_contribution: The paper clarifies the concepts of institutional intermediaries, open system intermediaries, and the distinction between MID and BCD services. It extends institutional entrepreneurship and institutional voids research by showing how business incubators can create benefits beyond focal clients in emerging-market settings. It also contributes to sponsorship research by theorizing how sponsor motivations and skills affect the kinds of institutional-intermediation services incubators provide.
practical_implication: Policy makers and development actors should not treat incubators as interchangeable start-up support organizations. Incubators in weaker institutional environments may need to devote substantial effort to market infrastructure, while those in stronger environments can put more weight on firm-level capabilities. The findings also imply that sponsor diversity matters: private, academic, NGO, and government sponsors tend to bring different service emphases to the entrepreneurial ecosystem.
limitations: The authors caution that the World Bank infoDev survey may underreport incubators in some nations or overrepresent incubators connected to the World Bank. The analysis varies across rather than within nations and focuses on service-mix ratios rather than direct market or firm outcomes. The data also provide a snapshot of incubators and their services rather than longitudinal evidence on how service mixes evolve over time.
future_research: Future research could examine the nature and impact of MID and BCD services, including industry-wide MID services such as educational investment and contract enforcement legislation. The authors call for direct comparisons between OSIs and closed system intermediaries, studies of how incubator functions become embedded in markets, and longitudinal work on how BCD and MID services co-evolve. They also suggest investigating how legacy institutions such as political ties, organized crime, family ties, corruption, or religious norms impede entrepreneurial organizations after initial institutional advances.
abstract: In emerging-market countries, commercial institutions do not always develop sufficiently quickly or effectively to support ambitious entrepreneurs. How might intermediaries remedy these problems? We address this question by drawing on institutional literatures to develop the concept of “open system intermediaries.” Our research design involves examining business incubators in emerging markets as a form of open system intermediary. Empirically, we examine the relative emphasis that business incubators in emerging-market countries place on developing markets versus developing specific businesses. The study further examines how private, government, academic, and nongovernmental organization sponsorship of incubators influences the mix of services that incubators provide. In sum, this work contributes to our understanding of how, why, and when intermediaries emerge to address institutional failures.

title: Temporal Institutional Work
methods: Inductive qualitative case study of an institutional project to establish a foundation-based university and pace wider university reform, using interviews, archival reports, policy documents, speeches, pamphlets, and media coverage with iterative coding and Gioia-style abstraction.
industry: Higher education and university-sector reform.
time_period: The focal institutional project ran from September 2005 to August 2009; interviews took place from March 2008 to March 2010 with supplementary interviews in autumn 2013, and archival materials covered earlier reform attempts and policy processes.
units: Key stakeholders in the Innovation University project and university reform, including university leaders and staff, government officials, politicians, industry representatives, labor unions, students, reports, policy documents, speeches, and news stories.
n_sample: 44 interviews, three supplementary interviews, 74 reports and memos, 18 speeches and pamphlets, 10 legislative and policy documents, and 641 news stories.
authors: Granqvist, N.; Gustafsson, R.
theories: entrainment; institutional work; temporality in institutions; timing norms
keywords: constructing urgency; enacting momentum; entraining; institutional change; temporal institutional work; temporality; timing norms
research_question: How do actors engage in temporal institutional work during institutional change? The paper asks how actors construct, navigate, and capitalize on timing norms, and how those activities shape shared temporal beliefs that affect the unfolding of a wider institutional reform.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Temporal institutional work, timing norms, entrainment, constructed urgency, enacted momentum, windows of opportunity, synchronicity, irreversibility, and the tension between top-down timing norms and bottom-up issue construction.
- Process / phases: Actors first constructed urgency and entrained the Innovation University proposal with openings in wider reform, producing a perceived window of opportunity. They then enacted momentum and entrained the project with democratic and reform schedules, creating synchronicity between the project and university reform. In parallel, they used speed, prioritization, symbolic progress, and selective participation to create a perception of irreversibility.
- Practices: Articulating crisis, constructing societal transition, synchronizing the project with wider reform, responding to alternatives, articulating temporary power positions, projecting a radical vision, pacing movement, signaling progress, and preempting resistance through speed and exclusivity.
- Emergent outcomes: Shared temporal beliefs of window of opportunity, synchronicity, and irreversibility that helped the institutional project pace and stabilize wider university reform.
- Boundary conditions: The case concerns a nested political-institutional setting with a foundation-based university project tightly coupled to national university-sector reform.

The process is temporal and interpretive rather than a simple causal-variable model. Actors did not merely adapt to external schedules; they framed some timing norms as openings, used project pacing to modify wider reform rhythms, and transformed a future possibility into a current belief that change was already unavoidable. These temporal beliefs then organized participation, resistance, and the pace of institutional change.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops temporal institutional work as a perspective for explaining how temporality enters institutional work and institutional change. It identifies entraining, constructing urgency, and enacting momentum as forms of work through which actors produce shared temporal beliefs. It also reconceptualizes windows of opportunity, synchronicity, and irreversibility as socio-temporal constructs rather than external givens.
practical_implication: For actors trying to advance institutional change, timing is not only a constraint but also a resource that can be framed, paced, and made meaningful. The case shows that aligning a change project with political schedules, visible milestones, and stakeholder perceptions of urgency can accelerate reform, but it also shows that speed and exclusivity can preempt opposition and narrow participation.
limitations: The paper is based on one extreme case of unexpectedly rapid university-sector reform in a Northern-European political-institutional setting. Its process model is grounded in qualitative retrospective interviews, archival documents, and media evidence rather than comparative cases. The study does not fully elaborate how changing paces and rhythms disrupt existing activity patterns, which timing norms become dominant zeitgebers, or whether desynchronization is required for all institutional change.
future_research: Future research could examine temporal maintenance work in stable and turbulent institutional contexts. The authors call for studies of how synchronicity, asynchronicity, and desynchronization affect institutional change; how institutionalization unfolds as a flow of temporary projects; and how temporality acts as a carrier of institutional logics and a source of institutional complexity.
abstract: Time is inherently present in empirical research on institutional change—most studies sequence actions and events across stages of development, over time. Yet research has overlooked how temporality, as a negotiated organizing of time, shapes institutional processes, despite the fact that timing, duration, and tenor of relationships are their foundational elements. To unpack the role of temporality in institutions, we examine how actors engage in temporal institutional work—that is, how they construct, navigate, and capitalize on timing norms in their attempts to change institutions. We draw on an inductive study of an institutional project to establish a novel foundation-based university that subsequently came to pace major statewide university reform. We identify three forms of temporal institutional work: entraining—as a top-down, routinized, reproductive form—and constructing urgency, and enacting momentum—both as bottom-up, issuedriven and generative forms. We show that by engaging in these types of work, actors produce windows of opportunity, synchronicity, and irreversibility as shared beliefs of temporality. These beliefs, in turn, shape how the wider institutional change unfolds. Our study shows that temporal institutional work enables institutional change. We discuss the implications for reconceptualizing institutional research from a temporal perspective.

title: A Two-Phase Longitudinal Model of a Turnover Event: Disruption, Recovery Rates, and Moderators of Collective Performance
methods: Longitudinal quantitative study of bank branches using monthly branch sales data, employee survey measures of interdependence, personnel records of turnover events, and discontinuous random coefficient growth models estimated with SAS Proc Mixed and REML.
industry: Branch banking.
time_period: February 2010 to January 2011.
units: Bank branches with employees and managers nested within branches.
n_sample: 3,113 employees and 524 managers nested within 524 branches.
authors: Hale, Donald Jr.; Ployhart, Robert E.; Shepherd, William
theories: collective turnover theory; context-emergent turnover theory; team adaptability theory
keywords: branch-level performance; collective turnover; discontinuous random coefficient growth models; group adaptability; interdependence; turnover event
research_question: The paper asks how an individual turnover event affects collective performance over time, how long those consequences last, and why disruption and recovery rates differ. It specifically examines whether the position of the leaver and branch-level interdependence shape immediate disruption and subsequent recovery in branch sales performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a two-phase adaptation process linking individual exits to collective outcomes. In Phase 1, turnover disrupts branch routines, coordination, relationships, and role coverage, producing an immediate drop in sales performance. In Phase 2, remaining members adapt by reconfiguring routines, socializing replacements, and absorbing work, allowing recovery after employee turnover but not statistically significant recovery after manager turnover within the 12-month window. Interdependence slows recovery after employee turnover because more coordinated branch systems are harder to reconfigure after membership change.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends collective turnover research by shifting attention from aggregate turnover rates to discrete turnover events and their temporal consequences. It integrates context-emergent turnover theory with team adaptability theory to specify disruption and recovery as distinct phases with potentially different moderators. It also advances positional-distribution theorizing by showing that manager and employee turnover are not redundant and can have multiplicative consequences for collective performance.
practical_implication: Managers should treat turnover costs as dynamic rather than one-time losses, because branch performance can remain depressed for months after a turnover event. The findings imply that manager exits require especially swift higher-level intervention and that employee turnover is more damaging when paired with manager turnover. Branches with high interdependence may need cross-training and proactive coordination support to shorten the recovery period after employee turnover.
limitations: The authors note that the branch banking setting may have lower interdependence than more tightly coupled teams, so generalizability to other workflows requires caution. Interdependence was measured broadly and only once, limiting causal inference about changes in interdependence over time. The 12-month monthly data window obscures intra-month dynamics and cannot show longer-term consequences after sales goals reset.
future_research: Future research should test the two-phase model in settings with higher and lower interdependence, other occupations, and different cultural, organizational, and industry contexts. Studies should use repeated measures of interdependence and other collective states, finer-grained time windows, and longer performance windows. The authors also call for work on leaver and replacement quality, turnover functionality, alternative longitudinal models, and the net financial impact of turnover events.
abstract: Blending theory on collective turnover and group adaptability, this paper develops a two-phase longitudinal model that explains how and why an individual-level turnover event has effects on collective performance. Phase 1 (disruption) is marked by a sudden and negative change in unit-level performance, while Phase 2 (recovery) entails a gradual increase in unit performance over time. We further propose that the positional distribution (manager or employee) of the turnover event and the amount of interdependence within the collective will influence the consequences of a turnover event. Using a sample of 524 branches of a U.S. bank, the results largely support the hypotheses as a turnover event leads to an immediate and negative change in branch-level performance. Notably, there is an interaction between manager and employee turnover events that significantly decreases performance. In the recovery period, branches recover more quickly after losing an employee than they do after losing a manager. However, the moderating effect of branch-level interdependence depends on the position, and there is no statistically significant recovery from a manager turnover event within our performance window. These results highlight the insights of our two-phase model and the need to study collective turnover dynamics over time and across different positions.

title: Spilling Outside the Box: The Effects of Individuals’ Creative Behaviors at Work on Time Spent with their Spouses at Home
methods: Daily diary field study using worker-spouse dyads. Employees completed entry, afternoon, and evening surveys; spouses completed nightly paper surveys. The analysis uses hierarchical linear modeling with person-mean-centered daily predictors to test how variance-focused creative behaviors and idea validation predict same-evening time with spouse and spouse negative affect, with openness to experience as a cross-level moderator.
industry: Working adults from over 20 industries, including finance, construction, government, education, healthcare, transportation, business and financial operations, sales, management, and engineering.
time_period: A two-week workday diary study.
units: Worker-spouse dyad-days.
n_sample: 685 fully matched days from 108 worker-spouse pairings.
authors: Harrison, S. H.; Wagner, D. T.
theories: creativity theory; resource allocation theory; work-family conflict theory
keywords: creative behaviors; idea validation; openness to experience; resource allocation theory; time spent with spouse; work-family conflict
research_question: How do employees' daily creative behaviors at work affect the time they spend with their spouses at home and their spouses' evening affect? The paper asks whether variance-focused creative behaviors and selection-focused idea validation have distinct downstream consequences for home relationships.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that variance-focused creative behaviors absorb cognitive resources and can keep employees mentally engaged with work after they leave the workplace, reducing time allocated to spouses at home. Idea validation narrows possibilities and helps employees leave work cognitively bounded, making more resources available for spousal interaction and support. Openness to experience strengthens the time-allocation effects because highly open employees are especially engaged by variance-focused work and especially able to benefit from idea validation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts creativity research from treating creative ideas as the endpoint to examining the relational aftereffects of creative behaviors. It distinguishes variance-focused and selection-focused creative behaviors, showing that they can have opposite consequences for home relationships. It also extends work-family conflict and resource allocation theory by showing that desirable work behaviors can create or conserve resources that spill into the home domain.
practical_implication: Organizations and managers should consider the relational costs of creative work rather than assuming creativity is uniformly beneficial. Workers may benefit from ending the workday with idea validation or feedback-seeking practices that delimit open-ended creative work before going home. The findings also suggest that job design and creative-process norms should help employees manage transitions between intensive creative work and home life.
limitations: The study does not directly measure the cognitive resources that are central to its theoretical mechanism, so resource depletion and availability are inferred from behavior and moderation patterns. The results may not generalize to all forms of highly engaging work, all occupations, or all spouse characteristics because the study focuses on creative behaviors in a Singapore worker-spouse sample. The design also does not observe the quality of feedback during idea validation or the qualitative nature of time spent with spouses.
future_research: Future research could directly measure cognitive mediators and test whether similar patterns occur in other forms of highly engaging work. Studies could examine spouse attributes, spouse employment status, and whether spouses join or interrupt employees' continuing creative thought processes. Qualitative or observational work could also clarify what employees and spouses actually do during additional time together after idea validation.
abstract: Most research on creativity describes it as a net positive: producing new products for the organization and satisfaction and positive affect for creative workers. However, a host of anecdotal and historical evidence suggests that creative work can have deleterious consequences for relationships. This raises the question: how does creativity at work impact relationships at home? Relying on work–family conflict and resource allocation theory as conceptual frameworks, we test a model of creative behaviors during the day at work and the extent to which employees spend time with their spouses at home in the evening, using 685 daily matched responses from 108 worker–spouse pairings. Our results reveal that variance-focused creative behaviors (problem identification, information searching, idea generation) predict less time spent with a spouse at home. In contrast, selection-focused creative behaviors (idea validation) predict more time spent with a spouse. Further, openness to experience moderates these relationships. Overall, the results raise questions about the possible relational costs of creative behaviors at work on life at home.

title: Relational Changes During Role Transitions: The Interplay of Efficiency and Cohesion
methods: Longitudinal ego-network survey study of recently promoted service professionals in three professional service firms, using two-way clustered logit regression for tie loss and ordinary least squares estimates for trust in gained ties.
industry: Professional service firms: consultancy, audit company, and law firm.
time_period: Two survey waves roughly 1.5 years apart after promotion.
units: Respondent-contact ties and gained contacts.
n_sample: 1,084 contacts under risk of tie loss from 68 respondents; 499 gained contacts from 67 respondents.
authors: Jonczyk, Claudia D.; Lee, Yonghoon G.; Galunic, Charles D.; Bensaou, Ben M.
theories: network embeddedness; social capital; social embeddedness; structural holes
keywords: cohesion; efficiency; professional service firms; role transitions; social embeddedness; tie gain; tie loss; trust
research_question: The paper asks how recently promoted service professionals reconfigure workplace relationships during role transitions. It examines which node, relational, and structural features predict tie loss, and whether prior network structure shapes the cognitive and emotional trust of newly gained ties.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cross-level network process in which role transitions activate both efficiency and cohesion pressures. Efficiency appears in the retention of high-ranking and multiplex contacts, the substitution of redundant ties when competent alternatives exist, and the formation of cognitively trusted new ties from prior non-redundant networks. Cohesion appears in the retention of emotionally trusted and embedded ties, especially where third-party closure strengthens the relationship. The findings therefore frame relational change during promotion as an embedded compromise rather than a simple shift toward either instrumental efficiency or relational loyalty.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to social embeddedness and social capital research by showing that efficiency and cohesion operate together across node, dyadic, and structural levels during role transitions. It extends network dynamics research by examining both tie loss and tie gain in organizational promotion contexts rather than treating networks as static career resources. It also clarifies that prior network structure acts as a "shadow of the past" by shaping the cognitive trustworthiness of newly gained contacts.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that professionals who overemphasize cohesion may sacrifice efficiency, while those who ignore embedded ties may face social sanctions or performance costs. HR professionals can support role transitions by helping employees build multiplex and embedded ties when continuity is valuable, or by creating tools and events that help employees discover better-fitting alternative relations when rapid adaptation is needed.
limitations: The authors note that ego-network data may contain inaccuracies in assessments of second-order ties and that full network data would be preferable. The respondent sample is relatively small, even though the number of tie-level observations is adequate for the statistical analyses. They also could not systematically measure changing task requirements, prove agency for each tie loss or gain, or account for personality differences such as self-monitoring.
future_research: Future research could use full network designs to better assess second-order ties, homophily, and network-level structure during role transitions. Studies could collect larger longitudinal samples and more directly measure how changing task requirements affect tie loss and tie gain. The authors also call for designs that establish agency more clearly and incorporate personality differences in the propensity to change networks.
abstract: This study looks at what happens to the collection of relationships (network) of service professionals during a role transition (promotion to a management role). Our setting is three professional service firms, where we examine changes in relations of recently promoted service professionals (auditors, consultants, and lawyers). We take a comprehensive look at the drivers of two forms of network changes: tie loss and tie gain. Looking backward, we examine the characteristics of the contact, the relationship, and social structure and identify which forces are at play in losing ties, revealing an overarching tendency for both cohesion and efficiency forces to play a role. Looking forward, we identify the effect of previous network structures that act as a “shadow of the past” and impact the quality of newly gained relations during the role transitions. Findings demonstrate that role transitions are not only influenced by a few key contacts but that the entire (extant) network of professional relationships shapes the way people reconfigure their workplace relations during a role transition.

title: Delaying Change: Examining How Industry and Managerial Turbulence Impact Structural Realignment
methods: Longitudinal archival quantitative study of firms in the U.S. medical marketplace, using quasi maximum likelihood fixed-effects Poisson models with lagged predictors and robustness checks to estimate structural recombination counts.
industry: Medical device and pharmaceutical sectors.
units: Firm-period observations.
n_sample: 171 firm-period observations from 46 firms.
authors: Karim, Samina; Carroll, Timothy N.; Long, Chris P.
theories: contingency theory; decision avoidance and delay; group dynamics; organization design
keywords: contingency theory; decision avoidance; industry growth; industry turbulence; managerial turbulence; structural realignment; structural recombination; top management team
research_question: The paper asks how and when firms align their structures with environmental changes. It examines when firms initiate structural realignment through business unit recombination under industry growth, industry turbulence, declining turbulence, and managerial turbulence in the top management team.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism combines contingency theory with decision avoidance and group dynamics. Industry growth signals opportunities and encourages recombination, but industry turbulence makes cause-and-effect relationships harder to assess, leading decision makers to delay structural realignment. Declining turbulence makes recombination more likely because managers can process information and evaluate structural changes more effectively. Growth in TMT size also reduces recombination because a changing executive team has more difficulty reaching consensus around organizational design choices.
theoretical_contribution: The paper refines contingency theory by showing that environmental change does not automatically prompt structural realignment; turbulent conditions can delay action even when realignment might be expected. It contributes to organization design research by explaining when firms recombine business units, not only how recombination changes structure. It also links external industry turbulence and internal managerial turbulence as parallel constraints on decision makers' capacity to pursue structural change.
practical_implication: Executives should recognize that turbulent industry conditions may make structural realignment harder to evaluate, not simply more urgent. The findings suggest that firms may need to judge when turbulence has declined enough to make recombination decisions more tractable. Firms should also avoid abrupt changes in top management team size when structural redesign decisions require information processing and consensus.
limitations: The authors do not examine the performance implications of structural realignment through recombination. The sample is limited to 46 firms in pharmaceutical and medical device sectors because the study required detailed mapping of structural change over a 20-year period. Other sectors may show different patterns of organizational response to turbulence.
future_research: Future research could examine whether firms that pursue recombination under difficult environmental conditions perform better or worse than firms that delay. The authors also call for research on the capabilities that make unit recombination successful and on how top management team composition and executive histories shape consensus around structural change. Additional studies in other sectors would help assess the generalizability of the findings.
abstract: This paper examines when firms pursue structural realignment through business unit reconfiguration, specifically by recombining business units. Our results refine and extend contingency theory and studies of organization design by drawing on theories of decision avoidance and delay to describe environmental conditions when firms pursue or postpone structural realignment. Our empirical analysis of 46 firms from 1978 to 1997, operating within the U.S. medical device and pharmaceutical sectors, demonstrates that while decision makers initiate structural recombination during periods of industry growth (i.e., munificence), they reduce their recombination efforts during periods of industry turbulence (i.e., dynamism), and managerial turbulence (i.e., growth in top management team size). We also find evidence that firms delay realignment and bide their time for better environmental conditions of declining turbulence and industry growth before pursuing more structural realignment. Together, these findings suggest that decision makers often delay initiating structural recombination until they can effectively process information and assess how structural changes will help them realign the organization to the environment.

title: Turning their Pain to Gain: Charismatic Leader Influence on Follower Stress Appraisal and Job Performance
methods: Two quantitative field studies of U.S. Marines using survey and supervisor-rated task performance data; Study 1 used hierarchical linear modeling, and Study 2 used multilevel structural equation modeling to test dual-stage moderated mediation.
industry: Military / U.S. Marine Corps
time_period: Study 1 collected performance ratings approximately three months after the initial survey; Study 2 used an approximately three-week lag. Calendar collection dates are not reported in paper.
units: Enlisted U.S. Marines and unit leaders
n_sample: Study 1 analyzed 74 Marines with performance ratings from 33 unit leaders; Study 2 analyzed 270 enlisted Marines and 92 unit leaders.
authors: LePine, Marcie A.; Zhang, Yiwen; Crawford, Eean R.; Rich, Bruce Louis
theories: challenge-hindrance stressor framework; charismatic leadership theory; conservation of resources theory; transactional theory of stress
keywords: challenge appraisals; challenge stressors; charismatic leader behaviors; hindrance appraisals; hindrance stressors; task performance; transactional theory of stress
research_question: The paper asks whether and how unit-level charismatic leader behaviors alter followers' stress appraisal and reaction processes, thereby changing the effects of challenge and hindrance stressors on task performance. It focuses on whether charismatic leaders amplify the positive performance pathway from challenge stressors through challenge appraisals and buffer the negative pathway from hindrance appraisals to performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a dual-stage moderated mediation model. Transactional stress theory implies that demands affect performance through primary appraisals, and the challenge-hindrance framework distinguishes demands with potential for growth from demands that obstruct growth. Charismatic leaders are theorized to manage meaning, optimism, efficacy, and emotional resources so that followers appraise challenge stressors as more challenging and respond more productively to challenge and hindrance appraisals. The evidence supported stronger challenge stressor-to-appraisal and appraisal-to-performance pathways under more charismatic leadership, while charismatic leadership buffered the negative performance implications of hindrance appraisals without reducing hindrance appraisals themselves.
theoretical_contribution: The study embeds the stress process in a multilevel leadership context by showing that unit-level leader behavior can shape how individual followers appraise and respond to stressful demands. It extends the challenge-hindrance stressor framework by separating stressors from appraisals and testing cognitive appraisals as mediating mechanisms rather than assuming that demand categories automatically produce their expected meanings. It also contributes to charismatic leadership theory by identifying stress appraisal and stress-response processes as channels through which charismatic leaders affect follower task performance.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat stress management only as an HR, counseling, or employee assistance responsibility. The findings suggest that charismatic leadership behaviors, including role modeling, frame alignment, vision articulation, optimism, and displaying conviction, can help employees convert challenge stressors into stronger performance and reduce the performance damage associated with hindrance appraisals. Organizations may therefore incorporate charismatic behaviors into leader development, promotion criteria, team design, and stress-management practice.
limitations: The studies measured stressors and appraisals cross-sectionally, so the proposed causal direction from stressors to appraisals remains theory-based rather than experimentally established. Alternative explanations may exist, including individual characteristics such as cognitive ability or core self-evaluation, and the model did not include all potentially relevant contextual factors such as support, justice, or other leadership styles. The setting was the U.S. Marine Corps, so external validity to business organizations, higher organizational levels, and less structured settings requires further evidence.
future_research: Future research should use experimental, longitudinal, or experience-sampling designs to test the causal nature of the stressor-appraisal relationship and capture how appraisals shift across the workday. Scholars should examine cross-links between challenge stressors and hindrance appraisals, individual and group contingencies such as political skill, and contextual factors such as support, justice, transformational leadership, and transactional leadership. Additional research should test the model in business settings and compare whether charismatic leaders at different organizational levels use different behaviors or have different discretion over challenge and hindrance stressors.
abstract: We develop and test a theoretical model that explores how individuals appraise different types of stressful job demands and how these cognitive appraisals impact job performance. The model also explores how charismatic leaders influence such appraisal and reaction processes, and, by virtue of these effects, how leaders can influence the impact of stressful demands on their followers’ job performance. In Study 1 (n 5 74 U.S. Marines), our model was largely supported in hierarchical linear modeling analyses. Marines whose leaders were judged by superiors to exhibit charismatic leader behaviors appraised challenge stressors as being more challenging, and were more likely to respond to this appraisal with higher performance. Although charismatic leader behaviors did not influence how hindrance stressors were appraised, they negated the strong negative effect of hindrance appraisals on job performance. In Study 2 (n 5 270 U.S. Marines), charismatic leader behaviors were measured through the eyes of the focal Marines, and the interactions found in Study 1 were replicated. Results from multilevel structural equation modeling analyses also indicate that charismatic leader behaviors moderate both the mediating role of challenge appraisals in transmitting the effect of challenge stressors to job performance and the mediating role of hindrance appraisals in transmitting the effect of hindrance stressors to job performance. Implications of our results to theory and practice are discussed.
apa_citation: LePine, M. A., Zhang, Y., Crawford, E. R., & Rich, B. L. (2016). Turning their pain to gain: Charismatic leader influence on follower stress appraisal and job performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(3), 1036-1059. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0778

title: Venture Capital Ownership as a Contingent Resource: How Owner–Firm Fit Influences IPO Outcomes
methods: Longitudinal quantitative study of U.S. private firms attempting IPOs, using probit and OLS two-stage Heckman models to test how VC owner-firm fit predicts successful exit and 90-day post-IPO stock performance.
industry: U.S. private firms seeking to go public.
units: Private firms attempting IPOs, VC-backed private firms, and owner-firm dyads.
n_sample: 1,953 private firms attempted IPOs; 1,194 VC-backed firms and 11,955 unique owner-firm dyads were analyzed for VC fit.
authors: Lungeanu, Razvan; Zajac, Edward J.
theories: demands-abilities fit; expertise-based perspective; owners as contingent resources; resource dependence perspective
keywords: IPO outcomes; contingent resource; owner expertise; owner-firm fit; strategic needs; venture capital ownership
research_question: The paper asks whether, when, and how corporate owners affect firm performance through expertise rather than only through agency alignment, monitoring, or power. In the venture capital context, it examines whether fit between VC owners' evolving expertise and private firms' evolving strategic needs improves successful exit and short-term post-IPO performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an owner-as-contingent-resource process. VC owners accumulate expertise from prior investments, but that expertise becomes valuable only when it fits the portfolio firm's stage of development, industry, and time horizon at relevant financing rounds. Fit creates a channel for advice and experience transfer; misfit can lead owners to apply expertise in the wrong context. The results support positive effects of stage fit and time-horizon fit on both successful exit and short-term post-IPO performance, and partial support for industry fit on successful exit.
theoretical_contribution: The paper redirects corporate ownership research from differences in owner type, monitoring incentives, or power toward heterogeneity within a class of owners. It advances a contingency perspective in which ownership expertise is not inherently valuable, but becomes a resource-in-use when matched to firms' changing strategic needs. It also links corporate governance, strategy, and entrepreneurship by showing how the portfolio of investors surrounding a firm can shape venture outcomes.
practical_implication: For entrepreneurs and private firms, the findings imply that choosing VC investors should involve assessing fit between investor experience and the firm's current and future strategic needs, not only investor reputation or capital availability. For VC firms, the results suggest that value creation depends on deploying the right experience in the right portfolio-firm context and at the right stage of the investment relationship.
limitations: The authors note that expertise is captured at the VC firm or partner level and that the transfer process between individual VC partners, syndicate partners, and portfolio-firm executives is not directly observed. The study is also specific to VC owners and private firms attempting to go public, a setting chosen because expertise differences and owner involvement are visible. The authors acknowledge that other owner types and firm contexts may reveal additional dimensions of ownership expertise.
future_research: Future research should examine fit or misfit between the expertise of VC partners and portfolio-firm top executives, as well as the conditions under which expertise transfer is more or less effective. The authors also call for work on how owner-firm fit affects the type of exit chosen, such as IPO versus M&A, and on whether the contingent-resource perspective extends to other owners and firms beyond venture capital and IPO settings.
abstract: This study seeks to contribute to the literature on corporate ownership and firm performance by advancing an expertise-based perspective that views owners as a contingent resource. Specifically, we propose that heterogeneous prior experiences of corporate owners creates identifiable and evolving differences in owner expertise, and that these differences in expertise, when matched appropriately to firms’ specific and changing strategic needs, will be a source of value over the life cycle of a firm. We draw from the venture capital (VC) context to identify ex ante the meaningful differences in owner expertise, as well as the firmspecific situations in which we believe a fit or misfit would exist between VC owners and these private firms. We test and find support for our predictions regarding the performance benefits of well-matched owners and firms using an extensive longitudinal dataset of the population of U.S. private firms seeking to go public from 1997 to 2004, and their VC owners. We discuss the implications of our approach as they relate to future research opportunities across the corporate governance, strategy, and entrepreneurship literatures.
