title: How Does Leader Humility Influence Team Performance? Exploring the Mechanisms of Contagion and Collective Promotion Focus
methods: Three-study empirical design: a laboratory experiment manipulating leader humility in 31 undergraduate business student teams, a longitudinal CarCorp team simulation with 53 undergraduate business student teams, and a multistage field study of 77 health services work teams. The analyses use confirmatory factor analysis, SEM path analysis, and bootstrapped regression-based indirect-effects models.
industry: Laboratory business student teams, auto-manufacturing simulation teams, and health services work teams.
country: United States, with field-company offices and clientele in the United States, Puerto Rico, and Great Britain.
time_period: Study 1 laboratory session, Study 2 ten-week simulation, and Study 3 two survey waves approximately one month apart.
units: Teams.
n_sample: 607 subjects organized into 161 teams: 31 Study 1 teams, 53 Study 2 teams, and 77 Study 3 teams.
authors: Owens, B. P.; Hekman, D. R.
theories: regulatory focus theory; self-experience framework; social contagion
keywords: collective humility; collective promotion focus; leader humility; social contagion; team performance
research_question: How does leader humility influence team interaction patterns, emergent states, and team performance? The paper asks whether humble leader behavior spreads to followers as collective humility, generates collective promotion focus, and thereby improves team performance.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a two-stage team process. Humble leaders model admitting limits, appreciating others' strengths, and teachability; followers emulate these behaviors, creating collective humility as a shared interpersonal process. Collective humility then creates opportunity, motivation, and ability for a collective promotion focus. Study 1 tests this contagion path to collective humility and collective promotion focus, while Studies 2 and 3 test whether that emergent state links collective humility to team performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends leadership research by specifying how a nontraditional, character-based leadership construct affects team performance through imitable leader behavior. It introduces collective humility as a team-level interpersonal process and positions collective promotion focus as the motivational emergent state linking humble team interaction to performance. It also contributes to regulatory focus research by identifying leader humility and collective humility as antecedents of collective promotion focus in both laboratory and field settings.
practical_implication: The findings imply that leaders can influence team performance by modeling behaviors that followers can actually emulate, rather than only articulating values or visions. Teams may benefit when leaders openly acknowledge limits, highlight member strengths, and remain teachable, because these behaviors can normalize constructive interaction and growth-oriented striving. The field-study comparison also suggests that the leader humility pathway is distinct from transformational leadership.
limitations: Collective humility and team collective promotion focus were measured from the same sources at the same time, so their relationship may be inflated by common method variance. The studies were conducted with Western samples, leaving generalizability to Eastern contexts unclear. The authors also note the need to examine boundary conditions across task specialization, hierarchy, humility dispersion, time pressure, task interdependence, and contexts where directive leadership may be more appropriate.
future_research: Future research could replicate the findings with behavioral or extra-team observer measures of collective humility and collective promotion focus. Studies should test the model in Eastern contexts and in team settings with different levels of task specialization, hierarchy, interdependence, and time pressure. The authors also call for work on other antecedents of collective humility and on whether other virtues, such as courage or compassion, spread through similar leader-modeling processes.
abstract: Using data from 607 subjects organized into 161 teams (84 laboratory teams, 77 organizational field teams), we examined how leader humility influences team interaction patterns, emergent states, and team performance. We develop and test a theoretical model, positing that, when leaders behave humbly, followers emulate their humble behaviors, creating a shared interpersonal team process (collective humility). This, in turn, creates a team emergent state focused on progressively striving toward achieving the team’s highest potential (collective promotion focus), which ultimately enhances team performance. We test our model across three studies wherein we manipulate leader humility to test the social contagion hypothesis (Study 1), examine the impact of humility on team processes and performance in a longitudinal team simulation (Study 2), and test the full model in a multistage field study in a health services context (Study 3). Our findings collectively support our theoretical model, demonstrating that leader behavior can spread via social contagion to followers, producing an emergent state that ultimately affects team performance. We contribute to the leadership literature by suggesting the need for leaders to lead by example and showing how a specific set of leader behaviors influence team performance, providing a template for future leadership research on a wide variety of leader behaviors.

title: Micro-Foundations of Firm-Specific Human Capital: When Do Employees Perceive Their Skills to be Firm-Specific?
methods: Empirical quantitative study using two labor-survey data sources: an unbalanced KLIPS panel and a cross-sectional NLSY79 sample. The authors estimate ordered probit models of perceived firm-specific human capital, with robustness checks using ordered logit, generalized ordered logit, random-effects ordered probit, additional controls, fixed-effects OLS checks, and common-method-variance diagnostics.
industry: Cross-industry labor-market samples; industry is controlled using three-digit Korean Standard Industrial Classification codes and three-digit U.S. Census Industrial Classification codes.
time_period: KLIPS 2002-2007 surveys and NLSY79 1994 survey.
units: Employee observations and individual-year observations.
n_sample: KLIPS: 5,419 individuals and 16,580 individual-year observations; NLSY79: 2,438 individuals.
authors: Raffiee, J.; Coff, R.
theories: cognitive psychology; human capital theory; resource-based view; transaction cost economics
keywords: cognitive bias; firm-specific human capital; on-the-job training; organizational commitment; organizational tenure; perceived firm-specificity
research_question: When do employees perceive their skills to be firm-specific? The paper asks whether perceptions of firm-specific human capital follow strategy theory's assumptions about tenure, employer-provided on-the-job training, and organizational commitment, or whether they instead reflect cognitive biases in employee judgment.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that existing strategy theory assumes informational efficiency: employees should recognize when tenure, OJT, and commitment are associated with firm-specific investments. Raffiee and Coff relax that assumption and argue that ex-post assessments may be shaped by cognitive dissonance, choice-supportive bias, recall bias, availability bias, false consensus bias, and projection bias. These biases can lead longer-tenured and more committed employees to perceive their skills as more general and transferable, even if actual firm-specific human capital has accumulated.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a micro-foundational account of firm-specific human capital by distinguishing objective specificity from employees' perceived specificity. It challenges resource-based and human-capital arguments that treat firm-specific skills as observable and similarly understood by employees, firms, and other labor-market actors. It also extends transaction cost economics and strategy research by showing that assumptions about asset specificity may depend on biased and potentially misaligned perceptions.
practical_implication: Managers should not assume that employee tenure, training, or commitment automatically translate into employee awareness of firm-specific skill investments. Because perceived specificity may shape skill investment and turnover decisions, firms may need to manage how employees understand the portability and value of their human capital. The findings also imply that retention and human-capital strategies should account for employee beliefs rather than relying only on objective or managerial assessments of specificity.
limitations: The study does not include an objective measure of firm-specific human capital, so it cannot determine whether employee perceptions are inaccurate or whether common proxies such as tenure and OJT are weak measures of actual specificity. The KLIPS and NLSY79 measures capture the perceived share of skills that are firm-specific rather than the absolute stock of firm-specific human capital. The organizational commitment finding may also be partly affected by survivorship bias, although robustness checks suggest that this is unlikely to be the only mechanism.
future_research: Future research could compare perceived firm-specific human capital with objective measures or experimental manipulations of specificity. Scholars could examine whether perceptions of specificity affect skill acquisition, turnover, internal promotion, and wage outcomes, and whether employees, hiring managers, and firms hold aligned or divergent perceptions. Additional work could also distinguish ex-ante from ex-post perceptions and study how actors strategically shape others' beliefs about the portability of human capital.
abstract: Drawing on human capital theory, strategy scholars have emphasized firm-specific human capital as a source of sustained competitive advantage. In this study, we begin to unpack the micro-foundations of firm-specific human capital by theoretically and empirically exploring when employees perceive their skills to be firm-specific. We first develop theoretical arguments and hypotheses based on the extant strategy literature, which implicitly assumes information efficiency and unbiased perceptions of firm-specificity. We then relax these assumptions and develop alternative hypotheses rooted in the cognitive psychology literature, which highlights biases in human judgment. We test our hypotheses using two data sources from Korea and the United States. Surprisingly, our results support the hypotheses based on cognitive bias—a stark contrast to expectations embedded within the strategy literature. Specifically, we find organizational commitment and, to some extent, tenure are negatively related to employee perceptions of the firm-specificity. We also find that employer-provided on-the-job training is unrelated to perceived firm-specificity. These results suggest that firm-specific human capital, as perceived by employees, may drive behavior in ways unanticipated by existing theory—for example, with respect to investments in skills or turnover decisions. This, in turn, may challenge the assumed relationship between firm-specific human capital and sustained competitive advantage. More broadly, our findings may suggest a need to reconsider other theories, such as transaction cost economics, that draw heavily on firm-specificity and implicitly assume widely shared and unbiased perceptions.

title: Mediated Sensemaking
methods: Inductive multi-case qualitative study of six family firms and nine Most Trusted Advisors, combining longitudinal interviews, participant observation, documents, multiple-case analysis, Gioia-style coding, axial coding, and grounded process modeling.
industry: Family firms; specific industries are not reported to maintain anonymity.
country: Two North American cities; specific countries are not reported.
time_period: Access began in 2001; main fieldwork occurred in 2005 and 2007; site visits and symposium observations continued through 2010; final data collection occurred in March 2013.
units: Family firms, Most Trusted Advisors, Family Business Entrepreneurs, family members, and other informants.
n_sample: Six family firms, nine Most Trusted Advisors, and 45 interviews with 21 informants.
authors: Strike, Vanessa M.; Rerup, Claus
theories: adaptive sensemaking; boundary spanning; mediation; sensemaking theory
keywords: Most Trusted Advisors; adaptive sensemaking; doubt; family firms; mediated sensemaking; pause; voice and knowledge
research_question: The paper asks how outsiders in the broader context influence local sensemaking, specifically how Most Trusted Advisors slow down Family Business Entrepreneurs and help them doubt sense already made. It examines what social position, skills, and tactics enable mediated sensemaking and how these processes are associated with adaptive sensemaking.
mechanism_summary:
- Key actors: Most Trusted Advisors, Family Business Entrepreneurs, family members, board members, employees, and other stakeholders in family firms.
- Mediation structure: MTAs occupy trusted inside-outside positions across family and business boundaries, giving them access to FBEs and to marginal or weak cues.
- Disposition to mediate: MTAs combine prosocial orientation, objectivity, emotional understanding, and social skill.
- Actions of mediation: MTAs induce pause, insert doubt, and mediate voice and knowledge.
- Adaptive sensemaking outcomes: FBEs lower commitment to entrapped frames, attend to alternative perspectives, and expand their frames.

The process starts when FBEs move quickly within an entrapped frame and have little motive to slow down or question their own sensemaking. MTAs use their trusted boundary-spanning position to create pause, introduce doubt through questions and red flags, and bring forward voices or knowledge that might otherwise remain unheard. These actions recursively slow the FBE, lower commitment to the initial frame, and support a broader frame through reflection and integration of additional cues.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces mediated sensemaking as an overlooked form of adaptive sensemaking that unfolds across boundaries rather than only inside a local sensemaking group. It shows that mediators' social position, prosocial disposition, and skilled actions shape whether outsiders can redirect sensemaking. It also contributes to sensemaking theory by foregrounding pacing, temporality, pause, and doubt as mechanisms through which actors can simultaneously know, doubt, and still mobilize action.
practical_implication: The study suggests that executives and family business owners may benefit from trusted mediators who can slow action, surface weak cues, and create space for dissent without directly taking over the sensemaking process. It also implies that family firms should recognize the value of informal advisory roles that can bridge family and business concerns and help powerful owners hear voices that might otherwise remain silent.
limitations: The authors identify family firms as a special context and possible boundary condition, although they argue that the mediated sensemaking process may transfer to other ownership structures. They did not trace precise performance outcomes or test a causal link between mediated sensemaking and results. The paper also focuses on cases where pause and delay helped adaptive sensemaking, while acknowledging that delay can be harmful in other settings.
future_research: Future research should assess the causal link between mediated sensemaking and outcomes in other contexts and ownership structures. The authors call for work on the short- and long-term dynamics of mediated sensemaking, including how social position, disposition, and tactics sustain mediation over time. They also encourage research on when adaptive sensemaking should be fast, slow, or mixed, and on whether materiality, signs, symbols, artifacts, technology, and boundary objects can mediate sensemaking across boundaries.
abstract: We use a multi-case analysis of nine Most Trusted Advisors (MTAs) in six family firms to introduce the concept of mediated sensemaking—that is, the social position, orientation, and actions used by mediators to facilitate adaptive sensemaking that unfolds when someone begins to doubt the sense already made. Our data captures the mediation process through which MTAs help Family Business Entrepreneurs (FBEs) interrupt momentum in sensemaking by slowing down action and facilitating doubt. Interestingly, FBEs have no motive to slow down and doubt their own sensemaking, yet MTAs can induce them to do so. We unpack the social skills and tactics used by MTAs to accomplish this pacing. We synthesize our findings in a grounded theoretical process theory that captures how MTAs facilitate adaptive sensemaking by regulating the pacing and temporality of FBEs’ sensemaking.
apa_citation: Strike, V. M., & Rerup, C. (2016). Mediated sensemaking. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(3), 880-905. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0665

title: Managing the Consequences of Organizational Stigmatization: Identity Work in a Social Enterprise
methods: Inductive qualitative case study of Keystone, a social enterprise in Thetford, using participant observation, 70 formal interviews, informal interviews, field diary data, print media, internal documents, open coding, axial coding, peer debriefing, and member checking.
industry: Social enterprise and community development organization.
country: United Kingdom, specifically Thetford, Norfolk, in the East of England.
time_period: Participant observation from April to December 2011, with follow-up conversations over the next three years.
units: Keystone as an organization, Keystone members, community members, employers, public-sector representatives, and local stakeholders.
n_sample: 70 formal interviews, plus participant observation, informal interviews, field diary entries, print media, and internal documents.
authors: Tracey, Paul; Phillips, Nelson
theories: organizational identity; organizational identity work; organizational stigma; stigma transfer
keywords: identity work; image crisis; organizational identity; organizational stigmatization; social enterprise; stigma transfer
research_question: The paper asks what effects organizational stigmatization has on organizational identity, how those effects can be managed, and what outcomes follow for the organization. It examines these questions through Keystone, a social enterprise whose support for migrants transferred community stigma onto the organization and triggered an internal identity crisis.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Organizational stigmatization, image crisis, stigma mirroring, secondary stigmatization, empathy with stigmatizers, organizational identity, and identity work.
- Process / phases: Stigma transfer from migrants to Keystone; image crisis among established residents; internal identity crisis through secondary stigmatization and empathy with stigmatizers; identity work through advocacy and valorization; identity affirmation and resource augmentation.
- Practices: Keystone leaders advocated for migrants by reframing migration as part of Thetford's history, economically necessary, and important to public services; they valorized Keystone's social-justice mission by making migrant support a source of organizational pride.
- Emergent outcomes: Keystone deepened rather than reduced its alignment with migrants, strengthened internal clarity and solidarity, and gained visibility and resources from stakeholders who valued its migrant-support work.
- Boundary conditions: The authors frame the model as most transferable to organizations that experience sudden stigma transfer and operate among stakeholders with diverse value commitments.

The process argument is that external stigmatization can be mirrored inside an organization when members experience secondary stigma and identify partly with the stigmatizing community. Leaders can manage this identity crisis through identity work that changes the meaning attached to the stigma: advocacy builds internal support for the stigmatized group, while valorization reframes the organization's stigmatized position as evidence of its core values. Once the organization repairs identity enough to live with a tarnished image among some stakeholders, stigma can also generate positive outcomes by attracting support from other stakeholders who share the organization's values.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational stigma research by shifting attention from external reputation and image effects to the internal consequences of stigmatization for organizational identity. It develops a model of identity management in stigmatized organizations, showing how advocacy and valorization can repair identity crises created by stigma transfer. It also extends stigma theory by explaining how stigmatization can produce positive outcomes, including identity affirmation and resource augmentation, under some conditions.
practical_implication: For leaders of stigmatized organizations, the study suggests that managing external image is insufficient when stigma damages members' understanding of what the organization stands for. Leaders may need to engage directly in internal identity work, especially when frontline members experience stigma personally or sympathize with stigmatizing stakeholders. The Keystone case also suggests that organizations can sometimes convert a stigmatized association into a clearer mission and stronger support from value-aligned stakeholders.
limitations: The study is based on a single qualitative case, so the authors caution that transferability depends on the type and timing of stigmatization. The model is most applicable to sudden stigma transfer and may not apply directly to core-stigmatized organizations that are stigmatized from inception, such as abortion clinics, strip clubs, or arms manufacturers. The authors also note that positive resource outcomes are likely only when salient stakeholders hold diverse values.
future_research: Future research could test the model in other cases of stigma transfer and event stigma to clarify which forms of identity work are effective in different stigmatization contexts. Scholars could also examine how the speed of stigmatization shapes member disidentification, exit, and identity repair. Additional work should investigate when split images across stakeholder groups create resource opportunities rather than compounding identity and legitimacy problems.
abstract: In this inductive study, we shift the focus of stigma research inside organizational boundaries by examining its relationship with organizational identity. To do so, we draw on the case of Keystone, a social enterprise in the East of England that became stigmatized after it initiated a program of support for a group of migrants in its community. Keystone’s stigmatization precipitated a crisis of organizational identity. We examine how the identity crisis unfolded, focusing on the forms of identity work that Keystone’s leaders enacted in response in order to reframe the meaning that organizational members attached to the stigma. Interestingly, we show not only that the internal effects of stigmatization on identity can be managed, but also that they may facilitate unexpected positive outcomes for organizations.

title: When Experts Become Liabilities: Domain Experts on Boards and Organizational Failure
methods: Empirical quantitative longitudinal study of U.S. local banks. The authors link directors' professional biographies to bank failure data and estimate competing-risks regression models, with inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting to address observable differences in banks' propensity to have expert-heavy boards.
industry: Local banks, or community banks
time_period: Banks founded between 1996 and 2012, observed for an average of 9.5 years
units: Bank-year observations for local banks and their boards
n_sample: 1,307 banks; 9,957 bank-year observations after lagged independent variables
authors: Almandoz, J.; Tilcsik, A.
theories: board composition; decision uncertainty; domain experts and decision-making groups
keywords: bank failure; board composition; decision uncertainty; domain experts; organizational failure
research_question: How does the presence of domain experts on a corporate board affect organizational outcomes? The paper asks whether a higher proportion of directors with primary professional experience in the focal industry increases the probability of organizational failure under conditions of decision uncertainty.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that expert-heavy boards can become less effective strategic decision-making groups when uncertainty is high. Domain experts may bring cognitive entrenchment, group overconfidence, and reduced task conflict, while non-experts may be less able or willing to challenge high-status experts. Empirically, the domain-expert failure relationship is stronger under rapid asset growth and non-standard real estate lending; local competition is theorized as another uncertainty source, but its interaction is not statistically significant in the reported models.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts board-composition research from broad professional diversity to the relative representation of domain experts versus non-experts. It develops a contingency argument in which decision uncertainty determines when directors' professional backgrounds become consequential for organizational survival. The study also specifies cognitive entrenchment, group overconfidence, and reduced task conflict as mechanisms through which board composition can affect strategic decision making and organizational failure.
practical_implication: The findings caution against assuming that more domain experts always make boards more effective. For local banks, regulators, founders, and investors should consider whether expert-heavy boards may be risky when the organization faces substantial decision uncertainty. The implication is not that boards should have no domain experts, but that boards may need a non-trivial number of directors whose primary expertise lies outside the focal domain.
limitations: The sample is limited to local banks founded after 1996, so the observed effects may depend on organizational age, the banking context, and boards that are directly involved in strategic decision making. The 1996-2012 window includes the 2007-2008 financial crisis, although the authors report robustness checks excluding 2008 and 2009. The data do not distinguish which domain experts are more or less prone to cognitive entrenchment or overconfidence.
future_research: Future research could examine whether these effects fade in older organizations or vary in unusually volatile versus stable economic environments. Additional work could study heterogeneity among experts, including whether exposure to other domains or prior volatile conditions reduces entrenchment and overconfidence. The authors also call for research on whether the findings generalize beyond banking, especially where boards are less directly involved in strategic decisions or where expert-heavy boards confer stronger legitimacy benefits.
abstract: How does the presence of domain experts on a corporate board—directors whose primary professional experience is within the focal firm’s industry—affect organizational outcomes? We argue that under conditions of significant decision uncertainty, a higher proportion of domain experts on a board may detract from effective decision making and thus increase the probability of organizational failure. Building on exploratory interviews with board members and CEOs, we derive hypotheses from this argument in the context of local banks in the United States. We predict that the greater the level of decision uncertainty—due to rapid asset growth or operation in less predictable markets—the stronger the relationship between the proportion of banking expert directors and the probability of bank failure. Longitudinal analyses of 1,307 banks between 1996 and 2012 support this prediction, even after accounting for both the overall level of professional diversity among directors and banks’ different propensities to have an expert-heavy board. We discuss implications for the key dimensions of board composition, the conditions under which the professional background of directors is more or less consequential, and the mechanisms whereby board composition affects organizational outcomes.

title: Knowledge Inheritance, Vertical Integration, and Entrant Survival in the Early U.S. Auto Industry
methods: Quantitative historical study of early U.S. automobile entrants using probit models for engine vertical integration, IV OLS models for market segment positioning, and IV Tobit/probit models for survival outcomes.
industry: Early U.S. automobile manufacturing industry.
units: Automobile industry entrants, including employee spinoffs and non-spinoffs.
n_sample: 63 entrants with sufficient data; 60 entrants in the multistage survival estimations after right-censored acquisitions were dropped.
authors: Argyres, N.; Mostafa, R.
theories: firm capabilities; knowledge inheritance; strategic positioning; transaction cost economics
keywords: early U.S. auto industry; employee spinoffs; entrant survival; knowledge inheritance; strategic positioning; vertical integration
research_question: How does knowledge inherited from parent firms shape employee spinoffs' early vertical integration choices, strategic positioning, and survival in the early U.S. auto industry? The paper asks whether parent-firm integration of a key activity, engine production, makes spinoffs more likely to integrate that activity and whether this helps them establish defensible positions away from low-price competition.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that parent firms' in-house production of a key value chain activity signals and transmits activity-specific knowledge to employee spinoffs. Spinoffs inheriting engine-production knowledge are more likely to vertically integrate engine production, and this integration supports differentiated, higher-price market positioning. Such defensible positioning is then associated with longer entrant survival.
theoretical_contribution: The paper links knowledge inheritance, vertical integration, and strategic positioning, which prior work often treated separately. It contributes to the literature on firm boundaries by showing that early boundary choices can reflect inherited capabilities, not only contemporaneous transaction costs. It also refines spinoff-performance explanations by identifying a mechanism through which lineage affects strategic choices and survival.
practical_implication: For entrants in technologically progressive industries, inherited knowledge is most valuable when it concerns a value chain activity that becomes strategically central. Founders and investors should attend not only to whether a founding team comes from a strong incumbent, but to whether the inherited know-how maps onto activities that support defensible positioning. The findings also imply that early make-or-buy decisions can have long-run survival consequences.
limitations: The empirical setting is historically specific: early U.S. automobile manufacturing during 1917-1931, with engine production as the key activity and price segment as the positioning proxy. The authors note that the data do not conclusively distinguish all types of de alio entrants and that right-censored acquisitions reduce the survival-estimation sample. They also state that the empirical context tests whether integration enables differentiation, not whether a similar mechanism supports cost leadership.
future_research: Future research could isolate how much knowledge spillover comes from parent-firm employment versus founders' own prior education and work experience. The authors call for work on when spinoffs can exploit inherited knowledge through informal relationships or alliances rather than vertical integration. They also suggest examining whether cost leadership strategies require integration of key value chain activities in other settings.
abstract: A key finding in the literature on industry evolution and strategy is that knowledge “inherited” from the founder’s previous employer can be an important source of a new firm’s capabilities. We analyze the conditions under which knowledge that is useful for carrying out a key value chain activity is inherited, and explore the mechanism through which such an inheritance shapes an entrant’s strategies and, in the process, influences its performance. Evidence from the early U.S. auto industry indicates that employee spinoffs generated from incumbents that had integrated a key value chain activity were also more likely to integrate that activity than other entrants, which, we suggest, reflects the application of knowledge inheritance relative to that activity. Moreover, we find that the integration of this key activity, stimulated by knowledge inheritance, contributed to the establishment of defensible strategic positioning, thereby enhancing the survival duration of inheriting spinoffs. We thus link together the phenomena of knowledge inheritance, vertical integration, and strategic positioning to explain entrant performance. Previously, these three phenomena have tended to be treated disparately in the literature, rather than in combination.

title: Coordinating Knowledge Creation in Multidisciplinary Teams: Evidence from Early-Stage Drug Discovery
methods: Longitudinal qualitative single-site field study of early-stage drug discovery project teams at DrugCo, using semi-structured interviews, non-participant observations, archival data, open coding, axial coding, and iterative model development.
industry: Early-stage drug discovery in a global pharmaceutical company.
time_period: Spring 2011 until early winter 2012.
units: Five multidisciplinary drug discovery project teams, their sub-teams, specialists, meetings, and coordination practices.
n_sample: 68 interviews, 55 observations, 930 pages of interview transcripts, and 167 pages of field notes.
authors: Ben-Menahem, Shiko M.; von Krogh, Georg; Erden, Zeynep; Schneider, Andreas
theories: coordination theory; organizational design; practice-based perspective on coordination; structural contingency theory
keywords: conjectural interdependencies; early-stage drug discovery; formal coordination structures; informal coordination practices; knowledge creation; multidisciplinary teams; sub-teams
research_question: The paper asks how multidisciplinary teams engaged in knowledge creation combine formal and informal coordination mechanisms when they face unpredictable interdependencies among specialists' knowledge domains. It focuses on early-stage drug discovery teams, where uncertainty makes it difficult to know in advance which specialist domains must coordinate and when.
mechanism_summary:
- Core context: Multidisciplinary drug discovery teams work under high task uncertainty and unpredictable interdependencies among knowledge domains.
- Formal structuring: Project teams create and revise self-managed sub-teams around conjectural and later revealed interdependencies.
- Specialist roles: Sub-team insiders carry direct responsibility for knowledge creation, while sub-team outsiders question assumptions and suggest alternative approaches.
- Informal coordination practices: Specialists use anticipatory conforming, workflow synchronizing, and cross-domain triangulating to integrate domain-specific work.
- Structural adaptation: Newly revealed interdependencies trigger the inclusion or exclusion of knowledge domains in sub-team structures.

The process is recursive rather than linear. Formal sub-team structures reduce complexity, allocate responsibility, and make interdependencies visible enough for specialists to coordinate informally. Informal coordination then exposes new knowledge-domain interdependencies, which prompts project teams to redesign formal structures. Knowledge creation therefore depends on the mutual constitution of formal coordination structures and informal coordination practices.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates organizational design and practice-based coordination perspectives by showing how formal structures and informal practices co-evolve in multidisciplinary knowledge work. It extends structural contingency theory by replacing the image of an omniscient designer with a process in which specialists use conjectural representations of interdependence and adapt structures as new interdependencies are revealed. It also contributes to practice-based coordination research by showing that informal practices depend on formal sub-team structures that reduce complexity and create shared awareness.
practical_implication: Managers of multidisciplinary discovery work should provide autonomy, time, and slack resources for teams to restructure sub-teams and recruit relevant specialists as interdependencies change. Performance appraisal should recognize cross-domain contributions to collective outcomes, not only domain-specific standards of excellence. Managers should also encourage sub-team outsiders to ask questions and contribute expertise because these outsider interventions can reveal hidden assumptions and new coordination needs.
limitations: The authors note that the study focuses on self-managed teams with discretion to change their structures, making autonomy a boundary condition for the model. The drug discovery setting also involves a precautionary principle and strong safety awareness, which may shape how specialists respond to uncertainty. The observation window did not cover the complete five- to six-year trajectory of any one drug discovery project, and the single-site design limits claims about transferability to other firms or industries.
future_research: Future research should examine whether the observed structural adaptations and informal coordination practices affect project performance and ultimate drug discovery success. Studies could test the model in other firms in the same industry and in other multidisciplinary settings with similar coordination challenges. Further work could also examine how knowledge distance among specialist domains changes over time as teams create new knowledge.
abstract: Based on a multi-year field study of early-stage drug discovery project teams at a global pharmaceutical company, this paper examines how multidisciplinary teams engaged in knowledge creation combine formal and informal coordination mechanisms when faced with unpredictable interdependencies among specialists' knowledge domains. While multidisciplinary teams are critical for knowledge creation in increasingly specialized work environments, the coordination literature has been divided with respect to the extent to which such teams rely on formal coordination structures and informal coordination practices. Our findings show that when interdependencies among knowledge domains are dynamic and unpredictable, specialists design self-managed (sub-)teams around collectively held assumptions about interdependencies based on incomplete information (conjectural interdependencies). These team structures establish the grounds for informal coordination practices that enable specialists to both manage known interdependencies and reveal new interdependencies. Newly revealed interdependencies among knowledge domains, in turn, promote structural adaptation. Drawing on these findings, we advance an integrative model explaining how team-based knowledge creation relies on the mutual constitution of formal coordination structures and informal coordination practices. The model contributes to theory on organizational design and practice-based research on coordination in cross-disciplinary knowledge creation.

title: Different Views of Hierarchy and Why They Matter: Hierarchy as Inequality or as Cascading Influence
methods: Quantitative field study of 75 work teams using team member surveys for dyadic influence, task complexity, process conflict, and satisfaction, supervisor surveys for team performance, and regression plus bootstrapped conditional indirect-effect analyses.
industry: Existing work teams from 11 industries and multiple disciplinary areas, including information technology, hospitality, finance, agriculture, transportation, telecommunications, education, and government services.
time_period: All data were collected within a two-month period.
units: Work teams and team members
n_sample: 457 respondents from 75 work teams in 56 organizations.
authors: Bunderson, J. Stuart; van der Vegt, Gerben S.; Cantimur, Yeliz; Rink, Floor
theories: ethological hierarchy research; hierarchy as acyclicity; hierarchy as inequality; social hierarchy; social network theory
keywords: acyclicity; cascading relations of dyadic influence; group performance; hierarchy; inequality; member satisfaction; process conflict; task complexity
research_question: The paper asks whether the mixed findings on hierarchy in task groups reflect different conceptualizations of hierarchy rather than only contextual contingencies. It compares hierarchy as inequality in member influence, operationalized as centralization and steepness, with hierarchy as cascading dyadic influence relations, operationalized as acyclicity.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that acyclical influence relations clarify whose voice should carry weight when disagreements arise, reducing process conflict and improving team outcomes. By contrast, centralized or steep influence structures create inequality that can foster rivalry, jockeying, and conflict, especially when complex tasks produce more occasions for disagreement. Process conflict then transmits these hierarchy effects to group performance and member satisfaction.
theoretical_contribution: The study clarifies that hierarchy has been conceptualized in distinct ways and that those conceptualizations can have divergent implications for group process and performance. It challenges the dominant inequality view of hierarchy in organization and management research by showing that centralization and steepness can capture dysfunctions rather than benefits. It also advances hierarchy-as-acyclicity as a relational conceptualization that better captures how ordered influence can help task groups coordinate and resolve conflict.
practical_implication: Managers should distinguish between clear chains of influence and unequal concentrations of influence or status. The findings imply that teams may benefit when influence relations are ordered enough to settle disagreements, but may suffer when influence is concentrated or sharply unequal, particularly under complex task conditions. Team design and leadership interventions should therefore focus on clarifying influence and deference relations without simply increasing inequality among members.
limitations: The study measured influence through member ratings rather than direct behavioral indicators of influence or deference. Its cross-sectional design means causal ordering among hierarchy, conflict, performance, and satisfaction remains theory-based rather than conclusively established. The authors also note that the study did not examine a broader set of mediators or outcomes, such as information sharing, innovation, turnover, or citizenship behavior.
future_research: Future research should examine the antecedents of acyclical influence relations and whether acyclicity can be deliberately managed. Scholars should test boundary conditions such as reachable connectedness, distinguish acyclicity in influence from acyclicity in communication, and examine when centralization and steepness diverge rather than behave similarly. Additional work should use longitudinal or behavioral designs and study broader conflict forms, mediators, and outcomes.
abstract: Hierarchy is a reality of group life, for humans and for most other group-living species. However, there remains considerable debate about whether and when hierarchy can promote group performance and member satisfaction. We suggest that progress in this debate has been hampered by a lack of clarity about hierarchy and how to conceptualize it. Whereas prevailing conceptualizations of hierarchy in the group and organization literature have focused on inequality in member power or status (i.e., centralization or steepness), we build on the ethological and social network traditions to advance a view of hierarchy as cascading relations of dyadic influence (i.e., acyclicity). We suggest that hierarchy thus conceptualized is more likely to capture the functional benefits of hierarchy, whereas hierarchy as inequality is more likely to be dysfunctional. In a study of 75 teams drawn from a range of industries, we show that whereas acyclicity in influence relations reduces conflict and thereby enhances both group performance and member satisfaction, centralization and steepness have negative effects on conflict, performance, and satisfaction, particularly in groups that perform complex tasks. The theory and results of this study can help to clarify and advance research on the functions and dysfunctions of hierarchy in task groups.

title: Flourishing via Workplace Relationships: Moving Beyond Instrumental Support
methods: Mixed-methods program of studies combining critical incident qualitative coding, item-generation procedures, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses for the Relationship Functions Inventory, and regression and relative-weights analyses linking six relationship functions to job satisfaction, meaningful work, positive emotions at work, and life satisfaction.
industry: Multiple organizations and occupations; Study 1 included education, government, retail, banking, information technology, health care, human services, and manufacturing, and Study 2 drew from a wide variety of organizations and occupations.
country: United States or Canada for the Study 2 working-adult sample.
time_period: Calendar period not reported; Study 2 used two focal-participant surveys separated by approximately one month and a partner survey between them.
units: Employees' positive workplace relationships and coworker relationship functions; Study 2 uses matched focal-participant and partner pairs.
n_sample: Study 1 Phase 1 collected 287 participants and 283 coded stories; Study 1 Phase 3 surveyed 177 MBA students; Study 2 analyzed 151 matched participant pairs after attention checks.
authors: Colbert, A. E.; Bono, J. E.; Purvanova, R. K.
theories: attachment theory; employee flourishing; positive work relationships; social exchange lens; thriving through relationships
keywords: Relationship Functions Inventory; employee flourishing; life satisfaction; meaningful work; positive emotions at work; positive work relationships; relationship functions
research_question: How do positive workplace relationships support employee flourishing beyond instrumental support? The paper asks what functions good work relationships serve and whether distinct functions predict distinct flourishing-consistent outcomes.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / functions: Task assistance, career advancement, emotional support, friendship, personal growth, and giving to others.
- Process / scale development: Critical incident descriptions were coded into six functions, converted into the Relationship Functions Inventory, and validated through item-assignment, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis.
- Outcomes: Job satisfaction, meaningful work, positive emotions at work, and life satisfaction.
- Boundary / design features: The Study 2 evidence is cross-sectional and uses self and partner reports for several outcomes, with positive affectivity controlled in regressions.

The process argument is that positive work relationships provide multiple resources and identity-relevant experiences, not only task help or career advice. Giving to others is theorized to make work more meaningful by reinforcing caring identities and prosocial impact; friendship is expected to support positive emotions through closeness and enjoyable interaction; and personal growth can extend beyond the work role into broader life satisfaction. The empirical tests show differential associations rather than one uniform relationship-quality effect.
theoretical_contribution: The paper expands relationship theory by developing a six-function taxonomy of positive workplace relationships that includes personal growth, friendship, and giving to others alongside task assistance, career advancement, and emotional support. It contributes precision by showing that different functions align with different flourishing outcomes rather than treating relationship quality as a single broad predictor. It also introduces and validates the Relationship Functions Inventory as a measurement tool for future research.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that organizations benefit when workplace designs and reward structures allow employees to give and receive resources through positive relationships. The findings caution against systems that pit employees against one another because such systems may suppress less visible benefits of high-quality relationships, including information sharing, positive emotions, meaningful work, and potentially lower health-related costs. The paper also emphasizes that giving to others is valuable in itself, not only an input into social exchange.
limitations: The authors state that the data ordering is consistent with their theory but cannot test the implied causal associations because the data are cross-sectional. The taxonomy was developed from positive relationship stories involving bosses, peers, and subordinates, but later analyses focus on coworker relationships in aggregate, leaving open whether functions operate differently in single relationships or across networks. The study also does not examine whether work and nonwork relationships serve redundant or additive functions.
future_research: Future research should use longitudinal panel designs to test reciprocal and causal dynamics between relationship functions and employee outcomes. The authors call for studies on antecedents of specific relationship functions, including trust, emotional carrying capacity, resilience, and openness to new ideas. They also suggest work on the mechanisms linking relationship functions to positive identity, self-knowledge, self-esteem, and on whether negative workplace relationships can serve some basic functions.
abstract: In a series of qualitative and quantitative studies, we developed a model of the functions of positive work relationships, with an explicit focus on the role that these relationships play in employee flourishing. Stories that employees told about positive relationships at work revealed that relationships serve a broad range of functions, including the traditionally studied functions of task assistance, career advancement, and emotional support, as well as less studied functions of personal growth, friendship, and the opportunity to give to others. Building on this taxonomy, we validated a scale—the Relationship Functions Inventory—and developed theory suggesting differential linkages between the relationship functions and outcomes indicative of employee flourishing. Results revealed unique associations between functions and outcomes, such that task assistance was most strongly associated with job satisfaction, giving to others was most strongly associated with meaningful work, friendship was most strongly associated with positive emotions at work, and personal growth was most strongly associated with life satisfaction. Our results suggest that work relationships play a key role in promoting employee flourishing, and that examining the differential effects of a taxonomy of relationship functions brings precision to our understanding of how relationships impact individual flourishing.

title: Empowered to Perform: A Multilevel Investigation of the Influence of Empowerment on Performance in Hospital Units
methods: Multi-source, temporally lagged field study of hospital employees nested in units, analyzed with multi-level confirmatory factor analysis and multi-level structural equation modeling in MPlus7.
industry: Hospital healthcare units including respiratory care, nursing, and neurodiagnostics.
time_period: Two online surveys approximately 13 months apart, plus HR performance evaluations before and after the second survey.
units: Hospital employees nested in hospital units
n_sample: 544 individuals from 78 units
authors: D’Innocenzo, Lauren; Luciano, Margaret M.; Mathieu, John E.; Maynard, M. Travis; Chen, Gilad
theories: multi-level systems theory (Chen & Kanfer, 2006); psychological empowerment theory; unit empowerment
keywords: hospital units; job performance; multi-level systems theory; psychological empowerment; unit empowerment; unit voice climate
research_question: The paper asks how empowerment operates across levels in hospital units: whether unit empowerment conditions the relationship between individual psychological empowerment and job performance, and whether unit voice climate builds unit empowerment that in turn enhances individual psychological empowerment. The study focuses on the unique and synergistic effects of unit- and individual-level empowerment in a dynamic healthcare setting.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is cross-level and contextual. Unit voice climate creates a collective forum for speaking up, which fosters shared unit empowerment. Unit empowerment then both raises individual psychological empowerment and creates the conditions, or zones of discretion, under which individually empowered employees can translate motivation into improved job performance. The performance benefits of psychological empowerment were significant when unit empowerment was high, but not when it was low.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances a multi-level theory of empowerment by showing that unit empowerment is not only a higher-level antecedent of individual psychological empowerment, but also a contextual condition that changes how individual empowerment relates to performance. It extends empowerment research beyond a simple linear cause-and-effect model by identifying a cross-level moderated mediation process. It also introduces unit voice climate as a contextual antecedent of unit empowerment in hospital units.
practical_implication: Managers in hospitals and similar dynamic, interdependent settings should treat empowerment as both an individual and unit-level issue. Empowering individual employees may not improve performance unless the unit context also gives members discretion and support to act. The findings also support participatory systems and voice climates as practical routes for strengthening unit empowerment and, indirectly, individual psychological empowerment.
limitations: The sample came from hospitals in a single geographical region of the United States, so generalizability to other populations, industries, and organizational contexts is unknown. Although the design used multiple sources and temporally separated measures, reciprocal relationships and method effects may still affect some linear relationships. The study modeled empowerment as a higher-order construct, which leaves open whether specific dimensions such as competence, self-determination, impact, or meaning operate differently across contexts.
future_research: Future research should sample across settings that vary in contextual features likely to change empowerment effects, including industries beyond healthcare and organizational contexts with different levels of discretion and interdependence. Studies should compare different conceptualizations and subdimensions of empowerment across multiple levels. The authors also encourage broader models that include additional antecedents, such as employees’ knowledge, skills, abilities, social networks, unit and organizational features, and outcomes such as voice behaviors and patient safety.
abstract: Psychological empowerment has been studied extensively over the past few decades in a variety of contexts and appears to be especially salient within dynamic and complex environments such as healthcare. However, a recent meta-analysis found that psychological empowerment relationships vary significantly across studies, and there is still a rather limited understanding of how empowerment operates across levels. Accordingly, we advance and test a multi-level model of empowerment which seeks to better understand the unique and synergistic effects between unit and individual empowerment in hospital units. Analysis of data involving 544 individuals in 78 units, collected from multiple sources over three different time periods, revealed that unit empowerment evidenced a synergistic interaction with individual-level psychological empowerment as related to individuals’ job performance, as well as an indirect effect on performance via individual empowerment, while controlling for previous performance levels. Notably, these effects were significant at relatively high, but not at relatively low, levels of unit empowerment. Furthermore, we found that unit voice climate increased unit empowerment and thereby enhanced individual psychological empowerment. These findings suggest that, in complex and dynamic environments, empowering work units is an important means by which leaders can enhance individuals’ performance.

title: Doing More with Less: Innovation Input and Output in Family Firms
methods: Meta-analysis of 108 primary studies using Hedges and Olkin-type meta-analysis, meta-analytic structural equation modeling, and post hoc meta-analytic regression analysis to compare family and nonfamily firms on innovation input and output.
industry: Primary studies from economics, finance, and management, with additional controls for whether samples included high-tech industries.
units: Primary studies and firm-level effect sizes comparing family and nonfamily firms.
n_sample: 108 primary studies.
authors: Duran, Patricio; Kammerlander, Nadine; van Essen, Marc; Zellweger, Thomas
theories: behavioral agency theory; institution-based view; resource orchestration; resource-based view
keywords: MARA; MASEM; family CEO; family firms; founder CEO; innovation input; innovation output; meta-analysis
research_question: The paper asks how family firm status affects innovation input and innovation output, and why family firms can appear conservative in R&D investment while still producing substantial innovation output. It also asks how these relationships differ when a family CEO or founder CEO leads the firm and whether country-level institutions condition the input-output relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that family control, wealth concentration, and nonfinancial goals reduce willingness to invest in uncertain innovation projects, but also strengthen monitoring, resource orchestration, tacit knowledge, routines, and trusted network access. These same idiosyncrasies therefore reduce innovation input while improving conversion of input into innovation output. Later-generation family CEOs intensify the output advantage, whereas founder CEOs increase input but are associated with lower output, which the authors attribute to less developed routines, tacit knowledge, and trusted network access.
theoretical_contribution: The study separates innovation input from innovation output and shows that family control can affect them in opposite directions. It extends innovation research by shifting attention from the level of R&D investment to the conversion rate between innovation input and output. It also contributes to family business research by explaining heterogeneous effects of family CEOs and founder CEOs and by linking family firm innovation to institutional context.
practical_implication: Family firms should not interpret lower R&D input as evidence that they are necessarily less innovative; the findings suggest that monitoring, trusted networks, routines, and tacit knowledge can help them use innovation resources efficiently. Family firms with family CEOs may need incentives or governance systems that encourage sufficient investment in innovation. Firms with nonfamily professional managers should attend to preserving the social and human capital that supports innovation efficiency.
limitations: The authors note that the meta-analysis relies on modest effect sizes and on the design limitations of the primary studies. The operationalization of family firms varies across studies, and dichotomous family-versus-nonfamily measures may hide differences in ownership thresholds and family control intensity. Innovation input is usually captured through R&D expenditure measures, while innovation output measures such as patents and product introductions do not capture all types of innovation.
future_research: Future research should examine more specific family firm characteristics beyond CEO type and use continuous measures of family control. The authors call for more nuanced innovation output variables and for work linking leadership variables to different forms of innovation activity. They also encourage research on how founder-led firms' innovation input and output change as CEO tenure increases and how country-, firm-, and family-level factors shape the family firm innovation relationship.
abstract: Family firms are often portrayed as an important yet conservative form of organization that is reluctant to invest in innovation; however, simultaneously, evidence has shown that family firms are flourishing and in fact constitute many of the world’s most innovative firms. Our study contributes to disentangling this puzzling effect. We argue that family firms—owing to the family’s high level of control over the firm, wealth concentration, and importance of nonfinancial goals—invest less in innovation but have an increased conversion rate of innovation input into output and, ultimately, a higher innovation output than nonfamily firms. Empirical evidence from a meta-analysis based on 108 primary studies from 42 countries supports our hypotheses. We further argue and empirically show that the observed effects are even stronger when the CEO of the family firm is a later-generation family member. However, when the CEO of the family firm is the firm’s founder, innovation input is higher and, contrary to our initial expectations, innovation output is lower than that in other firms. We further show that the family firm–innovation input–output relationships depend on country-level factors; namely, the level of minority shareholder protection and the education level of the workforce in the country.

title: Grand Challenges and Inductive Methods: Rigor without Rigor Mortis
methods: Editorial commentary that develops an argument about why inductive methods are well suited to grand challenges and how qualitative researchers can preserve rigor without imposing rigid templates.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Eisenhardt, K. M.; Graebner, M. E.; Sonenshein, S.
theories: grounded theory building; inductive methods; theoretical sampling
keywords: grand challenges; grounded theory building; inductive methods; qualitative research; theoretical sampling
research_question: The editorial asks how inductive methods can help management scholars address grand challenges while producing rigorous theory. It focuses on why methods such as theory building from cases, interpretivist studies, and ethnography fit problems that are complex, uncertain, socially consequential, and not easily handled by conventional deductive approaches.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Inductive methods are especially useful for grand challenges because they generate theory from rich data in settings where existing theory is limited and clear answers are unavailable.
- Methodological elements: Deep immersion in focal phenomena, theoretical sampling, and grounded theory building.
- Grand-challenge affordances: Novel ideas, effective process explanations, attention to configurations and equifinality, hard-to-measure constructs, and extreme cases.
- Rigor conditions: Internal coherence and parsimony, compelling grounding in data, and rich, unexpected insights.
- Rigor mortis risks: Forced writing formats, rigid analytic recipes, and excessive process transparency that distract from theory.

The process argument is that inductive methods combine openness to emergent insight with disciplined data collection, sampling, and analysis. Because grand challenges involve uncertain, evolving mixes of technical and social elements, the authors argue that inductive work can reveal concepts, relationships, processes, and boundary conditions that deductive designs may overlook. Rigor comes from strong theory grounded in rich evidence, not from mechanical adherence to a single qualitative template.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial positions inductive methods as central to AMJ's grand-challenges agenda. It contributes by specifying how case-based theory building, interpretivist research, and ethnography can generate novel theory about complex social and organizational problems. It also clarifies quality criteria for inductive work by separating genuine rigor from template-driven "rigor mortis."
practical_implication: For authors, the editorial advises matching the research design, analysis, and presentation format to the focal question rather than forcing every qualitative paper into the same display or process template. For reviewers and editors, it implies that strong inductive work should be judged by theory quality, data grounding, and insight, not by ritual compliance with favored qualitative artifacts.
limitations: The piece is an editorial commentary rather than an empirical study, so it does not test its claims with a new sample or formal comparative evidence. Its examples are drawn from published inductive work and are used to illustrate methodological possibilities rather than establish systematic prevalence. The authors also caution that conventions such as data structures, process detail, and presentation formats can support some studies while constraining others.
future_research: The editorial points researchers toward inductive studies of grand challenges that surface novel ideas, processes, configurations, hard-to-measure constructs, and extreme cases. It also invites methodological reflection on how to preserve internal coherence, strong data grounding, and unexpected insight without imposing rigid qualitative templates. Future work could therefore examine how particular inductive designs and presentation choices help or hinder theory development in grand-challenge research.

title: Misfit and Milestones: Structural Elaboration and Capability Reinforcement in the Evolution of Entrepreneurial Top Management Teams
methods: Longitudinal quantitative panel study of high-technology entrepreneurial firms using monthly data on top management team roles and executives; the authors estimate panel-Poisson random effects regressions predicting counts of new TMT hires and new TMT roles, with robustness checks using alternative misfit measures, lag structures, fixed effects, and hurdle models.
industry: High-technology entrepreneurial firms in the 1990s across six industry categories, including computer, manufacturing, medical, research, semiconductor, and telecommunications.
time_period: From firm founding to December 2000 or until acquisition or failure.
units: Entrepreneurial firm top management teams, executives, job titles, hires, and new TMT roles.
n_sample: 167 high-technology entrepreneurial firms; 1,452 executives holding 1,918 TMT roles; 17,659 firm-month observations.
authors: Ferguson, A. J.; Cohen, L. E.; Burton, M. D.; Beckman, C. M.
theories: entrepreneurship theory; organizational role structures; person-environment fit; upper echelons
keywords: capability reinforcement; developmental milestones; firm development; overqualification; structural elaboration; top management team misfit; underqualification
research_question: How and when do entrepreneurial top management teams adjust people and roles in response to TMT misfit? The paper also asks how responses to misfit vary with the resources available as firms pass developmental milestones such as venture capital financing and IPO.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that underqualification represents a capability need relative to formal TMT roles, so firms should reinforce capabilities by hiring managers into existing roles. Overqualification represents unused capability relative to the current role structure, so firms should elaborate the structure by adding roles that make fuller use of existing managers. The study argues that these responses require attention and resources, making developmental milestones a contingency: before such milestones, even misfit teams may make few changes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to entrepreneurship theory by separating TMT composition from TMT role structure and modeling their misfit rather than treating people and roles as interchangeable. It identifies asymmetric responses to underqualification and overqualification, showing that capability needs are a stronger and more robust driver of TMT change than opportunities created by excess capability. It also contributes to upper-echelons, role-structure, and fit research by theorizing misfit at the team level and linking it to both change and inertia.
practical_implication: The findings imply that new venture leaders should attend early to fit between managerial capabilities and formal roles because later correction may depend on already having achieved resource-generating milestones. Overqualified teams may need to add roles to signal and use existing capability, whereas underqualified teams may need hires to fill skill gaps. The paper also cautions that firms may be unable to professionalize their TMTs before attracting the very resources that would enable such professionalization.
limitations: The authors state that the study cannot determine whether the net effects of misfit are good or bad for firms and top managers because it does not incorporate firm performance outcomes. They also note that the observed changes may reflect deliberate managerial strategies or more serendipitous processes, and the study does not isolate those mechanisms. Generalizability is limited by the relatively small sample, narrow industry sectors, regional setting, 1990s timing, and unusually high rates of venture capital financing and IPO.
future_research: Future research should examine whether TMT misfit and resulting hires or role additions improve or harm venture performance. Studies should assess managers' perceptions of TMT misfit to distinguish intentional responses from emergent alignment processes and should explore differences within overqualification and underqualification. The authors also call for research on external industry expectations, CEO power and founder constraints, other endogenous drivers of TMT change, and samples from other regions or periods with lower milestone-achievement rates.
abstract: We examine how “top management team (TMT) misfit,” or discrepancies between the TMT’s functional roles and the qualifications of the managers who fill those roles, affects the evolution of TMT composition and structure in a longitudinal study of entrepreneurial ventures. We distinguish two types of misfit—overqualification and underqualification— and study how each is associated with TMT changes. We further consider the moderating effect of firm development. Results reveal that underqualified TMTs hire new managers to reinforce existing capabilities whereas overqualified TMTs elaborate their role structures. However, achieving developmental milestones (i.e., obtaining venture capital funding and staging an initial public offering) is a critical contingency to TMT change: absent these milestones, firms neither hire new managers nor add roles, even when they seemingly need to do so. These findings contribute to knowledge of how TMTs and new ventures evolve by underscoring the importance of simultaneously attending to TMT composition and structure.

title: Managing the Risks of Proactivity: A Multilevel Study of Initiative and Performance in the Middle Management Context
methods: Empirical quantitative multilevel field study using survey data from middle managers and business-unit executives, year-end performance appraisal records, confirmatory factor analysis, and hierarchical linear modeling.
industry: Global transport and logistics service company
country: Not reported in paper; geographically dispersed business units of a large multinational corporation
time_period: Primary survey data collected mid-2010, with year-end job performance appraisals collected seven months later
units: Middle managers nested in business units
n_sample: 383 middle managers and 72 executives across 34 business units
authors: Glaser, L.; Stam, W.; Takeuchi, R.
theories: behavioral decision theory; organizational control; situational strength theory
keywords: job autonomy; job performance; performance management context; personal initiative tendency; risk propensity
research_question: The paper asks how middle managers' personal initiative tendency translates into job performance when proactive action is risky. It specifically examines whether risk propensity weakens the initiative-performance relationship and whether job autonomy and business-unit performance management context respectively amplify or attenuate that risk.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cross-level alignment argument. Personal initiative can improve middle managers' performance, but proactive managers with high risk propensities may underestimate downside risks, invest less in risk adjustment, and pursue initiatives that are poorly timed, misaligned, or difficult to control. High job autonomy creates a weaker situation that lets those risk tendencies shape behavior more strongly, while a strong performance management context supplies shared ambition, discipline, feedback, and accountability that help risk-seeking proactive managers channel initiative toward valued outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: The study qualifies the common view that proactivity and autonomy are uniformly beneficial by showing that personal initiative's performance payoff depends on individual risk propensity and organizational control. It integrates behavioral decision theory with situational strength theory to explain why proactive employees differ in their need for control. It also distinguishes formal job-level autonomy from informal business-unit performance management context as control mechanisms with different implications for low- and high-risk-propensity managers.
practical_implication: Organizations should not assume that encouraging initiative requires simply maximizing autonomy. Proactive middle managers with lower risk propensities may benefit from autonomy, whereas proactive managers with higher risk propensities may need stronger performance management contexts that clarify expectations, provide feedback, and discipline initiative. The practical implication is to align control mechanisms with managers' risk profiles rather than treating all proactive employees as needing the same freedom or constraint.
limitations: The authors note that the study relies mostly on cross-sectional data, despite a seven-month lag between predictor measures and performance appraisals, so reverse causality cannot be fully ruled out. The paper does not directly observe the behavioral risk-adjustment mechanisms it theorizes. It also studies middle managers in a single multinational corporation, which limits generalizability across jobs, hierarchical levels, organizations, and industries.
future_research: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify the interplay between personal initiative, risk propensity, aspiration levels, and job performance over time. Studies should directly measure risk perceptions and risk-reduction behaviors, compare different forms of proactivity, and examine domain-specific risk propensity. The authors also call for research across wider jobs, organizations, and industries, including work that compares perceptual and objective autonomy and multiple dimensions of job performance.
abstract: Drawing on theories of behavioral decision making and situational strength, we developed and tested a multilevel model that explains how the performance outcomes of personal initiative tendency depend on the extent of alignment between organizational control mechanisms and proactive individuals' risk propensities. Results from a sample of 383 middle managers operating in 34 business units of a large multinational corporation indicated that risk propensity weakens the positive relationship between personal initiative tendency and job performance. This negative moderating effect was further amplified when middle managers receive high job autonomy but was attenuated in business units with a strong performance management context. We discuss the implications of these findings for research on proactivity, risk taking, and organizational control.
