title: Cooperation vs. Competition: Alternative Goal Structures for Motivating Groups in a Resource Scarce Environment
methods: Quasi-experimental field experiment assigning rural Sri Lankan school-construction communities to competition or cooperation conditions, analyzed with hierarchical linear models and Monte Carlo indirect-effect tests, followed by qualitative focus groups coded in NVivo.
industry: Base-of-the-pyramid school construction and community infrastructure projects
time_period: 2012 calendar year field experiment; follow-up qualitative study shortly after completion
units: Rural communities and school construction committees participating in Edubuild school projects
n_sample: 44 communities; 452 construction committee members in the baseline survey; approximately 200 focus-group participants
authors: Kistruck, Geoffrey M.; Lount, Robert B., Jr.; Smith, Brett R.; Bergman, Brian J., Jr.; Moss, Todd W.
theories: goal interdependence theory; institutional economics; social interdependence theory
keywords: base-of-the-pyramid; competitive goal structures; cooperative goal structures; goal attainment; group motivation; inter-group familiarity; resource scarcity
research_question: The paper asks whether cooperative or competitive goal structures better motivate groups when resources are scarce and opportunity costs are high. It also asks whether inter-group familiarity changes how goal structure affects group motivation and subsequent goal attainment in a base-of-the-pyramid field setting.
mechanism_summary:
- Design / treatment: Rural Sri Lankan communities building schools were paired and assigned to competition or cooperation conditions around their community contribution targets.
- Focal process: Goal structure shapes group motivation, which in turn predicts goal attainment.
- Moderating condition: Inter-group familiarity moderates the effect of goal structure on motivation and the indirect path from goal structure to goal attainment.
- Follow-up explanation: Focus groups distinguish intrinsic excitement from competition, opportunity costs of cooperation, and extrinsic knowledge benefits from cooperating with unfamiliar groups.

The paper argues that resource scarcity changes the motivational implications of cooperation and competition. Competition can feel aspirational and emotionally energizing in a context where scarce-resource competition is part of daily life, whereas cooperation can impose costly inter-group coordination unless it provides access to rare knowledge. Quantitative results support higher motivation under competition on average, but the qualitative follow-up shows that cooperation with unfamiliar communities can also motivate because unfamiliar partners offer new information.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends social interdependence theory by identifying resource scarcity as a boundary condition for the usual claim that cooperative goal structures outperform competitive ones. It also shows that inter-group familiarity is not uniformly beneficial for cooperation: familiarity can expose negative traits and reduce willingness to cooperate, while unfamiliarity can make cooperation valuable as a route to new knowledge. Beyond social interdependence theory, the paper contributes to institutional economics in base-of-the-pyramid contexts by showing how organizations can use relational mechanisms among existing actors when formal enforcement is weak.
practical_implication: Organizations working in resource-scarce communities can use inter-group competition to encourage participation in collective infrastructure projects, especially when communities must allocate scarce labor, materials, and time across competing demands. Cooperation may still be useful when paired groups are unfamiliar and can exchange valuable knowledge, but managers should not assume that familiarity automatically creates shared responsibility.
limitations: The authors selected an extreme resource-scarce context rather than experimentally varying resource scarcity, so the exact point at which cooperation and competition reverse in motivational effectiveness remains untested. The inter-group familiarity measure used a single item, and the goal-attainment measure did not capture other performance outcomes such as task quality, creativity, sabotage, or animosity. The authors also note possible omitted variables despite random assignment and controls, and the competition manipulation may have been dampened by allowing a tied prize split.
future_research: Future research should test where along the resource-scarcity continuum the motivational advantage of competitive versus cooperative goal structures changes. It should also measure inter-group familiarity more richly, examine whether changing resource conditions alter intrinsic and extrinsic motivation over time, and study additional performance consequences of competition and cooperation, including task quality, creativity, destructive competition, and omitted-variable concerns in matched-pair designs.
abstract: There is a growing consensus that cooperative goal structures are more effective at motivating groups than competitive goal structures. However, such results are based largely on studies conducted in highly-controlled settings where participants were provided with the necessary resources to accomplish their assigned task. In an attempt to extend the boundary conditions of current theoretical predictions, we undertook a field experiment within a base-of-the-pyramid setting where resource scarcity is extremely high. Specifically, we collected data on 44 communities within rural Sri Lanka who were tasked with contributing a portion of their resources to the construction of a school building; 24 were assigned to a competition condition and 20 to a cooperation condition. The results of our field experiment, and subsequent follow-up interviews and focus groups, collectively suggest that competitive goal structures generally lead to higher levels of motivation within a resource scarce environment. However, our results also suggest that cooperative goal structures can be highly motivating when groups are unfamiliar with one another, as cooperating with unfamiliar groups can provide access to valuable and rare knowledge within such settings.
apa_citation: Kistruck, G. M., Lount, R. B., Jr., Smith, B. R., Bergman, B. J., Jr., & Moss, T. W. (2016). Cooperation vs. competition: Alternative goal structures for motivating groups in a resource scarce environment. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(4), 1174-1198. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0201

title: When in Rome, Look Like Caesar? Investigating the Link between Demand-side Cultural Power Distance and CEO Power
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of publicly traded, U.S.-incorporated pharmaceutical and semiconductor firms. The authors construct demand-side cultural power distance from country-level sales and GLOBE/Hofstede cultural power distance data, measure CEO power as a summative board-level index, and test hypotheses using generalized estimating equation models with controls, lagged independent variables, and selection-bias adjustment.
industry: Pharmaceutical and semiconductor manufacturing industries.
time_period: 2003 through 2012, inclusive.
units: Firm-year observations for publicly traded, U.S.-incorporated firms with country-specific sales data.
n_sample: 801 observations from 151 firms.
authors: Krause, R.; Filatotchev, I.; Bruton, G. D.
theories: agency theory; institutional multiplicity; neo-institutional theory; resource dependence theory
keywords: CEO power; board legitimacy; corporate governance; cultural power distance; demand-side legitimacy
research_question: The paper asks whether firms exposed to customers in high cultural power distance markets exhibit greater CEO power on their boards. It also asks when this demand-side cultural-cognitive legitimacy relationship is stronger, focusing on customer dependence, variance in demand-side cultural power distance, and industry bargaining power.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a demand-side legitimacy process. Customers in high power distance cultures may see a powerful CEO as more culturally comprehensible and legitimate, so firms selling heavily into those markets have reason to align board power structures with customers' cultural-cognitive expectations. The relationship should strengthen when sales are geographically concentrated, when demand-side cultural expectations are less varied, and when firms have less bargaining power over large institutional customers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper expands board-legitimacy research beyond capital market assessors by treating customers as grantors of firm legitimacy. It extends comparative corporate governance by showing that foreign product-market institutions, not only home-country institutions, can be associated with firm-level governance. It also complicates agency-theory assumptions about CEO power by showing that powerful CEOs may be legitimacy-enhancing in some customer environments.
practical_implication: The findings caution investors, proxy advisors, and regulators against treating low CEO power as universally good governance. For firms competing in foreign product markets where power distance is accepted, CEO-dominated boards may provide demand-side legitimacy benefits. Governance evaluations should therefore consider product-market culture, geographic sales concentration, cultural variance, and industry context.
limitations: The authors acknowledge possible ambiguity about whether firms adjust CEO power to match markets or target markets that fit existing CEO power. They also note that geographic segment sales data assume that purchasers are located in the reported country, which may not always hold. The study focuses on demand-side legitimacy among large institutional customers, so other stakeholder groups and other customer types remain outside the empirical scope.
future_research: Future research could use more granular customer-location data to assess the cultural-cognitive influence of actual purchasing agents. Additional studies could extend the demand-side legitimacy framework to suppliers, employees, or other salient stakeholders. The authors also call for work on whether the framework generalizes beyond firms that sell primarily to large institutional customers.
abstract: Agency theory-grounded research on boards of directors and firm legitimacy has historically viewed CEO power as de-legitimating, often taking this fact for granted in theorizing about external assessors’ evaluations of a firm. With few exceptions, this literature has focused exclusively on capital market participants (e.g., investors, securities analysts) as the arbiters of a firm’s legitimacy and has accordingly assumed that legitimate governance arrangements are those derived from the shareholder-oriented prescriptions of agency theory. We extend this line of research in new ways by arguing that customers also externally assess firm legitimacy, and that firms potentially adjust their governance characteristics to meet customers’ norms and expectations. We argue that the cultural-cognitive institutions prevalent in customers’ home countries influence their judgments regarding a firm’s legitimacy, such that firms competing heavily in highpower distance cultures are more likely to have powerful CEOs, with CEO power a source of legitimacy—rather than illegitimacy—among customers. We also argue that the more dependent a firm is on its customers and the more salient cultural power distance is as a demand-side institutional norm, the greater this relationship will be. Data from 151 U.S. semiconductor and pharmaceutical firms over a 10-year period generally support our predictions.

title: Why Are Abusive Supervisors Abusive? A Dual-system Self-control Model
methods: Three-study design combining two experimental-causal-chain studies with full-time supervisors and a multi-wave, multi-source field study of supervisor-subordinate teams analyzed with multilevel structural equation modeling.
industry: Study 1 and Study 2 used full-time supervisors recruited from Amazon's Mechanical Turk; Study 3 used full-time employees at four financial institutions in China.
country: Study 1 and the hostile-attribution pretest sampled supervisors living in the United States or Canada; Study 3 was conducted in China.
time_period: Study 3 collected supervisor and subordinate data at two time points separated by one week; calendar dates are not reported.
units: Full-time supervisors, subordinates, and supervisor-subordinate teams.
n_sample: Study 1 analyzed 92 full-time supervisors; Study 2 analyzed 101 full-time supervisors; Study 3 analyzed complete data from 50 supervisors and 206 subordinates.
authors: Liang, L. H.; Lian, H.; Brown, D. J.; Ferris, D. L.; Hanig, S.; Keeping, L. M.
theories: dual-system theoretical framework of self-control; hostile attribution bias; mindfulness; victimization perspective of abusive supervision
keywords: abusive supervision; hostile attribution bias; mindfulness; self-control; subordinate performance; supervisor hostility
research_question: Why and when does subordinate poor performance lead supervisors to engage in abusive supervision? The paper asks whether supervisor hostility explains this relationship and whether hostile attribution bias and mindfulness shape the two stages of the self-control process.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a dual-system self-control account. Poor-performing subordinates are theorized as provocateurs who trigger supervisor hostility; this hostility creates an impulse to behave abusively, while reflective control can constrain whether the impulse becomes abusive supervision. Study 1 supports the effect of poor performance and hostile attribution on hostility, Study 2 supports the effect of hostility on abusive-supervision intentions especially under low mindfulness, and Study 3 supports the conditional indirect effect in the field when hostile attribution is high and mindfulness is low.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances abusive-supervision research by specifying why victim-precipitating subordinate behavior can elicit abuse: poor performance can generate supervisor hostility that becomes abusive behavior when self-control fails. It also integrates subordinate behavior with supervisor traits, showing that victimization processes depend on both the subordinate's performance and the supervisor's attributional and mindfulness tendencies. More broadly, it contributes to self-control theory by modeling both the strength of hostile desire and the regulation of that desire.
practical_implication: The authors argue that organizations may reduce abusive supervision by reducing hostile interpretations and by strengthening supervisors' awareness and acceptance of hostile feelings. They suggest cognitive reappraisal training and mindfulness training as interventions that may prevent hostility from becoming abusive behavior. They also note a selection implication: organizations may benefit from supervisors and subordinates who are better able to regulate behavior.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that they controlled for trickle-down antecedents but did not compare their self-control model against all possible antecedents of abusive supervision. They also note that abusive supervision may sometimes be effortful and intentional rather than a self-control failure, although their own evidence did not support that interpretation. The experimental studies used visualizations and intentions, while the field study strengthened external validity but did not support every main-effect hypothesis.
future_research: Future research could compare the self-control model with other frameworks for abusive-supervision antecedents beyond trickle-down accounts. The authors call for work relaxing the assumption that abusive supervision is always self-control failure by examining supervisory beliefs about the instrumental value of aggression. They also suggest using the dual-system framework to identify additional moderators of workplace victimization, including reappraisal tendencies, negative relationship histories, self-control capacity, sleep deprivation, and social norms.
abstract: Building on prior work which has shown that abusive supervision is a reaction to subordinates’ poor performance, we develop a self-control framework to outline when and why supervisors abuse poor-performing subordinates. In particular, we argue that poorperforming subordinates instill in supervisors a sense of hostility toward the subordinate, which in turn leads to engaging in abusive supervision. Within this self-control framework, poor performance is more likely to lead to abusive supervision when (a) the magnitude of the hostility experienced is higher (e.g., for those with a hostile attribution bias), or (b) the translation of hostility into abusive supervision is unconstrained (e.g., for those who are low in trait mindfulness). In two experimental studies with full-time supervisors where we manipulated the independent variable (Study 1) and the mediator (Study 2), and in a multi-wave and multi-source field study with data collected from supervisor–subordinate teams (50 supervisors and 206 subordinates) at two time points (Study 3), we found overall support for our predictions. Implications for how to reduce the occurrence of abusive supervision in the workplace are discussed.
apa_citation: Liang, L. H., Lian, H., Brown, D. J., Ferris, D. L., Hanig, S., & Keeping, L. M. (2016). Why are abusive supervisors abusive? A dual-system self-control model. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(4), 1385-1406. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0651

title: Local Partnering in Foreign Ventures: Uncertainty, Experiential Learning, and Syndication in Cross-Border Venture Capital Investments
methods: Empirical quantitative study using Thomson Reuters VentureXpert data on VC firm-venture dyads. The authors model local partnering in foreign ventures as a multilayered decision using sequential logit models, with multinomial logit, Heckman two-stage, sensitivity, and alternative-measure robustness tests.
industry: Global venture capital investments.
country: Global sample spanning 61 countries, including domestic and cross-border investments.
units: VC firm-venture dyads from first-round investments.
n_sample: 30,395 first-round investments, including 2,673 VC firms and 20,885 ventures; cross-border subsample models report 3,858 observations.
authors: Liu, Yu; Maula, Markku
theories: experiential learning in international partnering; knowledge-based arguments on partnering in foreign ventures; organizational learning literature
keywords: country-level uncertainty; cross-border venture capital; experiential learning; foreign ventures; local partnering; syndication; uncertainty; venture-level uncertainty
research_question: Why do firms not always partner with local firms in uncertain foreign ventures, despite the intuitive value of local partnering for mitigating uncertainty? The paper asks how venture-level uncertainty, country-level uncertainty, and corresponding forms of international experience shape VC firms' propensity to syndicate cross-border investments with local VC partners.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism contrasts the need for local partnering with the feasibility of forming local partnerships. Venture-level uncertainty increases the value of local information and therefore increases local syndication. Country-level uncertainty also creates a need for local knowledge, but weak institutional environments make dependable local partners and enforceable cooperation harder to secure, reducing local partnering. Experience generally reduces the need for partners, but host-country experience increases local embeddedness and makes local partnering more feasible.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to cross-border VC and international business research by unbundling uncertainty into venture-level and country-level sources with different effects on local partnering. It extends organizational learning arguments by showing that experience does not simply reduce reliance on partners: host-country experience can increase local partnering by improving feasibility, legitimacy, and local network access. Methodologically, it treats local partnering as a multilayered market-entry and partner-choice decision rather than a single binary choice.
practical_implication: For firms entering foreign countries, the paper implies that local partnering decisions should distinguish uncertainty about the venture from uncertainty about the host country. Local partners may be most valuable when venture-level uncertainty is high, but country-level institutional weakness can make local cooperation harder and riskier. For policy makers seeking foreign investment, improving formal institutional environments may increase the feasibility of cooperation between foreign investors and local partners.
limitations: The authors note that the VC sector is a professional service industry that relies on intense social relationships and limited physical infrastructure, so generalizability to manufacturing or other organizational populations requires further study. The focal country-level institutional dimension is the regulatory/legal environment, leaving broader institutional configurations and interactions for future work. The authors also acknowledge remaining opportunities to disentangle knowledge-based need and feasibility effects from alternative explanations such as risk sharing.
future_research: Future research should test whether the findings generalize beyond international VC to other organizational populations with project- and country-level uncertainty. The paper calls for studies examining a broader set of institutions and their interactions, as well as contextual factors at the country level and dyadic country-pair level. It also points to further work on the complex drivers and interactions shaping partnering decisions in foreign ventures.
abstract: If partnering with local firms is an intuitive strategy with which to mitigate uncertainty in foreign ventures, then why don’t organizations always partner with local firms, especially in uncertain settings? We address this question by unbundling the effects of uncertainty in foreign ventures at the venture and country levels. We contend that, while both levels increase the need for partnering with local firms in foreign ventures, country-level uncertainty increases the difficulty of partnering with local firms and decreases the likelihood of such partnerships. We also posit that experiential learning helps firms manage the two types of uncertainty, and thereby reduces the need for partnering—yet, experience in the host country makes partnering more feasible and increases the likelihood of such partnerships. To test our hypotheses, we conceptualize the decision to partner with a local firm in a foreign venture as a multilayered decision, and model it accordingly. Using a global sample of venture capital investments made between 1984 and 2011, we find support for the distinct effects of ventureand country-level uncertainty as well as for corresponding levels of experiential learning. These findings have implications for the literature on cross-border venture capital investment and international business in general.

title: Creative, Rare, Entitled, and Dishonest: How Commonality of Creativity in One’s Group Decreases an Individual’s Entitlement and Dishonesty
methods: Empirical quantitative multi-study design combining four experiments, a pilot study, and a supervisor-subordinate field survey. The studies use identity and rarity manipulations, behavioral dishonesty tasks, psychological entitlement measures, mediation tests, ANOVA, logistic regression, bootstrapping, and moderated regression.
industry: Experimental student and MBA participant pools plus a field sample drawn from a variety of organizations and jobs.
country: United States for at least the university student experiments; not consistently reported across all samples.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individuals and supervisor-subordinate dyads.
n_sample: Study 1: 139 students; Study 2: 131 students; Study 3: 153 MBA students; pilot study: 104 MBA students; Study 4: 202 MBA students; Study 5: 83 subordinate-supervisor pairs.
authors: Vincent, Lynne C.; Kouchaki, Maryam
theories: psychological entitlement; role identity theory; scarcity principle; social evaluation theory
keywords: creative role identity; dishonesty; prevalence of creativity; psychological entitlement; rarity of creativity; unethical behavior
research_question: When and why does creative role identity lead individuals to feel entitled and engage in dishonest or unethical behavior? The paper asks whether this relationship depends on whether creativity is perceived as rare rather than common in the relevant group.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that creative identity can derive value from creativity being viewed as rare, special, and unique. When individuals see their creative identity as rare in their group, that perceived rarity increases psychological entitlement, which then increases willingness to lie, steal, or engage in unethical behaviors. When creativity is framed as common in the group, the entitlement pathway and the link between creative identity and dishonesty are reduced.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends creative role identity theory by showing that creative identity can have negative moral consequences, not only positive links to creative behavior. It distinguishes creative identity from creative ability: prior work emphasized cognitive flexibility and rationalization, whereas this study theorizes entitlement as the pathway from creative identity to dishonesty. It also contributes to identity theory by showing that altering a defining component of an identity, here the rarity of creativity, can change the identity's behavioral implications.
practical_implication: Organizations that encourage creative identities should avoid framing creativity as a rare possession of a few special employees. The authors suggest emphasizing the common, everyday, and accessible nature of creativity so that employees can value creativity without inferring that they deserve special treatment. This is especially relevant for organizations or departments that label some roles as creative and others as noncreative.
limitations: The authors state that the experimental studies may limit generalizability even though they provide control over the psychological mechanism. They also note that the field study is correlational, so causal ordering in that sample cannot be inferred strongly. Another limitation is that supervisors' judgments of unethical behavior may vary with how creative they perceive an employee to be.
future_research: Future research should test the effect with different methods, samples, and manipulations of creative identity. The authors call for work comparing stable creative identity with primed creative identity and examining interactions between creative identity and creative ability. They also suggest studying cultural variation in the meaning of creative role identity and other rare identities or attributes, such as wealth, status, leadership, or hierarchical position.
abstract: We examine when and why creative role identity causes entitlement and unethical behaviors, and how this relationship might be reduced. We found that the relationships among creative identity, entitlement, and dishonesty are contingent on the perception of creativity being rare. Four experiments showed that individuals with a creative identity reported higher psychological entitlement and engaged in more unethical behaviors. Additionally, when participants believed that their creativity was rare rather than common, they were more likely to lie for money. Moreover, manipulation of the rarity of creative identity, but not of practical identity, increased psychological entitlement and unethical acts. We tested for the mediating effect of psychological entitlement on dishonesty using both measurement of mediation and experimental causal chain approaches. We further provide evidence from organizations. Responses from a sample of supervisor–subordinate dyads demonstrated that employees reporting strong creative identities who perceived creativity as rare in their work group, rather than common, were rated as engaging in more unethical behaviors by their supervisors. This paper extends prior theory on negative moral consequences of creativity by shedding new light on assumptions regarding the prevalence of creativity and the role psychological entitlement plays.
apa_citation: Vincent, L. C., & Kouchaki, M. (2016). Creative, rare, entitled, and dishonest: How commonality of creativity in one’s group decreases an individual’s entitlement and dishonesty. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(4), 1451-1473. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.1109

title: When Justice Promotes Injustice: Why Minority Leaders Experience Bias When They Adhere to Interpersonal Justice Rules
methods: Empirical quantitative full-cycle design combining a field survey and a controlled laboratory experiment. Study 1 uses supervisor-subordinate dyads from varied industries to test whether supervisor race and interpersonal justice interact to predict fairness perceptions and helping behavior. Study 2 uses a 2x2 between-subjects experiment manipulating supervisor race and interpersonal justice to test stereotype application, fairness perceptions, and undermining outcomes.
industry: Study 1 sampled full-time employees from a diverse set of industries, including financial services, banking, information technology, engineering, telecommunications, healthcare, and pharmaceuticals; Study 2 used undergraduate students in organizational behavior and human resource management classes.
country: United States for Study 2; Study 1 country not reported in paper.
time_period: Not reported in paper.
units: Study 1 supervisor-subordinate pairs; Study 2 undergraduate student participants.
n_sample: Study 1: 165 subordinate-supervisor pairs after listwise deletion. Study 2: 296 participants after excluding 11 participants who failed the message attention check.
authors: Zapata, C. P.; Carton, A. M.; Liu, J. T.
theories: fairness heuristic theory; organizational justice; social exchange perspectives on justice; stereotype application and inhibition
keywords: fairness perceptions; interpersonal justice rules; minority supervisors; stereotyping; upward-directed bias
research_question: The paper asks when and why minority supervisors experience bias from subordinates despite adhering to interpersonal justice rules. It tests whether interpersonal justice reduces threat and attention to supervisors' individuating characteristics, thereby allowing stereotypes to influence fairness judgments and subordinate behavior toward minority supervisors.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an alternating pattern of stereotype application and inhibition. When supervisors violate interpersonal justice rules, subordinates attend more closely to supervisors as possible sources of threat, which inhibits reliance on racial stereotypes. When supervisors adhere to interpersonal justice rules, subordinates feel less threat and divert attention elsewhere, making fairness judgments more vulnerable to stereotypes that minority supervisors are deceitful. These fairness judgments then translate into less helping and more undermining toward minority supervisors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper challenges the assumption in organizational justice and social exchange perspectives that supervisors who treat subordinates well reliably receive better treatment in return. It adds an attention-based account of when fairness heuristics become vulnerable to stereotyping. It also extends research on racial bias by theorizing upward-directed bias from subordinates toward minority supervisors.
practical_implication: The authors caution that minority supervisors face a lose-lose situation: violating interpersonal justice harms subordinates, but adhering to it can make stereotypes more influential. They suggest structural and situational interventions that increase subordinates' attention to supervisors' individuating characteristics, such as smaller units, proximity, one-on-one meetings, small group caucuses, and relationship-building routines. They also recommend that organizations supplement global fairness ratings with questions about specific justice behaviors.
limitations: The Study 1 field design remains vulnerable to spurious effects and did not include multiple subordinates from each organization, limiting assessment of group and interpersonal dynamics. Study 2 allows causal inference but used an electronically mediated supervisor who was not physically present. The authors also examined Black and Hispanic supervisors together and did not use a within-person design in which individuals had multiple supervisors of different races.
future_research: Future research can examine how bias may snowball through social contagion or be buffered by third parties who speak out against it. Scholars could test whether expectations for unjust behavior vary by supervisor race and whether lower expectations cause employees to perceive more injustice. The authors also call for more work on attention as a mechanism linking interpersonal justice, stereotyping, organizational structure, and other organizational outcomes.
abstract: Accumulated knowledge on organizational justice leaves little reason to doubt that organizational members benefit when leaders adhere to interpersonal justice rules. However, upon considering how justice behaviors influence subordinates’ cognitive processes, we predict that interpersonal justice has a surprising, unintended negative consequence. Supervisors who violate interpersonal justice rules trigger subordinates to search for reasons why their supervisors are threatening them, causing subordinates to be more attuned to supervisors’ individual characteristics and therefore unlikely to use stereotypes when evaluating them. In contrast, supervisors who adhere to interpersonal justice rules allow subordinates to divert attention away from them, leading subordinates’ judgments of their supervisors to be influenced by stereotypes. Consistent with these predictions, using field data we found that minority supervisors faced bias relative to Caucasian supervisors when supervisors adhered to—but not when they violated— interpersonal justice rules. We replicated this effect in an experiment and established that it is explained by an alternating pattern of stereotype application and inhibition: the stereotype that minority supervisors are more deceitful than Caucasians influenced fairness judgments when supervisors adhered to—but not when they violated— interpersonal justice rules. We then conducted exploratory analyses and identified one factor (unit size) that mitigates this troubling pattern.

title: Come Aboard! Exploring the Effects of Directorships in the Executive Labor Market
methods: Empirical quantitative study using BoardEx, Execucomp, Compustat, institutional ownership, and Fama-French industry data. The authors use propensity score matching to construct treated and counterfactual executive groups, then test promotion outcomes with event history and multinomial logit models, title promotion with multiple-failure event history analysis, and pay with OLS regression.
industry: Large, publicly traded companies.
units: Top executives of large, publicly traded companies, comparing first-time directors with matched non-director counterfactual executives.
n_sample: 2,104 top executives, consisting of 1,052 executives with first-time directorships and 1,052 matched counterfactual executives without directorships.
authors: Boivie, S.; Graffin, S. D.; Oliver, A. G.; Withers, M. C.
theories: certification theory; human capital; signaling theory; social capital
keywords: board service; certification; directorships; executive compensation; executive labor market; promotion to CEO
research_question: What do executives gain from serving on boards? The paper asks whether first-time board appointments benefit non-CEO executives in the executive labor market by increasing promotion to CEO, promotion in title, and pay at the executive's home firm.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that a first-time board appointment acts as a visible third-party certification of executive quality in an information-poor labor market. Board service also gives non-CEO executives access to board-level knowledge, governance experience, and social connections. These certification and capital-building benefits make executives more attractive for CEO and title promotions and may lead home firms to raise compensation to retain them.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to executive labor market research by theorizing and testing board service as a predictor of non-CEO executives' promotion and compensation outcomes. It extends certification theory beyond CEOs by showing that directorships can certify non-CEO executive quality. It also contributes to corporate governance research by identifying career benefits that may help explain why busy executives accept board appointments.
practical_implication: For boards and firms evaluating CEO succession candidates, first-time directorships may operate as visible signals of executive quality, but the paper also implies that such signals should be interpreted alongside other evidence of capability. For executives, board service can carry career returns beyond director fees, including promotion opportunities and higher compensation. For governance practice, these career incentives may shape directors' motivation to seek and retain board seats.
limitations: The authors state that endogeneity cannot be ruled out completely, although they use propensity score matching to reduce this threat. They also note that board appointments and subsequent CEO promotions may partly reflect stages of one promotion process, despite the study's lag structure and controls for COO and president positions. The analysis is also limited by the lack of large-scale data on executive search firms.
future_research: Future research could examine whether multiple board appointments and director-network centrality affect subsequent executive promotion. The authors also suggest studying whether prior director experience shapes the decisions and performance of executives after they become CEOs. Additional work could examine how executive search firms influence promotion to CEO and longer-term career trajectories.
abstract: In this study, we examine the following question: What do executives gain from serving on boards? We propose that board service benefits non-CEO-level executives in the executive labor market by acting as a certification mechanism and by providing access to unique knowledge, skills, and connections. We argue that non-CEO executives who gain directorships will be more likely to be promoted to CEO both inside and outside their home firm, will be more likely to be promoted internally, and will receive higher pay from their home firms. To test our ideas, we employ propensity score matching to construct a longitudinal sample of 2,104 top executives of large, publicly traded companies in the United States over the period 1996 to 2012. The results provide consistent support for our theory.

title: My Family Made Me Do It: A Cross-Domain, Self-Regulatory Perspective on Antecedents to Abusive Supervision
methods: Two empirical quantitative studies: a lagged survey study of supervisors and subordinates in a Fortune 500 financial services organization, followed by an experience sampling study of supervisors across multiple organizations and industries. Analyses include moderated regression in Study 1 and random coefficient modeling for nested daily data in Study 2.
industry: Study 1 used a Fortune 500 financial services organization; Study 2 used a multi-organization, multi-industry supervisor sample representing 22 industries.
country: Study 1 sampled the firm's North America offices; Study 2's country is not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 collected three survey waves across roughly four months; Study 2 collected 10 consecutive daily surveys during a two-week work period. Calendar dates are not reported in paper.
units: Supervisors, subordinates, and supervisor-day observations.
n_sample: Study 1: 134 supervisors and 580 subordinates after exclusions; Study 2: 92 supervisors retained, with 857 daily observations.
authors: Courtright, Stephen H.; Gardner, Richard G.; Smith, Troy A.; McCormick, Brian W.; Colbert, Amy E.
theories: ego depletion; resource drain theory; self-regulatory resource depletion
keywords: abusive supervision; ego depletion; family-work conflict; gender; resource drain theory; situation control
research_question: The paper asks whether family-work conflict helps explain why supervisors behave abusively toward subordinates. It examines whether FWC predicts abusive supervision through ego depletion and whether gender and situation control condition the strength and stage of this process.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that competing family and work demands drain supervisors' finite self-regulatory resources. When ego depletion reduces supervisors' capacity to restrain aggressive impulses, abusive supervision becomes more likely. The paper finds that gender matters mainly because daily FWC is more strongly associated with ego depletion for female supervisors, while situation control matters because ego depletion is more strongly associated with abusive supervision when external sanctions are weaker.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to abusive supervision research by shifting attention from work-domain antecedents, social learning, displaced aggression, and moral exclusion toward a cross-domain self-regulatory explanation. It argues that abusive supervision can arise from depleted self-control caused by family-work conflict, not only from purposeful targeting, learned behavior, or workplace frustration. It also extends resource drain theory by showing a maladaptive work-domain outcome of FWC and by specifying gender and situation control as distinct moderators in the ego-depletion process.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that organizations seeking to reduce abusive supervision should address supervisors' family-work dynamics, not only select leaders or improve immediate workplace conditions. Flexible work arrangements may help reduce FWC, and policies or climates that make sanctions for abusive behavior salient may weaken the translation of ego depletion into abuse. The authors also point to recovery of self-regulatory resources, including leisure and sleep-related interventions, as a possible prevention route.
limitations: The authors note that Study 2's daily variables were collected from the same source at the same time of day, so same-source bias may have affected the mediation results despite supplementary lagged analyses. Study 2's multi-industry sample helped generalizability but did not allow industry or macro-level moderation tests. The authors also acknowledge possible overlap between cognitive ego depletion and emotional mood-spillover processes, even though they controlled for daily hostility.
future_research: Future research could examine how abusive supervision and its antecedent relationships vary across industries and other macro-level conditions. The authors call for more precise work separating cognitive ego-depletion processes from emotional reactions to FWC. They also suggest studying antecedents of FWC and using more extensive panel and event studies to test chronic effects of life events and FWC on abusive supervision.
abstract: Drawing on resource drain theory, we introduce self-regulatory resource (ego) depletion stemming from family–work conflict (FWC) as an alternative theoretical perspective on why supervisors behave abusively toward subordinates. Our two-study examination of a cross-domain antecedent of abusive supervision stands in contrast to prior research, which has focused primarily on work-related factors that influence abusive supervision. Further, our investigation shows how ego depletion is proximally related to abusive supervision. In the first study, conducted at a Fortune 500 company and designed as a lagged survey study, we found that, after controlling for alternative theoretical mechanisms, supervisors who experienced FWC displayed more abusive behaviors toward subordinates, and that this relationship was stronger for female supervisors and for supervisors who operated in environments with greater situation control. These results were then replicated and expanded in an experience sampling study using a multi-organization sample of supervisors. This allowed us to study the FWC–abusive supervision relationship as it emerged on a day-to-day basis and to examine ego depletion as an explanatory mechanism. Consistent with our hypotheses, we found that FWC was associated with abusive supervision, ego depletion acted as a mediator of the FWC–abusive supervision relationship, and that gender and situation control served as moderators.

My family made me do it: A cross-domain, self-regulatory perspective on antecedents to abusive supervision. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1630-1652. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1009

title: Managing Coordination in Multiteam Systems: Integrating Micro and Macro Perspectives
methods: Empirical quantitative study of 236 fourteen-person United States Air Force multiteam systems in a realistic computer-based Leadership Development Simulation. The authors used behavioral log measures and hierarchical linear regressions with bootstrapped moderated-mediation tests at the multiteam-system level.
industry: Military leadership development / United States Air Force officer training simulation
time_period: Five-week leadership development course; third Leadership Development Simulation session analyzed after first two sessions developed IFD.
units: Fourteen-person multiteam systems comprising component teams and an integration team
n_sample: 236 multiteam systems comprising 3,304 United States Air Force officers
authors: de Vries, Thomas A.; Hollenbeck, John R.; Davison, Robert B.; Walter, Frank; van der Vegt, Gerben S.
theories: intrapersonal functional diversity; multiteam systems theory; organization theory; organizational behavior
keywords: aspirational behavior; horizontal coordination; intrapersonal functional diversity; multiteam system performance; multiteam systems; vertical coordinated action
research_question: How does intrapersonal functional diversity shape multiteam system performance through horizontal coordination and aspirational behavior? The paper asks whether vertical coordinated action by an integration team enables multiteam systems to capture IFD's coordination benefits while reducing its downside for aspirational behavior.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a moderated mediation model. IFD gives members broader knowledge across functional domains, which can help component teams coordinate horizontally, but it can also reduce specialized task focus and thereby constrain aspirational behavior. Vertical coordinated action supplies top-down integration: when high, it strengthens the IFD-to-horizontal-coordination path and attenuates the negative IFD-to-aspirational-behavior path; when low, IFD's negative performance implications through reduced aspirational behavior become more salient.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates micro-level organizational behavior and macro-level organization theory perspectives on multiteam systems. It shows that IFD is not simply beneficial or harmful; instead, its performance implications depend on whether vertical coordinated action helps component teams use broad functional knowledge while sustaining complex, specialized activities. The contribution is a cross-level account of how bottom-up component-team capacities and top-down integration-team action jointly shape multiteam system effectiveness.
practical_implication: Managers can improve multiteam system performance by developing broad functional experience through job rotation, personnel transfer, career development, or cross-training, but the paper cautions that IFD alone is insufficient. Integration teams need to actively align their work with component teams through vertical coordinated action. The practical recommendation is to combine IFD-building interventions with coordination support, such as frame-of-reference training and interventions that help integrative leaders provide feedback on system effectiveness.
limitations: The authors note that ethical and practical issues prevented random assignment or experimental manipulation of IFD, so stronger causal inference requires future experimental evidence. The study uses a controlled military simulation, which provides psychological realism and comparable systems but limits generalization to longer-term and non-military multiteam contexts. The behavioral log measures also do not capture finer-grained cognitive, affective, communication, or micro-process mechanisms through which IFD and vertical coordinated action operate.
future_research: Future research could examine antecedents of IFD, including whether voluntary functional rotation differs from forced rotation after poor performance. The authors also call for work on alternative contingencies such as interteam task interdependence, environmental uncertainty, and task complexity, which may change when IFD helps coordination or harms aspirational behavior. Additional studies could investigate antecedents and microfoundations of vertical coordinated action, including integration teams' task orientations, goal orientations, dominance, and assertiveness.
abstract: Multiteam systems (i.e., teams of teams) are frequently used to deal with complex and demanding challenges that require several teams' joint efforts. However, achieving effective horizontal coordination across component teams in these systems remains difficult. Using insights from organizational behavior research, we argue that horizontal coordination between component teams can benefit if a multiteam system is composed of generalist members who are acquainted with the multiple functions present in the overall system (i.e., high intrapersonal functional diversity [IFD]). At the same time, however, such IFD may have detrimental side effects because generalists' broad focus may distract them from high-impact, specialized activities (i.e., aspirational behavior). Building on insights from organization theory, we propose that coordination across a multiteam system's hierarchical layers (i.e., vertical coordinated action between a team tasked with system-wide integration and task-specialized component teams) is critical for reaping IFD's benefits while avoiding its costs. These notions are supported in a sample of 236 14-person multiteam systems engaged in a realistic decision-making simulation. Our findings illustrate how combining insights from organizational behavior and organization theory can advance academic knowledge on multiteam systems and offer practical solutions for managing such systems.

title: Dual Directors and the Governance of Corporate Spinoffs
methods: Empirical quantitative study of corporate spinoffs using hand-collected director data from SEC filings, Compustat and CRSP financial and stock-market data, deal fixed effects regressions, treatment effects models, and switching regressions.
industry: Fortune 500 firms undertaking corporate spinoffs across industries.
time_period: Spinoffs announced and completed between January 1, 1995 and December 31, 2009; Fortune 500 membership assessed between 1995 and 2009, inclusive.
units: Parent-spinoff firm pairs and four-year post-spinoff panels for parent and spinoff firms.
n_sample: 228 spinoffs undertaken by 196 Fortune 500 firms.
authors: Feldman, Emilie R.
theories: resource dependence theory; transaction cost economics
keywords: corporate spinoffs; dual directors; parent firms; resource dependence theory; sales dependence; spinoff firms; stock market returns; transaction cost economics
research_question: The paper asks how dual directors enable firms undertaking corporate spinoffs to manage post-spinoff relationships with divested firms. It also asks what implications dual directors have for parent and spinoff firm performance, especially when spinoff firms depend on parent firms for sales.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that dual directors give parent firms power over spinoff firms by recreating some governance capacity after a shift from hierarchy to market. Drawing on transaction cost economics, the paper argues that this power can coordinate post-spinoff relationships and be value-creating on average. Drawing on resource dependence theory, it argues that when the spinoff firm is highly dependent on the parent firm as a buyer, dual directors have both the ability and incentive to exercise power in ways that benefit the parent firm at the spinoff firm's expense.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops corporate spinoff governance as a distinct domain rather than treating parent and spinoff firms as independent after divestiture. It extends transaction cost economics by showing that governance mechanisms can enable one firm to exercise power over a market counterparty, not only safeguard against opportunism. It also uses resource dependence theory to specify when that power becomes redistributive rather than merely coordinative.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that parent firms can use dual directors to coordinate post-spinoff relationships and improve average parent-spinoff returns. They also warn that dual directors may create distributional concerns when the spinoff firm depends heavily on the parent firm for sales. Thus, the same governance mechanism can appear value-creating on average while redistributing value toward the parent in high-dependence spinoff relationships.
limitations: The paper notes that it analyzes the static relationship between dual directors and performance rather than the dynamic evolution of dual director appointments and departures. It treats dual directors as a governance mechanism used by parent firms, while leaving their individual incentives, characteristics, and motivations largely unexplored. It also raises questions about generalizability beyond corporate spinoffs to other market-governed relationships where firms may appoint representatives to counterparties' boards.
future_research: Future research could examine why dual directors leave parent boards, spinoff boards, or both, and how those departures affect parent and spinoff firms. Additional work could study how dual director characteristics shape corporate governance quality in spinoff firms, including the meaning of director independence in this context. Researchers could also test whether similar power-preserving board appointments appear in other scope-reducing deals, buyer-supplier exchanges, ecosystems, top management teams, or large-shareholder relationships.
abstract: This paper investigates how “dual directors” enable firms that undertake corporate spinoffs to manage their post-spinoff relationships with the firms they divest, as well as the performance implications of dual directors serving simultaneously on these companies’ boards. While the presence of dual directors is positively associated with the average stock market returns of parent and spinoff firms, their presence is also increasingly positively associated with parent firm performance, but increasingly negatively associated with spinoff firm performance as the share of sales a spinoff firm makes to its parent firm rises. These findings show that, while dual directors give a parent firm power over its spinoff firm, dual directors only exercise that power at the spinoff firm’s expense when that company is highly dependent on its parent firm.

title: An Approach–Avoidance Framework of Workplace Aggression
methods: Two multi-wave field studies of employees in China; survey measures of workplace aggression, anger, anxiety, and approach- or avoidance-oriented counterproductive workplace behaviors analyzed with structural equation modeling in Mplus 6.1.
industry: Study 1: information technology, banking, electronic commerce, and telecom service; Study 2: banking, media, hospitality, retail, information technology, and real estate.
time_period: Study 1 used three survey waves approximately four months apart; Study 2 used three survey waves approximately two months apart.
units: Employees reporting on supervisor-related mistreatment, emotions, and counterproductive workplace behaviors.
n_sample: Study 1 final sample: 257 respondents; Study 2 final sample: 357 respondents.
authors: Ferris, D. L.; Yan, M.; Lim, V. K. G.; Chen, Y.; Fatimah, S.
theories: approach–avoidance framework of emotions; approach–avoidance motivation; workplace aggression theory
keywords: abusive supervision; anger; anxiety; approach–avoidance principles; counterproductive workplace behaviors; supervisor undermining; workplace aggression; workplace ostracism
research_question: The paper asks whether workplace aggression constructs that often appear empirically similar can be differentiated through an approach–avoidance framework. It examines whether abusive supervision, supervisor undermining, and workplace ostracism differentially elicit anger or anxiety and, through those emotions, different types of counterproductive workplace behavior.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that workplace aggression involving clear negative intent and responsibility, such as abusive supervision or supervisor undermining, elicits anger, an approach-oriented emotion, which then predicts approach-oriented counterproductive workplace behaviors. Workplace ostracism is theorized as more ambiguous about whether harm occurred and who is responsible, so it elicits anxiety, an avoidance-oriented emotion, which then predicts avoidance-oriented counterproductive workplace behaviors. The two studies test these differentiated indirect paths rather than treating workplace aggression constructs as interchangeable indicators of mistreatment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes an approach–avoidance model of workplace aggression that explains when aggression constructs should have distinct nomological consequences. It extends workplace aggression research by linking specific forms of mistreatment to distinct emotions and action tendencies rather than relying only on negative affect or broad CWB categories. It also contributes to emotion and CWB research by showing that negative emotions with different approach–avoidance properties predict different behavioral responses.
practical_implication: The paper argues that interventions should be matched to the emotional and behavioral pathway involved. Anxiety-reducing interventions are more relevant for workplace ostracism, whereas anger-reducing interventions are more relevant for abusive or undermining supervision and approach-oriented counterproductive behavior.
limitations: The authors note that the data came from one source, which raises common method concerns, although the studies used temporal separation between independent, mediator, and dependent variables. They also state that the data are not experimental, so the results should be viewed as consistent with, but not definitive evidence of, causality. A further limitation is that assumptions about how abusive supervision and ostracism are interpreted were not directly tested.
future_research: The paper calls for cross-lagged and experience-sampling designs to test temporal ordering and reciprocal effects among aggression events, emotions, and counterproductive behaviors. It also encourages research on moderators and boundary conditions, such as when abusive supervision does not elicit anger or when ostracism varies in causal clarity.
abstract: The number of constructs developed to assess workplace aggression has flourished in recent years, leading to confusion over what meaningful differences exist (if any) between the constructs. We argue that one way to frame the field of workplace aggression is via approach–avoidance principles, with various workplace aggression constructs (e.g., abusive supervision, supervisor undermining, and workplace ostracism) differentially predicting specific approach or avoidance emotions and behaviors. Using two multi-wave field samples of employees, we demonstrate the utility of approach– avoidance principles in conceptualizing workplace aggression constructs, as well as the processes and boundary conditions through which they uniquely influence outcomes. Implications for the workplace aggression literature are discussed.
apa_citation: Ferris, D. L., Yan, M., Lim, V. K. G., Chen, Y., & Fatimah, S. (2016). An approach–avoidance framework of workplace aggression. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1777-1800. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0221

title: Big Data and Data Science Methods for Management Research
methods: Editorial (From the Editors) primer and methods-guidance essay explaining how big data and data science can support management research through data scope, data granularity, and practical techniques for data collection, storage, processing, analysis, reporting, and visualization.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: George, Gerard; Osinga, Ernst C.; Lavie, Dovev; Scott, Brent A.
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: big data; data analysis; data collection; data granularity; data processing; data science; data scope; data storage; management theory; reporting and visualization
research_question: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Big data and data science can help management scholars produce better answers to existing questions and develop new questions by using greater data scope and data granularity.
- Key constructs: Big data; data science; data scope; data granularity; volume; velocity; variety.
- Data scope: The editorial reframes big data volume as the comprehensiveness of data available for examining a phenomenon, including wider variables, whole populations, and numerous observations.
- Data granularity: The editorial reframes data variety as theoretically proximal measurement, such as sensors, biometrics, messages, or digital traces rather than distal surveys or retrospective reports.
- Starter kit: The essay organizes practical guidance around data collection, data storage, data processing, data analysis, and reporting and visualization.
- Boundary conditions: The authors caution that the field is evolving rapidly and that privacy, data rights, construct validity, causal inference, robustness, and reporting transparency remain central challenges.

The process logic is editorial and methodological rather than empirical. George, Osinga, Lavie, and Scott argue that data science can expand management theory by improving the precision of answers to established questions and opening questions that were previously constrained by data access or analysis limits. They connect this opportunity to concrete methods, including sensors, web scraping, communications monitoring, SQL and NoSQL storage, text mining, variable selection, cross-validation, field experiments, parallelization, sequential updating, and visualization.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a new named theory. Its contribution is to translate big data's volume, velocity, and variety into management-research concepts of data scope and data granularity, then explain how those concepts can support theory testing, theory development, refined units of analysis, and clearer attention to mechanisms.
practical_implication: For management scholars, the editorial provides a starter kit for deciding how to collect, store, process, analyze, report, and visualize big data. It also advises authors to describe data sources, preprocessing, merging, model tuning, robustness checks, effect sizes, out-of-sample performance, and visualization choices carefully rather than treating large sample size or predictive validity as sufficient evidence.
limitations: The authors state that data science methods are evolving rapidly and that the editorial can only offer a primer rather than a definitive methods manual. They also note practical and ethical limits around privacy laws, research ethics, data ownership, data reliability, data storage tradeoffs, causal inference, spurious correlations, and context-sensitive measurement.
future_research: The editorial encourages scholars to use data scope and data granularity to revisit established management theories, generate more accurate answers, and pose new questions about mobility, communication, physical space, collaboration, decision making, social inclusion, public services, and organizational design. It also suggests that management research can enter a new phase as researchers adopt more refined units of analysis and use data science to illuminate mechanisms behind observed effects.

title: When Do Entrepreneurs Accurately Evaluate Venture Capital Firms’ Track Records? A Bounded Rationality Perspective
methods: Hybrid research design combining two waves of qualitative interviews with ordered-logit analysis of TheFunded.com entrepreneur ratings, LPJ venture-capital track-record scores, Alexa web-traffic prominence measures, and robustness tests including GEE, Heckman selection, alternative accuracy measures, and expanded VC samples.
industry: Early-stage U.S. venture capital firms and entrepreneurs seeking equity investments
units: Entrepreneur-VC rating dyads
n_sample: 1,278 quality perceptions of 153 VCs by 785 entrepreneurs
authors: Hallen, Benjamin L.; Pahnke, Emily Cox
theories: bounded rationality; firm reputation; signaling theory; social networks
keywords: bounded rationality; entrepreneurs; evaluative accuracy; firm reputation; prominence; track record; venture capital firms
research_question: The paper asks when entrepreneurs are more or less accurate in evaluating a venture capital firm's track record. It examines how evaluator characteristics, especially network centrality and motivation to search, combine with evaluated-firm characteristics, especially objective track record and prominence, to shape the match between entrepreneurs' perceptions and VC track-record quality.
mechanism_summary:
- Focal relationship: Entrepreneur evaluations of VC track records in an information-sparse fundraising context.
- Evaluator-side factors: Entrepreneur network centrality and motivation to search for information, operationalized through absence of prior community ratings and receipt of an offer.
- Evaluated-firm factors: VC objective track record, captured with the LPJ index, and VC prominence, captured with web traffic.
- Outcome: Accuracy of entrepreneur ratings, measured as the alignment between TheFunded track-record ratings and LPJ track-record scores.
- Process: Bounded rationality leads entrepreneurs to conserve effort, rely on accessible information, and use heuristics such as social proof, halo effects, and prominence cues.

The process is cross-level and dyadic: entrepreneurs do not simply read firm quality from an objective track record. They evaluate a VC through the information they can access, the effort they are motivated to expend, and the salience of VC-level cues. Centrality and motivation generally improve accuracy, stronger VC track records make accurate evaluation easier, and prominence can reduce accuracy by making incomplete or biased cues more available.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to firm reputation research by shifting attention from collective perceptions in information-rich settings to individual evaluative accuracy in information-sparse settings. It argues that reputation-relevant perceptions vary across evaluators and are shaped by both evaluator access/motivation and target-firm attributes. It also separates track record from prominence: stronger track records can improve accuracy by making information easier to pull, whereas high prominence can impair accuracy by pushing biased or incomplete cues.
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs may misjudge potential partners when they rely on visible prominence, prior community impressions, or narrow network information instead of systematically checking track-record evidence. The paper implies that entrepreneurs can benefit from better benchmarks, rankings, and education-oriented programs that help them compare VCs more rigorously before accepting investment partners.
limitations: The study examines entrepreneurs' perceptions of VCs they had met, not all possible entrepreneur-VC evaluations. The perceptual data use a coarser scale than the LPJ index, requiring assumptions about how to compare the two measures. TheFunded also collects limited information about entrepreneurs for privacy reasons, so the study uses indirect measures of centrality and motivation rather than richer direct measures.
future_research: Future research could use alternative designs to study entrepreneurs' evaluations of VCs they have not met, compare individual perceptions with collective field-level perceptions, test evaluative inaccuracy in other professional-service or information-rich contexts, and develop more direct measures of evaluator motivation, network access, bias, and reliability.
abstract: There has been substantial research on the value of young firms engaging high-quality partners. This literature, as well as the broader firm reputation literature, has tended to assume that individuals leading such firms find it relatively easy to accurately assess potential partner quality as reflected in their track record of past performance and behavior. Yet this prior work has largely focused on information-rich environments where potential partners are generally large and receive substantial public attention, and with whom evaluators may have high familiarity. In contrast, we draw on bounded rationality to theorize about how in information-sparse environments, individuals may misperceive the quality indicated by a firm’s objective track record. We argue that accurate evaluations depend not only on individuals’ motivation and ability to access information but on the convergence of these factors with attributes of the potential partner being evaluated. We test and find support for our framework using a novel dataset of 1,278 ratings of the quality of 153 early-stage venture capital firms by entrepreneurs that approached these firms for investments. Overall, this paper extends understanding of firm reputation dynamics to information-sparse contexts, and explores why individuals such as entrepreneurs may at times have difficulty accurately evaluating partners.
apa_citation: Hallen, B. L., & Pahnke, E. C. (2016). When do entrepreneurs accurately evaluate venture capital firms’ track records? A bounded rationality perspective. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1535-1560. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0316

title: The Quest for Originality: A New Typology of Knowledge Search and Breakthrough Inventions
methods: Empirical quantitative patent study of U.S. firm nanotechnology inventions. The authors construct patent-level measures of original search, local and boundary-spanning search types, path-breaking novelty, and high-impact breakthroughs, then estimate logit, negative binomial, and OLS models with robust standard errors clustered by firm, plus robustness checks with firm fixed effects, instrumental variables, alternative measures, expanded samples, and examiner-citation exclusions.
industry: U.S. nanotechnology patents classified under USPTO Class 977.
time_period: 1980 to 2006 for granted nanotechnology patents; forward citations measured through 2010.
units: Firm nanotechnology patents and patent-cited year observations.
n_sample: 1,848 nanotechnology patents granted to 504 U.S. firms, plus 7,006 patent-cited year observations for the post hoc citation analysis.
authors: Jung, H. J.; Lee, J.
theories: firm exploration; knowledge search; recombinant knowledge; technological uncertainty
keywords: high-impact breakthrough; knowledge search; nanotechnology patents; original search; path-breaking novelty; search boundary
research_question: How does the target of knowledge search, especially original knowledge, reshape the relationship between search boundary and breakthrough inventions? The paper asks whether original search affects two distinct inventive outcomes: path-breaking novelty and high-impact breakthrough.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that original knowledge carries unresolved technological uncertainty because it represents first-ever recombinations that remain primitive or underdeveloped. Searching original knowledge can produce path-breaking novelty by pushing firms toward new recombinations, and it can produce high-impact breakthroughs when subsequent inventions resolve uncertainty and make the searched knowledge useful to later inventors. The paper finds the strongest and most robust evidence for local original search producing high-impact breakthroughs; boundary-spanning original search is theorized to favor path-breaking novelty, but that comparison is weak in the main analysis and receives stronger support in robustness tests.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends knowledge-search theory by adding search target, original versus ordinary knowledge, to the conventional local versus boundary-spanning typology. It distinguishes path-breaking novelty from high-impact breakthrough and shows that their antecedents can differ. It also contributes to recombinant-knowledge research by separating the generation of new recombinations from the search and assimilation of prior original knowledge.
practical_implication: For R&D managers seeking high-impact breakthroughs, the paper suggests focusing attention on local search of original knowledge rather than treating boundary-spanning search as the only route to major invention. For managers seeking path-breaking novelties, extending search beyond the local domain may be more useful. The authors caution that this does not mean firms should only search locally, because boundary-spanning search can help generate original knowledge that later becomes useful through local search.
limitations: The authors note that the nanotechnology setting is emerging and under-commercialized, so the findings should be interpreted carefully for established fields or industries with traditional product classes. The study relies on patent citations and therefore omits knowledge-search channels such as consultants, customers, suppliers, and other non-patent sources. The authors also acknowledge possible unobserved heterogeneity and potential endogeneity in firms' search strategies, plus possible incompleteness in USPTO Class 977 nanotechnology classification.
future_research: Future research could test whether the theory generalizes to settings where patents are less useful or unavailable for tracing knowledge search. The authors suggest applying textual analysis to journal publications or other knowledge media to measure original search, topic centrality, and novelty. Additional work could examine established industries where complementary technologies and product classes make boundary-spanning search more important.
abstract: We re-examine firm exploration leading to breakthrough inventions by focusing on a new dimension of knowledge search: the search of originality. We conceptualize firm search types with two distinct dimensions—search target and search boundary—and propose contrasting effects of the search boundary in which firms search prior original knowledge on the propensities for firms to create path-breaking novelties and highimpact breakthroughs. In particular, we demonstrate that searching original knowledge and incorporating it into research and development makes local search outperform boundary-spanning search in generating high-impact breakthroughs. We argue that this advantage of local search arises from the originality that firms search and revitalize. We find robust support from the analysis of U.S. firm nanotechnology patents between 1980 and 2006. Our findings highlight the importance of searching original knowledge and the benefit of local search in creating breakthrough inventions, thereby suggesting a refinement of the conventional framework of knowledge search.
apa_citation: Jung, H. J., & Lee, J. (2016). The quest for originality: A new typology of knowledge search and breakthrough inventions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1725-1753. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0756
