title: Whatever It Takes to Win: Rivalry Increases Unethical Behavior
methods: Empirical quantitative multi-study design combining an archival analysis of professional soccer matches with experiments and recall-based negotiation scenarios. Study 1 uses Poisson and logistic regression models on Serie A misconduct data; Studies 2-4 experimentally manipulate or elicit rivalry and test deception, willingness to use unethical negotiation tactics, and mediation pathways.
industry: Professional soccer in Italy, university rivalry, and simulated car-dealership negotiation contexts with online adult participants.
country: Italy and the United States; MTurk participant country is not reported in paper.
time_period: Study 1 soccer matches were played between 2002 and 2009; Studies 2-4 report sample characteristics but not calendar dates of data collection.
units: Professional soccer matches and player-match observations; undergraduate participants; MTurk adult participants.
n_sample: Study 1: 2,788 Serie A matches and 100,310 player-match observations; Study 2: 70 Ohio State undergraduate students; Study 3: 101 MTurk adults; Study 4: 243 MTurk adults.
authors: Kilduff, G. J.; Galinsky, A. D.; Gallo, E.; Reade, J. J.
theories: achievement goal theory; contingency of self-worth; ethical decision-making cost-benefit models; rivalry theory; status concerns
keywords: competition; deception; performance-approach orientation; rivalry; unethical behavior; unsporting behavior
research_question: The paper asks whether actors engage in more unethical behavior when competing against rivals than when competing against non-rival competitors. It also asks what psychological mechanisms distinguish rivalry from general competition and explain its effect on unethical behavior.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that rivalry adds relational and historical psychological stakes to competition beyond the objective stakes of winning. Competing against rivals increases the extent to which outcomes matter for actors' self-worth and relative status, which then encourages a stronger performance-approach orientation focused on outperforming the rival. That orientation makes actors more willing to use deception, unsporting conduct, and other unethical tactics to improve competitive outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to rivalry research by identifying a dark side of rivalry: it can increase unethical behavior, not only motivation and effort. It contributes to unethical behavior research by identifying rivalry as a relational antecedent and by showing that competition's effects depend on prior relationships and histories between actors. It also extends models of competition by separating rivalry from structural competition and specifying psychological stakes and performance orientation as explanatory mechanisms.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that rivalry can motivate effort while also increasing ethical risk. The paper suggests caution with structures that repeatedly pit similar and evenly matched employees against one another or overemphasize outperforming rival companies. It also recommends using objective data, explicit decision criteria, and outside perspectives to reduce the risk that rivalry distorts strategic and moral judgment.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 is archival, uses an indirect co-location measure of rivalry, and cannot definitively rule out objective stakes or referee judgment as alternative explanations. They also note that yellow and red cards are face-valid but imperfect measures of unethical behavior. Study 4 relies on self-report measures for threat and challenge rather than physiological assessment, and the empirical evidence focuses on individual behavior rather than direct organization-level misconduct.
future_research: Future research could examine whether rivalry increases organization-level unethical behavior such as accounting fraud. The authors also call for work on different types of unethical behavior, including carryover effects beyond the rivalry domain and behavior less directly tied to performance goals. Additional research could examine rivalry's affective and physiological profiles, the deliberative versus automatic nature of its effects, other consequences of rivalry, and moderators that prevent rivalry from becoming harmful.
abstract: This research investigates the link between rivalry and unethical behavior. We propose that people will be more likely to engage in unethical behavior when competing against their rivals than when competing against non-rival competitors. Across an archival study and a series of experiments, we found that rivalry was associated with increased unsporting behavior, use of deception, and willingness to employ unethical negotiation tactics. We also explore the psychological underpinnings of rivalry in order to illuminate how it differs from general competition and why it increases unethical behavior. The data reveal a serial mediation pathway whereby rivalry heightens the psychological stakes of competition (by increasing actors’ contingency of self-worth and status concerns), which leads to the adoption of a stronger performance-approach orientation, which then increases unethical behavior. These findings highlight the importance of rivalry as a widespread, powerful, yet largely unstudied phenomenon with significant organizational implications. They also help to inform when and why unethical behavior occurs within organizations, and demonstrate that the effects of competition are dependent upon relationships and prior interactions between actors.
apa_citation: Kilduff, G. J., Galinsky, A. D., Gallo, E., & Reade, J. J. (2016). Whatever it takes to win: Rivalry increases unethical behavior. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1508-1534. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0545

title: Stories about Values and Valuable Stories: A Field Experiment of the Power of Narratives to Shape Newcomers’ Actions
methods: Field experiment in a large Asian technology firm using an incomplete 2 x 2 factorial design plus a control condition. Narrative conditions varied character level and whether stories upheld or violated values; outcomes were peer-rated helping and deviance behaviors, analyzed with ANOVA and planned contrasts, with a post-hoc LIWC content analysis of participant-generated stories.
industry: Large technology firm.
country: Asian technology firm; specific country not reported in paper.
time_period: Newcomers were in a five-and-a-half-month training program; the manipulation occurred 10 weeks into training, with final peer-rated outcomes collected later in the training period.
units: Individual organizational newcomers in entry-level programming training groups.
n_sample: Initial cohort of 632 newcomers; four manipulated groups contained 290 individuals, 342 served as control, and 307 completed the final survey with peer evaluations.
authors: Martin, Sean R.
theories: behavioral contagion; organizational narratives; social identity theory
keywords: behavioral contagion; deviance behaviors; helping behaviors; narratives; organizational newcomers; organizational values; social identity
research_question: The paper asks how organizational narratives shape newcomers' enactment of organizational values. Specifically, it examines whether stories about high- versus low-level organizational characters, and values-upholding versus values-violating behavior, influence newcomers' helping and deviance behaviors.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that narratives convey normative information about organizational values through characters whose social distance from newcomers affects whether the story is interpreted as an in-group behavioral guide or as an out-group signal of injunctive norms. Low-level characters are expected to be socially closer to newcomers and to show what people like them do, while high-level characters are expected to be more socially distant and to signal formal values. The results only partly match the predicted interaction: helping behavior showed main effects rather than the hypothesized interaction, while deviance behavior showed the predicted interaction between character level and narrative type.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates organizational narrative research with social identity theory and behavioral contagion to explain how stories can transmit values without direct observation of behavior. It contributes by showing that character level and story valence matter for whether narratives shape values-upholding or values-violating newcomer behavior. It also extends business and behavioral ethics research by treating stories as durable mechanisms for making values salient in organizational socialization.
practical_implication: Organizations can use newcomer storytelling exercises as a relatively low-cost socialization tool, but the content and protagonists of those stories matter. Positive stories about high-level members may make formal values salient, while values-upholding stories about socially closer, low-level members may better illustrate how values should guide everyday behavior. The findings also warn that some high-level or values-violating stories may have unintended effects on peer evaluations and behavior.
limitations: The author notes that two unexpected findings could not be fully explained because the design did not measure all possible organizational influences beyond social identity theory, behavioral contagion, and narrative. The outcomes were peer-rated perceptions rather than objective behavioral records, because ITECH was unwilling to share documented deviance evidence and extended observation was infeasible. The setting was a single values-driven Asian technology firm with low-level newcomers, limiting conclusions about other values, industries, organizational levels, and longer-tenured employees.
future_research: Future research could test how narratives convey values other than self-transcendent values, including openness to change and constructive deviance. Additional studies could examine whether stories influence longer-tenured employees, mid-level organizational members, and audiences at different hierarchical levels. The paper also calls for research on whether the storyteller's organizational level and the formality of story delivery change narrative effects.
abstract: This study draws on social identity theories of behavioral contagion and research concerning narratives in organizations to present and test a framework for understanding how narratives embed values in organizational newcomers’ actions. Employing a field experiment using newly hired employees in a large IT firm that prioritizes selftranscendent values, this study explores how narratives that vary in terms of the organizational level of main characters and the values-upholding or values-violating behaviors of those characters influence newcomers’ tendencies to engage in behaviors that uphold or deviate from the values. The results indicate that stories about low-level organizational characters engaging in values-upholding behaviors are more positively associated with self-transcendent, helping behaviors, and negatively associated with deviant behaviors, than are similar stories about high-level members of the organization. Stories in which high-level members of the organization violate values are more strongly negatively related to newcomers’ engagement in both helping and deviance than are values-violating stories about lower-level members. Content analyses of the stories suggest that they convey values in different and potentially important ways. Implications, future directions, and limitations are discussed.
apa_citation: Martin, S. R. (2016). Stories about values and valuable stories: A field experiment of the power of narratives to shape newcomers’ actions. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1707-1724. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0061

title: Better Together? Signaling Interactions in New Venture Pursuit of Initial External Capital
methods: Empirical quantitative study of nascent high-technology startups in Oklahoma using VDO records, NETS, Dun and Bradstreet, public records, logit models with county-clustered robust standard errors, average marginal effects, and bivariate probit robustness checks.
industry: Nascent high-technology startup firms.
time_period: Startups initiated between 1995 and 2010.
units: New technology startup firms seeking startup capital.
n_sample: 986 firms, of which 142 received external capital investment.
authors: Plummer, Lawrence A.; Allison, Thomas H.; Connelly, Brian L.
theories: sensemaking; signaling theory
keywords: commercial property; initial external capital; managerial experience; new ventures; product introduction; sensemaking; signaling theory; third-party affiliations; venture development organizations
research_question: The paper asks how third-party affiliation signals interact with other startup signals during the pursuit of initial external capital. Specifically, it examines whether affiliation with a venture development organization helps potential investors interpret otherwise ambiguous signals: founder managerial experience, product introduction, and operation from commercial property.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that early stage financing is noisy, uncertain, and ambiguous, so ordinary startup characteristics and actions may not be noticed or may invite multiple interpretations. VDO affiliation serves as a third-party signal that endorses the venture and provides substantive benefits. Through investor sensemaking, this affiliation helps investors interpret managerial experience, product introduction, and commercial property as positive signals of venture quality, viability, and commitment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends signaling theory by showing that signals in early stage financing are not merely additive or independent. It argues that third-party affiliations can activate weaker signals that would otherwise remain ambiguous or unnoticed. It also brings sensemaking into entrepreneurial signaling theory to explain how receivers interpret bundles of signals under high information asymmetry and noise, shifting attention from IPO-stage signaling to the earlier milestone of securing any external funding.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that startup founders may improve their chances of receiving external capital by combining VDO affiliation with credible signals of capability and commitment, such as prior managerial experience, product introduction, and commercial property. For investors, the results imply that third-party affiliation can help interpret otherwise blunt early stage signals, but those signals should be evaluated as combinations rather than as isolated indicators.
limitations: The paper notes that managerial experience is measured as a count of other Oklahoma businesses owned or principally managed, without distinguishing startup experience, senior managerial experience, success, failure, duration, or firm size. It also uses binary measures for product introduction and commercial property, which are crude indicators of signal presence rather than signal strength. The study cannot establish the timing or sequencing of signals relative to VDO affiliation. One robustness check for product introduction endogeneity did not converge in the full specification, although a reduced-controls specification did not indicate reverse causality.
future_research: Future research could examine how third-party affiliations shape sensemaking differently for competence signals versus integrity signals. Researchers could study additional early stage signals such as family endorsement, business-plan keywords, geography, and signals relevant before entrepreneurs seek formal external capital. Further work could measure signal strength more granularly, including sales, market penetration, number of products, property class, zoning, lease terms, or multiple locations, and test whether signals acquired before, during, or after third-party affiliation have different effects.
abstract: After new ventures have exhausted the limited financial resources of founders, family, and friends, they often pursue initial external capital. To secure investment, entrepreneurs can signal about their venture’s latent potential by aligning themselves with reliable third parties. Such affiliations affirm the new venture’s legitimacy and provide substantive benefits in the form of mentoring, access to resources, and ongoing monitoring. However, early stage financing is an especially “noisy” signaling environment owing to the large number of startups seeking funding, many of which will not survive. The real value of third-party affiliations in this context resides in their ability to unlock the potential of other more pedestrian signals, such as the entrepreneur’s characteristics and actions that might otherwise go unnoticed. We borrow from the sensemaking literature to explain how third-party affiliation signals disambiguate signals with multiple possible interpretations so that potential investors interpret them positively. Findings support our theory that a startup’s characteristics and actions are signals that remain relatively unnoticed unless a startup combines them with a third-party affiliation that enhances the signal’s value, thus increasing the likelihood of receiving external capital.
apa_citation: Plummer, L. A., Allison, T. H., & Connelly, B. L. (2016). Better together? Signaling interactions in new venture pursuit of initial external capital. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1585-1604. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0100

title: Beginning’s End: How Founders Psychologically Disengage From Their Organizations
methods: Inductive qualitative grounded-theory study using semi-structured narrative interviews, follow-up interviews with theoretically sampled participants, field notes, contact summary forms, research memos, first-order and second-order coding, axial coding, and iterative model development.
industry: Technology and life-science ventures based around a start-up office facility
time_period: Initial interviews plus follow-up interviews one year later; calendar dates not reported in paper
units: Founders and their voluntary successful exit experiences
n_sample: 34 founders; 60 interviews; voluntary successful exits from 30 organizations and 5 working-for-acquirer experiences
authors: Rouse, Elizabeth D.
theories: identity theory; organizational identification; psychological disengagement; role transitions; work orientations
keywords: entrepreneurial exit; founder psychological disengagement; founder work orientations; identity; portfolio path; serial path
research_question: The paper asks how founders manage psychological disengagement from their organizations when they choose to leave them. It also examines how psychological disengagement processes influence how founders begin again.
mechanism_summary:
- Focal process: Founder psychological disengagement during voluntary successful exit from one organization and movement toward another.
- Work orientations: Self-fortifying founders prioritize their own ideas, personal development, money, learning, and ego-gratification; stewarding founders prioritize people, organizational sustainability, customers, and social contribution.
- Portfolio path: Self-fortifying founders tend to use idea stockpiling and side business developing before physical departure, making anticipatory identification with the next venture more salient than deidentification from the current organization.
- Serial path: Stewarding founders tend to use empowering others and recruiting replacements before leaving, followed by idea searching after departure; deidentification and loss are more salient before anticipatory identification with the next venture.
- Emotional dynamics: The portfolio path is associated with excitement and enthusiasm around the next opportunity, whereas the serial path involves sadness, pain, loss, and later movement toward more positive emotions.

The process model links founders' work orientations to different behavioral tactics, identification dynamics, and emotional experiences during exit. Self-fortifying founders psychologically move forward by building attachment to future ideas before fully leaving the current organization. Stewarding founders psychologically separate by protecting the current organization, making room for successors, and only later searching for the next opportunity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops an experience-based process theory of psychological disengagement that integrates behavior, cognition, and emotion before and after physical exit. It extends identification and role-transition theory by showing how deidentification and anticipatory identification vary in timing and salience. It also contributes to entrepreneurship research by explaining differences between serial and portfolio habitual founders through founder work orientations rather than only formal patterns of ownership or involvement.
practical_implication: Founders may need explicit preparation for the emotional challenges of disengagement, even when exit is financially or strategically successful. The paper suggests that founders, employees, venture capitalists, and other stakeholders should attend to founder work orientations because these orientations shape whether founders prioritize organizational continuity or move attention toward side businesses and future ventures.
limitations: The study focuses on founders, who may have unusually strong identity connections to their organizations, so transferability to employees or other occupational roles is uncertain. It studies founder experience rather than the consequences for the organizations being left. The sample size also limited the paper's ability to examine demographic or organizational predictors of founder work orientations.
future_research: Future research could test whether the disengagement paths apply to other roles, occupations, and organizational-exit contexts. Longitudinal studies could examine how founders' self-fortifying and stewarding orientations shift across careers and organizations. Larger-sample research could investigate demographic, investor, cofounder, employee-competence, and organizational conditions associated with different orientations and tactics, and could assess consequences for both exited and newly started organizations.
abstract: Exit is a critical part of the entrepreneurial process. At the same time, research indicates that founders are likely to form strong identity connections to the organizations they start. In turn, when founders exit their organizations, the process of psychological disengagement might destabilize their identities. Yet, limited research addresses how founders experience exit or how they manage their identities during this process. Through a qualitative, inductive study of founders of technology-based companies, I developed a theoretical model of founder psychological disengagement that delineates how founder work orientations relate to the disengagement paths that founders follow when leaving one organization and starting another. In elaborating on theory of psychological disengagement, this study has implications for understanding the psychology of founders, how founders exit and begin again, and psychological disengagement more broadly.
apa_citation: Rouse, E. D. (2016). Beginning’s end: How founders psychologically disengage from their organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1605-1629. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1219

title: The Dark Side of Board Political Capital: Enabling Blockholder Rent Appropriation
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study of Chinese listed manufacturing firms. The authors use fixed-effects hierarchical regressions with Heckman two-stage correction, supplemented by Poisson regressions on regulatory sanctions and additional debt-financing and firm-performance analyses.
industry: Manufacturing firms listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange or Shenzhen Stock Exchange.
units: Chinese listed manufacturing firms and their directors.
n_sample: 1,046 firms, 2,854 firm-year observations, and 32,174 individual directors.
authors: Sun, P.; Hu, H. W.; Hillman, A. J.
theories: agency theory; corporate political strategy; principal-principal agency theory; resource dependence theory
keywords: China; blockholder rent appropriation; board political capital; corporate political strategy; principal-principal agency; resource dependence theory
research_question: The paper asks whether board political capital has a downside by enabling controlling blockholders to appropriate more firm wealth from minority shareholders. It also asks when this enabling effect is stronger or weaker across ownership-, industry-, and environment-level contingencies.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that political capital on the board can be used not only to secure resources for the firm but also to increase the bargaining power of controlling blockholders over minority shareholders. Politically connected boards can buffer blockholders from legal and regulatory oversight and can provide alternative financing channels, thereby reducing constraints that would otherwise discipline appropriation. The effect is expected to be stronger for private blockholders and regulated industries, and weaker in provinces with more developed market-supporting institutions.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to resource dependence theory by identifying a condition under which board cooptation can impose costs rather than simply provide resources for the whole firm. It integrates resource dependence and agency theory by asking "resource provision for whom" and showing how board capital can aggravate principal-principal agency conflicts. It also contributes to corporate political strategy research by specifying a mechanism through which political ties may become detrimental.
practical_implication: The findings imply that outside investors should not treat board political connections as uniformly valuable. Investors should evaluate whether the firm's ownership, industry regulation, and institutional environment make political capital more likely to facilitate blockholder appropriation. For policymakers, the paper suggests that political directors are not inherently harmful, but their value-creation role depends on institutions that prevent one party from using political ties against other stakeholders.
limitations: The authors caution that the findings are based on Chinese listed companies and should be generalized carefully to contexts without concentrated ownership, passive boards, and weak institutions. ORECTA captures a transparent form of tunneling but may miss less visible forms of rent appropriation. The study also uses a dichotomous additive measure of board political capital and lacks detailed director-level data on bureaucratic rank and years of service.
future_research: Future research could test whether board capital also worsens managerial agency problems in widely held public corporations. It could examine whether the same mechanism operates in developed economies with more robust institutions and stronger board independence. Further work could collect more granular director-level political-capital data, develop measures of less visible appropriation, and trace longer-term co-movement between equity and debt financing.
abstract: Resource dependence theorists argue that boards of directors with political capital can benefit focal firms by reducing uncertainty and providing preferential resources. Here, we develop theory regarding the downside of board political capital. The problem of principal–principal agency is evident in many parts of the world, and we argue that board political capital can further exacerbate it by enabling large blockholders to undertake more appropriation of firm wealth. Further, we explore how this enabling effect is moderated by ownership-, industry-, and environment-level contingencies. We find empirical support for our arguments using 32,174 directors in 1,046 Chinese listed firms over the period 2008–2011. Our study sheds light on new ways in which resource dependence and agency theories can be integrated to advance the extant research on board governance and corporate political strategy.
apa_citation: Sun, P., Hu, H. W., & Hillman, A. J. (2016). The dark side of board political capital: Enabling blockholder rent appropriation. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1801-1822. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0425

title: How do Firms Adapt? A Fuzzy-Set Analysis of the Role of Cognition and Capabilities in U.S. Defense Firms’ Responses to 9/11
methods: Mixed-methods study combining qualitative industry knowledge, archival sources, preliminary expert interviews, letters-to-shareholders content coding, asset acquisition and divestment data, an expert survey of firm adaptation, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis of 17 U.S. defense firms before and after 9/11.
industry: Large publicly traded U.S. defense firms producing weapon systems and accounting for about 75% of U.S. defense procurement.
time_period: Observation window from 1998 to 2005, bracketing the four years before and after 9/11.
units: Firms, with firm-level measures of defense dependence, attention timing, attention intensity, reconfiguration scope, reconfiguration intensity, and adaptation.
n_sample: 17 firms; adaptation ratings from five defense industry experts; 137 letters to shareholders; 275 reconfiguration-scope events; 485 reconfiguration-intensity events.
authors: Vergne, Jean-Philippe; Depeyre, Colette
theories: dynamic capabilities; managerial cognition / attention perspective; resource dependence theory
keywords: 9/11; U.S. defense firms; asset reconfiguration; dynamic capabilities; firm adaptation; fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis; managerial attention; strategic non-adaptation
research_question: In an industry experiencing an environmental shift, how do managerial attention and asset reconfiguration contribute to firm adaptation or lack of adaptation? The paper asks whether cognition and dynamic capabilities explain adaptation as competing, complementary, necessary, or substitutable conditions.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / causal conditions: Defense dependence, attention timing, attention intensity, reconfiguration scope, and reconfiguration intensity.
- Outcome: Firm adaptation to post-9/11 industry conditions, calibrated from expert assessments.
- Process / paths: Four equifinal adaptation configurations: anticipative, responsive, opportunistic, and decisive.
- Non-adaptation path: Haphazard non-adaptation among low-defense-dependence firms with delayed, low-intensity attention and high-intensity but narrow reconfiguration.
- Boundary conditions: The U.S. defense sector is a research- and technology-intensive, business-to-government setting shaped by Pentagon demand and the post-9/11 environmental shift.

The process argument is conjunctural rather than linear: attention and reconfiguration matter in different combinations, and neither superior cognition nor dynamic capabilities alone is required for adaptation. Anticipative adapters use early, intense attention with relatively lower-intensity reconfiguration; responsive adapters reconfigure substantially after later attention; opportunistic adapters leverage existing assets; and decisive adapters respond with broader and more intense post-shift reconfiguration. Strategic non-adaptation is possible when managers may be aware of change but judge adaptation as a low priority given the firm's revenue profile.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates cognition and capabilities perspectives by comparing their explanatory power in the same empirical setting. It shows that adaptation can occur without superior cognition and without intensified dynamic capabilities, recasting these literatures as sometimes substitutable and sometimes complementary rather than universally necessary. It also contributes a taxonomy of adaptation and non-adaptation paths and argues that adaptation and non-adaptation are asymmetric outcomes.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers should not treat adaptation as a single best-practice recipe. Depending on dependence on the affected market segment and the timing of managerial attention, firms may adapt through early anticipation, broad reconfiguration, opportunistic redeployment of existing assets, or rapid decisive reconfiguration. It also cautions that large-scale reconfiguration concentrated in a narrow set of business units may not produce adaptation when attention is delayed and industry dependence is low.
limitations: The authors note that the defense industry has distinctive features: it is research- and technology-intensive, dominated by government customers, and shaped by public tenders. They also note heterogeneity among sampled firms, including specialists, related diversifiers, and conglomerates, and acknowledge that some configurations group firms that may differ in corporate scope. The use of letters to shareholders captures top-management attention and may miss middle-manager cognition in industries where resource reallocation can occur without top-management approval.
future_research: Future research could replicate the study in larger samples and add causal conditions such as politics or leadership change. The authors also call for studies of middle-manager cognition, especially in settings where resource reallocation may occur without top-management approval. Additional work could examine how cognition variables drive the choice between internal and external asset reconfiguration.
abstract: How do firms adapt? In recent years, this old question has attracted new answers—albeit partial ones. On the one hand, cognition researchers have emphasized managerial attention to environmental change as a key driver of adaptation. On the other hand, dynamic capabilities scholars have underscored the role of asset reconfigurations implemented amid shifting environments. However, the explanatory powers of the two perspectives have not yet been assessed comparatively. This mixed methods study uses fuzzy-set analyses of defense firms’ responses to 9/11 to model the two perspectives as potentially competing or complementary, while our findings suggest that neither dynamic capabilities nor superior cognition must be present for firms to adapt. Instead, we identify four types of adapters (anticipative, responsive, opportunistic, and decisive), as well as the possibility of strategic non-adaptation. These results lead us to reassess the cognition and capabilities literatures and to outline a new, integrative framework to explain adaptation.

title: Engaged and Productive Misfits: How Job Crafting and Leisure Activity Mitigate the Negative Effects of Value Incongruence
methods: Empirical quantitative field study using three time points and two sources. Employees reported value congruence, job crafting, leisure activity, and later engagement; supervisors later rated task performance and citizenship behavior. The analysis integrates polynomial regression, response surface methods, moderated mediation, path analysis, and bootstrapped confidence intervals.
industry: Diverse organizations and industries; the four most common industries were finance and banking, information technology, education, and health care.
time_period: Three time points separated by three-week intervals; calendar dates not reported in paper.
units: Full-time employees and their supervisors
n_sample: 193 employee respondents after matching responses and addressing missing data and outliers
authors: Vogel, Ryan M.; Rodell, Jessica B.; Lynch, John W.
theories: attraction-selection-attrition model; need fulfillment; person-environment fit; self-determination theory; work/nonwork literature
keywords: job crafting; job engagement; job performance; leisure activity; misfit; value incongruence
research_question: The paper asks what proactive behaviors can buffer the performance detriments of value incongruence for organizational misfits. It examines whether job crafting and leisure activity mitigate the negative effects of value incongruence on job engagement, task performance, and citizenship behavior.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that value incongruence deprives employees of fundamental need fulfillment, making them less willing to invest themselves in work. Job crafting can substitute for unmet needs by reshaping task and social aspects of work, while leisure activity can provide nonwork sources of autonomy, competence, belonging, meaning, and psychological availability. The results indicate that job crafting and leisure activity buffer the negative engagement and performance consequences of value incongruence for misfits.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends person-environment fit and value congruence research by focusing on misfit rather than only fit, and by showing that misfits are not necessarily passive recipients of their environment. It adds nuance to the attraction-selection-attrition model by showing that proactive behavior can suppress the negative effects of value incongruence. It also brings a cross-domain work/nonwork perspective into value congruence theory by showing that leisure activity can compensate for unmet needs at work.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers should not rely only on hiring for value congruence or assume that value misfits will necessarily be disengaged and unproductive. Opportunities for employees to craft their jobs in meaningful ways may help misfits remain engaged and productive. The authors also suggest that involvement in fulfilling activities outside working hours can be especially useful for misfits whose needs are not fully satisfied by organizational values.
limitations: The authors note that assessing fit through participant ratings of both personal and organizational values may introduce reporting bias and may not capture objective fit. They also focus on incongruence around the employee's most important value, whereas future work could examine incongruence around the value ranked most important to the organization. A further limitation is that the study theorizes need fulfillment as the core process but does not directly test need satisfaction.
future_research: Future research could examine whether employees are labeled by others as misfits and what consequences follow from that experience. Scholars could test the specific needs through which value congruence, job crafting, and leisure activity operate, including whether different proactive actions satisfy different needs. The authors also call for more work on leisure activity, including specific forms such as exercise, entertainment, and community involvement.
abstract: The work life of “misfits”—employees whose important values are incongruent with the values of their organization—represents an under-researched area of the person– environment fit literature. The unfortunate reality is that these individuals are likely to be disengaged and unproductive at work. In this manuscript, we entertain the possibility that employees can protect themselves from this situation if they engage in alternative actions that supplement the fundamental needs that go unmet from value incongruence. We integrate theorizing about the motivational role of need fulfillment and work/nonwork behaviors in order to examine whether two actions in particular—job crafting and leisure activity—can potentially mitigate the negative effects of value incongruence on employee performance. The results from our field study of employees from diverse organizations and industries suggest that both job crafting and leisure activity do indeed act as a buffer, mitigating the otherwise negative effects of value incongruence on employee engagement and job performance (with regard to both task performance and citizenship behavior).
apa_citation: Vogel, R. M., Rodell, J. B., & Lynch, J. W. (2016). Engaged and productive misfits: How job crafting and leisure activity mitigate the negative effects of value incongruence. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1561-1584. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0850

title: The Impact of CEO Succession with Gender Change on Firm Performance and Successor Early Departure: Evidence from China’s Publicly Listed Companies in 1997–2010
methods: Empirical quantitative study of CEO successions in Chinese publicly listed companies. The authors use Heckman two-stage correction for succession and female-successor selection, generalized least square regression models for post-succession ROA, and multinomial-logistic regression models clustered at the firm level for successor early routine and non-routine departure.
industry: Publicly listed companies on China's Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges, excluding B-share issuers, interim CEO cases, and observations with missing critical successor, predecessor, moderator, or control data.
units: CEO successions in publicly listed companies.
n_sample: 3,320 CEO successions, including 289 with gender change.
authors: Zhang, Y.; Qu, H.
theories: CEO succession theory; gender leadership research; social categorization theory; social identity theory
keywords: CEO succession with gender change; Female corporate leadership; organizational attitudes toward female leadership; post-succession firm performance; successor early departure
research_question: How does CEO succession with gender change affect post-succession firm performance and the likelihood of successor early departure? The paper also asks whether other female leaders in the upper echelon and the successor's inside origin weaken the negative consequences of male-to-female succession.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that CEO succession is already disruptive, and a change in the CEO's gender may add disruption by changing gender-linked leadership styles and by making the successor more salient as an out-group member relative to the predecessor's established leadership context. This should harm post-succession performance and increase early departure risk. For male-to-female succession, the presence of other female leaders and inside origin are expected to reduce the female successor's gender-based status liability and make the transition less disruptive.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to CEO succession research by theorizing and testing a gender-change effect rather than treating successor gender alone as the focal explanatory variable. It also extends female leadership research by showing how gender inequality in CEO appointments may persist partly because firms anticipate disruption from gender change at the top. The study adds successor early departure as an outcome in CEO succession research and ties it to social identity and social categorization arguments.
practical_implication: The authors argue that firms can reduce the disruptive consequences of male-to-female succession by developing other female leaders on boards and top management teams and by grooming internal female CEO successors. These organizational contexts are presented as modifiable conditions that can help smooth the transition from a male predecessor to a female successor.
limitations: The authors state that the Chinese publicly listed-company context may limit generalizability, although supplementary analyses suggest the hypothesized effects hold in non-SOEs rather than SOEs. They also note that the study cannot directly observe whether and how disruption occurred across 3,320 CEO successions over 14 years.
future_research: Future research could test gender-change effects in CEO succession using data from other countries and institutional contexts. The authors also suggest that small-sample, survey, or case-study approaches could examine the processes through which disruption associated with gender change occurs in individual CEO successions.
abstract: Female corporate leadership has drawn increasing attention from academia and practitioners. We contribute to the literature by examining the impact of CEO succession with gender change—i.e., a male CEO succeeded by a female or vice versa. We propose that due to gender differences in executive leadership positions, CEO succession with gender change may amplify the disruption of the CEO succession process and thus adversely affect post-succession firm performance and increase the likelihood of successor early departure. Using data from 3,320 CEO successions in companies listed in China’s Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges from 1997 to 2010, we find evidence to support this argument. We also find that the negative (positive) impact of male-tofemale succession on firm performance (the likelihood of successor early departure) may be weakened by positive organizational attitudes toward female leadership as indicated by the presence of other female leaders on the firm’s board of directors and/or top management team, and the successor’s inside origin.
apa_citation: Zhang, Y., & Qu, H. (2016). The impact of CEO succession with gender change on firm performance and successor early departure: Evidence from China’s publicly listed companies in 1997–2010. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(5), 1845-1868. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0176

title: Management’s Science–Practice Gap: A Grand Challenge for All Stakeholders
methods: Mixed-methods study using grounded theory analysis of interviews and a focus group, a survey of academics and practitioners, and qualitative content analysis in ATLAS.ti with interrater reliability checks.
industry: Management research and practice stakeholders, including academics in OB/HR, strategy, entrepreneurship, and other management fields, plus practitioners, government employees, consultants, supervisors, managers, and working adults.
country: U.S. and international academics; practitioners were primarily U.S.-based, including MTurk respondents limited to U.S.-based respondents.
time_period: Academic author sampling frame covered publications between 2010 and 2014; exact interview and survey fieldwork dates are not reported in paper.
units: Academics, practitioners, working adults, interviewees, focus-group participants, survey responses, and organizational signatories.
n_sample: 38 interviewees; 7 focus-group participants; 1,767 survey participants, including 828 academics and 939 practitioners; 165 organizational signatories.
authors: Banks, G. C.; Pollack, J. M.; Bochantin, J. E.; Kirkman, B. L.; Whelpley, C. E.; O’Boyle, E. H.
theories: stakeholder theory
keywords: collaboration costs; grand challenges; grounded theory; knowledge creation; knowledge transfer; science–practice gap; stakeholder theory
research_question: The paper asks how management academics and practitioners can overcome collaboration challenges in knowledge creation and transfer, how information asymmetry and goal incongruence raise collaboration costs, and how grand challenges can reduce the science–practice gap. It also asks which grand challenges academics view as accomplished, which future challenges academics and practitioners identify, and how those challenges can be leveraged for collaboration.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: science–practice gap, information asymmetry, goal incongruence, collaboration costs, utility functions, grand challenges, knowledge creation, and knowledge transfer.
- Process / models: information asymmetry and goal incongruence increase collaboration costs; knowledge of utility functions and mutually valued grand challenges reduce those costs; lower collaboration costs enable knowledge creation with collaboration.
- Knowledge transfer: incentives and communication channels shape whether created knowledge is effectively transferred to management stakeholders.
- Empirical basis: grounded theory analysis produced theoretical models and propositions; survey-based qualitative content analysis identified 22 grand challenges, including overlapping academic and practitioner priorities.

The core process is that academics and practitioners often develop knowledge separately because they do not understand one another’s utility functions and do not always share aligned goals. Stakeholder theory is used to argue that reciprocal exchanges, mutual value creation, and attention to shared grand challenges can lower collaboration costs and create more valuable knowledge. The paper treats the science–practice gap as both a knowledge creation problem and a knowledge transfer problem.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends stakeholder theory by applying it to the management science–practice gap and by specifying how information asymmetry, goal incongruence, utility functions, grand challenges, and collaboration costs shape stakeholder collaboration. It contributes theoretical models and propositions for knowledge creation and knowledge transfer, arguing that collaboration between academics and practitioners can create more valuable knowledge by capitalizing on different perspectives and joint work.
practical_implication: The paper argues that management academics, practitioners, business schools, and the Academy of Management should build more durable collaboration structures around shared grand challenges. It recommends practitioner-oriented communication outlets, better use of conferences and executive education, organizational signatories for collaborative research, and business-school reward systems that explicitly value practical impact.
limitations: The authors identify sample-related limits: the academic respondents may not represent all active management researchers, and the practitioner survey respondents were largely mid-level U.S. managers. They also note unclear survey response rates, more practitioners than academics in the qualitative interviews and focus group, and a primarily for-profit framing that should be expanded.
future_research: Future research should use stratified random samples across academic and practitioner stakeholder groups, roles, occupational tenure, and management subfields. The authors also encourage more targeted work on the science–practice gap in domains such as social entrepreneurship and sustainability, plus empirical efforts that use the identified grand challenges as bases for collaborative research.
abstract: Despite multiple high-profile calls—across decades and from multiple stakeholders—to address the widening gap between science and practice, the relevance of research conducted in the management domain remains in question. To once again highlight this issue and, more importantly, identify solutions, we explore the grand challenge of the science–practice gap by applying stakeholder theory. Using a grounded theory approach, we conducted a series of interviews (n 5 38) and formed an interactive focus group with academics and practitioners (e.g., executives, entrepreneurs, government officials) in order to develop a set of theoretical models and propositions that extend stakeholder theory. We supplemented our inductive theory building approach with a survey of academics (n 5 828) and practitioners (n 5 939) and a qualitative content analysis to identify 22 grand challenges (i.e., eight shared, eight uniquely academic, and six uniquely practitioner). We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of our findings and illustrate multiple directions for future research to build permanent bonds—not just temporary links—between science and practice.
apa_citation: Banks, G. C., Pollack, J. M., Bochantin, J. E., Kirkman, B. L., Whelpley, C. E., & O’Boyle, E. H. (2016). Management’s science–practice gap: A grand challenge for all stakeholders. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(6), 2205-2231. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0728

title: Understanding Community Dynamics in the Study of Grand Challenges: How Nonprofits, Institutional Actors, and the Community Fabric Interact to Influence Income Inequality
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a seven-year panel of U.S. metropolitan statistical areas. The paper estimates fixed-effects models with instrumental-variable specifications, lagged independent and control variables, robustness checks using alternative inequality measures and controls, and additional sensitivity analyses for spatial effects and GMM estimation.
industry: Human-service welfare nonprofits and elite-oriented nonprofits in U.S. metropolitan statistical areas.
units: Metropolitan statistical areas and nonprofit organizations within those communities
n_sample: 245 U.S. communities
authors: Berrone, Pascual; Gelabert, Liliana; Massa-Saluzzo, Federica; Rousseau, Horacio E.
theories: community embeddedness; grand challenges literature; institutional theory; resource competition
keywords: community support; grand challenges; income inequality; institutional alignment; resource competition; welfare-oriented nonprofits
research_question: The paper asks which community-level competitive and institutional dynamics influence the effectiveness of welfare-oriented nonprofits in reducing community income inequality. It examines resource competition, local institutional actors, and community fabric as conditions shaping nonprofit effectiveness in addressing a grand challenge.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that welfare nonprofits can collectively reduce inequality by providing services, mobilizing resources, and building local legitimacy, but high density can also intensify competition for grants, volunteers, attention, and donors. Local institutional alignment conditions whether nonprofits gain support or face substitution, misalignment, or crowding-out dynamics. The findings suggest that government enforcement and conservative ideology operate largely as predicted, while weak social policy, financial presence, and racial diversity reveal more complex dynamics than the initial theory expected.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances grand-challenges research by specifying how community-level competition, institutional actors, and community fabric shape organizational effectiveness. It contributes to community and nonprofit studies by showing that nonprofit density is not monotonically beneficial: agglomeration benefits can be offset by resource competition and elite-oriented nonprofit density. It also extends institutional theory by showing that institutional alignment does not uniformly improve nonprofit effectiveness, because some institutions may substitute for or alter the perceived need for nonprofit action.
practical_implication: The authors caution policymakers against assuming that increasing the number of welfare nonprofits will automatically reduce inequality. They suggest that local governments may need to reduce inefficient competition by concentrating resources on nonprofits with demonstrated capacity and by helping nonprofits develop transparent performance measures. For nonprofit managers, the findings imply that local competitive and institutional dynamics should be assessed before choosing strategies for fundraising, collaboration, specialization, or cross-sector partnership.
limitations: The authors note that the broad community-level design requires relatively rough proxies for some constructs, including government enforcement capability. They also focus mainly on linear moderating effects, even though some community-fabric relationships, such as racial heterogeneity, may be nonlinear. Finally, they do not directly disentangle income inequality from poverty, despite recognizing that the two social problems are closely related.
future_research: Future research could use more granular measures of government enforcement and examine which government programs most influence nonprofit effectiveness. Scholars could analyze nonlinear community dynamics, especially different levels of racial heterogeneity and how they shape welfare nonprofits' impact. The authors also call for work that distinguishes income inequality from poverty and studies how welfare nonprofits affect each outcome differently.
abstract: This paper provides a conceptual model that explains how competitive and institutional dynamics at the community level influence the ability of welfare-oriented nonprofits to eradicate income inequality. To test our framework, we build a large and unique seven-year panel dataset consisting of data from 245 U.S. communities. We find that increasing the number of welfare nonprofits is beneficial for reducing community inequality, but only up to a point, after which resource competition decreases their effectiveness. This competition for resources is also present when a high density of elite-oriented nonprofits operates in the same community. Hypotheses focused on the institutional dimension receive mixed support. As predicted, welfare nonprofits are more effective when they operate in communities with strong law enforcement capabilities and less effective in politically conservative local contexts. Contrary to our expectations, however, we find that welfare nonprofits are less effective in demographically heterogeneous local contexts and when the government provides effective social policies, thus indicating a possible substitution effect. Surprisingly, nonprofit effectiveness is increased in highly financialized local contexts. Together, our results indicate that issues of competition, institutional alignment, and community support in the context of grand challenges are more complex than originally thought.

Understanding community dynamics in the study of grand challenges: How nonprofits, institutional actors, and the community fabric interact to influence income inequality. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(6), 1940-1964. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0746

title: Funding Financial Inclusion: Institutional Logics and the Contextual Contingency of Funding for Microfinance Organizations
methods: Empirical quantitative cross-sectional time-series study using proprietary MIX raw MFO funding data, ICRG country uncertainty measures, factor scores for MFO size, financial performance, and transparency, and OLS regression models with country- and year-fixed effects. Interviews with 34 industry informants support the theory-building around commercial and public funder logics.
industry: Global microfinance funding; loans from commercial and public funders to microfinance organizations.
units: MFO-year observations for microfinance organizations receiving traceable loans from commercial and public funders.
n_sample: 891 MFOs in 92 countries that borrowed from 1,490 funders; regression models report 1,746 MFO-year observations.
authors: Cobb, J. A.; Wry, T.; Zhao, E. Y.
theories: environmental uncertainty and organizational response (Audia, Locke, & Smith, 2000; Davis, Eisenhardt, & Bingham, 2009); institutional logics perspective (Thornton, Ocasio, & Lounsbury, 2012)
keywords: commercial and public funders; financial and development logics; funding; institutional logics; microfinance; microfinance organizations; uncertainty
research_question: The paper asks how commercial and public funders finance microfinance organizations, whether their lending practices differ according to financial and development logics, and how those practices change as country-level political and financial uncertainty rises. It examines whether institutional logics produce stable practice differences or contextually contingent convergence in MFO funding.
mechanism_summary: Commercial funders operate under a financial logic that prioritizes investment return, so they favor larger and financially stronger MFOs in stable contexts. Public funders operate under a development logic that supports sector health and poverty alleviation, so they are expected to favor smaller and less financially strong MFOs that commercial lenders overlook. As political or financial uncertainty rises, both types of funders shift attention toward MFO size as a visible signal of stability, causing their lending practices to converge even though their underlying logics remain different. This convergence directs capital toward larger MFOs and away from smaller MFOs that may be more committed to social outreach.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the institutional logics perspective by showing that the relationship between logics and organizational practices is contextually contingent rather than fixed across settings. It links institutional logics to environmental uncertainty, arguing that decision makers use logics as lenses for adapting behavior when the action-outcome link becomes less predictable. It also contributes to microfinance and foreign-aid research by shifting attention from aggregate funding flows to organization-level funding decisions that shape social-sector capacity.
practical_implication: The findings imply that smaller MFOs may struggle to finance loan portfolios precisely when country uncertainty increases and microfinance need intensifies. MFOs may improve funding access by growing, forming alliances, or improving transparency before uncertainty rises. Public funders and policymakers may need loan guarantees, reserve capital pools, or subsidized insurance mechanisms to keep capital flowing to smaller, socially oriented MFOs during volatile periods.
limitations: The analysis is limited to debt financing and does not include grants, equity, capacity-building funds, or regulatory-infrastructure funding. The study also cannot fully assess how national regulatory capacity conditions the effects of funding on microfinance outcomes. Finally, although the authors rule out several alternatives, they cannot directly observe whether external audiences interpret public funders' shifts toward larger MFOs as mission drift.
future_research: Future studies should examine other funding instruments, including grants and equity, as more data become available. Research should also study how regulatory capacity, safeguards against overborrowing, and competition among MFOs shape whether additional funding improves or harms microfinance sectors. The authors also suggest studying conflicts among internal and external audiences over how the same institutional logic should be interpreted, especially in organizations pursuing both financial and social aims.
abstract: Microfinance is a promising tool for addressing the grand challenge of global poverty. Yet, while many studies have examined how microfinance loans affect poor borrowers, we know little about how microfinance organizations (MFOs) themselves finance their lending activities. This is a significant oversight because most MFOs do not self-fund their lending, but, rather, rely on loans from external funders. To better understand microfinance funding, we apply and extend the institutional logics perspective to analyze the lending practices of commercial and public funders, who together provide most of the capital for global microfinance. We argue that these funders adhere to financial and development logics, respectively, and that this leads them to invest in different types of MFOs. Yet, in the face of uncertainty, we suggest that the practices motivated by these logics will start to converge in ways that are problematic for a nation’s microfinance sector. Using a proprietary database of all traceable loans to MFOs from 2004 to 2012, we find strong support for our hypotheses. In particular, our findings show that the relationship between institutional logics and organizational practices is contextually contingent, and this insight contributes important understanding about the efficacy of microfinance as a poverty-reduction tool.

title: Some Things Can Never Be Unseen: The Role of Context in Psychological Injury at War
methods: Ethnography of a military medical team, combining predeployment training observation, a six-week embedded tour in Camp Bastion, fieldnotes, headnotes, reports, hospital records, morbidity and mortality data, photographs, and interpretive coding of distress themes, context, and coping strategies.
industry: Military medicine / damage control surgery field hospital
time_period: April 2010-August 2011, including an embedded tour from June 14 to July 29, 2011
units: Damage control surgery team members and fieldwork events in Camp Bastion
n_sample: At any one time, around 4-5 general surgeons, 6-7 orthopedic surgeons, 1 plastic surgeon, and 5-6 anesthetists, alongside operating department practitioners, theater nurses, and theater coordinators
authors: de Rond, M.; Lok, J.
theories: context theory (Johns, 2006); coping and normalization; existentialism; institutional theory
keywords: existential grounding; futility; institutional context; psychological injury; senselessness; surreality; war
research_question: The paper asks what role cultural, professional, and organizational contexts play in the experience of psychological distress at war. It examines how institutional context shapes what deployed medical personnel experience as traumatic beyond direct exposure to combat threat.
mechanism_summary:
- Key contexts / expectations: cultural expectations of innocence and normality, professional role identity as medical caregivers, and organizational military protocol.
- Distressing experience themes: senselessness, futility, and surreality.
- Process / dissonance: contextual expectations clash with lived experience in Camp Bastion, especially around children’s suffering, compromised patient care, and surreal juxtapositions of routine and human injury.
- Coping responses: avoiding, bracketing, humor, recovering the familiar, and reclaiming control.
- Emergent outcome: sustained contextual dissonance threatens existential grounding and makes improvised coping strategies only temporarily effective.

The process account is interpretive rather than variable-causal. The authors argue that institutional context filters and amplifies exposure to war by producing dissonance between what medics understand as meaningful, good, and normal and what they encounter in practice. Because the same professional and organizational contexts also inhibit open processing of distress, medics rely on improvised coping strategies that may temporarily distance them from distress but do not resolve its contextual sources.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a contextual explanation of psychological distress at war that complements individual-level trauma accounts. It contributes to organizational research by showing how context theory and institutional theory can explain existential threat in organizations: institutional context socializes expectations, produces dissonance when those expectations clash with lived experience, and supplies coping resources that may fail or even amplify distress.
practical_implication: Interventions for psychological injury at war should not assume universal trauma triggers or purely individual coping deficits. The paper suggests that prevention and support need to be tailored to the situated cultural, professional, and organizational contexts through which different military groups experience distress.
limitations: The evidence comes from an ethnographic case of rear-located medical personnel in Camp Bastion, so the mechanisms may differ for frontline soldiers, other national militaries, or nonmedical personnel. The authors also frame some implications for PTSD prevention and treatment as suggestions for future research rather than as tested intervention effects.
future_research: Future research should compare how institutional context shapes psychological distress across different military groups, such as frontline troops, reservists, rear-located medics, and personnel leaving service after deployment. It should also examine whether coping strategies that normalize extreme environments can amplify distress by increasing the contrast between life at war and life at home.
abstract: Recent wars in Iraq and Afghanistan have reignited debates on how to prevent and manage psychological injury among returning troops. These debates point to the psychological cost of war as a grand challenge whose scale and complexity stretch far beyond the already large and growing number of veterans affected. We use a unique ethnography of a military medical team’s tour of duty in Camp Bastion, Afghanistan, to explore the role of institutional context as a contributing factor to psychological injury from war. We find that exposure to war and its consequences invokes sustained experiences of senselessness, futility, and surreality that are partially rooted in cultural expectations, professional role identity, and organizational protocol, and can threaten people’s existential grounding in this institutional context. We argue that what makes work at war traumatic for some and not others is likely affected by the specific context through which people filter, frame, and cope with their experience. A contextual understanding of psychological injury at war that is based in organizational research can thus form an important part of better addressing this grand challenge.

title: Management Research in AMJ: Celebrating Impact While Striving for More
methods: From the Editors editorial reflecting on management research impact, AMJ Best Paper Award exemplars, dissemination beyond publication, business-school impact expectations, and the 20th AMJ editorial team's closing record.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: George, Gerard
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: AMJ editorship; actionability; business schools; grand challenges; management research; research dissemination; research impact; responsible science
research_question: The editorial asks how management research can have greater impact beyond publication, citation, and internal scholarly recognition. It reflects on how AMJ scholarship can remain rigorous while becoming more significant, actionable, visible, and useful to managers, policy makers, business schools, and society.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Management scholarship should celebrate the robust knowledge it already produces while pushing harder toward broader managerial, organizational, and societal impact.
- Topic choice: Impact begins with bolder research topics that emphasize significance, novelty, curiosity, scope, and actionability rather than only literature gaps or methodological refinements.
- Exemplars: AMJ Best Paper Award finalists illustrate how significant phenomena, multiple levels of analysis, rich methods, and practical relevance can coexist with theory-driven research.
- Phenomenon focus: New or changing phenomena such as climate change, aging societies, digital money, digital workforces, risk, resilience, big data, and grand challenges create opportunities for stronger theory and impact.
- Dissemination: Research impact increasingly depends on follow-up work after publication, including digital formats, social media, media outlets, teaching, books, cases, and AMJ's Dynamic Edition.
- Institutional context: Business schools, funders, accrediting bodies, and responsible-science initiatives are putting impact at the center of research evaluation and mission.

The process is editorial and agenda-setting rather than empirical. George argues that impact grows from selecting consequential phenomena, using rigorous and varied methods, communicating research beyond the published article, and aligning business-school research with societal usefulness. The editorial closes by connecting this impact agenda to the outgoing AMJ team's service record and the journal's transition into its 60th year.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial does not develop a new named theory. Its contribution is to reframe AMJ's research-impact agenda around bolder topic selection, phenomenon-driven theorizing, methodological richness, active dissemination, and business-school accountability for societal relevance.
practical_implication: For management scholars, the editorial recommends choosing topics with significance and actionability, studying emergent phenomena, and treating publication as the start rather than the end of impact work. For business schools and journals, it highlights the need to support dissemination, responsible science, and evidence of research usefulness for organizations and society.
limitations: The editorial is a reflective essay by the outgoing AMJ editor rather than a systematic empirical study or formal review. Its examples come mainly from AMJ Best Paper Award finalists, AMJ editorials, and the author's editorial and dean experience, so the claims are illustrative rather than comprehensive.
future_research: The editorial calls for more management research on significant organizational and societal problems, including grand challenges and emergent phenomena whose managerial implications are not yet well understood. It also encourages scholars to examine how research can create impact through practice, policy, teaching, dissemination, and responsible-science initiatives beyond conventional citation metrics.

title: Understanding and Tackling Societal Grand Challenges through Management Research
methods: Editorial and conceptual Special Research Forum essay that defines societal grand challenges, reviews accepted AMJ studies on grand challenges, and develops a multilevel framework for future management research.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: George, Gerard; Howard-Grenville, Jennifer; Joshi, Aparna; Tihanyi, Laszlo
theories: Not reported in paper
keywords: Sustainable Development Goals; collaborative effort; coordinated effort; grand challenges; management research; multilevel actions; socially inclusive society; societal grand challenges
research_question: How can management research help formulate, articulate, coordinate, and empirically study societal grand challenges that individuals, organizations, communities, and nations face? The editorial asks how management scholars can convert persistent global problems into tractable organizational and managerial research questions.
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: Grand challenges require coordinated and collaborative effort across multiple stakeholders, levels, and institutional contexts.
- Articulation and participation: Collective goals need to be framed in ways that inspire voice, identification, purpose, and stakeholder engagement.
- Actor needs and barriers: Grand challenges reflect actor needs and aspirations, while individual, sociocultural, technological, and structural barriers block socioeconomic progress and well-being.
- Organizational constraints: Coordination costs, goal conflict, incentive conflict, information asymmetry, and transaction costs can frustrate sustained action.
- Institutional and multilevel context: Societal logics, regulatory environments, community settings, organizations, governments, and multilateral actors shape how action unfolds.
- Coordinating architectures and reinforcement: Platforms, shared norms, resourcing, advocacy, social attention, exogenous events, and goal-directed progress can sustain collaborative effort.
- Outcomes and impact: Success can appear as resilience, innovation, sustainability, behavioral change, goal attainment, and measurable societal impact.

The process is conceptual and editorial rather than causal-variable based. George, Howard-Grenville, Joshi, and Tihanyi argue that management research can study how grand challenges are formulated, how actors participate, what barriers and constraints shape action, and how multilevel coordinating architectures influence outcomes. The framework is meant to help scholars break large social problems into smaller empirical questions that remain connected to broader societal impact.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes a management-oriented definition of grand challenges and a higher-order framework for studying them through organizational and multilevel lenses. It positions grand challenges as managerial as well as societal problems, emphasizing articulation, stakeholder coordination, institutional context, reinforcing mechanisms, and outcomes. Rather than offering a new named theory, it provides a structure for developing theory and empirical research around societal problems.
practical_implication: For management scholars, the editorial frames societal grand challenges as legitimate and publishable research domains in leading journals. It encourages researchers to generate systematic, unbiased, and empirically robust evidence that can assist coordinated efforts toward socially inclusive growth. For educators, it also argues that management academics have responsibilities in social inclusion, skills retraining, and preparing business leaders for persistent global problems.
limitations: The authors explicitly state that their goal is not to provide a comprehensive review of prior work. The framework is offered as an architecture for thinking about complex, global, and multilevel challenges rather than as a set of specific constructs or measures. Because the article is an editorial and Special Research Forum introduction, it does not test the framework empirically.
future_research: The editorial identifies representative empirical questions around who articulates grand challenges, how actors align around shared goals, how barriers shape opportunity, how organizations coordinate or disclose action, and how progress can be measured. It calls for micro, meso, and macro theoretical lenses that produce empirical analysis capable of assisting collective efforts toward societal grand challenges.
abstract: “Grand challenges” are formulations of global problems that can be plausibly addressed through coordinated and collaborative effort. In this Special Research Forum, we showcase management research that examines societal problems that individuals, organizations, communities, and nations face around the world. We develop a framework to guide future research to provide systematic empirical evidence on the formulation, articulation, and implementation of grand challenges. We highlight several factors that likely enhance or suppress the attainment of collective goals, and identify representative research questions for future empirical work. In so doing, we aspire to encourage management scholars to engage in tackling broader societal challenges through their collaborative research and collective insight.
