title: Selective Regulator Decoupling and Organizations’ Strategic Responses
methods: Empirical quantitative study using patient- and hospital-level panel data from California nonprofit hospitals. The paper estimates prosecution likelihood and settlement amount models for regulatory enforcement, then uses seemingly unrelated regressions for upcoding across three Medicare DRG families, with robustness checks using alternative timing and econometric specifications.
industry: California nonprofit general acute care hospitals, with empirical focus on Medicare DRG upcoding in the hospital industry.
time_period: 1996-2007; the main post-leniency upcoding tests also analyze 2001-2007.
units: Hospital-year observations and patient-level DRG coding records
n_sample: 215 nonprofit hospitals and 2,063 hospital-year observations for Hypothesis 1; 186 nonprofit hospitals and 1,140 hospital-year observations for the main Hypothesis 2 tests.
authors: Heese, Jonas; Krishnan, Ranjani; Moers, Frank
theories: decoupling theory; institutional logics; institutional theory; nonmarket strategy
keywords: hospital industry; institutional pressures; nonmarket strategies; regulatory decoupling; selective decoupling; upcoding
research_question: The paper asks whether regulatory agencies themselves decouple from the rules they are charged with enforcing, and whether this decoupling is selective across regulated organizations. It then asks how hospitals that benefit from selective regulatory leniency respond strategically through nonmarket activity and upcoding behavior.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that regulators face conflicting institutional pressures, complex goals, and fragmented internal structures. In health care, these pressures push regulators to balance fraud enforcement against community access, charity care, and medical education. Hospitals that provide these beneficent services receive more lenient enforcement and use nonmarket strategies to maintain that status. After observing regulatory leniency, beneficent hospitals selectively decouple service ethics from pricing ethics by continuing unprofitable services while increasing upcoding.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends decoupling theory by moving the locus of decoupling from regulated organizations to regulatory agencies themselves. It introduces selective regulator decoupling, in which regulators symbolically enforce rules for favored organizations while enforcing them more rigorously for others. It also links institutional theory and nonmarket strategy by showing how regulated organizations can respond to regulator decoupling by shaping the enforcement climate and selectively decoupling their own norms.
practical_implication: The paper cautions that uniform enforcement can be difficult when regulators face real tradeoffs between fraud control and socially valued service provision. For regulators, reducing upcoding may require stronger fraud-control resources, better insulation from stakeholder pressure, and direct subsidies for organizations that provide socially important but underfunded services. For nonprofit hospitals, the findings show that nonmarket strategies and cost-shifting through upcoding may preserve beneficent services but create ethical and regulatory exposure.
limitations: The enforcement analysis has missing settlement amounts for some settlement-hospital-years, which the authors address with additional tests but cannot fully eliminate as a data limitation. The empirical setting is California nonprofit hospitals and selected Medicare DRG families, so the evidence is strongest for health care reimbursement regulation rather than all regulatory domains.
future_research: The discussion suggests examining selective regulatory decoupling in other domains where regulators balance enforcement against social, economic, or political costs, such as environmental regulation and financial regulation. Future research could also study how regulatory agency structure, stakeholder pressure, and social-norm change alter the boundary between symbolic and actual enforcement. Additional work could examine when subsidies or institutional redesign reduce the need for selective leniency.
abstract: Organizations often respond to institutional pressures by symbolically adopting policies and procedures but decoupling them from actual practice. Literature has examined why organizations decouple from regulatory pressures. In this study, we argue that decoupling occurs within regulatory agencies and results from a combination of conflicting institutional pressures, complex goals, and internal fragmentation. Further, regulatory decoupling is selective—that is, regulators fail to adequately enforce standards only for one set of organizations. Regulated organizations that benefit from selective regulatory decoupling use nonmarket strategies to maintain their favorable regulatory status, and, in the process, selectively decouple their norms in one organizational activity but not others. As an empirical context, we use the hospital industry in which regulators have to balance conflicting pressures to be tough on fraud while maintaining the community’s access to essential but unprofitable services, such as charity care and medical education. In response, hospital regulators selectively decouple and exhibit leniency in enforcement of mispricing practices toward “beneficent hospitals,” defined as hospitals that provide more charity care and medical education. In turn, beneficent hospitals selectively decouple their service and profit goals by providing unprofitable services to uninsured patients, while mispricing insured patients to earn higher reimbursements.

title: Challenges for Global Supply Chain Sustainability: Evidence from Conflict Minerals Reports
methods: Archival quantitative study of SEC conflict minerals reports using ordered logit models, with supplementary binary logit and robustness analyses; interviews with supply chain managers, lawyers, and activists informed the theory and interpretation.
industry: SEC filing companies whose products used conflict minerals, spanning major SIC industry groups including electronics, machinery, transportation equipment, chemicals, metals, wholesale trade, apparel, and business services.
country: Domestic and foreign corporations listed on U.S. stock markets; models distinguish U.S., EU, and non-U.S./non-EU headquarters.
time_period: Conflict minerals reports from the first two rounds of submissions in 2014 and 2015, with the main analysis using 2015 reports.
units: Companies submitting Form SD conflict minerals reports to the SEC.
n_sample: 1,179 companies in the final 2015 analytic sample.
authors: Kim, Y. H.; Davis, G. F.
theories: organization theory; supply chain complexity; transaction cost economics
keywords: conflict minerals; corporate social responsibility; global supply chains; supply chain sustainability; supply chain visibility
research_question: What organizational factors distinguish corporations that are able to vouch for their supply chains from those that are not? The paper examines why some SEC-filing companies could determine whether their products were free of DRC conflict minerals while most could not.
mechanism_summary: The core mechanism is supply chain visibility under organizational complexity. International diversification and larger supplier bases expand the number of geographies, suppliers, and indirect relationships that firms must trace, reducing their ability to know the origin of conflict minerals. Power over direct suppliers offers limited help because the relevant information often lies several tiers away, while reputation matters only after accounting for supply chain complexity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends organization theory and CSR research by showing how disaggregated supply chains create a responsibility paradox: demands for corporate accountability rise while firms' capacity to monitor dispersed production shrinks. It contributes systematic large-sample evidence to a domain previously dominated by cases and anecdotes, identifying organizational and supply chain complexity as central barriers to accountability beyond firm boundaries.
practical_implication: Managers should not assume that CSR motivation, visibility, or resources are sufficient to verify supply chain sustainability when supplier networks are broad and multi-tiered. The study suggests that stronger enforcement, collective verification infrastructure, and industry-certified sources may be needed because individual firms often cannot cheaply trace each direct and indirect supplier.
limitations: The authors note that the two-period disclosure sample does not support a strong panel design, so the main analysis uses cross-sectional models. They are also tentative about the reputation finding because it is sensitive to inclusion of two admired companies that declared their products conflict-free with great certainty. The study observes firms' disclosure outcomes rather than independently auditing the material origins of every supply chain.
future_research: Future research could examine how regulatory enforcement, collective supplier-verification systems, and market reactions alter firms' ability and incentives to achieve supply chain accountability. The paper also points to unresolved questions about when reputation operates as a burden that motivates verification rather than as a buffer against stakeholder scrutiny.
abstract: The vertically integrated corporation of the 20th century has been replaced by disaggregated global supply chains across many industries. Dis-integration can reduce costs, but also limits the ability to monitor and control critical processes, including labor practices and the sourcing of supplies. This article asks: What organizational factors distinguish corporations that are able to vouch for their supply chains from those that are not? Section 1502 of the Dodd–Frank Act of 2010 gave companies over three years to determine and report on whether their products contained “conflict minerals” from the Democratic Republic of Congo area. Our analysis of every conflict minerals report submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission by over 1,300 corporations found that almost 80% admitted they were unable to determine the country of origin of such materials, and only 1% could certify themselves conflict-free with certainty beyond reasonable doubt. Internationally diversified firms and those with large and more dispersed supply chains were less likely to declare their products conflict-free: complexity reduces the visibility of a firm’s supply chain. Our results suggest that widespread outsourcing may have reduced the corporate sector’s capacity to account for the practices that yield its products.

title: Engage Me: The Mature-Age Worker and Stereotype Threat
methods: Three-wave survey of mature-age employees, analyzed with hierarchical multiple regression, relative weight analysis, and PROCESS bootstrapping.
industry: Wide variety of jobs and industries.
time_period: Three surveys over a threeyear period, from 2011 to 2013.
units: Mature-age employees aged 45 years or older.
n_sample: 666 employees who participated in all three waves and worked for the same employer.
authors: Kulik, C. T.; Perera, S.; Cregan, C.
theories: stereotype threat framework
keywords: employee engagement; high performance practices; mature-age practices; mature-age workers; stereotype threat
research_question: How do threat-inducing contextual cues and threat-inhibiting organizational practices shape stereotype threat and later engagement among mature-age workers? The paper asks whether high performance practices and mature-age practices reduce stereotype threat and whether they buffer the threat associated with young managers.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that mature-age workers monitor workplace cues to judge whether they may be evaluated through negative age stereotypes. Threat-inducing cues increase stereotype threat, which depletes psychological resources and reduces later engagement. High performance practices affirm personal identity, while mature-age practices affirm age-group identity; both reduce stereotype threat, but mature-age practices are especially useful for counteracting cues from young managers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends stereotype threat research into an organizational, mature-age worker setting and shows that chronic workplace cues are associated with later engagement, not only immediate task performance. It also contributes to diversity management by showing that identity blind high performance practices and identity conscious mature-age practices operate independently and additively rather than as substitutes.
practical_implication: Organizations should treat young managers, young workgroups, and manual occupations as contextual cues that can heighten stereotype threat among mature-age workers. The paper recommends adopting both high performance practices and mature-age practices because they can reduce stereotype threat and support engagement through different pathways.
limitations: The study relies on employee self-reports for organizational practices and psychological experiences, although the authors argue self-report is unavoidable for stereotype threat. High performance practices and stereotype threat were measured in the same wave, and manager age and workgroup age composition were perceptual rather than archival measures.
future_research: Future research should replicate the findings using both manager and employee reports of organizational practices and objective records for manager and workgroup age. It should distinguish among different mature-age practice bundles, use repeated longitudinal measurement of practices, stereotype threat, and engagement, and examine behavioral outcomes such as absenteeism, exit, performance appraisals, and health.
abstract: As the workforce ages, and people retire later in life, organizations will need to develop strategies to engage their mature-age workers. We used a stereotype threat framework to investigate the impact of threat-inducing (young manager, young workgroup, manual occupation) and threat-inhibiting (high performance practices, mature-age practices) contextual cues on mature-age worker engagement. A total of 666 mature-age employees in Australia described their work experiences in three surveys administered over a threeyear period. Results indicated that mature-age employees who experienced stereotype threat in the workplace reported lower engagement 11–12 months later. All of the contextual cues had an impact on stereotype threat and exerted indirect (mediated by stereotype threat) effects on engagement. However, the effects of manager age were moderated by organizational practices. Diversity conscious mature-age practices moderated the indirect effect of manager age, so mature-age practices were particularly beneficial in counteracting negative cues associated with young managers. But diversity blind high performance practices moderated the direct effect of manager age, so high performance practices were especially helpful in generating engagement among matureage workers with older managers. We recommend that organizations adopt both diversity blind and diversity conscious practices into their diversity management portfolios. The two types of practices are complementary and have additive effects on mature-age worker engagement.

title: Mobilization in the Internet Age: Internet Activism and Corporate Response
methods: Event history analysis of corporate donation timing, using Gompertz models with firm-clustered robust standard errors and propensity score weighting; supplementary OLS and Heckman models examine total donation amount.
industry: Large publicly listed Chinese firms across industries, with state-controlled and private firms plus publicly listed financial institutions.
time_period: Daily donation spells from the May 12, 2008 Sichuan earthquake through June 30, 2008.
units: Large publicly listed Chinese firms
n_sample: 613 firms
authors: Luo, X. R.; Zhang, J.; Marquis, C.
theories: political opportunity structure; social comparison theory; social movement theory
keywords: Internet activism; authoritarian regimes; corporate donations; corporate response; public image vulnerability; social comparison
research_question: The paper asks whether and how Internet activism can pressure large corporations to respond to social demands in authoritarian regimes where traditional civil society, organized protest, and press freedom are constrained. It examines this question through Chinese firms' donation responses after the 2008 Sichuan earthquake.
mechanism_summary: Internet activism is theorized to focus public attention rapidly, make corporate donation comparisons salient, and threaten firms' public image. Firms that compare unfavorably in online rankings, or that are vulnerable because of reputation, industry culpability, ownership, or political status, are expected to respond faster to preempt or repair image damage.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a theory of Internet activism as a mobilizing structure that can pressure corporations in authoritarian contexts despite weak formal civil society channels. It extends social movement and organization research by identifying online rankings, rapid information diffusion, and social comparison as mechanisms through which dispersed Internet users can create corporate image threat and elicit firm response.
practical_implication: The findings imply that firms operating in tightly controlled societies may still face rapid public pressure through online activism, especially when their public image is vulnerable. Managers should monitor online comparisons and recognize that delayed or inadequate responses to social demands can intensify reputational exposure.
limitations: The authors note that they did not directly capture the interactive features of online media, such as comments or article forwarding, which may mean the study underestimates Internet activism's impact. They also study one form of Internet activism in one post-earthquake setting, limiting direct evidence about other online tactics and contexts.
future_research: Future research can examine how newer online tactics, including microblogging and social-networked communication through platforms such as Twitter, Weibo, and WeChat, affect corporate responses. The paper also points to the need to study Internet activism's constraints, including government monitoring, false information, and the limits of online mobilization in tightly controlled settings.
abstract: Civil society’s inability to hold powerful businesses accountable in authoritarian regimes is a grand challenge in today’s global environment. We propose that the development of Internet activism provides a novel mechanism to pressure for corporate response in those societies. Internet activism is dispersed, fast moving, and interactive, and hence can effectively focus public attention and potentially undermine a company’s public image by generating social comparison. In addition, firms with public image vulnerability may experience magnified pressure from Internet activism, as well as more intense social comparison. We explore this framework in the setting of corporate donations made in the wake of the 2008 earthquake in the Sichuan Province of China, which triggered Internet activism that challenged corporations to contribute to the good of the community. Analysis based on 613 large publicly listed Chinese firms supports our framework.

title: Scaffolding: A Process of Transforming Patterns of Inequality in Small-Scale Societies
methods: Qualitative case study of Gram Vikas's Rural Health and Environment Program in rural Odisha, using interviews, internal and external reports, film material, participant observation, shadowing, and iterative coding over a decade.
industry: Non-governmental development organization and rural water and sanitation program
time_period: Over the course of ten years, with fieldwork, interviews, observation, and archival data from 2004-2015
units: Gram Vikas, the Rural Health and Environment Program, rural villages, staff members, village leaders, villagers, reports, films, and observations
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Mair, J.; Wolf, M.; Seelos, C.
theories: development studies on local intervention; institutional theory and institutional change; organizational theory on societal challenges; social anthropology of small-scale societies
keywords: development programs; patterns of inequality; scaffolding; small-scale societies; social inequality
research_question: The paper asks how development programs can be used as organizing tools to transform entrenched patterns of inequality in small-scale societies. It focuses on how Gram Vikas's water and sanitation program reshapes behavior and interaction patterns in rural Indian villages.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: entrenched inequality in caste, class, and gender; manifest goals of water and sanitation; concealed goals of transforming local social order.
- Process / phases: rationalizing interaction by coopting local norms and power structures; routinizing interaction by redesigning local governance structures; solidifying interaction through collective construction.
- Practices: mobilizing institutional, social organizational, and economic resources; stabilizing new patterns through formal and informal enforcement; concealing contested transformation goals behind an uncontested program goal.
- Emergent outcomes: new patterns of interaction across social divides, revised access to resources and power, and more robust alternative local social orders.
- Boundary conditions: scaffolding varies across caste and tribal villages and depends on local heterogeneity, resource availability, consensus around inclusion, and active organizational planning.

The process operates by keeping villagers focused on the manifest goal of clean water and sanitation while Gram Vikas organizes conditions for a deeper shift in interaction patterns. Mobilizing resources unlocks participation across social groups, stabilizing protects emerging routines from reversal, and concealing limits resistance from groups that would oppose the social-order transformation if it were foregrounded.
theoretical_contribution: The paper specifies scaffolding as a process that enables and organizes institutional transformation rather than using it only as a metaphor. It links organizational efforts to alleviate social problems with the transformation of social systems, showing how manifest and concealed goals can jointly support local social change.
practical_implication: Programs addressing inequality should not only deliver technical benefits, such as water or sanitation, but also attend to the local normative and social structures that reproduce exclusion. The study suggests that durable progress requires supported, temporary structures that mobilize resources, stabilize new interaction patterns, and protect contested transformation goals until alternative local orders become robust.
limitations: The study centers on one organization, one program, and rural villages in Odisha, so the transferability of scaffolding to other societal challenges remains to be tested. The authors also note variation across villages and call for designs that examine sources of variance and enabling or disabling conditions more systematically.
future_research: Future research should examine how resources are combined and configured in scaffolding across different small-scale societies. The authors also encourage work on boundary conditions and on whether scaffolding helps explain progress on other relationally rooted societal challenges, such as microfinance or refugee integration.
abstract: This study advances research on organizational efforts to tackle multidimensional, complex, and interlinked societal challenges. We examine how social inequality manifests in small-scale societies, and illustrate how it inheres in entrenched patterns of behavior and interaction. Asking how development programs can be organizing tools to transform these patterns of inequality, we use a program sponsored by an Indian non-governmental organization as our empirical window and leverage data that we collected over a decade. We identify “scaffolding” as a process that enables and organizes the transformation of behavior and interaction patterns. Three interrelated mechanisms make the transformation processes adaptive and emerging alternative social orders robust: (1) mobilizing institutional, social organizational, and economic resources; (2) stabilizing new patterns of interaction that reflect an alternative social order; and (3) concealing goals that are neither anticipated nor desired by some groups. Through this analysis, we move beyond conventional thinking on unintended consequences proposed in classic studies on organizations, complement contemporary research about how organizations effect positive social change by pursuing multiple goals, and develop portable insights for organizational efforts in tackling inequality. This study provides a first link between the study of organizational efforts to alleviate social problems and the transformation of social systems.

title: Echoes of Our Upbringing: How Growing Up Wealthy or Poor Relates to Narcissism, Leader Behavior, and Leader Effectiveness
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a multisource, cross-sectional survey of active-duty U.S. Army leaders and followers, archival USMA application data for parental income and demographics, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling with maximum likelihood estimation, and bootstrap confidence intervals for serial mediation.
industry: Military leadership in the United States Army.
country: United States Army; respondents served in the United States and abroad.
time_period: Online survey active for 12 weeks; exact calendar dates not reported in paper.
units: USMA alumni in leadership roles and nominated followers.
n_sample: 229 USMA alumni leaders with complete focal and control-variable data, drawn from 579 self-assessment respondents; 444 nominated followers responded.
authors: Martin, S. R.; Côté, S.; Woodruff, T.
theories: integrative trait-behavioral model of leadership effectiveness (DeRue et al., 2011); self-sufficiency hypothesis (Miller et al., 2015; Piff, 2014; Vohs et al., 2006); social learning theory (Bandura, 1977)
keywords: integrative trait-behavioral model; leader behavior; leader effectiveness; leadership behaviors; narcissism; parental income; social learning theory
research_question: The paper asks how parental income during an individual’s upbringing is associated with later leadership effectiveness after entering an organization. It specifically examines whether higher parental income relates to higher adult narcissism, reduced relational-, task-, and change-oriented leadership behaviors, and lower follower-rated effectiveness and workgroup behavior outcomes.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is serial and cross-level: higher parental income is theorized to foster self-sufficiency and self-focused behavioral learning, which is associated with higher narcissism in adulthood. Higher narcissism is then associated with lower engagement in relational-, task-, and change-oriented leadership behaviors. The serial indirect effects are significant for selected behavior-outcome paths: relational and change behaviors for effectiveness, change behavior for citizenship, and task and change behaviors for counterproductive behavior.
theoretical_contribution: The paper connects research on parental income and the psychological consequences of income with leadership effectiveness theory. It extends the integrative trait-behavioral model by identifying parental income as a developmental antecedent of narcissism and by showing how that trait is associated with leadership behavior and outcomes. It also brings social learning and self-sufficiency arguments into an organizational leadership setting.
practical_implication: The authors argue that organizations may benefit from attenuating the entitlement and grandiosity that can accompany some wealthy backgrounds, for example by eliciting compassion or valuing humility. They caution against selecting leaders on parental income, emphasizing instead that the negative pathways through narcissism and subsequent leadership behaviors should be mitigated.
limitations: The authors note that the cross-sectional survey design prevents conclusive causal claims for some reported relationships. They also acknowledge possible omitted variables, same-source ratings for leadership behaviors and effectiveness outcomes, few participants in the highest income bracket, and the use of one strong-norm organization where ongoing leader-follower relationships may make narcissism especially costly.
future_research: Future research should examine other pathways through which parental income relates to leadership, including potentially positive effects through educational opportunities, competencies, or technical abilities. Scholars could also study other leadership behaviors such as servant leadership, test the model in organizations with weaker norms or less frequent interaction, and assess whether narcissistic leaders fare differently in contexts where they are fast-tracked or where self-oriented behavior is viewed more favorably.
abstract: We investigate how parental income during an individual’s upbringing relates to his or her effectiveness as a leader after entering an organization. Drawing on research on the psychological effects of income, social learning theory, and the integrative trait-behavioral model of leadership effectiveness, we propose a negative, serially mediated association between higher parental income and lower future leader effectiveness via high levels of narcissism and, in turn, reduced engagement in behaviors that are viewed as central to the leadership role. We test our model using multisource data collected from active soldiers in the United States Army. Results reveal that parental income exerts indirect effects on leadership effectiveness criteria because (a) parental income is positively related to narcissism as an adult, (b) narcissism relates negatively to engaging in task-, relational-, and change-oriented leadership behaviors, and (c) reduced engagement in these behaviors relates to lower leader effectiveness. Our investigation advances theory by identifying pathways through which parental income relates to the effectiveness of leaders in organizations, and by illuminating the origins of a trait—narcissism—that predicts the behavior and effectiveness of leaders.

title: Coordinated Exploration for Grand Challenges: The Role of Advocacy Groups in Search Consortia
methods: Empirical quantitative study of FP7 grant applications. The paper combines content analysis of call texts, a first-stage probit selection model for advocacy group inclusion, fixed-effects OLS models for evaluation scores, an inverse Mills ratio correction, instrumental-variable logic, and robustness checks including alternative measures and coarsened exact matching.
industry: European FP7 grand challenge funding calls across themes including food and agriculture, health, ICT, nanotechnologies, energy, environment, transportation, security, and socio-economic and humanities-related issues.
country: European Commission Seventh Framework Program context, with participating organizations across multiple regions.
units: Search consortia submitting FP7 Cooperation applications and the European Commission calls to which they applied
n_sample: 35,249 consortia applying to solve 2,349 grand challenge problems; 1,284 consortia included at least one advocacy group.
authors: Olsen, Anders Ørding; Sofka, Wolfgang; Grimpe, Christoph
theories: coordinated exploration in organizational search; organizational legitimacy; signaling theory; stakeholder theory
keywords: advocacy groups; coordinated exploration; grand challenges; joint search; legitimacy; search consortia; stakeholder theory
research_question: The paper asks why search consortia include advocacy groups and how advocacy groups help consortia obtain funding to implement proposed solutions to grand challenge problems. It focuses on whether stakeholder-related task environments make advocacy group inclusion more likely and whether advocacy group involvement improves proposal evaluation through search and legitimacy mechanisms.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that advocacy groups bring stakeholder knowledge into coordinated exploration and help consortia identify solutions that are more acceptable to affected stakeholders. Their involvement can also signal legitimacy to evaluators because credible advocacy groups are unlikely to lend their reputation to proposals that ignore stakeholder interests. These benefits are theorized and found to be stronger when technological knowledge is highly dispersed, increasing coordination difficulty, and when the consortium lacks experience, increasing the value of legitimacy.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends coordinated exploration theory by showing that useful search partners need not contribute primarily through technological expertise. Advocacy groups can shape joint search by contributing stakeholder understanding, coordination, and legitimacy. It also extends stakeholder theory by modeling advocacy groups as active partners in innovation-oriented search rather than only as external actors who pressure firms through resistance, protest, or political intervention.
practical_implication: For governments and foundations, the findings imply that the wording of grand challenge calls can influence whether consortia include advocacy groups and stakeholder concerns. For firms, universities, and other consortium members, cultivating credible advocacy group relationships may improve proposal quality and evaluation, especially when the consortium is technologically dispersed or inexperienced. For advocacy groups, participation can be a way to shape solutions to grand challenges in line with stakeholder interests.
limitations: The study observes expert evaluations of grant applications rather than whether funded consortia ultimately solved the underlying grand challenge problems. The authors use multiple approaches to address endogeneity in advocacy group inclusion, but they do not observe an exogenous shock that would create a natural experiment. The data also do not systematically capture heterogeneity among advocacy groups, such as size, power, public attention, agenda conflict, or network position.
future_research: Future work could connect ex-ante proposal evaluations to ex-post project outcomes to test whether advocacy group involvement improves actual solution development and implementation. Studies in similar grant-application settings could exploit exogenous shocks to advocacy group availability or inclusion rules to strengthen causal identification. Additional research could examine how differences among advocacy groups affect coordination, legitimacy, information flow, and conflict within search consortia.
abstract: Grand challenges are among the most complex problems for modern societies. Many governments and foundations provide substantial resources to encourage the search for solutions. Due to the significance of these problems, organizations often form partnerships in what we call search consortia to engage in joint search and compete for funding. Prior research on joint search highlights the role of specialized organizations, mainly regarding technological domains, to identify a superior solution. However, stakeholder theory leads us to believe that the success of any solution depends on the acceptance and support of important stakeholders. In this study, we suggest that search consortia are more likely to receive funding when they include representatives of stakeholder concerns, so-called advocacy groups. We extend theory on coordinated exploration in joint search by integrating mechanisms from stakeholder theory and argue that advocacy groups improve the generation of potential solutions and provide legitimacy. We test our theory with a unique dataset of 35,249 consortia that proposed solutions to 2,349 grand challenge problems as part of a large European funding program. Our results show that advocacy groups benefit search consortia, particularly when consortia exhibit a high dispersion of technological knowledge and when they are inexperienced.

title: Health Care’s Grand Challenge: Stimulating Basic Science on Diseases that Primarily Afflict the Poor
methods: Empirical quantitative study using global disease-year analyses and local country-disease-year panel analyses. The paper links TRIPS compliance, disease burden measured by DALYs, and citation-weighted Scopus publications, with OLS models, country-disease and year fixed effects in local models, robustness checks, and basic/applied science classifications.
industry: Health care and biomedical science on neglected and nonneglected diseases.
time_period: 1990-2010 for the main publication analysis, with 1985-1989 publications used to construct cumulative controls.
units: Disease-year for the global response analysis; country-disease-year for the local response analysis.
n_sample: 82 diseases.
authors: Vakili, K.; McGahan, A. M.
theories: economic logic of intellectual property protections; managerial theories of institutions and innovation
keywords: Grand Challenge; Trade-Related Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS); basic science; intellectual property protections; managerial institutions; neglected diseases
research_question: The paper asks whether intellectual property protections under TRIPS stimulated research on neglected diseases, especially the basic science needed before drug development can occur. It also asks why the scientific response to TRIPS differs between neglected and nonneglected diseases and between global and local scientific communities.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that TRIPS changed the expected returns to science by increasing the protected market for diseases prevalent in compliant countries, but the response depended on the institutional readiness of scientific communities. For nonneglected diseases, prior basic science and commercialization institutions made applied research more responsive. For neglected diseases in low-income countries, the response appeared mainly in basic science, because drug development required earlier-stage knowledge and institutional development before clinical or commercial outcomes could emerge.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends economic accounts of intellectual property by showing that incentives alone are insufficient to explain scientific responses to grand challenges. It contributes to management theory by positioning TRIPS as a managerial institution of science whose effects depend on scientific infrastructure, institutional development, collaboration, and capability building. It also argues that management theories of institutions, innovation, and entrepreneurship are relevant to health-care grand challenges, not only to corporations.
practical_implication: Managers and policymakers should not treat intellectual property protections as a complete solution for neglected diseases. TRIPS may stimulate basic science, but translation into therapies requires institutional support for scientists in low-income countries, international collaboration, applied research, clinical trials, manufacturing, distribution, and commercialization. The paper suggests that WTO, WHO, governments, NGOs, and private organizations should complement TRIPS with support for the full scientific and drug-development ecosystem.
limitations: The authors caution that data limitations prevent them from directly observing the institutional and managerial processes through which TRIPS affected science. They cannot determine whether the relevant mechanisms were financial, technical, social, or some combination of these. They also urge caution in interpreting the local-response analysis causally because implementation timing and scientific activity could be linked to broader political, economic, legal, or social changes.
future_research: The paper calls for deeper qualitative and quantitative research on how scientific institutions emerge and how basic science on neglected diseases becomes applied science and commercialized medicine. It also calls for research on whether TRIPS was the most humane, efficient, or appropriate intervention, and on how global scientific institutions interact with local health-care alternatives. Further work should examine performance heterogeneity, capability development, governance structures, rivalry, and collaboration across the institutional ecosystem.
abstract: Perhaps the most compelling Grand Challenge in health care is addressing diseases that primarily afflict the poor. Policies and practices conceived in high-income countries for improving the lives of patients in low-income countries have been criticized as ineffective or harmful. We examine the impact of one such policy, the World Trade Organization’s 1994 Trade-Related Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS), which was partly justified by a claim that patents and other intellectual property protections would improve the availability of drugs for “neglected diseases” such as malaria and tuberculosis. There is little evidence associating TRIPS with clinical trials, patents, or trade-in drugs for these diseases. One explanation for this is that basic science is required as a prerequisite to drug development. We theorize, test for, and find evidence that TRIPS encouraged the time-consuming and complex development of managerial institutions required for basic science on neglected diseases. The results indicate an increase in basic science on neglected diseases and in applied science on nonneglected diseases as countries became TRIPS compliant. In newly TRIPS-compliant, low-income countries, scientists intensified basic research on locally relevant diseases. We call for the application of management theories to grand challenges, and to the evaluation of policies such as TRIPS.

title: Building Resilience or Providing Sustenance: Different Paths of Emergent Ventures in the Aftermath of the Haiti Earthquake
methods: Qualitative inductive multiple-case study of six Haitian-led ventures created after the 2010 Haiti earthquake, using interviews, observation, field notes, archival sources, follow-up exchanges, and Gioia-style iterative coding.
industry: Local post-disaster ventures focused on alleviating suffering
time_period: After the January 12, 2010 Haiti earthquake, with field interviews in Port-au-Prince in 2012 and primary data collection spanning nearly two years
units: Six anonymized ventures, associated founders, employees, customers, support-service informants, field notes, interviews, archival sources, and follow-up exchanges
n_sample: Six ventures
authors: Williams, T. A.; Shepherd, D. A.
theories: emergent response groups; entrepreneurial opportunity; resilience to adversity; social resources and resourcefulness
keywords: disaster response; emergent organizations; local ventures; resilience; suffering; venture creation
research_question: The paper asks how post-disaster new ventures acquire, combine, and use resources, and how venture creation facilitates community members' resilience after disaster. It focuses on why some Haitian-led local ventures after the 2010 earthquake became more effective than others in moving victims beyond immediate survival.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: potential opportunities to alleviate suffering; social resources; founding mindset; resourcefulness; sustaining versus transforming paths.
- Process / phases: locals first act on immediate suffering, identify opportunities, mobilize social and material resources, and then follow either a sustaining path of continued relief or a transforming path of staged recovery.
- Practices: sustaining ventures rely on transactional outside resources, lobbying, long-term appropriation, and sometimes deviant resource acquisition; transforming ventures use local and international ties, temporary resource use, customized services, and legal creative resourcing.
- Emergent outcomes: sustaining ventures preserve survival but can deepen dependency; transforming ventures move victims toward housing, work, psychological support, autonomy, and self-reliance.
- Boundary conditions: the model is induced from Haitian-led ventures in a least developed country after a major natural disaster, where weak institutions, outside aid, property-right uncertainty, and local social ties shaped venture paths.

The process model links venture founders' social resources and mindset to the kinds of opportunities they recognize and the resourcefulness practices they enact. Sustaining ventures interpret opportunity as long-term relief and resource claims, which keeps victims in a basic-needs cycle. Transforming ventures interpret opportunity as an obligation to help people progress through recovery stages, using relationships and staged investments to support resilience and self-reliance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a venturing model of disaster resilience that distinguishes survival-oriented sustaining from autonomy-oriented transforming. It extends resilience, disaster-response, and entrepreneurship research by showing how emergent ventures' social ties, founding mindsets, and resourcefulness practices shape different gradients of post-disaster functioning.
practical_implication: Disaster responders, NGOs, and policymakers should not treat all emergent local ventures as equivalent. Supporting grassroots ventures requires attention to whether their practices create pathways to self-reliance or reinforce long-term dependency, and external actors may need to help local ventures manage difficult transitions from relief to recovery.
limitations: The study is an inductive qualitative study of six ventures in the specific context of post-earthquake Haiti, so transferability to other disasters, countries, and institutional settings requires further evidence. The authors also note that the apparent superiority of transforming ventures may depend on the study's time horizon, because sustaining ventures could have longer-run institutional effects on property rights or redistribution.
future_research: Future research should examine how to support transforming ventures through disaster-preparation and response programs, compare disaster types and economic environments, and study how ventures sequence survival, speed, autonomy, and self-reliance. The authors also call for work on network development, prosocial mindset, long-term institutional change, and comparisons between post-disaster venturing and more traditional entrepreneurial contexts.
abstract: Disaster events threaten the lives, economies, and wellbeing of those they impact. Understanding the role of emergent organizations in responding to suffering and building resilience is an important component of the grand challenge of how to effectively respond to disasters. In this inductive case study we explore venture creation initiated by locals in response to suffering following the 2010 Haiti earthquake. In exploring six ventures we found that two distinctive groups emerged in terms of their identification of potential opportunities to alleviate suffering, their access to and use of key resources, the action they took, and ultimately their effectiveness in facilitating resilience. We offer an inductive, grounded theoretical model that emerged from our data that provides insight into and an extension of literature on resilience to adversity and the disaster literature on emergent response groups, opening pathways for management scholarship to contribute in a meaningful way to this grand challenge.
apa_citation: Williams, T. A., & Shepherd, D. A. (2016). Building resilience or providing sustenance: Different paths of emergent ventures in the aftermath of the Haiti earthquake. *Academy of Management Journal*, 59(6), 2069-2102. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2015.0682

title: Not All Inequality Is Equal: Deconstructing the Societal Logic of Patriarchy to Understand Microfinance Lending to Women
methods: Empirical quantitative cross-national panel study using MIX microfinance organization data, country-level patriarchy indicators, factor analysis, generalized least squares models with country fixed effects, and supplementary interviews with microfinance professionals.
industry: Global microfinance organizations, treated as social enterprises addressing poverty through lending.
units: MFO-year observations for microfinance organizations, with dependent variables for women borrowers served, female employees, and local funding.
n_sample: 2,326 MFOs in 115 developing countries.
authors: Zhao, E. Y.; Wry, T.
theories: institutional contrast and change (Seo & Creed, 2002); institutional logics perspective (Thornton, Ocasio, & Lounsbury, 2012); patriarchy as a societal-level logic; societal logics
keywords: gender inequality; institutional logics; lending to women; microfinance organizations; patriarchy; social outreach; societal logics
research_question: The paper asks how patriarchy, understood as a societal-level institutional logic, affects microfinance organizations' outreach to women. It specifically examines whether patriarchy suppresses lending through family, religion, professions, and state sectors, and whether uneven patriarchy across sectors can instead catalyze support for women's lending.
mechanism_summary: Patriarchy in family and religion can reduce the supply of women borrowers by shaping gender roles, domestic authority, and women's self-perception as economic actors. Patriarchy in professions and the state can reduce the supply of female employees and local subsidies needed for women-focused outreach. However, when women gain ground in professions or the state while patriarchy persists in family and religion, the resulting institutional contrast makes gender inequality more visible, motivates redress efforts, and increases resources for MFOs that lend to women.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends institutional logics research by showing that societal logics should not be treated only as uniform national characteristics or single aggregate indexes. By deconstructing patriarchy across societal sectors, it shows that a logic's organizational effects depend on where and how strongly it manifests. The study also adds to research on prosocial organizations by showing that the institutional causes of a social problem can constrain or support organizations that try to address it.
practical_implication: MFOs seeking to serve women in highly patriarchal countries may need to rely more heavily on foreign investment because local support is unlikely to be strong. In countries with relatively lower visible gender inequality, MFOs and funders may need to make persistent inequality more salient to build support for women-focused lending. Development agencies should consider cross-sector patterns of patriarchy when deciding where microfinance support can most effectively expand outreach to women.
limitations: The analysis includes major MFOs covered by MIX but not the entire population of MFOs in every country. The paper cannot directly test all mechanisms because it lacks data on female loan applications and cannot observe discrimination in lending decisions directly. The cross-national design also relies on coarse country-level indicators, and the employee and local-funding analyses are constrained by more limited data coverage.
future_research: Future research should directly study female loan applications, borrower access, and discrimination in lending decisions to better test the mechanisms through which patriarchy affects MFOs. Case-based research could add detail on how professional women, state actors, and other groups support microfinance under uneven patriarchy. The authors also suggest extending the cross-sector societal-logics approach to other forms of categorical inequality, including class, race, religion, sexual orientation, and environmental degradation.
abstract: Many social problems reflect sets of beliefs and practices—or “institutional logics”— that operate at the societal level and rationalize the marginalization of certain categories of people. Studies have examined the consequences this has for individuals, but have largely overlooked how organizations that address such issues are affected. To understand this, we apply and extend the institutional logics perspective. Our approach recognizes that practices within different sectors of a society may be shaped by different organizing principles. However, we suggest practices are also likely to reflect—to varying degrees—broader societal logics. Based on this, we argue that societal logics may work through multiple influence channels and affect organizations in non-obvious ways, depending on how, where, and with what intensity they manifest in society. We test our theory by analyzing how patriarchy, as a societal-level logic, affects outreach to women by microfinance organizations in 115 nations. We find that patriarchy supports practices in the family, religion, professions, and state that suppress this outreach. Yet, in some nations, patriarchy is differently evident across sectors. The resulting contrasts draw attention to women’s issues, motivate redress efforts, and catalyze resource flows to microfinance organizations. The greatest outreach to women is in these nations.

title: Collective Organizational Engagement: Linking Motivational Antecedents, Strategic Implementation, and Firm Performance
methods: Survey-based, firm-level empirical study of small- to medium-sized U.S. credit unions, using aggregated employee and TMT ratings, archival ROA, moderated regression, and bootstrapped moderated mediation tests.
industry: Credit unions
time_period: Employee survey data with firm performance collected six months after the survey
units: Small- to medium-sized credit unions
n_sample: 83 firms; 302 TMT members, 301 mid-level managers, and 300 entry-level employees
authors: Barrick, M. R.; Thurgood, G. R.; Smith, T. A.; Courtright, S. H.
theories: engagement theory (Kahn, 1990); resource management model (Sirmon et al., 2007)
keywords: CEO transformational leadership; HRM practices; collective organizational engagement; engagement theory; firm performance; motivating work design; resource management model; strategic implementation
research_question: The paper asks whether employee engagement can operate as a shared firm-level motivational capability, which organizational practices foster that shared engagement, and how executives' strategic implementation affects the link between those resources and collective organizational engagement.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that motivating work design, HRM practices, and CEO transformational leadership jointly support psychological meaningfulness, safety, and availability, producing shared perceptions that organizational members are collectively engaged. Collective organizational engagement then functions as an organization-level capability that links these resources to firm performance. Strategic implementation strengthens the resource-to-engagement relationships by aligning and monitoring organizational effort around the firm's objectives.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends engagement theory by conceptualizing engagement as a firm-level collective construct rather than only an individual-level state. It contributes to resource management theory by specifying collective organizational engagement as a motivational capability through which bundled organizational resources create firm value, and by showing that TMT strategic implementation is a boundary condition that strengthens this capability-building process.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that leaders can improve firm performance by deliberately creating shared engagement across the organization rather than relying on isolated engagement initiatives. It points to enriched entry-level work design, fair and developmental HRM practices, transformational CEO leadership, and active TMT monitoring of strategy as mutually reinforcing levers.
limitations: The authors note that much of the research design is cross-sectional, so causal inference rests primarily on theory rather than a fully longitudinal empirical design. They also note that the study focuses on one level of analysis, relies heavily on survey measures for constructs other than firm performance, and uses small- to medium-sized credit unions, which may limit generalizability to larger firms.
future_research: The authors call for longitudinal research to test causal relationships and examine whether collective organizational engagement is dynamic over time. They also suggest multilevel research on whether collective engagement influences individual or group motivational states and further work on the complexity of strategic implementation.
abstract: We present a comprehensive theory of collective organizational engagement, integrating engagement theory with the resource management model. We propose that engagement can be considered an organization-level construct influenced by motivationally focused organizational practices that represent firm-level resources. Specifically, we evaluate three distinct organizational practices as resources—motivating work design, human resource management practices, and CEO transformational leadership—that can facilitate perceptions that members of the organization are as a whole physically, cognitively, and emotionally invested at work. Our theory is grounded in the notion that, when used jointly, these organizational resources maximize each of the three underlying psychological conditions necessary for full engagement; namely, psychological meaningfulness, safety, and availability. The resource management model also underscores the value of top management team members implementing and monitoring progress on the firm's strategy as a means to enhance the effects of organizational resources on collective organizational engagement. We empirically test this theory in a sample of 83 firms, and provide evidence that collective organizational engagement mediates the relationship between the three organizational resources and firm performance. Furthermore, we find that strategic implementation positively moderates the relationship between the three organizational resources and collective organizational engagement. Implications for theory, research, and practice are discussed.

title: Diplomas, Photos, and Tchotchkes as Symbolic Self-Representations: Understanding Employees' Individual Use of Symbols
methods: Qualitative grounded theory study using semi-structured employee interviews, workspace inventories, observations, photographs, and iterative coding.
industry: Cross-industry employees from varied settings, including marketing/design, software, financial services, automotive, education, government, real estate, and power/utilities.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Employees with personalized or minimally personalized workspaces across 14 organizations.
n_sample: 28 employees/interviews; initial 13 employees at 2 firms plus 15 additional employees selected through theoretical sampling.
authors: Byron, K.; Laurence, G. A.
theories: emotion regulation; self-regulation; sociomaterial perspective; symbols as representations of self
keywords: physical work environment; relationship development; self-regulation; symbolic representations of self; workspace personalization
research_question: The paper asks what prompts employees to personalize or not personalize their workspaces, how employees personalize, and what consequences personalization has. It examines workspace objects as symbolic self-representations that may shape both interpersonal relationships and intrapersonal self-regulation at work.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / distinctions: Workspace personalization, symbolic expressions of self, symbolic reminders of self, work and nonwork identities, future selves, relationship development, and self-regulation.
- Relational process: Public symbolic expressions of self can initiate conversations, increase role clarity, and encourage self-disclosure, but excessive or norm-violating distinctiveness can create negative impressions.
- Regulatory process: Symbolic reminders of self can focus attention on goals and values and help employees enact desired work-nonwork boundaries, but too much personalization can distract attention and generate negative affect.
- Boundary conditions: The model is grounded in employees' accounts across varied workspaces and organizations, not in a statistical test of causal effects.

The process model distinguishes symbols used for others from symbols used for the self. Personalization directed toward others helps employees communicate similarity, difference, role identity, and personalistic information, thereby building or sometimes inhibiting relationships. Personalization directed toward the self helps employees remember goals, values, and work-nonwork boundaries, thereby supporting or sometimes impeding regulation of attention, behavior, and emotion.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends research on symbols at work by showing that individually chosen physical objects do more than communicate status or distinction to others; they also provide or deplete regulatory resources for the self. It contributes to workplace relationship theory by showing how material objects help employees find common ground, clarify roles, and disclose personalistic information. It also extends self-regulation theory by showing how symbolic self-representations can focus attention, support affect regulation, and shape boundary management.
practical_implication: Organizations should be cautious about placing excessive limits on workspace personalization, because moderate personalization can help employees regulate emotion, orient effort toward goals, and build relationships. Employees and managers should also recognize that personalization can have relational and attentional costs when it violates norms, conveys too much distinctiveness, or creates distracting clutter. The practical implication is not unlimited personalization, but a middle ground that permits meaningful self-representation while preserving professionalism and focus.
limitations: The authors note that interview data may be affected by retrospective sensemaking and that participants' accounts of motives and effects cannot be fully verified. The study focuses mainly on visual physical objects, leaving other sensory features of personalization such as touch, smell, and taste underexamined. The analysis also does not provide fine-grained evidence about how symbolic self-representations operate under specific conditions such as identity threat.
future_research: Future research should test the grounded theory model with complementary designs and diverse samples. The authors call for work on nonvisual sensory inputs from symbolic self-representations and on whether personalization helps employees cope with identity threats. They also suggest examining whether physical spaces that reflect desired goals improve goal achievement, whether personalization helps employees acquire desired identities, and how employees can facilitate disclosure when they lack a personalizable workspace.
abstract: Most employees personalize their workspaces with photos, memorabilia, and other items—even in the face of constraints such as rules prohibiting personalization. This prevalent use of objects likely reveals much about intrapersonal and interpersonal processes at work. By analyzing employee interviews and workspace inventories and observations, we discover that the objects with which employees personalize their workspaces (and even the absence of such objects) symbolize who they are and who they want to be. Through their symbolic representations of self, they find common ground (often through shared nonwork experiences), establish a common understanding of employees’ work roles, and share personalistic information about the self—all of which contribute to relationship development among employees and their coworkers, customers, and clients. With symbolic representations of self that offer an optimal amount of stimulation, they focus their attention on their goals and values and establish a desired boundary or integration between work and nonwork—both of which contribute to employees’ self-regulation. Our findings support the importance of examining micro-level processes related to the physical work environment, as we find that employees shape their work environment in ways that affect both their relationships at work and their self-regulatory functions.

title: How Early Implementations Influence Later Adoptions of Innovation: Social Positioning and Skill Reproduction in the Diffusion of Robotic Surgery
methods: Multilevel empirical mixed-method study of robotic surgery diffusion in Italy, combining qualitative interviews and archival reconstruction of organization-level adoption and implementation processes with quantitative tracking of field-level adoption patterns from 1999 to 2010.
industry: Italian health care system, focused on hospitals adopting or considering robotic surgery.
units: Hospital-level adoptions and implementations of robotic surgery, with interviews from adopters, non-adopters, distributors, policymakers, foundations, and health care experts.
n_sample: 50 robotic-surgery adoptions in 43 hospitals, plus interviews with 124 adopters, 43 other relevant actors, and 24 non-adopters.
authors: Compagni, Amelia; Mele, Valentina; Ravasi, Davide
theories: institutional theories of diffusion; isomorphic diffusion; rational action theories of diffusion; social positioning
keywords: diffusion of robotic surgery; early implementations; exemplary users; isomorphic diffusion; later adoptions; skill reproduction; social gains; social positioning
research_question: The paper asks how early adopters' implementation experiences influence later adoption decisions during the early diffusion of an innovation. It focuses on why some actors adopt robotic surgery under high technical and economic uncertainty, how their social positions shape those motivations, and how their later dissemination practices affect field-level diffusion.
mechanism_summary:
- Key actors: Central hospitals, peripheral hospitals, surgeons, hospital managers, patients, professional associations, and technology distributors.
- Motivational drivers: Central actors adopted to preserve organizational or reputational imperatives, while peripheral actors adopted to gain social standing and professional prominence.
- Process / phases: Phase I involved pioneering adoptions under uncertainty; Phase II involved imitation of apparently successful exemplary users; Phase III involved coercive patient pressure, bandwagon effects, and renewed social-gain motives in peripheral regions.
- Dissemination practices: Exemplary users used peer-oriented and public-oriented narratives, codification, mediated exposure, schooling, migration, and proctoring.
- Emergent outcomes: These practices enabled skill reproduction, reassured later adopters about implementation feasibility, and supported isomorphic diffusion despite unresolved uncertainty about technical and economic benefits.

The process is that peripheral early adopters treated robotic surgery as a chance to improve their field position, then constituted themselves as exemplary users by publicizing positive experiences and transferring implementation know-how. Their discursive persuasion helped frame the innovation as viable and desirable, while skill reproduction reduced later adopters' uncertainty about how to implement it. As adoption accumulated, patient demand, media visibility, and competitive fear shifted diffusion toward coercive and bandwagon pressures.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends diffusion theory by showing that early diffusion depends not only on how many actors have adopted, but also on how earlier adopters implemented the innovation and disseminated those experiences. It links social position to adoption motives, arguing that central and peripheral actors may both adopt early but for different reasons: central actors protect their position, whereas peripheral actors seek social gains. It also adds micro-level mechanisms, especially discursive persuasion and skill reproduction, to institutional accounts of isomorphic diffusion.
practical_implication: The findings imply that managers evaluating complex innovations should examine not only adoption counts or promotional narratives, but also the implementation experience and skill-transfer infrastructure behind those adoptions. For hospitals and policymakers, the study warns that technologies can diffuse rapidly under social and competitive pressure even when technical and economic benefits remain uncertain. It also shows that proctoring, schooling, and codified protocols can materially affect whether late adopters believe they can implement a complex technology.
limitations: The authors note that the single-case design prevents direct comparison with other fields, so claims about which contextual conditions generalize remain speculative. The medical setting may heighten reputational dynamics because technological innovation is central to the status of hospitals and surgeons. The observability and complexity of robotic surgery may also amplify the importance of mediated exposure and skill reproduction relative to less visible or easier-to-implement innovations.
future_research: Future research could test whether similar social-positioning and exemplary-user dynamics occur for innovations that matter less for actors' reputations or provide clearer direct economic gains. Studies could examine whether early adopters disclose implementation knowledge differently when doing so risks helping direct competitors. The authors also encourage research on how knowledge exchanges between early and late adopters, including the mechanisms and kinds of knowledge transferred, shape diffusion patterns.
abstract: We report on a multilevel study investigating the diffusion of robotic surgery in the Italian health care system between 1999 and 2010. A combination of qualitative and quantitative methods allowed us to link organization-level processes associated with the adoption and implementation of the innovation to its diffusion at the population level. Our findings advance the understanding of how early experiences with the implementation of an innovation influence later adoptions, and they draw attention to how the search for social gains drives some peripheral actors to pioneer an innovation and engage in practices of discursive persuasion and skill reproduction that, in turn, constitute them to be "exemplary users." These practices eventually trigger and support the isomorphic diffusion of the innovation, even in the presence of persistent uncertainty about its technical or economic benefits.
apa_citation: Compagni, A., Mele, V., & Ravasi, D. (2015). How early implementations influence later adoptions of innovation: Social positioning and skill reproduction in the diffusion of robotic surgery. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(1), 242-278. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.1184

title: Ostracism, Self-Esteem, and Job Performance: When Do We Self-Verify and When Do We Self-Enhance?
methods: Empirical quantitative research using two field samples with multi-wave, multi-source designs. Sample A tested workplace ostracism, self-esteem level, importance of performance to self-esteem, in-role behaviors, and organizational citizenship behaviors; Sample B tested the same moderated mediation logic for organizational and interpersonal deviance. The authors used multiple regression, simple effects analysis, and bootstrapped tests of moderated mediation.
industry: Employed individuals from diverse occupations and industries, including business and finance, computers and mathematics, education, sales, and government.
time_period: Sample A used two online surveys approximately one week apart plus peer ratings; Sample B used focal-participant and work-peer surveys. Exact calendar dates are not reported.
units: Focal employees and nominated work peers.
n_sample: 158 matched focal participant/work peer datasets in Sample A and 273 complete datasets in Sample B.
authors: Ferris, D. L.; Lian, H.; Brown, D. J.; Morrison, R.
theories: self-enhancement motivation; self-verification theory (Swann, 1983, 2012); sociometer theory (Leary & Baumeister, 2000; Leary et al., 1995)
keywords: contingent self-esteem; importance of performance to self-esteem; job performance; self-enhancement; self-esteem level; self-verification; workplace ostracism
research_question: The paper asks when ostracized employees self-verify through behavior consistent with lowered self-esteem and when they self-enhance by maintaining strong job performance. It examines whether the importance of performance to self-esteem determines when self-esteem level mediates the relationship between workplace ostracism and job performance outcomes.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is that workplace ostracism lowers self-esteem, and lower self-esteem can lead employees to act in ways that verify negative self-perceptions through poorer performance or more deviance. The paper argues that this self-verification path is strongest when employees' self-worth is not contingent on workplace performance. When performance is important to self-esteem, employees are motivated to self-enhance in that domain, so self-esteem level no longer predicts poorer job performance in the same way.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to ostracism research by explaining why prior findings on ostracism, self-esteem, and performance were mixed: the indirect effect depends on contingent self-esteem. It also contributes to motivation theory by positioning contingent self-esteem as a boundary condition separating self-verification from self-enhancement. More broadly, it offers a moderated mediation model that can extend to other negative interpersonal behaviors carrying rejection and self-worth threats.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that organizations should understand workplace ostracism as a threat to employees' self-esteem and job behavior, not only as an interpersonal discomfort. Interventions that support employee self-esteem may reduce performance costs of ostracism, but the authors caution that developing high performance-contingent self-esteem may have downsides for well-being.
limitations: The authors note that the samples were convenience samples, so generalizability to the broader working population should be treated cautiously. They also state that the field data are cross-sectional for some theoretical paths, limiting causal inference. A further limitation is that performance could influence ostracism or self-esteem, and the available data are not well suited to test those reciprocal possibilities.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether relationship-contingent self-esteem moderates ostracism's effect on self-esteem. They also suggest examining other moderators of ostracism's direct performance effects, including task interdependence and situational interventions that reduce ambiguity or improve affect after ostracism. Future studies could also integrate behavioral and well-being outcomes to test when contingent self-esteem buffers performance damage while worsening well-being.
abstract: Self-esteem level has been positioned as a key mediating mechanism accounting for the effects of ostracism on behaviors, invoking the notion that individuals seek to verify their self-perceptions by behaving in a way that is consistent with those self-perceptions. However, evidence supporting the relation of ostracism and self-esteem level to behavioral outcomes has been mixed. We argue that such mixed effects arise because individuals may engage in behaviors alternately to verify their self-perceptions (suggesting a relation between self-esteem level and behavioral outcomes) or to self-enhance (suggesting no relation between self-esteem level and behavioral outcomes). Within this framing, the question becomes: When do we self-verify and when do we self-enhance? To that end, we position contingent self-esteem—or the extent to which individuals base their self-worth on outcomes in a particular domain—as a determining factor in whether we self-verify or self-enhance, and present a moderated mediation model to account for varying relations between ostracism and job performance. Our predictions regarding self-verification and self-enhancement motivation are fully supported across two field samples using multi-wave, multi-source study designs. Theoretical and practical implications for self-verification and self-enhancement motivation, as well as negative interpersonal behaviors at work, are discussed.
