title: Fashion with a Foreign Flair: Professional Experiences Abroad Facilitate the Creative Innovations of Organizations
methods: Empirical-quantitative archival panel study of high-end fashion houses using Journal du Textile creativity ratings, creative-director career histories, two-stage least squares regressions with instrumental variables, and fashion-house fixed effects.
industry: Global high-end fashion industry
country: Global fashion houses presenting in Paris, New York, Milan, and London
time_period: 2000-2010, covering 21 fall/winter and spring/summer fashion seasons
units: Fashion house-season observations, creative directors, and fashion collections
n_sample: 2,427 house-season observations from 270 fashion houses
authors: Godart, Frédéric C.; Maddux, William W.; Shipilov, Andrew V.; Galinsky, Adam D.
theories: blind variation and selective retention model of creativity; foreign experience model of creative innovations; social embeddedness perspective on creativity; theory of international adjustment
keywords: breadth; creative innovations; cultural distance; depth; fashion houses; foreign professional experiences
research_question: The paper asks whether creative directors' foreign professional experiences predict the creative innovations of the fashion houses they lead. It further asks how three dimensions of those experiences--breadth, depth, and cultural distance--independently and jointly shape firm-level creative output.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that foreign professional experiences expose leaders to novel inputs, require psychological adaptation to foreign cultural and work environments, and embed them in diverse professional networks. Moderate breadth and cultural distance provide variety without overwhelming adaptation, while depth supplies sustained exposure, adaptation, and embeddedness. The results indicate that depth is the most critical dimension; breadth and cultural distance matter primarily when depth is low and can substitute for one another as sources of variety.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces the foreign experience model of creative innovations to connect individual executives' international work histories to organization-level creative output. It integrates blind variation and selective retention, international adjustment, and social embeddedness perspectives to explain why foreign work experience can enhance creative innovations but may show diminishing or negative returns at high levels. It also extends creativity research by demonstrating curvilinear and interactive effects of breadth, depth, and cultural distance in historical field data.
practical_implication: Organizations seeking creative innovations may benefit from hiring or developing leaders with substantial professional experience abroad. The findings suggest that international rotational programs can build such experience internally, especially when assignments provide enough duration for adaptation rather than only brief exposure. Individuals seeking to enhance creative capacity may also benefit from substantial work abroad, not merely travel or shallow multicultural exposure.
limitations: The authors note that the archival design cannot directly observe creative teams' thought processes, conversations, or collective cognition. The study assumes that foreign professional experiences affect both idea generation and implementation, but it cannot separate ideas generated from ideas implemented in final collections. The measure of depth is duration abroad, which captures quantity more than the quality of immersion, network intensity, or local cultural learning.
future_research: Future research could test the model with experiments, surveys, participant observation, or interviews that directly observe exposure, adaptation, embeddedness, and implementation processes. Studies could examine whether the findings generalize to other creative or knowledge-intensive industries such as music, publishing, cinema, art, technology, or pharmaceutical R&D. Future work could also measure depth through language learning, local network size and intensity, and the quality of immersion abroad rather than duration alone.
abstract: This research explores whether the foreign professional experiences of influential executives predict firm-level creative output. We introduce a new theoretical model, the foreign experience model of creative innovations, to explain how three dimensions of executives’ foreign work experiences—breadth, depth, and cultural distance—predict an organization’s “creative innovations,” which we define as the extent to which final, implemented products or services are novel and useful from the standpoint of external audiences. We examined 11 years (21 seasons) of fashion collections of the world’s top fashion houses and found that the foreign professional experiences of creative directors predicted the creativity ratings of their collections. The results revealed individual curvilinear effects for all three dimensions: moderate levels of breadth and cultural distance were associated with the highest levels of creative innovations, whereas depth showed a decreasing positive effect that never turned negative. A significant three-way interaction shows that depth is the most critical dimension for achieving creative innovations, with breadth and cultural distance important at low but not high levels of depth. Our results show how and why leaders’ foreign professional experiences can be a critical catalyst for creativity and innovation in their organizations.
apa_citation: Godart, F. C., Maddux, W. W., Shipilov, A. V., & Galinsky, A. D. (2015). Fashion with a foreign flair: Professional experiences abroad facilitate the creative innovations of organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(1), 195-220. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0575

title: Help-Seeking and Help-Giving as an Organizational Routine: Continual Engagement in Innovative Work
methods: Inductive qualitative field study of help-seeking and help-giving among AdvanteQ engineers. The study uses ethnographic observations, semi-structured interviews, and archival materials, coded with grounded-theory techniques to identify 189 helping interactions, 2,344 moves, four subroutines, cognitive and emotional engagement moves, helping clusters, and contextual variation.
industry: Software and hardware engineering in a large technology company developing servers, workstations, software development tools, and infrastructure software.
country: Teams were distributed across California's Silicon Valley, Southern California, Massachusetts, and/or India; observations were limited to Silicon Valley and Massachusetts.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: AdvanteQ engineers, temporary project teams, helping interactions, moves within interactions, interviews, field notes, and archival materials.
n_sample: 19 initially shadowed AdvanteQ workers; 59 site visits; 184 observation hours; 602 pages of field notes; 32 brief semi-structured interviews; 189 identified helping interactions; and 2,344 coded moves.
authors: Grodal, Stine; Nelson, Andrew J.; Siino, Rosanne M.
theories: group engagement; interaction ritual chains; organizational routines perspective
keywords: cognitive engagement; coordination; emotional engagement; help-giving; help-seeking; innovative work; organizational routine
research_question: How does helping behavior unfold in organizations doing innovative work? The paper asks how help-seeking and help-giving proceed beyond initial consent when work is highly interdependent, innovative, and marked by pervasive helping.
mechanism_summary:
- Core process: Help-seeking and help-giving unfold as an organizational routine rather than a discrete exchange.
- Subroutines: Establishing mutual attention, orienting towards the issue, striving towards a resolution, and concluding the encounter.
- Engagement moves: Cognitive moves such as attracting attention, asking process or issue questions, invoking representational tools, and proposing solutions; emotional moves such as urgency, humor, excitement, interest, sympathy, and appreciation.
- Collective pattern: Helping can expand from dyads into helping clusters when additional help-givers become engaged.
- Contextual shaping: Well-defined versus ambiguous tasks, meetings versus impromptu encounters, and face-to-face versus technologically mediated interaction alter how the routine is enacted.

The process begins when a help-seeker and potential help-giver establish mutual attention, then build shared understanding of the issue and work toward resolution. Cognitive and emotional engagement moves keep participants involved, overcome impasses, accelerate interaction, and prepare for future help. Because the routine is recognizable but flexible, participants can recombine moves, involve additional people, and coordinate interdependent work even when the technical problem is ambiguous.
theoretical_contribution: The paper shifts helping research from an exchange-and-cost framing centered on the initial decision to help toward a process view of joint cognitive and emotional engagement. It shows that helping may be an organizational routine, may involve groups rather than only dyads, and is shaped by work context. It also extends routines research by showing that emotional engagement, not only cognitive scripts or schemas, can be central to routine enactment.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers in innovative and interdependent work settings should build psychological safety and rewards around seeking and giving help. It also implies that managers should consider whether meetings, technological mediation, or lack of colocation make engagement harder, especially when tasks are ambiguous and require sustained joint problem solving.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that this is a single case study of AdvanteQ, so transferability to other settings can only be speculated. They note possible limits in newer organizations where helping routines may not yet be established, across occupational boundaries where routines may not be shared, for personal rather than work-related helping, and in settings where routines are more formally articulated and less flexible.
future_research: Future research could examine how cognitive and emotional engagement across repeated helping encounters contributes to the emergence of organizational routines. The authors also call for comparative work between organizations where helping is prevalent and organizations where it is not, and for studies of how communication technology, meetings, occupational boundaries, and organizational change shape helping routines over time.
abstract: The literature on help-giving behavior identifies individual-level factors that affect a help-giver’s decision to help another individual. Studying a context in which work was highly interdependent and helping was pervasive, however, we propose that this emphasis on the initial point of consent is incomplete. Instead, we find that workplace help-seeking and help-giving can be intertwined behaviors enacted through an organizational routine. Our research, therefore, shifts the theoretical emphasis from one of exchange and cost to one of joint engagement. More specifically, we move beyond the initial point of consent to recast help-seeking and help-giving as an interdependent process in which both the help-seeker and the help-giver use cognitive and emotional moves to engage others and thereby propel a helping routine forward. In contrast to the existing literature, an organizational routines perspective also reveals that helping need not be limited to dyads, and that the helping routine is shaped by the work context in which help is sought. Finally, we extend these insights to the literatures on routines and coordination and debate how our results might generalize even if helping is not part of an organizational routine.

title: Managing by Design
methods: Editorial and conceptual essay that contrasts design-led, business-led, and engineering-led innovation, applies design thinking to the new workplace experience, and identifies opportunities for management scholarship.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Gruber, Marc; de Leon, Nick; George, Gerard; Thompson, Paul
theories: design thinking; experience economy
keywords: customer journey; design thinking; employee experience; innovation; new workplace experience
research_question: The editorial asks how leaders might manage by design: that is, how design thinking can be applied beyond products and services to work itself, workplace systems, physical and virtual environments, and employee experience. It also asks what research opportunities this shift creates for management scholars.
mechanism_summary:
- Design thinking: A human-centered, iterative, collaborative, and interdisciplinary approach that starts from observation of users and context, then moves through discovery, definition, ideation, prototyping, testing, and delivery.
- Service and workplace experience: The editorial argues that managers should frame service and workplace design around customer and employee journeys rather than only workflows, tools, and process optimization.
- New workplace experience: The proposed design principles emphasize real needs, value and values, employee journeys, co-creation, sensory and emotional engagement, and narrative sequencing.
- Scholarly agenda: The editorial calls for empirical work and theory development on performance effects, measurement of workplace experience, tensions between experience design and economic pressures, organizational redesign, HR practices, and motivation.

The process is editorial and agenda-setting rather than a tested causal model. Gruber, de Leon, George, and Thompson use design thinking to reframe management work around intentionally designed experiences, arguing that organizations can improve customer and employee outcomes when leaders design the systems, processes, environments, and interactions that shape those experiences.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial extends design thinking from product and service innovation into management science by treating the workplace and employee experience as design objects. Its contribution is to connect design thinking, the experience economy, organizational design, HR practices, motivation, and firm performance as a research agenda for studying the new workplace experience.
practical_implication: Managers should design employee and customer experiences intentionally rather than allowing them to emerge as by-products of workflows, tools, and organizational structures. The editorial suggests using co-creation, journey thinking, emotional and sensory design, and narrative sequencing to align work systems with user needs, employee values, and organizational goals.
limitations: The editorial does not report empirical tests, sample evidence, or validated measures. Its claims about performance, employee experience, and organizational redesign are presented as conceptual arguments and research opportunities rather than demonstrated findings.
future_research: The editorial calls for research on the performance effects of workplace design initiatives, measures that capture the quality of employee work experience, tensions between favorable work experiences and economic pressures, and the role of organizational forms, HR practices, and motivation in the new workplace experience.

title: If They Can Do It, Why Not Us? Competitors as Reference Points for Justifying Escalation of Commitment
methods: Event-history analysis using Cox semiparametric gap-time models on Taiwanese IT firms' repeated strategic actions in Chinese locations, supplemented by three waves of field interviews for theory development and illustration.
industry: Leading Taiwanese companies in personal computer, mainboard, and network device manufacturing.
country: China, with Taiwanese firms investing across Chinese provinces and municipalities.
units: Firm-location-quarter observations based on firm-location histories of Taiwanese IT companies in Chinese locations.
n_sample: 1,920 firm-location-quarter observations based on 131 firm-location histories of 51 firms in 16 locations.
authors: Hsieh, K.-Y.; Tsai, W.; Chen, M.-J.
theories: competitive dynamics; competitors as reference points; escalation of commitment
keywords: competitive dynamics; competitive market conditions; competitors as reference points; escalation of commitment; overseas expansion
research_question: The paper asks how competitive market conditions shape firms' escalation of commitment to underperforming initiatives. Specifically, it examines whether larger and smaller competitors function as reference points that enable or disable justification for continued investment in loss-incurring Chinese locations.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is that competitor cues alter the perceived justification for continuing investment despite negative performance feedback. Larger competitors' high action volume signals opportunities and competitive pressure, while smaller competitors' positive performance suggests that the focal firm should also be capable of succeeding. Larger competitors' negative performance instead provides an unsupportive cue, reducing the expected return to additional commitment.
theoretical_contribution: The paper links escalation of commitment research with competitive dynamics by identifying competitive market conditions as structural determinants of escalation behavior. It extends work on competitive relativity and asymmetry by showing that larger and smaller rivals have different informational value as reference points under adverse performance conditions. It also complicates purely bias-based accounts of escalation by showing that unsupportive external cues can reduce commitment.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that competitors' actions and performance can become justifications for continued resource commitment, even when a focal initiative is underperforming. Advantaged firms' aggressive moves may unintentionally encourage weaker rivals to escalate if those moves are read as evidence of attractive opportunities. Competitor analysis should therefore consider how rivals may interpret visible actions, not only how those actions affect direct market position.
limitations: The study focuses on competitors as external reference points and does not model internal mechanisms such as top management teams, political dynamics, organizational practices, inertia, or status quo preferences. Its empirical setting combines factor-market and product-market rivalry in Chinese locations, so it does not disentangle whether those two arenas have distinct implications. It also does not examine alternative entry modes such as greenfield investment, joint ventures, acquisitions, or conversions between ownership forms.
future_research: Future research can link micro-level psychological biases with macro-level firm behavior by examining how internal organizational factors amplify or attenuate competitor-based cues. Studies could distinguish factor-market from product-market rivalry and examine how different entry modes shape subsequent commitment to loss-incurring locations. Additional work could also compare escalation under negative performance with behavior under positive performance, where competitor cues may operate through different logics.
abstract: This study highlights competitive market conditions as an important structural determinant of escalation of commitment. Bridging escalation behavior literature and competitive dynamics research, we argue that reference to certain rivals may enable or disable decision makers to justify continuing investment in an underperforming initiative, thereby influencing a firm’s tendency toward escalating commitment. We test our ideas using data on a set of leading companies in the information technology industry and their investment activities in China. Empirical analysis reveals strong evidence that a firm’s escalating tendency is increased by larger competitors’ high action volume and smaller competitors’ positive performance. In contrast to prior research focus on decision makers’ persistence irrespective of external cues, we also find that a firm’s escalation behavior is decreased by larger rivals’ negative performance.

title: Who Defers to Whom and Why? Dual Pathways Linking Demographic Differences and Dyadic Deference to Team Effectiveness
methods: Multi-period survey and archival study using Kenny's social relations model to analyze directed dyadic deference, perceptions of task contributions, and social affinity; team performance was modeled with quasi-Poisson regression on publication and conference-output counts.
industry: Multidisciplinary academic research laboratories in a large public university research center.
time_period: Data from a larger project collected between 2009 and 2012 in multiple waves; surveys at Time 1 and Time 2, with archival performance data approximately 18 months after Time 2.
units: Research teams/labs, scientists and engineers, and directed dyadic ratings.
n_sample: 55 labs, 619 individuals, and 9430 directed dyadic ratings; team performance data for 46 labs.
authors: Joshi, A.; Knight, A. P.
theories: self-categorization theory; status characteristics theory
keywords: demographic differences; dyadic deference; social affinity; task contributions; team effectiveness
research_question: The paper asks how demographic differences shape who defers to whom in multidisciplinary research teams, and why those dyadic deference patterns affect team effectiveness. It focuses on whether deference emerges through perceptions of task contributions, social affinity, or both.
mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a dual-pathway model. In the task-contributions pathway, demographic attributes operate as status cues that shape perceived task competence, producing deference toward partners viewed as valuable contributors. In the social-affinity pathway, demographic similarity produces interpersonal affinity and mutual deference. These dyadic processes aggregate upward: task-based deference supports team research productivity, whereas affinity-based deference can divert influence toward socially close partners rather than task-relevant expertise.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends status research in teams by showing that demographic attributes shape deference not only through competence-based status expectations but also through social affinity. It contributes a multilevel account in which dyadic deference processes become bottom-up mechanisms linking demographic composition to team effectiveness.
practical_implication: Team leaders in knowledge-intensive settings should make task-relevant expertise more salient when teams coordinate across disciplinary boundaries. The findings suggest that leaders should reduce reliance on diffuse demographic cues and intervene when influence patterns appear to reflect affinity rather than task-relevant contribution.
limitations: The authors note that the team-level sample was relatively small, reducing power for some team-level effects. They also relied on single-item measures for dyadic task contributions, social affinity, and deference, and studied an academic research setting where education may be more salient than tenure or other status cues.
future_research: The paper calls for further dyad-level research on how demographic differences shape deference and other team processes. Future work should examine additional task-specific status cues, whether social affinity and task-competence perceptions overlap differently across high- and low-status groups, and how deference trajectories unfold from team inception to final performance outcomes.
abstract: We develop and test predictions about how demographic differences influence dyadic deference in multidisciplinary research teams, and how differential patterns of dyadic deference emerge to shape team-level effectiveness. We present a dual pathway model that recognizes that two distinct mechanisms—task contributions and social affinity— account for how team members’ demographic attributes contribute to deference. Furthermore, we propose that the extent to which these different mechanisms are prevalent in a team has implications for the team’s research productivity, with deference based on social affinity detracting from it and deference based on task contributions enhancing it. Using longitudinal data from a sample of 55 multidisciplinary research teams comprising 619 scientists, we found general support for our conceptual model. Our findings underscore the importance of accounting for multiple interpersonal mechanisms to understand the complex, multilevel nature of deference in teams.
apa_citation: Joshi, A., & Knight, A. P. (2015). Who defers to whom and why? Dual pathways linking demographic differences and dyadic deference to team effectiveness. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(1), 59-84. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0718

title: Real Options Logic Revisited: The Performance Effects of Alternative Resource Allocation Regimes
methods: Empirical quantitative study using Mannheim Innovation Panel / German Community Innovation Survey data; the authors estimate OLS regression models of new product sales on sequencing, low initial commitment, reallocation, fit, and controls.
industry: Product-innovating firms across diverse industries in the German CIS sample.
units: Firms with at least 10 employees and more than 5 product innovation projects.
n_sample: 436 firms
authors: Klingebiel, Ronald; Adner, Ron
theories: real options logic; resource allocation theory
keywords: innovation performance; low initial commitment; new product sales; real options logic; reallocation; resource allocation regimes; sequencing
research_question: The paper asks whether resource allocation behavior consistent with real options logic improves product innovation performance relative to alternative resource allocation regimes. It specifically examines whether sequencing, low initial commitment, reallocation, and the fit between low commitment and reallocation explain differences in new product sales.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that sequencing gives firms repeated decision points to adapt innovation projects as information about market and technical viability develops. Low initial commitment is valuable only when paired with later resource reallocation, because otherwise firms may escalate weak projects or cull projects without maintaining enough alternatives. The authors find sequencing and fit improve performance, but real options logic as the full Type D regime does not outperform other regimes once sequencing and fit are controlled.
theoretical_contribution: The paper clarifies real options logic as a multidimensional resource allocation regime requiring sequencing, low initial commitment, and reallocation rather than any one element alone. It contributes to real options theory by showing that prior mixed performance findings may reflect misidentification of real options logic. It also situates real options logic within broader resource allocation theory by showing that other regimes can combine sequencing and fit to achieve similar innovation performance.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat a single practice, such as stage-gated sequencing or low initial funding, as sufficient evidence of a real options approach. The results suggest that firms benefit from sequential resource allocation and from aligning initial commitment policies with later reallocation behavior. Low-commitment experimentation without disciplined reallocation, or culling without enough alternative projects, can reduce innovation performance.
limitations: The study uses survey-based CIS measures and does not provide fine-grained evidence on firms' rationales for adopting or discontinuing projects. The authors also note that they could not control for varying lag effects between innovation investment and returns. Additional limitations include limited observation of reallocation efficiency, formalization, centralization, uncertainty type, and possible inflection points in the number of allocation stages.
future_research: Future research could inspect firms' reported rationales for adopting or discontinuing product innovation projects in more detail. The authors also identify opportunities to study reallocation efficiency, formalized and routinized resource allocation, centralization, uncertainty conditions, allocation-stage inflection points, and longitudinal lag structures in more narrowly specified settings.
abstract: We delineate three dimensions of resource allocation behavior that allow us to distinguish between real options logic and alternative resource allocation regimes: sequencing, low initial commitment, and reallocation. We then measure these in a product innovation context to test for the performance effect of real options logic vis-à-vis its alternatives. Sequencing, which distinguishes dynamic allocation regimes more generally, is associated with higher new product sales. Low initial commitment and reallocation do not show individual direct effects on new product sales. However, when assessed as a match, we find that the fit between low initial commitment and reallocation (yes–yes; no–no) increases performance significantly. After controlling for such fit as well as sequencing, we find no significant performance difference between real options logic and other regimes. Our findings imply that insufficient identification of real options logic picks up confounding effects, which may provide an explanation for the inconclusive results in prior studies of real options and performance. In addition to bounding the concept more precisely, we contribute to theory by situating real options logic within the broader set of allocation regimes conducive to innovation performance in uncertain, competitive markets.
apa_citation: Klingebiel, R., & Adner, R. (2015). Real options logic revisited: The performance effects of alternative resource allocation regimes. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(1), 221-241. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0703

title: Professional Image Maintenance: How Women Navigate Pregnancy in the Workplace
methods: Mixed-method empirical study combining qualitative grounded-theory interviews, scale development and validation with exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, and a time-lagged survey study using path analysis.
industry: Working pregnant women across varied jobs and organizations, not a single industry.
country: Primarily United States; Study 3 also included a small number of respondents from Canada and outside North America.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Working pregnant women navigating pregnancy at work.
n_sample: Four samples: Study 1 n = 35; Study 2 final samples n = 199 and n = 133; Study 3 final sample n = 200.
authors: Little, L. M.; Smith Major, V.; Hinojosa, A. S.; Nelson, D. L.
theories: professional image construction (Roberts, 2005); regulatory focus theory (Higgins, 1997, 2000); self-regulation of behavior (Carver & Scheier, 1998); social identity-based impression management (Roberts, 2005)
keywords: burnout; decategorization; image maintenance; perceived discrimination; pregnancy; professional image; returning to one's job; social identity-based impression management
research_question: The paper asks how pregnancy affects working women's professional experiences and how pregnant workers use social identity-based impression management to maintain professional image. It also asks how SIM motives and strategies relate to perceived discrimination, burnout, and returning to one's job after maternity leave.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / motives: Legitimacy preservation and devaluation reduction.
- Key constructs / strategies: Image maintenance and decategorization.
- Process / sequence: Qualitative identification of motives and strategies, scale development and validation, then time-lagged testing of links to workplace outcomes.
- Emergent outcomes: Perceived discrimination, burnout, and return to one's job.
- Boundary conditions / controls: Pregnancy stage, number of pregnancies at the organization, pregnancy risk, workplace gender composition, self-image at work, self-verification striving, and prior burnout.

The paper argues that pregnancy can make a new and potentially devalued social identity salient at work, threatening women's prior professional image. Pregnant workers respond through approach-oriented image maintenance, such as maintaining pace, avoiding accommodations, going the extra mile, or shortening leave, and through avoidance-oriented decategorization, such as passing or downplaying pregnancy. In Study 3, legitimacy preservation predicted image maintenance, which was associated with lower perceived discrimination, lower burnout, and greater likelihood of returning to the job; devaluation reduction predicted decategorization but was directly associated with higher perceived discrimination and burnout rather than being improved by avoidance strategies.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends professional image construction and SIM theory by showing that changing social identities can produce non-loss-focused image maintenance rather than the gain-focused positive distinctiveness emphasized in work on stable identities. It also develops and validates measures of SIM during pregnancy and integrates self-regulation theory to distinguish approach-related image maintenance from avoidance-related decategorization. The results show that approach-oriented SIMp strategies can have beneficial outcomes, whereas avoidance motives may be more consequential than avoidance behaviors.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that organizations should focus less on whether pregnant workers' priorities shift and more on reducing the devaluation concerns that make pregnancy feel professionally risky. Supportive supervisors and workplaces may reduce the perceived need for avoidance strategies and help pregnant workers maintain professional image without burnout or perceived discrimination. The paper also indicates that image maintenance behaviors can be linked to retention after maternity leave.
limitations: The authors note possible common-method bias because the data came from the same source, although outcomes were collected in a separate time-lagged survey. They also state that the time lag may not have been long enough to observe meaningful changes in some SIMp constructs and that causality cannot be definitively established. The sample was largely U.S.-based, limiting claims about international generalizability.
future_research: The authors call for research on individual-level traits, additional mediators, and robust within-person designs across pregnancy stages and numbers of pregnancies. They also recommend testing whether the findings generalize to other new social identities, including chronic illness and other temporary or permanent identity changes. Future work should examine international differences in stereotypes of pregnant workers and the outcomes of gain-focused versus non-loss-focused SIM motives.
abstract: Women now constitute a significant portion of the workforce, making the effects of pregnancy on professional image (others’ perceptions of competence and character at work) more salient. While opinions regarding how pregnant women should manage others’ impressions and the consequences of doing so abound (Noveck, 2012) research to substantiate or disconfirm these opinions has lagged. In this paper, we present three studies that develop and test a model of social identity-based impression management (SIM) techniques used by pregnant workers. In Study 1 (n ⴝ 35), we utilized qualitative methods to identify the motives and strategies used by pregnant women to manage their professional images. In the second study, we collected two samples (n ⴝ 199 and n ⴝ 133) to develop and validate two scales based on the motives and strategies identified in Study 1. In Study 3 (n ⴝ 200), we employed a time-lagged design to examine how SIM motives and strategies affect important workplace outcomes: perceived discrimination, burnout, and returning to one’s job after maternity leave. Our findings demonstrate both positive and negative outcomes of the motives and strategies women use to manage their images at work when pregnant.

title: Investor Perceptions of Financial Misconduct: The Heterogeneous Contamination of Bystander Firms
methods: Event-study analysis of cumulative abnormal returns around financial restatement announcements, using multiple regression models with bystander-firm, perpetrator-firm, event, industry, and governance variables.
industry: S&P 1500 firms covering 219 industries around financial restatement events.
time_period: Financial restatement events in 2004, with financial and firm data from fiscal year 2003.
units: Bystander firms and restatement events.
n_sample: 725 S&P 1500 firms across 84 financial misconduct events.
authors: Paruchuri, S.; Misangyi, V. F.
theories: agentic attribution; generalization-instantiation process; industry categorization processes; social view of financial markets
keywords: bystander firms; contamination; corporate governance; financial misconduct; generalization-instantiation process; industry categorization; investor perceptions
research_question: The paper asks whether financial misconduct by one firm lowers investors' valuations of other firms in the same industry, and why this contamination varies across misconduct events and bystander firms. It focuses on how investors generalize culpability to an industry category and then perceive that generalized culpability as instantiated in particular bystander firms.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that investors use industry categories to make sense of financial misconduct under uncertainty. When a restatement reveals misconduct, investors generalize culpability from the perpetrator to the industry, lowering valuations for industry bystanders. The strength of that category-level generalization depends on perpetrator and event characteristics, while the degree to which particular bystander firms are penalized depends on their familiarity and governance signals.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the social view of financial markets by showing that investor valuation processes involve categorical social judgments, not only firm-specific financial information. It extends research on organizational misconduct by separating contamination into generalization and instantiation, which clarifies why innocent third parties suffer heterogeneous market penalties. It also contributes to corporate governance research by treating governance structures as signals that shape investor perceptions during misconduct events.
practical_implication: The study implies that firms may suffer valuation losses from peer misconduct even when they are not directly involved. It suggests that investor-facing governance signals and the visibility of both perpetrator and bystander firms can affect the magnitude of contamination after financial restatement announcements.
limitations: The paper's empirical context is accounting-related financial restatements in 2004, shortly after SOX-related governance changes, so the findings may not generalize unchanged to other misconduct forms or regulatory periods. The design identifies market reactions around events but infers the investor cognition behind generalization and instantiation from observable valuation patterns. The paper also notes that board vigilance operated opposite to the authors' prediction, indicating context-specific ambiguity in how investors read governance signals.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether similar generalization-instantiation processes operate for other forms of organizational misconduct and for other stakeholder audiences. They also encourage work on positive or ambiguous events, such as innovation, CEO charisma, mergers, acquisitions, and diversification, to test whether investor generalization works similarly outside negative judgments. Further research is needed on how contamination becomes stigmatization and how different investor types may perceive perpetrator, event, and bystander characteristics differently.
abstract: We suggest that, when one firm reveals financial misconduct, others in the industry suffer lower valuations, but do so heterogeneously. To understand this heterogeneity, we conceptualize such contamination as a generalization–instantiation process: investors generalize the culpability to the industry category and perceive the instantiation of generalized culpability within the industry bystander firms. This theoretical separation allows us to hypothesize the factors that affect the degree to which both of these elements of the contamination process occurs. Specifically, we predict that characteristics of the misconduct firm or event—factors that lend to investors’ familiarity with the misconduct firms, or that prompt attributions of blame for the misconduct—affect the potency of the generalization of culpability to the industry, while characteristics of the industry bystander firms—investors’ familiarity with such firms, or factors that lend to investors’ perceptions that they have strong governance—affect the firms’ vulnerability to being perceived as instantiating the generalized culpability. We tested our hypotheses on a sample of 725 firms across 84 financial misconduct events, and the results of our event analyses broadly support our predictions. Our study thus has implications for future research on the social view of financial markets, organizational misconduct, and corporate governance.
apa_citation: Paruchuri, S., & Misangyi, V. F. (2015). Investor perceptions of financial misconduct: The heterogeneous contamination of bystander firms. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(1), 169-194. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0704

title: I Need Time! Exploring Pathways to Compliance under Institutional Complexity
methods: Mixed-method study combining an experimental vignette study with Dutch childcare managers, ANCOVA and post-hoc comparisons of intended compliance delay, and inductive analysis of follow-up semi-structured interviews about planned responses.
industry: Dutch childcare sector.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Childcare managers responding to a hypothetical coercive regulatory demand.
n_sample: 100 respondents participated; 99 were retained after one failed manipulation check, with ANCOVA reported on n=96.
authors: Raaijmakers, A. G. M.; Vermeulen, P. A. M.; Meeus, M. T. H.; Zietsma, C.
theories: institutional complexity; institutional theory; sensemaking
keywords: childcare managers; coercive institutional demand; institutional complexity; pathways to compliance; time to compliance
research_question: The paper asks when and how organizational decision makers respond to coercive institutional demands when important constituents contest the demand's legitimacy. It focuses on whether institutional complexity delays intended compliance and what pathways to compliance decision makers plan before complying.
mechanism_summary:
- Key pressures: A coercive government demand to adopt a new childcare practice, combined with varying support or opposition from parents and employees.
- Timing outcome: Delay of intended compliance with the mandated digital wall.
- Response pathways: Early adoption, delay, accommodative responses such as neutralizing opposition and partial compliance, resistant responses such as fighting the practice and stimulating opposition, and exit.
- Interpretive conditions: Decision makers' interpretations of institutional complexity and their personal beliefs toward the mandated practice.
- Field process: Time before compliance is used either as a buffer against uncertainty or as a resource for action to reduce complexity.

The central process is that conflicting constituent pressures make the path to legitimacy ambiguous, so decision makers delay compliance rather than simply obeying the most coercive actor. During the delay, they may wait for others to clarify the situation or actively try to reshape pressures by influencing parents, employees, government actors, or the practice itself. Personal beliefs shape which responses they choose, especially whether they move toward accommodative or resistant pathways.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional complexity research by showing that coercive pressure does not automatically produce fast compliance when other constituents contest the practice. It adds microfoundations to institutional theory by explaining how decision makers interpret conflicting pressures, use time strategically, and engage in sensemaking and institutional work before compliance. It also extends work on institutionalization pace by showing that force-driven adoption can be slowed by influence-based efforts to construct a clearer path to legitimacy.
practical_implication: The findings imply that regulators and powerful constituents should not assume that coercive mandates will be implemented quickly when target organizations face opposition from other salient constituents. Managers can use implementation windows to negotiate with stakeholders, experiment with partial adaptations, and reduce uncertainty before full compliance. The paper also suggests that delays may be active attempts to preserve legitimacy rather than mere resistance or passivity.
limitations: The study uses hypothetical vignettes and anticipated responses rather than observed organizational implementation behavior. Its empirical setting is the Dutch childcare sector, where coercive regulation, parents, employees, and managers' pedagogical beliefs create a specific form of institutional complexity. The authors caution that generalizability is strongest for similar contexts where actors cannot ignore coercive pressure but also depend on important constituents who may oppose compliance.
future_research: Future research should identify contingencies affecting responses to institutional pressures under complexity, including when actors can safely ignore pressures, when fields sustain differentiated meanings, and when complexity resolves into shared understandings. Further work could examine how personal beliefs condition flexibility or inflexibility in responses to contested practices. The paper also argues that experimental approaches can help investigate the microfoundations of institutional theory and institutionalization processes.
abstract: In this study, we examined responses to institutional complexity by analyzing when and how organizations respond to a coercive institutional demand from a powerful constituent when other important constituents do not accept the demand as legitimate. We experimentally manipulated institutional complexity and gauged the time to compliance of 100 childcare managers in the Netherlands, and then asked them to describe and explain their anticipated responses to multiple pressures. We found that institutional complexity leads decision makers to delay compliance, but usually not passively: decision makers used the time before compliance to attempt to reduce institutional complexity by neutralizing opposing pressures, challenging the coercive pressure, adapting the practice to suit opponents and their own personal beliefs, and/or waiting to see how the situation would unfold as multiple parties influenced one another. We found two factors influenced decision makers' choice of responses: (1) their interpretation of institutional complexity and (2) their personal beliefs toward the practice itself. Our findings contribute to an emerging understanding of how decision makers interpret and respond to institutional complexity, and thus complement recent studies in the institutional complexity literature.
apa_citation: Raaijmakers, A. G. M., Vermeulen, P. A. M., Meeus, M. T. H., & Zietsma, C. (2015). I need time! Exploring pathways to compliance under institutional complexity. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(1), 85-110. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0276

title: West Meets East: New Concepts and Theories
methods: Conceptual essay and special research forum introduction comparing Eastern and Western contextual traditions, reviewing management theory development over time, and using the six papers in the forum as exemplars for generating concepts and theories from Eastern contexts.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Barkema, Harry G.; Chen, Xiao-Ping; George, Gerard; Luo, Yadong; Tsui, Anne S.
theories: agentic view of theory creation; construct equivalence; construct infusion; construct salience; normal science; theory development
keywords: East and the West; agentic view; construct equivalence; construct infusion; construct salience; cultural values; institutions; new concepts and theories; philosophies
research_question: Why have Eastern contexts generated relatively few new concepts and theories in leading management journals despite substantial differences between East and West in institutions, philosophies, cultural values, and management practices? How can researchers, journals, and management schools reduce normal-science bias and create theories grounded in new management puzzles from Eastern contexts?
mechanism_summary:
- Core problem: Management research has internationalized in authorship and samples, but still often applies Western concepts and theories to Eastern settings rather than generating new theory from those settings.
- Contextual foundations: Eastern institutions, philosophies, cultural values, and contemporary management practices differ from Western contexts and may surface distinct management puzzles.
- Theory-development process: New theories are more likely when researchers start from observed empirical puzzles, local management problems, and lived or multicultural experience rather than from narrow gaps in existing paradigms.
- Contribution threshold: Eastern constructs need to be assessed through construct equivalence, construct salience, and construct infusion to distinguish real theoretical contribution from relabeling.
- Agentic actors: Researchers, journals, and management schools can deliberately select, support, review, and publish work on novel management problems and social concerns.

The process argument is conceptual rather than variable-causal. Barkema and colleagues argue that management theory becomes more novel and globally relevant when scholars actively attend to the worldviews embedded in particular institutions, philosophies, and cultural beliefs, then use inductive and phenomenon-focused research to explain puzzles those contexts make visible. The paper positions construct equivalence, salience, and infusion as diagnostic criteria for judging whether an Eastern concept merely renames a Western construct, highlights an especially important attribute in an Eastern context, or adds new theoretical nuance. It also argues that journal and school-level choices can reduce normal-science pressures that otherwise keep theoretical contributions close to existing Western paradigms.
theoretical_contribution: The article contributes a conceptual account of how Eastern contexts can enrich management theory rather than only supply new empirical settings for Western theories. It synthesizes contextual differences between East and West, historical patterns in AMJ theory development, and the six special research forum papers to articulate construct equivalence, construct salience, and construct infusion as contribution criteria. It also advances an agentic view of theory creation in which researchers, journals, and management schools deliberately create variation in the field by supporting research on new puzzles, problems, and worldviews.
practical_implication: For researchers, the paper recommends starting from locally grounded management puzzles, using inductive or phenomenon-focused methods, and building on lived and multicultural experience to identify what is theoretically novel. For journals, it recommends review procedures, multicultural reviewer pools, and special research fora that reduce bias toward existing paradigms. For management schools, it recommends recognizing, funding, and rewarding research on local and emerging economic, social, and environmental problems, even when such work takes longer to publish.
limitations: The paper is a conceptual essay and special research forum introduction rather than a systematic empirical test of its claims about theory development, reviewer bias, or the production of new concepts from Eastern contexts. Its East-West comparisons are presented as indicative rather than exhaustive, so the authors frame them as broad contextual contrasts rather than complete coverage of all countries, institutions, or traditions.
future_research: The authors call for further work on communication in Asian organizations, leadership in Asian contexts, outward direct investment by Asian firms, composition-based strategy, and organizations addressing poverty, healthcare, education, and other grand challenges. They also encourage research that tests Eastern concepts across contexts, identifies boundary conditions and mechanisms, and examines whether concepts developed in Eastern settings can evolve into more universal theories.
abstract: Management scholarship has grown tremendously over the past 60 years. Most of our paradigms originated from North America in the 1950s to the 1980s, inspired by the empirical phenomena and cultural, philosophical, and research traditions of the time. Here following, we highlight the contextual differences between the East and the West in terms of institutions, philosophies, and cultural values and how they are manifest in contemporary management practices. Inspired by theory development in management studies over time, we offer insights into the conditions facilitating new theories, and how these might apply to emergent theories from the East. We discuss the contributions of the six papers included in this special research forum as exemplars of integrating Eastern concepts and contexts to enrich existing management theories. We highlight the difficulty with testing Eastern constructs as distinct from Western ones by discussing the properties of equivalence, salience, and infusion in constructs. We provide directions for future research and encourage an agentic view to creating new theories and paradigms.

title: Family- versus Lone-Founder-Controlled Public Corporations: Social Identity Theory and Boards of Directors
methods: Empirical quantitative study of large publicly traded firms using firm-year panel regressions for board interlocks, director experience, and institutional ownership, plus event-history analysis for outside director exit. The study draws on Compustat, proxy statements, Form 10-Ks, SEC EDGAR and Q-file filings, CRSP, and Bushee institutional investor classification data.
industry: Largest publicly traded firms listed on Compustat; industry controls are included.
time_period: Sample frame 1991-2005; board and officer data gathered from 1989-2005; the abstract describes publicly traded corporations between 1991 and 2006.
units: Firm-years and individual outside-director years.
n_sample: 742 firms; 10,533 firm-year observations; institutional ownership analyses use 6,090 observations.
authors: Cannella, Albert A., Jr.; Jones, Carla D.; Withers, Michael C.
theories: director identity; organizational identification; social identity theory
keywords: boards of directors; director experiences; director tenures; directorship interlocks; family companies; institutional investors; lone-founder companies; organizational identification; social identity theory
research_question: The paper asks how family-controlled and lone-founder-controlled public corporations differ in organizational identity and how those identities shape board structure, outside director experience, director tenure, and institutional investor ownership. It also asks whether treating family and lone-founder firms as a single category obscures meaningful governance differences.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that family and lone-founder firms have distinct organizational identities even though both controlling owners seek to preserve control. Family firms' familial identity motivates ties to other family firms and directors with family-firm experience, while lone-founder firms' individualistic and entrepreneurial identity motivates ties to other lone-founder firms and directors with lone-founder experience. These identity-consistent board structures reduce perceived threats to owner control, lengthen matched directors' tenure, and signal different governance and shareholder orientations to dedicated institutional investors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to corporate governance research by separating family-controlled firms from lone-founder-controlled firms rather than treating both as a single family-firm category. It extends social identity theory and organizational identification into board research by showing how owner and director identities shape interlocks, director selection, and director exit. It also links director identity to institutional investor behavior, arguing that outside directors' family- or lone-founder-firm experience signals a firm's openness to outside investor influence and shareholder-value priorities.
practical_implication: For boards and controlling owners, the findings imply that director selection is not merely a matter of generic independence or expertise; prior experience in similar ownership contexts can affect trust, control preservation, and director retention. For institutional investors, director experience in family firms versus lone-founder firms may serve as a governance signal because outside-director experience indicates a firm's governance and shareholder orientation. The results also imply that researchers and practitioners should avoid pooling family and lone-founder firms when assessing board structure and investor reactions.
limitations: The authors state that the sample is limited to publicly traded companies, so the findings are not generalizable to private firms. They also note that identifying family and lone-founder ownership is difficult and may not capture every qualifying firm, especially family firms with informal family involvement or late-stage generational complexity. The study only observes directors' experience within the sample firms and does not directly measure organizational identity, relying instead on theoretically grounded ownership and experience classifications.
future_research: Future research could examine other governance mechanisms through which family and lone-founder firms preserve control, including leadership structure, CEO duality, and the types of directors they recruit. The paper also calls for research on generational transitions in family firms and how board configurations differ across first-, second-, and third-generation family control. Additional work could directly measure organizational identity and test whether directors with family- or lone-founder-firm experience behave differently in monitoring, advising, and strategic decision making.
abstract: We distinguish between “family companies,” involving multiple family members as owners and/or managers, and “lone-founder companies,” involving only the founder and no other family members. We apply social identity theory and organizational identification to elucidate the differences between these two types of firms, and how their differing organizational identities reflect unique desires for control and influence. We then consider how these differences are reflected in a firm’s board structure (i.e., directorship interlocks, director experiences, and director tenures). Specifically, we predict that family firms are more likely to interlock with other family firms, select directors with more experience in family firms, and keep directors on their boards longer. Correspondingly, we posit that family firms are less likely to interlock with lone-founder firms or to select directors with experience in lone-founder-controlled firms. Lone-founder firms follow a similar pattern. We also consider the consequences of family and lone-founder ownership and board structures on the investment behavior of three classes of institutional investors. We test our hypotheses with a sample of publicly traded corporations between 1991 and 2006, and report strong support for most of our predictions.

title: Modernizing without Westernizing: Social Structure and Economic Action in the Indian Financial Sector
methods: Empirical quantitative archival study of analyst forecast accuracy in India. The authors merge I/B/E/S Detail History data with Prowess firm data and hand-coded CEO and analyst affiliation measures, then estimate OLS regressions with year dummies and robust standard errors adjusted using two-way clustering at firm-CEO and analyst levels.
industry: Indian financial markets and equity analyst coverage of publicly listed Indian firms; no single firm industry restriction is reported.
units: Analyst-firm-year earnings forecasts linked to equity analysts, CEOs, and focal Indian firms.
n_sample: 1,552 earnings forecasts issued by 296 equity analysts, covering 141 firms and 191 CEOs after exclusions.
authors: Chen, Guoli; Chittoor, Raveendra; Vissa, Balagopal
theories: efficient market hypothesis; embeddedness perspective; foci of affiliation; imprinting
keywords: analyst forecast accuracy; business groups; caste; embedded network ties; multinational corporations; regional language; school ties
research_question: The paper asks whether Asia's transition toward market economies follows the Western path of disembedded market relations, or whether economic action remains shaped by historically specific social structures. Empirically, it examines how caste, regional-language, and school ties between Indian equity analysts and CEOs affect analysts' EPS forecast accuracy, and whether CEO generation and organizational form change which ties matter.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that shared caste, language, or school affiliation can create trust and mutual understanding between analysts and CEOs, making private information more likely to flow and improving forecast accuracy. The macro institutional shift after India's 1991 reforms changes the salient basis of affiliation: prereform-generation CEOs are expected to rely more on caste and language ties, while postreform-generation CEOs rely more on school ties. The micro organizational context further shapes the process because BGs legitimate particularistic information exchange, whereas Western MNC subsidiaries dampen such transfers.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends the embeddedness perspective by showing that the institutional bases of network ties are not fixed and that economic action in transitional economies can remain embedded in historically specific social structures. It contributes to business group research by portraying BGs as repositories and carriers of behavioral norms that blend modern management practices with particularistic social patterns. It also broadens relational demography by examining caste, language, and school similarity across a market interface rather than only within hierarchical organizational relationships.
practical_implication: For financial-market actors in emerging economies, analyst forecast accuracy may depend on social access to CEOs, not only on formal disclosure infrastructure or analyst skill. Firms and regulators should recognize that weak public disclosure can make private interpersonal pathways consequential for capital-market information flows. The findings also imply that BGs and Western MNC subsidiaries can create different expectations about whether executives should engage with external market intermediaries through particularistic ties.
limitations: The authors state that the study is based on archival sources and does not directly observe private information flowing from CEOs to analysts or the development of interpersonal relationships. They also lack data on the total pool of caste and language groups, cannot test brokerage-house location based assortative matching, and infer caste and language ties from last names using a relatively novel methodology with unknown bias. The final sample is biased toward larger firms and more experienced analysts because public information was easier to find for them.
future_research: The authors suggest examining whether BGs and MNC subsidiaries differ in human resource practices, including possible nepotism in top management teams. Future work could identify other foci that support high-quality interpersonal network pathways, such as voluntary organizations or prestigious work organizations, and study analysts' ties to suppliers, customers, rivals, and other value-chain actors. They also call for research on English-language proficiency, regional-language affiliation, and whether the findings generalize to other Asian emerging economies such as Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka.
abstract: To better understand whether the transition by Asian countries toward market economies mirrors the path taken in the West, we ask how embedded network ties between equity analysts and the chief executive officers (CEOs) of the firms that they follow in India influence the accuracy of analysts’ earnings forecasts. We contrast traditional institutions of caste and regional language with contemporary institutions, such as universities, as the locus of such ties. We posit that CEOs from the postreform generation are more likely to transfer material private information via their school ties, while prereform-generation CEOs favor caste or language ties. Contrasting domestic business groups (BGs) with Western multinational corporations (MNCs) as organizational contexts, we argue that BGs legitimate the transfer of private information along particularistic ties, whereas MNCs mitigate such transfers. Our conceptual framework is supported by analyses that draw on a sample of 1,552 earnings forecasts issued between 2001 and 2010 by 296 equity analysts. Our findings suggest that the embeddedness perspective should be broadened to incorporate the influence of the larger historical social structures within which economic action is embedded, and to view BGs as carriers and repositories that blend modern management practices with particularistic behavioral patterns among top executives.

title: Does West “Fit” with East? In Search of a Chinese Model of Person–Environment Fit
methods: Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews, critical incident technique, purposive and theoretical sampling, line-by-line open coding, axial coding, cognitive mapping, and NVivo 9.0 analysis.
industry: Diverse industries including banking, media, retail, transportation, and service industries
time_period: 15-week data collection period
units: Chinese working adults and PE fit episodes
n_sample: 30 Chinese informants; 611 usable episodes
authors: Chuang, A.; Hsu, R. S.; Wang, A.-C.; Judge, T. A.
theories: Confucian relationalism; Confucian selfhood; person-environment fit theory
keywords: Chinese model of PE fit; Confucian relationalism; appropriateness; person-environment fit; qualitative study; selfhood
research_question: The paper asks how Chinese individuals interpret their experiences of person-environment fit at work. It specifically examines whether PE fit theories developed largely in Western contexts can explain fit experiences in a Chinese cultural setting.
mechanism_summary:
- Cultural grounding: Confucian relationalism, selfhood, and appropriateness.
- PE fit themes: Competence at work, harmonious connections at work, balance among life domains, cultivation, and realization.
- Process structure: Input, throughput, and output processes through which informants locate the person and environment, interpret their interaction, and evaluate fit.
- Temporal structure: Retrospective and prospective temporal frames, plus diachronic attention to personal and environmental transformation.
- Core tension: Western PE fit emphasizes congruence, while the Chinese model emphasizes appropriateness and can include incongruence-yet-fit.

The process account argues that Chinese informants interpret fit not only as a match between personal attributes and work demands, but as appropriate engagement with work, relationships, life domains, self-cultivation, and environmental transformation. Relation-related fit provides a foundation for task-related fit because Chinese workers understand the self as embedded in multiple relationships. Cultivation and realization extend PE fit beyond static congruence by showing how individuals can experience fit while learning from incongruence or transforming work environments.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a contextualized Chinese model of PE fit that challenges the assumption that fit is best understood as congruence between separable person and environment attributes. It extends PE fit theory by introducing relationalism, selfhood, and appropriateness as cultural foundations and by identifying cultivation and realization as fit themes that are underdeveloped or absent in Western PE fit models. It also contributes temporal theorizing by providing empirical evidence for psychological time and proposing diachronic time as relevant to PE fit.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers in Chinese contexts should design HR practices that support competence, relational harmony, work-family balance, learning, and opportunities to make meaningful changes at work. It highlights the value of feedback and approval for competent performance, interpersonal and team-management training, family-supportive work practices, developmental opportunities, and spaces for employees to realize constructive aspirations.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that whether the Chinese PE fit themes replicate in other cultural settings or are unique to Chinese contexts is an empirical question. They also note that the study identifies meaningful themes but does not yet provide psychometrically sound measures or quantitative tests of validity, incremental validity, antecedents, consequences, mediating mechanisms, or boundary conditions.
future_research: The authors encourage qualitative inquiry into PE fit in other parts of the world and further work on how misfit meanings vary across cultural settings. They call for measure development for the five Chinese PE fit themes and empirical tests of their validity, relationships, interactions, antecedents, consequences, and boundary conditions. They also encourage future research on how different time perspectives evolve in PE fit experiences.
abstract: Extant theorizing concerning person–environment fit (PE fit) is culture bound in that it focuses predominantly on PE fit phenomena in the Western world. We enrich the PE fit literature by exploring the interpretations of PE fit in a prevailing Eastern context (Chinese) using a qualitative study. We interviewed 30 Chinese working adults with diverse backgrounds, and our findings suggest an integrated Chinese model of PE fit that constitutes five dominant PE fit themes: competence at work, harmonious connections at work, balance among life domains, cultivation, and realization. In addition, our research finds empirical evidence of both psychological time and diachronic time with regard to PE fit. With reference to cultural grounding, we reason that Confucian relationalism, selfhood, and appropriateness are particularly helpful in explaining our findings. Other implications and future research are also discussed.
apa_citation: Chuang, A., Hsu, R. S., Wang, A.-C., & Judge, T. A. (2015). Does West “fit” with East? In search of a Chinese model of person-environment fit. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(2), 480-510. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.1076

title: Lessons from a Martial Arts Dojo: A Prolonged Process Model of High-Context Communication
methods: Five-year participant observation ethnographic study of a Japanese martial arts dojo, analyzing three physicality norm violation cases through Hall's contexting model and the culture in interaction model.
industry: Japanese martial arts dojo within a large global martial arts organization
time_period: Roughly 1995-2000
units: Three physicality norm violation cases involving non-Japanese practitioners
n_sample: 3 cases
authors: Cole, Benjamin M.
theories: Hall's contexting model; culture in interaction model; focus theory of normative conduct
keywords: content management; context management; contexting model of communication; continuum staggering; continuum straddling; high-context communication; physicality norms; time giving
research_question: The paper asks whether communicators actively use context to communicate messages, and how they mix context and content to convey meaning to targets. It examines these questions through norm violations in a Japanese martial arts dojo where high-context communication depends on shared understandings, hierarchy, and face-saving interaction.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: high-context communication, low-context communication, shared understandings, tacit common ground, physicality norms, group boundaries, group bonds, and speech norms.
- Cases: the visitor, Ringo, and Einstein each violate physicality norms in different ways, creating opportunities to observe how instructors and senior members guide targets toward norm compliance.
- Context management practices: context reliance through time giving, and context nonreliance through tearing or reprogramming shared understandings.
- Content management practices: continuum staggering shifts from implicit to more explicit messages over time, while continuum straddling uses implicit and explicit messages simultaneously for different audiences.
- Process outcome: communicators begin with less interactive, face-saving guidance and escalate only when time giving and implicit cues do not resolve the violation.

The process model shows high-context communication as prolonged and staged rather than as a one-shot choice between implicit and explicit speech. Communicators rely on shared understandings first, monitor whether the target self-corrects, and then adjust message content or the context itself when the target fails to interpret the intended meaning. The central process is not direct causal control of behavior but guided self-realization and norm restoration with minimal loss of face.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to cross-cultural communication theory by showing that context is not merely an exogenous national or individual characteristic; communicators can actively use, tear, and reprogram context as part of communication. It develops a prolonged process model that links context management practices with content management practices across time. It also argues that micro-level contexts such as dojo norms, hierarchy, and ongoing relationships can shape communication more directly than broad national stereotypes.
practical_implication: Managers working across high-context and low-context communication styles should attend to indirect guidance, silence, altered routines, and contextual changes as possible communicative acts rather than treating only explicit statements as meaningful. The paper suggests that attentiveness to workplace dissatisfaction and interpersonal friction can help managers respond before problems become visible conflicts. It also warns low-context communicators that direct messages from high-context communicators may come only after earlier indirect efforts have failed.
limitations: The paper explicitly notes that its single-organization design raises questions about generalizability across other organizations. Its evidence comes from one Japanese martial arts dojo and three physicality norm violation cases, so the model should be treated as theory-building rather than as a statistically generalizable test. The setting is also not a conventional firm, although the author argues that the observed processes parallel phenomena in organizational and managerial contexts.
future_research: The paper calls for research on whether low-context communicators understand high-context messages but intentionally avoid acknowledging that understanding, for example to evade responsibility or signal defiance. It also suggests studying whether expatriate experiences in high-context locales improve managers' later ability to manage employees after returning home. Future work could also test whether continuum staggering and continuum straddling operate with content characteristics other than explicitness.
abstract: Rather than treat the context of communication as an exogenously determined factor, I investigate the extent to which communicators actively utilize context as a vehicle of communication. Focusing on three cases of “physicality norm” violations observed during a five-year ethnographic study of a Japanese martial arts dojo, I document the use of specific context management and content management practices on the part of the instructors to reconcile the situations in which they found themselves. The prolonged process model of high-context communication that I develop shows how communicators manipulate the two key dimensions of the contexting model of communication—the message content (via continuum staggering and continuum straddling), and the shared understandings that constitute the context in which messages are being delivered and interpreted (via context reliance, i.e., time giving, and context nonreliance, i.e., tearing and reprogramming)—often over extended periods of time.
apa_citation: Cole, B. M. (2015). Lessons from a martial arts dojo: A prolonged process model of high-context communication. *Academy of Management Journal, 58*(2), 567-591. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0986
