title: Managing Digital Money
methods: From the Editors editorial and agenda-setting essay that frames digital money as a transformational innovation, reviews platforms and readiness indexes, and identifies research opportunities for management scholars in innovation, entrepreneurship, trust, business models, competitiveness, regulation, and inclusive growth.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Dodgson, Mark; Gann, David; Wladawsky-Berger, Irving; Sultan, Naveed; George, Gerard
theories: dynamic capabilities theory; innovation ecosystems; institutional theory; resource-based view; transaction cost economics
keywords: business models; digital money; inclusive innovation; innovation ecosystems; trust
research_question: The editorial asks why digital money matters for management scholarship and what research questions it raises about innovation, entrepreneurship, trust, business models, competitiveness, regulation, and social inclusion. It also asks how digital money may reshape transactions among individuals, organizations, financial institutions, governments, and societies.
mechanism_summary:
- Digital money: A dematerialized medium of exchange, measure, and store of value that moves payments, transfers, and receipts from physical to digital environments.
- Platforms and ecosystems: Apple Pay, Alipay, bitcoin, mobile Internet infrastructure, banks, telecommunications firms, Internet service providers, developers, regulators, and open source communities form competing and evolving digital money ecosystems.
- Innovation and entrepreneurship: Digital money creates opportunities for disruptive financial services, inclusive innovation, bottom-up entrepreneurship, new platforms, and new forms of consumer experience.
- Trust and governance: Disintermediation heightens concerns about privacy, cybersecurity, fraud, identity, distributed authenticity, regulation, and ethical service-provider behavior.
- Business models and competitiveness: Efficiency gains, new customer engagement models, transaction data, lower cash-handling costs, digital readiness, and capabilities for virtual transactions affect business growth and national competitiveness.

The process is conceptual and agenda-setting rather than a tested causal model. Dodgson, Gann, Wladawsky-Berger, Sultan, and George argue that digital money dematerializes transactions, reduces frictions, shifts intermediation, and creates new data flows, thereby opening research opportunities across innovation ecosystems, business model innovation, trust, regulation, and competitive advantage.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial contributes by positioning digital money as a globally significant phenomenon for management research rather than only a financial-technology topic. It links digital money to innovation ecosystems, transaction cost economics, organizational design, coordination costs, institutional theory, resource-based view, dynamic capabilities, trust, governance, and inclusive innovation as candidate lenses for future empirical and theoretical work.
practical_implication: Managers, financial institutions, technology firms, and regulators should treat digital money as a strategic and institutional shift, not merely a payments tool. The editorial suggests that organizations will need capabilities for platform partnership, cybersecurity, privacy protection, data analytics, regulatory adaptation, open collaboration, and business model experimentation.
limitations: The editorial does not provide an empirical test, systematic review, or comprehensive research agenda. Its examples and forecasts are illustrative, and the authors repeatedly emphasize uncertainty, technological fluidity, contested regulation, and the unpredictability of digital money's adoption trajectory.
future_research: Future research should examine how digital money affects business growth, competition, entrepreneurship, innovation ecosystems, technology standards, regulatory balance, auditing, trust, privacy, cybersecurity, business model innovation, national competitiveness, and financial inclusion. The editorial also calls for research on institutional readiness and adaptability as digital money changes technology, individual behavior, and the context of management.

title: An Inductive Study of Feedback Interactions over the Course of Creative Projects
methods: Inductive grounded theory study of feedback meetings in two creative-project contexts: modern dance and product design. The authors coded observed, transcribed, and video-recorded feedback interactions, supplemented by interviews and a focus group, to build a process model of feedback moves, response moves, and problem-space co-construction.
industry: Modern dance and product design/R&D for outdoor technical products.
time_period: Dance observations covered four cycles over 2 years; product-design teams were filmed over 8 months.
units: Feedback interactions, creative-worker groups, and two product-design teams.
n_sample: The text reports 88 feedback interactions; Table 1 summarizes 53 observed dance meetings and 33 video-recorded product-design meetings.
authors: Harrison, Spencer H.; Rouse, Elizabeth D.
theories: feedback and creativity; grounded theory; problem space; process theory
keywords: adjustments; creative projects; creative prototypes; excavations; feedback interactions; problem space
research_question: How do feedback providers and creative workers interact during creative projects, and how do those feedback interactions influence changes to prototypes over time? The paper asks how feedback content, two-way interaction, and evolving project stage jointly shape whether creative workers make comprehensive excavations or incremental adjustments.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / moves: Feedback providers use personalizing, puzzling, measuring, and prescribing; creative workers use backgrounding, forecasting, and opening.
- Process / phases: Early feedback interactions tend to emphasize puzzling and backgrounding around retrospective problem space; later interactions tend to emphasize measuring and forecasting around prospective problem space.
- Emergent outcomes: Excavations are comprehensive changes that return to previously considered ideas; adjustments are incremental refinements to the current prototype.
- Boundary conditions: The model is grounded in creative projects with formal feedback meetings, unfinished prototypes, and knowledgeable feedback providers.

The process is interactive rather than one-way. Feedback providers and creative workers jointly make sense of prototypes by co-constructing a problem space; creative workers' openings signal when providers can move from understanding to prescription. Early in projects, puzzling and backgrounding help surface retrospective problem space, making it possible for feedback to legitimate old ideas and trigger excavations. Later in projects, measuring and forecasting help define prospective problem space, allowing prescriptions to refine the prototype through adjustments.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a process theory of feedback interactions in creative work by treating creative workers as active shapers of the feedback they receive rather than passive recipients. It reframes feedback content as a pattern of interaction moves, showing how moves often labeled informational and controlling can work together when creative workers create openings for prescription. It also advances problem-space co-construction as the mechanism linking feedback interactions to prototype change over time.
practical_implication: The study suggests that feedback providers and creative workers should treat feedback meetings as a two-way search for understanding newness, not as unilateral evaluation of unfinished work. Managers can use the model to set expectations about the creative process: early feedback may legitimately return teams to old ideas, while later feedback may focus on smaller refinements. The findings also imply that norms around feedback can make review meetings more generative and less affectively threatening for creative workers.
limitations: The authors note that using two contexts strengthens theoretical comparison but also introduces complexity that the study cannot fully resolve. The dance and product-design settings differed in the number and spacing of feedback meetings, project length, and whether feedback providers were external observers or embedded team members. These differences limit claims about optimal feedback timing and about how insider versus outsider feedback providers affect problem-space construction.
future_research: Future research could examine the optimal amount of time between feedback meetings and creative work, especially across projects with different rhythms and review structures. It could also compare whether feedback providers inside a creative team enhance feedback by understanding the problem space more deeply or constrain feedback by being attached to existing outcomes. The authors further suggest examining when wholesale rejection of a prototype, rather than excavation or adjustment, is necessary and what consequences such rejection has.
abstract: While there is a large amount of literature on feedback, it is unclear how well traditional prescriptions for feedback apply during creative projects, since creativity often relies on nonlinear and ambiguous work patterns. We conducted an inductive study of feedback meetings in creative projects in two contexts—modern dance and product design—to understand how feedback might influence the development of creative prototypes. Our emergent findings reframe current theorizing on feedback by revealing its interactive nature: feedback providers and creative workers co-construct a problem space that provides openings for changing prototypes. Our analysis revealed sets of moves that feedback providers (personalizing, puzzling, measuring, and prescribing) and creative workers (backgrounding, forecasting, and opening) use to interact. We also found evidence that patterns among these moves helped guide one of two responses: (1) excavations, when feedback spurs comprehensive changes by prompting creative workers to return to old ideas, and (2) adjustments, when feedback spurs incremental refinements to the prototype. We integrate these findings into a process model that describes how feedback influences creative projects over time.

title: A Confucian Social Model of Political Appointments among Chinese Private-Firm Entrepreneurs
methods: Two-study empirical quantitative design: a cross-sectional survey of private-firm CEOs and chairs using OLS regression with interaction terms, and a longitudinal archival study of Chinese publicly listed private firms using lagged GEE logistic regression.
industry: Chinese private firms, including publicly listed private-owned companies; financial companies were excluded from Study 2.
time_period: Study 1 survey timing was two waves separated by two months; Study 2 covered 2006-2012.
units: Private-firm CEOs/chairs in Study 1; listed private firms and chair-years in Study 2.
n_sample: Study 1 surveyed 166 private-firm CEOs and chairs; Study 2 used 1,323 listed private companies and 4,578 firm-year observations.
authors: Li, X.-H.; Liang, X.
theories: Confucian doctrine of role transition; Western theories of life career development
keywords: Chinese private-firm entrepreneurs; Confucian social model; political appointments; proself motive; prosocial motive
research_question: The paper asks why successful Chinese private-firm entrepreneurs increasingly pursue PC or PPCC political appointments despite declining economic returns to political connections. It examines whether proself and prosocial motives condition the relationship between business success and entrepreneurs' desire for, and attainment of, political appointment.
mechanism_summary: The proposed Confucian social model argues that business success gives entrepreneurs discretion to act on salient motives. When proself motives dominate, successful entrepreneurs are less likely to pursue costly political appointments because marginal economic benefits are limited. When prosocial motives dominate, successful entrepreneurs are more likely to pursue appointments as legitimate channels for influencing policy, addressing social problems, and serving the broader society.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends political-connection research beyond the dominant economic lens by showing that personal motives, especially prosocial motives rooted in Confucian role-transition doctrine, help explain political appointment-seeking. It also links Western life-career development theories with an Eastern Confucian account of movement from self-orientation to social orientation, offering a cross-cultural model of how entrepreneurs define life goals after business success.
practical_implication: The findings suggest that political appointment among successful Chinese private-firm entrepreneurs should not be interpreted only as self-interested rent seeking. Policymakers selecting PC or PPCC members may need to distinguish entrepreneurs motivated by public contribution from those primarily seeking private or firm-level economic benefits.
limitations: The authors note that political appointment is only one possible channel for expressing prosocial motives, and its meaning may vary by cultural and institutional context. Study 1 may suffer from sample-selection bias, with women underrepresented and possible generational differences among entrepreneurs. The authors also caution that CSR disclosure may become institutionalized over time and may then be a weaker proxy for prosocial motive.
future_research: Future research should examine other channels through which entrepreneurs pursue prosocial life goals, including social entrepreneurship and other social outcomes. It should test the proself and prosocial motive scales in other cultural contexts, compare them with related psychological measures, and develop better objective indicators of prosocial motive. Further work should also compare political appointments with other forms of political connection and investigate inauthentic prosocial motives.
abstract: In China, many successful private-firm entrepreneurs hold representational appointments in political councils such as the People’s Congress (PC) or People’s Political Consultative Conference (PPCC). By considering Western theories of life career development and Confucian doctrines of personal development, we seek to understand the complex motivations of successful entrepreneurs for joining political councils. We propose a Confucian social model of role transition to explain the pursuit and attainment of political appointment in China. We hypothesize that the “proself” and “prosocial” motives for seeking political connections will, respectively, attenuate or strengthen the relationship between private-firm entrepreneurs’ business success and their intention and attainment in seeking political appointment. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 166 private-firm chief executive officers (CEOs) and chairs, and a longitudinal archival study of 1,323 Chinese publicly listed private firms from 2006 to 2012. The findings support our hypotheses on the moderating effect of the proself and prosocial motives. The study offers insights into how Confucian cultural values may explain the dynamic between business success and political appointments among private-firm entrepreneurs in China.

title: The Dark Side of Socialization: A Longitudinal Investigation of Newcomer Alcohol Use
methods: Empirical quantitative study using multisource, multilevel, and longitudinal survey data from newcomers, veteran teammates, and supervisors. The authors use multilevel CFA, multilevel modeling in Mplus 6.0, logistic regression for hazardous and harmful alcohol use, and Monte Carlo simulation for indirect effects.
industry: Sales and client service teams in two manufacturing companies.
time_period: Three waves: Wave 1 at less than six months of employment, Wave 2 three months later, and Wave 3 six months after Wave 1.
units: Newcomers nested in sales and client service teams, with veteran teammate and supervisor reports.
n_sample: 147 newcomers at the individual level and 57 teams at the team level.
authors: Liu, Songqi; Wang, Mo; Bamberger, Peter; Shi, Junqi; Bacharach, Samuel B.
theories: organizational sensemaking theory (Weick, 1995)
keywords: alcohol misuse; client alcohol use norms; newcomer socialization; performance drinking motives; sensemaking; veteran alcohol use norms; work-based heavy drinking
research_question: How do veteran peers' and clients' alcohol use norms shape newcomers' performance drinking motives, work-based heavy drinking, and later alcohol misuse? The paper asks whether informal socialization can produce a "dark side" in which newcomers infer that risky behaviors are legitimate and effective ways to meet job-related objectives.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cross-level sensemaking process. Newcomers face uncertainty about how to achieve performance goals, observe veteran peers' and clients' descriptive alcohol-use norms, and form accounts that drinking is an effective and legitimate way to improve job performance. These accounts appear as performance drinking motives, which are associated with more frequent heavy drinking with clients; work-based heavy drinking is then associated with subsequent alcohol misuse. The evidence supports the indirect paths from veteran and client norms to work-based heavy drinking through performance motives, but it does not support the full hypothesized indirect paths from norms to alcohol misuse.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends newcomer socialization research by showing that informal socialization can generate dysfunctional outcomes, not only adjustment and performance gains. It contributes to sensemaking theory by treating motives as an operational manifestation of newcomers' accounts and by showing that both internal stakeholders and external clients provide inputs to those accounts. It also adds to workplace alcohol research by theorizing how permissive drinking cultures emerge through norm-based sensemaking rather than only documenting their effects.
practical_implication: Managers should attend to informal socialization processes, especially in client-facing roles where newcomers may infer that risky practices are required for performance. The findings imply that laissez-faire reliance on peer and client norms can impose long-run health and organizational costs even when the behavior seems performance-enhancing in the short run. Organizations may need to clarify acceptable means of relationship building and guide newcomers away from risky client-service routines.
limitations: The paper notes that its measures of workplace alcohol-use norms may not capture all relevant sources or forms of normative influence, including injunctive norms and norms from other newcomers or competitors. Work-based heavy drinking is measured with a single self-report item, and performance drinking motives and work-based heavy drinking are measured at the same wave, so the causal ordering between motives and drinking cannot be fully ruled out. The sample is limited to sales and client service employees in China, where business drinking is culturally salient, so generalizability to other occupations and national contexts requires replication.
future_research: Future research should examine other sources and forms of workplace drinking norms, including injunctive norms and normative cues from newcomers, competitors, and other socialization agents. The authors call for experience-sampling designs, cross-lagged panel designs, and experimental designs to better capture drinking behavior over time and clarify reciprocal relationships between motives and behavior. They also encourage research on boundary conditions such as job demands, alcohol tolerance, age, first-job status, newcomer turnover, and replication in other cultural settings.
abstract: Organizational veterans and external stakeholders such as clients often play an important and informal role in newcomer socialization, influencing newcomer cognition and behavior and providing learning opportunities and social support that facilitate employee adjustment and performance enhancement. However, from a sensemaking perspective, newcomers may also draw insight from stakeholder behavior in order to better understand how to best meet job-related objectives and expectations. These understandings may manifest as performance-related motives, leading to the adoption of risky behaviors that can be detrimental to newcomer health and organizational effectiveness. Using multisource, multilevel, and longitudinal data, we demonstrate that the alcohol use norms of both organizational veterans and clients are significantly associated with the performance drinking motives of newcomers in sales and client service teams, suggesting that veteran and client norms signal to newcomers that drinking alcohol is an effective and legitimate means to improve job performance. In addition, we demonstrate that performance drinking motives mediate the positive relationship between veteran and client alcohol use norms and newcomers’ frequency of work-based heavy drinking. Finally, we find that the frequency of work-based heavy drinking is positively related to newcomer alcohol misuse and mediates the positive relationship between performance drinking motives and newcomer alcohol misuse.

title: Weathering a Meta-Level Identity Crisis: Forging a Coherent Collective Identity for an Emerging Field
methods: Longitudinal qualitative grounded-theory study of the iSchools field, using a cross-level organization-field design, semi-structured interviews, archival data, iConference attendance, non-participant observation, field notes, and open, axial, and theoretical coding.
industry: Academic information schools and the emerging iSchools field.
time_period: More than seven years, with primary data collection from 2004 through 2011 and archival coverage of earlier field formation.
units: Member iSchools, deans, faculty, staff, students, alumni, archival documents, and field events.
n_sample: 46 information schools in the consortium; 74 formal interviews; deans of all 31 schools in the population at the end of data collection.
authors: Patvardhan, Shubha D.; Gioia, Dennis A.; Hamilton, Aimee L.
theories: collective identity; identity work; institutional identity work; optimal distinctiveness; social construction view of identity
keywords: coherent identity; collective identity; consensual identity; emerging field; identity-work processes; meta-level identity crisis
research_question: By what processes do organizations in an emerging field develop a collective identity? The paper examines how organization-level and collective-level identity formation co-evolve in the iSchools field, why these dynamics precipitated a meta-level identity crisis, and how the crisis was resolved through coherent rather than consensual identity.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: legacy identities, nested identities, optimal distinctiveness, collective identity claims, meanings of claims, field boundaries, identity crisis, consensual identity, and coherent identity.
- Process / phases: member schools first reconfigured local identities around the iSchool label; the collective then pursued consensus on common identity claims and meanings; disagreements over meanings, core identity, and boundaries produced an identity crisis; deans later reframed identity around shared problems, interests, practices, and coherence.
- Triggering conditions: members came from older library science, computer science, information systems, and related fields, while also remaining embedded in universities, regions, and professional communities with their own identity expectations.
- Emergent outcomes: a coherent field-level identity became workable without full agreement on the meaning of every identity claim, and younger cohorts became more comfortable identifying with the iSchools field.
- Boundary conditions: the authors emphasize emerging issue-oriented fields, collectives with strong legacy and nested identities, and collectives linked by shared fate more than by shared task interdependence.

The process is interpretive rather than variable-causal. Patvardhan and colleagues show that member schools used the iSchool label to gain local legitimacy and distinctiveness, but they filled that label with meanings shaped by legacy fields and nested institutional settings. These local identity adaptations made consensus at the collective level harder, especially when the field tried to define its common core and membership boundaries. The crisis became manageable when actors shifted from trying to discover common meanings to creating coherence through shared problem domains, mutual interests, ongoing interaction, and acceptance of ambiguity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes a cross-level grounded model of collective identity formation in an emerging field, showing that organization-level and field-level identities evolve in tandem rather than in a simple sequence. It extends identity research beyond individual and organizational levels by conceptualizing a meta-level identity crisis and specifying how legacy identities, nested identities, and local optimal distinctiveness can destabilize collective identity formation. It also advances the distinction between consensual and coherent identity, arguing that meta-level collectives may require coherence around shared domains and practices rather than full consensus on identity meanings.
practical_implication: For leaders of emerging fields, the findings suggest that forcing early consensus on identity meanings can intensify conflict when members have heterogeneous histories and institutional embeddings. Field leaders may instead make progress by building shared agendas, common problem domains, and recurring practices that allow members to work together while retaining local variation. The study also suggests that ambiguity can be useful when it creates room for multiple member identities to fit within a broader collective identity.
limitations: The authors note that the study ended before the iSchools achieved a definitive collective identity, so the ultimate identity outcome remained a work in progress. They also studied an emerging issue-oriented academic field rather than an industry-oriented organizational field, and they caution that identity formation may differ in collectives with more concrete category features, stronger task interdependence, or entirely greenfield organizations. The case therefore supports theoretical elaboration and transferability judgments rather than statistical generalization.
future_research: The paper calls for deeper study of identity as a process of becoming rather than as a stable thing. It also points to future work on identity crises in other emerging fields, especially fields formed by breakaway groups with strong legacy identities or collectives held together by shared fate rather than shared task interdependence. Further research could compare issue-oriented and industry-oriented fields, examine greenfield collectives, and investigate how coherent identities later evolve into more explicit consensus or remain fluid.
abstract: We employed a longitudinal, grounded-theory approach to investigate the occurrence of an identity crisis in an emerging collective of organizations attempting to form a new academic field. The findings indicate that legacy identities and the nested structure of such organizations have implications for the formation of identity at this level. Specifically, the co-evolution of organization-level and collective-level identities, and the interdependencies between the levels, rendered the collective identity formation process as multiphased, complex, contentious, and continuously precarious—ultimately leading to an identity crisis that was resolved not by arriving at a “consensual identity,” but, rather, a “coherent identity.” The findings contribute to the nascent stream of literature on collective identity beyond the organizational level by explicating identity-work processes involved in the precipitation, manifestation, and resolution of an identity crisis in an emerging field.

title: When Times Collide: Temporal Brokerage at the Intersection of Markets and Developments
methods: Inductive qualitative process study based on a six-month organizational ethnography of Fairtrade International, participant observation, in-depth and follow-up interviews, archival documents, media articles, and iterative coding in NVivo.
industry: Fairtrade and ethically certified agricultural commodities.
country: Fairtrade International's secretariat in Bonn, Germany, with producer networks in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
time_period: Fieldwork between July and December 2007, with documentary data from 2006 to 2012.
units: Fairtrade International, including FLO, FLO-CERT, staff, liaison officers, managers, licensees, external consultants, and standards committee deliberations.
n_sample: More than 1,100 hours of participant observation, 39 in-depth interviews, 9 follow-up interviews, about 100 media articles, and internal and public documents.
authors: Reinecke, Juliane; Ansari, Shaz
theories: ambitemporality; clock time and process time; temporal brokerage; temporal structuring
keywords: ambitemporality; clock-time orientation; development temporalities; market-based models for human development; process time; temporal brokerage; temporal structures
research_question: The paper asks how organizations positioned between temporally asymmetric worlds negotiate conflicting temporalities. It examines how Fairtrade International handled the collision between market-oriented clock time and development-oriented process time in its attempt to connect Northern ethical markets with Southern producer development.
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs / tensions: Clock-time orientation, process-time orientation, temporal structures, temporal conflict, temporal reflexivity, mutual appreciation of interdependencies, temporal brokerage, and ambitemporality.
- Process / phases: Disrupting the temporal commons through ISO 65 certification; negotiating moving picture versus snapshot, temporal asymmetry versus symmetry, and long versus short temporal depth; reconstituting the temporal commons toward ambitemporality.
- Organizational actors: FLO as standards setter and producer liaison, FLO-CERT as market-oriented certifier, and Fairtrade's standards committee as a site of explicit temporal contestation.
- Emergent outcomes: Revised standards and certification practices that made room for producer-owned development plans, more flexible timelines, process-oriented criteria, and certification consistency.

The process begins when FLO-CERT imports product-certification templates and time-bound compliance criteria to make development legible to Northern markets. FLO contests this temporal structuring because it turns development into certifiable snapshots and risks excluding producers whose empowerment unfolds unevenly over longer horizons. Through confrontation, both units become temporally reflexive, recognize that development credibility in the South and market credibility in the North are interdependent, and jointly rework Fairtrade's model toward ambitemporality rather than choosing either clock time or process time alone.
theoretical_contribution: The paper advances an agentic view of time by showing that temporal structures are not merely background conditions but cultural resources that actors can use to frame phenomena as manageable products or unfolding processes. It develops the concept of ambitemporality to explain how organizations can accommodate seemingly contradictory temporal orientations when they broker between discrepant temporal environments. It also contributes to research on market-based development by showing how clock-time assumptions in Western management models can truncate efforts to address complex social problems.
practical_implication: The paper implies that organizations using market-based models for development should avoid treating linear metrics, deadlines, and certification cycles as neutral tools. They need temporal structures that satisfy market demands for credibility while still preserving attention to locally variable, long-term, and intangible development processes. For standards organizations, this means combining auditable criteria with flexibility, producer-owned development plans, and support activities between formal audits.
limitations: The paper is based on an extreme qualitative case: Fairtrade International at a specific moment of ISO 65-driven certification change. The authors use the case because temporal conflict is unusually visible in an organization wrestling with contrasting temporalities of markets and development.
future_research: Future research could examine temporal brokerage in other pluralistic organizations, including science-industry collaborations, hybrid organizations, sustainability initiatives, and organizations balancing exploitation and exploration. Studies could also investigate how temporal assumptions shape social and environmental performance measurement, where clock-based metrics may miss long-horizon or intangible outcomes, and how organizations use temporal structuring to make emergent processes appear as static objects.
abstract: We study the influence of a pervasive Western organizational mentality—clock-time orientation—in market-based models for human development. While a linear, clocktime orientation optimized for markets is meant to enhance efficiency, coordination, and control, it may be unsuitable for managing emergent, complex, and indeterminate processes such as development. To examine how the tension between market and development temporalities plays out at the organizational level, we draw on an ethnography of Fairtrade International, an organization connecting markets in the North with low-income community development in the South. We examine intra-organizational contestation over different temporal structures needed to entrain to discrepant temporal environments. We explain how contestation, temporal reflexivity, interpretive shifts, and mutual appreciation of interdependencies led to the reconstitution of Fairtrade’s development model to bridge competing temporal structures. We contribute by (a) elucidating an agentic view of time, where time is used as a cultural resource to regulate attention and render social phenomena amenable to particular types of managerial action; (b) developing the notion of “ambitemporality,” where organizations accommodate seemingly contradictory temporal orientations; and (c) explaining how deep-seated Western organizational mentalities truncate the power of development models, and how these models may benefit from embracing processual approaches associated with Eastern thought.

title: Asymmetric Learning Capabilities and Stock Market Returns
methods: Empirical quantitative event study of R&D alliance announcements. The authors use SDC Platinum and rDNA alliance data, Lexis/Nexis and Factiva announcement dates, CRSP stock returns, Compustat and Bioscan firm data, USPTO patent citations, Heckman two-stage selection correction, ordinary least squares regressions, and robust standard errors clustered by firm.
industry: U.S. computing and biopharmaceutical industries.
time_period: Alliance formations and patent-citation windows covering 1984-2003.
units: Public-firm observations nested in 610 R&D alliances; each alliance contributes two firm-level observations.
n_sample: 610 R&D alliances with complete data; 1,140 firm-level observations in the CAR regressions.
authors: Yang, Haibin; Zheng, Yanfeng; Zaheer, Akbar
theories: alliance learning; learning race; partner-specific absorptive capacity; private and common benefits in alliances
keywords: R&D alliances; alliance learning; cumulative abnormal returns; equity alliance governance; learning race; market similarity; specific learning capability; stock market returns
research_question: The paper asks whether a firm's superior alliance learning capability relative to its partner yields higher stock market returns, and under what conditions those market returns vary with the learning capability gap. It focuses on whether asymmetric partner-specific learning capability creates performance gains through the learning race in R&D alliances.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that a focal firm with higher partner-specific learning capability than its partner is expected to extract more private benefits from the alliance and signal stronger future learning-race performance to the stock market. Equity governance weakens this effect because equity stakes align interests, discourage opportunism, and shift attention toward common alliance benefits. Market similarity strengthens the effect because partners competing in similar product and knowledge markets face greater private-benefit incentives, making superior learning capability more valuable to investors.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to alliance learning research by conceptualizing and operationalizing specific learning capability as a competitive, partner-specific capability distinct from partner-specific absorptive capacity. It empirically links asymmetric learning capabilities to stock market performance, showing that the market rewards firms whose specific learning capability exceeds that of their partners. It also clarifies boundary conditions for the learning race by showing that equity governance attenuates, while market similarity amplifies, the performance effect of the learning capability gap.
practical_implication: For managers forming R&D alliances, the findings imply that relative learning capability matters for investor expectations, not only general alliance experience or partner resources. Firms with weaker learning capability may benefit from equity governance as a protective arrangement, whereas stronger learners may face market penalties when equity governance constrains their ability to appropriate private benefits. The results also warn managers that alliances with market-similar partners intensify competitive learning pressures.
limitations: The authors state that the sample is limited to public firms in two knowledge-intensive sectors, which may limit generalizability to private firms or other industries. They also note that cumulative abnormal returns capture only one dimension of performance and that patents provide a conservative measure because they cannot capture the full extent of interfirm learning in alliances. Potential endogeneity in alliance governance remains difficult to address because instrumenting interaction terms is both econometrically and theoretically challenging.
future_research: The authors suggest testing whether the conclusions hold for private firms and for alternative performance outcomes such as new product introduction or new market entry. They call for research on whether firms' learning rates change after previous alliances and how those changes affect innovation and alliance instability. They also encourage work on cross-national alliances, alliance portfolios, network-level contingencies, and how competitive learning can be reconciled with trust and relational capability in interfirm relationships.
abstract: Drawing on the alliance learning literature, we propose that a firm’s relative capability to learn partner-specific know-how holds the key to understanding the learning race phenomenon and its performance consequences. Specifically, we argue that a firm with higher specific learning capability relative to its partner’s will be rewarded with superior stock performance. We also contend that equity alliance governance and market similarity between partners moderate this relationship in opposite directions. Equity alliance governance motivates firms to suppress competitive learning and thus reduces the positive impact of the specific learning capability gap on abnormal stock returns, while market similarity between partners aggravates the learning race and strengthens the positive impact of the specific learning capability gap. Results of an event study of 610 R&D alliances in the U.S. computing and biopharmaceutical industries in the period 1984–2003 support our hypotheses. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the learning race, its contingencies, and its performance implications.
apa_citation: Yang, H., Zheng, Y., & Zaheer, A. (2015). Asymmetric learning capabilities and stock market returns. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(2), 356-374. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0675

title: Paradoxical Leader Behaviors in People Management: Antecedents and Consequences
methods: Two-study quantitative design: Study 1 develops and validates a multidimensional paradoxical leader behavior scale using EFA, CFA, test-retest reliability, and discriminant, convergent, predictive, and incremental validity tests across five Chinese samples; Study 2 uses a time-lagged multilevel field survey and hierarchical linear modeling.
industry: Privately owned technical or engineering services companies for Study 2; Study 1 also uses continuing-education respondents and five manufacturing and service firms.
time_period: Study 2 collected data twice, with supervisors rating subordinate work-role behavior three weeks after Time 1.
units: Supervisors, subordinates, work units, and firms.
n_sample: Study 1 uses five samples of 228, 204, 193, 186/172/116, and 478 respondents; Study 2 uses 76 supervisors and 516 subordinates from 6 firms.
authors: Zhang, Y.; Waldman, D. A.; Han, Y.-L.; Li, X.-B.
theories: organizational paradox theory; yin-yang philosophy
keywords: holistic thinking; integrative complexity; paradoxical leader behavior; people management; work role performance
research_question: How can paradoxical leader behavior in people management be conceptualized and measured, and what cognitive and contextual antecedents explain its occurrence? The paper also asks whether paradoxical leader behavior is associated with subordinate proficiency, adaptivity, and proactivity.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that leaders with a both-and cognitive basis can accept, connect, and integrate contradictory structural and follower demands over time. Paradoxical leader behavior then provides both bounded and discretionary work environments: followers understand work roles and standards while retaining autonomy, flexibility, dignity, and individualized consideration. This combination is theorized to model openness to contradictions and support proficiency, adaptation, and proactive change behavior. The field evidence supports holistic thinking and integrative complexity as antecedents, rejects organic structure as a significant antecedent in the controlled model, and links paradoxical leader behavior to all three subordinate outcomes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends organizational paradox research from macro strategic tensions to supervisory people management, arguing that leaders face paradoxes in structural and follower demands. It contributes a five-dimensional measure of paradoxical leader behavior and shows construct and predictive validity beyond established leadership constructs. It also bridges Eastern yin-yang philosophy with Western paradox and leadership literatures to theorize both-and leader behavior.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that leaders should be trained not only to choose situationally among behavioral alternatives, but also to handle competing demands through long-term paradoxical thinking and action. For international and complex organizational contexts, a paradox-based lens may help managers respond to uncertainty without reducing every tension to an either-or choice.
limitations: The empirical setting is China, so the authors caution that findings may reflect Chinese-specific ways of integrating opposites and should be tested in Western and cross-cultural contexts. Study 2 uses a small firm-level sample and supervisor-rated organizational structure, which may explain the unsupported organizational-structure finding. The validation samples also include evening students from one university and professional, college-educated workers, and some Study 1 relationships may be vulnerable to common method effects.
future_research: Future research should test paradoxical leader behavior in Western and cross-cultural contexts, examine whether different cultures display different paradoxical behaviors, and extend the construct beyond people management to stakeholder, globalization, and strategic leadership domains. Researchers could also examine downsides such as leader cognitive strain and subordinate discomfort when followers hold black-white views, and expand the nomological network to include open-mindedness, learning orientation, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation, environmental uncertainty, work characteristics, and group-level outcomes.
abstract: As organizational environments become increasingly dynamic, complex, and competitive, leaders are likely to face intensified contradictory, or seemingly paradoxical, demands. We develop the construct of “paradoxical leader behavior” in people management, which refers to seemingly competing, yet interrelated, behaviors to meet structural and follower demands simultaneously and over time. In Study 1, we develop a measure of paradoxical leader behavior in people management using five samples from China. Confirmatory factor analyses support a multidimensional measure of paradoxical leader behavior with five dimensions: (1) combining self-centeredness with other-centeredness; (2) maintaining both distance and closeness; (3) treating subordinates uniformly, while allowing individualization; (4) enforcing work requirements, while allowing flexibility; and (5) maintaining decision control, while allowing autonomy. In Study 2, we examine the antecedents and consequences of paradoxical leader behavior in people management with a field sample of 76 supervisors and 516 subordinates from 6 firms. We find that the extent to which supervisors engage in holistic thinking and have integrative complexity is positively related to their paradoxical behavior in managing people, which, in turn, is associated with increased proficiency, adaptivity, and proactivity among subordinates.

title: Hot Buttons and Time Sinks: The Effects of Electronic Communication During Nonwork Time on Emotions and Work-Nonwork Conflict
methods: Seven-day experience sampling study of working adults receiving work-related electronic communication during nonwork time, analyzed with hierarchical linear modeling / random coefficient modeling to test within-person effects, cross-level moderation, and mediated relationships.
industry: Variety of industries including technology, finance, manufacturing, government, and healthcare
time_period: Seven-day survey period
units: Daily work-related electronic communication events nested within working adults
n_sample: 341 working adults; 1,572 daily surveys involving work-related electronic communication during nonwork time
authors: Butts, Marcus M.; Becker, William J.; Boswell, Wendy R.
theories: Byron's model of emotion in e-mail; affective events theory; appraisal theory of emotion; boundary theory; positive-negative asymmetry effects; relational schemas
keywords: abusive supervision; affective tone; anger; electronic communication during nonwork time; happiness; segmentation preference; time required; work-to-nonwork conflict
research_question: How do the affective tone and time required by work-related electronic communications received during nonwork time shape employees' anger, happiness, and work-to-nonwork conflict? The paper also asks whether abusive supervision, communication sender, and segmentation preference condition these within-person relationships.
mechanism_summary: The paper treats electronic communications during nonwork time as affective work events that employees appraise as favorable or unfavorable. Negative affective tone and greater time demands are associated with anger, while affective tone is also associated with happiness; the reported indirect effects on work-to-nonwork conflict operate through anger, not happiness. Relational context matters because abusive supervision and supervisor-sent messages shape appraisals of affective tone, while segmentation preference makes time-demanding intrusions into nonwork time more conflictual.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends work-nonwork and electronic communication research by shifting attention from overall communication volume to event-level properties of individual messages. It integrates affective events theory, appraisal theory, electronic communication emotion theory, positive-negative asymmetry, relational schemas, and boundary theory to explain why anger mediates the effects of affective tone and time required on work-to-nonwork conflict. It also shows that abusive supervision, sender status, and segmentation preference are boundary conditions for these processes.
practical_implication: Managers should be careful about affective tone, timing, and effort demands when sending electronic communications after normal work hours. The findings suggest value in training employees to communicate clearly and constructively after hours, limiting unnecessary time demands, and recognizing that employees with stronger segmentation preferences may experience time-consuming after-hours messages as especially intrusive. The paper also implies that supervisor behavior is consequential because abusive supervisory relationships can intensify anger responses to negatively toned messages.
limitations: The study used convenience and snowball sampling rather than random population sampling, so the authors caution against overgeneralizing to a defined population. The daily measures were collected concurrently, which prevents the design from fully eliminating alternative causal orderings such as anger shaping perceived tone. The focal within-person measures of affective tone and time required were single-item self-reports, leaving room for reliability limits, retrieval errors, and common method concerns.
future_research: Future work should test the model in more controlled settings or a single organization and use time-separated measures of emotions and work-nonwork conflict across the end of the workday, evening communications, and the next morning. Research could examine additional message features such as salutations, closings, capitalization, response timing, emoticons, and time of day. The authors also call for research on other relational and receiver factors, including leader-member exchange, career ambition, empowerment, daily work-at-home expectations, and perceptual accuracy in affective tone interpretation.
abstract: As advances in communication technologies have made organizations more easily connected to their workforce outside of normal work hours, there is increased concern that employees may experience heightened work-nonwork conflict when away from the office. The current study investigates the effects of electronic communication received during nonwork time using an experience sampling methodology to examine within-person relationships among elements of electronic communication (affective tone, time required), emotional responses (anger, happiness), and work-to-nonwork conflict in a sample of 341 working adults surveyed over a seven-day period. Hierarchical linear modeling results suggested that both affective tone and time required were associated with anger, but only affective tone was associated with happiness. Further, anger was associated with work-to-nonwork conflict and mediated the effects of affective tone and time required on work-to-nonwork conflict. Results also revealed cross-level moderating effects of abusive supervision and communication sender together, as well as segmentation preference. Implications of these findings for future theorizing and research on electronic communication during nonwork time are discussed.
apa_citation: Butts, M. M., Becker, W. J., & Boswell, W. R. (2015). Hot buttons and time sinks: The effects of electronic communication during nonwork time on emotions and work-nonwork conflict. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 763-788. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0170

title: Social Networks, Cognitive Style, and Innovative Performance: A Contingency Perspective
methods: Empirical quantitative complete-network survey study in one Italian design and manufacturing firm. The authors measure employees' cognitive style with Kirton's Adaption-Innovation Inventory, workplace advice-network brokerage with UCINET structural holes routines, innovative performance with supervisor-rated RBPS innovation items, and estimate OLS regressions with robustness checks using clustered standard errors, department controls, and nested-data specifications.
industry: Design and manufacturing firm; ItalianSofa is described as a leading designer and producer of sofas.
time_period: Cross-sectional; data collection dates are not reported in paper.
units: Employees in the complete organization, including first-line managers and the CEO; innovative performance ratings cover employees with supervisors.
n_sample: 68 persons in the organization; innovative performance data pertain to 67 employees.
authors: Carnabuci, Gianluca; Diószegi, Bálint
theories: adaption-innovation theory; complementary fit; network theory of social capital
keywords: adaption-innovation theory; closed networks; cognitive style; complementary fit; innovative performance; social capital; social networks; structural holes
research_question: The paper asks which workplace network structure is most conducive to individual employee innovative performance once employees' cognitive styles are taken into account. It examines whether brokering versus closed networks have opposite performance implications for adaptors and innovators.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a complementary fit between social capital and information-processing style. Brokering networks supply heterogeneous information and compensate for adaptors' weaker idea generation, while adaptors' implementation orientation helps them turn these ideas into innovations. Closed networks supply coordination, consensus, and support, which compensate for innovators' implementation weakness while allowing their stronger idea-generation capability to translate into implemented innovation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to social network theory by showing that the innovation value of brokerage and closure depends on employee cognitive style rather than operating uniformly across actors. It integrates the brokerage and closure views of social capital in a single contingency explanation, arguing that social networks shape information access while cognitive style shapes what information individuals need and how they process it. It also advances psychologically informed network research by identifying adaptive-innovative cognitive style as a key contingency in employee innovation.
practical_implication: Managers seeking to increase employee innovativeness should assess both employees' social networks and their cognitive styles. The findings suggest that adaptors may benefit from brokering ties that expose them to diverse ideas, whereas innovators may perform better in closed networks that help coordinate support and implementation. The paper warns against assuming that structural holes are always beneficial for innovation, because placing innovators in highly brokering networks may reduce their innovative performance.
limitations: The authors identify the cross-sectional design as a key limitation because it makes endogeneity and alternative explanations difficult to rule out. The study is based on a single organization, which limits confidence about generalizability across firms, industries, and more or less creativity-intensive contexts. The authors also note that the setting's premium on creativity may affect the main effects of brokerage and cognitive style, even if the contingency logic should be more robust.
future_research: The authors call for panel or quasi-experimental research that can test the theorized causal mechanisms more conclusively. They suggest extending the argument to interorganizational ties and gatekeeper roles, where cognitive style may shape how external information is translated and disseminated. They also encourage research on similarity fit, network homophily, social network activation, and whether the findings hold in less creative settings and across multiple organizations and sectors.
abstract: Integrating insights from cognitive psychology into current network theory on the social capital of brokering and closed networks, we argue that cognitive style is a critical contingency explaining the relation between social network position and innovative performance. Based on a “complementary fit” argument, we posit that a social network rich in structural holes enhances the innovative performance of employees with an adaptive cognitive style; however, individuals with an innovative cognitive style are most innovative when embedded within a closed network of densely interconnected contacts. Using data on the individual cognitive styles and complete workplace social networks of all employees within a design and manufacturing firm, we show that our theorized contingency mechanism accounts for a large share of empirical variation in employee innovative performance over and above existing social network explanations.

title: Sanctioning in the Wild: Rational Calculus and Retributive Instincts in Gourmet Cuisine
methods: Mixed-method field study: inductive qualitative interviews and content analysis with gourmet chefs, followed by a randomized scenario-based field experiment using chef responses to manipulated norm-violation scenarios.
industry: Gourmet cuisine and high-end restaurants.
country: Italy for the field experiment; Italy and the United States for the qualitative interviews.
time_period: Qualitative interviews ran from winter 2008 through fall 2010; the experiment used the 2009 Italian Michelin Guide sampling frame.
units: Gourmet chefs, restaurants, and chef-scenario responses.
n_sample: 23 qualitative informants; 534 returned surveys, of which 492 were complete; regression tables report 3,036 experimental observations.
authors: Di Stefano, G.; King, A. A.; Verona, G.
theories: norm-based intellectual property systems; social norms; strong reciprocity theory; weak reciprocity theory
keywords: gourmet cuisine; norm violations; sanctioning behavior; social exchange; strong reciprocity; weak reciprocity
research_question: Why do individuals sanction norm violations in real-world social exchange, and under what conditions are they more likely to administer sanctions based on rational calculus versus retributive instincts?
mechanism_summary:
- Mediating relationship: Propensity to sanction is analyzed as a link between scenario treatments and willingness to transfer knowledge.

The paper argues that sanctioning combines weak-reciprocity and strong-reciprocity processes. Chefs calculate the social cost of sanctioning by anticipating whether peers will see the sanction as legitimate, so they sanction less when a high-reputation violator may receive the benefit of the doubt and more when physical proximity increases the stakes. At the same time, severe misuse of recipes and signature dishes triggers a retributive response that makes sanctioning feel obligatory. Anticipating this costly obligation, chefs sometimes avoid knowledge exchange before any violation occurs.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the strong- versus weak-reciprocity debate by showing that both logics predict sanctioning behavior in a field setting. It also extends legitimacy research by showing that legitimacy loss can arise not only from violating a norm but also from sanctioning a norm violation when observers cannot reconstruct the prior offense. Finally, it contributes to work on norm-based intellectual property systems by examining how sanctions maintain norms governing transferred culinary knowledge.
practical_implication: Communities that rely on informal norms need ways to make violations and legitimate sanctions interpretable to peers; otherwise, potential enforcers may avoid sanctioning or avoid exchange altogether. In professional communities where reputation is valuable, actors may withhold knowledge not because they reject cooperation but because they anticipate the social and emotional costs of enforcing cooperation later.
limitations: The study measures intended action rather than observed sanctioning behavior, so actual behavior may differ from respondents' scenario-based responses. The models explaining propensity to sanction also have limited explanatory power, suggesting missing variables and the need to study individual characteristics. The authors note that the social legitimacy mechanism may be especially salient in status-based industries and professional elites.
future_research: Future research could examine how network structures, agglomeration, and dense relationships influence the propensity to sanction in field settings. The paper also calls for research on individual attributes that explain who becomes willing to police norm violations, especially because a decomposition analysis suggests that individual-level characteristics explain substantial variance in sanctioning behavior.
abstract: Why do we sanction norm violations? Despite near universal agreement on the role of sanctions for maintaining norms of cooperation, scholars hotly dispute whether individuals sanction based on a rational calculus or because of strong retributive instincts. In this paper we report on a mixed-method field study examining sanctioning behavior. Our goal is to extend theories of sanctioning by evaluating the conditions under which individuals are more likely to administer a sanction in response to a norm violation. To guide the development of our hypotheses, we engage in a qualitative examination of sanctioning decisions in the context of gourmet cuisine. We then test our predictions in a field experiment involving more than 500 gourmet chefs in Italy. Our results suggest that individuals follow retributive instincts, but they also engage in cost–benefit calculations. Indeed, we find that the two logics of sanctioning jointly influence participation in social exchange. Recognizing their own tendency to sanction at a cost, individuals avoid circumstances that could trigger the need for costly sanctions.

title: Same Page, Different Books: Extending Representational Gaps Theory to Enhance Performance in Multiteam Systems
methods: Field experiment with random assignment to frame-of-reference training, behavioral coordination and performance measures, hierarchical moderated regression, and moderated mediation analyses in Mplus with bootstrapped confidence intervals.
industry: Military leadership development and simulation training context.
country: United States; United States Air Force context.
time_period: Multiyear research program; specific calendar years not reported.
units: Fourteen-person multiteam systems of USAF captains.
n_sample: 249 multiteam systems; 3,486 officers.
authors: Firth, B. M.; Hollenbeck, J. R.; Miles, J. E.; Ilgen, D. R.; Barnes, C. M.
theories: information processing theory; representational gaps theory
keywords: Multiteam systems; between-team coordination; frame-of-reference training; multiteam system performance; representational gaps; within-team coordination
research_question: The paper asks what enhances between-team coordination and subsequent multiteam system performance, and when these effects are most likely to occur. It tests whether frame-of-reference training improves coordination and performance through an intervention theorized to reduce representational gaps, and whether within-team coordination in point and support teams changes the effect of that intervention.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that frame-of-reference training provides standardized criteria and a common language for interpreting task information, an intervention theorized to reduce representational gaps between specialized teams. This improves between-team coordination, which integrates point-team, support-team, and leadership-team actions toward system-level goals. Within-team coordination changes how strongly the training translates into between-team coordination: point-team coordination enhances the intervention's benefits, while support-team coordination shows a compensatory pattern.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends representational gaps theory from specialized members within teams to specialized component teams within multiteam systems. It also extends information processing theory by arguing that reducing uncertainty from multiple sources can interact, rather than merely add, when shaping between-team coordination and system performance. The study further clarifies how team-level processes can affect system-level coordination in multiteam systems.
practical_implication: Managers of multiteam systems can use frame-of-reference training to create standardized confidence ratings and a common language for translating functionally specific judgments across team boundaries. The paper also cautions that intervention design should account for component-team functions, because point and support teams condition the training-performance pathway differently.
limitations: The study uses behavioral indicators and does not directly measure psychological constructs such as shared cognition, representational gaps, or the specific cognitive and motivational mechanisms changed by training. The context is a USAF simulation with working professionals and career-relevant stakes, so extrapolation to non-military, non-simulated, or more uncertain environments requires caution. Several effects are statistically significant but small.
future_research: Future research should examine the specific cognitive and motivational mechanisms altered by frame-of-reference training in multiteam systems. It should also test alternate training designs, such as different duration, feedback intensity, target audience, or levels of representational gaps. The authors further call for research on other interventions that enhance between-team coordination and on contexts with different multiteam system types, sizes, goals, cultures, and uncertainty levels.
abstract: Multiteam systems are increasingly used by organizations, but are difficult to coordinate effectively. Building from theory on representational gaps, we explain why coordination between teams in multiteam systems can be hindered by inconsistencies that exist between them regarding the definition of shared problems. We argue that frame-of-reference training, an intervention that is theorized to reduce representational gaps, can facilitate coordination and subsequent performance in multiteam systems. We studied the effects of frame-of-reference training on multiteam system coordination and performance in 249 multiteam systems comprised of specialized teams. Supporting our expectations, we found that: (a) frame-of-reference training had a positive effect on multiteam system performance by enhancing between-team coordination; (b) within-team coordination improved the relationship between frame-of-reference training and between-team coordination, ultimately improving multiteam system performance; and (c) the patterns by which within-team coordination leveraged our intervention depended on teams' specific functions. Our findings extend representational gaps theory, highlight the interdependencies between team-level and system-level coordination, and demonstrate the utility of frame-of-reference training in a new setting.
apa_citation: Firth, B. M., Hollenbeck, J. R., Miles, J. E., Ilgen, D. R., & Barnes, C. M. (2015). Same page, different books: Extending representational gaps theory to enhance performance in multiteam systems. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 813-835. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0216

title: Which Problems to Solve? Online Knowledge Sharing and Attention Allocation in Organizations
methods: Rare-event logit models with choice-based sampling and weighted exogenous sampling maximum-likelihood estimation on provider-problem dyads from an intraorganizational online discussion forum; the authors also used a Heckman selection correction and clustered standard errors by provider.
industry: Structural engineering online discussion forum in a global engineering firm.
country: Global firm headquartered in London with offices across 26 countries.
time_period: January 2003-August 2005; 32-month forum observation window.
units: Provider-problem dyads among knowledge providers and posted problems.
n_sample: 13,761 dyads: 1,251 realized and 12,510 nonrealized provider-problem matches.
authors: Haas, M. R.; Criscuolo, P.; George, G.
theories: attention-based view of the firm; matching theory; selective attention
keywords: attention allocation; expertise matching; online knowledge sharing; problem characteristics; problem crowding; provider-problem matching
research_question: The paper asks why organization members allocate attention to some online knowledge-sharing problems rather than others. It specifically shifts the explanation from provider-seeker relationships to provider-problem matches in an intraorganizational online discussion forum.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an attention-allocation process in which knowledge providers compare the expected benefits and costs of responding to specific problems. Closer expertise matching increases the expected value of responding and lowers cognitive costs, making providers more likely to respond. Problem length, breadth, and novelty attract attention up to a point but can become costly when cognitive load is high; problem crowding increases forum salience, with expertise matching amplifying providers' willingness to attend to the focal problem.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes by theorizing attention allocation as a matching process between providers and problems inside organizations. It extends online knowledge-sharing research beyond interpersonal provider-seeker ties by showing that expertise fit, problem characteristics, and problem crowding shape which problems receive attention. It also brings matching theory into an intraorganizational setting where the match is between an actor and an issue rather than between two actors.
practical_implication: The findings imply that organizations using online discussion forums should not assume that making problems visible is enough for knowledge sharing. The study highlights provider-problem expertise fit, problem presentation, and competing problems as attention-allocation conditions that matter for managerial attention, while stopping short of a detailed forum-design prescription.
limitations: The study is based on a single professional services organization, so the generalizability of the patterns to smaller firms, less dispersed organizations, or settings with stronger participation pressure is uncertain. The study measures attention allocation mainly as whether a provider posted a response; its supplementary response-length analysis is suggestive but cannot fully capture time, effort, or response quality.
future_research: Future research could examine attention intensity with richer measures than response length and study the quality or helpfulness of responses, including peer-rated online contributions. Further work could also investigate why knowledge seekers post some problems to online forums, which individuals are more likely to post problems, and which problem types are more likely to be posted.
abstract: Why do individuals allocate attention to specific problems in organizations? Viewing online knowledge sharing as a matching process between knowledge providers and problems, we examine attention allocation in the context of an online community within which knowledge providers respond to problems posted by other organization members. We argue that knowledge providers are more likely to allocate attention to solving problems that more closely match their expertise, but that decisions to allocate attention are also influenced by problem characteristics such as length, breadth, and novelty, as well as by problem crowding. Analyzing 1,251 realized matches and 12,510 nonrealized matches among knowledge providers and problems posted over a 32month period on an online discussion forum within a global engineering firm, we find evidence to support our claim that attention allocation is driven by the features of a particular provider–problem match, thereby shifting the discourse from knowledge provider–seeker relationships to knowledge provider–problem matches. The implications for theories of knowledge sharing, matching processes, and managerial attention are discussed.
apa_citation: Haas, M. R., Criscuolo, P., & George, G. (2015). Which problems to solve? Online knowledge sharing and attention allocation in organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 680-711. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0263
