title: The Threshold Effect of Participative Leadership and the Role of Leader Information Sharing
methods: Two empirical quantitative studies using subordinate and supervisor survey data, objective performance records in Study 2, and multilevel analyses of linear, quadratic, interaction, and mediated moderation effects.
industry: Study 1: textile manufacturing and telecommunication services; Study 2: garment manufacturing.
time_period: Calendar data-collection period not reported; Study 2 objective performance records were obtained one month after the paper surveys.
units: Subordinate-supervisor dyads; employees nested within supervisors/groups.
n_sample: Study 1: 625 subordinates rated by 203 supervisors; Study 2: 148 subordinates supervised by 19 supervisors.
authors: Lam, C. K.; Huang, X.; Chan, S. C. H.
theories: adaptive resonance theory (Grossberg, 1999); implicit leadership theory (Brown & Lord, 2001; Eden & Leviatan, 1975)
keywords: adaptive resonance theory; employee performance; implicit leadership theory; information sharing; leadership effectiveness; participative leadership
research_question: The paper asks whether participative leadership has a threshold, J-shaped relationship with employee performance rather than a simple positive linear effect. It also asks whether leader information sharing strengthens this curvilinear relationship and whether perceived leadership effectiveness explains its effect on objective performance.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on implicit leadership theory, the paper argues that low or moderate participative leadership may not activate employees' participation schema because it does not sufficiently match a participative-leader prototype. When participative leadership passes a threshold, employees are more likely to interpret the leader as genuinely participative and respond with higher performance. Adaptive resonance theory extends this logic: high information sharing provides consistent cues that reinforce the participative-leader prototype, whereas low information sharing creates ambiguity and weakens the performance response. In Study 2, leadership effectiveness is the cognitive pathway through which high participative leadership combined with high information sharing predicts objective work performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to participative leadership research by theorizing and testing a threshold effect: participative leadership becomes performance-relevant mainly after it exceeds a moderate level and is paired with high information sharing. It extends implicit leadership theory and adaptive resonance theory by showing how multiple leader behaviors jointly activate leader prototypes and participation schemas. It also identifies perceived leadership effectiveness as a proximal cognitive mechanism linking the moderated curvilinear pattern to objective employee performance.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat partial or symbolic participation as enough to improve performance; employees respond more strongly when leaders demonstrate a sufficiently high level of participative leadership. Leaders should also share information about goals, reasons, expectations, and decision requirements so participation is interpreted as genuine rather than ambiguous. Organizations can support this by training leaders in two-way communication and building procedures, policies, and systems that support leadership accountability and a culture of sharing.
limitations: The study's correlational design precludes causal conclusions, even though the authors argue that theory and time-lagged performance data make reverse causality less likely. Common method variance may still be a concern, although multisource performance data, CFA and AVE evidence, and the complexity of the quadratic-by-linear interaction reduce this threat. Generalizability is also limited because all studies were conducted in China, where high power distance and collectivism may shape employee responses to participative leadership.
future_research: Future work should use experimental or longitudinal designs to test the causal direction of participative leadership, information sharing, leadership effectiveness, and performance. Researchers could examine employee attributes and dispositional factors, such as experience, knowledge, readiness, need for closure, pessimism, causal attribution, commitment to the leader, and romanticized beliefs about leadership, as additional moderators of the threshold effect. The authors also call for studies of other performance outcomes, especially innovative behavior, and for research on leaders' well-being and emotional responses as possible consequences of participative leadership and information sharing.
abstract: Drawing on implicit leadership theory (Brown & Lord, 2001; Eden & Leviatan, 1975), we hypothesize that the relationship between participative leadership and employee performance is curvilinear (J-shaped), suggesting that participative leadership is unrelated to employee performance when participative leadership is below a moderate level (i.e., a threshold). Above this threshold, increased participative leadership is related to higher employee performance. Building on adaptive resonance theory (Grossberg, 1999), a variant of implicit leadership theory, we further hypothesize that leaders' information-sharing behavior will moderate this curvilinear relationship. We test this model using two independent samples: office and call-center employees (Study 1) and factory workers (Study 2). Results from Study 1 reveal that this curvilinear relationship is stronger when leaders' information sharing is high and weaker when information sharing is low. Furthermore, in Study 2, we find that leadership effectiveness mediates the interactive effect of participative leadership and information sharing on objective work performance.
apa_citation: Lam, C. K., Huang, X., & Chan, S. C. H. (2015). The threshold effect of participative leadership and the role of leader information sharing. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 836-855. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0427

title: Discrimination in Selection Decisions: Integrating Stereotype Fit and Interdependence Theories
methods: Four studies: a lab experiment, a field experiment, and two online experiments; randomized manipulations of task requirement and competition/cooperation; OLS/logistic regression and bootstrapped moderated mediation tests.
industry: Not reported in paper
country: United Kingdom, South Korea, and U.S.-representative online samples
time_period: Study 2 Winter Boot Camp in January 2013; other study dates not reported
units: Male participants/decision makers making selection decisions about male candidates
n_sample: Study 1: 98 White male participants; Study 2: 78 male association members; Study 3: 122 males with work experience; Study 4: 121 male participants
authors: Lee, S. Y.; Pitesa, M.; Thau, S.; Pillutla, M. M.
theories: interdependence theory (Deutsch, 1949); statistical theory of discrimination (Arrow, 1973; Phelps, 1972); stereotype fit theory (Dipboye, 1985; Heilman, 1983)
keywords: discrimination; instrumentality; interdependence; selection decisions; stereotype fit
research_question: How do stereotype-based inferences about task fit and expected competition or cooperation with a candidate jointly shape discrimination in selection decisions? The paper asks when decision makers favor candidates from their own social group and when self-interested interdependence leads them to prefer candidates from a different social group.
mechanism_summary: Decision makers use stereotypes to infer whether a candidate has the ability required for the focal task. When the decision maker expects competition, a candidate stereotyped as more able becomes a more threatening future competitor and is perceived as less instrumental; when cooperation is expected, the same candidate becomes a more useful future collaborator and is perceived as more instrumental. Selection preference follows this perceived instrumentality, producing discrimination for or against the stereotypically stronger candidate depending on interdependence.
theoretical_contribution: The paper qualifies the dominant in-group favoritism account of discrimination in selection decisions by specifying conditions under which decision makers discriminate against members of their own social group. It contributes by integrating stereotype fit theory with interdependence theory, showing that task requirements and expected intra-organizational relationships jointly determine whether stereotypes produce favorable or unfavorable treatment.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat discrimination risk as only a matter of generalized prejudice or similarity attraction. The paper suggests that selection systems should account for whether evaluators expect to compete or cooperate with the candidate, and that accountability practices may reduce self-interested reliance on stereotypes in hiring and assignment decisions.
limitations: The studies used all-male decision makers and candidates, and Studies 1-3 focused on White-Asian racial comparisons, so generalization to other gender and race combinations requires caution. The experiments also focused on choices between equally qualified candidates; stereotype-based effects may be weaker when candidates clearly differ in qualifications or when decision-maker-candidate interdependence is weak.
future_research: Future research should test the model with other gender, race, religion, and sexual-orientation combinations, and examine individual differences in self-interest, prejudice, and organizational orientation. The authors also call for large-scale passive observational studies of hiring committees and for research on how the strength of interdependence affects the model's explanatory power.
abstract: We integrate stereotype fit and interdependence theories to propose a model that explains how and why decision makers discriminate in selection decisions. Our model suggests that decision makers draw on stereotypes about members of different social groups to infer the degree to which candidates possess the specific ability required for the task. Decision makers perceive candidates that have a greater ability required for the task as less (more) instrumental to their personal outcomes if they expect to compete (cooperate) with the candidate, and they discriminate in favor of candidates that are perceived as more instrumental to them. We tested our theory in the context of racial (Studies 1–3) and age (Study 4) discrimination in selection decisions with all-male samples and found evidence consistent with our predictions. By explaining when and why decision makers discriminate in favor of, but also against, members of their own social group, this research may help to explain the mixed support for the dominant view that decision makers exhibit favoritism toward candidates that belong to the same social group. In addition, our research demonstrates the importance of considering the largely overlooked role of interdependent relationships within the organization in order to understand discrimination in organizations.
apa_citation: Lee, S. Y., Pitesa, M., Thau, S., & Pillutla, M. M. (2015). Discrimination in selection decisions: Integrating stereotype fit and interdependence theories. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 789-812. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0571

title: Distant Search, Narrow Attention: How Crowding Alters Organizations’ Filtering of Suggestions in Crowdsourcing
methods: Longitudinal Cox proportional hazard models on weekly suggestion-level risk-set records, using proprietary crowdsourcing-platform data, text-analysis measures of content distance, network measures of structural distance, contributor-history measures of personal distance, and Huber-White clustered standard errors at the individual level.
industry: Organizations using a website-embedded suggestion tool across different industries, with the clientele dominated by web companies.
country: Software company located on the west coast of the United States; most customer organizations were located in America and Western Europe.
time_period: November 2007-June 2011.
units: Crowdsourced suggestions submitted by external contributors to organizations, observed as weekly risk-set records until selection or censoring.
n_sample: 105,127 suggestions submitted to 922 organizations; 10,629 selected suggestions over 5,039,413 weekly observations.
authors: Piezunka, H.; Dahlander, L.
theories: attention-based view (Ocasio, 1997); crowdsourcing as solution to distant search; distant search
keywords: crowding; crowdsourcing; distant knowledge; distant search; organizational attention
research_question: The paper asks whether organizations that solicit suggestions from external contributors in order to access distant knowledge actually pay attention to suggestions that are distant. It also asks whether crowding makes organizations more or less likely to attend to distant knowledge during suggestion filtering.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an attention-filtering process under bounded organizational attention. When crowding increases, organizations simplify and rationalize filtering, which steers attention toward suggestions that are familiar in content, structurally connected to other supported suggestions, or submitted by contributors with prior attention from the organization. The evidence most strongly supports crowding as amplifying the negative effects of content and structural distance, while personal distance has a negative main effect but less robust moderation by crowding.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to attention research by showing that crowding changes what organizations attend to, not only how much attention any single suggestion receives. It contributes to search research by separating access to distant knowledge from attention to distant knowledge, showing that organizations may collect distant suggestions but filter them out when the pool becomes crowded. It also contributes to crowdsourcing research by shifting attention from the solicitation stage to the filtering stage and by distinguishing content, structural, and personal distance empirically.
practical_implication: Organizations using crowdsourcing should not assume that larger suggestion pools automatically improve innovation search. Managers may need to constrain the generation of alternatives, design filters that deliberately preserve distant suggestions, and establish criteria or ratios that prevent familiar suggestions from crowding out more distant ones. They can also begin by examining suggestions from contributors from whom the organization has not previously heard.
limitations: The authors state that their theory depends on settings in which all suggestions and ideas are visible to the organization and to external contributors. It also depends on social mechanisms that allow external contributors to vote, comment, or refine suggestions; a simple suggestion box without these mechanisms would not provide the same relationship cues for filtering suggestions.
future_research: Future research could examine how crowding affects organizations' relationships with ignored or rejected contributors, including whether disappointed contributors publicly harm organizational reputation or future search efforts. The authors also point to settings such as suggestion boxes, where social mechanisms among external contributors are absent, as contexts where the theory's assumptions may not hold in the same way.
abstract: In their search for innovation, organizations often invite suggestions from external contributors. Soliciting suggestions is a form of distant search, since it allows organizations to tap into knowledge that may not reside within their organizational boundaries. Organizations engaging in distant search often face a large pool of suggestions, an outcome we refer to as crowding. When crowding occurs, organizations, given a limited attention span, can attend to only a subset of suggestions. Our core argument is that crowding narrows the attention of organizations; that is, despite organizations’ efforts to reach out to external contributors and access suggestions that capture distant knowledge, they are more likely to pay attention to suggestions that are familiar, not distant. We test our theory with a unique longitudinal dataset that captures how 922 organizations responded to 105,127 crowdsourced suggestions from external contributors. After distinguishing between three different dimensions of distance (content, structural, and personal), we find that (a) all three types of distance have independent negative effects on the likelihood of attention, (b) crowding amplifies these negative effects, and (c) there are differences among the effects’ magnitudes. We elaborate on the broader implications of these findings for the literatures on attention, search, and crowdsourcing.
apa_citation: Piezunka, H., & Dahlander, L. (2015). Distant search, narrow attention: How crowding alters organizations’ filtering of suggestions in crowdsourcing. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 856-880. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0458

title: Seeing the Forest for the Trees: Exploratory Learning, Mobile Technology, and Knowledge Workers’ Role Integration Behaviors
methods: Four-study quantitative design combining an archival analysis of Enron emails, two online experiments with working adults, and a three-wave field survey of knowledge workers; analyses include linguistic abstraction coding, t-tests, hierarchical regressions, and bootstrapped mediation tests.
industry: Knowledge-work contexts, including Enron email communication and varied job functions such as information technology, human resources, and administrative functions
country: United States for the Study 4 screening panel; country is not reported for the Study 2 and Study 3 online working-adult samples
time_period: Study 1 covers Enron emails from 1997 to 2002; Study 4 surveys knowledge workers across three waves over a four-month period
units: Employees, working adults, and knowledge workers whose role integration, construal level, and exploratory learning behavior are measured or experimentally manipulated
n_sample: Study 1 analyzes 236 Enron employees; Study 2 includes 97 participants; Study 3 includes 99 participants; Study 4 includes 80 respondents completing all three waves
authors: Reyt, Jean-Nicolas; Wiesenfeld, Batia M.
theories: boundary theory; bounded rationality; construal level theory; organizational learning research
keywords: boundary theory; construal level theory; exploratory learning activities; mobile technologies; role integration behaviors
research_question: How does role integration, enabled by mobile technologies and blurred boundaries across work and nonwork roles, shape knowledge workers’ construal level and exploratory learning behavior? The paper asks whether role integration behaviors move workers toward more abstract work representations and whether that abstraction explains greater exploratory learning.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism starts from boundary theory: role integration makes multiple role demands simultaneously salient and weakens temporal, spatial, and social boundaries. Because people have bounded cognitive resources, these overlapping demands push workers toward higher-level, more abstract construals that emphasize central goals and transferable meanings rather than local details. Higher construal then supports exploratory learning by helping workers generate, compare, and search across more distant alternatives. Across the studies, the authors treat role integration as a behaviorally grounded antecedent of abstract work cognition, which in turn predicts exploratory learning.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends boundary theory by identifying construal level as a cognitive mechanism through which role integration affects work behavior, moving beyond prior emphasis on stress, satisfaction, and work-family conflict. It extends construal level theory by applying abstraction to social roles rather than only to discrete objects, events, or temporal distance. It also contributes to organizational learning research by opening the cognitive black box of exploratory learning and linking individual role integration to distant search and exploratory activity.
practical_implication: Managers should recognize that mobile-technology-enabled role integration can shape how abstractly knowledge workers think, not only how available they are. The paper suggests that role integration may be useful for employees whose work benefits from exploratory learning, innovation, and broader search, but may be costly where effectiveness depends on focus, detail-orientation, and execution. It also implies that managers can shape construal through work design, technology expectations, time horizons, and reward systems.
limitations: Study 1 is archival and cannot establish causal direction, and its email-based measures are noisy proxies for role integration and construal level. Study 4 reduces common-method concerns through a multi-wave design, but its dependent variable is self-reported exploratory learning. The authors also limit the model to cumulative micro-role integration and leave open whether momentary role integration, macro-role transitions, role-integration preferences, or non-mobile forms of integration operate similarly.
future_research: Future research should identify when the benefits of role integration for exploratory learning outweigh its costs for attention, stress, and focused performance. The authors call for more dynamic work on momentary versus cumulative integration, comparisons across temporal, spatial, and social boundaries, and tests of whether mobile technology is a boundary condition or one example of a broader integration process. They also suggest examining role preferences, macro-role transitions, and managerial tools for monitoring or shaping employees’ role integration.
abstract: Role integration is the new workplace reality for many employees. The prevalence of mobile technologies (e.g., laptops, smartphones, tablets) that are increasingly wearable and nearly always “on” makes it difficult to keep role boundaries separate and distinct. We draw upon boundary theory and construal level theory to hypothesize that role integration behaviors shift people from thinking concretely to thinking more abstractly about their work. The results of an archival study of Enron executives’ emails, two experiments, and a multi-wave field study of knowledge workers provide evidence of positive associations between role integration behaviors, higher construal level, and more exploratory learning activities.
apa_citation: Reyt, J.-N., & Wiesenfeld, B. M. (2015). Seeing the forest for the trees: Exploratory learning, mobile technology, and knowledge workers’ role integration behaviors. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(3), 739-762. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0991

title: When the Leader Follows: Avoiding Dethronement through Imitation
methods: Quantitative analysis of GPS, wind, race-order, and outcome data from America’s Cup World Series match races; probit regression models with heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors clustered by leader-follower dyad, using GARCH-based environmental-uncertainty measures and controls for penalties, positioning, experience, prior performance, race order, and event.
industry: America’s Cup World Series professional sailing match races.
country: Multiple countries across six international venues.
time_period: 2011–12 America’s Cup World Series.
units: Upwind legs in leader-follower match-race dyads.
n_sample: 148 upwind-leg observations from 74 match races among 11 teams.
authors: Ross, J.-M.; Sharapov, D.
theories: Austrian School perspective; competitive dynamics
keywords: Austrian School perspective; action imitation; competitive dynamics; environmental uncertainty; positioning imitation
research_question: The paper asks whether, and under what conditions, a leader’s imitation of follower actions can be an effective competitive strategy for avoiding dethronement. It focuses on how action imitation and positioning imitation shape the likelihood that the leader remains ahead under uncertainty, initial advantage, and follower capability differences.
mechanism_summary: The core mechanism is that follower actions create disequilibrium and opportunities to catch the leader, while leader imitation can equilibrate those moves and preserve the status quo. Action imitation aligns the leader’s tactical trajectory with the follower’s moves, and positioning imitation reduces longer-term differences in exposure to environmental shifts. The results support positive direct effects of both imitation strategies and their complementarity, but the moderation results are mixed: environmental uncertainty strengthens action imitation and weakens positioning imitation, initial advantage strengthens both, and follower capability advantage weakens action imitation but not positioning imitation.
theoretical_contribution: The paper redirects competitive dynamics research from the familiar question of followers imitating leaders to the less examined possibility that leaders imitate followers to defend leadership. It uses the Austrian School view of competition as movement toward and away from equilibrium to explain imitation as an equilibrating response to follower disruption. It also advances competitive dynamics as a predictive theory by specifying endogenous and exogenous boundary conditions around imitation: environmental uncertainty, initial advantage, and capability differences.
practical_implication: For market leaders, the findings imply that selective imitation of follower moves can be a defensive strategy, especially when the environment is uncertain and the leader has a strong head start. The paper also warns that imitation has costs: if followers possess superior capabilities, leader imitation can release information that helps them exploit those capabilities and catch up. Managers therefore need to weigh the defensive benefits of matching follower moves against reputational concerns and the risk of strengthening a capable challenger.
limitations: The empirical setting provides fine-grained data from match racing, but the authors state that generalizability to business settings still needs validation. The study examines head-to-head competition, so the theory also needs testing in settings with more than two rivals. The authors further note the difficulty of separating imitation from shared reactions to environmental shocks, and they discuss possible sailing-specific aerodynamics and right-of-way concerns.
future_research: Future work should test the theory in business contexts with multiple rivals and more complex competitive interdependence. Researchers should use more fine-grained approaches to distinguish imitation from common responses to environmental shocks. The paper also points to settings where firms receive low-lag information about exogenous conditions, such as oil prices, foreign exchange rates, stock prices, commodity prices, airlines, and trading, as useful contexts for studying uncertainty and imitation.
abstract: When is imitation of follower actions an effective competitive strategy for a leader? Building on prior work in competitive dynamics from the Austrian School perspective, we propose that imitation can be an effective means of staying ahead, even in the absence of mimetic social pressures. This is because the leader’s imitation of follower actions represents equilibrating moves to maintain the status quo in reaction to the disequilibrating actions that the follower undertakes to catch up with the leader. Furthermore, reduction of difference in competitive positioning between leader and follower serves the same purpose, and both imitation strategies are complementary. These effects of “action imitation” and “positioning imitation,” we argue, are moderated by the degree of environmental uncertainty, by the extent of the leader’s initial advantage, and by the difference between leader and follower capabilities. Our theoretical arguments are supported by an analysis of data on head-to-head boat races from the America’s Cup World Series. By developing mechanisms that take endogenous and exogenous contingencies of competitive interactions into account, this paper advances competitive dynamics as a predictive theory of performance outcomes.

title: Reinsurance Trading in Lloyd’s of London: Balancing Conflicting-yet-Complementary Logics in Practice
methods: Yearlong ethnographic study of reinsurance underwriting in Lloyd’s of London across the 2009-2010 reinsurance cycle, using field observations, interviews, documentary data, NVivo coding, and abductive theorizing.
industry: Reinsurance trading in Lloyd’s of London.
time_period: 2009-2010 reinsurance cycle.
units: Reinsurance underwriters across seven Lloyd’s reinsurance firms, plus brokers and Lloyd’s representatives.
n_sample: 26 underwriters shadowed.
authors: Smets, M.; Jarzabkowski, P.; Burke, G. T.; Spee, P.
theories: institutional logics; institutional theory; practice theory
keywords: bridging; community logic; demarcating; institutional complexity; institutional logics; market logic; practice lens; segmenting
research_question: The paper asks how actors facing long-standing institutional complexity enact both the contradiction and the interdependence between coexisting logics in everyday work. It studies how Lloyd’s reinsurance underwriters balance market and community logics while trading risks as both employees of profit-seeking firms and members of the Lloyd’s community.
mechanism_summary:
- Key logics: Market logic emphasizes profitability, share price, firm performance, and competitive status; community logic emphasizes Lloyd’s membership, trust, reciprocity, reputation, and long-term relationships.
- Segmenting: Underwriters assign market-oriented analytic work to the office and community-oriented broker interaction to the Lloyd’s trading floor, reinforced by schedules, spaces, dress codes, and privacy practices.
- Bridging: Underwriters import community information into commercial pricing and import commercial rationale into broker-facing interactions, allowing the two logics to inform one another without collapsing into a single hybrid logic.
- Demarcating: Underwriters use peer review, risk-review meetings, cynicism, protected analysis, price boundaries, delayed decisions, and sanctions to prevent either logic from being over-privileged.
- Process relationship: Segmenting creates distinct logics, bridging reconnects them in particular situations, and demarcating reasserts their boundaries when bridging risks slippage.

The process is not a variable-based causal model. Individuals maintain market and community logics as conflicting-yet-complementary by iteratively separating and integrating them in practice. The balance shifts across tasks and situations, so the paper theorizes dynamic, moment-by-moment balancing rather than a fixed organizational settlement.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to institutional complexity research by moving attention from structural organizational responses to frontline actors’ everyday practices. It theorizes segmenting, bridging, and demarcating as a cyclic system through which individuals keep coexisting logics distinct enough to remain conflicting and connected enough to become complementary. It also shows that, in a long-standing hybrid context, institutional complexity can itself become institutionalized and routinely enacted in practice.
practical_implication: For organizations facing durable institutional complexity, the study suggests that formal structural separation is insufficient if everyday work requires actors to move between logics. Work arrangements, peer scrutiny, and interaction routines can help practitioners connect competing demands while still maintaining boundaries that prevent drift toward one logic.
limitations: The authors derive the model from Lloyd’s of London, a persistent hybrid with market and community logics, repeated transactions, diffuse enforcement, and relatively autonomous professionals. They argue that these institutional and organizational conditions make the mechanisms especially visible but may also moderate how well the model travels to contexts with more rigidly codified demands, less complementarity in the work, fewer repeated interactions, or lower actor autonomy.
future_research: The authors encourage future research on how the nature of work and the nature of institutional demands affect the experience of institutional complexity and the type, order, and salience of balancing mechanisms. They also identify scope for examining contexts where logics are more centrally enforced, where referent audiences are differently present across spaces, or where actors have less discretion to balance competing logics in the moment.
abstract: Drawing on a yearlong ethnographic study of reinsurance trading in Lloyd’s of London, this paper makes three contributions to current discussions of institutional complexity. First, we shift focus away from structural and relatively static organizational responses to institutional complexity and identify three balancing mechanisms—segmenting, bridging, and demarcating—that allow individuals to manage competing logics and their shifting salience within their everyday work. Second, we integrate these mechanisms in a theoretical model that explains how individuals can continually keep coexisting logics, and their tendencies to either blend or disconnect, in a state of dynamic tension that renders them conflicting-yet-complementary logics. Our model shows how actors are able to dynamically balance coexisting logics, maintaining the distinction between them while also exploiting the benefits of their interdependence. Third, in contrast to most studies of newly formed hybrids and/or novel complexity, our focus on a long-standing context of institutional complexity shows how institutional complexity can itself become institutionalized and routinely enacted within everyday practice.

title: Watching You Watching Me: Boundary Control and Capturing Attention in the Context of Ubiquitous Technology Use
methods: Qualitative grounded theory-building study using semistructured interviews and archival data on U.S. Navy ICT use; interviews were transcribed, imported into NVivo, and coded through open, selective, and axial coding rounds to develop aggregate dimensions and a process model.
industry: Military / naval organization
time_period: Interview data collected in four rounds from fall 2003 through spring 2013, supplemented by more than 15 years of archival data
units: Navy members, spouses, supervisors, information professionals, and archival materials on Navy ICT use
n_sample: 73 interviews: 14 high-level officers or information professionals, 6 lower-level officers, 25 enlisted sailors, and 27 spouses; two individuals were interviewed twice
authors: Stanko, Taryn L.; Beckman, Christine M.
theories: attention and control; boundary control; organizational control; situational controls
keywords: boundary control; contextualization; deflection; individual attention; monitoring; situational controls; ubiquitous technology use; work–nonwork interactions
research_question: How do organizations attempt to shape individual attention and divert attention from nonwork activities in the face of ubiquitous ICT use? The paper asks how boundary control operates when work and nonwork interactions are continually interwoven by communication technologies.
mechanism_summary:
- Core attention problems: Nonwork ICT use during work creates productivity problems when attention shifts away from work and security problems when employees forget organizational rules and norms.
- Situational controls: The Navy monitors employees to track attention, contextualizes technology use to cultivate attention, and deflects access to restrict attention.
- Individual responses: Artful use of controls elicits simultaneity, rule accommodation, and refocusing; underuse elicits work-arounds, dismissal, and desensitization; overuse elicits forced compliance through disconnection and powerlessness.
- Control dynamics: Effective boundary control is dynamic, layered across global and situational controls, and only temporarily effective because new threats to attention continually emerge.

The process account shows organizations trying to capture attention rather than merely regulate employees' physical presence or time at work. Monitoring identifies where attention is going, contextualization keeps organizational norms salient during technology use, and deflection removes or limits access when productivity or security risks require stronger intervention. These controls work best when combined transparently and flexibly: too little control invites rejection, while excessive monitoring or restriction without contextualization damages morale and trust.
theoretical_contribution: The paper redefines boundary control as the ways managers at multiple organizational levels capture and shape employee attention during the daily flow of work–nonwork interactions. It develops situational controls as a core organizational-control concept, identifying monitoring, contextualization, and deflection as mechanisms that track, cultivate, and restrict attention in the moment. It also contributes a process model showing how different configurations of situational controls generate cooperation, rejection, or forced compliance.
practical_implication: Organizations facing ubiquitous ICT use should not rely only on global rules, blanket bans, or surveillance. The Navy case suggests that monitoring needs transparent contextualization and intermittent, targeted deflection so employees understand why attention is being managed and can keep organizational norms in mind while using technology. Managers should also avoid permanent or unexplained restrictions because they may reduce morale, trust, and employees' ability to manage nonwork responsibilities.
limitations: The study is based on an extreme case: the U.S. Navy, a total institution with strong socialization, expected monitoring, and unusual control over physical space during deployment. The qualitative single-case design clarifies the process of boundary control, but the authors caution that the findings need examination in less controlled organizations and in settings where employees have more control over physical space.
future_research: Future research should examine situational boundary control in settings where organizations have less control over physical space and where personal devices make deflection harder. The paper points to comparative work on corporate security, state control, technology-enabled monitoring tools, e-mail timeouts, social media shutdowns, and other interventions that capture attention. It also calls for research on how situational controls shape productivity and safety across work tasks beyond the work–nonwork boundary.
abstract: As information communication technologies proliferate in the workplace, organizations face unique challenges managing how and when employees engage in work and nonwork activities. Using interview and archival data from the U.S. Navy, we explore one organization’s attempts to shape individual attention in an effort to exert boundary control. We describe the organizational productivity and security problems that result from individual attention being engaged in nonwork activities while at work, and find that the organization manages these problems by monitoring employees (tracking attention), contextualizing technology use to remind people of appropriate organizational use practices (cultivating attention), and diverting, limiting, and withholding technology access (restricting attention). We bring together research on attention and control to challenge current definitions of boundary control, and we detail the understudied situational controls used by the organization to shape work–nonwork interactions in the moment. We highlight how situational control efforts must work together in order to capture attention and shape behavior, and we develop a model to explicate this ongoing process of boundary control. Our findings offer insight into the evolving challenges that organizations face in executing boundary control, as well as of organizational control more broadly, in the modern workplace.

title: Information, Attention, and Decision Making
methods: From the Editors thematic editorial introducing a set of AMJ articles on information, attention, and decision making in the information age and developing future research directions across individual, group, organizational, and institutional levels.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: van Knippenberg, Daan; Dahlander, Linus; Haas, Martine R.; George, Gerard
theories: bounded rationality (Cyert & March, 1963; Simon, 1957); managerial attention and information processing (Ocasio, 2011); motivated information processing (De Dreu et al., 2008)
keywords: attention; bounded rationality; decision making; information; information age; information overload
research_question: The editorial asks how management in the information age challenges existing theories of information processing, attention, and decision making. It focuses on how expanded information access, information overload, and scarce attention reshape individual, group, organizational, and institutional behavior.
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial frame: The article introduces a thematic issue on information, attention, and decision making and positions the information age as a context that may require management scholars to revisit established theoretical assumptions.
- Information abundance and attention scarcity: The authors argue that information now scales faster than human and organizational attention, creating overload, bias, distraction, and costly information-management demands.
- Cross-level scope: The issue articles are presented as examples of information-processing problems across individuals, teams, multiteam systems, organizations, markets, and institutions.
- Thematic research agenda: The editorial identifies future research opportunities around creativity, innovation, talent management, unstructured content analysis, strategic value and costs of information, attention quality, workplace well-being, and social change.
- Theoretical refresh: The closing argument encourages scholars to revisit bounded rationality, managerial attention, absorption, and information processing in an information-rich, networked world.

The process is editorial and agenda-setting rather than empirical. The authors connect classic bounded rationality and attention arguments to a changed information context in which digital technologies, big data, social media, and ubiquitous communication expand information access while intensifying demands on scarce attention. They use the thematic issue's articles to show that these pressures operate across levels and to organize a future research agenda for management scholarship.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial's contribution is to reposition information, attention, and decision making as a renewed management research agenda for the information age. It argues that classic assumptions about bounded rationality and managerial attention remain important but need to be refreshed for contexts marked by information abundance, digital technologies, open information systems, and cross-level information flows.
practical_implication: For managers, the editorial implies that more information is not automatically better; organizations must design practices that help people filter, share, protect, and use information without overwhelming attention. It also points to practical challenges around knowledge sharing systems, crowdsourcing, feedback, information-related burnout, social media, and information governance.
limitations: The article is an editorial introduction rather than a systematic review or empirical study. Its claims are organized around selected articles in the thematic issue and illustrative examples, so the coverage of information, attention, and decision-making research is explicitly agenda-setting rather than exhaustive.
future_research: The editorial calls for research on how information-rich contexts affect creativity, innovation, talent management, content analysis, business models, attention quality, workplace well-being, leadership, distributed teams, institutions, and social change. It especially encourages scholars to study information, attention, and decision making across levels of analysis and to revisit established theories under new technological and social conditions.

title: The Dynamic Nature of Collective Turnover and Unit Performance: The Impact of Time, Quality, and Replacements
methods: Longitudinal empirical study using quarterly unit-level data from a Fortune 100 U.S. retail chain; hypotheses are tested with random effects regression models and robust standard errors clustered by unit.
industry: Retail stores in a prominent U.S. retail chain.
time_period: Four quarters in 2003 and one quarter in 2004, spanning over 15 months.
units: Retail employees nested within stores/units.
n_sample: 2,592 unit-quarter observations across 988 units; the article text also reports 108,357 employees.
authors: Call, M. L.; Nyberg, A. J.; Ployhart, R. E.; Weekley, J.
theories: context-emergent turnover theory (Nyberg & Ployhart, 2013)
keywords: collective turnover; context-emergent turnover theory; replacement hires; turnover dispersion; turnover rate change; unit performance
research_question: The paper asks how turnover rate change affects unit performance over time, above and beyond static turnover rates. It also asks when this relationship is strengthened or weakened by turnover quality, turnover dispersion, and the quality and quantity of replacement hires in a human capital resource flow system.
mechanism_summary: The paper theorizes turnover as part of a dynamic human capital resource flow system rather than as an isolated rate. Increasing turnover rate change is expected to disrupt unit workload, coordination, routines, and psychological processes, thereby lowering unit performance. The results support the distinct negative effect of turnover rate change, show that losses are stronger when departing employees are higher quality, and show that more dispersed turnover weakens the negative effect. The predicted moderating benefits of replacement quality are not supported under two-tailed tests, and replacement quantity moderates in the opposite direction from the prediction.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends collective turnover research by distinguishing static turnover rates from turnover rate change and showing that both matter for unit performance. It provides an empirical test of context-emergent turnover theory by modeling turnover quantity, turnover quality, turnover dispersion, and replacement hires within one longitudinal human capital resource system. It also shows that the timing and quality of turnover events add explanatory value that static turnover-rate models miss.
practical_implication: Managers should monitor changes in turnover rates, not only average turnover levels, because small changes can be especially consequential in units with lower baseline turnover. The findings imply that firms should pay particular attention to retaining higher-quality employees and to avoiding clustered turnover events. Staffing forecasts should integrate turnover timing and replacement patterns, while also avoiding overstaffing that may erode profit.
limitations: The study uses one Fortune 100 U.S. retail chain with high turnover and relatively low job complexity, so the findings may not generalize to lower-turnover, higher-complexity, or non-retail contexts. The sample covers five quarters and may be affected by seasonality, and the study cannot fully rule out omitted managerial ability despite including a replacement manager quality control. Replacement quality and turnover dispersion are measured with specific operationalizations, and the sample consists exclusively of new hires.
future_research: Future research should directly measure the workload, workflow, routine, climate, and cohesion processes that the paper theorizes but does not observe. Additional studies should test turnover quality and dispersion in other industries, lower-turnover settings, and more complex jobs. Research should also refine turnover dispersion measures and examine the timing of replacement hires relative to turnover events.
abstract: This study builds from context-emergent turnover theory to examine the dynamic properties of turnover rates, including: (a) the changing quality and quantity of the human capital resources that depart, (b) the changing turnover dispersion (i.e., how distributed turnover events are over time), and (c) the changing quality and quantity of replacement hires. We examine these properties using data drawn from a sample of retail employees nested within stores of a prominent U.S. retail chain over five quarters, and show that the turnover rate (level) is conceptually and empirically distinct from turnover rate change, and that the two interact with each other to influence changes in unit performance. We also find that the relationship between turnover rate change and change in unit performance is moderated by both the quality of those who leave as well as turnover dispersion. Overall, we contribute to turnover rate, staffing, and human capital resource literatures by testing core context-emergent turnover theory propositions to show when, why, and how turnover rate change and replacement hires, as part of a holistic human capital resource system, influence unit performance.
apa_citation: Call, M. L., Nyberg, A. J., Ployhart, R. E., & Weekley, J. (2015). The dynamic nature of collective turnover and unit performance: The impact of time, quality, and replacements. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(4), 1208-1232. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0669

title: Learning Through the Distribution of Failures within an Organization: Evidence from Heart Bypass Surgery Performance
methods: Longitudinal panel study of California hospitals offering CABG surgery, using lagged predictors and feasible generalized least squares regression to estimate risk-adjusted mortality rates, with supplemental analyses of hospital responses, surgeon turnover, and IMA graft usage.
industry: Hospitals offering coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.
time_period: 2003 through 2010, organized into four two-year reporting periods; estimation uses lagged predictors from 2005 through 2010.
units: Hospital-period observations.
n_sample: 468 hospital-period observations in the study panel; final FGLS models report N = 315 after lagging and model restrictions.
authors: Desai, V.
theories: attribution theory (Burger, 1981; Ford, 1985); organizational learning theory (Argote & Miron-Spektor, 2011; Levitt & March, 1988)
keywords: CABG surgery; attribution theory; failure concentration; learning from failures; organizational learning; risk-adjusted mortality rate
research_question: The paper asks whether organizations with similar overall failure experience learn differently depending on how failures are distributed internally across individuals or units. It also asks whether organizational size and performance relative to aspiration levels intensify or weaken the relationship between failure concentration and subsequent failure rates.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that concentrated failures make it easier for organizational decision makers to attribute problems to a narrow set of individuals or units. Those attributions encourage localized responses, such as focusing on culpable surgeons, rather than broader investigations of shared routines, procedures, technologies, or structural conditions. Dispersed failures are harder to explain as the fault of one party, so they are more likely to prompt systemwide learning and process change. The panel results support the main prediction that higher failure concentration predicts higher subsequent risk-adjusted mortality; size strengthens this relationship, performance above aspirations weakens it, and performance below aspirations receives only partial support as a weakening condition.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to organizational learning theory by showing that the internal distribution of failure events can matter even when organizations have similar aggregate failure rates. It integrates attribution theory with organizational learning by explaining how decision makers' causal interpretations of where failures occur shape whether learning remains localized or becomes systemwide. It also shifts attention from the benefits of experience to the possibility that some patterns of experience generate overly simple or misleading lessons.
practical_implication: Managers should not assume that repeated failures tied to the same individual or unit are fully explained by that local source. Even when removal, discipline, or retraining seems appropriate, leaders should also examine whether shared procedures, technologies, routines, or organizational conditions contributed to the failures. The hospital evidence suggests that dispersed failures are more likely to trigger procedural change, whereas concentrated failures may encourage turnover without equivalent process improvement.
limitations: The study cannot directly observe managerial attributions, so the proposed attribution mechanism is supported indirectly through archival patterns, anecdotal hospital responses, surgeon turnover, and IMA graft usage. The focal predictor and outcome both concern failure information, which raises the possibility that related information is used on both sides of the model, although the study lags predictors and treats concentration and rate as distinct constructs. The measure of failure location is limited to distribution across surgeons, which is defensible for standardized CABG surgery but less adequate for settings where failures arise through interactions among units, technologies, or complex systems.
future_research: Future research should test similar processes in settings where failures can originate across units, technologies, routines, or more complex interdependencies. Additional work could examine other micro-processes that shape learning from failure and study the consequences, not only the benefits, of organizational experience.
abstract: While research has suggested that organizations can improve by investigating and learning from failures, some work has found that they may generate incorrect lessons or fail to learn. This study addresses the debate by turning attention to the processes that underlie learning, using attribution theory to highlight the way in which decision makers interpret information about where failures occurred or who was involved. This approach is notable because it suggests that different organizations with similar experiences may have quite distinct reactions based on where that experience originates. Specifically, I predict that organizations learn less effectively when their failures are relatively concentrated in origin, meaning that failures typically involve a particular unit or even a specific individual, compared to when failures are more broadly dispersed. I also examine factors that intensify or ameliorate this effect, including an organization's size or its performance relative to aspirations. I test related hypotheses on a panel of hospitals that offered a specific surgical procedure within California from 2003 through 2010.
apa_citation: Desai, V. (2015). Learning through the distribution of failures within an organization: Evidence from heart bypass surgery performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(4), 1032-1050. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0949

title: Motivated to Acquire? The Impact of CEO Regulatory Focus on Firm Acquisitions
methods: Longitudinal archival panel study using LIWC content analysis of CEO shareholder letters to measure promotion and prevention focus, SDC acquisition data, Execucomp compensation data, fixed-effects Poisson models for acquisition counts, and random-effects Tobit models for acquisition value.
industry: Publicly traded corporations from 73 six-digit NAICS industries with varying degrees of volatility.
time_period: Fiscal years 1997-2006; independent and control variables were lagged one year to predict acquisition activity in the following year.
units: Firm-year observations for publicly traded corporations and CEOs' annual shareholder letters.
n_sample: 512 firms and 3,250 observations in the primary analysis; value-of-acquisitions models use 2,522 observations.
authors: Gamache, D. L.; McNamara, G.; Mannor, M. J.; Johnson, R. E.
theories: agency theory (Eisenhardt, 1989); regulatory fit (Higgins, 2000); regulatory focus theory (Higgins, 1997, 1998)
keywords: CEO regulatory focus; firm acquisitions; regulatory fit; regulatory focus theory; stock option pay
research_question: The paper asks whether CEOs' promotion and prevention regulatory focus shape firms' proclivity to undertake acquisitions. It also asks whether stock option pay moderates these regulatory focus-acquisition relationships through regulatory fit.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that promotion-focused CEOs attend more to accomplishment, growth, opportunity search, and the gains available from acquisitions, making them more inclined toward more and larger acquisitions. Prevention-focused CEOs attend more to security, responsibility, possible losses, and due diligence, making them less inclined toward more and larger acquisitions. Stock option pay creates a gain-oriented compensation context that can attenuate prevention-focused CEOs' conservative acquisition tendencies, although the paper does not find that it further amplifies promotion-focused CEOs' acquisition activity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends regulatory focus theory from individual and non-executive leadership outcomes to firm-level strategic actions by showing that CEO regulatory focus predicts acquisition quantity and scale. It contributes to strategic leadership research by treating regulatory focus as a motivation-based CEO attribute distinct from self-concept traits such as hubris or narcissism. It also contributes to executive compensation and acquisition research by showing that stock option pay interacts with CEO prevention focus, qualifying simple incentive-compensation accounts of acquisition risk taking.
practical_implication: CEOs can use awareness of their own regulatory focus to counterbalance tendencies that might push them toward overly aggressive or overly cautious acquisition behavior. Boards may need to provide more cautious oversight for highly promotion-focused CEOs and more encouragement for highly prevention-focused CEOs when risk taking is warranted. The findings also suggest that stock option pay can be a tool for encouraging acquisition risk taking among prevention-focused CEOs, but not necessarily for further increasing the acquisition activity of already promotion-focused CEOs.
limitations: The paper's measure of CEO regulatory focus depends on an unobtrusive content analysis of annual-report letters rather than direct observation of CEO cognition or acquisition decision processes. The authors discuss concerns that shareholder letters may involve public relations staff, although they cite prior evidence and supplemental analyses to support the measure's validity. The empirical scope is acquisitions and stock option pay, so the findings do not by themselves establish whether regulatory focus similarly affects other strategic actions or other compensation designs.
future_research: Future research could examine whether CEO regulatory focus affects acquisition performance and whether promotion- and prevention-focused CEOs pursue different types of acquisitions. The authors also call for studies of other strategic outcomes, including research and development, greenfield investment, capital investment, international expansion, divestitures, and conformity to industry practices. Additional work could test other moderators, such as top management team or board regulatory focus, industry dynamism, munificence, and other combinations of CEO traits and compensation elements.
abstract: Regulatory focus theory proposes that decision making and goal pursuit occur via either a promotion focus (a sensitivity to gains and a desire for advancement and growth) or a prevention focus (a sensitivity to losses and a desire for stability and security). Recent theorizing in strategic management research suggests that there may be important firm-level outcomes influenced by the regulatory focus of top executives. We expand research on regulatory focus theory by testing whether chief executive officers’ (CEOs’) regulatory focus impacts the proclivity of firms to undertake acquisitions. Furthermore, regulatory focus theory suggests that the effects of people’s promotion and prevention foci are magnified when their regulatory focus is congruent with salient situational characteristics, a phenomenon known as regulatory fit. As a test of this idea, we demonstrate how the effects of CEO promotion and prevention foci are differentially impacted by one such characteristic, namely incentive compensation. Our findings indicate that CEO regulatory focus impacts both the quantity and scale of acquisitions undertaken by a firm. We also find some support for our arguments that these relationships are moderated by stock option pay.

title: “I Put in Effort, Therefore I Am Passionate”: Investigating the Path from Effort to Passion in Entrepreneurship
methods: Two-study quantitative design: a weekly field study of entrepreneurs using cross-lagged hierarchical linear modeling, followed by a fully crossed 2 x 2 x 2 laboratory experiment manipulating entrepreneurial effort, new venture progress, and free choice; a supplemental experiment tested reward-contingency as an alternative explanation.
industry: Entrepreneurship in the pre-launch phase; Study 1 entrepreneurs pursued opportunities in retail, manufacturing, services, and counseling/consulting, while Study 2 used business administration students working on entrepreneurial tasks.
country: Germany in Study 1; Singapore in Study 2; the supplemental reward-contingency experiment included students from Singapore and Germany.
time_period: Study 1 followed entrepreneurs weekly over 8 weeks; Study 2 and the supplemental experiment were laboratory sessions with no calendar dates reported.
units: Individual entrepreneurs and undergraduate students working on entrepreneurial venture tasks.
n_sample: Study 1: 54 German entrepreneurs and 341 usable weekly observations; Study 2: 136 undergraduate students; supplemental reward-contingency experiment: 111 students.
authors: Gielnik, M. M.; Spitzmuller, M.; Schmitt, A.; Klemann, D. K.; Frese, M.
theories: self-perception theory (Bem, 1972); theories of self-regulation (Bandura, 1997; Carver & Scheier, 1982; Locke & Latham, 2002); theory of emotion as a feedback system (Baumeister et al., 2007)
keywords: entrepreneurial effort; entrepreneurial passion; free choice; new venture progress; self-perception; self-regulation
research_question: Does entrepreneurial effort predict changes in the positive emotion of entrepreneurial passion, and do new venture progress and free choice explain why and under which conditions effort affects passion?
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that effort can generate passion rather than only result from it. From self-regulation theories, effort helps entrepreneurs make progress and achieve small wins, which increases positive affect. From self-perception theory, people infer their emotions from their own behavior when that behavior is experienced as freely chosen. Thus, effort increases entrepreneurial passion most clearly when it produces new venture progress and is invested under free choice.
theoretical_contribution: The paper reverses the dominant passion-to-effort framing in entrepreneurship by showing that entrepreneurial effort can also be an antecedent of entrepreneurial passion. It contributes to work on antecedents and dynamics of entrepreneurial passion by identifying new venture progress and free choice as mechanisms that help explain the effort-to-passion path. It also extends behavior-emotion and self-regulation perspectives by showing that positive entrepreneurial emotion can be shaped by prior action.
practical_implication: The findings imply that entrepreneurial effort is more likely to sustain passion when it produces visible venture progress and is experienced as freely chosen. The paper does not test intervention designs, so this implication should be read as a boundary on the demonstrated effort-to-passion mechanism rather than direct evidence about a specific training or support program.
limitations: The authors note that Study 1 used a one-week lag and retrospective weekly reports, which may introduce memory bias and may miss finer-grained reciprocal dynamics between effort and passion. Study 2 measured short-term entrepreneurial passion in a laboratory setting, so its connection to enduring passion over longer entrepreneurial processes remains open. The authors also acknowledge the small entrepreneur sample in Study 1 and the use of undergraduate students in Study 2, although they argue that combining a field study with an experiment balances external and internal validity.
future_research: Future studies could use experience sampling to reduce memory bias and examine more fine-grained temporal dynamics between entrepreneurial effort and passion. The authors also suggest distinguishing anticipated entrepreneurial passion from actually experienced passion, because anticipated emotions may motivate future entrepreneurial effort. Growth-curve or similar longitudinal approaches could identify different patterns of growth or decay in entrepreneurial effort and passion across individuals.
abstract: Most theoretical frameworks in entrepreneurship emphasize that entrepreneurial passion drives entrepreneurial effort. We hypothesize that the reverse effect is also true, and investigate changes in passion as an outcome of effort. Based on theories of self-regulation and self-perception, we hypothesize that making new venture progress and free choice are two factors that help to explain why and under which conditions entrepreneurial effort affects entrepreneurial passion. We undertook two studies to investigate our hypotheses. First, we conducted a weekly field study with 54 entrepreneurs who reported entrepreneurial effort and passion over 8 weeks (341 observations). The results showed that entrepreneurial effort predicted changes in entrepreneurial passion. Second, we conducted an experiment (n 5 136) to investigate the effect of effort on passion and the underlying psychological processes in a laboratory setting. The results revealed that new venture progress mediated the effect of entrepreneurial effort on passion, and that free choice moderated the mediated effect. Overall, our findings provide a new theoretical perspective on the relationship between entrepreneurial effort and passion.
apa_citation: Gielnik, M. M., Spitzmuller, M., Schmitt, A., Klemann, D. K., & Frese, M. (2015). "I put in effort, therefore I am passionate": Investigating the path from effort to passion in entrepreneurship. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(4), 1012-1031. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0727

title: Network Defense: Pruning, Grafting, and Closing to Prevent Leakage of Strategic Knowledge to Rivals
methods: Empirical quantitative study using longitudinal German board-interlock and Eastern European investment data from 1990 to 2003. The dyadic tie-termination and tie-formation analyses use fixed-effects logit models with robust standard errors; the ego-network closure analysis uses system generalized method-of-moments dynamic panel estimation.
industry: Large publicly traded German corporations listed in the DAX 100, with rivalry measured using primary six-digit GICS industry codes.
country: Germany, with firms' strategic experience measured through foreign direct investment in former Warsaw Pact countries.
units: Firm-partner dyads for tie termination and formation; focal firms' ego networks for closure.
n_sample: 71 German firms, with 4,583 firm-partner years for tie termination models, 5,626 firm-partner years for tie formation models, and 803 firm-years for closure models.
authors: Hernandez, E.; Sanders, W. G.; Tuschke, A.
theories: behavioral theory of the firm; knowledge-based theory of the firm; social network theory
keywords: board interlocks; indirectly connected rivals; knowledge spillover; network closing; network grafting; network pruning; strategic knowledge
research_question: The paper asks how firms protect strategic knowledge from leaking to indirectly connected rivals through interorganizational networks. It examines whether firms with more strategic experience respond to indirect competitor links by terminating existing board interlocks, avoiding new risky interlocks, and increasing ego-network closure.
mechanism_summary: The central mechanism is defensive network adaptation. Indirect links to rivals create extra-dyadic leakage risk because partners can transmit strategically sensitive knowledge beyond the focal dyad. As firms accumulate strategically valuable experience, the cost of leakage rises, making them more likely to prune existing risky ties, graft by forming safer new ties, and close their networks to increase monitoring and circumscribe information flows.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to network and strategy research by identifying indirect ties to rivals as a distinct source of knowledge-spillover risk, not merely a channel for learning or intelligence. It shows that dyadic safeguards such as legal protections, trust, and embeddedness may be insufficient for extra-dyadic leakage risks. It also offers a defensive explanation for network evolution: firms may close structural holes and alter network composition to preserve strategic knowledge rather than only to access resources.
practical_implication: The findings imply that firms should assess not only direct partners but also the second-order competitor paths those partners create. In board networks and other interorganizational settings, firms may need to manage tie termination, tie formation, and network closure as knowledge-protection tools when strategic knowledge becomes competitively sensitive.
limitations: The authors do not directly observe firms' motives for dissolving or forming board ties, nor the exact strength and content of knowledge exchanged through those ties, so the design cannot conclusively prove the proposed knowledge-leakage mechanism. The study is also limited by its focus on German board interlocks, projection of a two-mode director-firm network into an interfirm network, and available measures of Eastern European investment experience.
future_research: The paper suggests studying whether direct and indirect links to rivals create different leakage risks in other networks, such as alliances, where direct competitor ties are more common. It also calls for research on different path lengths to rivals, the possible intelligence benefits of indirect competitor links, and heterogeneity in the size and mode of investments that shape perceived leakage threats.
abstract: We explore how firms protect themselves from the risks of knowledge spillover to indirectly connected rivals in a network of interorganizational ties. We argue that the safeguards to limit opportunistic behavior by directly linked firms in a dyad, which have been the focus of extant research, are insufficient to overcome extra-dyadic leakage risks. Instead, firms terminate or avoid ties that expose their knowledge to indirectly linked rivals (“pruning” and “grafting”) and embed themselves in dense networks (“closing”) to prevent strategic knowledge spillover. Through a longitudinal study of German board interlocks during 1990–2003, we find that firms are more likely to prune, graft, and close their networks as they accumulate strategic knowledge and as the firms to which they are interlocked increasingly generate indirect ties to competitors, even when controlling for dyadic safeguards discussed by prior research. We capture strategic knowledge by tracking firms’ experience in the former Warsaw Pact countries from immediately after the sudden fall of communism in 1990 until 2003. The study introduces indirect links to rivals as a source of knowledge spillover in networks, shows how firms deal with extra-dyadic risks, and provides a defensive explanation for the evolution of network composition and structure.

title: Making a Difference in the Teamwork: Linking Team Prosocial Motivation to Team Processes and Effectiveness
methods: Two-study quantitative design: Study 1 used three-source, four-wave field data from work teams and multilevel structural equation modeling with bootstrapped indirect effects; Study 2 used a fully crossed 2 x 2 laboratory experiment manipulating team prosocial motivation and task interdependence, again analyzed with MSEM and bootstrapped indirect and conditional indirect effects.
industry: Study 1: traditional work teams from diverse industries including construction, information technology, legal services, marketing, accounting, and customer services; Study 2: undergraduate business students in a consulting-task laboratory setting
country: Study 1: United States and China; Study 2: Midwestern United States university
time_period: Study 1 data collected at four time points: T1, T2 one month after T1, T3 three months after T1, and T4 one year after T1; Study 2 occurred in a laboratory session
units: Work teams, team members, upper-level managers, HR records, and four-person student consulting teams
n_sample: Study 1: 310 individual members in 67 work teams and 24 upper-level managers; Study 2: 496 undergraduate business students assigned to 124 four-person teams
authors: Hu, Jia; Liden, Robert C.
theories: motivated information processing perspective (De Dreu & Carnevale, 2003); prosocial motivation (Grant, 2007); team effectiveness theory (Hackman, 1987)
keywords: task interdependence; team OCB; team cooperation; team effectiveness; team performance; team prosocial motivation; team viability; team voluntary turnover
research_question: How does team prosocial motivation relate to team effectiveness, and through which team processes are these effects realized? The paper also asks when these indirect relationships are stronger or weaker, focusing on task interdependence as the team-context condition.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that teams sharing a desire to benefit others are more willing to cooperate, share ideas, reduce social loafing, and coordinate work toward collective outputs. This task-driven cooperation transmits team prosocial motivation into higher team performance and OCB. In parallel, team prosocial motivation can build stronger emotional ties and team viability, which mainly explains lower team voluntary turnover. Task interdependence strengthens these pathways because highly interdependent work gives prosocially motivated members more opportunity to interact, coordinate, and translate prosocial purpose into team processes.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends prosocial motivation from the individual level to the team level by defining team prosocial motivation as a shared collective belief about working to benefit others. It contributes to team effectiveness theory by showing that task-oriented cooperation and affect-based viability are distinct mediating processes linking team motivation to different team outcomes. It also identifies task interdependence as a boundary condition that determines when team prosocial motivation is more likely to improve effectiveness.
practical_implication: Managers should cultivate team prosocial motivation when team outcomes depend on coordinated action, because concern for others can support smoother cooperation, stronger interpersonal ties, higher performance, more OCB, and lower voluntary turnover. The paper suggests combining prosocial motivation with work designs that create real task interdependence; high prosocial motivation without interdependence gives members fewer opportunities to translate their motives into effective teamwork. Interventions such as increasing beneficiary contact, modeling prosocial behavior, and selecting or introducing members with high prosocial motivation may help create a prosocial team culture.
limitations: Study 1 is time-lagged but not experimental, so reverse causality and omitted organizational or team-level factors remain possible. Study 2 improves causal inference but uses temporary undergraduate student teams in a laboratory task, which differs from permanent work teams in organizations. The authors also note some inconsistencies across the studies, especially in whether mediation is full or partial for team OCB and team voluntary turnover.
future_research: Future research should examine additional task-based and affect-based mechanisms, such as whether a prosocial motivation climate creates positive affective tone or work engagement that improves team outcomes. The paper also calls for research on other boundary conditions, including opportunities for team members to contact beneficiaries. Further studies could test whether task processes and affective processes differ systematically in predicting performance, OCB, and turnover across team contexts.
abstract: Although the importance of team motivation has been increasingly emphasized, few studies have focused on prosocial motivation. Integrating theories on team effectiveness with prosocial motivation, we propose a theoretical model that links team prosocial motivation to team effectiveness as mediated by team processes. Team process is captured through the task-driven process of team cooperation and the affect-based team viability, and team effectiveness is operationalized as team performance, team organizational citizenship behavior (OCB), and team voluntary turnover. The model is tested in Study 1, a field study with three-source data collected from 310 members of 67 work teams over four time periods, and Study 2, a laboratory experiment with 124 four-person teams in which team prosocial motivation is manipulated. In Studies 1 and 2, we find support for indirect effects of team prosocial motivation on team performance and team OCB through the mediating role of team cooperation. Team voluntary turnover is indirectly affected by team prosocial motivation through team viability. Furthermore, in both studies the indirect effects of team prosocial motivation on team performance and team OCB through team cooperation and on team voluntary turnover through team viability are stronger when the nature of the teams’ work requires greater task interdependence.
apa_citation: Hu, J., & Liden, R. C. (2015). Making a difference in the teamwork: Linking team prosocial motivation to team processes and effectiveness. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(4), 1102-1127. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.1142
