title: When Can Women Close the Gap? A Meta-Analytic Test of Sex Differences in Performance and Rewards
methods: Meta-analysis of individual-level sex differences in performance evaluations and organizational rewards, using random-effects meta-analytic regression, Monte Carlo permutation tests, a semipartial correlation mediation test, and exploratory crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis.
industry: Field studies across varied work settings and industries, including examples from IT, healthcare, utilities, manufacturing, retail banking, automotive retail, science and engineering, and professional services.
country: Country coverage is not fully reported for all primary studies; externally matched occupation, industry, and job-context analyses used U.S.-based samples and excluded non-U.S. samples.
time_period: Primary studies conducted between 1985 and 2013.
units: Effect sizes from primary field studies reporting individual-level effects of gender on performance evaluations or organizational rewards.
n_sample: 190 effect sizes and 474,732 individuals from 142 studies.
authors: Joshi, A.; Son, J.; Roh, H.
theories: institutional and structural perspectives on gender inequality; macro and micro domains in gender research; role congruity theory; social dominance theory
keywords: gender inequality; meta-analysis; organizational rewards; performance evaluations; sex differences
research_question: The paper asks when women can close the gap in workplace performance evaluations and organizational rewards. It tests whether occupation-, industry-, and job-level attributes mitigate or exacerbate sex differences in performance evaluations, salary, bonuses, and promotions.
mechanism_summary: The paper argues that gender inequality is shaped by cross-level work contexts rather than only by individual human capital or overt discrimination. Male-dominated occupations and complex jobs strengthen gendered status cues, ambiguous evaluation criteria, and discretionary reward allocation, while prestigious occupations can operate as hierarchy-enhancing settings in which women perform equally but receive lower rewards. Industries with more women in executive or senior managerial roles provide a contrasting context, because greater representation and scrutiny can reduce or reverse sex differences in both performance evaluations and rewards.
theoretical_contribution: The study bridges macro institutional and structural perspectives on gender inequality with micro sociopsychological perspectives on gender bias. Its central contribution is showing that sex differences in rewards are much larger than sex differences in performance evaluations and are not explained by performance gaps, making reward allocation a distinct site of gender inequality. It also adds a configurational account of how occupation, industry, and job attributes jointly produce settings where men or women receive higher evaluations and rewards.
practical_implication: The paper recommends that diversity management focus on accountability structures in performance management and compensation, job designs that reduce inequitable discretion in complex work, and industry-wide mentoring networks for women. It argues that scrutiny by neutral observers or advisors can help move calibration and reward-allocation discussions away from stereotypes and toward performance-relevant information.
limitations: The authors note that the meta-regression analyses used smaller samples than the overall meta-analysis because some primary studies lacked information needed to code external context variables. They could not test a full model with all key and control variables simultaneously, incorporate consistent organization-level variables such as culture or HR policies, include fine-grained human-capital controls, or isolate selection effects into jobs and occupations. They also acknowledge possible file-drawer bias for null or politically uncomfortable gender findings.
future_research: The paper calls for research on how high-involvement performance management and compensation practices affect gender inequality in male-dominated versus gender-integrated settings. It also proposes work on whether promotion practices that avoid zero-sum choices reduce hierarchy-enhancing reward allocation, how job complexity shapes social comparison and scrutiny, and how organizational attributes operate within broader occupational or industry contexts. Future meta-analyses could compare selection-biased and selection-corrected estimates and extend the argument to contextual performance, creativity, turnover, and specific reward types.
abstract: Drawing on macro and micro domains in gender research, we meta-analytically test whether occupation-, industry-, and job-level factors mitigate or exacerbate differences in performance evaluations (k 5 93; n 5 95,882) and rewards (k 5 97; n 5 378,850) between men and women. Based on studies conducted across a variety of work settings and spanning nearly 30 years, we found that the sex differences in rewards (d 5 .56) (including salary, bonuses, and promotions) were 14 times larger than sex differences in performance evaluations (d 5 .04), and that differences in performance evaluations did not explain reward differences between men and women. The percentage of men in an occupation and the complexity of jobs performed by employees enhanced the male– female gap in performance and rewards. In highly prestigious occupations, women performed equally, but were rewarded significantly lower than men. Only a higher representation of female executives at the industry level enabled women to reverse the gender gap in rewards and performance evaluations. Our configurational analysis also revealed that some occupation-, industry-, and job-level attributes of the work context jointly contributed to differences in rewards and performance evaluations.
apa_citation: Joshi, A., Son, J., & Roh, H. (2015). When can women close the gap? A meta-analytic test of sex differences in performance and rewards. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(5), 1516-1545. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0721

title: All Aspirations are not Created Equal: The Differential Effects of Historical and Social Aspirations on Acquisition Behavior
methods: Empirical quantitative archival study using event history analysis and piecewise exponential models of repeat acquisitions; acquisition performance is measured with acquirer cumulative abnormal returns, split around historical and social aspiration levels, with interactions for prior acquisition performance variability.
industry: U.S. commercial banking industry; horizontal acquisitions among commercial banking institutions, including banks, thrifts, savings banks, and bank holding companies.
units: Publicly traded commercial banking institutions, horizontal acquisitions, and yearly event-history spells.
n_sample: 3,010 acquisitions made by 642 publicly traded banks, transformed into 8,799 yearly spells.
authors: Kim, J.-Y. (J.); Finkelstein, S.; Haleblian, J. (J.)
theories: aspiration-level theory; behavioral theory of the firm (Cyert & March, 1963); performance feedback theory
keywords: U.S. commercial banking industry; acquisition behavior; acquisition performance variability; historical aspirations; performance aspirations; performance feedback; social aspirations
research_question: The paper asks whether historical and social aspiration levels produce different effects on firms' subsequent acquisition behavior. It also asks how variability in prior acquisition performance changes the relationship between acquisition performance relative to aspirations and the probability of making another acquisition.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an interpretation-based performance feedback process. Historical aspirations compare current acquisition performance with the firm's own acquisition record, making capability assessments more internally grounded and encouraging caution when performance greatly exceeds prior standards. Social aspirations compare performance with other banks in the same core geographic market; because peer performance is more ambiguous, managers are more likely to interpret above-social-aspiration performance as evidence of their own capability and continue acquiring. High prior performance variability makes performance signals less reliable, intensifying acquisition persistence below aspirations but attenuating acquisition persistence above aspirations.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends behavioral theory of the firm and performance feedback research by showing that historical and social aspirations are not interchangeable reference points. It theorizes and tests why aspiration sources differ in the information they encode and in the cognitive and organizational processes through which managers interpret them. It also adds performance variability as a moderator of feedback-based learning, showing how variability can change whether managers treat performance shortfalls or successes as reliable signals for future acquisition behavior.
practical_implication: Managers should not treat acquisition performance feedback as a simple success-or-failure signal. The same market reaction to a deal can motivate different future acquisition behavior depending on whether managers compare it with the firm's own history or with peer banks. Acquisition decision makers should also account for the variability of prior deal performance, because highly variable records can make both unusually good and unusually poor outcomes less diagnostic of underlying acquisition capability.
limitations: The authors note that omitted variables may affect both acquisition performance and subsequent acquisition likelihood, even though they include extensive controls and year fixed effects. The study examines only horizontal acquisitions in U.S. commercial banking, so the findings may not hold for other acquisition types, industries, or institutional settings. It also proposes psychological processes such as self-enhancement and attention to variability but does not directly test those processes.
future_research: Future research could examine when managers attend more to historical aspirations, social aspirations, absolute performance, relative performance, or performance variability. Studies could broaden the acquisition context beyond horizontal banking acquisitions and test whether the findings apply to different acquisition types. Laboratory or richer behavioral studies could isolate the causal psychological processes linking aspiration feedback, performance variability, and subsequent strategic action, and future acquisition work could model aspirations and expectations together.
abstract: Research on performance aspirations has tended to assume that historical and social aspirations work in parallel and influence strategic behavior in a similar manner. We posit that these two distinct modes of performance comparison in fact lead to dissimilar firm behavior. We also explore how variability in prior acquisition performance influences the relationship between aspiration levels and subsequent strategic behavior. We examine our questions in the context of mergers and acquisitions within the U.S. commercial banking industry from 1988 to 2005. Consistent with our opening prediction, we find that firms’ acquisition behavior varies significantly depending on whether historical or social comparisons are used. We also find that high variability in the previous acquisition performance of a firm intensifies the relationship between acquisition performance relative to aspirations and the probability of the firm making acquisitions below historical and social aspirations, but attenuates the relationship above such aspirations.

title: Status and Corporate Illegality: Illegal Loan Recovery Practices of Commercial Banks in India
methods: Longitudinal panel study of commercial banks in India using Banking Ombudsman complaint data, Prowess preferred-banker affiliation networks, RBI financial data, and Karmayog CSR ratings; hypotheses are tested with GEE negative binomial models with AR1 error structure and robustness checks for endogeneity and reporting bias.
industry: Commercial banking.
time_period: 2004-2009; complaints span 2005-2009 and independent variables are observed from 2004-2008.
units: Commercial bank-year observations.
n_sample: 82 commercial banks and 396 bank-year observations.
authors: Krishnan, R.; Kozhikode, R. K.
theories: behavioral theory of the firm (Cyert & March, 1963); loss aversion (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979); status theory (Podolny, 1994, 2005; Phillips & Zuckerman, 2001)
keywords: commercial banks; corporate illegality; financial asset quality; illegal loan recovery practices; reputation for integrity; status theory
research_question: The paper asks why high-status organizations, which status theory often treats as relatively secure, engage in corporate illegality. It examines whether insecurity about meeting associates' expectations for quality explains illegal loan recovery practices among commercial banks in India, and whether associates' integrity expectations weaken that tendency.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that high-status banks face strong expectations to maintain financial asset quality. When their asset quality deteriorates relative to their own past performance or their status peers, potential status loss creates insecurity and makes illegal recovery practices more attractive as a way to reduce bad assets. The results show a positive status-illegality relationship, stronger effects when financial asset quality declines, and weaker effects when associated BSE500 firms place greater emphasis on CSR and integrity.
theoretical_contribution: The study challenges the status-theory assumption that high-status organizations are relatively secure once they occupy privileged positions. It shows that reputation for quality remains consequential for high-status organizations because associates can evaluate whether the organization continues to meet quality expectations. It also extends status and reputation research by showing that affiliates' integrity expectations can condition whether high-status organizations respond to status insecurity through illegal action.
practical_implication: The findings imply that high-status banks should not be assumed to be less likely to engage in illegal practices. High-status banks facing declining asset quality can face stronger pressure to preserve status, increasing misconduct risk. The paper also suggests that associates with strong CSR and integrity expectations can deter illegality by making unethical means more reputationally costly.
limitations: The study focuses on commercial banks in India, where financial asset quality is a salient quality signal and illegal loan recovery practices are observable through Banking Ombudsman complaints. The authors note that financial asset quality was appropriate in this context, but other industries may evaluate quality through different attributes. The evidence also relies on complaint data, which the paper treats carefully through robustness checks but cannot make immune to all underreporting concerns.
future_research: Future research should examine how high-status organizations manage conflicting role expectations when reputation for quality and reputation for integrity point in different behavioral directions. The paper calls for more work on conditions, beyond peers' integrity concerns, that deter high-status organizations from using illegality to protect status. It also suggests extending the argument to other industries where different quality dimensions, such as product quality, may drive status insecurity.
abstract: Why might high-status organizations, presumably secure in their positions, resort to illegality? This study considers the possibility that status theory might have overestimated the relative security of high-status organizations. We examine our theory that an inability to meet associates' expectations about quality might be the source of insecurity, using data on the illegal loan recovery practices employed by commercial banks in India between 2005 and 2009. High-status banks were found to be particularly likely to engage in illegal recovery practices. This was especially true when a high-status bank had experienced a decline in its financial asset quality or had fallen behind the financial asset quality of its peers. However, when a bank's business partners placed greater emphasis on corporate social responsibility (CSR), it minimized a bank's tendency to resort to illegal loan recovery practices.

title: Leadership Over-Emergence in Self-Managing Teams: The Role of Gender and Countervailing Biases
methods: Longitudinal quantitative field study of MBA students in self-managing teams; peer ratings were collected across three time periods and hypotheses were tested with multilevel multivariate analyses in Mplus using a cluster approach.
industry: Full-time MBA program and self-managing student teams.
time_period: Seven months, with three survey waves spanning pre-team measurement, behavior ratings after approximately six weeks, and leadership ratings approximately four months later.
units: MBA students nested in 5-person self-managing teams.
n_sample: 181 students; hypothesis models report Level 1 n = 177 and 37 clusters.
authors: Lanaj, K.; Hollenbeck, J. R.
theories: Expectancy Violation Theory (Jussim et al., 1987); Gender Role Theory (Eagly, 1987; Eagly & Karau, 1991)
keywords: Expectancy Violation Theory; Gender Role Theory; countervailing bias; gender; leadership effectiveness; leadership emergence; leadership over-emergence; self-managing teams
research_question: The paper asks when leadership emergence exceeds leadership effectiveness in self-managing teams and whether gender helps explain that mismatch. It specifically examines whether men over-emerge because gender stereotypes favor men as leaders, and whether women over-emerge when they perform agentic task and boundary-spanning behaviors that violate gendered expectations.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a perceptual-bias process in which leadership emergence and leadership effectiveness are related but distinct judgments. Gender Role Theory predicts that men receive more emergence credit than effectiveness credit because male gender roles are more congruent with leader roles. Expectancy Violation Theory predicts a countervailing bias: women who engage in agentic task and boundary spanning behaviors receive more emergence credit than equivalent men, while those behaviors do not produce a corresponding gender-contingent difference in effectiveness. Social behaviors increased effectiveness but did not produce the predicted male over-emergence effect.
theoretical_contribution: The study introduces leadership over-emergence as a distinct problem in self-managing teams: the person seen as most leaderlike may not be the person judged most effective. It contributes to Gender Role Theory by showing that men over-emerge under baseline conditions, while also showing that agentic women can receive a countervailing emergence advantage. It contributes to Expectancy Violation Theory by supporting the counter-stereotypic benefit for agentic women but not the predicted gender-neutral benefit for men who perform communal social behaviors.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that organizations relying on self-managing teams should not assume informal leadership emergence identifies the most effective leader. Teams may need 360-degree feedback, after-action reviews, or rotational leadership schemes to surface discrepancies between emergence and effectiveness. For individuals, especially women seeking to emerge as leaders in small groups, task and boundary-spanning behaviors may increase emergence, although the authors emphasize that this is not a structural solution to gender stereotypes.
limitations: Leadership emergence was measured through subjective perceptions, which may be more vulnerable to bias than objective indicators such as coded video behavior. Gender was also confounded with minority status because the MBA sample contained more men than women. The study did not measure likeability or other indicators of social backlash, and it did not examine other possible predictors such as cognitive ability or prior leadership experience.
future_research: Future research should develop more objective and direct measures of leadership over-emergence and examine whether agentic and social behaviors matter differently across stages of group development. The authors also call for research on leadership under-emergence, male- versus female-dominated group composition, and whether other-advocating versus self-oriented agentic behavior produces different over-emergence patterns. Additional work should test whether agentic women who over-emerge are liked less than men who perform the same behaviors.
abstract: We examine leadership over-emergence, defined as instances when the level of one’s leadership emergence is higher than the level of one’s leadership effectiveness, in a sample of intact self-managing teams who worked together for a period of seven months. We draw from Gender Role Theory and Expectancy Violation Theory to examine the role of gender in predicting leadership over-emergence. Building on arguments from Gender Role Theory, we find that all else equal, men over-emerge as leaders. However, Expectancy Violation Theory suggests that women are likely to benefit from a countervailing bias. Specifically, women are attributed with higher levels of leadership emergence than men when they engage in agentic leadership behaviors—even if the level of the behaviors exhibited by men is exactly the same. Because the impact of these behaviors on leadership effectiveness is not contingent on gender, however, women who engage in more task behaviors and boundary spanning behaviors in self-managing teams also over-emerge as leaders. We discuss the implications of this study for Gender Role Theory and Expectancy Violation Theory, along with practical implications for managing the problem of leadership over-emergence in work groups.

title: Folding Under Pressure or Rising to the Occasion? Perceived Time Pressure and the Moderating Role of Team Temporal Leadership
methods: Field survey of software project teams with repeated team-member measures and leader-rated project performance; regression, moderated regression, moderated-mediation, and instantaneous indirect-effect analyses tested the nonlinear mediated effect of perceived time pressure.
industry: Customized software development project work.
time_period: Projects were launched around the same time and expected to be completed in two months; time pressure and temporal leadership were measured at the project midpoint, team processes two weeks later, and performance after client delivery.
units: Software project teams and their members.
n_sample: 1,115 employees in 111 project teams.
authors: Maruping, L. M.; Venkatesh, V.; Thatcher, S. M. B.; Patel, P. C.
theories: activation theory (Gardner, 1990); challenge-hindrance stressor framework (LePine et al., 2005); temporal leadership theory (Mohammed & Nadkarni, 2011)
keywords: Team temporal leadership; moderated mediation; perceived time pressure; project teams; team performance; team processes
research_question: The paper asks when perceived time pressure helps rather than harms project team performance. It specifically examines whether team processes mediate the nonlinear relationship between perceived time pressure and team performance, and whether team temporal leadership changes that mediated relationship.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is that time pressure changes team members' engagement in interdependent task-management processes. At low to intermediate levels, time pressure can activate teams to plan, coordinate, monitor progress, and manage interpersonal demands; at higher levels, especially under weak temporal leadership, teams may abandon those processes and focus narrowly on task completion. Strong team temporal leadership shifts this pattern by directing attention to deadlines, sequencing, milestones, and temporal resources, so the indirect effect of time pressure through team processes is positive rather than harmful.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances time-pressure theory by showing that team-level perceived time pressure has nonlinear effects rather than a uniformly positive or negative relationship with performance. It integrates time-pressure research with temporal leadership theory by identifying team temporal leadership as a condition that shapes whether time pressure is translated into effective team processes. It also broadens team-process theory by treating transition, action, and interpersonal processes as the pathway through which temporal context affects project performance.
practical_implication: Managers should direct teams' attention to temporal constraints early enough for teams to respond with planning, coordination, and prioritization rather than panic. The findings suggest that temporal leadership behaviors such as setting interim milestones, synchronizing tasks, pacing work, and allocating time for contingencies can help teams continue using effective processes under deadline pressure. Organizations should also build teams' temporal-management capability before deadlines become acute.
limitations: The study focuses on perceived rather than actual time pressure, so the findings may not transfer directly to settings where objective time constraints are experimentally manipulated. The field design also leaves some possibility of reverse causality, including the possibility that temporal leadership changes perceived time pressure rather than only shaping responses to it. The authors note that the software development context may explain why strong temporal leadership allowed teams to benefit even under high time pressure.
future_research: Future research should examine whether actual time pressure has similar effects on team processes as a function of team temporal leadership.
abstract: “Team temporal leadership” orients teams toward managing the time-related aspects of their work. We examine how perceived time pressure affects team processes and subsequent performance under weak versus strong team temporal leadership. The results of our field study of 111 project teams show that the mediated relationship between perceived time pressure and team performance is non-linear. Moreover, this non-linear mediated relationship is moderated by team temporal leadership such that, under strong team temporal leadership, the indirect effect of perceived time pressure on team performance is mostly positive, while, under conditions of weak team temporal leadership, the indirect effect is positive at low levels of perceived time pressure and negative at intermediate to high levels. Implications for current and future time pressure research are also discussed.
apa_citation: Maruping, L. M., Venkatesh, V., Thatcher, S. M. B., & Patel, P. C. (2015). Folding under pressure or rising to the occasion? Perceived time pressure and the moderating role of team temporal leadership. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(5), 1313-1333. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0468

title: Women on Boards and Firm Financial Performance: A Meta-Analysis
methods: Quantitative meta-analysis of 140 studies on female board representation, firm financial performance, and board activities. The authors coded firm-level studies, country-level shareholder protection and gender parity moderators, effect sizes, study characteristics, and board activity measures, then used random-effects meta-analysis and weighted least squares meta-regression.
industry: Firm-level studies of corporate boards across varied industry sectors; studies using nonprofit samples were excluded.
country: Firms in 35 countries across five continents.
time_period: Studies published or completed by May 2014; journal hand searches covered January 1989 through May 2014.
units: Independent samples/effect sizes from firm-level studies of female board representation, firm financial performance, and board activities.
n_sample: 140 studies, 144 independent samples, and a combined sample size of 90,070 firms.
authors: Post, C.; Byron, K.
theories: agency theory; upper echelons theory
keywords: accounting returns; board monitoring; board strategy involvement; female board representation; firm financial performance; gender parity; market performance; meta-analysis; shareholder protections; women on boards
research_question: The paper asks whether female board representation is related to firm financial performance and whether legal/regulatory and socio-cultural national contexts explain mixed findings in the literature. It also asks whether female board representation is related to board monitoring and strategy involvement as more proximal board activities.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on upper echelons theory, the paper argues that female directors may bring different cognitive frames, experiences, knowledge, and values to board decision making. These differences can expand the information considered by boards, increase deliberativeness, and support monitoring and strategy involvement. The relationships are contingent: shareholder protections may motivate boards to leverage diverse perspectives, while gender parity may affect the legitimacy and market interpretation of female board representation.
theoretical_contribution: The study develops and tests a contingency model of female board representation and firm financial performance. It contributes to women-on-boards and corporate governance research by distinguishing accounting returns from market performance, identifying national shareholder protections and gender parity as moderators, and showing that female board representation relates positively to board monitoring and strategy involvement. The paper also advances upper echelons theory by treating national context as a condition under which board gender diversity is more or less likely to shape firm outcomes.
practical_implication: The paper argues that board gender diversity is not a simple numbers game. For female directors to be associated with higher accounting returns, boards need a culture in which dissenting voices are heard and considered. It also suggests that firms in contexts with limited supplies of potential female directors should diversify boards in ways that capture relevant experiences, knowledge, and values, and that the market value of gender-diverse boards may depend on broader socio-cultural gender parity.
limitations: The meta-analysis is constrained by the available primary studies and by uneven reporting of board-, firm-, and industry-level moderators. The authors rely on country-level shareholder protection and gender parity because other plausible moderators were not reported often enough for meta-analysis. They also note that they cannot claim causality because reverse causality and omitted variables remain difficult to eliminate in a meta-analysis of primary studies.
future_research: The paper calls for research on why women on boards affect some performance indicators but not others, including operational performance, growth, and other theoretically relevant outcomes. It also encourages studies of additional moderators such as environmental uncertainty, munificence, ownership, consumer proximity, industry context, and critical mass. Future work should examine whether board monitoring, strategy involvement, advice to the CEO, and resource linkages mediate the relationship between female board representation and firm performance.
abstract: Despite a large body of literature examining the relationship between women on boards and firm financial performance, the evidence is mixed. To reconcile the conflicting results, we statistically combine the results from 140 studies and examine whether these results vary by firms’ legal/regulatory and socio-cultural contexts. We find that female board representation is positively related to accounting returns and that this relationship is more positive in countries with stronger shareholder protections—perhaps because shareholder protections motivate boards to use the different knowledge, experience, and values that each member brings. We also find that, although the relationship between female board representation and market performance is near zero the relationship is positive in countries with greater gender parity (and negative in countries with low gender parity)—perhaps because societal gender differences in human capital may influence investors’ evaluations of the future earning potential of firms that have more female directors. Lastly, we find that female board representation is positively related to boards’ two primary responsibilities: monitoring and strategy involvement. For both firm financial performance and board activities, we find mean effect sizes comparable to those found in meta-analyses of other aspects of board composition. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of our findings.
apa_citation: Post, C., & Byron, K. (2015). Women on boards and firm financial performance: A meta-analysis. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(5), 1546-1571. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0319

title: Strategic Responses to FDI in Emerging Markets: Are Core Members More Responsive than Peripheral Members of Business Groups?
methods: Empirical quantitative archival panel study of Indian public limited companies using Prowess, CapEx, and Bombay Stock Exchange Directors Database data. The authors estimate logistic regressions of local firm expansion on MNE investment announcements and interactions with business group affiliation, group professionalization, group density, promoter ownership, control-cash flow rights wedge, and group affiliate centrality; they report negative binomial, first-entry, mixed-effects, penalized-likelihood, rare-event logit, and alternative dependent-variable robustness checks.
industry: 1,118 unique industries in India, classified at the most detailed available CMIE industry level.
units: Firm-industry-year observations for public limited Indian companies, excluding foreign-owned and government-owned firms.
n_sample: 3,531 public limited companies; 1,433 business group members affiliated with 435 groups and 2,098 stand-alone firms; 6,414 unique firm-industry observations each year and 70,826 observations in the main full-sample models.
authors: Ayyagari, M.; Dau, L. A.; Spencer, J. W.
theories: business group theory; competitive dynamics awareness-motivation-capability framework (Chen, 1996; Chen et al., 2007); identity domain (Livengood & Reger, 2010)
keywords: business groups; directorship network; emerging markets; foreign direct investment; identity domain; investment announcements; strategic responses
research_question: The paper asks whether local emerging-market firms respond to MNE investment announcements by announcing expansions of their own, and whether that response differs between stand-alone firms and business group affiliates. It further asks whether a business group's professionalization, directorship-network density, and a member firm's prominence within the group shape its responsiveness to FDI threats.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a competitive-response process in which MNE investment creates a strategic threat, and local firms differ in their awareness of the threat, motivation to respond, and capability to expand. Business group affiliation can supply resources and coordination, but group heterogeneity matters: professionally managed groups and central member firms are more likely to support expansion responses, while dense interlocks and larger control-cash flow wedges can dampen response. The empirical results support stronger responsiveness among group affiliates, professionally managed groups, and central group members, but do not support promoter ownership and run counter to the predicted positive role of group density.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to FDI spillover research by shifting attention from longer-run productivity outcomes to local firms' immediate strategic responses to MNE investment announcements. It links spillover research with competitive dynamics and business group theory, showing that the governance and relational structure of local firms helps explain heterogeneous responses to FDI in emerging markets. It also extends the identity-domain concept to business groups by arguing and showing that core group members, especially those central in directorship networks, are more responsive than peripheral members.
practical_implication: For managers of emerging-market firms, the findings imply that response to foreign entry depends not only on firm-level resources but also on the firm's position in a wider business group. Business group leaders should recognize that professional management and the allocation of attention and resources to core member firms can shape whether affiliates respond assertively to MNE threats. Policy makers seeking to understand FDI effects should expect heterogeneous local responses rather than assuming a uniform productivity or crowding-out effect.
limitations: The authors note that the data do not allow them to identify entry deterrence scenarios in which aggressive pre-positioning by incumbent firms deters MNE investment altogether. Their dependent variable captures announced expansion projects, so it may miss other strategic responses, although robustness tests using R&D and marketing expenses did not show evidence of those alternatives. The setting is Indian public limited companies during 1995-2010, so the results may not generalize to private firms, other emerging economies, or later institutional periods without further evidence.
future_research: The paper calls for research on whether increasingly capable emerging-market firms respond to MNE entry at home by making strategic moves in other markets where the MNE operates. It also suggests examining how relational embeddedness within business groups shapes such global strategic interaction. Future work could further investigate entry deterrence and compare how different emerging-market governance structures condition local firm responses to FDI.
abstract: With increasing foreign direct investment (FDI) into emerging markets, local firms must make critical strategic decisions in order to remain competitive. When faced with multinational enterprises (MNEs) announcing FDI into their industry, local firms can expand operations and challenge the MNE head on, or refrain from responding directly, effectively ceding market share to the MNE investor. We propose that local firms’ responses are shaped by their affiliation with, and position in, a business group. Using data on investment announcements by MNEs and local firms in India from 1995 to 2010, we find that firms that are affiliated with business groups tend to be more sensitive to MNE investment announcements than are stand-alone firms. More professionally managed group affiliate firms are more likely to respond to MNE threats. Furthermore, firms that are in the group’s identity domain—that is, those holding more prominent positions within their group (especially as measured by centrality in the group’s directorship network)—appear more likely to respond to MNE investment announcements. Overall, our results highlight the importance of business group affiliation in examining FDI spillovers in emerging markets.
apa_citation: Ayyagari, M., Dau, L. A., & Spencer, J. W. (2015). Strategic responses to FDI in emerging markets: Are core members more responsive than peripheral members of business groups? *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1869-1894. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0521

title: Uneasy Lies the Head that Bears the Trust: The Effects of Feeling Trusted on Emotional Exhaustion
methods: Three-wave, multi-source quantitative field study of public transit bus drivers; employee surveys measured feeling trusted, pride, perceived workload, reputation maintenance concerns, and emotional exhaustion, supervisor surveys measured job performance, and hypotheses were tested with structural equation modeling in Mplus using corrections for supervisor-level nonindependence.
industry: Public transit bus driving in a large London transportation company.
time_period: Three data collection waves; Time 2 occurred six weeks after Time 1, followed by Time 3 supervisor job-performance ratings.
units: Bus drivers, with supervisor-rated job performance.
n_sample: 219 bus drivers with complete data; 20 supervisors provided Time 3 performance ratings.
authors: Baer, M. D.; Dhensa-Kahlon, R. K.; Colquitt, J. A.; Rodell, J. B.; Outlaw, R.; Long, D. M.
theories: Conservation of resources theory (Hobfoll, 1988, 1989, 2001); trust dynamics
keywords: conservation of resources theory; emotional exhaustion; feeling trusted; job performance; perceived workload; pride; reputation maintenance concerns; trust dynamics
research_question: The paper asks whether feeling trusted by a supervisor is uniformly beneficial or whether it can also deplete employees. It specifically examines how feeling trusted affects emotional exhaustion and job performance through pride, perceived workload, and reputation maintenance concerns.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a conservation-of-resources process in which feeling trusted creates both resource gains and resource drains. Feeling trusted increases pride, which reduces emotional exhaustion and indirectly supports job performance. It also increases perceived workload and reputation maintenance concerns, which heighten emotional exhaustion and indirectly reduce job performance. Pride further amplifies the exhausting effect of reputation maintenance concerns because a valued positive image becomes more threatening to lose.
theoretical_contribution: The study challenges the prevailing assumption that feeling trusted is simply beneficial for employees and shows that it can operate as a double-edged sword. It extends trust research by using conservation of resources theory to distinguish resource gains, resource losses, and resource threats in the experience of being trusted. It also contributes to conservation of resources theory by simultaneously operationalizing gains, losses, and threats and showing that pride can intensify, not only buffer, stress processes.
practical_implication: The paper suggests that managers should recognize that trusted employees may still become emotionally exhausted, especially when trust brings more responsibilities or pressure to protect a positive image. Managers can accentuate the positive meaning of trust, redistribute or remove other tasks when trusted employees receive extra responsibilities, and reassure employees that their reputation does not rise or fall with every stretch assignment. Social support is also presented as a way to reduce emotional exhaustion.
limitations: The design used two sources and three waves, but pride, perceived workload, reputation maintenance concerns, and emotional exhaustion were measured in the same wave, so those links may still contain common-method inflation. The data established temporal precedence but did not measure all variables at all time periods, limiting causal authority compared with a panel design. The sample was predominantly male and had a final complete-data sample of around 200 participants, so larger replications would strengthen generalizability.
future_research: Future research should examine additional mediators linking feeling trusted to performance, including psychological empowerment, idiosyncrasy credits, and different forms of managerial risk-taking behavior such as delegating tasks, promoting ideas, or requesting favors. The authors also call for research on outcomes beyond traditional job performance, including creativity and adaptive performance. Further work should test whether the effects of feeling trusted vary by job control, work-unit dispersion of trust, and individual differences such as conscientiousness and prosocial motives.
abstract: The construct of feeling trusted reflects the perception that another party is willing to accept vulnerability to one’s actions. Although this construct has received far less attention than trusting, the consensus is that believing their supervisors trust them has benefits for employees’ job performance. Our study challenges that consensus by arguing that feeling trusted can be exhausting for employees. Drawing on Stevan Hobfoll’s conservation of resources theory, we develop a model in which feeling trusted fills an employee with pride—a benefit for exhaustion and performance—while also increasing perceived workload and concerns about reputation maintenance—burdens for exhaustion and performance. We test our model in a field study using a sample of public transit bus drivers in London, England. Our results suggest that feeling trusted is a double-edged sword for job performance, bringing with it both benefits and burdens. Given that recommendations for managers generally encourage placing trust in employees, these results have important practical implications.

Uneasy lies the head that bears the trust: The effects of feeling trusted on emotional exhaustion. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1637-1657. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0246

title: Harnessing Productive Tensions in Hybrid Organizations: The Case of Work Integration Social Enterprises
methods: Mixed-method empirical study. The quantitative component uses a panel of French work integration social enterprises and random-effects GLS regressions, with mediation and robustness checks, to test relationships among social imprinting, economic productivity, and social performance. The qualitative component uses a longitudinal comparative case analysis of two socially imprinted recycling WISEs to unpack how spaces of negotiation can help manage the paradox.
industry: French work integration social enterprises, with qualitative case evidence from two socially imprinted WISEs in the recycling industry.
time_period: Quantitative panel from 2003 to 2007; qualitative case histories traced from founding through 2008.
units: WISE establishment-year observations and two WISE case organizations
n_sample: 641 establishment-year observations with complete information; qualitative evidence from two WISE cases, 20 onsite interviews, 4 follow-up phone interviews, and 11 broader field interviews.
authors: Battilana, J.; Sengul, M.; Pache, A.-C.; Model, J.
theories: coordination in organizations; hybrid organizing; organizational imprinting; paradox theory
keywords: economic productivity; hybrid organizations; social imprinting; social performance; spaces of negotiation; work integration social enterprises
research_question: The paper asks whether work integration social enterprises can sustainably achieve their social mission despite dependence on commercial customers and the risk of neglecting beneficiaries. It further asks how social imprinting and economic productivity jointly shape social performance, and how socially imprinted WISEs may mitigate the productivity costs of that imprint.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is paradoxical. Social imprinting keeps WISEs focused on beneficiaries by shaping hiring, routines, and social-mission-oriented systems, which improves social performance. The same imprint can reduce economic productivity because socially oriented staff and routines may underemphasize commercial discipline, thereby lowering the resources and signals that support beneficiary placement. The case comparison shows that structural differentiation alone does not resolve the paradox; it becomes productive when paired with spaces of negotiation that force social counselors and production supervisors to coordinate trade-offs while maintaining their distinct commitments.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to hybrid organizing by identifying social imprinting and economic productivity as empirically supported antecedents of social performance in WISEs. It advances the imprinting literature by showing that founding social imprints can have contradictory effects: directly supporting social performance while indirectly weakening it through lower productivity. It also contributes to coordination research by theorizing spaces of negotiation as formal arenas through which structurally differentiated groups in hybrid organizations can maintain productive tension rather than collapse into unresolved conflict.
practical_implication: For leaders of social enterprises, the paper implies that protecting the social mission does not require ignoring commercial productivity, because weak productivity can itself undermine beneficiary outcomes. Hybrid organizations can assign social and economic responsibilities to distinct groups, but they also need formal interaction arenas, shared planning routines, and appraisal processes that require those groups to negotiate trade-offs. The BETA case suggests that retreats, general assemblies, communication, training, and job shadowing can help build the common goal and mutual respect needed for these spaces to work.
limitations: The study focuses on French WISEs, a setting where state accreditation, subsidies, and monitoring shape the balance between social and commercial objectives. Its qualitative evidence comes from two socially imprinted recycling WISEs, so the process findings clarify mechanisms but do not establish the full generality of spaces of negotiation across all hybrid organizations. The authors also note that spaces of negotiation consume resources, and their costs may limit usefulness in larger or differently structured organizations.
future_research: Future research should test whether these relationships hold in WISEs and other hybrids operating under different public-authority regimes and institutional settings. The paper calls for more work on how social enterprises and other hybrids sustain both mission focus and productive operations, including the roles of decision rights, incentives, financial structure, governance, and new legal forms such as community interest companies and benefit corporations. It also calls for research on when spaces of negotiation generalize to other hybrids such as hospitals and universities, and on the costs, benefits, and size-related boundary conditions of these coordination mechanisms.
abstract: We examine the factors that influence the social performance of hybrid organizations that pursue a social mission and sustain their operations through commercial activities by studying work integration social enterprises (WISEs). We argue that both social imprinting, defined as a founding team’s early emphasis on accomplishing the organization’s social mission, and economic productivity are important drivers of a WISE’s social performance. However, there is a paradox inherent in the social imprinting of WISEs: Although social imprinting directly enhances a WISE’s social performance, social imprinting also indirectly weakens social performance by negatively affecting economic productivity. Results based on panel data of French WISEs gathered between 2003 and 2007 are congruent with our predictions. To understand how socially imprinted WISEs may mitigate this negative relationship between social imprinting and economic productivity, we also conduct a comparative analysis of case studies. We find that one effective approach is to assign responsibility for social and economic activities to distinct groups while creating “spaces of negotiation”—arenas of interaction that allow members of each group to discuss the trade-offs that they face. We conclude by highlighting the conditions under which spaces of negotiation can effectively be used to maintain a productive tension in hybrid organizations.

title: Paying the Price? The Impact of Controversial Governance Practices on Managerial Reputation
methods: Panel study of large U.S. industrial firms from 1985 to 1989 using Fortune Most Admired Companies management-quality ratings by analysts and executives, poison pill and board data from Jerry Davis and the Investor Responsibility Research Center dataset, COMPUSTAT financial data, Wall Street Journal media coverage, an inverse Mills control for poison-pill selection, and GLS cross-sectional time-series regression.
industry: Large U.S. industrial firms appearing on either the 1985 or 1980 Fortune 500 list by sales.
units: Publicly traded Fortune 500 firm-years.
n_sample: 266 firms and 1,108 firm-years with all key data available; reported regression models use 1,103 firm-years.
authors: Bednar, M. K.; Love, E. G.; Kraatz, M.
theories: agency theory (Fama & Jensen, 1983; Jensen & Meckling, 1976); attribution theory (Heider, 1958; Jones & Davis, 1965; Kelley, 1967); intergroup bias research (Hewstone et al., 2002)
keywords: controversial governance practices; firm performance; managerial reputation; media coverage; peer executives; poison pill; prior adoptions; reputational penalties; stock analysts
research_question: The paper asks whether managers pay reputational penalties when their firms use controversial governance practices, and whether those penalties differ across evaluating audiences. It examines poison pills to test when stock analysts and peer executives penalize managerial reputation and how media coverage, firm performance, and prior adoption shape those penalties.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is an audience-specific attribution process. Analysts, positioned as investor-oriented outsiders, are expected to interpret poison pills as signs of managerial self-interest and impose stronger reputational penalties, especially when firms are performing well and when few peers have adopted poison pills. Peer executives, positioned closer to the managerial in-group, are expected to attribute poison pills more to external pressures and impose weaker penalties, although negative media coverage can make specific managers appear more self-serving. The findings support stronger analyst penalties, media-related executive penalties, stronger analyst penalties for high-performing firms, and dissipation of analyst penalties as poison pills diffuse.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to corporate governance research by directly testing the assumption that controversial governance practices damage managerial reputation. It shows that reputational sanctions are not uniform: they vary by audience, media attention, firm performance, and diffusion of the practice. It also extends reputation-as-social-control theory by showing that audience heterogeneity and causal attributions help explain when reputational penalties are meaningful and when they dissipate.
practical_implication: The findings imply that controversial governance practices may not deter managers through reputation loss as reliably as governance theory assumes. Managers may face strong penalties from investment-community audiences under some conditions, but relatively neutral judgments from peer executives can weaken the overall social-control effect. Media coverage matters because public attention can increase reputational sanctions, while low-visibility practices may allow managers to avoid stronger peer penalties.
limitations: The study focuses on one controversial governance practice, poison pills, in a historically specific period when the practice was highly contested. The data cannot directly measure the causal attributions that the theory argues are central to reputational penalties. The sample is also a relatively open community of large U.S. industrial firms, which may limit comparison with closed communities where reputation might operate as a stronger social-control mechanism.
future_research: Future research could examine how reputational penalties translate into managers' subsequent choices and whether this process varies across audiences, firms, and time. The authors also call for work that directly measures evaluators' causal attributions about questionable behavior. Additional studies could test whether other controversial governance practices, such as CEO duality or option repricing, still generate reputational penalties after they become widely adopted.
abstract: This study directly examines the reputational penalties that managers pay when they engage in controversial governance practices that raise questions about managerial selfinterest. These penalties should deter questionable behavior and enable reputation to serve a social control function, yet we know little about how and when these penalties are actually imposed. Unlike prior research in this vein, we account for the fact that reputational penalties associated with such practices may differ across audiences because of differences in interpretations of the practice and differences in causal attributions about its use. Specifically, we develop theory to explain how and when stock analysts and peer executives applied reputational penalties to managers when firms used a poison pill, a prominent anti-takeover device. We find that the reputational penalties associated with poison pills differed substantially between these two groups and that these groups applied different penalties depending on the media coverage that the poison pill received, the performance of the firm, and the extent to which the practice had already been adopted. The findings suggest that reputational penalties for questionable behaviors may be more contingent and harder to sustain than previously thought.
apa_citation: Bednar, M. K., Love, E. G., & Kraatz, M. (2015). Paying the price? The impact of controversial governance practices on managerial reputation. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1740-1760. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.1091

title: Dealing with Failure: Serial Entrepreneurs and the Costs of Changing Industries Between Ventures
methods: Original face-to-face survey of serial entrepreneurs in or near Beijing, China, analyzed with propensity score matching, logit models for industry-change outcomes, and OLS models for growth; appendix robustness tests use U.S. VentureXpert data on VC-backed ventures.
industry: Cross-industry entrepreneurial ventures in China, with a U.S. robustness sample of VC-backed ventures across six industry categories.
time_period: Chinese survey data collected between September and December 2012; U.S. VentureXpert data cover VC-backed ventures through 2009 and focus on ventures founded before 2006.
units: Serial entrepreneurs and their previous and subsequent ventures.
n_sample: 253 usable Chinese survey responses; main matched regressions use 219 observations; U.S. appendix reports 1,562 serial-entrepreneur observations for industry-change models and 27,472 venture observations for performance models.
authors: Eggers, J. P.; Song, L.
theories: Behavioral Theory of the Firm; attribution theory; learning from failure
keywords: attribution; industry change; learning from failure; serial entrepreneurship; subsequent venture performance
research_question: The paper asks whether serial entrepreneurs learn equally from prior venture experience, or whether previous failure changes what they do in their next venture and thereby affects subsequent performance. It focuses on whether failed founders change industries rather than internal choices such as strategy, planning, or management style.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is attribution-based. Failed entrepreneurs are expected to blame external conditions, especially the industry environment, and therefore to change industries when starting the next venture. That move sacrifices industry-specific experience, so the subsequent venture loses knowledge that could otherwise improve performance, while founder-controlled features such as strategy, planning, and management style are less likely to change after failure.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to serial entrepreneurship research by shifting attention from whether prior experience or prior success predicts later performance to how entrepreneurs behaviorally respond after failure. It integrates the Behavioral Theory of the Firm, learning-from-failure research, and attribution theory to explain why failure may trigger a costly industry switch rather than useful learning. It also qualifies revealed-quality explanations by showing that industry-specific experience and post-failure choices can shape performance persistence across ventures.
practical_implication: For serial entrepreneurs, the study implies that leaving an industry after a failed venture may feel like a corrective response but can discard useful industry-specific knowledge. Founders should distinguish between problems caused by an industry environment and problems that can be addressed without abandoning accumulated industry experience.
limitations: The authors note limits common to survey designs, including potential non-response and retrospective bias, although they argue these are mitigated by focusing on actions and descriptions. They also note that the study measures only a limited set of internal and external changes between ventures and that the results remain correlational because they do not use an instrumental-variable or natural-experiment design.
future_research: Future research should disentangle the many learning and behavioral responses that occur between closing one venture and creating the next. The authors specifically call for work on which aspects of experience are mutable versus lost when context changes, other internal and external factors founders may change between ventures, and stronger identification strategies for testing causality.
abstract: As part of the recent interest in serial entrepreneurship, studies have investigated the presence (or absence) of learning benefits from a previous to a subsequent venture. We extend this literature by integrating behavioral concepts on attribution and learning from failure that highlight the differences in behavioral responses to success versus failure. We theorize that serial entrepreneurs whose previous venture failed are likely to blame the external environment and change industries for their subsequent venture, and that this industry change is costly in that it invalidates potentially useful industry experience, thereby hindering their subsequent venture. In contrast, founders of failed ventures are unlikely to change aspects of their previous business (when starting their subsequent venture) that would be attributable to their leadership—that is, strategy, decision-making, and planning style. Using data on entrepreneurs in China and the U.S., we find support for our theory. The results have important implications for the study of serial entrepreneurship, and more broadly for research on behavioral responses to failure.

title: Inherently Relational: Interactions between Peers’ and Individuals’ Personalities Impact Reward Giving and Appraisal of Individual Performance
methods: Two-study quantitative design. Study 1 used a field round-robin dyadic design in intact management-course teams and hierarchical linear modeling to test peer-by-actor personality interactions. Study 2 used a randomized virtual-team experiment with electronic confederates, ANOVA/MANOVA, logistic regression, and bootstrapped moderated mediation to test performance evaluations, promotion recommendations, rewards, trait sensitivity, and person impressions while holding objective performance constant.
industry: Management-course team and virtual-team settings.
time_period: Study 1 was introduced around the midpoint of the semester; Study 2's second phase occurred about one week after the personality questionnaire.
units: Dyadic peer ratings in student teams and individual participant evaluations of manipulated virtual confederates.
n_sample: Study 1 included 178 participants in final analyses; Study 2 analyzed 135 participants across agreeableness and extraversion conditions.
authors: Erez, A.; Schilpzand, P.; Leavitt, K.; Woolum, A. H.; Judge, T. A.
theories: Realistic Accuracy Model of personality judgment (Funder, 1995); information utilization model of interpersonal dyadic evaluation
keywords: agreeableness; extraversion; interpersonal dyadic evaluation; introversion; negative person impressions; peer performance evaluations; reward giving; trait sensitivity
research_question: The paper asks whether an observing peer's personality changes how that peer evaluates and rewards coworkers with different interpersonal traits. Specifically, it tests whether introverted peers are more likely than extraverted peers to penalize extraverted and disagreeable actors in performance evaluations, reward allocations, and promotion-related judgments.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is an information-utilization process in dyadic evaluation. Drawing on the Realistic Accuracy Model of personality judgment, the authors argue that introverted peers are more sensitive to interpersonal trait cues and more likely to use those cues when forming general person impressions. Those impressions then shape ratings and rewards: introverted peers evaluate and reward extraverted or disagreeable actors more negatively, even when the experiment holds objective task performance constant. The results support this pattern in both the field dyadic team study and the virtual-team experiment, with trait sensitivity and person impressions mediating parts of the Study 2 effects.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to dyadic workplace-interaction theory by showing that peer evaluations are not only properties of actors or raters but can emerge from actor-by-peer personality combinations. It extends personality research by applying introversion-linked sensitivity to interpersonal traits in work settings. It also contributes to performance appraisal theory by identifying a dyadic source of rating variance that may be hidden when evaluations are modeled only as rater bias or ratee performance.
practical_implication: Organizations using peer evaluations, peer bonuses, or 360-degree feedback should monitor whether actor-peer personality combinations systematically shape ratings and rewards. The findings suggest that highly extraverted or disagreeable employees may need feedback about how their trait-relevant behaviors affect introverted peers' experiences of dyadic work encounters. Managers can also design team interactions and workspaces to reduce overwhelming interpersonal exposure for introverted employees.
limitations: The authors note that hidden psychological processes are difficult to observe directly, and Study 2 holds task output constant but cannot fully resolve whether introverted peers are biased or are evaluating broader interpersonal performance more holistically. The studies focus on dyads, so full-team processes could buffer or alter the effects. The experiment also uses salient personality manipulations, limited interaction time, and an introversion manipulation that may partly signal shyness or social anxiety.
future_research: Future work should test whether introverted peers make more accurate judgments of interpersonal performance or whether accurate personality judgments spill into biased performance ratings. Research could examine larger team contexts, three-way combinations of actor extraversion and agreeableness with peer introversion, and longer interactions where trait-consistent behaviors emerge without explicit personality descriptions. Additional work could also identify threshold levels at which introversion or extraversion begins to change dyadic evaluation patterns.
abstract: Introverted individuals may experience and evaluate their dyadic work relationships differently than extraverts. In two studies, we investigated the interaction effect of an individual’s and observing peer’s personality traits on performance evaluations and reward giving. Results from Study 1 showed that introverted (but not extraverted) peers consistently evaluated extraverted and disagreeable (but not introverted and agreeable) individuals’ performance as lower. Study 2 replicated these findings with regard to performance evaluation and reward giving using an experimental design that manipulated actor personality and held objective performance constant. The results also showed that introverts’ trait sensitivity and negative person impressions mediated these relationships. Overall, our results support an information utilization model of interpersonal dyadic evaluation, wherein introverts are more sensitive to interpersonal personality traits than are their extraverted counterparts, incorporating interpersonal traits in person impressions and subsequent evaluations and reward distributions. Our paper concludes with implications for dyadic workplace interactions, personality, and sources of emergent dyadic influences on performance evaluation.
apa_citation: Erez, A., Schilpzand, P., Leavitt, K., Woolum, A. H., & Judge, T. A. (2015). Inherently relational: Interactions between peers’ and individuals’ personalities impact reward giving and appraisal of individual performance. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1761-1784. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0214

title: Emotional Labor Dynamics: A Momentary Approach
methods: Laboratory call center simulation with 76 undergraduate participants, manipulated customer civility across three phases, continuous participant ratings of felt emotions, surface acting, and deep acting every 200 milliseconds during call playback, third-party ratings of vocal tone, multilevel growth models, and within-person path analysis with 10-second lags.
industry: Simulated call center service interaction.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Undergraduate participants acting as call center employees in a single customer-service call.
n_sample: 76 participants after eight exclusions from 84 recruited participants.
authors: Gabriel, A. S.; Diefendorff, J. M.
theories: control theory models of behavioral self-regulation (Carver & Scheier, 1998); self-regulatory view of emotional labor (Diefendorff & Gosserand, 2003; Diefendorff & Richard, 2008); social interaction model of emotion regulation (Cote, 2005)
keywords: call center simulation; continuous measures; customer incivility; deep acting; emotional labor; felt emotions; surface acting; vocal tone; within-episode emotional labor dynamics
research_question: The paper asks whether emotional labor varies moment to moment within a single customer interaction and how shifts in customer incivility shape felt emotions, surface acting, deep acting, and vocal tone. It also examines the within-episode causal ordering among felt emotions, emotion regulation, and vocal tone, including whether surface acting and deep acting are used as alternatives or simultaneously.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a self-regulatory emotional labor process. Customer incivility signals a discrepancy from the goal of satisfying the customer and creates a mismatch between felt emotions and display rules, leading employees to regulate through surface acting and deep acting while trying to maintain positive vocal tone. Lagged models show that felt emotions primarily precede regulation and vocal tone, surface acting and vocal tone influence each other reciprocally, and surface acting tends to precede later deep acting. The findings also show that surface and deep acting co-occur within moments rather than operating only as mutually exclusive strategies.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to emotional labor theory by providing a direct within-episode test of a process that prior theory had described dynamically but prior empirical work usually measured at the person, day, or interaction level. It shows that customer behavior can causally alter trajectories of employee feelings, regulation, and vocal tone during a single interaction. It also refines emotion regulation theory by showing that surface acting and deep acting can be complementary, simultaneously used strategies, with surface acting sometimes preceding deep acting.
practical_implication: The findings imply that customer incivility in call centers and service work can quickly increase employees' negative feelings and regulation demands, even within a brief interaction. They also suggest that service recovery can restore more positive affect and reduce regulation needs after incivility. Managers may therefore benefit from training employees in service recovery, providing respite after difficult encounters, and helping employees detach from negative experiences or process them with coworkers.
limitations: The study used one simulated call with undergraduate participants rather than multiple calls handled by actual call center workers, which limits direct generalization to full call center work. The continuous ratings were made retrospectively while participants listened back to recordings, raising the possibility of slight retrospection bias. The authors also note that the 10-second lag used to model causal ordering was partly arbitrary, even though supplemental analyses showed similar patterns across other lag lengths.
future_research: Future research should examine multiple calls to test carryover between interactions and changing trajectories across a work shift. The authors encourage studies using actual call center workers and recordings of real customer calls, paired with postshift continuous ratings and customer or supervisor evaluations. They also call for work on emotional authenticity, separate continuous ratings of faking and suppression, display-rule perceptions, individual differences, micro-events within interactions, and thresholds at which incivility leads employees to abandon display rules.
abstract: Emotional labor has been described as a dynamic self-regulatory process that unfolds over the course of customer interactions, with employees continuously monitoring and adjusting their felt and expressed emotions via two emotion regulation strategies: surface acting and deep acting. Despite dynamic theory on the topic, empirical tests have largely ignored within-episode variability in emotional labor, relying on assessments of emotional labor focused on the person, day, or interaction level of analysis. The current study elaborated on theory pertaining to within-episode emotional labor dynamics, utilizing a call center simulation to examine how shifts in customer incivility impacted on continuous measures (captured every 200 milliseconds) of participants’ felt emotions, surface acting, deep acting, and vocal tone during a single interaction. Results provided evidence that customer behavior causally influences within-episode changes in emotions, emotion regulation, and vocal tone, and that these key emotional labor variables significantly relate to each other at the momentary level of analysis. Further, by modeling lagged effects, we were able to gain insight into the causal direction in the relationships among these continuously measured variables. Moreover, we showed for the first time that surface acting and deep acting are used simultaneously to manage emotional labor demands.
apa_citation: Gabriel, A. S., & Diefendorff, J. M. (2015). Emotional labor dynamics: A momentary approach. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1804-1825. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1135
