title: The Management of Natural Resources: An Overview and Research Agenda
methods: From the Editors editorial and research agenda that reviews prior AMJ work on resources and natural resources, uses illustrative natural-resource scarcity cases, and develops practice-oriented themes from discussions with Teng Lit Liak.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: na
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: George, Gerard; Schillebeeckx, Simon J. D.; Liak, Teng Lit
theories: institutional theory; population ecology; resource dependence theory; resource-based view (Barney, 1991)
keywords: grand challenges; management research; natural resource scarcity; natural resources; resource scarcity; sustainability
research_question: The editorial asks why management scholarship has paid limited attention to natural resources despite the centrality of resource scarcity, sustainability, and resource access to organizations, governments, industries, and societies. It develops a research agenda for studying how natural resource scarcity reshapes business models, regulation, stakeholder engagement, technology adoption, governance, and sustainability.
mechanism_summary:
- Editorial frame: The article positions natural resources as a grand challenge for management research and argues that AMJ has used "resources" extensively while paying scant attention to physical and natural resources.
- Review of AMJ work: The authors distinguish people as resources, organizational assets as resources, and interorganizational and societal resources, then show that natural resources usually appear only as context rather than as focal theoretical objects.
- Scarcity reframing: The editorial treats scarcity as causally ambiguous and shaped by technology, regulation, market imperfections, supply risks, environmental externalities, and social conflict rather than only by biophysical depletion.
- Managerial and institutional responses: It organizes examples around organizational responses to scarcity, government intervention, social impacts of natural resources, and the movement from scarcity to sustainability.
- Practice-based agenda: Discussions with Teng Lit Liak are used to identify future research themes around attitudes and behaviors, technology substitution and adoption, agenda shaping, leadership and governance, and pragmatic experimentation.

The process is editorial and agenda-setting rather than empirical. George, Schillebeeckx, and Liak argue that natural resource scarcity creates constraints and opportunities that cut across firms, governments, civil society, and individuals. They call for management scholars to examine how organizations innovate, collaborate, govern, and lead under resource constraints, and how scholarship can help shift attention from scarcity toward sustainable management of natural resources.
theoretical_contribution: The editorial's contribution is to make natural resources a focal domain for management theory rather than a background context. It argues that existing resource theories have emphasized human, relational, knowledge, and organizational assets, while physical and natural resources require more explicit attention to scarcity, externalities, regulation, market imperfection, social impact, and cross-sector governance.
practical_implication: For managers and policymakers, the editorial implies that natural resource scarcity should be treated as a strategic and governance problem, not only as an environmental or engineering issue. It points to practical responses including supply-chain innovation, material efficiency, recycling and urban mining, frugal innovation, stakeholder engagement, public-private collaboration, and leadership that combines idealism with pragmatic experimentation.
limitations: The article is an editorial overview and research agenda rather than a systematic review or empirical study. Its claims are grounded in selected AMJ patterns, illustrative resource-scarcity cases, and practice-oriented discussion, so it is designed to open research questions rather than test causal relationships.
future_research: The editorial calls for research on how natural resource scarcity affects organizational responses, business-model innovation, government intervention, stakeholder engagement, social conflict, technology substitution, sustainability leadership, and cross-sector governance. It particularly encourages management scholars to study business, government, and civil society together as they respond to the scarcity and sustainability of Earth's natural resources.

title: Entrepreneurship in Regulated Markets: Framing Contests and Collective Action to Introduce Pay TV in the U.S.
methods: Inductive comparative historical case study of two attempts to introduce pay TV in the U.S. broadcasting industry: over-the-air pay TV and pay cable TV. The analysis uses archival data, regulatory reports, historical books, trade and industry communications, 204 New York Times articles, 20 law and economics journal articles, and 15 Cable Center interviews, with iterative case-history development and coding of framing and collective action.
industry: U.S. broadcasting and pay TV.
units: Two technologies and market-entry attempts: OTA pay TV and pay cable TV.
n_sample: Two comparative cases, supported by archival documents, 204 New York Times articles, 20 law and economics articles, and 15 interviews.
authors: Gurses, K.; Ozcan, P.
theories: framing theory and framing contests; institutional entrepreneurship; public interest theory of regulation
keywords: collective action; entrepreneurship in regulated markets; framing contests; institutional entrepreneurship; pay TV; public interest; regulatory void
research_question: The paper asks how entrepreneurs and incumbents advance or protect their interests and shape a regulated market in their favor. It examines why over-the-air pay TV failed while pay cable TV succeeded, despite both facing incumbent resistance and regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. broadcasting market.
mechanism_summary:
- Key actors / contestants: Pay TV entrepreneurs, broadcasting and theater incumbents, the FCC, courts, legislators, executive-branch actors, public-interest groups, schools, churches, and consumers.
- Process / phases: Initial entry through alignment with incumbents and the regulator's public-interest frame; incumbent resistance that frames the new service against public interest; entrant creation and diffusion of an alternative public-interest frame; collective action that moves from private groups to public and institutional actors; institutional pressure on the regulator and eventual frame consensus.
- Practices: Frame alignment, new frame creation, frame multiplicity, frame consensus, industry association activity, public campaigns, coalition building, lobbying, and indirect pressure on regulators.
- Emergent outcomes: OTA pay TV remained constrained and eventually disappeared, whereas pay cable TV built support, benefited from deregulation, and became institutionalized.

The process centers on framing contests over what counts as the public interest in a regulated market. Incumbents can protect their position by persuading regulators that an entrant's technology threatens public welfare. Entrepreneurs are more likely to succeed when they avoid direct dependence on the regulator early, mobilize groups that benefit from the new technology, diffuse a broader public-interest frame, and use collective action to create pressure across public and institutional arenas.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to entrepreneurship and institutional entrepreneurship research by showing how entrepreneurs in regulated markets can shape rather than simply accept their institutional environment. It develops framing as both a market-entry strategy and a mechanism through which entrants and incumbents battle over institutional change. It also extends work on framing contests by tracing how frames coevolve over time among entrepreneurs, incumbents, regulators, courts, legislators, and public groups.
practical_implication: Entrepreneurs entering regulated markets should not rely only on direct petitions to regulators, especially when incumbents have strong institutional ties. The study suggests that entrants can build legitimacy by aligning initially with dominant public-interest frames, then mobilizing beneficiaries and coalition partners who can help diffuse a new frame. Incumbents and regulators should also recognize that public-interest claims may be strategic attempts to preserve or contest market positions.
limitations: The authors acknowledge that the broader political context of deregulation in the 1970s and 1980s may have contributed to the success of pay cable TV, even though it does not fully explain the case. The theory is built from two historical cases in one U.S. regulated industry, so its transferability is strongest for settings where regulation is tied to public-interest interpretations. The archival design reconstructs long-term processes from historical documents and retrospective interviews rather than observing actors in real time.
future_research: Future research could examine whether similar public-interest framing contests occur in other regulated markets such as automotive, biotechnology, food, healthcare, telecommunications, or VOIP. Additional work could also study how incumbents and entrants learn from prior framing contests and adapt their strategies across technologies and regulatory regimes.
abstract: In their endeavor to establish new products and services, entrepreneurs can face strong resistance from market incumbents whose resources and market position they threaten. This paper looks at the battles between entrepreneurs and market incumbents in a regulated market where various institutional actors (e.g., regulators, courts) have the power to protect the incumbents by hindering the entrepreneurs. Our comparison of one failed and one successful attempt to introduce pay TV in the U.S. reveals how entrepreneurs can first enter a regulated market without facing resistance, and then introduce a new frame to legitimize their product or service despite growing resistance from incumbents. Our framework highlights framing as a strategy and framing contests as a mechanism through which entrepreneurs and incumbents can battle to enable or disable institutional change. As part of this process, we also uncover how entrepreneurs evolve from self-serving actors with no field-level intentions to powerful groups that create a ripple effect in their environment by moving their target of influence from private to institutional actors. Our work constitutes a step toward a more “realistic” tale of institutional change.

title: You Don’t Forget Your Roots: The Influence of CEO Social Class Background on Strategic Risk Taking
methods: Empirical quantitative panel study. The authors surveyed current S&P1500 CEOs about childhood social class background, combined those responses with CEO biographical data and CRSP/Compustat firm data, and estimated endogeneity-corrected 2SLS instrumental-variable panel regressions with extensive firm-, CEO-, industry-, and year-level controls plus Heckman self-selection robustness checks.
industry: Cross-industry S&P1500 firms.
country: North American context, centered on S&P1500 CEOs.
time_period: CEO-firm panel from 2002 to 2011, with CEO survey data collected in August 2012.
units: CEO-firm-year observations.
n_sample: 1,042 regression observations from 265 executives and 308 unique CEO-firm combinations after missing data.
authors: Kish-Gephart, J. J.; Campbell, J. T.
theories: imprinting theory (Marquis & Tilcsik, 2013); prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979); social class theorizing; upper echelons theory (Hambrick & Mason, 1984)
keywords: CEO social class background; elite education; general management functional background; imprinting theory; social class origins; strategic risk taking; upper echelons
research_question: The paper asks whether CEOs' perceived childhood social class origins shape firm-level strategic risk taking after they have reached the corporate elite. It further asks whether later career experiences, specifically elite education and general management functional background, strengthen or weaken the influence of those social class imprints.
mechanism_summary: The proposed mechanism is an imprinting process linking childhood social class experiences to later executive risk preferences. Upper-class origins provide safety nets, perceived control, and opportunity orientation, while lower-class origins can make middle-class status maintenance less central and increase willingness to accept downside risk; both are theorized to produce more strategic risk taking than middle-class origins. Elite education reduces risk taking among lower-class-origin CEOs in the main endogeneity-corrected models, while general management functional background amplifies the risk-taking tendency for CEOs from both upper and lower social class origins by broadening networks, experience, and perceived strategic options.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to upper echelons theory by directly testing CEO social class background as an early-life managerial characteristic that predicts firm strategy, rather than treating elite education as a proxy for class origin. It integrates imprinting theory with social class theorizing to argue that childhood access to resources and societal rank can persist into executive decision making. It also contributes to research on executive risk taking by showing that social class origins and later career experiences jointly condition firm-level strategic risk preferences.
practical_implication: The findings imply that executives' formative social class experiences may shape their comfort with risky resource commitments. Elite education and broad general management careers do not have uniform effects across executives; their implications depend partly on the CEO's class-origin imprint. The paper cautions against treating visible credentials alone as capturing the formative backgrounds shaping strategic behavior.
limitations: The authors identify the North American setting as a limitation and note that social class structures may operate differently in other institutional contexts. They also focus on CEOs because of data availability, leaving open how the social class backgrounds of other TMT members or the diversity of social class backgrounds within the TMT may affect strategy. Finally, although the study uses direct measures of perceived social class background and endogeneity-corrected models, it measures strategic risk taking from firm-level archival outcomes rather than observing executive decision processes directly.
future_research: Future research could examine other firm-level outcomes shaped by CEO social class origins, including employment programs, cooperative strategies, strategic alliances, and responses to compensation incentives. The authors call for work on how upward mobility affects executives' identity, organizational connection, and interactions with coworkers, leaders, and subordinates. They also encourage more proximal studies of executive decision making through scenario analysis, computer simulation, policy capturing, or samples of smaller firms and executive MBA populations.
abstract: Social class is increasingly recognized as a powerful force in people’s lives. Yet despite the long and extensive stream of research on the upper echelons of organizations, we know little about how executives’ formative childhood experiences with social class influence their strategic choices. In this study, we investigate the influence of chief executive officers’ (CEOs’) perceived social class origins on firm risk taking. We also explore the moderating influences of other important career experiences, in the form of elite education and diverse functional backgrounds. Our theory and findings highlight that an executive’s social class origins have a lasting and varying impact on his or her preferences, affecting his or her tendency to take risks. By examining this novel managerial characteristic, we offer important implications for theorizing about social class and upper echelons.
apa_citation: Kish-Gephart, J. J., & Campbell, J. T. (2015). You don’t forget your roots: The influence of CEO social class background on strategic risk taking. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1614-1636. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.1204

title: Isolating Trust Outcomes from Exchange Relationships: Social Exchange and Learning Benefits of Prior Ties in Alliances
methods: Empirical quantitative study using a web-based survey of strategic alliance professionals. The authors develop measures for institutionalization-based trust, affect-based trust, partner knowledge, prior ties, market overlap, and cultural similarity; assess measurement reliability and validity with partial least squares; and estimate seemingly unrelated regression models with interaction terms and sector fixed effects.
industry: Strategic alliances.
country: Respondents came from Association of Strategic Alliance Professionals members, most representing U.S. firms, and executive-program alumni at a major European business school; the final alliance sample included both international and domestic alliances.
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Alliance agreements reported by single key informants.
n_sample: 189 observations in the final analyses.
authors: Lioukas, C. S.; Reuer, J. J.
theories: learning and knowledge-based perspectives; social exchange theory; transaction cost economics
keywords: affect-based trust; cultural similarity; institutionalization-based trust; learning; market overlap; partner knowledge; prior ties; social exchange theory; strategic alliances; trust
research_question: The paper asks whether prior alliance ties between firms generate the trust outcomes presumed by social exchange theory, or whether they more generally generate learning about a partner's anticipated behavior. It also asks when prior ties are more likely to produce institutionalization-based and affect-based trust, focusing on market overlap and cultural similarity as boundary conditions.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism separates social exchange from learning. Prior ties create opportunities for reciprocal benefits and emotional attachments, but those trust-building processes require stronger behavioral conditions than repeated contact alone. Repeated alliances more readily create partner knowledge because firms observe how partners behave across circumstances and learn to anticipate opportunism and coordination needs. The results support this distinction: prior ties predict partner knowledge overall, while affect-based trust emerges from prior ties mainly when market overlap is low and cultural similarity is high.
theoretical_contribution: The paper tightens social exchange theory by showing that repeated exchange should not automatically be treated as evidence of trust. It distinguishes trust rooted in reciprocity from learning-based knowledge about a partner's future behavior, thereby separating social exchange outcomes from learning and knowledge-based outcomes in strategic alliances. It also identifies partner competition and cultural fit as boundary conditions for when the trust predictions of social exchange theory apply.
practical_implication: Researchers and managers should be cautious about treating prior ties as a simple proxy for trust in alliance relationships. Prior collaborations may give partners useful knowledge about how the other firm will behave, including when opportunism or coordination problems may arise, without necessarily producing institutionalized or affective trust. Alliance managers seeking trust from repeated ties should attend to competitive overlap and cultural similarity because these conditions shape whether reciprocal, trust-building behavior is likely to develop.
limitations: The authors note that they focus only on prior ties, leaving other routes to trust or partner knowledge, such as common third-party ties, industrial clusters, or technical committees, for future work. The study also uses a cross-sectional design, which limits tests of mediation from prior ties through trust and learning outcomes to alliance performance. Its survey design relies on single key informants for alliance agreements, although the authors use procedural and statistical checks to mitigate common method concerns.
future_research: Future research could examine how firms develop trust or partner knowledge through common third-party ties and generalized exchange among multiple firms. Longitudinal studies could test whether trust and learning outcomes mediate the relationship between prior ties and alliance performance and compare prior-tie effects with trust and learning that develop inside a focal alliance. Additional work could extend the boundary-condition logic to other social exchange outcomes and to other intraorganizational or interorganizational settings.
abstract: Social exchange theory is a broad theory that has been used to explain trust as an outcome of various exchange relationships, and research commonly presumes trust exists between exchange partners that have prior relationships. In this paper, we contribute to research on social exchange theory by isolating the trust outcomes of interorganizational exchanges from other outcomes emphasized by learning and knowledge-based perspectives, and by specifying important boundary conditions for the emergence of trust in interorganizational exchanges. We make such a theoretical contribution within the domain of strategic alliances by investigating the effects of previous alliance agreements, or prior ties, between the partnering firms. We find that prior ties generally lead to learning about a partner’s anticipated behavioral patterns, which helps a firm predict when self-interested behavior may occur and know how to interact with the partner during the coordination and execution of the alliance tasks. By contrast, the kind of trust emphasized in social exchange theory is not generally rooted in prior ties and only emerges from prior relationships under certain conditions. We discuss the implications of these findings for research on social exchange theory.
apa_citation: Lioukas, C. S., & Reuer, J. J. (2015). Isolating trust outcomes from exchange relationships: Social exchange and learning benefits of prior ties in alliances. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1826-1847. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0934

title: Does Seeing “Eye To Eye” Affect Work Engagement and Organizational Citizenship Behavior? A Role Theory Perspective on LMX Agreement
methods: Empirical quantitative multi-source survey study of leader-subordinate dyads. The authors test LMX agreement and LMX quality using polynomial regression and response surface methodology; they test indirect effects on supervisor-rated OCBO through employee-rated work engagement with a block-variable mediation approach and Mplus bootstrapping, and report supplemental coworker-rated OCBI analyses.
industry: Diverse jobs and organizations; the paper does not restrict the sample to one industry.
country: Not directly named in paper; participants were recruited through a large Midwestern university.
time_period: Three separate data collection periods; calendar dates are not reported.
units: Leader-subordinate dyads, with employee self-reports and immediate supervisor reports; supplemental OCBI analyses use coworker ratings in the final sample.
n_sample: 280 matched employee-supervisor dyads for the main analyses; supplemental OCBI analysis uses 139 focal employees.
authors: Matta, F. K.; Scott, B. A.; Koopman, J.; Conlon, D. E.
theories: leader–member exchange theory; role theory
keywords: LMX quality; leader–member exchange (LMX) agreement; organizational citizenship behavior (OCB); polynomial regression; response surface methodology; role theory; work engagement
research_question: The paper asks whether agreement versus disagreement between leader and subordinate perceptions of LMX quality affects employee work engagement and subsequent organizational citizenship behavior. It further asks whether agreement at high LMX quality differs from agreement at low LMX quality, and whether the two forms of disagreement differ depending on whether the leader or subordinate rates the relationship more positively.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a role-theoretic congruence process. When leaders and subordinates agree about LMX quality, role consensus reduces expectation discrepancies and allows employees to invest physical, cognitive, and emotional energy in their work roles. When they disagree, misaligned expectations around socio-emotional versus transactional roles consume attention and resources, reducing engagement. Engagement then carries these dyadic role effects into OCBO by broadening how employees enact discretionary work roles.
theoretical_contribution: The study challenges the common LMX practice of treating either leader or subordinate ratings as sufficient to describe the relationship. It contributes by showing that LMX agreement is substantively important beyond LMX quality, and that even low-quality agreement can be associated with better engagement and citizenship than disagreement. Methodologically, it advances LMX research by using polynomial regression and response surface methodology rather than dichotomized agreement categories or difference scores.
practical_implication: The findings imply that leaders should attend not only to building high-quality LMX relationships but also to whether both parties understand the relationship similarly. When high-quality relationships are not feasible with every subordinate, clarifying roles and expectations may still improve outcomes by moving the dyad from incongruence to congruence. Leaders may therefore benefit from communicating their view of the relationship and aligning expectations rather than assuming that their own perception is shared.
limitations: The authors note that the design cannot establish causality, so alternative causal orderings remain plausible, including the possibility that work engagement or OCB shapes later LMX quality. The study focuses on work engagement and OCB, leaving other LMX-related outcomes such as job satisfaction, commitment, fairness perceptions, task performance, supervisor performance, and career advancement for future work. The OCBI analysis is limited because coworker ratings were collected only in one of the three samples.
future_research: Future research could collect longitudinal data to examine how LMX agreement and quality change over time and whether supervisor perceptions tend to move dyads toward shared high- or low-quality relationships. The authors also call for work on boundary conditions, including interaction intensity, dyadic performance, and LMX differentiation within work groups. Additional research could compare objective agreement with subjective perceptions of agreement and test why and when those two forms align.
abstract: Despite meta-analytic evidence demonstrating that leader–member exchange (LMX) agreement (consensus between leader and subordinate perceptions) is only moderate at best, research on LMX typically examines this relationship from only one perspective: either the leader’s or the subordinate’s. We return to the roots of LMX and utilize role theory to argue that agreement between leader and subordinate perceptions of LMX quality has meaningful effects on employee motivation and behavior. In a polynomial regression analysis of 280 leader–subordinate dyads, employee work engagement—and subsequent organizational citizenship behavior (OCB)—was maximized (at each level of LMX quality) when leaders and subordinates were in agreement about the quality of their LMX relationship, but suffered when they did not see “eye to eye.” Indeed, situations in which both leaders and subordinates evaluated their relationship as low quality were associated with higher work engagement (and subsequent OCB) than were situations of disagreement in which a single member evaluated the relationship as high quality. Further, this effect was consistent regardless of whether the leader or the subordinate evaluated the relationship highly. We conclude that, to fully understand the implications of our only dyadic leadership theory, we must consider the perspectives of both members of the LMX dyad simultaneously.
apa_citation: Matta, F. K., Scott, B. A., Koopman, J., & Conlon, D. E. (2015). Does seeing “eye to eye” affect work engagement and organizational citizenship behavior? A role theory perspective on LMX agreement. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1686-1708. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2014.0106

title: What Drives Trickle-Down Effects? A Test of Multiple Mediation Processes
methods: Two empirical quantitative survey studies of supervisor-subordinate dyads. Study 1 uses cross-sectional dyadic data and structural equation modeling with bootstrapped multiple-mediation tests; Study 2 uses a three-wave longitudinal dyadic design, alternative mediator measures, and the same multiple-mediation approach.
industry: A broad range of organizations, including aerospace and defense, education, transportation, government, financial services, hospitality and entertainment, retail, manufacturing, and health care.
country: United States, specifically the Southeastern United States sampling context.
time_period: Study 1 is cross-sectional; Study 2 separates independent variables, mediators, and dependent variables across three waves with three-week lags.
units: Supervisor-subordinate dyads.
n_sample: Study 1: 200 matched supervisor-subordinate dyads; Study 2: 270 matched supervisor-subordinate dyads.
authors: Wo, D. X. H.; Ambrose, M. L.; Schminke, M.
theories: displaced aggression (Marcus-Newhall et al., 2000; Tedeschi & Norman, 1985); social exchange theory (Blau, 1964); social learning theory (Bandura, 1977, 1986)
keywords: displaced aggression; informational justice; interactional justice perceptions; interpersonal justice; organizational justice; social exchange theory; social learning theory; trickle-down effects
research_question: The paper asks which theoretical mechanisms explain trickle-down effects in interactional justice perceptions from managers to supervisors to subordinates. It specifically examines whether interpersonal and informational justice perceptions trickle down through the same or different processes: social exchange, social learning, and displaced aggression.
mechanism_summary: The mechanism is a cross-level trickle-down process in which supervisors' treatment by managers shapes how supervisors treat subordinates. The two studies show different processes for the two justice facets: interpersonal justice trickles down through anger or anger/irritation, consistent with displaced aggression, while informational justice trickles down through perceived organizational support or felt obligation, consistent with social exchange. The studies do not find support for social learning as the mediating process for either justice facet.
theoretical_contribution: The study contributes to trickle-down and organizational justice research by directly testing, rather than merely invoking, three major theoretical explanations for trickle-down effects in a single multiple-mediation framework. It shows that the mechanism depends on the justice facet: interpersonal justice follows a more affective displaced-aggression route, whereas informational justice follows a more cognitive social-exchange route. It also challenges the common use of social learning theory as a default explanation for trickle-down effects by finding no support for role model influence or interactional efficacy as mediators.
practical_implication: The findings imply that supervisors are not only transmitters of higher-level treatment but may also serve as buffers who can stop negative treatment from cascading downward. Because interpersonal justice trickles down through anger and irritation, organizations may reduce harmful spillovers by helping supervisors manage emotional responses to unfair treatment. The separate informational-justice pathway through felt obligation also shows that different forms of justice may cascade through different mechanisms.
limitations: The authors note that they test three major trickle-down theories but do not exhaust all possible justice theories, such as relational, deontic, or needs-based accounts. They also caution that the evidence speaks directly only to interpersonal and informational justice, not every kind of trickle-down phenomenon. Additional limitations include potential unfairness in how the Study 2 mediators were operationalized, relatively fair samples that may understate displaced aggression, and the possibility that other operationalizations of the mechanisms could yield additional insight.
future_research: The paper calls for research on additional mediating mechanisms from other justice theories, including self-identity, moral identity, and needs for autonomy or control. It also suggests examining whether the same affective and cognitive mechanisms generalize to other kinds of trickle-down effects beyond interpersonal and informational justice. Future studies should use more parallel mediator operationalizations and samples that include both fair and unfair environments.
abstract: Organizational research has established the existence of trickle-down effects, wherein the perceptions, attitudes, or behavior of one person in an organization affects those of another person at a lower level. Although current research has explained the phenomenon using several different theoretical perspectives, prior studies have not explicitly tested the theorized mechanisms. This paper develops and tests a model that incorporates three theories of trickle-down effects for interactional justice perceptions: social exchange theory, social learning theory, and displaced aggression. Using crosssectional data from 200 supervisor–subordinate dyads in Study 1 and longitudinal data from 270 supervisor–subordinate dyads in Study 2, we test this multiple mediator model. The results demonstrate that the two aspects of interactional justice perceptions— interpersonal and informational justice perceptions—trickle down from supervisors to subordinates through two different mechanisms. Specifically, displaced aggression accounts for the trickle-down effects of interpersonal justice perceptions and social exchange accounts for the trickle-down effects of informational justice perceptions. We discuss the implications of the findings for research on trickle-down effects and organizational justice.
apa_citation: Wo, D. X. H., Ambrose, M. L., & Schminke, M. (2015). What drives trickle-down effects? A test of multiple mediation processes. *Academy of Management Journal*, 58(6), 1848-1868. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2013.0670

title: Corporate Governance and Investors' Perceptions of Foreign IPO Value: An Institutional Perspective
methods: Archival study of foreign IPOs (SDC New Issues database; SEC S-1 filings and final prospectuses); fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fs/QCA) with truth-table reduction (consistency cutoff .80, frequency threshold 2); asymmetric low-premium analysis and extended-condition robustness tests
industry: Multiple industries; high-tech (Internet-related, electronics, software) vs. non-high-tech; utilities excluded
country: United States (listing venue); foreign IPO firms from 36 home countries
units: Foreign firms making first-time firm-commitment IPOs on US exchanges
authors: Bell, R. G.; Filatotchev, I.; Aguilera, R. V.
theories: agency theory (contrasted baseline); institutional logics (Dunn & Jones, 2010); neoinstitutional theory (Meyer & Rowan, 1977; Kraatz & Zajac, 1996; Scott, 2001); nested legitimacy framework (Holm, 1995; Deephouse & Suchman, 2008)
keywords: corporate governance; foreign IPOs; fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis; institutional logics; investor perceptions; nested legitimacy; price premium
research_question: Can different bundles of governance mechanisms in foreign IPO firms lead to the same perceived valuation outcomes, and how do differences between a foreign IPO firm's home and host country institutional contexts affect this process of gaining legitimacy through governance mechanisms?
hypotheses:
H1: The effect of a foreign IPO's governance mechanisms on investor value perceptions is contingent on the legitimacy of its home country regulatory institutions, and the value of multiple mechanisms does not accumulate for foreign IPOs originating from countries with strong legal protection for minority investors.
H2: To achieve high investor value perceptions, foreign IPOs from countries with weak legal protection for minority investors must employ a larger number of mechanisms in their governance bundles than IPOs from countries with strong protection for minority investors.
mechanism_summary: Investor valuation of foreign IPOs is theorized as a socially constructed legitimation process rather than a purely rational, efficiency-centered assessment. Firm-level governance mechanisms confer cognitive legitimacy, but this process is nested within US investors' perceptions of the regulatory legitimacy of the firm's home country institutions, so overall legitimacy falls at the intersection of the cognitive and regulatory institutional domains. Foreign IPOs from jurisdictions that surpass a minimal regulatory legitimacy threshold (strong minority shareholder protection) can obtain legitimacy flexibly from different, limited governance combinations, because under conditions of "cognitive economy" additional signals become redundant and their marginal effect declines. Firms from weak-protection countries face divergent institutional logics, institutional duality, and heightened investor uncertainty, so investors demand a wider range of standard, institutionalized governance practices before granting the same level of legitimacy and valuation.
data_measures: Sample: 198 foreign firms from 36 countries that made first-time "firm commitment" IPOs in the US between 1996 and 2006, identified from the Security Data Corporation (SDC) New Issues database, with each firm's S-1 registration filing and final prospectus obtained from the SEC; listings from mergers/acquisitions or spin-offs, unit trusts, warrants, rights offerings, utilities, and firms incorporated in Bermuda, the Bahamas, or the Cayman Islands were excluded. Outcome condition: price premium = (offer price - book value)/offer price, calibrated with full non-membership below a 66 percent premium, full membership at a 95 percent premium (the sample's highest decile, following Fama and French, 2002), and the midpoint at the average of the two breakpoints; a variant using the first-day closing price controls for underpricing and does not change results. Governance conditions: board independence (independent directors identified from the prospectus; fully in at 70 percent independent members, fully out at 30 percent), CEO stock (crisp set: stock options offered to the issuing firm's CEO prior to IPO), and venture capital backing (crisp set: VCs among a firm's principal pre-IPO shareholders). Country condition: strong home country investor protection = the product of the standardized Djankov et al. (2008) revised antidirector index and the International Country Risk Guide law and order index, with countries above the sample median fully in (97 weak-protection vs. 101 strong-protection firms). Contextual conditions: prestigious underwriter (Carter and Manaster index of 8 or higher fully in, below 5 fully out), mature IPO (at least 20 years old fully in, 1 year or less fully out, 5-year crossover), and high-tech industry (Internet-related, electronics, and software firms). Analysis: fs/QCA truth-table reduction with a consistency cutoff of .80 and a frequency threshold of two (capturing 84 percent of cases); the design is set-theoretic and configurational (sufficiency analysis), not a causal-identification design.
key_findings: Six solution configurations showed acceptable consistency (consistency >= .80; overall solution consistency = .88, overall coverage = .54) for high foreign IPO price premiums. In line with Hypothesis 1, foreign IPOs from countries with strong legal protection of minority investors (solutions 1-3) achieved high price premiums with only one governance mechanism: incentive alignment (with prestigious underwriters) for mature technology firms, venture capital monitoring for younger technology firms, and an independent board for non-technology firms. Supporting Hypothesis 2, IPOs from countries without strong legal protection (solutions 4-6) needed multiple governance mechanisms — incentive alignment combined with venture backing, incentive alignment combined with an independent board, or all three — to reach comparably high perceived values. The asymmetric analysis of low perceived value complements these results: strong-protection IPOs suffer low perceived value when they adopt multiple governance mechanisms, while weak-protection IPOs experience poor perceived value when they adopt very few. Robustness analyses adding insider retained ownership, Big Five auditor backing, and founder-CEO status are consistent with both hypotheses; the presence of an international auditor appears in all configurations leading to high perceived value, and a hot IPO market was a necessary condition for high foreign IPO perceived value.
theoretical_contribution: The study shows there is no universal governance bundle leading to high levels of investors' value perceptions: different and limited combinations of monitoring and incentive-related mechanisms are equifinal, challenging agency-grounded assumptions that governance mechanisms act independently, additively, and cumulatively. It offers a nested model of legitimacy in which investor perceptions of a foreign IPO's overall legitimacy fall at the intersection of the cognitive and regulatory institutional domains, with home country minority investor protection acting as a first-order regulatory legitimacy threshold that shapes the size and composition of firm-level governance bundles. Methodologically, the paper introduces fs/QCA to IPO governance research, relaxing assumptions of permanent causality, additivity, and causal symmetry inherent in most IPO research.
practical_implication: For foreign firms going public on US exchanges, IPOs originating from countries with weak minority investor protection must deploy both monitoring and incentive-related governance to bolster US investor confidence in their governance quality and their potential to achieve high valuations. IPOs from strong-protection countries can achieve high perceived value with a single salient governance mechanism, and having too many governance practices may actually undermine their IPO valuations.
limitations: fs/QCA is constrained by the number of variables researchers can include, so the analysis does not utilize all possible controls typically used in IPO research. Investor protection is a formal-institution proxy for institutional differences between home countries, so informal institutional characteristics (e.g., networks, trust relationships) that US investors may also weigh are not captured by the operationalization. The price premium measure reflects the commingling of the value perceived by institutional investors and underwriters, and the study does not tease out how different groups of investors perceive foreign IPO quality; normative sources of legitimacy are likewise not isolated.
future_research: The authors call for research isolating which governance bundles are associated with prestigious underwriters and auditors, which bundles attract "dedicated" institutional investors, and whether institutional factors affect these bundles. They suggest applying the configurational framework to IPO survival studies, to host capital markets whose institutional environments differ from the US, and to firms listing on two or more national capital markets. They also point to developing a broader theoretical approach to nested legitimacy, including its formative and boundary conditions and normative and other institutional aspects of legitimation.
abstract: This article investigates stock market responses to different constellations of firm-level corporate governance mechanisms by focusing on foreign initial public offerings (IPOs) in the United States. We build on sociology-grounded research on financial market behavior and use a “nested” legitimacy framework to explore US investor perceptions of foreign IPO value. Using a fuzzy set theoretic methodology, we demonstrate how different combinations of monitoring and incentive-based corporate governance mechanisms lead to the same level of investor valuation of firms. Moreover, institutional factors related to the strength of minority shareholder protection in a foreign IPO’s home country represent a boundary condition that affects the number of governance mechanisms required to achieve high value perceptions among US investors. Our findings contribute to the sociological perspective on comparative corporate governance and the dependencies between organizations and institutions.
apa_citation: Bell, R. G., Filatotchev, I., & Aguilera, R. V. (2014). Corporate governance and investors' perceptions of foreign IPO value: An institutional perspective. *Academy of Management Journal*, *57*(1), 301-320. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0146

title: Competitive Parity, Status Disparity, and Mutual Forbearance: Securities Analysts' Competition for Investor Attention
methods: Natural experiment (enactment of Regulation Fair Disclosure); archival panel of analyst earnings estimates from Thomson IBES (1995-2007) merged with Institutional Investor rankings, SDC Platinum underwriting data, and CRSP; three-stage least squares (3SLS) fixed-effect simultaneous linear probability regressions of boldness and accuracy
industry: Sell-side securities analysis (equity analysts at brokerage firms covering publicly traded companies)
time_period: January 1, 1995 to December 31, 2007
units: Analyst-stock earnings estimates
n_sample: 1,229,872 estimates (473,649 by 4,784 analysts pre-Reg-FD; 756,223 by 6,670 analysts under Reg-FD)
authors: Bowers, A. H.; Greve, H. R.; Mitsuhashi, H.; Baum, J. A. C.
theories: mutual forbearance theory (Simmel, 1950; Barnett, 1993; Baum & Korn, 1996); status-based model of market competition (Podolny, 1993)
keywords: Regulation Fair Disclosure; bold earnings estimates; competitive parity; investor attention; multipoint contact; mutual forbearance; securities analysts; status disparity
research_question: How do two dimensions of competitive relationships, multipoint contact and status, influence securities analysts' responses to a regulatory change (Regulation Fair Disclosure) that abruptly eliminates privileged access to firm information as a critical source of competitive advantage?
hypotheses:
H1: An analyst's likelihood of issuing bold earnings estimates on a stock is lower if the analyst experiences high multipoint contact with other analysts.
H2: The effect stated in Hypothesis 1 is stronger under Reg-FD and may be exclusive to the period after its enactment.
H3: Analysts with Institutional Investor's ranking are less likely to issue bold estimates after Reg-FD.
H4: The effect stated in Hypothesis 1 is stronger for analysts with II (Institutional Investor) ranking.
mechanism_summary: Bold earnings estimates are competitive actions that attract investor attention and threaten rival analysts. Multipoint contact through co-coverage of the same stocks lets analysts recognize their mutual interdependence, develop reciprocal dominance over separate spheres of influence, and convey mutual threats of retaliation, raising the cost of boldness and inducing forbearance. Forbearance presupposes competitive parity: before Reg-FD, analysts with privileged access to corporate information had little incentive to enter reciprocal dominance relationships, so multipoint contact should suppress boldness mainly after Reg-FD leveled access to material information. Because the distress of losing status exceeds the pleasure of gaining it, high-status (II-ranked) analysts forbear more strongly when multipoint contact permits it, stabilizing the existing status order.
data_measures: Data: Thomson IBES earnings estimates issued by all named sell-side analysts for publicly traded US companies between January 1, 1995 and December 31, 2007 (final sample 1,229,872 estimates), augmented with Institutional Investor All-Star rankings, SDC Platinum underwriting data, and CRSP stock data. DVs: analyst positive/negative boldness = dummy coded 1 when an estimate differs from the consensus (mean of all active estimates the day before the focal estimate) by more than 1.5 standard deviations above/below it; accurate positive/negative boldness = bold estimates closer to actual earnings than the consensus. IVs: multipoint contact = average proportional portfolio overlap between the focal analyst and the other analysts covering the focal stock; Reg-FD = dummy coded 1 for dates after October 1, 2000; analyst status = years listed as an Institutional Investor All-Star since 1990, weighted by recency. Identification: the enactment of Reg-FD is treated as a natural experiment satisfying the three conditions for causal inference; estimation uses three-stage least squares (3SLS) simultaneous linear probability regressions with analyst-stock dyad fixed effects and analyst, brokerage, and stock controls.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: coefficients for analyst multipoint contact are negative and significant for both positive boldness (-0.027, p < .001) and negative boldness (-0.018, p < .001) in Model 2, and as expected the effect is stronger for positive bold estimates.
- H2 supported: the Reg-FD x multipoint contact interactions are negative and significant (-0.006, p < .10 for positive boldness; -0.048, p < .001 for negative boldness). Prior to Reg-FD, analysts issued more negative bold estimates on high multipoint contact stocks (main effect +0.014, p < .001), showing a breakdown of forbearance under unequal information access; the sum of the main effect and the Reg-FD interaction is negative and significant.
- H3 supported: high-status analysts were more likely to issue bold estimates before Reg-FD but had the same likelihood as low-status analysts under Reg-FD (the sum of coefficients before and after is not significantly different from zero).
- H4 supported: the multipoint contact x analyst status interaction is negative and significant (-0.011, p < .001 for positive boldness; -0.004, p < .01 for negative boldness); in split-period regressions this interaction falls below standard significance levels for positive boldness under Reg-FD.
- Accuracy: pre-Reg-FD bold estimates display uncanny accuracy (above 0.8 for both directions); under Reg-FD accuracy drops to 0.395 (positive) and 0.251 (negative), far below the 0.5 coin-toss threshold, and multipoint contact increases the accuracy of bold estimates.
theoretical_contribution: The study establishes competitive parity and status disparity as boundary conditions of mutual forbearance theory, making one theoretical premise explicit: equal footing. When some actors hold a substantial informational competitive advantage, structural conditions that would otherwise facilitate mutual forbearance do not foster it; indeed, multipoint contact sharpened certain competitive actions (negative bold estimates) when information was restricted, a full reversal of the result under public information circulation. The paper also extends multipoint contact research, which had treated actors as equal and ignored the social structure of markets, by showing that high-status actors are more willing to forbear in order to stabilize the status order, placing the work at the intersection of the mutual forbearance, competitive parity, and status research traditions.
practical_implication: For the policy makers who drafted and passed Reg-FD, the findings show that a regulatory crackdown on one form of collusion (companies' private disclosure of information to preferred analysts) was effective in its own right but led to an increase in another form of collusion (mutual forbearance among analysts linked by multipoint contact). The rise in mutual forbearance suggests that market information may not be conveyed as directly or efficiently as actors focus on each other as sources of competitive advantage rather than individual skill, which has implications for the information analysts provide to investors.
limitations: The authors cannot rule out quiet releases of material information after Reg-FD, although they found no evidence of such leaks in analysts' estimates and argue that consistently accurate estimates are visible and arouse suspicion. The Sargan test indicated that bold estimates were not fully exogenous in the accuracy regression, indicating potential bias in the accuracy (though not the boldness) regressions used for hypothesis testing. The trade-offs analysts make between attention gains and inaccuracy risk cannot be directly observed and are examined only indirectly through the accuracy models.
future_research: The authors point to studying the effects of public information circulation on competition in other settings, such as safety-intensive industries (airlines, railroads, nuclear power plants) and industries subject to fair competition regulations, and to the reverse process, in which an industry characterized by relative homogeneity in competitive strength becomes more heterogeneous (e.g., through deregulation or transitions from dominant designs to technological ferment). They propose examining analysts' expansion and contraction of coverage (entry and exit behaviors) and alternative observable outcomes of multipoint contact such as the accuracy and timeliness of estimates. They also call for research into the microcognitive processes through which actors learn to compete under novel conditions.
abstract: Most studies of responses to change in competitive environments focus on competitor-specific adaptations. However, rivals are often acutely aware of one another, and this awareness should influence their competitive behavior. In this study, we focus on three market structures that affect competitive behavior: competitive parity, status disparity, and multipoint contact. In particular, we examine how securities analysts responded to a regulatory discontinuity, Regulation Fair Disclosure ("Reg-FD"), which promotes competitive parity by eliminating privileged access to proprietary firm information as a critical source of competitive advantage. We predict and find that Reg-FD activated mutual forbearance among analysts linked through multipoint contact. We also predict and find that high-status analysts forbear more strongly. Analysts' responses to heterogeneity in competitive advantage thus depend importantly on their competitive overlap and status, which has implications for both their behavior and the information they provide to investors.

title: What Goes Around Comes Around: Knowledge Hiding, Perceived Motivational Climate, and Creativity
methods: Two-study multimethod design: multilevel field survey analyzed with hierarchical linear (random coefficient) modeling (Study 1); 3 x 2 between-persons factorial experiment analyzed with random coefficient modeling and multilevel moderated mediation (Study 2)
industry: Aluminum manufacturing and metal processing (Study 1); university HRM course (Study 2)
time_period: August-October 2011 (Study 1); not reported for Study 2
units: Employees rated by their direct supervisors (Study 1); undergraduate students working in dyads (Study 2)
n_sample: 240 employees in 34 groups (Study 1); 132 undergraduates (Study 2)
authors: Černe, M.; Nerstad, C. G. L.; Dysvik, A.; Škerlavaj, M.
theories: achievement goal theory (Ames, 1992a; Nicholls, 1984, 1989); norm of reciprocity (Gouldner, 1960); regulatory focus theory (Higgins, 1997); social exchange theory (Blau, 1964)
keywords: creativity; knowledge hiding; mastery climate; motivational climate; performance climate; reciprocal distrust loop; social exchange theory
research_question: How does knowledge hiding affect the knowledge hider's own creativity, and how do perceived mastery and performance climates moderate this relationship? The study proposes a reciprocal distrust loop, grounded in social exchange theory and the norm of reciprocity, as the interpersonal mechanism explaining why hiding knowledge backfires on the hider.
hypotheses:
- H1: Knowledge hiding is negatively related to a knowledge hider's creativity.
- H2: A coworker's distrust mediates the negative relationship between knowledge hiding and a knowledge hider's creativity.
- H3: A perceived mastery climate moderates the relationship between knowledge hiding and creativity; the higher the perceived mastery climate, the less negative the relationship.
- H4: A perceived performance climate moderates the relationship between knowledge hiding and creativity; the higher the perceived performance climate, the more negative the relationship.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on social exchange theory and the norm of reciprocity, the authors argue that when employee A intentionally hides knowledge that employee B has requested, distrust is created and B retaliates by hiding knowledge from A. This reciprocated hiding denies the initial knowledge hider access to the alternatives, example solutions, and relevant ideas needed for creative work, so knowledge hiding backfires on the hider's own creativity. A mastery climate (valuing effort, cooperation, learning, and skill development) overrides these reciprocity norms and attenuates the creativity penalty, whereas a performance climate (emphasizing normative ability, social comparison, and intrateam competition) strengthens adherence to reciprocity norms and makes the negative relationship stronger.
data_measures: Study 1: field survey of 240 employees and their 34 direct supervisors in two Slovenian companies (an aluminum manufacturer and a metal-processing firm), with data collected in August, September, and October 2011. Knowledge hiding was self-reported on Connelly et al.'s (2012) 12-item scale (alpha = .89); creativity was supervisor-rated on Zhou and George's (2001) 13-item scale (alpha = .95); perceived mastery and performance climates used Nerstad et al.'s 14-item instrument (alpha = .79 and .84), aggregated to the group level; the creative requirement of each position, rated by an independent HRM expert blind to the study, served as a control. Estimation used hierarchical linear (random coefficient) modeling on employees nested in groups. Study 2: a 3 (mastery climate / performance climate / no climate induced) x 2 (knowledge hiding low / high) between-persons factorial experiment with 132 second-year undergraduates working in dyads on a two-stage marketing scenario; creativity was rated by two independent expert raters (ICC2 = .83); distrust was rated by the other dyad member; prevention focus was measured with nine adapted items from Lockwood et al.'s (2002) general regulatory focus measure; analyses used random coefficient modeling (HLM 7, MPlus 6) and multilevel moderated mediation procedures (Bauer et al., 2006). Study 1 is cross-sectional and associational; the randomized manipulations in Study 2 were added to strengthen causal inferences.
key_findings: Study 1: H1 supported, knowledge hiding was negatively and significantly related to creativity (γ = -.21, p < .01). H3 supported: a significant positive knowledge hiding x mastery climate interaction (γ = .17, p < .05); knowledge hiding predicted lower creativity when the mastery climate was low (γ = -.39, p < .01) but not when it was high (γ = -.01, n.s.). H4 received only marginal support: the knowledge hiding x performance climate interaction was marginally significant (γ = -.12, p = .07), with the slope more negative in groups perceiving a higher performance climate. Study 2: the knowledge-hiding manipulation significantly decreased a respondent's own creativity (γ = -.26, p < .01); knowledge hiding decreased creativity in the performance climate and control conditions but not in the mastery climate condition (supporting H3). Three-path mediation analysis supported the reciprocal distrust loop (H2), with distrust mediating the knowledge hiding-creativity relationship in all motivational climate conditions; prevention focus also uniquely mediated the relationship, so interpersonal (social) and intrapsychic mechanisms represent different sides of the same coin.
theoretical_contribution: The study's first contribution to the creativity literature is establishing the existence of a distrust loop between knowledge hiding and creativity: the very actions deemed by knowledge hiders as self-protective can backfire by undermining their own creativity, answering calls to enrich knowledge about social influences on creativity. Second, it introduces the moderating role of motivational climate: a mastery climate overrides the reciprocity norms underlying the social exchange in the knowledge hiding-creativity relationship, shifting explanation from personal dispositions to context. The findings also extend research on help seeking and help giving (Mueller & Kamdar, 2011) by showing positive gains, in the form of personal creativity, from giving knowledge and information to others.
practical_implication: Managers can mitigate the negative influence of knowledge hiding on a knowledge hider's creativity by facilitating a mastery climate, which fosters trust rather than distrust; stimulating a performance climate (emphasizing competition and goal achievement at any cost) leads to even worse scenarios, so providing incentives for employees to "betray" their coworkers should be avoided. For employees who intentionally hide knowledge, the two studies show that "what goes around comes around": hiders receive reciprocated selfish treatment from coworkers that ultimately decreases their own creativity, so they should engage in less knowledge-hiding behavior to facilitate their own creative processes.
limitations: Knowledge hiding was self-reported and, as a low-base-rate and undesirable behavior, may be underreported; Study 1 is cross-sectional, so reverse causality cannot be excluded (less creative employees may be more inclined to hide knowledge), and sequential data on the distrust loop could not be collected. In Study 2, the mastery climate manipulation may have confounded cooperation and learning with the knowledge-hiding manipulation, rating distrust after the first stage of the task may have affected behavior in the second stage, and participants were not randomly assigned to dyads. The student sample poses a potential threat to generalizability, although the authors argue that knowledge hiding and creativity are relevant for all workers.
future_research: The authors call for research exploring work situations and factors beyond motivational climate (for example, perceived supervisor support, decision autonomy, and goal orientation) that stimulate or hinder the negative relationship between knowledge hiding and creativity. They ask future studies to rule out potential confounds by producing cleaner manipulations of the three mastery climate dimensions (cooperation, the important role each individual plays, and learning) and to vary the measurement order of distrust. Because the performance climate findings were not consistent across the two studies, that moderation should be interpreted with caution and warrants further research.
abstract: Knowledge hiding prevents colleagues from generating creative ideas, but it may also have negative consequences for the creativity of a knowledge hider. Drawing on social exchange theory, we propose that when employees hide knowledge, they trigger a reciprocal distrust loop in which coworkers are unwilling to share knowledge with them. We further suggest that these effects are contingent on motivational climate, in such a way that the negative effects of an individual’s hiding knowledge on his/her own creativity are enhanced in a performance climate and attenuated in a mastery climate. A field study of 240 employees nested in 34 groups revealed a negative relationship between knowledge hiding and knowledge hiders’ creativity as well as a moderating role of a mastery climate. Study 2 replicated these findings in an experimental study of 132 undergraduate students, testing a reciprocal distrust loop and comparing it with an alternative intrapsychic explanatory process based on situational regulatory focus. Implications for practice and future research are discussed.

title: Newcomers Abroad: Expatriate Adaptation during Early Phases of International Assignments
methods: Longitudinal survey study; four monthly web surveys (times 1-4) during the first months of international assignments; two-level random coefficient (growth) models in HLM 6; mediated regression with indirect-effect tests; hierarchical regressions; measurement invariance tests and CFA in LISREL 8.8
industry: Energy (expatriates of one large multinational Global 100 company)
country: Host countries: US, Canada, UK, and Australia (expatriates of 25 nationalities)
time_period: First four months of new international assignments; participants recruited on a rolling basis over 18 months (calendar dates not reported in paper)
units: Expatriate managers who had recently begun a new international assignment
n_sample: 70 (times 1-3 analyses; 61 provided complete data through time 4; 118 initially surveyed)
authors: Firth, B. M.; Chen, G.; Kirkman, B. L.; Kim, K.
theories: challenge-hindrance stressor framework (Cavanaugh et al., 2000; LePine et al., 2005); control theory (Carver & Scheier, 1982); work motivation framework (Carver & Scheier, 1982; Kanfer & Heggestad, 1997; Kuhl, 1985)
keywords: assignment satisfaction; challenge stressors; cross-cultural motivation; expatriate adjustment; hindrance stressors; newcomer socialization; premature return intention; psychological empowerment; work adjustment
research_question: The paper examines the nature, antecedents, and outcomes of changes in expatriate work adjustment: why and how motivational states (cross-cultural motivation, psychological empowerment) and stress cognitions (challenge and hindrance stressors) relate to initial levels of, and changes in, expatriates' work adjustment during the first months of an international assignment, and how adjustment change in turn relates to assignment satisfaction and premature return intention.
hypotheses:
- H1: Expatriates' (a) psychological empowerment and (b) cross-cultural motivation positively relate to initial levels of work adjustment.
- H2: Expatriates' initial work adjustment mediates a negative relationship between expatriates' (a) psychological empowerment and (b) cross-cultural motivation and changes in work adjustment over time.
- H3: Challenge stressors positively relate to changes in expatriates' work adjustment over time (expatriates with higher challenge stressors exhibit more positive, or less negative, adjustment change).
- H4: Hindrance stressors negatively relate to (a) initial levels of and (b) changes in expatriates' work adjustment over time.
- H5a: Changes in work adjustment positively relate to assignment satisfaction.
- H5b: Changes in work adjustment negatively relate to premature return intention.
mechanism_summary: Building on Kanfer and Heggestad's (1997) work motivation framework integrated with control theory (Carver & Scheier, 1982), the paper argues that motivational states and stress-related cognitions trigger motivation control and emotion control strategies that direct and sustain effort toward assignment goals. Expatriates higher in cross-cultural motivation and psychological empowerment immediately devote effort toward work goals and therefore experience higher initial work adjustment; per control theory's negative feedback cycle, the resulting positive discrepancies between actual and desired adjustment lead them to divert subsequent effort elsewhere, producing steeper declines in work adjustment over time. Challenge stressors lead expatriates to gradually increase effort to attain associated benefits, mitigating this decline, whereas hindrance stressors were expected to drain regulatory resources away from adjustment. Because adjustment perceptions reflect a sensemaking process, the rate and direction of adjustment change inform expatriates' appraisals of their assignment, shaping assignment satisfaction and premature return intention.
data_measures: Data came from expatriates of a large multinational Global 100 company in the energy industry; for 18 months the firm provided monthly contact lists of expatriates who had recently begun a new international assignment, and participants completed four confidential web surveys one month apart (times 1-4). Of 118 expatriates, 70 (59 percent) provided complete times 1-3 data (Hypotheses 1-4) and 61 provided complete data at all four time points (Hypothesis 5). Measures (1 "strongly disagree" to 5 "strongly agree" unless noted): cross-cultural motivation = Ang et al.'s (2007) five-item scale (time 1); psychological empowerment = Spreitzer's (1995) 12-item scale reworded to the current assignment (time 1); challenge and hindrance stressors = six- and five-item scales from Cavanaugh et al. (2000), rated 1 "produces no stress" to 5 "produces a great deal of stress" (time 1); work adjustment = three-item Black and Stephens (1989) scale (times 1-3); assignment satisfaction = Hackman and Oldham's (1976) four-item job satisfaction scale reworded to the assignment (time 4); premature return intention = three-item Kraimer and Wayne (2004) scale (time 4). Controls: organizational tenure, host-country language skills, prior international experience, and days on assignment before time 1. Analyses used two-level random coefficient models in HLM 6 (with Bayes-estimated work adjustment change scores), mediated regression with indirect-effect tests (MacKinnon et al., 2004), and hierarchical regressions; the design is an associational longitudinal self-report survey, with no causal identification strategy claimed.
key_findings:
- H1a and H1b supported: psychological empowerment (beta = 0.73, p < .05) and cross-cultural motivation (beta = 0.23, p < .05) related positively to initial levels of work adjustment.
- H2a and H2b supported: initial work adjustment negatively and uniquely predicted work adjustment change (b = -.17, p < .05), and the indirect effects of cross-cultural motivation (-.04) and psychological empowerment (-.09) on adjustment change through initial adjustment were both statistically significant.
- H3 supported: challenge stressors related positively to work adjustment trajectories over time (beta = 0.12, p < .05); the challenge stressor x time interaction accounted for 3 percent of the variance in adjustment change.
- H4a and H4b not supported: hindrance stressors related to neither initial levels of work adjustment (beta = -0.08, n.s.) nor adjustment trajectories (beta = -0.02, n.s.).
- H5a and H5b supported: work adjustment change positively predicted assignment satisfaction (beta = 2.76, p < .05; delta R-squared = .14) and negatively predicted premature return intention (beta = -1.98, p < .05; delta R-squared = .08), above and beyond controls, antecedents, and initial work adjustment; results held when controlling for average adjustment levels instead.
- On average, work adjustment decreased over the study period (beta = -0.08, p < .05), with significant individual differences in linear change.
theoretical_contribution: First, the study shows that the impact of expatriates' motivational states and stressor experiences on work adjustment is time dependent, and it is among the first to demonstrate control theory's utility in explaining adjustment patterns over time, providing a motivational explanation for why expatriates with higher initial adjustment experience subsequent decreases. Second, it provides theoretical rationale and empirical evidence for the unique role of changes in work adjustment as antecedents of subsequent expatriate attitudes, above and beyond initial and average adjustment levels. Third, by viewing expatriates as newcomers, it integrates the expatriate adjustment and newcomer socialization literatures into a more complete account of how and why employees adapt to novel and challenging work demands.
practical_implication: Managers might survey potential expatriates to select those exhibiting higher cross-cultural motivation and psychological empowerment, and organizations can take actions to improve cross-cultural motivation prior to assignment and empower expatriates in their new assignments. Because expatriates with higher initial motivation are more likely to experience decreases in work adjustment, managers should take care to maintain high levels of expatriate motivation over time. The paper also identifies challenge stressors, which are largely under the control of organizational leadership (e.g., time pressures, responsibility for multiple challenging projects, making international assignments prerequisites for promotion), as a lever for maintaining higher rates of work adjustment and keeping expatriates satisfied and focused on completing their assignments.
limitations: The sample was limited to four well-developed, Western host countries, so generalizability to more culturally diverse settings is untested. The study did not directly measure the underlying motivation and emotion control processes posited to account for the hypothesized relationships, and it measured only initial levels of the motivational and stress-related antecedents, which may fluctuate over time. The authors also caution against overgeneralizing findings from the first several months of assignment to adjustment processes that unfold over longer periods, and the study relies on longitudinal self-report data capturing only expatriates' perceptions.
future_research: The authors call for process-oriented research that formally tests the posited motivation and emotion control mechanisms, including intrapersonal processes such as effort, goal setting, and goal striving. They recommend collecting repeated measures of motivation and stress-related variables to model how fluctuations dynamically impact adjustment (using mixed-effects or latent growth modeling), examining whether findings generalize to more culturally diverse countries and to longer or varying assignment durations, and studying other adjustment forms (e.g., interaction, general) and behavioral effectiveness criteria (e.g., job performance, citizenship behavior, turnover, career success) longitudinally. They also suggest measuring adjustment from multiple sources and incorporating additional stakeholders such as spouses and local coworkers.
abstract: Integrating work from the expatriate adjustment and newcomer socialization literatures within a motivational framework, we propose that motivational states and stress cognitions impact expatriates’ work adjustment patterns over time, which in turn influence important assignment attitudes. In accordance with our theorizing, analyses of longitudinal data collected from 70 expatriates during their first four months of international assignment indicated that cross-cultural motivation and psychological empowerment related positively to initial levels of adjustment, and indirectly and negatively to work adjustment change. Challenge stressors positively related to changes in work adjustment over time. In turn, changes in work adjustment significantly related to expatriates’ assignment satisfaction and premature return intention, explaining variance above and beyond that explained by average levels of work adjustment. These findings extend understanding of how and why expatriate work adjustment evolves over time, as well as the unique influence that differences in adjustment change have on important expatriate outcomes.
apa_citation: Firth, B. M., Chen, G., Kirkman, B. L., & Kim, K. (2014). Newcomers abroad: Expatriate adaptation during early phases of international assignments. *Academy of Management Journal*, 57(1), 280–300. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0574
