title: Making the Most of Where You Are: Geography, Networks, and Innovation in Organizations
methods: Longitudinal firm-year panel; intraorganizational inventor networks from patent co-inventorship data; conditional fixed-effects quasi-maximum-likelihood Poisson regression with robust standard errors, random-effects Poisson with bootstrapped standard errors, probit selection model (inverse Mills ratio), and robustness checks (alternative lags, Burt's constraint, pre-1990 non-relocating subsample, Box-Cox OLS).
industry: Nanotechnology (firms engaged in commercial nanotechnology R&D)
units: Firms (firm-year observations; networks and outcomes measured at each firm's main research facility)
n_sample: 454 firms; 2,760 firm-year observations
authors: Funk, R. J.
theories: community social capital (Coleman, 1988; Lin, 1999; Putnam, 2000); social network theory: brokerage and cohesion (Burt, 2004; Coleman, 1988; Obstfeld, 2005; Lazer & Friedman, 2007); theories of geography and innovation / localized knowledge spillovers (Audretsch & Feldman, 1996; Bathelt, Malmberg, & Maskell, 2004)
keywords: cohesion; geographic proximity; inefficiency; innovative performance; intraorganizational networks; knowledge spillovers
research_question: How does the makeup of firms' local environments influence their ability to generate innovations? Specifically, the paper theorizes and tests whether the innovative-performance benefits of geographic proximity to companies performing related R&D are moderated by the structure of intraorganizational collaboration networks among a firm's inventors.
hypotheses:
H1: Increases in proximity to other companies that perform related R&D are positively associated with a firm's innovative performance.
H2a: As proximity to companies that perform related R&D increases, a firm has greater innovative performance if the cohesiveness of its intraorganizational collaboration network also increases.
H2b: As proximity to companies that perform related R&D decreases, a firm has greater innovative performance if the inefficiency of its intraorganizational collaboration network increases.
mechanism_summary: Geographic proximity to industry peers increases access to localized knowledge spillovers (through monitoring competitors, chance encounters, informal networks, and shared local institutions), supplying the diverse knowledge that fuels novel recombination but also raising the volume of information firms must internalize, adapt, and use. Cohesive intraorganizational networks promote frequent communication, trust, and joint problem solving, so they help highly proximate firms process large volumes of complex spillover knowledge, while local interaction offsets the knowledge-stagnation risks of dense ties. Inefficient networks, which have low connectivity and diffuse information slowly, preserve diverse ideas internally, create brokerage opportunities, and facilitate parallel problem solving, thereby compensating geographically isolated firms for their diminished access to spillovers. Innovative performance is therefore greatest when the structure of a firm's inventor network fits its geographic milieu.
data_measures: Longitudinal panel of 454 US firms engaged in nanotechnology R&D, 1990-2004 (2,760 firm-year observations after firm entry and exit). Intraorganizational networks are built from co-inventorship ties formed when two or more of a firm's employees work on a patent together (a unipartite projection of the inventor-patent bipartite network from the Patent Network Dataverse; ties dropped after five years), restricted to each firm's main research facility, whose annually updated location was hand-collected from SEC filings, archived company websites, press releases, and trade publications. DVs: impact = citation-weighted sum of nanotechnology patents applied for at t + 1 and t + 2 (five-year citation window); new combinations = count of such patents first combining a previously uncombined set of USPTO subclasses. IV: firm proximity = inverse-distance-weighted measure across all other sample firms, weighted by their logged annual nanotechnology patent counts. Moderators: cohesion = the network clustering coefficient scaled by that of a simulated random network with an identical bipartite degree distribution; inefficiency = average path length within connected components scaled by the random-network expectation. Estimation is associational: conditional fixed-effects quasi-maximum-likelihood Poisson models with robust standard errors plus random-effects Poisson models with bootstrapped standard errors, with a first-stage probit selection model supplying an inverse Mills ratio; fixed effects, the lag structure, and extensive controls (e.g., local university ties, local inventor hires, distant inventors, patent stocks) are used to alleviate endogeneity concerns, supported by robustness checks (pre-1990 non-relocating facilities, one-year lags, Burt's constraint, unweighted proximity, Box-Cox OLS).
key_findings: In sum, all three hypotheses receive strong support. H1 supported: firm proximity has a positive and significant effect on both patent impact and new combinations (models 2 and 10). H2a supported: the cohesion x firm proximity interaction is positive and significant for both dependent variables (0.01, p < .01, models 6 and 14); as proximity to other nanotechnology firms increases, more cohesive inventor networks lead to greater innovative performance. For high-proximity firms, a two-standard-deviation increase above mean cohesion predicts increases of 25 percent in impact and 28 percent in new combinations, whereas for low-proximity firms the same increase predicts declines of 8 and 6 percent. H2b supported: the inefficiency x firm proximity interaction is negative and significant (-0.01; p < .05 for impact, p < .01 for new combinations), meaning that as proximity decreases, inefficient networks become beneficial; firms with much lower proximity see a 22 percent increase in impact and a 29 percent increase in new combinations for a two-standard-deviation increase in inefficiency. An unhypothesized finding is that firms combining high proximity with very cohesive networks have the greatest absolute performance; the main effect of inefficiency is positive and significant for both innovation measures.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances theories of geography and innovation by showing that the benefits firms derive from their local environments are moderated by the structure of collaboration networks among their employees, accounting both for how highly proximate firms filter and process large volumes of spillover knowledge and for how geographically isolated firms create and sustain diversity internally. It contributes to network theory by examining contingencies in the overall (global) structure of relations rather than ego networks, showing that ego-level insights favoring increased connectivity do not translate cleanly to the global level, where less connectivity can be advantageous for groups that seek diverse ideas but have limited exposure to external knowledge. The finding that less connected networks can improve collective innovation also pushes community social capital research, and ecological and institutional work on local community effects, toward a more nuanced, contingency-based perspective.
practical_implication: Managers seeking to stimulate innovation should consider structuring teams in ways that limit overall ties among their R&D employees when those employees have little exposure to new knowledge from peers at proximate organizations, for example by creating formal units housing separate project teams or skunk-works separations; by contrast, managers operating in settings proximate to industry peers should increase cohesion among R&D employees, for example through frequent meetings that bring together employees from diverse projects for collective problem solving. For entrepreneurs or managers choosing a location for a new venture or relocating an existing one, the findings help evaluate the trade-offs of different kinds of locations, and closely monitoring patterns of collaboration among employees might attenuate some of the innovation disadvantages of isolation.
limitations: The proximity measure is based on distance to other firms, whereas universities, nonprofit research institutes, and government laboratories active in nanotechnology may also provide spillover benefits, and for some firms distance to a key partner could matter more than overall proximity. In addition, models that derive network and innovation data from archival sources like patents miss collaborative ties and innovations that leave no paper trail and do not account for informal contributions, a problem the author mitigates by studying a field in which patenting is commonplace.
future_research: The paper calls for more nuanced measures of regional composition to better understand the effects of geography and intraorganizational ties; for alternative data on intraorganizational ties and performance, such as scientific publications or surveys, including better documentation of employees' interpersonal connections outside the organization and the human resource practices that facilitate or constrain the persistence of those ties; and for systematic research explaining the success of geographically isolated firms. It also urges research on how intraorganizational collaboration patterns shape the geographic diffusion of knowledge and regional economies, and on identifying the applicability of different network contingencies across ego and global levels of analysis.
abstract: Drawing on insights from macro- and microlevel research, I develop and test a theory of how the makeup of firms’ local environments influences their ability to generate innovations. I propose that although geographic proximity to industry peers can enhance performance, such effects are moderated by intraorganizational network structures. Data on collaborations among inventors and the geographic locations of 454 US companies active in nanotechnology R&D between 1990 and 2004 are used to show that as proximity to industry peers decreases—and knowledge spillovers become less common—inefficient networks are beneficial because they create and sustain diversity internally. For firms with high proximity, more cohesive network structures that facilitate information processing are desirable.

title: Rethinking Management Scholarship
methods: Editorial essay (From the Editors); no empirical design or analysis.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: George, G.
keywords: context; grand challenges; management scholarship; relevance; rigor; theoretical contribution
research_question: Not reported in paper
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: rebalance relevance with rigor by promoting strong empirical work that informs practice, bringing the context center stage and moving the organizational problem to the forefront.
- Problem focus: manuscripts should be motivated by clearly articulated problem statements or research questions rooted in managerial challenges, rather than by smaller literature "gaps" or by adding untested moderators, mediators, and moderated mediators.
- Context: context shapes the boundary conditions and assumptions of the theories being examined; authors should integrate the setting (e.g., an organization's culture and policies, or industry characteristics) into the motivation and framing of the study.
- Embedding practices: a new reviewer evaluation criterion ("Engages an important problem for organizations"), reviewer education, editorials coauthored with a senior executive, thought leader, or scholar from a different field, and experimentation with the "house style."
- Workflow changes: shorter first-round reviews (2-3 pages with 4-6 major points), guidance to keep "Response to Reviewers" documents to about 20 pages, earlier "conditional accept" decisions, and a goal of keeping the first-submission-to-in-press cycle under 500 days.

This inaugural editorial by the 20th editorial team of the Academy of Management Journal argues that the dominant paradigm of motivating studies through a rather elusive "theoretical contribution," often achieved by adding moderators and mediators without regard to an organizational problem or phenomenon, has shifted the field's focus away from relevance and its applied nature. The team's proposed remedy is to make organizational problems and contexts the starting point of empirical research, and to embed that philosophy through reviewer criteria, author guidance, coauthored editorials, and workflow reforms.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The editorial reframes what counts as a theoretical contribution: rather than deftness of theoretical manipulation using constructs, moderators, and moderated mediators, contribution should be a coherent explanation of how, when, and why phenomena occur. It positions problem-focused framing and context, which shapes theories' boundary conditions and assumptions, as the route to theoretical and empirical contribution, shifting discussion from smaller "gaps" in the literature to managerial, organizational, and societal problems that need to be addressed.
practical_implication: For authors submitting to AMJ, the editorial signals that manuscripts should engage important organizational problems and integrate the context into their framing; authors may suggest action editors and five potential reviewers from the editorial review board, should disclose prior use of a dataset and individuals who commented on earlier versions, and are advised to keep "Response to Reviewers" documents to roughly 20 pages. Reviewers are asked to score manuscripts on the new criterion of engaging an important problem for organizations and to write shorter, more focused first-round reviews (2-3 pages with 4-6 major points).
limitations: The editorial acknowledges that an incoming editor is not the reviewer: without consensus and guidance, reviewers will likely revert to habit, so the team's efforts in informing and educating reviewers will only slowly take hold. It also notes that it is difficult to define turnaround targets given author response time, reviewer speed, and editorial engagement.
future_research: The editorial encourages pursuing bold ideas and "Grand Challenges" in management, adopting less conventional approaches to address significant, unresolved problems. It announces editorials coauthored with senior executives, thought leaders, or scholars from different fields as stage setters for opening up fresh new areas of inquiry, with the stated aim of making AMJ less formulaic, more interesting, and decidedly relevant in tackling managerial, organizational, and societal problems.

title: Courage as Identity Work: Accounts of Workplace Courage
methods: Narrative analysis supplemented by grounded theory coding and constant comparison; four-phase analysis of 89 written courage accounts with an independent second-coder reliability check
industry: Multiple industries (respondents employed in a wide range of jobs, occupations, and industries)
time_period: 2009 (participants recruited during April and June 2009)
units: Written narrative accounts of workplace courage (one account per respondent)
authors: Koerner, M. M.
theories: identity theory (Burke & Stets, 2009); identity work (Sveningsson & Alvesson, 2003; Alvesson & Willmott, 2002); sensemaking (Weick, 1995)
keywords: identity processes; identity tensions; identity work; narratives; workplace courage
research_question: The study asks three questions: (1) How do identity tensions influence acts of workplace courage? (2) How does courage-based identity work unfold in the storylines reflected in courage narratives? (3) How does courage-based identity work help to reconcile identity tensions in accounts of courage?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Triggering conditions: identity tensions, i.e., incompatibilities among identities (self-identity vs. position/role identity, self-identity vs. relational identity, self-identity vs. group/organizational identity, one social identity vs. a different social identity, and opposing values within one's self-identity) that produce uncertainty, dissonance, anxiety, distress, and sometimes excitement (sensebreaking).
- Process / storylines: five storylines ordered by the courageous actor's level of proactivity, from low to high: endurance, reaction, opposition, creation, plus a no-courage storyline.
- Identity work forms: preserving an identity by withstanding unchangeable situations (endurance); repairing an identity by admitting fault or strengthening it by responding to a challenge or crisis (reaction); strengthening, revising, asserting, or reaffirming an identity by opposing more powerful individuals or organizational forces (opposition); creating a new identity or strengthening one by seizing risky opportunities (creation); no identity work performed (no courage).
- Contextual forces: relationships, power imbalances, and organizational norms, rules, and standards both foster and inhibit courage-based identity work.
- Emergent outcomes: reconciliation of identity tension, in which current identities are verified or modified, new identities are adopted, self- and social identities become coherent, and the actor's authentic self is revealed, accompanied by a sense of integrity, pride, joy, relief, and confidence; in no-courage accounts there is no reconciliation, and shame, regret, and frustration follow.

In the proposed model, identity tension operates as a sensebreaking mechanism: incompatibilities among a person's self- and social identities create dissonance and lead individuals to question which of their identities are most central. Courage-based identity work is the corresponding sensemaking mechanism, a courageous act through which individuals weigh contrasting alternatives, select the most salient identity, and reduce the tension. The process works as an identity distillation in which more salient identities are separated from less salient ones in the pursuit of a coherent identity; acts of no courage involve no identity work and leave the tension unreconciled.
data_measures: Data are 89 written narrative accounts of workplace courage (one per respondent; 92 to 2,672 words, mean 470 words) submitted anonymously through an online data collection tool by business professionals enrolled in an evening MBA program at a western US liberal arts college; respondents described an incident of workplace courage they personally experienced or observed, rated the degree of courage demonstrated, and explained how they defined courage. The narrative was the unit of analysis. Analysis combined narrative analytic techniques with grounded theory coding and constant comparison across four phases: microanalysis and open coding of the first 25 accounts; development of preliminary categories (storylines, identity tensions, characters, organizational context); recoding of all 89 accounts using operational definitions, with an independent reliability check by a colleague holding a Ph.D. in business administration; and storyline-by-storyline analysis using story skeletons.
key_findings: Five storylines organize the accounts: opposition (56%), reaction (19%), no courage (17%), creation (5%), and endurance (4%). The three components of courage (morally worthy goal; risk, threat, or obstacle; and intentional action) were present in all but two narratives. Identity tensions precipitated the courageous acts, and courage-based identity work reconciled them; the four forms of identity work varied by the actor's level of proactivity, from low (endurance) to high (creation). In courage accounts, protagonists were described as having strong, salient personal values (93%), identifying strongly with their occupation, work group, or company (85%), and being high in self-efficacy (96%). References to relationships appeared in 93% of narratives, power imbalances in 81%, and organizational norms, rules, and standards in 77%; these forces both fostered and inhibited courage, and in 80% of accounts the act was intended to benefit others rather than just the actor. Courageous acts were followed by a sense of integrity, pride, joy, relief, and confidence, whereas no-courage accounts involved no identity work, left identity tensions unreconciled, and were followed by shame, regret, and frustration.
theoretical_contribution: The main contribution is a model depicting the identity dynamics reflected in accounts of workplace courage: a three-step identity distillation process in which identity tension is aroused (sensebreaking), courage-based identity work is performed (sensemaking), and identity tension is reconciled. The study conceptualizes courage as a form of identity work, a conceptualization not proposed in prior research, adding a distinctive and more intense tactic to the identity work repertoire for situations in which two or more highly valued identities conflict, and showing how courageous acts help individuals manage discrepancies among self- and social identities. It also extends theory on the process of courage by proposing self- and social identity as crucial constructs in a courageous act and identifies four forms of courage-based identity work (endurance, reaction, opposition, creation) that broaden the oppositional focus of prior workplace courage research.
practical_implication: For organizational leaders, courageous acts can serve as a signal that identity boundaries have been crossed; when those boundaries were crossed significantly or repeatedly, perceived negative outcomes followed, including individuals seeking new employment, no longer identifying with the organization, or actively disidentifying with it. Because respondents generally viewed courage-based identity work as a healthy response to organizational demands perceived as inappropriate, the paper's stated implication is that organizational leaders should welcome, support, and even promote courageous acts at work.
limitations: All participants had college degrees, so low-skilled and uneducated workers are not represented; the average age was 30, ethnicity mirrored a predominately Caucasian community, and males were overrepresented. Written accounts may lack the depth of a lengthy interview, preclude follow-up questions, and may emphasize what respondents believed the researcher or other readers wanted to hear. Because the accounts are retrospective narratives, storytellers may have omitted, added, or changed details; the findings reflect how people make sense of courageous acts rather than how courageous acts occur objectively, some respondents may have fabricated identity tensions to explain courageous acts, and some positive feelings may have been self-enhancing rationalizations.
future_research: The paper states that the endurance and creation forms of workplace courage deserve closer examination, and that courage focused on creation is likely an important type of workplace courage that warrants more attention given the importance of innovation and the attention entrepreneurship is receiving in business. It also notes that narratives offer promise as a method of gaining insight about both courage and identity, since sensemaking is integral to understanding both phenomena.
abstract: This study focuses on the intersection of identity dynamics and workplace courage. I examine accounts of courage submitted by business professionals and articulate the identity processes underlying the accounts. The narratives illustrate four storylines that reflect four distinct forms of courage and one storyline that reflects a lack of courage. In the accounts, identity tensions precipitate courageous acts, and courage-based identity work is used to reconcile the tensions. The findings suggest that in accounts of workplace courage, courageous behavior is viewed as an important form of identity work that helps individuals to minimize incongruities between their self- and social identities.

title: Power to the Principals! An Experimental Look at Shareholder Say-On-Pay Voting
methods: Two fully crossed 2x2 between-subjects lab experiments simulating shareholder say-on-pay votes; logistic regression with marginal effects, OLS regression, and Baron and Kenny (1986) mediation tests
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual MBA students voting as shareholders in a simulated say-on-pay vote
n_sample: 93 (Study 1); 88 (Study 2)
authors: Krause, R.; Whitler, K. A.; Semadeni, M.
theories: agency theory (Jensen & Meckling, 1976; Eisenhardt, 1989); loss aversion in riskless choice (Tversky & Kahneman, 1991); prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)
keywords: CEO compensation; agency theory; agency-normative assessment; loss aversion; prospect theory; say-on-pay; shareholder voting
research_question: What impacts shareholders' preferences and ultimate voting behavior in nonbinding say-on-pay votes on CEO compensation? The authors propose that shareholders' frame of reference, determined jointly by CEO rewards and firm performance, determines their preferences regarding the link between CEO pay and firm performance.
hypotheses:
- H1: With firm performance held constant, higher CEO rewards decrease the probability that shareholders vote to approve CEO pay.
- H2: With CEO rewards held constant, poorer firm performance decreases the probability that shareholders vote to approve CEO pay.
- H3: Higher CEO rewards decrease the probability that shareholders vote to approve CEO pay only when firm performance is poor.
- H4: The effect of high CEO rewards on the probability shareholders vote to approve CEO pay is mediated by shareholders' agency-normative assessment.
- H5: The effect of poor firm performance on the probability shareholders vote to approve CEO pay is mediated by shareholders' agency-normative assessment.
mechanism_summary: Shareholders, as principals, are assumed to want the strongest firm performance for the lowest CEO compensation (agency theory), but following Tversky and Kahneman's (1991) model of loss aversion in riskless choice, agency losses (high CEO rewards paired with poor firm performance) loom larger in shareholders' minds than commensurate agency gains. Firm performance and CEO rewards jointly determine whether shareholders occupy a loss, neutral, or gain position, and CEO rewards reduce approval only when shareholders vote from a loss position. The proximal mechanism is shareholders' agency-normative assessment, an evaluation of the appropriateness of the CEO's rewards from an agency perspective that is disproportionately impacted by a loss position and mediates the effects of CEO rewards and firm performance on the vote.
data_measures: Two fully crossed two-by-two between-subjects lab experiments with random assignment simulated a say-on-pay vote using a notice modeled after a Fortune 500 firm's actual say-on-pay notice (Aflac Incorporated, 2010). Study 1: 93 of 107 full-time students in a first-year MBA strategy course at a large research university with a BusinessWeek "Top 20" MBA program (results validated on a convenience sample of 63 experienced investors). Study 2: 88 full-time first- and second-year MBA students prompted to act as mutual fund managers whose fund held 15 percent of its assets in the focal firm. DV: approval, coded 1 for a vote to approve and 0 for a vote to reject (logistic regression; marginal effects reported). Mediator: agency-normative assessment, measured in Study 1 with the single item "To what extent do you agree that the CEO's pay is justified, given the performance of the firm?" (7-point scale, standardized) and in Study 2 with a three-item average. Manipulations: CEO pay increase (pay rising from about $9 million to $11 million vs. falling from $13 million to $11 million) in Study 1, high vs. low CEO pay (95th vs. 5th percentile of Fortune 500 CEO pay) in Study 2, and shareholder return deficit (return 20 percentage points below vs. above the S&P 500 average in Study 1, the industry average in Study 2). Mediation was tested with Baron and Kenny's (1986) three-step method (logit and OLS); the authors note that experiments enable researchers to draw conclusions about the causal direction between related variables.
key_findings: Study 1: H1 not supported (an increase in CEO pay had no significant marginal effect on approval); H2 supported (a shareholder return deficit decreased the probability of approval by 20 percentage points, p < .05); H3 supported (a CEO pay increase decreased approval by 27 percentage points when shareholder return was below the S&P 500, p < .05, but had no significant effect when shareholder value was above the S&P 500); H4 and H5 supported (agency-normative assessment, marginal effect 0.23, p < .001, accounted for all of the overall effects of both treatments). Study 2: all five hypotheses supported; high CEO pay reduced approval by 18 percentage points (p < .05), a shareholder return deficit reduced it by 36 percentage points (p < .001), high CEO pay decreased approval by 29 percentage points only in the loss vs. neutral frame (p < .05), and including agency-normative assessment (marginal effect 0.27, p < .001) eliminated any effect of either treatment. Overall, shareholders value pay for performance but exhibit loss aversion, reacting to CEO rewards only when facing a potential loss, not when facing a potential gain.
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates agency theory and prospect theory, via Tversky and Kahneman's (1991) model of loss aversion in riskless choice, to explain shareholder voting behavior more completely than either theory alone, applying prospect theory to shareholders' side of the agency contract rather than to CEOs' response to incentives. It introduces a new construct, shareholders' agency-normative assessment, as the mediating mechanism, and contributes theory-based, experimental evidence on causal mechanisms to a shareholder voting literature that remains underdeveloped and dominated by archival studies.
practical_implication: Boards of directors should take shareholders' frame of reference into account when presenting CEO pay for a say-on-pay vote: shareholders react very negatively to raising CEO pay in times of poor firm performance, so boards should be wary of doing so. Because a decrease in CEO pay, or simply low CEO pay, only alters shareholders' behavior in times of poor performance, symbolically low compensation should be adopted with caution, since raising it later may be difficult if performance is weak. Boards can also proactively educate shareholders and justify CEO compensation ahead of annual shareholder meetings, especially since a no-vote may register displeasure with the board's compensation committee rather than the CEO.
limitations: Lab experiments are less generalizable because they are conducted in controlled settings, and the study offers no indication of how the individual-level loss aversion identified maps onto communities of investors, who routinely exhibit herding behavior. Only a few variables could be manipulated in any given study, and common method variance may still be present given the high correlations between the mediator and outcome, especially in Study 2. Because several conditions changed between Study 1 and Study 2 (the institutional investor prompt, extreme CEO pay values, the industry performance benchmark, and the high-salience 15 percent portfolio stake), the authors cannot identify which altered condition explains the support for H1 found only in Study 2.
future_research: The authors call for analysis of actual say-on-pay vote outcomes once data become available, testing the hypotheses on institutional investors, and joining work on collective investor biases to understand how individual-level loss aversion aggregates into shareholder vote outcomes. They suggest replicating the studies while altering the pay mix (stock options, restricted stock, bonus pay, salary), using alternative reference points and conditions (past firm performance, environmental conditions, CEO tenure, board monitoring activity, the CEO's past compensation), and shifting the decision frame to relative deprivation by contrasting CEO pay with an average worker's pay. They also encourage techniques such as measuring variables at different times to study agency-normative assessment without common method variance.
abstract: With recent legislation mandating that publicly traded corporations submit their CEOs' compensation for a nonbinding shareholder vote, a systematic understanding of shareholder preferences has never been so important. In spite of this, relatively little is known about what impacts shareholders' preferences and, subsequently, their ultimate voting behavior. We integrate two theories to help frame the question and to help predict shareholder behavior. Per agency theory, shareholders, as principals, will disapprove of high CEO rewards and poor firm performance, symmetrically assessing gains and losses. Per prospect theory, shareholders will be loss averse, responding much more strongly to being in a loss position than to being in a gain or neutral position. We combine these theories' predictions in two lab experiments in which we simulate a shareholder "say-on-pay" vote, hypothesizing that shareholders will be concerned with agency costs, but only when they are in a loss position. The results of these simulated votes suggest that shareholders do value "pay for performance," in keeping with agency theory. However, shareholders exhibit this focus on agency-normative prescriptions asymmetrically, showing loss aversion in keeping with prospect theory. This finding has significant implications for both theory and practice as shareholder votes become a regular and high-profile occurrence.

title: Abusive Supervision and Retaliation: A Self-Control Framework
methods: Two multi-wave online field surveys (three time points separated by approximately one week); confirmatory factor analyses (AMOS 19.0); hierarchical multiple regression (SPSS 19.0); moderated mediation via Edwards and Lambert's (2007) approach with 1,000 bootstrapped samples
industry: Diverse industries (e.g., computers and mathematics, business and finance, sales, production, education, government, health care support)
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Full-time employees who interacted regularly with their supervisors
n_sample: 196 (Study 1); 188 (Study 2)
authors: Lian, H.; Brown, D. J.; Ferris, D. L.; Liang, L. H.; Keeping, L. M.; Morrison, R.
theories: bases of social power (French & Raven, 1959); emotion regulation (Gross, 2001); self-control theory (Baumeister & Vohs, 2007)
keywords: abusive supervision; hostility toward supervisor; motivation to self-control; retaliatory behavior; self-control capacity; supervisor coercive power; supervisor reward power; supervisor-directed aggression
research_question: The paper addresses the paradox of whether subordinates will or will not aggress against an abusive supervisor. It asks how subordinates' self-control capacity and motivation to self-control (perceived supervisor coercive and reward power) jointly determine hostile emotional reactions and supervisor-directed aggression following abusive supervision.
hypotheses:
- H1a: In a significant three-way interaction, the relation between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression is strongest when subordinates neither have self-control capacity nor perceive that their supervisor has coercive power.
- H1b: In a significant three-way interaction, the relation between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression is strongest when subordinates neither have self-control capacity nor perceive that their supervisor has reward power.
- H1c: The three-way interaction between abusive supervision, self-control capacity, and supervisor coercive power (H1a) is stronger than the three-way interaction between abusive supervision, self-control capacity, and supervisor reward power (H1b) in the prediction of supervisor-directed aggression.
- H2: Hostility toward supervisors mediates the relation between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression.
- H3: The relation between abusive supervision and hostility toward supervisors is moderated by self-control capacity: the relation is weaker when self-control capacity is high rather than low.
- H4: The relation between hostility toward supervisors and supervisor-directed aggression is strongest when subordinates neither have self-control capacity nor perceive their supervisor as having coercive power.
- H5: The indirect relation between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression through the mediating role of hostility toward supervisors is strongest when subordinates neither have self-control capacity nor perceive their supervisor as having coercive power.
mechanism_summary: Abusive supervision is theorized as an interpersonal provocation that elicits hostility toward the supervisor, a hostile impulse that must be controlled. Whether that impulse becomes supervisor-directed aggression depends jointly on self-control capacity (the ability to restrain retaliatory urges, which also mitigates the extent to which hostile feelings are experienced) and motivation to self-control, operationalized as perceived supervisor power to punish (coercive power) or reward. Subordinates who possess neither the capacity nor the motivation to self-control reciprocate supervisory abuse with abuse in kind, whereas possessing either ingredient enables them to override their natural inclination to retaliate. Following the principle that bad is stronger than good, punishment-based coercive power is expected to outweigh reward power as a motivator of self-control.
data_measures: Two multi-wave online surveys of full-time employees who interacted regularly with their supervisors, each with three measurement points separated by approximately one week (Study 1: n = 196, recruited through advertisements on online forums; Study 2: n = 188, recruited through University of Waterloo alumni offices and public advertisements). Measures: abusive supervision = Tepper's (2000) 15-item scale; supervisor coercive and reward power = Hinkin and Schriesheim's (1989) four-item scales; self-control capacity = 25-item scale (Ciarocco, Twenge, Muraven, & Tice, 2007); supervisor-directed aggression = Mitchell and Ambrose's (2007) ten-item scale; hostility toward supervisor (Study 2) = adapted hostility subscale of the PANAS-X (Watson & Clark, 1994). Controls: age, tenure with supervisor, and gender, plus impression management (Paulhus, 1991) in Study 1. Analyses: confirmatory factor analyses (AMOS 19.0), hierarchical multiple regression (SPSS 19.0), and Edwards and Lambert's (2007) moderated path-analysis approach with 1,000 bootstrapped samples. The design is associational: the authors state that the cross-sectional design does not allow causal inferences.
key_findings: Study 1: the three-way abusive supervision x self-control capacity x supervisor coercive power interaction significantly predicted supervisor-directed aggression (b = .23, p < .01), and the abusive supervision-aggression relation was strongest when subordinates were low in self-control capacity and perceived coercive power was low, supporting H1a. The parallel three-way interaction with supervisor reward power was not significant (b = -.21, n.s.), failing to support H1b; usefulness analyses showed the coercive-power interaction added explained variance (delta R-squared = .02, p < .01) while the reward-power interaction did not (delta R-squared = .01, n.s.), supporting H1c. Study 2: the abusive supervision x self-control capacity interaction predicted hostility toward supervisors (b = -0.14, p < .05, Table 4), the relation being weaker when self-control capacity was high rather than low, supporting H3. The indirect effect of abusive supervision on supervisor-directed aggression through hostility toward supervisor was significant (.19, p < .01), supporting H2. The hostility x self-control capacity x supervisor coercive power interaction was significant (b = .23, p < .01), with the hostility-aggression relation strongest when coercive power was low and self-control capacity was low, supporting H4; the reward-power three-way interaction was again not significant (b = .07, n.s.). The indirect effect was strongest under low coercive power and low self-control capacity (.77, p < .01, significantly stronger than the other three conditions), supporting H5.
theoretical_contribution: The paper presents a self-control model of retaliation that reconciles theoretical frameworks in which supervisory power mitigates retaliatory responses with empirical results showing abused subordinates frequently do retaliate: aggression toward supervisors is a joint function of self-control capacity, motivation to self-control, and their interaction, a framework that also maps previously disparate and disconnected moderation findings onto common self-control theory constructs. It extends the abusive supervision literature's treatment of power by directly measuring perceived power rather than indirect proxies and by differentiating supervisory reward power from coercive power, showing punishment-based motivation is more effectual than reward-based motivation, in accordance with the principle that bad is stronger than good. By situating hostility toward supervisors as the mediating mechanism, the model is among the first to link the abusive supervision literature to the emotion literature and contributes to understanding of discrete emotions in the workplace.
practical_implication: For organizations and individual employees, the findings suggest selection procedures that directly assess self-control capacity and training that develops it (e.g., self-control exercises such as physical exercise programs or financial management training), as well as mindfulness training to reduce feelings of hostility in response to abusive supervision. Organizations can also maximize motivation to self-control by raising employees' awareness of the negative consequences of retaliatory actions and by strengthening workplace norms for civil behavior through training or formal civility interventions. Because abusive supervisors are provocateurs, the most straightforward route is to remove or alter aggressive supervisor behavior, including selecting individuals with high self-control capacity for supervisory positions, training supervisors' self-control, and informing supervisors of the negative consequences of engaging in abusive acts.
limitations: The authors note that the studies did not employ random population sampling, so generalizability should be viewed with some caution, and that single-source self-report data raise common-source concerns, although interactive effects offer persuasive evidence against common source effects and self-reports are considered valid for perceptual outcomes and internal states. The cross-sectional design does not allow causal inferences, and it is plausible that supervisor-directed aggression leads to abusive supervision rather than the reverse. The studies also did not directly assess the reappraisal and suppression strategies implied by the emotion-regulation account of their findings.
future_research: The paper encourages examining the model in other settings and populations, using multisource data, and using cross-lagged panel designs to untangle the causal relation between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression. It calls for directly testing reappraisal and suppression strategies and related individual differences (e.g., hostile attribution bias), examining alternative motivational factors (e.g., agreeableness, traditionality, negative reciprocity, performance-contingent self-esteem, or directly assessed motivation to self-control), and exploring downsides of the self-control process such as decreased job performance and organizational citizenship behaviors. It also suggests experience-sampling designs to examine the model at the intraindividual level and generalizing the framework to other aggression targets (organizations, coworkers, family members), covert retaliation, and displaced aggression.
abstract: There are conflicting perspectives on whether subordinates will or will not aggress against an abusive supervisor. To address this paradox we develop a self-control model of retaliatory behavior, wherein subordinates’ self-control capacity and motivation to self-control influence emotional and retaliatory reactions to provocations by enabling individuals to override their hostile impulses. In Study 1, we demonstrate that self-control capacity, motivation to self-control (supervisor coercive power), and abusive supervision interact in such a way that the strongest association between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression occurs when subordinates are low in self-control capacity and perceive their supervisor to be low in coercive power. In Study 2, we extend this finding, testing a moderated mediation model, wherein hostility toward a supervisor represents the hostile impulse resulting in retaliatory behavior, mediating the relation between abusive supervision and supervisor-directed aggression. Results from Study 2 indicate that self-control capacity allows individuals to regulate the hostile feelings experienced following abusive supervision, while self-control capacity and supervisor coercive power jointly moderate the tendency to act on one’s hostile feelings toward an abusive supervisor. We discuss implications for retaliatory behaviors at work.

title: Falling from Great (and Not-So-Great) Heights: How Initial Status Position Influences Performance after Status Loss
methods: Multi-study design: archival field study of Major League Baseball final-offer salary arbitrations analyzed with multilevel (mixed-effects) regression (Stata 12 xtmixed), plus two randomized between-participants laboratory experiments (2x2 designs) analyzed with ANOVA and Poisson regression
industry: Professional baseball (Major League Baseball) in Study 1; university-affiliated participant pools in Studies 2-3
time_period: Study 1: arbitrations from 1974 to 2011; Studies 2-3: Not reported in paper
units: Individual players (Study 1) and individual participants (Studies 2-3)
n_sample: Study 1: 199 nonpitchers who went through arbitration once, complete data on 186; Study 2: 86 participants (77 in main analyses); Study 3: 76 participants (73 in main analyses)
authors: Marr, J. C.; Thau, S.
theories: psychology of the self (Alicke & Sedikides, 2011; Steele, 1988); self-affirmation theory (Steele, 1988; Sherman & Cohen, 2006); self-threat (Baumeister, Smart, & Boden, 1996)
keywords: initial status position; self-affirmation; self-threat; status hierarchy; status loss; task performance quality
research_question: How does a person's initial position in a status hierarchy influence the quality of their task performance in the aftermath of status loss? Specifically, the authors ask whether high- or low-status individuals have more difficulty executing tasks proficiently and accurately after losing an objectively comparable amount of status.
hypotheses:
H1: The negative effect of status loss on performance quality for high-status individuals is stronger than it is for low-status individuals.
H2: Self-affirmation moderates the effect of initial status position on performance quality after status loss: high- (but not low-) status individuals perform better when they are given an opportunity for self-affirmation.
mechanism_summary: Because people strive to maintain and enhance positive self-views, high-status individuals define their superior position as a relatively more central component of the self than low-status individuals do. Losing status therefore triggers more self-threat (challenges or contradictions to a central view of the self) for high-status individuals, and self-threat interrupts the information processing necessary to execute subsequent tasks proficiently and accurately by directing attention toward the self and away from the task. As a result, high-status individuals' performance quality declines after status loss while comparable status loss leaves low-status individuals' performance unaffected. Because self-affirmation protects against threats to the self, giving high-status individuals an opportunity to self-affirm restores the quality of their performance.
data_measures: Study 1 (field): archival data on all nonpitchers who went through Major League Baseball final-offer salary arbitration once between 1974 and 2011 (n = 199; complete data on 186 players). Initial prearbitration status = composite of All-Star Game selections and four major awards (alpha = .72); status loss = losing the arbitration (dummy: 1 = loss, 0 = win); postarbitration performance quality = standardized composite of on-base percentage and slugging percentage (alpha = .90). Multilevel regressions (players nested in teams; Stata 12 xtmixed) with controls including prior performance (linear and squared), team performance and postseason play, year, player age, injuries, share of games on the current team, and the financial opportunity cost of the loss; the design is associational, and the authors state that causality cannot be determined from these results. Study 2 (lab): 2 (initial status: high vs. low) x 2 (status loss vs. no status loss) between-participants group experiment (86 participants; 77 after excluding suspicious participants) using confederates, respect-point ratings, and role titles; all participants received identical above-average performance feedback so status loss was not confounded with negative performance feedback; performance quality = summed errors on a word-search task (independent-rater reliability r = .90); Poisson regression. Study 3 (lab): 2 (initial status) x 2 (self-affirmation vs. no affirmation) between-participants computer-mediated design (76 participants; 73 after exclusions) in which all participants lost 50 percent of their respect points; affirmation was manipulated by writing about a valued personal relationship versus a trip to the grocery store; performance quality = number of low-quality responses in generating adjectives describing the taste of chocolate chip cookies (independent-rater reliability r = .92); Poisson regression.
key_findings: Study 1: a significant negative interaction between initial status position and status loss on performance quality (gamma = -.19, s.e. = .08, p = .01). Simple slopes showed that when initial status was low (-1 s.d.), status loss had no effect on performance quality (b = -0.08, p = .77), but when initial status was high (+1 s.d.), status loss had a significant negative effect (b = -0.76, p = .002); the main effect of status loss was marginally significant and negative (gamma = -.42, p = .08) and initial status position was positively related to performance quality (gamma = .17, p = .001). H1 supported. Study 2: a significant initial-status-by-status-loss interaction on errors (b = -1.17, s.e. = 0.45, p = .01); high-status participants who lost status performed more poorly (mean errors = 4.21) than high-status participants who had not lost status (mean = 1.53, p = .001) and than low-status participants who lost a comparable amount of status (mean = 0.62, p = .001), while low-status participants' performance quality was unaffected by status loss (p = .69); output quantity did not differ (p = .11), suggesting impaired ability rather than reduced motivation. H1 supported. Study 3: a significant status-by-affirmation interaction (b = -0.15, s.e. = 0.08, p = .05); high-status participants who were not affirmed gave more low-quality responses (mean = 10.67) than affirmed high-status participants (mean = 7.84, p = .005), whereas low-status participants were unaffected by affirmation (means = 9.56 vs. 9.56, p = .99). H2 supported: self-affirmation restored the quality of high-status individuals' performance.
theoretical_contribution: The paper contributes to the status literature by examining the understudied phenomenon of status loss: to the authors' knowledge it is the first series of studies investigating how high- and low-status people behave after actually losing status, rather than reacting to the prospect of losing it. The findings challenge traditional models of status in which more status is equated with greater resources and better outcomes, highlighting status loss as a negative life event in which more status resources are a liability because the self becomes implicated in holding a high-status position. Whereas research on prospective status loss suggests people increase effort to avoid loss, this research shows that those with the most status are least careful and proficient after actual loss, a self-defeating reaction that may produce further status loss and thwart status regain.
practical_implication: For understanding status loss in organizations, the authors note that high-status individuals such as star performers and high-ranking executives are the most likely to experience impaired performance after losing status yet are probably also less likely to admit or show that they feel threatened, so bad decisions and errors made in the immediate aftermath of status loss may go unrecognized by coworkers, clients, and shareholders until they have serious and potentially irreversible consequences. Study 3 gives reason for optimism: thinking about a significant relationship that makes one feel respected and worthy can restore high-quality performance, although the authors question whether those at the top of a hierarchy will seek out the affirmation they need. Because status can often be regained, finding other ways to appear worthy of a high-status position (e.g., helping one's group members) might help high-status individuals regain their position after status loss.
limitations: The authors state that causality cannot be determined from Study 1's field data, and that unobservable factors (e.g., arbitrators being more aware of high-status players' deficits, or the public visibility of high-status players increasing the magnitude of their loss) could have influenced results. In Study 1, status loss was negatively correlated with prior-year performance (r = -.14), so losing arbitration may partly have been perceived as negative performance feedback, and the on-base/slugging composite feeds into team performance; Study 2 addressed these issues with controlled feedback and an individual task. Study 2's hierarchy was zero-sum, so reactions to status loss may also have been reactions to a specific group member gaining status, and its design could not examine the role of self-threat, which the authors describe as difficult to measure accurately and which was therefore assessed only indirectly through Study 3's self-affirmation moderation-of-process design.
future_research: The authors propose investigating how those in the middle of a status hierarchy (e.g., the middle class, midlevel managers) respond to losing status; how different types of status hierarchies (bimodal, flat, zero-sum) and gradual versus abrupt losses of achieved versus ascribed status influence reactions and their downstream consequences; and extending the scope of outcomes to other organizationally relevant behaviors (organizational citizenship behaviors, counterproductive behaviors, adaptive and proactive behaviors) and to behaviors outside the context in which the status loss occurred. They also call for exploring moderators such as the centrality of status to the self and affective commitment to one's role, and alternate processes (e.g., thwarted status-striving motivation, cognitive inconsistency, inequity reduction) that might contribute to performance declines after status loss.
abstract: We investigate how initial status position influences the quality of task performance in the aftermath of status loss. We argue that despite the benefits of having status, high-status individuals experience more “self-threat”—challenges or contradictions to a central view of the self—and, consequently, have more difficulty performing well after status loss than do low-status individuals who experience a comparable loss of status. In a field study of professional baseball players (Study 1), we found that although low-status players’ performance quality was unaffected by status loss, the quality of high-status players’ performance declined significantly after losing status. In a high-involvement group experiment (Study 2), we found that high-status individuals who lost status were less proficient than both high-status individuals who did not lose status and low-status individuals who lost a comparable amount of status. However, supporting self-threat as the proposed psychological process, self-affirmation restored the quality of high-status individuals’ performance (Study 3). We discuss the practical and theoretical implications of these findings.
apa_citation: Marr, J. C., & Thau, S. (2014). Falling from great (and not-so-great) heights: How initial status position influences performance after status loss. *Academy of Management Journal*, 57(1), 223-248. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0909

title: On Melting Summits: The Limitations of Field-Configuring Events as Catalysts of Change in Transnational Climate Policy
methods: Longitudinal qualitative study of a field-configuring event series (UNFCCC COPs 1-17); participant observation, 39 semistructured interviews, and archival documents (204 Earth Negotiations Bulletin issues, UNFCCC secretariat archives, New York Times coverage) coded in ATLAS.ti
industry: Transnational climate policy field (UNFCCC climate conferences)
country: Transnational (Parties from more than 190 countries; COPs hosted worldwide)
units: UN climate conferences (COPs) in a field-configuring event series; interviews, observations, and documents
n_sample: 17 COPs; 39 semistructured interviews; 204 COP-related ENB issues
authors: Schüssler, E.; Rüling, C.-C.; Wittneben, B. B. F.
theories: field-configuring events (Lampel & Meyer, 2008; Hardy & Maguire, 2010); institutional theory (field structuration and issue-based fields; DiMaggio & Powell, 1983; Hoffman, 1999); transnational field structuration (Djelic & Quack, 2008)
keywords: field maintenance; field-configuring events; institutional change; interactional openness; temporal boundedness; transnational climate policy
research_question: The paper poses two research questions in its own words: (1) What are the causes and effects of temporal boundedness and interactional openness in a field-configuring event series? (2) How and why do field-configuring events change in the context of an evolving organizational field? Both are asked to explain why the UN climate conferences (COPs) have failed to bring about regulations to combat human-induced climate change.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: temporal boundedness (deadlines, multiyear negotiation cycles, media attention) and interactional openness (overlapping formal and informal discursive spaces among diverse field members)
- Event types: regular COPs (technical, incremental negotiation with more open interaction) versus high-stakes COPs (COP 3 Kyoto, COP 13 Bali, COP 15 Copenhagen: milestone deadlines, high expectations, strong media coverage)
- Aggregate dimensions from the coding: event staging (event calendar; issues and positions; general audience awareness) and event enactment (opportunities and spaces for interaction; negotiation tactics; observer roles)
- Process / phases: Phase 1 (1995-2005), negotiating and implementing the Kyoto Protocol; Phase 2 (2005-2012), defining the future of the UNFCCC amid growing field complexity and issue multiplication
- Triggering conditions: entry into force of the Kyoto Protocol in 2005; US withdrawal from the Kyoto process; entry of diverse new actors; multiplication of negotiation tracks
- Emergent outcomes: the event series shifts from field-endogenous catalyst of institutional change to mechanism of field maintenance; failure of the 2009 Copenhagen summit

Regular events created interactional openness through multiple formal and informal opportunities for participant exchange, supporting trust building and the incremental advancement of rules, whereas the few high-stakes events induced a stronger sense of temporal boundedness through deadlines and media attention, generating momentum. In the early phases of field development, the interaction of regular and high-stakes events facilitated institutional change by allowing for both trust building and momentum creation. After the Kyoto Protocol entered into force, growing field complexity and issue multiplication meant that the COPs ceased to be interactionally open and temporally bounded, and the event series came to maintain the field rather than change it. Deliberately staging the 2009 Copenhagen COP as a high-stakes event under these conditions prevented institutional change and resulted in an ongoing delay of substantive policy decisions.
data_measures: Longitudinal qualitative data on the UNFCCC COP event series: participant observation (one author has attended 13 major international climate policy events since 2000; two authors attended COP 14 in Poznan in 2008 and the subsequent subsidiary bodies meeting in Bonn in 2009); 39 formal semistructured interviews (28 at events, 11 follow-ups; 34 audio-taped and fully transcribed); and documents comprising 204 COP-related Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB) issues (187 daily issues plus 17 COP summaries), 58 academic articles, UNFCCC secretariat electronic archives (participant directories, press releases, official speeches, side-event registration data, budget reports), and New York Times coverage (3 articles sampled per COP plus per-COP article counts). All 204 ENBs, interviews, and observations were coded with ATLAS.ti qualitative data analysis software: a first round of descriptive coding yielded an initial scheme with 60 codes, the data were additionally coded for temporal boundedness and interactional openness, and iterative analysis produced a data structure of six second-order themes under two aggregate dimensions (event staging and event enactment).
key_findings: First, events in the series were staged and enacted in different ways: regular COPs created more interactional openness by providing multiple formal and informal opportunities for participant exchange, whereas the few high-stakes events (Kyoto, Bali, Copenhagen) induced a stronger sense of temporal boundedness through deadlines and media attention; high-stakes events led to highly visible outcomes, either new agreements (Kyoto, Bali) or a widely shared sense of failure (Copenhagen), while regular events favored incremental advancement of rules. Second, in the early phases of field development the interaction of regular and high-stakes events facilitated institutional change by allowing for both trust building and momentum creation. Third, over time the COPs ceased to be interactionally open and temporally bounded as diverse actors with vested interests entered the field, power coalitions shifted, and the events became platforms for issues not strictly related to emission reduction: growing field complexity and issue multiplication compromised the change potential of the event series in favor of field maintenance, and the deliberate staging of the Copenhagen high-stakes event in 2009 prevented institutional change and resulted in an ongoing delay of substantive policy decisions. The authors attribute the Copenhagen failure at least in part to organizers' futile attempt to stage a high-stakes event in a situation of insufficient interactional openness among field constituencies.
theoretical_contribution: The study makes two contributions to research on field-configuring events, institutional change, and the structuration of transnational fields. First, it identifies variations among different events within a series (regular versus high-stakes) that allow the authors to define the processes by which the temporal boundedness and interactional openness of field-configuring events can lead to institutional change, extending scholarly work on discursive spaces and field-configuring events (Hardy & Maguire, 2010). Second, it detects field-level conditions that limit the capacity of field-configuring events to bring about institutional change: when an issue-based field fragments into increasingly diverse membership and subissues as a result of the fluid and complex dynamics of transnational field structuration, the role of field-configuring events shifts from field-endogenous catalysts of change to mechanisms of field maintenance.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that organizers of field-configuring events need to take field structures into account when designing their events, specifically considering the complexity and diversity of issues at stake and the boundaries and authority structures of a field. Event formats such as "unconferences" or "barcamps" could be integrated into a field-configuring event series to better balance coordination with the creativity needed to imagine possible futures, which also raises the practical question of how effective a template for structuring transnational fields the UN system is. For climate policy, a shift into smaller policy forums and the breaking down of complex issues into more concrete and tangible policy arenas could reintroduce some of the boundaries within which field-configuring events can support the development of a new, encompassing climate agreement.
limitations: The authors state that they focused on one specific and in many ways unique transnational policy field, so the findings may not be directly applicable to other field settings; they note, however, that other fields share characteristics of the climate policy field (formation around a contested issue, absence of clear structures of domination, increasing field complexity and issue multiplication) and suggest their findings will apply to such settings. In addition, their choice to highlight the temporal aspects of boundedness meant that they largely neglected the role of spatial proximity or distance.
future_research: The paper proposes that further research could build on its idea of field maintenance and track national and community activities resulting from and related to field-configuring events, illuminating the trickle-up and trickle-down processes occurring between transnational and local arenas. It also calls for research on the spatial and temporal dimensions of field-configuring events at group and individual levels of analysis (for instance, how high-stakes staging affects objective and subjective representations of time and space among event participants, or how different time frames affect group processes during events), for investigating how elements of creativity and spontaneity could be reinstalled in highly complex and fragmented decision-making processes (for example, through "unconferences" or "barcamps"), and for paying attention to the two-sided role of emotions at field-configuring events to enrich understanding of the emotional dimension of institutional work.
abstract: Although field-configuring events have been highlighted as catalysts of institutional change, scholars still know little about the specific conditions that allow such change to occur. Using data from a longitudinal study of United Nations climate conferences, we analyze how regular and high-stakes events in an event series interacted in producing and preventing institutional change in the transnational climate policy field. We uncover variations in event structures, processes, and outcomes that explain why climate conferences have not led to effective solutions to combat human-induced global warming. Results in particular highlight that growing field complexity and issue multiplication compromise the change potential of a field-configuring event series in favor of field maintenance. Over time, diverse actors find event participation useful for their own purposes, but their activity is not connected to the institutions at the center of the issue-based field. In discussing how events configuring a field are purposefully staged and enacted but also influenced by developments in the field, our study contributes to a more complete understanding of field-configuring events, particularly in contested transnational policy arenas.
apa_citation: Schüssler, E., Rüling, C.-C., & Wittneben, B. B. F. (2014). On melting summits: The limitations of field-configuring events as catalysts of change in transnational climate policy. *Academy of Management Journal*, 57(1), 140–171. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0812

title: It's Not Easy Being Green: The Role of Self-Evaluations in Explaining Support of Environmental Issues
methods: Mixed methods: Study 1 inductive qualitative study (29 semi-structured interviews plus field observations, grounded-theory coding); Study 2 inductive quantitative observational study (survey scales, bootstrapped confirmatory factor analysis, Ward's hierarchical cluster analysis, one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc comparisons of observed behaviors)
industry: Various industries (issue supporters in business, nonprofit, and government roles; Study 2 recruited members of environmental groups)
country: North America (Study 1: program at a North American university; Study 2: major North American city)
time_period: Study 1 field observations in 2006 and 2007; other data collection dates not reported
units: Individual environmental / climate change issue supporters
n_sample: Study 1: 29 interviewees; Study 2: 91 participants (construct-validity pretest n = 58)
authors: Sonenshein, S.; DeCelles, K. A.; Dutton, J. E.
theories: goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham, 1990); issue selling (Dutton & Ashford, 1993); self-affirmation theory (Steele, 1988; Sherman & Cohen, 2006); self-determination theory / self-concordance (Deci & Ryan, 1985; Sheldon & Elliot, 1999); situated self-work (theory induced in this paper)
keywords: environmental issues; issue-supportive behaviors; mixed selves; self-assets; self-doubts; self-evaluations; situated self-work; social issue supporters
research_question: The paper poses two emergent research questions in its own words: Study 1 asks "How do issue supporters' everyday experiences influence their self-evaluations?"; Study 2 asks "How do patterns of self-evaluations relate to levels of issue-supportive behaviors?"
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Key constructs: issue support challenges (relational, cognitive, organizational); self-assets (value assets, knowledge assets, experience assets); self-doubts (doing questioning, doing constraints); situated self-work; mixed-self profiles (self-affirmers, self-equivocators, self-critics)
- Process / phases: supporters interpret issue support challenges across life domains (work, home, school); challenges prompt ongoing self-evaluation around two questions (Do I have the assets needed to be an issue supporter? How am I performing as an issue supporter?); the resulting mixed self-evaluations combine into profiles that relate to different levels of issue-supportive behavior
- Triggering conditions: complacency and skepticism of others (relational); the issue's scope, complexity, and interconnectivity (cognitive); getting organizational buy-in and the economic challenges of organizational support (organizational)
- Emergent outcomes: real issue-supportive behaviors (composting, interpersonal influence attempts, signing an Earth Hour pledge)

The induced theory of situated self-work holds that being an issue supporter confronts individuals with relational, cognitive, and organizational challenges in multiple contexts, prompting ongoing, effortful evaluation of the self. Supporters respond by claiming self-assets (values, knowledge, experience) that position them as capable of supporting the issue while simultaneously harboring self-doubts about the sufficiency of their actions. Study 2's motivation-based account suggests that self-assets foster self-concordance and self-efficacy; high self-doubts without accompanying assets may function as externally imposed burdens that decrease motivation, whereas low-level doubts combined with high assets might function as reminders of important goals and standards rather than as burdens.
data_measures: Study 1: 29 hour-long semi-structured interviews with self-identified climate change issue supporters (14 current students and 15 working alumni of the Environment and Business Program at a North American university), supplemented by field observations at two annual student gatherings (2006 and 2007) and program information; grounded-theory analysis moved from open codes to theoretical categories to three aggregate dimensions. Study 2: 91 environmental issue supporters recruited through 19 environmental groups in a major North American city; self-doubts measured with three items (e.g., "I don't do enough to be called a good environmentalist"; alpha = .88) and self-assets with nine items spanning knowledge, experience, and values (alpha = .88), validated in a 58-student pretest and a bootstrapped confirmatory factor analysis; issue-supportive behavior was the sum of three concealed-observation behaviors (composting leftover food, a written or verbal interpersonal influence attempt about the study's environmental practices, and signing a WWF Earth Hour pledge). Profiles were derived inductively with Ward's hierarchical cluster analysis, and behavior differences were tested with one-way ANOVA and Tukey post hoc comparisons; the design is observational and associational, not a causal-identification design.
key_findings: Study 1 finds that informants interpret three categories of issue support challenges (relational, cognitive, organizational) and respond with mixed self-evaluations: positive self-assets (value, knowledge, and experience assets) and negative self-doubts (doing questioning, doing constraints), theorized together as situated self-work. Study 2's cluster analysis yielded three profiles: 38 self-affirmers (low self-doubts, high self-assets), 33 self-equivocators (high self-doubts, high self-assets), and 20 self-critics (high self-doubts, low self-assets). Self-affirmers engaged in the most issue-supportive behaviors (mean = 1.21 actions), followed by self-equivocators (mean = 0.61) and self-critics (mean = 0.45); the ANOVA was significant (F = 10.56, p < .01), with self-affirmers significantly higher than both self-critics (mean difference = 0.76, p < .01) and self-equivocators (mean difference = 0.60, p = .01), while the self-equivocator versus self-critic difference did not reach statistical significance. Even the most dedicated issue supporters had doubts, which the authors argue may be enabling or damaging depending on the composition of the mixed self.
theoretical_contribution: The paper's theory of situated self-work offers an alternative to the outward-looking, image-risk-focused self of issue-selling research: supporters evaluate whether they have the assets to support an issue and how they are performing on it, rather than how others construe them. It documents a decidedly mixed self of simultaneous self-assets and self-doubts and, in contrast with self-affirmation theory, shows that individuals can generate self-assets in the same domain in which they perceive a threat, with no posited sequential order between doubts and assets. It also embeds self-processes in multiple contexts (work, home, school), explaining how contexts shape ongoing self-evaluations and joining scholarship on spillover between work and nonwork contexts.
practical_implication: The findings help explain why it is difficult to be a social issue supporter and present guidance for strengthening social issue supporters, for whom burnout and depression are a key concern: because self-doubts question the self across multiple contexts, bolstering self-assets may not be a sufficient remedy, and supporters may also need to devise ways to mitigate their self-doubts. The authors also note that supporters can develop self-assets outside their work context, which may be particularly important for those who lack access to tangible resources or who sit in less politically legitimate parts of an organization, such as a corporate social responsibility department.
limitations: The authors note that their studies raise, but do not resolve, the question of how mixed self-evaluations influence social issue support, with existing research split between an ambivalence-resolution view and a view of contradictory beliefs as a foundation for wisdom. They examined social issue support only vis-a-vis the natural environment, so it is not clear the findings will generalize to other social issues, and the profiles represent self-evaluations at a single point in time. Study 2 also faced statistical issues, including low power/sample size and restricted range on the dependent variable.
future_research: The authors call for longitudinal research to unpack how self-evaluations change over time and relate to ongoing issue-supportive behaviors: whether individuals end up with more self-doubts as they burn out, accrue more self-assets as they capture small wins, or move through profiles as stages of working through an ambivalent self. They also note that self-evaluations induced by issue support challenges may vary for different kinds of social issues, and that additional empirical work can help disentangle the relationship between a mixed self and issue-supportive behaviors.
abstract: Using a mixed methods design, we examine the role of self-evaluations in influencing support for environmental issues. In Study 1—an inductive, qualitative study—we develop theory about how environmental issue supporters evaluate themselves in a mixed fashion, positively around having assets (self-assets) and negatively around questioning their performance (self-doubts). We explain how these ongoing self-evaluations, which we label “situated self-work,” are shaped by cognitive, relational, and organizational challenges individuals interpret about an issue from a variety of life domains (work, home, or school). In Study 2—an inductive, quantitative, observational study—we derive three profiles of environmental issue supporters’ mixed selves (self-affirmers, self-critics, and self-equivocators) and relate these profiles to real issue-supportive behaviors. We empirically validate key constructs from Study 1 and show that even among the most dedicated issue supporters, doubts play an important role in their experiences and may be either enabling or damaging, depending on the composition of their mixed selves. Our research offers a richer view of both how contexts shape social issue support and how individuals’ self-evaluations play a meaningful role in understanding the experiences and, ultimately, the issue-supportive behaviors of individuals working on social issues.
apa_citation: Sonenshein, S., DeCelles, K. A., & Dutton, J. E. (2014). It's not easy being green: The role of self-evaluations in explaining support of environmental issues. *Academy of Management Journal*, *57*(1), 7–37. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2010.0445
