title: Exploring the Locus of Invention: The Dynamics of Network Communities and Firms' Invention Productivity
methods: Longitudinal network panel; Girvan-Newman community detection on yearly alliance networks; negative binomial regression with conditional firm-level fixed effects; three-level Poisson models with random intercepts and random coefficients
industry: Global computer industry (technology alliances; about 60% manufacturing, 30% services, 10% embedded systems)
time_period: Partnership data 1981-2001; yearly networks 1985-2001; patents filed 1986-2002
units: Firm-year observations
n_sample: 918 firm-year observations across 192 unique computer firms (720 firm-years in fixed-effects estimation; 410 firms in the full network sample)
authors: Sytch, M.; Tatarynowicz, A.
theories: ego network perspective (Burt, 1992; Ahuja, 2000); global network perspective (Schilling & Phelps, 2007; Uzzi & Spiro, 2005); network community perspective
keywords: interorganizational partnerships; invention productivity; knowledge heterogeneity; membership turnover; network communities
research_question: How do the membership dynamics of network communities (the turnover of community members and a firm's own rate of movement across different communities) affect the invention productivity of member firms, and how do these effects vary with a firm's core/periphery location in its community and with global network reach?
hypotheses:
H1: The turnover of community members in a firm's network community has an inverted U-shaped effect on the firm's invention productivity; the firm attains the highest invention productivity at a moderate rate of membership turnover.
H2: A firm's movement across different network communities has an inverted U-shaped effect on the firm's invention productivity; the firm attains the highest invention productivity if it moves across network communities at a moderate rate.
H3a: The inverted curvilinear relationship between membership turnover and invention productivity is moderated by the firm's core/periphery location in the community; a core firm benefits more from a moderate rate of membership turnover than a peripheral firm.
H3b: The inverted curvilinear relationship between a firm's movement across network communities and invention productivity is moderated by the firm's core/periphery location in the communities it encounters; a firm occupying a core position benefits more from a moderate rate of movement than a firm occupying peripheral positions.
H4a: The membership turnover relationship is moderated by global network reach; the positive effect of a moderate rate of membership turnover is weaker at higher levels of global network reach.
H4b: The movement relationship is moderated by global network reach; the positive effect of a moderate rate of movement is weaker at higher levels of global network reach.
mechanism_summary: Network communities are dense, nonoverlapping structural groups whose internal connectivity homogenizes knowledge within community boundaries while sparse between-community connectivity preserves knowledge heterogeneity across them. Membership dynamics update the knowledge base that is locally accessible to member firms: moderate membership turnover opens up and updates a community's knowledge base without imposing the trust, collaboration, and stability costs of excessive turnover, and moderate movement across communities gives a firm direct exposure to diverse knowledge inputs while avoiding integration costs, permanent newcomer status, and an incoherent collaborative profile. Core positions in a community provide broader and quicker access to the community's updated knowledge base, so core firms are expected to capture more of these benefits.
data_measures: Data: interorganizational technology partnerships in the global computer industry, 1981-2001, from the MERIT-CATI database; 410 unique computer firms; yearly networks reconstructed for 1985-2001 (17 annual observations, partnership duration set to five years). The effective sample included 918 firm-year observations across 192 unique computer firms; the conditional fixed-effects estimation truncated this by about 20 percent to 720 firm-year observations because firms that never patented were eliminated. DV: number of patents in t+1, the count of a firm's eventually approved patent applications from the NBER database of US patents, category 2 "computers & communications" (143,500 patents). IVs: membership turnover, measured as the inverse of community overlap across contiguous years; prior community affiliations, the number of distinct communities the firm belonged to before t, excluding the current community. Moderators: within-community coreness (Borgatti and Everett continuous core/periphery model, including its firm-history average) and global network reach (average inverted network distance, including its firm-history average). Communities were identified each year with the Girvan and Newman (2002) modularity-maximization method (average modularity 0.63). Estimation: negative binomial regression with conditional firm-level fixed effects plus three-level Poisson models with random intercepts and random coefficients; controls include headcount, net income, return on assets, R&D spending, ego network measures, and community characteristics. The design is an observational longitudinal panel; firm-level fixed effects are used to eliminate unobserved heterogeneity in firms' propensity to patent, and no experimental identification is claimed.
key_findings: H1 supported: membership turnover has an inverted U-shaped effect on invention productivity (inflection at 47 percent turnover); a member of a moderately dynamic community (retaining about 55 percent of its members year to year) files 19.5 percent more patents than a member of a static community and 4.2 percent more than a member of a highly dynamic one. H2 supported: movement across communities has an inverted U-shaped effect (inflection at five prior community affiliations); a firm with about five prior affiliations files approximately twice as many patents as a firm with none and about 50 percent more than a firm with nine. H3a consistently supported: the positive effect of moderate turnover is amplified for core firms, who file about 5 percent more patents than peripheral members of a moderately dynamic community. H3b only partially supported: the interaction is not supported in the partial models but is supported in the fully specified models, with the inflection point shifting from five to three prior communities for core firms. H4a and H4b not supported: the negative binomial models show null interaction effects and the multilevel Poisson models yield estimates opposite to expectations. Supplementary analyses indicate that two firms in the same community are on average twice as likely to cite each other's patents as outsiders' patents, and that community dynamics are substantially driven by the behaviors of other firms rather than the focal firm's own new alliance formation.
theoretical_contribution: The study advances a network community perspective as a third lens, beyond the ego network and global network perspectives, on how social structure shapes firms' invention: community boundaries demarcate homogeneous knowledge inputs, and the membership dynamics of communities have fundamental implications for firms' invention outcomes, casting doubt on the conclusion that only ego networks matter for actor outcomes. It contributes to research on network dynamics by identifying membership dynamics as an influential dimension of network change and by showing that community dynamics are significantly driven by other firms' behaviors rather than a firm's own pursuits, suggesting constrained individual agency over network positions. It also shows that ego network properties interact with features of network communities, a step toward a more integrative, multilevel approach to the relationship between network structures and actors' behaviors and outcomes.
practical_implication: For firms in interorganizational partnership networks such as the computer industry studied here, the results imply that invention productivity is greatest in moderately dynamic network communities and at a moderate rate of movement across communities, and that firms located in community cores capture more of these benefits than peripheral members. The authors frame this as a tension between deep integration and search across only a few network communities as a core member versus a quick scan and peripheral entry into numerous network communities, and note that network communities tend to allow rich firms and firms in their cores to get even richer.
limitations: The authors note that their theory and results are tailored to sparsely connected interorganizational systems in which network communities do not overlap, and that the network community lens is of limited applicability where a global network resembles a random network or displays a strong core/periphery structure; its use is contingent on a robust community structure being present. In addition, the conditional fixed-effects estimator eliminated firms that never patented during the 17-year window, truncating the sample by about 20 percent, a limitation addressed with alternative full-sample models in robustness tests.
future_research: The authors propose extending the analysis to systems with overlapping network communities and to actors who are members of more than one community at a time, and applying the network community lens to a broader range of industrial, national, and institutional systems, including economies organized around business groups. They also suggest that ego network studies attend to whether an ego's alters sit in the same or different communities; that research explore how network communities form and evolve in industrial districts and regional economies; that industry analyses combine network communities of collaborators with groups of rivals, adding a cognitive lens on executives' and influential third parties' (such as financial analysts') perceptions of collaboration and rivalry; and that future work more systematically analyze how firm-level attributes interact with community membership dynamics.
abstract: Departing from prior research analyzing the implications of social structure for actors’ outcomes by applying either an ego network or a global network perspective, this study examines the implications of network communities for the invention productivity of firms. Network communities represent dense and nonoverlapping structural groups of actors in a social system. A network community lens helps identify new ways to study firms’ access to diverse knowledge inputs in a dynamic system of interorganizational relationships. Specifically, we examine how the membership dynamics of a network community affect the invention productivity of member firms by either enabling or constraining access to broad, diverse knowledge inputs. Our findings suggest, first, that a firm reaps the greatest invention benefits in a network community with moderate levels of membership turnover. Second, a firm attains the greatest invention productivity when its own rate of movement across different network communities is moderate. Third, we find that community members located in the core of their network community can benefit more from membership dynamics and prior community affiliations than those on its periphery. In empirical analyses, we use the evolving community structure of the network of interorganizational partnerships in the global computer industry over 1981–2001 to predict firms’ patenting rates.

title: The Riddle of Heterarchy: Power Transitions in Cross-Functional Teams
methods: Mixed methods: preliminary qualitative field illustration (five 2-hour teamwork observations and 21 semi-structured interviews across 12 teams); three-round laboratory experiment with 45 cross-functional teams and 516 directional dyads; generalized mixed-effects model for Hypothesis 1 and team-level hierarchical OLS regression for Hypotheses 2-3
industry: Diverse organizational settings in the field illustration; a cell-phone marketing task in the laboratory study
country: United States for the laboratory study; field illustration country not reported
time_period: Three sequential laboratory task rounds; calendar data-collection dates not reported
units: Directional member-to-member dyads nested in cross-functional teams, with team-level creativity outcomes
n_sample: 516 directional dyads in 45 laboratory teams (131 participants); 21 field interviewees from 12 teams and five observed teamwork events
authors: Aime, F.; Humphrey, S. E.; DeRue, D. S.; Paul, J. B.
theories: approach-inhibition theories of power (Keltner, Gruenfeld, & Anderson, 2003; Magee & Galinsky, 2008); legitimacy as propriety (Dornbusch & Scott, 1975; Suchman, 1995); power-dependence theory (Emerson, 1962); social exchange theory (Emerson, 1962, 1969)
keywords: cross-functional teams; interpersonal power expressions; perceived legitimacy; power heterarchy; power transitions; shared leadership; situational demands; team creativity
research_question: How do changes in situational task demands shift relative power and interpersonal power expressions among members of cross-functional teams, and when do those shifts enhance team creativity? Specifically, does a concomitant shift in perceived legitimacy condition the effect of shifts in power expression on team creativity?
hypotheses:
H1: As situational demands shift, those members whose resources better fit the new demands will express relatively more power than other members of the team.
H2: Positive shifts in interpersonal power expressions by members with the resources to resolve the current situational demands will be positively related to team creativity.
H3: The positive effect of incremental shifts in interpersonal power expression on team creativity will be moderated by shifts in perceived legitimacy, such that shifts in power expression that are seen as legitimate (illegitimate) will strengthen (weaken) the effect on team creativity.
mechanism_summary: A power heterarchy is a relational system in which members' relative power shifts as their resources become more or less relevant to changing task demands. Approach-inhibition theories predict that members whose resources become more relevant will feel more powerful and express more power, while other members become more inhibited and grant that power. Social-exchange rebalancing then brings members' diverse information and expertise into the creative process, but these inputs foster creativity only when the team regards the accompanying shift in power expression as legitimate.
data_measures: The field illustration comprised five 2-hour teamwork observations and 21 semi-structured interviews with members of 12 teams in diverse organizational settings; recordings and notes were analyzed for situational power shifts, behavioral responses, and legitimacy perceptions. The laboratory study randomly assigned 131 business-school participants to 45 cross-functional teams containing two confederates and two or three participants; teams completed three sequential cell-phone marketing tasks while marketing expertise, access to client information, and presentation expertise made different members' resources situationally relevant. Confederates rated each participant's directed power expressions toward teammates through two items, "expressed influence" and "applied pressure," on 7-point scales; participants rated each teammate's right to influence others because of expertise or access to information, and focal-versus-nonfocal change scores captured power-expression and legitimacy shifts. Three independent marketing subject-matter experts rated each team's output from 1 to 10 using a consensual creativity assessment. H1 was tested with a generalized mixed-effects model that nested directional relationships within teams and receivers; H2-H3 were tested with team-level hierarchical OLS regressions of creativity on the shift scores and their interaction.
key_findings:
- H1 supported: in Time 2, the contact member expressed more power than other members (t = 9.16, p < .01) and more than that same member did in the other tasks (t = 4.16, p < .01); in Time 3, the presentation expert expressed more power than other members (t = 6.65, p < .01) and more than that same member did in the other tasks (t = 4.02, p < .01).
- H2 supported: shifts in power expression by the member with situationally relevant resources positively predicted team creativity and explained 6% of its variance (beta = .24, p < .05).
- H3 supported: the power-expression-shift by legitimacy-shift interaction was positive and significant (beta = .26, p < .05, change in R-squared = .04). High shifts in power expression positively affected creativity only when accompanied by a shift in legitimacy; without that legitimacy shift, power-expression shifts had no effect on creativity.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a meso-level theory of power heterarchy that bridges micro accounts of abrupt power transitions and macro accounts of stable hierarchy by explaining how task demands produce repeated shifts in relative power and power expression within teams. It challenges the assumption that unstable power relations are inherently dysfunctional, showing instead that dynamic power expression can enhance team creativity, and identifies perceived legitimacy as the boundary condition that determines whether those shifts improve team functioning. The model also gives shared-leadership research a concrete account of what shifts among members, how those shifts occur, and why members without formal authority can step up when their resources fit the team's needs.
practical_implication: Managers and team leaders should rapidly identify the resources required by changing task demands and enable the members who hold those resources to express power, while providing autonomy, empowerment, and resource alignment. The authors also recommend assembling teams with diverse resources, allowing fluid membership or access to external resource holders when needed, and creating reward systems, trust, and team cultures in which situationally appropriate power shifts are regarded as legitimate rather than threatening.
limitations: The laboratory study used newly formed ad hoc teams in a U.S. business-school setting, with clear power bases and no organizational embedding; the field illustration supports external relevance but does not replace replication in organizational settings. The design minimized redundancy among members' resources and examined only expertise and information power over a limited set of transitions, leaving overlapping resources, other power sources, repeated shifts toward the same member, and formal authority insufficiently tested. The outcome was limited to team creativity, and the theory is expressly bounded to teams with diverse knowledge, skills, and abilities and reciprocal interdependence.
future_research: The authors call for research on how formal authority constrains or enables power transitions, how members step up and back effectively, and whether heterarchical dynamics extend to top-management teams, other organizational forms, and cross-organizational groups. They propose examining resource redundancies, additional power sources, repeated opportunities for the same member to exercise power, national culture, compensation and evaluation systems, psychological safety, and trust as conditions shaping power shifts and their legitimacy. They also encourage studies of outcomes beyond creativity, including speed, quantity, and team viability, and direct tests of the motivational, approach-inhibition, leadership-granting, and group-identification explanations for why members express more power when their resources become situationally relevant.
abstract: In this paper, we develop the concept of a power heterarchy, which is a conceptualization of power structures in groups that is more dynamic and fluid than traditional hierarchical structures. Through a study of 516 directional dyads in 45 teams, we demonstrate that heterarchical structures in which the expression of power actively shifts among team members to align team member capabilities with dynamic situational demands can enhance team creativity. Our results indicate that this positive effect of power heterarchies on team creativity is contingent on the team perceiving the shifts in interpersonal power expressions as legitimate. We discuss the implications of this heterarchical power structure for research on group functioning, power, and legitimacy in organizations.

title: Relational Pluralism in De Novo Organizations: Boards of Directors as Bridges or Barriers to Diverse Alliance Portfolios?
methods: Longitudinal firm-month event history study using semiparametric Cox proportional-hazards models; robustness checks use alternative diversity measures, lagged specifications, Hausman tests, and Heckman-like two-stage models.
industry: De novo merchant semiconductor producers
time_period: Firms founded January 1978-December 1985; board and alliance data through 1990 and outcomes through December 2002
units: De novo semiconductor firms; firm-month observations
n_sample: 104 firms; 4,741 firm-months in the alliance-portfolio models
authors: Beckman, C. M.; Schoonhoven, C. B.; Rottner, R. M.; Kim, S.-J.
theories: connectionist and structuralist perspectives of networks; relational pluralism
keywords: asymmetry; board of directors; de novo organizations; diverse alliance portfolio; heterogeneity; multiplexity; relational pluralism
research_question: How does the board of directors, as a collective instantiation of relational pluralism, shape diverse alliance portfolio emergence among de novo technology organizations? The paper also asks whether forming a diverse alliance portfolio speeds attainment of major revenue milestones.
hypotheses:
- H1: The greater the heterogeneity of the board, as indicated by the diversity of board experiences, the greater the rate of diverse alliance portfolio emergence in de novo organizations.
- H2: The greater the multiplexity of the board, as indicated by board members' multiple types of ties, the higher the rate of diverse alliance portfolio emergence in de novo organizations.
- H3: The greater the asymmetry of the board, as indicated by the distribution of board member centrality, the lower the rate of diverse alliance portfolio emergence in de novo organizations.
- H4a: The greater the asymmetry of the board, with outside directors having dominance, the greater the rate of diverse alliance portfolio emergence in de novo organizations.
- H4b: The greater the asymmetry of the board, with investor board members having dominance, the lower the rate of diverse alliance portfolio emergence in de novo organizations.
- H5: Forming a diverse alliance portfolio will speed the attainment of important revenue milestones in a de novo organization.
mechanism_summary: Heterogeneous board experiences broaden the information, expertise, and alliance opportunities available to a new venture, while multiplex ties deepen information and trust through multiple points of connection. The distribution of board-member centrality allocates attention and influence: central non-investor outsiders provide broad knowledge without discouraging attention to other members, whereas dominant investor directors may narrow alliance choices toward their own networks and preferred strategies. A diverse alliance portfolio is theorized to give the venture access to resources, know-how, innovative capabilities, and external legitimacy that help it attain revenue milestones more quickly.
data_measures: The study follows 104 de novo merchant semiconductor producers founded in the continental United States between January 1978 and December 1985. Structured interviews, supplementary financial forms, subsequent telephone waves, and archival research provide annual board measures, monthly alliance data through 1990, and annual revenue outcomes through 2002 or firm death. Diverse portfolio emergence is the time to obtaining three alliance types; an alternative specification uses a Blau diversity index, and the revenue models use the monthly cumulative number of alliance types. Board heterogeneity is the geometric mean of Blau indices for outside directors' regions, two-digit industries, and organization types; multiplexity sums investor, customer, and parent board ties; asymmetry uses board-member degree-centrality skewness and differences between the most central outside and investor directors. Semiparametric Cox event history models estimate time to portfolio emergence and to the US$10 million, US$20 million, and US$50 million revenue milestones.
key_findings:
- H1 was supported: board heterogeneity increased the rate of diverse alliance portfolio emergence (b = 1.587, p < .05; full model b = 1.500, p < .05).
- H2 was supported in its standalone model: board multiplexity increased portfolio-emergence rates (b = 0.560, p < .05), although the positive effect was only marginally significant in the full model (b = 0.517, p < .10).
- H3 received only partial support and not in the predicted simple direction. Overall centrality skewness was nonsignificant; negative skewness, reflecting multiple highly central members and few low-centrality members, increased portfolio-emergence rates (b = 3.148, p < .001; full model b = 2.702, p < .001), while positive skewness was nonsignificant.
- H4a was supported in Model 6: outside-director dominance increased portfolio-emergence rates (b = 62.060, p < .01), with the positive effect becoming marginally significant in the full model (b = 45.950, p < .10).
- H4b had the predicted negative direction but was nonsignificant in Model 6 (b = -28.680) and only marginally significant in the full model (b = -54.600, p < .10).
- H5 received milestone-specific support: alliance portfolio diversity increased the rate of attaining US$10 million in annual revenue (b = 0.236, p < .05), was positive but marginal for US$20 million (b = 0.229, p < .10), and was nonsignificant for US$50 million (b = 0.023).
theoretical_contribution: The paper conceptualizes relational pluralism as a collective construct instantiated in the board of directors and develops heterogeneity, multiplexity, and asymmetry as its dimensions, adding asymmetry to prior formulations. It combines connectionist attention to tie content with structuralist attention to network position and power distribution, showing how board relationships shape both the emergence of diverse alliance portfolios and their revenue consequences in de novo organizations.
practical_implication: For de novo ventures, the paper indicates that board composition and the balance of influence matter for developing diverse alliance portfolios: heterogeneous and multiplex experience and central non-investor outsiders can help, whereas dominance by central investor directors can impede portfolio formation. Early alliance portfolio formation is associated with reaching US$10 million and US$20 million revenue milestones more quickly, milestones the paper identifies as providing credibility to retain existing investor support and attract new investors.
limitations: The average board contained only four members, with a maximum of ten, and almost half of the firms had no multiplex board ties, limiting empirical power. The single-industry setting and the concentration of 75 percent of firms in northern California leave open whether the dimensions and effects of relational pluralism depend on an industry's network structure, development stage, and geographic concentration.
future_research: Future research could examine a larger collective to refine analysis of relational pluralism's dimensions and compare settings such as biotechnology, where alliances are more prevalent, and nanotechnology, where board networks may be sparse and span more knowledge domains. The paper also calls for examining how industry network structure, stage of development, geographic agglomeration, and region-specific network path dependencies condition relational pluralism.
abstract: This paper develops relational pluralism as a collective construct whose dimensions are heterogeneity, multiplexity, and asymmetry. Relational pluralism is instantiated in the board of directors, whose network of relationships influence a new venture’s ability to establish external links beyond the networks of the founding team. We argue that relational pluralism speeds the establishment of a diverse alliance portfolio, which, in turn, speeds the attainment of major revenue milestones in a new firm. We examine these ideas in a population of de novo semiconductor firms and find that diverse alliance portfolios emerge faster when a board includes members with heterogeneous, multiplex relationships, as well as central network positions. However, the asymmetric influence of outside board members can have both positive and negative effects: the alliance formation process is aided by outsiders in central network positions, but impeded when central investors dominate the board. We discuss implications for our understanding of relational pluralism as a collective construct.

title: The Impact of Social Context on the Relationship Between Individual Job Satisfaction and Absenteeism: The Roles of Different Foci of Job Satisfaction and Work-Unit Absenteeism
methods: Two longitudinal, correlational multilevel field studies using employee surveys, archival short-term absence records, and HLM cross-level interaction models.
industry: Residential elderly care (Study 1); tax and revenue public administration (Study 2)
time_period: Absenteeism records for 6 months before and 6 months after each questionnaire survey
units: Employees nested in work units
n_sample: Study 1: 412 employees in 63 work units; Study 2: 330 employees in 53 work units
authors: Diestel, S.; Wegge, J.; Schmidt, K.-H.
theories: attitude representation theory; situational strength; social information processing theory
keywords: externally focused satisfaction; individual absenteeism; internally focused satisfaction; social context; work-unit absenteeism
research_question: How do the mean and dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism jointly moderate the individual relationships between externally and internally focused job satisfaction and subsequent individual absenteeism?
hypotheses:
- H1: The mean and dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism jointly moderate the negative relationship between externally focused job satisfaction and individual absenteeism: the relationship is strongest when both work-unit absenteeism mean and dispersion are high, and weaker when either or both are low.
- H2: The mean and dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism jointly moderate the negative relationship between internally focused job satisfaction and individual absenteeism: the relationship is strongest when both work-unit absenteeism mean and dispersion are low, and weaker when either or both are high.
mechanism_summary: Externally focused satisfaction concerns job conditions, management, and career opportunities and serves an instrumental function. When work-unit absence mean and dispersion are both high, the context is weak and tolerant enough for employees' own external dissatisfaction to translate into more absence; when absence patterns are uniform, employees instead align with the unit's absence level. Internally focused satisfaction concerns colleagues and supervisors and indicates social integration, so satisfied employees tend to align with work-unit absence patterns, whereas dissatisfied employees tend to withdraw. Accordingly, the negative internal satisfaction-absence relationship is predicted to be strongest when work-unit absence mean and dispersion are both low.
data_measures: Study 1 included 412 health-care employees in 63 work units at a German residential elderly care organization; Study 2 included 330 employees in 53 work units at a German tax and revenue organization. Externally focused satisfaction was measured with three items on working conditions, organization and management, and career opportunities; internally focused satisfaction was measured with two items on colleagues and the work-unit supervisor. Archival absence frequency counted short-term absence events of fewer than four consecutive workdays during the six months before and after the survey; work-unit absence mean and dispersion were the aggregated mean and within-unit standard deviation of pre-survey absence frequency. The authors estimated HLM cross-level interaction models, controlling for prior individual absenteeism, health disorders, demographics, team size, and local unemployment; the longitudinal design remained correlational.
key_findings: Study 1 supported both hypotheses. For H1, externally focused satisfaction was negatively related to subsequent absence only when work-unit absence mean and dispersion were both high (γ = -0.34, p < .01); for H2, internally focused satisfaction was negatively related to absence only when both were low (γ = -0.42, p < .01), with the other simple slopes nonsignificant. Study 2 strongly supported H1: the high-mean, high-dispersion slope was negative and significant (γ = -0.43, p < .01), while the other slopes were nonsignificant. H2 was not fully supported in Study 2 because the three-way interaction was nonsignificant; internal satisfaction was negatively related to absence when work-unit absence mean was low (γ = -0.20, p < .01) but not when it was high (γ = 0.01, n.s.), and dispersion did not moderate this relationship.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a cross-level, context-based account of when job satisfaction predicts individual absenteeism by combining satisfaction focus with the mean and dispersion of work-unit absence. It shows that contextual strength has different implications for an instrumental attitude toward job conditions and a social-adjustive attitude toward the work unit. This distinction extends social information processing arguments by identifying attitude function and work-unit behavioral patterns as joint boundary conditions of the satisfaction-absenteeism relationship.
practical_implication: The authors recommend that HR practices simultaneously increase internally focused satisfaction and reduce work-unit absenteeism. Managers should foster social integration and supportive relationships among teammates and supervisors while using group-level practices such as clear supervisory instructions, formalized attendance procedures, feedback systems, or unit-level incentives to control work-unit absence patterns.
limitations: Although the data were longitudinal, the design was correlational and did not permit strong causal inferences. The satisfaction measure covered only five job aspects, the absence measure did not explicitly distinguish voluntary from involuntary or excused from unexcused cases, and unmeasured confounding remained possible. The studies also did not test the proposed mediating processes or directly measure the unit-level mechanisms producing work-unit absenteeism.
future_research: Future studies should model changes in satisfaction and absenteeism over time and develop more explicit measures of satisfaction components and attitudinal functions. They should test mediating processes such as calculative judgment and social identification, distinguish voluntary from involuntary and excused from unexcused absences, and consider further relevant controls. The paper also calls for research that integrates behavioral patterns at higher structural levels when explaining relationships between job attitudes and individual behavior.
abstract: Building upon recent conceptualizations of different foci of job satisfaction and theories of social-contextual influence, we develop and test an integrative cross-level model of the individual relationships between both “externally focused satisfaction” (referring to job conditions) and “internally focused satisfaction” (referring to the work unit) and absenteeism. For both of these foci, we hypothesize differential three-way interactive effects of work-unit absenteeism patterns as characterized by their mean and dispersion levels, as well as individual satisfaction levels on subsequent individual absenteeism. Based on two German multi-level samples, our analyses demonstrate that the negative relationship between externally focused satisfaction and individual absenteeism is strongest in the presence of high mean and dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism, whereas this relationship is weaker when either the mean or dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism, or both, are low. In contrast, the negative relationship between internally focused satisfaction and individual absenteeism is strongest under conditions of low mean and dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism, whereas this relationship is weaker when either the mean or dispersion levels of work-unit absenteeism, or both, are high. The present findings suggest that simultaneously improving individual internally focused satisfaction and reducing work-unit absenteeism is the most promising approach to reducing individual absenteeism.

The impact of social context on the relationship between individual job satisfaction and absenteeism: The roles of different foci of job satisfaction and work-unit absenteeism. *Academy of Management Journal, 57*(2), 353–382. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2010.1087

title: Big Data and Management
methods: Editorial essay (From the Editors); no empirical design or analysis.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: George, G.; Haas, M. R.; Pentland, A.
keywords: big data; causality; consilience; data sharing; microfoundations; privacy
research_question: Not reported in paper
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: the defining feature of big data is its fine-grained nature rather than dataset size alone, enabling granular analysis of individual actions and behaviors.
- Data sources: public data, private data, data exhaust, community data, and self-quantification data.
- Analytical progression: identify correlational patterns, use theory to develop causal arguments, test those arguments in subsequent research, ideally through field experiments, and seek consilience across independent sources.
- Evidence standards: emphasize effect sizes, variance explained, and informative outliers rather than relying on p values that become unhelpful in extremely large datasets.
- Enabling conditions: link data-sharing agreements to data protection and privacy mechanisms, including anonymization, access control, rights management, and data usage control.

The editorial presents big data as fine-grained, high-volume information that can expose variables, relationships, and contextual conditions unavailable in conventional management datasets. Because most big data are unstructured and not designed to establish causality, observed correlations can have multiple causal explanations. The proposed progression combines theory-guided explanation, subsequent field experimentation, and convergence of evidence from independent sources, while data-sharing and privacy arrangements make access possible.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The editorial reframes big data from a question of dataset size to one of fine-grained information and develops an agenda for its use in management scholarship. It argues that such data can reveal overlooked variables, relationships, boundary conditions, microfoundations, and dynamic organizational processes, while theory-guided tests and consilience can strengthen conclusions drawn from initially correlational patterns.
practical_implication: Management scholars entering big-data research should integrate data sharing and privacy into their research methodology, emphasize effect sizes, variance explained, and outliers rather than p values alone, and use theory followed by field experiments to investigate causality. For scholars and managers interested in action research, the editorial presents "management engineering" as an opportunity to shorten the cycle between identifying a promising theoretical insight and testing it through a well-designed intervention.
limitations: The authors state that the editorial is neither a systematic review of big-data applications nor a definitive guide for future research. Specialized analytical techniques are beyond its scope, and the authors caution that unstructured big data are generally not designed for causal identification and can support multiple possible causal explanations.
future_research: The editorial calls for research questions that integrate data sharing and privacy into research methodology, with the aim of refining future models of data sharing and data rights. It urges scholars to use theory to explain causal processes and test those explanations in subsequent research, ideally through field experiments, and to examine how ubiquitous data generate value, the routes through which value is created, and how that value is captured and apportioned. It also identifies opportunities to study microfoundations, organizational processes, individual and team behavior, and network dynamics using granular, near-real-time data.

title: Why Are Job Seekers Attracted by Corporate Social Performance? Experimental and Field Tests of Three Signal-Based Mechanisms
methods: Two-study design: a randomized longitudinal web-page experiment analyzed with ANOVA and regression-based multiple mediation, plus an associational job-fair field study using participant perceptions and independent recruitment-material ratings; confirmatory factor analyses and 5,000-sample bootstrap indirect-effect tests
industry: Study 1: fictitious clothing manufacturers and distributors; Study 2: engineering, technology, agriculture, nonprofit, and government organizations
time_period: Study 1: two sessions separated by one week; Study 2: November 2008 and March 2009
units: Study 1: senior undergraduate students; Study 2: active job seekers attending job fairs
n_sample: Study 1: 180; Study 2: 171 (153 for recruitment-material analyses)
authors: Jones, D. A.; Willness, C. R.; Madey, S.
theories: person–organization fit theory (Kristof, 1996); signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Rynes, 1991); social identity theory (Ashforth & Mael, 1989; Tajfel & Turner, 1992)
keywords: anticipated pride; corporate social performance; expected treatment; organizational attractiveness; organizational prestige; perceived value fit
research_question: Why do an organization’s community involvement and pro-environmental practices increase its attractiveness to job seekers, and are these relationships explained by anticipated pride or organizational prestige, perceived value fit, and expectations about favorable employee treatment?
hypotheses:
H1: The positive relationships between CSP pertaining to (a) community involvement and (b) pro-environmental practices and organizational attractiveness are mediated by anticipated pride (Study 1) and beliefs about organizational prestige (Study 2).
H2: The positive relationships between CSP pertaining to (a) community involvement and (b) pro-environmental practices and organizational attractiveness are mediated by perceived value fit.
H3a: An organization that engages in community involvement is more attractive to individuals higher in communal orientation, and this relationship is mediated by perceived value fit.
H3b: An organization that engages in pro-environmental practices is more attractive to individuals with stronger pro-environmental attitudes, and this relationship is mediated by perceived value fit.
H4: The positive relationships between CSP pertaining to (a) community involvement and (b) pro-environmental practices and organizational attractiveness are mediated by expectations about favorable employee treatment.
mechanism_summary: CSP sends job seekers signals about organizational prestige, organizational values, and prosocial orientation. These signals respectively inform anticipated pride in affiliation, perceived fit between personal and organizational values, and expectations that the organization treats employees favorably; those inferences then shape organizational attractiveness. H3 further proposes that CSP is especially attractive when the relevant personal orientation or attitude aligns with the organization’s community or environmental practices, with perceived value fit transmitting that relationship.
data_measures:
Study 1 was a longitudinal experiment with 180 senior undergraduates at a Western Canadian university. Participants completed two sessions one week apart and were randomly assigned in equal groups to review a fictitious clothing company’s web pages containing community-involvement CSP, pro-environmental CSP, or no CSP information. Communal orientation used Clark et al.’s 14-item measure; pro-environmental attitudes used six adapted items; anticipated pride used three Cable and Turban items; perceived value fit used three Cable and DeRue items; expected treatment used five author-created items; and organizational attractiveness used Highhouse et al.’s five-item measure. Analyses included CFA, ANOVA and contrasts, regression-based multiple mediation with 5,000 bootstrap samples, and a blind content analysis of employment-choice rationales.

Study 2 surveyed 171 active job seekers at two three-hour job fairs held at a Northeastern U.S. university in November 2008 and March 2009; 153 cases had independent recruitment-material ratings. A research assistant rated community and environmental CSP content on four-point scales, while job seekers completed four-item seven-point perceived-CSP measures. Organizational prestige used a five-item Highhouse et al. measure, and perceived value fit, expected treatment, and organizational attractiveness used the Study 1 measures. Bootstrap multiple-mediator models controlled for familiarity with the organization and the other CSP dimension; this field design was associational, whereas Study 1 supported causal inference from the randomized CSP manipulation.
key_findings:
In Study 1, organizational attractiveness was significantly higher in both CSP conditions than in the no-CSP condition. H1a/H1b and H2a/H2b were supported: unique indirect effects through anticipated pride were .47 for community involvement and .27 for pro-environmental practices, and those through perceived value fit were .22 and .21, respectively. H4a/H4b were not supported in the simultaneous three-mediator models (expected-treatment indirect effects were .01 and −.02), although post hoc analyses found both expected-treatment effects significant when anticipated pride was removed; H3a/H3b were supported, with indirect effects through perceived value fit of .34 and .11.

In Study 2, both perceived community CSP and independently rated community CSP in recruitment materials had significant total indirect effects on organizational attractiveness (.20 and .17) and significant unique indirect effects through organizational prestige, perceived value fit, and expected treatment, supporting H1a, H2a, and H4a. For environmental CSP, none of the indirect effects through the three mediators was significant for either CSP operationalization, so H1b, H2b, and H4b were not supported in Study 2 despite significant correlations and some significant component paths.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops and tests a signal-based account of why CSP attracts job seekers by specifying the inferences that connect CSP signals to organizational attractiveness rather than treating mediation as assumed. It distinguishes signals about prestige, values, and prosocial orientation from the mechanisms they inform—anticipated pride, perceived value fit, and expected treatment—and provides complementary experimental and field evidence across three CSP operationalizations. The contrast between community involvement and pro-environmental practices also shows that signal-based effects depend on the nature and co-occurrence of CSP practices.
practical_implication: Companies may benefit from communicating CSP initiatives through websites, recruitment materials, and recruiters because job seekers must be aware of CSP before receiving its signals. The paper specifically suggests promoting external CSP recognition to signal prestige, explaining links between company values and CSP practices to inform value fit, and explicitly linking CSP to concern for employees to inform expected treatment.
limitations: The relatively young participants may limit generalizability, and the studies address early recruitment stages, so whether the findings extend to later stages remains unknown. In Study 1, the no-CSP web pages contained less information and fewer positive statements than the CSP pages, making information amount and positivity alternative explanations; analogous differences could also affect Study 2. In the field study, substantial co-occurrence of community and environmental CSP increased the potential for suppression when both dimensions were modeled together, particularly for environmental CSP.
future_research: The authors call for tests of whether the effects differ for older job seekers, persist into later recruitment stages or after hiring, and depend on prior knowledge about the employer. They recommend examining other signals from CSP, whether more people-oriented CSP practices produce stronger expected-treatment signals, and boundary conditions involving social-approval needs, internalized CSP values, fairness sensitivity, and attributions of disingenuous motives. They also propose assessing whether CSP changes applicant-pool size and quality by measuring general mental ability, conscientiousness, and other predictors of job performance.
abstract: Research on employee recruitment has shown that an organization’s corporate social performance (CSP) affects its attractiveness as an employer, but the underlying mechanisms and processes through which this occurs are poorly understood. We propose that job seekers receive signals from CSP that inform three signal-based mechanisms that ultimately affect organizational attractiveness: job seekers’ anticipated pride from being affiliated with the organization, their perceived value fit with the organization, and their expectations about how the organization treats its employees. We hypothesized that these signal-based mechanisms mediate the relationships between CSP and organizational attractiveness, focusing on two aspects of CSP: an organization’s community involvement and pro-environmental practices. In an experiment (n ⴝ 180), we manipulated CSP via a company’s web pages. In a field study (n ⴝ 171), we measured CSP content in the recruitment materials used by organizations at a job fair and job seekers’ perceptions of the organizations’ CSP. Results provided support for the signal-based mechanisms, and we discuss the implications for theory, future research, and practice.

title: Reputation and Decision Making under Ambiguity: A Study of U.S. Venture Capital Firms' Investments in the Emerging Clean Energy Sector
methods: Longitudinal archival panel study; discrete-time random-effects panel logistic regression for sector entry; random-effects panel linear regressions for syndication and later-stage investment; panel GEE with a probit link for commitment; Heckman two-stage correction for selection; one-year-lagged predictors and supplementary robustness analyses
industry: Venture capital investments in clean energy startups
units: U.S.-based VC firms and VC firm-year observations
n_sample: 3,574 VC firms (37,293 firm-years); risk-reduction panel: 172 VC firms (709 firm-years)
authors: Petkova, A. P.; Wadhwa, A.; Yao, X.; Jain, S.
theories: legitimacy theory; social cognition and behavioral theories
keywords: clean energy sector; decision making under ambiguity; reputation; risk reduction strategies; sector legitimation; venture capital firms
research_question: How does a firm’s reputation affect its decision making under ambiguity through pressures to pursue risky opportunities and to preserve consistent performance, and how does the legitimation of an emerging sector directly and interactively shape these decisions? The study examines these questions in U.S. VC firms’ investment decisions concerning the emerging clean energy sector.
hypotheses:
H1: The higher the reputation of a VC firm, the higher the likelihood that it will invest in an emerging sector.
H2: The higher the reputation of a VC firm, the greater its use of (a) syndication and (b) later-stage investment, and (c) the lower its levels of commitment when investing in an emerging sector.
H3: Sector legitimation will increase the likelihood of a VC firm investing in an emerging sector.
H4: Sector legitimation will reduce the use of (a) syndication, (b) later-stage investment, and (c) lower levels of commitment among VC firms investing in an emerging sector.
H5: Sector legitimation will strengthen the relationship between a VC firm’s reputation and its likelihood to invest in an emerging sector.
H6: Sector legitimation will weaken the relationship between a VC firm’s reputation and its use of (a) syndication, (b) later-stage investment, and (c) lower levels of commitment when investing in an emerging sector.
mechanism_summary: Reputation creates dual pressures under ambiguity. High stakeholder expectations raise reputable VC firms’ aspirations, while reputation also supplies resources and access to startups, making these firms more likely to interpret an emerging sector as an opportunity and invest in it. At the same time, the greater reputational cost of being wrong makes reputable firms manage exposure through syndication, later-stage investment, and lower commitment. Sector legitimation attracts attention, supplies information and structure, and provides social proof, thereby increasing entry and altering how reputation relates to both entry and risk reduction.
data_measures: The archival data cover the population of 3,574 U.S.-based VC firms active from 1990 through 2008, yielding 37,293 firm-year observations for the sector-entry analysis; a second panel follows the 172 firms that invested in 181 clean energy startups, yielding 709 firm-years for the risk-reduction analyses. Investment data came from VentureXpert, with sector data from the Earth Policy Institute, U.S. Department of Energy, LexisNexis Academic, and DSIRE; 13 semi-structured exploratory interviews with clean energy VC investors informed the characterization of ambiguity. Entry equals whether a focal firm first invested in a clean energy startup; syndication is the average number of co-investment partners across clean energy rounds; later-stage investment is the average stage of the clean energy startups funded; and commitment is the number of clean energy startups funded divided by all startups funded by the VC firm in that year. Reputation is a annually updated composite of five standardized five-year indicators—portfolio companies, amount invested, funds raised, number of funds, and portfolio-company IPOs—transformed to a 100-point scale. Sector legitimation combines standardized media attention, federal financial incentives, and cumulative peer investments (Cronbach’s alpha = .97). The authors use observational longitudinal panel models with one-year-lagged predictors, random effects, time-period dummies, and a two-stage selection correction; the design is not a natural or randomized experiment.
key_findings: H1 was supported: VC firm reputation had a positive and significant effect on entry, with a one-standard-deviation increase in reputation multiplying the odds of clean energy investment by 1.25. H2a, H2b, and H2c were supported: reputation positively predicted syndication and later-stage investment and negatively predicted level of commitment, indicating greater use of lower commitment as a risk-reduction strategy. H3 was supported: a one-standard-deviation increase in sector legitimation multiplied the odds of entry by 2.33. H4a was not supported because sector legitimation had no significant effect on syndication; H4b was not supported and the result ran contrary to its prediction because legitimation positively affected later-stage investment; H4c was supported because legitimation positively affected level of commitment, thereby reducing the use of lower commitment. H5 was supported: sector legitimation positively strengthened the reputation–entry relationship. H6a and H6b were not supported and ran contrary to prediction because the interactions of legitimation with reputation were positive and significant for syndication and later-stage investment; H6c was not supported because the interaction for commitment was not significant.
theoretical_contribution: The study moves beyond the self-reinforcing reputation–performance relationship by showing that, under ambiguity, reputation simultaneously promotes risky exploration and more extensive risk reduction rather than only conservative persistence. It identifies aspirations and concern for reputation preservation as mechanisms producing these dual pressures and distinguishes decision making under ambiguity from decision making under uncertainty. It also shows that sector legitimation does not affect all firms uniformly: its influence on investment strategies depends on firm reputation, extending reputation, legitimacy, and VC decision-making research.
practical_implication: In the clean energy setting, the authors argue that reputable VC firms’ ability to legitimate new activity is tempered by extensive use of risk-reduction strategies; given the sector’s large capital requirements, small-scale commitments may be inadequate to accelerate its development. They state that policymakers and clean energy protagonists seeking faster sector development may need to identify alternative funding sources or find ways to encourage greater involvement by the VC community.
limitations: The VC reputation index aggregates firm-level data and does not capture partners’ individual reputations, which could confound firm and individual reputation in other samples even though excluding the two such cases identified here did not change the results. The study does not analyze VC firms’ choices among syndication partners, and the small number of reputable clean energy investors prevents conclusions about the roles of prospective partners’ reputation and sector experience. The observation window ends in 2008 before a major policy-induced change in the sector, and generalizability may be limited because VC firms routinely take risks, make a restricted set of investment decisions, and are knowledge-intensive organizations.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether reputable firms’ ability to recognize institutional change produces long-term performance benefits, on how reputation and experience differ under uncertainty versus ambiguity, and on the rationales, benefits, drawbacks, and combined use of syndication, later-stage investment, and lower commitment. They recommend examining confounding between individual and firm reputations, as well as the sector-specific experience and reputation of prospective syndication partners. They also propose using the post-2008 institutional shock as a natural-experiment opportunity to study new clean energy investment models and subsequent investment trajectories, and testing the identified mechanisms in less knowledge-intensive contexts.
abstract: This study examines the role of reputation on decision making under ambiguity. Drawing on social cognition and behavioral theories, we propose that a firm’s reputation exerts dual pressures on its decision making under ambiguity. On the one hand, a firm’s reputation increases its aspirations for future performance and promotes its engagement in risky strategies to achieve them. On the other hand, preserving the already established reputation requires a firm to deliver consistent performance over time, which promotes greater use of risk reduction strategies. Our analyses of the U.S. venture capital firms’ investments in the clean energy sector from 1990 to 2008 demonstrate that while reputable firms are more likely to invest in the emerging sector, they also employ risk reduction strategies more extensively. The sector’s legitimation further influences these firms’ investment decisions both directly and through its interaction with firm reputation.

title: Turnkey or Tailored? Relational Pluralism, Institutional Complexity, and the Organizational Adoption of More or Less Customized Practices
methods: Concurrent mixed-method triangulation using a survey, archival data, interviews, a focus group, and conference observations; separate logit regressions in STATA 12.
industry: Multiple industries: services, retail, financial, utilities and transportation, manufacturing, wholesale trade, and other
units: Fortune 500 firms
authors: Raffaelli, R.; Glynn, M. A.
theories: institutional complexity; institutional theory (normative and mimetic isomorphism); relational pluralism
keywords: employee volunteering programs; institutional complexity; mimetic isomorphism; normative conformity; practice adoption; practice customization; relational pluralism
research_question: How do organizations’ ties to extra-industry professional networks and industry peers, together with organizational filters, influence whether firms adopt less customized turnkey practices or more customized tailored practices?
hypotheses:
- H1: Organizational adoption of a turnkey practice will be positively affected by participation in an extra-industry network that exposes the organization to the practice.
- H2: Organizational adoption of a tailored practice will be positively affected by the interaction between participation in an extra-industry professional network that normatively sanctions the practice and the practice’s intra-industry prevalence, which legitimates customized adaptation.
- H3: Organizational adoption of a CSR practice will be positively influenced by organizational infrastructure, governance and leadership involvement, organizational identity, and the organization’s elite standing in its field.
mechanism_summary: Professional networks expose firms to normatively sanctioned practices and ready-made templates, which the paper argues is sufficient for adoption of the less customized DOS practice. Tailored SBV adoption instead depends on relational pluralism: normative pressure from the professional network combines with mimetic legitimation from industry peers to support customized adaptation. Organizational filters shape firms’ receptivity to these pressures, with infrastructure and identity playing different roles across practice variants.
data_measures:
- Data and design: A 2008 survey of senior executives responsible for CSR at 161 Fortune 500 firms (33% response rate), supplemented by public archives, interviews with 12 expert informants, a focus group with 12 community-involvement directors, and CSR-conference observations.
- Outcomes: Three dummy variables coded adoption as 1 and nonadoption as 0 for any EVP, turnkey DOS, and tailored SBV.
- Relational predictors: Industry diffusion was the percentage of firms in the focal firm’s two-digit SIC industry adopting the same practice and was mean-centered. Practice-network participation indicated attendance at one or both CECP and BCCCC annual conferences; H2 used its interaction with industry diffusion.
- Institutional filters: Infrastructure summed four binary items on written CSR processes and standards (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.72); governance and leadership involvement indicated public CSR-event participation by at least 30% of the top two management levels; identity was GRI reporting; and elite standing was Fortune 100 membership in 2008.
- Analysis: Separate associational logit models in STATA 12 predicted EVP, DOS, and SBV adoption, with controls for explicit business benefit, organizational age, and whether EVP practices were based only in the United States.
key_findings:
- H1 was supported: Participation in the CSR practice network positively predicted turnkey DOS adoption (b = 0.78, p < .05), while industry diffusion was not significant.
- H2 was supported: The practice-network-by-industry-diffusion interaction positively predicted tailored SBV adoption (b = 0.16, p < .05). The corresponding interaction was not significant for any EVP or for DOS.
- H3 received partial support. Infrastructure positively predicted all three outcomes (EVP b = 0.55, p < .05; DOS b = 0.38, p < .05; SBV b = 0.61, p < .01). Identity positively predicted EVP (b = 1.19, p < .05) and SBV (b = 0.93, p < .05), but not DOS. Governance and leadership involvement positively predicted any EVP (b = 2.76, p < .01), was only marginal for DOS (b = 0.79, p < .10), and was not significant for SBV. Elite field position was marginally negative for EVP (b = -1.20, p < .10) and nonsignificant for DOS and SBV, so it did not support H3’s predicted positive direction.
theoretical_contribution: By distinguishing turnkey from tailored practice variants, the study shows that relational ties do not operate uniformly: professional-network participation predicts turnkey adoption, whereas tailored adoption depends on the joint normative and mimetic pressures created by relational pluralism. It integrates institutional, network, and innovation accounts by showing how organizational embeddedness in practice and industry fields, together with organizational filters, produces heterogeneous responses to institutional complexity.
practical_implication: CSR practitioners should consider both internal organizational capabilities and external relational influences when deciding whether to adopt emerging CSR practices. The paper specifically highlights managers’ active involvement in CSR professional conferences and communities of practice as relevant to EVP adoption and to decisions about when to devote organizational resources to a new practice.
limitations: The study examines 161 Fortune 500 firms, so adoption patterns may differ for smaller, younger, or less prestigious firms. Elite standing is measured through Fortune 100 membership based on revenue, and the authors note that more fine-grained subjective or qualitative status measures may reveal different effects. The 2008 cross-sectional design does not examine temporal waves or the leading and lagging effects of relational ties and institutional filters.
future_research: The authors call for time-series research on temporal waves of practice diffusion and the leading or lagging effects of relational ties and institutional filters. They also propose distinguishing leaders who act as knowledgeable practice champions from symbolic figureheads and examining how internal and external audiences construe organizational identity in relation to practice adoption. Further work should test smaller, younger, or less prestigious firms and other organizational fields, using more fine-grained measures of elite status.
abstract: We examine how the organizational adoption of new practices is influenced by relational pluralism, i.e., an organization’s multiple ties to actors inside and outside its industry. We theorize that institutional mechanisms of practice diffusion underlying relational networks and filtered by organizational characteristics influence the adoption of practices that are more customized (tailored) or less customized (turnkey). We hypothesize, first, that organizations participating in extra-industry professional networks will, through normative conformity, be more likely to adopt turnkey practices; second, that the normative pressure of professional networks will interact with the mimeticism of industry peers such that organizations will be more likely to adopt tailored practices; and third, that organizational filters will affect adoption of all practices. Using unique survey data from 161 Fortune 500 organizations, supplemented by archival and qualitative data, we focus on two corporate social responsibility practice variants. We find significant support for our first two hypotheses and mixed support for our third: Organizational infrastructure and identity significantly affect practice adoption, albeit in different ways, but only marginal support for leadership and elite organizational status. Our results point to how a complex web of relational ties affects the organizational adoption of practice variants that differ in their degree of customization.

title: Do Ties Really Bind? The Effect of Knowledge and Commercialization Networks on Opposition to Standards
methods: Longitudinal firm-vote data; ordered logistic regression with firm and year fixed effects, ballot fixed effects in the fully specified models, one-year-lagged predictors, and robustness checks.
industry: Computer industry; INCITS T10, T11, and T13 peripheral-interface standards subcommittees
time_period: 14-year study period, 1994 through 2008
units: Firm-vote observations across 135 firms and 241 ballot measures
n_sample: 9,120 firm-vote observations
authors: Ranganathan, R.; Rosenkopf, L.
theories: alliance network multiplicity; exploration–exploitation duality; relational pluralism
keywords: commercialization ties; interorganizational relationships; knowledge linkages; opposition to the standard
research_question: How do firms’ positions in knowledge and commercialization networks independently and jointly influence their opposition to a coordinated technological standard?
hypotheses:
H1: The more central a focal firm is within the knowledge network of member firms, the lower its opposition to the standard.

H2: The more central a focal firm is within the commercialization network of member firms, the higher its opposition to the standard.

H3: Knowledge network centrality negatively moderates the effect of commercialization network centrality on opposition to the coordinated standard; the more peripheral the firm’s knowledge network position, the greater the positive effect of commercialization centrality on opposition.
mechanism_summary: Knowledge network centrality indicates that a firm’s knowledge is foundational to other committee members and therefore likely to be reflected in the emerging standard, reducing its opposition. Commercialization network centrality captures a firm’s ability to appropriate rents from complementary ties built around current technologies; a system-wide interoperability standard can devalue those investments, increasing opposition. Consequently, firms peripheral in the knowledge network but central in the commercialization network have the most to lose and are most likely to delay the standard.
data_measures:
The study combines INCITS archival records with alliance announcements from Factiva, NBER patent-citation data, Derwent patent data, and firm data from Compustat, Hoover’s, and Corptech. The dependent variable is a firm’s ballot vote, coded 0 for yes, 1 for abstain, 2 for yes with comments or conditions, and 3 for no, so higher values indicate greater opposition.

Knowledge network centrality is the weighted degree centrality of a firm in a five-year moving network of knowledge-generating alliances; an alternative measure uses in-degree centrality in a five-year patent cross-citation network. Commercialization network centrality is weighted degree centrality in a five-year moving network of alliances involving existing technologies, including interoperability, marketing, licensing, and production agreements. The authors estimate ordered logistic regressions at the firm-vote level with one-year-lagged predictors, firm and year fixed effects, and ballot fixed effects in the fully specified models; the design is observational rather than experimental.
key_findings:
H1 was supported: knowledge network centrality was negatively associated with opposition, and a one-unit increase decreased the odds of not voting yes by 0.41 times. H2 was supported: commercialization network centrality was positively associated with opposition, and a one-unit increase increased the odds of not voting yes by 1.85 times.

H3 was supported: the interaction between knowledge and commercialization network centrality was negative and significant, so the positive commercialization-centrality effect increased as knowledge centrality decreased. The likelihood of not voting yes was approximately three times higher for a firm central in the commercialization network and peripheral in the knowledge network than for a firm with the reverse positions.
theoretical_contribution: The study shows that network-position effects depend on tie function: knowledge and commercialization centrality have opposing, interacting, and nonadditive effects on firms’ standards-setting conduct. Pooling the two alliance types yields no discernible centrality effect because their influences counterbalance, demonstrating why relational pluralism and alliance network multiplicity must be modeled explicitly. It further shows that central network positions can either promote or impede technological coordination depending on the network, industry context, and strategic behavior examined.
practical_implication: In voluntary technology standards committees, firms peripheral in the knowledge network but central in the commercialization network are most likely to cast opposing votes because they have the most to lose from changes to current technology. Their opposition can delay the standard and allow them to continue exploiting current network positions.
limitations: The authors caution that the findings may be particular to a systemic industry in which substantial technological competition occurs within a standards forum, limiting their scope. Opposition to a standard is also a context-specific behavioral dependent variable, so the findings should not be assumed to generalize to other outcomes or settings.
future_research: Future research should incorporate other forms of relational pluralism, including interpersonal networks formed through mobility or common institutional affiliations, and assess differentiation within and commonality across tie classifications. The authors also call for extensions to other industries and context-specific dependent variables, including studies of diverging votes or changing committee participation among longstanding alliance partners.
abstract: We examine how the multiplicity of interorganizational relationships affects strategic behavior by studying the influence of two such relationships—knowledge linkages and commercialization ties—on the voting behavior of firms in a technological standards-setting committee. We find that, while centrally positioned firms in the knowledge network exhibit lower opposition to the standard, centrally positioned firms in the commercialization network exhibit higher opposition to the standard. Thus, the influence of network position on coordination is contingent upon the type of interorganizational tie. Furthermore, when we consider these relationships jointly, knowledge centrality moderates the opposing effect of commercialization centrality, such that the commercialization centrality effect increases with decreasing levels of knowledge centrality. In other words, firms most likely to delay the standard are peripheral in the knowledge network yet central in the commercialization network, which suggests that they have the most to lose from changes to current technology.
