title: Executive Departures Without Client Losses: The Role of Multiplex Ties in Exchange Partner Retention
methods: Longitudinal archival event-history study; discrete-time hazard models with a complementary log-log link, merger fixed effects, and robust standard errors clustered by advertising parent firm-client parent firm dyad; robustness checks include client-industry fixed effects and a Lee (1983) selection correction
industry: Advertising agencies (SIC 7311)
time_period: 2000-2003 (three-year postmerger observation window)
units: Agency-client relationship dyad-years (2,313 relationships with complete independent-variable data)
n_sample: 4,117 dyad-years
authors: Rogan, M.
theories: economic multiplexity and structural embeddedness (Gimeno & Woo, 1996; Granovetter, 1985); multiunit organizational perspective (Cyert & March, 1963; March, 1962); triadic theory (Simmel, 1950; Krackhardt, 1998; Shipilov & Li, 2012)
keywords: across-agency multiplex ties; client tie loss; convergent interests; distributed control; exchange partner retention; executive departures; interorganizational multiplexity; within-agency multiplex ties
research_question: How do within-agency and across-agency multiplex ties affect agency-client tie dissolution, and when do across-agency multiplex ties reduce the positive effect of executive departures on client loss? Specifically, how do the distribution of control and the convergence of interests among intraorganizational units condition relationship retention?
hypotheses:
H1: The likelihood of agency-client tie dissolution decreases the more the tie is embedded in within-agency multiplex ties.
H2: The likelihood of agency-client tie dissolution decreases the more the tie is embedded in across-agency multiplex ties.
H3: The positive effect of executive departures on tie dissolution decreases the more the tie is embedded in across-agency multiplex ties.
H4: The negative interaction effect of across-agency multiplex ties and executive departures on tie dissolution increases with the proportion of non-competitive ties.
mechanism_summary: Multiplex ties are theorized to improve retention through reputational enforcement of behavioral norms and through learning and information transfer across ties. Within-agency multiplex ties combine convergent interests with concentrated control, so they can stabilize ties generally but do not insulate the relationship from executive departures. Across-agency ties distribute control, reducing individual executives' influence and bargaining power; when those ties connect non-competing agencies, convergent interests also permit learning across units. Ties spanning competing agencies lack this convergence, limiting their additional stabilizing effect when executives depart.
data_measures: The study uses archival data on client relationships following 10 advertising-firm mergers completed in 2000, yielding 108 agencies. Mergers came from SDC Platinum; agency characteristics, executives, and client relationships came from REDBOOKS; and client information came from Bureau Van Dijk's Amadeus, Osiris, and Orbis databases. The final analysis contains 2,313 relationships observed over 2000-2003, or 4,117 dyad-years. Tie dissolution equals one in the first year an agency no longer lists the client account in REDBOOKS. Executive departures equal the number of previously listed executives absent from the current-year listing divided by the prior executive count. Within-agency multiplexity is the number of accounts an agency has with a client relative to its total accounts, excluding the focal tie; across-agency multiplexity is the density of possible ties to the same client across agencies in the parent firm. The proportion of non-competitive ties is the share of across-agency multiplex ties involving agencies in the same network. The multiplexity measures are logged, interaction components are mean-centered, and hypotheses are tested with discrete-time complementary log-log hazard models, merger fixed effects, and dyad-clustered robust standard errors. The postmerger design reduces the relative influence of general client dissatisfaction but is associational rather than a causal-identification design; robustness checks address client-industry heterogeneity and selection into merger.
key_findings: Executive departures are positively and significantly related to tie dissolution. H1 is supported: within-agency multiplex ties have a negative, significant association with dissolution (Model 4: b = -0.11, p < .05). H2 and H3 are only conditionally supported: their constituent effects are significant in Models 2 and 3, respectively, but lose significance in Model 4 because across-agency multiplex ties reduce dissolution, including the increase associated with executive departures, only when the ties connect non-competing agencies. H4 is supported by a negative, significant three-way interaction (b = -73.96, p < .05); when executive departures and non-competitive ties are high, a one-standard-deviation increase in across-agency multiplex ties decreases the predicted probability of tie dissolution by 80%, whereas the effect is negligible when non-competitive ties are low. The within-agency multiplexity-executive departures interaction is not significant. Most robustness analyses reproduce the main pattern, but the agency-level aggregation did not reproduce moderation by the proportion of non-competitive ties. The proposed alternative in which multiplexity reduces client loss by preventing executive departures is rejected as a mediation explanation.
theoretical_contribution: The study relaxes the assumption that firms in multiplex relationships are unitary actors, showing that the distribution of control across intraorganizational units and the convergence or divergence of those units' interests determine whether multiplexity stabilizes exchange. It conceptualizes relationships spanning units as multiplex hybrids between dyads and triads: non-competitive hybrids combine distributed control with convergent interests, whereas competitive hybrids behave more like multiplex triads. The findings extend research on executive mobility by identifying firm-level multiplex bonds that reduce dependence on particular individuals and offer a relational-retention rationale for holding-company structures in professional services.
practical_implication: For advertising firms, multiple client ties spread across non-competing agencies can reduce vulnerability to client-account loss when executives leave, because control is distributed while unit interests remain convergent. The paper extends this implication only to firms with comparable multiunit structures, including investment-banking divisions, consulting-firm country offices, and hospital networks, where control over a client relationship is distributed rather than concentrated in one unit.
limitations: The data do not identify which executives served particular clients or where departing executives moved, so the study cannot observe whether clients followed them or distinguish fully between solo and collective departures. It examines only advertising-firm-side multiplexity in a postmerger sample; client-side multiplexity remains untested, and acquisition selection is not entirely exogenous despite the reported selection correction. The arguments assume relationships are maintained for economic value and examine ownership ties joining units that share market ties to a client, leaving affective commitments and other multiplex tie types outside the study.
future_research: The paper calls for studies that track executives' destinations and whether their clients follow, and that compare the retention effects of multiplexity under solo versus collective executive departures. It also proposes empirical investigation of client-side multiplexity. Further research could examine which multiplex ties generate affective commitments, how those commitments affect retention, and whether multiplexity composed of ties such as alliances rather than ownership or market ties produces similar stability.
abstract: To reduce vulnerability to exchange relationship loss when executives leave, firms often form multiple ties to the same exchange partners. Despite the assumed importance of interorganizational multiplexity for relationship retention, theory and evidence of its effect are lacking. Analysis of a longitudinal sample of client ties of advertising firms confirms that, in general, multiplexity improves retention. However, only relationships that span intraorganizational units with convergent interests reduce the positive effect of advertising agency executive departures on client tie loss. The findings highlight the need to consider the implications of intraorganizational structure for theories of interorganizational relationship retention, and suggest an additional rationale for the persistence of the holding company structure in professional services firms despite limited returns to scale.
apa_citation: Rogan, M. (2014). Executive departures without client losses: The role of multiplex ties in exchange partner retention. *Academy of Management Journal*, *57*(2), 563-584. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.1049

title: Relational Pluralism Within and Between Organizations
methods: Conceptual literature synthesis and a two-dimensional typology of relational pluralism, followed by a narrative review of the special issue's studies.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Shipilov, A.; Gulati, R.; Kilduff, M.; Li, S.; Tsai, W.
theories: identity theory; social network theory
keywords: multiple identities; multiple kinds of relationships; network ties; relational pluralism
research_question: How can relational pluralism, understood through actors' multiple identities and heterogeneous network ties, be classified, and what opportunities and constraints does it create within and between organizations?
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core construct: Relational pluralism involves multiple kinds of relationships and multiple identities.
- Typology dimensions: Single versus multiple identities and single versus multiple kinds of ties.
- Enabling outcomes: Flexibility in network tie formation, stable exchange relationships, and tailored innovation adoption.
- Constraining conditions: Identity incoherence, external audience dependence, and the coordination of multiple relationships.

Multiple relationship types and multiple identities give actors additional bases for action and tie formation. Multiple identities can increase flexibility once an actor is intelligible to relevant audiences, whereas incoherent identities under audience dependence can produce an illegitimacy discount. Because relational pluralism operates within and between organizations, its opportunities and constraints also depend on how ties and identities are coordinated across levels.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The paper integrates identity theory and social network theory by organizing research along two dimensions: whether actors have single or multiple identities and whether they maintain single or multiple kinds of ties. It frames relational pluralism as an inherently multi-level phenomenon and uses the typology to connect its enabling and constraining consequences within and between organizations.
practical_implication: For organizations, relational pluralism can provide flexibility in building network ties, support more stable exchange relationships, and enable the adoption of tailored innovations. It can also constrain an organization when external audiences have difficulty classifying it and the organization depends on those audiences for resources.
limitations: Not reported in paper
future_research: Future studies should examine multiple ties and multiple identities simultaneously, assess how each shapes the other, and investigate how they interact in affecting performance. The authors call for multi-level analyses of how interpersonal and interorganizational relationships develop into one another and how relational pluralism at one level affects another. They also identify organizational coordination of information and resource exchange, temporal multiplexity, relationship dynamics, and change across two-mode networks as research priorities.
abstract: Relational pluralism exists when actors maintain multiple kinds of relationships with one another and develop multiple identities as a result. The outcomes of relational pluralism can include greater flexibility in building network ties, more stable exchange relationships, and the ability to adopt tailored innovations. We develop a typology of relational pluralism and examine both the positive and negative features of relational pluralism inside and across organizations. We conclude with a discussion of future directions for research.

title: Friends and Foes: The Dynamics of Dual Social Structures
methods: Longitudinal interorganizational network analysis using rare-events logit models with dyad-level network autocorrelation, configuration-model comparisons against 1,000 randomized networks, and agent-based simulations linking dyadic and triadic tie formation to global network segregation.
industry: Pharmaceutical and biotechnology industry
units: Firm dyad-years
n_sample: 760,250 dyad-years
authors: Sytch, M.; Tatarynowicz, A.
theories: Structural balance theory (Heider, 1946, 1958)
keywords: balanced dyadic and triadic structures; collaboration; conflict; dual social structure; network segregation; structural balance theory
research_question: How do collaborative and conflictual relationships among corporate actors coevolve to produce balanced and unbalanced dyadic and triadic structures, and how do these micro-level formation dynamics aggregate to shape the global industry-wide network?
hypotheses:
- H1a: The number of current collaborative relationships between two firms will be positively related to a new collaborative relationship and negatively related to a new conflictual relationship.
- H1b: The number of current conflictual relationships between two firms will be positively related to a new conflictual relationship and negatively related to a new collaborative relationship.
- H2a: The number of third parties to which both firms hold collaborative ties will be positively related to a new collaborative relationship between the firms.
- H2b: The number of third parties to which one firm holds a collaborative tie and the other a conflictual tie will be positively related to a new conflictual relationship between the firms.
- H2c: The number of third parties to which both firms hold conflictual ties will be positively related to a new collaborative relationship between the firms.
- H3a: The number of third parties to which both firms hold collaborative ties will be negatively related to a new conflictual relationship between the firms.
- H3b: The number of third parties to which one firm holds a collaborative tie and the other a conflictual tie will be negatively related to a new collaborative relationship between the firms.
- H3c: The number of third parties to which both firms hold conflictual ties will be negatively related to a new conflictual relationship between the firms.
mechanism_summary: Structural balance implies that same-type relationships perpetuate while collaboration and conflict crowd one another out, increasing balanced uniplex dyads and reducing unbalanced multiplex dyads. At the triadic level, common third-party relationships were expected both to pull firms toward balanced triads and away from unbalanced triads, through cognitive alignment or tension and third-party intervention. The supported dyadic perpetuation and crowding-out dynamics, together with avoidance of unbalanced triads, aggregate into segregation of the global network into collaborative and conflictual segments.
data_measures:
The study combines partnership records from MERIT-CATI and BioScan with patent-infringement and antitrust litigation records from Lex Machina and PACER for a population of 2,200 companies in the global pharmaceutical and biotechnology industry during 1996-2006. Because partnerships were modeled with a five-year duration window, annual dual networks were analyzed from 2000 to 2006; the full risk set contained 760,250 dyad-years, and the rare-events logit estimation used a matched sample of 7,908 dyad-years comprising 1,318 realized relationships matched 1:5 to nonmaterialized relationships. Litigation data covered all 93 U.S. federal district courts, although antitrust cases filed only in state courts were not captured.

The collaboration and conflict dependent variables equaled 1 when a dyad entered at least one partnership or initiated at least one lawsuit, respectively, in year t + 1, and 0 otherwise. Current collaborative ties were counts of joint partnerships; current conflictual ties were counts of active patent-infringement and antitrust lawsuits; and the triadic predictors counted shared third parties linked to both firms by collaborative ties, conflictual ties, or one tie of each type. Models included year fixed effects, dyad-level network-autocorrelation terms, and controls for firm assets, long-term debt, profit, patents, joint patent citations, prior collaboration and conflict experience, and past dyadic ties. Complementary analyses compared observed motif formation with 1,000 configuration-model random networks and used agent-based simulations to assess global network segregation.
key_findings:
- H1a was supported. A one-standard-deviation increase in current collaborative relationships raised the probability of a new collaborative relationship by 27.1% and reduced the probability of a new conflictual relationship by 13.9%.
- H1b was supported. A one-standard-deviation increase in current conflictual relationships raised the probability of a new conflictual relationship by 14.9% and reduced the probability of a new collaborative relationship by 10.5%.
- H2a, H2b, and H2c were not supported: collaborative third parties and conflictual third parties had no effect on new collaboration, and mixed third parties had no effect on new conflict. The results therefore did not show a pull toward balanced triads.
- H3a was supported in the rare-events logit analysis: collaborative third parties reduced the likelihood of a new conflictual tie by 16.3%. The computational motif comparison was consistent (z = -3.36, p < .001).
- H3b was supported in the rare-events logit analysis: mixed third parties reduced the likelihood of a new collaborative tie by 9.8%. The computational motif comparison was consistent (z = -8.06, p < .001).
- H3c was supported in the rare-events logit analysis: conflictual third parties reduced the likelihood of a new conflictual tie by 15.8%. In the computational motif comparison, however, formation of the all-conflictual unbalanced triad was statistically indistinguishable from the random case.

The real network was segregated into collaborative and conflictual segments (S = -0.520). The agent-based scenario using the empirically estimated perpetuation, crowding-out, and unbalanced-triad effects provided the best fit (E(S) = -0.507, z = -0.359), while a scenario with a weaker pull away from unbalanced triads also fit well; this indicated that dyadic perpetuation and crowding out were more consequential for segregation than the triadic effect.
theoretical_contribution: The study extends structural balance theory from the stability of interpersonal cognitive structures to the formation of balanced and unbalanced structures among organizations. It conceptualizes collaboration and conflict as interdependent elements of one social space and links their dyadic and triadic coevolution to an emergent global network property, showing how balanced dyads and avoidance of unbalanced dyads can produce structural segregation. It also restores agency to common third parties by distinguishing their role as actors that can mediate or inhibit tie formation from their treatment as objects in the original balance formulation.
practical_implication: An apparent gap in collaborative connectivity can mask a fully fledged conflictual relationship, so examining collaborative ties alone can provide an incomplete picture of interorganizational social structure. In the paper's biotechnology and pharmaceutical setting, considering partnership and litigation ties jointly reveals how firms become separated into collaborative and conflictual network segments.
limitations: The authors cannot directly evaluate the generalizability of the findings to a broader range of social systems. The setting isolates extreme, emotionally charged patent-infringement and antitrust conflicts that are highly consequential and share a locus of managerial control with collaborative relationships, so variation in the nature of conflict across other settings may alter the documented dynamics. The short observation period and limited within-dyad variance also prevented dyad fixed-effects estimation, although dyad random-effects models produced consistent results.
future_research: Future work could distinguish brokerage by a mediator between conflicting parties from brokerage that spans two otherwise unconnected parties, and further evaluate the agency of common third parties in forming triadic structures. It could test effects on global network properties beyond segregation, such as small-world or core-periphery structure, and model reciprocal effects from the global system or institutional environment to micro-level tie formation. The theory could also be examined in broader social systems and across relationships where conflict and collaboration are more closely intertwined, including early interactions between venture-capital firms and targets or between acquirers and hostile-takeover targets.
abstract: This paper investigates the evolutionary dynamics of a dual social structure encompassing collaboration and conflict among corporate actors. We apply and advance structural balance theory to examine the formation of balanced and unbalanced dyadic and triadic structures, and to explore how these dynamics aggregate to shape the emergence of a global network. Our findings are threefold. First, we find that existing collaborative or conflictual relationships between two companies engender future relationships of the same type, but crowd out relationships of the different type. This results in (a) an increased likelihood of the formation of balanced (uniplex) relationships that combine multiple ties of either collaboration or conflict, and (b) a reduced likelihood of the formation of unbalanced (multiplex) relationships that combine collaboration and conflict between the same two firms. Second, we find that network formation is driven not by a pull toward balanced triads, but rather by a pull away from unbalanced triads. Third, we find that the observed micro-level dynamics of dyads and triads affect the structural segregation of the global network into two separate collaborative and conflictual segments of firms. Our empirical analyses used data on strategic partnerships and patent infringement and antitrust lawsuits in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals from 1996 to 2006.

title: Lunch Breaks Unpacked: The Role of Autonomy as a Moderator of Recovery during Lunch
methods: Multi-source experience sampling over 10 workdays; daily employee reports matched to coworker fatigue ratings; multilevel random-coefficient modeling using HLM 6.06 with restricted maximum likelihood, person-centered Level 1 predictors, and temporal controls.
industry: Higher education administration
time_period: 10 workdays
units: Administrative employees; daily observations nested within employees
n_sample: 78 employees
authors: Trougakos, J. P.; Hideg, I.; Cheng, B. H.; Beal, D. J.
theories: ego depletion theory (EDT); self-determination theory (SDT)
keywords: ego depletion; end-of-workday fatigue; lunch break activities; lunch break autonomy; self-determination theory; work recovery
research_question: How do daily social, work, and relaxing activities during lunch breaks relate to end-of-workday fatigue, and how does employees' daily lunch break autonomy moderate these within-person relations?
hypotheses:
- H1a (SDT): Higher levels of social activities during the lunch break will result in lower end-of-workday fatigue.
- H1b (EDT): Higher levels of social activities during the lunch break will result in higher end-of-workday fatigue.
- H2: Higher levels of lunch break autonomy will result in lower end-of-workday fatigue.
- H3: Lunch break autonomy will moderate the effect of social activities on end-of-workday fatigue, such that social activities result in more fatigue when autonomy is low and less fatigue when autonomy is high.
- H4: Higher levels of work activities during the lunch break will result in higher end-of-workday fatigue.
- H5: Lunch break autonomy will moderate the effect of work activities on end-of-workday fatigue, such that work activities result in more fatigue when autonomy is low and less fatigue when autonomy is high.
- H6: Higher levels of relaxing activities during the lunch break will result in lower end-of-workday fatigue.
- H7: Lunch break autonomy will moderate the effect of relaxing activities on end-of-workday fatigue, such that the effect is stronger when autonomy is lower and weaker when autonomy is higher.
mechanism_summary: Ego depletion theory predicts that social interaction and continued work require effortful self-regulation and consume limited energy, whereas relaxation permits regulatory resources to recover. Self-determination theory predicts that social and work activities can satisfy relatedness and competence needs and restore energy when those activities are autonomously chosen. Integrating the theories, the paper argues that autonomy determines whether social and work activities deplete or restore energy, while low autonomy combined with little relaxation is especially depleting.
data_measures: Employees reported their lunch break activities and autonomy immediately after lunch, and coworkers rated focal employees' fatigue near the end of each workday for 10 workdays. The final multilevel sample comprised 78 administrative employees and 444 matched daily responses. Relaxing activity used three Work Recovery Experience Questionnaire items; work activity used three modified break-activity items; social activity used two adapted items; and lunch break autonomy used three Work Recovery Experience Questionnaire items, all on 7-point scales. Coworker-rated fatigue used the PANAS items "tired" and "sluggish." The authors estimated multilevel random-coefficient models with restricted maximum likelihood, person-centered Level 1 predictors, and controls for day, sine, cosine, and lagged fatigue; the observational design provides temporally ordered associations rather than experimental causal identification.
key_findings:
H1b, H4, and H6 were supported, whereas H1a was not: social activity (B = .17, beta = .23) and work activity (B = .12, beta = .18) predicted higher fatigue, while relaxing activity predicted lower fatigue (B = -.11, beta = -.15; all p < .05 in Step 2). H2 was not supported because lunch break autonomy had no significant main effect on fatigue.

H3 and H5 were supported: the social activity by autonomy (B = -.20, beta = -.14) and work activity by autonomy (B = -.21, beta = -.14) interactions were significant (p < .05). Social activity significantly increased fatigue at autonomy scores at or below .13 and reduced fatigue at scores at or above 1.80; work activity increased fatigue at scores at or below -.06 and reduced fatigue at scores at or above 1.89.

H7 was supported: the relaxing activity by autonomy interaction was positive (B = .16, beta = .12, p < .05), so relaxation's negative association with fatigue was significant at autonomy scores at or below .04 and weakened as autonomy increased. Low autonomy combined with low relaxing activity was especially fatiguing; high autonomy did not add to the benefit of high relaxation.
theoretical_contribution: The study integrates ego depletion theory and self-determination theory in work recovery research, showing that autonomy reconciles their competing predictions by changing whether social and work lunch activities deplete or restore energy. It also advances a dynamic, within-person view of autonomy and extends recovery research to lunch breaks as consequential within-workday recovery episodes.
practical_implication: Employees should attend to how they use lunch breaks: work and social activities may produce poorer immediate recovery, whereas relaxing activities can aid recovery. Managers and organizations should avoid pressuring employees to work during breaks or to join lunch activities they do not freely choose, because autonomy over personal break time can offset the fatigue associated with work, social activity, or insufficient relaxation.
limitations: Coworker ratings captured externally observable fatigue and may have missed internal aspects, although supplemental self- and coworker-rated fatigue correlated at r = .30. The study theorized resource depletion, resource restoration, and psychological need fulfillment but did not measure those mechanisms directly. Autonomy was measured for the lunch break as a whole rather than for each activity, and the design did not cover other work breaks, after-work time, or weekends; the social measure also did not identify interaction partners or interaction content.
future_research: Future studies should measure regulatory resources, need fulfillment, and how resources are depleted or restored, and could examine conservation of resources theory as an alternative account. Research should track recovery across other work breaks, after-work periods, weekends, and longer-term outcomes, including how one break shapes later activity choices. The paper also calls for greater specificity about social interaction partners and content and for research on nutritional choices and nutrient consumption during lunch.
abstract: Work recovery research has focused mainly on how after-work break activities help employees replenish their resources and reduce fatigue. Given that employees spend a considerable amount of time at work, understanding how they can replenish their resources during the workday is critical. Drawing on ego depletion (Muraven & Baumeister, 2000) and self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 1985), we employed multi-source experience sampling methods to test the effects of a critical boundary condition, employee lunch break autonomy, on the relation between lunch break activities and end-of-workday fatigue. Although specific energy-relevant activities had a main effect on end-of-workday fatigue, each of these was moderated by the degree of autonomous choice associated with the break. Specifically, for activities that supported the psychological needs of relatedness and competence (i.e., social and work activities, respectively), as lunch break autonomy increased, effects switched from increasing fatigue to reducing fatigue. To the extent that lunch break activities involved relaxation, however, lunch break autonomy was only important when levels of relaxation were low. We conclude that lunch break autonomy plays a complex and pivotal role in conferring the potential energetic benefits of lunch break activities. Contributions to theory and practice are discussed.

title: Knowledge Networks, Collaboration Networks, and Exploratory Innovation
methods: Longitudinal patent-data network analysis with negative binomial regressions; knowledge- and collaboration-network predictors precede the 1996-2000 outcome period.
industry: Microprocessor manufacturing
time_period: 1976-1995 knowledge-network history; 1991-1995 collaboration-network predictor window; 1996-2000 outcome observation period
units: Researchers at one firm
n_sample: 844 researchers
authors: Wang, C.; Rodan, S.; Fruin, M.; Xu, X.
theories: knowledge embeddedness; knowledge-based search; structural holes
keywords: collaboration networks; degree centrality; exploratory innovation; knowledge networks; structural holes
research_question: How do structural holes and degree centrality in a firm’s knowledge network and researcher collaboration network differently affect a researcher’s exploration of knowledge elements new to the firm’s extant stock of knowledge?
hypotheses:
- H1: A researcher whose knowledge elements have more structural holes in a firm’s knowledge network tends to explore fewer knowledge elements new to the firm’s extant stock of knowledge.
- H2: The degree centrality of a researcher’s knowledge elements in a firm’s knowledge network has an inverted-U-shaped relationship with the number of explored knowledge elements new to the firm’s extant stock of knowledge.
- H3: A researcher with more structural holes in a firm’s collaboration network among researchers tends to explore more knowledge elements new to the firm’s extant stock of knowledge.
- H4: A researcher with higher degree centrality in a firm’s collaboration network tends to explore fewer knowledge elements new to the firm’s extant stock of knowledge.
mechanism_summary: Knowledge-network structural holes indicate unexploited combinatorial opportunities among extant knowledge elements; exploiting those opportunities draws limited attention, resources, and motivation away from exploring knowledge elements outside the firm and can create a competency trap. Additional analyses separate a direct negative effect on exploration from an indirect positive effect mediated through the number of new patents, with the overall effect remaining negative. Increasing knowledge-element degree centrality initially raises perceived combinatorial potential and search efficiency, but high centrality brings diminishing returns as combinatorial value is exhausted. In the collaboration network, structural holes provide timely information and autonomy that facilitate exploration, whereas degree-central researchers benefit from current opportunities, are immersed in prevailing paradigms, and have status interests tied to extant knowledge elements.
data_measures: The study uses USPTO patent data from one leading U.S. microprocessor manufacturer and follows 844 researchers who patented during 1991-1995 and remained active during 1996-2000. The authors constructed a 1976-1995 knowledge network in which nodes were industrial subclasses and ties indicated their joint use in patents, and a 1991-1995 collaboration network in which researchers were tied through patent co-authorship. The dependent variable was the number of industrial subclasses in a researcher’s 1996-2000 patents that had not appeared in the firm’s 1976-1995 patent stock. Knowledge-network structural holes and degree centrality were calculated for each knowledge element and averaged across the researcher’s knowledge portfolio; collaboration-network structural holes used Burt’s constraint-based measure, and collaboration degree centrality counted collaboration partners. Negative binomial regressions modeled the overdispersed count outcome with researcher, knowledge, network, geography, and observation-period controls; the longitudinal design is observational.
key_findings: All four hypotheses were supported in the primary Model 3. H1 was supported: knowledge-network structural holes had a negative effect (b = -1.30, p < .001), and a one-unit increase multiplied the exploration rate by 0.27. H2 was supported: knowledge-network degree centrality had a positive first-order coefficient (b = 0.07, p < .001) and a negative squared coefficient (b = -0.001, p < .05), producing an inverted-U relationship with an inflection point around 39. H3 was supported: collaboration-network structural holes had a positive effect (b = 0.56, p < .05), and a one-unit increase multiplied the exploration rate by 1.75. H4 was supported: collaboration-network degree centrality had a negative effect (b = -0.05, p < .01), and a one-unit increase multiplied the exploration rate by 0.95. In sensitivity analyses, omitting three observation-period controls made the H3 coefficient nonsignificant; using the number of patents containing a new knowledge element as the outcome preserved the other directions but made knowledge centrality linear and positive rather than significantly inverted-U-shaped.
theoretical_contribution: The paper develops a multilevel account of knowledge embeddedness by showing that researchers are embedded both in a collaboration network of researchers and in a network of knowledge elements, and that these two networks are decoupled. It demonstrates that structural holes and degree centrality have different meanings and effects across the two networks, qualifying accounts that treat social networks primarily as conduits for heterogeneous knowledge. By theorizing knowledge-based search, it connects the combinatorial structure of knowledge to exploratory innovation and explains how knowledge-network structural holes can produce a competency trap in which exploitation displaces exploration.
practical_implication: For firms big and old enough to accumulate a stock of knowledge and separate the two networks, the findings indicate that knowledge and collaboration networks provide distinct signals about where researchers search for discoveries. The paper does not prescribe a specific managerial intervention.
limitations: Patent data do not capture tacit knowledge or trade secrets, so the mapped knowledge network may be incomplete. The longitudinal design uses one earlier and one later period rather than panel observations, lacks researchers’ functional affiliations, and examines a single firm whose characteristics may affect the estimates. The outcome counts new knowledge elements without weighting their relative importance, and the arguments require a firm large and old enough for its knowledge and collaboration networks to separate.
future_research: Future studies should examine how researchers acquire knowledge elements that are rich in structural holes or central, including the roles of socioeconomic background and social networks, and whether knowledge-network positions shape interactions with other researchers. The authors call for firm-level studies using industry-wide knowledge and collaboration networks, tests of network decoupling and other inventive outcomes such as idea quality, and panel designs that capture change over multiple periods. They also propose multi-firm research on how administrative structures, control systems, cultures, leadership, and strategies condition the effects, together with research on significant new knowledge elements and the large-and-old-firm scope condition.
abstract: Innovation in firms is doubly embedded: in a social network of collaborations between researchers, and in a knowledge network composed of linkages between knowledge elements. The two networks are decoupled. Their structural features are distinct and influence researchers’ exploratory innovation differently. Using the patent data of a leading U.S. microprocessor manufacturer, we constructed the firm’s collaboration and knowledge networks, and examined the effects of two structural features in the two networks—structural holes and degree centrality—on researchers’ exploratory innovation. Our findings show that a researcher with knowledge elements rich in structural holes in the knowledge network tends to explore fewer new knowledge elements from outside the firm, while structural holes in the collaboration network increase exploratory innovation. The average degree centrality of a researcher’s knowledge elements in the knowledge network has an inverted-U-shaped relationship with his or her exploratory innovation, while degree centrality in the collaboration network has a negative effect. This study suggests that knowledge and social networks influence where researchers search for discoveries.

title: With or Without You: When Does Managerial Exit Matter for the Dissolution of Dyadic Market Ties?
methods: Longitudinal study of 232 advertiser–agency dyads (1,130 dyad-years, 1986–1998); logistic regression estimated via generalized estimating equations (GEE, SAS GENMOD) on pooled cross-sectional time-series data; supplemented by seven exploratory interviews with advertiser and agency exchange managers.
industry: Advertising — dyadic advertiser–agency market ties (a professional service industry)
country: United States (advertising agencies headquartered in the greater New York City area)
units: Dyadic advertiser–agency market ties
n_sample: 232 dyads (84 agencies, 135 advertisers); 1,130 dyad-years observed; 151 tie dissolution events
authors: Broschak, J. P.; Block, E. S.
theories: social capital theory; social embeddedness
keywords: advertiser–agency relationships; dyadic market ties; managerial exit; market tie dissolution; relationship-specific assets; social capital
research_question: From which firm—advertisers or agencies—is managerial exit more detrimental to dyadic market ties, from which role—exchange managers or executives—is exit more likely to disrupt ties, and under what conditions are these exits more or less disruptive?
hypotheses:
H1. The number of executives exiting from advertisers will have a stronger effect on the likelihood of dyadic market tie dissolution than will the number of executives exiting from agencies.
H2. The number of exchange managers exiting from agencies will have a stronger effect on the likelihood of dyadic market tie dissolution than will the number of exchange managers exiting from advertisers.
H3. In advertisers, the number of executives who exit will have a stronger effect on the likelihood of dyadic market tie dissolution than the number of exchange managers who exit.
H4. In agencies, the number of exchange managers who exit will have a stronger effect on the likelihood of dyadic market tie dissolution than the number of executives who exit.
H5. In advertisers, the effect of the number of executives and exchange managers who exit on dyadic market tie dissolution will be greater the poorer the advertiser's financial performance.
H6a. In agencies, the effect of the number of executives and exchange managers who exit on dyadic market tie dissolution will decrease the longer the duration of market ties.
H6b. In advertisers, the effect of the number of executives and exchange managers who exit on dyadic market tie dissolution will decrease the longer the duration of market ties.
mechanism_summary: Managers and executives occupying roles related to market ties invest role-based social capital—relationship-specific assets, formal control, and the timing and intensity of interaction—that keeps advertiser–agency ties embedded and continuous. When managers exit, that role-based social capital is lost and ties become more likely to dissolve. Because roles differ in what they contribute and buyers (advertisers) hold more control than sellers (agencies) over forming and breaking ties, exit effects are theorized to differ by side of the market, by hierarchical level, and with tie strength (advertiser performance and tie duration).
data_measures: Data were hand-collected annually (1986–1998) from two public directories: The Standard Directory of Advertising Agencies ("Agency Red Book") and The Standard Directory of Advertisers ("Advertiser Red Book"). DV (dissolution): a dyad is coded 1 when an advertiser and agency are listed as exchange partners in year t but not in year t+1. IVs: counts of executive and exchange-manager exits, where an individual is listed as employed in year t but not t+1, aggregated to the firm level; executives are those holding Chairman/CEO/President titles (advertisers) or Chairman/CEO/President/Chief Creative Officer titles (agencies), and exchange managers are marketing managers (advertisers) and account services or creative managers (agencies). Moderators: advertiser performance = year-to-year change in the log of advertiser gross revenue; tie duration = number of continuous years the advertiser and agency reported working together. Controls include advertiser/agency size, agency mortality, agency reputation, advertiser industry, market orientation, and year effects. Models are logistic regressions estimated via generalized estimating equations (GEE, SAS GENMOD) on pooled cross-sectional time-series data; the design is observational/associational, with no causal-identification strategy claimed.
key_findings: Main effects (Model 2): each advertiser executive who exits increases the likelihood of tie dissolution by roughly 75% (exp(0.56)) and each advertiser marketing manager by roughly 23% (exp(0.21)); for agencies, only creative-manager exits have a positive, significant main effect (about 8%, exp(0.08) per exit), while agency executive and account-services exits are not significant. H1 receives strong support—advertiser executive exits are positive and significant while agency executive exits are negative and non-significant. H2 is not supported and runs contrary to prediction: advertiser marketing-manager exits have a greater effect than either agency creative-manager (p < .05) or account-services-manager (p < .01) exits. H3 is supported—within advertisers, the executive-exit coefficient is significantly larger than the marketing-manager coefficient (p < .05). H4 is supported—within agencies, creative-manager exits have a significantly greater effect than executive exits (p < .05), and account-services vs. executive exits are marginally greater (p < .10). H5 is supported—the advertiser-exit × advertiser-growth interactions are negative and significant for both executives and marketing managers (exit is most disruptive when advertiser revenues are declining, negligible when the advertiser is growing). H6a receives partial support—the agency executive-exit × tie-duration interaction is negative and significant (Model 5), the creative-manager × duration interaction is only marginally significant, and the account-services interaction is non-significant. H6b is not supported—the advertiser executive- and marketing-manager × tie-duration interactions are not significant.
theoretical_contribution: The study develops a more balanced, role- and side-differentiated theory of how managerial mobility disrupts inter-organizational market ties, moving beyond the assumption that exit effects are symmetric across buyers and sellers. It shows that the loss of role-based social capital operates through different mechanisms depending on whether exit occurs among advertiser or agency executives versus exchange managers, and it specifies conditions (advertiser performance, tie duration/fragility) that amplify or dampen those effects. In doing so it contributes to research on the dynamics of interfirm relationships and on the organizational consequences of managerial mobility.
practical_implication: Identifying the conditions under which market ties are more or less likely to end can help managers in buyer (advertiser) and seller (agency) firms improve firm performance and enhance chances of survival. The results suggest which departures most threaten client–service-firm relationships—advertiser executive exits and agency creative-manager exits—and when they matter most, namely when advertiser performance is poor and when market ties are new.
limitations: The authors study dyadic market ties in only one setting—advertising, a professional service marked by complex interactions and buyer–seller informational asymmetries—so it is unclear whether the findings generalize to other professional-service contexts or to settings where ties are less strategic or sustained by physical or financial rather than social capital. They also cannot identify the extent to which specific executives and exchange managers are directly involved in the observed dyads, which prevents measuring the investments particular individuals make or lose and thus testing the individual-actor mechanism. Finally, the data do not reveal which individual account services managers attend to particular buyers' accounts, possibly weakening the account-services results.
future_research: The paper calls for pairing individual exchange managers with specific market ties to gain richer insight into how investments in particular types of social capital magnify or diminish the disruptive effects of managerial exit. It also urges disentangling the relative influence of different types of social capital and the conditions under which disruptions to social capital affect ties, extending the framework of mechanisms to other contexts to understand when market ties fail, and investigating why creative managers strongly affect specific dyadic relationships but not a firm's overall portfolio of relationships.
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between managerial exit from advertising agencies and advertisers and the dissolution of dyadic market ties. We examine how the amount and locus (advertiser vs. agency) of managerial exit and the hierarchical level from which exit occurs (executives vs. exchange managers) influence the likelihood that dyadic market ties will dissolve. We theorize that managerial exit disrupts dyadic market ties through its effect on three mechanisms of social capital: investments in relationship-specific assets; formal control over market ties; and the intensity of interaction with exchange partners. We consider how market tie fragility, the financial performance of advertisers, and the duration of market ties condition the effects of managerial exit on market tie dissolution. In short, we theorize about which managerial roles matter more to market tie dissolution, why they matter and when they matter. Using longitudinal data on 232 dyadic ties between advertisers and New York City advertising agencies, we find that the number of executives and exchange managers who exit on both sides of market ties affects tie dissolution. However, these effects are neither symmetrical between exchange partners nor uniform across the hierarchical levels from which exit occurs, and vary with the strength of market ties.

title: CEO Career Variety: Effects on Firm-Level Strategic and Social Novelty
methods: Longitudinal panel of Fortune 250 CEOs; hypotheses tested with population-averaged generalized estimating equations (GEEs) specifying a Gaussian family, identity link, and AR(1) within-CEO correlation, with robust (Huber-White) standard errors; two-stage residual models run as an endogeneity robustness check.
industry: Large public U.S. firms spanning a wide range of industries (Fortune 250; 10 GICS sectors)
time_period: New non-interim CEOs entering office January 1999-December 2005, each tracked over their first five years in office (plus pre-entry-year data)
units: CEOs and firm-years (plus 2,624 TMT members for the social-novelty tests)
n_sample: 183 CEOs / 776 CEO-years (475 firm-years for corporate strategic change; 678 firm-years for the TMT tests)
authors: Crossland, C.; Zyung, J.; Hiller, N. J.; Hambrick, D. C.
theories: upper echelons theory (Hambrick, 2005; Hambrick & Mason, 1984)
keywords: CEO career variety; social novelty; strategic distinctiveness; strategic dynamism; strategic novelty; top management team; upper echelons theory
research_question: Does a CEO's career variety—the array of distinct professional and institutional experiences accumulated before becoming CEO—shape firm-level strategic novelty (strategic dynamism and strategic distinctiveness) and social novelty (top management team membership change and heterogeneity)?
hypotheses:
Hypothesis 1. CEO career variety will be positively associated with firm-level strategic dynamism.
Hypothesis 2. CEO career variety will be positively associated with firm-level strategic distinctiveness.
Hypothesis 3. CEO career variety will be positively associated with TMT membership change.
Hypothesis 4. CEO career variety will be positively associated with TMT heterogeneity.
mechanism_summary: Adopting upper echelons logic, the paper argues that career variety reflects two personal attributes: an ingrained dispositional preference for change and experimentation, and accumulated cognitive breadth (awareness of multiple paradigms and exemplars). High-variety CEOs are therefore predisposed to generate and favor novel, distinctive options and to perceive a wider range of options as feasible, directing their firms toward strategic and social novelty; low-variety CEOs, preferring stability and incrementalism, keep firms closer to industry norms.
data_measures: Career histories were hand-collected from multiple archival sources (e.g., Marquis Who's Who, Dun & Bradstreet, Standard & Poor's Register, BoardEx, corporate sites and press releases); strategic-choice variables came from Compustat and TMTs from firms' annual 10-K reports. The focal independent variable, CEO career variety, is the sum of distinct industry sectors, distinct firms, and distinct functional areas the individual had worked in prior to becoming CEO, divided by pre-CEO career length (inter-rater ICC1 = .91; Cronbach's alpha = .76; EFA supported convergent/discriminant validity). Strategic dynamism was operationalized as resource reallocation (year-on-year absolute change across six Winsorized, logged, standardized strategic-choice variables: advertising, R&D, overhead efficiency, capital intensity, plant/equipment newness, and financial leverage) and as corporate strategic change (year-on-year change in an entropy diversification measure). Strategic distinctiveness was the standardized absolute difference of the same six variables from the industry mean (logged and summed). TMT membership change was the annual sum of additions and deletions divided by prior-year TMT size; TMT heterogeneity was captured for age and tenure (coefficient of variation) and education and gender (Herfindahl-Blau index). Models included a comprehensive control set (instrumented pre-entry condition, CEO age/education/MBA/experience, incentive compensation, CEO ownership, duality, outsider, previous CEO dismissal, firm departures, board independence, institutional blockholding, firm size/age/performance, industry dynamism, and calendar-year, tenure-year, and industry dummies). Estimation used population-averaged GEEs (Gaussian, identity link, AR(1)) with robust standard errors; the design is associational, and a two-stage residual model addressed potential endogeneity in board selection of CEOs.
key_findings: Strategic novelty received strong support. Hypothesis 1 was supported: career variety was positively related to resource reallocation (β = 3.43, p < .05) and to corporate strategic change (β = 2.88, p < .01). Hypothesis 2 was supported: career variety was positively related to strategic distinctiveness (β = 2.91, p < .05). Social novelty received mixed support. Hypothesis 3 was supported: career variety was positively related to TMT membership change (β = 0.42, p < .01). Hypothesis 4 was not supported for any of the four TMT heterogeneity measures (age, tenure, education, gender), where the career-variety effect was non-significant. Practically, moving from a CEO one SD below to one SD above the mean in career variety corresponded to an increase of about 37% of one SD in resource reallocation (roughly a $34 million annual change in advertising and $149 million in SG&A for the median firm) and about one additional TMT addition or removal per year. A limited post-hoc analysis suggested that strategic novelty brings about subsequent performance volatility but is not related to the subsequent performance level.
theoretical_contribution: The paper introduces and validates "CEO career variety" as a distinct behavioral construct — reliably measurable and not redundant with openness to experience, risk propensity, age, or education — that reflects both dispositional preferences for change and accumulated cognitive breadth. It extends upper echelons theory by showing that the breadth of an executive's pre-CEO experiences is systematically associated with firm-level strategic novelty and, in part, social novelty, and it responds to calls for research on the antecedents of TMT composition.
practical_implication: The authors suggest that boards of directors might benefit from explicitly considering a candidate's career variety when making CEO selection decisions: if a firm's strategy has become too predictable, conventional, or inertial, hiring a high-variety CEO might help promote rapid, large-scale change and greater strategic distinctiveness, whereas if a firm's strategy has been too erratic and volatile, hiring a low-variety CEO might contribute to a more consistent, steady approach. They caution that high-variety CEOs may seek novelty for its own sake, shaking up strategies and TMTs whether or not the firm needs it.
limitations: The study does not demonstrate the underlying psychological content of career variety, relying on prior research to argue what the construct reflects; survey and/or experimental methods would be needed to confirm and clarify what career variety actually indicates about a CEO. The measure is archivally derived, the analysis is restricted to the first five years of each CEO's tenure, and the focus is strictly on CEOs.
future_research: The authors point to confirming the psychological content of career variety through survey/experimental work; examining whether accumulated career-variety experiences reinforce novelty-seeking behaviors; exploring implications for CEO tenure length and succession (e.g., whether high-variety CEOs have shorter tenures, depart even when performance is satisfactory, or are especially likely to be multi-time CEOs); refining or developing more fine-grained measures of prior experiences; studying the effects of career variety during later phases of CEO tenure; and extending the construct to employees at other organizational levels (e.g., high-variety sales representatives, R&D scientists, or country managers, and links to individual creativity, deviance, and supervisory styles). They also note it would be interesting to explore whether high-variety CEOs attract and retain other high-variety individuals to their TMTs, and to examine the prescriptive and performance implications of career variety.
abstract: We introduce the concept of “CEO career variety”—defined as the array of distinct professional and institutional experiences an executive has had prior to becoming CEO. Using a longitudinal sample of Fortune 250 CEOs, we hypothesize, and find strong evidence for the assertion, that CEO career variety is positively associated with firm-level strategic novelty—manifested in strategic dynamism (period-on-period change) and strategic distinctiveness (deviance from industry central tendencies). We also find mixed evidence that CEO career variety is positively associated with social novelty—manifested in top management team turnover and heterogeneity.

title: Climate Change and Management
methods: Editorial essay (From the Editors); no empirical design or analysis.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Not reported in paper
n_sample: Not reported in paper
authors: Howard-Grenville, J.; Buckle, S. J.; Hoskins, B. J.; George, G.
keywords: adaptation; climate change; grand challenges; mitigation; organizational resilience; value chains
research_question: Not reported in paper
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Core argument: climate change is so pervasive that its causes and consequences show up at every level of analysis of interest to organizational scholars, and responses to it will fundamentally reshape many of the phenomena, interactions, and relationships central to management scholarship.
- Dual role of organizations: the rise of organizations and industrialized production set us on this path, yet organizations are equally critical to mitigating and adapting to climate change, engaging a suite of approaches under the broad banners of adaptation and mitigation.
- Implication 1 — Reshaping value chains: climate change will reshape supply networks, production arrangements, and the provision of energy and water, prompting industrial symbiosis, circular-economy models, and production closer to the point of consumption.
- Implication 2 — Organizational resilience and adaptation: high, non-linear uncertainty favors ways of organizing that foreground resilience and responsiveness rather than scale or growth, making proactive adaptability a possible "new normal."
- Implication 3 — Shifts in work and life: resource-efficient cities and the decentralization and de-synchronization of activity will alter where and how individuals live, work, and move, reshaping employment practices and how employees identify with organizations.
- Implication 4 — Societal shifts: infrastructure change and less predictable exposure to extreme events place adaptation burdens on society, raising questions of governance, distributional responsibility, climate migration, and social mobilization.

The editorial offers a primer on the science and policy of climate change and then argues that, because climate impacts will impinge on value chains, organizational resilience, individual work patterns, and broader governance systems, the topic poses pressing questions across the typical levels of analysis and range of methodologies that management scholars employ. It frames organizations as both drivers of and responders to climate change, and uses four illustrative domains of implication to open avenues for research and engagement.
data_measures: Not reported in paper
key_findings: Not reported in paper
theoretical_contribution: The editorial establishes climate change as a pervasive, multi-level phenomenon whose causes and consequences appear at every level of analysis of interest to organizational scholars, arguing that it will fundamentally reshape the phenomena, interactions, and relationships that are of central concern to management scholars. By pairing a brief primer on the science and policy of climate change with four illustrative domains of organizational implication — value chains, organizational resilience and adaptation, work and life, and societal shifts — it positions the issue as ripe for study across the typical levels of analysis and within the range of methodologies that management scholars employ.
practical_implication: Addressing management and organizational scholars, the editorial calls on them to use their expertise to better understand the challenges climate change poses to organizations, individuals, and societies, and to study how business, society, and public entities mobilize for and navigate these challenges. It notes that private, public, and not-for-profit organizations will need to engage a suite of approaches under the broad banners of adaptation and mitigation to cope with the implications of climate change.
limitations: The authors frame the piece as a brief primer intended to offer insight into the science and policy of climate change and to outline potential implications for organizations and organizational scholars, rather than as a comprehensive treatment. They note that the four highlighted implications are neither exhaustive nor exclusive, but are meant to illustrate a wide range of questions ripe for study.
future_research: Across four domains, the editorial maps research directions it explicitly invites. On value chains, it asks how governance, coordination, and risk-mitigation arrangements can anticipate and respond, and how shifts such as sourcing "waste" material as an input alter interorganizational relationships, the boundaries of the firm, and organizational identities. On resilience and adaptation, it calls for developing theory on what adaptation and resilience look like under the assumption of significant disruption to "business as usual." On work and life, it invites study of whether motivation, commitment, identification, or pro-social behaviors are differently manifested, and how altered patterns of mobility, co-presence, and communication change collaboration, creativity, or productivity, including in the developing world. On societal shifts, it asks what new models of social mobilization and change might be occasioned by efforts to respond to climate change, and to what degree a response demands shifts in cultural or institutional values or logics.

title: A Social–Structural Perspective on Employee–Organization Relationships and Team Creativity
methods: Two-wave onsite survey of Chinese high-technology firms; clustered regression with White correction (clustered on organization) and nested-equations path analysis (Edwards & Lambert, 2007) with 1,000-sample bootstrap; first- and second-stage moderated mediation.
industry: High-technology organizations (functional teams in R&D, product design, technical support, manufacturing, quality testing, and customer service)
time_period: 2009–2010 (first-wave survey March–August 2010; second wave two to four months later)
units: Work teams (functional teams within organizations)
n_sample: 229 teams (1,807 employees) across 55 organizations
authors: Jia, L.; Shaw, J. D.; Tsui, A. S.; Park, T.-Y.
theories: employee–organization relationship framework (Tsui, Pearce, Porter, & Tripoli, 1997); social capital theory (Nahapiet & Ghoshal, 1998; Coleman, 1988); social exchange theory
keywords: employee–organization relationships; mutual investment; social capital; task complexity; team creativity; work-related communication density
research_question: How, and under what conditions, do employee–organization relationship (EOR) forms relate to team creativity? The authors theorize the EOR–creativity link at the work-team level, positing team members' work-related communication density as the mediating mechanism and task complexity as a boundary condition.
hypotheses:
H1. The relationship between expected contributions and team members' work-related communication density will be positive and significant when offered inducements are high, but attenuated when offered inducements are low.
H2. Team members' work-related communication density will relate positively to team creativity.
H3. The relationship between EORs and team creativity will be mediated by team members' work-related communication density, such that the mediated effect will be strongest for the mutual investment EOR approach.
H4. The relationship between team members' work-related communication density and team creativity will be moderated by task complexity, such that the positive relationship will be stronger when task complexity is high.
H5. The strength of the mediated relationship between EORs and team creativity (through work-related communication density) will depend on task complexity; the indirect and total effects of EORs (specifically, mutual investment) on team creativity will be stronger when task complexity is high.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on Nahapiet and Ghoshal's (1998) social capital theory, the authors argue that offered inducements supply the opportunity and capability to build dense work-related communication networks, while expected contributions supply the motivation and value expectancy to do so; only the mutual investment form satisfies all four preconditions for dense networks. Dense communication networks in turn enable the knowledge transfer and combination that generate team creativity, but this social capital is effectively mobilized into creativity mainly under high task complexity. The result is a first- and second-stage moderated mediation model linking EOR forms to team creativity via communication density.
data_measures: Data source: a two-wave onsite survey of high-technology organizations in an eastern province of China, with firms drawn from a government-accredited list; the final analytic sample is 55 organizations, 229 teams, and 1,807 employees. EOR (offered inducements and expected contributions): supervisor-rated Time 1 items adapted from Hom et al. (2009) and Wang et al. (2003), with a good-fitting second-order factor structure (offered inducements α = .90; expected contributions α = .92), and mutual investment defined as high on both continua. Work-related communication density (mediator): team members' Time 1 ego-centered networks (up to five alters), binary-coded ties, Scott's (2000) density formula, aggregated to the team level. Task complexity (second-stage moderator): seven items from Dean and Snell (1991), supervisor-rated at Time 1 (α = .80). Team creativity (DV): a six-item supervisor rating at Time 2 (four items from Farmer et al. 2003, two from Leenders et al. 2003; α = .86). Controls include team size, average team tenure, communication network size, percentage female, average education, outside-network percentage, perceived supervisor support (a social-exchange proxy), and team performance. Estimation used clustered regression with a White correction (clustered on organization) and nested-equations path analysis (Edwards & Lambert, 2007) with a 1,000-sample bootstrap for indirect and total effects; the design is associational (two-wave), and the authors state they cannot firmly establish causality.
key_findings: H1 supported: the expected-contributions × offered-inducements interaction on communication density was significant (b = .16, p < .01); the expected-contributions → communication-density slope was positive and significant under high offered inducements (b_high OI = .45, p < .01) but not under low (b_low OI = .13, n.s.). The authors note the observed pattern departed somewhat from the predicted form in that the lowest density occurred in the overinvestment type. H2 not supported: work-related communication density was not significantly related to team creativity overall (b = .11, n.s.). H3 supported: the mediated (indirect) effect of expected contributions on team creativity via communication density was significant under high offered inducements (indirect = .05, p < .05; total = .26, p < .05) but not under low, consistent with mediation being strongest under mutual investment. H4 supported: the communication-density → team-creativity link was moderated by task complexity — positive under high complexity (b = .29, p < .01), not under low (b = -.05, n.s.); this crossing explains the null H2 main effect. H5 supported: the conditional indirect and total effects were positive and significant only when both offered inducements and task complexity were high (indirect = .13, p < .01; total = .36, p < .01), and slope-difference tests showed this high–high combination differed significantly from the others, though its difference from the high-inducement/low-complexity slope was marginal (t = 1.91, p = .06).
theoretical_contribution: The study reorients the EOR literature beyond its dominant social-exchange mechanism by advancing a social–structural (social capital) account in which organizational decisions about offered inducements and expected contributions shape the density of work-related communication networks—and thereby team creativity—over and above social exchange. It integrates the EOR, social capital, and team creativity literatures into a single moderated-mediation model and identifies task complexity as the key contextual condition under which the value latent in dense communication networks is realized as team creativity.
practical_implication: For organizational decision makers, the mutual investment EOR—pairing high offered inducements with high expected contributions—is the form most conducive to the dense work-related communication networks that support team creativity. The authors caution, however, that in relatively simple task environments decision makers may not fully realize these creativity benefits; the payoff is concentrated in teams performing highly complex tasks.
limitations: The authors cannot firmly establish causality; despite the two-wave design, the model should be read as suggesting rather than confirming the presumed causal sequence. Unmeasured variables could relate to both EOR and creativity (though several confounds were controlled), and the cognitive processes presumed to link EOR to communication-seeking were not measured. The communication-density measure relied on fixed-format egocentric network data (a maximum of five alters) aggregated to the team level, and its team-mean reliability (ICC(2) = .46) fell below the conventional .70 benchmark.
future_research: The authors call for study of other social network types (e.g., advice or friendship ties) and possible curvilinear network–creativity relationships, and for concurrently assessing intra-team and extra-team networks under different employment forms. They also point to examining the nature and stability of ties (including instrumental/affective and kinship-like ties in the Chinese context), the cognitive processes linking EOR to communication, whether financial incentives enhance or mitigate the EOR–creativity effect, and whether cultural diversity or team members' cultural identity moderates the EOR–creativity relationship.
abstract: We develop a social–structural perspective on the relationship between employee–organization relationships (EORs) and team creativity. We argue that the mutual investment EOR approach, in which employers expect high levels of employee contributions and offer extensive inducements, will be associated with higher team creativity relative to other EOR approaches. We also advance the argument that this relationship will be mediated by team member work-related communication density and that the mediated relationship will be stronger when team members’ tasks are complex. We find support for the model in a two-wave study of 1,807 employees in 229 teams in 55 Chinese high-technology organizations. We discuss the implications for future employment relationship research and practice.
