title: Do Interviewers Sell Themselves Short? The Effects of Selling Orientation on Interviewers' Judgments
methods: Two studies. Study 1: randomized laboratory experiment with 32 mock interviewer-applicant dyads (64 participants); selling orientation manipulated high vs. low; accuracy analyzed with OLS regression testing an applicant-self-rating x selling-orientation interaction. Study 2: multi-wave observational field study with two samples of professional interviewers, analyzed with multilevel (random-intercept) regression (applicants nested in interviewers) plus multilevel Poisson regression for job-offer counts.
industry: Study 1: simulated retail customer-service-manager hiring (supermarket role, El Fresco); Study 2 Sample A: MBA program admissions; Sample B: K-12 international teacher placement
country: United States (Study 2 Samples A and B); Study 1 laboratory study (payments in GBP)
time_period: Multi-wave field data across four time points (application, interview, and post-entry outcomes at roughly 9 months, 18 months, and up to two years); published 2014
units: Interviewers and their dispositional judgments of job/program applicants in first-meeting interviews (applicants nested within interviewers in Study 2)
n_sample: Study 1: 64 participants (32 interviewer-applicant pairs). Study 2 Sample A: 10 interviewers, up to 1,003 rated applicants (analytic n = 142 and 109). Sample B: 35 interviewers, 1,102 rated applicants (analytic n = 125 and 98).
authors: Marr, J. C.; Cable, D. M.
theories: automaticity of dispositional judgments (thin-slice social perception); inattentional blindness; motivated social cognition
keywords: core self-evaluations; dispositional judgments; employment interviews; judgment automaticity; motivated social cognition; person perception; predictive validity; selling orientation
research_question: Does an interviewer's motivation to attract the applicant (a "selling orientation") during an interpersonal first meeting such as a job interview help or hinder the accuracy and predictive validity of that interviewer's dispositional judgments about the applicant — specifically, judgments of the applicant's core self-evaluations?
hypotheses:
The paper advances two competing (alternative) hypotheses drawn from opposing perspectives on judgment automaticity:
H1 (automaticity prediction): When interviewers adopt a stronger selling orientation during an interview, their judgments regarding interviewees' core self-evaluations will be more accurate.
H2 (motivated-cognition prediction): When interviewers adopt a stronger selling orientation during an interview, their judgments regarding interviewees' core self-evaluations will be less accurate.
mechanism_summary:
- Moderator: Interviewer selling orientation (Study 1: manipulated high vs. low; Study 2: measured with a two-item scale)

A selling orientation is theorized as a motivation that directs the interviewer's limited attentional resources toward attracting the applicant and away from the process of forming dispositional judgments. Two accounts make opposite predictions: if such judgments are automatic (best made with little explicit attention), distraction by selling should improve accuracy; if they require effortful, controlled processing, diverting attention should degrade accuracy and predictive validity. Empirically, selling orientation operates as a moderator that weakens the link between an applicant's true disposition and the interviewer's rating (Study 1) and between the interviewer's rating and the applicant's later newcomer outcomes (Study 2).
data_measures: Study 1 (lab experiment): 64 participants recruited from a university research pool were randomly assigned to interviewer vs. applicant roles and to high vs. low selling-orientation conditions, then completed a 15-minute mock interview for a customer-service-manager role (materials adapted from Van Iddekinge, Raymark, & Roth, 2005). Core self-evaluations were measured with Judge et al.'s (2003) 12-item CSES: applicant self-ratings collected one week before the interview, interviewer ratings collected afterward, and friend/family contact ratings used to build a robustness "true-score" composite. Selling orientation was manipulated through role instructions and checked with a two-item interviewer-rated measure (alpha = .85). Analysis: OLS regression with an applicant-self-rating x selling-orientation interaction; random assignment supports causal inference. Study 2 (field): two samples of professional interviewers rated applicant CSES (adapted Judge et al. 2003 12-item scale) and reported selling orientation with the same two-item measure. Sample A (MBA admissions, 10 interviewers): DVs were school advocacy (2 items) and count of full-time job offers. Sample B (international teacher placement, 35 interviewers): DVs were organizational citizenship/helping behavior (Van Dyne & LePine, 1998), value congruence (Cable & DeRue, 2002), and principal-rated organizational contributions. Analysis: multilevel random-intercept regression with applicants nested in interviewers, and multilevel Poisson regression for the job-offer count, each testing an interviewer-CSES-rating x selling-orientation interaction. The Study 2 field design is associational (no manipulation).
key_findings: Results supported H2 (the motivated-cognition prediction) and rejected H1 (the automaticity prediction) across all three samples. Study 1: a significant negative interaction between applicants' self-ratings of core self-evaluations and selling orientation on interviewers' ratings (b = -.66, t = -2.12, p < .05, R-squared = .25); when selling orientation was low, interviewer ratings tracked applicants' self-rated core self-evaluations (b = .46, t = 2.81, p < .01), but when it was high there was no significant relationship (b = -.19, t = -.74, n.s.). The pattern held using the applicant-plus-contact composite "true score" (interaction b = -.76, t = -2.36, p < .05). Study 2 Sample A: selling orientation negatively moderated the predictive validity of interviewer core-self-evaluation judgments for school advocacy (gamma = -.04, p < .05) and job offers (gamma = -.17, p < .05) — low selling meant interviewer ratings positively predicted outcomes, high selling meant no relationship. Study 2 Sample B: significant negative moderation for citizenship behavior (gamma = -.06, p < .05) and value congruence (gamma = -.07, p < .05); for organizational contributions the interaction was negative but not significant by a 95% standard (gamma = -.04, p < .06), which the authors report as not supported unless a one-tailed test is applied. Across studies, a stronger selling orientation consistently reduced the accuracy and predictive validity of interviewers' dispositional judgments.
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes two contributions. First, it brings competing motivations (judgment vs. selling) into the study of organizational interviews, broadening "selling orientation" from an organization-induced recruitment stance or a sales-specific behavior into an individual-level motivation to attract another person in any interpersonal first meeting. Second, it probes the boundaries of judgment automaticity during naturally occurring social interactions where real outcomes are at stake, showing that forming accurate dispositional judgments in first meetings is not an effortless automatic process but requires dedicated cognitive attention — evidence favoring a motivated-social-cognition view over a pure automaticity view, and an organizational demonstration of inattentional blindness in social judgment.
practical_implication: To maximize the utility of selection and placement interviews, the authors argue that firms should formally separate the applicant-evaluation process from the applicant-attraction (selling) process — either by having evaluation and selling conducted by different people or at different stages of the hiring process. They further suggest that interviewers should assess applicants' core self-evaluations and that firms should incorporate those judgments into their hiring decisions, since interviewers who are least distracted by selling make the most predictive judgments about which applicants will succeed.
limitations: The studies do not test judgment automaticity directly. Study 1 relied on a mock-interview setting with non-professional (novice) interviewers and used a self/contact composite as the core-self-evaluation "true score," which may not perfectly reflect applicants' dispositions. The research examined only one trait (core self-evaluations); interview structure was measured with a single item and selling orientation with a two-item scale, so sub-facets and specific enactments of selling were not captured. The field evidence came from only 45 interviewers across just two organizations (Sample A had only 10 interviewers), and the studies cannot establish when or why a selling orientation is triggered.
future_research: The authors call for research on whether the effect generalizes to other dispositional traits and other future work behaviors; on the components and enactments of selling orientation (e.g., thinking about selling vs. specific selling behaviors); on when and why a selling orientation is triggered in real interactions; on larger and more varied samples of organizations that would permit examining the organizational expectations and incentives shaping interviewers' propensity to sell versus evaluate; and on extending the theory to other interpersonal first meetings, such as dating.
abstract: Drawing on alternative perspectives about the automaticity of dispositional judgments, we examine whether the motivation to attract the other (i.e., selling orientation) in interpersonal first meetings (e.g., job interviews) helps or hinders the accuracy and validity of dispositional judgments. In a laboratory study (Study 1), we found that selling orientation reduced the accuracy of interviewers’ judgments about applicants’ core self-evaluations. Then, we investigated the real-world implications of selling orientation in a field study (Study 2) with two different samples (Samples A and B) and found that a selling orientation negatively influenced the predictive validity of interviewers’ judgments. Specifically, when selling orientation was low, interviewers’ judgments accurately predicted which applicants would be most (and least) successful as newcomers in the organization (in terms of citizenship, performance, and fit). However, when selling orientation was high, interviewers’ judgments no longer predicted applicant outcomes. Together, these results suggest that making dispositional judgments in interpersonal first meetings is an effortful process that is hindered by focusing on other goals (e.g., selling). We discuss the practical and theoretical implications of these findings.
apa_citation: Marr, J. C., & Cable, D. M. (2014). Do interviewers sell themselves short? The effects of selling orientation on interviewers' judgments. *Academy of Management Journal, 57*(3), 624–651. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0504

title: “Defining What We Do—All Over Again”: Occupational Identity, Technological Change, and the Librarian/Internet-Search Relationship
methods: Qualitative longitudinal study; interpretive/grounded discourse analysis of 199 articles (1980–2010) from two U.S. library-field journals (American Libraries and Library Journal), retrieved via EBSCO Academic Source Premiere and coded iteratively into first-order categories, second-order themes, and aggregate dimensions to build a process model (Langley, 1999; Strauss & Corbin, 1998).
industry: Librarianship / the U.S. library field (an occupation), read through trade-journal discourse
time_period: 1980–2010 (~22 years of Internet-search discourse)
units: Journal articles, each coded for its discursive response toward Internet search
n_sample: 199 articles
authors: Nelson, A. J.; Irwin, J.
theories: occupational identity (Ashcraft, 2013; Barley, 1989; Pratt et al., 2006); paradox of expertise (Nelson & Irwin, 2014); sociology of occupations and professions (Abbott, 1988); technology interpretation and enactment (Leonardi & Barley, 2010; Orlikowski & Gash, 1994)
keywords: Internet search; occupational identity; occupations and professions; paradox of expertise; technological change; technology interpretation
research_question: How does an occupation’s identity — the overlap between “who we are” and “what we do” — shape, and how is it shaped by, its interactions with a new technology? The authors pursue this through the mutually shaping relationship between librarians (as an occupation) and Internet search.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Focal construct: Occupational identity — the conjunction of “who we are” and “what we do” for an occupation (here, librarianship), defined relationally and treated as dynamic rather than static.
- Focal technology: Internet search, whose core function (information search) overlaps librarians’ identity-central task, making it an unusually direct “foil” for the occupation.
- Core mechanism — “paradox of expertise”: librarians’ deep mastery of (non-Internet) searching led them to judge Internet search against their own criterion (a search returns the single “correct” answer), dismiss it as a flawed niche, and miss innovation opportunities around it.
- Process (four eras / discursive responses): “Masters of Search” (describe-and-question / dismiss) → “Masters of Interpretation” (differentiate) → “Teachers of Search” (engage) → “Connectors of People and Information” (leverage).
- Co-shaping loop: occupational identity refracts how the technology is interpreted; using and interacting with the technology reshapes the identity; the changed identity then refracts the technology differently — a cycle that repeats and, in later eras, enables librarian-led innovation.
- Boundary conditions for the paradox: it is apt to arise when (1) the technology’s task overlaps a task closely tied to the occupation’s identity, (2) the technology performs that task in a way inconsistent with members’ understanding of how it should be done, and (3) the occupation has a strong, stable identity.

The paper models occupational identity as a lens (“like a lens that bears the imprint of the light it refracts”): identity conditions the interpretation and adoption of a technology, but sustained interaction with that technology then alters the identity, which in turn changes subsequent interpretations and innovation activity. Because librarians’ mastery of searching was central to who they were, an overlapping technology first triggered dismissal and differentiation (the paradox of expertise) and only later — as search improved and diffused — appropriation and leveraging, through a series of small steps that each opened space for the next.
data_measures: Interpretive, process-oriented qualitative design. Data corpus: 199 articles (final dataset) drawn from American Libraries (the ALA’s official journal) and Library Journal, the two most widely read U.S. library-field journals, whose authors and audience are librarians. Articles were retrieved via EBSCO’s Academic Source Premiere using the keywords “Internet,” “search,” and “web” for 1980–2010, excluding advertisements, book reviews, and Internet-filtering-only pieces. Each author independently read every article and coded its overall “discursive response,” yielding four response types (describe-and-question, differentiate, engage, leverage). Iterative grounded coding then moved from detailed codes to first-order categories (Table 1), second-order themes, and three aggregate dimensions (understanding of search, search tasks, and innovation activities); the prevalence of the four responses was traced over time (Figure 2) to bracket four eras. No quantitative measures or hypothesis tests; the output is a grounded process model (Figure 4).
key_findings: The study surfaces a grounded process model of occupational-identity change rather than hypothesis tests. Initially (“Masters of Search,” through the mid-1990s), librarians discounted Internet search as a flawed, disorganized niche that violated their notion of a successful search (the single correct answer) and saw no identity threat — a paradox of expertise led them to miss innovation opportunities even though they had the technical capability to build search tools. As search technology improved and diffused, librarians’ identity shifted through three further eras — “Masters of Interpretation” (differentiate from search), “Teachers of Search” (engage with users and search firms), and “Connectors of People and Information” (leverage search into new work) — progressively ceding searching to Google and reorienting around user-focused connecting. The response mix tracked Internet diffusion: “differentiation” dominated when fewer than half of the U.S. population used the Internet, whereas “leveraging” dominated once the majority did. Throughout, occupational identity both shaped interpretations of the technology and was reshaped by interactions with it, and the redefined identity ultimately enabled librarian-led innovations (e.g., LibraryThing, Reference Extract, link resolvers, and data mining of library records).
theoretical_contribution: The paper makes three contributions. First, it shows that occupational identity serves as an interpretive lens for a new technology, and that these interpretations shape both adoption decisions and ongoing interactions — linking technology interpretation to adoption and tracing interpretation over time (answering Leonardi and Barley’s call for longitudinal work). Second, it introduces the concept of a “paradox of expertise”: an occupation’s mastery of a task can, ironically, lead its members to dismiss innovation opportunities around that same task, adding to explanations (beyond cannibalization or lack of capability) for why insiders fail to innovate. Third, it demonstrates that technology can reshape occupational identity — identity defined not only by contrast but by appropriation — with implications for the literatures on occupations, professions, professionalization, and de-professionalization.
practical_implication: Staying within the paper’s stated scope (occupations whose core tasks overlap an emerging technology), the case suggests that deep occupational expertise can become a liability, blinding members to innovation opportunities around a technology that mimics their core task. The authors speculate — explicitly tentatively — that occupations may be better equipped to avoid this paradox if they regularly refresh their ranks with new entrants (who are more open to outside innovations) and if they have a history of frequent identity shifts, so that the fluidity of occupational identity becomes an opportunity rather than a liability.
limitations: The authors note that their model rests on a single case — librarians and Internet search — which bounds its transferability. Internet search itself expanded enormously over the period, a pattern that may have shaped librarians’ approaches and their success at narrowly focused innovation. Two features of the librarian case may not generalize: librarians had the technical skill to engage with and even shape search technology, and their practice and skills were not bound up in a single, replaceable technology, leaving them “room to maneuver.” The analysis is also confined to occupational identity, setting aside the multiple identities individuals hold simultaneously.
future_research: The authors highlight two directions they find particularly intriguing: examining occupational-identity/technology dynamics outside the information-technology context (e.g., materials, transportation, or biotechnologies), and studying multiple identities — how individuals’ several simultaneous identities interact with one another as they engage technological change. They also point to studying occupations with less skill or less room to maneuver, and to how technology may drive de-professionalization, as avenues opened by their boundary conditions.
abstract: Although a growing literature explores occupational identity, or the overlap between “who we are” and “what we do,” this literature has not fully considered how occupational identity may interact with technological change. In this paper, we explore this interaction, asking how an occupation’s identity shapes and is shaped by its interactions with a new technology. We focus, specifically, on the relationship between librarians and Internet search. Drawing on an analysis of 22 years of articles from library journals, we demonstrate how and why librarians initially discounted Internet search and differentiated themselves from it. We argue that these responses were associated with a “paradox of expertise,” by which librarians missed innovation opportunities around one of the most important information technologies in history precisely, and ironically, because of their deep knowledge of non-Internet searching. Later, however, we demonstrate how librarians engaged with this same technology, drawing upon it to redefine their occupational identity. Our findings demonstrate how occupational identity conditions the interpretation of a technology, while also showing how these interpretations can change with ongoing interactions. We also illustrate how occupational identity itself can change in response to new technology. Finally, we elaborate upon why expert insiders may not actually be best positioned to pursue emerging technologies.
apa_citation: Nelson, A. J., & Irwin, J. (2014). “Defining what we do—all over again”: Occupational identity, technological change, and the librarian/Internet-search relationship. *Academy of Management Journal, 57*(3), 892–928. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0201

title: Human Capital Flows: Using Context-Emergent Turnover (CET) Theory to Explore the Process by Which Turnover, Hiring, and Job Demands Affect Patient Satisfaction
methods: Longitudinal unit-month panel (838 observations, 12 nursing units, 2003-2008); fixed effects panel regression with product-of-coefficients (Sobel) mediation tests for short-term effects, and panel vector autoregression (PVAR) estimated via system GMM with forward de-meaning, impulse response functions, and 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations for dynamic long-term effects.
industry: Hospital nursing units (health care); one Midwestern U.S. university hospital system
time_period: 2003-2008 (monthly observations)
units: Nursing units (unit-month observations)
n_sample: 12 nursing units; 838 unit-month observations
authors: Reilly, G.; Nyberg, A. J.; Maltarich, M. A.; Weller, I.
theories: context-emergent turnover (CET) theory (Nyberg & Ployhart, 2013); dynamic systems theory (Sims, 1980; Steel, 2002); human capital resource theory (Becker, 1964; Ployhart, Weekley, & Ramsey, 2009)
keywords: context-emergent turnover theory; employee transfers; hiring rates; human capital flows; job demands; patient satisfaction; unit performance; voluntary turnover rates
research_question: How and why do unit-level human capital flows — voluntary turnover, hiring, and employee transfers (in and out) — affect unit performance (patient satisfaction) over time? The study asks how changes in job demands mediate these effects, and how the relative magnitude and duration of each flow's effect unfold within a dynamic, mutually causal, and co-evolving system.
hypotheses:
H1. The negative effects of (a) voluntary turnover rates and (b) transfer-out rates on patient satisfaction are partially mediated by job demands.
H2. The positive effects of (a) hiring rates and (b) transfer-in rates on patient satisfaction are partially mediated by job demands.
H3a. The immediate effect of voluntary turnover rates on job demands is more strongly negative than the immediate effect of transfer-out rates on job demands.
H3b. The immediate effect of voluntary turnover rates on patient satisfaction is more strongly negative than the immediate effect of transfer-out rates on patient satisfaction.
H3c. The immediate effect of transfer-in rates on patient satisfaction is more strongly positive than the immediate effect of hiring rates on patient satisfaction.
H4a. The negative effect of voluntary turnover rates on patient satisfaction has a longer duration than the negative effect of transfer-out rates on patient satisfaction.
H4b. The positive effect of hiring rates on patient satisfaction has a longer duration than the positive effect of transfer-in rates on patient satisfaction.
H5. The effect of voluntary turnover rates on patient satisfaction has a longer duration than the effect of voluntary turnover rates on job demands.
mechanism_summary:
- Mediator(s): Job demands (required output relative to staffing; work intensity per nurse)
- Moderator(s): None formally tested; the study instead models the timing and duration of effects through a dynamic PVAR system

In CET theory's dynamic-systems view, human capital flows change a unit's stock of human capital, which shifts job demands — the amount of work faced by remaining nurses. Outflows (voluntary turnover and transfers-out) raise job demands, whereas inflows (hiring and transfers-in) can lower them, and job demands in turn drive patient satisfaction because nurses have more or less time for patient care. Because managers can counteract these flows (adjusting patient loads, timing transfers, accelerating hiring) and the system is mutually causal and co-evolving, the different flows are expected to differ in both the magnitude and the duration of their reverberations through the system.
data_measures: Data are 838 unit-month observations from 12 nursing units of one Midwestern U.S. university hospital system, observed 2003-2008; individual nurse career-path records (hire, turnover, transfer events) were aggregated into monthly unit-level rates. Patient satisfaction (DV): six nursing-focused items from the HCAHPS survey administered after each stay, aggregated to monthly unit level (ICC(1) = 0.12, ICC(2) = 0.94). Voluntary turnover rate: nurses voluntarily leaving the organization in a month / nurses at month start. Hiring rate: new external nurse hires / nurses at month start. Transfer-out and transfer-in rates: nurses transferred out of / into a unit / nurses at month start. The four flow-rate variables were transformed via the inverse hyperbolic sine. Job demands (mediator): monthly-adjusted patient-days / nurses employed that month. Prior staffing level (control): nurses employed at month start. Estimation: fixed effects panel regression with product-of-coefficients (Sobel) mediation tests for short-term effects, and panel vector autoregression (PVAR) via system GMM (forward de-meaning / Helmert procedure, impulse response functions, 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations for 90% confidence intervals, variance decompositions) for dynamic long-term effects. The design is observational panel data; "mutual causality" is inferred from the dynamic-systems PVAR model, not from randomization.
key_findings: Short-term mediation (fixed effects, Table 3): voluntary turnover raised job demands (b = 13.30, p < .001) and so did transfer-out (b = 7.89, p < .001); hiring lowered job demands (b = -6.53, p < .001); transfer-in was not significant (b = 0.18, n.s.); job demands lowered patient satisfaction (b = -0.72, p < .01). Indirect effects on patient satisfaction through job demands were significant for voluntary turnover (a x b = -9.58, p < .05) and transfer-out (a x b = -5.68, p < .05), supporting H1a and H1b, and for hiring (a x b = 4.70, p < .05), supporting H2a; the transfer-in indirect effect was not significant (a x b = -0.13, n.s.), so H2b was not supported. Relative-magnitude comparisons (Chow tests) were in the predicted direction but had overlapping confidence intervals and non-significant z-values (z = 1.39, 0.36, 0.85), so H3a, H3b, and H3c were not supported. Dynamic duration (PVAR / impulse responses): voluntary turnover's negative effect on patient satisfaction emerged about month 3 and persisted through the 12-month window, whereas transfer-out's effect was immediate (month 0) but dissipated and was non-significant thereafter — supporting H4a; hiring's positive effect on patient satisfaction was significant from month 2 through month 12, whereas transfer-in was significant only in months 1, 3, and 5 — supporting H4b. Voluntary turnover's effects on both patient satisfaction and job demands persisted throughout the 12 months, so the satisfaction effect did not outlast the job-demands effect and H5 was not supported. The system accounted for about 24% of the variance in patient satisfaction over time.
theoretical_contribution: The study tests and extends context-emergent turnover (CET) theory. It validates the quantity dimension of collective turnover as a driver of unit performance; situates voluntary turnover within a broader, mutually causal system of human capital flows by distinctly modeling hiring and transfers (in and out); adds temporal precision by showing that different flows differ in the duration of their effects; and identifies job demands as the previously omitted causal mechanism linking quantity changes in human capital to unit outcomes. Methodologically, it introduces panel vector autoregression (PVAR) to management research as a way to model dynamic, co-evolving human-capital systems.
practical_implication: For managers, unit-level voluntary turnover is negatively related to patient satisfaction while hiring is positively related to it, and much of each effect runs through job demands. Managers can therefore mitigate turnover's effects by managing job demands — using transfers and hiring, ideally before or concurrent with expected turnover, and by holding some slack human capital resources so remaining nurses' workloads do not spike. Hiring ahead of anticipated human capital degradation (and, for some outcomes, favoring external hiring over transfers-in despite higher cost) can reduce performance declines, a decision that is likely more important for highly complex or team-oriented tasks.
limitations: The study could not incorporate individual differences or the quality of the human capital flowing in and out; 76% of the variance in patient satisfaction remained unexplained. Data came from a single hospital and a single job (nurse), which aids internal comparability but limits generalizability across industries and contexts. The 2003-2008 window excluded events such as the post-2008 downturn, and month-long observation units may be too coarse to capture the full process (weeks might reveal stronger, finer-grained effects). The small number of units (12) creates power limitations that may mask relationships, and standard significance testing could not establish whether the observed duration differences (e.g., 12 months vs. one month) were statistically different.
future_research: Future research should quantify the quality of the human capital resource flowing in and out, not just its quantity, including measuring firm-specific knowledge and the social integration of interdependent work units. Research is also needed on how different contexts and industries — with different levels of workflow controllability, replacement timelines, opportunities to use transfers, and standardization of procedures — alter the relationships among these constructs.
abstract: The dynamic systems view of voluntary turnover rates advocated in context-emergent turnover theory is used to explore how and why human capital flows impact unit performance over time. We examine hiring rates and employee transfer rates as distinct system components that work alongside voluntary turnover rates to affect job demands, and ultimately patient satisfaction. Our work explores this dynamic system of interrelated constructs, and explains and compares their mutual causality over time. The sample examined consists of 12 nursing units in a large hospital over 72 monthly observations, with patient satisfaction as the measure of unit performance.

Human capital flows: Using context-emergent turnover (CET) theory to explore the process by which turnover, hiring, and job demands affect patient satisfaction. *Academy of Management Journal, 57*(3), 766-790. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2012.0132

title: How Organizations Foster the Creative Use of Resources
methods: Single-site inductive case study (theory elaboration) of one fast-growing U.S. specialty retailer ('BoutiqueCo'); grounded-theory analysis (open/in-vivo then second-order/axial coding via the Gioia methodology) of 60 interviews, 62.5 hours of participant observation, and 151 documents, coded in NVivo 8.0.
industry: Specialty retail (clothing, jewelry, accessories, gift items); pseudonymous 'BoutiqueCo'
time_period: Family era 1999–Feb 2010; investor era Feb 2010 onward; fieldwork/observations 2008–2010
units: One organization; corporate managers and store employees
n_sample: 60 interviews (19 home-office/regional managers, 41 store employees); 62.5 hrs observation; 151 documents
authors: Sonenshein, S.
theories: bricolage (Baker & Nelson, 2005); creativity theory (Amabile, 1988, 1996); resourcing (Feldman, 2004; Feldman & Worline, 2012)
keywords: autonomous resourcing; creative resourcing; creativity; directed resourcing; resourcing
research_question: How do resources shape creative activities inside organizations over time? The paper asks how managers foster ongoing creative activity as an organization's perceived resource endowment changes, shifting attention from the quantity of resources to the actions through which managers and employees turn objects into resources.
hypotheses: Not reported in paper
mechanism_summary:
- Aggregate dimensions (grounded data structure): perceived resource endowment, resourcing identity, regulating objects, creative resourcing, problem solving.
- Creative resourcing forms: manipulating (altering a single object) and recombining (altering the relationships among a set of objects) in novel and useful ways to solve problems.
- Autonomous resourcing (perceived limited resources; family era): managers foster a "resourcing identity" through cultivating ownership schemas and cultivating creator schemas, after which creative resourcing proceeds with minimal ongoing managerial control, yielding original solutions.
- Directed resourcing (perceived abundant resources; investor era): managers "regulate objects" by withholding fixed objects (e.g., planograms) and provisioning dynamic objects (e.g., trend alerts, stories, broad guidelines), exerting more control while sustaining creative resourcing, yielding heterogeneous solutions.
- Transition: problem solving under autonomous resourcing improves managers' perceived resource endowment (via resource-conservation, endogenous-resourcefulness, and knowledge-based mechanisms), prompting a shift toward directed resourcing.

The study elaborates a process model in which the link between resources and creativity runs through the actions and interpretations of managers and employees rather than through resource quantity. Under a perceived limited endowment, managers shape employees' identities as creative owners, and employees enact that identity by manipulating and recombining available objects. Under a perceived abundant endowment, managers instead regulate the flow of objects—withholding those employees would read as fixed and provisioning those they would read as dynamic—so that creativity persists but is more guided. Both processes are recursive: solving problems reinforces the identity or generates new objects to resource, and can itself raise the perceived resource endowment.
data_measures: Single-site, longitudinal inductive case study of "BoutiqueCo" (pseudonym), a fast-growing U.S. specialty retailer transforming from a family business into a large public chain. Data: 60 interviews (19 home-office employees and regional managers, including most of the top management team, plus 41 store employees), 62.5 hours of (mostly participant) observation, and 151 documents. Analysis followed a grounded-theory approach (Charmaz; Glaser & Strauss) using the Gioia methodology: open/in-vivo coding, then second-order/axial coding into five aggregate theoretical dimensions, with memo writing, constant comparison, triangulation across data sources, member checking, and peer debriefing, managed in NVivo 8.0. The design is interpretive and theory-elaborating; no causal identification is claimed.
key_findings: The study induces two organizational processes through which managers foster creative resourcing, contingent on their perceived resource endowment. Under autonomous resourcing (perceived limited resources, family era), managers foster creativity indirectly by shaping employees' resourcing identity through ownership and creator schemas; employees then creatively resource—manipulating and recombining objects—with minimal managerial control, producing original solutions "not imaginable by corporate managers." Under directed resourcing (perceived abundant resources, investor era), managers exert more control by regulating objects—withholding fixed objects (planograms) and provisioning dynamic objects (trend alerts, stories, broad guidelines)—which sustains creative resourcing but yields more heterogeneous (somewhat less fully original) solutions. Problem solving under autonomous resourcing can improve the perceived resource endowment, moving the organization toward directed resourcing. The overarching finding is that both limited and abundant resource endowments can foster creativity; what matters is how managers and employees interpret and act on those endowments, not the quantity of resources per se.
theoretical_contribution: The paper elaborates theory that integrates creativity and resourcing research, reorienting creativity scholarship away from variance-explanation models (resource quantity → creative output) toward organizational processes and the situated actions of managers and employees over time. Adopting a resourcing lens, it treats resources not as fixed entities but as objects individuals act on, and shows that managerial action—fostering a resourcing identity (autonomous resourcing) and regulating objects (directed resourcing)—shapes how creative resourcing unfolds as an organization grows. To the resourcing literature it adds creativity as a foundational skill for resourcing and shows that resourcing is not only a bottom-up employee process but is also permitted and guided by managers.
practical_implication: The paper offers two practical implications for managers. First, rather than focusing on the amount of resources available, managers can focus on the actions they and their employees take in response to their perceived resource endowment, choosing between autonomous resourcing (less ongoing managerial involvement and control, but more potential for original solutions) and directed resourcing (greater control, but dependent on a repertoire of objects to provision). Second, managers can spark creative activity by fostering a resourcing identity and by regulating—withholding and provisioning—objects, adding new levers for influencing employee creativity beyond personal characteristics, intrinsic motivation, and leader–member exchange.
limitations: The study is a single-site case study of one retailer, chosen as an extreme case to elaborate theory by compressing the time frame of organizational growth. The author notes that relying on a key informant risks a partial interpretation of the organization, a risk mitigated by drawing on multiple data sources. Several claims—notably the shift from autonomous to directed resourcing and the suggested tradeoff whereby directed resourcing may favor usefulness over novelty—are described as only suggestive, tentative, or speculative and are flagged as needing further research.
future_research: The paper explicitly invites further work on how managers learn to resource in more helpful ways, and on a closer dialogue between resourcing scholars and more psychologically oriented scholars who study the antecedents of creative acts. It also calls for more research to substantiate the tentative tradeoff between novelty and usefulness across autonomous versus directed resourcing, and for further exploration of how the usefulness of creative solutions is contextually dependent on an organization's lifecycle stage.
abstract: Using a multi-year qualitative study, I explain how employees at a fast-growing retail organization used creative resourcing—that is, the manipulation and recombination of objects in novel and useful ways to solve problems. I induce two core organizational processes (autonomous resourcing and directed resourcing) that explain how organizations foster ongoing creative activities in response to different perceived resource endowments. In doing so, I add clarity to a mixed literature that argues on the one hand that limited resources foster creativity, and on the other, that abundant resources foster creativity. Instead, I reorient the questions that scholars ask by shifting the conversation away from variance-explanation models and towards understanding organizational processes, specifically around how employees use resources in dynamic ways and how managers enable them to do so. My study unpacks how the link between resources and creativity is rooted deeply in the actions of managers and employees embedded in organizations over time. In elaborating theory around these actions, I contribute to scholarly and practitioner understanding around how organizations foster creativity in a variety of resource environments.

title: Managers and Analysts: An Examination of Mutual Influence
methods: Longitudinal firm-quarter panel of large US firms (S&P 500 as of January 2002, excluding financials). Simultaneous-equation models of three impression management activities: probit with firm dummies and endogeneity corrections for forecast guidance; two-stage least squares with firm fixed effects and robust standard errors for (log) press releases and conference calls; 50-dataset multiple imputation for missing press-release data. Change in analysts' subsequent forecasts modeled with firm fixed-effects regression interacting each activity with above-target and below-target.
industry: Large publicly traded firms across industries (S&P 500 as of January 2002), excluding financial-industry firms (SIC 5999-7000) and unclassified firms (SIC 9999)
time_period: January 2002 - December 2007
units: firm-quarters
n_sample: 116 firms in the hand-collected press-release subsample; roughly 2,300-2,447 firm-quarters for hand-collected data and about 7,000-7,400 firm-quarters for the archival variables
authors: Washburn, M.; Bromiley, P.
theories: impression management (Elsbach, 2003; Pfarrer, Pollock, & Rindova, 2010; Rindova, Williamson, Petkova, & Sever, 2005); information asymmetry and signaling in manager-analyst exchange (Sanders & Carpenter, 2003; Basdeo et al., 2006); information intermediaries and the social construction of reputation (Rindova, Pollock, & Hayward, 2006; Bitektine, 2011)
keywords: conference calls; earnings per share; forecast guidance; impression management; press releases; securities analysts
research_question: How does a firm's performance relative to prior analyst earnings-per-share targets influence managers' impression management activities — issuing forecast guidance, holding conference calls, and issuing press releases — and how do those activities in turn influence analysts' subsequent forecasts, given that managers and analysts engage in a recursive, dyadic process in which neither party fully controls the outcome?
hypotheses:
H1: The extent earnings diverge above or below analyst forecasts decreases the likelihood managers issue forecast guidance.
H2a: The extent that earnings diverge (above or below) analyst forecasts increases the number of press releases that managers subsequently issue.
H2b: The divergence of earnings from analyst forecasts has a larger influence on the number of press releases when earnings are below rather than above analyst forecasts.
H3a: The extent that earnings diverge (above or below) analyst forecasts positively influences the number of conference calls that managers subsequently undertake.
H3b: The divergence of earnings from analyst forecasts has a larger influence on the number of conference calls when earnings are below rather than above analyst forecasts.
H4: For firms with earnings significantly above analyst targets, forecast guidance, press releases, and conference calls negatively influence the change in subsequent analyst forecasts.
H5: For firms with earnings significantly below analyst targets, forecast guidance, press releases, and conference calls negatively influence the change in subsequent analyst forecasts.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on impression management theory, the paper models a recursive, dyadic process: analysts set EPS targets, firms report performance relative to those targets, and managers respond with impression management activities whose intensity varies with the magnitude and direction of the performance-target divergence; these activities then feed back into analysts' subsequent forecast revisions. Larger deviations — especially shortfalls below target — heighten a firm's need to explain itself and so raise press releases and conference calls, whereas divergence in either direction discourages forecast guidance because guidance puts managers' reputations as accurate, competent forecasters at risk. Because neither party fully controls the process, the authors use the language of "influence" rather than direct causal control.
data_measures: Data sources: analyst quarterly EPS forecasts from I/B/E/S; forecast guidance from the First Call database; conference calls from the BestCalls database; financial data from Compustat Fundamentals Quarterly; institutional ownership from Thomson Reuters CDA/Spectrum (13F); press-release counts hand-collected from Lexis Nexis and verified against Hoover's Pro Online. Key dependent measures: forecast guidance = 1 if the firm provided point or interval estimate forecasts or made a material statement about an existing analyst forecast, else 0 (about 44% of firm-quarters); conference calls = count of management-analyst calls (values 0-17); press releases = natural log of the total number of press releases per period (mean 37, maximum 1,794). Independent variables of theoretical interest: above target = announced EPS minus the analyst consensus forecast when earnings exceeded the forecast (else 0); below target = consensus forecast minus announced EPS when the forecast exceeded earnings (else 0); differences greater than $1 were excluded. Second-model outcome: forecast change = mean analyst EPS forecast for quarter t generated in quarter t-1 minus the mean forecast for quarter t generated in quarter t-2. Controls: analyst consensus (SD of prior-period forecasts), fourth-quarter effect, change in and number of analyst forecasts, earnings management (deferred component of income tax expense scaled by quarterly assets), firm size (log market capitalization), and transient / quasi-indexer / dedicated institutional ownership. Estimation and identification: firm dummies / fixed effects with corrections for endogeneity among the three activities (probit for forecast guidance; two-stage least squares with robust standard errors for press releases and conference calls; fixed-effects regression for forecast change), plus 50-dataset multiple imputation for missing press-release data and Cook's D / dbeta outlier trimming. The design is an observational panel; the authors deliberately use "influence" language, noting the lack of direct control (associational, not an experimental identification strategy).
key_findings: Managers' impression management activities varied systematically with performance relative to analyst targets. H1 was strongly supported: divergence both above target (b = -2.72, p < .001) and below target (b = -3.14, p < .001) reduced the likelihood of issuing forecast guidance. H2a was supported: divergence increased press releases for both above target (b = 0.40, p < .01) and below target (b = 0.55, p < .01). H2b was not supported: the below-target parameter exceeded the above-target parameter, but the difference just missed significance (χ²(1) = 2.48, p = .12). H3a was partially supported: divergence increased conference calls for below target (b = 0.505, p < .01) but not for above target (b = -0.039, n.s.). H3b was supported: the below-target influence on conference calls was significantly greater than the above-target influence across all 50 imputed datasets. H4 and H5 (effects of the activities on subsequent forecast revisions) were only partially supported, and only through conference calls: conference calls significantly reduced (smoothed) the increase in subsequent forecasts for firms with performance well above or well below target (negative interactions with above target and below target, significant in most windows). Forecast guidance had no significant effect on forecast change (H4/H5 not supported for forecast guidance). Contrary to H4/H5, press releases most strongly and negatively influenced forecast change when performance was near the target, becoming insignificant at extreme divergence.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends impression management theory from a predominantly one-directional view — firms projecting impressions onto passive audiences — to a two-way, continuing process of mutual influence in which managers and analysts each react to the other and neither fully controls the outcome. It advances a relational view of how stakeholders negotiate the value of socially constructed assets such as legitimacy, reputation, and status, and shows that the medium of transmission itself conveys information: how messages are communicated, not only their content, shapes their reception. Empirically, it demonstrates that firms' impression management activities vary systematically with performance relative to analyst targets and that some activities — notably conference calls — shape subsequent analyst forecasts under extreme performance.
practical_implication: Managers may manage impressions more effectively if they systematically adapt their communication behavior — the choice among forecast guidance, press releases, and conference calls — to their firm's performance relative to analyst targets and to the target audience.
limitations: The analysis examined only the media and channels of impression management, not the specific content of managers' messages. It lacked direct measures of analysts' sensitivity to influence, so the modest effects on forecast revision may reflect variation in the content or intent of the activities, variation in analysts' ability to discount them, or problems in the study's ancillary theoretical assumptions. By focusing solely on the manager-analyst relation, the study de-emphasized analysts' indirect influence on firms' access to external resources and the role of other intermediaries such as journalists and outside directors. The study also stops short of a normative analysis of whether managers should attempt to influence forecasts.
future_research: The authors call for examining how the influence of firms' messages changes as those messages move through networks of intermediaries (for example, journalists and other analysts) to provide a more complete representation of managerial impression management. They also call for a normative analysis of whether managers should attempt to influence forecasts — one that allows for divergence between managers' and the firm's motivations, and that considers whether impression management activities systematically bias analyst forecasts and how such biases affect the firm.
abstract: Securities analysts' predictions of firms' earnings per share constitute important performance targets for those firms. Firm managers attempt to both influence analysts' targets and achieve the targets. We draw on the impression management literature to offer hypotheses regarding how a firm's performance relative to prior targets influences the impression management activities of issuing forecast guidance, having conference calls with analysts, and issuing press releases. We also consider the influence of these impression management activities on subsequent analysts' targets. We test this dyadic representation of impression management activities using a longitudinal panel of large firms. Findings suggest managers take a variety of actions that vary with firm performance, and that some of those actions influence subsequent analyst targets under some conditions.

title: Conscience without Cognition: The Effects of Subconscious Priming on Ethical Behavior
methods: Three randomized experiments (Studies 1 and 3 in the laboratory; Study 2 online via Amazon mTurk) manipulating subconscious priming through a sentence-unscrambling task; analyses include t-tests, chi-square tests, bootstrapped multiple-mediation (Preacher & Hayes, 2008), and a three-way ANOVA.
industry: Not reported in paper
time_period: Not reported in paper
units: Individual participants (undergraduate students in Studies 1 and 3; online adult mTurk workers in Study 2)
n_sample: Study 1: 103; Study 2: 291 (plus 168 in a supplementary comparison); Study 3: 312 (final analyzed samples)
authors: Welsh, D. T.; Ordóñez, L. D.
theories: goal-setting theory (Latham, Stajkovic, & Locke, 2010); neurocognitive model of ethical decision making (Reynolds, 2006); self-concept maintenance theory (Mazar, Amir, & Ariely, 2008)
keywords: behavioral ethics; ethical behavior; monitoring; moral standards; performance goals; self-concept maintenance theory; subconscious priming
research_question: Can subconscious, automatic processes—not just conscious, deliberate reasoning—shape ethical behavior? Specifically, does subconscious ethical and unethical priming activate moral standards and thereby increase ethical categorization and reduce unethical behavior, even under conflicting conscious objectives such as high performance goals and external monitoring?
hypotheses:
H1a: Priming subconscious ethical and unethical content will activate moral standards.
H1b: Priming subconscious ethical and unethical content will increase the likelihood that morally ambiguous situations will be categorized as unethical.
H1c: Activation of moral standards will mediate the relationship between priming subconscious ethical and unethical content and the categorization of morally ambiguous situations.
H2a: People will behave more unethically when they have high performance goals than when they have "do your best" (DYB) goals.
H2b: Priming subconscious ethical and unethical content will reduce unethical behavior when people are given high performance goals.
H3a: People will behave more unethically when they are not monitored than when they are monitored.
H3b: Priming subconscious ethical and unethical content will reduce unethical behavior when people are unmonitored.
mechanism_summary: Integrating Reynolds' (2006) neurocognitive dual-process model with self-concept maintenance theory, the authors argue that subconscious stimuli containing moral content are implicitly matched to moral schemas through the automatic "X-system," activating an individual's moral standards. Activated standards raise the propensity to categorize morally ambiguous situations as unethical and to align behavior with self-concept, thereby reducing unethical conduct. Because the mechanism runs through internal psychological processes, subconscious priming can counteract conscious pressures—high performance goals that divert attention from moral standards—especially when external monitoring is absent.
data_measures: Study 1 (lab, final n = 103 undergraduates): subconscious priming manipulated with a 20-sentence unscrambling task (12 ethics-related sentences in the ethical condition; 8 in the unethical condition); categorization coded dichotomously from whether participants raised any ethics issue in Butterfield et al.'s (2000) mystery-shopper dilemma; activation of standards measured as moral sensitivity (two items, α = .74) and Aquino and Reed's (2002) 10-item moral identity scale (α = .75); a funnel-debrief awareness check excluded participants who detected the prime; mediation tested with Preacher and Hayes' (2008) bootstrapped multiple-mediation (1,000 resamples, bias-corrected 95% CIs). Study 2 (online mTurk, final n = 291 adults; 3 subconscious-prime × 2 conscious-recall design): DV was self-reported likelihood of unethical behavior on a seven-point scale using Gino, Norton, and Ariely's (2010) toxic-pesticide scenario; an additional 168 participants compared the unscrambling prime against a Ten Commandments recall prime. Study 3 (lab, final n = 312 business students; 3 prime × 2 goal × 2 monitoring design): DV was actual cheating measured as over-reported correct answers on Mazar et al.'s (2008) 20-matrix addition task, analyzed with a three-way ANOVA. Random assignment was used across the laboratory and online experiments, and the authors state the laboratory design let them "infer causality" between subconscious priming and ethics-related outcomes.
key_findings: All hypotheses were supported. Study 1: H1a supported—ethical and unethical priming raised moral sensitivity (5.30 and 4.92 vs. 4.00 neutral) and moral identity (5.73 and 5.65 vs. 5.23 neutral); H1b supported—ethics-issue categorization was 58% (ethical) and 56% (unethical) vs. 28% (neutral); H1c supported—activation of moral standards fully mediated the priming→categorization effect (significant bootstrapped indirect effects; the direct effect dropped from significant to non-significant). Study 2: participants whose standards were activated (subconsciously, consciously, or both) reported significantly less unethical behavior than the neutral/neutral control (3.59 vs. 2.61–2.84); subconscious priming reduced unethical behavior under neutral recall but was attenuated when combined with conscious recall (a ceiling on activation), and the subconscious prime was less consciously detected than the Ten Commandments prime. Study 3: H2a supported—high goals nearly doubled over-reporting (mean .61 vs. .35 DYB; F = 5.15, p < .05); H2b supported—ethical/unethical priming reduced cheating under high goals (priming main effect F = 4.21, p < .05); H3a supported—monitoring reduced cheating (F = 5.61, p < .05); H3b supported—when unmonitored, over-reporting was more than double under neutral (1.02) vs. ethical (.35) and unethical (.45) priming (priming × monitoring interaction F = 3.84, p < .05), while priming had little effect when participants were monitored; the three-way interaction was non-significant.
theoretical_contribution: The paper extends self-concept maintenance theory (Mazar et al., 2008) by integrating it with Reynolds' (2006) neurocognitive dual-process model to show that subconscious primes—not only conscious moral reminders—can activate existing moral standards and reduce unethical behavior. It advances four points: it tests the mediating mechanism linking subconscious processes to ethical behavior; shows ethical and unethical priming operate similarly by triggering schemas people already possess rather than changing their values; provides a first demonstrated mechanism for reducing goal-induced unethicality; and shows subconscious priming is most effective when individuals are unmonitored.
practical_implication: For organizations, the authors suggest that subconsciously priming ethical behavior—through the images, symbols, stories, and slogans that comprise organizational culture (e.g., a fire-alarm poster calling attention to unethical conduct on campus, or In-N-Out's discreet Bible-verse notations)—may activate employees' existing moral standards and reduce unethical behavior. This may matter because today's organizations have fewer resources to monitor employees, and priming reduced dishonesty even for unmonitored individuals strongly committed to difficult performance goals. Priming works by activating standards employees already hold rather than by altering their moral values.
limitations: The mediated process was tested in Studies 1 and 2 but not in Study 3. The studies could not test how long the effects of subconscious priming persist over time. Subconscious ethical priming also requires that individuals already possess the appropriate moral schemas, so effects may be attenuated in contexts lacking widely accepted norms for ethical behavior.
future_research: The authors call for research on how long subconscious priming effects last; on the effectiveness of other forms of subconscious primes (images, symbols, words, and sounds across a variety of contexts); on the effects of subconscious priming on unethical behaviors of various types and magnitudes; on individual-level characteristics (e.g., people who rely more on intuition than cognition); and on links between subconscious priming and other organizational theories, including whether priming increases prosocial behaviors such as organizational citizenship behaviors (altruism, civic virtue, and voice).
abstract: Research in the field of behavioral ethics has traditionally viewed ethical decision making as rational and deliberate. However, some recent research has proposed a dual process model of ethical decision making that has both conscious and subconscious components (Reynolds, 2006). We extend current theory by using subconscious ethical and unethical priming to test the effects of subconscious processes on ethical behavior through an automatic process of schema activation and implicit association. Studies 1 and 2 extend self-concept maintenance theory (Mazar, Amir, & Ariely, 2008) by exploring the mediated process through which subconscious ethical and unethical primes trigger the activation of moral standards, thereby influencing categorization and subsequent responses to morally ambiguous situations. Study 3 demonstrates that both subconscious ethical and unethical priming reduce dishonesty even when participants are unmonitored and are given difficult performance goals that previously have been shown to lead to unethical behavior.
apa_citation: Welsh, D. T., & Ordóñez, L. D. (2014). Conscience without cognition: The effects of subconscious priming on ethical behavior. *Academy of Management Journal*, 57(3), 723–742. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.1009

title: It's Not Fair … Or Is It? The Role of Justice and Leadership in Explaining Work Stressor–Job Performance Relationships
methods: Multilevel moderated-mediation study. Two-source, time-lagged survey: employees self-reported stressors, strain, justice, and leadership; supervisors rated five job-performance dimensions about three weeks later. Analyzed with multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM) in Mplus 6.11, level-1 stressors group-mean centered and level-2 leadership grand-mean centered, controlling for job tenure and industry; bias-corrected 95% CIs for indirect effects from 20,000 Monte Carlo re-samples. Cross-sectional (associational) design.
industry: Automobile-manufacturing and pharmaceutical organizations
time_period: Two survey waves about three weeks apart; calendar dates not reported
units: Full-time white-collar employees nested in work units / supervisors
n_sample: 339 employees; 88 supervisors
authors: Zhang, Y.; LePine, J. A.; Buckman, B. R.; Wei, F.
theories: challenge–hindrance stressor framework (Cavanaugh et al., 2000); fairness theory (Folger & Cropanzano, 1998, 2001); social exchange theory (Blau, 1964); transactional theory of stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984); transformational–transactional leadership theory (Bass, 1985)
keywords: challenge stressors; hindrance stressors; job performance; organizational justice; social exchange; transactional leadership; transformational leadership; work stressors
research_question: How and why do challenge and hindrance stressors differentially relate to employee job performance? Specifically, does organizational justice operate as an intervening mechanism linking the two stressor dimensions to five job-performance dimensions over and above strain, and how do unit-level transformational and transactional leadership moderate the stressor–justice relationships?
hypotheses:
H1a. Organizational justice perceptions mediate the negative relationship between hindrance stressors and job performance.
H1b. Organizational justice perceptions mediate the positive relationship between challenge stressors and job performance.
H2a. Transactional leadership moderates the (negative) hindrance stressor–justice relationship such that it is less negative when transactional leadership is high.
H2b. Transactional leadership moderates the negative indirect effect of hindrance stressors on job performance via justice such that it is less negative when transactional leadership is high.
H3a. Transactional leadership moderates the (positive) challenge stressor–justice relationship such that it is more positive when transactional leadership is high.
H3b. Transactional leadership moderates the positive indirect effect of challenge stressors on job performance via justice such that it is more positive when transactional leadership is high.
H4a. Transformational leadership moderates the (negative) hindrance stressor–justice relationship such that it is less negative when transformational leadership is high.
H4b. Transformational leadership moderates the negative indirect effect of hindrance stressors on job performance via justice such that it is less negative when transformational leadership is high.
H5a. Transformational leadership moderates the (positive) challenge stressor–justice relationship such that it is more positive when transformational leadership is high.
H5b. Transformational leadership moderates the indirect effect of challenge stressors on job performance via justice such that it is more positive when transformational leadership is high.
mechanism_summary: Grounded in social exchange theory (Blau, 1964) and Folger and Cropanzano's (1998) fairness theory, the model argues that employees appraise stressful demands against the reciprocity norms of their exchange relationship with the organization. Hindrance stressors imply contributions with little prospect of return, violating reciprocity, so they are perceived as unfair and prompt employees to withhold performance contributions. Challenge stressors carry the promise of future benefits and growth, are consistent with reciprocity, and are therefore perceived as fair and reciprocated with performance. This justice pathway is proposed to operate over and above the conventional strain/energy-depletion pathway. Leaders, as sense-givers and resource allocators, shape how stressors are interpreted with regard to fairness: transactional (contingent-reward) behavior frames demands as "part of the deal," buffering the hindrance–justice link, whereas transformational behavior fosters a meaning-and-growth framing that strengthens the challenge–justice link.
data_measures:
Data: 339 full-time white-collar employees and their 88 supervisors from automobile-manufacturing and pharmaceutical firms in eastern China; surveys translated and back-translated into Chinese. Two-wave, two-source lagged design (employee survey first; supervisor performance ratings about three weeks later).

Measures (employee-reported unless noted):
- Challenge stressors: 6 items (workload, time pressure, task complexity, responsibility); frequency-rated 1–5.
- Hindrance stressors: 7 items (role ambiguity, role/interpersonal conflict, politics, hassles, red tape); frequency-rated 1–5.
- Strain: 4 exhaustion items from the Maslach Burnout Inventory (Maslach et al., 1996).
- Organizational justice: Colquitt's (2001) 19-item measure (distributive, procedural, interpersonal, informational), modeled as a second-order overall-justice factor.
- Transformational / transactional leadership: MLQ Form 5X (Bass & Avolio, 1995) — transformational = 20 items across four dimensions; transactional = 4-item contingent-rewards subscale; aggregated to unit-level means (L2).
- Job performance (supervisor-rated): task performance (4 items; Williams & Anderson, 1991), helping (4) and voice (4) (Van Dyne & LePine, 1998), counterproductive behavior (5; Bennett & Robinson, 2000), and creative behavior (5; George & Zhou, 2001; Scott & Bruce, 1994).

Analysis: multilevel SEM (MSEM) in Mplus 6.11 with level-1 stressors group-mean centered and level-2 leadership grand-mean centered; job tenure and industry controlled on all endogenous variables; bias-corrected 95% CIs for indirect effects from 20,000 Monte Carlo re-samples. The design is cross-sectional/associational — the authors do not claim causal identification.
key_findings:
Justice pathway (H1). Hindrance stressors were negatively related to organizational justice (γ = −.57, p < .05); challenge stressors were unrelated to justice (γ = .10, p > .05). Justice predicted all five performance dimensions (task β = .37; helping β = .32; voice β = .30; creative β = .32; counterproductive β = −.19; all p < .05). **H1a supported** — hindrance stressors' average indirect effects via justice were significant for all five outcomes (task ρ = −.21; helping −.18; voice −.17; creative −.18; counterproductive +.11; all p < .05). **H1b not supported** — challenge stressors' indirect effects via justice were nonsignificant (ρ ≈ .02–.04; all p > .05).

Strain pathway (comparison). Both stressors related to strain (hindrance γ = .50; challenge γ = .17; both p < .05), but in the full model strain predicted only counterproductive behavior (β = .12, p < .05); strain-mediated indirect effects were significant only for counterproductive behavior.

Leadership moderation. **H2a supported** — transactional leadership moderated the hindrance–justice link (γ = .32, p < .05; simple slope −.24 when high vs −.78 when low). **H2b supported** — the hindrance→justice→performance indirect effects differed by transactional leadership for all five outcomes (e.g., task diff = .24, p < .05). **H3a and H3b not supported** (transactional × challenge: γ = −.28, p > .05; indirect-effect differences ns). **H4a and H4b not supported** (transformational × hindrance: γ = −.22, p > .05; indirect-effect differences ns). **H5a supported** — transformational leadership moderated the challenge–justice link (γ = .32, p < .05; simple slope .28 when high vs .03 when low). **H5b supported** — the challenge→justice→performance indirect effects differed by transformational leadership for all five outcomes (e.g., task diff = .24, p < .05).

Summary — supported: H1a, H2a, H2b, H5a, H5b; not supported: H1b, H3a, H3b, H4a, H4b. The unexpected asymmetry (transactional leadership matters for hindrance stressors, transformational leadership for challenge stressors) suggests a contingency rather than a simple augmentation view of leadership; results also held for a single overall-performance latent factor.
theoretical_contribution: The study positions organizational justice as a new intervening mechanism — beyond the conventional strain/energy-depletion account — that explains how challenge and hindrance stressors translate into job performance, integrating the stress, organizational-justice, and leadership literatures through social exchange theory. It shows that leadership's role in the stress process is contingent on stressor type: transactional leadership is more influential in buffering the negative effect of hindrance stressors on justice, whereas transformational leadership is more effective in enhancing the positive effect of challenge stressors on justice. This asymmetric, contingency pattern reframes the augmentation view of transformational–transactional leadership, and the authors advance regulatory-focus theory as a post hoc explanation for it.
practical_implication: The authors argue organizations should take steps to minimize hindrance stressors — for example, using employee task forces to identify and resolve them — since justice's encompassing effects may make such initiatives more valuable than previously thought. They suggest stress management can be improved by shaping how employees judge the fairness of demands, leveraging "justice rules" and more transparent, informative communication about why demands exist and how coping is acknowledged and rewarded. Finally, because leaders shape stressor–justice appraisals, they argue for leadership training and development that fosters both transformational and transactional behaviors and helps leaders identify challenge versus hindrance stressors and apply the fitting style.
limitations: The relationships are cross-sectional, so alternative pathways and feedback loops cannot be ruled out, though the multi-source, multilevel, lagged, moderated design mitigates this concern. Employees provided ratings of the independent variables, moderators, and mediators, raising a common-source-variance concern, though the outcomes were rated by a second source (supervisors). The study did not include a direct measure of the social-exchange process presumed to transmit stressor effects to justice. The broad, averaged conceptualization of justice is somewhat atypical, complicating direct comparison with prior dimension-specific research and potentially masking source-specific justice effects.
future_research: The authors call for longitudinal and experimental designs to further rule out alternative pathways, and for measures from additional sources to further address common-source concerns. They suggest extending the mediational chain to include a direct measure of social exchange and examining the "micro-mediations" within the model. They encourage studying features of stressful demands that evoke different fairness perceptions and contextual factors such as leadership that shape them, better understanding the offsetting moderating effects (the compatibility of work demands and leader behaviors), and testing the regulatory-focus explanation directly. They also point to testing the mediating role of narrower, specific justice dimensions and to examining how strain/energy-depletion processes drive counterproductive behavior.
abstract: We develop and test a theoretical model of multilevel moderated mediation in which organizational justice serves as an intervening mechanism that explains associations among two dimensions of work stressors (challenges and hindrances) and five dimensions of job performance (task performance, helping, voice, counterproductive behavior, and creativity) over and above the intervening role of strain. We also consider how leadership influences the intervening role of justice in the stressor–job performance relationships by virtue of the effect it has on how stressors are interpreted with regard to fairness. Results of a study of 339 employees and their supervisors provide support for this model across dimensions of performance. Somewhat unexpectedly, the moderating effect of leadership is found to be contingent on the type of leadership and the type of stressors. Transactional leaders reduce the negative effect of hindrance stressors on job performance because they weaken the negative link between hindrance stressors and justice perceptions. Alternatively, transformational leaders enhance the positive effect of challenge stressors on job performance because they foster a positive link between challenge stressors and justice perceptions. We discuss how this intriguing pattern of moderated mediation could be explained by using theory and research on regulatory focus.
