title: FDI Spillovers Over Time in an Emerging Market: The Roles of Entry Tenure and Barriers to Imitation
methods: Firm-fixed-effect ('within') panel regression of a log-linear Cobb–Douglas production function on an unbalanced domestic firm–year panel; one-year-lagged industry-level predictors, a squared entry-tenure term, and three interaction terms; year, industry, and region dummies; standard errors clustered at the firm level; survival-bias correction via an inverse Mills ratio (xtprobit). Robustness via Gompertz survival models, alternative firm/foreign definitions, longer lags, geographic/country-origin splits, and random subsamples.
industry: Manufacturing (511 four-digit SIC industries)
units: Domestic firms (100% domestically owned); foreign firms (100% foreign owned) used to compute industry-level FDI variables
n_sample: 945,553 domestic firm–year observations (301,667 domestic firms); 223,382 foreign firm–year observations (64,946 foreign firms)
authors: Zhang, Y.; Li, Y.; Li, H.
theories: absorptive capacity (Cohen & Levinthal, 1990); competitor imitation / barriers to imitation (Lippman & Rumelt, 1982; Reed & DeFillippi, 1990); organizational learning perspective (Cyert & March, 1963; Kogut & Zander, 1992; Winter, 2000)
keywords: FDI spillovers; barriers to imitation; domestic firm productivity; emerging markets; entry tenure; organizational learning
research_question: How do FDI spillovers to domestic firms in an emerging market occur over time, and how do barriers to imitation—shaped by attributes of the foreign firms—affect the role of time in these spillovers?
hypotheses:
H1. The entry tenure of foreign firms in an industry has a positive relationship with the productivity of an individual domestic firm in the same industry.
H2. That positive relationship becomes weaker (i.e., increases at a diminishing rate) as the foreign firms' entry tenure continues to increase.
H3. The positive relationship is stronger when the foreign firms have lower export intensity.
H4. The positive relationship is stronger when the foreign firms have lower intangible asset intensity.
H5. The positive relationship is stronger if the foreign firms have followed a more rhythmic (i.e., less irregular) pattern of entering the industry.
mechanism_summary: From an organizational-learning view, as foreign firms' entry tenure in an industry lengthens, domestic firms have more time to observe, imitate, and assimilate the foreign firms' advanced technologies and management practices, raising their productivity—but at a diminishing rate, because obvious learning opportunities gradually dry up and remaining foreign advantages become tacit and idiosyncratic. Drawing on the competitor-imitation/barriers-to-imitation argument, the speed of this learning ("imitation from a distance") depends on how imitable the foreign firms are: lower export intensity, lower intangible-asset intensity, and a more rhythmic entry pattern reduce information asymmetry and causal ambiguity, thereby strengthening the tenure–productivity relationship.
data_measures: Data source: the Chinese National Bureau of Statistics (CNBS) Annual Industrial Survey Database (1998–2007), covering all state-owned firms and larger non-state-owned firms (annual sales of RMB 5 million or above) in manufacturing. DV: domestic firm productivity measured as log output—firm annual sales deflated to year-2000 constant prices—within a log-linear Cobb–Douglas production function that also includes log capital and log labor inputs. IV: industry-level entry tenure of foreign firms = asset-weighted mean of individual foreign firms' years since founding in China. Moderators: export intensity = foreign firms' export sales divided by total sales; intangible asset intensity = foreign firms' intangible assets divided by total assets; rhythm of entry pattern = kurtosis of the entry-tenure distribution (recoded ×−1 so higher values indicate more rhythmic entry). Estimation: firm-fixed-effect ("within") transformation with year, industry, and region dummies and one-year-lagged predictors; standard errors clustered at the firm level; an inverse Mills ratio included to correct survival bias. Identification is associational (a fixed-effects panel design), not a natural or randomized experiment.
key_findings: All five hypotheses are supported in the main firm-fixed-effect model (Table 2, Model 3). H1 supported: entry tenure of foreign firms is positively related to domestic firm productivity (b = 0.016, p < .001). H2 supported: the squared entry-tenure term is negative (b = −0.002, p < .001), so the positive effect diminishes as tenure grows (the slope flattens but does not turn negative); as entry tenure rose from 1 to 10 years, a domestic firm's output increased by about 14.4%. H3 supported: entry tenure × export intensity is negative (b = −0.006, p < .001)—the relationship is stronger when foreign export intensity is lower. H4 supported: entry tenure × intangible asset intensity is negative (b = −0.032, p < .001)—stronger when foreign intangible-asset intensity is lower. H5 supported: entry tenure × rhythm is positive (b = 6.95E-04, p < .001)—stronger when foreign firms entered more rhythmically. Robustness: results hold using domestic firm survival (Gompertz model) as an alternative outcome (H1–H4 consistent; H5 not supported there), a post-1998 left-censoring subsample, within-/outside-region and country-origin splits, alternative ownership cut-offs, and random subsamples; with longer lags H1–H2 stay robust, H3 is the most robust moderator and H5 the least (none of the three moderators holds at a 5-year lag).
theoretical_contribution: This is, to the authors' knowledge, the first empirical study to explicitly examine the role of time—the inter-temporal dynamics—in FDI spillovers, shifting the literature from a static "snapshot" view of FDI presence to a dynamic view centered on foreign firms' entry tenure. By integrating the organizational-learning perspective with the competitor-imitation/barriers-to-imitation argument, it shows that domestic firms' learning "from a distance" accrues over time but only up to a limit. It also repositions foreign firms—previously treated as "black boxes" and studied mainly through domestic firms' absorptive capacity—as knowledge-source firms whose attributes (export intensity, intangible-asset intensity, entry-pattern rhythm) govern the speed at which spillovers occur.
practical_implication: The findings speak to MNC managers, domestic managers, and policy makers in emerging markets. For MNC managers, the results clarify how, and under what conditions, host-country domestic firms learn from them over time and when the MNCs are more or less vulnerable to domestic imitation. For domestic managers in emerging markets, the benefits of FDI spillovers take time to materialize (roughly a 10–12-year window before additional learning gains flatten) and are greatest when the "targets" for learning are foreign firms with a local-market focus and high tangible-asset intensity. For policy makers in emerging markets, bringing in FDI at a more rhythmic pace helps domestic firms observe and learn from entrants, and pressuring foreign firms to export may delay domestic firms' learning.
limitations: The authors note that they captured the role of time only through foreign firms' entry tenure, which gives an overall picture but not more specific temporal dimensions (e.g., time elapsed since particular FDI milestone events). They also examined only three foreign-firm attributes that shape barriers to imitation, leaving other potential sources of such barriers unexamined. Finally, the study is confined to FDI spillovers in China, so whether the findings generalize to other emerging markets remains unanswered.
future_research: The authors call for research that (a) examines more specific dimensions of time, such as time elapsed since milestone events—for example, a major MNC's significant investment in an industry, or the point at which foreign firms begin purchasing from local suppliers; (b) investigates other sources of barriers to imitation, such as foreign firms' strategic alliances with domestic firms, through which knowledge may be passed on to domestic non-partner firms; and (c) replicates the study with firms in other emerging markets (e.g., Romania, Kenya, Ecuador) to test whether the core ideas generalize beyond China.
abstract: In this study, we examine how foreign direct investment (FDI) spillovers to domestic firms in an emerging market occur over time. From the organizational learning perspective, we propose that, as entry tenure of foreign firms in an industry increases, domestic firms can learn from the foreign firms over time and improve their productivity. We further build upon the competitor imitation argument to propose that this effect will be stronger when barriers to imitation faced by the domestic firms are lower. Based upon a comprehensive panel dataset on manufacturing firms in China in 1998–2007, our findings strongly support these arguments. We find that entry tenure of foreign firms in an industry has a positive relationship with the productivity of individual domestic firms in the same industry, albeit at a diminishing rate. We also find that this positive relationship is stronger when the foreign firms have lower export intensity, lower intangible asset intensity, and have followed a more rhythmic (i.e., less irregular) entry pattern—situations characterizing lower barriers to imitation.

title: How Directors' Prior Experience with Other Demographically Similar CEOs Affects Their Appointments onto Corporate Boards and the Consequences for CEO Compensation
methods: Longitudinal (1995-2006) observational study of Fortune 500 new director appointments and subsequent CEO compensation; feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) regressions with firm-wise heteroscedasticity; Heckman two-stage sample selection model (inverse Mills ratio); focal indices constructed via discrete principal components analysis; OLS with clustered robust errors and a three-level multilevel model as robustness checks.
industry: Largest industrial and service companies on the 1995 Fortune 500 list (cross-industry)
units: New director appointments (director-firm) and firm-year CEO compensation decisions
n_sample: 275 companies; 1,114 new director appointments; 613 CEO compensation decisions
authors: Zhu, D. H.; Westphal, J. D.
theories: similarity-attraction paradigm; social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954); upper echelons theory
keywords: CEO compensation; CEO power; corporate governance; demographic difference; interlock ties; new director appointments; social comparison theory; triads
research_question: How do CEOs resolve the dilemma of appointing demographically dissimilar new directors, under external pressure to do so, despite their preference for similar individuals who are likely to support their leadership and decision making? The study further asks how such appointments, working through directors' prior interlock ties to other similar CEOs, affect subsequent CEO compensation.
hypotheses:
H1. The focal CEO's power will be positively associated with a new director's prior experience with other CEOs who are demographically similar to the focal CEO.
H2. The demographic difference between a new director and the focal CEO will strengthen the positive relationship between the focal CEO's power and the new director's prior experience with other CEOs who are demographically similar to the focal CEO.
H3. New directors' demographic difference from the CEO will reduce the CEO's compensation to a smaller degree when new directors have more prior experience with other CEOs who are demographically similar to the focal CEO.
mechanism_summary: Drawing on social comparison theory, the paper argues that a focal CEO estimates a new director's social acceptability (the likelihood that the director will support the CEO's leadership and evaluate the CEO's decisions fairly) by observing whether the director has previously served with other CEOs who are demographically similar to the focal CEO, treating those similar CEOs as a reference group. Powerful CEOs are better able to appoint such directors, and they give these prior ties more weight when a director is demographically more different from them. Because prior contact with similar or different others can also reduce reliance on stereotypes, a dissimilar director's prior work with other similar CEOs mitigates the director's less favorable view of the focal CEO, thereby weakening the otherwise negative effect of CEO-director demographic difference on CEO compensation.
data_measures:
- Sample and sources: 275 companies drawn from the 1995 Fortune 500, yielding 1,114 new director appointments and 613 subsequent CEO compensation decisions over 1995-2006. Board membership from the Compact Disclosure database (all U.S. SEC-filing public companies); CEO compensation from COMPUSTAT ExecuComp; executive characteristics mainly from Capital IQ, supplemented by the Social Register, Marquis' Who's Who, proxy statements, and annual reports; additional data from COMPUSTAT, CRSP, Thomson Financials, and RiskMetrics.
- New director's prior experience with other similar CEOs (DV1): the director's other Fortune board appointments in the prior three years, scored for CEO similarity on seven characteristics (gender, ethnicity, age, highest degree earned, Ivy League background, functional background, industry of employment) and combined into a single index via discrete principal components analysis.
- CEO compensation (DV2): logarithm of the focal CEO's total compensation (salary, bonus, options valued by the Black-Scholes method, and grants) in year t+1.
- CEO power (IV): index of four indicators - CEO tenure, number of board appointments held, CEO ownership, and whether the CEO is board chair - combined via discrete PCA.
- New director's demographic difference from the CEO (moderator): coded 1 for a difference on each of the seven characteristics and combined via discrete PCA.
- Identification and design: observational/associational. A Heckman two-stage sample selection model (inverse Mills ratio from a first-stage model on all 6,135 new Fortune directors) addresses selection because prior experience is observable only for directors with earlier Fortune appointments; estimation uses FGLS with firm-wise heteroscedasticity, extensive firm-, CEO-, and director-level controls, and industry and year dummies.
key_findings:
All three hypotheses were supported (one-tailed tests for hypothesized variables).
- H1 supported: CEO power is positively associated with a new director's prior experience with other similar CEOs (β = 0.09, p < .05; Table 2).
- H2 supported: the CEO power × new director's demographic difference interaction is positive (β = 0.11, p < .05; Table 2, Model 3), indicating that powerful CEOs rely more on these prior ties when the new director is demographically more different from them.
- H3 supported: the interaction between new directors' demographic difference and their prior experience with other similar CEOs on CEO compensation is positive (β = 5.69, p < .05; Table 4, Model 2); the negative effect of CEO-director demographic difference on CEO compensation is significantly weakened and can disappear entirely when prior experience with other similar CEOs is relatively high.
- Robustness: results held under OLS with clustered robust standard errors, two alternative measures of prior experience, alternative aggregations of demographic difference, and a three-level (director/CEO/firm) multilevel analysis.
theoretical_contribution: The study identifies a new role for directors' interlock ties in corporate governance: beyond serving as information conduits or resource-dependence mechanisms, a director's prior ties to other demographically similar CEOs act as a social cue that the focal CEO uses to gauge the director's social acceptability. By extending social comparison theory to director selection and showing how a director's ties to third-party CEOs (triads) shape the dyadic CEO-director relationship and its consequences, it redirects behavioral governance research from dyad-level factors to triadic social structure. It further contributes to CEO compensation research by identifying a mechanism through which powerful CEOs can secure compensation despite externally demanded increases in CEO-director dissimilarity.
practical_implication: The authors caution that when a CEO is powerful within the firm, it is especially important for the public and shareholders to attend to a broad range of new directors' characteristics, including their prior experience with other similar CEOs. Shareholders and governance reform advocates in particular should be wary when a powerful CEO appears to conform to demands for greater formal board independence or CEO-director dissimilarity, because such appointments can reflect impression management rather than a substantive improvement in board monitoring and control.
limitations: The study examines only two consequences of directors' prior ties to other similar CEOs, namely their appointment onto boards and subsequent CEO compensation, and does not examine other consequences of such third-party ties. The data cannot completely rule out that a small number of directors' prior experiences with other CEOs were perceived as negative, though the authors argue this makes the test conservative. They also cannot fully exclude alternative indicators a CEO might use to infer a new director's social acceptability.
future_research: The authors call for examining how new directors' prior ties to other similar CEOs influence board control over other major decisions such as CEO dismissal, CEO succession, acquisitions, and diversification, and whether such ties affect the board's advice-and-counsel function. They suggest adopting more refined, longitudinal measures of a director's prior experience, and applying the social comparison perspective to other strategic decisions, such as the choice of alliance partners.
abstract: In recent years, new director appointments have increasingly posed a dilemma for corporate leaders: while CEOs prefer individuals who have similar backgrounds to them, they face increased pressure to appoint new directors who have a different demographic profile. We suggest that CEOs may resolve this dilemma by appointing new directors who have prior experiences working with other demographically similar CEOs. We then explain why this tendency is stronger when new directors are demographically more different from CEOs. Moreover, we posit that new directors’ prior experiences with other similar CEOs will reduce the negative effect of their demographic differences from the CEO on CEO compensation. Longitudinal analysis of Fortune 500 companies’ new director appointments and subsequent CEO compensation provided support for our theoretical expectations. This study identifies an important new role that interlock ties to other CEOs can play in corporate governance and leadership. In particular, we suggest that such ties are a means by which CEOs evaluate whether a new director will support their leadership and decision making. In explaining the role of directors’ ties to other CEOs in influencing director appointments and CEO compensation, this study also highlights the important influence of triads on CEO-director dyadic relations.

How directors' prior experience with other demographically similar CEOs affects their appointments onto corporate boards and the consequences for CEO compensation. *Academy of Management Journal, 57*(3), 791–813. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.0590
